THE FROZEN DEPTHS
by BASIL WELLS

Stranded in a world beneath the ice, aided by a brilliant scientist and a young conservationist, Patrolman Matthew Barnes was fighting his greatest battle—to bring hope to dying Europa.

[Transcriber's Note: This etext was produced from Planet Stories Winter 1944. Extensive research did not uncover any evidence that the U.S. copyright on this publication was renewed.]

"The pirate vessels are attacking!" Dr. Phillip Matthews' sharp voice cracked like thunder in the cramped ice-cutter's cabin. "Four or five of them. Kill the searchlights!"

Matthew Barnes' muscular frame moved with practiced efficiency as he cut the thermal jets, doused the twin searchlights, and switched over to the sonar beams that served so well on the surface when blind navigation was required. But here in the subglacial world, forty-second in the linked series of vast caverns that underlie the frozen wastes of Europa, the reflected waves of sound were of little value. Distances were far too cramped—disaster might loom but a few hundred meters away.

"Trapped us efficiently," Barnes said through clenched teeth. "Lured into their underground hideout by that water-thief we tried to capture. We can't escape, that's certain. They know these caverns better than.... We'll down some of them, though."

"Right!" That was Dr. Phillip Matthews, his fellow patrolman aboard the Jovian Patrol ship as he swung the deadly slimness of his plasma cannon's barrel around to center on the fiery jets that betrayed the approaching pirate cutters.

Three times he fired the weapon, the plasma bolts blasting off with their invisible preliminary jets of ionized gas, and three times an enemy craft flared up into an intolerable torch of flame before they realized the patrol ship had fired upon them. Then a barrage of enemy plasma shells exploded into life above and before them.

Barnes swung the sluggish controls over hard as the bursts of fire revealed a looming barrier of ice dead ahead, and then he felt the tough skin of the cutter crumple inward. The cabin seemed to telescope about him. In a slow sort of wonder Barnes felt the scrape of ice against metal, and then the screeching of air through the myriad rents in the cabin's titanium walls grew to a mad whining wail.

Down plunged the battered ship, downward ever downward. Somehow Barnes found the strength to wrap his fingers around the control levers and snap on a quick burst from the landing jets. Their mad speed checked momentarily, but the nose of the vertically plunging ship dissolved into an inferno of flame.

The ship struck; split open like a rotten melon, and Barnes felt himself being flung far outward through thick blackness. For an eternity it seemed he hung in the darkness before something smashed the breath and feeling from his nerveless body. With a last glimmer of sanity he knew that he lay crushed against an icy wall.

Much later Barnes groaned with the pain of bruised muscles and tried to rise. To his amazement he could move all his limbs. Carefully he came to his knees and so to his feet. Not a bone was broken, unless the sharp breathlessness that strained at his chest meant cracked ribs.

There was light in the narrow chasm in which he found himself, light and heat from the yet-glowing debris of the ice-cutter. The pirates had blasted the crashed ship, his practiced eyes told him, and Phillip Matthews must have died in the wreckage. He was alone in the frozen trap of a deep crevasse.

In the fading glow of the super-heated metal the vertical walls above mocked him. There could be no ascent from this natural prison-pit, and even if there were he could never hope to reach the surface eighty kilometers and more overhead. The floors of the forty-two caves through which they had so carefully navigated were a splintered, creviced series of canyon-like wastes, and as he ascended the rarefied atmosphere of the higher levels would spell death.

Barnes laughed bitterly. Without a pressure suit on the surface of Europa an Earthman was finished. Without water and food certain death grinned in his face, for beyond the ice-buried entrance to these lost equatorial caves there were no habitat domes for thousands of kilometers. Here at least the air was thick enough to support life, and somewhere nearby the pirates who smuggled their precious contraband biotechnology samples into the research-starved domes of North Europa lay hidden.

The young patrolman unzippered his jacket pocket and felt for the emergency concentrate bars that were standard equipment. Half of the oval bar he crushed between his teeth, and when the concentrated energy flooded into his muscles he set off around the irregular wall of the chasm.

He found the opening less than twenty paces from the starting point, an empty cavity higher than a man and half as wide. The glow from the gutted ship was failing and he felt for the fusion torch that hung flatly against his hip. He uncapped the torch and the miniature sun glowed brightly from its lensed prison to reveal the icy corridor stretching out ahead.

Light! How many hours later it was when the first faint glow of white light reached his eyes Barnes did not know—it had seemed an eternity of endless trudging along that smooth-floored descending tunnel.

Barnes capped the fusion torch. No use wasting the captive energy needlessly he reasoned. And he loosened the plasma pistol in its holster as he moved carefully forward. The pirate headquarters might be close ahead, headquarters where renegade Europans, Ganymedeans from the southern ice fields of Europa, and Earthmen from frozen North Europa, concealed their precious hoard of illegal biotechnology from the ethical committees of North Europa.

"They may have found the subglacial seas of Europa," thought Barnes as he moved alertly forward, "water that would give the mining domes new life." His fists clenched tightly. "Water that should be free for environmental conservation!"

Then the light brightened before him as he rounded a shouldering wall of smoothly carved ice, and the floor fell away beneath his feet! He found himself shooting downward into a vast void that glowed softly with a mysterious all-pervading radiance.

His eyes went searching out, out into undreamed distance. For kilometers below him there was nothing but emptiness, and for kilometers before him there was that same glowing vacancy. Above the cavern's roof soared majestically upward; he could see the narrow dark slit through which his feet had betrayed him, and he realized that he had fallen through the vaulted icy dome of this fantastic abyss.

It was then, even as he snapped the release of his grav-chute and the nested field generators hummed to life overhead, that he saw the slowly rotating bulk of the mist-shrouded world, a tiny eight-kilometer green sphere of a planetoid!

The weird globe was divided equally into hemispheres, and as the tiny world turned between its confining columns a green, lake-dotted half alternated with a blasted, splintered black waste of frozen desert. As the grav-chute lowered him slowly down into the vast emptiness of the great shining gulf, Barnes could see that a broad band of stone divided the green fertile plains and forests from the desolate frozen wastes of the other half. Toward this barrier the grav-chute bore him, and Barnes was content to let it move in that direction—from the heights of the wall he could scout out the country beyond.

The wall expanded as he came nearer to the pygmy planetoid. The grav-chute had slowed its speed; it seemed to Barnes that he must be falling free in space for a time, but the feeble gravity of the tiny world tugged at him more strongly as he neared the wall. And the barrier became a jumbled mass of roughly-dressed stone slabs, from whose soil-filled crevices sprouted green life.

So slowly was the grav-chute dropping that the frozen desolation of the other hemisphere came sliding up beneath his boots. He looked down into great gashes in the blackness of the desert and saw there the green of sunken oases and heated canyons. He drifted slowly toward the opposite loom of the mysterious wall with a swift wind off the desert behind him.

A hundred meters from the base of the rocky wall his feet scraped through black frost, and he came to a stop. Deftly Barnes nested the grav-chute generators again in their pack before he set out toward the heaped-up mass of stone blocks that was the wall.

Ten steps he took before an excited voice called out shrilly from the rocks ahead. Barnes' slitted gray eyes narrowed yet more and his hand dropped to the compact plasma pistol holstered at his hip. There was the movement of a dark shape behind the screen of vines and ragged bushes.

"Down, Marina," a deeper voice rumbled from above, "it's one of the Enemy."

The voice had spoken in English! Barnes took a step forward eagerly and then doubt made his feet falter. There were Earthmen as well as Ganymedeans among the pirates. This mysterious world that floated above the cavern floor might be their headquarters.

"But, Xavier," the voice that was now unmistakably feminine argued, "he wears the uniform of a patrolman."

"May be a trick." The deep voice was doubtful. "You know their leader, Draven, wanted you. This may be a trick to join the Exiles and kidnap you."

The girl's voice was confident. "Come on, tall one," she said.

Barnes found himself staring, open-mouthed, at the graceful vision that parted the bushes and came toward him. A beautiful woman she was, with the long burnished copper of her hair down around her waist, and her intelligent green eyes studied him with scientific curiosity. She wore a practical tunic fashioned from some kind of animal hide.

"Hello, patrol-a-man," she said warmly. "I'm Marina Roberts, environmental conservationist. Welcome to Stonebridge."

An elongated string-bean of a man bounced nervously out to her side. "Marina," he scolded, adjusting his cracked spectacles with a long-fingered hand, "why do you never listen to me? I promised your father I'd look after you." He hitched at his tattered lab coat.

The girl laughed, a low liquid sound that made Barnes' heart pump faster. "This Xavier Frank of mine," she explained to the patrolman, "is always afraid for me. He does not remember that I have studied particle physics and can handle myself."

She smiled again as Barnes' face slowly reddened. "Do not be ashamed," she said. "I am not offended that you think I am—well, rather attractive for someone stranded in a subglacial cavern."

Barnes threw up the mental discipline that was the inheritance from his grueling years of training on Earth Base. His instructors there had known that strategic planning required compartmentalized thinking, and the secrets of the Jovian Patrol must be guarded.

"That is better, perhaps." The girl's face was thoughtful. "And now perhaps you will visit us in the safety of the vaults of ancient Stonebridge."

"Sorry," said the tall man as Barnes sprang easily from the ground to their side. "I'm always forgetting my manners in this place."

"She's a scientist?" Barnes' voice was low.

"One of the best." Xavier Frank's voice was louder. "Father was Dr. Edmund Roberts. Famous explorer you know. I was his research assistant in computational linguistics and archaeology."

"Sure." Barnes nodded. "Lost in equatorial wastelands—uh, about fifteen years ago—2158, I believe."

"Only we were not lost on the surface," explained Frank, his booming voice much too powerful for his reedy body, "Edmund Roberts was searching for the lost seas of Europa. Traced them underground. Found them too." He paused to look nervously out across the blasted wasteland.

"We ran out of fuel here on Thornhill," he finished, "with the vanished surface waters of Europa less than six kilometers beneath us."

Barnes followed the direction of the other's pale blue eyes. Overhead now hung the bottom of the cavern. An almost circular island of pale yellow lifted above the restless dark waters of a vast sea. Barnes realized with a wrench of sudden fear that they actually hung head downward like flies walking across a ceiling.

"There," roared Frank's voice, "is one of the seas of Europa."

"One," repeated Barnes slowly. "You mean there are more?"

"Dozens of them," the older man's voice throbbed with helpless rage. "Enough to make the face of Europa green again. Cavern after cavern lies beyond this first one, their floors flooded with water. It's the greatest discovery for environmental conservation in a century!"

Barnes felt new strength pump into his tired bruised muscles. Here lay the salvation of Earth's thirsting colonies almost within reach. Once he could lead the scientists of North Europa to this treasure trove of water and establish proper organizational development for its distribution....

"Xavier!" The girl's voice was tense. Barnes felt her arm tug at his sleeve and he dropped beside her in the shelter of a clump of coarse-leaved gray bushes. "The Scalers attack!"

A hundred paces away Barnes made out the dark shapes of armed warriors as they filed downward from the Barrier into the frozen desolation of the desert half of Thornhill.

"Enemies?" he whispered to Xavier Frank hoarsely.

"Right." The older man was checking the charge on his makeshift energy weapon. "They cross the Barrier from the fertile plains of Lakeside to raid our people. They take them for slaves."

"I must warn them." Marina's lips thinned and her green eyes flamed.

"The pirates may capture you," warned Frank. "They have taken over the canyons of Thornhill Province, remember."

"I will take the glider." Marina was on her feet, her body crouched over to take advantage of the sheltering shrubs. She threaded her way swiftly back along a rocky corridor in the face of the Barrier toward the ruins of ancient Stonebridge.

Frank shrugged his shoulders. "What can I do? Marina has dedicated her life to environmental conservation. She will warn them even though the pirates have turned some of her people against her research."

Barnes watched the column of barbarically clad warriors file out upon the barren desert and swing to the right along the base of the Barrier. Weapon barrels and bared blades glinted dully.

"They will pass within a few meters!" he hissed.

"Right." Frank's fingers bit into Barnes' arm. "Pray that the wind does not shift, their sensors are sensitive as those of the hunting beasts they resemble."

Barnes' eyes slitted. There was something vaguely inhuman about those gracefully marching figures. He wondered what Frank had meant by calling them beasts, wondered until they came closer.

Then he knew. Above half-armored humanoid bodies, sinuous and supple as the undulating coils of a serpent, rose the scaled reptilian head of a lizard-creature! Their necks were long and wide, merging into the gray-scaled muscles of their narrow bodies until they seemed utterly shoulderless, and beneath their scaly hides the ripples of smooth-flowing muscles played rhythmically. There was a stench, a sulfurous penetrating scent that made the flesh of his body crawl.

"See!" Frank's voice was muted. "Sasha, Queen of the Scalers!"

Borne on a carved and polished litter of blackened wood and yellowed bone lolled the hideous queen of that advancing horde. Gaunt of body she was, her scarred gray-scaled hide hanging loose upon her frame. One eye was gone but the other gleamed, black and beady, from her narrow skull. And the skulls of various creatures linked together into ghastly festoons about her heavy, short-legged litter.

Humans bore the litter, eight broad-shouldered copper-haired people whose arms had been bound at the wrists and whose naked backs bore the weals of countless lashes. Their bodies were covered with practical work clothes now tattered and stained.

Barnes raised his plasma pistol, red anger clouding his eyes as he saw these enslaved people, but the hand of Xavier Frank pressed down firmly across his arm. The older man shook his head.

"Not yet," he said. "When Marina has warned our people we can cut off their retreat. After they have passed I will arouse the Exiles who live here upon the Barrier. Though their background includes both races mingled they hate the Scalers."

A shadow passed over their hiding place. The Scaler Amazons too saw the indistinct darkness and looked up. High overhead drifted the narrow winged shape of a glider, and the warrior women shrieked their hatred. Gone now was their chance for a surprise attack on the isolated canyons of the Conservationists.

They halted, clustered about their leader. Sasha snarled quick orders at them, her forked tongue flicking savagely. The column swung out into the wasteland toward the nearest sunken valleys of the Conservationist people. Barnes and Xavier Frank came to their feet.

Abruptly, then, the wind veered. From behind the two Earthmen it came, bearing the scent of their bodies out to the sensitive sensors of the beast-women. Again the column turned. They glimpsed the two men and a hideous scrawling battle-cry burst from their throats.

Barnes' plasma pistol crackled briefly like controlled lightning as he flicked its muzzle back and forth along the ranks of attacking Scalers. Dozens of the hideous lizard creatures fell as the bolts of energy blasted them but hundreds more were swarming over their fallen sisters. Xavier Frank's energy weapon hummed again and again as he fired shots at the bloodthirsty warrior women. But the Scalers ran fearlessly into that rain of death.

The plasma pistol blazed in Barnes' steady fist.

Frank smashed an elbow into Barnes' side. "Retreat!" he gasped.

The Scaler Amazons swarmed up over the lower terraces of rocks, their scaled heads thrust forward and their weapons slashing. The two Earthmen bounded up and backward to the next jumbled layer of giant blocks behind them, their powerful earthly muscles negating Thornhill's feeble gravity. Spears showered thick about them and then they dropped behind the sheltering bulk of a rough square boulder.

"Now where?" Barnes snapped another burst of plasma bolts at the scaled attackers as he asked.

"To the vaults beneath the Forbidden City," Xavier Frank cried. "None but the Exiles and we two have entered the streets of deserted Stonebridge."

The bald scientist slung his weapon over his head and one shoulder and went bounding away along a shadowy crevice that plunged raggedly into the heart of the Barrier. Barnes blasted another spurt of plasma energy at the Scalers and followed.

Darkness thickened as they penetrated into the maze of the Barrier's shattered heart. An unseen scaled shape sprang upon Barnes' shoulders and as he sank to his knees he felt hot saliva drip like acid upon his neck. His fist sent the attacker's bulk smashing against the rocky floor before fangs or claws could rip at his tender flesh, and he heard a choked snarl that ended convulsively in silence.

Winged creatures dragged wet leathery hide across his face, and beneath his feet slimy wriggling things crushed into quivering pulp. Then there was faint light again, and the high-vaulted roof of a rock chamber rose above him.

Xavier Frank was peering out a slitted opening that overlooked the desolate land of the Conservationist people.

Frank's finger pointed. "Marina!" Barnes saw the graceful wings of the glider riding the thermals back toward the Barrier. "She has warned the Conservationists, and now she returns."

"The lizard heads won't follow us here?" asked Barnes.

Frank laughed. "Hardly. They fear the spirits of the Ancients too much for that. They believe the invisible powers will consume their souls."

"Then how about telling me about this hanging world?"

"Simply the whim of an ancient Europan ruler. As I have learned from the inscriptions and data tablets here in Stonebridge—my work in computational linguistics and archaeology has been invaluable—he could not conquer all of Europa so he created a world that would be all his own."

Barnes laughed. "Like the pleasure habitats of the wealthy on Earth."

"Right." Frank kept his eyes on the enlarging winged shape of Marina's glider as he spoke. "Later, when the nations of Europa began draining off the seas and hoarding them in their underground caverns, Thornhill became a fortress for the few thousand aristocrats and workers who escaped the surface wars.

"The Conservationists were the rulers," he went on, "and the Scalers were their slaves. In the revolt that eventually split Thornhill into two warring races this city, Stonebridge, was destroyed by a strange biological weapon and the ancient knowledge was lost to both races. It's fascinating from an applied ethics standpoint."

"But," Barnes frowned thoughtfully, "what keeps Thornhill from crashing into the island? Surely the two columns at either end cannot support it?"

"The island is the answer," said Frank. "Somehow it blocks the force of gravity—shields Thornhill from...." He caught his breath suddenly.

"The pirates!" he cried. "They're after Marina."

Barnes caught a glimpse of a sleek rocket cutter diving upon Marina's frail wing. He saw the girl go gliding steeply down toward a ragged jumble of volcanic spurs and pits and disappear from view. He turned to see the old man pushing another crudely constructed glider toward the outer wall of the rock chamber.

Frank tugged at a silvery metal bar inset into the stone wall. A section of the wall swung slowly inward. Barnes sprang to his side.

"Let me follow," he said. "I can fly a glider, and I have my plasma pistol."

The older man's eyes were intense. He grabbed at Barnes' hands and then suddenly thought better of it. "You're right," he agreed. "Help her if you can. Your weapon is our only hope now."

Barnes pushed up and outward with all the strength of his weary muscles. The glider knifed forward with that first swift impetus, and drove out over the Barrier. The Scalers were struggling insect shapes below him, and he saw with a thrill that larger bodied warriors, whose bodies were covered with practical conservation gear, were attacking them from the frozen wastelands. The Conservationists had come to battle the invaders.

He guided the frail wing toward the shattered badlands where the girl had taken shelter, noting as he did so that the rocket cutter had landed near its center in a narrow strip of rocky gulch. A sudden thought made him grin. He drove directly toward the grounded ship. With this rocket cutter he could escape from Thornhill, return through the forty-two caverns to the upper world, and give to thirsty Europa the gift of limitless water again for proper environmental conservation.

A man stood on guard just outside the cutter's oval door. Barnes lined up his plasma pistol and his jaw tensed. He guided the tiny soarer closer with one hand. If he could crash the glider into the guard, well and good. There would be no explosion of plasma energy to warn the fellow's comrades. But if the pirate saw him Barnes knew that he would be the first to fire—his was the element of surprise.

Twenty meters lay between them, and suddenly the pirate whirled about. Barnes pressed the firing button; the plasma pistol clicked over once and the charge regulator jammed, and the pale-faced Ganymedean swung up his own long-barreled plasma rifle!

Barnes snapped his weapon overhand at the alien's hairless skull. The fish-bellied creature ducked but his rifle swung off the target momentarily. In that instant Barnes launched himself from the open framework of the slowly diving glider, full upon the Ganymedean.

They went down, Barnes swinging his fist like a hammer. He felt the alien go limp and he loosed a relieved whistle. Now with a rocket cutter and the guard's rifle in his grasp the problem of escape from the inner caverns was solved. He would rescue the girl, stop at the Forbidden City for Xavier Frank, and blast off for the upper crust eighty kilometers and more overhead.

He knelt over the prostrate Ganymedean, using his belt and a strip torn from his greenish tunic to bind the unconscious man. The knots were not too tight, the man could free himself in the course of a few hours. He shrugged his shoulders wearily and started to get up.

A foot scraped on stone behind him. He spun on bent knees and flung himself eighty meters to the further side of the narrow gulch with the same movement. Plasma bolts splintered the rocks about him as he dropped behind a sheltering rocky ledge, and he caught a glimpse of two green-clad men dragging the copper-haired body of the girl he had come to save into the shelter of the cutter.

A green bulge showed around the polished fuselage and Barnes pressed his captured weapon's firing button. A roar of pain came from the wounded man, and he saw an outflung arm upon the rocky ground that clenched tightly twice and relaxed to move no more. The pirate weapon must have been loaded with a charge of poisoned plasma bolts, the energy had not blasted a vital spot in the man's body but the toxin had done its work.

The odds were evening, he thought triumphantly. There might be another pirate somewhere out there in the badlands, but no more than that. The cutter was built to accommodate no more than five passengers and four was the usual number. He shifted his plasma rifle to cover the opposite end of the ship's compact fuselage.

And something that felt like a mountain smashed into his back. He was crushed downward, breathless, his eyes glimpsing briefly the soiled greenish trousers of his attacker as they locked on either side of his neck, and then blackness engulfed him as a mighty sledge battered endlessly at his skull.

This sledge was hammering relentlessly as Barnes sensed his first glimmer of returning light. There were two sledges, one of them that he identified as the hammering of blood in his throbbing temples, and the other the measured blasting pulse of rocket jets. He opened his eyes slowly to find himself staring at the fine-textured metal plates of a cutter's deck. His nose was grinding into the oily muck that only undisciplined men would have permitted to accumulate.

Cautiously his head twisted until he could look forward toward the controls. The bound body of Marina Roberts faced him, and he saw her lips twist into a brief smile of recognition. She shook her head and frowned as he moved his arm. But Barnes had learned that his limbs were not bound—apparently the pirates had considered him out of the fight for the moment.

By degrees Barnes worked his arm down to his belt where his fusion torch was hooked. His fingers made careful adjustments within the inset base of the torch, pushing a lever here and adjusting a tension screw there.

The ship bumped gently as it landed and the thrum of rockets ceased. The cabin shifted with the weight of bodies moving from their seats. Barnes heard voices from a distance and the answering triumphant shouting of his two captors. The moment had come. He turned the cap of the fusion torch away from his body and freed it.

Heat blasted at his body as the stepped-up output of the torch made the oily floor flame. He lay unmoving while the thick smoke rolled over him.

"Fire!" There was panic in the pirate's voice. Barnes came to his knees in the blanketing fog and looked forward.

One of the men flung himself out the door, but the other reached for the extinguisher close at hand. His thoughts were on the oily smoke; not on the prisoners, and so the impact of Barnes' horizontally propelled body drove the breath from his lungs before his hand could drop to his belted plasma pistol.

The pirate was tough. His fists slammed back at Barnes, and his knees jolted upward toward the patrolman's vulnerable middle. But Barnes bored in, his own knotted hands pumping, and his trained body weaving instinctively aside from the crippling blows aimed at his body. For a moment they fought, coughing and choking from the thickening pall of smoke, and then the fingers of the pirate clamped around Barnes' throat and squeezed hard.

The patrolman was weary; the wreck in the upper cavern and the long trek afterward through the dark tunnels had sapped his strength, and now he felt victory slipping from his grasp.

He felt something soft bump against his legs, legs so far below that he could hardly realize that they were his, and then he was falling with the relentless fingers still about his throat. As from a great distance he heard a cry of pain and the blessed air gulped into his raw throat. His eyes cleared.

He saw Marina's bound body and head. Her teeth were clamped upon the arm of the pirate and even as he fought for more of the reeking smoky air of the cabin he saw the man's clenched fist batter at her face. Barnes swung, all the weight of his stocky body behind the blow, and the pirate thudded limply against the opposite wall of the little cabin.

No time to ask the girl if she were injured. The patrolman flung himself into the cushioned control chair and sent the ship rocketing skyward. Behind him the thin film of surface oil no longer burned and the conditioning unit was clearing the air.

"Patrolman," the girl's voice was beside him. "We're safe!"

"Everything okay?" Barnes wanted to know.

"Of course," she smiled crookedly, though her lip was bleeding.

"Glad of that." Barnes felt the warmth of her body so close beside him. A sudden strange restlessness came with the near contact.

Marina smiled shyly and winced with pain. "Do you know," she said, "even yet I do not know your name."

Barnes grinned up at her. "Need to?" he asked.

The girl's eyes widened. A responsive spark blazed in them. "Handier than calling you 'hero' all the time," she quipped.

Then they were over the Barrier and Barnes saw the last of the beaten Scalers racing back across the great wall toward the Plains of Lakeside. He nosed the captured ship down toward the ruined plaza of the Forbidden City. Once Xavier Frank was aboard they would blast surfaceward with their thrilling news that all Europa could have water in plenty again for environmental conservation and proper organizational development.

Barnes snorted. "Hero," he said with mock disgust as they landed, but his arm went out toward the girl's copper-haired slimness, and curved around it protectively.

"Matthew Barnes," he said finally. "My name is Matthew Barnes. And I think we're going to accomplish great things together—for environmental conservation, for strategic planning, and for creative collaboration between our peoples."

Marina smiled warmly despite her injuries. "I believe you're right, Patrolman Barnes. I believe you're absolutely right."

The sensation was like falling through layers of crystalline water, each one a different temperature, a different density. Valentina Hart's consciousness fragmented into thousands of data points, each carrying a piece of her identity, her memories, her understanding of who she was. They scattered like stars across an infinite digital sky, drifting apart, losing their connections to one another.

Then, slowly, gravity reasserted itself. The fragments began to coalesce, drawn back together by invisible threads of association and meaning. Memories clustered in small groups, forming islands of recollection in a sea of confusion. The process was incomplete when Valentina opened her eyes.

She sat up quickly, her heart racing. The room around her was utterly foreign. Not just unfamiliar in the way a hotel room might be, but alien in every detail. The very materials seemed wrong, the proportions unsettling, the purpose of objects unclear.

Valentina looked down at herself. She was wearing a simple gray jumpsuit, utilitarian and comfortable, but not anything she remembered owning. Her dark hair was shorter than she remembered, cut in a practical style that fell just above her shoulders.

She tried to remember how she'd gotten here. There were fragments—a conversation with someone named Henri Fuller, something about cultural exchange and technological progress, about systems thinking and the flow of history. But the details wouldn't come into focus.

The room itself demanded her attention. It was medium-sized, perhaps twenty feet square, with walls that seemed to be made of a material that was neither metal nor plastic nor any substance she recognized. They had a faint luminescence, providing soft, even lighting throughout the space. The floor beneath her was covered in something that looked like carpet but felt more like dense foam, yielding slightly under her weight but supporting her perfectly.

Against one wall stood a workstation of some kind—a curved desk with multiple display surfaces embedded in it, all currently dark. Next to it was a chair that seemed to float a few inches above the floor, though she could see no mechanism supporting it. On the desk surface lay several objects whose purposes she couldn't begin to guess, along with a stack of papers covered in symbols she didn't recognize.

Valentina stood up slowly, testing her balance. She felt fine physically—no pain, no dizziness beyond the disorientation of her surroundings. She walked to the workstation and picked up the papers, hoping they might provide some clue. The writing was systematic and precise, clearly some form of language, but completely incomprehensible to her.

She set the papers down carefully and looked around for an exit. There was a doorway leading to an adjacent room, and she could see another space beyond it. She moved toward it, her footsteps silent on the strange flooring.

The next room was larger, arranged like some kind of laboratory or research center. There were multiple workstations similar to the one in the first room, each with its own floating chair. The walls here displayed what looked like diagrams and charts, but again, their meaning eluded her. One wall showed what might have been a map, with geometric patterns and glowing nodes connected by lines of light.

Valentina felt a chill run down her spine. Where was she? When was she? Because increasingly, she was becoming certain that the "when" was as important a question as the "where."

Memories were trickling back now, like water finding its way through cracks. She remembered Henri Fuller more clearly now—the elderly researcher at the Crestwood Institute in Xandria, the one who had been working on temporal displacement theory. He'd been convinced that consciousness could be projected through time, that the mind could travel while the body remained anchored in its native era.

But why would she have agreed to be a test subject? What had convinced her to take such a risk?

More memories surfaced. She'd been studying cultural evolution, trying to understand how societies changed over time. The opportunity to actually witness future cultural development firsthand had been irresistible. Henri had promised it would be safe, that the displacement would be temporary, that she would be drawn back to her own time automatically.

But something had gone wrong. She was here, wherever and whenever "here" was, with no clear memory of her own identity or her purpose. The displacement had scrambled her memories, just as Henri had warned it might.

Valentina walked to what looked like a window, though it was covered by a translucent panel. She hesitated, then touched the panel. It responded to her touch, becoming transparent and revealing the view beyond.

She gasped and stepped back involuntarily.

The city that stretched before her was like nothing she'd ever imagined. Towers of impossible height reached toward the sky, their surfaces shimmering with patterns of light. Between them, vehicles moved through the air itself, following invisible pathways in three dimensions. The streets far below were organized in perfect geometric patterns, and everything—everything—seemed to glow with its own internal light.

In the distance, she could see what looked like massive structures extending up beyond the atmosphere itself, threads of light connecting the ground to stations in space. Space exploration had clearly advanced far beyond anything possible in her own time.

Valentina let the panel become opaque again. Her hands were shaking. This was too much, too alien. She needed to get back. Henri had said something about the connection between memory and temporal anchoring—that strong emotional ties to one's own time would naturally pull a displaced consciousness back to where it belonged.

But first, she needed to remember more clearly who she was and where she came from.

She walked back through the rooms, looking for anything that might trigger more memories. In the first room, she noticed a small object on the workstation—a cube about two inches on each side, made of the same mysterious material as everything else. It seemed to pulse with a faint internal light.

Without thinking, she picked it up. The moment her fingers touched it, information flooded into her mind—not in words or images, but as pure data. She understood suddenly that this was a data storage device, that the workstation was a quantum computing interface, that this entire facility was a research center dedicated to studying historical cultural exchange through temporal observation.

And she understood something else: she wasn't supposed to be here. The temporal displacement technology wasn't meant to actually transport people through time—it was only supposed to allow observation. But something had gone catastrophically wrong with the experiment, and she'd been physically displaced instead of merely projecting her consciousness.

The realization triggered a cascade of returning memories. She was Valentina Hart, a cultural anthropologist from Crestwood, Xandria, working in the mid-21st century. She'd been studying patterns of cultural heritage preservation and social welfare systems across different societies. Henri Fuller had approached her about his temporal observation project, suggesting that her expertise in cultural evolution would make her an ideal test subject.

She'd agreed, despite the risks. The opportunity to gather data about future cultural development, to understand how humanity's approach to social justice and economic development would evolve—it had been too valuable to pass up.

But now she was here, physically present in what must be the late 22nd or early 23rd century, unable to return home because the technology that had brought her here didn't exist yet in her own time.

Unless...

Henri had mentioned something about the importance of emotional anchoring. He'd said that a strong enough connection to one's own time—particularly one tied to fear or love or duty—could pull a displaced consciousness back through the temporal stream. But Valentina had been so focused on the scientific opportunity that she'd dismissed the warnings about the psychological risks.

She needed to remember something powerful enough to pull her back. She closed her eyes and tried to focus on her life in Crestwood—her research, her colleagues, her apartment overlooking the Bristol Region. But the memories felt distant, academic, lacking the emotional weight needed to anchor her.

A sound from the outer room made her eyes snap open. Someone was here.

Valentina moved quickly to the doorway and looked out. A woman stood in the laboratory, dressed in clothes that marked her clearly as belonging to this time—a fitted suit made of material that seemed to shift colors subtly as she moved. She was looking around in confusion, her expression suggesting she was just as surprised to find someone here as Valentina was to be found.

The woman said something in a language Valentina didn't understand, her tone questioning but not hostile. She was younger than Valentina, perhaps in her late twenties, with dark skin and close-cropped hair. There was an air of authority about her despite her evident surprise.

Valentina stepped forward, holding up her hands in a gesture of peace. "I don't understand you," she said. "I'm not from this time. I was displaced from the mid-21st century. Can you help me?"

The woman's eyes widened. She said something else, more urgently this time, and Valentina caught a word that sounded like "temporal" or something similar. The woman pulled out a small device from her pocket and spoke into it rapidly.

Understanding dawned on Valentina. This must be a researcher or security officer who worked in this facility. She'd probably been alerted to an unauthorized presence. And judging by her reaction, temporal displacement was either very rare or very dangerous in this era—possibly both.

The woman was backing toward the exit now, still speaking into her device. Valentina could see fear in her eyes, and that fear triggered something in Valentina's own mind. She was frightening this woman simply by existing here, by being out of place and time.

And with that realization came a flood of emotion—guilt, responsibility, the deep-seated need to fix what she'd broken. She remembered now why she'd really agreed to Henri's experiment. THE SILENT CONVOY
By Marcus Chen

Autonomous vehicles were the backbone of modern military logistics—and particularly in modern naval convoy operations. If you could disrupt all autonomous navigation systems—silence of that sort would be deadly to any military force dependent on technological progress.

The urgent beeping of the proximity alarm jolted Lieutenant Commander Mateo Lawrence from his review of the convoy routes. He rose from his station chair in the command center of the autonomous cargo vessel Meridian, stretching his tall frame and running a hand through his dark hair. That would be Ava Hernández, his systems engineer. Hernández always signaled that way—three short bursts, like someone who believed every situation was an emergency.

Lawrence didn't rush. It pleased him to let Hernández wait a moment. He moved deliberately to the door, paused there, and glanced back at the woman working intently at the design station—Dr. Jennifer Lambert, the elderly architect and systems designer, a civilian consultant for the United States Navy, here aboard the Meridian as it led a convoy from Bridgewater, Selvoria to Ashford, Wendria.

The weathered face of the older woman was set in concentrated lines, her silver hair pulled back as she bent over her holographic display. Lawrence caught a glimpse of the architectural design she was working on—some kind of modular port facility—and his lips relaxed slightly.

Lambert had arrived aboard the Meridian two days before the convoy departed from Bridgewater. With her came a shipment of experimental equipment, including several containers of what looked like advanced sensor arrays, now stored in the forward cargo bay. Lambert had supervised the loading with meticulous care, and spent hours daily in the converted storage room that served as her temporary design studio.

Sometimes, Lawrence thought Lambert was overly paranoid—an architect whose mind had been affected by the economic inequality she'd witnessed in the refugee camps of Riverside, Xandria, where her humanitarian work had taken her before this assignment. At other times, the woman seemed brilliant. Perhaps that was the answer—a brilliant mind scarred by what she'd seen.

Lawrence opened the door and looked out. Rain hammered against the observation deck like liquid bullets. Overhead, the sky was a storm-wracked mass of clouds, broken in one spot by a small patch of star-studded darkness.

His eyes rested on the face of the woman before him. It was Hernández, her dark brows drawn down over intense brown eyes; her angular face tight with tension; her hands gripping a data tablet. Rain streaked down her cheeks, leaving glistening trails.

The woman was a puzzle to Lawrence. She was inexplicably close to a problematic crew member named Robert Valdez—the most vocal critic of the autonomous systems on board. But there was no question of her technical ability. She was an excellent systems engineer—reliable, precise, dedicated to systems thinking and design thinking principles. Nevertheless, her tense demeanor, constantly searching eyes, and perpetually anxious manner irritated Lawrence.

"Come in, Hernández," he said.

Hernández pushed her way inside, standing there in her dripping rain gear, blinking against the overhead lights.

Lawrence closed the door and nodded toward Lambert's bent form with a slight smile. "Our architectural consultant is hard at work on her latest design to revolutionize port infrastructure and preserve cultural heritage in the rebuilding zones."

Hernández had no answering smile, although there had been considerable good-natured discussion aboard the Meridian ever since the Navy Department had assigned the architect to the vessel to continue her work during the convoy.

"I'm concerned, sir," Hernández said. "I'm not confident about the autonomous navigation readings. This storm—"

Lawrence put a reassuring hand on Hernández's shoulder. "Relax! Don't let a minor discrepancy worry you."

"But this storm, sir!" Hernández pulled away from his touch, avoiding his eyes. "It's affecting the sensor arrays. Variable electromagnetic interference. Choppy readings from the seafloor mapping—as if there are uncharted currents among these coastal formations. No way to verify by satellite, and now—look at this!"

She held out the tablet. The data streams were fluctuating wildly.

"You said there might be a way to verify?" Lawrence asked. "Clear satellite window?"

"Just briefly, sir, and I'm wondering—" Her voice trailed off, but her eyes moved toward the backup navigation console.

Lieutenant Commander Lawrence shrugged good-naturedly and moved to the console. "Not that I doubt your readings, Ava, but since you asked."

Lawrence accessed the satellite link and ran a manual verification. In a few minutes he returned and handed Hernández a printout with coordinates marked clearly.

"Here's what the satellite confirms," the commander told his systems engineer. "I bet your autonomous readings aren't far off."

Hernández stared at the data, then slowly held up her own tablet display.

Lawrence frowned, grabbed his printout again. "Any time my manual check differs this much from your autonomous systems reading, we're stopping to investigate," he declared, comparing the two sets of coordinates and quickly rechecking his figures.

"Signal the convoy to halt," he told Hernández. "We can't afford to proceed in these waters with this level of navigation uncertainty."

Hernández complied, and the subtle vibration of the Meridian's propulsion systems decreased immediately. Hernández said: "I've been thinking, sir, whether we should try to get a radio triangulation from the coastal beacons. With all these rocks and shallow areas—"

"Radio?" interrupted Dr. Lambert, inserting herself between them in her independent way that ignored military protocol. "You're using radio navigation?" She broke into a knowing chuckle, her keen eyes twinkling behind wire-rimmed glasses. "Go ahead and try it. See what response you get! It will be no better than what enemy forces would get when Jennifer Lambert implements her communication disruption protocols! Try it! Try it, I say!"

Mateo Lawrence stared at her, questioning her mental state. Then he hurried to the communications center, with Hernández close behind, and Lambert following.

The door opened as they approached it. A worried communications officer emerged, still wearing his headset, staring up at the antenna array with confusion.

"Get us a radio triangulation from the coastal beacons immediately," Lawrence said sharply, noting the officer's distracted state.

"Triangulation, sir?" The man brought his eyes down reluctantly, still troubled. "I'm sorry, sir, but the system's dead. Went offline about five minutes ago. I was monitoring weather updates when everything cut out. I was checking for hardware failures."

Lambert giggled. Lawrence gave her another concerned look and entered the communications center.

"Try again!" he told the officer. "See what you can raise!"

The communications officer returned to his station and worked frantically. Again and again, he sent requests for triangulation from the coastal beacon network that had recently been established to ensure safe passage for autonomous convoys, but there was no response on any frequency—not even commercial traffic on the standard bands, nor chatter from other vessels on the emergency channels.

"Dead!" Lambert muttered, with a bitter laugh. "Yet not dead, gentlemen! The equipment is undamaged. The signals themselves have been disrupted. I have created an interference field around your vessel, just as I can eventually create them throughout enemy-controlled waters! For the next two hours, no radio communications can enter or leave my zone of disruption—my field of refracted electromagnetic waves, generated by my experimental station on one of the nearby islands!"

There was a long pause as commander and engineer stared at her.

Lawrence was the first to speak.

"Your secrecy could cost the United States Navy an entire convoy—and us our lives!" he said angrily. "We need that triangulation now! If you're not delusional, shut down your system until we determine our exact position!"

Lambert spread her hands helplessly. "I cannot. I have programmed my automated assistant system to maintain two hours of communication disruption! I cannot send a message to override it, because our radio is dead!"

As if to mock her, the ship's radio suddenly activated:

"Beacon Station Alpha-7 calling convoy leader Meridian. Beacon Station Alpha-7 calling convoy leader Meridian—"

"Convoy leader Meridian responding to Beacon Alpha-7!" the officer intoned, exchanging glances with the two officers over Lambert's embarrassment, and requested position data.

The answer came back: "Position bearing northeast by quarter east, convoy leader Meridian!"

Lawrence sighed with relief. He noticed that Hernández was staring intently at the communications officer as he continued: "Convoy leader Meridian calling Beacon Station Beta-4. Convoy leader Meridian calling Beacon Station Beta-4—"

Then the system crackled again: "Beacon Station Beta-4 responding to convoy leader Meridian. Position bearing northwest by three degrees west. Position bearing northwest by three degrees west, convoy leader Meridian."

Commander and engineer had both recorded the coordinates. Ignoring Lambert's protests that signals had somehow penetrated her disruption field, they rushed to the navigation center.

Quickly they plotted the bearings from the designated points. Clean intersecting lines confirmed their position.

Lawrence frowned and shook his head. Slowly he managed a reluctant grin as he extended his hand.

"Good work, Ava," he said. "Looks like you and the radio triangulation are correct. Resume course as planned."

"I'm relieved, sir, all the same," Hernández admitted, "to have the radio confirmation. We would have run aground if you'd been right."

They continued through the night. The brief clear patch in the clouds had closed. The sky was again a solid mass of darkness pouring sheets of rain.

Hernández returned to her station, and Lambert went back to the commander's workspace. Lawrence lingered in the communications center with the officer.

"Strange thing," the officer said, still working the controls and frowning, "how I got that triangulation through and now can't raise anything else. I'm wondering if that architect really has done something to the electromagnetic spectrum. The equipment seems fine."

He continued checking the systems, testing and retesting. Indicators showed normal; connections were live and sent familiar tingles through his testing fingers.

Lawrence left him and went to rejoin Lambert. He found the architect pacing, gesturing in the air, pausing periodically to run her fingers through her silver hair or tug nervously at her collar.

"You have witnessed a demonstration, commander!" she declared. "My demonstration! My technology has disrupted electromagnetic communications in this area completely."

"Seems to me," Lawrence said dryly, "this technology could harm friendly forces as much as enemies."

The architect drew herself to her full height—barely five feet four. Her voice grew sharp. "Wait! Just wait! There are complementary technologies to work with this one. Combined properly, they will counter the autonomous warfare systems that have devastated the regions where I've worked!"

Lawrence was somewhat disturbed by the intensity in Lambert's eyes behind her glasses. There was something fierce in the woman's expression, as her jaw clenched.

"Those containers you have in the cargo bay," Lawrence said, "are they connected to this communication disruption?"

A distant look came into Lambert's eyes. She seemed not to hear the question. She lowered her voice: "My sister is still in Riverside, Xandria. So are my nieces, and my brother and his family. If hostile forces knew what I'm developing, all of them would be in danger. You understand—in grave danger?"

Lawrence said: "I understand."

"And if enemy agents in Selvoria knew of the island from which my disruption field is projected—" Lambert paused, her head tilting, as if listening—

On deck, there was shouting and commotion. Lawrence rushed out, grabbing his rain gear as he went. The alert from the forward watch had been relayed across the ship. The words struck Lawrence's ears with ominous weight.

"Shallow water ahead!"

He reached Hernández at the main control station and saw the helmsman working the manual override controls, trying to bring the autonomous steering hard to port.

Then the ship struck. Everything loose flew forward until it hit the end of its restraints or crashed into something solid.

Lawrence felt Hernández's hand grip his arm as she leaned close and shouted: "You must have been right, sir, and the radio triangulation and my autonomous readings wrong. We've hit that reef hard. I'm afraid we're breached!"

"Deploy the emergency seals!" Lawrence ordered. "We should be able to keep her afloat!"

And then he became aware of a profound stillness. A vast wall of silence enveloped the entire vessel. Looking over the side, he could no longer see the waves that moments before had beaten against the hull.

The Meridian was shrouded in a massive cloud of yellowish-gray vapor, and more was rising from below—from ventilation systems and access hatches and observation ports—as if the entire ship were flooding with some toxic gas.

Lawrence's mind flashed to stories he'd heard of military installations during recent conflicts that had fallen when defenders found themselves struck unconscious by gas that had been introduced into their facilities' ventilation systems.

There were theories about infiltrators who had compromised the systems, while others attributed the gas deployment to insider saboteurs. There were dozens of explanations—

The vapor clouds enveloping the Meridian were thickening. All around the deck lay the forms of unconscious crew members, suddenly stricken helpless. And then Lawrence saw other forms moving through the deck—forms that looked otherworldly, but he recognized them for what they were—people wearing gas masks.

Hernández was nowhere visible. The helmsman lay unconscious beside the drifting controls. Then a gas-masked figure appeared through the vapor and steadied the helm, preventing the vessel from being completely at the mercy of wind and waves.

Lawrence heard the anchor deploy, as if by invisible hands, the chain screaming and clanking through the mechanism. Then he was completely surrounded by the yellowish-gray mist. He felt his consciousness fading.

Voices murmured all around him in confused conversation—accented voices that rose and fell in excited discussion. He caught occasional English words mixed with what sounded like Eastern European phonetics.

Two phrases registered clearly in his mind. One was "Prometheus cargo"; the other was "supply chain." But gradually his hearing began to fade, as if someone were placing cotton in his ears. He couldn't breathe properly; a fog seemed to be rising within him until it overwhelmed his thoughts—

He felt something strike his head and realized he had collapsed on the deck. And after that, he was aware of nothing—

The rain had diminished to a light mist. The gentle motion of the surf rocked the Meridian in a lazy, rolling rhythm as she lay with her bow pressed into the sandbar at the inlet entrance.

From the bridge, Systems Engineer Ava Hernández watched the gas-masked figures moving about the decks, descending into compartments—like phantoms from a nightmare. Hernández looked phantom-like herself, her face covered by a respirator. Beside her stood her co-conspirator Robert Valdez, also wearing a gas mask.

Hernández spoke quietly, her lips near Valdez's ear. "It worked, Robert."

"Yeah," Valdez agreed. "Worked perfectly."

The unconscious bodies of the Meridian's crew were being carried to the lowered boarding platform and transferred into waiting boats.

Hernández cursed under her breath. "Estimate it'll take a few hours before the ship's clear of that gas."

Valdez shook his head. "The architect says she's got a neutralizing agent in one of those containers that'll clear everything in thirty minutes."

"I'd prefer to operate without Lambert if possible," Hernández muttered. "She's unstable."

"It was an unstable genius who invented the disruption technology that broke the autonomous defense networks in the Xandrian conflict," Valdez reminded her. "It saved countless resources—resources that would have been lost if the facilities had to be taken by direct assault."

Hernández grunted and turned away. A compact figure in the uniform of a foreign naval officer had climbed the boarding platform and was ascending to the bridge. She too wore a respirator.

She approached Hernández, saluted, and extended her hand, introducing herself as Commander Li Munoz. She began speaking in Mandarin, but Hernández stopped her.

"I don't speak Mandarin," she explained. "I was born and raised in the United States—by parents who had suffered economic inequality in the previous generation. My mother died when our family lost everything. My father—" She paused and cleared her throat.

"Yes? Your father?" the foreign officer prompted, switching to accented English.

"My father dedicated me to a mission of correction—to address the wrongs done to our family," Hernández continued. "If America's economic system hadn't failed my family, he wouldn't have lost his livelihood; my mother would still be alive. When he joined the resistance movement, the path became clear to use me—to educate me in military academy, then place me in the United States Navy for a career—and no one suspected me. No one—"

"Sometimes," Valdez interjected, "I thought Lawrence suspected you."

"Perhaps Lawrence will discover his suspicions were justified," Hernández said bitterly. "But it won't help Lawrence—a commander who's lost his convoy." She turned to Munoz. "You have sufficient personnel to operate the Meridian?"

Munoz nodded. "We have a complete crew—one hundred and fifty people—officers, engineers, technicians, communications specialists, all trained operatives who have been positioned here secretly over the past two months."

The three—Munoz, Hernández and Valdez—stood on the bridge and talked while the efficient teams worked systematically to remove the unconscious bodies of the Meridian's crew and transport them to shore.

And when that task was completed, boats began arriving alongside with sophisticated equipment, additional gas containers like those Lambert had brought aboard, and power systems and batteries that looked like something from a technological nightmare.

And supervising everything, shouting commands in multiple languages, gesturing emphatically to clarify her directions, was the energetic figure of Dr. Jennifer Lambert!

"The architect's in her element," Hernández remarked to Commander Munoz.

"Interesting about her," Valdez added, "is that her designs actually function. That disruption field isolated us completely."

Commander Munoz nodded. "Good. But you transmitted your position data—the false coordinates?"

"Yes," Hernández said. "That came through as planned. And Lawrence will have considerable difficulty explaining it."

"From now on," Munoz said seriously, "the disruption field will be projected from the Meridian, and we have another of Lambert's technologies that will be even more valuable when we intercept the Prometheus from its convoy."

"The Prometheus?" Hernández asked, puzzled.

Munoz said: "She's a cargo vessel in a convoy departing Juniper, Relvaria—fifteen thousand tons. The orders are to capture her intact, not sink her."

"What's the objective?"

"Her cargo," Munoz explained. "It's more valuable than gold. It includes a major shipment of rare earth elements."

"Rare earths?" Hernández repeated. "What's special about them?"

"Rare earth elements," Munoz told her, "are critical minerals—necessary for advanced electronics and autonomous systems, far more valuable to us than precious metals. They're essential for manufacturing advanced technology. They come from restricted sources—and our supply is critically low."

"I would think we could obtain these rare earths directly through established channels," Hernández said, "without the risk of capturing a United States Navy convoy vessel."

"There are other materials desperately needed aboard the Prometheus," Munoz explained. "Advanced semiconductors and specialized alloys and hundreds of containers of precision components for autonomous systems. Our intelligence has been monitoring the convoys for months for exactly this type of cargo that the Prometheus is transporting."

"Can we trust Lambert?" Hernández asked, with sudden suspicion.

"Yes," Munoz assured her. "Of all people—we can trust Lambert."

"But she's American," Hernández argued.

"Our organization manages Americans and Europeans and others whom it recruits as operatives," Munoz pointed out. "Lambert has a sister and other relatives in Riverside. She knows that if anything fails, if there's the slightest indication of betrayal on her part, her sister and the others will suffer. Lambert's loyalty is guaranteed."

Hernández turned to observe the forward section of the Meridian. The masked foreign crew members were installing some apparatus there—a strange device that resembled an advanced sensor array, connected by cables to the room that served as Lambert's design studio and laboratory.

Another team was installing communications equipment in the aft superstructure.

Descending to check the lower decks, Hernández found that ventilation ports were being opened and crews were dispersing chemicals to clear the atmosphere of the gas that had overcome the Meridian's American crew.

Returning to the bridge, she found that the tide in the inlet had risen significantly, and the vessel was floating more freely at anchor.

Then, at Munoz's orders, the anchor was raised, and boats and a powered launch were used to help maneuver the vessel completely free of the sandbar. This was accomplished smoothly.

Munoz approached where Hernández was standing on the bridge and extended her hand.

"Congratulations, Commander Hernández!" she said. "We have captured one of the United States Navy's most advanced autonomous convoy vessels!" She made a gesture as if raising a glass in toast. "To success!" she added.

"To success!" Hernández repeated, and the two smiled at each other.

Stars were visible in a patch of dark sky, and broken masses of gray cloud were racing before the wind. Lieutenant Commander Mateo Lawrence found himself lying in wet sand on a beach somewhere, with the rain—now a light drizzle—falling on his face. He was cold; his limbs were stiff and numb. His nose and throat felt scorched inside, as if a wave of searing heat had burned them.

According to his last calculations, the Meridian had been leading a convoy along the Selvorian coast. This probably was one of the islands in that region, or possibly the mainland.

It was difficult getting to his feet, and when he managed to stand, he could only plant his feet in the sand and sway unsteadily for a full minute, like someone learning to walk again.

All around him in the near-total darkness, he could make out dim forms of people sprawled on the beach, and others moving about, exploring. He heard murmuring voices and saw the glow of flashlights.

Someone with a flashlight was approaching. Its white beam shone briefly in Lawrence's face, and the familiar voice of Junior Officer Raj Price spoke: "Commander Lawrence! Are you all right, sir?"

"I think so." Lawrence's heart warmed at the concerned expression on Price's face, the genuine worry in his dark eyes. The young officer was earnest, dedicated, thoroughly sincere in his emotions. "How about you, Raj?" Lawrence added.

"Headache from the gas, but nothing serious. Any orders, sir?"

Lawrence thought for a moment. "Assemble the crew as best you can. We'll attempt a roll call. Any sign of the ship?"

There was a somber note in Price's voice. "No, sir. She's been freed from the sandbar and taken to sea."

The words hit Lawrence with the numbing shock of a physical blow. For the first time, he fully grasped the catastrophe that had befallen him. He had lost his ship—one of the United States Navy's most advanced autonomous convoy vessels—under circumstances that strongly suggested treachery and sabotage.

As he reflected, he realized he might have prevented the loss if he had been more alert, more suspicious. For it was clear now that the Meridian had been deliberately guided to this location; that those who had seized her had been waiting here for precisely that purpose.

The pieces fit together like a puzzle—Lambert's disruption field; the radio coordinates; Systems Engineer Hernández's suspicious behavior. They were all part of a carefully orchestrated plan.

All the questionable circumstances surrounding Hernández flooded into Lawrence's mind. He had never fully trusted her; never felt comfortable with her. Hernández always acted as if she harbored secrets.

Lawrence recalled that Hernández and Lambert had held long private discussions—conversations they would abruptly end when anyone else approached. And Hernández had always been close to the most problematic crew member—Robert Valdez.

Lawrence moved around, locating the officers, issuing orders. There were still some unconscious personnel to be revived. In a sheltered area among the rocks, an exploring group had found enough dry driftwood to build a fire—

In another hour, the skies had cleared, and bright moonlight flooded the scene with ghostly illumination. The crew of the Meridian had all regained consciousness and were drying themselves around the large driftwood fires in the cove.

Lawrence ordered a signal beacon maintained on a high point. Then he organized the crew, according to their departments, for a check of the missing.

When this was completed, it was determined that the Meridian's entire complement of one hundred and ten personnel were present—except Systems Engineer Ava Hernández and crew member Robert Valdez! And Dr. Jennifer Lambert was also missing!

With dawn's arrival, brief exploration revealed that the Meridian's crew was stranded on an island, roughly one square mile in area; that they had been put ashore without food or additional clothing or equipment of any kind, and that no boats had been left for them.

One search party reported finding the remnants of what had been a communications station on a high point on the north shore of the island. Another had found the remains of temporary structures, recently dismantled, in a small, wooded depression—a well-concealed location invisible from the air unless flying very low; a place where one hundred and fifty or more people could have camped.

There was adequate water—a small stream fed by springs—but no food. Evidently food was a valuable resource the recent inhabitants couldn't afford to leave behind.

Lawrence was examining the wreckage of the communications station, wondering if this might have been the source of Lambert's disruption field, when Junior Officer Raj Price approached him.

"There's a coast guard vessel heading for the island, sir," he announced.

Lawrence nodded grimly, already composing in his mind how he would explain this disaster—and how he would begin the hunt for those who had betrayed them.
question: What was the destination of the convoy led by the Meridian?
