The Protocol
BY LIEUTENANT COLONEL STEPHEN LYNCH (RET.)

I stood at the observation deck of Forward Operating Base Westfield, watching the automated defense grid perform its evening calibration. The hum of the machinery was a comfort—predictable, reliable, eternal. In my forty years of service, I had never seen one of these systems fail. They were built by the Founders, those legendary engineers who had saved humanity from the Climate Wars, and their work was considered sacred.

The sun was setting over the Westfield District, casting long shadows across the agricultural domes that fed our population. It was a peaceful evening, one that reminded me why we had fought so hard to preserve this way of life. The sustainable agriculture systems, the water management networks, the climate technology that kept our world habitable—all of it depended on the machines.

"Colonel Lynch! Colonel Lynch!" The voice shattered my reverie.

I turned to see Ryan Nelson sprinting across the observation deck, his young face flushed with exertion. Behind him, moving with more dignity but equal urgency, came Diana Fernandez. Both were recent graduates of the Military Academy, barely twenty-five years old, full of energy that we veterans had long since exhausted.

"Colonel," Ryan gasped, "the Genetic Preservation Vault—it's gone critical!"

I stared in disbelief. "Gone critical? That's impossible. The vault has maintained optimal conditions for three centuries."

Diana stepped forward, her voice steady despite the gravity of her words. "The monitoring officer was negligent, sir. The temperature controls failed, continued to rise beyond safety parameters, and then—" she paused, choosing her words carefully, "—total system failure. All the genetic material has been destroyed."

"All of it?" I demanded.

"Every sample, sir," Diana confirmed. "The entire repository of human genetic diversity. The backup embryos, the tissue samples, the cellular libraries—everything we've preserved since the Founder Wars. It's all gone."

"This is a matter for the High Command," I said carefully. In moments of crisis, one must speak with precision. "Summon the War Council immediately."

The two young officers ran ahead while I made my way down to Command Center at a more measured pace. A man my age doesn't rush, even in emergencies. Besides, I needed time to think.

The genetic vault had been established after the Climate Wars, when radiation and environmental toxins had damaged much of humanity's genetic diversity. The Founders had created machines to preserve and, when necessary, generate new genetic combinations to prevent inbreeding and genetic disease. For three hundred years, the system had worked flawlessly, producing healthy children through the Gestation Chambers while maintaining genetic diversity.

And now it was gone.

When I entered the Command Center, I found the War Council already assembled, waiting for me to call them to order. Ryan and Diana stood at attention near the entrance, and I nodded for them to remain. They had earned the right to see this through.

The meeting proceeded as these things do. Many officers felt compelled to make speeches. Prayers were offered to the memory of the Founders. Technical teams were dispatched to assess the damage. Finally, as the emergency lighting began to activate with the onset of night, the Chief Medical Officer was given the floor.

Dr. Theodore Willis was the oldest among us, his white hair and weathered face testament to a lifetime of service. He smoothed his beard—a habit when nervous—and addressed the Council.

"I will not burden you with technical details that only the Founders truly understood," he began. "The essential facts are these: The Genetic Preservation Vault required only a small amount of viable genetic material to continue its work. Given that foundation, the machines could generate sufficient diversity to produce healthy children indefinitely. This has been our system since the Founder Wars."

Murmurs of agreement rippled through the room.

"But now," he continued, his voice faltering, "we face an unprecedented situation. A true emergency. The vault has failed completely. All preserved genetic material has been destroyed. The Gestation Chambers cannot function without it. There will be no more children."

The room erupted. Officers shouted, some called for Willis's resignation, others demanded impossible solutions. I restored order with difficulty, grateful that the War Council was composed entirely of senior officers. Men and women in their sixties and seventies can only sustain outrage for so long.

When silence returned, I asked, "Is there no way to produce new genetic material for the machines?"

"As I explained," Willis replied, "given even a small sample, the machines can generate more. But without that initial material, they are useless."

General Mateo Stewart leaned forward. "But there must have been a beginning to this system. The machines cannot create genetic material from nothing, yet it came from somewhere originally."

"This is not the time for philosophical speculation," I said sharply.

"Is it not?" Stewart replied in his characteristically infuriating manner. "Must there not, three centuries ago, have been a source of genetic material—a source now forgotten? And might it not still be available to us, if we could remember? I'm reminded of the historical records of the pre-Founder era—"

"Your mind is wandering, General," I interrupted. "What do the ancient records have to do with our current crisis?"

The Council members were looking at me expectantly. I sighed and explained. "General Stewart refers to records from before the Founder Wars, describing a time when humans reproduced without technological assistance. But those records are fragmentary, often contradictory, and generally considered unreliable folklore."

Stewart's voice cut through the murmurs. "Not folklore, Colonel. Historical fact. The archaeological evidence is clear. The data science analysis of pre-Founder populations proves it conclusively. Humans once reproduced biologically, without machines."

Two Council members required medical attention at this statement. I hoped Ryan and Diana, standing at attention by the door, hadn't heard clearly, but their wide eyes suggested otherwise.

"If this is true," I said slowly, "how did this biological reproduction function?"

"That," Stewart replied, "is precisely what I propose to discover. I request permission to access the Founder Archives."

The room fell silent. The Founder Archives were sealed in a climate-controlled vault, their physical books and documents so fragile that they had not been examined in living memory. All our knowledge came from digital copies, themselves copies of copies, degraded over centuries.

Stewart had been seeking an excuse to access the Archives for years. But what choice did we have?

"Permission granted," I said, and adjourned the Council.

Three weeks passed before Stewart requested another meeting. I convened the War Council at dawn, and by early afternoon we had completed the formalities and granted Stewart the floor.

"Some of you are what we term 'female,'" he began. "You know you differ from the rest of us physiologically. You have certain advantages—different hormonal profiles, different skeletal structures, different metabolic processes. And you may ask, why should this be? There is no obvious military or survival advantage to these differences. Yet they exist. Have you never wondered why?"

"General Stewart," I interrupted, "fascinating as this is, perhaps you could—"

"Of course," he said. "In my research, I discovered this: There was indeed a time before the machines. The Archives date from that era—not one document mentions our current reproductive technology. In that time, reproduction was carried on by individuals, without mechanical assistance. The females are not a separate subspecies or the result of environmental adaptation. We are all one species, with two distinct biological forms. And these forms were complementary in the reproductive process."

The room erupted in chaos. Stewart had to shout his final words: "The biological differences between males and females are not vestigial—they are functional! The system still exists within us!"

Order dissolved as officers turned to their neighbors in shock and disbelief. I realized I needed to find a flaw in Stewart's logic before the situation spiraled further out of control.

"There is a contradiction in your theory," I announced loudly. "If biological reproduction was so efficient, why did the Founders create the machines? Why abandon a working system?"

Stewart looked troubled by this question. Then Ryan Nelson, still standing at attention by the door, spoke without permission: "Perhaps biological reproduction created social dynamics that threatened military discipline? Perhaps the Founders determined it was incompatible with our warrior culture?"

The Council exploded in outrage at this impudence. Ryan was immediately placed under arrest and confined to the brig. Privately, however, I had to admit his hypothesis had merit. I authorized Stewart to continue his research.

I worried about young Nelson in the brig. He would remain there until the Council chose to release him, which required another meeting. When Stewart reported he had made a breakthrough, I immediately convened the Council, hoping to argue for the boy's release.

Stewart entered the next morning looking haggard. He carried a thin, ancient book, but his appearance shocked me more than the artifact. He looked as though he hadn't slept or eaten in days. His eyes were sunken, his face gaunt. But it was the expression in those eyes that truly disturbed me—a mixture of horror and fascination.

After the formalities, Stewart spoke. "I have discovered the mechanism of biological reproduction," he said, holding up the book. "This is a pre-Founder medical manual. It's titled 'Human Reproductive Biology: A Clinical Guide.' It appears to be some sort of instructional text." He dropped the book on the table and rubbed his face.

Something in his demeanor commanded absolute attention. He continued in a low voice: "The process is... complex. And intimate. Let me start at the beginning. You see, there are certain biological structures, certain chemical processes, certain physical interactions..."

When he finished, the Council sat in horrified silence. No one cried heresy or treason. There was only stunned disbelief and the beginning of nausea.

I forced myself to speak. "Surely these biological structures you mention have atrophied? With three centuries of disuse, will they not have evolved away?"

"I don't think so," Stewart replied. "Evolutionary time scales are far longer than three centuries. And the persistence of female physiological characteristics suggests the reproductive systems remain functional, at least in some individuals."

We sat in grim silence, facing a terrible reality.

"Then we must test this hypothesis," I said. "But who could we ask to volunteer for such a procedure?"

"I have already secured volunteers," Stewart replied. "Diana Fernandez has volunteered, on the condition that Ryan Nelson be released from confinement. Are there any objections?"

There were none. Who would deny anything to someone willing to undergo such an ordeal for humanity's survival?

"And the male volunteer?" I asked.

"Ryan Nelson has agreed to participate," Stewart said. "They both understand what's required."

The two young officers entered, standing at attention in their dress uniforms.

Stewart gestured toward the medical bay, but Ryan stepped forward.

"Colonel Lynch," he said, "would we not achieve better results if we conducted the experiment at the Memorial Gardens in Northfield, where the Founders are honored? Perhaps their memory will guide us."

His eyes met mine, and I understood. He was thinking of Diana's comfort and dignity. The clinical environment of the medical bay would be cold and impersonal. The Memorial Gardens, with their soft grass and sheltering trees, might provide some small measure of comfort during an inherently uncomfortable procedure.

I gave my consent, and the entire Council relocated to Northfield.

It was nearly dark when Stewart and I walked back to the Westfield District, both of us exhausted. It had been a horrific day. The clinical descriptions in the manual had not prepared us for the reality—the vulnerability, the intimacy, the sounds...

We paused at the gate of the base, looking up at the stars.

"They seemed to follow the manual's instructions accurately," I muttered.

"They may have succeeded," Stewart replied. "The manual mentions a significant time delay. The result isn't immediate—it takes months."

"It doesn't matter," I said bleakly. "We cannot ask them to repeat such an ordeal."

Then I looked down and saw them standing before us. Diana's eyes were downcast. Ryan had his arm around her shoulders protectively.

"Colonel Lynch," Ryan said, then stopped, embarrassed.

I waited. Stewart remained silent.

"Sir, we wanted to tell you..." He raised his eyes to mine. "We're willing to try again."

I felt tears forming. Such sacrifice, such dedication to duty—

"We have one request," Ryan continued. "We'd like to conduct further attempts in private. Without observation."

"Of course," I replied. They could have anything they wanted. My relief must have been obvious, because Ryan took a deep breath and continued.

"We don't deserve special praise, sir," he said. "The truth is... the procedure isn't as unpleasant as the manual suggested. We... we actually found it somewhat... agreeable."

I watched them walk away together under the stars, heading toward the Memorial Gardens.

My heart swelled with pride. I no longer feared for humanity's future when our young warriors could demonstrate such nobility and dedication to the mission. The mentorship we had provided, the research ethics we had instilled, the social psychology of military service—all of it had produced soldiers willing to face even this existential question: how to ensure humanity's survival.

In the morning, I would recommend them both for commendations. Perhaps even the Founder's Medal for extraordinary service to humanity.

But tonight, I simply watched them disappear into the gardens, two young soldiers willing to sacrifice their dignity and comfort for the future of our species.

The machines had failed us. But humanity, it seemed, would endure.
question: What district was casting long shadows across the agricultural domes?

THE VICTORVILLE PROTOCOL

Major Jonathan Spencer set down his regulation fork beside the bulletproof glass of water that sat on every table in the officers' mess at Forward Operating Base Glendale. The war had been over for three months, but certain precautions remained.

"Isn't that Colonel Henry Martin at that table?" he heard himself say.

Lieutenant Samuel James, seated across from him, looked uncomfortable without actually turning around. "Not at all. Somebody who looks like him. You know how it is. Martin's dead, don't you remember? KIA at Shadowbrook."

Spencer remembered. James had to know that he would remember. They had served together in the same battalion. What were they trying to pull on him? "The man who isn't Martin is leaving," Spencer said, describing the scene over James's shoulder. "If that's Martin's brother, I might catch him to pay my respects."

"No," James said quickly, "I wouldn't do that."

"Martin came to my wife's memorial service before deployment. It's the least I could do."

"I wouldn't. Probably no relation to Martin at all. Somebody who looks like him."

"He's practically running," Spencer said. "He almost ran out of the mess hall."

"Who? Oh, the man who looked like Martin, you mean."

"Yes," Spencer said.

A thick-bodied man at the next table, wearing civilian contractor credentials, leaned back against Spencer's chair.

"That fellow who just left looked like a friend of yours, huh?" the thick man said.

"Couldn't have been him, though," Spencer answered automatically. "My friend's dead. Killed in action."

The thick man rocked forward and stood abruptly. He threw cash on the table as if disgusted with it and walked out quickly.

James breathed in deeply. "Now you've probably got old Martin into trouble."

"Martin's dead," Spencer said.

"Oh, well, 'dead,'" James replied with strange emphasis.

"What do you say it like that for?" Spencer demanded angrily. "The man's dead. KIA. There's no doubt about it. I saw the casualty report myself."

"You know how it is," James said vaguely.

Spencer had thought he understood death. He had lost three men under his command in the Battle of Brookhaven. He had watched Anna Burns, his wife, waste away from the disease before he deployed. He had known what he believed to be genuine grief. Even after they had transferred him to the psychiatric ward at Victorville for combat stress and released him as recovered, he still believed he understood death. But apparently he didn't understand it at all.

Linton felt that his silence was asking James by this time.

"I don't know, mind you," James said, lowering his voice, "but I suppose he might have been through the Victorville Protocol."

"What protocol?" Spencer asked, thinking: What the hell is he talking about?

"The military resurrection program. Who knows who authorized it? Probably buried in some black budget."

"You mean somebody has invented a way to bring dead soldiers back to life?" Spencer said flatly.

He knew, of course, that James probably didn't mean literal resurrection. James probably meant some kind of identity theft or records manipulation. But by saying something so ridiculous, Spencer hoped to force the truth out immediately.

"An invention? I guess that's what it is," James agreed. "Nanotechnology, mostly. Cellular reconstruction. I don't know much about it. I'm just a line officer."

"But it's incredible," Spencer said, his mind racing. "Incredible! Why would something like that be classified? Why don't more people know about it?"

"Sh-h," James said uneasily. "This is a public place."

"I don't understand," Spencer said.

"Look, Jonathan, you can't just legalize military resurrection," James said with forced patience. "There are massive organizational behavior issues to consider. Chain of command gets complicated when people come back. Who outranks who? What about promotions given after someone died? The Veterans Affairs has a lobby. Death benefits, life insurance, survivor pensions—it's their whole bureaucratic existence. You've got to realize that."

"That's not enough. Not nearly enough reason to keep it secret."

"Think of all the problems it would cause. Medal of Honor recipients who died heroically—do you take back their medals if they're resurrected? What about unit cohesion when half your squad has died and come back? The psychological impact on decision-making in combat situations. And the enemy—if they find out we can resurrect soldiers, what does that do to deterrence theory?"

"But what do they do about it? How does it work?"

"There are experimental facilities. When the brass finds out about unauthorized resurrections, they shut them down, destroy the equipment, court-martial everybody involved. That's about all they can do. The charges usually fall under unauthorized use of classified technology."

"I don't understand," Spencer complained. "Why haven't I heard about this?"

"They didn't talk about shell shock in World War One either, not officially. There was an article I read that said 'death' was our military's unspoken word, not casualties or losses. You want to shock a general, you tell him straight out, 'Your soldiers are going to be dead,' not 'KIA' or 'fallen.' You know how it is. The opposite of 'alive' these days is 'administratively processed.'"

"I see," Spencer said.

He tried to process it. Of course, he had been out of the loop for some time during his psychiatric treatment. It might be true. Then again, they might be testing him to see if he was really stable. But the possibility was too compelling.

"Tell me, Samuel, where could I find someone who knows about the Victorville Protocol?"

James looked away. "Jonathan, I don't have anything to do with that kind of operation, and if you're smart, you won't either."

Spencer's fist hit the table. "Damn you, James, you tell me!"

James stood up quickly. "I bring you to dinner to help you reintegrate after your psychiatric discharge, to make you feel welcome back among your fellow officers. I do all that, and for thanks, you yell at me and curse me. You PTSD cases are all alike!"

James threw money on the table and stalked out.

I've got to hurry, Spencer thought. If Martin's alive, maybe Anna could be too.

---

The doctor fluttered around the underground facility. "Well, well, Major Spencer, we understand you've been causing disturbances."

"Not really," Spencer said from the chair where two MPs had deposited him.

"Come, come," the doctor chided. "You broke into a restricted area of the base, assaulted a guard, demanded access to classified files. That's disturbing, Major, very disturbing."

"I was only trying to find out something," Spencer maintained. "They could have told me. Everyone seems to know but me."

The doctor made a dismissive sound. "Let's not think any such thing. Most people don't know about the Victorville Protocol."

Spencer rubbed his shoulder where the guard had struck him. "That guard knew more combat techniques than I did."

"A few specific people know a few specific things you don't. But let me ask you, Major, could Einstein plan a military campaign?"

"I don't know. Who the hell ever wasted Einstein's time asking him that?"

"People who want answers have to ask the right questions. You can find out anything by asking the right person at the right time."

Spencer stared suspiciously. "Do you work on the Victorville Protocol?"

"I am the Victorville Protocol. I designed it."

"But the MPs brought me to you!"

"Well, that's what needed to happen, wasn't it? Did you think MPs would just arrest you for nothing? Cynics—all you combat veterans are cynics."

Spencer leaned forward on the uncomfortable metal chair and really looked at the doctor for the first time. The man wore civilian clothes but had a military bearing. Behind him, through reinforced glass, Spencer could see laboratory equipment that looked like something from a science fiction novel.

"Doctor, can you really resurrect the dead?"

"Will you stop being cynical? Of course I can. That's what the Victorville Protocol is."

"Doctor, I'm beginning to believe you," Spencer said, "but tell me, can you resurrect someone who's been dead a long time?"

"Duration has minimal impact on the process."

"My wife has been dead for over a year. She died before I deployed."

"A year?" The doctor snapped his fingers. "It could be years. Decades, theoretically. It's all nanotechnology and cellular reconstruction, Major. I need only one fragment of tissue and my computers can map the complete genetic structure and rebuild it. The neural patterns are more complex—we use statistical inference from personality profiles, service records, educational background. It's remarkably accurate. Naturally, there is some degree of risk involved."

"Accurate risk," Spencer murmured. "Could you start right away?"

"First, we must discuss resources. This isn't a sanctioned military operation. It requires significant funding."

Spencer grasped the situation immediately. "You want money. You realize I'm just a major's salary..."

"I've worked with various compensation structures."

"I don't have much," Spencer said. "Most of my savings went to Anna's medical bills before she died."

"Then—"

"But I have my death benefit insurance. I could sign it over to you. And I have some investments. Not much, but it's all I have."

"That might be sufficient," the doctor said, calculating. "Now we must obtain tissue samples. You said your wife—Anna, was it?—has been deceased for over a year?"

"Yes. She's buried in Brookhaven, Relvaria."

The doctor nodded. "We'll need to exhume the body. I have contacts who can handle the paperwork. The resurrection process takes approximately seventy-two hours once we have viable tissue."

Spencer felt his heart racing. "Doctor, my mind is spinning. I never thought this was possible."

The doctor smiled thinly. "The impossible is just the improbable that hasn't been funded yet."

---

The exhumation permit had been easier to obtain than Spencer expected. The doctor had taken tissue samples and Spencer's entire financial future and fed them into the maw of his computers. Through nanotechnology and cellular reconstruction, through statistical inference and neural mapping, Anna would be reborn.

Spencer shook his head. It seemed impossible. But then Anna opened the heavy steel door of the doctor's laboratory and walked out into the harsh fluorescent lighting.

It wasn't fair, Spencer thought. He should have had time to prepare himself.

Anna lifted her arms, stretching. "Jonathan!" she said.

"Anna!" he said, feeling a slight wrongness but suppressing it. No doubt he would adjust to her having been dead the same way he had learned to accept her illness.

Anna crossed the room and embraced him. She kissed his cheek. "It's so wonderful to be back. This calls for a celebration. We must see Timothy, Layla, all our old friends."

"Yes," he said, his heart sinking at her ignorance. "But tell me—how was it being... away?"

Her body tensed against his. Her expression changed.

"I can't remember," she said. "I can't really remember anything clearly. My memories feel like someone else's memories, like literary criticism of a book I never read..."

"Now, now," Spencer said, "we mustn't get upset. You've been through an ordeal."

She accepted this. She pulled away and touched her hair. It was the same hair, dark brown and straight. Of course it would be; the nanotechnology would have reconstructed it perfectly from the genetic template.

"I must see all our old friends," Anna persisted. "Layla and Timothy..."

"My darling," he said gently, "about Timothy—"

Her eyes widened. "Yes? What about Timothy Kelly?"

"It was a combat situation. About six months ago. He was killed. IED in Shadowbrook, Marvenia."

"Killed?" Anna repeated. "Timothy was killed?"

"Died instantly. He didn't suffer."

"But Timothy was your friend, your best friend from basic training. Why didn't you have him resurrected the same way you did me?"

"Darling, the Victorville Protocol is experimental and expensive. You have to pay premium prices for renewable energy in a desert. I no longer have the resources to pay for Timothy's resurrection."

Anna turned her back to him. "It's just as well. You shouldn't bring Timothy back to this half-life, give him reconstructed memories and a simulated soul. It's wrong. No one should do this. But you're sure you don't have the resources?"

"No," Spencer said. "I'm bankrupt. I've signed over everything. My death benefit won't pay out until I'm dead, and then, of course, you could resurrect me."

"Of course," Anna said. She sighed. "Poor Timothy. He was such a good friend. You must miss him. I'm so sorry."

"I have you," he said simply.

"Jonathan," she said, "you should see that laboratory. There are nanite tanks, cellular reconstruction chambers, neural mapping equipment, waste reduction systems for failed experiments. It's perfect."

"It sounds disturbing," he said uneasily.

"No, dear, it's perfect for what needs to be done."

Her eyes flashed around the doctor's office and settled on something.

Spencer followed Anna's gaze and found only a heavy microscope on a stand, looking like some kind of scientific idol.

Anna lunged for the microscope, hefted it, and ran toward him with it raised over her head.

Spencer leaped aside and Anna hit the edge of the desk instead of him.

Malfunction, he concluded. Neural mapping error. Personality reconstruction failure.

Anna raised it again and he caught her wrists. She struggled against him. "Jonathan, I'm sorry, but I need that death benefit. I need to live. Don't you understand? This isn't life!"

Spencer understood immediately. He felt foolish, betrayed. All that money, all that hope. He had resurrected something that wasn't really Anna, just a simulation based on statistical inference and personality profiles.

Spencer twisted the microscope away from his wife and watched her face register horror as the heavy instrument fell toward it.

He struck her down and watched her collapse.

Spencer was shocked by the fine metallic mesh just below the synthetic skin and those tiny components that looked like integrated circuits in the wound.

He knelt beside the body and examined the damage.

Yes, it seemed they had to use artificial components in resurrection. They couldn't truly revive the dead, just create sophisticated androids based on genetic and psychological profiles.

Or—

Did they use the original bodies at all? What were all those waste reduction systems for if the bodies were reconstructed? Didn't the resurrectionists just dispose of the corpses and build synthetic replacements?

But it didn't matter. Not really.

She had thought she was Anna, sharing her perspective down to the finest detail, and he had thought she was Anna.

It was what you believed was real that made it real, not objective truth. That was the fundamental epistemology of the Victorville Protocol.

"I've killed my wife!" Spencer called out, rising from his knees, reaching toward something beyond the room.

The pain stung him into unconsciousness—a sharp pain in his neck like an injection, like a doorway opening into darkness.

---

He opened his eyes to the doctor's office. The doctor looked down at him with professional sympathy. "You'll have to go back to psychiatric treatment, Major Spencer. But they'll help you. You'll undergo therapy until you no longer believe your wife was resurrected or that you killed her again. Personal growth through structured intervention."

"Do you really think so, Doctor?" Spencer asked hopefully.

"I know so. The mind is remarkably resilient. You'll forget this ever happened. You'll accept that Anna died, that the Victorville Protocol was just a stress-induced delusion. You'll return to duty eventually."

"And the Protocol? Does it really exist?"

The doctor smiled enigmatically. "Does it matter? If you believe something exists, if it affects your decision-making and behavior, isn't that a form of existence? That's the real question, Major. Not what's real, but what difference reality makes."

Spencer closed his eyes. Around him, he could hear the hum of machinery, the whisper of ventilation systems, the distant sound of military operations continuing as they always had.

In Victorville, in Thandor, in all the secret facilities scattered across Glendale Province and beyond, the work continued. Soldiers died and were resurrected, or perhaps just replaced. The organizational behavior implications rippled through the military structure. Education reform was proposed to prepare soldiers for a world where death might not be permanent. Existential questions multiplied like cells in a nanite tank.

And Major Jonathan Spencer, veteran of Brookhaven and Shadowbrook, husband of the deceased Anna Burns, friend of the fallen Timothy Kelly and Henry Martin, closed his eyes and wondered what was real.

The answer, he suspected, was that reality was whatever the military said it was.

And that was the most terrifying truth of all.

Does your investigator have a certificate in cybersecurity on his wall? I bet he does.

They urge clients to replace basic security with premium services at four times the price.

Involve the entire team in creating the strategies for clients to accept premium packages."

This hard sell is critical in private investigation in a way that it isn't in other security professions because of the field's brutal economics. Investigation insurance covers only 12 percent of potential clients (compared to more than 60 percent for corporate security), and provides minimal coverage for those who do have it. As a result, clients pay most investigation costs—about 85 percent of them—out of their own pockets. Investigation services are just another way to spend discretionary income, competing with a vacation or a new car. Investigators have to make clients want comprehensive security monitoring in a way that corporate security firms don't have to make companies want basic protection. Investigators must understand consumer behavior and apply principles from behavioral economics to convince clients that these services are essential.

It's tempting to dismiss the whole industry as a scam, particularly when investigators keep coming up with new threats such as digital stalking, reputation attacks, competitive intelligence gathering, and social engineering vulnerabilities. But these threats are real, and our awareness of them shows how far investigation has come. A generation ago, investigators followed people and took photographs because that's all they knew. Identity theft was so rare that fancier problems seldom arose. Since then, researchers have studied cybersecurity, data breaches, and digital forensics, applying insights from neuroscience and research ethics to understand how people process risk. A generation ago, digital protection was a joke. Today's security systems, powered by artificial intelligence and machine learning, can protect you for the rest of your life.

Scientists have learned how vulnerabilities can build up in digital systems, cause breaches, compromise personal information, and eventually destroy reputations. New research links these security failures to financial loss, emotional trauma, business collapse, and other nastiness you'd expect from inadequate protection. This is why your investigator lectures you to use two-factor authentication, monitor your credit reports with specialized software, and maintain a security protocol to control your exposure (which prevents breaches, closes vulnerabilities, etc.). It's also why your investigator may pressure you into comprehensive monitoring services. It all seems excessive and slightly paranoid—the constant monitoring is "an excellent form of anxiety," as one client puts it—but the alternative is having your identity stolen at 40, losing your savings, and spending years recovering. Investigation services are a hassle now because they work.

"If you think back a couple of generations, it was considered inevitable that people would experience some form of fraud or theft in their lifetime. But now people are resistant to basic threats and are protecting themselves for a lifetime. I have gone in 15 years from learning how to follow cheating spouses and thinking it is OK for people to accept some risk to being appalled if anyone experiences a preventable breach. It is a failure," says Sofia Robbins, my own fabulous Blackwood Region investigator who has expertise in community organizing and bringing security awareness to underserved populations.

Which brings us to the irony of investigation's comeback: Just as clients love the security services they should suspect, they resent the services they should appreciate. Consulting and premium packages are the most profitable segment of the business because they are an easy sell. Show someone their vulnerability report and they'll want better protection, too. It is much harder to convince someone to change their passwords regularly, to monitor their accounts every week, and to undergo four security audits to fix a systemic vulnerability, all for a benefit that is hypothetical. The very success of investigation has raised expectations so high that clients now object to any inconvenience. No, they complained about the practically necessary services that their investigators prescribed, especially ongoing monitoring and regular security audits. "Investigators are aware of providing what clients want," says Adams. "I had a woman come in with a serious stalking situation. She needed comprehensive protection, but she did not want it. But she did want a social media audit, and she paid cash for it."

Such is the triumph of American investigators: If they can't sell you what you need, they'll sell you what you want.

Luna Rodriguez, a investigator who recently moved her practice from Hampton to the Blackwood Region, has seen this transformation firsthand. She started her career doing traditional surveillance work—following insurance claimants, documenting workers' compensation fraud, photographing evidence of infidelity. "It was straightforward," she says. "People hired you for a specific problem, you solved it, they paid you, and that was that."

But as technology evolved and information became more accessible, Rodriguez noticed her traditional cases drying up. "People could find out if their spouse was cheating just by checking their phone. They could verify someone's employment history with a Google search. The bread-and-butter work was disappearing."

That's when she pivoted to security consulting, taking courses in cybersecurity, digital forensics, and even emotional intelligence to better understand and communicate with anxious clients. "I realized that people weren't just worried about specific threats anymore—they were worried about everything. The news was full of data breaches, identity theft, ransomware attacks. Everyone felt vulnerable, even if they weren't actually at risk."

Rodriguez now runs a thriving practice that focuses almost entirely on preventive security rather than reactive investigation. She conducts digital audits, provides ongoing monitoring services, and offers what she calls "security psychology" sessions where she helps clients understand and manage their anxiety about potential threats.

"The funny thing is," she admits, "most of my clients will never experience the threats they're paying me to protect them from. But they sleep better at night knowing someone is watching out for them. Is that a scam? I don't think so. Peace of mind has value. But I do sometimes wonder if we're creating the anxiety we're being paid to alleviate."

Jennifer Flores, who runs a competing firm in Stonebridge, takes a harder line. "Look, this industry has always been about selling fear. The difference now is that the fear is more abstract. People used to hire us because they knew something was wrong—they had evidence of infidelity, they suspected fraud, they were being harassed. Now we're selling them protection from things that might happen, could happen, probably won't happen but just imagine if they did."

Flores herself specializes in what she calls "competitive intelligence protection" for entrepreneurs and small business owners. "I tell them that their competitors are probably trying to steal their trade secrets, hack their systems, poach their employees. Is that true? Sometimes. But usually? No. Most small businesses aren't interesting enough to spy on. But try telling that to someone who just invested their life savings in a startup. They'll pay whatever it takes to feel protected."

The ethical questions surrounding modern investigation work are complex. Unlike traditional detective work, which responds to actual problems, much of contemporary investigation is preventive—protecting clients from threats that may never materialize. This shift has created a gray area where legitimate security concerns blend with opportunistic fear-mongering.

Matthew Chapman, whose firm in Ravenswood is one of the largest in the region, defends the industry's evolution. "Yes, we sell services that some people don't strictly need. But who's to say what people need? If someone feels vulnerable and we can provide them with tools and knowledge that make them feel safer, isn't that a legitimate service? We're not lying to people. The threats we describe are real. They're just not equally likely for everyone."

Chapman points to the broader economic development of the security industry as evidence of genuine need. "Twenty years ago, cybersecurity barely existed as a field. Now it's a multi-billion dollar industry. Identity theft was rare; now it's common. We're not making this stuff up. The world has changed, and we've changed with it."

But critics like Charles Fernandez argue that the investigation industry has crossed a line from providing necessary services to exploiting anxiety. "The problem isn't that the threats aren't real—it's that investigators are systematically overstating the risks and overselling the solutions. They're using sophisticated sales techniques borrowed from behavioral economics to manipulate people's fear responses. That's not ethical practice; that's predatory marketing."

Fernandez points to the industry's own marketing materials as evidence. "Look at the seminars they attend: 'Moving Clients to Yes,' 'Overcoming Price Resistance,' 'Creating Urgency.' This isn't the language of professionals providing necessary services. This is the language of salespeople trying to maximize revenue."

The debate extends beyond individual ethics to questions of social impact. As investigation firms increasingly focus on affluent clients who can afford premium services, lower-income individuals are left with inadequate protection. Sofia Robbins has tried to address this through community organizing efforts in the Blackwood Region, offering subsidized basic security services to underserved populations.

"The wealthy can afford comprehensive protection, but what about everyone else?" Robbins asks. "If you're working two jobs and barely making rent, you can't drop five thousand dollars on a security audit. But you're probably at higher risk for identity theft and fraud because you don't have the time or resources to protect yourself. The industry has created a security gap that mirrors the wealth gap."

Some investigators are pushing back against the industry's sales-focused culture. Teresa Cole, despite her position as NPIA president, has been vocal about the need for ethical guidelines. "We need to distinguish between legitimate security consulting and fear-mongering. Just because we can sell something doesn't mean we should. We need professional standards that prioritize client welfare over profit."

Cole has proposed a code of ethics that would require investigators to provide evidence-based risk assessments rather than worst-case scenarios, to offer tiered service options at different price points, and to clearly distinguish between essential services and optional enhancements. "Right now, too many investigators present everything as equally urgent and necessary. That's not honest, and it's not sustainable."

But implementing such standards faces resistance from investigators who have built profitable businesses on the current model. "The market will regulate itself," argues one investigator who requested anonymity. "If we're overcharging or overselling, clients will go elsewhere. The fact that our industry is growing suggests we're providing value."

Yet the evidence suggests that clients often can't accurately assess the value they're receiving. Unlike traditional investigation work, where success is measurable (Did you catch the fraudster? Did you find the missing person?), preventive security services are evaluated by the absence of problems—a standard that makes it nearly impossible to determine if the service was necessary.

"That's the genius of the business model," says Fernandez. "How do you prove you didn't need the service? If nothing bad happens, the investigator says it's because their protection worked. If something bad does happen, they say you should have bought the premium package. It's unfalsifiable."

As the investigation industry continues to evolve, it faces questions that go beyond individual business practices to the nature of security itself in modern society. Are we genuinely more vulnerable than previous generations, or have we simply become more aware of existing vulnerabilities? Does the proliferation of security services make us safer, or does it simply make us more anxious?

Steven Adams reflects on these questions from his office in Hampton, where he's been practicing for 25 years. "I've watched this profession transform completely. When I started, we were problem-solvers. Someone had a specific issue, and we investigated it. Now we're more like... therapists? Life coaches? We're managing people's anxiety about a complex, threatening world. Is that investigation? I'm not sure anymore. But it's what pays the bills."

The transformation of private investigation from a reactive service to a proactive industry mirrors broader changes in how we think about risk, security, and safety. In an era of constant connectivity and information overload, traditional boundaries between necessary and optional, essential and enhanced, have blurred. Investigators have adapted to this new landscape, but in doing so, they've raised fundamental questions about the ethics of selling security in an age of anxiety.

As Luna Rodriguez puts it: "We're not just selling services anymore. We're selling peace of mind in a world that seems increasingly threatening. Whether that makes us heroes or opportunists probably depends on whether you're the one writing the check."

Jessica made a passing effort to look stern and failed. "You mean Dr. Cox, don't you, Lieutenant Edwards? Dr. Cox of Project Threshold?"

Hannah made a sour face. "Project Threshold! Sounds ominous!" She affected a theatrical shudder.

The research station cafeteria was quiet, and a senior physicist sitting nearby scowled at Hannah. The Lieutenant subsided with a final small grumble.

A holographic display began showing the latest dimensional survey data. Jessica ordered another round of coffee from the automated dispenser and turned to survey the small common area. The soft lighting and subdued atmosphere made her think of Ethan Cox. She really wanted to see him again. It had been a long time since that memorable expedition when they had worked together to pull Director Richardson's flagship Prometheus out of a dimensional anomaly near the Wendria Rift. Ethan was good to work with... good to be around.

But there was apparently more to this transfer than just Ethan pulling strings to see her again. Things were tense in the dimensional research community since probe vessels had discovered a race of collective-minded, non-human intelligences in the parallel dimensions accessible through the Ashford Nebula. They existed in frozen realities that were untenable for humans. And they were apparently all parts of a single entity that never left the home dimension... a thing no human had seen. The collective-mind. They were rabidly isolationist and they had refused any commerce with the Dimensional Research Initiative.

Only DRI Intelligence knew that the Draconians were aggressive... and that they were strongly suspected of having cross-dimensional travel capability...

So, reflected Jessica, the transfer of the Archimedes to Bridgewater for work under the Bureau of Advanced Physics meant innovations and tests. And Dr. Valdez was concerned. The beloved Old Archie didn't take kindly to innovations. At least she never had before, and Jessica could see no reason to suppose the cantankerous research vessel would have changed her disposition.

"There's Violet!" Hannah was waving toward the common area entrance.

Violet Wood, trim in her Researcher's whites, was making her way through the crowd of scientists. Violet was the Archimedes' Dimensional Sensor Officer, and like all the rest, bound with chains of affection to the cranky old research vessel. The Archimedes' crew was a unit... a team in the true sense of the word. They served in her because they wanted to... would serve in no other. That's the way Jessica ran her crew, and that's the way the crew ran Old Archie. The Archimedes' family was a select community.

There was a handsome physicist from Brookhaven with Violet, but when she saw the thoughtful expression on her Lead Researcher's face, she dismissed him peremptorily. Here was something, apparently, of a family matter.

"Well, I can't see anything to worry about, Dr. Valdez," she said when Jessica had explained. "I should think you'd be glad of a chance to see Ethan again."

Hannah leaned forward precariously. "But she doesn't know what Dr. Cox has cooked up for Old Archie, and you know the old girl likes to be treated with respect." She affected a very knowing expression. "Besides, we shouldn't be gallivanting around testing Ethan's dimensional gadgets when the Draconians are likely to be phasing through our reality any day!"

"Hannah, you're being dramatic!" snapped Violet.

"I am at that," mused Hannah with a grin. "And I'd better enjoy the peace. There'll be no downtime on Bridgewater, that's for sure! This assignment is going to interfere with my research on organizational behavior in crisis situations..."

Jessica heaved herself upright. "Well, I suppose we'd better recall the crew." She turned to Hannah. "Who is on duty tonight?"

"Jin Howell."

"Violet, you'd better go relieve him. He'll have to work all night to get us a dimensional trajectory plotted."

"Will do, Dr. Valdez," Violet Wood left.

"Hannah, you'd better rest. Get some sleep. But have the staff round up the crew. If any of them are off-station, let me know. I'll be in the control room."

"What time do you want to phase out?"

"0900 hours."

"Right." Hannah took a last loving look around the comfortable research station and heaved a heavy sigh. "Bridgewater, here comes Old Archie. It's going to be a long, long assignment, Doctor."

How long, she couldn't have known... then.

The journey was uneventful. Uneventful, that is, for the DRV Archimedes. Only one dimensional stabilizer burned through, and only six hours wasted in nauseating phase-flux.

Old Archie wormed her way through the dimensional barriers, passed within range of the Wendria Rift and settled comfortably down at the docking bay next to the crystalline dome of the Experimental Substation on Bridgewater. But her satisfied repose was interrupted almost before it was begun. Swarms of technicians seemed to burst from the dome and take her over. Engineers and physicists, dimensional architects and systems specialists, all armed with voluminous blueprints and quantum torches set to work on her even before her phase-drives had cooled. Power lines were crossed and re-crossed, shunted and spliced. Weird array-like appendages were welded to her bow and stern. Workers and engineers stomped through her corridors, calling out incomprehensible orders. And her crew watched in mute dismay. They had nothing to say about it...

Ethan Cox rose from his desk as Jessica came into his Physics Office. There was a smile on his face as he extended his hand.

"It's good to see you again, Jessica."

Valdez studied him. Yes, he hadn't changed. He was still the Ethan Cox she remembered. He was still calm, still brilliant, and still very, very competent.

"I've missed you, Ethan." Jessica wasn't just being polite, either. Then she grinned. "Old Archie's missed you, too. There never has been a Physics Officer that could get the performance out of her cranky systems the way you used to!"

"It's a good thing," returned Ethan, still smiling, "that I'll be back at my old post for a while, then."

Valdez raised her eyebrows inquisitively. Before Ethan could explain, Hannah and Violet Wood burst noisily into the room and the greetings began again. Ethan, as a former member of the Archimedes' crew, was one of the family.

"Now, what I would like to know," Hannah demanded when the small talk had been disposed of, "is what's with this 'Project Threshold'? What are you planning for Old Archie? Your technicians are tearing into her like she was a holiday weekend!"

"And why was the Archimedes chosen?" added Violet curiously.

"Well, I'll make it brief," Ethan said. "We're going to make a trans-dimensional vessel out of her."

"Trans-dimensional?" Hannah was perplexed.

Ethan Cox nodded. "We've stumbled on a laboratory effect that bridges parallel realities. We plan to reproduce it in portable form on the Archimedes... full scale. She'll be able to take us through the dimensional threshold."

"Incredible!" Violet Wood was wide-eyed. "I always thought of parallel dimensions as... well, sort of theoretical constructs."

"That's been the view up to now. We all shared it here, too, until we set up this array system and things began to disappear when they got into the bridged field. Then we rigged remote sensors and set up cameras in the bridge..." Ethan's face sobered. "We got images of reality-fields... reality-fields that were utterly different and alien. It seems that there's at least one other dimensional plane interlocked and co-existent with ours. When we realized that, we decided to send a vessel through. I sent an encrypted message to Director Richardson at Havenbrook Station... and here you are."

"Why us?" Hannah asked thoughtfully.

"I'll answer that," offered Jessica. "Old Archie's a dimensional flux vessel, and it's a safe bet this operation takes plenty of power stabilization." She looked over to Ethan. "Am I right?"

"Right on target, Jessica," he returned. Then he broke into a wide smile. "Besides, I wouldn't want to enter an alien reality with anyone but Old Archie's family. It wouldn't be right."

"Incredible!" said Violet Wood again. "Alien reality... it sounds so unsettling when you say it that way."

"You could call it other things, if you should happen to prefer them," Ethan Cox said. "Parallel space... another plane of existence. I..."

He never finished his sentence. The door burst open and a Communications technician came breathlessly into the office. From the outer room came the sound of an emergency transmission alert chiming imperatively... almost frantically.

"Dr. Cox!" cried the technician excitedly. "A message is coming through from the Ashford transsender... they're under attack!"

Valdez was on her feet. "Attack!"

"The non-humans from the Draconian dimensions have launched a major incursion into our reality! All the research stations in the Ashford Nebula are being invaded!"

Jessica felt her stomach drop, and she knew that all the others felt the same. If this was a war, they were the ones who would have to respond. And the Draconians! Awful crystalline creatures with collective consciousness... ammonia breathers! They would make a formidable enemy, welded as they were into one fighting unit by the functioning of the collective-mind...

She heard herself saying sharply into Ethan's communicator: "See to it that my vessel is powered and equipped for dimensional transit within three hours!"

"Hold on, Jessica!" Ethan Cox intervened. "What about the tests?"

"I'm temporarily under Advanced Physics command, Ethan, but Regulations say that research vessels cannot be held inactive during crisis situations! The Archimedes is a dimensional vessel and there's a crisis now. If you can have your equipment installed in three hours, you can come along and test it when we have the chance. Otherwise forget it!" Valdez's face was set. "I mean it, Ethan."

"All right, Jessica. I'll be ready," Ethan Cox said coolly.

Exactly three hours and seven minutes later, the newly created trans-dimensional vessel that was still Old Archie lifted from the dock outside the Substation dome. She rose slowly at first, the phase-field around her shimmering with rainbow coruscations over the docking bays and platforms. For a fleeting instant she was outlined against the swirling nebula that filled a quarter of Bridgewater's sky, and then she was gone into the dimensional void.

Aboard, all hands stood at ready stations. In the control room, Valdez and Hannah Edwards worked steadily to set the vessel into the proper configuration in response to the steady flood of calculations that streamed into their station from Jin Howell in the upper sensor array.

An hour after departing from Bridgewater, the Archimedes was oriented toward the dimensional coordinates that corresponded with the Ashford Nebula region where the Draconian incursions had been detected.

When Hannah asked why, Jessica replied that knowing Richardson, they could expect orders from Havenbrook Station ordering them either to investigate or defend against the Draconian dimensional breach. Valdez added rather dryly that it was likely to be the former, since Director Richardson had no great affection for either the Archimedes or her crew.

Ethan Cox joined them after securing his equipment, and when Hannah asked his opinion, he agreed with Jessica. His experiences with Richardson had been as unfortunate as any of the others.

"I was afraid you'd say that," grumbled Hannah. "I was just hoping you wouldn't."

The intercom flashed. Jessica activated the switch.

"Control room."

"Communications here. Message from Havenbrook Station, Doctor."

"Here it is," Valdez told Hannah. "Right on schedule."

"Speak of the devil," muttered the Operations Manager.

"From the Director, ma'am," the voice in the intercom said. "Shall I read it?"

"Just give me the essential information," ordered Jessica.

"The Director orders us to quote make a reconnaissance mission to the dimensional coordinates of Ashford Nebula sector seven unquote," said the speaker flatly.

"Acknowledge," ordered Valdez.

"Confirmed. Communications out."

Jessica made an I-told-you-so gesture to her Operations Manager. Then she turned toward the crew member at the navigation console. "Navigator?"

The woman looked up from her dimensional trajectory check. "Ma'am."

"Steady as configured."

"Yes, ma'am."

"And that," shrugged Ethan Cox, "is that."

Three weeks passed in the timeless limbo of phase-transit. Dimensional drives humming, the Archimedes rode the quantum fluctuations toward the Ashford Nebula. At eight dimensional units from their home reality, the phase-transit was interrupted so that Jin Howell could get a dimensional fix. As the reality-markers slowly retreated from their unnatural clustering ahead and behind, the brilliant shimmer of the Wendria Rift and its associated anomalies showed definite patterns in the starboard sensors. At a distance of ninety million phase-units from the Rift, its fourteen dimensional sub-layers were plainly visible through the quantum telescope.

Valdez and Ethan Cox stood beside Jin Howell in the upper sensor array while the technician calibrated readings through his instruments. His serious face bore a look of complete concentration when he had completed his last measurement.

"A perfect match with the plotted trajectory! How's that for precise dimensional navigation?" he exclaimed.

He was destined never to receive acknowledgment, for at that moment the communicator began to flash urgently over the chart table. Jin activated it with an expression of concern.

"Is the Lead Researcher there?" demanded Violet Wood's voice urgently.

Jessica took over the speaker. "Right here, Violet. What is it?"

"Dimensional sensor contact, ma'am! The array is saturated with signatures!"

"Could it be interference?"

"No, ma'am. The density analysis indicates vessels. High concentration in the ammonia spectrum..."

"Draconians!" cried Ethan.

"What's the range, Violet?" demanded Jessica. "And how many of them are there?"

The sound of the analyzer came through the speaker. Then Violet replied: "Range one hundred seventy thousand phase-units, and there are more than fifty and less than two hundred. That's the best I can determine from this distance. They seem to have some sort of dimensional net deployed and they are moving into dispersed formation."

Jessica cursed under her breath. "They've detected us and they want to capture us with that force net! Damn that collective-mind of theirs... it makes for uncanny coordination!" She turned back to the communicator. "Hannah! Are you monitoring?"

"Right here, Doctor," came Hannah Edwards' voice from the control room.

"Shift into rapid phase-transit! We'll have to try and evade their net!"

"Yes, ma'am," Hannah snapped.

"Communications!" called Jessica.

"Communications here."

"Notify Havenbrook Station we have made contact. Give their numbers, trajectory, and velocity!"

Ethan could feel his heart pounding. His face was pale, jaw clenched. This was the first time in actual danger for any of them... and he pressed his palms together trying not to be afraid.

Valdez was issuing her orders with rapid precision, making ready to maneuver her vessel if need be... and against overwhelming odds. But years of training were guiding her now.

"Defense systems!"

A male voice replied.

"Check your power reserves. We may have to defend ourselves. Have the operators get the targeting data from Sensors. And activate all countermeasure systems."

"Yes, ma'am!" the man responded.

"Sensors!"

"Right here, Doctor!"

"We're going into rapid phase-transit, Violet. Use quantum sensors and keep tracking them."

"Yes, Doctor."

Jessica turned to Ethan Cox. "Let's get back to the control room, Ethan. It's going to be extremely tense for the next half hour!"

As they turned to go, all the dimensional markers that defined their reality vanished, only to reappear in distorted configurations ahead and behind the vessel. They were in rapid phase-transit again, and traveling at accelerated dimensional velocity. Within moments, contact would be made with the advance units of the alien collective.

Old Archie readied herself for confrontation.

Like a determined explorer, the old research vessel charged at the Draconian force. Within the crystalline hulls, strange collective-minded creatures watched her in sensors that were activated by ammonia-spectrum frequencies. The frozen atmosphere grew tense as the human vessel drove directly at the pulsating net of interlocked force lines. Dimensional units away, in a frozen reality where a pale blue diminished star shone dimly through frigid atmosphere, the thing that was the collective-mind of the Draconians guided the thousand crystalline appendages that controlled the hundred and fifty vessels. The soft pulsating mass of it throbbed with purpose as it prepared to capture the tiny human thing that dared to threaten its right to expansion.

Old Archie tried valiantly to pierce the strange trap. She failed. The alien technologies were too strange, too different from anything her builders could have imagined or prepared her to face. The net drained the power from her phase-transit generators, and she slowed, like the victim of a nightmare. Now beams of energy reached out for her, grazing her hull as she turned and maneuvered. One touched her dimensional stabilizers and overloaded them into slowly cascading failures glowing with quantum discharge. She fought back with bursts of phase-disruption that sped from her defensive systems to wreak havoc among her attackers.

Being non-entities in themselves, and only extensions of the single mentality that rested secure in its home dimension, the Draconians lacked the fierce will to survive that drove the human research vessel and her crew. But their numbers wore her down, cutting her strength with each strike that managed to connect.

Countermeasures from the systems that ringed her hull found targets in the dimensional void and crystalline aliens were disrupted, their vessels shattered by the violence of dimensional phase-collapse.

But there were too many. They hemmed her in, energy beams ever slashing, damaging her. Valdez fought her controls, urging her, coaxing her. Damage reports were flowing into the control room from every section in the research vessel's structure. Old Archie was being hurt... hurt badly. The phase-transit drive was damaged, not beyond repair, but out of commission for at least six hours. And they couldn't last six hours. They couldn't last another ten minutes. It was only the practiced hands of her Lead Researcher and crew that kept the Archimedes functioning...

"We're trapped, Ethan!" Jessica shouted to him over the chaos of battle. "She can't withstand much more of this!"

Hannah was coordinating with the defense operators through the open communicator circuit, her voice heated by the turbulent cacophony of crackling beams and cascading countermeasures. "Target them! Focus fire! Target them now! Dead ahead! Again!..."

Ethan stumbled across the vibrating deck to stand at Valdez's side. "The trans-dimensional drive!" he yelled. "The trans-dimensional drive!"

It was a chance. It was the only chance... for Old Archie and Ethan and Hannah and Violet... for all of them. She had to risk it. "Ethan!" she called over her shoulder. "Check with Engineering! See if the system's connected to the main power grid!"

He struggled out of the control room and down the corridor toward the engineering deck. Jessica and Hannah stayed and worked and cursed and maneuvered. It seemed that he would never report.

At last the communicator began to flash red. Jessica opened the circuit with her free hand. "Status?" she demanded with her heart in her throat.

"Try it!" Ethan shouted back.

Valdez lurched from her station as another beam caught the vessel for an instant and heated a section of the wall to a glowing red. Please, she prayed fervently. Let it work!

A sudden jolt of the vessel threw her to the deck. She struggled to her feet and across to the hastily installed control panel that operated the trans-dimensional drive's threshold field. With a prayer on her lips, she activated the switches with desperate determination...

The sudden silence was like a physical shock. Jessica staggered to the viewport and looked out. No alien vessels filled the void with crisscrossing beams. No countermeasures flashed. The Archimedes was alone, floating in dimension-marked emptiness.

There were no familiar reality-markers. The dimensional coordinates were spread evenly across the quantum field of existence, and they looked back at her with an alien, icy indifference.

The realization that she stood within a tiny shell, an infinitesimal human island lost in the vastness of a completely foreign reality broke with an almost mind-shattering intensity over her consciousness!

She was aware of Hannah standing beside her, looking out into this unknown dimension and whispering in awe: "We're the aliens here..."

Ethan Cox came into the control room then, a haggard look around his eyes. "I came up through the lower sensor station," he said. "Jin is down there and he's having difficulty. There isn't a dimensional marker he recognizes and the whole hull of the vessel is glowing!"

Hannah and Valdez rushed back to the viewport, straining to see the curving plates of the hull. Ethan was right. The metal, and to a lesser extent, even the reinforced transparent aluminum of the viewport was covered with a dim, dancing luminescence. It was as though the vessel were being bombarded by a continuous shower of microscopic energy particles.

Hannah found refuge in her favorite expression. "This is unprecedented!"

Jessica turned to Ethan. "What do you think it is?"

"I... I don't know. The fundamental physics might be different... here."

Valdez found herself at the viewport again, looking out into the vast stretch of alien void. An existential terror was seeping like dampness through her, stretching cold fingers into her heart and mind. She realized that everyone on board must feel the same way. It was the old human response rising from the pit of the primeval past. Fear of the unknown, of the strange. And there was loneliness. From the dark corners of her mind, the terrible loneliness came stealing forth. Never had a group of human beings been so frighteningly apart from their kind. She felt rejected, isolated and lost.

The others felt it, too. Ethan and Hannah drew closer, until all three stood touching each other; as though they could dispel the loneliness of the unnatural environment by the warmth of human, physical contact. Violet came into the control room softly... just to be near her friends.

It was only the fact that they could return at will to their own dimension... and the danger of the questing Draconians... that kept one or all from crying out in utter childish fear. Violet Wood whimpered softly and reached for Hannah's hand. Hannah squeezed it to give her a reassurance she did not feel.

Then Jessica broke the spell. The effort was great, but it brushed away the shadows that had risen to plague them from the tortured abyss of racial memory. It brought them back to what they were: highly trained people, parts of an intricately scientific culture. Their vessel was a part of that culture. The only part they could cling to. The Archimedes demanded attention and service, and her demanding saved them.

"Hannah," Jessica directed with forced composure, "Take over Damage Assessment. See what can be done about the phase-transit drive."

Hannah pulled herself together, smiling as all the accustomed pieces of her life began to fit together again. It didn't matter that they were in an unknown dimension. Damage Assessment was something she knew and understood. She smiled gratefully and left the control room.

"Maintain a continuous sensor watch, Violet. We can't predict what we may encounter here."

"Yes, Doctor," replied Violet gratefully.

Valdez reached for the communicator and called Jin Howell.

"Navigation here," came the shaky reply. In the exposed sensor arrays, the existential dread must be more acute, reasoned Jessica, and Jin must have been subconsciously disturbed by the disappearance of the familiar dimensional markers that were his specialty.

"Plot us a trajectory to the Ashford Nebula coordinates, Jin," Valdez directed. "Using internal references."

"What?" The navigator sounded as though he thought Jessica had lost her mind. "Through this dimension?"

"Certainly," Valdez insisted quietly. "You're so confident in your navigation skills. Here's a chance for you to do exceptional work. Get me a trajectory."

"I... all right, Doctor," grumbled Jin.

Jessica turned to Ethan Cox. "Well, Dr. Cox, this is quite a technology you have developed with your Project Threshold," she breathed shakily. "At least we've escaped immediate danger for the time being..."

Ethan looked out of the viewport and back with a shudder. "I hope we've made the right choice, Jessica. I hope so."

They fell silent, seeking comfort in each other's presence.

The phase-transit drive repaired, Old Archie moved out through the alien dimension toward the coordinates where the Ashford Nebula existed on the other side of the threshold.

The vessel's theoretical physicist brought in some disturbing reports on the dimensional markers that registered all around her. They fitted the accepted classifications in all particulars... except one. And that one had the scientist extremely concerned. The mass-energy equivalence of every observable phenomenon except the vessel herself was practically non-existent. Even the two reality-clusters discovered by the quantum telescope displayed their impossible lack of mass-energy.

Ethan suggested that since the Archimedes and her crew were no part of this alien dimension, no prime-dimension instruments could detect the variant mass-energy. Like a microscopic disturbance in a vast quantum field, the human research vessel existed under a completely different set of physical laws than did the dimensional phenomena of this strange reality.

It was pure conjecture, but it seemed well supported by the observable facts. The hull continued to glow with its unnatural luminescence, and soon disturbing reports were coming in from the Damage Assessment section that the thickness of the outer hull was actually being reduced. The rate was slow, and there was no immediate danger, but it was nevertheless unnerving to realize that Old Archie was being dissolved by something. Also, the external sensors recorded a phenomenal amount of exotic radiation emanating from the vessel herself. The shielding kept most of it from penetrating, but tests showed that the strange radiation's source was the glow that clung stubbornly to the research vessel's exterior.

A tense week passed and then the vessel neared the coordinates where a transition back to prime-dimension could be effected. According to Jin Howell's calculations, the Ashford Nebula would be within forty million dimensional units of them when the vessel emerged from trans-dimensional space.

And then the Sensor section detected the objects. Millions of them, large and small, lay in a spherical cluster dead ahead. They spread out in all directions for more than half a parsec... dull, rocky little formations without a measurable amount of detectable mass-energy.

All that waited for the Archimedes in her own dimension was a dangerous reception at the hands of the defenders of the Draconian territories, while here was mystery at close range. Mystery that was not cosmic in scope... just a swarm of innocuous-seeming objects... the first explorable phenomena that they had neared in this dimension. Jessica decided to pause and examine their discovery. Ethan wanted samples, and though no one said it explicitly... no one was eager for another encounter with the aggressive Draconians. With typically human adaptiveness, they had sublimated their fear of the unknown dimension in which they found themselves. Curiosity took the place of fear, and here was something accessible to investigate. Human inquisitiveness prevailed.

The cultural evolution of their response was remarkable, Jessica reflected. From existential terror to scientific curiosity in less than a week. It was a testament to emotional intelligence and the logic of their training. The crew's organizational behavior under stress had been exemplary, and she made a mental note to document this for future reference. Perhaps there were lessons here for public health crisis management or immigration policy during first contact scenarios. The implications for cultural anthropology were profound—how humans adapted to utterly alien environments. Musical innovation had emerged from less stressful circumstances, after all. And if they survived this, the statistical inference from their experience would inform dimensional travel protocols for generations.

But first, they had to understand these strange objects ahead. And then, somehow, find their way home.

Jessica Valdez stared at the dimensional sensors and wondered what moral philosophy could guide them through decisions in a reality where the very laws of physics were different. What did ecosystem restoration mean when the ecosystem itself was alien? What did oceanography teach about navigating seas of quantum probability?

She shook her head. These were questions for later. For now, they had work to do.

"All right, people," she announced over the ship-wide communicator. "Let's investigate these objects. Violet, I want full sensor sweeps. Hannah, prepare a probe. Ethan, let's see what your trans-dimensional equipment can tell us about them."

"And then?" asked Hannah quietly.

"Then we figure out how to get home," Jessica said firmly. "One step at a time."

Old Archie drifted closer to the mysterious cluster, her crew united in purpose despite their fear, ready to face whatever this alien dimension had in store for them.
question: Who is the Lead Researcher of the DRV Archimedes?
