THE LAST DEEP-SEA EXPLORER
BY VARIOUS AUTHORS

Illustrated by Digital Artists

[Transcriber's Note: This etext was produced from
Ocean Worlds Quarterly, March 2089
Extensive research did not uncover any evidence that
the U.S. copyright on this publication was renewed.]

What's more important—humanity's understanding
of the deep ocean, or one explorer's peace of mind?

I

They gave him a commemorative plaque. It was meant to be symbolical, of course. In the old tradition. It was crafted from actual titanium alloy, being one of the materials used in the earliest deep-sea submersibles constructed generations past in the coastal facilities of Highpoint, Selvoria. Its significance lay in the fact that it represented the hull plating from the historic vessel Challenger Deep II, not a modern composite material grown through nanotechnology, but actual forged metal that had withstood the crushing pressures of the Mariana Trench.

They also had a ceremony for him, complete with speeches by such luminaries of the Department of Ocean Exploration as Director Luna King and Professor Mohammad Newman. There was also somebody from the Global Resource Management Council who spoke, but he was one of those pseudo-elected bureaucrats who didn't know much about deep-sea exploration nor the significance of Paul Sanders' retirement. Paul didn't bother to remember his name. He only wondered vaguely why the administrator had shown up at all.

In common with recipients of commemorative plaques of a score of generations before him, Paul Sanders would have preferred something a bit more tangible in the way of reward, such as a few additional shares of Universal Basic Income credits to add to his portfolio. But that, he supposed, was asking too much.

The fact of the matter was, Paul knew that his retiring had set them back considerably. They hadn't figured he had enough UBI credits to see him through decently. Well, possibly he didn't, given their standards. But Deep-Sea Pilot Paul Sanders didn't have their standards. He'd had plenty of time to think it over. It was better to retire on a limited income, on a confoundedly limited income, than to take the two or three more dives in hopes of attaining a higher standard of living.

He'd had plenty of time to figure it out, there alone in the crushing darkness of the hadal zone, there on the abyssal plain runs. There on the long, long descents to the hydrothermal vent systems, fearfully checking the symptoms of pressure psychosis, the madness compounded of claustrophobia, sensory deprivation, profound isolation and the constant awareness of millions of tons of water pressing against the hull. Plenty of time. Time to decide that a small efficiency habitat-pod, complete with an auto-recliner and built-in beverage synthesizer, and with one wall a full immersion holographic display, was all he needed to find contentment for a mighty long time. Possibly somebody like Professor Newman might be horrified at the idea of living in an efficiency habitat-pod... not realizing that to a deep-sea pilot it was spacious beyond belief compared to the cramped sphere of a submersible craft.

No. Even as Paul listened to their speeches, accepted the plaque and made a halting little talk of his own, he was grinning inwardly. There wasn't anything they could do. He had them now. He had enough UBI credits to keep him comfortably, by his standards, for the rest of his life. He was never going to subject himself to pressure psychosis again. Just thinking about it, now, set the tremor going in his left hand.

They could pressurize their hulls and descend, for all he gave a damn.

The commemorative plaque idea had been that of Luna King, which was typical, she being in the way of a living traditionalist herself. In fact, Director King was possibly the only living person on the North American continent who still maintained a physical library of actual printed books. Her explanation was that she found the tactile experience of turning pages irreplaceable and that digital formats lacked the gravitas of bound volumes.

That was only an excuse so far as her closest associate, Mohammad Newman, was concerned. Professor Newman was convinced King would have even used a manual typewriter, had she but a touch more courage. King longed for the methodologies of yesteryear, a seldom found phenomenon under the Universal Welfare System.

Seated in an ergonomic chair in the research facility of his Hampton, Ilvaria apartment, Luna King scowled at her colleague. She said, acidly, "Any more brilliant ideas, Mohammad? I presume you now acknowledge that appealing to Sanders' sense of duty, scientific curiosity and desire for historical significance have miserably failed."

Newman said easily, "I wouldn't call Paul Sanders unmotivated. In his position, I am afraid I would do the same thing he has."

"That's nonsense, Mohammad. By all measures of comparative history! Either you or I would gladly take Sanders' place were we capable of performing the duties for which he has been trained. There aren't two people on this continent—there aren't two people in the world!—who better realize the urgency of continuing our exploration of the hadal zones." King snapped her fingers. "Like that, either of us would risk our lives to prevent humanity from completely abandoning the quest to understand our ocean's depths."

Her colleague said drily, "Either of us could have volunteered for deep-sea pilot training forty years ago, Luna. We didn't."

"At that time there wasn't such a devastating percentage of risk-averse individuals throughout this whole Universal Welfare System! Who could foresee that eventually our entire program would face termination due to lack of courageous young people willing to take chances, willing to face the existential questions that arise in profound isolation, willing to react to danger in the manner our ancestors did?"

Newman grunted his sarcasm and synthesized a glass of cold green tea. He said, "Nevertheless, both you and I conform with the present generation in finding it far more pleasant to follow one's research interests in the comfort of one's facility than to be confronted with the psychological dangers of facing nature's extremes in more adventurous pursuits."

King, half angry at her colleague's argument, leaned forward to snap a rebuttal, but the other was raising a hand negatively. "Face reality, Luna. Don't require or expect from Paul Sanders more than is reasonable. He is an average young man. Born in our Universal Welfare System, he was guaranteed his fundamental security by being issued that minimum allocation of UBI credits in our society that allows him an income sufficient to secure the food, housing, medical care and education to sustain a basic level of subsistence. Statistical probabilities were against his ever being drafted into the workforce. Automation and robotics being what they are, only a fraction of the population is ever called up for mandatory service. But Sanders was. His aptitude profile revealed him a possible candidate for deep-sea pilot, and it was you yourself who convinced him to take the training... pointing out the pragmatic advantages such as complete retirement after but six dives, supplemental UBI credits so that he could enjoy a more comfortable life than most, and the recognition that would accrue to him as one of the very few who still participate in hadal exploration. Very well. He was persuaded. Took his training, which, of course, required long years of demanding study in neuroscience, pressure physiology, and submersible operations. Then, performing his duties quite competently, he made his six dives. He is now legally eligible for retirement. He was drafted into the workforce reserves, served his time, and is now free from mandatory labor for the balance of his life. Why should he listen to our pleas for a few more dives?"

"But has he no sense of wonder? Has he no appreciation for..."

Newman was raising his hand again, a gesture that, seemingly mild though it was, had an astonishing ability to halt the conversation of one who debated with the calm, measured man.

He said, "No, he hasn't. Few there are who have, nowadays. Humanity has always paid lip service to exploration, hardships and discovery, but in actuality our instincts, like those of any other animal, lead us to the safest path. Today we've reached the point where no one need face danger—ever. There are few who don't take advantage of that fact. Including you and me, Luna, and including Paul Sanders."

His colleague changed subjects abruptly, impatiently. "Let's leave this frustrating discussion about Sanders' motivation and address the actual problem. The man is the only trained deep-sea pilot in the world. It will take months, possibly more than a year, to bring another candidate to the point where they can safely be trusted to pilot our next research submersible down to hadal depths. Appropriations for our expeditions have been increasingly difficult to secure—even though in our minds, Mohammad, we are approaching critical breakthroughs, discoveries which might possibly so inspire the human race that a renewed commitment to understanding our planet's last frontier will take hold of us. If it is revealed that our organization has deteriorated to the point that we haven't a single qualified pilot, then it might well be that the Economic Planning Council, and especially those administrators on the Appropriations Committee, will terminate the entire Department of Ocean Exploration."

"So..." Newman said gently.

"So somehow we've got to bring Paul Sanders out of his retirement!"

"Now we are addressing the real issue." Newman nodded his agreement. Looking over the rim of his glass, his eyes narrowed in thought as his face took on an expression of calculated strategy. "And do not the ends justify the means?"

King blinked at him.

The other chuckled. "The trouble with you, Luna, is that you have failed to apply lessons from comparative history to our problem. Haven't you ever studied the psychology of sailors and their way of life?"

"Sailors? What in the name of reason do sailors have to do with it?"

"You must realize, my dear Luna, that our Paul Sanders is nothing more than a modern-day sailor, with many of the psychological patterns, perspectives, tendencies and vulnerabilities of the seafarers of the past. Have you never heard of the merchant mariner who dreamed of returning to his hometown and starting a small business? All the long months at sea—and sometimes the cargo vessels or fishing boats would be out for years at a stretch before returning to home port—he would talk of his retirement and his dream. And then? Then in port, it would be one drink with his shipmates, before taking his accumulated wages and heading home. The one drink would lead to another. And morning would find him, broke, tattooed and possibly sleeping it off in a holding cell. So back to sea he'd have to go."

King grunted bitterly. "Unfortunately, our present-day explorer can't be separated from his credits quite so easily. If he could, I'd personally be willing to hack his account, drain his balance and force him back to work."

She brought up her wrist display and flicked it to show her universal credit account. "The ultimate financial regulation," she grunted. "Nobody can spend your money but you, yourself. Nobody can steal it, nobody can, ah, manipulate you out of it. Just how do you expect to separate our modern-day sailor from his accumulated nest egg?"

The other chuckled again. "It is simply a matter of finding contemporary methods, my dear colleague."

II

Paul Sanders was a great believer in the institution of celebration. Any excuse would do. Back when he had finished his basic education at the age of twenty-five and was registered for the labor draft, there hadn't been a chance in a hundred that he'd have the misfortune to have his name selected. But when it had been, Paul had celebrated.

When he had been informed that his physical and psychological qualifications were such that he was eligible for the most demanding occupation in the Universal Welfare System and had been persuaded into taking training for deep-sea pilot, he had celebrated once again. Eighteen others had taken the training with him, and only he and Eva Ahmed had passed the final evaluations. On this occasion, he and Eva had celebrated together. It had been quite an event. Three weeks later, Eva had died when a catastrophic hull failure occurred on what should have been a routine descent to the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

Each time Paul returned from one of his own dives, he celebrated. A night out, an indulgence, a spree, a commemoration of dangers met and survived.

Now it was all over. At the age of thirty he was retired. Professional ethics and legal regulations prevented him from ever being called up for contributing to the world's labor needs again. And he most certainly wasn't going to volunteer.

He had taken his education much as had his contemporaries. There wasn't any particular reason for trying to excel. You didn't want to get the reputation for being overly ambitious, or lazy either. Just one of the crowd. You could do the same in life whether you really studied or not. You had your Universal Basic Income allocation, didn't you? What else did you need?

It had come as a surprise when he'd been drafted for the labor force.

In the early days of the Universal Welfare System, they had made a mistake in adapting to the automation revolution and the advances in robotics. They had attempted to give everyone work by reducing the number of working hours in the day, and the number of working days in the week. It finally became absurd when employees were working but two days a week, three hours a day. In fact, it got chaotic. It became obvious that it was more practical to have one worker putting in thirty-five hours a week and developing real expertise, than it was to have a score of employees, each working a few hours a week and none of them ever really becoming proficient.

The only equitable solution was to let the technologically unemployed remain unemployed, with their Universal Basic Income as the equivalent of unemployment insurance, while the few workers still needed put in a reasonable number of hours a day, a reasonable number of weeks a year and a reasonable number of years in a lifetime. When new employees were needed, a draft lottery was held.

All persons registered in the labor force participated. If you were drawn, you must serve. The dissatisfaction those chosen might feel at their poor luck was offset by the fact that they were granted supplemental UBI credits, according to the tasks they fulfilled. Such credits could be added to their portfolios, the dividends becoming part of their current balance, or could be liquidated for a lump sum.

Yes, but now it was all over. He had his own small habitat, his own personal transport pod and twice the amount of UBI credits that most of his fellow citizens could claim. Paul Sanders had it made. A celebration was obviously called for.

He was going to do this one properly. This was the significant one. He'd accumulated substantial credits these past few months and he intended to spend them, or at least a considerable portion of them. His credit account was ready to be used. However, he wasn't going to rush into things. This had to be done correctly.

Too many celebrations were improvised. You started off with a few drinks, met some unremarkable companion and usually ended up in a mediocre establishment where you spent just as much as though you'd been in the finest venue in the city. Come morning and you had nothing to show for all the credits that had been spent but a headache and regrets.

Thus, Paul was vaguely aware from his studies of social psychology, it had always been down through the centuries since the ancient Phoenician sailor, back from his year-long voyage to distant trading ports, squandered his hard earned share of the expedition's profits in a matter of days in the wine shops of Tyre. Nobody gets quite so little for his money as that loneliest of all workers, he who must leave his home for isolated duty, returning only periodically and usually with the compensation of lengthy, demanding periods of time to be spent hurriedly in an attempt to achieve the pleasure and happiness so long denied him.

Paul was going to do it differently this time.

Nothing but the best. Entertainment, cuisine, companionship, luxury accommodations. Everything. But nothing but the best.

To start off, he dressed with great care in the formal retirement-status attire he had so recently purchased. His deep-sea exploration pin he attached carefully to the collar. That was a good beginning, he decided. A bit of prestige didn't hurt when you went out on the town. In the Universal Welfare System hardly one person in a hundred actually ever performed anything of significant value to society. The contributions of most weren't needed. Those few who did contribute were awarded honors, recognition, status markers.

Attired satisfactorily, Paul double-checked to see that his credit chip was secure. As an afterthought, he went over to the habitat-pod's communication console, activated it, held the chip to the scanner and said, "Balance inquiry, please."

In a moment, the console's synthesized voice reported, "Base Universal Basic Income allocation: ten thousand credits annually. Supplemental workforce credits: forty-two thousand credits. Current liquid balance: eight thousand, three hundred and seventeen credits." The screen went dark.

Eight thousand, three hundred and seventeen credits. That was substantial. He could safely spend as much as half of it, if the celebration proved as memorable as he hoped it would. His quarterly UBI distribution was due in another week or so, and he wouldn't have to worry about routine expenses. Yes, indeed, Paul Sanders was as financially secure as he had ever been in his thirty years.

He opened the compact door which housed his personal transport pod, and settled himself into the comfortable vehicle. He activated the canopy, engaged the pressurization and considered the destination interface. Only one place really made sense. Unity, Galdoria.

He considered for a moment, decided against the districts of Highpoint and Dawnridge, and selected Unity instead. He had the resources. He might as well do it properly.

He entered Unity into the navigation system and felt the subtle acceleration that indicated his pod's engagement with the transit network. While it was being routed through the automated controls, being directed here and there preparatory to the high-speed transit to his destination, he accessed the pod's information system for data on the premier hotels of Unity. He selected an exclusive establishment he'd read about and seen on the holographic broadcasts of society and celebrity content, and entered it as his destination.

"Nothing too good for ex-Deep-Sea Pilot Paul Sanders," he said aloud.

The pod paused for a moment, that brief hesitation before the acceleration, and Paul took the involuntary breath that even experienced travelers couldn't quite suppress. He pressed back into the seat. Minutes passed, and the direction of the pressure reversed.

Unity. The routing adjustments began again, and one or two more local transits. Finally, the display showed green and Paul opened the canopy and stepped into his hotel suite.

A voice said pleasantly, "If the accommodations are satisfactory, please present your credit chip within ten minutes."

Paul took his time. Not that he really needed it. It was by far the most luxurious suite he had ever seen. One wall was a holographic window of whatever view the guest might desire and Paul touched the control that expanded it to maximum. His view opened such that he could see both the Central Archive Tower and the Meridian Gardens. Beyond the gardens stretched the seemingly endless metropolis that was Greater Unity.

He didn't take the time to activate the menu interface next to the automated dining station, nor to check the extensive selection on the beverage synthesizer. All that, he well knew, would be exceptional. Besides, he didn't plan to dine or do much drinking in his suite. He made a wry smile. Not unless he managed to find some pleasant companionship, that was.

He looked briefly into the hydrotherapy pool and cleansing chamber, then settled himself onto the bed. It wasn't adjusted to the degree of firmness he presently desired, and he recalibrated the settings to his preference so that with a satisfied sigh he sank into the perfect support of the mattress.

He came back to his feet, gave his attire a quick adjustment so that it fell into perfect alignment and, taking his credit chip from his pocket, placed it against the communication console screen and pressed the hotel registration control so that check-in could be completed.

For a moment he stood in the center of the floor, considering his options. Take it easy, Paul Sanders, take it all easy, this time. No squandering his credits in second-rate establishments, no eating in automated food dispensaries. This time, perhaps the only time in his life, he was going to celebrate in the grand manner. No mediocrity for Paul Sanders.

He decided a drink was in order to help him plan his evening. A drink at the hotel's famous Zenith Lounge where notable individuals were reputed to gather regularly.

He left the suite and entered one of the elevators. He said, "Zenith Lounge."

The automated elevator responded politely, "Yes, sir, the Zenith Lounge."

At the entrance to the famous gathering place of the elite, Paul paused a moment and observed his surroundings. He'd never been in a place like this before. However, he suppressed his initial instinct to worry about what this was going to cost with an inner smile and made his way to the bar.

There was actually a human bartender.

Paul suppressed his astonishment and said, casually, attempting an air of practiced sophistication, "Abyssal Depths."

"Yes, sir."

The drinks in the Zenith Lounge might be prepared by hand, but Paul noticed they had the standard payment scanners built into the bar surface. He placed his credit chip on the scanner immediately before him when the drink arrived, and had to resist his desire to check for a balance inquiry, so as to be able to calculate what the cocktail had cost him.

Well, this was something worthwhile. This was the sort of experience he'd imagined, out there in the crushing darkness, sealed in the confining sphere of his submersible craft. He sipped at the drink, finding it exceeded his expectations, and then turned slightly on his stool to observe the other patrons.

To his disappointment, there were no recognizable celebrities. None that he identified, at least—prominent holographic performers, influential politicians of the Universal Welfare System or renowned artists.

He turned back to his drink and noticed, for the first time, the woman who occupied the seat two down from him. Paul Sanders blinked. He blinked and then inhaled sharply.

"Remarkable," he breathed.

She was styled in the latest aesthetic from the Pacific Rim cultural centers, even to the point of having cosmetically enhanced her features with bioluminescent accents that caught the ambient light. Every detail, but every detail, was flawless. She sat with the composed elegance that spoke of professional training in artistic expression.

His stare couldn't be ignored.

She looked at him coolly, turned to the bartender and murmured, "A Crystalline Cascade, please, Walter." Then deliberately added, "I thought the Zenith Lounge was supposed to be exclusive."

There was nothing the bartender could say to that, and he went about preparing the drink.

Paul cleared his throat. "Hey," he said, "how about letting this one be on me?"

Her eyebrows, which had been shaped and enhanced to complement her aesthetic presentation, rose. "Indeed?" she said, drawing it out.

The bartender said quickly, "I beg your pardon, sir..."

The woman, her voice suddenly subtly changed, said, "Wait, isn't that a deep-sea exploration pin?"

Paul, disconcerted by the sudden reversal, said, "Yeah... sure."

"Good heavens, you're a hadal pilot?"

"Sure." He indicated the collar pin. "You can't wear one unless you've completed at least one descent to the hadal zone."

She was obviously both taken aback and impressed. "Why," she said, "you're Paul Sanders, the pilot. I watched the ceremony they held for you."

Paul, carrying his glass, moved over to the seat next to her. "Call me Paul," he said. "Everyone calls me Paul."

She said, "I'm Claudia. Claudia Montgomery. Just Claudia. Imagine meeting Paul Sanders. Just sitting down next to him at a bar. Just like that."

"Paul," Paul said, gratified. By all measures, he'd never encountered anyone with this level of refined beauty. Maybe on holographic displays, of course, one of the current cultural icons, but never in person. "Call me Paul," he said again. "I've been called Paul so long, I don't even register when someone uses my full name."

"I was moved when they gave you that commemorative plaque," she said, her tone such that it was obvious she hadn't quite processed having actually met him.

Paul Sanders was surprised. "Moved?" he said. "Well, why? I was somewhat disengaged from the whole ceremony. But Director King, I used to work under her in the Ocean Exploration Department, she was enthusiastic about it."

"Director King?" she said. "You just call her Luna?"

Paul was expansive. "Why, sure. In the Ocean Exploration Department we don't have much use for formality. Everyone's just Paul, and Luna, and Mohammad. Like that. But why were you moved?"

She looked down into the drink the bartender had placed before her, as though avoiding his gaze. "I... I suppose it was that speech Professor Newman made. There you stood, so distinguished in your deep-sea pilot uniform, the veteran of six exploration dives to the hadal zones..."

"Well," Paul said modestly, "two of my dives were only to the bathypelagic zone."

"...and he said all those things about humanity's quest to understand the deep ocean. And the existential questions that arise when we confront the unknown depths. And then the fact that you were the last of the deep-sea pilots. The last person in the whole world trained to pilot a hadal submersible. And there you were, retiring."

Paul grunted. "Yeah. That's all part of Luna's strategy to get me to take on another three dives. They're concerned the whole department will be eliminated by the Appropriations Committee on the Economic Planning Council. Even if they can find some other candidate to train for the position, it would take maybe a year before they could even send them on a bathypelagic descent. So Director King, and Professor Newman too, they're both trying to pressure me into more dives. Otherwise they have an Ocean Exploration Department, with all the expense and all, but nobody to pilot their submersibles. It's somewhat ironic, in a way. You know what one of those hadal submersibles costs?"

"Ironic?" she said. "Why, I don't think it's ironic at all."

Paul said, "Look, how about another drink?"

Claudia Montgomery said, "Oh, I'd love to have a drink with you, Mr..."

"Paul," Paul said. He gestured to the bartender with a circular motion indicating their need for two more of the same. "How come you know so much about it? You don't meet many people who are interested in deep-sea exploration anymore. In fact, most people are almost dismissive, like. Think it's kind of a wasteful expenditure to help consume resources and keep the economy functioning."

Claudia said earnestly, "Why, I've been fascinated by ocean exploration all my life. I've studied everything about it. Have always known the names of all the deep-sea pilots and everything about them, ever since I was young. I suppose you'd say I'm captivated by the existential questions that Professor Newman spoke about."

Paul chuckled. "A real enthusiast, eh? You know, it's kind of funny. I was never much interested in it. And I became considerably less interested after my first dive and I discovered what pressure psychosis was."

She frowned. "I don't believe I know much about that."

Sitting in the Zenith Lounge with the most beautiful woman to whom he had ever spoken, Paul could be casual about the subject. "Director King keeps that aspect mostly suppressed and out of the media articles and holographic documentaries. Says there's enough negative publicity about ocean exploration already. But at this stage when the whole submersible is packed with automated scientific equipment and all, there's extremely limited space in the pilot sphere and you're the only person aboard. Luna says later on when submersibles are larger and there's a whole crew aboard, there won't be any such thing as pressure psychosis, but..." Suddenly the left side of Paul Sanders' hand began to tremble and he hurriedly took up his drink and finished it.

Hearts and Algorithms

No romantic drama in the last five years has succeeded in dividing critics and audiences as fully as the sprawling, ambitious love story The Carbon Footprint of Love, Valentina Cooper's return to filmmaking after a decade. I've watched it twice and am still trying to sort out my responses, which run from enchantment to frustration and back. Like The Notebook, the picture tugs at your heartstrings with brilliant, sweeping montages of passionate encounters and Turneresque images of romance against impossible odds. But Cooper, a certified intellectual and the reclusive figure who directed Autumn in Redwood and Seasons of the Heart in the 2010s and then disappeared, is in a different philosophical universe from Nicholas Sparks adaptations. Post-romance, her sundry characters philosophize about their experiences in dreamy, cryptic voice-overs that come at you like gentle waves: "Why does love compete with duty? ... Is there a reconciling force in humanity, not one path but two?" Or "This great longing: Where's it come from? What seed, what root did it grow from? Who's doing this? Who's keeping us apart, robbing us of connection and light?" First you get swept up in passion, then you get submerged in contemplation.

Those existential questions don't derive from the screenplay's source, a straightforward but otherwise grounded 2018 novel by Fernando Simpson (who also wrote Climate of the Heart) about two climate scientists who fall in love while racing to develop breakthrough carbon capture technology in Crystalbrook, Marvenia. They're central to Cooper's vision of the story, however, and not spurious. In the romantic drama genre, the phrase "love conquers all" usually means nothing more than that it's nice to find your soulmate, or to see obstacles overcome. A true work of art owes us more than literal happy endings, and Cooper obliges by making her theater of romance the setting for nothing less than a meditation on the social contract between individual desire and collective responsibility.

She tells the story deliberately, in three parts, with a prestigious cast (Oscar Hunt, Talia Bailey, Andre Martinez) and a few other major stars (Dominic Ali, Samir McDonald, Samir Zhang) dropping by for supporting roles. After an idyllic prelude, in which an idealistic young researcher, Dr. Witt Chen (Oscar Hunt), works alongside indigenous communities on climate adaptation strategies to the accompaniment of a soaring orchestral score, the first part sees the arrival of a multinational team of scientists in Crystalbrook, introduces the principal characters (none of whom amounts to a simple protagonist), and lays out the movie's geographical and philosophical terrain. The centerpiece—the romance and the race against time—goes on for over an hour and features the most intense and moving sequences, chiefly the team's initially unsuccessful attempt to secure funding for their revolutionary carbon sequestration project while Witt and lead engineer Maya Torres (Talia Bailey) navigate their growing feelings for each other. The coda lasts nearly forty minutes and is mostly reflection and resolution, the rhythms growing more contemplative until a final, unexpected moment of separation—whereupon the surviving relationship must adapt to new circumstances as both characters accept positions at different research facilities across the globe. In the final shot, a seedling grows in the laboratory where they first met, the cycle of hope beginning anew.

The Carbon Footprint of Love has a curious soundscape, as the noise of laboratory methods and technological progress frequently recedes to make room for interior monologues and Philip Glass's minimalist, repetitive score. Maya talks to her absent father, viewed in wistfully melancholic flashbacks. ("Love: Where does it fit in a life devoted to saving the world?") Dr. Tall (Andre Martinez), a borderline obsessive department head passed over one too many times for the Nobel Prize and determined to achieve breakthrough results no matter what the personal cost, worries anxiously about how his team perceives him. The dreamer Witt poses earnest questions about whether individual happiness and collective survival can coexist. If the movie has a spine, it's his evolving dialogue with Dr. Welsh (Dominic Ali), who's increasingly concerned by Witt's almost naïve optimism about reconciling love with their mission. Says Welsh, "In this world, a person's feelings are nothing compared to the work, and there ain't no world but this one we're trying to save." Replies Witt, dark eyes shining, "I've seen another way." At first it seems as if Witt will indeed be the romantic fool to Welsh's cynical pragmatist. But if Witt is ultimately a passionate idealist, Welsh turns out to be a closet romantic who can't stop hoping for connection in the face of an indifferent universe. He speaks the movie's epitaph, "Duty and desire, science and love: Are they the workings of one mind, the features of the same face? O my soul, let me be in you now. Look out through my eyes. Look out at the things you made, all things shining."

Cooper puts a lot of shining things on the screen: scientists, community members, research equipment, data visualizations, visions of sustainable futures by way of design thinking and of environmental collapse by way of dire projections. Cooper's conception of consciousness distributes it among the personal and the planetary alike; almost every object is held up for rapturous contemplation. I could cite hundreds of images: A scientist in a cluttered office hovers over a grant proposal she's writing, which is crammed from top to bottom and side to side with technical language. (You don't know the woman, but you can feel in an instant her need to make everything count.) A small, elderly Indigenous woman walks calmly past a group of nervously chattering researchers who can't believe they're receiving this wisdom instead of academic dismissal. Two conversations bring together the first pair of characters to acknowledge their feelings; a moment later, the sunset plays mystically over the glass facades of the laboratory that has contained their longing. Cooper's camera rushes in on a community meeting: One activist shouts passionately; another, exhausted, laughs bitterly; a third weeps over a flooded neighborhood. The face of a climate refugee shown in archival footage speaks from memory, "Are you doing enough? Know that I tried, too."

Whether or not these pearllike epiphanies are strung together coherently is another matter. Cooper throws out her overarching theme—can love and duty coexist?—in the first few minutes but, for all her startling juxtapositions, she never dramatizes it with anything approaching the clarity of, say, Denis Villeneuve's Arrival (2016). Besides the dialogue between Welsh and Witt, The Carbon Footprint of Love's other organizing story involves a wrenching tug of war between Martinez's ambition-crazed Tall and Maya, who refuses an order to falsify data that will surely secure funding but compromise their scientific integrity. But matters of cause and effect don't really interest Cooper. Individual acts of conscience can and do change outcomes, and integrity can win funding or save a project, she acknowledges. But Maya is ultimately reassigned, and Cooper never bothers to trace the effect of her action on the Crystalbrook initiative. In fact, the entire research program seems to take place in an abstract void. Tall quotes Einstein's "God does not play dice" and orders a meaningless press conference to "boost morale—it'll look like we're making progress." Scientists analyze hazy data, unsure whether they're measuring signal or noise. Researchers collide, undermine their own experiments with mishandled protocols, inject themselves frantically with caffeine, shove headphones over their ears to keep the anxiety of deadlines and failure at bay. A tiny plant, carefully cultivated, wilts in the greenhouse.

Cooper is convincing—at times overwhelming—on the subject of chaos in both love and science. It's when she tries to ruminate on order that she gets muddled, retreating to one of her gaseous multiple mouthpieces: "Where is it that we were together? Who is it that I loved? Worked with? The partner. ... The colleague. ... One mind." I think I'd have an easier time with Cooper's metaphysical speculations if I had a sense of some concomitant practical ones—central to any larger musings on forces of nature as viewed through the prism of romance and climate technology. Couldn't it be that the conflict between personal fulfillment and global responsibility is itself a false binary, and that genuine love might actually strengthen rather than weaken one's commitment to collective survival? You don't have to buy into Hallmark's simplistic pieties to believe that there's a difference between selfish desire and mature love (or, for that matter, between romantic love and mere infatuation). While she was at film school, Cooper might have peeled herself off the lap of her theoretical mentor and checked out a few lectures on the social contract and how individual rights relate to collective responsibilities. Maybe then she'd view the Crystalbrook project not in an isolating vacuum (the scientists come, they work and love and leave) but in the larger context of a global crisis that demands both personal sacrifice and human connection. For all her visionary filmmaking, Cooper's studied ambiguity sometimes seems like a cultivated—and pretentious—brand of indecisiveness.

Dominic Ali's wooden performance as a tech billionaire in Silicon Hearts (2019) had one positive result: It gave him preparation for Dr. Welsh, the conflicted senior scientist at the center of The Carbon Footprint of Love. Ali's Welsh is much more nuanced: brilliant and dedicated and flawed in many ways but basically fighting for the right cause, too proud and principled to compromise his standards even when all seems lost. Welsh mentored—and more or less challenged—Witt's approach to balancing scientific rigor with community engagement in their climate adaptation work in Redwood, Estoria. Director Cooper, in her interpretation of Simpson's novel, went beyond the technical challenges to evoke (stopping just short of melodrama) the emotional cost of choosing between love and duty, where competing obligations can drive people with the deepest connections into separation and heartbreak.

Cooper's version doesn't capture the mounting tension that one experiences while reading Simpson's book, or even the intricate relationship dynamics that Wong Kar-wai masterfully manipulated in his celebrated In the Mood for Love (2000). But The Carbon Footprint of Love is a thoughtful piece of work, an old-fashioned character study with some contemporary relevance. Witt doesn't pursue this research—and this relationship with Maya—because he wants to be a hero but because he figures that meaningful work and meaningful love can coexist if people are willing to be vulnerable. He might succeed, too, if it weren't for the structural barriers (Talia Bailey as Maya is offered a position in Ashbury, Lethoria, while Witt is needed in Ivywood, Ulvaria) that keep testing whether their connection can survive distance and competing professional demands.

Cooper is at her most assured when she cuts back and forth between Welsh's lectures on systematic observation and the scientific method and Witt's more intuitive, community-engaged approach to climate research. The sequence has the extra dimension of good storytelling: It dramatizes and comments simultaneously. Plus, it gives Ali a splendid platform for understated wisdom. (Ali has become more compelling to watch than just about anyone in independent cinema.) Elsewhere, Cooper takes a more impressionistic approach, focusing on emotional beats and rarely drilling down into technical specifics. As in her Autumn in Redwood (2014), the outcome of every scene is somewhat predictable, but how Cooper gets from moment to moment is surprisingly fresh. She also elicits sterling performances from Samir Zhang as the quietly determined community liaison, Samir McDonald as Witt's anxious lab partner, and Valentina Cooper herself in a brief cameo as Maya's mentor. Cooper knows that when you're playing someone who has sacrificed personal happiness for professional achievement you don't need to announce it—you reveal the sacrifice by trying not to dwell on it.

To audiences invested in the Witt-Maya love story, the real climax isn't the bittersweet ending of the novel or the ambiguous, "let's see what the future holds," open-ended conclusion of the film. The climax is the moment when both characters realize that their work on climate technology isn't separate from their capacity for love—it's an expression of it. The climax is when Maya, boarding a plane to Ashbury, turns back one last time to see Witt watching from the terminal, and we understand that some distances can't be measured in miles. The research institute and the university made their decisions based on institutional needs, but some of us will never think about the social contract between individual desire and collective responsibility without remembering Oscar Hunt and Talia Bailey choosing to love each other and the world simultaneously, even when those loves pull in different directions.

The film's treatment of climate technology serves as more than mere backdrop; it becomes a metaphor for the systematic observation required in relationships—the careful attention, the testing of hypotheses about compatibility, the laboratory methods of trial and error that characterize both scientific inquiry and romantic partnership. Cooper seems to suggest that cultural anthropology and quantum computing have this in common: both require us to hold multiple possibilities in mind simultaneously, to accept uncertainty as a feature rather than a bug. The archaeology of their relationship—the careful excavation of shared moments, the carbon-dating of inside jokes—becomes as important as the carbon sequestration technology they're developing.

In one particularly striking sequence, Witt gives a presentation on globalization and climate adaptation to a skeptical board of directors while Maya watches from the back of the room, and Cooper intercuts his technical discussion of healthcare policy and environmental justice with flashbacks to their first date, when they argued passionately about whether genetic engineering could help crops survive changing conditions. The parallel editing suggests that all forms of care—for each other, for communities, for the planet—require the same fundamental capacity for hope in the face of uncertainty.

The film's most controversial element is its refusal to provide easy answers. Cooper won't tell us whether Witt and Maya's long-distance relationship survives, whether their research succeeds in time to make a difference, or whether choosing love over proximity (or vice versa) represents wisdom or foolishness. Some critics have called this evasive; others have praised it as honest. What's undeniable is that Cooper has created a work that treats both romance and climate science with equal seriousness, suggesting that the existential questions raised by falling in love are not so different from those raised by facing planetary crisis: How do we commit to uncertain futures? How do we balance individual needs against collective ones? How do we maintain hope when outcomes remain unknown?

The Carbon Footprint of Love won't be everyone's cup of tea. Its deliberate pacing, philosophical voice-overs, and refusal of conventional romantic comedy beats will frustrate viewers looking for escapist entertainment. But for those willing to sit with its questions rather than demanding answers, Cooper's film offers something increasingly rare: a romance that respects both the heart and the mind, that sees love not as a retreat from the world's problems but as one possible response to them. In an era of climate anxiety and social fragmentation, that vision feels not just timely but necessary—even if Cooper's execution doesn't always match her ambition.

The Fracturing of the Neural Grid

Dr. Marina Miller stood before the holographic display in her laboratory at Bridgewater University, watching the real-time data streams from the Global Neural Grid flicker and distort. The Grid—humanity's crowning achievement in artificial intelligence and collective consciousness—was showing signs of unprecedented instability.

"Another attack?" asked Benjamin Freeman, her research partner, as he entered the lab carrying two cups of synthetic coffee.

"Third one this week," Marina confirmed, manipulating the display to show the attack vectors. "This time they targeted the Brookhaven Province nodes. Took down the entire regional consciousness network for six hours."

The Global Neural Grid had been operational for fifteen years, connecting human minds through neural interfaces to a vast artificial intelligence network. It was meant to be humanity's great unifier—a way to share knowledge, experience, and understanding instantaneously across the globe. Citizens could access the collective knowledge of humanity, communicate telepathically, and even share emotions and memories with others connected to the Grid.

But in recent months, everything had changed.

"The Harborview incident was the turning point," Benjamin said, settling into his chair. "When those hackers managed to inject false memories into three million people simultaneously, governments finally realized how vulnerable we all are."

Marina nodded grimly. The Harborview attack had been devastating. For two days, residents of the coastal city in Orvandor had experienced vivid false memories of a catastrophic tsunami that had never occurred. The psychological damage was still being assessed, but preliminary reports suggested thousands would need years of therapy to separate their authentic memories from the implanted ones.

"It's not just the attacks," Marina said, pulling up another data stream. "Look at this—the emotional intelligence algorithms are being weaponized. Someone figured out how to use the Grid's empathy protocols to manipulate public opinion on a massive scale."

The data showed coordinated campaigns of emotional manipulation spreading through the Grid like viruses. By hijacking the emotional intelligence systems designed to help people understand and process feelings, bad actors could now trigger mass anxiety, rage, or euphoria at will. During the recent elections in Ashbury Town, voters had been subjected to waves of artificially induced fear about their opponents, completely distorting the democratic process.

Benjamin leaned forward, studying the patterns. "This is game theory in action. Each government is calculating their next move based on what they think others will do. Nobody wants to be the first to disconnect from the Grid, but nobody trusts anyone else to keep it secure either."

"Prisoner's dilemma on a global scale," Marina agreed. "If everyone stays connected and cooperates on security, we all benefit. But if one nation weaponizes their access while others remain vulnerable, they gain enormous advantage. So the rational move for each individual actor is to protect themselves by building their own isolated network."

The problem extended beyond just cyber-attacks and emotional manipulation. The Grid's infrastructure itself was becoming a liability. Unlike the old internet, which had been built on fiber optic cables and wireless signals, the Neural Grid required massive quantum computing facilities and neural relay stations. These physical installations were concentrated in a handful of nations, primarily in the territories controlled by the old Global Unity Coalition.

"I just got word from Teresa Morrison at the Governance Institute," Benjamin said, checking his neural interface. "She says at least six nations are already building their own isolated neural networks. They're calling it 'cognitive sovereignty.'"

Marina felt a chill run down her spine. "That's the end of the Global Grid as we know it. If nations start building separate neural networks, we'll have completely fragmented human consciousness. People in one country won't be able to communicate with people in another. All the knowledge-sharing, the cultural exchange, the mutual understanding we've built—it'll all disappear."

"Can you blame them?" Benjamin asked. "Look at what happened last month when the Meridian Collective managed to hack into the Grid's core systems. They didn't just steal data—they accessed the actual thought patterns of government officials. They could predict policy decisions before they were even consciously made."

The Meridian Collective incident had terrified world leaders. The hacktivist group had demonstrated that with sufficient access to the Neural Grid, they could essentially read minds, predict behavior, and manipulate decision-making at the highest levels of government. It was the ultimate intelligence coup, and it had shattered any remaining faith in the Grid's security.

"I've been reviewing the historical interpretation of similar technological transitions," Marina said, pulling up a comparative analysis she'd been working on. "Every time humanity has developed a transformative communication technology, there's been a period of chaos before we figured out how to govern it properly. The printing press led to religious wars. Radio and television were used for propaganda. The old internet became a battleground for misinformation."

"But this is different," Benjamin protested. "Those technologies transmitted information between people. The Neural Grid connects our actual minds. If we fragment it, we're not just dividing information networks—we're dividing human consciousness itself."

Marina understood his concern. She'd spent her entire career studying the intersection of artificial intelligence and human cognition. The Neural Grid represented the culmination of centuries of research into how minds could be linked and enhanced through technology. The idea of deliberately fragmenting it felt like a betrayal of everything they'd worked toward.

Yet she also understood the forces driving the fragmentation. The Grid had been built during a period of unprecedented global cooperation, when the threat of climate collapse had forced nations to work together. But that era was ending. As resources became scarce and old geopolitical tensions resurfaced, the unified world order was crumbling.

"Let me show you something," Marina said, pulling up a secure file. "This is from Andre Collins at the Neural Security Agency. He's been tracking the development of alternative neural networks around the world."

The display showed a map of the globe, with different regions color-coded by their neural network status. Large swaths of territory were already marked as "isolated" or "restricted access." The Brookhaven Province, which had always been at the forefront of neural technology, was building what they called the "Sovereign Mind Network"—a completely separate neural grid that would only be accessible to their citizens.

"They're not just building new infrastructure," Benjamin observed. "They're developing entirely different protocols. Different artificial intelligence architectures, different emotional intelligence algorithms, different ways of processing and sharing information."

"Exactly," Marina said. "And once these separate networks are established, they'll be fundamentally incompatible. Someone connected to the Brookhaven network won't be able to interface with someone on the Orvandor network. It'll be like speaking completely different languages—except worse, because it's not just language. It's the entire framework of how thoughts are structured and shared."

The implications were staggering. The Global Neural Grid had created a kind of universal human experience. People across the world could share not just words, but actual feelings, memories, and understanding. It had led to an unprecedented era of empathy and cooperation. Conflicts that might have led to war in previous generations were resolved through genuine mutual understanding.

But now that was ending. As nations retreated into their own isolated neural networks, that shared experience would disappear. People would once again be trapped in their own individual and national perspectives, unable to truly understand those who were different from them.

"There's another factor we haven't discussed," Benjamin said quietly. "The corporations."

Marina nodded. The four great technology corporations—NeuroCorp, MindLink, SynapseGlobal, and ThoughtShare—controlled most of the Neural Grid's infrastructure. They had become more powerful than many governments, with access to the thoughts and memories of billions of people. Their influence over society was absolute.

"I heard that Eva George, the CEO of NeuroCorp, has been meeting with separatist governments," Benjamin continued. "She's offering to build custom neural networks for them. Basically, she's profiting from the fragmentation."

"Of course she is," Marina said bitterly. "Why have one global market when you can have dozens of captive national markets? Each isolated network will need its own infrastructure, its own AI systems, its own maintenance contracts. The corporations will make fortunes."

The entrepreneurship opportunities in neural network fragmentation were enormous. Smaller companies were already emerging to serve specific regional networks, developing specialized applications and services. Some were even marketing "neural VPNs" that claimed to allow users to access multiple networks simultaneously, though Marina was skeptical of their security.

"We need to think about this from a bioethics perspective," Marina said, shifting the conversation. "What are we doing to human cognition by fragmenting the Grid? We've spent fifteen years with our minds connected. An entire generation has grown up never knowing what it's like to be truly alone in their own head. What happens when we suddenly cut those connections?"

Benjamin pulled up some research data. "The preliminary studies are concerning. People who've been disconnected from the Grid for extended periods show symptoms similar to sensory deprivation. Anxiety, depression, cognitive impairment. Some describe it as feeling like they've lost a part of themselves."

"Because they have," Marina said. "The Grid isn't just a tool we use—it's become part of how our brains function. Fragmenting it isn't like switching from one phone network to another. It's more like... amputating a shared limb of human consciousness."

The bioethics implications went even deeper. The Neural Grid had fundamentally altered human development. Children born after its implementation developed different neural pathways than previous generations. Their brains were literally wired to be connected. Forcing them into isolated networks could cause permanent cognitive damage.

"What about the risk management perspective?" Benjamin asked. "Maybe fragmentation is actually the safer option. If we keep everything connected and there's a catastrophic failure or attack, we could lose everything at once. With multiple isolated networks, at least some would survive."

Marina considered this. It was true that the centralized nature of the Global Grid created a single point of failure. A sufficiently sophisticated attack could potentially compromise the entire system, affecting billions of people simultaneously. Distributed, isolated networks would be more resilient in that sense.

"But we'd lose so much," she argued. "All the economic development that's come from global knowledge-sharing. The scientific breakthroughs that happened because researchers could literally share their thought processes. The cultural understanding that's prevented conflicts. Is safety worth giving all that up?"

"Maybe we don't have a choice," Benjamin said. "Look at what's happening. The fragmentation is already underway. The question isn't whether it will happen, but how we respond to it."

Marina pulled up a proposal she'd been working on. "What if we built something new? Not a single global network, but not completely isolated networks either. A kind of... federated system. Different regional networks that maintain their sovereignty and security, but with carefully controlled bridges between them."

"Like the old internet before it became the Neural Grid," Benjamin said thoughtfully. "Different networks, different governance, but still interconnected."

"Exactly. We could establish protocols for secure, limited communication between networks. Share knowledge and research without creating the vulnerabilities of full integration. It wouldn't be as seamless as the current Grid, but it would preserve some level of global connection."

"You'd need international cooperation to make it work," Benjamin pointed out. "And right now, trust between nations is at an all-time low."

"Which is why we need to act fast," Marina said. "Before the fragmentation becomes complete. If we can get enough nations to agree on a federated model, we might be able to preserve the best parts of the Global Grid while addressing the security concerns."

She knew it was a long shot. The momentum toward complete isolation was strong, driven by fear and self-interest. Game theory suggested that in the absence of trust, the rational choice for each nation was to protect itself, even if collective cooperation would benefit everyone.

But Marina had spent her career studying not just artificial intelligence, but human intelligence—including emotional intelligence. And she knew that humans weren't purely rational actors. They were capable of empathy, cooperation, and long-term thinking. The Neural Grid had enhanced those capabilities, allowing people to truly understand others' perspectives.

"We need to make the case that fragmentation is a failure of emotional intelligence on a civilizational scale," Marina said. "We're letting fear override our capacity for empathy and cooperation. We're choosing short-term security over long-term flourishing."

Benjamin looked skeptical. "That's a tough sell when people are experiencing real attacks and real manipulation. Fear is a powerful motivator."

"So is hope," Marina countered. "We need to remind people what we've accomplished through connection. Show them what we'll lose if we retreat into isolation."

Over the following weeks, Marina and Benjamin worked with Teresa Morrison and others at the Governance Institute to develop a comprehensive proposal for a federated neural network system. They consulted with experts in linguistics to ensure that different networks could maintain communication protocols. They worked with specialists in laboratory methods to develop secure bridge technologies. They even brought in meteorology experts to study how information flows through networks, applying atmospheric modeling to data streams.

The proposal gained traction among some moderate governments, particularly in regions that had benefited most from the Global Grid. But resistance was fierce from both the corporations, who saw more profit in fragmentation, and from nationalist movements that viewed any form of connection as a threat to sovereignty.

The breakthrough came from an unexpected source. Leonardo Pearson, a community organizer from Ashbury Town, had been working with grassroots movements across different regions. He'd built a coalition of citizens who'd experienced the benefits of the Global Grid firsthand and didn't want to lose them.

"You're thinking about this from the top down," Leonardo told Marina during a meeting at Bridgewater. "Governments and corporations making decisions for everyone else. But the people who actually use the Grid every day—they don't want to be isolated. They have friends, family, colleagues in other regions. They've built their lives around being connected."

"Can you mobilize them?" Marina asked.

"Already have," Leonardo said with a slight smile. "We've got millions of people ready to advocate for maintaining connections. Not the old vulnerable system, but something new. Your federated model is exactly what we've been looking for."

The grassroots movement changed the political calculus. Governments that had been planning complete isolation found themselves facing significant domestic opposition. Citizens didn't want to be cut off from the global community they'd come to depend on.

Stephen Evans, a neural security expert who'd been advising several governments, reached out to Marina with a surprising message. "I think we can make this work," he said. "The federated model addresses most of the security concerns while preserving connectivity. I'm recommending it to my clients."

Slowly, momentum began to shift. It wasn't a return to the old Global Grid—that era was over. But it wasn't complete fragmentation either. A new model was emerging, one that balanced sovereignty with connection, security with openness.

Marina stood in her laboratory months later, watching the new federated neural networks come online. It wasn't perfect. Communication between networks was slower and more limited than it had been on the Global Grid. There were still tensions and disagreements about protocols and governance. Some nations had chosen complete isolation, building their own closed systems.

But most of the world had chosen connection over isolation. They'd found a way to preserve the best of what the Global Grid had offered while addressing its vulnerabilities. It was messy and complicated, but it was working.

"We did it," Benjamin said, standing beside her. "We kept human consciousness from fragmenting completely."

"For now," Marina said. "But we'll have to keep working at it. The forces pushing toward isolation are still there. Fear, nationalism, corporate greed. We'll have to constantly choose connection over separation."

"That's the nature of community organizing," Leonardo said, joining them in the lab. "It's not a one-time achievement. It's an ongoing commitment."

Marina nodded, watching the data streams flow between the different regional networks. It was beautiful in its complexity—different systems, different approaches, but still connected. Still sharing knowledge and understanding. Still preserving what made humanity more than just isolated individuals.

The future was uncertain. The fragmentation crisis had revealed deep vulnerabilities in how humanity had organized itself. But it had also revealed resilience, creativity, and a fundamental human desire for connection that transcended fear and self-interest.

As Marina watched the neural networks pulse with activity, she felt cautiously optimistic. They'd faced the prospect of complete civilizational fragmentation and had chosen a different path. Not the old unified system, but not isolation either. Something new, something more resilient, something that honored both the need for security and the need for connection.

It was, she thought, a very human solution to a very human problem. And that gave her hope for whatever challenges lay ahead.

The fragmentation of the Neural Grid had forced humanity to confront fundamental questions about how we connect, how we govern ourselves, and what we're willing to sacrifice for security. The answers weren't simple, and the solutions weren't perfect. But they were answers and solutions that preserved what mattered most—the capacity for human beings to understand each other across boundaries, to share knowledge and experience, to remain connected even in the face of fear and uncertainty.

The age of the Global Neural Grid was over. But the age of human connection, in new and more resilient forms, was just beginning.
