The neural interface hummed softly against Sebastian Knight's temples as he reviewed the genetic modification protocols one more time. Beside him, Nina Ramos adjusted her own interface, her dark eyes scanning the holographic displays that floated in the air before them.

"Are you sure about this?" Nina asked, her voice tight with a mixture of excitement and apprehension. "Once we sign those contracts with the Consciousness Integration Institute in Springfield, there's no turning back."

Sebastian reached over and took her hand, feeling the familiar warmth of her skin against his. They'd been partners for three years now—both in their research and in life. "We've talked about this a hundred times, Nina. Earth's cognitive development crisis isn't going to solve itself. Someone has to do the fieldwork."

The crisis had started subtly, almost imperceptibly. As humanity had pushed further into genetic engineering and neural enhancement technologies, something unexpected had happened. The newest generation—those born with standard genetic modifications meant to enhance intelligence and longevity—were experiencing a plateau in consciousness studies metrics. Their cognitive development stalled at adolescence, unable to progress to the higher-order thinking that had defined human advancement for millennia.

The Consciousness Integration Institute had traced the problem to a missing element, something that couldn't be replicated in Earth's carefully controlled biospheres and cities. They needed researchers willing to go to the frontier colonies—places like Springfield in the Galdoria system, where humanity was still struggling to terraform hostile worlds and where the environmental pressures might hold the key to understanding what had gone wrong.

"I know," Nina said, squeezing his hand back. "It's just—Springfield. It's not exactly Maplewood, is it?"

Sebastian smiled despite himself. Maplewood, in the Estoria system, was known as the jewel of the outer colonies. Comfortable, civilized, with art galleries that rivaled Earth's best and universities where aesthetic philosophy was debated with the same passion as neuroscience. Springfield, by contrast, was a hardscrabble mining colony on Galdoria-7, where the primary exports were rare earth elements and the primary imports were survival equipment.

"No," he admitted. "But that's where the Institute needs us. The correlation data is undeniable—the frontier colonies show different patterns in cognitive development. The children born there don't experience the plateau. Something about the environmental stress, the social dynamics of survival communities, the constant adaptation required—it's triggering something in human consciousness that we've lost back home."

Nina nodded slowly. She knew he was right. They both did. That's why they'd volunteered in the first place.

The compensation wasn't great—the Institute was a non-profit research organization, funded by a consortium of governments desperate to solve the crisis before an entire generation was lost to cognitive stagnation. But Sebastian and Nina had never been motivated by money. They were motivated by the same thing that had driven them into consciousness studies in the first place: the belief that understanding the human mind was the most important work anyone could do.

"When do we leave?" Nina asked.

"Transport leaves in three days. We'll have forty-eight hours to settle in Springfield before we start the field research."

Nina pulled up her own data streams, reviewing the mission parameters one more time. They would be conducting a longitudinal study of cognitive development in frontier colony children, comparing their neural patterns and genetic expression profiles to those of Earth-born children. The work would involve extensive field observation, neural scanning, and genetic sampling. It would be exhausting, potentially dangerous, and absolutely critical.

"I suppose I should tell my mother," Nina said with a wry smile. "She's going to be thrilled that we're leaving for a mining colony instead of accepting that position at the Rosewood Territory Institute."

Sebastian winced. The Rosewood Territory position had been prestigious—a comfortable research post studying aesthetic philosophy and its relationship to neural architecture. Safe. Respectable. Boring.

"Your mother will understand eventually," he said, though he wasn't entirely sure that was true.

"Will she?" Nina laughed. "You don't know my mother very well if you think that. She's already convinced we're throwing our careers away."

Three days later, they stood in the departure bay of Newbridge City's orbital station, their belongings compressed into two storage pods and their neural interfaces updated with the latest consciousness monitoring software. The transport ship loomed before them, a utilitarian vessel designed for cargo and personnel transfer, not comfort.

"Last chance to back out," Sebastian said, only half-joking.

Nina punched his shoulder lightly. "Don't even think about it, Knight. We're in this together."

The journey to Galdoria-7 took four weeks, most of which they spent in cryo-sleep. When they finally arrived at Springfield, Sebastian's first thought was that the colony looked even more desolate than the briefing materials had suggested.

Springfield was built into the side of a massive crater, its domed habitats connected by pressurized tunnels that snaked across the rust-red landscape. The atmosphere outside was barely breathable, toxic with sulfur compounds and too thin to sustain human life without assistance. The mining operations that sustained the colony scarred the surrounding terrain, great gouges in the earth where extraction machines had torn out the valuable minerals that made the colony economically viable.

"Welcome to paradise," Nina muttered as they disembarked.

Their contact at the colony was a gruff administrator named Giovanni Ward, who met them at the arrival dock with a harried expression and a data pad clutched in one weathered hand.

"Knight and Ramos?" he asked without preamble. "Good. We've got your quarters ready, but I need to brief you on the situation here before you settle in."

"Situation?" Sebastian asked, exchanging a glance with Nina.

Ward led them through the pressurized tunnels toward the residential sector, talking as he walked. "The Institute didn't tell you? Figures. We've been having some problems with one of the mining supervisors. Name's Nicholas Black. He's—well, he's been sabotaging research operations."

"Sabotaging?" Nina stopped walking. "What do you mean?"

Ward sighed. "Black used to work for one of the big genetic engineering firms back on Earth. Got caught up in the Sadlerville Incident—you heard about that?"

Sebastian nodded grimly. Everyone had heard about Sadlerville. A genetic engineering facility that had experienced a catastrophic containment failure, releasing experimental organisms into the surrounding area. Hundreds had died. Thousands more had been affected by the genetic contaminants. The incident had led to massive reforms in how genetic engineering was regulated, and several major firms had been dissolved or reorganized.

"Black was there," Ward continued. "Lost both his legs to the genetic contaminants. They gave him prosthetics, of course, but something broke in him. He blames the whole field of genetic engineering for what happened. And by extension, he blames consciousness researchers like you who use genetic modification data in their work."

"That's insane," Nina said. "Consciousness studies and genetic engineering are related fields, but we're not—we didn't have anything to do with Sadlerville."

"Try telling him that," Ward said. "He's been here for five years, ever since he left Earth. Built himself a little isolated habitat out in the Rosewood Territory sector—that's the mining region about fifty kilometers from here. He's been picking off research teams that venture out there. Nothing fatal, thank God, but he's destroyed equipment, contaminated samples, even held a few researchers at gunpoint until we could negotiate their release."

Sebastian felt a chill run down his spine. "And the Institute sent us here anyway?"

"The Institute needs the data," Ward said bluntly. "And Black hasn't actually killed anyone. We've increased security, and we're monitoring his movements as best we can. Just—be careful out there. Don't go into the field alone, and always keep your emergency beacon active."

Their quarters were small but functional, carved out of the rock of the crater wall and pressurized against the hostile atmosphere outside. Nina collapsed onto the narrow bed and stared at the ceiling.

"This is going to be harder than we thought," she said.

"Maybe," Sebastian agreed, settling into the desk chair and pulling up the research protocols on his neural interface. "But we knew it wouldn't be easy. The question is whether we're committed enough to see it through."

Nina sat up, her expression serious. "Of course we are. This isn't about us, Sebastian. This is about every child back on Earth who's trapped in cognitive stagnation, who'll never reach their full potential unless we figure out what's gone wrong. That's worth a little danger."

Sebastian smiled. That was the Nina he knew—fierce, dedicated, unwilling to back down from a challenge. "Then let's get to work."

The first few weeks were productive. They established their field research protocols, began conducting neural scans of the colony children, and collected genetic samples for analysis. The data was fascinating—the frontier-born children showed significantly different patterns of neural development compared to Earth-born children, with enhanced plasticity in regions associated with problem-solving and social adaptation.

"It's the environment," Nina theorized as they reviewed the data one evening. "The constant stress, the need to adapt to new challenges—it's triggering evolutionary biology mechanisms that we've suppressed back on Earth with all our safety measures and controlled environments."

"That would explain the cognitive development differences," Sebastian agreed. "But it raises uncomfortable questions about trade policy and resource allocation. If we need environmental stress to maintain healthy cognitive development, what does that mean for how we structure our societies?"

They were so absorbed in their work that they almost forgot about Nicholas Black. Almost.

It was on their fourth week in Springfield that they ventured out to the Rosewood Territory sector to collect environmental samples. The mining region was even more desolate than the main colony, a wasteland of excavated craters and abandoned equipment. They wore full environmental suits, their neural interfaces monitoring their vitals and maintaining constant communication with the colony.

They'd been working for about three hours when Sebastian's proximity alarm went off.

"Someone's approaching," he said, his hand instinctively moving to the emergency beacon on his belt.

A figure emerged from behind a massive ore processor, moving with an odd, mechanical gait. As it came closer, Sebastian could see it was a man in an old-style environmental suit, the kind that had been standard twenty years ago. The figure's legs moved with the distinctive hydraulic hiss of prosthetics.

Nicholas Black.

"Turn off your beacon," Black's voice crackled over the comm channel. "I'm not going to hurt you. I just want to talk."

Nina's hand was already on her own beacon. "Why should we trust you?"

"Because if I wanted to hurt you, you'd already be hurt," Black said flatly. "I've been watching you for three weeks. I know your research schedule, your routes, your protocols. I could have sabotaged your equipment a dozen times over. But I haven't. Because I've been reading your research papers, and I think—I think maybe you're different."

Sebastian exchanged a glance with Nina through their helmet visors. Against his better judgment, he was curious. "Different how?"

Black moved closer, and Sebastian could see his face through the helmet's faceplate. It was weathered and lined, with the haunted look of someone who'd seen too much suffering.

"You're not just doing genetic engineering for profit," Black said. "You're trying to understand consciousness itself. You're trying to help people. I've read your work on cognitive development and social dynamics. You actually care about the ethical implications of what you're doing."

"Of course we care," Nina said. "That's why we're here."

Black was silent for a long moment. Then he said, "I've been wrong. About a lot of things. I thought—after Sadlerville, after what happened to me—I thought all genetic engineering was evil. That everyone in the field was just chasing profit, not caring about the consequences. But I've been watching the children here in Springfield. I've seen how different they are from the children back on Earth. And I've been reading the consciousness studies literature, trying to understand why."

"And what did you conclude?" Sebastian asked carefully.

"That the problem isn't genetic engineering itself," Black said. "It's how we've been using it. We've been trying to optimize for intelligence without understanding what intelligence really means. We've been treating consciousness like a machine we can tune up, instead of recognizing it as an emergent property of complex systems interacting with complex environments."

Nina's eyes widened. "That's—that's actually very close to our own hypothesis."

Black nodded. "I know. That's why I wanted to talk to you. I've been sabotaging research operations because I was angry, because I wanted revenge against the field that took my legs. But you're not the enemy. You're trying to fix the mistakes that people like me made."

Sebastian felt something shift in his understanding of the situation. Black wasn't just a madman seeking revenge. He was a broken man who'd been consumed by guilt and anger, lashing out at a field he blamed for his suffering. But underneath that anger was someone who still cared about the science, who still wanted to understand.

"Mr. Black," Sebastian said carefully, "what happened to you at Sadlerville was a tragedy. And you're right that the genetic engineering industry made terrible mistakes. But the solution isn't to destroy research. It's to do better research. To approach these questions with humility and care, to always consider the ethical implications of our work."

"I know that now," Black said. "But I've done so much damage. I've set back research by years with my sabotage. I've—" His voice broke. "I've become the very thing I hated. Someone who causes harm without considering the consequences."

Nina stepped forward. "It's not too late to change that. You clearly have a deep understanding of the science. You could help us. Contribute to the research instead of fighting against it."

Black laughed bitterly. "You want my help? After everything I've done?"

"We want to solve the cognitive development crisis," Sebastian said. "And that's going to take all the brilliant minds we can get—including yours. What you did was wrong, but you're not beyond redemption. The question is whether you're willing to do the work to make things right."

Over the following months, Nicholas Black became an unlikely ally in their research. His insights into genetic engineering, combined with their expertise in consciousness studies, led to breakthrough after breakthrough. They discovered that the cognitive development plateau wasn't caused by the genetic modifications themselves, but by the sterile, stress-free environments in which modified children were raised. The human brain, shaped by millions of years of evolutionary biology, needed challenge and adaptation to develop properly.

The solution wasn't to abandon genetic engineering, but to redesign Earth's social environments to provide the kind of developmental challenges that frontier colonies provided naturally. It would require a massive shift in how humanity thought about child-rearing, education, and social structure—but it was possible.

When Sebastian and Nina finally returned to Earth with their data, they brought Nicholas Black with them. He would face consequences for his actions—mandatory psychological treatment and community service—but he would also have a chance to contribute to the solution he'd once tried to destroy.

On the transport ship home, Nina leaned against Sebastian's shoulder, watching the stars drift by through the viewport.

"Do you think we made the right choice?" she asked. "Coming to Springfield, I mean. We could have taken that safe position in Rosewood Territory. We could have avoided all of this."

Sebastian thought about the children they'd studied, the breakthrough they'd achieved, the broken man they'd helped to heal. He thought about the future they'd helped to secure—a future where human consciousness could continue to grow and evolve, where the mistakes of the past could be learned from and corrected.

"Yes," he said simply. "We made the right choice. Not because it was easy, but because it was necessary. Because someone had to do the work, and we were able to do it. That's what being a researcher means—not chasing prestige or comfort, but going where the questions lead you, even when it's hard."

Nina smiled and squeezed his hand. "Fellow hero," she said softly.

"Fellow hero," he agreed.

As Earth grew larger in the viewport, Sebastian felt a deep sense of satisfaction. They'd gone to Springfield not for glory or wealth, but because they believed in the importance of the work. They'd faced danger and uncertainty, but they'd never lost sight of what mattered: understanding consciousness, helping humanity, and advancing knowledge for its own sake.

That was why they'd really decided to go to Springfield. Not because they had to, but because they chose to. And that choice had made all the difference.

The research vessel Prometheus groaned as its landing struts settled into the marshy terrain of Kepler-442b. The planet's thick atmosphere pressed against the hull, making the ship's metal framework protest with sharp pings and low moans. It was an unwelcoming sound, two hundred light-years from the cramped cities of Earth.

Commander Henry Martin rolled out of his bunk, his body heavy under the planet's 1.3g gravity. He was a lean man in his early forties, with the kind of weathered face that came from years managing impossible missions. The burden of Earth's desperate gamble had carved deep lines around his eyes. He shuffled toward the control room, already dreading the coffee.

Dr. Kara Perry glanced up from her console, tucking a strand of red hair behind her ear. "Morning, Henry. You look terrible."

"Thanks." He poured himself a cup of the bitter synthetic brew. "Anything new overnight?"

"The luminescent spheres—we're calling them 'orbs' now—had another gathering about three klicks north. They dispersed at dawn. And our two junior researchers snuck out again. Bruno tracked them but lost their signal in the fog. I've been running a beacon to guide them back."

Henry cursed under his breath. Earth's biotech programs were so desperate for field researchers that they were sending kids barely out of secondary school. The two assigned to his mission, Jordan Martinez and Stella Ahmed, seemed to have no survival instinct whatsoever.

Not that there was obvious danger here. The orbs appeared harmless, just curious. The local fauna were docile herbivores—strange six-legged creatures that looked like a nightmare fusion of mammals and arthropods. Nothing had shown aggression.

But something had happened to Dr. Chen's expedition twelve years ago, and to the follow-up mission under Captain Reeves five years back.

He moved to the viewport. The planet's sun was rising somewhere above the perpetual cloud cover, turning the thick fog from black to grey. In the distance, the yellow-green canopy of the scrub forest was barely visible. Shapes moved among the undergrowth—probably a herd of the native grazers. Through the haze, details were impossible to make out. Even the deep ravine where they'd discovered Reeves' deliberately buried ship was completely obscured.

Three of the orbs were hovering over the grazing animals now, pulsing with soft bioluminescence. Henry stared at them, trying to understand their purpose. If he had time to study them properly...

But there was no time.

Earth's Global Migration Authority had ordered him to check this site after delivering his cargo of colonists to Stonegate Territory on World-designate Clinton Province. He'd already overstayed by ten days. If there was no explanation within another forty-eight hours for what happened to the researchers who'd abandoned their ship and equipment, he'd have to report back and recommend the planet be marked as hostile.

He would have left already, except a recent landslide had exposed enough of Reeves' ship for their metal detectors to catch it from aerial survey. It had been buried deep enough to fool the original search.

"Henry!" Kara's voice was sharp. "Henry, there are the kids!"

Before he could turn to her pointing finger, movement caught his peripheral vision.

The orbs had abandoned the herd. Now all three were racing at incredible speed toward a spot near the ship, hovering excitedly above something in the fog.

He saw the two researchers then, running back toward the Prometheus, just beyond the disturbance in the mist.

Something was emerging from lower ground. The fog swirled and parted. Henry grabbed the radio microphone, shouting a warning to the researchers.

They must have seen it the same moment his call reached them. Jordan grabbed Stella's arm and they spun around together.

Then the fog cleared completely.

Under the dancing orbs, a group of figures was advancing toward the researchers. Bipedal forms, roughly humanoid but wrong in every detail. One stood nearly seven feet tall, leading the others in a direct line toward the two young people in their environment suits. Some carried tools or weapons. The leader raised one arm—the gesture was unmistakably a command.

"Get the rovers out!" Henry yelled at Kara. He yanked open the officers' lift and hammered the descent button. The lift crawled downward with agonizing slowness. He burst out at the vehicle bay. Crew members were scrambling in confusion, but someone—one of the engineers—was taking charge. The rovers were lining up. The lead vehicle was already running, and Henry sprinted for it as the exit ramp deployed.

No time for full environment suits. The air here was breathable, if unpleasant—high in sulfur compounds and low in oxygen. He jumped into the passenger seat and saw that Dr. Bruno Singh was driving. At Henry's nod, the rover rolled down the ramp, its electric motors whining as it accelerated. Two more rovers followed.

The researchers had disappeared into the fog. Then Henry spotted them, surrounded by the humanoid figures. Up close, the beings looked grotesque—distorted proportions, covered in coarse hair, faces that suggested human features filtered through some alien lens.

The tall leader suddenly gestured toward the approaching rovers. He made an impossible leap backward, covering twenty feet. Others turned, two of them seizing the researchers. The rover was doing forty kilometers per hour, but the group began pulling away, despite carrying their captives. They descended into a depression, vanishing into the mist.

"Follow the orbs," Henry commanded. He regretted not wearing his suit—the radio would have let him coordinate with the other rovers. Too late now.

The orbs pursued the humanoids. Bruno drove the rover down into a gully with remarkable skill, but had to slow as the fog thickened. Then it cleared to reveal the group had doubled back to confuse pursuit.

No time to stop. The rover plowed through them. Henry glimpsed five-foot bodies diving aside. Faces covered in thick hair, eyes that seemed almost human. A spear clattered against the windshield from behind—the point was beautifully worked stone, impossibly sharp.

The humanoids vanished as Bruno fought to turn. The other rovers were catching up, but too late to help intercept. They had to reach the group holding the researchers before they all disappeared into the broken terrain.

An orb descended, nearly touching Henry's head. He raised his hand instinctively. There was a tingling sensation as the orb seemed to flow around his fingers. It rose a few inches and drifted away.

Suddenly, Bruno slammed the brakes. Henry lurched forward against his restraint. The seven-foot leader was standing directly ahead, a researcher on each shoulder.

The wheels locked and the rover skidded forward. The humanoid leaped back, dropping both researchers with a surprised grunt.

Henry was out before the rover stopped, diving at the figure. It had thin, elongated arms below massively developed shoulders, but incredible strength. Henry felt those arms wrench at him as his hands found the thick neck. An overwhelming stench filled his nostrils as the being fell backward. Bruno hit it a second after Henry's tackle. Its head struck rocky ground with a heavy thud, and it went limp, though still breathing.

Another rover arrived. Crew members were checking the researchers—both unharmed, Stella laughing or crying, Jordan trying to kick the unconscious humanoid. The two were loaded into one rover while others helped Bruno and Henry secure the captive before heading back.

"No skull fracture. Incredibly dense bone structure," Bruno said, shaking his head. "Remarkable physiology."

"I hope it survives," Henry told him. "You're assigned to keep it alive and conscious. Find out if it can communicate—signs, drawings, anything. I need to know what happened to Chen and Reeves, and why that ship was buried. This thing might have answers."

Bruno nodded grimly. "I'll try, though I can't risk pharmaceutical intervention on an unknown metabolism." He pulled out a cigarette, then grimaced. "Henry, none of this makes sense. We've surveyed this planet with thermal imaging—no settlements, no infrastructure, no signs of organized culture. We should have found something."

"Cave dwellers, maybe," Henry suggested. "Just call me when you learn anything. We need to get back to Earth. We're already past our window."

The researchers' reports were straightforward—they'd been grabbed and carried, but not harmed. Now they were enjoying their moment of drama. Henry confined them to quarters, knowing their accounts would only grow more embellished with each retelling.

If they could communicate with the captive, they might learn more than they could from excavating Reeves' ship. That vessel was probably stripped clean by now. The only logical conclusion was that both expeditions had been overcome by these humanoids.

But it raised troubling questions. How could primitives breach Reeves' ship? Why was the fuel dumped? Only trained personnel would know how to do that. And who taught these beings that a ship's metal detectors could be fooled by enough rock? They'd buried it with sophisticated understanding of human technology.

Maybe there would never be complete answers, but he had to find something—and quickly. Earth needed every marginally habitable world. The planet was dying, not from war or disaster, but from success. Twelve billion people, resources exhausted, ecosystems collapsed. Humanity had to spread to the stars or face extinction through slow suffocation on an overcrowded homeworld.

The race had survived its nuclear age, prevented interplanetary conflicts, developed faster-than-light travel, and found dozens of worlds that could—with massive terraforming—support human life.

But none were perfect. None were Earth. The explorers went out in desperation. The biotech teams did what they could with genetic engineering and environmental conservation. And the great colony ships began filling worlds with desperate volunteers.

Nearly seventy worlds now. The nearest a three-month journey from Earth and three months back.

If this world could be used, it would be among the closest. If not, no more time could be wasted here.

Primitives could be displaced, perhaps. It would be ruthless and morally questionable to take their world, but survival was the first law.

But how could primitives do what these had apparently done?

He studied the recovered spear. The shaft was laminated from strips of the local scrub wood, expertly crafted. The point was delicately knapped flint, done with a skill that modern humans had lost centuries ago.

"Beautiful primitive work," he muttered.

Kara pulled her coffee away from her lips and snorted. "You can see more of it outside."

He returned to the viewport. About fifty of the humanoids were squatting in the clearing fog, holding spears and staring at the ship. They waited perhaps eight hundred meters away. Waiting patiently. For what? The return of their leader? Or for an opportunity to take the ship?

Henry grabbed the comm and called Bruno. "Status on the captive?"

Bruno's voice sounded strange. "Physically stable. You should come down. But—"

Henry dropped the comm and headed for the medical bay. He cursed Bruno for not calling immediately, then cursed himself for not checking sooner. Then he stopped at the sound of voices.

Bruno was asking a question. A thick, harsh vocalization answered—a sound that made Henry's skin crawl. Bruno seemed to understand, responding as Henry entered.

The captive was sitting on the examination table, unrestrained and somehow unthreatening now. The heavy features were relaxed but focused. It made a gesture like a salute when it saw Henry enter, its eyes fixing on the insignia on his uniform.

"Haaroo, Commmaander," it said.

"Commander Martin, meet your predecessor, Commander Chen," Bruno said. His smile was forced, his face pale with strain.

The being nodded slowly and pulled something from the thick hair on its head. A tarnished silver eagle—a commander's insignia.

"He didn't mean to frighten the researchers—just wanted to talk," Bruno said quickly. "I've got some of the story. He's changed. Speech is difficult. They've had to modify language to fit their new vocal structures, and he's forgotten most standard English. But it gets easier. It's really Chen. I'm certain."

Henry had his doubts. An alien could have taken the insignia from a captured human, learned some words. But Chen had been his mentor.

"What was your daughter's name? What was your wife's profession? What was your research focus?"

The lips contorted into something like a smile, and the strangely proportioned fingers spread out.

"Maaree. Daaata anaalysis. Cuuultural sociooology."

The answers were correct.

By the time Chen finished his story, Henry and Bruno sat in stunned silence. Finally Henry stood. "Is it possible, Bruno?"

"No," Bruno said flatly. "Not by any biology I know. But it happened. I've examined tissue samples. The cellular changes are there. Hard to believe about their offspring. Mature in six years, but smaller. It shouldn't be hereditary—somatic changes don't alter germ cells. But in this case, the mechanism that changed Chen is real, so maybe the inheritance is equally real."

Henry escorted Chen to the exit. The waiting orbs descended to touch the transformed man, then leaped up again. The crowd of humanoids moved forward toward their leader. A few were nearly as tall as Chen, but most stood around five feet.

The children of the original expedition.

Back in the control room, Henry found the fuel purge controls, entered the authorization codes, and activated the sequence. There was a hiss and gurgle as the ship's fuel tanks discharged their contents onto the ground, where no technology could recover it to power the ship again.

He'd have to tell the crew eventually, after organizing his explanation so they could accept it, however much they might resist. But first he had to tell Kara.

"It was the orbs," he summarized. "They seem fascinated by humans. They don't need anything from us, but they enjoy our presence. Chen doesn't understand why. They can modify our cells, adapt us. Before humans came, all life here had six legs. Now they're changing that, as we've seen.

"And they don't need physical contact to do it. We've all been outside the hull. The changes don't show yet—but we're altered. In another month, Earth food would kill us. We have to stay. We'll bury the ship deeper, and Earth won't find us. They can't risk a colony where three ships disappear, so we'll vanish. And they'll never know."

No one would know. Their children—strange children who matured in six years—would be primitive in three generations. Earth tools would be useless for their changed hands. Nothing from the ship would last. Books would be unreadable to their new eyes. Eventually, Earth wouldn't even be a memory.

Kara stared out the viewport at what would be her home. Then she sighed. "You'll need to practice your presentation, but the others don't know you like I do, Henry. We can make them believe it. And it's too late now. But we haven't actually been changed yet, have we?"

"No," he admitted. Damn his voice—he'd never been good at deception. "No. They have to touch us directly. I've been touched, but the others could still return."

She nodded. He waited for her anger, but saw only confusion. "Why?"

Then, before he could answer, understanding dawned on her face. "The spawning ground."

It was the only option. Earth needed places to plant humanity's seed, but no world except Earth could be trusted to preserve that seed across generations. Some colonies were already showing instability.

Here, though, the orbs had adapted humans to the alien world instead of humans having to terraform the entire planet. Here, humanity's strange children could grow, develop, and begin the long climb back to civilization. The technology would be lost temporarily. But perhaps some of humanity's cultural values would remain to make the next rise better.

"We're needed here," he told her, his voice pleading for understanding he couldn't fully give himself. "These people need genetic diversity to give the new race strength. The forty-eight people on this ship will provide that foundation. We can't return to Earth, where no one would believe or accept this—or allow us to come back. We have to stay."

She smiled and moved toward him, seeking his strength. "Be fruitful," she whispered. "Be fruitful and multiply and replenish a world."

"No," he told her. "Replenish the stars."

But she was no longer listening, and that part of his vision could wait.

Someday, their children would find their way back to space exploration, seeking other worlds. With the orbs to help them adapt, they could claim most worlds. The unchanged human spirit would drive them through all space, and the changing bodies would conquer worlds beyond counting.

Someday, the entire galaxy would be a spawning ground for the children of humanity.
