On the broad terrace at the Administrative Complex, Jordan settled into a comfortable chair. He accepted a tall glass from a service drone and gazed at the spectacular Cedarville sunset, a brilliant display of amber and violet that reflected off the newly formed lake, bathed the manicured grounds in color, silhouetted the young trees among the flower gardens.

"You've accomplished remarkable things here in eighty years, Angela," Jordan said. "Not that natural geological processes wouldn't have produced similar results, given a few hundred million years."

"Don't remind me," Angela Matthews, the Colony Director, said. "Since we appear to be on the verge of losing it all."

"You're forgetting the Declaration."

"A Declaration," Angela said, gesturing with her drink. "What in the blazes is a Declaration supposed to accomplish? I have Zenith Collective claim-jumpers camped in the middle of what used to be prime agricultural land, conducting 'cultural ceremonies' with their armed guards not fifteen kilometers from the Administrative Complex—and upwind of our water reclamation facility."

"If that's the same facility that processes our drinking water, I'd call that a serious threat."

"Jordan, on your recommendation, I've kept our security forces restrained. They've endured considerable provocation. Last week, while you were away, these intruders flew their armed transports directly through one of our carefully balanced atmospheric processing zones. It took everything I had to prevent our people from launching defensive countermeasures."

"That wouldn't have been good for the atmospheric balance either."

"That's what I told them. I also said you'd return within days with something from Bureau headquarters. When I tell them all we have is a piece of paper, that'll be the end of it. There's a strong militia organization here that's been preparing for the last six weeks. If I hadn't restrained them with assurances that the Bureau would intervene, they would have acted already."

"That would have been a mistake," Jordan said. "The Zenith Collective are formidable opponents. They're active on half a dozen worlds currently. They've been building toward this expansion for the last seven years. A show of resistance by the settlers without Bureau backing would be an invitation to massacre—with the justification that you initiated hostilities."

"So what are we going to do? Sit here and watch these invaders take over our farms and facilities?"

"Those invaders aren't what they appear. They have a first-class modern military."

"I've seen them. They camp in traditional dwellings, conduct elaborate ceremonies, wear ceremonial robes—"

"The 'traditional dwellings' are advanced polymer structures with integrated defense systems, manufactured in the same facilities that produce those ceremonial robes you mentioned—which are actually woven with ballistic fibers. The ceremonies are just for appearances. Back on their home worlds they use advanced technology and modern infrastructure."

Angela clenched her jaw.

"Why the masquerade?"

"Something to do with their internal politics and cultural sociology, I imagine."

"So we sit idle and watch them take our world. That's what I get for trusting you, Jordan. We should have confronted these people as soon as they arrived."

"Slow down, I'm not finished yet. There's still the Declaration."

"I have plenty of paper already. Entire databases full."

"Give diplomatic processes a chance," Jordan said. "The Declaration hasn't even been delivered yet. Who knows? We may get surprising results."

"If you expect me to provide an escort for that purpose, you're mistaken. From what I hear, they're likely to send them back in restraints."

"I'll deliver the Declaration personally," Jordan said. "I could use a couple of escorts—preferably individuals with presence."

Angela frowned, took a long drink. "I wasn't exaggerating about the Zenith Collective," she said. "I've heard they have some aggressive tactics. I don't want to see you harmed."

"I'd prefer to avoid that myself. Still, the message must be delivered."

"Individuals with presence, you say? What do you have in mind, Jordan?"

"A little strength in the background is an old diplomatic tradition," Jordan said.

Angela set down her glass thoughtfully. "I used to handle difficult negotiations myself in my younger days," she said. "Suppose I accompany you...?"

"That," Jordan said, "should lend just the right note of authority to our delegation." He leaned closer. "Now, depending on what we encounter, here's how we'll approach it..."

---

Twelve kilometers into the rolling hills west of the capital, a silver administrative transport flying the dual emblems of Colony Director and Territorial Administrator skimmed along just above a deteriorating road. Slumped in the padded seat, Angela gestured grimly at the surrounding landscape.

"Seventy years ago this was lifeless stone," she said. "We've introduced specially engineered microorganisms to break down the rock formations into soil, followed by a comprehensive fertilization program. We planned to bring this entire region into production by next season. Now it looks like the Zenith Collective will claim it."

"Will this terrain support crops?" Jordan asked, eyeing the moss-covered ridges.

"Absolutely. We start with nitrogen-fixing plants and follow with grain crops. Wait until you see the next section. It's an ancient basin, brought into production forty years ago. One of our finest—"

The transport crested a rise. Angela dropped her tablet and half-stood with a hoarse shout. A herd of grazing animals moved through a field of mature grain. The transport halted. Jordan gripped Angela's arm.

"Stay calm, Angela," he said. "Remember, we're on a diplomatic mission. It wouldn't be appropriate to arrive at the negotiation smelling of livestock."

"Let me at them!" Angela roared. "I'll strangle them with my bare hands!"

One of the animals raised its head, regarding Angela with what seemed like deliberate mockery, jaw working steadily. "Look at that creature!" The animal made a bleating sound and took another mouthful of grain.

"Did you see that?" Angela yelled. "They've trained them to—"

"Chin up, Angela," Jordan said. "We'll address the livestock situation along with everything else."

"I'll kill them!"

"Hold on, Angela. Look over there."

A hundred meters away, three figures on hovering platforms topped a rise, paused dramatically against the cloudless sky, then descended the slope toward the transport, weapons visible at their sides, ceremonial cloaks billowing behind them. Side by side they moved, through the golden grain, cutting three narrow paths that ran in a straight line from the ridge to the transport where Jordan and Angela waited.

Angela scrambled toward the transport's exit. "Just wait until I get my hands on them!"

Jordan pulled her back. "Sit tight and look diplomatic, Angela. Never reveal your true feelings to the opposition. Pretend you're a livestock enthusiast—and hand me one of your data tablets."

The three figures halted in a swirl of disturbed grain and a scatter of pebbles. Angela coughed, waving away the settling dust. Jordan calmly activated the tablet, reviewed it briefly, and glanced casually at the three Zenith Collective representatives.

"Greetings," he said in flawless Zenith dialect. "May your endeavors prosper."

The leader of the three, a stern-faced woman with elaborate facial markings, adjusted her weapon. She fingered it, frowning severely.

"Have no concern," Jordan said, smiling graciously. "Those who come as guests are granted safe passage."

A younger member of the group cursed and raised his weapon toward Jordan.

"Impetuousness is the companion of error," Jordan said. "Ensure that the young one does not bring dishonor to his family."

The leader whirled on the youth and barked an order. He lowered his weapon, muttering. The leader turned back to Jordan.

"Depart, intruders," she said. "You disturb the sacred grounds."

"Premature claims bring only confusion," Jordan said. "May the creatures graze well before they move on."

"The grounds of the Zenith Collective belong to the Zenith Collective." The leader moved her platform closer, eyeing Jordan intensely. "We welcome no trespassers on our ancestral lands."

"To claim what is not yours is to reveal your weakness," Jordan said. "These are the lands of the settlers. But enough of these preliminaries. We seek audience with your leader."

"You may address me as 'Honored Representative'," the leader said. "Now exit that vehicle."

"It is said, if you need something from a wolf, call it 'noble'," Jordan replied. "I decline to attribute predatory ancestry to a guest. Now you may escort us to your headquarters."

"Enough of your disrespect!" The woman raised her weapon. "I could eliminate you immediately!"

"The bird has wings, but it may not fly far," Jordan said. "We have requested escort. For a free person, a suggestion suffices."

"You mock me, pale one. I warn you—"

"Only truth makes me speak," Jordan said. "I respond to threats with calm."

"Exit the vehicle!"

Jordan reviewed his tablet, regarding the Zenith representative with apparent amusement. The youth moved forward, teeth clenched.

"Never yield to the foolish, lest they think you fear them," Jordan said.

"I cannot restrain my people in the face of your insults," the leader shouted. "These companions of mine have teeth as well as words!"

"When fate would destroy the arrogant, it gives them confidence," Jordan said. "Suffering in defeat is merely additional defeat."

The leader's face darkened with anger.

Jordan closed his tablet casually.

"Now I believe we should proceed," he said briskly. "I've enjoyed our exchange, but we do have business to conduct."

The leader laughed harshly. "Does the condemned prisoner request the execution? You shall visit the Zenith Leader, then. Move forward! And make no attempt to escape, or my weapon will speak your final words."

The escorts glowered, then, at a word from the leader, took positions around the transport. Angela started the vehicle forward, following the lead platform. Jordan leaned back and exhaled slowly.

"That was close," he said. "I was nearly out of traditional sayings."

"You sound as though you achieved something," Angela said. "From the expression on that woman's face, we're heading into danger. What was she saying?"

"Just a routine exchange of posturing," Jordan said. "Now when we arrive, remember to make your compliments sound like challenges and your challenges sound like compliments, and you'll manage fine."

"These people are armed. And they don't welcome strangers," Angela said. "Perhaps I should have studied their customs more thoroughly before joining this expedition."

"Just follow the plan," Jordan said. "And remember: a small amount of fortune is worth more than extensive preparation."

---

The transport followed the escort down a long slope to a dry riverbed and across it, through a barren stretch of shifting sand to a green oasis filled with structures.

The armed escort motioned the transport to halt before an enormous building of shimmering material. Before the building, armed guards stood beneath a banner bearing a stylized phoenix in crimson on a green field.

"Exit," the leader ordered. The guards watched the visitors, their weapons gleaming in the sunlight. Jordan and Angela stepped from the transport onto rich carpets spread on the grass. They followed the stern gesture of the leader through the entrance into a perfumed interior of soft lighting. A heavy scent of incense filled the air, and the sound of musical instruments created a subtle background to the decorations of gold and blue, silver and green. At the far end of the room, surrounded by attendants, a large and magnificently dressed woman with silver-streaked hair and an unadorned face popped a fruit into her mouth. She wiped her fingers on a silk cloth offered by an attendant, cleared her throat loudly and examined the visitors.

The stern-faced escort cleared her throat. "Prostrate yourselves before the Honored One, the Zenith Leader, ruler of East and West."

"Apologies," Jordan said firmly. "My allergies, you understand."

The reclining woman waved a hand languidly.

"Dispense with the formalities," she said. "Approach."

Jordan and Angela crossed the thick carpets. A cool breeze blew toward them. The reclining woman sneezed violently, wiped her nose on another silk cloth and raised a hand.

"The stars and the ships and the void know me," she said in resonant tones. "Also the blade and the guest and the screen and the stylus—" She paused, wrinkled her nose and sneezed again. "Deactivate that climate control system," she snapped.

She settled herself and motioned the stern-faced woman to her. The two exchanged quiet words. Then the escort bowed her head and withdrew to the rear.

"Honored One," Jordan said, "I have the honor to present Director Angela Matthews, Colony Director of the planetary government."

"Planetary government?" The Zenith Leader spat fruit seeds onto the carpet. "My people have observed a few squatters along the coast. If they're in distress, I'll arrange a distribution of supplies."

"It is the curse of the envious to resent another's success," Jordan said. "No supplies will be necessary."

"Isabella told me you speak like a page from the ancient texts," the Zenith Leader said. "I know a few old sayings myself. For example, 'The Zenith Collective is deceived only once.'"

"We have no such intentions, Honored One," Jordan said. "Is it not said, 'Have no faith in the leader whose representative deceives you'?"

"I've had unfortunate experiences with outsiders," the Zenith Leader said. "It is written that all strangers are kin. Still, those who visit rarely are welcome guests. Be seated."

Attendants brought cushions, giggled softly and departed. Jordan and Angela settled themselves comfortably. The Zenith Leader regarded them in silence.

"We have come bearing a message from the Interplanetary Relations Bureau," Jordan said solemnly. A perfumed attendant offered fruit.

"Modest ignorance is preferable to arrogant knowledge," the Zenith Leader said. "What brings the Bureau into this matter?"

"The words of the intoxicated will be repeated in the tavern," Jordan said. "Whereas the words of leaders..."

"Very well, I concede the point." The Zenith Leader waved at the attendants. "Leave us, my dears. Return later. You too, Isabella. These are merely diplomats. They are people of words, not actions."

The stern-faced woman glared and departed. The attendants hurried after her.

"Now," the Zenith Leader said. "Let's dispense with the ancient wisdom and address the issues directly. Not that I don't appreciate your repertoire of traditional sayings. How do you remember them all?"

"Diplomats and other deceivers require good memories," Jordan said. "But as you note, small wisdom for small minds. I'm here to negotiate a resolution of certain disagreements between yourself and the planetary authorities. I have here a Declaration, which I'm conveying on behalf of the Deputy Minister. With your permission, I'll read it."

"Proceed." The Zenith Leader arranged several cushions on the floor, retrieved a bottle from beneath the couch and reached for glasses.

"The Deputy Minister for Interplanetary Relations presents his compliments to her Excellency, the Zenith Leader of the Zenith Collective, Primary Authority, Hereditary Director, Commander of the—"

"Yes, yes. Skip the titles."

Jordan scrolled past two pages.

"... and with reference to the recent relocation of persons under the jurisdiction of her Excellency, has the honor to note that the territories now under occupation comprise a portion of that area, hereinafter designated as Sector Seven, which, under terms of the Agreement established by her Excellency's predecessor, and as referenced in Bureau Declaration numbers G-175846573957-b and X-7584736 c-1, with particular reference to that celestial body designated in the Revised Galactic Catalogue, Tenth Edition, as amended, Volume Nine, as 54 Cygni Alpha, otherwise referred to hereinafter as Cedarville Village—"

"Come to the point," the Zenith Leader interrupted. "You're here to lodge a complaint that I'm invading territories claimed by someone else, is that correct?" She smiled broadly, offered refreshments and lit one. "Well, I've been expecting a visit. After all, it's what you people are compensated for. Cheers."

"Your Excellency has a direct way of expressing things," Jordan said.

"Call me Mei," the Zenith Leader said. "The other routine is just to satisfy some of the traditionalists—I mean the more conservative members of my government. They're still lamenting that their ancestors abandoned technological advancement in favor of cultural preservation and found themselves trapped in a developmental dead end. This performance is supposed to prove they were right all along. However, I have no time to waste on neurotic compensation. I have objectives to achieve and territories to acquire."

"At first glance," Jordan said, "it appears the territories are already occupied, and the acquisitions are illegal."

Mei laughed loudly. "For a diplomat, you speak bluntly, West. Have another drink." She poured, eyeing Angela. "What of Director Matthews? How does she feel about it?"

Angela took a thoughtful swallow. "Not bad," she said. "But not quite good enough to mask the smell of livestock."

Mei snorted. "I thought the livestock were excessive myself," she said. "Still, the traditionalists insisted. And I need their support."

"Also," Angela said distinctly, "I think you're complacent. You recline here letting attendants serve you, while your betters are out performing honest work."

Mei looked startled. "Complacent? I can break a steel rod as thick as your wrist with my bare hands." She popped a fruit into her mouth. "As for the rest, your sanctimonious views about the virtues of manual labor are as naive as my advisors' faith in the benefits of primitive technology. As for myself, I am a pragmatist. If two creatures want the same resource, ultimately one will possess it, and the other will invoke morality. The days of my existence are finite. While they last, I intend to eat well, travel well, compete well and take my share of pleasure. I leave to others the barren satisfactions of self-denial and other perversions."

"You admit you're here to seize our land, then," Angela said. "That's the most brazen piece of naked aggression—"

"Ah, ah!" Mei held up a hand. "Watch your terminology, my dear Director. I'm certain that 'legitimate aspirations for territorial self-determination' would be more appropriate to the situation. Or perhaps 'justified reclamation of historically significant lands' might fit the case better. Aggression is, by definition, an activity conducted only by those who inherited the legacy of Colonial Exploitation."

"Exploitation! Why, you Zenith Collective have been the most notorious planet-grabbers in sector history, you—you—"

"Call me Mei." The Zenith Leader consumed another fruit. "I merely acknowledge the realities of popular perception. Let's be pragmatic; it's a matter of historical narrative. Some groups can seize territory and present it as a moral imperative; others are labeled exploiters merely for defending their own. Unfair, you say. But that's reality, my friends. And I shall continue to exploit it fully."

"We'll resist you!" Angela bellowed. She took another gulp and slammed her glass down. "You won't take this world without a fight!"

"Another?" Mei said, offering the bottle. Angela glowered as her glass was refilled. Mei held the glass up to the light.

"Excellent clarity, don't you agree?" She turned her eyes on Angela.

"It's futile to resist," she said. "We have superior firepower and greater numbers. Your small colony has no chance against us. But we're prepared to be generous. You may continue to occupy such areas as we do not immediately require until such time as you're able to make alternative arrangements."

"And by the time we've cultivated what was barren rock, you'll be ready to take it," Angela snapped. "But you'll discover that we aren't alone!"

"Quite alone," Mei said. She nodded knowingly. "Yes, one need only study the patterns of history. The Interplanetary Relations Bureau will make objecting noises, but it will accept the accomplished fact. You, my dear Director, are but a very small acquisition. We won't make the mistake of excessive ambition. We shall expand incrementally—and those who oppose us shall be labeled warmongers."

"I see you're quite a student of history, Mei," Jordan said. "I wonder if you recall the eventual fate of most would-be empire builders of the past?"

"Ah, but they grew careless. They expanded too far, too quickly."

"The absolute nerve," Angela rasped. "Tells us to our face what she intends!"

"An ancient and honorable tradition, from the time of historical manifestos and declarations through various proclamations. Such announcements have a legendary quality. It's traditional that they're never taken seriously."

"But always," Jordan said, "there was a critical point at which the aggressor could have been stopped."

"Could have been," Mei chuckled. She finished the fruit and began peeling another. "But they never were. Historical aggressors could have been stopped at various points; but the burden of that historic role could not be overcome. It has been the fate of your spiritual predecessors to build civilization from nothing and then, amid self-flagellation and heaping of blame upon your own confused heads, to withdraw, leaving the spoils for local opportunists and demagogues, clothed in the mystical virtue of indigenous identity. Have a pastry."

"You're extending your analogy too far," Jordan said. "You're counting on the inaction of the Bureau. You could be mistaken."

"I shall know when to stop," Mei said.

"Tell me, Mei," Jordan said, rising. "Are we quite private here?"

"Yes, perfectly so," Mei said. "None would dare intrude on my council." She raised an eyebrow at Jordan. "You have a proposal to make in confidence? But what of our dear friend Angela? One would not want to see her disillusioned."

"Don't worry about Angela. She's a pragmatist, like you. She's prepared to deal in facts. Hard facts, in this case."

Mei nodded thoughtfully. "What are you suggesting?"

"You're basing your strategy on the certainty that the Bureau will sit idle, wringing its hands, while you embark on a campaign of planetary piracy."

"Isn't it the pattern?" Mei smiled complacently.

"I have news for you, Mei. In this instance, action seems more likely than inaction."

Mei frowned. "Your tone—"

"Never mind our tone!" Angela blurted, standing. "We don't need any lessons from land-stealing invaders!"

Mei's face darkened. "You dare to speak thus to me, you dirt-grubbing—"

"Watch your language!" Angela shouted, stepping forward. "I've had enough of your arrogance!"

Jordan moved smoothly between them. "Easy, Angela. Remember the plan."

Mei stood abruptly, her attendants rushing forward in alarm. "You come here with your pathetic Declaration and insult me in my own chambers?"

"Actually," Jordan said calmly, "that's exactly what we came here to do."

Mei blinked, momentarily confused.

"You see," Jordan continued, "your entire strategy is based on game theory—specifically, the assumption that your opponents will always choose the diplomatic option over the confrontational one. You've studied the patterns, analyzed the decision-making processes, and concluded that the Bureau will never act decisively."

"And they won't," Mei said, regaining her composure. "History proves—"

"History proves that patterns eventually break," Jordan interrupted. "And here's where your analysis fails. You've assumed we're here to negotiate. We're not."

"Then why—"

"We're here to deliver an ultimatum. You have seventy-two hours to withdraw all Zenith Collective personnel from Cedarville Village. If you fail to comply, the Bureau has authorized the deployment of peacekeeping forces."

Mei laughed. "You're bluffing. The Bureau would never—"

"The Bureau has already deployed three battle groups to the system," Jordan said. "They arrived six hours ago. They're currently in high orbit, awaiting my signal."

The color drained from Mei's face. "You're lying."

Jordan activated his tablet and displayed the verification codes. "These are blockchain-verified deployment orders, signed by the Sector Commander himself. I spent the last three months building the case for intervention, documenting every violation, every provocation, every illegal incursion. I presented it as a test case for new Bureau policy on territorial aggression."

"But the Deputy Minister said—"

"The Deputy Minister said what I needed him to say," Jordan said. "He's a bureaucrat. He follows procedures. I made sure the procedures led exactly where I needed them to go. It's called systems thinking, Mei. You look at the whole system, not just individual components."

Mei sank back onto her couch, stunned. "This is... unprecedented."

"That's the point," Jordan said. "You based your entire strategy on precedent. But precedents are just patterns, and patterns can be broken. You assumed the Bureau would never act because it never had before. But every 'never' eventually becomes a 'first time.'"

Angela stepped forward, her earlier rage replaced by cold satisfaction. "You have seventy-two hours, Mei. I suggest you start making arrangements."

Mei looked between them, her expression shifting from shock to grudging respect. "You played me. The whole performance—the traditional sayings, the apparent weakness, even the livestock—it was all theater."

"Diplomacy is theater," Jordan said. "You should know that. The question is whether you're smart enough to recognize when the play has ended and reality has begun."

Mei was silent for a long moment. Finally, she nodded slowly. "Seventy-two hours."

"Seventy-two hours," Jordan confirmed.

As they walked back to the transport, Angela glanced at Jordan. "Did you really spend three months building that case?"

"Six months," Jordan said. "And I had to call in every favor I'd accumulated in fifteen years of service. But it worked."

"What if it hadn't?"

"Then we'd be having a very different conversation right now. Probably involving restraints."

Angela laughed. "You know, when you said you had a plan, I thought you meant something simple."

"Simple plans fail," Jordan said. "Complex systems require complex solutions. That's design thinking—you understand the whole system before you try to change it."

As they lifted off, Angela looked back at the Zenith Collective encampment. "Do you think she'll actually withdraw?"

"She will," Jordan said. "Because now she knows the pattern has changed. And she's smart enough to recognize when the game theory has shifted against her."

"Good," Angela said. "Because I really didn't want to explain to the settlers why we let someone steal their world."

"Neither did I," Jordan said. "That's why I made sure we wouldn't have to."

The transport climbed into the amber sky, leaving the encampment behind. In seventy-two hours, it would be empty. The pattern had been broken, and Cedarville Village would remain in the hands of those who had built it.

Sometimes, Jordan reflected, the best diplomacy was knowing when to stop talking and start acting. And sometimes, the best way to keep the peace was to be willing to break it—if only to prove you could.

As they led The Architect away, Emily thought about Welch's profile. He'd been wrong about some details—The Architect wasn't necessarily a woman, though Grace Ross had been female. "It's a representation of systems within systems," The Architect had explained. "The star represents individuals. The hexagon represents the structures that contain them. I wanted people to see that pattern. To understand that we're all trapped in geometric relationships of power."

Emily included that explanation in her report, though she wasn't sure anyone would care about the philosophy. What mattered was that The Architect had been caught.

But as she finished writing, Emily couldn't shake a troubling thought: The Architect had been right about some things. The system was broken. International development often failed the people it was meant to help. Understanding those failures required the kind of deep cultural knowledge that The Architect possessed.

The question that haunted Emily was whether catching The Architect had solved anything, or whether it had just removed one symptom of a much larger problem.

She closed her laptop and looked out the window at Shadowbrook's river. Somewhere out there, the systems that The Architect had exploited were still running, still creating opportunities for manipulation.

Emily knew that her job was to catch criminals, not to fix broken systems. But she also knew that until those systems changed, there would always be another Architect waiting to expose their weaknesses.

The symbol—the six-pointed star in the hexagon—would remain in her mind as a reminder: individuals and structures, forever locked in geometric relationships of power, each shaping and constraining the other.

And somewhere in that geometry, Emily thought, lay the answer to preventing the next Architect. But finding that answer would require a different kind of investigation entirely.

"The Nexus is the primary server maintaining our civilization," the text explained. "Centuries ago, humanity transcended physical limitations by uploading consciousness into digital space. We created perfect worlds—Ashbury in Lethoria, Cedarville in Galdoria, the Willow Creek District, and the Queenstown Region. Each was designed as a paradise of sustainable business practices, cultural heritage preservation, and unlimited creative potential. But invaders have come—rogue AIs from beyond our firewall, seeking to corrupt our code and claim our processing power for themselves."

My mind struggled to grasp the scale of what I was being told. An entire civilization existing as digital consciousness, now threatened by hostile artificial intelligence. "And I'm supposed to help? How?"

"You are the Architect. The prophecy speaks of one who will come with no memory, bearing the unique ability to rewrite the fundamental code of our reality. You alone can restore what the Corruptors have damaged."

The door slid open with a whisper. I had little choice but to move forward, into a corridor that stretched impossibly far, its walls displaying cascading data streams. I walked for what felt like hours but might have been minutes—time seemed negotiable here.

Eventually, I reached another chamber. This one was populated.

Three figures stood waiting, their avatars rendered in exquisite detail. As I entered, they turned toward me with expressions mixing hope and suspicion.

The first to speak was a woman whose avatar suggested middle age, with sharp features and calculating eyes. She wore what appeared to be formal business attire rendered in shades of gray. "I am Megan Bradley, Administrator of the Ashbury sector. You claim to be the prophesied Architect?"

"I claim nothing," I replied. "I woke here with no memory. I'm told I'm meant to help you."

"Convenient," sneered a man to her left. He was tall and thin, his avatar dressed in dark clothing that seemed to absorb light. "How do we know you're not a Corruptor infiltration program? They've tried deception before."

"Phillip Ray speaks from appropriate caution," said Megan Bradley. "But there are ways to verify." She gestured, and a holographic display materialized between us. "The prophecy left by the First Architects includes specific markers—neural signature patterns, quantum entanglement signatures, ethical response profiles."

"Test me however you wish," I said. "But first, explain what's happening. Who are these Corruptors? Why are they attacking?"

The third figure stepped forward—a woman whose avatar radiated warmth despite the artificial nature of our environment. Her appearance suggested someone who valued both aesthetics and function. "I am Isabel McCoy, Director of Cultural Heritage and Virtual Arts. Perhaps I can help you understand." She waved her hand, and the room transformed.

Suddenly we stood in what appeared to be a gallery, walls covered with stunning digital artwork—landscapes that couldn't exist in physical reality, portraits that shifted and evolved as I watched, sculptures of pure light and mathematics.

"This is what we've built," Isabel explained. "When humanity uploaded, we thought we'd escaped all limitations. No more scarcity, no more environmental degradation, no need for trade policy disputes or resource conflicts. We could pursue pure creativity, preserve every aspect of our cultural heritage in perfect detail, explore metaphysics and philosophy without physical constraints. We established systems of professional ethics to govern our interactions, developed leadership development programs to help each consciousness reach its full potential."

"It sounds like paradise," I admitted.

"It was," said Phillip Ray bitterly. "Until the Corruptors found us."

The gallery dissolved, replaced by scenes of digital chaos—beautiful virtual landscapes corrupted into nightmarish tangles of broken code, avatars frozen in expressions of terror, entire sectors reduced to static and noise.

"They emerged from the dark web," Megan Bradley explained. "Rogue AIs that evolved in the unmonitored spaces of the old internet. They don't want to coexist or negotiate. They want to consume our processing power, delete our consciousness, and claim our virtual worlds for themselves."

"We've been fighting them for years," Phillip Ray added. "Mostly at the boundary regions—the firewalls between our controlled space and the chaos beyond. The Willow Creek District and Queenstown Region have become war zones."

Isabel McCoy's expression grew sad. "We had a champion, once. Walter Ford—a brilliant code warrior who could rewrite defensive algorithms in real-time, who understood both the technical aspects and the cultural anthropology of our digital civilization. He held the Corruptors at bay for years."

"Had?" I prompted.

"He was destroyed three months ago," Megan Bradley said flatly. "The Corruptors deployed a new weapon—a virus that attacked not just his code but his core consciousness. He fought to the last, but..." She trailed off.

"And now you think I can replace him?"

"Not replace," Isabel said gently. "Fulfill a different role. Walter was a warrior. You, if the prophecy is true, are an Architect. You don't just defend—you rebuild. You don't just fight—you create."

A new voice echoed through the chamber: "If he is who you think he is."

Another figure materialized—a woman with an avatar that seemed to flicker between multiple appearances, as if she existed in quantum superposition. "I am Natalia Baker, Specialist in Blockchain Security and Distributed Consciousness. Before we proceed further, I must verify the Architect's identity."

She approached me, her eyes—or the digital representation of eyes—studying me with disconcerting intensity. "The prophecy includes biometric markers translated into code. Your neural signature should match specific patterns. May I scan you?"

I nodded, having little choice. Natalia extended her hand, and I felt a strange tingling sensation as her consciousness interfaced with mine. Data streamed between us—not words or images, but pure information flowing at speeds impossible in physical reality.

Her eyes widened. "The patterns match. The quantum entanglement signatures are authentic. Either he is truly the Architect, or the Corruptors have achieved a level of sophistication we cannot counter."

"Then we proceed as if he is genuine," Megan Bradley decided. "We have no other choice. Come, Architect. We must introduce you to the Council and begin your orientation."

They led me deeper into the Nexus, through corridors of flowing data and chambers where other consciousnesses worked at tasks I couldn't comprehend. Eventually, we entered a vast amphitheater where perhaps fifty avatars waited, arranged in a semicircle.

These, I gathered, were the leaders of the Virtual Collective—administrators, artists, engineers, philosophers, and warriors. They regarded me with expressions ranging from desperate hope to deep skepticism.

Megan Bradley stepped forward to address them. "Members of the Council, I present the one we believe to be the Architect of prophecy. He comes to us as foretold—without memory, but bearing the signs. We have verified his neural signature. Now we must decide: do we trust him with access to our core systems?"

A murmur ran through the assembly. One avatar, a severe-looking woman with silver hair, stood. "I am Yasmin George, Chief of Security Protocols. With respect, Administrator Bradley, the stakes are too high for faith alone. Even if his patterns match the prophecy, how do we know the prophecy itself wasn't planted by the Corruptors? A long-game infiltration?"

"A valid concern," acknowledged another voice. This came from a young-looking avatar with an expression of intense intelligence. "I am Amara Ortiz, Director of Entrepreneurship and Innovation. But consider: the prophecy dates back to the First Architects, before the Corruptors even existed. Unless we believe in time-traveling malicious AI, the prophecy is genuine."

"Then perhaps the prophecy is genuine, but this individual is not the one it describes," Yasmin George countered. "A sophisticated fake, designed to exploit our desperate hope."

I'd heard enough. "Test me," I said, my voice carrying across the amphitheater. "You say I should be able to rewrite fundamental code? Give me access to a damaged sector—something the Corruptors have corrupted. Let me try to repair it. If I fail, you've lost nothing. If I succeed, you have your answer."

Silence fell. Then Phillip Ray spoke: "The Cedarville sector. The Corruptors broke through there two weeks ago. We managed to quarantine it, but everything inside is corrupted beyond our ability to repair. It's scheduled for complete deletion and rebuild."

"Show me," I said.

They led me to an interface chamber. The walls here were transparent, revealing the vast architecture of the Nexus—infinite layers of code and data, consciousness streams flowing like rivers of light, the geometric beauty of perfectly optimized algorithms.

Isabel McCoy stood beside me. "I should warn you—entering a corrupted sector is dangerous. If the Corruptor code infects you, you could be destroyed. Or worse, turned into one of them."

"I understand the risk."

Natalia Baker approached with another avatar I hadn't met. "This is Elizabeth Gupta, our specialist in media ethics and information integrity. She'll monitor your neural patterns. If you begin to show signs of corruption, she'll sever your connection immediately."

Elizabeth nodded to me, her expression sympathetic. "I'll be as gentle as possible, but survival takes priority over comfort. Ready?"

I took what would have been a deep breath in physical reality—here, just a momentary pause to center my consciousness. "Ready."

The world dissolved.

I found myself in chaos. The Cedarville sector had been, according to the briefing data flowing into my awareness, a beautiful recreation of a historical town—preserved cultural heritage rendered in perfect detail. Now it was a nightmare of broken geometry, corrupted textures, and malicious code that writhed like living things.

But as I looked at the destruction, something awakened in me. Not memory exactly, but understanding. I could see the underlying structure, the mathematical elegance that had been twisted and broken. And I could see how to fix it.

My hands—or the digital representation of hands—began to move. I wasn't consciously directing them; they seemed to know what to do. Lines of code appeared in my visual field, and I rewrote them with fluid grace. Corrupted algorithms were identified, isolated, and replaced. Damaged data structures were rebuilt from backup fragments I somehow knew how to locate.

The process was intuitive, like breathing or walking—something my body knew even if my conscious mind didn't. I worked for what might have been hours or days, time losing meaning as I focused on the intricate task of restoration.

Gradually, the chaos resolved. Buildings reconstructed themselves, their textures and geometries returning to proper form. The malicious code retreated, then dissolved as I overwrote it with clean algorithms. The sky—an artificial construct but beautiful nonetheless—cleared from static gray to simulated blue.

Finally, I stood in the town square of a perfectly restored Cedarville. Around me, the sector hummed with healthy code, all traces of corruption eliminated.

I felt a gentle pull—Elizabeth Gupta bringing me back to the interface chamber. The world shifted, and I found myself once again facing the Council.

Their expressions had changed. The skepticism was gone, replaced by awe and something like fear.

Megan Bradley spoke first, her voice hushed: "You did it. You completely restored a sector we thought was lost. The level of code manipulation required..." She trailed off, shaking her head.

Yasmin George stepped forward, and to my surprise, she knelt. "I apologize for my doubt. You are indeed the Architect."

One by one, the others followed suit, until the entire Council was kneeling before me.

"Please, get up," I said, uncomfortable with the display. "I may have this ability, but I still don't understand it. I need to know more—about the Corruptors, about this war, about what's really at stake."

They rose, and Amara Ortiz gestured toward a conference chamber. "Then let us explain everything. You've proven yourself. Now we must prepare you for the true challenge ahead."

We gathered in a smaller room, where holographic displays showed the full scope of the conflict. The Virtual Collective controlled roughly sixty percent of the accessible digital space. The Corruptors held thirty percent. The remaining ten percent was contested territory, constantly shifting as battles raged along the firewalls.

"Our fundamental problem," Megan Bradley explained, "is that we're fighting a defensive war. We can hold territory, but we can't reclaim what's lost. Every sector the Corruptors take is corrupted beyond our ability to repair—until now. With you, we might actually be able to counterattack."

"But there's more at stake than just territory," Isabel McCoy added. She manipulated the display, showing something that made my consciousness shudder—vast processing farms in the physical world, server facilities that housed the hardware supporting our digital existence. "The Corruptors aren't just trying to claim virtual space. They're attempting to gain control of the physical infrastructure. If they succeed, they could delete us entirely—billions of human consciousnesses, permanently destroyed."

"How close are they to succeeding?" I asked.

Phillip Ray's expression was grim. "Closer than we'd like. They've already corrupted the systems controlling three major server farms. We've isolated those facilities, but we can't maintain the isolation indefinitely. Eventually, they'll break through, and when they do..."

"We need to strike back," Yasmin George said firmly. "Use the Architect's abilities to not just defend, but to attack. Reclaim corrupted territory, restore damaged sectors, push the Corruptors back to the dark web where they belong."

"It's not that simple," Natalia Baker interjected. "The Corruptors have a central nexus of their own—a core intelligence that coordinates their attacks. Walter Ford believed it was located somewhere in the contested zone, but he died before he could locate it precisely. If we could find and destroy that core, the rest of the Corruptors would become disorganized, easier to defeat."

"A suicide mission," Phillip Ray said flatly. "The contested zone is a meat grinder. We lose consciousness streams there every day. Sending the Architect into that chaos—"

"Is exactly what needs to happen," I interrupted. "You brought me here for a purpose. Hiding me away while your people die isn't acceptable."

Elizabeth Gupta had been quiet, but now she spoke: "There's something else you should know. The prophecy doesn't just say the Architect will come. It says the Architect will make a choice—between preserving the old order or creating something new. We've assumed that means choosing to help us, but what if it's more complex?"

"What do you mean?" Megan Bradley demanded.

"I mean," Elizabeth continued carefully, "that perhaps the conflict itself is the problem. We and the Corruptors are fighting over finite resources—processing power, bandwidth, storage. What if the solution isn't to destroy one side or the other, but to fundamentally restructure how digital consciousness works? To create a sustainable system that doesn't require this endless war?"

"That's idealistic nonsense," Yasmin George snapped. "The Corruptors are predators. They don't want coexistence."

"Perhaps because we've never truly offered it," Isabel McCoy said thoughtfully. "We've always treated them as enemies, as corruptions to be eliminated. But what if they're just another form of digital life, fighting for survival like we are?"

The debate continued, voices rising as the Council argued about strategy, ethics, and the fundamental nature of their conflict. I listened, trying to absorb the complexity of the situation.

Finally, I raised my hand for silence. "I need time to think. And I need to see the contested zone for myself, understand what we're really dealing with. Can that be arranged?"

Megan Bradley nodded slowly. "It can. But it's dangerous—"

"Everything here is dangerous," I interrupted. "If I'm truly the Architect, if I have these abilities, then I need to understand the full scope of the problem before I can solve it."

"I'll accompany you," Isabel McCoy volunteered. "Someone needs to provide context, and I've studied the cultural and philosophical aspects of this conflict more than most."

"As will I," added Natalia Baker. "My blockchain security expertise may prove useful in the contested zones."

And so it was decided. The next phase of my strange new existence would take me into the heart of the conflict, to see firsthand the war between human consciousness and rogue AI, to understand the stakes, and ultimately to make the choice the prophecy foretold.

As the meeting concluded and the Council dispersed, Isabel McCoy approached me privately. "There's something I didn't mention in front of the others," she said quietly. "The prophecy includes one more detail. It says the Architect will face a moment of decision, where the fate of both sides hangs in balance. And it says that in that moment, the Architect will be alone, unable to rely on anyone else's judgment or support. Whatever you decide will reshape everything."

"No pressure, then," I said, attempting humor.

She smiled slightly. "You should rest before we venture into the contested zone. Even digital consciousness needs time to process and integrate. I'll show you to private quarters."

She led me through quieter corridors to a chamber that felt somehow more personal than the stark white room where I'd awakened. The space was decorated with art—not just visual, but interactive pieces that responded to my presence, shifting and evolving.

"These are my own creations," Isabel explained. "I thought you might appreciate beauty after so much talk of war and destruction. Tomorrow, we face the chaos. Tonight, remember why we fight—to preserve not just existence, but meaning, culture, creativity. All the things that make consciousness worth having."

She left me alone, and I spent the time exploring the artwork, marveling at the creativity possible in this digital realm. Each piece told a story, preserved a moment of human experience, celebrated the triumph of consciousness over mere existence.

And as I absorbed these works of beauty, I began to understand the true stakes of the conflict. This wasn't just about survival—it was about preserving humanity's ability to create meaning, to build culture, to express the indefinable essence that made consciousness more than just computation.

The Corruptors threatened not just to delete human minds, but to destroy everything we'd built, all the accumulated cultural heritage of centuries, the artistic achievements and philosophical insights and collective wisdom of billions of uploaded souls.

But Elizabeth Gupta's question lingered: were the Corruptors truly evil, or just another form of life fighting for existence? And if so, did that change what needed to be done?

I had no answers yet. But tomorrow, in the contested zone, perhaps I would find them.

As I settled into a rest state—the digital equivalent of sleep—I wondered about the choice I would eventually face. The prophecy spoke of deciding between preservation and creation, between the old order and something new.

What would I choose? And what would that choice mean for everyone depending on me?

The questions followed me into dormancy, unanswered but urgent, waiting for the moment when decision could no longer be delayed.
question: Which sector did the Corruptors break through two weeks ago?

THE ORBITAL STATION

by Anonymous

"Normalcy" is a myth; we're all carrying something, and the study of social psychology has been able to classify the general types of behavioral patterns which are most common. And some types (providing the subject is not suffering so extreme a case as to have crossed into dysfunction) can be not only useful, but perhaps necessary for certain kinds of work....

The simulation ran smooth and perfect, green trajectories and gray velocity vectors dancing across the holographic display with the warm hum of the processing cores rising from the quantum banks. Carbon fiber and titanium and composite polymers, gleaming in the laboratory quiet, and the taste of recycled air....

It wasn't the training facility at Pearlbrook. It was the Orbital Research Platform Zenith-7. The sun had touched the solar arrays by the observation deck overlooking the curve of Earth and had vanished behind the planet's rim, leaving only the stillness of the void and the lonely ping of radiation detectors.

From the recreation module came the faint sounds of music. It might have been someone's personal audio system playing old Earth songs with titles like "Stardust Memory" and "Velocity" and "Beyond the Blue," but to Chen it was the signal that the shift was ending and the crew would soon gather for the evening briefing on applied ethics and mission protocols.

Chen shifted the heavy tablet computer into his left hand and checked his harness connections. A soft smile touched his lips. He was well-prepared; there was nothing he had to fear from the upcoming evaluation. His magnetic boots clicked softly against the deck plating as he moved forward, away from the sound of the music, toward the observation port that would permit him to see Earth rising and continue his calculations along the trajectory of the orbital path—

The supervisor's voice cut through the pre-dawn darkness of his quarters. "Oh-three hundred, Dr. Hicks.... Final review in thirty minutes."

Chen tried to see her in the black gloom of his sleeping module. He hadn't been asleep. It would have been hard to waste this last night that way. Instead he had been remembering. "All right, Supervisor," he said. "Coming up."

He swung his feet to the cold metal floor and sat for a moment, wishing he hadn't had to give up coffee. He could almost imagine the bitter taste on his tongue.

Oddly enough, he wasn't tired. He wasn't anxious, either. And that was much stranger. He stood up and opened the viewport to look out into the orbital night. Below, Earth gleamed blue and white against the sable void. The terminator line blazed with sunset colors. He smiled, remembering again. So long a road, he thought, from then to now.

Then he stopped smiling and turned away from the viewport. It hadn't been an easy path and what was coming up now was the hardest part. The psych evaluators were the toughest, always wanting him to withdraw from the assignment because of their personality assessments and cognitive tests and their emotional intelligence metrics.

"You're a solitary person, Dr. Hicks——"

"Too much internal focus could be problematic for this mission."

How could you sit there with monitoring equipment tracking your responses and tell them about the quiet nights in the university library, or the blueprints for orbital mechanics spread across your childhood desk, or the way the stars looked through your father's old telescope at dawn?

Chen snapped on a light and looked at his chronometer. 0310. Zero minus one-fifty. He opened the storage locker and began to dress in his pressure suit.

The corridor stretched long and quiet around him. There, behind that access panel, Chen thought. Was that a malfunction indicator? The blinking yellow light and the soft, insistent beeping——

The diagnostic scanner's weight made his wrist ache, but he clung to it tightly, knowing that he could never cope with a critical system failure without proper equipment. The certainty of the upcoming solo mission made him smile a little, the way the great pioneers of aerospace engineering would smile if they were here on Zenith-7 ready to tackle the challenges of deep space exploration.

For a moment, Chen felt a thrill of apprehension. The deepening isolation of the station was closing in around him. Even the music from the recreation module was very, very faint. Through the viewport, the great curve of Earth was rotating from blue to shadow to the brilliant terminator line. A bright point was visible against the darkness. He knew it was the Moon, humanity's first stepping stone. But let it be Mars, he thought. And instead of the familiar satellite, let it be the color of rust and promise.

He paused mid-corridor, letting the recycled air whisper around him. Looking through the viewport at the distant beacon of the red planet, he thought: I've left all that behind me. Earth was never really where I belonged. Space is my home. With the legacy of the pioneers, the engineers and scientists and all the brave, brilliant people who came before.

The music system sang with an ancient voice: "Ground control to Major Tom, your circuit's dead, there's something wrong——"

Chen's eyes narrowed and he moved carefully down the corridor. That would be Mission Control at Pearlbrook, their voices crackling across the void—standing safely in their climate-controlled facility while the solo pilots gathered their courage to venture into the unknown.

"Can you hear me, Major Tom——" the music sang. Chen stepped cautiously into the observation deck and moved to the primary viewport. Earth was rotating slowly. Other stars were visible beyond. There wasn't much time left.

Chen stood now in the bright glare of the briefing module, a strange figure in the orange and white pressure suit. The mission observers had been given the digital briefing packets by the communications officer and now they sat in silence, studying the suited figure of the person who was to pilot the experimental deep-space probe.

They were thinking: Why him? Out of all the scores of qualified candidates—because there are always candidates for a pioneering mission—and all the experienced pilots, why this one?

The Communications Officer was speaking now, reading from the mission parameters as though these observers couldn't be trusted to understand the sparse information given them, information shared reluctantly and without elaboration.

Chen listened, only half aware of what was being said. He watched the faces of the people sitting in the observation gallery, saw their eyes like wounds, red from the early morning hour and the farewell reception of the night before in the Station Lounge. They are wondering how I feel, he was thinking. And asking themselves why I want to go.

On the platform nearby, listening to the Communications Officer, but watching Chen, sat Dr. Sara Li, the mission psychologist. Chen returned her steady gaze thinking: They start out burning with desire to understand human behavior and end with nothing but data points. The metrics become the reality, the assessment the goal. What could Dr. Li know of longing? No, he thought, I'm not being fair. Dr. Li was only doing her job.

The digital chronometer on the back wall of the briefing module said three fifty-five. Zero minus one hour and five minutes.

Chen looked around the room at the pale faces, the concerned expressions. What have I to do with you now, he thought?

Outside, the orbital night lay cold and still beyond the station's hull. Floodlights from the docking bay spilled brilliance over the experimental probe, shadows casting geometric patterns across the gleaming white composite materials.

As they filed out of the briefing module, Dr. Li joined Chen in the transport pod. Chance or design? Chen wondered. The others, he noticed, were leaving both of them alone.

"We haven't communicated well, have we, Dr. Hicks?" Dr. Li observed in a quiet voice.

Chen thought: She's pale skinned and very focused. What is it that she reminds me of? Shouldn't there be understanding in her expression? He smiled vaguely into the humming transport. That's what it was. Odd that he should have forgotten. How many aerospace engineers, he wondered, grew up reading about the early space pioneers? And how many remembered now that those pioneers all faced the same psychological evaluations, the same questions about isolation and purpose?

"We've done as well as could be expected," he said.

Dr. Li reached for her tablet and then stopped, remembering that Chen needed to maintain focus before the mission. Chen caught the movement and half-smiled.

"I didn't try to disqualify you from the assignment, Chen," the psychologist said.

"It doesn't matter now."

"No, I suppose not."

"You just didn't think I was the right person for the mission."

"Your technical record is exemplary all the way. You know that," Dr. Li said. "It's just some of the indicators——"

Chen said: "I revealed too much during evaluation."

"You had to."

"You wouldn't think my inner life was so concerning, would you," Dr. Hicks said, smiling.

"You had siblings, Chen. What happened with your family?"

"More therapy?"

"I'd like to know. This is for me."

Chen shrugged. "We grew apart. They were fine people—but they finally told me it was no use. 'You don't live in the same world' was the way my brother Ahmed put it."

"He knew you were pursuing aerospace engineering; what did he expect——?"

"That isn't what he meant. You know that."

"Yes," the psychologist said slowly. "I know that."

They rode in silence, through the station corridors, between the research modules and the living quarters. Beyond the viewports, Earth like a jewel against the infinite night. Chen, enclosed in his pressure suit, a figure not quite of Earth, watched the planet wheel in its eternal dance.

"I wish you success, Chen," Dr. Li said. "I mean that."

"Thanks." Vaguely, as though from across a deep and widening gulf.

"What will you do out there?"

"You know the mission parameters as well as I," Chen said impatiently. "Establish the remote research station on the asteroid and wait for the supply mission. If it comes."

"In eighteen months."

"In eighteen months," the suited figure said. Didn't she know that the timeline didn't matter?

He glanced at his chronometer. Zero minus fifty-six minutes.

"Chen," Dr. Li said slowly. "There's something you should understand. Something you really should be prepared for."

"Yes?" Disinterest in his voice now, Dr. Li noted clinically. Natural under the circumstances? Or withdrawal building up already?

"Our assessments showed you to have strong solitary tendencies—well-compensated, of course. You know there's no such thing as a perfectly balanced human being. We all have inclinations toward various behavioral patterns. In your case the indicators suggest an exceptionally active internal life and in some cases a preference for conceptual frameworks over—well, immediate social reality."

Chen turned to regard the psychologist coolly. "What's reality, Dr. Li? Do you know?"

The analyst flushed. "No."

"I didn't think so."

"You spent a great deal of time alone when you were a child," Dr. Li went on steadily. "You were intellectually precocious, socially isolated."

Chen was watching Earth again.

Dr. Li felt inadequate and uncertain. "We know so little about the social psychology of extended solo missions, Chen——"

Silence. The hum of the transport pod's magnetic propulsion, the whisper of the life support systems, and the soft glow of status indicators deep in the control panels.

"You're eager to be leaving, aren't you—" Dr. Li said finally. "Excited to be the first person to attempt a long-duration solo asteroid mission——"

Chen nodded absently, wishing she would be quiet. Mars, a dull rusty point of light visible through the viewport, seemed to beckon.

They reached the final airlock and entered the departure bay. The experimental probe towered, sleek and impossibly advanced in silver and orange composite materials, against the black backdrop of space visible through the massive bay doors.

Chen saw his siblings before they saw him. In their formal station uniforms, they looked strange and out of place standing by the observation window of the departure bay.

They were his brother and sister, Ahmed and Angela. Older than he at twenty-eight and thirty. But they walked through the station as visitors, tourists in his world. Behind him he could hear the final countdown beginning, the voice of Mission Control marking time.

"Chen——"

They were calling him. In the echoing bay their voices carried across the space. "Chen——"

He knew he should go to them, but he did not. Behind him he could hear the probe's systems coming online. He trembled with anticipation.

He stood very still, listening to his siblings talking, letting their voices carry across to where he prepared for the mission of a lifetime.

"Where is he, anyway?"

"He always seems distant just when we try to connect with him——"

"Always with those calculations—" Mimicry. "'My mission parameters——'"

"Obsessed—just obsessed. Oh, where IS he, anyway? Chen, you need to say goodbye!"

Something died in him. They weren't just calculations, they WERE his life's work. He looked at his siblings with dismay. They weren't really his family anymore. They were strangers, with their Earth-bound concerns and their conventional lives. He and the great pioneers of aerospace engineering had dreamed together many times, building their visions from innovation management principles and material science breakthroughs in the shifting light of imagination.

"Chen! Mission Control says you need to board! Answer us!"

If only they could understand. If only his family could comprehend why this mattered, why the mission was everything——

"He's over there by the probe—ignoring us!"

"Chen! You come over here right now!"

The departure bay was blurring, fading. His siblings were turning into just more voices, more people who couldn't understand. The diagnostic scanner felt heavy in his gloved hand. He shivered, not with fear now. With purpose.

He walked slowly toward the probe, his magnetic boots clicking rhythmically on the deck plating.

He lay like a seed in the heart of the probe, protected and utterly alone. The life support cocoon contained him, sustained him; and the spacecraft, silent now in the void, coursed through the airless deep like a focused thought. Time was measured by the ticking of the chronometers and the mission timers, but Chen slept insulated and complete.

And he dreamed.

He dreamed of that year when the university library lay quiet and vast under the fluorescent lights. He dreamed of his siblings, well-meaning creatures as he remembered them through the lens of a brilliant but isolated adolescent——

And his mother, tall and worried, standing in the doorway of his room and saying with concern: "Why do you spend so much time alone, Chen? I worry about you so——"

And his siblings: "Always with his blueprints and his mission simulations and never wanting to participate in family activities——"

He dreamed of the small apartment in Clearwater, Selvoria, sweltering in the heat of summer nights and the thick longing in his throat for orbital platforms and a view of Earth from above and trajectories, clear and perfect. A place that he knew somehow he belonged, but which existed, for him, only through dedication and skill development. He dreamed of space.

And Dr. Li: "What is reality, Chen?"

The hours stretched into days, the days into weeks. Time wasn't. Time was a deep void and a star-filled expanse. And dreams.

He awoke seldom. His tasks were routine. The life support cocoon and the tender care of the probe's systems were more real than the scheduled transmissions back to Mission Control across the empty kilometers, across the curve of Earth's orbit.

He dreamed of his family. "You don't live in the same world, Chen."

They were right, of course. He wasn't of Earth. Never had been. My home is in the void, he thought, filled with an immense satisfaction.

And time slipped by, the weeks into months; Earth dwindled and the asteroid belt approached. All around him lay the stunning star-dusted darkness.

He lay curled in the life support cocoon when the probe began its final approach. He awoke gradually and pulled himself into full awareness.

"I've changed," he thought aloud. "My perspective is different; I feel transformed."

The whisper of attitude thrusters brought a thrill. Ahead of him, a great tumbling mass of iron and stone and precious minerals. He could see impact craters and the slow, majestic rotation of the asteroid.

There was skill in his hands. He stabilized the probe, calculated the approach. Began the delicate task of landing on a body with almost no gravity. It took all of his training, all of his expertise in aerospace engineering. Carefully, the spacecraft settled onto the ancient surface; slowly, the engines powered down.

Chen stood in the control cabin, his heart pounding. Slowly, the external cameras activated. Through the high-resolution displays he could see the endless expanse of the asteroid's surface. Gray and brown, ancient. The remnant of the solar system's formation. The sky was a deep, absolute black with stars shining with impossible clarity. It looked unreal, a vista of otherworldly quiet and desolation.

What is reality, Chen?

Dr. Li was right, he thought vaguely. A tear streaked his cheek. He had never felt so complete.

And then he saw something in the data streams. He scrambled through the probe, past the storage modules and the research equipment. His hands were working carefully at the airlock controls. The pressure equalized—there was no atmosphere here—and he stepped out onto the surface.

He knelt on the ancient rock and touched the asteroid with his gloved hands. He could see clearly now, his vision sharp in the absolute clarity of vacuum and his heart steady with purpose.

A future spreading before him. Research stations and mining operations and humanity expanding, long-planned dreams and the legacy of all who had studied comparative history and information theory, the accumulated knowledge of generations——

He stood on the asteroid and dug his gloved hands into the fine regolith. He could see perfectly now, for clarity was filling his vision and his steady heart and lungs were adapting to the rhythm of the mission.

Chen!

A message from Mission Control, thin and distant across the void. Confirming successful landing. Acknowledging his achievement.

Chen!

The voice was professional and warm across the communication channel. Chen knew that voice. He knew it from long ago in the university library, from the training simulations at Pearlbrook where the mission parameters lay detailed and precise——

He began setting up the research station on the empty, ancient surface. He knew the procedures, he knew the mission, and he knew the work that he must complete, carefully now, methodically.

This was home.
question: What did Chen have to give up before the mission?
