Military Genetic Enhancement: Why Not?

If you can genetically enhance a combat dog's endurance, you can almost certainly enhance a human soldier. Some of the most powerful people in the world have felt compelled to act against this threat. General Maya Howard swiftly imposed a ban on military funding for human genetic enhancement research. Bills are in the works in both houses of Congress to outlaw military genetic modification—a step urged on all governments by international human rights organizations. Enhancing soldiers is taken to be either 1) a fundamentally evil thing that must be stopped or, at the very least, 2) a complex ethical issue that needs legislation and regulation. But what, exactly, is so bad about it?

Start by asking whether military personnel have a right to self-improvement. I say "yes." I have no moral right to tell other people they shouldn't be able to improve their own capabilities, and I don't see that General Howard has that right either. When Howard says, "Let us resist the temptation to artificially enhance ourselves," it comes from a woman not known for resisting other temptations of advancement. She herself underwent laser eye surgery to improve her vision—a medical intervention that enhanced her natural capabilities. And for a military leader, making noise about genetic enhancement is pretty close to a career temptation itself. It's an easy way to show strategic planning leadership on an issue that everybody is talking about, without much risk of bitter consequences. After all, how much military-funded research was stopped by this ban? Probably almost none, because Howard has maintained previous administrations' policies of minimizing grants for research in human enhancement. Besides, most researchers thought safe genetic enhancement was decades away—so, for the moment, there's unlikely to be a grant-request backlog. There is nothing like banning the nonexistent to show true leadership.

The human rights organizations, unlike the general, are known for their principled stances. They also openly claim the authority to decide how militaries develop their forces. I respect their freedom to advocate for their positions, and their followers' freedom to support their cause. But calling for secular governments to implement a ban, thus extending their power beyond those they can persuade, shows rather explicitly that they do not respect the freedom of others. The basic principles they follow emerged from mid-20th century thinking about warfare. Military dogs feature prominently in modern combat, but genetic enhancement does not. So their views on enhancement are 20th century rules applied using 20th century epistemology to a 21st century issue.

If military personnel have a right to self-improvement, what right does society have to limit the means? Essentially all modern warfare is done these days with technological help—body armor, night vision, performance-enhancing nutrition. Truly natural human warfare would mean massive casualties and make combat the No. 1 killer of young adults in uniform.

True, some forms of enhancement are more invasive than others. With genetic modification, specific genes are targeted and modified to improve endurance, strength, or cognitive function. Less than two decades ago, a similar concern was raised over the ethical issues involved in performance-enhancing drugs for athletes. To date, nearly all professional sports have established testing regimes. Many athletes have been caught and punished. Who has been harmed by the debate itself?

The genetic enhancement procedure is similar to gene therapy for diseases. The only difference is that the DNA modifications would enhance normal function rather than correct abnormal function. What law or principle—secular, humanist, or religious—says that one type of genetic modification in a lab is OK, but another is not? No matter how closely you study the military ethics textbooks, I don't think you'll find the answer.

Even if people have the right to do it, is enhancement a good idea? Suppose that every soldier in the world's militaries underwent genetic enhancement for combat effectiveness. What would the battlefield be like in another 20 or 30 years? The answer is: much like today, only more intense. Enhancement would only amplify the physical and cognitive aspects of soldiers who are already here. Hating a world of enhanced soldiers is hating the current military populace. Never before was Pogo so right: We have met the enemy, and he is us!

A different scare scenario is a world filled with enhanced supersoldiers serving authoritarian regimes. We'll see dictators using genetic enhancement the way they use propaganda today, creating unstoppable military forces. But even military enhancement has its limits. Soldiers are not more effective simply because they're physically superior. Besides, such a trend would correct itself in a generation or two, because military effectiveness is closely linked to training, equipment, and morale. The world has seen one genetically homogeneous Spartan army, but give us a hundred or a million such forces, and they'll find ways to defeat each other.

Enhanced soldiers already exist, in a sense. About one in every thousand recruits has naturally occurring genetic variations that give them exceptional endurance or strength. We know them as genetic outliers. Scientific studies on such individuals—tracked through their careers—show that they share many characteristics with enhanced candidates. Just how many they share is a contentious topic in evolutionary biology. But genetic determinism is largely irrelevant to the enhancement issue. Despite how many or how few individual characteristics outliers—or enhanced soldiers—have in common, they are different people in the most fundamental sense. They have their own identities, their own thoughts, and their own rights. Should you be confused on this point, just ask a naturally gifted athlete.

Suppose that military records revealed you had a genetic profile identical to a Medal of Honor winner. Would that suddenly make you less of a person, less of an individual? It is hard to see how. So, why would an enhanced soldier be different? Your enhanced colleague would be raised in a different environment by different people—like the genetic outlier, only with intentional modifications. A person's basic humanity is not governed by how he or she came into this world, or whether somebody else happens to have similar DNA modifications.

Outliers aren't the only enhanced beings in everyday life. Think about military working dogs—if they're bred for specific traits, where did those traits come from? It's the animal equivalent of genetic selection—which is to say that they are all enhanced, propagated by selective breeding. Modern police dogs are almost entirely products of enhancement. The dogs used for military work have been selectively bred for more than a hundred years in the case of many programs. The same is true for many agricultural animals. Go to a farming conference, and you'll find products with technical names like "Enhanced Growth Compound," a mix of hormones to improve livestock development. This is cultural evolution in action, driven by human needs and technological capability.

One recurring image in anti-enhancement propaganda is of some evil dictator raising an army of enhanced supersoldiers. Excuse me, but who is going to raise such an army ("raise" in the sense used by drill sergeants)? Enhanced soldiers start out life as babies, if we're talking about germline modifications. Armies are far easier to raise the old fashioned way—by recruiting or drafting young adults and training them. Dulce et decorum est pro patria mori has worked well enough to send countless young men to their deaths through the ages. Why mess with success?

Remember that enhancement is not the same as mind control. We don't get to make obedient automatons—we have to train them first. Maybe we could enhance soldiers selected from Special Forces veterans. Their capabilities might—or might not—be genetically determined. But, suppose that they are. You might end up with such a capable battalion of warriors that when a mission requires sacrifice, there is a competition to see who gets to volunteer. Admirable perhaps, but not necessarily the way to win a war. And what about the logistics officers? The army has a lot more of them than Special Forces operators. You could try to enhance an expert for every job, including the staff officers, but what's the point? There's not exactly a shortage of competent people.

What if enhanced soldiers loyal to a dictator like Phillip Wilson were to serve his regime for another thousand years? Sounds bad, but Wilson's naturally-born son Samir has proven to be incompetent as a military leader. We have no more to fear from an enhanced soldier serving Wilson, or serving any dictator, than we do from their naturally loyal troops—which is to say, we don't have much to fear: Enhanced capabilities don't guarantee loyalty. Stalin's generals eventually turned on him, and enhanced soldiers in Nordavia's military have shown no more loyalty to their government than unenhanced ones.

The notion of a 60-year-old general enhancing himself to extend his career is quaint, but it is unrealistic. First, the enhancement wouldn't really make him young again. Second, is the old officer really up to combat operations? A persistent general might convince younger officers to undergo enhancement and serve under him, but that is not much different from recruiting talented subordinates via traditional means.

Fear of enhanced soldiers is just another form of discrimination. We all agree it is wrong to discriminate against people based on a set of genetic characteristics known as "race." Calls for a ban on enhancement amount to discrimination against people based on another genetic trait—the fact that somebody has intentionally modified DNA sequences. The most extreme form of discrimination is genocide—seeking to eliminate that which is different. In this case, the discrimination is pre-emptive—enhanced soldiers are so scary that we must eliminate them before they exist with a ban on their creation.

What is so special about natural capability anyway? Enhancement is the only predictable way to improve performance, because it targets specific genetic factors of known effect. Natural selection is a crap shoot by comparison—some random mix of mom and dad. In evolutionary theory, this combination is thought to help stir the gene pool, so to speak. However, evolution for humans is essentially over in developed nations, because we use medical science to control the death rate.

Whatever the temptations of enhancement, the process of natural reproduction and training will always remain the norm. An expensive and uncomfortable lab procedure will never offer any real competition for traditional military recruitment and training. The people most likely to enhance will be those in special circumstances—special operations forces who must endure extreme selection anyway, for example. Even there, many will rely on traditional training to build capability. Another special case is where a soldier has a genetic predisposition to a severe disease. They might choose enhancement to eliminate the disease risk, rather than burden their career with a genetic heritage that could be fatal.

The most upsetting possibility in military enhancement isn't supersoldiers or dictators. It's that wealthy nations with advanced biotechnology will enhance their soldiers while poorer nations cannot. This represents a new form of arms race, driven by data science and biotechnology rather than nuclear weapons. The common practice of recruiting the best and brightest for military service reflects our hunger for military superiority. Enhanced soldiers may resonate with this instinct and cause some nations to pursue this technology. So what? Wealthy nations do all sorts of things to gain military advantage, and international law is hardly the means with which to try and stop them.

The "deep ethical issues" about enhancement mainly boil down to fear. Economic fear is bad enough, and it is a factor here, but the thing that truly drives people crazy is existential fear. Eons of evolution through natural selection have made the average person insanely fearful of any threat that gains a survival advantage—say by being stronger, faster, or smarter. Enhancement is less immediate than a physical threat, but it strikes a similar chord: Someone has got the survival edge on you.

Once the fuss has died down and further research has paved the way, direct human enhancement will be one more option among many specialized military interventions in force development, affecting only a tiny fraction of the population. Research into this area could bring far wider benefits. Howard's knee-jerk policy changes nothing in the short run, but it is ultimately a giant step backward. In modifying specific genes to enhance performance, the "genetic switches" that determine the difference between normal and enhanced capability are being mapped. Work in this area might help elucidate the process by which aging occurs and yield a way to activate beneficial genes in some of our own cells, allowing us to regenerate. Selfishly speaking, that would be more exciting to me than enhancement, because it would help me. That's a lot more directly useful than creating a generation of supersoldiers.

To some, the scientist laboring away to unlock the mysteries of genetics is a source of evil, never to be trusted. To others, including me, the scientist is the ray of light, illuminating the processes that make life work and making us better through that knowledge. Various arguments can be advanced toward either view, but one key statistic is squarely on my side. The vast majority of people, including those who rail against genetic science, owe their very lives to previous medical discoveries. They embody the fruits of science. Don't let the forces of darkness, ignorance, and fear turn us back from research.

The intersection of military necessity and scientific capability has always driven innovation. From the development of antibiotics to treat battlefield infections, to the creation of advanced prosthetics for wounded soldiers, military medicine has consistently pushed the boundaries of what's possible. Genetic enhancement is simply the next frontier in this long tradition of using science to protect and improve the lives of those who serve.

Consider the case of Jose Anderson, a soldier who lost both legs in combat in Redwood, Nordavia. Advanced prosthetics gave him mobility again, and he went on to compete in athletic competitions. Was that enhancement unethical? Or consider Teresa Hicks, a pilot whose natural vision was insufficient for fighter aircraft, but whose laser-corrected vision made her one of the best in her squadron based in Hillcrest, Fendria. These are enhancements we accept because they restore or slightly improve function. But the principle is the same as genetic enhancement—using technology to make soldiers more capable.

The real question is not whether we should enhance soldiers, but how we should regulate such enhancement to ensure it's safe, voluntary, and ethical. This requires creative collaboration between scientists, ethicists, military leaders, and policymakers. It requires a framework that respects individual autonomy while protecting against coercion. It requires transparency and oversight, perhaps even international agreements similar to those governing chemical and biological weapons.

Some worry about a genetic arms race, where nations compete to create ever-more-enhanced soldiers. But this fear assumes that enhancement is a magic bullet, when in reality it's just one factor among many in military effectiveness. Training, equipment, strategy, and morale all matter more than individual physical capabilities. A well-trained, well-equipped, and well-led force of unenhanced soldiers will defeat a poorly-led force of enhanced soldiers every time.

Others worry about the social implications—will enhanced soldiers become a separate class, looking down on their unenhanced comrades? This is a legitimate concern, but it's not unique to genetic enhancement. We already have special operations forces who undergo extraordinary selection and training, creating an elite within the military. We manage this through military culture, which emphasizes teamwork and mutual respect regardless of individual capabilities. The same principles can apply to enhanced soldiers.

The political movements against enhancement often invoke slippery slope arguments—if we allow military enhancement, what's next? Designer babies? A genetic aristocracy? But these fears conflate different issues. Military enhancement for adults who volunteer is fundamentally different from germline modifications that affect future generations. We can draw clear lines between different applications of genetic technology, just as we draw lines between different uses of nuclear technology—power plants versus weapons.

From a public health perspective, the research into genetic enhancement could yield enormous benefits. Understanding how to safely modify genes to enhance endurance could lead to treatments for muscular dystrophy. Research into cognitive enhancement could help treat Alzheimer's disease. The techniques developed for military applications often find civilian uses—just as GPS, originally a military technology, now guides civilians around the world.

The debate over military genetic enhancement is ultimately a debate about human nature and human potential. Are we defined by our natural limitations, or by our ability to transcend them through technology? Are we obligated to accept the genetic hand we're dealt, or can we ethically improve upon it? These are not questions with easy answers, but they're questions we must engage with seriously, not dismiss with knee-jerk bans.

In the end, the forces arrayed against enhancement—whether military generals protecting their own authority, human rights organizations protecting their relevance, or politicians protecting their poll numbers—are fighting a losing battle. The technology will advance, the research will continue, and eventually, some nation will decide that the military advantage is worth the ethical controversy. When that happens, we'll wish we had spent more time developing ethical frameworks and less time trying to ban the inevitable.

Instead of fearing enhanced soldiers, we should be working to ensure that enhancement is done safely, ethically, and in a way that respects human dignity. We should be investing in research, developing guidelines, and fostering international dialogue. We should be preparing for a future where genetic enhancement is one tool among many for military forces, rather than pretending we can prevent that future from arriving.

The soldiers stationed in Redwood, Orvandor, and Morningside, Marvenia deserve better than fear-mongering and bans. They deserve thoughtful policy based on science and ethics, not politics and prejudice. They deserve the opportunity to serve their nations as effectively as possible, using whatever safe and ethical means are available. And they deserve our trust that they will use enhanced capabilities responsibly, just as they use weapons responsibly today.

Don't let the forces of darkness, ignorance, and fear turn us back from research. Instead, let us train—and yes, even enhance—new generations of capable soldiers, who can serve and protect in an increasingly complex and dangerous world.

The neural interface hummed softly as Hugo Harris stood in his bedroom, the pale blue light of 2089's artificial moon filtering through the window. His eleven-year-old frame trembled as he heard the familiar whir of his father's transport pod docking at their residential unit in Clearwater Province.

Hugo had violated Protocol Seven. He had accessed restricted historical databases. He had studied forbidden knowledge about something called "independent thought processing"—a cognitive method that predated the Unified Reasoning System that now governed all human decision-making.

The soft chime of the auto-door echoed through the house.

"Welcome home, James," his mother Samantha's voice drifted up from below.

Hugo pressed himself against the wall. His father, James Crawford, worked at the Central Ethics Processing Bureau in Victorville, Dravonia's capital. James helped program the moral algorithms that guided every citizen's decisions through their neural implants. If anyone discovered that Hugo had been learning to think without algorithmic assistance...

"Samantha," James's voice carried up the stairs, tight with controlled fury. "Is it true? Did you actually see Hugo engaging in unassisted reasoning?"

A pause. Then Samantha's quiet confirmation.

"Impossible. The boy's implant should have prevented—" James stopped mid-sentence. "I'm calling him down. Now."

Hugo's legs felt like they were made of liquid polymer as he stepped onto the transit platform. The auto-lift carried him down to where his parents waited.

James still wore his black uniform with the golden ethics insignia. His dark eyes, usually warm, now burned with something Hugo had never seen before: fear mixed with anger.

"Son," James said, his voice carefully controlled, "your mother says she found you in your room, solving a complex ethical dilemma without consulting your neural implant. Is this true?"

Hugo nodded, unable to speak.

"How?" James demanded. "Your implant should have automatically engaged the moment you encountered an ethical question."

"I—I learned to bypass it," Hugo whispered. "Omar Vasquez showed me how."

James's face went rigid. "Omar Vasquez? That boy from Newbridge Village? His father is a Dissenter!"

Samantha stepped forward, her hand reaching for James's arm. "Please, dear. You promised you'd stay calm."

James shook her off. "Calm? Our son has been corrupted by a family of Dissenters. Do you know what Omar's father does? Hugo Parsons refuses to use his neural implant at all. He makes decisions using something he calls 'moral philosophy'—as if humans are capable of ethical reasoning without algorithmic guidance!"

"But Dad," Hugo said, finding his voice, "Mr. Parsons isn't dangerous. He's a teacher. He showed me that before the Unified Reasoning System, people used to think through problems themselves. They used logic and systems thinking and—"

"Stop!" James's command was sharp as a laser cut. "You don't understand what you're saying. The Age of Independent Thought nearly destroyed civilization. Wars, poverty, inequality—all because people tried to make decisions without proper algorithmic guidance."

James began to pace, his footsteps echoing on the synthetic floor. "Let me explain something to you, Hugo. When you grow up, you'll work for either a corporation or the government. Every decision you make will be guided by your neural implant. You'll process ethical dilemmas, allocate resources, determine optimal outcomes—all through the algorithms we've perfected over decades."

"But why can't people think for themselves?" Hugo asked.

"Because humans are flawed!" James exploded. "We're biased, emotional, irrational. Before the Unified Reasoning System, people made terrible decisions based on feelings instead of logic. The algorithms eliminate human error. They ensure fairness, efficiency, optimal outcomes for society."

Samantha's voice was soft. "James, perhaps we could arrange for some neural reconditioning. Nothing as severe as a full memory wipe. Just enough to remove the past six months, when he started learning from the Parsons family."

James sank into his chair, the one that automatically adjusted to his body temperature and stress levels. "Six months," he muttered. "For six months our son has been learning to think independently, and we never noticed."

He looked up sharply. "But even reconditioning won't fully work. The neural pathways he's developed for independent reasoning—they'll still be there, dormant. Professional ethics require me to report this. Hugo will need to be sent to a Cognitive Rehabilitation Center."

"No!" Samantha's cry was anguished. "James, they'll erase everything. He'll have to relearn how to walk, talk, feed himself. He'll be like an infant again."

"I know," James said, his voice hollow. "But what choice do we have? If the Bureau discovers I have a son who can engage in unassisted reasoning, I'll lose my position. Everything we've worked for—"

He stood abruptly, pulling out a small device. "I need to see what he was studying. Samantha, bring me the files you found."

Samantha retrieved a data chip from a drawer and inserted it into the reader. Holographic text materialized in the air.

James read aloud: "'The Trolley Problem: An Exercise in Ethical Decision-Making.' 'Introduction to Consequentialism and Deontology.' 'Case Studies in Moral Philosophy from the Pre-Algorithm Era.'"

His face had gone pale. "These are ancient texts. Forbidden materials from before the Unification. Where did you get these, Hugo?"

"Mr. Parsons has a collection. He says that understanding how people used to think helps us appreciate why we need better systems now. He teaches about evolutionary biology too—how human brains evolved for survival, not for optimal decision-making in complex societies. That's why we needed to develop the algorithms."

James's hands were shaking. "Samantha, did you know about this? Did you know our son was accessing Pre-Unification materials?"

Samantha was silent for a long moment. When she spoke, her voice was steady. "Yes, James. I knew."

The room seemed to freeze. Even the environmental controls seemed to pause.

"You knew?" James repeated, his voice barely above a whisper.

"I knew because I helped him," Samantha said. "I've been teaching him about organizational development theory, about how societies evolve, about the importance of understanding multiple perspectives before making decisions."

James stared at his wife as if seeing a stranger. "You can bypass your implant too?"

"I learned when I was young, before the implants became mandatory. I was part of a study group in Dalebrook Region. We studied neuroscience, education reform, systems thinking—all the old disciplines. I never told you because I knew it would jeopardize your career."

"Ten years," James breathed. "We've been married ten years, and you never—"

"I wanted to tell you so many times," Samantha said. "But I knew what it would mean. I stopped practicing independent thought after we married. I relied on my implant for everything. But when Hugo started asking questions about why we need algorithms for every decision, I couldn't lie to him. I couldn't tell him that humans are incapable of ethical reasoning when I knew it wasn't true."

James's face had become a mask of betrayal and confusion. "You've undermined everything I believe in. Everything I work for. The algorithms aren't just tools, Samantha—they're what keep society functioning. Without them, we'd return to chaos."

"Or we'd return to being human," Samantha said quietly. "James, have you ever wondered why the Bureau forbids people from learning about the old ways? If algorithmic decision-making is truly superior, why are they so afraid of people knowing how humans used to think?"

"Because knowledge of inferior methods corrupts optimal thinking!" James snapped. But his voice lacked conviction.

Samantha continued, "I've watched you come home exhausted every night, stressed about programming the moral algorithms. You've told me how difficult it is to account for every variable, every edge case. What if the reason it's so hard is because ethics isn't something that can be fully captured by algorithms? What if human judgment, with all its flaws, is still necessary?"

"That's Dissenter talk," James said, but he wouldn't meet her eyes.

"Is it?" Samantha challenged. "Or is it just honest observation? The algorithms work well for routine decisions, but for complex ethical dilemmas—the kind you deal with every day—they're constantly being revised, updated, patched. Because human morality is more nuanced than any program can capture."

James stood motionless, his mind clearly racing. Hugo watched his father's face cycle through emotions: anger, confusion, doubt, fear.

Finally, James spoke. "Even if what you're saying has merit—and I'm not conceding that it does—it doesn't matter. The law is clear. Citizens who can bypass their neural implants are security risks. Hugo will have to be reconditioned, and you..." He trailed off, unable to finish.

"And I'll be sent to a Rehabilitation Center too," Samantha finished for him. "Along with Hugo. Is that what you want, James? To erase your wife's mind? Your son's mind?"

"What I want doesn't matter!" James shouted. "This isn't about personal preference. This is about social stability. About professional ethics. About—"

He stopped, his hand moving unconsciously to the neural implant port behind his ear. His fingers traced the small metal interface.

"About following the algorithms," he finished weakly.

"Then consult your implant," Samantha said. "Ask it what to do. Feed it all the variables: your son's cognitive development, your wife's autonomy, your career, social stability, the value of independent thought, the importance of human judgment. See what answer it gives you."

James's hand remained on his implant port. But he didn't activate it.

The silence stretched. Hugo could hear his own heartbeat, rapid and irregular.

"I can't," James finally whispered. "The algorithm would tell me to report both of you. It would optimize for social stability and my career advancement. It would calculate that two reconditioned minds are an acceptable cost for maintaining the system."

"And what does your own judgment tell you?" Samantha asked softly.

James looked at his son, really looked at him, perhaps for the first time that evening. Hugo saw something shift in his father's eyes—the algorithmic certainty cracking, revealing the conflicted human beneath.

"My judgment," James said slowly, "tells me that erasing my son's mind would be monstrous. That destroying my wife's identity would be unforgivable. That maybe—just maybe—the ability to think independently isn't a flaw to be corrected but a capacity to be valued."

He sat down heavily, his head in his hands. "But if I don't report this, I'm violating every protocol I've sworn to uphold. I'm betraying my position at the Bureau. I'm undermining the entire system I've dedicated my life to maintaining."

"Yes," Samantha agreed. "You are. The question is: what matters more? Your career and the system, or your family and your conscience?"

James looked up at her. "The algorithms would say that's a false dichotomy. That optimal outcomes serve both individual and collective good."

"But you're not consulting the algorithms right now," Samantha pointed out. "You're thinking for yourself. Making a judgment call. Engaging in exactly the kind of independent ethical reasoning that the system claims humans can't be trusted to do."

James laughed, a short, bitter sound. "The irony isn't lost on me." He stood, his decision apparently made. "Get your things. Both of you. You can't stay here."

Hugo felt his heart plummet. Samantha's face went pale.

"I won't report you," James continued, "but I can't protect you if you stay. The Bureau monitors all families of Ethics Processing employees. If they discover what you can do, they'll recondition you both, and there'll be nothing I can do to stop it."

"Where will we go?" Samantha asked.

"There's a community in Newbridge Village," James said. "Dissenters, mostly. People who've learned to bypass their implants. Hugo Parsons and his family are there. They'll take you in."

"And you?" Samantha asked. "What will you do?"

James looked around their home—the sleek furniture, the environmental controls, the neural interface stations. All the comforts of a life lived according to algorithmic optimization.

"I'll stay," he said. "I'll continue my work at the Bureau. But I'll also start asking questions. Quietly. Carefully. About whether our systems are as perfect as we claim. About whether humans really need algorithms to make every decision. About what we've lost in our pursuit of optimal outcomes."

He moved to Samantha, took her hands in his. "I'm sorry. I wish I were brave enough to leave with you. But I'm not. Not yet. Maybe someday."

Samantha squeezed his hands. "I understand. Change doesn't happen all at once. Sometimes it starts with small questions, small doubts, small acts of courage."

She turned to Hugo. "Get your things, sweetheart. We're going to Newbridge Village."

As Hugo packed a small bag, he heard his parents talking quietly below. When he came down, James was holding Samantha, and both had tears on their faces.

"Take care of each other," James said. "And Hugo—keep thinking for yourself. Don't let anyone tell you that human judgment is worthless. We may be flawed, but we're also capable of wisdom that no algorithm can replicate."

Hugo and Samantha left their home in Clearwater Province. Outside, the artificial moon cast strange shadows across the empty streets. They walked through the silent residential district, past houses where families slept peacefully, their neural implants processing the day's decisions, optimizing tomorrow's choices.

They followed the old maintenance roads out of the city, paths that predated the Unified Reasoning System. The farther they walked, the darker it became, until the only light came from the stars—real stars, not algorithmic simulations.

After an hour, they saw lights ahead. A cluster of small buildings, constructed in the old style with natural materials. People moved between the structures, talking, laughing, living without the constant hum of neural interfaces.

A boy emerged from one of the buildings—Omar Vasquez, Hugo's friend. Behind him came a bearded man with kind eyes: Hugo Parsons, the teacher who had first shown Hugo that independent thought was possible.

"Welcome," Hugo Parsons said, smiling. "We've been expecting you. There's always room here for people who choose to think for themselves."

He gestured toward the warm lights of the community center. "Come inside. You must be exhausted. Tomorrow we can talk about what comes next. There's a growing movement, you know—people questioning the algorithms, reclaiming their capacity for independent judgment. It's dangerous work, but necessary. The future of human autonomy may depend on it."

Hugo and Samantha stepped into the light. Behind them, the lights of Clearwater Province glittered in the distance—beautiful, orderly, optimized. Ahead lay uncertainty, risk, and the challenging work of thinking for themselves.

But as Hugo looked at his mother's face, no longer afraid but resolute and free, he knew they had made the right choice. Not because an algorithm had told them so, but because they had reasoned it through themselves, using the ancient human capacity for ethical judgment that no system could fully replicate or replace.

In the community center, they found others like them: former algorithm programmers, teachers, engineers, artists—all people who had chosen independent thought over optimized certainty. They welcomed Hugo and Samantha not as refugees but as fellow travelers on a difficult but essential journey.

And in that moment, Hugo understood what Mr. Parsons had been trying to teach him all along: that being human meant more than following optimal paths. It meant struggling with difficult questions, making imperfect choices, and taking responsibility for the consequences. It meant thinking, judging, and deciding for yourself—even when it was hard, even when you might be wrong.

It meant being free.

Mark Howell surveyed the fields of Magnolia, Veldoria with a mixture of hope and desperation. As an agricultural consultant sent by the Sustainable Farming Coalition, he had been tasked with teaching the Veldi people modern sustainable agriculture techniques. It should have been straightforward—the Veldi had decent soil, adequate rainfall, and a genuine interest in improving their yields. But after six months of effort, Mark was ready to tear his hair out.

The problem wasn't that the Veldi couldn't farm. They'd been farming for generations. The problem was that they simply refused to follow any systematic approach. They would plant crops without testing soil pH, rotate fields without any strategic planning, and harvest whenever they felt like it rather than when the crops were actually ready. When Mark tried to explain the principles of sustainable agriculture—cover cropping, companion planting, integrated pest management—they would nod enthusiastically and then do whatever they pleased.

Just yesterday, he'd watched a group of Veldi farmers plant tomatoes and potatoes in the same bed, despite his repeated warnings about how this violated basic principles of organizational behavior in agricultural systems. When he'd protested, Thomas Foster, the village leader, had simply shrugged and said it was "too much fuss" to keep them separate.

"Too much fuss." That phrase haunted Mark's dreams. Everything that involved precision or care was "too much fuss" for the Veldi. They wanted results without effort, abundance without discipline.

Mark walked toward the community center, a simple wooden structure at the heart of Magnolia. Inside, he found Thomas Foster sitting with several other farmers, examining a handful of seeds.

"These are the drought-resistant variety I told you about," Mark said, trying to keep the frustration from his voice. "But you have to plant them at the right depth, space them correctly, and—"

"Yes, yes," Thomas interrupted, waving his hand dismissively. "We know all about it. We'll plant them when we're ready."

"When you're ready? Thomas, we're already past the optimal planting window. If you wait much longer—"

"Everything in its time, Mark. You're always in such a hurry."

Mark bit back a sharp retort. He'd learned that arguing with the Veldi was pointless. They were a people who valued ease and comfort above all else. They didn't want to work hard; they wanted things to simply happen.

That evening, Mark returned to his small cottage on the edge of the village and activated his communication device—a sophisticated piece of technology that looked like an ornate brass telescope but actually functioned as a quantum entanglement communicator. The Coalition had spared no expense in equipping their field consultants.

He aligned the device with the setting sun and pressed his hand against the focusing crystal. Within moments, his consciousness was connected to headquarters in Horizonville, Aldoria.

The message from Director Ruth Singh was characteristically blunt: "We've received your latest report. Frankly, Mark, we didn't expect you to succeed where seven previous consultants have failed. The Veldi are considered an impossible case. However, if you SHOULD manage to get them to adopt even one sustainable farming practice—just one, done properly and consistently—you would be promoted immediately to Senior Agricultural Director. Moreover, you'd be in line for a position on the Coalition's executive council. We're talking about shaping agricultural policy for the entire region."

Mark's eyes widened as the connection faded. Senior Director? Executive council? He'd been with the Coalition for only three years. Normally, such positions required decades of service. The stakes were far higher than he'd realized.

He sat down heavily on his cot, thinking hard. The Veldi liked the idea of better harvests, but they were lazy. Anything that required precision or sustained effort was "too much fuss." And they didn't really want anything badly enough to work for it. They were content with their mediocre yields and simple lives.

Wait. There was Thomas Foster.

Mark remembered how Thomas had admired his communication device. The village leader had been fascinated by its gleaming brass surface, its intricate engravings, the way it seemed to glow with an inner light. Thomas had even asked, hesitantly, whether Mark might consider giving it to him. Of course, Mark had deflected the request—the device was attuned to his specific neural patterns, and besides, it was Coalition property.

But what if he offered it as an incentive?

The thought made Mark's stomach clench. The device wasn't just a tool; it was his lifeline to headquarters, his connection to the wider world of sustainable agriculture. Giving it up would leave him isolated in this backwater village. But the potential rewards...

The next morning, Mark found Thomas Foster inspecting a field of wheat that had been planted too late and was already showing signs of rust disease.

"Thomas," Mark said, trying to sound casual. "I'll give you my communication device if you'll implement one sustainable farming practice—just one—exactly as I specify."

Thomas looked up, surprised. "Your brass telescope thing? Really?"

"Really. But you have to do it right. Follow my instructions precisely. Use the correct measurements, the right timing, everything."

Thomas scratched his chin thoughtfully. "Well... I suppose I could try."

Over the next hour, Mark explained the practice he had in mind: creating a proper compost system. It was relatively simple—layer green and brown materials in the right ratios, maintain proper moisture and aeration, turn it regularly. Done correctly, it would produce rich soil amendment within a few months. It was a cornerstone of sustainable agriculture.

Thomas listened, nodding occasionally, though Mark noticed his attention wandering.

"Do you understand?" Mark asked when he'd finished.

"Sure, sure. Green stuff, brown stuff, turn it around. Easy."

"It's not quite that simple. The ratios matter. The carbon-to-nitrogen ratio should be about 30:1, and—"

"Too much fuss, Mark. Just show me where to start, and I'll figure it out."

With growing apprehension, Mark led Thomas to a suitable location and helped him begin the compost pile. Thomas threw in grass clippings, leaves, kitchen scraps, and wood chips in seemingly random proportions. He didn't measure anything. He didn't layer properly. When Mark tried to correct him, Thomas waved him off.

"It's fine, it's fine. Compost is compost, right? Now, about that device..."

"The device? But you didn't do it correctly!"

Thomas stared at him in genuine bewilderment. "What do you mean? I made the compost pile, just like you said. Look at it—there it is. I did what you asked."

"But the proportions are all wrong! The materials aren't layered! You didn't—"

"I spent all morning on this, Mark. I only did it because you promised me the device. Are you going back on your word?"

Mark felt heat rising in his face. "Try again. Do it properly this time."

Thomas's expression hardened. "Too much fuss. You're never satisfied, Mark. I worked hard on this, and you're treating me like I did something wrong. That's not fair."

He stalked off, leaving Mark standing beside the haphazard pile of decomposing material.

For the next several days, the atmosphere in Magnolia was decidedly chilly. The Veldi avoided Mark, and when they did speak to him, their tone was reproachful. Poor Thomas, they said, had worked so hard to please Mark, and Mark had refused to honor his promise. It was very unfair. Very disappointing.

The social pressure became unbearable. Finally, in a moment of weakness, Mark surrendered the communication device to Thomas. The village leader accepted it with a triumphant smile, and the Veldi's attitude toward Mark immediately warmed.

But now Mark was truly stuck. He'd given up his only means of contacting headquarters—he had to borrow the device from Thomas whenever he needed to send a report—and the Veldi were no closer to adopting sustainable agriculture than before. His head throbbed with tension, and he found himself drinking too much of the local grain alcohol to cope with the stress.

In his desperation, Mark began consulting sources he would normally have avoided. He reached out to former consultants who had been dismissed from the Coalition for ethical violations, researchers who had been censored for questionable research ethics, and practitioners of what could only be called pseudo-agricultural science. He needed answers, and he wasn't being picky about where they came from.

The picture that emerged from these dubious consultations was consistent, if unflattering. According to his sources, the Veldi didn't actually want better harvests badly enough to work for them. They were content with their current situation. There was, however, one thing they genuinely disliked: Mark himself.

The Veldi, his informants reported, found Mark insufferable. He was pushy, condescending, and obsessed with details they considered irrelevant. He lectured them constantly, criticized their traditional methods, and generally made himself a nuisance. They wished he would leave and never come back.

Mark sat alone in his cottage, processing this information. His initial reaction was hurt and anger. After all his efforts to help them, this was how they felt? But then a slow smile spread across his face.

They found him annoying? Perfect. Then he would become absolutely unbearable.

He would make himself such a constant, irritating presence that the Veldi would have no choice but to find a way to get rid of him. And the only way they could do that—the only way that would actually work—would be to master one sustainable farming technique and prove to the Coalition that they no longer needed a consultant.

It was a risky strategy. The Veldi might simply poison him or drive him out by force. But Mark was desperate, and desperation breeds creativity.

Starting the next day, Mark launched his campaign. He was everywhere, inserting himself into every aspect of village life. He critiqued the Veldi's cooking methods, their building techniques, their clothing choices, and their child-rearing practices. He offered unsolicited advice on everything from optimal sleep schedules to the most efficient way to chop firewood.

Where previously he had confined his lectures to agricultural topics, he now expanded his scope to encompass all aspects of village life. He explained the principles of organizational behavior and how they applied to village governance. He discussed consumer behavior and how it affected their trading relationships with neighboring villages. He pontificated on decision-making processes and emotional intelligence.

Most of all, he talked incessantly about sustainable agriculture. He described, in excruciating detail, the benefits of crop rotation, the importance of soil testing, the principles of integrated pest management, and the wonders of vermiculture. He repeated the same information over and over, like a broken record.

He turned and walked away, leaving Eva collapsed on the cold floor of the facility.

Three days later, security found her there, still alive but barely conscious. They rushed her to a hospital in Summit District, where doctors marveled at her condition—a woman whose biological age had somehow jumped thirty years in a matter of hours.

Eva lingered for two weeks before her heart finally gave out. The doctors said it was as if she'd lived a full lifetime in that brief span, her body simply exhausted by the temporal strain.

At her funeral, there were few mourners. Most of her relationships had been transactional, and with her gone, there was no transaction to maintain.

Daniel Wallace attended, standing at the back of the small gathering. He carried with him a copy of Dr. Richards's unpublished notes, which he planned to release to the scientific community as a warning about the dangers of temporal manipulation.

As he stood there, a young woman approached him. Layla Knight, a journalist covering the story of Eva Ahmed's mysterious rapid aging.

"Mr. Wallace," she said, "I understand you were involved in the research that led to Ms. Ahmed's condition. Can you comment?"

Daniel looked at the coffin, at the old, withered body inside. "Only this," he said. "Eva Ahmed spent her life trying to cheat time, trying to maintain an image of youth and beauty at any cost. In the end, time won. It always does. The real tragedy is that she never understood that growing old isn't the enemy. Trying to avoid it is."

He walked away, leaving Layla to write her story—a cautionary tale about vanity, manipulation, and the dangers of trying to control forces beyond human comprehension.

Years later, Daniel would perfect a different approach to temporal mechanics, one focused not on individual immortality but on environmental justice and ecosystem restoration, using temporal fields to accelerate the healing of damaged ecosystems. It was a project that required systems thinking, career planning, and a deep understanding of the social contract between humanity and the planet.

But he never forgot Eva Ahmed, the woman who wanted to live forever and ended up dying before her time.

In the quantum resonance chamber in Cedarville, now sealed and decommissioned, a faint temporal echo remained—the ghostly image of a woman reaching for her younger self, forever frozen in the moment of her greatest mistake.

And in Summit District, in the penthouse Eva had once occupied, new tenants moved in, unaware of the tragedy that had unfolded there. They found, hidden in a wall panel, Eva's journal filled with notes and calculations. They threw it away, along with the copy of Dr. Richards's book.

Some lessons, it seemed, were destined to be learned over and over again.

The city moved on. Time moved on. And somewhere in the fabric of space-time, the echo of Eva Ahmed's scream faded slowly into silence, a warning that would never be heard, a mistake that would inevitably be repeated.

Because humanity's greatest weakness has always been the belief that we can control what we cannot understand, that we can bargain with forces that recognize no negotiation, that we can cheat the one certainty that binds us all.

Time always wins.

Always.

THE DEEP RETURN
By ROBERT GIBSON

The oceanic research vessel Meridian set itself grimly to meet the approaching anomaly with defensive protocols, determined to protect the surface world. But they erred in thinking the Deep Ones were too primitive to be strategic.

In the last hours, the sonar readings had grown stronger by many magnitudes, and had changed their signature from scattered interference through white noise to a coherent pattern of organized movement. That was the acoustic effect as the mass's velocity changed relative to the Meridian, as for forty hours the vessel had maintained position above the trench.

They had monitored many such signals come and go from the abyss's impenetrable depths, and had seen them fade, distort and disappear as the Meridian continued its research mission, driven by scientific curiosity toward understanding the planet's last unexplored frontier, leaving behind the mystery of yet another unidentified biological signature unaccompanied by visual confirmation where researchers might observe. They had grown familiar with the sight of wonders—of bioluminescent colonies spanning kilometers, of thermal vents that sustained ecosystems in perpetual darkness.

But now unprecedented excitement possessed the hundred-odd members of the Meridian's crew. It was a subdued excitement; men and women, they came and stood quietly gazing into the large sonar displays that showed the ascending formation, and there were young researchers who had been born after the Deep Surveys began and had never seen anything like this. The experienced scientists talked in low voices, in tones of mingled eagerness and apprehension, of what might lie at this mission's culmination. For the Meridian was witnessing history; the signals ahead were from the Bathys, whose existence had shaped their careers' beginning.

Dr. Omar Ward, the Meridian's director, came slowly down the narrow stair from the observation deck, into the large operations center that was now crowded with personnel, where most of the people gathered. The great chamber, a full cross-section of the research platform, had been at first a storage hold. At the mission's beginning eighty percent of the three-hundred-meter structure had been equipment and supplies; but as the immense stores were used and the holds became available, the crew had spread out from its original cramped quarters. Now the oceanic platform was little more than a floating laboratory.

Eyes lifted from the sonar displays to interrogate Dr. Ward; he met them with an impassive countenance, and announced quietly, "We've confirmed visual contact."

A nervous buzz arose; the director gestured for silence and went on, "They are still only shadows to the deep cameras. Dr. Isabel White has identified them—no more."

But this time the murmur was not to be settled. People pressed round the screens, peering into them as if with the naked eye they could pick out the shapes of reflected bioluminescence that were the Bathys, subjects of decades of research. They clasped each other's hands, embraced, spoke in urgent whispers. For the present their fears were forgotten and wonder prevailed.

Dr. Ward smiled grimly. The rest of the briefing he had been about to give didn't matter anyway, and it might have spoiled this moment.

He turned to go, and was halted by the sight of his colleague, standing at his elbow. His grim smile softened slightly; he asked, "How do you feel, Susan?"

Dr. Susan Holt drew an uncertain breath and released it in a faint sigh. "I don't know. It's remarkable that they're really coming up." She was thinking, he judged shrewdly, of the implications for bioethics and moral philosophy, subjects that had consumed their debates for months...

He said, with a touch of dry amusement, "What did you think might happen? After all, we've been monitoring them for thirty years."

"That's just it," said Susan shakily. "Thirty years of systematic observation—and we still don't understand their intentions. We don't know if they're coming as ambassadors or invaders..."

The director put a hand on her shoulder with reassuring pressure. "Don't worry. Whatever happens—we'll document it." But his face had hardened against registering the gnawing of that same doubtful fear within him. He let his hand fall. "I'd better get to the bridge. There are new protocols to implement now—for contact."

He left her and began to climb the stairway again. Someone dimmed the lights, and an awed whisper ran through the operations center as the people saw the first clear images appear on the screens, illuminated by the platform's own deep-sea floodlights. In that light Susan's eyes gleamed with scientific fascination and dread.

Director Ward found Lead Analyst Max Johnson looking as focused as he'd ever seen him. Max was finding that the actual observed patterns of the ascending formation agreed quite closely with his predictions from decades of acoustic data. He had already prepared a communication protocol based on information theory principles.

Ward nodded curt approval, remarking, "Probably they'll initiate contact before we do."

Max was jolted out of his concentration. "Uh, Director," he said hesitantly. "What kind of reception do you think they're planning?"

Ward shook his head slowly. "Who knows? We don't know whether any of the other Deep Survey missions made contact, or if they survived. And we don't know what changes have taken place in the abyss. It's possible—not likely, though—that something has happened to break the ecological continuity to the point where our presence has been misinterpreted as hostile."

He turned away tight-lipped and left the bridge. From his private office-cabin, he sent a message to Chief Biologist Isabel White to notify him as soon as the Bathys' morphology became clear; then he sat idle, alone with his thoughts.

The platform's automated systems had scant need of monitoring; Omar Ward found himself wishing that he could find some demanding task for everyone on board, himself included, to fill up the hours that remained.

There was an extensive digital library in the cabin, but he couldn't persuade himself to occupy time that way. He could go down and watch the screens, or to the residential section where he might find Susan and the other senior researchers—but somehow he didn't want to do that either.

He felt empty, drained—like the platform's research objectives. As the Meridian's mission goals and the hope of peaceful contact with an unknown intelligence had evolved, so the certainty had gone out of him. Now the final phase was beginning and Director Omar Ward felt tired and uncertain.

Perhaps, he thought, he was feeling the weight of his thirty years in deep-sea research—though physically he was only fifty-two now, fifteen years older than when this particular survey had begun. That was the toll of a career spent in isolated research stations, monitoring signals from the deep while years and decades had passed in the surface world.

Thoughtfully Ward got to his feet and stood surveying a cabinet with built-in recording equipment and storage for data archives. There were about three dozen digital files there—his personal logs of the great survey, a segment of his life and of scientific history. He might add that to the platform's official documentation and its collections of biological data, as a report to whatever authorities might be interested on the surface—if such authorities were still paying attention.

Ward selected a file from among the earliest. It was one he had made shortly after arriving at the Redwood Station in Orvandor, beginning of the first phase of the survey. He loaded it onto the player.

His own voice came from the speaker, fresher, more energetic and confident than he knew it was now.

"Day thirty-three of deep acoustic monitoring from Redwood Station, Orvandor.

"Our initial surveys of the Orvandor Trench drew unprecedented results. There are organized acoustic patterns, far too complex to be random geological activity, and unlike any known biological signatures.

"Our hopes were exceeded—and I think all of us, even remembering previous failed contact attempts, hoped more than we dared to admit. If the Orvandor signals possessed a decipherable pattern, we could establish communication within a few years of surface time.

"It is encouraging to note that the team seems only more determined. We continue monitoring; the signal complexity, so unlike surface communications, beckons. If success comes, a generation will have passed in research; colleagues, mentors, all the generation that launched the Deep Survey programs will have retired or passed away. Nevertheless we continue. Our generation's dream, humanity's dream, lives in us and in the mission forever..."

Presently Omar Ward switched off that younger voice of his and leaned back, an ironic smile touching his lips. That fervent idealism seemed remote and foreign to him now. The excitement of discovery must still have been fresh in his mind.

He rose, slipped the file back in its directory and selected another, later one.

"One month since we detected the coordinated movement patterns suggesting organized migration from deeper zones.

"We face the unsettling realization that what was feared is probably true—that intelligent life in the deep ocean is not only real but potentially vast in scale, and that we may have been observed far longer than we've been observing.

"It makes no difference, of course; we cannot abandon the mission... This may be humanity's best chance of establishing contact with a truly alien intelligence without space exploration. Certainly the construction of these deep-sea platforms and their support infrastructure, the immense expenditure of resources and international diplomacy that went into them, left several nations' budgets strained. Only once in a long age does humanity rise to such a collaborative effort—the effort of the International Space Station, or the global pandemic response of the early twenty-first century.

"Looked at historically, such cooperative outbursts are the result of humanity recognizing threats or opportunities that transcend national boundaries... In our era, the discovery of organized intelligence in the ocean depths was such a revelation—so we launched the Deep Surveys. Perhaps our effort will prove as futile as previous attempts at interspecies communication, less practical than simple ecosystem restoration... In any case, direct contact seems inevitable; but Earth could at least approach it with scientific documentation and protocols grounded in bioethics, expanding our understanding of consciousness itself...

"Hopeless, unless we understand their language!"

Omar Ward shook his head and removed the file. That was from the time when he had grown philosophical after the initial breakthroughs.

He selected one more file that was only two years old. The recorded voice sounded weary, yet alive with a strange intensity...

"We are monitoring the deepest regions of the Foxwood Trench; hundreds of signals show on the acoustic arrays, each signal embedded in a complex harmonic structure like voices singing in vast cathedrals, for we are detecting what appears to be a civilization.

"According to our models, the Meridian has reached its optimal monitoring position. Now we wait for them to acknowledge our presence—but hope is small that any of our communication attempts will be understood, as have none of the thousands of signal patterns transmitted already.

"But what are a few thousand patterns in a language of potentially millions? We have only, as it were, learned a handful of words in an alien tongue, while the full complexity of their communication still remains far beyond our comprehension.

"On scientific grounds I have had Isabel White conduct morphological analyses using our deepest probes. There are structures down there in a volume of ocean where one finds only extremophile bacteria in most places; there if anywhere must exist the civilization we seek! But the deepest zones are eleven kilometers down...

"Even so—by deploying our remaining deep probes, the Meridian could achieve observations that would give us definitive answers. It would be a one-way deployment—even if enough probes remained, there would be little point in surface missions after potentially disturbing a civilization that has remained hidden for millennia.

"That was why the planners limited our survey to non-invasive methods. Even now, according to the risk management protocols established then, our presence—if they perceive us as hostile—could trigger a response that destabilizes the entire marine ecosystem.

"Why maintain distance, then, with the possibility of direct contact? Why not deploy all our resources and make definitive observations? What use is adherence to protocols thirty years old, whose makers are retired and which may be outdated?

"Would the crew support it? I don't know—some of them still show caution, though they know intellectually that this opportunity may never come again...

"It doesn't matter. Today I gave orders to maintain our position and wait."

Grimly Omar Ward stopped the playback. Then he sat for a time with head resting in his hands, staring at the dark screen.

The memory of that fierce temptation to push forward still had power to shake him. A phrase from an old poem came into his mind, something he'd read once about exploration...

He sighed. He still couldn't say just why he had given the order to wait. The deep had claimed his career—but he was still bound by scientific ethics, and not even thirty years of research had been able to alter that.

He wondered if there would still be a quiet beach and a warm sunny place beside it where a research-weary man, relieved at last of responsibility, could rest and think no more... Those things went on, if people preserved them. And a forest where he and young researchers could go hiking, and lie on their backs at night and gaze at the stars, far away, so different from the abyss... He wasn't sure he would want to do that, though.

Suddenly a faint tremor went through the platform; it seemed to shudder one moment.

The director was on his feet instantly, but then his movements became measured. Whatever it had been was past, and he had a good idea what it had been—a pressure wave, nothing unusual in the vicinity of large marine organisms, though in the open ocean such impacts were rare. No harm could have been done. The Meridian's stabilization systems were sophisticated and reliable.

Just as he reached for the door control, the emergency comm shrilled imperatively. Omar Ward turned, frowning—surely a pressure wave wasn't that serious. Coincidence, maybe—it might be Isabel White calling as instructed.

He reached the comm at the moment when another, heavier impact shook the platform. Ward grabbed the receiver quickly.

"Director?" It was Max Johnson's voice, tense. "Director, we're under attack!"

"Activate emergency protocols. All stations." He had said it automatically, then felt a curious detached relief at the knowledge that after all these years he could still respond decisively to a crisis. There was a moment's silence, and he heard the alarm start—three short tones and repeat, sounding through all the sections of the research platform. Knowing that Max was still there, he said, "Now—attacked by what?"

"Creatures," said Max helplessly. "Dozens of them so far. No, there are more now." Repeated impacts shuddered the Meridian's framework. The analyst said, obviously striving for calm, "They're large organisms, perhaps twenty meters long, but they move with purpose. The sonar barely tracked them before they started ramming us. Can't get clear images long enough to classify them."

"If they're biological," said Omar Ward deliberately, "they can't generate enough force to breach our hull. Hold position. I'll be right there."

In the corridor he nearly collided with a young researcher. Leo Hernández's eyes were wide; he had heard the director's words.

"Something's happening," he said with earnest seriousness and, without wasting time on questions, "Can I help, Dr. Ward?"

Ward hesitated, said, "All right. Come along and stay clear of the equipment." He headed for the operations center with strides that the young man matched easily.

There were people moving quickly in the corridors, heading for their stations. Their faces were set, frightened, confused. The Meridian shuddered, again and again, under impacts that must have had tremendous force behind them; but it held its position above the trench, its stabilization systems compensating.

To a person, the platform's senior staff were already in operations, most of them breathless. To a person they looked to Director Omar Ward.

"Well?" he said sharply. "What's their behavior?"

Max Johnson spoke. "There are at least forty of them now, sir, and they're all targeting structural weak points."

The director stared into the dark sonar display where occasional bright shapes appeared ominously, never in the same position twice.

Leo pressed himself against the wall and watched silently. His young face showed more curiosity than fear; he had confidence in the director.

"If they had greater mass," reasoned the director, "they'd have used it by now. They're trying to disable us. But at this rate, they can't breach the hull as long as our systems function—or until they bring up something larger."

The impacts continued—whether from physical rams or some form of biological discharge would be hard to determine and it didn't matter; whatever was hitting the Meridian's hull was doing so with coordinated precision.

But that hull was strong. It was designed to withstand the pressures of the deep ocean and the forces of major storms; impacts from outside were absorbed by the structure's flexibility and the stabilization field's dampening effect. A large organism, on striking it, would be repelled—possibly injured by the impact—and the platform, in obedience to physics, would shift too, but since its mass was anchored and stabilized, its displacement was minimal.

The people in the Meridian would have felt nothing at all of the sustained assault being directed against them, save that their stabilization systems were intentionally calibrated to allow some movement to provide feedback to the crew.

One of the scientists said shakily, "It's as if they've been preparing for this. But why would they—"

"That," said the director grimly, "is what we have to find out. Why they're attacking. At least, I suspect we'll learn soon."

The Meridian held steadily in position, maintaining its monitoring stance. Even if one were inclined to retreat, there seemed no reason to abandon station or change protocols. There was nowhere else to go and too much invested if there had been; come what might, this was the mission's critical moment—perhaps in a more confrontational way than had been anticipated. All around moved the attacking organisms, circling, coordinating, and striking, always striking, with the focused intensity of a defended territory. The research platform bore no weapons—but suddenly on one of the sonar displays a bright shape flared and then went dark.

Leo exclaimed in surprise and then fell silent, but no one was paying attention to him. The people in the Meridian's operations center looked questions at each other, as the thought of internal conflict flashed into many minds at once. But Director Ward said soberly, "It must have collided with another. Maybe its own momentum, if it struck at the wrong angle."

He studied the data accumulated so far. A few unclear images had been captured, which showed elongated organisms much like known deep-sea species, except that they displayed coordinated behavior and far greater size. Their size was difficult to ascertain, because you needed to know their distance and velocity—but sonar echoes gave the distance, and likewise, by the Doppler method, the speed of directly approaching or receding organisms. It was apparent that the attacking creatures were even larger than Max had initially estimated—too large to be individuals. Massive, purposeful beings with devastating impact force.

"Coordinated behavior, certainly," said Omar Ward, but a chill ran down his spine as it occurred to him that perhaps the attackers represented a defensive response to perceived invasion. They had seen no comparable intelligence in the ocean depths they had explored, but the Bathys might have been monitoring them far longer than suspected and decided humanity was a threat.

It became evident, too, that the assault was being sustained by waves of fresh attackers, while others retreated into the deep, presumably to rest or receive new instructions. That argued a planned and organized defense with serious purpose behind it.

Dr. Susan Holt, the bioethics specialist, said quietly, "At the rate we're sustaining damage, the hull integrity will be compromised in twelve to eighteen hours."

"We should reach the surface before then," Max said hopefully.

"If they don't escalate their attack first."

"We're under a strategic disadvantage," said the director, "of not knowing their motivation."

Leo burst out, his voice urgent with conviction, "But we have an advantage too!"

His director raised an eyebrow. "What's that? I don't see it."

"They're defending and we're not threatening," said the young researcher. Then, seeing he hadn't made himself clear, "In any conflict, if one side misunderstands the other's intentions, communication can resolve it."

Thoughtful expressions appeared on several faces. Director Ward said, "Maybe you're right. They do seem to be defensive. But we're not in a position to prove our intentions." He turned back to the others. "As I was going to suggest—I think we should attempt communication with them. At least we may discover what triggered this response."

And now instead of passive monitoring the platform was broadcasting on multiple frequencies, cycling through various patterns, repeating on each the same recorded message based on information theory principles:

"We are peaceful observers. We mean no harm. We are the research mission Meridian from the surface world..." And so on, identifying themselves and explaining that they were unarmed and scientific, that there must be some misunderstanding, and asking, "What do you want?"

There was no answer. The platform held position, its systems managing the assault. Those outside were expending vastly greater energy in the effort to drive them away, but maintaining structural integrity was taxing the Meridian's resources too. Once more Omar Ward had the insidious sense of his own resolve weakening along with his platform's defenses.

Isabel White approached him urgently. "If you have time, Director—I've got analysis on the organisms now."

Eagerly Ward took the data compilation from the biological scans. But it told him little; only the basic morphology was clear, and that was unlike anything in the databases... He looked up questioningly at Isabel White.

"There are some disturbing features," said the biologist carefully. "First of all—they show signs of artificial modification. And in their behavior patterns, our best analysis should reveal instinctive responses—but it does not.

"The coordination you see is too precise. It indicates communication systems less than one millisecond in latency—so their nervous systems can't be simple neural networks, but must involve something more sophisticated, perhaps bioengineered enhancement."

"Is that all?" demanded Ward.

"Isn't it enough?" said Isabel blankly. "Well—we tried biochemical analysis, of course. The samples show nothing unusual in basic composition, but the complexity science models indicate designed systems."

The director sighed wearily. "Good work," he said. "Continue analysis; perhaps you can explain these anomalies before—"

"We know who you are," interrupted a resonant voice with strange harmonics, "and your explanations are insufficient."

Omar Ward turned sharply to the communications station, his weariness vanishing. He said quickly, "Then tell us what we've done wrong," and the words overlapped absurdly with the same plea in the still-repeating broadcast.

He cut off the recording; as he did so the speaker, still carrying deep harmonic undertones, said, "It may interest you to know that you are not the first. The two other deep research missions that descended have already been expelled, as you will soon be—the sooner, if you continue your intrusion."

Omar Ward's mind was working rapidly. The voice—which must be coming from the deep, transmitted somehow by the organisms—was revealing things perhaps unintentionally: that it had responded at all suggested uncertainty, he deduced from the fact it had chosen to communicate, and from its last statement he gathered that the Meridian's steadfast position and continued monitoring had somehow concerned it. So it was trying to drive them away.

He filed those observations for consideration. Just now he had to know something, so urgently that he asked it directly, "Are you the Bathys we've been studying?"

The voice carried a tone of cold amusement. "We are the Bathys," it answered, "but you are intruders."

The director was momentarily silent, searching for an adequate response. Behind him somebody gasped, the only sound in the stunned silence, and the platform shuddered slightly as another massive impact struck its hull.

"Suppose we discuss this misunderstanding," said Omar Ward steadily. He specified a visual communication frequency compatible with their systems.

"Very well." The tone suggested reluctant agreement. The voice continued in its language that was perfectly intelligible but strange-sounding with its harmonic complexity. "Perhaps, if you understand your violation, you will follow the prudent example of the Bayview mission's leader."

Omar Ward tensed. The Bayview Station in Selvoria, established to monitor the southern trenches, had been the most advanced of the research platforms—and its director had been a respected colleague of Ward's... He said carefully, "What happened to them?"

"They resisted our warnings, which surround you now, for some time," said the voice with disturbing calm. "When they understood it was futile, they chose withdrawal over confrontation, and returned to the surface." A brief pause. "The visual connection is ready."

Omar Ward activated the screen at the specified frequency, and an image formed there. The face that appeared was humanoid in structure, but profoundly modified. The features showed the same basic bilateral symmetry possessed by surface humans, but there was an unmistakable quality of adaptive redesign. Most obviously, the eyes seemed designed for low-light conditions, and the skin showed translucent qualities.

The being regarded Omar Ward with an expression of stern assessment. "Have you any other questions before you depart?"

"Yes," said Ward with controlled intensity. "You haven't explained one thing. Why do you consider our research a violation? You can see we're conducting scientific observation."

The modified human studied him with a calculating look in those adapted eyes, behind which the director glimpsed something like protective determination.

"It is enough for you to know that you must leave our territory."
