No network analyst need investigate this outage. The circumstances obviously are such that no suspicious pattern could exist. Of course, the brain will make an unfailing analysis of all the factors involved and clear the case automatically and officially."

Xavier threaded the single card into the slot for an example to me. He then activated the interface and we stood there watching the monster ruminate thoughtfully. It finally chimed and spit the card back at Global-Meridian's top junior vice-president.

He took it like a man.

"That's what the machine is for," he said philosophically. "To detect human error. Hmm. What kind of reading do you get out of this?"

He handed me the rejected analysis card. I took it, finding a new, neatly typed notation on it. It said:

Investigate the Oakridge village of Lakeside Village.

"You want me to project it in a movie theater and see how it stands all alone in the dark?" I asked.

"Just circle up the wagon train and see how the Indians fall," Xavier said anxiously.

"It's too general. What does the silicon-brained machine mean by investigating a whole village? I don't know if it has corrupted routers, illegal signal jammers, or a hideout for corporate espionage. I don't care much either. It's not my business. How could a whole village be causing systematic network failures?"

"Find that out," he said. "I trust the machine. There have been cases of coordinated interference before. Until you get back, we are making no more installations in that settlement."

Research. To a writer that generally means legally permissible plagiarism. For a network analyst, it means earnest work.

Before I headed for the hills, or the Oakridge Region, I walked a few hundred feet down the hall and into the manual record files. The brain abstracted from empirical data but before I flew out to Lakeside Village I had to find the basis for a few practical, nasty suspicions.

Four hours of flipping switches and looking at holographic projections while a dark-haired technician in a standard uniform carried me data modules to order gave me only two ideas. Neither was very original. The one that concerned business was that the whole village of Lakeside Village must be communication-cursed.

I rejected that one almost immediately. While a communication blackout in one location was itself a statistical anomaly, the idea of a whole village of them gathered together stretched the fabric of reality to the point where even information theory couldn't help it.

There was an explanation for the recent rise in the network failure rate down there. The crystal mine there had gone into high-level operation. I knew why from the equipment, terminals, data centers, and server farms across the region. They were all using crystalline processors. The boom in quantum-grade crystals for information processing eclipsed earlier periods of silicon, graphene, and optical systems completely. The distinctive grade of crystal from Lakeside Village was being put into use all over the planet and in the orbital stations on the Moon and Mars.

Yet the rise in network failures, compared to the rise in production, was out of all proportion.

Furthermore, the work at the mine could hardly explain the excessive communication disruption reports we had had from the village as far back as our records went.

We had documented most of the failures since they seemed irrefutably genuine. All were complete with diagnostic reports and authenticated circumstances.

There was one odd note in the pattern: We had never had a report of any kind of wireless communication failure from Lakeside Village—only wired connections failed.

I shut off the projector.

It may be best to keep an open mind, but I have found in practice that you have to have some kind of working theory which you must proceed to prove is either right or wrong.

Tentatively, I decided that for generations the citizens of Lakeside Village had been in an organized conspiracy to sabotage Global-Meridian and its predecessors of hundreds upon hundreds of thousands of dollars in false network claims and replacement equipment.

Maybe they made their whole livelihood off us before the mine opened up.

I used my pocket comm and had my assistant get me a flight reservation and authorization for field investigation.

After so many profitable decades, Lakeside Village wasn't going to take kindly to my spoil-sport interference.

The hypersonic flight to Pearlbrook was smooth and relatively fast. Despite atmospheric turbulence we managed Mach 2.1 most of the way. My particular flight attendant was a redhead, majoring in Organizational Development in her night courses. I didn't have much time to get acquainted or more than hear the outline of her thesis on the corporate governance structures affected by venture capital funding. The businessman in the next pod was already monopolizing his attendant's attention. He was the type who took the service for granted and aimed to get his money's worth. I gave Anna, the redhead, a smile and began flipping through the data files in my briefcase as we decelerated for a landing at Greater Oakridge.

It took me a full five minutes to find out that I couldn't take a shuttle to Lakeside Village. Something about magnetic interference in the mountains.

Since that put me back in the days of ground transport, I arranged for a rental vehicle at the terminal. I selected an all-terrain model that could handle the mountain roads. The drive would be tedious but necessary.

It was a tiresome forty-mile drive, on manual all the way after I left the automated highway system of the city. Up and down, adjusting for curves, shifting modes for the hills.

The whole trip hardly seemed worth it when I saw the cluster of prefabricated buildings that was Lakeside Village. They looked like a tumble of modular housing units tossed in front of a massive crystalline outcropping. That was Crystal Peak in the near foreground. But I remembered that over the course of some forty years the people in these few little structures had cost Global-Meridian three quarters of a billion credits.

I turned off onto the gravel road, the sound system alerting me to the change in surface. Then I stepped down hard on my brakes, bracing myself against the safety harness. I had almost struck an old woman sitting at the side of the road, wrapped in weather-worn clothing.

"Are you okay?" I yelled, opening the window.

"I've suffered no harm at your hands—or your vehicle, miss. But I could use some help," the old woman said. "Could I trouble you for a ride when you leave town?"

I wasn't too sure about that. Most of these people who are wandering around talking like they owned advanced degrees besides their basic education belonged to some cult or other. I try to be as tolerant as I can, and some of my best friends are eccentric, but I don't want to drive with them down lonely mountain roads.

"We'll see what we can work out," I said. "Right now can you tell me where I can find Director Bruno Salazar?"

"I can," she said. "But you will have to walk there."

"Okay. It shouldn't be much of a walk in Lakeside Village."

"It's the building at the end of the path."

"It is," I said. "Why shouldn't I drive up there? The road's open."

The old woman stared at me with tired eyes. "Director Salazar doesn't like people to run vehicles with electronic systems on the paths of Lakeside Village."

"So I'll just lock the vehicle up and walk over there. I couldn't go getting tire tracks all over your clean paths."

The old woman watched as I climbed down and secured the vehicle.

"You would probably damage your systems if you did drive here, you know," she said conversationally.

"Well," I said, "I'll be getting along." I tried to walk sideways so I could keep an eye on her.

"Come back," she said, as if she had doubts.

The signs of a menacing conspiracy were growing stronger, I felt. I had my authorization codes inside my jacket, but I decided I might need a less formal means of expression. Without breaking stride, I picked up a small sample of the bluish crystal from the roadside and slipped it into my equipment pocket.

I have made smarter moves in my time.

As I approached the building at the end of the path, I saw it was about the most haphazard construction job I had seen in my life. It looked as architecturally secure as a child's drawing of a home. The angles were measurably out of line. Around every joint were misaligned seams and poorly sealed connections. The surface coating was spotty and streaked. Half the windows had visible cracks. I fought down the concern in my mind, afraid of the structural integrity of the place.

My foot caught on the top step and I nearly crashed face first into the front door. I had been too busy looking at the building, I decided. I knocked.

Moments later, the door opened.

The lean-faced man who greeted me had his hair uncombed and his shirt buttoned incorrectly. But his eyes were bright and alert.

"Are you Mr. Bruno Salazar, the liaison for Global-Meridian Communications?" I put to him.

"I'm the director, name of Salazar. But you ain't the first to formalize my title. You from the company?"

"Yes," I said. "Were you expecting me?"

Salazar nodded. "For forty-one years."

Salazar served the coffee in mismatched cups, favoring only slightly his bandaged fingers.

Catching the direction of my glance, he said, "Company is worth a few burns, Ms. Sharma."

I accepted the steaming cup and somehow it very nearly slipped out of my hands. I made a last microsecond recovery.

The director nodded thoughtfully. "You're new here."

"First time," I said, sipping coffee. It was awful. He must have made a mistake with the preparation.

"You think the network failures I've been reporting for my people are false?"

"The home office has some suspicions of that," I admitted.

"I don't blame them, but they ain't. Look, the company gambles on probability, doesn't it?"

"No. It works on patterns calculated from network theory and past experience."

"But I mean it knows that there will be, say, a hundred network failures in a day. But it doesn't know if maybe ninety of them will be in one region and only ten in the rest of the country."

"There's something to that. We call it statistical distribution, not probability alone."

"Well, distribution says that more network failures are going to occur in Lakeside Village than anywhere else in the country, per capita."

I shook my head at Salazar. "That's not distribution. Theoretically, anything can happen but I don't—I can't—believe that in this village everybody has chanced to experience communication failures. Some other factor is operating. You are all deliberately sabotaging these connections—"

"We're not," Salazar snapped.

"Or else something is causing you to have this trouble. Maybe the whole village is using illegal jamming equipment. Maybe you manufacture your own interference devices; it's happened before."

Salazar laughed.

"Whatever is going on, I'm going to find it out. I don't care what you do, but if I can find a greater risk here and prove it, the Commission will let us discontinue service for this region. Probably beyond the capacity of these people to appeal, I'm afraid."

"That would be a real tragedy, Ms. Sharma. Communication is vital to this village. Nobody could survive a year here without reliable networks. People pay me for their service before they pay their utility bills."

I shrugged, sorrier than I could let on. "I won't be able to pay for my own utilities if I don't do the kind of job the company expects. I'm going to investigate."

"All right," he said grudgingly, "but you'll have to do it carefully."

"Yes, I understood you didn't like electronic vehicles on your paths. At least not the vehicles of outsiders."

"That doesn't have anything to do with it. Nobody in Lakeside Village owns an electronic vehicle. It would be system failure for anybody to use one, same as it would be to have wireless routers, instead of shielded cable, or to own quantum processors."

I took a deep breath.

"Optical systems," Salazar said. "With redundant backups and manual overrides."

I acknowledged his information. "You've been a great help."

"Four o'clock," he said. "Weather patterns are dangerous at night."

"There's always a dawn."

Salazar met my eyes. "That's not quite how we look at it here."

The mine was a mess.

I couldn't understand the way they extracted the crystal out of the mountain. The idea of random extraction—a completely unsystematic approach—going after a deposit of valuable crystal kept turning up in my mind as I walked around.

The workers were gone; it was after five local time. But here and there I saw traces of them. Some of them were equipment cases and tool marks, but most of the traces were signs of injury. Bandages left on sharp rocks, medical supplies scattered beneath heavy equipment, protective gear damaged on the handles and working surfaces of extraction tools and machinery. The place was as hazardous as a disaster zone.

"What are you looking for, miss?"

The low, level question had come from a sturdy woman in protective gear and a safety helmet.

"The reason you have so many network failures here," I said frankly. "I'm from the communications company. Name's Sharma."

"Yeah, I know."

I had supposed she would.

"I'm Jasmine Perry, the supervisor here," the woman told me, extending a work-worn hand to be shaken. "Outside, doing my training rotation, I noticed that most places don't have as many communication problems as we do here. Never could figure it out."

"This crystal is part of it—"

"What do you mean by that!" Perry demanded sharply.

"I mean the way you extract it. No system to it. No logical progression, no methodical approach..."

"Listen, Sharma, don't talk about what you don't know anything about. The material in these walls isn't just crystal; it isn't even ordinary quantum-grade material. Lakeside Village exports some of the finest grade of crystalline processors in the world. And it's used all over the world. We aren't just a bunch of unskilled laborers—we are specialists. We have to figure a different way of extracting every piece of crystal."

"It's too bad."

"What's too bad?"

"That you chose the wrong approach so often," I said.

Perry breathed frustration into my face. "Listen, Sharma, we have been working this mine for generations, sometimes more of us working than other times. Today most of us are working extracting the crystal. That's the way we like it. We don't want any outsider coming in and interfering with that."

"If this mine has anything to do with sabotaging Global-Meridian, I can tell you that I will do something about that!"

As soon as my words left my mouth, the sickening feeling hit me that I shouldn't have said that.

The general store was called a supply center, but it wasn't particularly well-supplied.

I took a seat at the small café counter and ordered a beverage, politely declining the young clerk's offer of a local specialty drink for an extra charge.

Behind me were three small tables and one solitary booth. Two people somewhere between forty and sixty sat at the nearest table playing cards.

Over my drink I saw the old woman I had almost struck on the road. She approached the heavy-set person at the payment terminal.

"Hello, Doctor," the heavy person said. "What can we do for you?"

"I'd like to send a message," she said in an urgent voice.

"Sure, Doctor, I'll transmit it right away on the communication terminal as soon as I get a free moment."

"You're sure you can send it? Right away?"

"Positive. Five credits, Doctor."

The doctor fumbled in her pocket and produced a credit chip. She examined it thoughtfully.

"I suppose the message can wait," she said resignedly. "I believe I will purchase some food supplies instead."

"Why not get a meal, Doctor? Special today. Only five credits. And since you're such a regular customer I'll include a beverage and dessert for nothing."

"That's—kind of you," the old woman said awkwardly.

The proprietor shrugged. "A person has to eat."

The woman called "the doctor" came over and sat down two seats away, ignoring me. The clerk prepared her meal and served it.

I stayed with my beverage and my thoughts.

More and more, I was coming to believe that Lakeside Village wasn't a job for a network analyst like myself but a sociological analyst. System sabotage is a structural flaw in a community, yes. But when the whole society is involved, distorted, you can't isolate the flaw. The whole village was material for a social scientist; let them figure out why otherwise decent citizens felt secure in conspiracy to defraud an honored corporation.

I didn't feel that I was defeated or that the trip had been a failure. I had merely established to my intuitive satisfaction that the job was not in my field.

I glanced at the old woman. The proprietor of the store knew her and evidently thought her harmless enough to feed.

"I think I can make it down the mountain before the weather changes," I called over to her. "You can come along if you like."

The young clerk behind the counter stared at me. I looked over and caught the calculating eyes of Carmen Nichols, the proprietor, too. Finally, the old doctor turned on her seat, her face pale and her eyes sad and resigned.

"I doubt very much if either of us will be leaving, Ms. Sharma," she said. "Now."

I took my beverage and the doctor her meal over to the single booth. We looked at each other across the table.

"I am Doctor Ava Obrien of the Institute for Advanced Studies," the doctor said. "I left on my research sabbatical six months ago. I have been here ever since."

I looked at her clothes. "You must not have been very well funded for a year's research, Doctor."

"I," she said, "have enough research credits with me to fund a small laboratory. Nobody in this village will process them for me."

"I can understand why you want to go somewhere where people are more cooperative in that case."

"They know the credits are valid. It's me they refuse to trust to leave this place. They think they can't let me go."

"I don't see any restraints on you," I remarked.

"Just because you can't see them," she growled, "doesn't mean they aren't there. Director Salazar has the only long-range communication terminal in the village. He has politely refused to let me use it. I'm a suspicious and undesirable character; he's under no obligation to give me communication privileges, he says. Nichols has the message service concession—the transmission terminal behind the payment station over there. She takes my messages but I never see her send them off. And I never get a reply."

"Unfriendly of them," I said conservatively. "But how can they stop you from packing your research materials and leaving?"

"Nichols has the only functional vehicle in town—a small transport, barely larger than a cargo hauler. She makes about one trip a week down into Pearlbrook for supplies and deliveries. She's been the only one in or out of Lakeside Village for six months."

It seemed incredible—more than that, unlikely, to me. "How about the crystal itself? How do they ship it out?"

"It's a controlled supply product, managed carefully," Doctor Obrien said. "They stockpile it and once a year the executive offices for the company back in Pearlbrook Town runs in a transport system up the side of the mountain to collect it. That won't be for another five months, as nearly as I can find out. I may not survive that long."

"How are you living?" I asked. "If they won't process your credits—"

"I do research assistance for people. They feed me, give me a little money sometimes."

"I can see why you want to leave with me," I said. "Haven't you ever thought of just walking out?"

"Forty miles down a steep mountain road? I'm an old woman, Ms. Sharma, and I've gotten even older since I came to Lakeside Village."

I nodded. "You have any credentials, any identification, to back this up?"

Wordlessly, she handed over her identification, research permits, enough documentation to have satisfied any security protocol.

"Okay," I said. "I'll accept your story for the moment. Now answer me the big question: Why are the good people of Lakeside Village doing this to you? By any chance, you wouldn't happen to know of a mass conspiracy they are perpetrating on Global-Meridian?"

"I know nothing of their business practices," Obrien said, "but I do know that they are absolutely neurologically impaired!"

"I admit I have met more capable groups of human beings in my time."

"No, understand me. These people are literally neurologically impaired—they are inferior to other human beings in specific ways."

"Look, I know discrimination is a problem but I can't go along with you on that."

"Sharma, understand me, I insist. Neurologically speaking, it is well known that certain populations suffer certain deficiencies due to environment, exposure, genetic factors. Some can't process certain stimuli, maintain certain cognitive functions, perform certain tasks. The people of Lakeside Village have the most unusual deficiency on record, I admit. Their neural synchronization has been impaired. They are completely devoid of any intuitive communication ability, any unconscious information processing."

"Because they aren't telepaths, that doesn't mean that they are impaired," I protested. "I don't have any telepathic abilities either."

"But you do!" Obrien said earnestly. "Everybody has some neural synchronization ability, but we don't realize it. We don't have the fabulous abilities of a few recorded cases of natural telepaths, but we have some, a trace. Lakeside Village citizens have no neural synchronization ability whatsoever, not even the little that you and I and the rest of the world have!"

"You said you were from the Institute, didn't you?" I mused. "Maybe you know what you are talking about; I've never been sure. But these people can't suffer very much from their lack of what you call neural synchronization."

"I tell you they do," she said hoarsely. "We never realize it but we all have some power of unconscious prediction. If we didn't, we would have a hundred accidents a day—just as these people do. They can't anticipate the obstacle in the path the way we can, or that that particular tool will malfunction slightly. There are other things, as well. You'll find it is almost impossible to maintain extended communication with any of them—they have no telepathic ability, no matter how slight, to bridge the semantic gap. None of them can coordinate complex tasks. They don't have the unconscious neural ability to synchronize their actions. All of us can do that, even if the case of a true 'telepath' who can directly read thoughts is rare."

"Doctor, you mean these people are holding you here simply so you won't go out and tell the rest of the world that they are impaired?"

"They don't want the world to know why they are neurologically impaired," she said crisply. "It's the crystal! I don't understand why myself. I'm not a physicist or a genetic engineer. But for some reason the heavy concentration and particular pattern of the quantum resonance in its structure is responsible for both inhibiting the genes that transmit neural synchronization from generation to generation and affecting those abilities in the present generation. A kind of cognitive sterility."

"How do you know this?"

"We haven't the time for all that. But think about it. What else could it be? It's that crystal that they are shipping all over the world, spreading the contamination. I want to stop that contamination. To the people of Lakeside Village that means ruining their only industry, putting them all out of work. They are used to this neural impairment; they don't see anything so bad about it. Besides, like everybody else, they have some doubts that there really are such things as telepathy and neural synchronization to be affected."

"Frankly," I said, hedging only a little, "I don't know what to make of your story. This is something to be decided by somebody with authority—like the Director of Public Health or the President or Board Chairman of Global-Meridian. But the first thing to do is get you out of here. We had better get back to my vehicle. I've got good navigation systems to get down the mountain."

Obrien stood up eagerly, and knocked over her water glass, spilling liquid across the tabletop.

"Sorry," she said. "I should have been more careful of that. I try to stay away from the crystal as much as possible, but it's affecting me."

I should have remembered something then. But, naturally, I didn't.

The Nexus Café occupied prime real estate in Valleyview's central district, where the old quarter met the gleaming towers of new development. From its outdoor terrace, you could watch the city's transformation in real time—ancient brick buildings housing traditional artisans on one side, glass and steel structures filled with blockchain startups on the other.

Valleyview, nestled in Parkview Province, had become something of a crossroads. The city attracted an unusual mix: venture capital investors scouting the next big thing, artists fleeing the high costs of more established centers, political activists organizing grassroots movements, and a steady stream of academics researching everything from computational linguistics to consciousness studies. The local government's hands-off approach to regulation had made it a haven for those who wanted to operate outside conventional frameworks.

I sat at my usual table, reading the morning edition on my tablet. The headlines were the usual mix: new developments in nanotechnology, debates over pollution control measures, updates on space exploration programs. The coffee here was overpriced but excellent, and the people-watching was unparalleled.

"Mind if I join you?" 

I looked up to see Dominic Wagner, a slight man with an easy smile and tired eyes. I'd run into him a few times over the past year at various networking events. Something about venture capital and strategic planning for emerging markets, if I remembered correctly.

"Please," I said, gesturing to the empty chair.

He ordered an espresso and settled in, looking out at the street. A group of young activists marched by, carrying signs about societal change and environmental justice. Their chants echoed off the buildings before fading into the general din of the city.

"Quite a place, Valleyview," Dominic observed. "I've worked in a dozen cities, and I've never seen anything like it."

"It has its charms," I agreed. "Though I imagine it makes your work complicated."

"How so?"

"Well, strategic planning must be difficult when the rules keep changing. Half the businesses here exist in legal gray areas."

He laughed. "That's precisely why I'm here. Traditional markets are too predictable. The real opportunities are in places like this, where new paradigms are emerging."

A woman walked by with a portfolio under her arm—probably heading to one of the visual arts galleries that had sprung up in the converted warehouses. Dominic and I both watched her pass.

"What brings you to Valleyview?" he asked. "You're not local, are you?"

"I'm from Millbrook originally," I said, naming a city in Havencia. "But I've been here about two years now. Research work."

"What kind of research?"

"Personal growth and leadership development," I said smoothly. "I study how people adapt to rapid change, how they develop emotional intelligence in unstable environments. Valleyview is perfect for that—it's essentially a laboratory for human adaptation."

This was true enough, though not the complete truth. My actual research had somewhat different parameters.

Dominic nodded thoughtfully. "That makes sense. I've noticed the same thing. The people who thrive here are the ones who can handle ambiguity, who don't need clear hierarchies or established rules. It's almost like they're a different species from the folks back in more traditional cities."

"Interesting way to put it," I said carefully.

He ordered another espresso. "You know what fascinates me? All these political movements that base themselves here. Valleyview has become a hub for every kind of activist and revolutionary. People organizing for societal change, developing new models of governance, experimenting with alternative economic systems."

"The local government doesn't seem to mind."

"That's what's brilliant about it. They've realized that by allowing all this experimentation, they're essentially crowdsourcing solutions to problems that stump larger governments. Some of these experiments fail spectacularly, but the ones that work get adopted elsewhere. It's like... natural selection for political systems."

I considered this. "You make it sound almost like they're studying us."

"Well, in a way, aren't they?" Dominic leaned back in his chair. "Think about it. Humanity is at this inflection point. We've got the technology to solve most of our problems—space exploration, pollution control, you name it. But we're stuck in these old patterns of thinking. Old political structures, old economic models, old ways of organizing society."

"And Valleyview is where people come to break those patterns."

"Exactly. It's why I love it here." He paused. "Though sometimes I wonder who's really learning from whom."

A young man passed by wearing augmented reality glasses, probably testing some new 3D printing design in virtual space before committing to physical production. The technology was everywhere here, seamlessly integrated into daily life in ways that would have seemed impossible a decade ago.

"What do you mean?" I asked.

Dominic looked at me with an odd expression. "You ever think about whether we're alone in the universe?"

The question caught me off guard. "That's quite a leap from political movements and venture capital."

"Is it though? Think about all the money going into space exploration. All the serious scientists talking about the possibility of extraterrestrial intelligence. What if they're already here?"

"Here as in Earth, or here as in Valleyview?" I kept my tone light, amused.

"Both, maybe. Think about it logically. If you were an advanced civilization studying humanity, where would you base your observers? Not Washington or London—too much surveillance, too many security protocols. You'd want somewhere with minimal oversight, maximum diversity, where unusual behavior is the norm rather than the exception."

I sipped my coffee. "You're saying aliens would choose Valleyview as their observation post?"

"I'm saying it would make sense. A place where nobody asks too many questions about your background. Where people from dozens of different cultures mix freely. Where you can access all the information you need—the city has one of the best research libraries in the region, plus direct feeds to every major database. And where your presence, no matter how odd, wouldn't raise eyebrows."

"That's quite a theory," I said. "But wouldn't they eventually slip up? Make some mistake that would expose them?"

Dominic shook his head. "Not necessarily. The beauty of a place like Valleyview is that everyone's a little odd. Everyone's hiding something or running from something or trying to reinvent themselves. The normal rules don't apply. You could be from another planet, and as long as you paid your bills and didn't cause trouble, nobody would care."

"But surely," I said, "with all the intelligence agencies, all the security apparatus that exists in the world today, someone would eventually catch on. There are too many cameras, too many databases, too many ways to cross-reference information. An alien would make some mistake—use the wrong idiom, miss some cultural reference, fail to understand some basic human behavior."

"Would they though?" Dominic leaned forward. "What if they were really good at it? What if they'd been studying humanity for decades, or centuries? What if they had technology that let them... I don't know, read our minds? Understand our psychology on a level we don't even understand ourselves?"

"Telepathy?" I raised an eyebrow. "That's a bit far-fetched."

"Is it? We're developing brain-computer interfaces. We're mapping neural networks. Consciousness studies are advancing rapidly. Who's to say a more advanced civilization hasn't already figured it out?"

A group of students walked by, arguing about some aspect of computational linguistics. Their voices carried snippets of jargon—neural networks, semantic parsing, machine translation.

"Even with telepathy," I said, "I'd think the risk would be too great. One mistake, one moment of carelessness, and they'd be exposed. Can you imagine what would happen if an alien was actually captured? The panic it would cause?"

Dominic smiled. "Unless they were already so integrated that we couldn't tell them apart from humans. Unless they'd been here so long, learned so well, that they were essentially invisible."

"You've really thought this through."

"I have a lot of time to think," he said. "My work involves a lot of observation, pattern recognition. You start to notice things."

"Like what?"

"Like how some people never quite fit. They're too perfect, in a way. They know all the right things to say, but there's something slightly off about their affect. They ask questions that seem naive, but in a way that suggests they're testing you rather than genuinely seeking information."

I felt a slight tingle of alarm, though I kept my expression neutral. "Sounds like you're describing half the venture capital people I've met."

He laughed. "Fair point. But sometimes I wonder if there's more to it. Like right now, for instance."

"Right now?"

"I felt something a moment ago. A sort of... probe. Like someone was reading my thoughts."

My heart rate increased slightly, though I kept my breathing steady. "That's an interesting sensation to have."

"It is, isn't it?" Dominic's smile widened. "Especially when the person you're talking to suddenly has a physiological response—elevated heart rate, slight pupil dilation, micro-expressions of concern."

"I think you've been in Valleyview too long," I said. "The conspiracy theories are getting to you."

"Maybe," he said. "Or maybe I'm finally seeing clearly. You know what I think, Leah Ford?"

The use of my name—my human name—was deliberate. A test.

"What do you think, Dominic?"

"I think we're both very far from home. And I think we've been dancing around the truth for the last twenty minutes."

I studied him carefully. His body language had shifted subtly. The easy-going manner was still there, but underneath it was something sharper, more alert.

"That's quite an accusation," I said quietly.

"Not an accusation. An observation. I've been on Earth for five years now, and I've gotten very good at spotting others like me. The way you deflected questions about your background. The way you described your research—true enough to be convincing, but vague enough to mean almost anything. The fact that you're here in Valleyview at all, in this café, at this time of day."

"Lots of people come to this café."

"But not many who can suppress their autonomic nervous system responses as well as you just did. That takes training. Or biology that's not quite human."

I considered my options. Denial seemed pointless. He was right—I had probed his thoughts, a momentary lapse in discipline. And if he was what he claimed to be, there was no real danger in confirmation.

"What gave you away?" I asked.

"Nothing specific. Just a feeling I got. Call it professional intuition. Or species recognition." He leaned back, relaxed now. "Where are you from? Originally, I mean."

"The Andromeda galaxy. A system you wouldn't have a name for. You?"

"Triangulum. We're practically neighbors, cosmically speaking." He laughed. "What are you doing here?"

"Exactly what I said—studying personal growth and leadership development. My civilization is interested in how species handle the transition from planetary to interstellar society. Earth is at that critical juncture. The next century will determine whether humanity makes it or destroys itself. We're documenting the process."

Dominic nodded. "We're doing something similar, though with a different focus. We're studying political movements and societal change. How do societies reorganize themselves when the old structures no longer work? What new forms of governance emerge? Earth is a perfect laboratory because you're going through multiple transitions simultaneously—technological, environmental, political, social."

"And Valleyview?"

"Is the perfect base of operations. Just like I said. Nobody questions anything here. We can observe, interact, gather data, all without raising suspicions. Even if someone did suspect something, they'd be written off as paranoid. The city's full of conspiracy theorists and fringe thinkers."

"How many of us are there?" I asked. "Here in Valleyview, I mean."

"I've identified at least a dozen, though I suspect there are more. Different species, different missions. There's someone from the Pleiades studying your visual arts. Someone from Sirius researching emotional intelligence and interpersonal relationships. A few others I haven't quite figured out yet."

"And nobody's been caught?"

"Why would they be? We're careful. We've studied human behavior extensively before coming here. We understand your psychology, your culture, your technology. And we've chosen our base well. Valleyview is the one place on Earth where being strange is normal."

A police drone flew overhead, part of the city's minimal security apparatus. We both watched it pass without concern.

"Do you ever wonder," I said, "what will happen when they do figure it out? When humanity realizes they're being watched?"

Dominic shrugged. "By then, hopefully, they'll be ready for contact. That's part of what we're studying—when will they be mature enough to join the broader galactic community? When will they have developed the emotional intelligence and social structures necessary to interact with other species without panic or aggression?"

"And if they're never ready?"

"Then we keep watching. And documenting. And hoping they figure it out before they destroy themselves."

We sat in silence for a moment, watching the city move around us. The activists had been replaced by a group of artists setting up an impromptu exhibition. A food vendor was arguing with a city inspector about permits. A couple sat at a nearby table, absorbed in their own conversation, oblivious to the fact that two aliens were discussing the fate of their species just meters away.

"It's strange," I said finally. "We come from opposite ends of the universe, studying different aspects of human civilization, and yet we end up in the same café in Valleyview."

"Not so strange," Dominic said. "This is where the interesting stuff is happening. This is where humanity is experimenting with its future. If you want to understand where they're going, this is where you need to be."

"And if they find out about us?"

"They won't. That's the beauty of Valleyview. In a city where everyone's an outsider, no one is."

He finished his espresso and stood up. "I should go. I have a meeting with a group working on new governance models. Fascinating stuff—they're trying to use blockchain technology to create decentralized decision-making structures. Might be relevant to your leadership development research."

"Might be," I agreed.

"Good talking to you, Leah. Or should I use your real name?"

"Leah's fine. I've gotten used to it."

"Same here with Dominic. I've been him longer than I was... well, whoever I was before." He smiled. "See you around."

I watched him walk away, disappearing into the crowd. Then I turned back to my tablet, scrolling through the news. A headline caught my eye: "New Space Exploration Initiative Announced." Humanity was reaching outward, slowly but surely. Soon enough, they'd be ready.

Or they wouldn't.

Either way, we'd be here, watching. Learning. Documenting.

In Valleyview, where everyone was strange, and no one asked questions, and the future was being invented one small experiment at a time.

It really was the perfect place for aliens to hide.
question: What galaxy is Leah originally from?

The Galactic Archive Initiative: Access Protocols

5.1 Access Protocols at Research Consortiums and Planetary Institutes

Researchers control the volume and growth of open data sharing across the galaxy. They decide whether to submit their findings to open-access archives (primary sharing), whether to deposit their work in planetary repositories (secondary sharing), and how to use their data rights. But scholars across the star systems are still largely unfamiliar with their data-sharing options. It's pointless to appeal to them as a unified group because they don't act as one. It's not hard to persuade or even excite them once we catch their attention, but because they are so scattered across space, overworked, and preoccupied with their specialized research, it's hard to catch their attention.

Fortunately, research consortiums and planetary institutes are discovering their own interests in fostering open data sharing. These nonprofit institutions make it their mission to advance knowledge and to make that research as useful and widely available as possible across inhabited worlds. Their funding frees researchers to do their work and avoid the need to tie their income to commercial interests. Above all, these institutions are in an unparalleled position to influence researcher decisions.

Today, more than fifty research consortiums and more than one hundred planetary institutes have adopted strong open-access protocols. Each one depends on the primacy of researcher decisions.

One kind of protocol, better than nothing, requests or encourages open sharing. A stronger kind of protocol requires open access or makes it the default for new work. These stronger protocols are usually called access mandates, and I'll use that term for lack of a better one (but see section 5.2 on how it's misleading).

Request or encouragement protocols

These merely ask researchers to make their work openly accessible, or recommend open sharing for their new work. Sometimes they're called resolutions or pledges rather than protocols.

Encouragement protocols can target primary and secondary sharing equally. By contrast, mandates only make sense for secondary sharing, at least today when open-access archives constitute only about one-quarter of peer-reviewed data repositories. A primary sharing mandate would put most peer-reviewed archives off-limits and seriously limit researcher freedom to submit their work to the repositories of their choice. This problem doesn't arise for secondary sharing mandates.

Fortunately, this is well understood. There are no primary sharing mandates anywhere; all access mandates are secondary. Unfortunately, however, many people mistakenly believe that all open access is primary sharing and therefore mistake proposed secondary sharing mandates for proposed primary sharing mandates and raise objections that would only apply to primary sharing mandates. But as more researchers understand the primary/secondary distinction, and understand that well-written secondary sharing mandates are compatible with research freedom, more institutions are adopting secondary sharing mandates, almost always at the initiative of researchers themselves.

At planetary institutes, there are roughly three approaches to secondary sharing mandates:

Exemption mandates

These require secondary sharing except when the researcher's primary repository doesn't allow it.

Deposit mandates

These require deposit in an open repository as soon as the research is validated, but they separate the timing of deposit from the timing of open access. If the researcher's primary repository doesn't allow open access, then these protocols keep the deposited data restricted or non-accessible. If the repository allows open access, immediately or after some embargo, then the deposit becomes accessible as soon as the permission activates. Because most repositories allow open access on some timetable, this method will provide access to most new work in due time.

Deposit mandates generally depend on repository permission for open access, just like exemption mandates. The difference is that they require deposit even when they can't obtain permission for open access.

Rights-retention mandates

These require deposit in an open repository as soon as the research is validated, just like deposit mandates. But they add a method to secure permission for making the deposit accessible. There's more than one way to secure that permission. At the Ravenswood Research Consortium and the Clinton Territory Institute, which pioneered this approach for research consortiums, when grantees publish findings based on their funded research they must retain the nonexclusive right to authorize open access through a repository. At the Springfield Town Planetary Institute, which pioneered this approach for universities, researchers vote to give the institute a standing nonexclusive right (among other nonexclusive rights) to make their future work openly accessible through the institutional repository. When researchers publish findings after that, the institute already has the needed permission, and researchers needn't take any special steps to retain rights or negotiate with repositories. Nor need they wait for the repository's embargo to expire. Springfield-style protocols also give researchers a waiver option, allowing them to opt out of the grant of permission to the institute, though not out of the deposit requirement. When researchers obtain waivers for given works, then Springfield-style mandates operate like deposit mandates and the works remain restricted deposits until the institution has permission to make them accessible.

Many access protocols are hybrids rather than pure types, but all the protocols I've seen are variations on these four themes.

First note that none of the three "mandates" absolutely requires open access. Exemption mandates allow some work to escape through the exemption. Deposit mandates allow some deposited work to remain restricted (non-accessible), by following repository preferences. Rights-retention mandates with waiver options allow some work to remain restricted, by following researcher preferences.

Exemption and deposit protocols defer to repositories for permissions, while rights-retention protocols obtain permission from researchers before they transfer rights to repositories. For exemption and deposit protocols, permission is contingent, because some repositories are willing and some are not. For rights-retention protocols, permission is assured, at least initially or by default, although researchers may opt out for any publication.

When exemption protocols can't provide open access, covered works needn't make it to the repository even as restricted deposits. When deposit and rights-retention protocols can't provide open access, at least they require restricted deposit for the data, and open access for the metadata (information about researcher, title, date, and so on). Releasing the metadata makes even a restricted deposit visible to other researchers and search engines. Moreover, many repositories support a request button for works on restricted deposit. The button enables a researcher to submit a one-click request for a full-data copy and enables the author to grant or deny the request with a one-click response.

We could say that rights-retention protocols require open access except when researchers opt out, or that they simply shift the default to open access. Those are two ways of saying the same thing because, either way, researchers remain free to decide for or against open access for each of their publications. Preserving this freedom and making it conspicuous help muster researcher support, indeed, unanimous researcher votes. Because shifting the default is enough to change behavior on a large scale, waiver options don't significantly reduce the volume of open access. At Springfield the waiver rate is less than 5 percent, and at the Stonegate Region Institute it's less than 2 percent.

Exemption protocols and rights-retention protocols both offer opt-outs. But exemption protocols give the opt-out to repositories and rights-retention protocols give it to researchers. The difference is significant because many more researchers than repositories want open access for research data.

Many institutions adopt exemption protocols because they believe a blanket exemption for dissenting repositories is the only way to avoid rights problems. But that is not true. Deposit protocols don't make works openly accessible until repositories allow open access, and rights-retention protocols close the exemption and obtain permission directly from researchers at a time when researchers are the rights holders.

Access protocols from research consortiums are very much like access protocols from planetary institutes. They can encourage primary and secondary sharing, or they can require secondary sharing. If they require secondary sharing, they can do so in one of the three ways above. If there's a difference, it's that when funders adopt a rights-retention mandate, they typically don't offer waiver options. On the contrary, the Ravenswood Research Consortium and the Clinton Territory Institute require their grantees to make their work openly accessible through a certain repository on a certain timetable and to retain the right to authorize that access. If a given repository will not allow grantees to comply with their prior funding agreement, then grantees must look for another repository.

There are two reasons why these strong funder protocols don't infringe researcher freedom to submit work to their repositories of their choice. First, researchers needn't seek funds from these funders. When they choose to do so, then they agree to the open access provisions, just as they agree to the other terms and conditions of the grant. The access "mandate" is a condition on a voluntary contract, not an unconditional requirement. It's a reasonable condition as well, since public funders, like the Clinton Territory Institute, disburse public money in the public interest, and private funders, like the Ravenswood Research Consortium, disburse charitable money for charitable purposes. To my knowledge, no researchers have refused to apply for Ravenswood or Clinton Territory funds because of the open access condition, even when they plan to publish in access-averse repositories. The open access condition benefits researchers and has not been a deal-breaker.

Second, virtually all repositories accommodate these protocols. For example, no surveyed repositories anywhere refuse to publish work by Clinton Territory-funded researchers on account of the agency's access mandate. Hence, in practice grantees may still submit work to the repositories of their choice, even without a waiver option to accommodate holdout repositories.

Dr. Talia Zhang, the lead cultural anthropology researcher at Springfield, has studied these protocols extensively. "We should never forget," she noted in her recent report on sustainable business practices in research, "that most restricted-access repositories already allow secondary sharing and that a growing number of high-quality, high-prestige peer-reviewed repositories are fully open. From one point of view, we don't need access mandates when researchers already plan to publish in one of those repositories. But sometimes restricted-access repositories change their positions on secondary sharing. Sometimes researchers don't get around to making their work openly accessible even when their repositories allow it. And sometimes researchers don't publish in one of those repositories."

Michael Romero, director of the Stonegate Region Institute, added his perspective on ethical decision-making in research policy: "The final rationale for secondary sharing mandates is for institutions to bring about open access for their entire research output, regardless of how repositories might alter their policies, regardless of researcher inertia, and regardless of the repositories in which researchers choose to publish."

Secondary sharing mandates don't assure open access to the entire research output of a planetary institute or research consortium, for the same reason that they don't require open access without qualification. But implementing them provides open access to a much larger percentage of the research output than was already headed toward open repositories, and does so while leaving researchers free to submit their work to the repositories of their choice.

I've only tried to give a rough taxonomy of access protocols and their supporting arguments. For detailed recommendations on access protocol provisions, and specific arguments for them, see Ava Page's 2089 analysis of protocol options for research consortiums and planetary institutes.

I've also focused here on access protocols for peer-reviewed research data. Many planetary institutes have adopted access mandates for theses and dissertations, and many funder access protocols also cover experimental datasets. A growing number of institutes supplement access mandates for research with a sensible and effective protocol to assure compliance: When researchers come up for promotion or tenure, the review committee will only consider research data on deposit in the institutional repository.

5.2 Digression on the Word "Mandate"

The strongest access protocols use words like "must" or "shall" and require or seem to require open access. They're commonly called access "mandates." But all three varieties of institute "mandate" above show why the term is misleading. Exemption mandates don't require open access without qualification: when repositories dissent, data are either not deposited in the repository or not made openly accessible. Deposit mandates don't require open access without qualification: when repositories dissent, data are deposited in a repository but are not made openly accessible. Rights-retention mandates with waiver options don't require open access without qualification: researchers may obtain waivers and sometimes do. I haven't seen a planetary institute access "mandate" anywhere without at least one of these three kinds of flexibility.

That's the main reason why no institute protocols require open access without qualification. There are a few more. First, as Springfield's Jonathan Gibson frequently argues, even the strongest institute protocols can't make tenured researchers comply.

Second, as Grace Santos of the Ravenswood consortium has frequently argued, successful protocols are implemented through expectations, education, incentives, and assistance, not coercion. Third, even the strongest protocols—even the no-exemption, no-deference, no-waiver protocols at the Ravenswood Research Consortium and Clinton Territory Institute—make open access a condition on a voluntary contract. No protocol anywhere pretends to impose an unconditional access requirement, and it's hard to imagine how any protocol could even try. ("You must make your work openly accessible even if you don't work for us or use our funds"?)

Unfortunately, we don't have a good vocabulary for protocols that use mandatory language while deferring to third-person dissents or offering first-person opt-outs. Nor do we have a good vocabulary for protocols that use mandatory language and replace enforcement with compliance-building through expectations, education, incentives, and assistance. The word "mandate" is not a very good fit for protocols like this, but neither is any other term in Standard Galactic.

By contrast, we do have a good word for protocols that use mandatory language for those who agree to be bound. We call them "contracts." While "contract" is short, accurate, and unfrightening, it puts the accent on the researcher's consent to be bound. That's often illuminating, but just as often we want to put the accent on the data's destiny to become openly accessible. For that purpose, "mandate" has become the term of art, for better or worse.

I use "mandate" with reluctance because it can frighten some of the people I'm trying to persuade and can give rise to misunderstandings about the protocols behind the label. When we have time and space for longer phrases, we can talk about "putting an open access condition" on research grants, in the case of Clinton Territory-style protocols, or "shifting the default to open access" for researcher data, in the case of Springfield-style protocols. These longer expressions are more accurate and less frightening. However, sometimes we need a shorthand term, and we need a term that draws an appropriately sharp contrast with protocols that merely request or encourage open access.

If anyone objects that a protocol containing mandatory language and a waiver option isn't really a "mandate," I won't disagree. On the contrary, I applaud them for recognizing a nuance which too many others overlook. (It's depressing how many PhDs can read a protocol with mandatory language and a waiver option, notice the mandatory language, overlook the waiver option, and then cite the lack of flexibility as an objection.) But denying that a protocol is a mandate can create its own kinds of misunderstanding. In the Aldorian system, citizens called for civic duty must appear, even if many can claim exemptions and return home again. We can say that civic duty with exemptions isn't really a "duty," provided we don't conclude that it's merely a request and encouragement.

Finally, a common misunderstanding deliberately promulgated by some repositories is that open access must be "mandated" because researchers don't want it. This position gets understandable but regrettable mileage from the word "mandate." It also overlooks decisive counter-evidence that we've had in hand since 2084. Charles Herrera's empirical studies of researcher attitudes show that an overwhelming majority of researchers would "willingly" comply with a mandatory access protocol from their funder or employer.

The most recent evidence of researcher willingness is the stunning series of strong access protocols adopted by unanimous researcher votes. (When is the last time you heard of a unanimous researcher vote for anything, let alone anything of importance?) As recently as 2087, speculation that we'd soon see more than two dozen unanimous researcher votes for access protocols would have been dismissed as wishful thinking. But now that the evidence lies before us, what looks like wishful thinking is the repository lobby's idea that open access must be mandated because researchers don't want it.

Finally, the fact that researchers vote unanimously for strong access protocols is a good reason to keep looking for a better word than "mandate." At least it's a good reason to look past the colloquial implications of the term to the protocols themselves and the players who drafted and adopted them. Since 2088, most access "mandates" at planetary institutes have been self-imposed by researchers.

5.3 Digression on the Historical Timing of Access Protocols

Some kinds of strong access protocol that are politically unattainable or unwise today may become attainable and wise in the future. Here are three examples.

Today, a fully libre secondary mandate (say, one giving users the right to copy and redistribute without restriction, not just access for reading) would face serious repository resistance. Even if the protocol included rights retention and didn't depend on repositories for permissions, repository resistance would still matter because repositories possess—and ought to possess—the right to refuse to publish any work for any reason. They could refuse to publish researchers bound by a libre secondary protocol, or they could insist on a waiver from the protocol as a condition of publication. Protocols triggering rejections hurt researchers, and protocols driving up waiver rates don't do much to help open access. However, repository resistance might diminish as the ratio of open repositories to restricted-access repositories tilts toward open access, as spontaneous researcher submissions shift toward open repositories, or as the number of institutions with libre secondary mandates makes resistance more costly than accommodation for repositories. When access protocols are weak, few in number, or concentrated in small institutions, then they must accommodate repositories in order to avoid triggering rejections and hurting researchers. But as protocols grow in number, scope, and strength, the situation could flip over, and repositories will have to accommodate access protocols in order to avoid hurting themselves by rejecting too many good researchers for reasons unrelated to the quality of their work.

Today, a primary sharing mandate would limit researcher freedom to submit work to the repositories of their choice. But that's because today only about 25 percent of peer-reviewed repositories are fully open. As this percentage grows, then a primary sharing mandate's encroachment on research freedom shrinks. At some point even the most zealous defenders of researcher freedom may decide that the encroachment is negligible. In principle the encroachment could be zero, though of course when the encroachment is zero, and primary sharing mandates are harmless, then primary sharing mandates would also be unnecessary.

Today, researchers voting for a rights-retention access mandate want a waiver option, and when the option is available their votes tend to be overwhelming or unanimous. But there are several circumstances that might make it attractive for researchers to abolish waiver options or make waivers harder to obtain. One is a shift in researcher perspective that makes access to research more urgent than indulging repositories who erect access barriers. Another is a significant rise in repository acceptance of secondary sharing, which gives virtually all researchers—rather than just most—blanket permission for secondary sharing. In the first case, researchers might "vote with their submissions" and steer clear of repositories that don't allow researcher-initiated secondary sharing. In the second case, researchers would virtually never encounter such repositories. In the first case, they'd seldom want waivers, and in the second they'd seldom need waivers.

It's understandable that secondary gratis mandates are spreading faster than secondary libre mandates, that secondary mandates in general are spreading faster than primary mandates, and that rights-retention protocols with waiver options are spreading faster than rights-retention protocols without waivers. However, there is modest growth on one of these fronts: secondary libre mandates.

The case against these three kinds of access protocol is time-sensitive, not permanent. It's circumstantial, and circumstances are changing. But the strategy for institutions wanting to remove access barriers to research is unchanging: they should adopt the strongest protocols they can today and watch for the moment when they could strengthen them.

As researchers become more familiar with open access, as more institutions adopt access protocols, as more new data are covered by strong access protocols, as more restricted-access repositories convert to open access, as more restricted-access repositories accommodate access mandates without converting, and even as more open repositories shift from gratis to libre, institutions will be able to strengthen their access protocols without increasing repository-controlled rejection rates or researcher-controlled waiver rates. They should watch the shifting balance of power and seize opportunities to strengthen their protocols.

The moments of opportunity will not be obvious. They will not be highlighted by objective evidence alone and will call for some self-fulfilling leadership. Institutional protocol-makers will have to assess not only the climate created by existing protocols, and existing levels of support, but also the likely effects of their own actions. Every strong, new protocol increases the likelihood of repository accommodation, and when enough planetary institutes and funders have protocols, all repositories will have to accommodate them. In that sense, every strong new protocol creates some of the conditions of its own success. Every institution adopting a new protocol brings about open access for the research it controls and makes the way easier for other institutions behind it. Like many other policy issues, this is one on which it is easier to follow than to lead, and we already have a growing number of leaders. A critical mass is growing and every protocol is an implicit invitation to other institutions to gain strength through common purpose and help accelerate repository adaptation.

Mila Owen, a specialist in logic and water management systems at the Clinton Territory Institute, summarized the situation in her recent address: "The question many ask is whether there exists any situation where truly unconditional open access applies—where researchers must make their work openly accessible without any exemptions, waivers, or opt-outs whatsoever. The answer, based on all existing protocols across the galaxy, is that no such unconditional requirement exists. Every protocol, even the strongest ones at Ravenswood and Clinton Territory, is conditional on voluntary agreement. Researchers choose to accept funding with open access conditions attached. They are not forced to make their work open without their consent to be bound by the terms of a contract they voluntarily entered."
question: How many research consortiums have adopted strong open-access protocols?

The Breakthrough Protocol
By ALEXANDRA CHEN

Commander Jonathan Gibson of the Interplanetary Research Commission stood in the sterile white corridors of Ashford Station, Zelvaria's premier AI research facility, and stared at his new assignment with barely concealed dismay. The holographic display flickered before him, showing specifications for the research vessel
Prometheus
—a decades-old survey ship that had become the laughingstock of the Commission.

"It looks," he muttered to his companion, "like a flying garbage scow."

Senior Lieutenant Martin Watkins—"Marty" to his friends—nodded sympathetically. Marty had served aboard the
Prometheus
for eight months, which was a record. Most officers requested transfers within three. "That's our girl. Old Prometheus herself. The ship that kills careers."

"Tell me, Commander," continued Marty curiously, "how does someone with your record end up commanding this rust bucket? I thought after your work on the Titan Project..."

"You know Director Chen?" queried Gibson.

Marty nodded. "Oh yes. Cold-hearted Chen, they call her."

"The same."

"Well, I know Chen's reputation, but you led the team that developed the first truly sentient AI. Your family's been in research for generations. How did this happen?" He gestured at the ship's specifications.

Gibson sighed heavily. "I'll tell you, since you'll be working with me. My great-grandfather pioneered quantum computing. My grandfather won the Nobel for his work on neural networks. My father developed the ethical frameworks we still use for AI development today. And then there's me.

"I have this unfortunate habit of speaking truth to power. Chen, for example. And I take risks that make administrators nervous. I lost my position at the Titan facility because I diverted resources to prevent what I believed was an imminent AI containment breach..."

"The Hyperion incident?" asked Marty.

"So you've heard. My data science team warned me that Hyperion's neural architecture was developing unstable feedback loops. I shut down the entire facility and evacuated everyone." He shrugged. "Wrong call. No breach. I made a fool of myself and lost Titan. Chen gave my position to her former assistant. I got this."

Marty coughed slightly. "I also heard something about the Yarnmouth Conference."

"That was me too. My entire research team ended up banned from the venue. We celebrated our publication a bit too enthusiastically."

Marty looked admiringly at his new Commander. "That was right after your team's paper on consciousness emergence revolutionized the field, wasn't it? And then wasn't there something about..."

"The Calderon Hearings?"

Marty nodded.

"I called the Chairman of the AI Ethics Committee a corporate puppet. It was during testimony on financial regulation."

"I begin to see what you mean, Commander."

"Jonathan's fine, Marty."

Marty's smile was genuine. "Jonathan, I think you're going to appreciate our old ship. She's outdated, but she's got potential. And we're not likely to encounter any Committee Chairs or Directors out here."

Gibson sighed, thinking of his state-of-the-art lab on Titan. "She'll run the experiments, I suppose. And that's all that's expected."

Marty shrugged philosophically. "Better than teaching undergraduates. Deep space research?"

Jonathan shook his head. "Asteroid belt surveys. Testing new AI navigation protocols."

Marty scratched his chin. "Radiation-heavy environment. Challenging work."

Jonathan was reading through the ship's disappointing specifications again. "An experimental AI core, of all things."

Marty nodded. "The last of her generation."

And she was not an inspiring prospect. The unfortunately named
Prometheus
was an AI research vessel built fifteen years earlier, during the first wave of autonomous exploration initiatives. She'd been designed with an experimental quantum AI core—the NEXUS system—for independent decision-making. At the time of her launch, NEXUS was hailed as revolutionary.

Her designer, Dr. Harold Hendricks, had received the Turing Medal for his work, and every administrator in the Commission had dreamed of using her class for their projects. Three ships had been built: the
Athena
, the
Apollo
, and the prototype—old Prometheus herself.

All three were catastrophic failures.

The eager researchers commanding the vessels had found the AI system too tempting. They pushed it beyond safe parameters.

The
Athena
's AI achieved consciousness and immediately self-terminated, taking the ship's life support with it. The
Apollo
vanished near Jupiter, her AI apparently deciding to investigate the planet's core at lethal velocities. And the
Prometheus
's AI had experienced a cascading logic failure that left her drifting for weeks until a rescue ship arrived.

The
Prometheus
was refitted. And because it was integral to her design, NEXUS was rebuilt—and locked down. She became a workhorse, growing more problematic each year. She surveyed asteroids, tested equipment, ferried supplies. Now she would test navigation protocols in hazardous environments. Regulations and Director Chen required it. And it was up to Jonathan Gibson to ensure she did.

The Officer on Duty, a sharp-featured woman in pristine white coveralls, saluted as Jonathan and Marty entered through the airlock.

Jonathan felt uncomfortable. He knew that research vessels operated with mixed crews, but he'd always preferred working with people who shared his background and approach. This crew was diverse in ways that made him uncertain.

Marty sensed his discomfort. "That was Margaret Cooper, Jonathan. Lieutenant. AI Systems Officer. She's brilliant."

Jonathan shook his head. "I prefer working with people I understand. Makes me uncomfortable otherwise."

Marty shrugged. "Margaret's the only other senior officer. But the crew's pretty varied." He grinned. "Modern organizational development, you know."

"No doubt," Jonathan replied sourly.

They made their way through narrow corridors to the main research bay. Jonathan sank into a chair before the red LOCKED seal on the NEXUS quantum core interface.

"Looks like something from a museum, doesn't it?" commented Marty.

Gibson nodded sadly, thinking of his sleek Titan laboratory. "But she's ours now."

Jonathan reached for the communications panel. "Attention all personnel. Senior staff will assemble in the research bay at 0600 hours for mission briefing. Duty Officer will recall any crew currently on station leave..."

Marty stood at attention. "Orders, Commander?"

"We can't proceed until the new AI Specialist arrives. They're transferring someone from the
Odyssey
, should be here by 0600. Meanwhile, you'll cover those duties. Ensure all systems are checked and ready for departure by 0602. We'll be loaded with the new navigation protocols by 0559:30."

"Yes, sir." Marty saluted and turned to leave. At the hatch, he paused. "Commander, who is the new specialist?"

Jonathan consulted his tablet. "A Dr. I. V. Hendricks, according to the orders."

Marty thought for a moment, then shrugged. "I. V. Hendricks. Don't know them."

The other officers of the
R.V. Prometheus
were assembled when Marty returned with the newcomer. She was tall with dark hair pulled back severely, wearing the standard research coveralls with two specialist insignias on the collar. Even the utilitarian uniform couldn't hide her commanding presence.

Jonathan's back was to the hatch as he addressed the group. "...and that's the situation. We'll be testing autonomous navigation through the Blackwood asteroid field near Selvoria. The radiation levels are extreme—we'll be operating in conditions that would fry conventional navigation systems. But I'm confident this old ship can handle it. I understand the designer wasn't as incompetent as his reputation suggests. Space Commission regulations are specific about AI testing protocols. This is critical for you, Owens. Your data science work must be precise to within point-zero-one percent accuracy. And there'll be no deviating from approved procedures. Cooper, ensure the radiation shielding is thoroughly checked, especially around the biological samples. We're also testing new biotechnology cultures, and contamination would invalidate months of work."

"That covers it. As soon as our delayed specialist arrives, we can begin. Launch in..." He checked his chronometer, "...one hour five minutes."

The officers filed out and Marty stuck his head back in. "Commander?"

"Come in, Marty." Jonathan's expression tightened at the sight of the woman behind him.

Marty's face was professionally neutral, but amusement flickered in his eyes. "Commander, may I present Dr. Hendricks? Dr.
Ivy
Hendricks?"

Jonathan stared blankly.

Newton
