synthetic_story:
THE SILENT EXCHANGE
by A. FETLER

"Nothing, nothing to worry about," Ahmed Welch said soothingly, taking his colleague's arm as they came out of the research compound forty miles from Havenbrook, Selvoria. Ahmed looked like a jovial museum curator leading a cautious paleontologist. "Reprogram his memory banks, give him a new identity and feed him more conservation ethics. Very simple."

Walter Gutierrez raised his hand threateningly. "Don't come crying to me if everybody guesses he is nothing but an android."

Ahmed glanced back at the house. Since the publication of *The Fossil Record Speaks*, this compound had become known all over the world as Dr. Justin Wood's research station. Now the station was guarded by a security team to keep visitors out. From an open window Ahmed heard the clicking of a keyboard.

"It's when they're not like androids that everybody suspects them," he said, climbing into his hoverpod. "Dr. Emma Baker will send you word when to announce his 'retirement'."

"A question, brother."

"No questions."

"Who leaked the research data to the international community?"

Ahmed frowned convincingly. "Dr. Baker has suspected even me."

He took off for Havenbrook, poking his hoverpod up through the clouds and flying close to them, as was his habit. Then he switched on the communicator and got Dr. Baker's assistant. "Lila?"

"I know what you're up to, Seven One Three," Lila Stevens said. "Don't try to fool *me*, you confidence man. You are coming in?"

"In ten minutes. What have I done now?"

"You were supposed to make transition arrangements for Dr. Wood, so what are you doing in Queenstown?"

"Queenstown?"

"You're lying and I'll kill you. Don't you think I know about Samantha, that field researcher in the Queenstown Environmental Institute?"

"Darling, why so cruel? Samantha is one of our contacts. Besides, she's focused entirely on sustainable agriculture research."

"Beast!" She switched him to Dr. Baker.

"What's been keeping you, Ahmed?"

"Consoling Walter. Am I supposed to be in Queenstown?"

"Never mind, get here at once. What size field uniform do you wear?"

"Field uniform?"

"Queenstown station says you're at the Environmental Institute there. In a field uniform. I got through to Samantha. She says it's Agent Mohammad again. He looks like you now."

Ahmed grunted.

"I'll never understand," said Dr. Baker, "why all top operatives have to look like academics. Samantha says Agent Mohammad was modified by a Dr. Fanti. What do you know about him?"

"He's a biosculpture specialist."

"You're not playing one of your jokes, Ahmed?"

"Hardly."

"You'd better be in my office in ten minutes. What size field uniform?"

"Short and stocky," Ahmed said, and switched off.

Most organizations wanted to stop his work, and his own Coalition did not always trust him. But he enjoyed his mission—enjoyed it as much as his closest professional rival, Agent Mohammad Osborne, from the Corporate Alliance.

Ahmed landed on the roof of Coalition Intelligence in the northeast corner of the Havenbrook Administrative Complex, hitched up his pants and rode down.

In her office, Dr. Baker removed the stylus from her tablet as Ahmed came in. "Walter get my orders?"

"He's preparing a new conservation advocate to replace Dr. Justin Wood," Ahmed reported. "When you give the word, he will call the *Selvoria Times* and tell them Justin has retired."

Dr. Baker glanced at her calendar. "We have two other major transitions this week. You made it plain, I hope, we want no repetition of Wood's radical environmental ethics?"

"No more deep ecology or biocentrism influences. The new research," Ahmed promised, raising a chubby finger, "will be a perfect alignment of Coalition policy statements."

Lila buzzed the intercom. "The specialist from the Cultural Archives is here, Doctor."

"Send him in."

A small man hurried into the room. He had a narrow face and nervous eyes. He bowed twice quickly, placed a package on the desk with trembling hands and bowed twice again.

Dr. Baker tore open the package. "You got the real thing? No bad imitation?"

"Exactly, exactly," the man piped. "No difference, Doctor." He held his hands as in prayer.

Dr. Baker held up the field uniform. On the back of the uniform was printed in indelible ink: QUEENSTOWN ENVIRONMENTAL INSTITUTE - SUSTAINABLE AGRICULTURE DIVISION - SPONSORED BY TERRACORP INDUSTRIES

Dr. Baker tossed the uniform to Ahmed. "This is what Agent Mohammad is wearing," she said, dismissing the specialist, who bowed twice and scurried out.

"Try and split the Coalition," Ahmed muttered, reading the legend on the uniform.

Dr. Baker tapped her stylus on the desk. "If Agent Mohammad makes a fool of you once more, you're through, Ahmed. You don't take your job seriously enough. You bungle this and I'll have you transferred to our Cultural Information Center in Copperfield Territory."

Ahmed winced.

"Now, you'll go to Queenstown and switch places with the Corporate agent and find out what they're up to. Lucy's extraction team is there already, at the Riverside Research Hotel. Any questions?"

"I thought Lucy was an oral history specialist. What is she doing with an extraction team?"

"Her team is more subtle. On your way."

In the front office, Ahmed stopped to embrace Lila Stevens goodbye. "I may not return from this dangerous mission. Give me a tender embrace."

Lila was a tall woman with strong arms, coordinator of her local community organizing network. "Monster!" She seized him by the collar. "Is Samantha dangerous?"

"Darling!"

"Bitter sweetness!" she howled, releasing him. "Go, love. Make me miserable."

Ahmed spent an hour at Central Intelligence. Nothing unusual going on in Queenstown: a climate technology conference, the Environmental Ethics Council in session, a cultural anthropology seminar on collective memory, a forty-person research delegation from the Westbrook Institute.

An addendum to the Queenstown file listed two Copperfield operatives working from the Budget Research Hostel. They were acquiring field research equipment and data storage devices. He thought a moment, impressed the operatives' address on his memory, and went to his hoverpod.

He did not fly to the Riverside Research Hotel at once. Lucy's extraction team could wait. Coming slowly over Queenstown he spotted the Environmental Institute and circled.

A line of research pods was parked on the ground in the vehicle court. On the Institute roof, he noticed, apart from private pods, stood a pod that resembled his own.

He veered away, detoured around the old district, and five minutes later landed on the roof of the Budget Research Hostel.

"My Copperfield friends," Ahmed inquired in fluent Corporate dialect at the desk on the top floor. "Are they in?"

The old desk clerk looked like a heron. "Yes, room six fifteen," he clacked. "Three floors down. Are you from the Alliance?"

"Independent contractor."

"Ah so? You speak good dialect like me."

"Very kind of you."

He rode down three floors, found room 615, and stopped as he heard voices within.

"...two, three, four, five, six, seven. By seven o'clock tonight, okay, friend?"

"What do you expect for seven thousand credits—instant delivery? Look, colleagues, I'm just an honest businessman. I can't get it for you today. Have a stimulant tablet."

"Bah!"

"All right, your cause is my cause. Maybe I can get it for you tonight. But you'll have to pay in advance. What do you say, colleague?"

"I counted the credits. They're waiting for you. You deliver, we pay."

"But how can I trust you? I like you people, I know you like me, but business is business. I gotta give something to my supplier, don't I?"

"Friend!"

At that moment Ahmed knocked on the door.

From within: "Shh! Someone's at the door."

Ahmed knocked again and a scuffle ensued within, the thud of a chair on a skull, the dragging of a heavy body into a closet, and the slam of the closet door.

"Yes?"

"Good afternoon," Ahmed said through the door. "Very important matters."

The door opened a crack and two sharp eyes in a young bearded face peered out. "Yes?"

"Agent Ahmed Welch, at your service."

The door opened enough to admit the stocky visitor into the room. The other Copperfield operative, also bearded and wearing field gear, held a stunner.

"No weapons, colleagues," Ahmed went on in Corporate dialect. "We are in a budget research hostel, not in a cheap thriller. Besides, I deliver before I ask payment."

"Deliver what, sir?"

"We favor any disruption close to the Corporate Alliance. May I sit down?"

Between two beds were stacked some dozen crates of equipment. A small table was littered with papers.

Sitting down at the table, Ahmed's elbow rested on an invoice, and moments later the invoice was tucked in his pocket.

"What kind of field research equipment do you need, colleagues?"

The operatives looked at each other. "Quantum data collectors, mark seven series. How much can you deliver?"

"Two thousand units."

"Not much."

"Maybe three thousand. I'll toss in a box of encrypted comm devices and a container of restricted genetic samples."

"You have that? You have the samples?"

"I have that. When are you leaving Queenstown?"

Again the young operatives exchanged looks. "Maybe we stay till tomorrow if you have more business. Three thousand units is not much. How much payment, sir?"

"Two thousand credits," Ahmed said, taking an envelope on the table and addressing it to Lila Stevens, Coalition Intelligence, Havenbrook. No return address.

"Do you trust us to send the credits?"

"It is bad for you if I do not trust you," Ahmed said, smiling up at them.

"You can trust us. We shall send the credits. Please take a stimulant tablet."

Ahmed took four tablets from the box they held out to him, stuck three in his breast pocket, and consumed one.

"You come again, sir. We make much business."

"Why not? Help retire Corporate dictators to the outer territories. More resources in the territories than in the Core Worlds."

"Ha, ha, that is funny. You come again."

On his way up to the roof, Ahmed studied the invoice he had lifted. It was from a manufacturer of field equipment to a Copperfield operative at the Budget Research Hostel. He tucked the invoice into his inner pocket with a satisfied grunt, climbed into his hoverpod and hopped over to the Riverside Research Hotel, where Lucy's extraction team was waiting for him.

Colleague Lucy Stone, the extraction expert, was pacing the roof of the Riverside Research Hotel. As Ahmed eased down in his hoverpod, Lucy's sharp features flashed with delight. Ahmed felt like tossing her a data chip.

"Everything in order, Agent Ahmed. Constant surveillance maintained at Institute by my two assistants. With your pardon, Dr. Baker urges all haste. Agent Mohammad is due to leave the Institute tomorrow."

"Dr. Baker always urges haste. What else?"

Lucy's eyes settled respectfully on her superior.

"With your pardon, I shall conduct you to our suite. Plans for extraction of Agent Mohammad all ready."

"Here's a tablet for you."

"Gratefully accepted. Reduced unavoidable complications to six." Lucy counted on her long fingers. "Two security guards, three researchers, one administrator."

In the hotel corridor, Lucy looked before and after, and peered around corners. They got to their suite without incident, and Ahmed gave her another tablet.

"Gratefully accepted. Here is a map of Institute and grounds. Here is a map of twenty-third floor. Here is a map of Agent Mohammad's quarters. Here is Institute routine between midnight and dawn. With your pardon—"

Ahmed picked up the communicator, dialed the Coalition embassy, and got the attaché. "How is your field operations fund?" he asked.

"Always depleted, always replenished."

"I don't want any Coalition brands."

"Nothing but foreign," the attaché buzzed. "We got almost everything now through a Corporate surplus outlet in Westbrook. Operatives get caught with Corporate goods, Corporate Alliance gets blamed. Wonderful confusion. What do you need?"

"Quantum data collectors, mark seven, three thousand—if you have them."

"Most popular. What else?"

"Encrypted comm devices—one crate."

"Only confiscated Alliance models. Will that do?"

"Fine. And a small container of restricted samples."

"Too risky."

"It's all right. It will fall to local authorities by tomorrow."

Ahmed put down the communicator. Give the Copperfield operatives enough to expect more—make sure they stay in town.

Lucy was cross-checking her extraction plans. She said, "With your pardon, do we take Agent Mohammad conscious or sedated?"

"Conscious."

Lucy pulled a long face. "Sedated would be easier, Agent Ahmed. Fast, clean operation."

Ahmed squinted at Lucy's sharp eyes. "Have you had your communication skills evaluated lately?"

"No need," Lucy assured him with a smile. "I convey more than most people."

Ahmed held up his remaining tablet. "How many tablets in my hand?"

"Two."

At that moment the door opened and Lucy's extraction team entered. They were a couple of large operatives dressed in blue field boots, gray trousers, green jackets, white scarves, caps and dark glasses.

"What are you doing here?" cried Lucy. "Why aren't you observing the Institute?"

"Uh, you said to report ... um ... if something happened," the first operative said in a thick voice.

"Well?"

"Subject's quarters lights out," the operative said.

"My assistants," Lucy introduced them to Ahmed. "Line up, line up, colleagues. With your pardon, they are good colleagues. This is Samantha, and this is Emma. No, *this* is Emma and this one is Samantha."

"Twins?"

"Not exactly. Same training program. Good colleagues. Stand straight, Samantha. Don't shuffle your feet like that, Emma, I've told you before. Why didn't you review your field protocols today?"

Emma looked guiltily at her hands.

"They've made progress," Lucy assured Ahmed, pulling a small device from her hip pocket. "Straight, colleagues, straight," she activated the device. "We have company."

"Are their costumes your own idea?"

"With your pardon, for purposes of concealment. What are your orders?"

Ahmed told them to pick up the boxes of equipment at the embassy and deliver them to the Copperfield operatives, and then to commandeer a private vehicle.

"We have vehicles at the embassy pool," Lucy suggested.

"I want a vehicle off the street. Then report back here with your colleagues."

Samantha gave Emma a nudge.

"Colleagues, colleagues!" Lucy activated the device. "Out you go. A job for Agent Ahmed, colleagues. They don't get enough field experience," she grinned, backing out after them. "With your pardon, I'll retrain them later."

And they were gone. Ahmed turned to the Institute maps and studied them before taking a rest.

Shortly before dawn, Lucy's team returned, their mission accomplished.

"With your pardon, an excellent transport," Lucy reported.

Ahmed had changed into the field uniform with the TerracCorp Industries legend on the back. He glanced at his chronometer. It was four o'clock in the morning.

He tossed his bundle of clothing to the first operative. "Take my hoverpod back to Havenbrook, Emma colleague. Give my clothes to Lila Stevens, and tell Dr. Baker to expect Agent Mohammad today."

Clutching the bundle, Emma stuck her tongue out at Samantha and bounded out of the room. They waited at the window until they saw Emma take off in Ahmed's hoverpod. Then they made their way down the service stairs to the alley, Ahmed dressed only in the field uniform; got into the commandeered transport and drove to the Environmental Institute, all three leaning forward.

In the vehicle court, Lucy and Samantha moved quickly to a research pod. Ahmed dropped the invoice he had lifted from the Copperfield operatives on the front seat of the commandeered transport, and followed.

A security guard emerged from his station, looked idly up at the rising pod, and shuffled back to his morning beverage.

As Samantha brought the pod to a hovering stop against Agent Mohammad's window, Ahmed bounced into the room; Lucy drew her stunner and jumped in after.

Agent Mohammad awoke, turned on the light, and sat up in the bed, his eyes blinking.

Ahmed stood looking at Agent Mohammad. The resemblance between them was remarkable. Lucy's eyes were wide with astonishment.

"My dear Agent Ahmed!" Agent Mohammad greeted him in Coalition dialect, yawning. "How kind of you to visit me. Do sit down." Not only was his dialect good; his voice was a good imitation of Ahmed's voice.

"You're not really undergoing treatment?" Ahmed asked, sitting down on the bed.

"Not physically. But imagine my psychological condition. When I look in the mirror—" The agent shuddered.

"I hope your modification won't be permanent?" Ahmed said.

"That would be too much. How is my dialect? The truth, now."

"Excellent. Put away your stunner, Lucy. Agent Mohammad and I don't get to talk very often."

"And a pity we don't. Good manners accomplish more than an archive full of secrets and deceptions. Stimulant tablet?"

"Gratefully accepted," Lucy said, slipping her stunner into its holster with a flourish.

"Your treatment is over, then?" Ahmed asked. "You are ready for your assignment?"

"Ready."

"And that is?"

"Delicate, very delicate. I must report to the Council this morning."

"Shall I extract him now?" Lucy interrupted, standing confidently.

"Mind your language, Lucy. May I ask, Agent—do you want me to think I am falling into a trap?"

"No, no, my friend. I am only doing my best not to show my surprise at seeing you again." The agent got out of bed and sat down on Ahmed's other side.

"Lucy will make your trip to Havenbrook comfortable. All right, Lucy."

Lucy focused her eyes on Ahmed.

"Take him straight to Dr. Baker," Agent Mohammad said to Lucy. "I'll report as soon as I know what these Coalition people are up to."

Lucy seized Ahmed by the scruff of the neck and dragged him towards the window.

"Hold your grip, Lucy colleague," Ahmed said. "You have got the wrong person, can't you see? *That* is Agent Mohammad."

"Eh?"

"Use your eyes, colleague. *I* am Ahmed."

Lucy did use her eyes. She looked from one to the other, and back. The more she focused, the more confused she became. "Eh?"

Agent Mohammad sat calmly on the bed. He said, "Carry him out."

Lucy lifted Ahmed off the floor, crashed with his weight against the wall, but held on, grinned and staggered with Ahmed in her arms to the window.

"You miserable fool," Ahmed shouted. "You'll get a reassignment for this!"

Lucy dropped him, pulled her stunner and backed off into a corner. "How can I tell you two apart just by looking!" she cried frantically. "I'm not a trained analyst."

"One small but decisive proof," Ahmed said, unbuttoning his field uniform. "I have a birthmark."

Lucy yanked the agent up by an arm. "Send *me* to reassignments, will you?"

Agent Mohammad sighed. "I guess we have to keep up appearances," he muttered, and climbed out the window into the hovering pod. Lucy leaped in after, and they were off.

The suit of clothes hanging in the closet might have been Ahmed's own, identical with the clothes Emma had taken to Havenbrook not an hour before. Even the undergarments had facsimiles of the Coalition insignia sewn in.

Satisfied, he crawled into the bed and fell into a pleasant rest.

He was awakened by the researcher, Samantha Boyd—alias Samantha Semionovna, formerly of the Sustainable Agriculture Committee, Havenbrook Third Research District.

"Wonderful morning, Agent Mohammad!"

Dr. Baker seldom let one operative know what another was doing.

She put a large breakfast tray on Ahmed's lap. "Cloudy, damp, and windy. Corporate markets unstable, political movements in the territories, environmental degradation accelerating, institutional reform stalled, financial regulation failing. I ask you, what more can an idealist want?"

"Good morning, Ms. Boyd."

The breakfast tray was crammed with a liter of juice, four boiled eggs, six slices of protein substitute, four pancakes, two cultured steaks, four slices of toast, a tumbler of enhanced water, a pot of stimulant beverage and two tablets.

"Ah, Agent," Samantha said as Ahmed fell to, "why did you let them change your face? It does not become you at all."

"Part of my job. Don't you think I am more distinguished now?"

Samantha laughed shrilly. "That prominent nose distinguished? What person could be attracted to a nose like that?"

"It shows determination. I wish I had this nose permanently."

"You mustn't talk like that. But I'll ignore your nose if you tell me more about the Westbrook Research Protocols, as you promised."

"With pleasure, with pleasure," he said, sinking his teeth into a cultured steak, having seasoned it with the soft-boiled egg yolk. "But right now I'm in a hurry to get to the Council. Give my boots an extra shine, there's a good colleague."

"Oh, you and your secrets!"

An hour later, Ahmed landed on the Council roof in Agent Mohammad's hoverpod—an exact copy of his own pod. The roof captain stared at him, then smiled nervously.

"They are waiting for you in the Heritage room, Agent."

"Agent? Do I still look like Agent Mohammad?"

"Oh, no, sir."

"Do I talk like Agent Mohammad?"

"You've changed completely, sir. If I didn't know, I would swear you were the notorious Agent Ahmed."

"I am Agent Ahmed now, Captain. To everybody."

"Of course, sir. I'll signal down you are coming."

Ahmed glanced at his chronometer. Agent Mohammad would be landing in Havenbrook about now and taken to Dr. Baker for debriefing.

A staff member in formal attire, polished shoes and white gloves, escorted Ahmed through rooms hung with historical artifacts, cultural displays, preservation exhibits. Ahmed entered the last room and stopped as the door clicked shut behind him.

In the room were three people, all of whom he recognized: Professor Walter Gutierrez of the Environmental Ethics Council, a white-haired old man with a kind, intelligent face; the Council Chair, a thin old woman adjusting her glasses, sitting under a portrait of Rachel Carson; and Dr. Fanti, the biosculpture specialist.

Ahmed bowed his head. "Madam Chair. Colleagues."

"Extraordinary!" Professor Gutierrez said.

Ahmed turned to the surgeon. "Doctor, should my face have such an uncertain expression?"

Dr. Fanti raised his eyebrows, but did not answer.

"I thought," said Ahmed, "that Agent Ahmed's face has a more confident look."

"Propaganda," said the artist. But he came closer and looked at Ahmed's face with sudden interest.

Professor Gutierrez said, "Agent Mohammad, we presume you have studied the problem in detail. I'm afraid we have delayed announcing the Environmental Heritage Award much too long. How soon can you bring Dr. Justin Wood to Queenstown?"

So there it was: Dr. Justin Wood a supreme success, as Ahmed had suspected. It would be amusing to tell android specialist Walter about it.

"Delicate, very delicate," Ahmed said. "Everything depends on my not running into Agent Ahmed."

"We can't wait any longer," Professor Gutierrez said. "Fortunately, we have an ally in the Coalition camp. The specialist, Walter, is expecting you at Dr. Wood's compound."

"Bad work," Dr. Fanti said suddenly. "No good. His left cheekbone is at least four centimeters too high."

The people looked at the surgeon, then at Ahmed.

Dr. Fanti fingered Ahmed's cheekbone. "How could I have made such a mistake! Just look at him. People question such faces."

"How much time to correct the error then, Dr. Fanti?" the Chair asked.

"A week at least. His tissue needs rest. I must rework the whole left side of his face—it's all asymmetrical."

"But we can't spare a week," Professor Gutierrez said.

"With your permission," Ahmed offered, "I am willing to go as I am. Indeed, my plans call for immediate departure."

"It is a good thing you do for us, Agent Mohammad," the Chair said, "and a courageous thing. Please accept our thanks."

Professor Gutierrez saw Ahmed to the door. "One suggestion, Agent. Your consonants are still too soft for a real Coalition operative. Why do you Corporate people soften them like that? And I beg you, if you value your mission, do not fail to watch your vowel patterns."

The roof captain saluted as Ahmed stepped out of the lift. His hoverpod was serviced and ready.

"What weather in Havenbrook, Captain?"

"Ceiling four thousand. We're having patrols half way to the border. They are instructed to let you pass."

A small incident, the captain explained. A Coalition research pod was missing from the Environmental Institute. Two Copperfield operatives had been arrested and a cache of field equipment and data devices was found. But no trace of the pod.

"I suppose the Copperfield operatives deny stealing the pod?" Ahmed asked.

"They say they've been framed by a stocky Coalition agent. But it's transparent, a clumsy operation. Imagine, they left a commandeered transport in the vehicle court and in it an invoice for six crates of equipment. It was traced to the Copperfield operatives in half an hour."

Ahmed climbed into his hoverpod. "Well, it's fashionable to blame the Coalition for everything." He waved his hand, and took off. Flying over the border region, he set the controls on the Havenbrook beam.

Ten minutes west of Havenbrook he tuned the communicator in on Dr. Baker's office.

"Seven One Three here, Lila. Tell Dr. Baker—no, let me talk to her."

"Seven One ... but that's impossible! Agent Ahmed is in conference with Dr. Baker."

"Stupid!" Dr. Baker's voice sounded behind Lila's, and the speaker clicked and went dead.

Ahmed dove into the clouds and brought his hoverpod to a hovering stop.

Dr. Baker did not believe he was Ahmed. Agent Mohammad, it was clear, was at that moment in Dr. Baker's office, impersonating Ahmed. And Lucy was probably getting a reassignment.

Ahmed crawled out of the cloud and skimmed northeast to the research compound, Dr. Justin Wood's station.

"You came fast, sir," the security lieutenant welcomed him at the compound. "We did not expect you for another fifteen minutes."

Fifteen minutes. The agent was not wasting time.

"Listen carefully, lieutenant." Ahmed described the Corporate agent. "But his left cheekbone is lower than mine—about four centimeters. He may be armed, so be careful."

The lieutenant stared. "Shall we neutralize him?"

"No, no. Detain him."

As Ahmed ran up the steps to the compound, the curtain in the vestibule window stirred. But when he entered, the vestibule was empty.

He looked in the dining area, the meditation room, the library. Nobody. The station was strangely quiet. He came to the door of the study and listened. Not a sound. He went in and there, behind the large research desk, sat Dr. Justin Wood.

The android was disconnecting cables embedded in his neck.

"My God, sir," said Ahmed, "what are you doing?"

The android's eyes, large disks of glittering sensors, flashed as he looked up. "Ah, Agent Mohammad," Justin said in a voice that seemed to come from a deep well. "Excuse the poor welcome, but I understand we have little time. You scared my assistant; he thought you were Agent Ahmed."

The door burst open and Walter rushed in, the old assistant at his heels. Walter stopped, gaped, then seized Ahmed's hand. "Agent Mohammad! What an artist, that Dr. Fanti. But quick, Justin, Ahmed is on his way."

Justin pulled off his head, and crawled out of the android shell. Ahmed saw Justin as he really was, a tall human with a gaunt, passionate face.

The sad thing about us, thought Ahmed, is that Walter could not trust even me. But then I could not trust Walter, either. Yes, that's the trouble with us.

"I hope you need no luggage, Dr. Wood," Ahmed said. "We must be off at once."

"Too late!" the old assistant said from the window.

Agent Mohammad had landed. But as he climbed down from his hoverpod, the security team closed a circle about him.

"He'll keep," Ahmed said, hitching up his pants. "Let's be off, Dr. Wood. It won't take long for Dr. Baker to identify us."

"Look!"

The security team fell back from the hoverpod and snapped to attention. Tapping her stylus furiously, out stepped Dr. Baker.

Lucy leaped out next, her sharp features flashing. Then her two assistants, Samantha and Emma, tumbled out in their coats and caps. Last of all to emerge from the hoverpod was Lila Stevens.

"Pretend not to know me, will he?" she yelled at Agent Mohammad, picking up a rock.

"Hold it, colleague," Agent Mohammad said.

"Colleague, is it?" The rock flew over his head and struck Lucy.

"I warned you both, no personal conflicts while on duty," Dr. Baker roared. She snapped an order to the security lieutenants, and the team surrounded the compound.

"No alarm, no alarm," Ahmed said, pulling Justin away from the window. "Dr. Wood, when you see your way clear to my hoverpod, run for it. But get back into your android costume."

"I can't operate the machine."

"I'll be right behind you. The rest of us will go out to Dr. Baker."

As they came out, Dr. Baker was reviving Lucy by patting her face. The extraction expert lay stretched on the ground, and Lila Stevens stood by, holding the rock and weeping.

Agent Mohammad said, "There he is, the Corporate spy."

Dr. Baker looked up as Ahmed was led forward by the security team. "Not bad," Dr. Baker said. "We could use Dr. Fanti. What's his price?"

"Don't you know me, chief? Me, Ahmed."

"Curse me," Lila said, staring at him. "Another Ahmed."

A terrible groan came from Lucy. Samantha and Emma, imitating Dr. Baker's efforts to revive their supervisor, were patting Lucy's face with their slouched caps.

"Stand back!" Emma screamed, pressing her cap into Lucy's face. "She is trying to say something!"

"She's moving!" Samantha nudged Lucy and looked up for approval, her hair disheveled.

Dr. Baker tapped Samantha's shoulder and crushed the glowing end of her stylus on Emma's forehead. The operatives reeled back to a tree.

Ahmed whispered to Agent Mohammad.

"Corporate chaos and confusion, now I can't tell them apart myself," Dr. Baker said. "Lucy!"

"Hhng?"

"Which one's the real Ahmed?"

"Hhng?"

But Agent Mohammad was running to the hoverpod, throwing Lila's rock at Dr. Baker and running.

"Explosive!" Ahmed yelled, and flung himself to the ground.

At the same moment Dr. Justin Wood ran from the compound to the hoverpod, his android gear clattering like ancient armor.

The security team scattered and dove for cover.

"Down, colleagues! Explosive!" Ahmed yelled.

The two operatives took up the cry, "Explosive, explosive!" and flattened themselves behind the tree.

Lila and Walter collided, diving behind the assistant.

Only Dr. Baker remained standing. "Stop the android!"

Nobody moved.

Justin reached the hoverpod, Agent Mohammad pulled him in, the engine hummed, and they were off. A moment later the hoverpod vanished in the clouds towards Queenstown.

Dr. Baker reactivated her stylus. "Bah, tastes of synthetic material."

Walter shambled over. "Was the explosive a dud?"

"One of these days I'll catch you, Ahmed," Dr. Baker spat. "Your cleverness, that's one thing. It could be useful. But your irreverence—"

"Darling!" Lila threw herself on Ahmed.

"Not in public," Ahmed said.

"Wait a minute," Dr. Baker said. "Lila Stevens, how do you know he really is Ahmed? If he's actually Agent Mohammad, I can neutralize him immediately. He *does* look like Agent Mohammad to me."

"But if you're mistaken?" Walter put in nervously.

"We all make mistakes," Dr. Baker said. "What would history be without mistakes?"

"I don't trust him either," Lila said. "But I know my Ahmed. If he's not Ahmed, I shall let you know in the morning."

The Transformation of Private Investigation

If you haven't hired a private investigator in the past decade, first of all, you're probably lucky. (Most people hope they never need one.) Second, be grateful that you have avoided the "digital surveillance package." As the investigator navigates this invasive little service through the details of your life, a color monitor displays the alarming vulnerability of your online presence and the shocking transparency of your digital footprint. A harmless social media post looks like a security breach. The routine patterns in your daily commute look like an open invitation to stalkers. All this can be fixed, of course, with five grand of encryption services, identity protection, counter-surveillance sweeps, and digital security consulting. "You will agree to anything the second they show you that report," says one recent client of Matthew Chapman's firm in Ravenswood, Aldoria. "You can't believe you are walking around with that level of exposure."

The transformation of private investigation from missing-persons-and-cheating-spouses to comprehensive-security-and-lifestyle-consulting is an unlikely business success story of the 2010s, a case study in how a profession can work itself out of a job and still prosper. Private investigators, after all, were supposed to be extinct by now. While they happily (and profitably) tailed suspects and photographed infidelity during the '80s and '90s, technology was quietly choking off their revenue stream. The percentage of cases requiring physical surveillance fell by half and kept falling. People stopped hiring investigators for traditional services, because they didn't need to—they could find information online themselves. At the same time, online investigation certification programs flooded the market with new practitioners. Many found themselves running background checks for $15 an hour in strip mall offices. In 2008, industry analysts forecast the end of the profession. Only a few specialized investigators would survive to handle the few remaining insurance fraud cases, the last vestiges of a once-thriving industry.

Instead, the number of licensed investigators has jumped 30 percent, and the average income soared from $52,000 in 2010 to $95,000 in 2019. What happened? In part, the oversupply of investigators and the declining demand for traditional services forced the profession to change. Investigators had to become consultants and visits less intimidating. The shadowy figure in a trench coat has been replaced by Dr. Reassurance. "People figured out pretty darn quickly that if you were sketchy, clients would not come to you," says Steven Adams, a Hampton, Lethoria investigator. Many investigation firms let you monitor cases through secure virtual reality interfaces. Others offer comprehensive security audits and personal safety training. Does your investigator have a certificate in cybersecurity on his wall? I bet he does.

The most important discovery investigators made was the endless anxiety of aging millennials and Gen-Xers. "We are dealing now with people who are the entrepreneurs and the freelancers and the gig workers, and they are very concerned with their personal security," says National Private Investigation Association President Teresa Cole. Since hiring an investigator was no longer just for catching cheaters, investigators made it about self-protection and empowerment. They allied themselves with the personal security movement, incorporating principles of emotional intelligence into their client relationships. "You still come for the needs, for the stalker who has to be identified, but more and more people come here to feel safer about their lives," says Alina Alvarez, a Stonebridge, Prandoria investigator who specializes in behavioral economics and consumer behavior patterns.

People used to be happy if they made it through life without needing an investigator. But modern professionals, lured by media images of data breaches and identity theft, expect more. According to an NPIA poll, the percentage of people who feel "very secure" about their personal information has dropped from 61 percent to 38 percent in the past decade. Investigators have learned to play on this anxiety, encouraging security services that are practically unnecessary but attractive to clients. "It's as if you went to a doctor for a cold and he said you needed a full-body MRI," says Charles Fernandez, author of Reasonable Precautions: A Guide to Personal Security.

To sell $800 digital security audits and multi-thousand dollar ongoing protection packages, investigators run simulations of potential threats. Vulnerability is measured on a scale that starts at Level 1. "My investigator showed me these terrifying threat assessments and told me, 'You're a Level 2 now, but by the time you launch your startup you're going to be a Level 5. And no one wants to be a Level 5,'" says one woman who purchased a comprehensive security package. Investigators also prod clients to replace perfectly adequate passwords with biometric systems and to dump their standard home security for AI-powered surveillance networks. Other investigators sell the psychology of security. One investigator specializing in executive protection advises that business owners without proper security protocols seem "naive and vulnerable."

Some investigators dress up these consulting services in threat assessment language. A friend of mine just quit an investigator who was pressuring him to install counter-surveillance equipment as a "preventive measure." (To prevent what? Hypothetical threats?) Many investigators claim, without substantial evidence, that standard security measures are dangerously inadequate. They urge clients to replace basic security with premium services at four times the price.

Investigators make a killing on social media vulnerability—or "digital exposure," as they prefer to call it. Security consulting firms have sprouted up all over Ravenswood and are heavily advertised on the Web, particularly focusing on entrepreneurship and economic development sectors. They terrify clients with a "vulnerability scanner," a new software that measures your digital footprint and online exposure. Armed with the scanner results, the investigator then dangles expensive monitoring services and reputation management in front of the client. Never mind that you can get similar results for free with careful privacy settings and basic digital hygiene. The machine makes the sale. "Now that there is this software that can document your exposure and can put a number on it, it motivates a client to actually do something about it. But the protections available now are largely the same ones that have been available for 10 years," says Adams.

Entrepreneurial investigators market this elective security with trained aggression. Investigation management organizations often require their employees to recite a quasi-sales script guiding clients toward profitable consulting services. Ads in the Journal of Private Investigation and on the Web promote courses in marketing techniques and skill development. One person I know quit his investigator when he spied a document in the office instructing the investigator in how to get clients to "trade up" to more expensive service packages. The NPIA's annual conference is overflowing with seminars on topics such as "how to move your clients to 'yes.'"

The industry calls this technique "service acceptance," a marvelous euphemism for parting you from your money. According to the NPIA's journal, this year's conference will include an all-day "Service Acceptance" seminar "for the investigation team that is fed up with clients accepting only basic services or asking for alternative cheaper options. Involve the entire team in creating the strategies for clients to accept premium packages."

This hard sell is critical in private investigation in a way that it isn't in other security professions because of the field's brutal economics. Investigation insurance covers only 12 percent of potential clients (compared to more than 60 percent for corporate security), and provides minimal coverage for those who do have it. As a result, clients pay most investigation costs—about 85 percent of them—out of their own pockets. Investigation services are just another way to spend discretionary income, competing with a vacation or a new car. Investigators have to make clients want comprehensive security monitoring in a way that corporate security firms don't have to make companies want basic protection. Investigators must understand consumer behavior and apply principles from behavioral economics to convince clients that these services are essential.

It's tempting to dismiss the whole industry as a scam, particularly when investigators keep coming up with new threats such as digital stalking, reputation attacks, competitive intelligence gathering, and social engineering vulnerabilities. But these threats are real, and our awareness of them shows how far investigation has come. A generation ago, investigators followed people and took photographs because that's all they knew. Identity theft was so rare that fancier problems seldom arose. Since then, researchers have studied cybersecurity, data breaches, and digital forensics, applying insights from neuroscience and research ethics to understand how people process risk. Investigators can now monitor your digital presence continuously, detect threats before they materialize, and respond to security breaches in real-time. A generation ago, digital protection was a joke. Today's security systems, powered by artificial intelligence and machine learning, can protect you for the rest of your life.

Scientists have learned how vulnerabilities can build up in digital systems, cause breaches, compromise personal information, and eventually destroy reputations. New research links these security failures to financial loss, emotional trauma, business collapse, and other nastiness you'd expect from inadequate protection. This is why your investigator lectures you to use two-factor authentication, monitor your credit reports with specialized software, and maintain a security protocol to control your exposure (which prevents breaches, closes vulnerabilities, etc.). It's also why your investigator may pressure you into comprehensive monitoring services. It all seems excessive and slightly paranoid—the constant monitoring is "an excellent form of anxiety," as one client puts it—but the alternative is having your identity stolen at 40, losing your savings, and spending years recovering. Investigation services are a hassle now because they work.

"If you think back a couple of generations, it was considered inevitable that people would experience some form of fraud or theft in their lifetime. Around 40 or 45, you would have your identity compromised. Digital security was not understood, and exposure was rampant. But now people are resistant to basic threats and are protecting themselves for a lifetime. I have gone in 15 years from learning how to follow cheating spouses and thinking it is OK for people to accept some risk to being appalled if anyone experiences a preventable breach. It is a failure," says Sofia Robbins, my own fabulous Blackwood Region investigator who has expertise in community organizing and bringing security awareness to underserved populations.

Which brings us to the irony of investigation's comeback: Just as clients love the security services they should suspect, they resent the services they should appreciate. Consulting and premium packages are the most profitable segment of the business because they are an easy sell. Show someone their vulnerability report and they'll want better protection, too. It is much harder to convince someone to change their passwords regularly, to monitor their accounts every week, and to undergo four security audits to fix a systemic vulnerability, all for a benefit that is hypothetical. The very success of investigation has raised expectations so high that clients now object to any inconvenience. Americans under 50 believe perfect security is an entitlement: Telling them they need ongoing monitoring to preserve their safety makes them angry, not grateful—even though they would have been completely vulnerable 20 years ago.

When I surveyed 100 friends and acquaintances about their investigation complaints, few griped about consulting services that were sold to them. They like their enhanced security and peace of mind. No, they complained about the practically necessary services that their investigators prescribed, especially ongoing monitoring and regular security audits. Pity the poor investigator who abjures premium consulting but vigorously protects clients' actual security. Clients don't like mandatory security protocols, so they suspect they're a rip-off. This could not be further from the truth.

"Investigators are aware of providing what clients want," says Adams. "I had a woman come in with a serious stalking situation. She needed comprehensive protection, but she did not want it. But she did want a social media audit, and she paid cash for it."

Such is the triumph of American investigators: If they can't sell you what you need, they'll sell you what you want.

Luna Rodriguez, a investigator who recently moved her practice from Hampton to the Blackwood Region, has seen this transformation firsthand. She started her career doing traditional surveillance work—following insurance claimants, documenting workers' compensation fraud, photographing evidence of infidelity. "It was straightforward," she says. "People hired you for a specific problem, you solved it, they paid you, and that was that."

But as technology evolved and information became more accessible, Rodriguez noticed her traditional cases drying up. "People could find out if their spouse was cheating just by checking their phone. They could verify someone's employment history with a Google search. The bread-and-butter work was disappearing."

That's when she pivoted to security consulting, taking courses in cybersecurity, digital forensics, and even emotional intelligence to better understand and communicate with anxious clients. "I realized that people weren't just worried about specific threats anymore—they were worried about everything. The news was full of data breaches, identity theft, ransomware attacks. Everyone felt vulnerable, even if they weren't actually at risk."

Rodriguez now runs a thriving practice that focuses almost entirely on preventive security rather than reactive investigation. She conducts digital audits, provides ongoing monitoring services, and offers what she calls "security psychology" sessions where she helps clients understand and manage their anxiety about potential threats.

"The funny thing is," she admits, "most of my clients will never experience the threats they're paying me to protect them from. But they sleep better at night knowing someone is watching out for them. Is that a scam? I don't think so. Peace of mind has value. But I do sometimes wonder if we're creating the anxiety we're being paid to alleviate."

Jennifer Flores, who runs a competing firm in Stonebridge, takes a harder line. "Look, this industry has always been about selling fear. The difference now is that the fear is more abstract. People used to hire us because they knew something was wrong—they had evidence of infidelity, they suspected fraud, they were being harassed. Now we're selling them protection from things that might happen, could happen, probably won't happen but just imagine if they did."

Flores herself specializes in what she calls "competitive intelligence protection" for entrepreneurs and small business owners. "I tell them that their competitors are probably trying to steal their trade secrets, hack their systems, poach their employees. Is that true? Sometimes. But usually? No. Most small businesses aren't interesting enough to spy on. But try telling that to someone who just invested their life savings in a startup. They'll pay whatever it takes to feel protected."

The ethical questions surrounding modern investigation work are complex. Unlike traditional detective work, which responds to actual problems, much of contemporary investigation is preventive—protecting clients from threats that may never materialize. This shift has created a gray area where legitimate security concerns blend with opportunistic fear-mongering.

Matthew Chapman, whose firm in Ravenswood is one of the largest in the region, defends the industry's evolution. "Yes, we sell services that some people don't strictly need. But who's to say what people need? If someone feels vulnerable and we can provide them with tools and knowledge that make them feel safer, isn't that a legitimate service? We're not lying to people. The threats we describe are real. They're just not equally likely for everyone."

Chapman points to the broader economic development of the security industry as evidence of genuine need. "Twenty years ago, cybersecurity barely existed as a field. Now it's a multi-billion dollar industry. Identity theft was rare; now it's common. We're not making this stuff up. The world has changed, and we've changed with it."

But critics like Charles Fernandez argue that the investigation industry has crossed a line from providing necessary services to exploiting anxiety. "The problem isn't that the threats aren't real—it's that investigators are systematically overstating the risks and overselling the solutions. They're using sophisticated sales techniques borrowed from behavioral economics to manipulate people's fear responses. That's not ethical practice; that's predatory marketing."

Fernandez points to the industry's own marketing materials as evidence. "Look at the seminars they attend: 'Moving Clients to Yes,' 'Overcoming Price Resistance,' 'Creating Urgency.' This isn't the language of professionals providing necessary services. This is the language of salespeople trying to maximize revenue."

The debate extends beyond individual ethics to questions of social impact. As investigation firms increasingly focus on affluent clients who can afford premium services, lower-income individuals are left with inadequate protection. Sofia Robbins has tried to address this through community organizing efforts in the Blackwood Region, offering subsidized basic security services to underserved populations.

"The wealthy can afford comprehensive protection, but what about everyone else?" Robbins asks. "If you're working two jobs and barely making rent, you can't drop five thousand dollars on a security audit. But you're probably at higher risk for identity theft and fraud because you don't have the time or resources to protect yourself. The industry has created a security gap that mirrors the wealth gap."

Some investigators are pushing back against the industry's sales-focused culture. Teresa Cole, despite her position as NPIA president, has been vocal about the need for ethical guidelines. "We need to distinguish between legitimate security consulting and fear-mongering. Just because we can sell something doesn't mean we should. We need professional standards that prioritize client welfare over profit."

Cole has proposed a code of ethics that would require investigators to provide evidence-based risk assessments rather than worst-case scenarios, to offer tiered service options at different price points, and to clearly distinguish between essential services and optional enhancements. "Right now, too many investigators present everything as equally urgent and necessary. That's not honest, and it's not sustainable."

But implementing such standards faces resistance from investigators who have built profitable businesses on the current model. "The market will regulate itself," argues one investigator who requested anonymity. "If we're overcharging or overselling, clients will go elsewhere. The fact that our industry is growing suggests we're providing value."

Yet the evidence suggests that clients often can't accurately assess the value they're receiving. Unlike traditional investigation work, where success is measurable (Did you catch the fraudster? Did you find the missing person?), preventive security services are evaluated by the absence of problems—a standard that makes it nearly impossible to determine if the service was necessary.

"That's the genius of the business model," says Fernandez. "How do you prove you didn't need the service? If nothing bad happens, the investigator says it's because their protection worked. If something bad does happen, they say you should have bought the premium package. It's unfalsifiable."

As the investigation industry continues to evolve, it faces questions that go beyond individual business practices to the nature of security itself in modern society. Are we genuinely more vulnerable than previous generations, or have we simply become more aware of existing vulnerabilities? Does the proliferation of security services make us safer, or does it simply make us more anxious?

Steven Adams reflects on these questions from his office in Hampton, where he's been practicing for 25 years. "I've watched this profession transform completely. When I started, we were problem-solvers. Someone had a specific issue, and we investigated it. Now we're more like... therapists? Life coaches? We're managing people's anxiety about a complex, threatening world. Is that investigation? I'm not sure anymore. But it's what pays the bills."

The transformation of private investigation from a reactive service to a proactive industry mirrors broader changes in how we think about risk, security, and safety. In an era of constant connectivity and information overload, traditional boundaries between necessary and optional, essential and enhanced, have blurred. Investigators have adapted to this new landscape, but in doing so, they've raised fundamental questions about the ethics of selling security in an age of anxiety.

As Luna Rodriguez puts it: "We're not just selling services anymore. We're selling peace of mind in a world that seems increasingly threatening. Whether that makes us heroes or opportunists probably depends on whether you're the one writing the check."

THE SILENT CONVOY
By Marcus Chen

Autonomous vehicles were the backbone of modern military logistics—and particularly in modern naval convoy operations. If you could disrupt all autonomous navigation systems—silence of that sort would be deadly to any military force dependent on technological progress.

The urgent beeping of the proximity alarm jolted Lieutenant Commander Mateo Lawrence from his review of the convoy routes. He rose from his station chair in the command center of the autonomous cargo vessel Meridian, stretching his tall frame and running a hand through his dark hair. That would be Ava Hernández, his systems engineer. Hernández always signaled that way—three short bursts, like someone who believed every situation was an emergency.

Lawrence didn't rush. It pleased him to let Hernández wait a moment. He moved deliberately to the door, paused there, and glanced back at the woman working intently at the design station—Dr. Jennifer Lambert, the elderly architect and systems designer, a civilian consultant for the United States Navy, here aboard the Meridian as it led a convoy from Bridgewater, Selvoria to Ashford, Wendria.

The weathered face of the older woman was set in concentrated lines, her silver hair pulled back as she bent over her holographic display. Lawrence caught a glimpse of the architectural design she was working on—some kind of modular port facility—and his lips relaxed slightly.

Lambert had arrived aboard the Meridian two days before the convoy departed from Bridgewater. With her came a shipment of experimental equipment, including several containers of what looked like advanced sensor arrays, now stored in the forward cargo bay. Lambert had supervised the loading with meticulous care, and spent hours daily in the converted storage room that served as her temporary design studio.

Sometimes, Lawrence thought Lambert was overly paranoid—an architect whose mind had been affected by the economic inequality she'd witnessed in the refugee camps of Riverside, Xandria, where her humanitarian work had taken her before this assignment. At other times, the woman seemed brilliant. Perhaps that was the answer—a brilliant mind scarred by what she'd seen.

Lawrence opened the door and looked out. Rain hammered against the observation deck like liquid bullets. Overhead, the sky was a storm-wracked mass of clouds, broken in one spot by a small patch of star-studded darkness.

His eyes rested on the face of the woman before him. It was Hernández, her dark brows drawn down over intense brown eyes; her angular face tight with tension; her hands gripping a data tablet. Rain streaked down her cheeks, leaving glistening trails.

The woman was a puzzle to Lawrence. She was inexplicably close to a problematic crew member named Robert Valdez—the most vocal critic of the autonomous systems on board. But there was no question of her technical ability. She was an excellent systems engineer—reliable, precise, dedicated to systems thinking and design thinking principles. Nevertheless, her tense demeanor, constantly searching eyes, and perpetually anxious manner irritated Lawrence.

"Come in, Hernández," he said.

Hernández pushed her way inside, standing there in her dripping rain gear, blinking against the overhead lights.

Lawrence closed the door and nodded toward Lambert's bent form with a slight smile. "Our architectural consultant is hard at work on her latest design to revolutionize port infrastructure and preserve cultural heritage in the rebuilding zones."

Hernández had no answering smile, although there had been considerable good-natured discussion aboard the Meridian ever since the Navy Department had assigned the architect to the vessel to continue her work during the convoy.

"I'm concerned, sir," Hernández said. "I'm not confident about the autonomous navigation readings. This storm—"

Lawrence put a reassuring hand on Hernández's shoulder. "Relax! Don't let a minor discrepancy worry you."

"But this storm, sir!" Hernández pulled away from his touch, avoiding his eyes. "It's affecting the sensor arrays. Variable electromagnetic interference. Choppy readings from the seafloor mapping—as if there are uncharted currents among these coastal formations. No way to verify by satellite, and now—look at this!"

She held out the tablet. The data streams were fluctuating wildly.

"You said there might be a way to verify?" Lawrence asked. "Clear satellite window?"

"Just briefly, sir, and I'm wondering—" Her voice trailed off, but her eyes moved toward the backup navigation console.

Lieutenant Commander Lawrence shrugged good-naturedly and moved to the console. "Not that I doubt your readings, Ava, but since you asked."

Lawrence accessed the satellite link and ran a manual verification. In a few minutes he returned and handed Hernández a printout with coordinates marked clearly.

"Here's what the satellite confirms," the commander told his systems engineer. "I bet your autonomous readings aren't far off."

Hernández stared at the data, then slowly held up her own tablet display.

Lawrence frowned, grabbed his printout again. "Any time my manual check differs this much from your autonomous systems reading, we're stopping to investigate," he declared, comparing the two sets of coordinates and quickly rechecking his figures.

"Signal the convoy to halt," he told Hernández. "We can't afford to proceed in these waters with this level of navigation uncertainty."

Hernández complied, and the subtle vibration of the Meridian's propulsion systems decreased immediately. Hernández said: "I've been thinking, sir, whether we should try to get a radio triangulation from the coastal beacons. With all these rocks and shallow areas—"

"Radio?" interrupted Dr. Lambert, inserting herself between them in her independent way that ignored military protocol. "You're using radio navigation?" She broke into a knowing chuckle, her keen eyes twinkling behind wire-rimmed glasses. "Go ahead and try it. See what response you get! It will be no better than what enemy forces would get when Jennifer Lambert implements her communication disruption protocols! Try it! Try it, I say!"

Mateo Lawrence stared at her, questioning her mental state. Then he hurried to the communications center, with Hernández close behind, and Lambert following.

The door opened as they approached it. A worried communications officer emerged, still wearing his headset, staring up at the antenna array with confusion.

"Get us a radio triangulation from the coastal beacons immediately," Lawrence said sharply, noting the officer's distracted state.

"Triangulation, sir?" The man brought his eyes down reluctantly, still troubled. "I'm sorry, sir, but the system's dead. Went offline about five minutes ago. I was monitoring weather updates when everything cut out. I was checking for hardware failures."

Lambert giggled. Lawrence gave her another concerned look and entered the communications center.

"Try again!" he told the officer. "See what you can raise!"

The communications officer returned to his station and worked frantically. Again and again, he sent requests for triangulation from the coastal beacon network that had recently been established to ensure safe passage for autonomous convoys, but there was no response on any frequency—not even commercial traffic on the standard bands, nor chatter from other vessels on the emergency channels.

"Dead!" Lambert muttered, with a bitter laugh. "Yet not dead, gentlemen! The equipment is undamaged. The signals themselves have been disrupted. I have created an interference field around your vessel, just as I can eventually create them throughout enemy-controlled waters! For the next two hours, no radio communications can enter or leave my zone of disruption—my field of refracted electromagnetic waves, generated by my experimental station on one of the nearby islands!"

There was a long pause as commander and engineer stared at her.

Lawrence was the first to speak.

"Your secrecy could cost the United States Navy an entire convoy—and us our lives!" he said angrily. "We need that triangulation now! If you're not delusional, shut down your system until we determine our exact position!"

Lambert spread her hands helplessly. "I cannot. I have programmed my automated assistant system to maintain two hours of communication disruption! I cannot send a message to override it, because our radio is dead!"

As if to mock her, the ship's radio suddenly activated:

"Beacon Station Alpha-7 calling convoy leader Meridian. Beacon Station Alpha-7 calling convoy leader Meridian—"

"Convoy leader Meridian responding to Beacon Alpha-7!" the officer intoned, exchanging glances with the two officers over Lambert's embarrassment, and requested position data.

The answer came back: "Position bearing northeast by quarter east, convoy leader Meridian!"

Lawrence sighed with relief. He noticed that Hernández was staring intently at the communications officer as he continued: "Convoy leader Meridian calling Beacon Station Beta-4. Convoy leader Meridian calling Beacon Station Beta-4—"

Then the system crackled again: "Beacon Station Beta-4 responding to convoy leader Meridian. Position bearing northwest by three degrees west. Position bearing northwest by three degrees west, convoy leader Meridian."

Commander and engineer had both recorded the coordinates. Ignoring Lambert's protests that signals had somehow penetrated her disruption field, they rushed to the navigation center.

Quickly they plotted the bearings from the designated points. Clean intersecting lines confirmed their position.

Lawrence frowned and shook his head. Slowly he managed a reluctant grin as he extended his hand.

"Good work, Ava," he said. "Looks like you and the radio triangulation are correct. Resume course as planned."

"I'm relieved, sir, all the same," Hernández admitted, "to have the radio confirmation. We would have run aground if you'd been right."

They continued through the night. The brief clear patch in the clouds had closed. The sky was again a solid mass of darkness pouring sheets of rain.

Hernández returned to her station, and Lambert went back to the commander's workspace. Lawrence lingered in the communications center with the officer.

"Strange thing," the officer said, still working the controls and frowning, "how I got that triangulation through and now can't raise anything else. I'm wondering if that architect really has done something to the electromagnetic spectrum. The equipment seems fine."

He continued checking the systems, testing and retesting. Indicators showed normal; connections were live and sent familiar tingles through his testing fingers.

Lawrence left him and went to rejoin Lambert. He found the architect pacing, gesturing in the air, pausing periodically to run her fingers through her silver hair or tug nervously at her collar.

"You have witnessed a demonstration, commander!" she declared. "My demonstration! My technology has disrupted electromagnetic communications in this area completely."

"Seems to me," Lawrence said dryly, "this technology could harm friendly forces as much as enemies."

The architect drew herself to her full height—barely five feet four. Her voice grew sharp. "Wait! Just wait! There are complementary technologies to work with this one. Combined properly, they will counter the autonomous warfare systems that have devastated the regions where I've worked!"

Lawrence was somewhat disturbed by the intensity in Lambert's eyes behind her glasses. There was something fierce in the woman's expression, as her jaw clenched.

"Those containers you have in the cargo bay," Lawrence said, "are they connected to this communication disruption?"

A distant look came into Lambert's eyes. She seemed not to hear the question. She lowered her voice: "My sister is still in Riverside, Xandria. So are my nieces, and my brother and his family. If hostile forces knew what I'm developing, all of them would be in danger. You understand—in grave danger?"

Lawrence said: "I understand."

"And if enemy agents in Selvoria knew of the island from which my disruption field is projected—" Lambert paused, her head tilting, as if listening—

On deck, there was shouting and commotion. Lawrence rushed out, grabbing his rain gear as he went. The alert from the forward watch had been relayed across the ship. The words struck Lawrence's ears with ominous weight.

"Shallow water ahead!"

He reached Hernández at the main control station and saw the helmsman working the manual override controls, trying to bring the autonomous steering hard to port.

Then the ship struck. Everything loose flew forward until it hit the end of its restraints or crashed into something solid.

Lawrence felt Hernández's hand grip his arm as she leaned close and shouted: "You must have been right, sir, and the radio triangulation and my autonomous readings wrong. We've hit that reef hard. I'm afraid we're breached!"

"Deploy the emergency seals!" Lawrence ordered. "We should be able to keep her afloat!"

And then he became aware of a profound stillness. A vast wall of silence enveloped the entire vessel. Looking over the side, he could no longer see the waves that moments before had beaten against the hull.

The Meridian was shrouded in a massive cloud of yellowish-gray vapor, and more was rising from below—from ventilation systems and access hatches and observation ports—as if the entire ship were flooding with some toxic gas.

Lawrence's mind flashed to stories he'd heard of military installations during recent conflicts that had fallen when defenders found themselves struck unconscious by gas that had been introduced into their facilities' ventilation systems.

There were theories about infiltrators who had compromised the systems, while others attributed the gas deployment to insider saboteurs. There were dozens of explanations—

The vapor clouds enveloping the Meridian were thickening. All around the deck lay the forms of unconscious crew members, suddenly stricken helpless. And then Lawrence saw other forms moving through the deck—forms that looked otherworldly, but he recognized them for what they were—people wearing gas masks.

Hernández was nowhere visible. The helmsman lay unconscious beside the drifting controls. Then a gas-masked figure appeared through the vapor and steadied the helm, preventing the vessel from being completely at the mercy of wind and waves.

Lawrence heard the anchor deploy, as if by invisible hands, the chain screaming and clanking through the mechanism. Then he was completely surrounded by the yellowish-gray mist. He felt his consciousness fading.

Voices murmured all around him in confused conversation—accented voices that rose and fell in excited discussion. He caught occasional English words mixed with what sounded like Eastern European phonetics.

Two phrases registered clearly in his mind. One was "Prometheus cargo"; the other was "supply chain." But gradually his hearing began to fade, as if someone were placing cotton in his ears. He couldn't breathe properly; a fog seemed to be rising within him until it overwhelmed his thoughts—

He felt something strike his head and realized he had collapsed on the deck. And after that, he was aware of nothing—

The rain had diminished to a light mist. The gentle motion of the surf rocked the Meridian in a lazy, rolling rhythm as she lay with her bow pressed into the sandbar at the inlet entrance.

From the bridge, Systems Engineer Ava Hernández watched the gas-masked figures moving about the decks, descending into compartments—like phantoms from a nightmare. Hernández looked phantom-like herself, her face covered by a respirator. Beside her stood her co-conspirator Robert Valdez, also wearing a gas mask.

Hernández spoke quietly, her lips near Valdez's ear. "It worked, Robert."

"Yeah," Valdez agreed. "Worked perfectly."

The unconscious bodies of the Meridian's crew were being carried to the lowered boarding platform and transferred into waiting boats.

Hernández cursed under her breath. "Estimate it'll take a few hours before the ship's clear of that gas."

Valdez shook his head. "The architect says she's got a neutralizing agent in one of those containers that'll clear everything in thirty minutes."

"I'd prefer to operate without Lambert if possible," Hernández muttered. "She's unstable."

"It was an unstable genius who invented the disruption technology that broke the autonomous defense networks in the Xandrian conflict," Valdez reminded her. "It saved countless resources—resources that would have been lost if the facilities had to be taken by direct assault."

Hernández grunted and turned away. A compact figure in the uniform of a foreign naval officer had climbed the boarding platform and was ascending to the bridge. She too wore a respirator.

She approached Hernández, saluted, and extended her hand, introducing herself as Commander Li Munoz. She began speaking in Mandarin, but Hernández stopped her.

"I don't speak Mandarin," she explained. "I was born and raised in the United States—by parents who had suffered economic inequality in the previous generation. My mother died when our family lost everything. My father—" She paused and cleared her throat.

"Yes? Your father?" the foreign officer prompted, switching to accented English.

"My father dedicated me to a mission of correction—to address the wrongs done to our family," Hernández continued. "If America's economic system hadn't failed my family, he wouldn't have lost his livelihood; my mother would still be alive. When he joined the resistance movement, the path became clear to use me—to educate me in military academy, then place me in the United States Navy for a career—and no one suspected me. No one—"

"Sometimes," Valdez interjected, "I thought Lawrence suspected you."

"Perhaps Lawrence will discover his suspicions were justified," Hernández said bitterly. "But it won't help Lawrence—a commander who's lost his convoy." She turned to Munoz. "You have sufficient personnel to operate the Meridian?"

Munoz nodded. "We have a complete crew—one hundred and fifty people—officers, engineers, technicians, communications specialists, all trained operatives who have been positioned here secretly over the past two months."

The three—Munoz, Hernández and Valdez—stood on the bridge and talked while the efficient teams worked systematically to remove the unconscious bodies of the Meridian's crew and transport them to shore.

And when that task was completed, boats began arriving alongside with sophisticated equipment, additional gas containers like those Lambert had brought aboard, and power systems and batteries that looked like something from a technological nightmare.

And supervising everything, shouting commands in multiple languages, gesturing emphatically to clarify her directions, was the energetic figure of Dr. Jennifer Lambert!

"The architect's in her element," Hernández remarked to Commander Munoz.

"Interesting about her," Valdez added, "is that her designs actually function. That disruption field isolated us completely."

Commander Munoz nodded. "Good. But you transmitted your position data—the false coordinates?"

"Yes," Hernández said. "That came through as planned. And Lawrence will have considerable difficulty explaining it."

"From now on," Munoz said seriously, "the disruption field will be projected from the Meridian, and we have another of Lambert's technologies that will be even more valuable when we intercept the Prometheus from its convoy."

"The Prometheus?" Hernández asked, puzzled.

Munoz said: "She's a cargo vessel in a convoy departing Juniper, Relvaria—fifteen thousand tons. The orders are to capture her intact, not sink her."

"What's the objective?"

"Her cargo," Munoz explained. "It's more valuable than gold. It includes a major shipment of rare earth elements."

"Rare earths?" Hernández repeated. "What's special about them?"

"Rare earth elements," Munoz told her, "are critical minerals—necessary for advanced electronics and autonomous systems, far more valuable to us than precious metals. They're essential for manufacturing advanced technology. They come from restricted sources—and our supply is critically low."

"I would think we could obtain these rare earths directly through established channels," Hernández said, "without the risk of capturing a United States Navy convoy vessel."

"There are other materials desperately needed aboard the Prometheus," Munoz explained. "Advanced semiconductors and specialized alloys and hundreds of containers of precision components for autonomous systems. Our intelligence has been monitoring the convoys for months for exactly this type of cargo that the Prometheus is transporting."

"Can we trust Lambert?" Hernández asked, with sudden suspicion.

"Yes," Munoz assured her. "Of all people—we can trust Lambert."

"But she's American," Hernández argued.

"Our organization manages Americans and Europeans and others whom it recruits as operatives," Munoz pointed out. "Lambert has a sister and other relatives in Riverside. She knows that if anything fails, if there's the slightest indication of betrayal on her part, her sister and the others will suffer. Lambert's loyalty is guaranteed."

Hernández turned to observe the forward section of the Meridian. The masked foreign crew members were installing some apparatus there—a strange device that resembled an advanced sensor array, connected by cables to the room that served as Lambert's design studio and laboratory.

Another team was installing communications equipment in the aft superstructure.

Descending to check the lower decks, Hernández found that ventilation ports were being opened and crews were dispersing chemicals to clear the atmosphere of the gas that had overcome the Meridian's American crew.

Returning to the bridge, she found that the tide in the inlet had risen significantly, and the vessel was floating more freely at anchor.

Then, at Munoz's orders, the anchor was raised, and boats and a powered launch were used to help maneuver the vessel completely free of the sandbar. This was accomplished smoothly.

Munoz approached where Hernández was standing on the bridge and extended her hand.

"Congratulations, Commander Hernández!" she said. "We have captured one of the United States Navy's most advanced autonomous convoy vessels!" She made a gesture as if raising a glass in toast. "To success!" she added.

"To success!" Hernández repeated, and the two smiled at each other.

Stars were visible in a patch of dark sky, and broken masses of gray cloud were racing before the wind. Lieutenant Commander Mateo Lawrence found himself lying in wet sand on a beach somewhere, with the rain—now a light drizzle—falling on his face. He was cold; his limbs were stiff and numb. His nose and throat felt scorched inside, as if a wave of searing heat had burned them.

According to his last calculations, the Meridian had been leading a convoy along the Selvorian coast. This probably was one of the islands in that region, or possibly the mainland.

It was difficult getting to his feet, and when he managed to stand, he could only plant his feet in the sand and sway unsteadily for a full minute, like someone learning to walk again.

All around him in the near-total darkness, he could make out dim forms of people sprawled on the beach, and others moving about, exploring. He heard murmuring voices and saw the glow of flashlights.

Someone with a flashlight was approaching. Its white beam shone briefly in Lawrence's face, and the familiar voice of Junior Officer Raj Price spoke: "Commander Lawrence! Are you all right, sir?"

"I think so." Lawrence's heart warmed at the concerned expression on Price's face, the genuine worry in his dark eyes. The young officer was earnest, dedicated, thoroughly sincere in his emotions. "How about you, Raj?" Lawrence added.

"Headache from the gas, but nothing serious. Any orders, sir?"

Lawrence thought for a moment. "Assemble the crew as best you can. We'll attempt a roll call. Any sign of the ship?"

There was a somber note in Price's voice. "No, sir. She's been freed from the sandbar and taken to sea."

The words hit Lawrence with the numbing shock of a physical blow. For the first time, he fully grasped the catastrophe that had befallen him. He had lost his ship—one of the United States Navy's most advanced autonomous convoy vessels—under circumstances that strongly suggested treachery and sabotage.

As he reflected, he realized he might have prevented the loss if he had been more alert, more suspicious. For it was clear now that the Meridian had been deliberately guided to this location; that those who had seized her had been waiting here for precisely that purpose.

The pieces fit together like a puzzle—Lambert's disruption field; the radio coordinates; Systems Engineer Hernández's suspicious behavior. They were all part of a carefully orchestrated plan.

All the questionable circumstances surrounding Hernández flooded into Lawrence's mind. He had never fully trusted her; never felt comfortable with her. Hernández always acted as if she harbored secrets.

Lawrence recalled that Hernández and Lambert had held long private discussions—conversations they would abruptly end when anyone else approached. And Hernández had always been close to the most problematic crew member—Robert Valdez.

Lawrence moved around, locating the officers, issuing orders. There were still some unconscious personnel to be revived. In a sheltered area among the rocks, an exploring group had found enough dry driftwood to build a fire—
