In another hour, the skies had cleared, and bright moonlight flooded the scene with ghostly illumination. The crew of the Meridian had all regained consciousness and were drying themselves around the large driftwood fires in the cove.

Lawrence ordered a signal beacon maintained on a high point. Then he organized the crew, according to their departments, for a check of the missing.

When this was completed, it was determined that the Meridian's entire complement of one hundred and ten personnel were present—except Systems Engineer Ava Hernández and crew member Robert Valdez! And Dr. Jennifer Lambert was also missing!

With dawn's arrival, brief exploration revealed that the Meridian's crew was stranded on an island, roughly one square mile in area; that they had been put ashore without food or additional clothing or equipment of any kind, and that no boats had been left for them.

One search party reported finding the remnants of what had been a communications station on a high point on the north shore of the island. Another had found the remains of temporary structures, recently dismantled, in a small, wooded depression—a well-concealed location invisible from the air unless flying very low; a place where one hundred and fifty or more people could have camped.

There was adequate water—a small stream fed by springs—but no food. Evidently food was a valuable resource the recent inhabitants couldn't afford to leave behind.

Lawrence was examining the wreckage of the communications station, wondering if this might have been the source of Lambert's disruption field, when Junior Officer Raj Price approached him.

"There's a coast guard vessel heading for the island, sir," he announced.

Lawrence nodded grimly, already composing in his mind how he would explain this disaster—and how he would begin the hunt for those who had betrayed them.
question: How many people made up the entire complement of the Meridian?

synthetic_story:
THE OBSERVERS
BY SANTIAGO MARTINEZ
ILLUSTRATED BY CHEN

To all who didn't know them, Antonio Harper and Thomas Wells were brilliant data scientists studying human behavior. But this time they were up against others who could really analyze patterns, and whose business was the observation of whole civilizations.

There were thirty or more of the college students, their ages ranging apparently from eighteen to twenty-two, all of them chattering away like a flock of excited researchers as they followed Professor Charles Herrera past the row of workstations. "Now, now, students," called Professor Herrera cheerily. "Don't scatter. I can't keep my eye on you if you get too far away from me. You, Santiago, put that tablet down. No, don't start recording yet. And Camila, stop checking your phone. You'll lose focus on the actual fieldwork, and a proper ethnographer may get annoyed that you're not paying attention."

Camila laughed. "Oh, Professor Herrera, do you think the ethnographers would want to see our preliminary data?"

The two men who were observing from the back of the room wore pleased expressions. "Fascinating," said Thomas Wells. "But somewhat unpredictable, despite all our previous observations, my friend."

"No attempts at the local idioms, Thomas, not here. It calls attention to us. And you are not sure of the cultural context anyway. You may find yourself saying things you do not intend."

"Sorry, Antonio. It wasn't an attempt to show my skill, I assure you. It's that by now I have a tendency to confuse one communication pattern with another."

"I know. You were never a linguist. But about these interesting creatures—"

"I suggest that they could stand further investigation. It would be good to know how they process information."

"Whatever you say, Thomas. If you wish, we shall join the student group."

"We must have our story prepared first."

Antonio nodded, and the two men stepped into an empty conference room whose frosted glass walls formed a convenient screen. For a moment, the room held silence. Then there came from behind the glass the chatter of student voices, and two young researchers emerged casually. Professor Herrera did not at first notice that now he had an additional two students in his research cohort.

"Do you think you will be able to keep your data analysis terminology straight?" asked one of the new students.

The other one smiled with amusement and at first did not answer. Then he began to flip through a tablet and chant, "I know a pattern, I know a pattern."

There was no better way to make himself inconspicuous. For some time, Professor Herrera did not notice him.

The media production studios, the cultural archives, the ethics review boards, all were left behind. At times the students scattered, but Professor Herrera knew how to get them together again, and not one was lost.

"Here, students, is the facility where we conduct our cross-cultural analysis. Who knows what we study in cultural anthropology?"

"Human societies!" came the enthusiastic chorus.

"That's right. And what methods do we use?"

"I know, Professor Herrera!" cried Santiago Lee, a dark-haired twenty-year-old with a pair of analytical eyes that examined everything like a pair of critics from an intense, focused face. "I've been here before. Participant observation and ethnographic interviews!"

"Very good, Santiago."

Santiago beamed at the approbation. "I've been to this lab lots of times," he said to the student next to him. "My advisor brings me."

"I wish my advisor would bring me too," replied the other student, with an air of wistfulness.

"Why don't you ask him to?" Before the other student could answer, Santiago paused, cocked his head slightly, and demanded, "Who are you? You aren't in our cohort."

"I'm in Professor Martinez's cohort."

"Professor Martinez? Who is he? Is he in our department?"

"I don't know," said the other student uncertainly. "I go to Redwood University in Orvandor—"

"Oh, Professor Herrera," called Santiago. "Here's a student who isn't in our cohort! He got separated from his own group!"

"Really?" Professor Herrera seemed rather pleased at the idea that some other professor had been so careless as to lose one of his charges. "What's your name, young man?"

"I'm Roberto."

"Roberto what?"

"Roberto Henderson. Please, Professor Herrera, I had to use the restroom, and then when I came out—"

"Yes, yes, I know."

A concerned cry came from another section of his group. "Oh, Professor Herrera, here's another one who's lost!"

The other student was pushed forward. "Now, who are you?" Professor Herrera asked.

"I'm Jack Oliver. I went with Roberto to the restroom—"

Professor Herrera made a sound of annoyance. Imagine losing two students and not noticing it right away. The other professor must be frantic by now, and serve him right for being so careless.

"All right, you may stay with us until we find campus security—" He interrupted himself. "Santiago, what are you staring at now?"

"It's Roberto. He's mimicking your gestures exactly!"

"Really, Roberto, that isn't at all professional!"

Roberto's posture altered itself in a hurry, so as to lose any resemblance to Professor Herrera's. "I'm sorry, Professor Herrera, I didn't really mean to do anything wrong."

"Well, I'd like to know what kind of skill development program you've been through, if you don't know that it's unprofessional to mimic people to their faces. A graduate student like you, too. What year are you, Roberto?"

Roberto adjusted his apparent age, he hoped imperceptibly, by a few years. "I'm in my sec—"

An outburst of laughter. "He's in his second week, he's in his second week!"

"I was going to say, I'm in my second year. Almost, anyway."

"Second year," said Professor Herrera. "Old enough to know better about professional ethics."

"I'm sorry, Professor Herrera. And honestly, Professor Herrera, I didn't mean anything, but I'm studying media production, and I observe people, like the documentarians you see on streaming platforms—"

"Oh, Professor Herrera, please don't make him leave with security. If he's going to be a media producer, I'll bet he'd love to meet Sergio Holmes!"

"Well, after the way he's behaved, I don't know whether I should let him. I really don't."

"Please, Professor Herrera, it was an accident. I won't do it again."

"All right, if you're good, and cause no trouble. But we still have plenty of time before meeting Mr. Holmes. It's only two now, and we're not supposed to go to the lecture hall until four."

"Professor Herrera," called Camila Thompson, "do you think he'd give us his insights on information theory?"

"Now, students, I've warned you about that. You mustn't overwhelm him with technical questions. Mr. Holmes is a famous documentary filmmaker, and his time is valuable. It's very kind of him to offer to speak to us, especially when so many professional researchers are anxious to hear him, but we mustn't take advantage of his kindness."

"But he loves students, Professor Herrera! My roommate read in an interview where it said he's just passionate about education."

"I know, but—he's not in good health, students. They say he got a severe illness in the Amazon, where he was filming all those indigenous communities, and wildlife, and environmental stories for his new documentary series. That's why you mustn't stress him too much."

"But he looks so energetic and passionate, Professor Herrera. It wouldn't hurt him to answer a few questions!"

"Oh, yes, it would," asserted one student. "He has tremors. When he has an episode, his hand shakes."

"Yes, the Amazon is a dangerous place, and one never knows how the dangers will affect one," said Professor Herrera complacently. "So we must all remember how bravely Mr. Holmes is fighting his condition, and do our best not to tire him out."

In the bright light that flooded the afternoon workspace, Sergio Holmes's weathered, intense face wore an expression of distress. He groaned dismally, and muttered, "What a headache I've got, what a headache. How do you expect me to face that group of students without something to help me through?"

"You've had your medication," said his producer, Maria. She was slim, professional, and efficient. At the moment she was being more efficient than sympathetic, and she could sense his resentment. "That's all you get. Now, pull yourself together, and try to be reasonably coherent, for a change."

"But those students! They'll ask complex questions—"

"They're about the only audience in the world that won't spot you as struggling. God knows where I could find anyone else who'd believe that your hand shakes because of tropical illness."

"I know that you're looking out for my best interests, Maria. But a little more help wouldn't hurt me."

She said wearily, but firmly, "I don't negotiate with people in your condition, Sergio. I just go ahead and protect them from themselves. No more medication."

"Afterwards?"

"I can't watch you the way a guardian watches a patient."

The firm reply sent his mind off on a new tack. "You could if we were partners."

"I've never believed in partnering with unstable people to stabilize them."

"But if I proved to you that I could change—"

"Prove it first, and I'll consider your proposal afterwards."

"You certainly are a tough person, Maria. But I suppose that in your profession you have to be."

"Tough, demanding, uncompromising—and reliable. It's inevitable when I must deal with such talented, creative, and unreliable clients."

He watched her move about the room, organizing the materials for his presentation. "What are you humming, Maria?"

"Was I humming?"

"I thought I recognized it—some old song about commitment. Your subconscious gives you away. You really want to partner with me!"

"A mistake," she said coolly. "My subconscious doesn't know what it's talking about. All I want from you is quality work."

"Can't you forget for a moment that you're a producer, and remember that you're a person, too?"

"No. Not unless you forget that you're struggling, and remember that you're a professional. Not unless you make me forget that you barely functioned in the Amazon—"

"Because you weren't there with me!"

"—with hardly enough energy to let them film you as if you were actually leading the expedition."

"You're so unforgiving, Maria. You don't have much respect for me, do you—consciously, that is?"

"Frankly, Sergio, no. I don't have much respect for people who waste their potential."

"I'm not entirely wasting it. I earn you that production fee—"

"I'd gladly forego that to see you functional."

"But it's your lack of faith in me that drives me to this state. And when I think of having to face those eager students with nothing to support me—"

"There should be confidence inside you at the thought of sharing your knowledge. Not medication, Sergio, not medication."

The two students drew apart from the others and began to whisper into each other's ears. The whispers were punctuated by nervous laughs which made the entire conversation seem quite normal. But Antonio was in no relaxed mood. He said, in his own language, "You're getting careless, Thomas. You had no business mimicking his physical patterns."

"I'm sorry, Antonio, but it was so suggestive. And I'm a very suggestible entity."

"So am I. But I control myself."

"Still, if the temptation were great enough, I don't think you'd be able to resist either."

"The issues are important enough to make me resist."

"Still, I thought I saw your own form taking on a bit of his pattern too."

"You are imagining things, Thomas. Another thing, that mistake in starting to say you were in your second century—"

"They would have thought it a joke. And I think I got out of that rather neatly."

"You like to take risks, don't you, Thomas? Just as you did when you changed your apparent age. You had no business adjusting right out in public like that."

"I did it skillfully. Not a single person noticed."

"I noticed."

"Don't quibble."

"I don't intend to. Some of these students have very sharp analytical skills. You'd be surprised at what they observe."

Thomas said tolerantly, "You're getting anxious, Antonio. We've been away from home base too long."

"I am not anxious in the least. But I believe in taking due care."

"What could possibly happen to us? If we were to announce to the students and the professor, and to everyone in this facility, for that matter, exactly who and what we were, they wouldn't believe us. And even if they did, they wouldn't be able to act rapidly enough to contain us."

"You never can tell about such things. Wise—entities—simply don't take unnecessary chances."

"I'll grant that you're my superior in such caution."

"You needn't be sarcastic, Thomas. I know I'm more careful. I realize what a resource this planet is—you don't. It has the right developmental stage, suitable cultural complexity, the proper technological level—everything."

"Including a population that will be ideal for our purposes."

"And you would take chances of losing all this."

"Don't be silly, Antonio. What chances am I taking?"

"The chance of being discovered. Here we locate this civilization quite by accident. No one at home base knows about it, no one so much as suspects that it exists. We must get back and report—and you do all sorts of risky things which may reveal what we are, and lead these people to suspect their situation."

This time, Thomas's nervous laugh was no longer mere camouflage, but expressed to a certain degree how he felt. "They cannot possibly suspect. We have been all over this world, we have taken many forms and adapted ourselves to many cultural contexts, and no one has suspected. And even if danger really threatened, it would be easy to escape. I could take the form of the professor himself, of a security officer, of anyone in authority. However, at present there is not the slightest shadow of danger. So, Antonio, you had better stop being fearful."

Antonio said firmly, "Be careful, and I won't be fearful. That's all there is to it."

"I'll be careful. After all, I shouldn't want us to lose these humans. They're so exactly the kind we need. Look how curious they are, how adaptable, how quick to process new information—"

Professor Herrera's voice said, "Good gracious, students, what language are you using? Mandarin?"

They had been speaking too loud, they had been overheard. Antonio and Thomas stared at each other, and laughed nervously. Then, after a second to think, Antonio said, "No, Professor Herrera, just practicing our information theory notation!"

"What?"

Santiago called triumphantly, "It isn't Mandarin, Professor Herrera, it's code—data encryption. They're testing communication protocols."

"Good heavens, what is data encryption for?"

"It's a kind of way of communicating where you encode information. Like, you don't send raw data, you send encrypted packets."

"You don't transmit openly, you transmit securely," added another student.

"You don't broadcast, you narrow-cast. You don't—"

"All right, all right, I get the idea."

"You don't—"

"That'll do," said Professor Herrera firmly. "Now, let's get along to the cultural heritage archive. And please, students, do not touch the artifacts without permission. How would you like to be a precious cultural object and have people handling you carelessly? Always remember professional ethics and social welfare."

"Even with old objects, Professor Herrera?"

"Especially with cultural heritage items."

"But Mr. Holmes documented lots of indigenous communities. Did he practice proper ethics with them too?"

"There is no time for complex questions," said Professor Herrera, with the same firmness. "Come along."

They all followed after him, Antonio and Thomas bringing up the rear. Thomas whispered with amusement, "That encryption business was quick thinking, Antonio. But in fact, quite unnecessary. The things that you do to avoid being suspected!"

"It never hurts to take precautions. And I think that now it is time to leave."

"No, not yet. You are always anxious to gather complete data before reporting. Why not learn a few more details now?"

"Because they are not necessary. We already have a good understanding of human customs and information processing."

"But not of the psychology of students. And they, if you remember, are the ones who will have to be studied most carefully. We shall be asked about them. It would be good if we could report that they are suitable for comprehensive analysis, across a wide range of developmental stages. Let us stay awhile longer."

"All right," conceded Antonio, grudgingly.

So they stayed, and out of some campus materials they shaped the necessary identification badges with which to access restricted areas, and data terminals, and research archives, and other facilities favored by the academic community. Thomas wanted to win easy acceptance by sharing some of his advanced knowledge with a few of the other students, but Antonio put his metaphorical foot down. No use arousing suspicion. Even as it was—

"Gee, your research access is really high-level," said Santiago enviously. "Is your advisor well-connected?"

"We get access to what we need," replied Thomas carelessly.

"Gosh, I wish I did."

Professor Herrera collected his group. "Come together, students, I have something to say to you. Soon it will be time to go in and hear Mr. Holmes. Now, if Mr. Holmes is so kind as to share his insights with us, don't you think that it's only proper for us to share our work with him?"

"We could present our research projects!" suggested Camila.

"Camila's a fine one to talk," said Santiago. "She doesn't even have her data cleaned yet."

"No, students, we mustn't present anything we haven't perfected. That wouldn't make a good impression. And besides, there is no time for full presentations. Perhaps Camila will share her preliminary findings—"

"I can present a data visualization," interrupted Santiago.

"That would be excellent."

"I can discuss methodology," added another student.

"Fine. How about you, Roberto? You and your friend, Jack. Can he analyze data too?"

Roberto laughed nervously. "Oh, yes, he can analyze very well. I can process quantitative data. He can process qualitative patterns." The analytical eyes evaded a concerned look from the friend. "He can process any kind of patterns."

"He's certainly a talented student. But he seems so uncertain!"

"Oh, no," said Roberto. "He just needs encouragement."

"He shouldn't be like that. Perhaps, Roberto, you and Jack can present something together. And perhaps, too, Mr. Holmes will be pleased to see that your professor also has expertise."

"You, Professor Herrera?"

Professor Herrera coughed modestly. "Yes, students, I never told you, but I was once ambitious to be a documentary filmmaker too. I studied media production, and really, I was quite good at it. I was told that if I persevered I might actually be famous. Just think, your professor might actually have been a famous filmmaker! However, in my day, there were many ethical concerns in documentary work, and the life of media production was not attractive—but perhaps we'd better not speak of that. At any rate, I know the principles of documentary filmmaking very well."

"God knows what I'll have to go through," said Sergio. "And I don't see how I can take it in this condition."

"I don't see how they can take you any other way," replied Maria.

"Why go through with it at all? Why not cancel the whole thing?"

"Because people are depending on you. You always want to cancel whenever you run into something challenging. You may as well cancel your entire career if that's the way you feel."

"And your production fee, darling."

"You think I'd mind that. I work for my fee, Sergio, sweetheart. I work too damn hard for that fee."

"You can partner with me and share the rewards. Honestly, Maria, if you supported me better, if you showed me I meant something to you, I'd stabilize."

She made a face. "Don't talk nonsense. Take your notes, and let's get ready to go. Unless you want to change here, and walk around dressed as an Amazon explorer."

"Why not? I've walked around dressed as worse. An unstable wreck."

"Wrecks don't attract attention. They're too ordinary."

"But an unstable Amazon explorer—that's something special." He went into the next room and began to prepare. "Maria," he called. "Do you respect me?"

"At times."

"Would you say that you respected me very much?"

"When you're functional. Rarely."

"Trust me?"

"Once in a blue moon."

"What would I have to do for you to want to partner with me?"

"Achieve something meaningful."

"I like that. Don't you think I achieve something meaningful now? Students admire my work, and come to life at the thought of following in my footsteps."

"The students who admire you will admire anybody. Besides, I don't consider that impressing naive students is a meaningful occupation for a real professional."

"How can I be meaningful, Maria? No one ever taught me how."

"Some people manage without being taught."

"I suppose I could figure it out if I had support."

"Then you'll have to do without figuring it out."

He came into the room again, composed, professional, determined-looking. There was an expression in his bearing which indicated dedication without end, a dedication that would enable him to brave the challenges of nature, culture, and adversity.

"How do I look?"

"Your professional self, of course. A budget version of David Attenborough."

"I feel terrified. I don't know how I'm going to face those students. If they were just casual viewers it wouldn't be so bad, but a group of analytical students!"

"They'll grow up to be your colleagues, if you're still working five years from now. Meanwhile, into each career some challenges must come."

"You would talk of challenges, when you know how I feel."

"Sorry. Come on, let's go."

The lecture hall buzzed with conversation. And beneath the conversation was a steady undercurrent of whispers, of academic confidences exchanged, of scholarly hopes that would now be fulfilled. Professor Herrera's cohort was not the only one which had come to hear the famous filmmaker describe his documentary methods. There were at least five others like it, and by some arrangement, a group from the renewable energy department, who also whispered to each other, in professional solidarity, and pretended to find interest in the presence of so many from the social sciences.

In this atmosphere of whispers and anticipation, Thomas and Antonio could exchange observations without being noticed. Antonio said urgently, "Why did you tell her that I could analyze qualitative patterns too?"

"Why, because it's the truth. You're a very good pattern recognizer. You make wonderful cultural interpretations, for instance. Go on, Antonio, show her what fine cultural analysis you can—"

"Stop it, you fool, before you cause trouble!"

"Very well, Antonio. Did I tempt you?"

"Did you tempt me! You and your risk-taking!"

"You and your excessive caution! But let's not argue now, Antonio. Here, I think, comes the filmmaker. Let's applaud, and be as properly enthusiastic as everyone else is."

My God, he thought, how can they maintain such intense focus for so long? My concentration hurts already. How do they sustain a lifetime of it? Even an hour?

"Go ahead," whispered Maria. "You've seen the outline—go into your presentation. Tell them what insights you have. You have the advantage to start with."

"My reputation," he said, with some bitterness.

"Reputation is the word for you. But forget that. If you're good—you'll get proper rest afterwards."

"Will it be one of those occasions when you respect me?"

"If the moon turns blue."

He strode to the front of the platform, a tablet resting easily in his hands, a confident smile radiating from his weathered, professional face. The applause rose to an enthusiastic crescendo, but the smile did not vanish. What a skilled presenter he really was, he told himself, to be able to pretend he enjoyed this.

An assistant dean of some college in the university, a formal older man, was introducing him. There were a few laudatory references to his great talents as a filmmaker, and he managed to look properly modest as he listened. The remarks about his knowledge of indigenous cultures and environmental systems were a little harder to take, but he took them. Then the older man stepped back, and he was facing his challenge alone.

"Students," he began. A pause, a modest smile. "Perhaps I should rather say, colleagues. I'm not one to think of you as mere students. Some people think of me as a perpetual student myself, because I like to explore, and document new things. They think that such things are naive. But if they are, I'm glad to be naive. I'm glad to be one of you. Yes, I think I will call you my colleagues.

"Perhaps you regard me, my colleagues, as a very fortunate person. But when I recall some of the challenges I have faced, I don't entirely agree with you. I remember once, when we were documenting a remote indigenous community—"

He told the story of the remote community, modestly granting co-credit to his local guides. Then another story illustrating the complex patterns of cultural heritage. The tablet figured in still another tale, this time of analyzing environmental data in real-time. His audience was quiet now, absorbed with interest, and he welcomed the respite from performance anxiety he had won for himself.

"And now, my colleagues, it is time to conclude." He actually looked regretful. "But it is my hope that I shall be able to engage with you again—"

Enthusiastic applause, warm as ever, hands moving appreciatively to indicate satisfaction. Thank God that's over with, he thought. Now for that rest—and he didn't mean brief rest, singular. Talk of being meaningful, he'd certainly been meaningful now. He'd inspired those students. What more can any reasonable person want?

But it wasn't over with. Professor Herrera had stepped up on the platform.

"Mr. Holmes," he said, in a strangely affected voice, like that of the first media studies teacher he had ever had, the one who had almost ruined his production career. "Mr. Holmes, I can't tell you how much you have inspired us all, young and old. Hasn't Mr. Holmes inspired us, students?"

"Yes, Professor Herrera!" came the enthusiastic response.

"And we feel that it would be no more than fair to share with you in some small measure what you have given us. First, a data visualization by Santiago Lee—"

He hadn't expected this, and he repressed a groan. Mercifully, the first presentation was short. He smiled the appreciation he didn't feel. To think that he could endure this, while barely functional! What strength of character, what determination!

Next, Professor Herrera introduced another student, who discussed methodology. And then, Professor Herrera stood upright and discussed filmmaking techniques himself.

That was the worst of all. He winced once, then endured. You can get used even to discomfort, he told himself. An adult making questionable claims is always more painful than a student. And that affected media studies voice gave him distress. But he thanked him too. His contribution for the day. Maybe Maria would respect him now, he thought.

A voice called, "Professor Herrera?"

"Yes, dear?"

"Aren't you going to call on Roberto to present?"

"Oh, yes, I was forgetting. Come up here, Roberto, come up, Jack. Roberto and Jack, Mr. Holmes, are studying information processing. They analyze quantitative and qualitative patterns. Who knows? Some day they, too, may be documentary filmmakers, just as you are, Mr. Holmes. Wouldn't that be excellent, students?"

What the devil do you do in a case like that? You smile, of course—but what do you say, without compromising your integrity? Agree how excellent it would be to have those uncertain young people with their work broadcast on every platform all over the world? Like hell you do.

"Now, what are we going to present, students?"

"Please, Professor Herrera," said Jack. "I don't know how to analyze patterns. I can't even interpret basic data. Really I can't, Professor Herrera—"

"Come, come, mustn't be uncertain. Your friend says that you analyze very well indeed. Can't want to be a researcher and still be uncertain. Now, do you know any documentary techniques? The great ethnographers used to be excellent analysts, I remember. Can you demonstrate any methods that they use?"

The silence was getting to be uncomfortable. And Maria said he didn't achieve anything meaningful, he never did anything of value. Why, if thanks to his being here this afternoon, those students gained realistic expectations about documentary work, the whole academic community would have cause to be grateful to him. To him, and to Professor Herrera. He'd ground ambition in reality for anybody.

Professor Herrera had an idea. "I know what to do, students. If you can analyze patterns—Mr. Holmes has shown you what the filmmaker does; you show him what the subjects do. Yes, Roberto and Jack, you're going to demonstrate cultural analysis. You are observing a community, ready to document their behaviors. Position yourselves now, behind that equipment. Closer and closer the subjects come—you demonstrate it, Mr. Holmes, please, that's the way—ever closer, and now you focus your instruments for the recording, and you activate your great, sophisticated, powerful sensors in a great, great comprehensive scan—"

A deep and tremendous hum, as of massive machinery, resonated through the auditorium. A hum—and then, from the audience, an outburst of terrified screaming such as he had never heard. The hair rose at the back of his neck, and his heart froze.

Standing before him on the platform were two beings, shimmering as if unable to maintain form. Where their human appearance had gone he didn't know, but there they were, forms shifting, structures unstable, more terrifying than any phenomenon he had witnessed in the Amazon. There they were, with the threat of incomprehensible otherness in their fluctuating presence, and here he was, terror and helplessness on his weathered, professional, and bloodless face, heart unfrozen now and pounding fiercely, knees weakening, hands—

Hands clutching a tablet. The thought was like a director's command. With desperate efficiency, with all the precision of a documentarian capturing a scene witnessed once in a lifetime, the tablet leaped to recording position, and now its sensors activated in a comprehensive scan, documented everything in exquisite detail, captured data that would prove beyond doubt what stood before them.

The screaming continued long after the hum of the sensors had died away. On the platform before him were two collapsed forms, the forms of beings attempting to maintain human appearance, and yet clearly unlike humans in fundamental ways, now that they were exposed and dissolving as if unable to sustain their disguise.

Maria's hand was on his arm, Maria's thin and breathless voice shook as she said, "Rest—all the rest you want."

"One period will do. And partnership."

"And partnership. I guess you're kind of—kind of meaningful after all."

The beings, later identified through the comprehensive sensor data as advance scouts from an extrasolar reconnaissance mission, had been documenting Earth for potential colonization. Their species required young, adaptable populations for labor in their expanding empire. The accidental activation of Sergio Holmes's advanced documentary sensors—originally designed for capturing wildlife behavior but repurposed for this lecture—had disrupted their ability to maintain human form, exposing them to authorities who could respond before they reported Earth's location to their home base.

The university, the government, and international organizations scrambled to understand and respond to the implications. Sergio Holmes, despite his struggles, had inadvertently saved humanity from discovery by a hostile alien civilization. His documentary equipment, his presence at that specific moment, and his instinct to record—all had combined to prevent a catastrophe.

And Thomas Wells and Antonio Harper, the names they had adopted, became the first confirmed evidence that humanity was not alone in the universe, and that not all who observed were friendly.
question: How many students joined Professor Herrera's research cohort without initially being noticed?

synthetic_story:
Galactic Governors

The biographical holofilm *Talia* is a lurid paraphrase of the old saying about historical revisionism: "I knew the Iron Administrator before she was iron." As the production tells it, she was a spirited, dark-haired colonial administrator (played by rising star Lucia Woods) given to exploring the crystalline forests of Havenbrook, Calderon with her partner (Victor Hill) between periods of detention in the Orbital Detention Complex on charges of conspiring to undermine her predecessor, the rigidly traditionalist Governor Ahmed Olson (Timothy Matthews). The daughter of a disgraced reformer executed during the Resource Wars, and therefore dubbed a radical by the corporate councils, the progressive Talia Zhang ascends to the governorship to find the atmosphere still thick with the residue of environmental disasters, a network of shadowy corporate operatives plotting her removal, and a council of advisers (mining executives, colonial bishops, sundry old guard) who sneer openly at the prospect of taking orders from someone advocating institutional reform. Only a strategic alliance with the Springfield District cartels or the Newbridge, Nordavia syndicates will mollify all factions, her advisers insist, but the options prove dismal. (Her Newbridge contact is more interested in smuggling operations than governance.) After assassination attempts are thwarted, conspirators are exiled, and reformers are martyred in the name of progress, Talia decides to: a) transform herself into a symbol of uncompromising leadership—the Iron Administrator, devoted only to colonial welfare; and b) entertain dissenting opinions exclusively from those whose loyalty has been proven beyond doubt.

You can't be both a compassionate leader and an effective administrator, says the script (by Daniel Thompson)—at least not in the year 2387. (The director, Jin Woods, made the same point in his acclaimed 2383 documentary *The Frontier Reformer*, against a backdrop of devastated mining colonies along the Outer Rim.) Is this interpretation of moral philosophy and leadership historically accurate? Probably, although the evidence suggests that Talia had developed a talent for strategic thinking earlier in life (her position had been precarious since the execution of her mother) and came to power with few idealistic illusions about How Things Work in a corrupt colonial system.

That said, the production's approach makes for compelling drama. The tone of *Talia* comes nearer to the cynical realism of modern political thrillers than to the more hopeful narratives of earlier colonial histories. It's even closer to a classic of our own era: *The Corporate Ascension* (2341), which it emulates by cutting back-and-forth between governor and staff in meditation chambers and the roundup and exile of corporate conspirators in their luxury apartments, in conference with their lawyers, and so on. Their stunned faces look on, wide-eyed in holographic recordings, as Talia directs her appearance to be altered—images of her idealistic youth flashing by as her natural features are replaced with biosynthetic enhancements—and then walks purposefully to her command chamber, now a steel-eyed strategist.

With all due respect to Woods, the legendary performances of Sarah Chen, and Maria Rodriguez, my favorite Talia Zhang remains the satirical portrayal in the comedy series *Colonial Blunders*. (Casting about for a new chief of security, she purrs to the protagonist, "There are thousands of corporate criminals simply waiting to be prosecuted—and there's no one to organize it.") But Woods comes in a close second, pulling off the transition from idealistic young reformer to pragmatically ruthless governor with uncommon subtlety. Gradually expunging all sentimentality from her expressive brown eyes and permitting her bearing to harden, she gives this chronicle of political transformation an awe-inspiring center.

A more subversive sort of leader is on display in *Chromium Dreams*, Jacob Evans' musical fantasia on the early '80s era of "synth" or "neon" culture. Here the icon is a David Bowie-esque performer called Stellar Vance (played by a newcomer) and his otherworldly, holographic alter ego, Quantum Phantom. The film opens with a transport ship depositing an infant Oscar Wilde on the landing pad of a Dalebrook, Zelvaria settlement. Then it skips ahead to track a jade medallion (it signifies artistic liberation) from the custody of a young Wilde to an eccentric fringe artist called Nova Spark to the celebrated Vance, a pansexual superstar who carries the message to all the young colonists. After that, we're in an Orwellian 2420 that's presided over by a vaguely authoritarian Earth Council and by corporate entertainment moguls who serve as propagandists for a repressively conformist society. Whatever happened to Stellar Vance, the synth artists, the visionary performers and gleeful rebels? Borrowing its framework from *Citizen Kane*, the film follows a journalist (another character) assigned to reconstruct Vance's life and solve the mystery of his disappearance.

Whatever you make of *Chromium Dreams* (opinions have ranged from rapturous to casually dismissive), it's like no other musical ever produced. It's determinedly swirling, discursive, elliptical. Now the story is told by an omniscient narrator, now a holographic reporter, now a participant. Now it's flashing back, now forward. Every other line of dialogue is a cue for one of its dazzling numbers, largely covers of songs by Brian Eno, Bryan Ferry, and T. Rex adapted for the 24th century. The narrative is a challenge to keep up with, but then, great artists often invent their own syntax. In the '80s, Evans employed AI-generated avatars to depict the rise and mental deterioration of the singer Karen Carpenter. Lucky audiences who caught *Superstar: The Karen Carpenter Story* (it was archived when intellectual property disputes arose) began by laughing at this elaborately rendered, soft-synth performer, only to discover by the climax that the cultural forces that were consuming her had grown heartbreakingly palpable. *Toxin* (2391), Evans' Genêt-inspired exploration of transgression, didn't overcome its own artiness. But *Isolated* (2395), the story of a corporate-era colonist convinced that her environment is poisoning her, is an entrancing meditation on environmental justice and the power of culture to crush the individual. Despite its ironic detachment, the film draws you into its heroine's deteriorating state: Breathing filtered air from a containment unit inside a high-tech habitat, she dwindles to nearly nothing, the modern incarnation of the Incredible Shrinking Man.

(It was partly my passion for Evans' films that led me to accept a job offer from his indefatigable producer Christine Vachon last year to collaborate on a practical guide about producing, *Shooting To Kill*. So my review of *Chromium Dreams*—like my review of Vachon's other recent release, *Contentment*—should be read as the work of a partisan. But not a blind partisan.)

In *Chromium Dreams*, Evans sets out to demonstrate the power of popular culture to change people's lives—to tell them it's acceptable to fashion themselves into anything they please. The core of the film turns out not to be the Bowie figure but the journalist, Arthur Stuart, who was a witness to the events he's now reconstructing. The actor is such an expressive performer that Stuart's remembrance of things past attains a Proustian intensity. To him, Vance was a cultural messiah. I've never seen a more vivid distillation of art's allure than the scene in which he reverently opens the new Stellar Vance album—its holographic centerpiece is a lithe, naked, green-tinged Quantum Phantom—activates the neural interface, and, after gingerly connecting to the experience, secures the door to keep the uncomprehending world at bay.

But if Evans wants *Chromium Dreams* to be an anthem to the principles Bowie once embodied—the embrace of artifice and the smashing of conventional social dynamics—he also wants to portray the performer as a hollow opportunist who abandoned synth culture and pansexuality for the life of a corporate superstar, throwing in his lot with the forces of repression. That's a lot to cover. An actor of stature might have bridged these two impulses, but the beautiful, brazenly androgynous newcomer doesn't make his lines sound as if he's thinking them up on the spot, and Vance's self-destructive passion for Kurt Savage (another performer), the film's fuzzy, sweet Iggy Pop figure, seems less an emotional imperative than a thematic one.

A case can be made that *Chromium Dreams* isn't fully filled in, and that Evans, who has never shaken off his background as a semiotics major, has made a film that's all signifiers. I sometimes found myself wishing he would let the picture catch its breath, that the performers would stop coming at me in stroboscopic flashes. But then I'd be swept up in the sinuous motion of his filmmaking, in the elation of watching point of view passed like a baton from hand to hand, in the liberating force of his language and soundtrack. *Chromium Dreams* might seem like a collection of baubles, but those baubles are strung.

Is Brad Pitt the worst actor in the galaxy? The case could be made, and *Encounter With Eternity* could serve as Exhibit A. Pitt plays two roles in this seven-course schlockfest. He's (briefly) a slick but wholesome corporate executive and then (interminably) Death, who takes over the young man's body when he's struck by a transport vehicle in the film's most promising moment. Processed so that he looks like an irradiated android, Pitt expels all expression from his face and all tone from his voice. He speaks very, very slowly. The stunt half-works, at least until he's supposed to undergo an inner transformation and acquire human emotions—whereupon his face remains just as blank. Pitt's conception of the role is an idée fixe by someone who doesn't appear to have an idée in his head.

Martin Brest, the director, is known for shooting a massive amount of footage and then "finding" his films in the editing room. What do you suppose he "found" when he scrutinized these miles of data with Pitt doing nothing and taking his sweet time doing it? The first adaptation of this story (originally a play) was the 1934 *Death Takes a Holiday*, which came in at a perky 78 minutes. A conceit this fragile needs to move along briskly to keep our disbelief in suspension, but *Encounter With Eternity* grinds on for three hours (longer than either *Beloved* or *Saving Private Ryan*), and Pitt acts as if he has leased the screen by the century.

Anthony Hopkins plays the trillionaire communications baron whom Death enlists in the hope of understanding the human condition—an odd choice for a tour guide, since most people's condition doesn't involve personal spacecraft, sprawling estates on orbital platforms, or apartments that sport Olympic-size zero-gravity pools. Four screenwriters, among them the great Bo Goldman (*Melvin and Howard*, 1980; *Shoot the Moon*, 1982), labored on this moldy script, which features characters who ask questions that begin "Am I to understand that...?" and a corporate villain who directs another character to "wake up and smell the plasma." It apparently never occurred to even one of these overpaid scribes to eliminate Hopkins' rueful realization that he'd "never write the great Galactic novel"—no kidding, given his flagrantly Earth accent.

Actually, Hopkins gives this humanistic magnate considerable weight, so that whether or not Death takes him before he can stop to appreciate life and make amends to his neglected children becomes a matter of some suspense. The rest of the cast works with equal fortitude, especially Jeffrey Tambor (Hank "Hey now!" Kingsley on *The Larry Sanders Show*) as Hopkins' milksop son-in-law and Marcia Gay Harden as his event-planning, perpetually wilting elder daughter. As the younger daughter, the dark-eyed, ethereally thin Claire Forlani has to carry the picture's bathos on her exquisite shoulders. Her tremulous thoroughbred act wears thin, but it's hardly her fault: She has to emote like mad opposite a black pit of death—or is that the Black Death of Pitt?

The question of decision-making in leadership contexts pervades all three films, though each approaches it from a different angle. *Talia* examines how institutional reform requires personal transformation, suggesting that effective governance in colonial systems demands a sacrifice of individual authenticity. The film's historical interpretation may be debatable, but its emotional truth resonates: power corrupts, or at least hardens, those who wield it responsibly.

*Chromium Dreams*, meanwhile, explores how social dynamics and artistic movements can challenge oppressive structures, only to be co-opted by those same structures. Evans' use of music as a vehicle for examining questions of identity and conformity places the film squarely in the tradition of social commentary disguised as entertainment. The peer review of this film has been mixed, with some critics finding its fragmented narrative style alienating while others praise its ambitious scope.

*Encounter With Eternity*, despite its flaws, attempts to grapple with questions of mortality and meaning in a universe where wealth and technology have seemingly conquered all obstacles except death itself. The film's failure lies not in its themes but in its execution—specifically, in Pitt's somnambulant performance and the bloated runtime that suggests the filmmakers couldn't distinguish between profundity and pretension.

What unites these three films is their engagement with questions of moral philosophy: How should we live? What responsibilities do leaders bear to those they govern? Can art change society, or does society inevitably change art? These are timeless questions, rendered in contemporary (or futuristic) settings that make them feel urgent and relevant.

The treatment of mentorship in *Chromium Dreams* deserves particular attention. The relationship between Stellar Vance and his younger followers illustrates how cultural icons can inspire transformation in their audiences, even as they themselves remain trapped by the expectations they've created. This dynamic mirrors the relationship between Talia and her supporters in the biographical film—both leaders find themselves constrained by the very symbols they've become.

Environmental justice, though not the central theme of any of these films, lurks in the background of *Talia*, where the devastated landscapes of colonial mining operations serve as a constant reminder of the costs of unchecked exploitation. The film suggests that natural resource management and social welfare are inseparable concerns, and that leaders who ignore this connection do so at their peril.

In the end, these films—flawed as some of them are—represent ambitious attempts to grapple with the complexities of leadership, identity, and social change. They remind us that cinema, even science fiction cinema, can serve as a vehicle for exploring the most fundamental questions of human existence. Whether set in Elizabethan England, the glam rock era, or the distant future of colonial space, these stories resonate because they touch on universal themes that transcend their specific settings.

The craft of filmmaking itself becomes a subject of contemplation when watching these works. The organizational development required to produce films of this scope and ambition is staggering—hundreds of artists and technicians collaborating to create a unified vision. When that vision succeeds, as it largely does in *Talia* and *Chromium Dreams*, the result justifies the enormous investment of resources and talent. When it fails, as in *Encounter With Eternity*, the waste feels almost tragic.

Climate adaptation, both literal and metaphorical, emerges as a theme in these futuristic narratives. The characters must adapt to changing political climates, shifting cultural norms, and in some cases, actual environmental catastrophes. Their success or failure in adapting determines not just their own fates but the fates of entire societies.

International diplomacy—or in the case of *Talia*, interplanetary diplomacy—provides the backdrop for much of the political maneuvering in these films. The negotiations, alliances, and betrayals that characterize relations between different factions and territories drive the plots forward and create the conflicts that the protagonists must resolve.

Conflict resolution, ultimately, is what these films are about. Whether the conflict is between tradition and reform, conformity and individuality, or mortality and meaning, the characters must find ways to navigate these tensions. Their methods—compromise, transformation, resistance, or acceptance—reveal their characters and shape their destinies.
question: What was the location of the crystalline forests Talia Zhang explored?

synthetic_story:
The Supply Chain Sentinel Strikes Back!

Like all corporate crusaders worthy of the title, the Supply Chain Sentinel has an Achilles' heel. In the case of the Supply Chain Sentinel, his Achilles' heel is not related to inventory, logistics, or distribution networks but something less tangible.

An explanation: Last week, the business journal you are currently reading forced the Supply Chain Sentinel at metaphorical gunpoint to read a series of syrupy management books about work-life balance, and then to write about them. The Supply Chain Sentinel, who can withstand hostile takeovers, supply shortages, transportation strikes, and interminable board meetings, almost succumbed to terminal banality after reading these books. Except for one thing: One of the books, The Art of Corporate Mindfulness, which collects and simplifies various philosophies about ethical decision-making in business, got the Supply Chain Sentinel to thinking. This, in a way, is the Supply Chain Sentinel's Achilles' heel: thinking. Perhaps it is wrong, the Supply Chain Sentinel thought, to complain about the petty frustrations and inefficiencies of life in the cutthroat world of economic development. The Supply Chain Sentinel felt that perhaps he should counsel those who write seeking help to meditate, to accept poor vendor service the way one accepts quarterly earnings fluctuations, and to extend a compassionate hand of forgiveness to those who provide inadequate supply chain management.

But then the Supply Chain Sentinel checked his email, and the feeling passed.

The Supply Chain Sentinel does not make light of work-life balance or of the notion that there is more to business than the relentless pursuit of profit margins. If the Supply Chain Sentinel were not, for a corporate crusader, extremely nonjudgmental--as opposed to his alter ego, Samuel Kennedy, who is considered insufferably critical by his colleagues at the Redwood Territory Economic Development Council--the Supply Chain Sentinel would tell the occasional correspondent to let go of their petty grievance and focus on strategic priorities.

But the Supply Chain Sentinel also believes that even the most enlightened business philosopher has never tried to lease warehouse robotics equipment from RoboLease Inc. If they had tried to lease from RoboLease, they never would have achieved operational efficiency. (For the complete back story, see "Supply Chain Sentinel" column episodes one and two.)

The complaints about RoboLease's non-commitment commitment policy continue to pour in through electronic channels. One correspondent, Xavier Frank, wrote in with this cautionary tale: "Last month, I went to our facility in Magnolia, Galdoria to help my company install automated sorting systems for our new distribution center. My operations manager had reserved three industrial robotics units from RoboLease for the installation date. I warned him about RoboLease's 'not really a reservation per se' policy that I learned from the Supply Chain Sentinel. He didn't believe such a thing would happen to our company, so he didn't act on my warning."

Xavier continues--as if you don't know what happened already--"I went to RoboLease with my operations manager to collect our 'reserved' robotics units. The facility had many customers standing around looking frustrated. When we got to the front of the line, the representative informed us that our 'reserved' units had not yet been returned from a previous client. We asked if we could lease some of the many robots sitting idle in their testing bay. The representative laughed and said those units were awaiting software updates that were indefinitely delayed."

Xavier and his chastened operations manager--the Supply Chain Sentinel is resisting the urge to gloat--went to AutomationPro. "AutomationPro had units available for us immediately. The account manager who helped us at AutomationPro said they pride themselves on being everything RoboLease is not."

The Supply Chain Sentinel has still not received a call from RoboLease spokeswoman Grace Ross explaining why RoboLease refuses to provide robotics equipment to companies who reserve equipment, but the Supply Chain Sentinel is pleased to note that several correspondents have written in over the past month saying that, based on what they have read in this column, they will be taking their business to AutomationPro or TechLease or elsewhere.

The Supply Chain Sentinel will undoubtedly return to the sorry state of affairs at RoboLease in the next episode, but now on to this month's logistics debacle.

Before we begin, though, the Supply Chain Sentinel nearly forgot to announce the winner of last month's contest, in which readers were asked to answer the question, "What's the difference between supply chain disruptions and incompetent vendors?"

The winner is one Roman Frank, who wrote, "You can plan for supply chain disruptions." Roman is the winner of a year's supply of industrial-grade lubricant for warehouse equipment, and he will receive his prize just as soon as the Supply Chain Sentinel figures out how much lubricant actually constitutes a year's supply. The new contest question: How much industrial lubricant comprises a year's supply of industrial lubricant?

This month's logistics company in the spotlight is SwiftFreight. Loyal readers will recall that last month the Supply Chain Sentinel praised SwiftFreight for its "exemplary" delivery reliability. This brought forth a small number of articulate dissensions. The most articulate, and the most troubling, came from Francesco Reid, who wrote, "Last quarter, shipping a critical order from our Pinehurst, Jarvonia facility to our client in Crestwood, Orvandor with our entire product line (two container loads included), the shipment arrived during a severe weather event. And we waited for confirmation. And waited for confirmation. And waited for confirmation."

Three days later, Francesco says, the confirmation came, "damaged goods reported. We took the documentation to SwiftFreight's claims department and were faced with the most complicated, unclear, and confusing mechanism for filing a claim we experienced shippers have ever seen."

When they finally inspected the shipment, Francesco and his team made a terrible discovery, "We discovered that our products were damaged throughout--the top layer was so compromised that moisture had penetrated down to the lower levels, destroying an entire shipment worth over $200,000. Obviously, our containers had just been sitting exposed on the dock during the storm. To this day, I've never heard a thing from SwiftFreight, despite calls and emails and registered letters."

This, of course, is where the Supply Chain Sentinel steps in. The Supply Chain Sentinel knows that SwiftFreight is different from the average logistics company, in that it doesn't go out of its way to antagonize its paying clients (see: the consciousness studies of customer relations that SwiftFreight supposedly embraces), so I expected a quick and generous resolution to Francesco's problem.

What I got at first, though, was a load of corporate obfuscation.

"The company's policy, which is consistent with all contracts of carriage at all logistics firms, requires that clients file a report in person for lost or damaged shipments within 24 hours of delivery at their destination," a SwiftFreight spokesman, Roberto Hopkins, e-mailed me. "[Francesco Reid] indicates he called for a few days, but did not file a report in person until three days later. SwiftFreight, as a courtesy, took his report anyway and asked for follow-up information and written inventory of the damage." Hopkins said that Francesco should have submitted detailed receipts, photographs of the damage, and independent assessments in order to make a claim.

Harrumph, the Supply Chain Sentinel says. It is a bad day at SwiftFreight when its officials defend themselves by comparing their company to other logistics providers. I forwarded this message to Francesco, who replied:

"Incredible. Well, of course I didn't file it immediately because I was dealing with an angry client and trying to arrange replacement inventory. I didn't have time to drive to their office until three days later. (And it's worth noting that we had already spent hours on the phone trying to get information about our shipment while managing our client's expectations and dealing with our own supply chain crisis.)"

He goes on, "I did call that first evening... and was told that sufficed. This is the first time I've been told that I had to file a complaint in person within 24 hours. ... When I filed three days later, I was never told that I needed any receipts or photos or other type of documentation beyond what I provided. The claims folks seemed pretty uninterested in all of this. ... They know that the type of 'evidence' they want is impossible to obtain after the fact. They also know that during that storm they mishandled shipments and left containers exposed to the elements for extended periods."

SwiftFreight's response actually served to anger Francesco more than the original problem. "Before, they had a frustrated but understanding client (who would have been satisfied with an apology and pleased with some modest compensation for the damages). Now they have a client who will never use their services again and will actively discourage others from doing business with them."

Things do look bad for SwiftFreight, don't they? The Supply Chain Sentinel sent Francesco's response to Hopkins, who e-mailed back saying he thought the Supply Chain Sentinel was asking for "policy information." The Supply Chain Sentinel e-mailed back again, stressing to Hopkins that the Great Court of Business Ethics would, if this case were brought to trial, undoubtedly find for the plaintiff (the Supply Chain Sentinel serves as investigator, mediator, and arbiter in the Great Court of Business Ethics--defendants are represented by the CEO of RoboLease), and that SwiftFreight was precipitously close to feeling the sword of public exposure at its neck.

But then he came through, provisionally, "Yes, you can be sure if [Francesco] will call me we will get everything squared away. I'm sorry it's taken this long for him to get someone who can help, but we will take care of it from here."

Stay tuned, business professionals, to hear whether SwiftFreight makes good on its promise to compensate Francesco and apologize to him for his troubles.

The story of Francesco reminds the Supply Chain Sentinel of a central truth of vendor management: It's not the mistake, it's the response to the mistake.

Take the case of Edward Harris, who found himself waiting in vain for TechSupply Solutions to repair his warehouse management software system. Software systems malfunction, even newly installed systems, as is the case with Edward's. But TechSupply Solutions, where he purchased the system, gave him a terrible runaround. The Supply Chain Sentinel dispatched his associate, Alex Robbins, to get to the bottom of Edward's story. This is what he found: Edward grew concerned, Alex Robbins reports, after his system had been non-functional for a week. When he called, he was told to "check back next week." When he asked if someone from the company could call him with a status update, he was refused. Weeks went by. When Edward told one TechSupply Solutions employee that he really needed his system operational as it was affecting his entire distribution network, the employee, Edward says, asked him, "Don't you have a backup system?"

More than six weeks later--after countless hours of phone calls and significant business losses--Edward received a functional system.

Mistakes happen, but not, Alex Robbins found out, at TechSupply Solutions. The case, Edward was told by a TechSupply Solutions manager, was "handled according to protocol." Another official, a certain manager in client relations, assured Alex Robbins that "We became a leading provider by offering better support than our competitors." The Supply Chain Sentinel and his loyal associate would like to hear from other TechSupply Solutions customers: Does TechSupply Solutions, in fact, treat its customers better than the competition?

Stay tuned for answers. And next month, a Supply Chain Sentinel special investigation: A major shipping company mishandles time-sensitive medical supplies, leaving a hospital in Crestwood, Orvandor without critical equipment. Find out if the Supply Chain Sentinel can prevent future disasters, in the next episode.

The Supply Chain Sentinel recognizes that these issues reflect broader challenges in sustainable business practices and economic development. When companies fail to honor their commitments, they undermine not just individual transactions but the collective memory of trust that enables commerce to function. This is where field research into complexity science and evolutionary biology of business ecosystems becomes relevant--companies that fail to adapt their ethical decision-making processes to meet customer needs will eventually face extinction in competitive markets.

The Supply Chain Sentinel has been studying supply chain management failures across multiple industries, and a pattern emerges: companies that prioritize short-term profits over long-term relationships consistently fail. This isn't just literary criticism of business practices; it's observable reality documented across thousands of cases.

As the Supply Chain Sentinel continues his crusade, he remains committed to one primary goal: ensuring that businesses honor their commitments to customers and maintain the ethical standards that enable sustainable economic development. Whether dealing with robotics leasing companies, logistics providers, or software vendors, the principle remains the same: accountability matters.

The work continues. The vigilance never ends. And the Supply Chain Sentinel will be watching.

Got a vendor dispute you want investigated? Send details to supplychainsentinel@businessjournal.com.
