THE WATER ARCHITECTS

by BASIL WELLS

Stranded in a hidden ecosystem within Zelvaria's forgotten zones, aided by a determined engineer and a veteran scientist, Inspector Steven Mason was fighting his greatest battle—to bring sustainable water management to the dying settlements of the Northern Territories.

[Transcriber's Note: This etext was produced from Planet Stories Winter 1944. Extensive research did not uncover any evidence that the U.S. copyright on this publication was renewed.]

"The illegal extractors are moving in!" Dr. Oscar Webb's urgent voice crackled through the cramped hydrocopter's cabin. "Five or six vehicles. Cut the spotlights!"

Steven Mason's compact frame moved efficiently as he powered down the turbines, doused the twin searchlights, and switched to the acoustic mapping system that served so well on the surface when visibility was compromised. But here in the sinkhole network, the forty-second in the linked series of vast underground cavities that underlie the water-starved plains of Northern Zelvaria, the reflected sound waves were of limited value. Distances were far too confined—disaster might loom mere meters away.

"Trapped us completely," Mason said through gritted teeth. "Lured into their underground operation by that tanker truck we attempted to intercept. We can't escape easily, that's certain. They know these caverns better than... We'll stop some of them, though."

"Agreed!" That was Dr. Oscar Webb, his fellow inspector aboard the Environmental Protection Agency craft as he swung the mounted water cannon around to target the bright headlights that revealed the approaching extraction vehicles.

Three times he fired the high-pressure jets, the water projectiles blasting forward with tremendous force, and three times an illegal vehicle flipped over into a cascade of metal and glass before they realized the EPA craft had engaged them. Then a barrage of debris and projectiles exploded around them.

Mason yanked the controls hard as the attacks revealed a looming barrier of limestone dead ahead, and then he felt the reinforced hull of the hydrocopter crumple inward. The cabin seemed to compress around him. In slow wonder Mason felt the scrape of rock against composite material, and then the screaming of air through the countless tears in the cabin's polymer walls grew to a mad shrieking wail.

Down plunged the damaged craft, downward ever downward. Somehow Mason found the strength to wrap his fingers around the control levers and engage a quick burst from the emergency thrusters. Their mad speed checked momentarily, but the nose of the vertically plunging vehicle dissolved into a shower of sparks and flame.

The craft struck; split open like overripe fruit, and Mason felt himself being flung far outward through thick darkness. For an eternity it seemed he hung in the darkness before something knocked the breath and sensation from his body. With a last glimmer of consciousness he knew that he lay crushed against a rocky wall.

Much later Mason groaned with the pain of bruised muscles and tried to rise. To his amazement he could move all his limbs. Carefully he came to his knees and so to his feet. Not a bone was broken, unless the sharp breathlessness that strained at his chest meant cracked ribs.

There was light in the narrow crevice in which he found himself, light and heat from the yet-glowing debris of the hydrocopter. The extractors had destroyed the crashed craft, his practiced eyes told him, and Oscar Webb must have died in the wreckage. He was alone in the waterless trap of a deep fissure.

In the fading glow of the super-heated metal the vertical walls above mocked him. There could be no ascent from this natural prison, and even if there were he could never hope to reach the surface eight miles and more overhead. The floors of the forty-two sinkholes through which they had so carefully navigated were a shattered, creviced series of canyon-like wastes, and as he ascended the increasingly toxic atmosphere of the higher levels would spell death.

Mason laughed bitterly. Without a respirator on the surface of Northern Zelvaria an inspector was finished. Without water and food certain death grinned in his face, for beyond the sand-buried entrance to these lost equatorial caverns there were no settlements for hundreds of miles. Here at least the air was breathable enough to support life, and somewhere nearby the extractors who smuggled their precious contraband water into the water-starved communities of the Northern Territories lay hidden.

The young inspector unzipped his jacket pocket and felt for the emergency nutrient bars that were standard equipment. Half of the compressed bar he crushed between his teeth, and when the concentrated energy flooded into his muscles he set off around the irregular wall of the crevice.

He found the opening less than twenty paces from the starting point, an empty passage higher than a person and half as wide. The glow from the gutted craft was failing and he felt for the LED torch that hung at his hip. He activated the torch and the bright beam glowed from its housing to reveal the rocky corridor stretching out ahead.

Light! How many hours later it was when the first faint glow of white light reached his eyes Mason did not know—it had seemed an eternity of endless trudging along that smooth-floored descending tunnel.

Mason capped the LED torch. No use wasting the battery needlessly he reasoned. And he loosened the tranquilizer gun in its holster as he moved carefully forward. The extractor headquarters might be close ahead, headquarters where renegade engineers, corrupt officials from the water management districts, and desperate settlers from parched Northern Zelvaria, concealed their precious hoard of water from the thirsty communities of the region.

"They may have found the ancient aquifers of Zelvaria," thought Mason as he moved alertly forward, "water that would give the settlements new life." His fists clenched. "Water that should be managed sustainably and distributed fairly!"

Then the light brightened before him as he rounded a protruding wall of smoothly carved stone, and the floor fell away beneath his feet! He found himself dropping downward into a vast void that glowed softly with a mysterious all-pervading radiance.

His eyes went searching out, out into undreamed distance. For hundreds of meters below him there was nothing but emptiness, and for hundreds of meters before him there was that same glowing vacancy. Above the cavern's roof soared majestically upward; he could see the narrow dark slit through which his feet had betrayed him, and he realized that he had fallen through the vaulted rocky dome of this fantastic abyss.

It was then, even as he deployed his emergency parachute and the canopy blossomed overhead, that he saw the slowly rotating structure of the cloud-wrapped habitat, a small kilometer-wide green sphere of an artificial ecosystem!

The strange sphere was divided equally into hemispheres, and as the tiny world turned on its axis a green, lake-dotted half alternated with a barren, shattered gray waste of rocky desert. As the parachute lowered him slowly down into the vast emptiness of the great shining gulf, Mason could see that a broad band of construction divided the green fertile plains and forests from the desolate desert wastes of the other half. Toward this barrier the parachute bore him, and Mason was content to let it move in that direction—from the heights of the wall he could scout out the territory beyond.

The wall expanded as he came nearer to the artificial habitat. The parachute had slowed its speed; it seemed to Mason that he must be falling free in space for a time, but the artificial gravity of the rotating world tugged at him more strongly as he neared the wall. And the barrier became a complex mass of precisely-engineered structural panels, from whose soil-filled sections sprouted green life.

So slowly was the parachute dropping that the barren desolation of the other hemisphere came sliding up beneath his boots. He looked down into great gaps in the grayness of the desert and saw there the green of sunken gardens and irrigated valleys. He drifted slowly toward the opposite side of the mysterious wall with a swift wind off the desert behind him.

A hundred meters from the base of the structural wall his feet scraped through gray dust, and he came to a stop. Deftly Mason collapsed the parachute and packed it away before he set out toward the towering mass of panels and girders that was the wall.

Ten steps he took before an excited voice called out clearly from the structures ahead. Mason's alert gray eyes narrowed and his hand dropped to the compact tranquilizer gun holstered at his hip. There was the movement of a figure behind the screen of vines and cultivated plants.

"Wait, Lila," a deeper voice called from above, "it might be one of the extractors."

The voice had spoken in Standard Zelvarian! Mason took a step forward eagerly and then doubt made his feet falter. There were corrupt officials as well as criminals among the extractors. This mysterious habitat that floated within the cavern might be their headquarters.

"But, Bruno," the voice that was now unmistakably feminine argued, "he wears the uniform of an EPA inspector."

"Could be a trick." The deep voice was doubtful. "You know their leader, Garrett, wanted access to our systems. This may be a trick to infiltrate the Architects and steal our designs."

The woman's voice was confident. "Come on, let's meet him," she said.

Mason found himself staring, amazed, at the professional figure that emerged from the vegetation and approached him. A striking woman she was, with short-cropped dark hair and intelligent eyes, wearing a functional engineer's jumpsuit marked with the insignia of the old Water Management Authority. Her skin had an unusual pale quality, as if she had spent years away from natural sunlight.

"Hello, Inspector," she said cautiously.

A tall, lean man with graying temples stepped nervously to her side. "Lila," he cautioned, adjusting his wire-rimmed glasses with a weathered hand, "why do you never listen to me? I promised your mentor I'd look after you." He tugged at his worn lab coat.

The woman laughed, a clear sound that made Mason's fatigue seem to lift slightly. "This Bruno Khan of mine," she explained to the inspector, "is always worried about security. He forgets that I can read the structural integrity sensors throughout the habitat."

She smiled as Mason's face showed confusion. "Don't be concerned," she said. "I'm not angry that you're wondering what this place is—and whether we're the criminals you're seeking."

Mason raised his mental guard, a habit from his extensive training at the EPA Academy. His instructors there had known that in field research situations, maintaining objectivity and proper investigative protocols was essential, and the mission of environmental protection must be preserved.

"That's better, perhaps." The woman's expression was professional. "And now perhaps you will visit us in the safety of the archives of old Cedarville Station."

"Sorry," said the tall man as Mason climbed easily up the embankment to their level. "I'm always forgetting that newcomers don't understand our communication skills here."

"She one of the original designers?" Mason's voice was low.

"Mother was." Bruno Khan's voice was clearer now. "Father was Jacob Evans. Famous hydrological engineer you know. I was his research assistant."

"Sure." Mason nodded. "Lost in the equatorial wastelands—uh, about twenty years ago—2053, I believe."

"Only we weren't lost on the surface," explained Khan, his resonant voice carrying easily, "Jacob Evans was researching sustainable water management systems. Traced the ancient aquifers underground. Found them too." He paused to look nervously out across the barren wasteland.

"We ran out of supplies here in the Sphere," he finished, "with the lost waters of Zelvaria less than six kilometers beneath us."

Mason followed the direction of the other's concerned eyes. Overhead now hung the ceiling of the cavern. An almost circular platform of pale construction materials lifted above the dark waters of a vast reservoir. Mason realized with a shock of sudden understanding that they actually stood on the inner surface of a rotating habitat, with artificial gravity holding them in place.

"There," Khan's voice resonated with emotion, "is one of the aquifers of Zelvaria."

"One," repeated Mason slowly. "You mean there are more?"

"Dozens of them," the older man's voice throbbed with restrained passion. "Enough to restore sustainable water management across Zelvaria. Cavern after cavern lies beyond this first one, their floors holding water reserves."

Mason felt new determination pump into his tired bruised muscles. Here lay the salvation of Zelvaria's thirsting settlements almost within reach. Once he could lead the water management scientists to this treasure trove of resources and help implement proper institutional reform...

"Bruno!" The woman's voice was tense. Mason felt her hand grip his sleeve and he dropped beside her in the shelter of a cluster of engineered support columns. "The extractor teams are attacking!"

A hundred meters away Mason saw the dark shapes of armed figures as they descended from the Barrier into the barren desolation of the desert half of the Sphere.

"Enemies?" he whispered to Bruno Khan hoarsely.

"Correct." The older man was checking the charge on his own tranquilizer weapon. "They cross the Barrier from the agricultural zones to raid our facilities. They want to steal our green infrastructure designs and water purification systems."

"I must warn the others." Lila's lips thinned and her dark eyes flashed with determination.

"The extractors may have blocked the passages," warned Khan. "They've taken over the sections near Bayview and Rosewood, remember."

"I'll take the transit pod." Lila was on her feet, her body crouched to take advantage of the sheltering structures. She threaded her way swiftly back along a maintenance corridor in the face of the Barrier toward the ruins of ancient Cedarville Station.

Khan shrugged his shoulders. "What can I do? Lila has dedicated her life to protecting this place. She will warn the other Architects even though the extractors have turned some of the outer settlements against us."

Mason watched the column of roughly dressed figures file out upon the barren desert and swing to the right along the base of the Barrier. Weapons and tools glinted dully in the artificial light.

"They will pass within meters!" he hissed.

"Correct." Khan's fingers gripped Mason's arm. "Pray that the air circulation doesn't shift our scent toward them—some of them have enhanced olfactory implants."

Mason's eyes narrowed. There was something vaguely threatening about those advancing figures. He wondered what Khan had meant about the extractors' desperation, wondered until they came closer.

Then he understood. These weren't just criminals—they were desperate people, gaunt and weathered from years of water scarcity. Above their ragged clothing, their faces showed the marks of dehydration and hardship. Their movements were purposeful but weary, and beneath their determined expressions lay the desperation of those who had lost everything to the water crisis.

"See!" Khan's voice was muted. "Garrett, leader of the extractor gang!"

Riding in a modified all-terrain vehicle of scavenged metal and salvaged parts sat the hardened leader of that advancing group. Lean of body he was, his scarred face showing years of exposure to Zelvaria's harsh environment. One eye was covered by a patch but the other gleamed, cold and calculating, from his weathered features. And the symbols of his crimes—confiscated water permits and broken treaties—hung like trophies about his reinforced vehicle.

Men and women bore equipment alongside the vehicle, eight broad-shouldered individuals whose arms showed the scars of hard labor and whose backs bore the marks of desperate survival. Their bodies, unlike Lila's pallor, were deeply tanned from surface exposure.

Mason raised his tranquilizer gun, anger clouding his judgment as he saw these victims of failed public health policy, but the hand of Bruno Khan pressed down firmly across his arm. The older man shook his head.

"Not yet," he said. "When Lila has warned the other Architects we can coordinate our response. After they have passed I will alert the Mediators who live here on the Barrier. Though their backgrounds span both communities they oppose the extractors' methods."

A shadow passed over their hiding place. The extractor group saw the movement and looked up. High overhead drifted the sleek shape of a transit pod, and the raiders shouted their frustration. Gone now was their chance for a surprise attack on the isolated facilities of the Water Architects.

They halted, clustered about their leader. Garrett barked quick orders at them, his voice harsh with determination. The column swung out into the wasteland toward the nearest maintenance valleys. Mason and Bruno Khan came to their feet.

Abruptly, then, the air circulation shifted. From behind the two men it came, carrying their scent out toward the enhanced senses of some in the extractor group. The column turned. They spotted the two men and a harsh battle cry burst from their throats.

Mason's tranquilizer gun fired in controlled bursts as he swept its barrel back and forth along the ranks of attacking extractors. Dozens of the desperate raiders fell as the sedative darts struck them but scores more were charging over their fallen comrades. Bruno Khan's weapon discharged again and again as he targeted the attackers. But the extractors ran fearlessly into that defensive fire.

Khan jabbed an elbow into Mason's side. "Retreat!" he gasped.

The extractors swarmed up over the lower terraces of structures, their weapons raised and their faces contorted with desperation. The two men bounded up and backward to the next level of platforms behind them, their conditioned muscles handling the artificial gravity easily. Projectiles showered around them and then they dropped behind the sheltering bulk of a large cylindrical tank.

"Now where?" Mason loaded another magazine of tranquilizer darts as he asked.

"To the archives beneath Cedarville Station," Bruno Khan cried. "None but the Architects and we few have entered the data vaults of the abandoned facility."

The scientist slung his weapon over his shoulder and went bounding away along a shadowy maintenance passage that plunged into the heart of the Barrier. Mason fired another burst of tranquilizer darts at the extractors and followed.

Darkness thickened as they penetrated into the maze of the Barrier's interior structure. An unseen figure lunged at Mason's shoulders and as he sank to his knees he felt rough hands grab at his equipment belt. His fist sent the attacker's bulk crashing against the metal floor before any weapon could be drawn, and he heard a choked gasp that ended in unconsciousness.

Automated maintenance drones brushed past his face with their sensor arrays, and beneath his feet loose wiring and discarded components crunched underfoot. Then there was faint light again, and the high-vaulted ceiling of an archive chamber rose above him.

Bruno Khan was peering out a narrow observation port that overlooked the desolate desert zone.

Khan's finger pointed. "Lila!" Mason saw the graceful form of the transit pod gliding on its magnetic rails back toward the Barrier. "She has warned the other Architects, and now she returns."

"The extractors won't follow us here?" asked Mason.

Khan laughed grimly. "Hardly. They fear the automated security systems too much for that. They believe the AI defenses will neutralize any intruders."

"Then how about explaining this rotating habitat?"

"Simply the vision of an ancient Zelvarian water management authority. As I have learned from the records and technical documentation here in Cedarville Station, they couldn't solve the surface water crisis so they created a self-sustaining ecosystem that would preserve the knowledge and technology."

Mason nodded thoughtfully. "Like the experimental design facilities of the old sustainability institutes."

"Correct." Khan kept his eyes on the approaching transit pod as he spoke. "Later, when the regions of Zelvaria began hoarding water and fighting over remaining resources, the Sphere became a refuge for the few hundred engineers and scientists who escaped the resource wars.

"The Water Architects were the designers," he went on, "and we've maintained this facility for twenty years. In the conflicts that eventually split Zelvaria into competing factions, Cedarville Station was abandoned due to a critical systems failure and the advanced knowledge was nearly lost."

"But," Mason frowned thoughtfully, "what keeps the Sphere rotating? Surely the structural supports at either end cannot maintain it indefinitely?"

"The central platform is the key," said Khan. "Somehow it generates the gravitational field—provides the Sphere with..." He caught his breath suddenly.

"The extractors!" he cried. "They're intercepting Lila."

Mason caught a glimpse of a fast-moving extractor vehicle pursuing Lila's transit pod. He saw the pod accelerate steeply toward a complex junction of maintenance tunnels and disappear from view. He turned to see the old man activating another transit pod near the archive chamber.

Khan gestured toward the vehicle. "Let me follow," Mason said. "I know emergency pursuit protocols, and I have my weapon."

The older man's eyes were intense. He grabbed at Mason's hands and then suddenly reconsidered. "You're right," he agreed. "Help her if you can. Your training is our best hope now."

Mason pushed forward with all the strength of his weary muscles. The pod accelerated smoothly with that initial command, and shot out beyond the Barrier. The extractor forces were struggling figures below him, and he saw with satisfaction that larger groups of defenders, whose uniforms showed the colors of the original Water Authority, were confronting them from the desert zones. The Mediators had come to oppose the raiders.

He guided the pod toward the shattered maintenance areas where Lila had taken shelter, noting as he did so that the extractor vehicle had stopped near its center in a narrow section of service tunnel. A sudden thought energized him. He drove directly toward the stopped vehicle. With this transit system he could navigate through the Sphere, return through the forty-two sinkholes to the upper world, and bring to water-starved Zelvaria the promise of sustainable water management again.

A figure stood guard just outside the vehicle's door. Mason lined up his tranquilizer gun and his jaw tensed. He guided the pod closer with one hand. If he could approach undetected, well and good. There would be no alert to warn the person's companions. But if the extractor saw him Mason knew he would need to act first—he had the element of surprise.

Twenty meters lay between them, and suddenly the extractor turned. Mason pressed the firing trigger; the gun clicked once and the safety jammed, and the suspicious guard swung up their own weapon!

Mason threw his gun at the figure's head. The extractor ducked but their weapon swung off target momentarily. In that instant Mason launched himself from the slowing pod, full upon the guard.

They went down, Mason using his training effectively. He felt the extractor go limp and he breathed a sigh of relief. Now with a transit vehicle and the guard's weapon in his possession the problem of escape from the inner caverns was manageable. He would rescue Lila, return to the archives for Bruno Khan, and navigate upward to the surface eight miles overhead.

He knelt over the unconscious extractor, using cable ties from his equipment belt to secure the person. The restraints were not too tight—they could free themselves eventually. He shrugged his shoulders wearily and started to rise.

A boot scraped on metal behind him. He spun on bent knees and threw himself several meters to the far side of the narrow tunnel with the same movement. Tranquilizer darts clattered against the walls around him as he dropped behind a sheltering structural beam, and he caught a glimpse of two figures dragging Lila's struggling form toward the shelter of the vehicle.

A figure appeared around the vehicle's edge and Mason pressed his captured weapon's trigger. A cry of pain came from the struck person, and he saw an outstretched arm on the metal floor that twitched twice and went still. The tranquilizer must have been loaded with a high-dose cartridge—the dart had delivered a powerful sedative.

The odds were improving, he thought grimly. There might be another extractor somewhere out there in the maintenance tunnels, but no more than that. The vehicle was built to accommodate no more than five passengers and four was typical. He shifted his weapon to cover the opposite end of the vehicle's frame.

And something that felt like a freight train smashed into his back. He was crushed downward, breathless, his eyes glimpsing briefly the worn work boots of his attacker as they locked on either side of his torso, and then darkness engulfed him as a powerful blow struck his skull repeatedly.

This pounding was hammering relentlessly as Mason sensed his first glimmer of returning consciousness. There were two sources of pain, one of them that he identified as the throbbing in his temples, and the other the measured vibration of vehicle engines. He opened his eyes slowly to find himself staring at the corrugated metal floor of a transport. His face was pressed into the accumulated grime that only careless operators would have permitted to build up.

Cautiously his head twisted until he could look forward toward the controls. The bound form of Lila Cole faced him, and he saw her lips move in a brief expression of recognition. She shook her head and frowned as he shifted his arm. But Mason had discovered that his limbs were not bound—apparently the extractors had considered him neutralized for the moment.

Gradually Mason worked his arm down to his belt where his LED torch was attached. His fingers made careful adjustments within the base of the torch, modifying settings and overriding safety protocols.

The vehicle bumped as it stopped and the vibration of engines ceased. The cabin shifted with the weight of bodies moving from their positions. Mason heard voices from nearby and the answering triumphant calls of his two captors. The moment had arrived. He turned the lens of the LED torch away from his body and activated it.

Intense light blazed as the overloaded output of the torch made the dirty floor smoke. He lay unmoving while the thick haze rolled over him.

"Fire!" There was panic in the extractor's voice. Mason came to his knees in the obscuring fog and looked forward.

One of the figures threw themselves out the door, but the other reached for the fire suppression system close at hand. Their attention was on the smoking haze; not on the prisoners, and so the impact of Mason's horizontally launched body drove the air from their lungs before their hand could reach their weapon.

The extractor was determined. Their fists struck back at Mason, and their knees drove upward toward the inspector's vulnerable abdomen. But Mason pressed forward, his own trained hands working efficiently, and his conditioned body moving instinctively aside from the disabling strikes aimed at his torso. For a moment they fought, coughing and choking from the thickening cloud of smoke, and then the fingers of the extractor clamped around Mason's throat and squeezed hard.

The inspector was exhausted; the crash in the upper sinkhole and the long trek afterward through the dark tunnels had depleted his strength, and now he felt success slipping from his grasp.

He felt something press against his legs, legs so distant that he could hardly recognize them as his own, and then he was falling with the relentless fingers still around his throat. As from a great distance he heard a cry of pain and the blessed air rushed into his burning throat. His vision cleared.

He saw Lila's bound form. Her teeth were clamped upon the arm of the extractor and even as he gasped for the acrid smoky air of the cabin he saw the person's free fist strike at her face. Mason swung, all the weight of his compact body behind the blow, and the extractor slumped unconscious against the opposite wall of the vehicle.

No time to check if Lila was injured. The inspector flung himself into the driver's seat and sent the vehicle accelerating toward the exit tunnel. Behind him the thin smoke from the overheated torch was dissipating and the ventilation system was clearing the air.

"Inspector," Lila's voice was beside him. "We're safe!"

"You alright?" Mason wanted to know.

"Of course," she smiled despite a swelling bruise on her cheek.

"Good to hear." Mason felt the warmth of her presence close beside him. A sudden unfamiliar feeling of connection emerged with the proximity.

Lila smiled cautiously and winced slightly. "Do you know," she said, "I still don't know your first name."

Mason grinned at her. "Does it matter?" he asked.

The woman's eyes widened. A responsive light appeared in them. "More professional than calling you 'the inspector' all the time," she replied.

Then they were approaching the Barrier and Mason saw the last of the defeated extractors retreating back across the great wall toward the desert zones. He guided the captured vehicle down toward the damaged plaza of Cedarville Station. Once Bruno Khan was aboard they would navigate surfaceward with their crucial news that all Zelvaria could have sustainable water management again.

Mason exhaled. "Steven," he said as they stopped, and his arm reached out toward the woman's determined presence, and curved around it.

Over the following weeks, Mason worked with Lila, Bruno, and the other Water Architects to document the Sphere's systems and the vast aquifer network. They developed plans for institutional reform of water management across Zelvaria, incorporating green infrastructure principles and human rights frameworks that would ensure equitable access to water resources. The extractors, it turned out, were mostly desperate settlers who had been failed by corrupt officials—many agreed to join the reform effort once they understood the Architects' vision.

The discovery led to the establishment of new water management protocols across Northern Zelvaria, with Cedarville Station becoming a training center for sustainable resource management. Mason remained as the liaison between the EPA and the Architects, working alongside Lila to implement the changes that would transform their world. And in the process, he found something he hadn't been searching for—a sense of purpose that went beyond enforcement, and a partnership that promised to reshape not just water policy, but his own future.
question: What year did Bruno Khan mention as the time Jacob Evans was researching aquifers on the surface?

synthetic_story:
The Gravity of Deception
by Alan E. Nourse (Adapted)

The chamber was cold and sterile, illuminated by harsh fluorescent lights that buzzed incessantly overhead. Miguel Ortiz followed the towering Crystalline guard down the polished corridor of the detention facility, his breath forming small clouds in the frigid air. He pulled his Earth-standard thermal jacket closer, shivering as his eyes took in the transparent holding cells lining both sides of the hallway. His polished shoes clicked against the smooth surface, echoing in the empty space.

"How much farther?" he called out irritably.

The guard gestured vaguely with one of its faceted appendages toward the end of the corridor. The hallway suddenly opened into a larger space, and the Crystalline stopped before a reinforced transparent barrier. "I still fail to comprehend the urgency," it chimed in its resonant, musical voice. "We have treated the prisoner with all appropriate protocols."

Miguel peered through the barrier into the holding cell. A figure huddled in the corner gradually came into focus—a thin, wiry man with sharp features and calculating eyes. "Isaac?" Miguel called sharply.

There was a startled gasp from within, and Isaac Hunt suddenly appeared at the barrier, his face breaking into a cunning smile beneath his unkempt hair. "Miguel! I knew they'd send you! I could count on it!" He performed an exaggerated bow. "Not much hospitality to offer, but it's the best I can manage under the circumstances."

Miguel frowned and turned to the guard. "Privacy, please. Interplanetary Protocol Article Seven. And leave the lighting."

The guard chimed its displeasure but departed. "About time you showed up!" Isaac cried. "Lucky they sent you, friend. I've been in here for weeks—"

"Look, Hunt, we're not friends," Miguel snapped. "And you've been here for exactly nineteen days, six hours, and approximately twenty minutes. You're getting as loose with facts as your Crystalline hosts." He studied Isaac's haggard appearance through the barrier. The man's eyes were bloodshot, his clothes disheveled. Miguel's expression softened slightly. "So Isaac Hunt's in trouble again. You look terrible."

Isaac snorted. "These silicon-based bureaucrats don't understand the concept of proper treatment. Synthetic nutrients and recycled water, nothing more. I thought you'd never arrive! I filed an appeal with the Earth Consulate the day I was detained. What took so long? All they had to do was process the extradition, sign the papers, and arrange transport off Lakeside Territory. Why the delay? I've been rotting here—" He stopped mid-sentence, his eyes widening. "You brought the papers, right? We can leave now?"

Miguel stared at the con artist with a mixture of pity and contempt. "You're a complete fool," he said finally. "Do you know that?"

Isaac's eyes narrowed. "What do you mean, fool? So I spend a few weeks in this freezer. The deal was worth it! I've got five million credits in the Earth Consulate account on Lakeside, Nordavia, just waiting for me to collect. Five million credits! That's enough to retire on!"

Miguel nodded grimly. "If you live long enough to collect them, that is."

"What do you mean, if?"

Miguel moved closer to the barrier, his voice dropping to an intense whisper. "I mean that right now you are essentially a dead man. You may not realize it, but you are. You waltz onto a newly colonized territory with your bag of tricks, arrive here with questionable credentials and no proper authorization, with no understanding of the Crystalline culture beyond a few paragraphs of misinformation in the Colonial Guide. And even then, you're not satisfied with selling something legitimate, something the natives might actually need. No, nothing so straightforward for you. You have to run your usual high-pressure scheme. And this time, Hunt, you're paying the price."

"You mean I'm not being extradited?"

Miguel smiled coldly. "Exactly that. You've committed a crime here—a serious crime. The Crystallines are furious about it. And the Earth Consulate isn't willing to sacrifice all future trade possibilities just to bail you out. You're going to stand trial—and these beings want your head. Personally, I think they're going to get it."

Isaac stood shakily. "You can't trust anything they say. They operate on completely different principles than we do. You should see the deals they tried to make with me! I've never encountered such a complex negotiation system." He glanced up at Miguel. "They'll probably impose a fine and release me."

"A fine measured in your lifespan." Miguel's smile was unpleasant. "You've committed what they consider the gravest possible offense, and they're determined to see justice done. I'm afraid your con-artist days are over."

Isaac fumbled for a cigarette, lighting it with trembling hands. "It's bad, then."

"It's very bad."

Some hint of Isaac's usual sly grin returned. "Well, at least they sent you. Nothing like a good lawyer to handle a trial."

"Lawyer? Not me! Absolutely not!" Miguel laughed harshly. "I'm your advisor, nothing more. I'm here to prevent you from making things worse for the Trading Commission. That's all. I wouldn't get involved in a legal proceeding with these beings for anything!" He shook his head. "You're your own lawyer, Mr. Master-Salesman. It's your show. And you'd better start thinking clearly, or you're going to lose in ways you can't imagine!"

Miguel watched Isaac's pale face and shook his head. In a way, it was tragic to see such a transformation in the smooth-talking, confident little man who had talked his way out of more jams than Miguel could count. Trade expansion attracted scammers; it was inevitable that wherever rich and unexploited territories were opened, they would fall prey to fast-talking operators. They spread out from Earth with the first wave of colonization—the slick con artists who could work new territories unfettered by the legal restrictions that governed established colonies. The first ones in were the richest ones out, and through some peculiar quirk of human psychology, they knew they could count on Earth protection, however dishonest their methods.

But occasionally a situation arose where the civilization and social practices of the alien inhabitants made interference unwise. Lakeside Territory had been recognized immediately by the Trading Commission as a commercial prize of tremendous value, but early reports had warned of the danger of wildcat trading on the crystalline world with its silicon-based, logic-driven inhabitants—warned specifically against the confidence tactics so frequently employed—but there was always someone, Miguel reflected bitterly, who didn't get the message.

Isaac puffed nervously on his cigarette, his narrow face troubled. "But I didn't do anything wrong!" he exploded. "So I ran a classic con. So what? Why are they so upset? So I made a few thousand credits, pulled some fast business." He shrugged eloquently. "Everyone does it. They do it to each other constantly. You should see how these beings operate with each other. My little scheme was nothing by comparison."

Miguel pulled out a pipe and began filling it methodically. "And precisely what sort of con game was it?" he asked quietly.

Isaac shrugged again. "The simplest, oldest scam in the book. Remember the old Earth story about selling the Brooklyn Bridge? Same concept. Only these beings didn't want bridges. They wanted energy—renewable energy sources for their expanding civilization. So I gave them what they wanted. I sold them energy rights."

Miguel nodded knowingly. "You certainly did. Exclusive rights to a hundred square kilometers of solar collection territory at a time. Only you sold the same hundred square kilometers to a dozen different Crystallines." Suddenly he threw back his head and laughed bitterly. "Of all the things you shouldn't have done—"

"But what's a patch of territory?"

Miguel shook his head hopelessly. "If you hadn't been so greedy, you'd have learned what territory means to these beings before you started peddling it. You'd have discovered other things about them, too. You'd have learned that despite all their logical processing and systematic behavior, they're not naive. You'd have found out that they're energy-dependent, and that three out of five newly formed Crystallines fail to secure sufficient energy sources to reach maturity. You'd have realized that they must compete for survival from the moment they crystallize. Anything goes, as long as it benefits them as individuals."

Miguel grinned at Isaac's horrified expression. "Never learned that, did you? And you've never learned other things, either. You probably never discovered that there are too many Crystallines here for the energy their territory can provide, and their energy requirements are so specific that they can't survive on anything that doesn't originate here. Consequently, territory is the fundamental factor in their economy, not currency; nothing but territory. To secure territory, it's every being for itself, and the loser dies, and their entire legal and economic system revolves around that principle. They've developed the most intricate and complex system of negotiation and exchange imaginable, aimed at individual survival, with territory as the value behind every transaction. That explains their approach to truth—of course they manipulate information, with an economy like that. They've completely redefined the concept of factual accuracy. Pathological? You bet they're pathological! Only a fool would present unvarnished truth when survival depends on being a more skillful negotiator than the next being! Information manipulation is their time-honored tradition, with their entire legal system built around it."

Isaac snorted. "But how could they possibly have a legal system? I mean, if they don't value straightforward truth?"

Miguel shrugged. "As we understand legal systems, I suppose they don't have one. They have only the vaguest notion what absolute truth represents, and they've dismissed the concept as impractical and useless." He chuckled maliciously. "So you went out and identified a section of solar collection territory, and sold exclusive rights to a dozen separate, self-centered, energy-starved Crystallines! Territorial encroachment is legal grounds for termination on this world, and twelve of them arrived at the same territory simultaneously, all armed with exclusive deeds." Miguel sighed. "You've got twelve furious Crystallines demanding justice. You've got an entire world demanding justice. And meanwhile, Earth's most valuable source of climate technology materials in decades is threatening to cut off supply unless they see you punished appropriately."

Isaac was visibly shaken. "Look," he said weakly, "so I made a mistake. What am I going to do? Are you going to stand by and let them destroy me? How could I defend myself in a legal system like this?"

Miguel smiled coolly. "You're going to get that devious little brain of yours working, I think," he said softly. "By Interplanetary Protocol, they have to give you a trial in Earth legal format—judge, jury, court procedure, all the standard elements. They think it's absurd—after all, what could a judicial oath mean to them?—but they agreed. The only problem is, they're determined to convict you, whatever it takes. So you'd better get those stunted wits of yours functioning—and if you try to implicate me, even slightly, I'll be gone so fast you won't know what happened."

With that, Miguel turned and walked toward the exit, leaving Isaac alone in the cold, sterile cell.

It certainly looked like a courtroom, at any rate. At the front of the large, temperature-controlled chamber was a bench with a seat behind it, and a small chair to the right. To the left was a platform with twelve seats—larger seats, with a railing along the front. The rest of the room was filled nearly to capacity with seats facing the bench. Isaac followed the Crystalline guard into the room, nodding approvingly. "Not a bad setup," he muttered. "They must have understood the concept quickly."

Miguel wiped the cold sweat from his forehead and shot Isaac a stern glance. "At least you've got a courtroom, a judge, and a jury. Beyond that—" He shrugged eloquently. "I can't make any promises."

At the back of the room, a door opened with a sharp hiss. Resonant, chiming voices filled the air as half a dozen Crystallines attempted to enter simultaneously. Isaac activated his translation device and watched the commotion in the anteroom with growing alarm. Finally, the question of precedence was resolved, and a group of Crystallines filed in, ordered by refraction index, moving across the room in flowing dark robes, their faceted faces gleaming with self-importance. They settled into the jury box, their crystalline bodies clicking against each other as they competed for front-row positions. The judge took his place with obvious satisfaction behind the heavy synthetic bench. Finally, the prosecuting attorney appeared, flanked by two assistants who took their positions beside him. The prosecutor fixed Isaac with a cold, multifaceted stare, then turned and performed what might have been a wink at the judge.

In moments, the room filled with the towering, geometric beings, their bodies refracting the harsh light as they jostled for seats, their chiming voices creating a cacophony of sound. Two minor altercations broke out in the rear but were quickly subdued by the security detail. Finally, the judge focused all his optical sensors on Isaac and struck the bench with a crystalline gavel until the activity subsided. The jurors shifted in their seats, exchanging what might have been knowing glances, then turned their attention forward.

"We are convening the case of the people of Lakeside Territory," the judge's voice resonated through the chamber, "against one Isaac Hunt—" he paused for a long, dramatic moment—"Earthman." The courtroom immediately erupted in angry chiming until the judge struck the bench several more times. "This—organism—is hereby accused of the following offenses," the judge announced. "Conspiracy to destabilize the government of Lakeside Territory. Deliberate termination of twenty-three law-abiding citizens of the settlement of Sunnydale, Ulvaria, during the third energy cycle following his arrival. Desecration of the Sacred Resonance Chamber of our revered Energy Matrix. Conspiracy with hostile elements to cause the unprecedented energy shortage in the Northern Sector. Deliberate exposure of his carbon-based physiology in a public space—" The judge struck the bench for order—"Espionage in coordination with the rival colony of Lakeside, Zelvaria, in preparation for territorial invasion."

Isaac's jaw dropped, the color draining from his face. He turned, wide-eyed, to Miguel, then back to the judge.

"The Jury Coordinator," said the judge efficiently, "will announce the verdict."

The Crystalline in the front of the jury box rose smoothly. "Defendant found guilty on all charges," it chimed.

"Defendant is guilty! The court will pronounce sentence—"

"Wait just a minute!" Isaac was on his feet, wild-eyed. "What kind of predetermined—"

The judge looked disappointedly at Miguel. "Not yet?" it asked, unhappily.

"No." Miguel's hands twitched nervously. "Not yet, Your Honor. Later, Your Honor. The trial comes first."

The judge appeared deflated. "But you indicated I should call for the verdict."

"Later. You must conduct the trial before you can have the verdict."

The Crystalline shrugged indifferently. "Now—later—" it chimed.

"Have the prosecutor call the first witness," said Miguel.

Isaac leaned over, his face ashen. "These charges," he whispered. "They're insane!"

"Of course they are," Miguel whispered back.

"But what am I going to—"

"Stay calm. Let them proceed."

"But those fabrications. They're all manipulating information, the entire system—" He broke off as the prosecutor resonated a name.

The Crystalline who took the stand was wearing a bright purple identification band that gleamed under the lights. It directed several optical sensors toward the prosecutor with what might have been anticipation. Then it began. "This Earthman criminal—"

"The oath," the judge interjected. "We must administer the oath."

The prosecutor nodded, and four Crystallines moved forward, carrying inscribed transparent tablets to the front of the court. One by one, the tablets were reverently stacked at the witness's base. The witness placed one faceted appendage on the stack, and the prosecutor said, "Do you swear to present information, complete information, and nothing but information, so help you—" he paused to consult the document in his appendage, finishing uncertainly, "—Energy Matrix?"

The witness removed the appendage from the tablets long enough to adjust its position, then replaced it and replied, "Of course," in an offended tone.

"Then present to this court what you have observed of the activities of this reprehensible being."

The witness settled back, focusing multiple sensors on Isaac's face, others on the prosecutor, and dimming a third set as if in contemplation. "I believe it occurred during the fourth cycle of the seventh rotation of Lakeside, Zelvaria (may the Energy Matrix deplete it)—or was it the seventh cycle of the fourth rotation?—" it directed a sensor apologetically at the judge—"when I was returning through the settlement toward my blessed territory, conducting my own affairs, Your Honor, after weeks of negotiating for the energy rights I was securing. Suddenly from the shadow of a structure, this creature—" it gestured an appendage at Isaac—"blocked my path with a threatening communication. He possessed a device I'd never encountered, and before I could process a response, he forced me against the wall. I could determine by the erratic patterns in his behavior that there was no logic, no systematic processing in his cognition, that I was—"

"Objection!" Isaac squealed, jumping to his feet. "This witness can't even remember what cycle he's talking about!"

The judge appeared startled. Then he searched frantically through his bundle of documents. "Overruled," he said abruptly. "Continue, please."

The witness directed all sensors at Isaac. "As I was stating before this disruptive interruption," it chimed, "I could determine that I was facing the most dangerous of criminal types, even for Earthmen. Note the asymmetry of his form, the irregularity of his features. I was paralyzed with concern. And then, helpless as I was, this two-legged abomination began to threaten harm to my blessed territory, dark threats of contaminating my energy sources unless I would reveal the location of our revered Energy Matrix—"

"I never encountered him before in my life," Isaac moaned to Miguel. "Listen to this! Why would I care where their Energy Matrix—"

Miguel gave him a hard look. "The Energy Matrix regulates everything here. It controls energy distribution. If it fails, someone's violated protocols. It's very straightforward."

"But how can I counter testimony like that?"

"I doubt you can counter it."

"But they can't verify any of it—" He looked at the jury, who were listening with rapt attention to the second witness. This one was testifying regarding the systematic destruction of twenty-three (or was it twenty-eight? Oh, yes, twenty-eight) Crystallines in the outlying settlement of Sunnydale. The massacre, it seemed, had been accomplished by a thermal weapon that caused catastrophic structural failure. A third witness took the stand, continuing the testimony as the room grew warmer and more oppressive. Isaac grew paler, his eyes becoming glassy as the accusations mounted. "But it's not true," he whispered to Miguel.

"Of course it isn't! Can't you understand? These beings have no regard for absolute truth. It's inefficient to them, foolish, a sign of poor processing. The only thing they respect is a negotiator more skillful and convincing than they are."

Isaac jerked around abruptly as he heard his name resonated. "Does the defendant have anything to present before the jury delivers the verdict?"

"Do I have—" Isaac was across the room in a flash, his pale cheeks suddenly flushed. He sat down carefully on the witness chair, facing the judge, his eyes bright with fear and excitement. "Your—Your Honor, I—I have information to present that will significantly impact this case. You must process it with the greatest attention." He glanced quickly at Miguel, then back to the judge. "Your Honor," he said in a hushed voice. "You are in the gravest danger. All of you. Your existence—your very territory is at stake."

The judge's optical sensors flickered, and he shuffled through his documents hurriedly as a murmur arose in the court. "Our territory?"

"Your existence, your territory, everything you value," Isaac said quickly, his words tumbling out. "You must attempt to understand me—" he glanced apprehensively over his shoulder—"now, because I may not survive long enough to repeat what I am about to reveal—"

The murmur quieted, all attention focused on his words through the translation devices. "These charges," he continued, "all of them—they're completely accurate. At least, they appear to be completely accurate. But in every instance, I was operating with full commitment, risking my existence, for the welfare of your magnificent territory."

There was a loud hiss of static from the back of the court. Isaac frowned and rubbed his hands together. "It was my misfortune," he said, "to arrive at the wrong colony when I first came to Lakeside from my homeland on Earth. I—I landed on Lakeside, Zelvaria, a serious error, but as it turned out, a very fortunate mistake. Because in attempting to establish trade in that hostile place, I made certain connections." His voice trembled and dropped lower. "I learned the terrible thing that is about to happen to this territory, at the hands of those rivals. The conspiracy is theirs, not mine. They have corrupted your Energy Matrix, manipulated it and deceived it, subverted its all-powerful regulation to their own malicious interests, preparing for the day when they could convince it to cast your territory into the catastrophic darkness of a ten-cycle energy blackout—"

Someone in the middle of the court burst into resonant laughter. One by one, the Crystallines nudged each other and chimed their amusement until the rising tide of noise drowned out Isaac's words. "The defendant is obviously manipulating information," the prosecutor resonated over the pandemonium. "Any properly functioning being knows that the Energy Matrix cannot be corrupted. How could it be an Energy Matrix if it could?"

Isaac grew paler. "But—perhaps they were very sophisticated—"

"And how could they manipulate it, when it processes, beyond any doubt, that it is the most perfectly calibrated system in all the Universe? And you dare to insult it, impugn its integrity."

The hisses grew louder, more hostile. Cries of "Terminate him!" and "Dissolve his structure!" rose from the courtroom. The judge struck for silence, his sensors angry.

"Unless the defendant wishes to consume more of our valuable processing time with these absurd manipulations, the jury—"

"Wait! Your Honor, I request a brief recess before I present my final statement."

"Recess?"

"A few moments to organize my thoughts, to structure my defense."

The judge settled back with a disgusted chime. "Must I?" he asked Miguel.

Miguel nodded. The judge shrugged, gesturing toward the anteroom. "You may use that chamber," he said.

Somehow, Isaac managed to stumble from the witness stand, amid riotous hisses and chimes, and staggered into the anteroom.

Isaac inhaled deeply from his cigarette and looked up at Miguel with haunted eyes. "It—it doesn't look promising," he muttered.

Miguel's eyes were troubled, too. For some reason, he felt a surge of sympathy and respect for the haggard con artist. "It's worse than I anticipated," he admitted grimly. "That was a good attempt, but you simply don't understand enough about them and their Energy Matrix." He sat down wearily. "I don't see what you can do. They want justice, and they're determined to get it. They simply won't believe you, no matter how skillfully you manipulate information."

Isaac sat in silence for a moment. "This information manipulation business," he said finally, "exactly how does it function?"

"The most skillful, most convincing negotiator wins. It's that simple. It doesn't matter how elaborate a construction you present. Unless, of course, they've determined that you simply aren't as skillful a negotiator as they are. And it appears that's exactly what they've concluded. It wouldn't matter what you present—unless, somehow, you could make them believe it."

Isaac frowned. "And how do they regard the—the most skillful negotiator? I mean, how do they respond to him?"

Miguel shifted uncomfortably. "It's difficult to say. It's been my experience that they respect him highly—perhaps even fear him somewhat. After all, the most convincing negotiator always wins in any transaction, so he secures more territory, more energy, more power. Yes, I think the most skillful negotiator could operate without any interference."

Isaac was on his feet, his eyes suddenly bright with excitement. "Wait a moment," he said tensely. "To present them with information that they'd have to accept—information they simply couldn't help but accept—" He turned on Miguel, his hands trembling. "Do they process the way we do? I mean, with logic, cause and effect, examining evidence and drawing conclusions? Given certain evidence, would they have to draw the same conclusions that we would draw?"

Miguel blinked. "Well—yes. Absolutely, they're perfectly logical."

Isaac's eyes flashed, and a huge grin broke across his haggard face. His thin body trembled. He started pacing excitedly, staring into space. "If I could only remember—" he muttered. "Someone—somewhere—something I studied."

"Whatever are you talking about?"

"It was a philosopher, I think—"

Miguel stared at him. "Oh, come now. Have you lost your mind completely? You have a serious problem here."

"No, no, I've solved the problem!" Isaac's cheeks flushed. "Let's return—I think I have the answer!"

The courtroom quieted the moment they opened the door, and the judge struck the gavel for silence. As soon as Isaac had taken his seat on the witness stand, the judge turned to the Jury Coordinator. "Now, then," he said with satisfied finality. "The jury—"

"Hold on! Just one moment more."

The judge stared down at Isaac as if he were a malfunctioning component. "Oh, yes. You had additional information to present. Well, proceed and present it."

Isaac looked sharply around the hushed room. "You want to convict me," he said softly, "in the most complete way possible. Isn't that correct?"

Sensors swung toward him. The judge's facets gleamed with anticipation. "That's correct."

"But you can't properly convict me until you've carefully processed any information I present in my own defense. Isn't that correct?"

The judge appeared uncomfortable. "If you have information to present, proceed and present it."

"I have just one statement to make. Brief and direct. But you'd better process it, and analyze it carefully before you decide that you really want to convict me." He paused and directed his gaze at the judge. "You don't value those who present unprocessed truth, it seems. Well, enter this statement in your record, then." His voice was loud and clear in the still room. "All Earthmen are absolutely incapable of presenting accurate information."

Puzzled expressions appeared on the jury's faceted faces. One or two exchanged startled glances, and the room was silent as death. The judge stared at him, then at Miguel, then back. "But you"—he stammered. "You're"—He stopped mid-sentence, his sensors flickering wildly.

One of the jurors let out a small chime and went completely dark. It took, all in all, about ten seconds for the statement to register.

And then chaos erupted in the courtroom.

"Really," said Isaac Hunt smugly, "it was so obvious I'm amazed it didn't occur to me immediately." He settled himself comfortably in the control cabin of the transport vessel and grinned at the outline of Lakeside, Nordavia growing larger in the viewscreen.

Miguel Ortiz stared stonily at the controls, his lips compressed angrily. "You might at least have informed me of your plan."

"And risk being monitored? Don't be ridiculous. It had to be a complete surprise. I had to establish myself as an information manipulator—the supreme manipulator of them all, but I had to present the sort of information that they simply could not process. Something that would throw them into such utter logical contradiction that they wouldn't dare convict me." He grinned impishly at Miguel. "The paradox of Epimenides the Cretan. It really stopped them cold. They knew I was an Earthman, which meant that my statement that Earthmen couldn't present accurate information was inaccurate, which meant that maybe I could present accurate information, in which case—oh, it was perfect."

"It sure was." Miguel's voice was a snarl.

"Well, it established me as a negotiator in a class they couldn't match, didn't it?"

Miguel's face was purple with anger. "Oh, indeed it did! And it classified all Earthmen in exactly the same category, too."

"So what's honor among thieves? I got off, didn't I?"

Miguel turned on him fiercely. "Oh, you got off just fine. You terrified them completely. And in an eon of information manipulation, they've never encountered a logical paradox like that. You've also completely destroyed any hope of ever establishing a trading alliance with Lakeside Territory, and that includes climate technology materials, too. Intelligent beings don't engage with loaded systems. You frightened them so thoroughly they want nothing to do with us."

Isaac's grin broadened, and he leaned back luxuriously. "Ah, well. After all, the Trading Alliance was your concern, wasn't it? What a shame!" He clicked his tongue sadly. "Me, I've got a fortune in credits sitting at the consulate waiting for me—enough to keep me comfortable for quite a while, I must say. I think I'll just take a nice, long vacation."

Miguel turned to him, and a glint of malicious satisfaction appeared in his eyes. "Yes, I think you will. I'm quite certain of it, in fact. Won't cost you a credit, either."

"What?"

Miguel grinned unpleasantly. He brushed an imaginary speck from his lapel and looked up at Isaac slyly. "That—uh—jury trial. The Crystallines weren't particularly happy to accommodate. They wanted to terminate you immediately. Thought a trial was completely inefficient—until they recovered their investment, of course. Not excessive—just five million credits."

Isaac went white. "But that money was in protected custody!"

"Is that so? My goodness. You don't suppose they could have misplaced those documents, do you?" Miguel grinned at the little con artist. "And incidentally, you're under arrest, you know."

A choking sound came from Isaac's throat. "Arrest!"

"Oh, yes. Didn't I mention it? Conspiring to undermine the authority of the Earth Trading Commission. Serious charge, you know. Yes, I think we'll take a nice long journey together, straight back to Earth. And there I think you'll face a jury trial."

Isaac spluttered. "There's no evidence—you've got nothing on me! What kind of setup are you trying to pull?"

"A beautiful setup. Airtight. A case from the ground up, and you're right in the center of it. And this time—" Miguel tapped a cigarette on his thumb with satisfied finality—"this time I don't think you'll get off."
question: Where was the five million credits Isaac Hunt mentioned held?
option_a: In a secret account on Earth
option_b: At the Earth Consulate at Lakeside, Nordavia
