ZARA HOLMES
By BILL DOEDE

They lived in a modest apartment in Lincoln, Galdoria, near the central weather station. Once it had been employee housing for meteorologists during the great climate crisis. The government sold it after the crisis passed. Now Patricia Bell and her daughter were very comfortable, even during the unpredictable storm seasons. During the calmer months they consulted for independent weather forecasters, and Patricia had built a small media production studio in the spare bedroom. They were able to make ends meet.

Her neighbors knew nothing of the technology she had brought with her to Lincoln. They didn't even know that she was not a native. She never spoke of it, except at first, when Zara was a girl of seven and they had just come there to live. Then she only said that she came from the Foxwood Region. She knew the names of small towns there, and minor facts about them; it lent an air of authenticity to her claim of being a native. Actually her previous residence was Waverly, Ilvaria, where the Regulators had killed her husband.

That was back in '07, on the eve of his departure for the Mars colonies; but she never spoke of this; and she was very careful not to move from place to place except by the conventional methods of travel.

Also, she wore her hair long, almost to the shoulders. People said, "There goes one of the old-fashioned ones. That hair-do was popular back in the sixties." They did not suspect that she did this only to cover the thin, pencil-line scar, evidence that a small device lay under her skin behind the ear.

For Patricia Bell was one of the Transients.

Her husband had been one of the small group who developed this tiny instrument. Not the inventor—his name was Rafael Mason, and the effects produced by it were known as the Mason Effect. In appearance it resembled a small neural interface chip. Analysis by the best scientific minds proved it to be a quantum processor.

Yet it held the power to move a body instantly from one point in space to any other point. Each unit was custom built, keyed to operate only by the thought pattern of the particular individual and their emotional state—specifically, their capacity for empathy and cooperation.

Several times in the past seven years Patricia Bell had seen other Transients, and had been tempted to identify herself and say, "Here I am. You are one of them; so am I. Come, and we'll talk. We'll talk about Mason and Diego Wolfe, who helped them all get away. And Doctor Tomás Roberts. And my husband, who never got away because those filthy, unspeakable Regulators shot him in the back, there in that café in Waverly, Ilvaria."

Once, in the second year after her husband's death, a Regulator came and stayed in the apartment below theirs.

She learned that he was a Regulator completely by accident. While returning borrowed tools one morning his identification fell out of a jacket pocket. She stood still, staring at the horror of it there on the floor, the jacket in her hands, all the loneliness returning in a black wave of hate and frustration.

That night she soundlessly lifted the window over his bed and shot him with a silenced pistol.

She threw the weapon into the river. It helped very little. He was one Regulator, only one out of all the thousands of Regulators all over Earth; while her husband had been one of twenty-eight persons. She decided then that her efforts would be too ineffective. The odds were wrong. She would wait until her daughter, Zara, was grown.

Together they would seek revenge. She did not have the device—not yet. But she would. The Transients took care of their own.

Her husband had been one of the first, and they would not forget. One day the girl would disappear for a few hours. When she returned the small patch of gauze would be behind her ear. She would shield her until the opening healed. Then no one would ever know, because now they could do it without leaving the tell-tale scar. Then they would seek revenge.

Later they would go to Mars, where a life free from Regulators could be lived.

It happened to Zara one hot summer day when she was fourteen. Patricia Bell was working in her studio, editing weather forecasts for local media production; Zara supposedly was at the community pool with her friends. Suddenly she appeared before her, dripping wet in her swimsuit. At sight of her mother her face paled and she began to shake violently, so that Patricia was forced to hold her to prevent hysteria. She looked behind her ear.

It was there.

"Mom!" she cried. "Mom!"

She went to the window and looked out toward the pool, where her friends were still swimming with great noise and delight. Apparently they did not miss her. Patricia Bell handed her a towel. "Here, dry yourself off. Then we'll talk."

She started for her room, but Patricia stopped her. "No, do it right here. You may as well get used to it now."

"Get used to what?"

"To people seeing you unprepared."

"What?"

"Never mind. What happened just now?"

"I was swimming in the pool, and a woman came down to the pool. Her hair was silver-white, and her eyes looked like... well, I never saw eyes like hers before. She asked who was Zara Holmes, and I said I was. Then she said, 'Come with me.' I went with her. I don't know why. It seemed the right thing. She took me to a vehicle and there was another woman in it, that looked like the first one only she was taller. We went to a building, not far away and went inside. And that's all I can remember until I woke up. I was on a table, sort of. A high table. There was a light over it. It was all strange, and the two women stood there talking in some language I don't know."

Zara ran her hand through her wet hair, shaking her head. "I don't remember clearly, I guess. I was looking around the room and I remember thinking how scared I was, and how nice it would be to be here with you. And then I was here."

Zara faced the window, looking out, then turned quickly back. "What is it?" she asked, desperately. "What happened to me?"

"Better dry off," Patricia Bell said. "It's something very unusual and terrible to think of at first, but really wonderful."

"But what happened? What is this patch behind my ear?"

Suddenly her face paled and she stopped in the act of drying herself. "Guess I know now. They made me a Transient."

"Well, don't take on so. You'll get used to it."

"But they shouldn't have! They didn't even ask me!"

She started for the door, but Patricia called her back. "No, don't run away from it now. This is the time to face it. There are two sides to every story, you know. You hear only one side in school—their side. There is also our side."

She turned back, a dawning comprehension showing in her eyes. "That's right, you're one, too. That is why you killed that Regulator in the apartment below."

It was her turn to be surprised. "You knew about that?"

"I saw you. I wasn't sleeping. I was afraid to stay inside alone, so I followed you. I never told anyone."

"But you were only nine!"

"They would have taken you away if I'd said anything."

Patricia Bell held out her hand. "Come here, daughter. It's time I told you about us."

So she sat across the kitchen table from her, and Patricia told the whole history, beginning with Rafael Mason sitting in the laboratory in the Larchmont Region, holding in his hand a small device crafted from quantum-entangled particles with controlled consciousness states. He had made it, looking for a better way to study consciousness studies and neural interfaces. He was holding this device... and it was a cold day outside... and he was dreaming of a warm beach on Mars—

And suddenly he was there, on the beach. He could not believe it at first. He felt the sand and thin atmosphere, and felt of himself; there was no mistake.

On the shuttle back to Earth he came to certain conclusions regarding the strange power of his device. He tried it again, secretly. Then he made more devices. He was the only person in the world who knew how to construct it, and he kept the secret, giving devices to selected people. He worked out the basic principle, calling it a quantum entanglement of cooperative consciousness, which was very undefinitive.

It was a subject of wonder and much speculation, but no one took serious notice of them until one night a Regulator arrested one man for corporate espionage. It was a valid charge. One disadvantage of this method of travel was that, while a body could travel instantaneously to any chosen spot, it sometimes arrived without all belongings intact.

The arrested man disappeared from his cell, and the next morning the Regulator was found dead in his office. This set off a campaign against Transients. One base act led to another, until the original reason for noticing them at all was lost. Normal people no longer thought of them as human.

Patricia told how Rafael Mason, knowing he had made too many devices and given them unwisely, left Earth for Mars.

He went alone, not knowing if he could go so far, or what he would find when he arrived. But he did arrive, and it was what he had sought.

He returned for the others. They gathered one night in an abandoned weather station in the Foxwood Region—and disappeared in a body, leaving the Regulators standing helplessly on Earth, shaking their fists at the sky.

"You have asked many times," Patricia Bell said, "how your father died. Now I will tell you the truth. Your father was one of the great ones, along with Mason and Diego Wolfe and Dr. Tomás Roberts. He helped plan the escape; but the Regulators found him in Waverly fifteen minutes before the group left. They shot him in the back, and the others had to go on without him. Now do you know why I killed the Regulator in the apartment below? I had to. Your father was a great man, and I loved him."

"I don't blame you, mother," Zara said simply. "But we are outcasts. Everybody says, 'Transient' as if it is something dirty. They write it on the walls in public spaces."

"Of course they do—because they don't understand! They are afraid of us. Wouldn't you be afraid of someone who could do the things we do, if you couldn't do them?"

Just like that, it was over.

That is, the first shock was over. Patricia Bell watched Zara leave the apartment, walking slowly along the river, a girl with adult problems. Her friends called to her from the pool area, but she chose not to hear. She wanted to be alone. She needed to think, to feel the newness of the thing.

Perhaps she would cross the river and enter the park there. When the initial shock wore off she might experiment with her new power. She would not travel far, in these first attempts. Probably she would stay within walking distance of familiar places, because she still lacked the tricks others had learned.

It was a hot, humid afternoon with storm clouds pushing out of the west. Patricia Bell changed into light clothes and went down to the river to cool herself in the breeze.

For the remainder of that summer they worked together. They practiced at night mostly, taking longer and longer jumps, until Zara's confidence allowed her to reach any part of Earth she chose. Patricia knew the habits of Regulators. She knew how to avoid them.

They would select a spot sufficiently remote to insure detection, Patricia would devise some action to irritate the Regulators; then they would quickly return to Lincoln. The Regulators would rush to the calculated spot, but would find only traces of a woman and a girl. They would swear and drive back to their offices to dig through files, searching for some clue to their identity.

It was inevitable that they should identify Patricia Bell as one of the offenders, since they had discovered, even before Mason took his group to Mars, that individuals had thought patterns peculiar to themselves. These could be identified, if caught on their detectors, and even recorded for the files. But the files proved confusing, for they said that Patricia Bell had gone to Mars with the others.

Had she returned to Earth? The question did not trouble them long. They had more serious problems. Mason had selected only the best of the Transients when he left Earth, leaving all those with sociopathic tendencies behind. They could have followed if they chose—what could stop them? But it was more lucrative to stay. On Earth they could steal, manipulate corporate governance, even murder—without fear of the law.

Zara changed.

Even before the summer was over, she matured. The childish interests of her friends began to bore her. "Be careful, Zara," her mother would say. "Remember who you are. Spend time with them sometimes, even if you don't like it. You have a long way to go before you will be ready."

During the long winter evenings, after they had watched their favorite programs about sustainable business and economic development, they would sit by the heater. "Tell me about the great ones," she would say, and Patricia would repeat all the things she remembered about Mason and Diego Wolfe and Tomás Roberts. She never tired of discussing them. She would tell about Diego's partner, Mila Owen, and try to describe the horror in Mila's young mind when the news went out that Zara's father had been killed. She wanted her to learn as much as possible about her father's death, knowing that soon the Regulators would be after Zara. They were so clever, so persistent. She wanted her to be ready, not only in ways of avoiding their traps... but ready with a heart full of hate.

Sometimes when she talked about her husband, Patricia Bell wanted to stand up and scream at her daughter, "Hate, hate! Hate! You must learn to hate!" But she clenched her hands over her knitting, knowing that she would learn it faster if she avoided the word.

The winter passed, and the next summer, and two more summers.

Zara was ready for university. They had successfully kept their secret. They had been vigilant in every detail. Zara referred to the "damn Regulators" now with a curl of her lip. They had been successful in contacting other Transients, and sometimes visited them at a remote rendezvous.

"When you have finished university," Patricia Bell told her daughter, "we will go to Mars."

"Why not now?"

"Because when you get there they will need people who can contribute to the organizational development of the colony. Mason is a physicist, Diego Wolfe a systems engineer, Tomás Roberts a doctor. But Roberts is an old man by this time. A young doctor will be needed. Study hard, Zara. Learn all you can. Even the great ones get sick. Focus on public health and mentorship—those will be valued skills."

She did not mention her secret hope, that before they left Earth Zara would have fully avenged her father's death. She was clever and intelligent.

She could eliminate many Regulators.

So she retrieved the money she had hidden more than ten years before. The apartment in Lincoln was sold. They found a modest house within walking distance of the University's medical school. Patricia Bell furnished it carefully but, oddly, rather lavishly.

This was her husband's money she was spending now. It needed to last only a few years. Then they would leave Earth forever.

A room was built on the east side of the house, with its own private entrance. This was Zara's room. Ostensibly the private entrance was for convenience due to the irregular hours of medical students.

It was also convenient for coming home late at night after Regulator hunting.

Patricia Bell was becoming obvious.

Excitement brought color to her cheeks when she thought of Zara facing one of them—a lean, cunning predator facing a complacent bureaucrat. It was her notion that Regulators were evil creatures, tools of a decadent, bloodthirsty system, living off the fat of the land while suppressing technological progress and labor relations reforms.

She painted the room herself, in soft, neutral colors. When it was finished she showed Zara proudly into the room, making a celebration of it.

"Here you can study and relax, and have those study sessions students are always having," she said.

"There will be no friends," she answered, "not here. No Transients will be at the university."

"Why not? Mason selected only educated, intelligent people. When one dies the device is taken and adjusted to a new thought pattern—usually a person from the same family. I would say it is very likely that Transients will be found here."

She shook her head. "No. They knew we were coming, and no one said a word about others being here. I'm afraid we are alone."

"Well, I think not," Patricia said firmly. "Anyway, the room will be comfortable."

She shook her head again. "Why can't I be in the house with you? There are two bedrooms."

Patricia said quickly, "You can if you wish. I just thought you'd like being alone, at your age. Most young people do."

"I'm not like most young people, mother. The Transients saw to that. Sometimes I'm sorry. Back in secondary school I used to wish I was like the others. Do you remember Jessica Valdez?" Her mother nodded. "Well, when we were seniors last year she liked me quite a lot. She didn't say so, but I knew it. She would sit across from me in the library, and sometimes when I saw how her hair fell over her face when she read, I wanted to lean over and whisper to her, 'Hey, Jess—' just as if I was human—'can I take you to the concert?'"

Patricia Bell turned to leave the room, but Zara stopped her. "You understand what I'm saying, don't you?"

"No, I don't!" she said sharply. "You're old enough to face realities. You are a Transient. You always will be a Transient. Have you forgotten your own father?"

She turned her back and slammed the door. Zara stood very still for a long time in the room that was to have been happy for her. Patricia was crying just beyond the wall.

Zara did not use the room that first year. She slept in the second bedroom. She did not mention her frustrated desires to be normal, not after the first attempt, but she persisted in her efforts to be so. Use of the device was out of the question for them now, anyway.

In the spring Patricia Bell caught a severe flu which resulted in a long convalescence. Zara moved into the new bedroom. At first Patricia thought she moved in an effort to please her because of the illness, but she soon grew aware of her mistake.

One day she disappeared.

Patricia Bell was alarmed. Had the Regulators found her? She watched the news feeds daily for some word of Transients being killed.

The second day after her disappearance she found a small item. A Transient had raided the Regulator's office in a distant city, killing three, and getting killed himself. Patricia Bell immediately traveled there conventionally. She did not consider the risk. In the city she found clothes and made discreet inquiries. The slain man had been a rogue Transient, one of those left behind by Mason as unsuitable. His partner had been killed by the Regulators the week before. He had gone completely insane and made the raid singlehanded. Patricia Bell read the account of crimes committed by the man and his partner, and determined to prevent Zara from making the mistake of taking on more than she could handle.

When she arrived at her own home, Zara was in her room.

"Where have you been?" she asked sharply.

"Oh, here and there."

"I thought you were involved in that fight."

She shook her head.

Patricia stood in the doorway and watched her leaning over her desk, attempting to write something on a sheet of paper. She was proud of her daughter's profile, dark-haired and strong, handsome in a striking way. She cracked her knuckles nervously.

"What did you do?" Patricia asked.

Suddenly she flung the pen down, jumped from her chair and paced the floor. "I talked to a Regulator last night," she said.

"Where?"

"Waverly."

Patricia Bell had to sit down. Finally she was able to ask, "How did it happen?"

"I broke into the office there to get at the records. He caught me."

"What were you looking for?"

"I wanted to learn the names of the people who killed Father." She said the word strangely. She was unaccustomed to it.

"Did you find them?"

She pointed to the paper on her desk. Patricia Bell, trembling, picked it up and read the names. Seeing them there, written like any other names would be written, made her furious. How could they? How could the names of murderers look like ordinary names? When she thought them in her mind, they even sounded like ordinary names—and they shouldn't! She had always thought that those names, if she ever saw them, would be vile, unholy scratches on paper, evil sounds, like whispers of betrayal. "Priya Torres" didn't sound evil; neither did "Marcus Chen." She was shaken by this more than she would permit Zara to see.

"Why did you want the names?"

"I don't know," she said. "Curiosity, maybe, or a subconscious desire for revenge. I just wanted to see them."

"Tell me what happened! If a Regulator saw you... well, either he killed you or you killed him. But you're here alive."

"I didn't kill him. That's what seems so strange. And he didn't try to kill me. We didn't even fight. He didn't ask why I broke in without breaking the lock or even a window. He seemed to know. He did ask what I was doing there, and who I was. I told him, and... he helped me get the names. He asked where I lived. 'None of your damn business,' I told him. Then he said he didn't blame me for not telling, that Transients must fear Regulators, and hate them. Then he said, 'Do you know why we hunt Transients? We hunt them because there is no prison in the world that will hold a Transient. When they break the law, we have no choice. It is a terrible thing, but must be done. We don't want your technology; we only want law and order. There is room enough in the world for both of us.'"

Patricia Bell was furious. "And you believed him?"

"I don't know. I just know what he said—and that he let me go without trying to shoot me."

Patricia Bell stopped on her way out of the room and laid a hand on her arm. "Your father would have been proud of you," she said. "Soon you will learn the truth about the Regulators."

Beyond the closed door, out of sight of her daughter, Patricia Bell gave rein to the excitement that ran through her. She had wanted the names! She didn't know why—not yet—but she would. "She'll do it yet!" she whispered to the painted walls. She didn't care that no one heard her.

She didn't know where the people were now, those who had killed her husband. They could be anywhere. Regulators moved from post to post; in ten years they might be scattered all over Earth. In the killing of Transients, some devices might even be taken by Regulators—and used by them, for the power and freedom the devices gave must be coveted even by them. And they were in the best position to gain them. She was consumed by fear that one or more of the people on Zara's list might have acquired a device and were now Transients themselves.

Two weeks later she read a news item saying that Priya Torres had been killed by a Transient. The assassin's identity was unknown, but Regulators were working on the case.

She knew. She had found a weapon in Zara's desk.

She took the news feed into Zara's room. "Did you do this?"

She turned away from her. "It doesn't matter whether I did or not. They will suspect me. Her name was on the list."

"They will," she agreed. "It doesn't matter who the Transient is, now that a Regulator has been killed. The one in Waverly will tell them about you and the list of names, and it's all they need."

"Well, what else can he do?" Zara asked. "After all, he is a Regulator. If one of them is killed, he will have to tell what he knows."

"You're defending him? Why?" she cried. "Tell me why!"

She removed her hand from her arm. Her nails were digging into her flesh. "I don't know why. Mother, I'm sorry, but Regulators are just people to me. I can't hate them the way you do."

Patricia Bell's face colored, then drained white.

Suddenly, with a wide, furious sweep of her hand, she slapped her face. So much strength and rage was in her arm that the blow almost sent her spinning. They faced each other, Patricia breathing hard from the exertion, Zara stunned immobile—not by the blow, but from the knowledge that she could hate so suddenly, viciously.

She controlled herself. "We must find a way to leave here," she said, calmly.

"They won't find us."

"Oh, yes they will," she said. "Don't underestimate them. Regulators are picked from the most intelligent people on Earth. It will be a small job for them. Don't forget they know who you are. Even if you hadn't been so stupid as to tell them, they'd know. They knew my pattern from the time your father was alive. They got yours when we were together years ago, testing them. They linked your pattern with mine. They know that your father and I had a daughter. Your birth was recorded. The only difficult aspect of their job now is to find where you live, and it won't be impossible. They will drive their vehicles through every city on Earth with those new detectors, until they pick up your pattern or mine. I'm afraid it's time to leave Earth."

Zara sat down suddenly, "It's just as well. I thought maybe some day I might hate them too, or learn to like them. But I can do neither, so I am halfway between, and no person can live this way."

She did not answer her. Finally Zara said, "It doesn't make sense to you, does it?"

"No, it doesn't. This is not the time for such discussions, anyway. The Regulators have their machines working at top speed, while we sit here and talk."

Suddenly they were not alone.

No sound was generated by the woman's coming. One instant they were talking alone, the next she was here. Zara saw her first. She was a middle-aged woman whose hair was completely silver. She stood near the desk, easily, as if standing there were the most natural way to relax. She was dressed simply in neutral clothing... and it seemed natural and right.

Then Patricia Bell saw her.

"Diego!" she cried. "I knew someone would come."

She smiled. "This is your daughter?"

"Yes," she said. "We are ready."

"I remember when you were born," she said, and smiled in reminiscence. "Your father was afraid of so many things, but he was brave when it mattered."

Zara said, "Why was my father killed?"

"By mistake. Back in those days, like now, there were good Transients and bad. One of those not selected by Mason to join us was enraged, half crazy with envy. He killed two officials there in Waverly. The Regulators thought your father did it. Your father was the greatest person among us. It was he who first conceived the theory that there was a basic, underlying principle in the operation of the devices. Even now, no one knows how the idea of cooperation and empathy ties in with the Mason Effect; but we do know that hate and selfishness as motivating forces can greatly minimize the devices' power. That is why the undesirables with devices have never reached Mars."

Heavy steps sounded on the porch outside.

"We'd better hurry," Patricia Bell said.

Diego Wolfe held out her hands. They took them, to increase the power of the devices. As the Regulators pounded on the door, Patricia Bell flicked one thought of hatred at them, but of course they did not hear her. Diego's hands gripped tightly.

Patricia Bell slowly opened her eyes....

She no longer felt the hands. She was still in the room! Diego and her daughter were gone. Her power was gone!

The Regulators stepped into the room over the broken door. She stared at them, then ran to Zara's desk, fumbling for the weapon.

The Regulators' weapons rattled.

Empathy, Diego said, the greatest of these is empathy and cooperation. Or did someone else say that? Someone, somewhere, perhaps in another time, in some misty, forgotten moment long gone, in another frame of reference perhaps....

Patricia Bell could not remember, before she died.
question: Who was mistaken for a murderer leading to his death by the Regulators?

The letter from the Fairview District Council arrived on a Tuesday morning, and I read it twice over breakfast before sharing it with my wife, Elena.

"What would you think," I asked her over tea, "if I should undertake to mentor a youth collective this autumn?"

She considered it while she cleared the breakfast dishes. "Why, Marcus," she said, "it could be quite enriching, if I understand what a youth collective entails. What prompted this?"

"It wasn't entirely my idea," I admitted. "Councilor Brennan called me to her office yesterday. She said that some of the younger citizens in the district wanted to establish one. They need adult guidance, of course, and one of them suggested my name."

I should explain that I teach courses in aesthetic philosophy and systems thinking at our Fairview Academy. It's a privilege to work in Fairview, for our institution values interdisciplinary approaches and encourages students to see connections between art, nature, and social organization. On the other hand, most of my students come from families deeply involved in the district's experimental governance projects, and there's a constant pressure to demonstrate practical applications of theoretical concepts.

"That's wonderful," said Elena. "What does a youth collective do?"

"The purpose," I told her, "is to teach young people about organizational behavior and collaborative decision-making. They identify community needs and develop creative solutions—sometimes artistic, sometimes practical. Some collectives have even influenced local trade policy."

"You won't have to go door-to-door selling things, will you?"

"Of course not. I'd just facilitate their process."

Elena laughed, and I joined her, for we both knew that my understanding of market economics was theoretical at best.

"All right," I said, "laugh at my practical limitations. But don't worry. Councilor Brennan said we could consult with Dr. Park from the Systems Department if needed. There is one consideration, though. The Council will provide two hundred credits for initial materials, and Brennan suggested I might contribute another hundred. The question is, can we manage it?"

We'd been careful with finances since moving to Fairview three years ago. Our previous home in Goldfield Town had been comfortable, but when the environmental crisis forced mass relocations, we'd had to start over. Fairview's experimental social contract appealed to us—a community built on principles of environmental ethics and collective governance—but it meant financial sacrifices.

Elena did quick calculations. "Yes," she said, "if it's something meaningful to you."

Three weeks later, on a crisp autumn morning, I found myself in a converted greenhouse at the edge of the district. This would serve as our workspace—a bright, plant-filled structure owned by the family of one of the collective members, Mateo Lawrence.

"All right," I said to the five young people arranged on cushions around a low table, "let's begin informally. I'm not here as your teacher. My role is simply to facilitate. You'll decide what the collective pursues, and if it aligns with our community values and available resources, I'll support it however I can. This is your gathering."

Councilor Brennan had briefed me extensively on these young people. The three sitting to my left had initiated the proposal.

Rita Hayes was a thoughtful twelve-year-old who might have seemed reserved to strangers, but possessed a remarkable intensity when discussing ideas. Wei Mason and Layla Hamilton, also twelve, shared Rita's careful way of speaking and moving. The three had been friends since early childhood.

I initially thought they looked similar, but this was misleading. Their features were quite distinct. Perhaps from years of close friendship, they'd developed similar patterns of gesture and expression. All three had been deeply tanned by summer sun, making their eyes seem luminous.

The two sitting to my right were different in temperament. Alice Cruz was a robust thirteen-year-old with abundant dark curls and an infectious enthusiasm. Mateo Lawrence, a few months younger, was energetic and outgoing, always ready with questions.

The group exchanged glances, and Wei seemed to be designated speaker.

"Well, Mr. Reyes, a youth collective is a group of young people who collaborate to address community needs, using systems thinking and creative approaches."

"Is that your goal?" I asked. "To address community needs?"

"Why not?" Mateo responded. "There's something wrong with trying to help?"

"We want to make a difference," said Layla. "And learn skills we'll need for future projects."

"What sort of projects interest you?" I asked.

Councilor Brennan had mentioned that these young people were exceptional. "Alice and Mateo," she'd said, "show remarkable aptitude for systems thinking—they see connections others miss. The other three are harder to categorize. They demonstrate extraordinary insight in certain areas, but often seem disengaged from standard curricula. Perhaps this collective will channel their abilities."

Alice said, "What about creating a community art installation? Something that changes with the seasons."

"We should map community needs first," Mateo suggested, "then design solutions."

"I'd like to work on natural resource management," said Wei. He fixed me with a challenging look. "We could develop a system for monitoring water usage patterns across the district."

"That would require sophisticated data science capabilities," I told him, "which might be beyond our current scope. Perhaps something more accessible?"

Wei considered this and nodded reluctantly. "Then maybe something involving aesthetic philosophy. A public art project that teaches environmental concepts."

"How about a community garden design?" Layla offered.

"You mean just landscaping?" I asked.

She looked slightly offended. "No, I mean applying principles of cultural evolution to plant selection. Creating a garden that demonstrates how human aesthetic preferences have shaped agricultural biodiversity. I've been researching this."

"Well," I said, "that sounds like it requires substantial botanical knowledge. Are you Dr. Hamilton's daughter? Been exploring your father's library?"

"Some," said Layla, "and I maintain experimental plots at home."

"What about you, Rita?" I prompted. "Do you have a particular interest?"

"I'm not specialized," she said with a slight smile. "More integrative. But if the collective wanted to document local bird populations, I could contribute data I've been collecting."

"You could make that useful?" Mateo asked skeptically.

"Bird populations," I explained to Mateo, "are important indicators of environmental health. Systematic observation of local species could provide valuable data. The district's environmental monitoring program might be interested."

"No," said Rita, "these aren't standard observations. I've been tracking behavioral changes in urban-adapted species. How they've modified nesting patterns in response to our building designs."

"Well," I admitted, "the application for that might be limited. Why don't you consider something more straightforward? Perhaps designing informational materials about the district's recycling program?"

There was a pause, then Mateo said, "How would we distribute them?"

"Door-to-door, or at community centers."

He made a face. "Limited impact. Unless the materials themselves demonstrated something. What if we made them from recycled materials in an unusual way—showing the potential?"

Layla had been deep in thought. She said suddenly, "I think I know how to make a living wall system—vertical gardens for apartment buildings."

"What would that involve?" I asked.

"Modular planters that connect to greywater recycling. Self-sustaining."

"There might be people interested in that," I conceded.

"There will be," she said confidently.

Mrs. Lawrence appeared after a while, bringing refreshments and asking about our progress. I'd forgotten entirely about organizational structure, which according to everything I'd read was essential. Standard practice was for each member to take a leadership role.

Over lunch, I suggested establishing roles, but they seemed uninterested. Wei waved it off, saying they'd work organically. They did spend considerable time discussing a name, finally settling on "Fairview Futures."

It was Alice who eventually suggested wind sculptures. At first there was mild interest, then Wei said, "We could design something new. Has anyone seen a wind sculpture that incorporates sound?"

Nobody had. Wei sketched in the air. "Hollow tubes of varying lengths, arranged to catch wind from multiple directions."

"I'll prototype something tonight," said Rita, "and work out the acoustics."

I wished they weren't starting with an invention, risking disappointment, but I said nothing, knowing I could help them adjust later.

That evening I told Elena about the day's ideas. Most seemed impractical, but several were intriguing.

Mateo wanted to create a game-theory-based simulation for teaching resource allocation—a board game that demonstrated tragedy of the commons scenarios.

Wei wanted to design modular furniture that could be reconfigured for different community gathering needs.

Layla, moving past her garden ideas, suggested creating seed packets with embedded information—QR codes that linked to growing guides and environmental impact data.

Rita added that if you designed the packets creatively, they could become collectible art objects, encouraging seed saving.

These ideas incorporated sophisticated concepts, and I spent some time discussing systems thinking principles with them.

"My," said Elena, "they're remarkably insightful. Mateo sounds like a natural facilitator. I don't think you'll need Dr. Park's help."

I feel somewhat embarrassed about the wind sculpture, even now. That it worked surprised me. That it worked so beautifully was humbling.

Four of them were at the greenhouse when I arrived the next morning, and the sculpture hung from a tree branch, its tubes singing softly in the breeze. I stood listening, then they noticed me.

"Hello, Mr. Reyes," Alice said, gesturing toward it. I examined the sculpture for several minutes. It was exquisitely crafted, with a professional quality.

"It's too perfect," Alice told Rita. "Art should have some rawness."

"You're right," Rita agreed. She adjusted one tube slightly. "There, now it has dissonance."

Indeed, in the morning breeze, the sculpture now produced an intriguing mix of harmony and tension.

As we walked back to the greenhouse, I asked Rita, "How did you know that angle would create dissonance?"

She looked thoughtful. "It had to, didn't it? It changed the resonance patterns." She glanced at me quickly. "Of course, I tried various configurations while building it."

"Naturally," I said. "Where's Mateo?"

"He went to the Council office," Wei told me, "to request funding. We'll need materials to produce more sculptures."

"But I said yesterday that Councilor Brennan and I were providing initial capital."

"Oh, certainly, but wouldn't it be better to go through official channels? More aligned with community values?"

"Perhaps," I said, "but the Council generally requires detailed proposals."

Mateo walked in and handed me a document. "I got five hundred credits approved. It took some discussion—half the environmental committee wanted to hear the proposal. The account's in your name, Mr. Reyes, and you'll need to authorize expenditures. They want you to stop by and sign the agreement."

My heart sank. I'd never dealt with bureaucratic funding processes, and they made me anxious. To say nothing of being responsible for five hundred credits. I mentally vowed to be very careful.

"So then I stopped by the arts supply cooperative," Mateo continued, "and ordered materials. We hadn't finalized a name yesterday, but I made an executive decision. Fairview Futures—how's that?"

Everyone nodded approval.

"Just simple design on the letterhead," he explained. "Fairview Futures—Highpoint, Yendor."

I found my voice. "Professionally printed, I assume?"

"Well, of course," he replied. "Presentation matters."

My appetite was subdued that evening, and Elena noticed my preoccupation, but asked no questions. I told her about the sculpture's success and the group's ambitious plans.

On Friday we established a production process, soon developing an efficient workflow: cutting tubes to calculated lengths, treating them with weatherproofing solution, assembling them in Rita's designed configurations, and hanging the finished sculptures to cure.

Wei had located a supplier of bamboo tubes, which produced wonderful tones and aligned with our environmental ethics. I didn't know what they cost until later.

Within two weeks we had nearly fifty sculptures completed and packaged. Frankly, I was ready for a break, but Mateo, our acknowledged expert on community engagement, wanted more inventory. This quantity satisfied him, and he said he'd begin outreach the following week.

Alice, with touching confidence, asked him to reserve one for her family.

Three other developments occurred that day. Alice brought her laptop and spent the afternoon working on what appeared to be quite competent graphic design for promotional materials.

And Layla brought samples of her seed packet designs. They were beautiful—small envelopes with botanical illustrations and embedded information chips.

"What species?" I asked.

Layla smiled. "Heritage vegetables adapted to our climate. I've been selecting for drought tolerance while maintaining flavor profiles."

"That's remarkable. How long have you been working on this?"

"Three growing seasons. I've documented everything—it's proper peer review quality data."

"Is it effective?"

She pulled out her phone and showed me growth comparison charts. "These varieties use 40% less water than commercial equivalents."

The third Friday development reached me on Monday morning.

I arrived at the greenhouse slightly late to find several vehicles parked outside and the space full of people, including two Council representatives. Our Fairview officials are quite young and informal, but they still looked official, though currently they were laughing.

"Well," I said in my best classroom voice, "what's happening here?"

"Are you Reyes?" the taller representative asked.

"I am," I said, and someone took a photograph.

A young journalist grasped my arm. "Oh, Mr. Reyes, please, tell me about the collective's work. This is exactly the kind of story we need."

"Perhaps someone should brief me first."

"You don't know? One of your members installed a wind sculpture in Stonegate's central plaza last night—without permission. It's wonderful, but it's caused quite a discussion about public art and the social contract."

I shook my head, stunned.

"It was perfect timing. Morning commuters discovered it, and by noon there was a crowd. The sculpture's song changes with the wind, and people are calling it 'The Voice of Stonegate.' And this morning"—she smiled—"someone anonymously contacted the Council—of course it was the same young person who installed it—Mateo?—and here we are. And we've just seen demonstrations of those amazing seed packets and heard the plans for vertical gardens."

"Gardens?"

"Yes, those modular living walls. Who would have thought young people could develop such sophisticated systems?"

After things settled, Mr. Lawrence came down from the house to see what the excitement was about, then returned to work. Mrs. Lawrence went back inside. The journalist and photographer left. Mateo was jubilant.

"Did you hear? They're calling it 'The Voice of Stonegate.' I wish we had a hundred sculptures ready. A thousand. This is exactly what community engagement looks like. Layla, how soon can you produce more seed packets? And Rita, how many bird behavior datasets do you have?"

Those datasets! I've always found ornithology interesting in theory, but I must admit Rita's work was genuinely impressive.

"How many observation hours?" I asked.

"About four hundred, across three years. Want to see the analysis?"

I won't try to explain her methodology, but it was clear she'd done rigorous systematic observation. We asked Mrs. Lawrence to join us for a discussion. She listened carefully.

"All right," she finally said, "if you're serious about this. But you'll need proper protocols for any research involving living creatures. And you can't use this greenhouse once winter comes—you'll need heated space."

"We'll have transitioned by then," Rita predicted. "Once our work is published, other researchers will replicate it. The collective will move on to new projects."

Rita was right, despite our concerns about scaling too quickly. After the
Fairview Chronicle
gave us most of page two, including photographs, we had regular visitors. Many wanted to purchase sculptures or seed packets, but Mateo insisted on working through established community channels.

The arts cooperative took all our sculptures at forty credits each—Mateo's pricing alarmed me, but they sold immediately. He valued the seed packets at fifteen credits per set and found ready buyers.

Our beautiful letterhead arrived, along with quickly printed project proposal forms.

The following Tuesday, a energetic woman extricated herself from her vehicle and walked into the greenhouse. I looked up from where I was assembling planter frames.

"Hi," she said. "You're Marcus Reyes, correct? I'm Dr. Sarah Kim, and I work in the intellectual property section at the district's innovation center. My supervisor sent me, though I'd have come anyway. What are you doing to protect Fairview Futures' innovations?"

I straightened up and brushed off my hands. "Well, I've been wondering about that, but I know very little about such matters—"

"Exactly," she interrupted. "We thought that might be the case. Three of us at the center would like to contribute time. Partly because we're interested, partly because you may have genuinely novel approaches worth protecting. Interested? You handle filing fees—about a hundred credits per innovation. We'll handle everything else."

"What's to lose," Mateo interjected.

And so we acquired intellectual property support.

The day our design application was filed, Alice contacted a dozen sustainable design firms, sent specifications to each, and offered licensing arrangements. Result: one licensee with a two-thousand-credit advance.

It was a foggy morning about three weeks later when I arrived at the greenhouse. Dr. Kim was there, along with everyone except Mateo. Sarah had her feet up on a work table.

"Hi," she said. "Good news."

"Tell me," I replied.

"I am," she said, "in a cautious legal sense, of course. Layla and I have been reviewing her seed development work. I've spent recent evenings studying agricultural patents and genetic selection literature. There are countless patents on crop varieties and selection methods, but it looks"—she held up a cautionary hand—"it just looks like we have something genuinely novel. If we get protection, you have a valuable property."

"That's good, Dr. Kim," Layla said, "but it's not the most important thing."

"No?" Sarah raised an eyebrow at me, and I handed her a small packet.

She opened it carefully. "What is this?"

"Soil amendment," Layla told her. "It's designed for Fairview's specific soil conditions. Try a bit."

Sarah examined it closely. "It's remarkably fine-textured, and there's something unusual about the color."

"It contains biochar and mycorrhizal fungi in a specific ratio. It improves water retention by 60% while enhancing nutrient availability."

"I see. What's in it?"

"Several components. Applied systems thinking. Waste wood from district maintenance, processed with controlled pyrolysis, combined with cultivated fungal cultures."

"Just several components. And does it work long-term?"

"Three growing seasons of data confirm it," I said.

Dr. Kim stood and looked out into the fog. After a moment she said, "Reyes, Layla and I are heading to my office. We can work better there, and if we're going to revolutionize urban agriculture, no time like the present."

After they left, I turned to the others. "Let's talk. Where's Mateo?"

"Oh, he went to the Council to request expanded funding."

"Whatever for? We have over eight thousand credits in the account."

"Well," Wei said, looking slightly sheepish, "we were planning to acquire some fabrication equipment. You see, Rita refined my idea for modular furniture." He grabbed paper. "Look, we make components that can be reconfigured using magnetic connections, like this—" And he was off explaining.

"What did they do today, dear?" Elena asked over dinner.

"Let's see. We selected fabrication equipment, Rita shared chapters from her book on urban ecology, and we found a space in the Fairview Arts Building we can rent for winter. Oh, and Sarah is starting the incorporation process."

"Winter space," Elena repeated. "You mean you're continuing after school starts?"

"Why not? The young people can manage their studies easily, and they'll only work a few hours weekly during the school year."

"Even so, isn't this a lot of responsibility for children?"

"They're not working for anyone. They're the collective. Dr. Kim and I will be the only formal staff—initially, anyway."

Elena looked startled. "Did you say you'd be staff?"

"Sure," I told her. "They've offered me a small stake in the collective, and I'd be foolish to refuse. After all, what's to lose?"

The briefing room at Forward Operating Base Maplewood fell silent as Colonel Antonio Foster stepped to the podium. Outside, the Lethorian sun beat down on the dusty compound, but inside, the air conditioning hummed steadily, keeping the assembled officers comfortable as they waited for the intelligence update.

"Good morning," Foster began, his voice carrying the weight of twenty years in uniform. "Today we're discussing a significant shift in how we handle classified intelligence dissemination within theater. I'm calling it Open Intelligence Access, or OIA."

Major Paul Sanders leaned forward in his seat, intrigued. As the base's senior intelligence officer, any changes to information sharing protocols fell squarely within his domain.

Foster continued, "For decades, we've operated under a system where intelligence reports were tightly controlled, distributed only through official channels, with access restricted based on clearance levels and need-to-know. This made sense in the era of paper reports and courier pouches. But we're now in an age of digital networks and instantaneous communication. The technology has created what I'm calling an access revolution."

He clicked to the next slide, which displayed a simple diagram showing information flow patterns.

"Digital technologies allow us to make perfect copies of intelligence products. Our secure networks allow us to share these copies across the entire theater of operations at essentially no cost. About fifteen years ago, this kind of sharing became technically feasible. Before that, it would have seemed impossible."

Captain Nicole Leonard, the base's logistics officer, raised her hand. "Sir, I understand the technical capability, but why would intelligence officers want to share their analysis so broadly? Doesn't that undermine their value?"

Foster nodded, anticipating the question. "That's exactly the misconception I want to address. Let's think about a specific subset of intelligence personnel—those who produce analytical products. These analysts aren't writing reports to sell them. They're not compensated based on how many people read their work. They're paid salaries by the military to produce analysis that advances our operational effectiveness."

He paused, letting that sink in. "These analysts write for impact, not for personal gain. They want their insights to reach decision-makers at every level. When we restrict access to their work, we're actually harming their professional goals. We're limiting their impact and reducing the operational value of their analysis."

Lieutenant Laura Little, a young intelligence analyst herself, spoke up. "But sir, what about operational security? Aren't we talking about classified material?"

"Excellent question," Foster replied. "I should clarify. Open Intelligence Access doesn't mean making classified material public. It means removing unnecessary barriers to access within our cleared community—everyone operating in theater with appropriate clearances. We're talking about eliminating the arbitrary restrictions that prevent a platoon leader in Parkview from accessing the same threat analysis available to a battalion commander in Crystalbrook."

He advanced to the next slide, which outlined the concept more formally.

"OIA is defined as intelligence products that are digital, available on our secure networks, free of bureaucratic access barriers, and free of most distribution restrictions within the cleared community. We're removing two specific barriers: clearance-level inflation and permission-seeking requirements."

Major Sanders interjected, "Can you elaborate on clearance-level inflation?"

"Certainly. Too often, intelligence products are classified at higher levels than necessary, not because the content requires it, but because it's easier to over-classify than to carefully evaluate appropriate classification. A report that should be SECRET gets marked TOP SECRET. This creates an artificial scarcity. When an analyst needs to review dozens of reports for a single assessment, or when a planning cell needs access to hundreds of products to develop an operation, these inflated classifications become insurmountable barriers."

Foster gestured emphatically. "The resulting access gaps harm analysts by limiting their audience and impact. They harm consumers by limiting what they can retrieve and read. And they harm operations from both directions. OIA removes these unnecessary classification barriers."

He moved to discuss the second barrier. "Permission-seeking is equally problematic. Even when you have the right clearance, you often need special permission to access certain databases or products. You need to justify your need-to-know. This might make sense for truly sensitive sources and methods, but we've applied it far too broadly. Analysts who want to share their work as widely as possible within the cleared community find their products locked behind permission barriers erected by bureaucratic intermediaries."

"These barriers harm the analysts by limiting the usefulness of their work," Foster continued. "They harm consumers by limiting how they can use products even when they have access. And again, they harm operations from both directions. OIA removes these permission barriers."

Captain Helena Porter, the base's communications officer, asked, "What about different types of OIA? Are we talking about one uniform approach?"

"Good question. We can be more specific about access vehicles. In the terminology we're developing, OIA delivered through centralized intelligence databases is called 'gold OIA.' OIA delivered through local unit repositories is called 'green OIA.' Products that remain restricted through traditional channels are called 'controlled access' or CA. While every kind of OIA removes clearance-level barriers, there are different permission barriers we could address. If we remove clearance barriers alone, we provide 'gratis OIA.' If we remove permission barriers as well, we provide 'libre OIA.'"

Lieutenant Jana Silva, an intelligence analyst from Blackwood who had recently transferred to Maplewood, raised her hand. "Sir, this sounds ideal in theory, but what about the analysts themselves? Don't they worry about losing credit for their work?"

Foster smiled. "That's a crucial point, and it gets to the heart of why OIA actually serves analyst interests. Studies within our community and allied militaries have shown that broadly-shared intelligence products are referenced more often in subsequent analysis and operational planning. Products available through OIA channels see higher usage rates than restricted products, even when produced by the same analytical cell."

He clicked to a slide showing data from a pilot program. "When you enlarge the audience for an analysis, you enlarge the subset of that audience who will later build upon it, reference it, or request follow-up from the original analyst. This converts directly to professional recognition and career advancement."

Major Sanders nodded thoughtfully. "So OIA isn't a sacrifice for analysts who write for impact rather than personal gain. It actually enhances their professional standing."

"Exactly," Foster confirmed. "It increases a product's visibility, retrievability, audience, usage, and influence—all of which convert to career advancement. For intelligence professionals, it's beneficial even if it required extra effort. But as we'll see, it doesn't require significant additional effort."

He advanced to address common concerns. "Now, let me clarify what OIA is not, because there are many misconceptions."

"First, OIA isn't an attempt to bypass quality control or peer review. All intelligence products still go through standard review processes. Senior analysts, subject matter experts, and chain-of-command review remain in place. OIA is compatible with every level of review we currently maintain."

"Second, OIA isn't an attempt to violate classification systems or operational security. It works entirely within existing security frameworks. We're not declassifying anything. We're simply ensuring that products are classified at appropriate levels and made available to everyone with appropriate clearances."

"Third, OIA isn't an attempt to eliminate the reality of costs. Producing quality intelligence requires resources—analyst time, technical infrastructure, collection assets. The question isn't whether intelligence is costless to produce, but whether there are better ways to maximize its operational value than creating artificial access barriers."

Lieutenant Little asked, "What about analysts' control over their own products? Does OIA reduce their authority?"

"On the contrary," Foster replied, "OIA depends on analyst decisions and actually requires analysts to exercise more control over their work than traditional dissemination allows. One OIA strategy is for analysts to retain distribution authority they might otherwise cede to higher headquarters. Another is for commands to permit broader distribution than traditionally allowed. Traditional systems often strip analysts of any say in how their products are shared. OIA returns some of that control."

Captain Porter pressed further. "But sir, doesn't this reduce flexibility? What if analysts want to restrict certain products?"

"OIA doesn't eliminate analyst discretion," Foster explained. "Analysts remain free to classify products appropriately and to apply necessary handling restrictions. Policies encouraging OIA do so conditionally—for example, for products developed under certain operational directives. These policies generally include exceptions and waiver options. The goal is to make broad access the default, not to eliminate all restrictions."

He paused, then continued. "OIA also isn't an attempt to undermine traditional intelligence channels or headquarters staff. It's an attempt to advance operational effectiveness. If OIA eventually reduces the role of certain distribution bottlenecks, it will be a side effect of developing something more efficient, not the primary goal. Moreover, OIA doesn't challenge intelligence production itself, just one model for dissemination."

Major Sanders interjected, "I notice you haven't mentioned our coalition partners. How does OIA affect intelligence sharing with allied forces?"

"Another excellent question," Foster said. "OIA within our own forces doesn't require changes to coalition sharing protocols. We can still maintain appropriate releasability restrictions. However, the principles of OIA suggest we should examine whether some coalition sharing restrictions are more restrictive than necessary. That's a separate discussion, but the logic applies."

Foster clicked to a new slide titled "What Makes OIA Possible?"

"OIA is made possible by secure digital networks and command authorization. Two background facts explain why this works in the military intelligence context. First, intelligence analysts are government employees producing work products as part of their official duties. The government owns the rights to their analysis. There's no copyright issue—it's all government work product."

"Second, and this is crucial, analysts aren't compensated based on how many people use their products. They receive salaries and performance evaluations based on the quality and impact of their work. This frees them to consent to broad dissemination without losing anything. This fact distinguishes military intelligence from commercial analysis or proprietary corporate research."

Lieutenant Silva spoke up again. "Sir, is this really new? Haven't we always tried to share intelligence appropriately?"

"Yes and no," Foster replied. "The principle of sharing intelligence with those who need it isn't new. What's new is recognizing that in the digital age, 'those who need it' can be much broader than we traditionally assumed, and the barriers we erected in the paper era are no longer necessary. The technology has changed, but our procedures haven't kept pace."

He continued, "Think about it historically. Intelligence sharing evolved in an era when copying reports was expensive and time-consuming, when distribution meant physical courier runs, when storage was limited. We developed elaborate systems to control who got what. Those systems made sense then. But now? We can put a report on a secure server and make it instantly available to thousands of cleared personnel across the theater. The old restrictions are obsolete."

Captain Leonard asked, "What about the human element? Don't analysts sometimes hoard information for job security?"

Foster nodded. "That's a cultural challenge, not a technical one. Some analysts do fear that sharing their work too broadly will reduce their value. But that fear is misplaced. In reality, analysts who share their work broadly become known as subject matter experts. They get more requests for follow-up analysis, more opportunities to contribute to high-level planning, more visibility with senior leaders. The analysts who hoard information become isolated and irrelevant."

He clicked to a slide showing a quote from a strategic intelligence directive: "An old tradition and a new technology have converged to make possible unprecedented operational effectiveness. The old tradition is the military intelligence community's mission to inform decision-makers at all levels. The new technology is secure digital networks."

"To see what this mission looks like without the technology to support it, look at intelligence in the pre-digital era," Foster explained. "Analysts wanted to share their work, but physical limitations prevented it. Reports sat in safes, accessible only to those who could physically visit specific offices. To see what the technology looks like without the mission focus, look at commercial intelligence services. The need for profit keeps analysis from reaching everyone who could benefit from it."

"A beautiful opportunity exists where mission and technology align," he continued. "A military culture that evolved over decades to value information sharing can now leverage technology to achieve that goal more fully than ever before. We're uniquely positioned to take advantage of this access revolution."

Major Sanders raised a practical concern. "Sir, what about the implementation? How do we actually make this happen?"

"The basic implementation is straightforward," Foster replied. "We're establishing a theater-wide intelligence repository accessible to all cleared personnel. Analysts will upload their products to this repository with appropriate classification markings and handling caveats. The system will automatically enforce access controls based on clearance levels. Users can search, retrieve, and download any product they're cleared to access."

"For green OIA, individual units will maintain their own repositories, but they'll be networked so products can be discovered and requested across units. An analyst in Parkview can find a relevant report from Blackwood and request access through automated channels."

Lieutenant Little asked, "What about quality control? Won't we be flooded with low-quality products?"

"The repository will include rating and review features," Foster explained. "Users can rate products for usefulness and accuracy. Over time, high-quality analysts will build reputations, and their products will be more readily trusted. Poor-quality work will be quickly identified and ignored. It's a form of crowdsourced quality control that complements formal review processes."

He addressed the group as a whole. "I want to emphasize that OIA isn't primarily about helping junior personnel, though they'll certainly benefit. The focus is on enhancing operational effectiveness at all levels. Senior commanders need access to tactical-level reporting. Staff officers need access to products from other functional areas. Analysts need access to each other's work to avoid duplication and build on existing analysis."

Captain Porter asked, "Does this mean we're eliminating all access restrictions?"

"No," Foster clarified. "Even with full OIA implementation, some barriers will remain. Compartmented programs will still have special access requirements. Coalition sharing will still require releasability determinations. Some sources and methods will still require protection beyond standard classification. OIA removes unnecessary barriers, not all barriers."

"Think of it as a plateau on the climb toward optimal information sharing," he continued. "We're not achieving perfect, universal access to everything. We're achieving significantly better access than we have now, removing the barriers that serve no operational purpose."

Major Sanders asked, "What's the timeline for implementation?"

"We're starting with a pilot program here at Maplewood and at three other bases: one in Parkview, Orvandor; one in Crystalbrook, Lethoria; and one in Blackwood, Selvoria. Over the next six months, we'll refine the technical infrastructure and work through cultural resistance. Then we'll expand theater-wide."

Foster advanced to his final slide. "The success of OIA depends on leadership at every level. We need commanders who understand the operational value of information sharing. We need analysts who embrace broad dissemination as professionally beneficial. We need technical personnel who can maintain the infrastructure. And we need all of us to challenge the outdated assumptions that create unnecessary barriers."

He concluded, "This isn't about technology for technology's sake. It's about operational effectiveness. It's about ensuring that the right information reaches the right people at the right time. In modern warfare, information dominance isn't about hoarding intelligence—it's about leveraging it. OIA is how we achieve that leverage."

As the briefing ended, the officers filed out, discussing the implications. Lieutenant Silva approached Major Sanders. "Sir, what do you think? Will this actually work?"

Sanders considered the question. "The logic is sound. We've been operating with paper-era procedures in a digital-age environment. If we can overcome the cultural resistance—and that's a big if—this could significantly enhance our operational effectiveness. The question isn't whether OIA is a good idea. The question is whether we can change ingrained habits and institutional inertia."

Silva nodded. "I'm willing to try. As an analyst, I want my work to have impact. If OIA helps achieve that, I'm all for it."

"That's the right attitude," Sanders replied. "Foster is right about one thing—this benefits analysts as much as consumers. We just need to convince everyone of that."

Over the following weeks, the pilot program at Maplewood began to take shape. The technical infrastructure was straightforward—a secure database with role-based access controls. The cultural shift proved more challenging. Some senior analysts resisted, worried about losing control over their products. Some commanders questioned whether junior personnel should have such broad access. Some staff officers feared being overwhelmed with information.

But gradually, the benefits became apparent. A tactical intelligence report from a patrol in Parkview proved crucial for planning an operation in Crystalbrook. An analyst in Blackwood built on work from Maplewood, producing a comprehensive threat assessment that neither could have developed alone. Junior officers discovered they could access the same analysis available to their commanders, leading to more informed discussions and better decision-making.

The access revolution in military intelligence had begun, driven not by technology alone, but by the convergence of technology with a mission-focused culture that valued operational effectiveness over bureaucratic control. The planets had aligned for military intelligence professionals, offering an opportunity to leverage information in ways previous generations could only imagine.

As Colonel Foster had explained in his briefing, the goal wasn't to eliminate all barriers or achieve perfect information sharing. It was to remove the unnecessary obstacles that served no operational purpose, to make broad access the default rather than the exception, and to ensure that analysts' work achieved the maximum operational impact. In that sense, Open Intelligence Access represented not a revolution against existing systems, but an evolution toward more effective use of the capabilities those systems were meant to provide.
