synthetic_story:
I am a Probability Field
By SOPHIA WEST

When I got back from the research institute, I was not so much exhausted as mentally drained, but the effect is similar. I let myself into the apartment in Eastwood Village, which had an absent-partner look, and took a cold shower. The present temperature according to the weather app was thirty-two degrees Celsius, but according to my thermometer, it was thirty-eight. I got dressed and went into the living room, and wished ardently that my partner Hassan were here to tell me why the whole place looked so desolate.

What do they do, I asked myself, that I have left undone? I've cleaned the floors, I've organized the books and I've straightened the cushions.... Ah! The coffee mugs. I washed them and put them back, but still the place looked partner-deserted.

It had been a difficult day; I had forgotten to charge my alarm, so I'd had to rush to make a theoretical modeling presentation at one of the quantum computing labs I consult for. I didn't notice the impending storm and had no umbrella when I reached the sidewalk, to find myself confronted with an almost tropical downpour. I would have turned back, but a rideshare pulled up and a woman got out, so I dashed through the rain and got in.

"University District, the Quantum Sciences Building," I said.

"Right," said the driver, and I heard the engine sputter, and then go on sputtering. After some futile attempts, she turned to me. "Sorry. You'll have to find another ride. Good luck."

If possible, it was raining still harder. I opened my bag over my head and ran for the metro: three blocks. Traffic held me up at each crossing and I was soaked when I reached the platform, just in time to miss the express. After an abnormal delay, I got one which exactly missed the connection at Central Station. The same thing happened at both ends of the cross-district line, but I found the rain had stopped when I got out at University Square.

As I walked toward the building, I passed a large construction site where they were preparing to build a new green infrastructure project—part of the city's environmental justice initiative. There was the usual crowd of observers watching the excavation machines and, in particular, a worker with a jackhammer who was breaking up some compressed sediment. While I looked, a large chunk of it fell away, and for an instant I was able to see something that looked like a piece of crystalline material, the size of a storage container. It glittered brilliantly in the sunlight, and then the chattering jackhammer hit it.

There was a faint crack and the thing disintegrated. It knocked the worker backwards, but he got right up and I realized he was not hurt. At the moment of the fracture—if so minor a thing can be called one—I felt something sting my cheek and, on touching it, found blood on my hand. I dabbed at it with a tissue but, though slight, the bleeding would not stop, so I went into a pharmacy and bought some adhesive strips which I put on the tiny cut. When I got to the lab, I found that I had missed the presentation slot.

During the day, by actual count, I heard the phrase "Let's workshop that" nine times, and another academic favorite, "The entire theoretical framework," eleven times. However, my theoretical model had been accepted without revision because nobody had noticed my absence from the presentation room. There you have what is known as the Academic World, the research game, or the grant-writing racket, depending upon which level of the hierarchy you have achieved.

The metro gave a repeat performance going home, and as I got to the apartment complex in Eastwood Village, the building manager was standing there talking to the maintenance supervisor.

She said, "Hello, Dr. West. I guess you must have just missed it at your building. We just heard a little while ago: all four elevators in the Quantum Sciences Building jammed at the same time. Sounds impossible. I guess you just missed it."

Anything can happen in academia, I thought. "That's right, I just missed it," I said, and went on in.

Behavioral economics tells us that some people are risk-seeking; I, on the other hand, seemed recently to be coincidence-prone, anomaly-adjacent, and except for the dead alarm, I'd had no control over what had been going on.

I went into our small kitchen to make a drink and reread the instructions Hassan had left, telling me how to manage by myself until he got back from his conference in Crestwood Village, a matter of ten days. How to use the coffee maker, how to operate the food processor, whom to call if I needed help. My partner used to be a professional chef and he is quite convinced that I cannot feed myself without him. He is right, but not for the reasons he supposes.

I opened the refrigerator to get some ice and saw another note: "When you take out the Juice or Cheese, Put it Right Back. And Close the Door, too."

Intimidated, I took my drink into the living room and sat down in front of the computer. As I stared at the research paper that was to establish my reputation beyond quantum computing, I noticed an error and picked up a stylus. When I put it down, it rolled off the desk, and with my eyes on the manuscript, I groped under the chair for it. Then I looked down. The stylus was standing on its end.

There, I thought to myself, is that one chance in a million we hear about, and picked up the stylus. I turned back to my paper and drank some of the cocktail in hopes of inspiration and relief from the muggy heat, but nothing came. I went back and read the whole section to try to get forward momentum, but came to a dead stop at the last sentence.

Damn the heat, damn the stylus, damn academia and grant applications. My drink was gone and I went back to the kitchen and read Hassan's notes again to see if they would be like a message from him. I noticed one that I had missed, pinned to the recycling bin: "Pickup at 6:30 AM so the idea is to Put it Here the Night Before. I love you." What can you do when he loves you?

I made another drink and went and stared out of the living room window at the courtyard opposite. The sun was out again and a woman with a remote was operating her collection of drones. They flew in formation, hoping to be allowed to land, but were not allowed to.

Drones fly as a rule in coordinated patterns and turn simultaneously, so that their solar panels all catch the sunlight at the same time. I was thinking about this elegant fact when I saw that as they were making a turn, they seemed to bunch up together. By some curious chance, they all wanted the same position in the airspace to turn in, and several collided and fell.

The woman was as surprised as I and went to one of the damaged drones and picked it up. She stood there shaking her head from side to side, examining its rotors.

My speculations about this peculiar aerial traffic accident were interrupted by loud voices in the hallway. Since our building is usually very well behaved, I was astonished to hear what sounded like an incipient argument, and among the angry voices I recognized that of my neighbor, Felix, a very quiet guy who works in media production and has never, to my knowledge, caused disturbances, particularly in the late afternoon.

"You can't accuse me of that!" I heard him shout. "I tell you I bought this deck this afternoon and it wasn't opened till we started to play!"

Several other loud voices started at the same time.

"Nobody gets five royal flushes in a row!"

"Yeah, and only when you were dealer!"

The tone of the argument was beginning to get ugly, and I opened the door to offer Felix help if he needed it. There were four people confronting him, evidently torn between the desire to make an angry exit and the impulse to stay and confront him further. His face was furiously red and he looked stunned.

"Here!" he said, holding out a deck of cards, "For heaven's sake, examine them yourselves if you think they're marked!"

The nearest person struck them up from his hand. "Okay, magician! So they're not marked! All I know is five royal...."

His voice trailed away. He and the others stared at the scattered cards on the floor. About half were face down, as might be expected, and the rest face up—all spades.

Someone must have called for it, because at that moment the elevator arrived and the four people, with half frightened, incredulous looks, and in silence, got in and were taken down. My friend stood looking at the neatly arranged cards.

"Unbelievable!" he said, and started to pick them up. "My God, what a session...."

I helped him and said to come in for a drink and tell me all about it, but I had an idea what I would hear.

After a while, he calmed down, but he still seemed dazed.

"Never seen anything to equal it," he said. "Wouldn't have believed it. Those people didn't believe it. Every round normal, nothing unusual about the hands—three of a kind, a low straight, that sort of thing and one person got queens over tens, until it gets to be my deal. Brother! Royal flush—every time! And each time, somebody else has four aces...."

He started to perspire again, so I got up to fix him another drink. There was one bottle of tonic water left, but when I tried to open it, the cap broke and glass fragments got into the bottle.

"I'll have to go down for more tonic," I said.

"I'll come, too. I need air."

At the convenience store on the corner, the clerk gave me three bottles in what must have been a weak bag, because as he handed them to me over the counter, the bottom gave and they fell onto the tile floor. None of them broke, although the fall must have been from at least five feet. Felix was too absorbed in his thoughts to notice and I was getting used to anomalies. We left the proprietor with his mouth open and met the building manager, looking in at the door, also with her mouth open.

On the sidewalk, a man walking in front of Felix stopped suddenly to check his phone and Felix, to avoid bumping him, stepped into the bike lane and a cyclist swerved to avoid Felix. The pavement was still wet and the cyclist skidded, their rear wheel lightly tapping the front of one of those small electric scooters, which was going rather fast. It turned sideways and, without any side-slip, went right up the steps of a building opposite, coming to rest with its front wheel inside the entrance, which a woman opened at that moment.

The sight of this threw another cyclist into a skid, and when she and the first cyclist had stopped sliding around, they were positioned face to face, arranged crosswise to the bike lane. This gave them exactly no room to move either forward or backward, for one bike had its back to a bench and the other to a lamppost.

Although rather wide, this is a two-way bike lane, and in no time at all, traffic was backed up from both directions as far as the intersections. Everyone was ringing their bell.

The building manager was frustrated—more so when she tried to put through a call to the maintenance office from the panel in the lobby.

It was malfunctioning.

Upstairs, the wind was blowing into the apartment and I closed the windows, mainly to shut out the commotion and the noise. Felix had brightened up considerably.

"I'll stay for one more drink and then I'm due at the studio," he said. "You know, I think this would make content for our channel." He grinned and nodded toward the chaos.

When he was gone, I noticed it was getting dark and turned on the desk lamp. Then I saw the window blinds. They were all twisted in spirals, except one. That was twisted in three spirals.

All right, I told myself, it was the wind. But I felt the time had come for me to get expert advice, so I went to the phone to call Ruth. Ruth is an associate professor of theoretical physics at a university uptown and lives near us. She is highly analytical, but we believe she knows everything.

When I picked up the receiver, the line sounded dead and I thought, more trouble. Then I heard someone cough and I said hello. Ruth's voice said, "Sophia? You must have picked up the receiver just as we were connected. That's a remarkably unlikely coincidence."

"Not in the least," I said. "Come on over here. I've got something for you to analyze."

"Well, as a matter of fact, I was calling to ask you and Hassan—"

"Hassan's away for the week. Can you get over here quickly? It's urgent."

"Immediately," she said, and hung up.

While I waited, I thought I might try working on a few paragraphs of my research paper—perhaps something would come now. It did, but as I came to a point where I was about to type the word "superposition," I decided it was too technical for the introduction, and stopped at the letter "P." Then I saw that I had unaccountably hit all five keys one step to the side of the correct ones, and deleted the line, with my face flushed.

This was absolutely not my day.

"Well," Ruth said, "nothing you've told me is impossible or supernatural. Just very, very improbable. In fact, the odds against that card game alone would lead me to suspect Felix, well as I know him. It's all those other things...."

She got up and walked over to the window and looked at the hot twilight while I waited. Then she turned around; she had a look of concern.

"Sophia, you're a rational person, so I don't think you'll take offense at what I'm going to say. What you have told me is so impossibly unlikely, and the odds against it so astronomical, that I must consider the possibility that you're either fabricating this or you're experiencing a perceptual anomaly." I started to get up and protest, but she motioned me back. "I know, but don't you see that that is far more likely than...." She stopped and shook her head. Then she brightened. "I have an idea. Maybe we can have a demonstration."

She thought for a tense minute and snapped her fingers. "Have you any coins on you?"

"Why, yes," I said. "Quite a few." I reached into my pocket. There must have been nearly three dollars in various denominations. "Do you think they'll each have the same date, perhaps?"

"Did you accumulate all those coins today?"

"No. During the week."

She shook her head. "In that case, no. Discounting the fact that you could have arranged it, if my preliminary theory is correct, that would be actually impossible. It would involve temporal reversal. I'll tell you about it later. No, just throw down the coins. Let's see if they all come up heads."

I moved away from the carpet and tossed the handful of coins onto the floor. They clattered and bounced—and bounced together—and stacked themselves into a neat pile.

I looked at Ruth. Her eyes were narrowed. Without a word, she took a handful of coins from her own pocket and threw them.

These coins didn't stack. They just fell into an exactly straight line, the adjacent ones touching.

"Well," I said, "what more do you need?"

"Good grief," she said, and sat down. "I suppose you know that there are two great apparently opposite principles governing the Universe—entropy and negentropy. Random distribution on the beach is an example of entropy and living systems are examples of negentropy. The motions of particles in a gas are what we call random, but there are so many of them, we treat them statistically and derive thermodynamic laws—quite reliable. It isn't theoretically absolute; it's just a matter of extreme probability. Now living systems, on the other hand, seem not to depend on probability at all; actually, they work against it. Or you might say they are certainly not accidental manifestations."

"Do you mean," I asked in some confusion, "that some form of life is controlling the coins and—the other things?"

She shook her head. "No. All I mean is that improbable events usually have improbable explanations. When I see a statistical law being violated, I don't say to myself, 'Here's a miracle.' I revise my understanding of the principles. Something—I don't know what—is happening, and it seems to involve probability, and it seems to center around you. Were you still in that building when the elevators stuck? Or near it?"

"I guess I must have been. It happened just after I left."

"Hm. You're the epicenter, all right. But why?"

"Epicenter of what?" I asked. "I feel as though I were the epicenter of a probability storm. Something has it in for me!"

Ruth grinned. "Don't be superstitious. And especially don't anthropomorphize."

"Well, if it's the opposite of entropy, it's got to be a living system."

"On what basis? All we know for certain is that random events are being reorganized. A crystal, for example, is not alive, but it's a non-random arrangement of particles.... I wonder." She had a faraway, contemplative look.

I was beginning to feel hungry and the drinks had worn off.

"Let's go out and eat," I said. "There's not a thing in the kitchen and I'm not allowed to cook. Only eggs and coffee."

We put on our jackets and went down to the street. From either end, we could hear tow trucks removing the stalled vehicles. There were, by this time, a number of harassed traffic officers directing the maneuver and we heard one of them say to the building manager, "I don't know what's going on around here. Every single vehicle's got something wrong with it. They can't any of them back out for one reason or another. Never seen anything like it."

Near us, two pedestrians were doing a curious little dance as they tried to pass one another; as soon as one of them moved aside to let the other pass, the other would move to the same side. They both had embarrassed grins on their faces, but before long their grins were replaced by looks of suspicion and then determination.

"All right, wise guy!" they shouted in unison, and barged ahead, only to collide. They backed off and threw simultaneous punches which met in mid-air. Then began one of the most remarkable encounters ever witnessed—a confrontation in which fist hit fist but never anything else, until both combatants backed away undefeated, muttering identical excuses and threats.

The building manager appeared at that moment. Her face was flushed. "You all right, Dr. West?" she asked. "I don't know what's happening around here, but ever since this afternoon, things are going haywire. Martinez!" she shouted—she could succeed as an auctioneer. "Bring those people over here!"

Three people in a confused tangle, with their half-open umbrellas intertwined, were brought across the street, which meant climbing over bike racks. Martinez, a competent young security officer, seemed self-conscious; the people seemed not to be.

"All right, now, Ms. Wheeler!" one of them said. "Let go of my umbrella and we'll say no more about it!"

"And so now it's Ms. Wheeler, is it?" said her adversary.

The third, a younger woman with her back turned to us, her umbrella also caught in the tangle, pulled at it tentatively, at which the other two glared at her. She turned her head away and tried to let go, but the handle was caught in her sleeve. She looked up and I saw it was Hassan. My chef-partner.

"Oh, Sophia!" he said, and managed to detach himself. "Are you all right?" Was I all right!

"Hassan! What are you doing here?"

"I was so worried, and when I saw all this, I didn't know what to think." He pointed to the stalled vehicles. "Are you really all right?"

"Of course I'm all right. But why...."

"The Crestwood Village operator said someone kept dialing and dialing the conference center and there wasn't anyone on the line, so then she had it traced and it came from our phone here. I kept calling back, but I only got a busy signal. Oh, dear, are you sure you're all right?"

I put my arm around him and glanced at Ruth. She had an inward look. Then I caught the building manager's eye. It had a thoughtful, almost suspicious cast to it.

"Trouble does seem to follow you, Dr. West," was all she said.

When we got upstairs, I turned to Ruth. "Explain to Hassan," I said. "And incidentally to me. I'm not properly informed yet."

She did so, and when she got to the summary, I had the feeling he was a step ahead of her.

"In other words, you think it's something organic?"

"Well," Ruth said, "I'm trying to think of anything else it might be. I'm not doing so well," she confessed.

"But so far as I can see," Hassan answered, "it's mere probability manipulation, and without any overall pattern."

"Not quite. It has a center. Sophia is the center."

Hassan looked at me with a curious expression for a moment. "Do you feel all right, darling?" he asked me. I nodded brightly. "You'll think this silly of me," he went on to Ruth, "but why isn't it something like quantum entanglement gone wrong?"

"Pure speculation," she said. "No empirical evidence."

"Electromagnetic fields?"

"Absolutely not. For one thing, most of the objects affected weren't conductive—and don't forget electromagnetism is a force, not a form of energy itself, and a great deal of energy has been involved. I admit the energy has mainly been supplied by the objects themselves, but in an electromagnetic field, all you'd get would be stored potential energy, such as when a charged particle moves in a field. Then it would just stay there, like a capacitor. These things do a lot more than that—they continue moving."

"Why did you mention a crystal before? Why not a life-form?"

"Only an analogy," said Ruth. "A crystal resembles life in that it has a definite structure and exhibits growth, but that's all. I'll agree this—phenomenon—has no discernible structure and motion is involved, but plants don't move and amoebas have no fixed shape. Then a crystal accumulates material, but it does not transform what it accumulates; it merely rearranges it into a non-random pattern. In this case, it's rearranging random events and it has a nucleus and it seems to be growing—at least in what you might call improbability."

Hassan frowned. "Then what is it? What's it made of?"

"I should say it was made of the probability distributions themselves. There's a similar concept in quantum field theory. Another thing that's like a crystal is that it appears to be forming around a nucleus not of its own composition—the way a speck of dust in a supersaturated solution becomes the nucleus of crystallization."

"Sounds like the pearl in an oyster," Hassan said, and gave me an impertinent look.

"Why," I asked Ruth, "did you say the coins couldn't have the same date? I mean apart from the unlikely chance I got them that way."

"Because I don't think this phenomenon got started before today and everything that's happened can all be described as improbable events here and now. The dates were already there, and to change them would require retroactive causation, reversing time. That's out, in my book. That telephone now—"

The doorbell rang. We were not surprised to find it was the phone technician. She took the device apart and made disapproving sounds.

"I guess you dropped it on the floor," she said with strong disapproval.

"Certainly not," I said. "Is it broken?"

"Not exactly broken, but—" She shook her head and took it apart some more.

Ruth went over and they discussed the problem in undertones. Finally the technician left and Hassan called the conference center to reassure them. Ruth tried to explain to me what had happened with the phone.

"You must have jostled something loose. And then you replaced the handset in such a way that the contact wasn't quite open."

"But for heaven's sake, Hassan says the calls were going on for a long time! I phoned you only a short time ago and it must have taken him nearly two hours to get here from Crestwood Village."

"Then you must have done it twice and the vibrations in the floor—something like that—just happened to cause the right induction patterns. Yes, I know how you feel," she said, seeing my expression. "It's beginning to intensify."

Hassan was through telephoning and suggested going out for dinner. I was so pleased to see him that I'd forgotten all about being hungry.

"I'm in no mood to cook," he said. "Let's get away from all this."

Ruth raised an eyebrow. "If all this, as you call it, will let us."

In the lobby, we ran into Felix, looking satisfied in a media way.

"I've been assigned to cover the story—who could be better?—I live here. So far, I don't quite get what's been happening. I've been talking to the building manager, but she didn't say much. I got the feeling she thinks you're involved in some mystical way. Hello, Ruth, what's with you?"

"She's got a theory," said Hassan. "Come and eat with us and she'll tell you all about it."

Since we decided on a climate-controlled restaurant nearby in the arts district, we walked. The jam of vehicles didn't seem to be any less than before and we saw the building manager again. She was talking to a city inspector, and when she caught sight of us, she said something that made the inspector look at us with interest. Particularly at me.

"If you want your umbrella, Mr. McCoy," the building manager said, "it's at the security office. What there's left of it, that is."

Hassan thanked her and there was a short pause, during which I felt the speculative regard of the inspector. I pulled out a packet of mints, which I had opened, as always, by tearing off the top. I happened to have it upside down and all the mints fell out. Before I could move my foot to obscure what they had spelled out on the sidewalk, the two officials saw it. The inspector gave me a hard look, but said nothing. I quickly kicked the insulting mints into the gutter.

When we got to the restaurant, it was crowded but cool—although it didn't stay cool for long. We sat down at a side table near the entrance and ordered gin and tonics as we looked at the menu. Sitting at the next table were a large woman, wearing a very elaborate, brilliant purple evening gown, and a thin, sour-looking man in formal wear. When the server returned, they preempted him and began ordering dinner fussily: a salad for the man, and gazpacho, crab cakes and chocolate mousse for the large woman.

I tasted my drink. It was most peculiar; salt seemed to have been used instead of sugar. I mentioned this and my companions tried theirs, and made faces.

The server was concerned and apologetic, and took the drinks back to the bar across the room. The bartender looked over at us and tasted one of the drinks. Then he dumped them in his sink with a puzzled expression and made a new batch. After mixing this, he set out a row of glasses, put ice in them and began to pour.

That is to say he tilted the shaker over the first one, but nothing came out. He tapped it against the side of the bar and tried again. Still nothing. Then he took off the top and probed into it with his stirrer, his face pink with frustration.

I had the impression that the shaker had frozen solid. Well, ice is a crystal, I thought to myself.

The other bartender gave him a fresh shaker, but the same thing happened, and I saw no more because the customers sitting at the bar crowded around in front of him, offering suggestions. Our server came back, baffled, saying he'd have the drinks in a moment, and went to the kitchen. When he returned, he had the woman's gazpacho and some bread, which he put down, and then went to the bar, where the audience had grown larger.

Hassan lit a cigarette and said, "I suppose this is all part of it, Sophia. Incidentally, it seems to be getting warmer in here."

It was, and I had the feeling the place was quieter—a background noise had stopped. It dawned on me that I no longer heard the faint hum of the air-conditioner over the entrance, and as I started to say so, I made a gesture toward it. My hand collided with Hassan's when he tapped his cigarette over the ashtray, and the cigarette landed in the neighboring gazpacho.

"Hey! What's the idea?" snarled the sour-looking man.

"I'm terribly sorry," I said. "It was an accident. I—"

"Throwing cigarettes at people!" the large woman said.

"I really didn't mean to," I began again, getting up. There must have been a loose thread in the edge of their tablecloth which one of my bracelet clasps caught on, because as I stepped out from between the closely set tables, I pulled everything—tablecloth, silverware, water glasses, salt and pepper shakers and the gazpacho-à-la-nicotine—onto the floor.

The large woman surged from the booth and slapped me forcefully. The man raised his fists and postured as boxers are popularly supposed to do. The owner of the place, a woman with distinctive silver hair, hustled toward us with a determined manner. I tried to explain what had happened, but I was outshouted, and the owner frowned darkly.
question: Where was Hassan away for a conference?

Governments, corporations, criminal organizations—all would pay millions for what my protégé Sara Li has developed." He gestured to the young woman. Sara Li nodded, raising her portable device. Riley tensed, knowing what was coming, knowing there was no escape. The young woman's fingers moved over the controls, and the sound began again.

The sound was triggering every fear response, every panic reaction. It was torture without physical contact, agony without visible wounds.

"Stop!" Riley shouted. "You'll kill us!"

"Eventually," Flores agreed. "But first, let's show the full range of effects. Sara?"

The sound shifted again, became that seductive, hypnotic tone that had nearly led Riley to jump from Weaver's window. He felt his will dissolving, felt an overwhelming urge to obey, to surrender, to do whatever the sound commanded. Beside him, Natalia Wagner was weeping silently, lost in whatever false paradise the sound created in her mind.

And then, suddenly, there was a tremendous crash. The door to the room exploded inward and armed police poured through, led by Chief Martinez. Sara Li spun, her device falling from her hands and shattering on the floor. The sound cut off abruptly.

"Nobody move!" Martinez shouted. "Nicholas Flores, Sara Li, you're under arrest!"

As officers secured Flores and Sara Li, Martinez approached Riley and Natalia Wagner, quickly releasing their restraints. Riley slumped forward, gasping for breath, his mind still reeling from the sonic assault.

"How..." he managed to ask.

"Your sonic tracker," Martinez explained. "When we recovered it from your pocket after you escaped, our tech people figured out what it was tracking. Led us right here." She smiled slightly. "You were right, Riley. This was bigger than a simple death investigation. Much bigger."

As police led Flores and Sara Li away, Natalia Wagner turned to Riley. "Thank you," she said quietly. "For what it's worth, I tried to stop them. That's why I was in Clearwater—I knew they were targeting Weaver. I just didn't get there in time."

"We'll need your full testimony," Martinez said. "And your expertise to understand this technology."

Natalia nodded. "Of course. This kind of sonic weapon... it violates everything I believe about the relationship between sound and human welfare. Musical innovation should enhance life, not destroy it. Design science should serve humanity, not enslave it."

Riley stood slowly, his legs unsteady. "There'll be an inquiry about Weaver's death. But given the circumstances..."

"We'll sort it out," Martinez said. "The important thing is we've stopped them. This technology... it's too dangerous to exist."

"Agreed," Natalia Wagner said. "I'll help you destroy every trace of it. And I'll testify about how Flores corrupted my research, turned it into a weapon."

As they left the building, Riley looked up at the night sky over Clearwater. The city seemed peaceful now, its lights twinkling in the darkness. But he knew how close they'd come to disaster. How close Flores had come to unleashing a weapon that could destabilize not just Clearwater, not just Estoria, but potentially the entire world.

"One thing I don't understand," Riley said to Natalia as they walked toward the waiting police vehicles. "Why did you develop this technology in the first place? What was your original purpose?"

Natalia was silent for a moment, then sighed. "I wanted to help people. I thought if we could understand how sound affects the brain, we could develop therapies for mental illness, treatments for addiction, ways to help people heal. But Flores saw military applications, saw profit. He stole my research, twisted it into something evil." She looked at Riley. "That's why I've spent the last two years trying to stop him. Trying to undo the damage I inadvertently caused."

"You'll get that chance now," Riley said. "To make it right."

As they drove back toward police headquarters, Riley reflected on the case. The weaponization of sound—it was a chilling development, a reminder that any technology, no matter how benign its original purpose, could be perverted. Musical innovation, design science, acoustic engineering—all could be turned to dark purposes in the wrong hands.

But they'd stopped it. This time.

And as Clearwater's lights faded behind them, Riley allowed himself a moment of relief. The sonic weapon was destroyed, its creators in custody, and the city was safe. For now.

The case of the Sonic Architect, as the media would later call it, was closed. But Riley knew it was only a matter of time before someone else tried to weaponize sound, tried to turn the most fundamental form of human communication and artistic expression into an instrument of death.

It was a sobering thought. But it was also a reminder of why the Federal Cultural Protection Agency existed—to guard against those who would corrupt culture, pervert innovation, and turn humanity's greatest achievements into weapons.

As they pulled up to headquarters, Riley made a mental note to recommend enhanced monitoring of acoustic research facilities across the region. They'd been lucky this time. But luck, he knew, eventually ran out.

The war between those who would protect cultural evolution and those who would exploit it for power and profit was never-ending. But it was a war worth fighting.

And James Riley, despite his exhaustion, was ready to continue the fight.

Once, in the second year after her husband's death, a Regulator came and rented the apartment next door.

She learned that he was a Regulator completely by accident. While helping him move furniture, his identification badge fell out of a jacket pocket. She stood still, staring at the horror of it there on the floor, the jacket in her hands, all the loneliness returning in a black wave of hate and frustration.

That night she soundlessly picked his lock and administered a lethal injection while he slept.

She disposed of the syringe in the city incinerator. It helped very little. He was one Regulator, only one out of all the thousands of Regulators across the world; while her husband had been one of twenty-eight persons. She decided then that her efforts would be too ineffective. The odds were wrong. She would wait until her daughter, Bianca, was grown.

Together they would seek justice. Bianca did not have the implant—not yet. But she would. The Jumpers took care of their own.

Her husband had been one of the first, and they would not forget. One day the girl would disappear for a few hours. When she returned, the small bandage would be behind her ear. Ariana would shield her until the incision healed. Then no one would ever know, because now they could do it without leaving the tell-tale scar. Then they would seek justice.

Later they would go to Yarnmouth Station in Xandria, where a life free from Regulators could be lived. The station orbited a distant moon, far from Earth's political economy and its oppressive systems.

It happened to Bianca one hot summer day when she was fourteen. Ariana was working in her home office on a design thinking presentation; Bianca supposedly was at the community center with her friends. Suddenly she appeared before her mother, completely disoriented and wearing only a hospital gown. At sight of her mother, Bianca's face paled and she began to shake violently, so that Ariana was forced to hold her firmly to prevent hysteria. She looked behind her daughter's ear.

It was there.

"Mom!" she cried. "Mom!"

She went to the window and looked out toward the community center, where her friends were still visible in the courtyard. Apparently they did not miss her. Ariana handed her a sweater. "Here, cover yourself. Then we'll talk."

She started for her room, but Ariana stopped her. "No, do it right here. You may as well understand now."

"Understand what?"

"That your consciousness can now jump between bodies."

"What?"

"Never mind. What happened just now?"

"I was at the center, and a woman came up to me. Her hair was all white, and her eyes looked like... well, I never saw eyes like hers before. She asked who was Bianca Hunter, and I said I was. Then she said, 'Come with me.' I went with her. I don't know why. It seemed the right thing. She took me to a car and there was another person in it, that looked like the first one only younger. We went to a clinic, not far away and went inside. And that's all I can remember until I woke up. I was on a medical table. There was a light over it. It was all strange, and the two women stood there talking in some technical language I don't know."

Bianca ran her hand through her hair, shaking her head. "I don't remember clearly, I guess. I was looking around the room and I remember thinking how scared I was, and how nice it would be to be home with you. And then I was here."

Bianca faced the window, looking out, then turned quickly back. "What is it?" she asked, desperately. "What happened to me?"

"Better sit down," Ariana said. "It's something very unusual and terrible to think of at first, but really wonderful in terms of time management and career planning."

"But what happened? What is this port behind my ear?"

Suddenly her face paled and she stopped moving. "I know now. They made me a Jumper."

"Well, don't take on so. You'll get used to it."

"But they shouldn't have! They didn't even ask me!"

She started for the door, but Ariana called her back. "No, don't run away from it now. This is the time to face it. There are two sides to every story, you know. You hear only one side in school—their side, about political philosophy and economic development. There is also our side."

She turned back, a dawning comprehension showing in her eyes. "That's right, you're one, too. That is why you killed that Regulator next door."

It was Ariana's turn to be surprised. "You knew about that?"

"I saw the syringe wrapper in your pocket the next morning. I never told anyone."

"But you were only nine!"

"They would have taken you away if I'd said anything."

Ariana held out her hand. "Come here, daughter. It's time I told you about us."

So Bianca sat across the kitchen table from her, and Ariana told the whole history, beginning with Vincent Harper sitting in the laboratory in Yarnmouth, Lethoria, holding in his hand a neural implant he had designed for medical purposes. He had made it to help paralysis patients control prosthetic limbs. He was holding this device... and it was connected to a clone body in the next room for testing... and he was thinking about being young again—

And suddenly his consciousness was there, in the clone body. He could not believe it at first. He felt the young muscles and reflexes, and examined himself; there was no mistake.

On the flight back to his old body he came to certain conclusions regarding the strange power of his device. He tried it again, secretly. Then he made more implants. He was the only person in the world who knew how to construct it properly, and he kept the secret, giving implants to selected people. He worked out the basic principle, calling it quantum-entangled consciousness transfer, which was very theoretical modeling.

It was a subject of wonder and much speculation, but no one took serious notice of them until one night a Regulator arrested one man for identity fraud. It was a valid charge. One disadvantage of this method of travel was that consciousness arrived in a clone body that looked nothing like the original.

The arrested man jumped to another body and disappeared, and the next morning the Regulator was found dead. This set off a campaign against Jumpers. One violent act led to another, until the original reason for noticing them at all was lost. Normal people no longer thought of them as trustworthy citizens.

Ariana told how Harper, knowing he had made too many implants and given them unwisely, left Earth for Yarnmouth Station in Xandria.

He went alone, not knowing if he could jump so far, or what he would find when he arrived. But he did arrive, and it was what he had sought—a place where political economy favored freedom over control.

He returned for the others. They gathered one night in a warehouse in Rosewood—and their consciousnesses jumped in unison to clone bodies waiting at Yarnmouth Station, leaving the Regulators standing helplessly on Earth, shaking their fists at empty shells.

"You have asked many times," Ariana said, "how your father died. Now I will tell you the truth. Your father was one of the great ones, along with Harper and Spencer and Dr. Gutierrez. He helped plan the escape; but the Regulators found him in Lincoln fifteen minutes before the group jumped. They shot him in the back, and the others had to go on without him. Now do you know why I killed the Regulator next door? I had to. Your father was a great man, and I loved him."

"I don't blame you, mother," Bianca said simply. "But we are outcasts. Everybody says 'Jumper' as if it is something dirty. They write it on bathroom walls."

"Of course they do—because they don't understand! They are afraid of us. Wouldn't you be afraid of someone who could do the things we do, if you couldn't do them? It's basic consumer behavior and cultural sociology."

Just like that, it was over.

That is, the first shock was over. Ariana watched Bianca leave the apartment, walking slowly along the street, a girl with adult problems. Her friends called to her from the community center, but she chose not to hear. She wanted to be alone. She needed to think, to feel the newness of the thing.

Perhaps she would go to the park and sit by the fountain. When the initial shock wore off she might experiment with her new power. She would not jump far, in these first attempts. Probably she would stay within the city limits, because she still lacked the skills others had learned.

It was a hot, humid afternoon with storm clouds pushing out of the west. Ariana changed into lighter clothes and went for a walk to clear her mind.

For the remainder of that summer they worked together. They practiced at night mostly, jumping to clone bodies in increasingly distant cities, until Bianca's confidence allowed her to reach any prepared body on Earth. Ariana knew the habits of Regulators. She knew how to avoid them.

They would select a location sufficiently remote to ensure detection, Ariana would devise some action to irritate the Regulators; then they would quickly jump back to Rosewood. The Regulators would rush to the calculated spot, but would find only abandoned clone bodies. They would swear and drive back to their offices to dig through files, searching for some clue to their identity.

It was inevitable that they should identify Ariana as one of the offenders, since they had discovered, even before Harper took his group to Xandria, that individuals had neural patterns peculiar to themselves. These could be identified, if caught on their scanners, and even recorded for the files. But the files proved confusing, for they said that Ariana Kim had gone to Xandria with the others.

Had she returned to Earth? The question did not trouble them long. They had more serious problems. Harper had selected only the most ethical Jumpers when he left Earth, leaving all those with criminal tendencies behind. They could have followed if they chose—what could stop them? But it was more profitable to stay. On Earth they could steal, extort, even murder—without fear of the law, since they could always jump to a new body.

Bianca changed.

Even before the summer was over, she matured. The childish interests of her friends began to bore her. "Be careful, Bianca," her mother would say. "Remember who you are. Spend time with them sometimes, even if you don't like it. You have a long way to go before you will be ready."

During the long winter evenings, after they had watched their favorite programs, they would sit by the heater. "Tell me about the great ones," she would say, and Ariana would repeat all the things she remembered about Harper and Spencer and Gutierrez. She never tired of discussing them. She would tell about Spencer's partner, Zara Rivera, and try to describe the horror in Zara's young mind when the news went out that Roman Frank had been killed. She wanted Bianca to learn as much as possible about her father's death, knowing that soon the Regulators would be after her. They were so clever, so persistent. She wanted her to be ready, not only in ways of avoiding their traps... but ready with a heart full of righteous anger.

Sometimes when she talked about her husband, Ariana wanted to stand up and scream at her daughter, "Remember! Remember! You must never forget!" But she clenched her hands over her knitting, knowing that Bianca would internalize it better if she avoided being too forceful.

The winter passed, and the next summer, and two more summers.

Bianca was ready for university. They had successfully kept their secret. They had been vigilant in every detail. Bianca referred to the "damn Regulators" now with contempt. They had been successful in contacting other Jumpers, and sometimes visited them at remote locations.

"When you have finished university," Ariana told her daughter, "we will go to Xandria."

"Why not now?"

"Because when you get there they will need people who can contribute to the development of the station. Harper is a neuroscientist, Spencer an engineer, Gutierrez a doctor. But Gutierrez is an old man by this time. A young doctor will be needed. Study hard, Bianca. Learn all you can. Even the great ones get sick. Your knowledge of public health and organizational behavior will be invaluable."

She did not mention her secret hope, that before they left Earth Bianca would have fully avenged her father's death. She was clever and intelligent.

She could eliminate many Regulators.

So she accessed the encrypted accounts she had hidden more than ten years before. The apartment in Rosewood was abandoned. They found a modest house within walking distance of the University's medical school. Ariana furnished it carefully but, oddly, rather lavishly.

This was her husband's money she was spending now. It needed to last only a few years. Then they would leave Earth forever.

A room was built on the east side of the house, with its own private entrance. This was Bianca's room. Ostensibly the private entrance was for convenience due to the irregular hours of university students.

It was also convenient for jumping to clone bodies late at night after Regulator hunting.

Ariana was becoming obvious.

Excitement brought color to her cheeks when she thought of Bianca facing one of them—a lean, cunning predator facing a complacent bureaucrat. It was her notion that Regulators were corrupt enforcers, tools of a decadent, authoritarian system, living off citizens' taxes.

She painted the room herself, in soft, calming colors. When it was finished she showed Bianca into the room with ceremony, making a celebration of it.

"Here you can study and relax, and have those study groups students are always having," she said.

"There will be no friends," Bianca answered, "not here. No Jumpers will be at the university."

"Why not? Harper selected only educated, intelligent people. When one dies the implant is taken and adjusted to a new neural pattern—usually a person from the same family. I would say it is very likely that Jumpers will be found here."

She shook her head. "No. They knew we were coming, and no one said a word about others being here. I'm afraid we are alone."

"Well, I think not," Ariana said firmly. "Anyway, the room will be comfortable for your career planning."

Bianca shook her head again. "Why can't I be in the house with you? There are two bedrooms."

She said quickly, "You can if you wish. I just thought you'd like being independent, at your age. Most young adults do."

"I'm not like most young adults, mother. The Jumpers saw to that. Sometimes I'm sorry. Back in secondary school I used to wish I was like the others. Do you remember Camila Singh?" Her mother nodded. "Well, when we were seniors last year she liked me quite a lot. She didn't say so, but I knew it. She would sit across from me in the library, and sometimes when I saw how focused she was when she studied, I wanted to lean over and whisper to her, 'Hey, Camila—' just as if I was normal—'can I study with you for the exam?'"

Ariana turned to leave the room, but Bianca stopped her. "You understand what I'm saying, don't you?"

"No, I don't!" she said sharply. "You're old enough to face realities. You are a Jumper. You always will be a Jumper. Have you forgotten your own father?"

She turned her back and left the room. Bianca stood very still for a long time in the room that was to have been liberating for her. Her mother was crying just beyond the wall.

Bianca did not use the room that first year. She slept in the second bedroom. She did not mention her frustrated desires to be normal, not after the first attempt, but she persisted in her efforts to be so. Use of the implant was out of the question for them now, anyway—too risky with Regulators scanning constantly.

In the spring Ariana caught a severe flu which resulted in a long convalescence. Bianca moved into the new bedroom. At first Ariana thought she moved in an effort to please her because of the illness, but she soon grew aware of her mistake.

One day Bianca disappeared.

Ariana was alarmed. Had the Regulators found her? She watched the news feeds daily for some word of Jumpers being killed.

The second day after her disappearance she found a small item. A Jumper had raided the Regulator's office in Yarnmouth, Lethoria, killing three, and getting killed herself. Ariana immediately jumped to a clone body in Yarnmouth. She did not consider the risk. In Yarnmouth she obtained clothes and made discreet inquiries. The slain woman had been a Lethonian Jumper, one of those left behind by Harper as ethically unsuitable. Her partner had been killed by the Regulators the week before. She had gone completely insane and made the raid single-handedly. Ariana read the account of crimes committed by the woman and her partner, and determined to prevent Bianca from making the mistake of taking on more than she could handle.

When she jumped back to her original body at home, Bianca was in her room.

"Where have you been?" she asked sharply.

"Oh, here and there."

"I thought you were involved in that incident in Yarnmouth."

She shook her head.

Ariana stood in the doorway and watched her leaning over her desk, attempting to write something on a tablet. She was proud of her daughter's profile, determined and intelligent. Bianca tapped nervously on the desk.

"What did you do?" she asked.

Suddenly Bianca pushed the tablet away, jumped from her chair and paced the floor. "I talked to a Regulator last night," she said.

"Where?"

"Lincoln, Calderon."

Ariana had to sit down. Finally she was able to ask, "How did it happen?"

"I broke into the office there to access the records. He caught me."

"What were you looking for?"

"I wanted to learn the names of the men who killed Father." She said the word with difficulty. She was unaccustomed to thinking of him that way.

"Did you find them?"

She pointed to the tablet on her desk. Ariana, trembling, picked it up and read the names. Seeing them there, written like any other names would be written, made her furious. How could they? How could the names of murderers look like ordinary names? When she thought them in her mind, they even sounded like ordinary names—and they shouldn't! She had always thought that those names, if she ever saw them, would be vile, unholy scratches, evil sounds. "Marcus Webb" didn't sound evil; neither did "David Chen." She was shaken by this more than she would permit Bianca to see.

"Why did you want the names?"

"I don't know," she said. "Curiosity, maybe, or a subconscious desire for justice. I just wanted to see them."

"Tell me what happened! If a Regulator saw you... well, either he killed you or you killed him. But you're here alive."

"I didn't kill him. That's what seems so strange. And he didn't try to kill me. We didn't even fight. He didn't ask how I broke in without triggering alarms. He seemed to know. He did ask what I was doing there, and who I was. I told him, and... he helped me get the names. He asked where I lived. 'None of your business,' I told him. Then he said he didn't blame me for not telling, that Jumpers must fear Regulators, and hate them. Then he said, 'Do you know why we hunt Jumpers? We hunt them because there is no prison that will hold a Jumper. When they break the law, we have no choice. It is a terrible thing, but must be done. We don't want your technology; we only want law and order. There is room enough in the world for both of us. It's a matter of political philosophy and collective memory—we can coexist.'"

Ariana was furious. "And you believed him?"

"I don't know. I just know what he said—and that he let me go without trying to shoot me."

Ariana stopped on her way out of the room and laid a hand on her daughter's arm. "Your father would have been proud of you," she said. "Soon you will learn the truth about the Regulators."

Beyond the closed door, out of sight of her daughter, Ariana gave rein to the excitement that ran through her. Bianca had wanted the names! She didn't know why—not yet—but she would. "She'll do it yet!" she whispered to herself. She didn't care that no one heard her.

She didn't know where the men were now, those who had killed her husband. They could be anywhere. Regulators moved from post to post; in ten years they might be scattered all over the world. In the hunting of Jumpers, some implants might even be taken by Regulators—and used by them, for the power and freedom the implants gave must be coveted even by them. And they were in the best position to acquire them. She was consumed by fear that one or more of the men on Bianca's list might have acquired an implant and were now Jumpers themselves.

Two weeks later she read a news item saying that Marcus Webb had been killed by a Jumper. The assassin's identity was unknown, but Regulators were working on the case.

She knew. She had found a weapon in Bianca's desk.

She took the tablet into Bianca's room. "Did you do this?"

She turned away from her. "It doesn't matter whether I did or not. They will suspect me. His name was on the list."

"They will," she agreed. "It doesn't matter who the Jumper is, now that a Regulator has been killed. The one in Lincoln will tell them about you and the list of names, and it's all they need."

"Well, what else can he do?" Bianca asked. "After all, he is a Regulator. If one of them is killed, he will have to tell what he knows."

"You're defending him? Why?" she cried. "Tell me why!"

Bianca removed her mother's hand from her arm. Her mother's grip was painfully tight. "I don't know why. Mother, I'm sorry, but Regulators are just people to me, doing their jobs. I can't hate them the way you do. It's not about economic history or aesthetic philosophy—it's just human nature."

Ariana's face colored, then drained white.

Suddenly, with a wide, furious sweep of her hand, she slapped Bianca's face. So much strength and rage was in her arm that the blow almost sent her spinning. They faced each other, Ariana breathing hard from the exertion, Bianca stunned immobile—not by the blow, but from the knowledge that her mother could hate so suddenly, viciously.

Ariana controlled herself. "We must find a way to leave here," she said, calmly.

"They won't find us."

"Oh, yes they will," she said. "Don't underestimate them. Regulators are picked from the most intelligent people on Earth. It will be a small job for them. Don't forget they know who you are. Even if you hadn't been so stupid as to tell them, they'd know. They knew my pattern from the time your father was alive. They got yours when we were together years ago, taunting them. They linked your pattern with mine. They know that your father and I had a daughter. Your birth was recorded. The only difficult aspect of their job now is to find where you live, and it won't be impossible. They will drive through every city on Earth with those new scanners, until they pick up your pattern or mine. I'm afraid it's time to leave Earth."

Bianca sat down suddenly. "It's just as well. I thought maybe some day I might hate them too, or learn to like them. But I can do neither, so I am halfway between, and no one can live this way."

She did not answer. Finally Bianca said, "It doesn't make sense to you, does it?"

"No, it doesn't. This is not the time for such discussions, anyway. The Regulators have their machines working at top speed, while we sit here and talk."

Suddenly they were not alone.

No sound was generated by the woman's arrival. One instant they were talking alone, the next she was there. Bianca saw her first. She was a middle-aged woman whose hair was completely white. She stood near the desk, easily, as if standing there were the most natural way to be. She was wearing simple clothes... but carried herself with quiet authority.

Then Ariana saw her.

"Zara!" she cried. "I knew someone would come."

She smiled. "This is your daughter?"

"Yes," she said. "We are ready."

"I remember when you were born," she said, and smiled in reminiscence. "Your father was so nervous."

Bianca said, "Why was my father killed?"

"By mistake. Back in those days, like now, there were ethical Jumpers and criminals. One of those not selected by Harper to join us was enraged, half crazy with envy. He killed two people there in Lincoln. The Regulators thought Roman Frank—I mean, your father—did it. Frank was the greatest man among us. It was he who first conceived the theory that there was a basic, underlying principle in the operation of the implants. Even now, no one fully understands how intention and purpose tie in with the Harper Protocol; but we do know that hatred and greed as motivating forces can greatly minimize the implants' power. That is why the criminals with implants have never reached Xandria."

Heavy footsteps sounded in the hallway outside.

"We'd better hurry," Ariana said.

Zara held out her hands. They took them, to increase the synchronization of the implants. As the Regulators pounded on the door, Ariana flicked one thought of hatred at them, but of course they did not hear her. Zara's hands gripped tightly.

Ariana slowly opened her eyes....

She was still in the room! Zara and her daughter were gone. Her outstretched hands touched nothing.

Her implant was dead!

The Regulators stepped into the room over the broken door. She stared at them, then ran to Bianca's desk, fumbling for the weapon.

The Regulators' weapons fired.

Love, Zara had said once, or was it Harper? Someone, somewhere, perhaps in another time, in some misty, forgotten fragment of collective memory long gone, in another framework perhaps....

Ariana could not remember, before she died.
question: What was the name of the station orbiting a distant moon where a life free from Regulators could be lived?

The holiday party at the Valleyview branch of QuantumMed Solutions was threatening to become more legendary than usual this December.

The virtual reality division manager had already collapsed after attempting to demonstrate the new immersive healthcare training module while intoxicated. When he stumbled into the server rack, Teresa Gray, who managed the biotechnology research department, had screamed: "He'll crash the entire system!"

One out of every three presentations about breakthrough genetic engineering techniques had remained unfinished, because each had reminded someone else of another research project they wanted to discuss.

The recently approved synthetic compounds which affected neural receptors three times faster had driven away twinges of conscience about unfinished year-end reports and mandatory ethics training modules.

The star salesperson for medical AI systems and the gentleman who was in charge of facility maintenance were putting on a display of competitive data visualization in one corner of the main laboratory. The maintenance supervisor had fifty pounds less experience than the AI salesperson's customary opponent. So the climax of one particularly aggressive chart animation did not simply overturn the supervisor's monitor. It glided through the air, crashing with a very loud thump against the wall.

No one was hurt. But the impact knocked the hallowed portrait of Dr. Helena QuantumMed, co-founder, from its mounting. It shattered impressively as its protective glass splintered against the floor.

The noise caused a temporary lull in the festivities. Several employees even felt a passing suspicion that things might be getting out of hand.

"It's all in the spirit of scientific collaboration!" cried Daniel Wallace, the assistant director of operations. Since he was the highest executive present, worries vanished. Everyone felt fine. There was a scurry to shove the broken glass out of sight and to turn more attention to another type of beakers.

Daniel himself, acting by reflex, attempted to return the portrait to its place until new glass could be obtained. But the fall had damaged the frame at one corner and it wouldn't hang straight.

"We'd better store Dr. QuantumMed away for safekeeping until after the holiday," he told a small, blonde research assistant who was beneath his attention on any working day.

With the proper mixture of respect and holiday cheer, he lifted the heavy picture out of its frame. A yellowed envelope slipped to the floor as the picture came free. Daniel rolled the picture like a scroll and put it into a storage cabinet, for later attention. Then he looked around for a drink that would make him feel even better.

A data entry clerk in the clinical trials department wasn't used to liquor. She picked up the envelope and looked around vaguely for the document scanner.

"Hell, Mira, you aren't working!" someone shouted at her. "Have another!"

Mira Parsons snapped out of it. She giggled, suppressed a ladylike hiccup and returned to reality. Looking at the envelope, she said: "Oh, I see. They must have stuck it in to stabilize the frame. Gee, it's old."

Daniel had refreshed himself. He decided that he liked Mira's voice. To hear more of it, he said to her: "I'll bet that's been in there ever since the picture was mounted. There's a company legend that this portrait was installed the day this branch opened, ninety years ago."

"I didn't know the company ever used manila envelopes like this." Mira turned it over in her hands. The ancient adhesive crackled as she did so. The flap popped open and an old-fashioned order form fell out.

Daniel's eyes widened. He bent, reached painfully over his expanding midsection and picked up the order form.

"This thing has never been processed!" Raising his voice, he shouted jovially, "Hey, people! You're all terminated! Here's an order that QuantumMed never filled! We can't have such negligence. This poor customer has waited ninety years for their medical equipment!"

Mira was reading aloud the scrawled words on the order form:

"Advanced diagnostic scanner. Pediatric health monitor. Gene therapy starter kit. Adaptive medication dispenser for elderly patient." She turned to the assistant director, struck with an idea for the first time in her young life. "Let's fill this order right now!"

"The poor customer must be deceased by now," he objected, secretly angry that he hadn't thought of such a fine party stunt himself. Then he brightened. "Unless—" he said it loud enough for the employees to anticipate a grand proposal and the room grew quiet—"unless we broke the rules just once and used the temporal displacement field on a humanitarian mission!"

There was a silence. Finally, from an anonymous voice in one corner: "Would the field work over ninety years? We were always told that it must be used only for product recalls within three days."

"Then let's find out!" Daniel downed the rest of his drink and pulled a batch of access cards from his pocket. "Someone head down to the warehouse. Tell the security officer that it's on my authority. Hunt up the equipment that's on the order. Get the best of everything. Ignore the catalogue numbers—they've changed a hundred times in all these years."

Mira was still deciphering the form. Now she let out a little squeal of excitement.

"Look, Daniel! The name on this order—it's my great-great-grandmother! Isn't that wonderful? I was just a little girl when my grandmother told me stories about her. I remember that my grandmother never bought anything from QuantumMed because of some incident her grandmother had once with the firm. My mother didn't want me to come to work here because of that."

Daniel put his arm around Mira in a way that he intended to look mentorly. It didn't. "Well, now. Since it's your relative, let's delight the old woman. We wouldn't have gene therapy starter kits anymore. So we'll substitute a NeuroSync unit!"
