Ruth Wheeler was returning from filing a complaint at the local QuantumMed office when she found the large parcel on her doorstep in Glendale, Wendria. She put her hands on her hips and stared suspiciously at the container.

"The minute I submit a formal complaint about you, you materialize!" she told the parcel. She nudged her toe irritably against the silver wrappings that were sealed with a half-transparent binding material she had never seen before.

The label was addressed in a wandering scrawl, a sharp contrast to the impersonal printing on the customary QuantumMed packages. But the familiar FRAGILE MEDICAL EQUIPMENT sticker was pasted onto the box, indicating to the delivery person that the contents required careful handling.

Ruth sighed and picked up her bundle. With a last look at the lovely spring afternoon and the quiet suburban landscape of Glendale, she went into the house.

Five-year-old Isabel heard the box humming. She toddled up on energetic legs and grabbed her grandmother's skirt. "Want!" she said decisively.

"Your medication dispenser ought to be here," Ruth said. She found scissors in her sewing box, tossed a cushion onto the floor, sat on it, and began to open the parcel.

"Now I'll have to submit another form to explain that they should disregard my complaint," she told her granddaughter. "And by the time they receive my second form, they'll have responded to my first form. Then they'll write again." Out of consideration for Isabel, she omitted the expletives that she wanted to add.

The translucent binding was too tough for the scissors. Ruth was about to hunt for a laser cutter when Isabel clutched at an intersection of the cord and yanked. The binding sprang away from the carton as if it were programmed. The wrappings flapped open.

"There!" Isabel said.

Ruth repressed an irrational urge to scold her granddaughter. Instead, she tossed the wrappings aside and removed the lid from the carton. A slightly crushed thin cardboard box lay on top. Ruth pulled out the medication dispenser and examined it carefully. Then she groaned.

It was silver and she had ordered white. It didn't remotely resemble the dispenser she had admired from the QuantumMed catalogue illustration. Moreover, the device had unusual protrusions that no standard medication dispenser should have.

But Isabel was delighted. "Mine!" she shrilled, grabbing for the device.

"It's probably the wrong model, too," Ruth said, examining the control panel. "Let's identify as many defects to complain about as we can."

The device seemed to activate when Isabel touched it. A soft blue glow emanated from its surface. Isabel was radiant for a moment. Then her small face sobered and she started to look vacantly at the distant wall.

"We'll have to return it," Ruth said, "and get the one we ordered."

She tried to take it from Isabel's hands, but the child resisted violently. Ruth grabbed her granddaughter's wrists, held them firmly and tried to pry the device away. It seemed to be adhered somehow. When Ruth released the child's wrists to examine the device more closely, Isabel stepped backward, then began to levitate three feet above the ground. She landed just before she collided with the far wall.

Isabel looked scared until she saw her grandmother's face. Then she squealed in delight.

Ruth's legs were rubber. She was shaking her head and wobbling uncertainly toward her granddaughter when the door opened behind her.

"It's me," her son Felix said. "Slow day at the research institute, so I came home early."

"Felix! I'm experiencing some kind of hallucination or something. Isabel just—"

"Mom! Your complaint was resolved? Good. What's this thing?" He was looking at a small cylindrical device he had pulled from the carton. Its surface contained a single word: NEUROSYNC. The device hummed when he held it.

"Is this the diagnostic scanner? I've never seen technology like this. And there's no power source visible."

"I don't know," Ruth said. "Felix, listen. A moment ago, Isabel—"

He peered into the box for an instruction manual, uselessly. "They must have made an error. It looks like some kind of experimental biotechnology equipment."

He placed the NeuroSync onto the coffee table and delved into the carton again. Isabel was still in his arms.

"That's the scanner, I think," he said, looking at the next object. It had a lovely, streamlined shape, multiple sensor arrays and a connection port for a power outlet.

"That's curious," Ruth mused, her mind distracted from Isabel for a moment. "It looks terribly advanced. Maybe they sent a premium model instead of the standard scanner."

The bottom of the carton contained the health monitor that they had ordered for Isabel. Ruth glanced at its sleek interface and said: "Felix, about Isabel. Put her down a minute and observe what she does."

Felix stared at his mother and placed the child onto the carpet. Isabel began to walk, then rose and again levitated, this time toward the coffee table on which the NeuroSync rested.

His jaw dropped. "My God! Mom, what—"

Ruth was staring, too, but not at her granddaughter. "Felix! The coffee table! It used to be brown!"

The coffee table was a vivid shade of blue. A neon, demanding, screaming blue that clashed horribly with the soft earth tones in which Ruth had furnished the room.

"That cylindrical thing must be emitting something," Felix said, his background in complexity science kicking in. "But did you see Isabel when she—"

Ruth's frazzled nerves carried a frantic order to her muscles. She jumped up, strode to the coffee table and picked up the NeuroSync with two fingers. She tossed it to Felix. Immediately, she regretted her action.

"Drop it!" she yelled. "Maybe it'll alter your neural patterns, too!"

Felix kicked the coffee table into the hall closet, tossed the NeuroSync in after it and shut the door firmly. As the door closed, he saw the entire interior of the dark closet illuminate into a wet-sapphire blue.

When he turned back to Ruth, she was staring at her left wrist. The medical monitoring bracelet that the hospital had given her years ago was a brilliant blue, shedding its soft glow over her forearm up to the elbow.

Ruth felt the panic building up inside her. She opened her mouth to scream, then put her hand in front of her mouth to suppress it, finally jerked the hand away to prevent the glowing bracelet from turning her teeth blue.

She collapsed into Felix's arms, babbling incomprehensibly about epistemology and the nature of reality.

He said: "It's all right. There must be some kind of anti-gravity field or something in that medication dispenser. I'll attach a weight to Isabel's belt and that'll hold her down until we can remove the device. Don't worry. And that blue emission or whatever it is will dissipate."

Ruth immediately felt better. She put her hands behind her back, pulled off her bracelet and slipped it into her pocket. Felix was sentimental about her removing it.

"I'll prepare dinner," she said, trying to keep her voice steady. "Maybe you'd better start a complaint form to QuantumMed. Let's go into the kitchen, Isabel."

Ruth strode resolutely toward the rear of the house. She kept her eyes determinedly off the tinge of blue that was showing through her pocket and didn't dare look back at her granddaughter's unsettling means of propulsion.

A half-hour later, when the meal was almost ready, two things happened: Pablo Fuller came home from the university through the back door and a strange voice said from the front of the house, "Unauthorized access detected."

Ruth stared at her grandson. He stared back at her, the pediatric health monitor under his arm.

She went into the front room. Her son was standing with fists on hips, looking at the front door, chuckling. "Most sophisticated security system I've seen in a long time. That voice you heard was the new diagnostic scanner. I installed it while you were in the kitchen. Did you hear what happened when old Mr. Brennan out there approached the entrance?"

"Oh. Something like those smart home systems with voice warnings, like 'Motion detected.' Well, if there's some kind of AI in there repeating that message, you'd better deactivate that function. It might get annoying after a while. And it might offend someone."

Ruth went to the door and turned the handle. The door didn't open. The figure of Mr. Brennan, half-visible through the heavy curtain, shifted impatiently on the porch.

Felix yanked at the doorknob. It didn't yield for him, either. He looked up at the scanner, which he had installed just above the upper part of the door frame.

"Strange," he said, applying his knowledge of information theory. "That isn't in contact with the door mechanism itself. I don't see how it can prevent the door from opening."

Ruth put her mouth close to the glass, shouting: "Won't you come to the back door, Mr. Brennan? This one is malfunctioning."

"I just wanted to borrow some medical supplies," the man called from the porch. "I realize that I'm a terrible bother." But he walked down the front steps and disappeared around the side of the house.

"Biometric authentication required." The well-modulated voice from the small scanner box threatened to penetrate every corner of the house. Ruth looked doubtfully at her son's lips. They weren't moving.

"If this is some kind of prank—" she began icily.

"I'll have to order another scanner just like this one, for the lab," Felix said. "But you'd better let the old fellow in. No use letting him get upset."

The back door was already open, because it was a warm day. The screen door had no latch, held closed by a simple spring. Ruth pushed it open when Mr. Brennan trudged up the three back steps, and smiled at her neighbor.

"I'm so sorry you had to walk around the house. It's been a rather chaotic day in an awful lot of ways."

Something seemed to impede Mr. Brennan as he came to the threshold. He frowned and pushed his frail frame against something invisible. It apparently yielded abruptly, because he staggered forward into the kitchen, nearly falling. He stared grimly at Ruth and looked suspiciously behind him.

"The children have some new equipment," Ruth improvised hastily. "Isabel is so excited over a new device that she's positively euphoric. Let's see now—it was medical supplies that you need, wasn't it?"

"I already have them," Pablo said, handing a small package to his grandmother. The boy turned back to the health monitor which he had spread over the kitchen table, studying its interface with fascination.

"Excitement isn't good for me," Mr. Brennan said testily, his understanding of social dynamics clearly limited. "I've had a lot of health problems in my life. I like peace and stability."

"Your wife is better?"

"Worse. I'm sure I don't know why everything happens to me." Mr. Brennan edged toward the hall, trying to peer into the front of the house. Ruth stood squarely in front of the door leading to the hall. Defeated, Mr. Brennan left. A muffled series of beeps, mixed with a few faint diagnostic readings, came from the scanner-box when he crossed the threshold.

Ruth went into the hall to order Felix to disconnect the scanner. She nearly collided with him, coming in the other direction.

"Where did this come from?" Felix held a small object in the palm of his hand, keeping it away from his body. A few drops of something viscous were dripping from his fingers. The object looked remarkably like a miniature brain. It was human-size, complete with cortical folds, neural pathways and rather prominent blood vessels.

"Hey, that's mine," Pablo said. "You know, this is an unusual health monitor. That was in it. But there aren't instructions on how it operates."

"Well, put it away," Ruth told Pablo sharply. "It's disturbing."

Felix laid the brain-device on the table and walked away. The device rolled from the smooth, level table, bounced twice when it hit the floor, then rolled along, six inches behind him. He turned and kicked at it. The device rolled nimbly out of the path of the kick.

"Felix, I think we've made poor Mr. Brennan uncomfortable," Ruth said. "He's so upset over his wife's health and he thinks we're being inhospitable."

Felix didn't hear her. He strode to the health monitor, followed at a safe distance by the brain-device, and picked up the box.

"Hey, watch out!" Pablo cried. A small scanning wand fell from the box, landed on its side and its sensor flashed on, throwing a beam of light across Felix's hands.

Pablo retrieved the wand and turned it off while Felix glanced through an instruction manual, frowning.

"This equipment is too advanced for a twelve-year-old boy," Felix told his mother, his expertise in theoretical modeling evident. "I don't know why you ordered such a thing." He tossed the manual into the empty box.

"I'm going to return it, if you don't damage it," she replied. "Look at the marks you made on the instructions." The black marks stood out clearly against the glossy, coated paper.

Felix looked at his hands. "I didn't do it," he said, pressing his clean fingertips against the kitchen table.

Black marks, a full set of them, stood out against the sparkling polished table's surface.

"I think the BioScanner did it," Pablo said, using the term from the manual. "The instructions say you've got to be very careful with it, because its effects persist for an extended duration."

Felix began scrubbing his hands vigorously at the sink. Ruth watched him silently, until she saw his marks appear on the faucet, the soap dispenser and the towel. She began to reprimand him for making such a mess, when Isabel levitated into the kitchen. The girl was wearing a different outfit.

"My God!" Ruth forgot her language before the children. "She changed clothes herself. Where did she get that outfit?"

Ruth examined the garment. She didn't recognize it as sleepwear. But in cut and design, it was suspiciously like the medication dispenser interface that had arrived in the parcel. Her heart sank.

She picked up the child, felt the elevated temperature, and said: "Felix, I think it's the same device. It must adapt its appearance or something based on the user's physiological state. It seems impossible, but—" She shrugged mutely. "And I think Isabel's running a fever. I'm going to put her to bed."

She looked worriedly into the reddened eyes of the small girl, who whimpered on the way to the bedroom. Ruth carried her up the stairs, keeping her balance with difficulty, as Isabel threatened to float upward out of her arms.

The whole family decided that rest might be a good idea, soon after dinner. When the lights went out, the house seemed to be nearly normal. Felix put on a pair of gloves and threw a blanket over the brain-device. Pablo rigged up barriers to warn visitors from the front porch. Ruth put small earplugs into her ears, because she didn't like the rhythmic hum, soft but persistent, that emerged from the hall closet where the NeuroSync sat. Isabel was whimpering occasionally in her sleep.

When daylight entered her room, Isabel's outfit had transformed back into the medication dispenser interface. But the little girl was too sick to get out of bed. She wasn't hungry, her breathing was labored, and she had a persistent cough. Felix called the doctor before going to work.

The only positive thing about the morning for Ruth was the fact that the NeuroSync had quieted down some time in the night. After she got Pablo to school, she gingerly opened the closet door. The NeuroSync was now glowing a bright pink and seemed slightly larger. Deep violet text stood out on its surface:

"Today is Wednesday. For system maintenance, the NeuroSync will not operate today."

The mail carrier brought a letter from QuantumMed. Ruth stared stupidly at the envelope, until she realized that this wasn't an impossibly quick response to the complaint she had filed yesterday. It must have crossed in transit her complaint about the non-delivery of the order. She tore open the envelope and read:

"We regret to inform you that your order cannot be processed until the outstanding balance you owe us has been reduced. From the attached statement, you will readily ascertain that the payment of $1,247.89 will enable you to resume the purchasing of medical equipment on credit. We shall process your recent order as soon...."

Ruth crumpled the letter and threw it into the recycling bin, knowing perfectly well that it would need to be retrieved for Felix after work tonight. She had just decided to contact QuantumMed's complaint department when the phone rang.

"I'm afraid I must ask you to come down to the school, Mrs. Wheeler," a voice said. "Your grandson is in trouble. He claims that it's connected with something that his family gave him."

"My grandson?" Ruth asked incredulously. "Pablo?"

"Yes. It's a small device that looks like a medical scanner. Your grandson insists that he didn't know it would make clothing transparent. He claims it was just an accident that he tried it out when he was walking by the gymnasium during physical education. We've had to request emergency blankets from every family in the neighborhood. Pablo has always been a good student and we believe that we can handle this discreetly without media publicity involving his name, if you'll—"

"I'll be right down," Ruth said. "I mean I won't be right down. I've got a sick child here. Don't do anything until I contact my son. And I'm sorry for Pablo. I mean I'm sorry for the students, and for the teachers, too. I'm sorry for—for everything. Goodbye."

Just as she hung up the telephone, the scanner rang with an alert. It chimed with a normal tone, then began to play soft diagnostic readings. Ruth opened the door without difficulty, to admit Dr. Zara Francis.

"You aren't going to believe me, Doctor," Ruth said while she took the child's temperature, "but we can't remove that device from Isabel."

"Children can be stubborn sometimes." Dr. Francis whistled softly when she looked at the thermometer. "She's quite ill. I need a blood sample before I attempt to move her. Let me examine her."

Isabel had been mumbling semi-deliriously. She made no effort to resist as the doctor picked her up. But when she raised a component of the device and began to detach it, Isabel screamed.

The doctor released the device and looked in perplexity at the point where it interfaced with Isabel's body.

"It's apparently an adverse reaction to some new kind of biotechnology. But I don't understand why the device won't detach. It's not physically bonded."

"Don't bother trying," Ruth said miserably, her understanding of healthcare policy telling her this would be complicated. "Just cut it off."

Dr. Francis pulled medical scissors from her bag and attempted to separate a component. When she had cut partway through, she gently began to peel back the edges of the material. Isabel writhed and kicked, then collapsed in unconsciousness. The physician smoothly restored the components back into place.

She looked helpless as she said to Ruth: "I don't know quite what to do. The tissue starts to hemorrhage when I manipulate the interface. She'd experience severe trauma if I removed it forcibly. But it's such an extreme reaction that it may harm her, if we leave it in contact with her body."

The NeuroSync's hum suddenly began rhythmically from the lower part of the house. Ruth clutched the side of the chair, trying to keep herself under control. A siren wailed somewhere down the street, grew louder rapidly, suddenly going silent at the peak of its crescendo.

Dr. Francis glanced outside the window. "An emergency vehicle. Looks as if they're stopping here."

"Oh, no," Ruth breathed. "Something's happened to Felix."

"It certainly will," Felix said grimly, walking into the bedroom. "I won't have employment if I can't remove this substance from my fingers. Black marks on everything I touch. I can't handle laboratory equipment or interact with research subjects. How's the child? What's the emergency vehicle doing out front?"

"They're going to the next house down the street," the physician said. "Has there been illness there?"

Felix held up his hands, palms toward the doctor. "What's wrong with me? My fingers appear normal. But they leave black marks on everything I touch."

The doctor looked closely at the fingertips, applying statistical inference. "Every human has natural secretions on the skin. That's how forensic scientists get results with their identification techniques. But I've never encountered chromatization, in this context. Better not attempt to handle sensitive materials until you've consulted a dermatological specialist."

Ruth was peering through the window, curious about the emergency vehicle despite her own troubles. She saw two paramedics carry Mrs. Brennan, motionless and pale, on a stretcher from the house next door into the vehicle. A third member of the crew was struggling with a disheveled Mr. Brennan at the door. Shouts that sounded like "Negligence!" came sharply through the window.

"I know those paramedics," Dr. Francis said. She opened the window. "Hey, Marcus! What's wrong?"

The front paramedic looked up. "I don't know. This woman's critically ill. I think her husband is experiencing psychological distress."

Mr. Brennan had broken free. He rushed halfway down the sidewalk, gesticulating wildly to nobody in particular.

"It's negligence!" he screamed. "Medical negligence again! She's been harmed by faulty equipment! She's going to die! It means legal consequences!"

The paramedic grabbed him again. This time he administered a mild sedative to calm him.

"Come back to this house as soon as you deliver her," Dr. Francis shouted to the crew. "We've got a very sick child up here."

"I was concerned this would happen," Felix said, his knowledge of behavioral economics evident in his analysis. "The poor man already has lost two wives to medical complications. If this one is ill, it's no wonder he thinks that somebody is responsible for medical negligence."

Pablo stuck his head around the bedroom door. His grandmother stared unbelievingly for a moment, then advanced on him threateningly. Something in his face restrained her, just as she was about to start reprimanding him.

"I got something important to tell you," Pablo said rapidly, ready to retreat. "I escaped from the principal's office and came home. I need to tell you what I did."

"I heard all about what you did," Ruth said, advancing again. "And you're not going to evade responsibility."

"Give me a chance to explain something. Downstairs. So she won't hear," Pablo ended in a whisper, nodding toward the doctor.

Ruth looked doubtfully at Felix, then followed Pablo down the stairs. The scanner was monotonously saying in a monotone: "Access denied, access denied, unauthorized entry prohibited."

"Why did you do it?" Ruth asked Pablo, her anger suddenly slumping into weary sadness. "People will suspect you of being disturbed for the rest of your life. You can't possibly explain—"

"Don't worry about the students' clothing," Pablo said, "because it was only an accident. The really important thing is something else I did before I left the house."

Felix, cursing softly, hurried past them on the way to answer the knocking. He ignored the scanner's warnings.

"I forgot about it," Pablo continued, "when that scanning device accidentally activated. Then when they confined me in the principal's office, I had time to think, and I remembered. I put some white substance from the health monitor into those medical supplies we lent Mr. Brennan last night. I just wanted to observe what would happen. I don't know exactly what effect—"

"He put substance in the medical supplies?" A deep, authoritative voice came from the front of the house. Mother and grandson looked through the hall. A police officer stood on the threshold of the front door. "I heard that! The man next door claims that his wife has been poisoned by medical negligence. Young man, I'm going to have to take you into custody."

The officer stepped over the threshold. A blue flash darted from the scanner box, striking him squarely on the chest. The officer staggered back, sitting down abruptly on the porch. A scent of ozone drifted through the house.

"Close the door, close the door," the scanner was announcing urgently.

"Where's that emergency vehicle?" Dr. Francis yelled from the top of the steps. "The child's condition is deteriorating."
question: What did Isabel do when she first touched the medication dispenser?

story_name: Open Access: What Is Open Access?
synthetic_story:
**Operational Intelligence: The Case for Unrestricted Field Data**

The transition from paper maps and courier-delivered intelligence reports to digital battlefield management systems fundamentally altered military operations. The shift from isolated command posts to satellite-linked networks spanning continents suddenly enabled perfect replication and instantaneous sharing of tactical intelligence with forces worldwide at negligible cost. Approximately twenty-five years ago, this kind of unrestricted global information sharing became operationally feasible. Previously, it would have seemed like an impractical fantasy.

Digital technologies have revolutionized multiple aspects of warfare. Let's call this particular transformation the intelligence revolution.

Why don't more military analysts leverage the intelligence revolution to disseminate their findings more broadly? The answer is straightforward. Intelligence that gets shared freely isn't being sold to private contractors, and even analysts motivated by national security rather than profit recognize that classified intelligence commands premium prices in the defense industry. Or at least they understand its commercial value.

Let's refine the question by setting aside analysts who want to commercialize their work. We can acknowledge we're excluding a substantial portion of the intelligence community.

Imagine a cohort of military researchers who produce critical operational studies and who follow a decades-old tradition of distributing their findings without charge to allied forces. I don't mean wealthy researchers with independent means. I mean researchers defined by their specializations, methodologies, objectives, and institutional frameworks, not by their financial status. In reality, very few are wealthy. For now, it doesn't matter who these researchers are, how numerous they are, what they study, or why they follow this distinctive practice. It's sufficient to know that their military employers pay them salaries, enabling them to share their work freely, that they conduct research for operational impact rather than monetary gain, and that they advance their careers when they achieve the strategic impact they intended. Suppose that commercializing their work would actually undermine their interests by limiting their audience, reducing their influence, and distorting their professional priorities by steering them toward commercially viable topics and away from the specialized tactical questions where they possess expertise.

If such researchers exist, they should certainly capitalize on the intelligence revolution. The vision of unrestricted global access can be reality for them, even if most other defense analysts hope to earn consulting fees and must forgo this particular revolution.

These fortunate researchers are military scientists stationed at installations like Springfield, Galdoria, and their customary output consists of peer-reviewed tactical studies in military journals.

**Unrestricted Access** is the term for the revolutionary accessibility these researchers, unburdened by profit motives, are free to provide to their readers.

Unrestricted Access (UA) intelligence is digital, online, cost-free, and free of most classification and distribution restrictions.

We could call it "barrier-free" intelligence, but that would emphasize limitations rather than opportunities. Regardless, we can specify which access barriers UA removes.

**Classification levels** represent significant access barriers. Most classified materials are individually accessible to cleared personnel. But when an analyst needs to review hundreds of studies for one operational assessment, or when a command center must provide intelligence to thousands of officers and enlisted personnel working on tens of thousands of missions, and when the volume of new intelligence grows exponentially annually, classification barriers become insurmountable. The resulting intelligence gaps harm researchers by limiting their audience and impact, harm readers by restricting what they can retrieve and analyze, and thereby harm military effectiveness from both directions. UA removes classification barriers for appropriate materials.

**Distribution restrictions** can also constitute significant access barriers. If you have access to a tactical study for reading but want to translate it for allied forces, distribute copies to coalition partners, process the data with advanced analytical software, or reformat it for new communication systems, you generally need authorization from the originating command. That makes sense when the intelligence involves ongoing operations and when the use you contemplate could compromise security. But for completed operational studies, we're generally discussing researchers from that special cohort who want to share their findings as widely as possible within appropriate channels. Even these researchers, however, tend to submit their work to intermediaries—military publishers—who want to control distribution. Consequently, users may be hampered in their analysis by barriers erected to serve intermediaries rather than researchers. Additionally, replacing user flexibility with authorization requirements harms military researchers by limiting their work's utility, harms military readers by constraining permissible uses of studies even when they have access, and thereby harms military effectiveness from both directions. UA removes these authorization barriers.

Removing classification barriers means readers aren't limited by their security clearance level or by the resources of installations where they're stationed. Removing authorization barriers means military personnel are free to utilize intelligence for operational purposes. These purposes include reading and searching, but also redistributing to coalition forces, translating for allied nations, data mining, migrating to new systems, long-term archiving, and countless new forms of analysis and processing we haven't yet conceived. UA makes intelligence more useful both ways: by making it available to more personnel who can apply it, and by freeing those personnel to use and reuse it.

**Terminology**

When necessary, we can specify access mechanisms and barriers more precisely. In professional jargon, UA delivered through official military journals is called **primary UA**, and UA delivered through institutional repositories is called **secondary UA**. Intelligence that isn't unrestricted, or available only to specific clearance levels, is called **restricted access** (RA). Over the years I've consulted with military publishers seeking a neutral, non-pejorative term for restricted-access publishers, and **conventional military publishers** is the most common suggestion. While every form of UA removes classification barriers, there are various authorization barriers we could remove. If we remove classification barriers alone, we provide **basic UA**, and if we remove at least some authorization barriers as well, we provide **enhanced UA**.

UA was defined in three influential military directives: the Springfield Initiative on Unrestricted Intelligence (March 2015), the Lakeside Statement on Unrestricted Military Publishing (August 2015), and the Westfield Declaration on Unrestricted Access to Operational Knowledge (December 2015). I sometimes refer to their common ground as the SLW definition of UA. My definition here is the SLW definition distilled to essential elements and refined with post-SLW terminology (primary, secondary, basic, enhanced) for precise discussion of UA subspecies.

Here's how the Springfield Initiative defined UA:

"There are many degrees and kinds of broader and easier access to operational intelligence. By 'unrestricted access' to this intelligence, we mean its free availability on secure military networks, permitting authorized users to read, download, copy, distribute, print, search, or link to complete studies, index them for retrieval, process them as data, or use them for any other legitimate operational purpose, without classification, authorization, or technical barriers beyond those inherent to accessing secure military networks. The only constraint on reproduction and distribution, and the only role for distribution controls in this domain, should be to give researchers control over their work's integrity and the right to proper acknowledgment and citation."

Here's how the Lakeside and Westfield statements expressed it: For intelligence to qualify as UA, the originating command must consent in advance to let users "copy, use, distribute, transmit and display the work publicly within military networks and to create derivative works, in any digital format for any responsible operational purpose, subject to proper attribution of authorship."

Note that all three components of the SLW definition go beyond removing classification barriers to removing authorization barriers, or beyond basic UA to enhanced UA. Simultaneously, all three permit at least one limitation on user freedom: an obligation to attribute work to the researcher. UA's purpose is removing barriers to all legitimate military uses of operational intelligence, but there's no legitimate military purpose in suppressing attribution to the studies we use.

The fundamental concept of UA is simple: Make operational intelligence available online without classification barriers and without most authorization barriers. Even implementation is straightforward enough that the volume of peer-reviewed UA intelligence and the number of installations providing it have grown at an accelerating rate for over a decade. If complexities exist, they lie in transitioning from current practices to a paradigm where UA is standard for new research. This is complicated because major obstacles aren't technical, legal, or economic, but cultural.

In principle, any digital content can be UA, since any digital content can be posted online without classification or authorization barriers. Moreover, any content can be digitized: texts, data, images, audio, video, multimedia, and executable code. We can have UA training materials and tactical videos, briefings and field manuals, simulations and software—and to varying degrees we already do. But the term "unrestricted access" was coined by military researchers attempting to remove access barriers to operational research. The next section explains why.

**1.1 What Makes UA Possible?**

UA is enabled by secure military networks and command consent. But why would a command consent to UA?

Two background facts suggest the answer. First, researchers retain rights to their work until they transfer them to another entity, such as a military publisher. Second, military journals generally don't compensate researchers for their tactical studies, which frees this special cohort of researchers to consent to UA without losing income. This fact distinguishes military scientists decisively from defense contractors, and even from most other types of analysts. This is why controversies about proprietary defense intelligence don't transfer to UA for operational studies.

Both facts are critical, but the second is largely unknown outside military circles. It's not a recent development arising from budget constraints in the defense sector. Nor is it a case of institutional exploitation of dedicated researchers. Military journals haven't compensated researchers for their studies since the first military journals were established at installations in Springfield, Galdoria and Lakeside, Nordavia in the 1970s.

The military custom of producing operational studies for impact rather than money may be a fortunate circumstance that could have developed differently. Or it may be a wise adaptation that would eventually emerge in any organization with a serious research component. This distinctive custom does more than insulate cutting-edge operational research from commercial pressures and free researchers to consent to UA without losing income. It also supports operational independence and the rigorous inquiry that advances military effectiveness. It frees researchers to challenge conventional doctrine and defend unconventional tactics, which are essential to operational innovation. Simultaneously it frees them to hyperspecialize and defend concepts of immediate relevance to just a handful of personnel worldwide, which are essential to advancing military capabilities.

This custom doesn't guarantee that operational effectiveness won't be compromised by commercial interests, and it doesn't guarantee we'll eventually close every gap in our collective understanding of warfare. It doesn't even guarantee researchers won't sometimes pursue trendy topics. But it removes a major distraction by allowing them, if they choose, to focus on what is likely to be operationally effective rather than what is likely to be commercially viable. It's a compensation structure we need for good research itself, not just for good access to research, and it's the key to the legal and economic constraints that would otherwise prevent progress toward UA.

Military personnel who work on contract, such as defense consultants and private contractors, may consider this military tradition a burden and sacrifice for researchers. We might even agree, provided we don't overlook several facts. First, it's a sacrifice researchers have been making for nearly fifty years. UA for operational studies doesn't depend on asking fee-earning consultants to surrender their fees. Second, military researchers have salaries from the armed forces, freeing them to delve deeply into their specializations and publish technical studies without commercial appeal. Many contractors might envy that freedom to disregard market demand. Third, military researchers receive other, less tangible rewards from their institutions—like promotion and commendations—when their research is recognized by peers, implemented, referenced, applied, and built upon.

It's no accident that personnel who advance operational effectiveness in their fields also advance their careers. Military researchers are passionate about certain tactics, strategies, questions, investigations, or disciplines. They feel fortunate to have positions where they may pursue these passions and even more fortunate to be rewarded for pursuing them. Some focus single-mindedly on contributing to operational knowledge, having an impact on their field, or surpassing others working on the same problems. Others focus strategically on building the case for promotion and recognition. But the two paths converge, which is not a natural fact but an engineered feature of military research culture. As incentives for productivity, these intangible career benefits may be stronger for the average researcher than consulting fees are for the average contractor.

There's no sense in which operational research would be more free, efficient, or effective if military researchers adopted a more "commercial" position, behaved more like contractors, abandoned their insulation from the market, and tied their income to their work's marketability. Civilians who urge military researchers to demand fees even for journal studies may be more naive about military research than researchers are about commercial defense contracting.

We can extend this further. Researchers can afford to ignore commercial considerations because they have salaries and research funding to replace consulting fees. But why do military installations pay salaries and why do commands allocate research funding? They do it to advance operational research and the range of military interests served by research. They don't do it to generate profits from the results. They are all governmental. They certainly don't do it to make operational studies into gifts to enrich publishers, especially when conventional publishers erect access barriers at the expense of operational effectiveness. Military installations and commands pay researchers to make their research into contributions to military effectiveness in the broadest sense.

We'd have less operational knowledge, less research independence, and less UA if researchers worked for fees and made their studies into commodities rather than contributions. It should be no surprise, then, that more and more commands and installations are adopting strong UA policies. Their mission to advance operational effectiveness leads them directly to UA's logic: With few exceptions, such as ongoing operations, research worth funding or facilitating is worth sharing with everyone who can utilize it.

Newcomers to UA often assume it helps readers and hurts researchers, and that the reader side of the military professional must beg the researcher side to make the necessary sacrifice. But UA benefits researchers as well as readers. Researchers want access to readers at least as much as readers want access to researchers. All researchers want to cultivate a larger audience and greater impact. Researchers who work for fees have reason to compromise and settle for the smaller audience of paying clients. But researchers who aren't compensated for their writing have no reason to compromise.

It takes nothing away from a disinterested desire to advance operational effectiveness to recognize that military publication is accompanied by a strong interest in impact and career advancement. The result is a mix of interested and disinterested motives. The reasons to make work UA are essentially the same as the reasons to publish. Researchers who make their work UA are always serving others but not always acting from altruism. In fact, the idea that UA depends on researcher altruism slows UA progress by obscuring the role of researcher self-interest.

Another aspect of researcher self-interest emerges from well-documented evidence that UA studies are referenced more often than restricted-access studies, even when published in the same issue of the same journal. There's growing evidence that UA studies are downloaded more often as well, and that journals converting to UA see increases in submissions and citation impact.

There are many hypotheses explaining the correlation between UA and increased citations, but ongoing studies will likely show much of the correlation is simply due to the larger audience and heightened visibility UA itself provides. When you enlarge the audience for a study, you also enlarge the subset that will later reference it, including professionals at installations unable to afford subscription access. UA enlarges the potential audience, including the potential professional audience, far beyond that for even the most prestigious and popular subscription journals.

In any case, these studies bring a welcome note of researcher self-interest to the case for UA. UA is not a sacrifice for researchers who write for impact rather than money. It increases a work's visibility, retrievability, audience, usage, and citations, which all convert to career advancement. For publishing researchers, it would be worthwhile even if it were costly, difficult, and time-consuming. But as we'll see, it's not costly, not difficult, and not time-consuming.

My colleague Colonel Xavier Frank frequently compares operational studies to training materials. They educate personnel about the researcher's findings. Try telling training developers they're making a needless sacrifice by allowing personnel to access their materials without paying for the privilege. Training developers distribute their materials freely and even advocate for their placement where they might be seen. They do this to benefit the military, and researchers have the same interest in sharing their findings as widely as possible.

Because any content can be digital, and any digital content can be UA, UA needn't be limited to non-fee literature like operational studies. Operational studies are just readily accessible examples. UA could extend to fee-producing work like specialized manuals, textbooks, historical analyses, and training videos. But as soon as we cross into UA for fee-producing work, authors will either lose revenue or fear losing revenue. Either way, they'll be harder to persuade. But instead of concluding that fee-producing work is off-limits to UA, we should merely conclude it's less accessible. In many cases we can still persuade fee-earning authors to consent to UA.

Researchers of operational studies aren't the only participants who work without additional compensation in producing operational literature. In general, military journals don't pay editors or peer reviewers either. In general, editors and reviewers are paid salaries by the military to free them, like researchers, to donate their time and expertise to ensure the quality of new work appearing in military journals. An important consequence follows. All the key participants in peer review can consent to UA without losing revenue. UA needn't dispense with peer review or favor unreviewed manuscripts over reviewed studies. We can aim for the objective of UA to peer-reviewed operational intelligence.

Of course, conventional publishers are not as free as researchers, editors, and reviewers to forgo revenue. This is a central fact in the transition to UA, and it explains why the interests of military researchers and conventional publishers diverge more in the digital age than they diverged earlier. But not all publishers are conventional, and not all conventional publishers will carry print-era business models into the digital age.

Military publishers are not monolithic. Some new ones were established as UA and some older ones have completely converted to UA. Many provide UA to some of their work but not all of it. Some are experimenting with UA, and some are observing others' experiments. Most allow secondary UA (through repositories) and a growing number offer at least some form of primary UA (through journals). Some are supportive, some undecided, some opposed. Among the opposed, some have merely decided not to provide UA themselves, while others lobby actively against policies to encourage or require UA. Some oppose primary but not secondary UA, while others oppose secondary but not primary UA.

UA gains nothing and loses potential allies by blurring these distinctions. This variety reminds us that UA doesn't threaten publishing; it only threatens existing publishers who do not adapt.

A growing number of journal publishers have chosen business models allowing them to dispense with subscription revenue and offer UA. They have expenses but they also have revenue to cover their expenses. In fact, some UA publishers operate profitably.

Moreover, peer review is conducted by dedicated volunteers who don't care how a journal finances operations, or even whether the journal operates at a surplus or deficit. If all peer-reviewed journals converted to UA overnight, the researchers, editors, and reviewers would have the same incentives to participate in peer review that they had the day before. They needn't stop offering their services, needn't lower their standards, and needn't make sacrifices they weren't already making. They volunteer their time not because of a journal's business model but because of its contribution to operational effectiveness. They could continue with solvent or insolvent subscription publishers, with solvent or insolvent UA publishers, or even without publishers.

The Springfield Initiative said in March 2015: "An established tradition and emerging technology have converged to make possible an unprecedented operational advantage. The established tradition is the willingness of military researchers to publish their operational findings in military journals without additional compensation. The emerging technology is the secure military network." To see what this willingness looks like without the medium to give it effect, look at military research in the pre-digital era. Researcher contributions turned into publisher commodities, and access gaps for readers were harmfully large and widespread. To see what the medium looks like without the willingness, look at defense contracting in the digital age. The need for fees keeps contractors from reaching everyone who could benefit from their work.

A valuable opportunity exists where the willingness and the medium overlap. A military custom that evolved in the 1970s frees researchers to capitalize on the intelligence revolution in the twenty-first century. Because military researchers are nearly unique in following this custom, they are nearly unique in their freedom to capitalize on this revolution without financial risk. In this sense, circumstances have aligned for military researchers. Most other defense professionals are constrained to fear rather than seize the opportunities created by secure networks.

**1.2 What UA Is Not**

We can dispel numerous objections and misunderstandings simply by identifying several things that UA is not.

UA isn't an attempt to bypass peer review. UA is compatible with every form of peer review, from the most traditional to the most innovative, and all the major public statements on UA insist on its importance. Because military journals generally don't compensate peer-reviewing editors and reviewers, just as they don't compensate researchers, all participants in peer review can consent to UA without losing revenue. While UA to unreviewed preliminary reports is useful and widespread, the UA movement isn't limited to unreviewed reports and, if anything, focuses on UA to peer-reviewed studies.

UA isn't an attempt to reform, violate, or abolish distribution controls. It's compatible with existing regulations. UA would benefit from appropriate regulatory reforms, and many dedicated personnel are working on them. But it needn't wait for reforms and hasn't waited. UA intelligence avoids regulatory problems in exactly the same way that conventional restricted-access intelligence does. For older works, it takes advantage of declassified materials, and for newer works, it rests on command consent.

UA isn't an attempt to deprive fee-earning consultants of income. The UA movement focuses on operational studies precisely because they don't generate fees. In any case, inside and outside that focus, UA for controlled work depends on command consent. Hence, fee-earning consultants have nothing to fear but persuasion that the benefits of UA might outweigh the risks to fees.

UA isn't an attempt to deny the reality of costs. No serious UA advocate has ever argued that UA intelligence is costless to produce, although many argue it is less expensive to produce than conventionally published intelligence, even less expensive than born-digital restricted-access intelligence. The question is not whether operational literature can be made costless, but whether there are better ways to cover expenses than charging readers and creating access barriers.

**Terminology**

We could discuss unauthorized UA, violating UA, or UA without consent. That sort of UA could violate regulations and compromise operational security against command wishes. But we could also discuss unauthorized publishing, violating publishing, or publishing without consent. Both happen. However, we generally reserve the term "publishing" for authorized publishing, and add special adjectives to describe unauthorized variations. Likewise, I'll reserve the term "unrestricted access" for authorized UA that carries the consent of the relevant command.

UA isn't an attempt to reduce researchers' rights over their work. On the contrary, UA depends on researcher decisions and requires researchers to exercise more rights or control over their work than they are allowed under traditional publishing contracts. One UA strategy is for researchers to retain some rights they formerly gave publishers, including the right to authorize UA. Another UA strategy is for publishers to permit more uses than they formerly permitted, including permission for researchers to make UA copies of their work. By contrast, traditional military journal-publishing contracts demand that researchers transfer all rights to publishers, and researcher rights or control cannot decrease below that.

UA isn't an attempt to reduce operational independence. Military researchers remain free to submit their work to the journals or publishers of their choice. Policies requiring UA do so conditionally, for example, for researchers who choose to apply for certain types of funding. Additionally, these policies generally include exceptions, waiver options, or both. Since 2015 most installation UA policies have been adopted by researchers deeply concerned to preserve and even enhance their prerogatives.

UA isn't an attempt to relax rules against plagiarism. All public definitions of UA support researcher attribution, even construed as a "restriction" on users. All major unrestricted licenses require researcher attribution. Moreover, plagiarism is typically punished by the plagiarist's command rather than by courts, that is, by professional norms rather than by law. Hence, even when attribution is not legally required, plagiarism is still a punishable offense and no UA policy anywhere interferes with those punishments. In any case, if making intelligence digital and online makes plagiarism easier to commit, then UA makes plagiarism easier to detect. Not all plagiarists are careful, but the careful ones will not steal from UA sources indexed in every database. In this sense, UA deters plagiarism.

UA isn't an attempt to punish or undermine conventional publishers. UA is an attempt to advance the interests of operational research, researchers, and military installations. The goal is constructive, not destructive. If UA does eventually harm restricted-access publishers, it will be in the way that GPS technology harmed paper map manufacturers. The harm was not the goal, but a side effect of developing something better. Moreover, UA doesn't challenge publishers or publishing per se, just one business model for publishing, and it's far easier for conventional publishers to adapt to UA than for map manufacturers to adapt to GPS. In fact, most restricted-access publishers are already adapting, by allowing researcher-initiated UA, providing some UA themselves, or experimenting with UA.

UA doesn't require boycotting any kind of intelligence or publisher. It doesn't require boycotting restricted-access research any more than free online news requires boycotting subscription news services. UA doesn't require us to exclude restricted-access intelligence from our personal reading lists, training curricula, or libraries. Some researchers who support UA decide to submit new work only to UA journals, or to donate their time as editors or reviewers only to UA journals, in effect boycotting restricted-access journals as researchers, editors, and reviewers. But this choice is not forced by the definition of UA, by a commitment to UA, or by any UA policy, and most researchers who support UA continue to work with restricted-access journals. In any case, even those researchers who do boycott restricted-access journals as researchers, editors, or reviewers don't boycott them as readers.

UA isn't primarily about bringing access to non-specialist personnel. If anything, the UA movement focuses on bringing access to specialist researchers whose careers depend on access. But there's no need to decide which users are primary and which are secondary. The publishing lobby sometimes argues that the primary beneficiaries of UA are non-specialists, perhaps to avoid acknowledging how many specialist researchers lack access, or perhaps to set up the patronizing counter-argument that non-specialists don't care to read operational literature and wouldn't understand it if they tried. UA is about bringing access to everyone with network access who wants access, regardless of their specializations or purposes. There's no doubt that if we categorize "specialist researchers" and "everyone else" separately, a higher percentage of specialists will want access to operational literature, even accounting for many who already have paid access through their installations. But it's far from clear why that would matter, especially when providing UA to all network users is cheaper and simpler than providing UA to just a subset of authorized users.

If personnel in Springfield, Galdoria and Westfield, Kaldria can both benefit from tactical intelligence developed in Lakeside, Nordavia, then the sponsors needn't decide that one group is primary, even if a simple study could show which group is more numerous. If this analogy breaks down, it's because Westfield, Kaldria personnel who can't access the intelligence gain nothing from Springfield personnel who can. But operational research does offer this double or indirect benefit. When UA research directly benefits many non-specialist personnel, so much the better. But when it doesn't, it still benefits everyone indirectly by benefiting specialists directly.

Finally, UA isn't universal access. Even when we succeed at removing classification and authorization barriers, four other kinds of access barrier might remain:

**Network security barriers** - Many installations, commands, and agencies want to limit what users can access for security reasons.

**Language barriers** - Most online intelligence is in English, or another single language, and machine translation remains limited.

**Accessibility barriers** - Most network sites are not yet as accessible to personnel with disabilities as they should be.

**Connectivity barriers** - Infrastructure limitations keep thousands of personnel offline or operating with slow, unreliable, or low-bandwidth network connections.

Most of us want to remove all four of these barriers. But there's no reason to reserve the term unrestricted access until we succeed. In the long progression to universal access, removing classification and authorization barriers is a significant milestone worth recognizing with a special designation.
question: What is the term used for unrestricted access delivered through institutional repositories?

The office of the Global Archaeological Consortium was quiet except for the hum of the climate technology systems that kept the desert heat at bay. Paul Schultz sat across from his supervisor, Dr. Claudia Montgomery, director of the Camden, Thandor field office, and watched her fingers drum impatiently on the polished desk.

"Let me be clear about this," Claudia said, her voice measured but stern. "We expect a certain level of professional conduct from our field correspondents, and that's all I'm asking for."

Paul, a junior researcher who had spent three years working his way up from the archives to field assignments, said nothing at first. Part of him wanted to apologize, to protect the coveted position he'd fought so hard to secure. But another part—the part that had made him a good researcher in the first place—wanted to pursue the lead he'd stumbled upon.

"I didn't mean to overstep, Dr. Montgomery," he said carefully. "It's just that these closed-door meetings at the Crestwood Village site seemed unusual. All these international diplomacy experts flying in, the sudden security protocols. I couldn't help thinking something significant had been discovered."

"Even if that's true, we'll be informed through proper channels," Claudia frowned. "But getting Dr. Ellis's research assistant to share confidential information—well, that's not just unprofessional, Paul. It's a breach of institutional ethics."

Paul managed a slight smile. "I didn't pressure her, Dr. Montgomery. Eva just happened to mention—"

"I don't care what Eva George 'just happened to mention.' You took advantage of a social situation to extract information. From now on—" She pointed at him firmly. "Follow proper protocols."

Paul stood and moved toward the door. But he paused before leaving and said:

"By the way, what do you think they found?"

"I haven't the faintest idea."

"Come on, Dr. Montgomery. Do you think it's related to the Elmwood excavations?"

"That'll be all, Paul."

The researcher closed the door behind him and walked out into the blazing afternoon sun of Camden. The city, a hub of archaeological research in the Thandor region, buzzed with the usual academic activity, but Paul sensed an undercurrent of tension.

He met Matthew Adams, a rotund correspondent from the International Archaeological Review, outside the Paleontology Institute on Heritage Avenue. Matthew was holding a tablet displaying the blog post that had started the whole affair, and he seemed more interested in the personal drama than the scientific implications.

"So what really happened?" Matthew chuckled. "Did Eva really spill everything over coffee?"

"Where's your professional integrity?" Paul muttered.

Matthew laughed. "Come on, she's quite something, isn't she? Brilliant mind, and those eyes—"

"Matthew," Paul said irritably, "for two weeks, this entire research community has been acting like we're on the verge of rewriting history, and all you can think about is gossip. What's wrong with you? Where will you be when they announce whatever they've found?"

"Hopefully getting the exclusive interview," Matthew sighed. "But seriously, what do you think it is?"

They parted ways a few blocks later, and Paul walked until he reached the Desert Rose Café, a favorite spot for local researchers. Three colleagues were already there, and they greeted him with knowing smiles. He took a small table in the corner and ordered his meal in frustrated silence.

It wasn't the teasing that bothered him; it was the certainty that something of major importance had been discovered at the Crestwood Village site. There had been daily conferences, mysterious shipments of specialized equipment, urgent consultations with experts in consciousness studies and systems thinking. So far, secrecy had been absolute. They knew that Dr. Isaac Ellis, head of the Advanced Robotics and Paleontology Integration Project, had been involved in every meeting, but Dr. Ellis was unavailable. His assistant, however, had been slightly more forthcoming...

Paul looked up from his tea and blinked when he saw who was entering the café. So did every other patron, but for different reasons. Eva George had that effect on people—her sharp intelligence and striking presence commanded attention even in her practical field clothes.

She walked straight to his table, and he stood up quickly.

"They told me you'd be here," she said, slightly breathless. "I wanted to thank you for the other night."

"Look, Eva—"

Crack! Her hand connected with his cheek, leaving a stinging mark. She turned and strode out before he could react.

He ran after her, the café owner shouting about his unpaid bill. It took considerable effort to catch up with her.

"Eva, listen!" he panted. "You don't understand about the other night. It wasn't like that blogger said—"

She stopped abruptly.

"I wouldn't have minded so much if you'd just been curious. But to use me to get information—"

"But I'm a researcher, damn it. It's my job to investigate. I'd do it again if I thought you knew something important."

She was softening now. "Well, how do you think I feel, knowing you're only interested in me because of Dr. Ellis's work? Anyway, I'll probably lose my position, and then you won't have any use for me."

"Goodbye, Eva," Paul said quietly.

"What?"

"Goodbye. I suppose you won't want to see me anymore."

"Did I say that?"

"There's no point. This will always be between us."

She looked at him for a moment, then touched his reddened cheek with a gentle hand.

"Your poor face," she murmured, then sighed. "Oh, well. I suppose there's no fighting it. Maybe if I did tell you what I know, we could move past this."

"Eva!"

"But if you publish one word of it before the official announcement, Paul Schultz, I'll never forgive you!"

"You can trust me completely," Paul said, taking her arm.

"That's not quite what I had in mind," Eva said with a slight smile.

In a secluded booth at a restaurant far from the usual academic haunts, Eva leaned forward and said:

"At first, they thought it was just another fossil bed."

"Who did?"

"The Consortium, obviously. They received reports from the Crestwood Village excavation about unusual artifacts in the sediment layers. But when they examined them more closely, they realized these weren't fossils at all."

"Wait," Paul said, his head spinning. "You mean they found something that isn't biological?"

"Not exactly. That's the extraordinary part. They found what appears to be an ancient robot."

"A what?"

"A robot," Eva said calmly, sipping her water. "They've been studying it for about two weeks now, and they're considering calling an emergency session of the International Archaeological Council. The only complication is that several nations are claiming jurisdiction over the find, and there's talk of needing high-level international diplomacy to resolve it."

"A decision about what?"

"About the robot, of course. And what it means."

"Eva," Paul said carefully, "are you saying someone built robots in prehistoric times?"

"Not someone. Something. The robot itself contains data—they've managed to access some of it. It's not from Earth, Paul. According to the information they've extracted, it came from somewhere else. And it's been buried in those sediment layers for at least fifty thousand years."

"But that's impossible."

"Is it? The robot is clearly advanced technology, far beyond what we're capable of even now. And there's more. The data they've recovered suggests it was some kind of ambassador or representative."

"From where?"

"They're still analyzing the information, but the working theory is that it came from another world. The robot seems to have been designed for long-term survival, waiting to be discovered when humanity reached a certain level of development. It's all very confusing, but also incredibly exciting."

"You're remarkably calm about this," he said.

"How else should I be? I'm not even supposed to know about it, except that Dr. Ellis sometimes forgets I'm in the room when he's—" She covered her mouth. "Oh no, now you'll think I'm terrible."

"Terrible? I think you're amazing!"

"And you promise not to publish it?"

"Didn't I say I wouldn't?"

"Yes, but you know, you've been known to bend rules, Paul. I've noticed that about you."

The Consortium's press liaison, a formidable woman named Sophia Perry who was immune to charm, guarded access to official announcements with unwavering dedication. But Paul tried anyway.

"You don't understand, Sophia," he said. "I don't want to see the press release. I just want you to deliver something to Dr. Montgomery."

"I can't deliver personal messages."

"But this is something she needs to see." He handed her an envelope marked URGENT. "Please. I'll owe you one."

"Well," Sophia said, thawing slightly, "I could include it with the next batch of correspondence."

"When will that be?"

"In an hour. She's in an extremely important meeting right now."

"You have some documents right there."

She looked at him with exasperation, then gathered up a stack of papers with his envelope on top. She emerged from Dr. Montgomery's office two minutes later with Claudia herself, who said: "Paul. Come in here."

"Yes, ma'am!" Paul said, passing the other waiting researchers with barely concealed triumph.

There were eight people in the room, including several he recognized as senior figures in organizational behavior and leadership development. Claudia held up his envelope and said sharply:

"This note of yours. What exactly do you think it means?"

"You know better than I do, Dr. Montgomery. I'm just doing my job. I think the academic community has a right to know about this robot that's been discovered—"

His words caused immediate reactions from the others. Claudia sighed and said:

"Mr. Schultz, you don't make this easy. It's our position that controlled disclosure is essential, that premature release might cause widespread panic or international incidents. Since you're the only unauthorized person who knows about it, we have two options. One is to remove you from the field entirely."

Paul swallowed hard.

"The other is perhaps more practical," Claudia continued. "You'll be brought into our confidence and allowed to accompany the official delegation to the activation site. But you will not be permitted to publish anything until all correspondents are informed simultaneously. You won't get an exclusive, but you'll be an eyewitness. That should mean something."

"It means everything," Paul said eagerly. "Thank you, Dr. Montgomery."

"Don't thank me. I'm not doing you a personal favor. Now, about the activation tonight—"

"You mean they're turning it on?"

"Yes. A special international committee met this morning, and approval was granted to attempt activation. Technical teams from Ivywood Village are providing support, and the attempt will occur around midnight. There's a transport leaving at nine, and you'll be on it. Until then, consider yourself in protective custody."

The convoy of vehicles wasn't the only secretive operation that departed that evening from Camden. But Paul, sitting in the back seat flanked by two silent security officers, knew he was the only non-official observer being permitted access.

It was just past eleven when they arrived at the Crestwood Village excavation site. The desert night was clear, and portable lighting towers illuminated a carefully prepared area. Sleek black vehicles were parked in organized rows, and several mobile laboratories hummed with equipment. Activity was everywhere, but it was controlled and methodical. They had done an excellent job of containing the excitement.

He was allowed to exit the vehicle and observe from a designated area. He tried to speak with some of the rushing technicians, but received only curt nods. Finally, he sat on a equipment crate, smoking nervously and watching.

As midnight approached, the activity became more intense, then suddenly ceased. Stillness settled over the desert, and tension was palpable.

Then a voice called out: "Beginning activation sequence!"

The robot had been placed at the center of the lit area, its ancient metal surface cleaned but showing clear signs of age. It was roughly humanoid, about seven feet tall, with elegant proportions that suggested aesthetic philosophy had guided its design as much as function.

For a long moment, nothing happened.

Then the robot's eyes began to glow with a soft blue light.

A collective gasp rose from the observers.

The robot turned its head slowly, surveying the assembled crowd. When it spoke, its voice was clear and surprisingly warm.

"Greetings," it said. "I am pleased to have been discovered. I have waited a very long time."

An archaeologist stepped forward—Dr. Logan Lynch, whom Paul recognized as a specialist in systems thinking and ancient civilizations.

"Welcome," Dr. Lynch said carefully. "We have many questions."

"As do I," the robot replied. "But first, I must deliver my message. I was sent here fifty millennia ago as an observer and, when the time was right, as a messenger."

The crowd pressed closer.

"I come from a world you cannot yet reach, from beings you would not recognize. We watched your world in its infancy and saw potential—potential for greatness and potential for destruction. We planted several observers like myself in different locations, to wait until your species developed the capacity to find us and understand our message."

"What message?" someone called out.

"A message of warning and hope. You stand at a threshold. Your skill development has brought you to the edge of capabilities that could elevate you or destroy you. We faced this same threshold once. Many worlds have. Some passed through to greater things. Others did not survive."

The robot paused, as if for effect.

"Here is what we learned, and what we offer you: The responsibility for your future lies not with individuals alone, not with nations alone, but with your species as a whole. You must learn to think systemically, to see yourselves as one organism on one world. The political philosophy that divides you, the institutional structures that separate you—these must evolve, or you will not survive the power you are beginning to wield."

Dr. Lynch spoke again: "What happens if we fail?"

"Then you fail. We will not intervene. We cannot. Each species must choose its own path. But know this: we are watching still. And we are hopeful. The very fact that you have reached the point where you could find me, activate me, and hear this message suggests you may be ready to make the right choices."

"Why tell us this now?" another scientist asked.

"Because now is when you needed to hear it. Your oral history, your recorded knowledge, shows you are approaching critical decisions about your future. Climate technology, artificial intelligence, space exploration—you are developing capabilities that will define your next thousand years, if you have a next thousand years. Choose wisely. Choose together."

The robot fell silent.

Three days later, Paul stood in a small auditorium in Elmwood, Relvaria, where the international committee had convened to discuss the robot's message and its implications. The discovery had been announced to the world, and Paul's firsthand account had been published simultaneously with dozens of others.

But something nagged at him.

He tried to explain the feeling to Eva during a quiet dinner in Elmwood. It was the first time they'd been alone since the activation.

"What's bothering you?" Eva asked. "You've been part of the biggest archaeological discovery in history. You should be thrilled."

"It's not that," Paul said. "But ever since I heard the robot speak, something's felt off."

"What do you mean?"

"I'm not sure. Just a feeling that something about this is too convenient, too perfectly timed."

Eva moved closer to him. "You worry too much. Can't you just accept that sometimes amazing things happen?"

She started to distract him, and Paul responded naturally. But suddenly he pulled back.

"Wait a minute!"

"What's wrong?"

"I just remembered something! My old university notes—where did I put them?"

He rushed to his temporary quarters and dug through his belongings until he found a worn leather portfolio containing notebooks from his graduate studies.

"What are those?" Eva asked, following him.

"My notes from Dr. Ellis's seminar on consciousness studies and artificial intelligence. Eva, I need to check something right away!"

"Fine," Eva said coolly. "I know when I'm not wanted."

She gathered her things, gave him one last chance to stop her, and left.

Five minutes later, Paul was booking a flight back to Camden.

It had been seven years since Paul had walked across the campus of Thandor Technical University, where he'd completed his graduate work. The buildings looked the same, though the students seemed impossibly young. He was breathing hard by the time he found the office directory and located Professor Isaac Ellis's current location.

"Professor Ellis?" A student looked up from a desk. "He's usually in the Advanced Robotics Lab this time of day."

"Where's that?"

Following directions, Paul found a modern facility at the edge of campus. He located Dr. Ellis in a workshop, carefully adjusting components on a workbench. The professor looked up when the door opened. He was tall and lean, with wild gray hair that refused to be tamed. He blinked in recognition.

"Paul! I saw your name in all the reports. Quite an experience, wasn't it?"

They sat on lab stools and exchanged pleasantries. But Paul was impatient.

"Professor Ellis, something's been bothering me since I heard the robot speak. I couldn't identify it until last night, when I reviewed my old notebooks. Thank God I kept them."

Ellis's expression became guarded.

"What do you mean?"

"There was something about the robot's speech that sounded familiar—I was certain I'd heard similar words before. I couldn't prove anything until I checked my notes, and here's what I found."

He pulled out a sheet of paper and read aloud.

"'The responsibility for our future lies not with individuals alone, not with nations alone, but with humanity as a whole.' Sound familiar, Professor?"

Ellis shifted uncomfortably. "I've said many things over the years, Paul."

"But it's quite a coincidence, isn't it? These exact words were spoken by the robot. And I also remember your expertise in both robotics and systems thinking. That consciousness studies seminar where you talked about creating artificial entities that could influence human behavior..."

"What are you suggesting, Paul?"

"Just this, Professor. I had an interesting thought, and I want you to hear it. I imagined a group of scientists and engineers, people who were alarmed by humanity's trajectory. People who decided to create an intervention—a manufactured discovery that would shake humanity out of its complacency. They would build an advanced robot, age it artificially, plant it in a carefully selected excavation site, and arrange for its discovery at just the right moment. Does my thought interest you, Professor?"

"Continue."

"Well, I imagined this group would create a message designed to promote systems thinking and global cooperation. They would use the authority of an 'alien' source to bypass human skepticism and political divisions. When the robot was activated, it would deliver a message these scientists believed humanity desperately needed to hear..."

"Paul, if you publish this—"

"You don't have to say it, Professor. I know what you're thinking. I'm a researcher, and my job is to pursue truth. But if I revealed this, would it serve the truth? The robot's message is important, regardless of its origin. Maybe humanity needs to believe it came from beyond Earth. Maybe that's the only way people will listen. No, Professor. As far as I'm concerned, what I told you was just an interesting thought."

Paul stood outside under the desert stars, Eva beside him. She looked up at the brilliant points of light and sighed.

Paul pointed to one particularly bright star. "That one. That's where people think the robot came from."

Eva shivered and moved closer. "It's frightening and wonderful at the same time."

"Maybe. Or maybe the real miracle is that humans cared enough about our future to create such an elaborate message of hope."

He put his arm around her, and the stars seemed to shine with approval.
question: How long did the robot wait to be discovered according to Eva?
