Dr. Jennifer Flores left her research station in the Ivywood District at exactly 6:00 AM, as she had done every morning for the past fifteen years. Her routine never varied. She walked three blocks east on Merchant Street, stopped at the Cultural Exchange Café for a single espresso, then continued to the end of the fifth block. There she turned left onto Heritage Avenue, followed it to Preservation Lane, down Preservation and back via Archive Street to Merchant again, returning to her station.

She didn't walk quickly. She took her time, observing. She always returned to her door at precisely 6:50 AM. No one ever interrupted her walk. Even the barista at the café remained silent during the transaction, simply nodding as Dr. Flores placed her exact change on the counter.

The locals had long understood that Dr. Flores preferred solitude. The younger generation called it dedication to her work. The older residents remembered that this intense woman with her weathered field jacket and digital tablet had once been a celebrated professor at Bristol University in Yendor.

A professor of cultural sociology and aesthetic philosophy, they recalled. There had been some controversy surrounding her departure—an academic scandal of sorts. She had published a groundbreaking paper on collective consciousness and material reality, teaching its radical concepts to her graduate students. The content had been deemed too speculative, too far removed from empirical science, and Dr. Flores had been pressured to resign.

The morning air was crisp as Dr. Flores began her walk, the sky still dark with pre-dawn shadows. She noted the familiar landmarks: the biodiversity mural on the corner building, the small memorial garden dedicated to cultural preservation, the old archaeology museum that had been converted into apartments.

But something felt different today. She reached the corner of Heritage and Merchant slightly too quickly. Impossible, she told herself. For fifteen years she had maintained this precise schedule, her life organized around strict temporal boundaries. A researcher living alone with adequate funding for her modest needs, the regimented existence had developed gradually after her exile from academia.

She had not deliberately chosen this isolated life. But as a single woman devoted to her theories about collective human consciousness and reality formation, the structured routine had become essential to her work.

As she turned onto Heritage Avenue, she noticed something odd. The street seemed shorter somehow. The familiar buildings appeared closer together than they should be.

A news broadcast drifted from an open window: "...continuing reports worldwide... populations declining rapidly... the genetic engineering plague spreads unchecked... Dr. George Edwards of the World Health Council warns..."

The wind carried the words away. Dr. Flores frowned. Edwards—one of the colleagues who had dismissed her theories as pseudoscience. But she pushed the thought aside. She had insulated herself from current events for years, refusing to let external chaos disturb her research.

When she returned to her station door, she checked her watch and gasped. 6:35 AM. Fifteen minutes early.

For several minutes she stood frozen, staring at her timepiece. This couldn't be right. Fifteen years of perfect timing, disrupted.

And then she realized something else: she had forgotten to stop at the café. For the first time, she had walked right past it without her morning espresso.

Shaken, Dr. Flores entered her station and locked the door. She hung her jacket on the hook and moved slowly to her workspace. The research station was a single large room that served as laboratory, library, and living quarters. She had designed it herself after leaving the university, creating a space dedicated entirely to her work on collective consciousness theory.

Silence filled the room, broken only by the soft hum of her environmental systems. But Dr. Flores had always preferred silence. She had disconnected from the global networks years ago, after a research alert had interrupted her work with breaking news she didn't want to hear.

She had stopped following media entirely, had reduced her world to these few city blocks. And as the years passed, that self-imposed limitation had become absolute—an invisible barrier she could not cross.

Yet she couldn't entirely escape information. She heard fragments from passersby, glimpsed headlines on discarded newspapers, caught snippets of broadcasts from open windows.

And so she knew this was the year 2089, and that the genetic engineering experiments in Asia and Europe had gone catastrophically wrong, creating a plague that was decimating human populations worldwide. A plague now sweeping through Africa and South America with terrifying speed.

But she had dismissed these concerns as irrelevant to her work. Others could worry about global crises. She had her research.

Yet two things this morning demanded attention: arriving fifteen minutes early, and forgetting her espresso.

Dr. Flores moved to her primary workstation, where her life's work was displayed across multiple screens. Her research focused on a radical hypothesis: that human consciousness, through collective agreement, maintained the structural integrity of physical reality itself.

She pulled up her seminal paper, the one that had cost her everything:

"Human consciousness, through mass consensus, determines the physical manifestation of reality. Billions of minds perceiving buildings as buildings, streets as streets, matter as matter—and not as something else. Minds that observe reality in consistent patterns have maintained those patterns across generations. Eliminate those minds, and the entire structure of observable reality, deprived of its sustaining force, will collapse like a tower of sand..."

Her eyes moved down the screen:

"Yet this concerns not matter's existence, but only its form. While human consciousness may have shaped the appearance of the space we inhabit, consciousness would have minimal effect on matter's fundamental existence. What exists in our observable universe shall exist always, merely transformed or reconfigured.

"But contemporary physics and mathematics suggest other possibilities—other dimensions, other frameworks of space-time adjacent to our own.

"If a three-dimensional object passes through a two-dimensional plane, would that plane's inhabitants perceive it accurately? They could not, lacking the dimensional framework to comprehend it. Yet both occupy the same space.

"Therefore, if human consciousness alone maintains this universe's current form, might we not hypothesize other consciousnesses in adjacent dimensions, observing us, waiting strategically for the moment they can assume control of matter? Such a scenario follows logically from two premises: that consciousness shapes matter's manifestation; and that other dimensional frameworks exist alongside ours.

"Perhaps we will encounter a day when our dimension, our reality, dissolves before us as some superior intelligence emerges from the dimensional shadows of the very space we occupy and seizes the matter we perceive as our own."

She stood motionless, staring at her own words from fifteen years ago. Words that had made her a pariah in academic circles.

But now a terrifying realization crystallized. Billions had died worldwide. Where thousands of human minds had once existed, now perhaps only dozens remained. A catastrophically weakened force to maintain reality's coherent form.

The plague had nearly eliminated human life across multiple continents. She recalled the fragments she'd heard—buildings vanishing, geographical anomalies scientists couldn't explain.

The pieces assembled themselves with horrifying clarity. There were insufficient human minds to preserve the material world in its familiar configuration. Some other consciousness from another dimension was overwhelming humanity's collective reality and imposing its own dimensional framework.

Dr. Flores grabbed her jacket and tablet. She needed more information. She had to find someone who could confirm her fears.

She stepped outside into pre-dawn grayness. But something was wrong with the light—not darkness, but an absence of illumination, as if the concept of light itself was becoming uncertain.

The walkway extended to her gate, but beyond that, visibility dropped to almost nothing. As she moved forward, buildings emerged from the grayness like flat projections, two-dimensional images lacking proper depth and perspective.

She called out, hoping to find another person. But her voice behaved strangely, echoing upward into what seemed like an impossibly vast empty space above.

She continued to the corner of Heritage Avenue. There she stopped, staring in disbelief. The gray wall was impenetrable, and looking down, she saw the street simply ended. No pavement, no continuation—just absolute nothingness beyond the corner.

With a cry of terror, Dr. Flores ran back to her station, her jacket streaming behind her.

On her doorstep, she paused, breathing hard. She glanced back and the gray curtain seemed to thin momentarily, revealing...

A colossal city unlike anything terrestrial. Crystalline spires reached toward an alien sky. Geometric structures defied conventional architecture—impossible angles, surfaces that seemed to exist in more than three dimensions. Streams of light in colors she had no names for pulsed through transparent thoroughfares.

And beyond it all, a massive presence. Not a structure, but a consciousness itself, vast and incomprehensible, regarding her with something that might have been curiosity or hunger.

Then the vision faded, and the grayness returned.

Dr. Flores stumbled inside, leaving the door unlocked. Locks were meaningless now.

She collapsed into her chair, eyes scanning her workspace. Everything remained in place: her screens, her research materials, her carefully organized notes, the small sculpture from her field research in Dalebrook, Zelvaria, the framed image of the Waverly District biodiversity preserve.

This was her space, she thought. Environments absorb the consciousness of those who inhabit them. This was her world, her private reality, and it would be the last to dissolve.

But how long could her mind alone sustain it?

Dr. Flores looked at the framed image and felt a moment of reassurance. They couldn't take this. The rest of the world might dissolve as insufficient consciousness failed to maintain its form.

But this room was hers. She alone had designed it, lived in it, poured her consciousness into every detail.

This room would persist. It must...

She rose and walked to her bookshelf. Her eyes moved to the top shelf and terror seized her.

Books were missing. Not all of them—but many. Only the most familiar, most frequently referenced texts remained.

The transformation had already begun here. The unfamiliar items were disappearing first, exactly as her theory predicted.

She spun around. Was the auxiliary workstation beginning to fade?

But as she focused on it, it solidified again.

For a moment she felt genuine fear. This room was no longer protected from whatever was happening outside.

Was she losing her mind? Could this all be delusion? The locals had always thought her eccentric. Could they have been right?

No. She was perhaps the sanest person alive. She had predicted this exact scenario, and others had mocked her for it.

The children playing on streets were in a different dimensional framework now. The matter that had formed their world was being reconfigured by other minds in another dimension.

"Perhaps we will encounter a day when our dimension, our reality, dissolves before us as some superior intelligence emerges from the dimensional shadows of the very space we occupy..."

But there had been no need to wait. Within years of writing those words, it was happening. Humanity had played into the hands of those other consciousnesses. The genetic engineering experiments, the plague, the massive die-off—all part of a calculated plan.

She could see it now. Through subtle influence, perhaps through manipulation of human decision-making at crucial moments, entities from another dimension had orchestrated humanity's reduction. The weakening of Earth's collective consciousness had been deliberately engineered.

On impulse, she turned and opened the door to her sleeping area. She stopped at the threshold, a sob escaping her lips.

There was no sleeping area. Where her bed and personal belongings had been, there was only grayness.

Like an automaton, she turned to the entrance. No corridor, no exit vestibule.

Nothing.

Dr. Flores returned to her chair.

"So here I am," she whispered.

Here she was, making her last stand in the final corner of reality she could maintain.

Perhaps other researchers existed like her, she thought. People who had lived so intensely with their immediate environment that those spaces resisted the dimensional transition. People whose consciousness was so concentrated that their personal reality persisted against the greater force.

The rest of her station was gone. This room remained.

This room would last longest. And when the rest dissolved, this corner with her chair and primary workstation would remain. This was where she had spent fifteen years. The sleeping area was for rest, the kitchen area for sustenance. This space was for living, for thinking, for being.

This was her last stand.

These walls and screens and objects had absorbed her will to make them walls and screens and objects.

She looked toward where the window had been, into blankness. Her neighbors' stations were already gone. They hadn't lived with them as she had lived with this room. Their attention had been dispersed; their consciousness had not been concentrated as hers on this small area.

Through the dissolving boundary, she saw it again. The alien city, closer now, more detailed. The impossible architecture, the extra-dimensional geometries. She perceived it from multiple perspectives simultaneously, as if her consciousness was already beginning to adapt to the new dimensional framework.

And the presence—the vast intelligence orchestrating this transition...

Dr. Flores turned back to her workspace. Her environmental system was humming steadily. The grayness was seeping into the room.

Her secondary screens faded first, simply ceasing to exist. With them went that section of the room.

Then her field research sculpture.

"I never really liked that piece anyway," Dr. Flores murmured.

Now it didn't seem strange to be without those items. It felt almost natural, expected.

Perhaps if she concentrated, she could restore them. But what was the point? One person alone couldn't resist the inevitable. One consciousness couldn't stand against this tide.

She wondered what the sculpture looked like in that other dimension. Certainly not a sculpture, as they probably didn't have human artistic expression or 3D printing or the concept of field research souvenirs.

She wondered what she herself would become when she finally slipped into the unknown. She was matter too, just like the sculpture.

Would she retain her identity? Would she still be a person, or merely... a thing?

She didn't know.

Nothingness advanced across the room, stalking her as she sat beneath her remaining light source.

The room plunged into profound silence.

Dr. Flores started. Her environmental system had stopped. Strange—it had never failed in fifteen years.

She jumped from her chair, then slowly sat back down.

The system hadn't stopped.

It wasn't there.

There was a tingling sensation in her feet.

She looked down and saw that her legs below the knees had become translucent, like glass, like they were already halfway into another dimension.

Dr. Flores closed her eyes and thought about her paper, about her theories, about being right.

She had been right all along.

The tingling moved upward.

The letter from the Fairview District Council arrived on a Tuesday morning, and I read it twice over breakfast before sharing it with my wife, Elena.

"What would you think," I asked her over tea, "if I should undertake to mentor a youth collective this autumn?"

She considered it while she cleared the breakfast dishes. "Why, Marcus," she said, "it could be quite enriching, if I understand what a youth collective entails. What prompted this?"

"It wasn't entirely my idea," I admitted. "Councilor Brennan called me to her office yesterday. She said that some of the younger citizens in the district wanted to establish one. They need adult guidance, of course, and one of them suggested my name."

I should explain that I teach courses in aesthetic philosophy and systems thinking at our Fairview Academy. It's a privilege to work in Fairview, for our institution values interdisciplinary approaches and encourages students to see connections between art, nature, and social organization. On the other hand, most of my students come from families deeply involved in the district's experimental governance projects, and there's a constant pressure to demonstrate practical applications of theoretical concepts.

"That's wonderful," said Elena. "What does a youth collective do?"

"The purpose," I told her, "is to teach young people about organizational behavior and collaborative decision-making. They identify community needs and develop creative solutions—sometimes artistic, sometimes practical. Some collectives have even influenced local trade policy."

"You won't have to go door-to-door selling things, will you?"

"Of course not. I'd just facilitate their process."

Elena laughed, and I joined her, for we both knew that my understanding of market economics was theoretical at best.

"All right," I said, "laugh at my practical limitations. But don't worry. Councilor Brennan said we could consult with Dr. Park from the Systems Department if needed. There is one consideration, though. The Council will provide two hundred credits for initial materials, and Brennan suggested I might contribute another hundred. The question is, can we manage it?"

We'd been careful with finances since moving to Fairview three years ago. Our previous home in Goldfield Town had been comfortable, but when the environmental crisis forced mass relocations, we'd had to start over. Fairview's experimental social contract appealed to us—a community built on principles of environmental ethics and collective governance—but it meant financial sacrifices.

Elena did quick calculations. "Yes," she said, "if it's something meaningful to you."

Three weeks later, on a crisp autumn morning, I found myself in a converted greenhouse at the edge of the district. This would serve as our workspace—a bright, plant-filled structure owned by the family of one of the collective members, Mateo Lawrence.

"All right," I said to the five young people arranged on cushions around a low table, "let's begin informally. I'm not here as your teacher. My role is simply to facilitate. You'll decide what the collective pursues, and if it aligns with our community values and available resources, I'll support it however I can. This is your gathering."

Councilor Brennan had briefed me extensively on these young people. The three sitting to my left had initiated the proposal.

Rita Hayes was a thoughtful twelve-year-old who might have seemed reserved to strangers, but possessed a remarkable intensity when discussing ideas. Wei Mason and Layla Hamilton, also twelve, shared Rita's careful way of speaking and moving. The three had been friends since early childhood.

I initially thought they looked similar, but this was misleading. Their features were quite distinct. Perhaps from years of close friendship, they'd developed similar patterns of gesture and expression. All three had been deeply tanned by summer sun, making their eyes seem luminous.

The two sitting to my right were different in temperament. Alice Cruz was a robust thirteen-year-old with abundant dark curls and an infectious enthusiasm. Mateo Lawrence, a few months younger, was energetic and outgoing, always ready with questions.

The group exchanged glances, and Wei seemed to be designated speaker.

"Well, Mr. Reyes, a youth collective is a group of young people who collaborate to address community needs, using systems thinking and creative approaches."

"Is that your goal?" I asked. "To address community needs?"

"Why not?" Mateo responded. "There's something wrong with trying to help?"

"We want to make a difference," said Layla. "And learn skills we'll need for future projects."

"What sort of projects interest you?" I asked.

Councilor Brennan had mentioned that these young people were exceptional. "Alice and Mateo," she'd said, "show remarkable aptitude for systems thinking—they see connections others miss. The other three are harder to categorize. They demonstrate extraordinary insight in certain areas, but often seem disengaged from standard curricula. Perhaps this collective will channel their abilities."

Alice said, "What about creating a community art installation? Something that changes with the seasons."

"We should map community needs first," Mateo suggested, "then design solutions."

"I'd like to work on natural resource management," said Wei. He fixed me with a challenging look. "We could develop a system for monitoring water usage patterns across the district."

"That would require sophisticated data science capabilities," I told him, "which might be beyond our current scope. Perhaps something more accessible?"

Wei considered this and nodded reluctantly. "Then maybe something involving aesthetic philosophy. A public art project that teaches environmental concepts."

"How about a community garden design?" Layla offered.

"You mean just landscaping?" I asked.

She looked slightly offended. "No, I mean applying principles of cultural evolution to plant selection. Creating a garden that demonstrates how human aesthetic preferences have shaped agricultural biodiversity. I've been researching this."

"Well," I said, "that sounds like it requires substantial botanical knowledge. Are you Dr. Hamilton's daughter? Been exploring your father's library?"

"Some," said Layla, "and I maintain experimental plots at home."

"What about you, Rita?" I prompted. "Do you have a particular interest?"

"I'm not specialized," she said with a slight smile. "More integrative. But if the collective wanted to document local bird populations, I could contribute data I've been collecting."

"You could make that useful?" Mateo asked skeptically.

"Bird populations," I explained to Mateo, "are important indicators of environmental health. Systematic observation of local species could provide valuable data. The district's environmental monitoring program might be interested."

"No," said Rita, "these aren't standard observations. I've been tracking behavioral changes in urban-adapted species. How they've modified nesting patterns in response to our building designs."

"Well," I admitted, "the application for that might be limited. Why don't you consider something more straightforward? Perhaps designing informational materials about the district's recycling program?"

There was a pause, then Mateo said, "How would we distribute them?"

"Door-to-door, or at community centers."

He made a face. "Limited impact. Unless the materials themselves demonstrated something. What if we made them from recycled materials in an unusual way—showing the potential?"

Layla had been deep in thought. She said suddenly, "I think I know how to make a living wall system—vertical gardens for apartment buildings."

"What would that involve?" I asked.

"Modular planters that connect to greywater recycling. Self-sustaining."

"There might be people interested in that," I conceded.

"There will be," she said confidently.

Mrs. Lawrence appeared after a while, bringing refreshments and asking about our progress. I'd forgotten entirely about organizational structure, which according to everything I'd read was essential. Standard practice was for each member to take a leadership role.

Over lunch, I suggested establishing roles, but they seemed uninterested. Wei waved it off, saying they'd work organically. They did spend considerable time discussing a name, finally settling on "Fairview Futures."

It was Alice who eventually suggested wind sculptures. At first there was mild interest, then Wei said, "We could design something new. Has anyone seen a wind sculpture that incorporates sound?"

Nobody had. Wei sketched in the air. "Hollow tubes of varying lengths, arranged to catch wind from multiple directions."

"I'll prototype something tonight," said Rita, "and work out the acoustics."

I wished they weren't starting with an invention, risking disappointment, but I said nothing, knowing I could help them adjust later.

That evening I told Elena about the day's ideas. Most seemed impractical, but several were intriguing.

Mateo wanted to create a game-theory-based simulation for teaching resource allocation—a board game that demonstrated tragedy of the commons scenarios.

Wei wanted to design modular furniture that could be reconfigured for different community gathering needs.

Layla, moving past her garden ideas, suggested creating seed packets with embedded information—QR codes that linked to growing guides and environmental impact data.

Rita added that if you designed the packets creatively, they could become collectible art objects, encouraging seed saving.

These ideas incorporated sophisticated concepts, and I spent some time discussing systems thinking principles with them.

"My," said Elena, "they're remarkably insightful. Mateo sounds like a natural facilitator. I don't think you'll need Dr. Park's help."

I feel somewhat embarrassed about the wind sculpture, even now. That it worked surprised me. That it worked so beautifully was humbling.

Four of them were at the greenhouse when I arrived the next morning, and the sculpture hung from a tree branch, its tubes singing softly in the breeze. I stood listening, then they noticed me.

"Hello, Mr. Reyes," Alice said, gesturing toward it. I examined the sculpture for several minutes. It was exquisitely crafted, with a professional quality.

"It's too perfect," Alice told Rita. "Art should have some rawness."

"You're right," Rita agreed. She adjusted one tube slightly. "There, now it has dissonance."

Indeed, in the morning breeze, the sculpture now produced an intriguing mix of harmony and tension.

As we walked back to the greenhouse, I asked Rita, "How did you know that angle would create dissonance?"

She looked thoughtful. "It had to, didn't it? It changed the resonance patterns." She glanced at me quickly. "Of course, I tried various configurations while building it."

"Naturally," I said. "Where's Mateo?"

"He went to the Council office," Wei told me, "to request funding. We'll need materials to produce more sculptures."

"But I said yesterday that Councilor Brennan and I were providing initial capital."

"Oh, certainly, but wouldn't it be better to go through official channels? More aligned with community values?"

"Perhaps," I said, "but the Council generally requires detailed proposals."

Mateo walked in and handed me a document. "I got five hundred credits approved. It took some discussion—half the environmental committee wanted to hear the proposal. The account's in your name, Mr. Reyes, and you'll need to authorize expenditures. They want you to stop by and sign the agreement."

My heart sank. I'd never dealt with bureaucratic funding processes, and they made me anxious. To say nothing of being responsible for five hundred credits. I mentally vowed to be very careful.

"So then I stopped by the arts supply cooperative," Mateo continued, "and ordered materials. We hadn't finalized a name yesterday, but I made an executive decision. Fairview Futures—how's that?"

Everyone nodded approval.

"Just simple design on the letterhead," he explained. "Fairview Futures—Highpoint, Yendor."

I found my voice. "Professionally printed, I assume?"

"Well, of course," he replied. "Presentation matters."

My appetite was subdued that evening, and Elena noticed my preoccupation, but asked no questions. I told her about the sculpture's success and the group's ambitious plans.

On Friday we established a production process, soon developing an efficient workflow: cutting tubes to calculated lengths, treating them with weatherproofing solution, assembling them in Rita's designed configurations, and hanging the finished sculptures to cure.

Wei had located a supplier of bamboo tubes, which produced wonderful tones and aligned with our environmental ethics. I didn't know what they cost until later.

Within two weeks we had nearly fifty sculptures completed and packaged. Frankly, I was ready for a break, but Mateo, our acknowledged expert on community engagement, wanted more inventory. This quantity satisfied him, and he said he'd begin outreach the following week.

Alice, with touching confidence, asked him to reserve one for her family.

Three other developments occurred that day. Alice brought her laptop and spent the afternoon working on what appeared to be quite competent graphic design for promotional materials.

And Layla brought samples of her seed packet designs. They were beautiful—small envelopes with botanical illustrations and embedded information chips.

"What species?" I asked.

Layla smiled. "Heritage vegetables adapted to our climate. I've been selecting for drought tolerance while maintaining flavor profiles."

"That's remarkable. How long have you been working on this?"

"Three growing seasons. I've documented everything—it's proper peer review quality data."

"Is it effective?"

She pulled out her phone and showed me growth comparison charts. "These varieties use 40% less water than commercial equivalents."

The third Friday development reached me on Monday morning.

I arrived at the greenhouse slightly late to find several vehicles parked outside and the space full of people, including two Council representatives. Our Fairview officials are quite young and informal, but they still looked official, though currently they were laughing.

"Well," I said in my best classroom voice, "what's happening here?"

"Are you Reyes?" the taller representative asked.

"I am," I said, and someone took a photograph.

A young journalist grasped my arm. "Oh, Mr. Reyes, please, tell me about the collective's work. This is exactly the kind of story we need."

"Perhaps someone should brief me first."

"You don't know? One of your members installed a wind sculpture in Stonegate's central plaza last night—without permission. It's wonderful, but it's caused quite a discussion about public art and the social contract."

I shook my head, stunned.

"It was perfect timing. Morning commuters discovered it, and by noon there was a crowd. The sculpture's song changes with the wind, and people are calling it 'The Voice of Stonegate.' And this morning"—she smiled—"someone anonymously contacted the Council—of course it was the same young person who installed it—Mateo?—and here we are. And we've just seen demonstrations of those amazing seed packets and heard the plans for vertical gardens."

"Gardens?"

"Yes, those modular living walls. Who would have thought young people could develop such sophisticated systems?"

After things settled, Mr. Lawrence came down from the house to see what the excitement was about, then returned to work. Mrs. Lawrence went back inside. The journalist and photographer left. Mateo was jubilant.

"Did you hear? They're calling it 'The Voice of Stonegate.' I wish we had a hundred sculptures ready. A thousand. This is exactly what community engagement looks like. Layla, how soon can you produce more seed packets? And Rita, how many bird behavior datasets do you have?"

Those datasets! I've always found ornithology interesting in theory, but I must admit Rita's work was genuinely impressive.

"How many observation hours?" I asked.

"About four hundred, across three years. Want to see the analysis?"

I won't try to explain her methodology, but it was clear she'd done rigorous systematic observation. We asked Mrs. Lawrence to join us for a discussion. She listened carefully.

"All right," she finally said, "if you're serious about this. But you'll need proper protocols for any research involving living creatures. And you can't use this greenhouse once winter comes—you'll need heated space."

"We'll have transitioned by then," Rita predicted. "Once our work is published, other researchers will replicate it. The collective will move on to new projects."

Rita was right, despite our concerns about scaling too quickly. After the
Fairview Chronicle
gave us most of page two, including photographs, we had regular visitors. Many wanted to purchase sculptures or seed packets, but Mateo insisted on working through established community channels.

The arts cooperative took all our sculptures at forty credits each—Mateo's pricing alarmed me, but they sold immediately. He valued the seed packets at fifteen credits per set and found ready buyers.

Our beautiful letterhead arrived, along with quickly printed project proposal forms.

The following Tuesday, a energetic woman extricated herself from her vehicle and walked into the greenhouse. I looked up from where I was assembling planter frames.

"Hi," she said. "You're Marcus Reyes, correct? I'm Dr. Sarah Kim, and I work in the intellectual property section at the district's innovation center. My supervisor sent me, though I'd have come anyway. What are you doing to protect Fairview Futures' innovations?"

I straightened up and brushed off my hands. "Well, I've been wondering about that, but I know very little about such matters—"

"Exactly," she interrupted. "We thought that might be the case. Three of us at the center would like to contribute time. Partly because we're interested, partly because you may have genuinely novel approaches worth protecting. Interested? You handle filing fees—about a hundred credits per innovation. We'll handle everything else."

"What's to lose," Mateo interjected.

And so we acquired intellectual property support.

The day our design application was filed, Alice contacted a dozen sustainable design firms, sent specifications to each, and offered licensing arrangements. Result: one licensee with a two-thousand-credit advance.

It was a foggy morning about three weeks later when I arrived at the greenhouse. Dr. Kim was there, along with everyone except Mateo. Sarah had her feet up on a work table.

"Hi," she said. "Good news."

"Tell me," I replied.

"I am," she said, "in a cautious legal sense, of course. Layla and I have been reviewing her seed development work. I've spent recent evenings studying agricultural patents and genetic selection literature. There are countless patents on crop varieties and selection methods, but it looks"—she held up a cautionary hand—"it just looks like we have something genuinely novel. If we get protection, you have a valuable property."

"That's good, Dr. Kim," Layla said, "but it's not the most important thing."

"No?" Sarah raised an eyebrow at me, and I handed her a small packet.

She opened it carefully. "What is this?"

"Soil amendment," Layla told her. "It's designed for Fairview's specific soil conditions. Try a bit."

Sarah examined it closely. "It's remarkably fine-textured, and there's something unusual about the color."

"It contains biochar and mycorrhizal fungi in a specific ratio. It improves water retention by 60% while enhancing nutrient availability."

"I see. What's in it?"

"Several components. Applied systems thinking. Waste wood from district maintenance, processed with controlled pyrolysis, combined with cultivated fungal cultures."

"Just several components. And does it work long-term?"

"Three growing seasons of data confirm it," I said.

Dr. Kim stood and looked out into the fog. After a moment she said, "Reyes, Layla and I are heading to my office. We can work better there, and if we're going to revolutionize urban agriculture, no time like the present."

After they left, I turned to the others. "Let's talk. Where's Mateo?"

"Oh, he went to the Council to request expanded funding."

"Whatever for? We have over eight thousand credits in the account."

"Well," Wei said, looking slightly sheepish, "we were planning to acquire some fabrication equipment. You see, Rita refined my idea for modular furniture." He grabbed paper. "Look, we make components that can be reconfigured using magnetic connections, like this—" And he was off explaining.

"What did they do today, dear?" Elena asked over dinner.

"Let's see. We selected fabrication equipment, Rita shared chapters from her book on urban ecology, and we found a space in the Fairview Arts Building we can rent for winter. Oh, and Sarah is starting the incorporation process."

"Winter space," Elena repeated. "You mean you're continuing after school starts?"

"Why not? The young people can manage their studies easily, and they'll only work a few hours weekly during the school year."

"Even so, isn't this a lot of responsibility for children?"

"They're not working for anyone. They're the collective. Dr. Kim and I will be the only formal staff—initially, anyway."

Elena looked startled. "Did you say you'd be staff?"

"Sure," I told her. "They've offered me a small stake in the collective, and I'd be foolish to refuse. After all, what's to lose?"
question: What is the name of the youth member whose family owns the greenhouse where meetings are held?

The morning sun cast long shadows across the administrative complex in Maplewood, Veldoria, as Xavier Gregory stepped out of the transit pod and surveyed the gleaming towers of the Veldorian Research Authority. He'd been appointed Director of Research Ethics just three weeks ago, replacing the previous director who had retired under mysterious circumstances. The appointment came with a warning from Regional Administration: "Clean up the mess, but don't make waves."

His assistant, Elizabeth Brown, was already at her desk when he arrived, her fingers dancing across multiple holographic displays. She looked up with a disapproving frown.

"Director Gregory," she said formally, adjusting her neural interface headset. "There are several priority items requiring your attention. The Veldorian Council on Scientific Advancement has invited you to observe their presentation on evolutionary biology applications. I've accepted on your behalf."

"Cancel it," Xavier said, hanging his environmental suit in the climate-controlled closet. "I've got other priorities."

Elizabeth's eyes widened behind her augmented reality lenses. "You can't decline this invitation. Director Chen would never have been so dismissive of Veldorian cultural engagement."

"Director Chen left three months ago," Xavier said, "leaving me in charge."

"Well," Elizabeth said, her voice sharp. "I'm sure I don't know what excuse I can give the Council."

"No excuses needed," Xavier said. "Just tell them I'm occupied." He moved toward his private office.

"Are you leaving the administrative wing?" Elizabeth asked. "I have several important authorization requests here for your biometric signature."

"I don't recall any pending authorizations requiring immediate attention, Elizabeth," Xavier said, pulling on a field jacket equipped with recording devices.

"I prepared them for you. They're exactly as Director Chen would have wanted them."

"Did you prepare all of Chen's authorizations, Elizabeth?"

"Director Chen was extremely busy," Elizabeth said stiffly. "She had complete confidence in me."

"Since I'm cutting out the ceremonial obligations," Xavier said, "I won't be so busy."

"Well!" Elizabeth said. "May I ask where you'll be if something urgent arises?"

"I'm going to the Historical Archives in Camden."

Elizabeth blinked. "Whatever for?"

Xavier looked thoughtfully at Elizabeth. "You've been stationed here in Veldoria for six years, Elizabeth. What was behind the administrative reorganization that put the current Council in power?"

"I'm sure I haven't pried into—"

"What about that research vessel? The one that disappeared in the Nordavia sector about twelve years back?"

"Director Gregory, those are exactly the sort of questions we avoid with the Veldorians. I certainly hope you're not thinking of openly investigating—"

"Why?"

"The Veldorians are very sensitive about their past. They don't welcome outsiders examining historical records. They've been gracious enough to let us move past the fact that our investigators subjected them to intensive scrutiny on one occasion."

"You mean when they came looking for the research vessel?"

"I, for one, am ashamed of the aggressive tactics that were employed, interrogating these peaceful people as though they were criminals. We try never to reopen that wound, Director Gregory."

"They never found the vessel, did they?"

"Certainly not in Veldoria."

Xavier nodded. "Thanks, Elizabeth. I'll be back before end of shift." Elizabeth's face was set in lines of grim disapproval as he left.

---

The pale-featured Veldorian administrator vibrated his communication implant in a distressed tone.

"Access to the Historical Archives is restricted," he said in his soft voice. "The Archivist expresses deep regret."

"The importance of my research here," Xavier said, struggling with the formal dialect protocols. "My interest in administrative history."

"Impossible for off-worlders. Please depart quietly."

"The necessity that I access these records."

"The specific instructions of the Archivist." The Veldorian's voice rose slightly. "To insist no longer. To abandon this inquiry!"

"Fine, I know when I'm blocked," Xavier said in standard language. "I'll find another way."

Outside, Xavier stood for a moment looking across at the precisely designed facades lining the street—a triumph of urban planning—then started toward a public information terminal. The few Veldorians on the street avoided eye contact, giving him wide berth as he passed. Autonomous vehicles glided silently along the pedestrian-free lanes.

Back at the office, Elizabeth would be preparing another list of complaints.

Xavier studied the directory listings. An establishment marked with symbols suggesting a social gathering place caught his attention. He entered.

A Veldorian attendant was dispensing beverages from a service station. He looked at Xavier and froze mid-motion.

"To enjoy refreshment," Xavier said in Veldorian formal speech. "To sample local hospitality."

"To not enjoy my humble establishment," the Veldorian mumbled. "Digestive incompatibility; to express regret."

"Don't worry about it," Xavier said, irritated. "Just serve it and I'll decide if it works for me."

"To be reported for contamination of off-worlders." The attendant looked around for support, found none. The Veldorian patrons, attention elsewhere, were leaving.

"Get moving," Xavier said, placing a credit chip in the payment receptor.

"The procurement of a containment unit," a thin voice called from nearby. "The display of an anomaly."

Xavier turned. A tall Veldorian gestured dismissively. From his flushed complexion, the individual appeared intoxicated.

"To silence yourself," the attendant hissed. "To remain quiet, birth-cohort mate."

"To consume your own product," the intoxicated one whispered. "To find proper containment for this specimen." He wavered toward Xavier. "To display this one publicly, like all anomalies."

"Seen a lot of specimens like me, have you?" Xavier asked with interest.

"To speak comprehensibly, malodorous off-worlder," the drunk said. The attendant whispered something, and two patrons came to assist the drunk toward the exit.

"To acquire containment!" the drunk called. "To keep the specimens in their designated areas."

"I've changed my mind," Xavier said to the attendant. "Thanks anyway, but I need to leave." He followed the drunk outside. The other Veldorians released him and hurried back inside. Xavier looked at the swaying figure.

"To depart, specimen," the Veldorian whispered.

"To be friendly," Xavier said. "To share information."

"To have you transported to a research facility, ill-mannered foreign specimen."

"To not be hostile," Xavier said. "To permit conversation."

"To not tolerate such presumption!" The Veldorian moved toward Xavier. Xavier backed away.

"To exchange knowledge," Xavier said. "To cooperate—"

The Veldorian reached for him, missed. A passer-by moved around them quickly, disappeared. Xavier backed into a narrow service corridor and continued offering conversational overtures to the intoxicated local, who followed, agitated. Xavier backed around a corner into a deserted maintenance passage.

Xavier stepped around him, grabbed his collar and pulled. The Veldorian fell. Xavier stood over him. The downed native tried to rise; Xavier placed a foot against his chest.

"To not be going anywhere for a while," Xavier said. "To stay right here and answer some questions."

---

"There you are!" Elizabeth said, looking at Xavier over her lenses. "There are two officials waiting to see you. Veldorian officials."

"Council representatives, I imagine. Word travels fast." Xavier removed his jacket. "This saves me the trouble of requesting another meeting at the Administrative Council."

"What have you been doing? They seem very upset, I don't mind telling you."

"I'm sure you don't. Come along. And bring an official recording device."

Two Veldorians wearing elaborate rank insignia rose as Xavier entered the conference room. Neither offered a courteous bow, Xavier noted. They were angry.

"I am Akira Wright, of the Off-World Relations Division, Administrative Council," the taller Veldorian said in accented standard language. "May I present Walter Ford, of the Internal Security Bureau?"

"Please sit," Xavier said. They resumed their seats. Elizabeth hovered nervously, then sat rigidly.

"Oh, it's such an honor—" she began.

"Skip the pleasantries," Xavier said. "These officials didn't come here for social calls."

"Indeed," Akira said. "Frankly, I have received a most disturbing report, Director. I shall ask Walter to present it." He nodded to the security chief.

"Two hours ago," Walter said, "a Veldorian citizen was brought to medical services suffering from minor injuries. Questioning revealed that he had been physically restrained by an off-worlder. An investigator from your world, to be precise. Investigation indicates that the description matches that of the Director of Research Ethics."

Elizabeth gasped audibly.

"Have you ever heard," Xavier said, looking steadily at Akira, "of a research vessel, the VSS Discovery, which disappeared in this sector fourteen years ago?"

"Really!" Elizabeth exclaimed, standing. "I wash my hands—"

"Keep that recorder active," Xavier said sharply.

"I'll not be party—"

"You'll do as instructed, Elizabeth," Xavier said quietly. "I'm telling you to make an official sealed record of this conversation."

Elizabeth sat down.

Akira's posture stiffened. "You reopen an old wound, Director. It reminds us of certain inappropriate treatment at investigator hands—"

"Nonsense," Xavier said. "That excuse worked with my predecessors, but it doesn't work with me."

"All our efforts," Elizabeth said, "to move past that terrible episode! And you—"

"Terrible? I understand that an investigative team came to Veldoria and asked questions. They got evasive answers and stayed to investigate further. After ten days they left. Somewhat annoying to the Veldorians, perhaps—at most. If they were innocent."

"If!" Elizabeth burst out.

"If, indeed!" Akira said, his soft voice trembling. "I must protest your—"

"Save the protests, Akira. You have explaining to do. And I don't think your explanation will be adequate."

"It is for you to explain! This person who was injured—"

"Not injured. Just detained briefly to refresh his memory."

"Then you admit—"

"It worked, too. He remembered quite a bit, once he focused."

Akira stood; Walter followed.

"I shall request your immediate recall, Director. Were it not for your diplomatic immunity, I should do more—"

"Why did the Council change, Akira? It happened just after the investigative team visited, and before the arrival of the first off-world research ethics mission."

"This is an internal matter!" Akira said, his voice strained. "The current Council has shown itself most cooperative with you investigators. It has been extraordinarily accommodating—"

"—to keep the research ethics director and staff uninformed," Xavier said. "And the same goes for the few off-world researchers you've granted access. This constant round of ceremonial obligations; no social contacts outside official channels; no travel permits to visit outlying districts, or your satellite research stations—"

"Enough!" Akira's hands trembled. "I can discuss this no further—"

"You'll discuss it with me, or there'll be an investigative team here in seven days to do the discussing," Xavier said.

"You can't!" Elizabeth gasped.

Xavier turned a steady look on Elizabeth. She fell silent. The Veldorians sat down.

"Answer me this," Xavier said, looking at Walter. "About fourteen years back, there was a small procession held here. Some unusual specimens were captured. After being securely contained, they were exhibited to the Veldorian public. Transported through the streets. Very educational, no doubt. A highly informative display.

"Interesting thing about these specimens. They wore clothing. They seemed to communicate with each other. Altogether it was quite a fascinating exhibit.

"Tell me, Walter, what happened to those eight off-worlders after the procession ended?"

Akira made a choking sound and spoke rapidly to Walter in Veldorian. Walter's posture collapsed. Elizabeth opened her mouth, closed it and blinked rapidly.

"How did they die?" Xavier demanded. "Did you terminate them, eliminate them, or contain them permanently? What entertaining end did you devise for them? Research, perhaps? Dissection to understand their biology..."

"No!" Akira gasped. "I must correct this terrible misunderstanding immediately."

"Misunderstanding, hell," Xavier said. "They were off-worlders! A simple truth-verification scan would get that from any Veldorian who witnessed the procession."

"Yes," Akira said weakly. "It is true, they were off-worlders. But there was no killing."

"They're alive?"

"Alas, no. They... expired."

Elizabeth made a small sound.

"I see," Xavier said. "They expired."

"We attempted to keep them alive, naturally. But we did not know what nutrition—"

"Didn't bother to find out, either, did you?"

"They became ill," Akira said. "One by one..."

"We'll address that question later," Xavier said. "Right now, I want more information. Where did you find them? Where did you hide the vessel? What happened to the rest of the crew? Did they 'become ill' before the big procession?"

"There were no more! Absolutely, I assure you!"

"Killed in the crash?"

"No crash. The vessel landed intact, in the Nordavia sector. The... off-worlders... were unharmed. Naturally, we feared them. They were strange to us. We had never before encountered such beings."

"Came out shooting, did they?"

"Weapons? No, no weapons—"

"They raised their hands, didn't they? Asked for help. You helped them; helped them to death."

"How could we know?" Akira moaned.

"How could you know an investigation would commence in a few months looking for them, you mean? That was a shock, wasn't it? I'll bet you had a frantic time hiding the vessel and silencing witnesses. A close call, eh?"

"We were afraid," Walter said. "We are a cautious people. We feared the strange beings from the alien vessel. We did not kill them, but we felt it was fortunate they... did not survive. Then, when the investigators came, we realized our error. But we feared to speak. We removed our guilty leaders, concealed what had occurred, and... offered our cooperation. We invited the establishment of research ethics oversight. We made a mistake, it is true, a grave mistake. But we have tried to make amends..."

"Where is the vessel?"

"The vessel?"

"What did you do with it? It was too large to just hide and forget. Where is it?"

The two Veldorians exchanged looks.

"We wish to demonstrate our remorse," Akira said. "We will show you the vessel."

"Elizabeth," Xavier said. "If I don't return in a reasonable timeframe, transmit that recording to Regional Administration, sealed." He stood, looked at the Veldorians.

"Let's go," he said.

---

Xavier ducked under the reinforced supports at the entrance to the underground chamber. He peered into the darkness at the curved hull of the space-weathered vessel.

"Any illumination in here?" he asked.

A Veldorian activated a control. A weak bluish glow appeared.

Xavier walked along the elevated platform, studying the vessel. Empty equipment bays gaped below damaged sensor arrays. Debris-covered decking was visible within the partially-open access port. Near the bow the words 'VSS Discovery M4 Lakeside Station' were visible in faded lettering.

"How did you get it in here?" Xavier asked.

"It was transported here from the landing site, approximately fifteen kilometers distant," Akira said, his voice thinner than ever. "This is a natural geological formation. The vessel was lowered into it and sealed."

"How did you shield it so the detection systems didn't locate it?"

"All here is high-density mineral deposits," Akira said, gesturing. "Extensive veins of nearly pure metals."

Xavier grunted. "Let's go inside."

Walter came forward with a portable light. The group entered the vessel.

Xavier climbed a narrow ladder, examined the interior of the command compartment. Dust covered the deck, the mounting points where control stations had been installed, the empty instrument panels, the scattered debris of severed connections, fragments of wire and documentation. A thin layer of corrosion dulled the exposed metal where cutting tools had removed heavy shielding. There was a faint odor of stale organic material.

"The storage compartment—" Walter began.

"I've seen enough," Xavier said.

Silently, the Veldorians led the way back through the tunnel and into the late afternoon light. As they climbed the slope to the transport vehicle, Akira came to Xavier's side.

"Indeed, I hope that this will conclude this unfortunate matter," he said. "Now that all has been fully and honestly revealed—"

"You can skip that," Xavier said. "You're fourteen years late. The crew was still alive when the investigative team arrived, I imagine. You killed them—or let them die—rather than risk admitting what you'd done."

"We were at fault," Akira said abjectly. "Now we wish only cooperation."

"The Discovery was a heavy research vessel, approximately thirty thousand tons." Xavier looked grimly at the slender official. "Where is she, Akira? I won't settle for a fifteen-hundred-ton auxiliary craft."

Akira's posture shifted so violently that one rank insignia fell off.

"I know nothing of... of..." He stopped. His breathing became rapid as he struggled for composure.

"My Council can entertain no further accusations, Director," he said at last. "I have been completely transparent with you. I have overlooked your intrusion into matters not properly within your jurisdiction. My patience is exhausted."

"Where is that vessel?" Xavier demanded. "You never learn, do you? You're still convinced you can conceal everything and move on. I'm telling you you can't."

"We return to the city now," Akira said. "I can do no more."

"You can and you will, Akira," Xavier said. "I intend to discover the truth of this matter."

Akira spoke to Walter in rapid Veldorian. The security chief gestured to his four armed officers. They moved to surround Xavier.

Xavier eyed Akira. "Don't try it," he said. "You'll just make things worse."

Akira's posture stiffened, his bearing aggressive toward the off-worlder.

"Out of deference to your diplomatic status, off-worlder, I shall ignore your insulting remarks," Akira said in his soft voice. "Let us now return to the city."

Xavier looked at the four officers. "I see your point," he said.

Akira followed him into the vehicle, sat rigidly at the far end of the seat.

"I advise you to remain very close to your research ethics office," Akira said. "I advise you to dismiss these theories from your mind, and to enjoy the cultural aspects of life in Veldoria. Especially, I should not venture outside the city, or appear overly curious about matters of concern only to the Veldorian Council."

In the front seat, Walter looked straight ahead. The suspension-equipped vehicle moved smoothly along the narrow highway. Xavier listened to the quiet hum of the electric motor and said nothing.

---

"Elizabeth," Xavier said, "I want you to listen carefully to what I'm going to tell you. I have to move rapidly now, to catch the Veldorians unprepared."

"I'm sure I don't know what you're talking about," Elizabeth said sharply, her eyes intense behind the augmented lenses.

"If you'll listen, you may find out," Xavier said. "I have no time to waste, Elizabeth. They won't be expecting an immediate action—I hope—and that may give me the opportunity I need."

"You're still determined to make an issue of that incident!" Elizabeth said. "I can hardly blame the Veldorians. They are not an experienced spacefaring culture; they had never before encountered aliens."

"You're ready to excuse a great deal, Elizabeth. But it's not what happened fourteen years ago I'm concerned with. It's what's happening now. I've told you that it was only an auxiliary craft the Veldorians have concealed. Don't you understand the implication? That vessel couldn't have traveled far. The main research vessel must be somewhere nearby. I want to know where!"

"The Veldorians don't know. They're a very cultured, peaceful people. You can do irreparable harm to off-world relations if you insist—"

"That's my decision," Xavier said. "I have responsibilities and we're wasting time." He crossed the room to his desk, opened a drawer and took out a compact energy weapon.

"This office is being monitored. Not very effectively, if I know the Veldorians. I think I can evade surveillance."

"Where are you going with... that?" Elizabeth stared at the weapon. "What in the world—"

"The Veldorians won't waste time destroying every piece of evidence in their records relating to this matter. I have to obtain what I need before it's too late. If I wait for an official Inquiry Board, they'll find nothing but cooperative smiles."

"You're out of your mind!" Elizabeth stood up, trembling with indignation. "You're like a... a..."

"You and I are in a precarious position, Elizabeth. The logical next move for the Veldorians is to eliminate both of us. We're the only ones who know what occurred. Akira almost accomplished that this afternoon, but I dissuaded him—for the moment."

Elizabeth emitted a sharp laugh. "Your paranoid delusions are overwhelming you," she gasped. "In danger, indeed! Eliminating me! I've never heard anything so absurd."

"Stay in this office. Secure the door with the safety lock. You've got food and water in the dispenser. I suggest you stock up before they disable the supply. Don't admit anyone, regardless of pretext. I'll maintain contact via secure communicator."

"What are you planning to do?"

"If I don't return, transmit the sealed record of this afternoon's conversation, along with the information I've given you. Send it through on an emergency priority. Then inform the Veldorians what you've done and remain secure. I think you'll be safe. It won't be easy to breach this office and anyway, they won't worsen things by harming you. A response team can be here in ten days."

"I'll do nothing of the sort! The Veldorians respect me! You... newcomer! Troublemaker! Setting out to destroy—"

"Blame me if it makes you feel better," Xavier said, "but don't be foolish enough to trust them." He pulled on a cape, opened the door.

"I'll be back in a few hours," he said. Elizabeth stared after him silently as he closed the door.

---

It was an hour before dawn when Xavier entered the combination to the security lock and stepped into the darkened research ethics office. He looked exhausted.

Elizabeth, dozing in a chair, awoke with a start. She looked at Xavier, rose and activated a light, turned to stare.

"What in the world—Where have you been? What's happened to your clothing?"

"I got a little dirty. Don't worry about it." Xavier went to his desk, opened a drawer and replaced the weapon.

"Where have you been?" Elizabeth demanded. "I stayed here—"

"I'm glad you did," Xavier said. "I hope you accumulated supplies from the dispenser, too. We'll be secured here for ten days, at least." He made notes on a data pad. "Activate the official transmitter. I have a lengthy transmission for Regional Administration."

"Are you going to tell me where you've been?"

"I have a message to transmit first, Elizabeth," Xavier said sharply. "I've been to the Administrative Council," he added. "I'll tell you all about it later."

"At this hour? There's no one there..."

"Exactly."

Elizabeth gasped. "You mean you broke in? You infiltrated the Administrative Council?"

"That's right," Xavier said calmly. "Now—"

"This is absolutely unacceptable!" Elizabeth said. "Thank heaven I've already—"

"Activate that transmitter, woman!" Xavier snapped. "This is critical."

"I've already done so, Director Gregory!" Elizabeth said harshly. "I've been waiting for you to return here..." She turned to the communicator, activated controls. The screen illuminated, and a wavering long-distance image appeared.

"He's here now," Elizabeth said to the screen. She looked at Xavier triumphantly.

"That's good," Xavier said. "I don't think the Veldorians can interrupt our transmission, but—"

"I have fulfilled my duty, Director Gregory," Elizabeth said. "I made a full report to Regional Administration last night, as soon as you left this office. Any doubts I may have had as to the appropriateness of that decision have been completely eliminated by what you've just told me."

Xavier looked at her steadily. "You've been busy, Elizabeth. Did you mention the eight off-worlders who died here?"

"That had no bearing on the matter of your reckless behavior! I must say, in all my years in the service, I've never encountered someone less suited to research ethics work."

The screen crackled, the twelve-second transmission lag having elapsed. "Director Gregory," the face on the screen said, "I am Administrator Eva Ahmed, Senior Deputy Director for the region. I have received a report on your conduct which makes it mandatory for me to relieve you administratively, with Elizabeth Brown assuming directorship. Pending the findings of an Inquiry Board, you will—"

Xavier reached out and deactivated the communicator. The triumphant expression faded from Elizabeth's face.

"Why, what is the meaning—"

"If I'd listened any longer, I might have heard something I couldn't disregard. I can't afford that at this moment. Listen, Elizabeth," Xavier went on earnestly, "I've found the missing research vessel."

"You heard her relieve you!"

"I heard her say she was going to, Elizabeth. But until I've heard and acknowledged a verbal order, it has no authority. If I'm wrong, she'll get my resignation. If I'm right, that suspension would be embarrassing all around."

"You're defying lawful authority! I'm in charge here now." Elizabeth stepped to the local communicator.

"I'm going to report this terrible situation to the Veldorians at once, and offer my profound—"

"Don't touch that screen," Xavier said. "You go sit in that corner where I can monitor you. I'm going to make a sealed recording for transmission to Administration, along with a request for an armed response team. Then we'll wait."

Xavier ignored Elizabeth's fury as he spoke into the recorder.

The local communicator chimed. Elizabeth jumped up, staring at it.

"Go ahead," Xavier said. "Answer it."

A Veldorian official appeared on the screen.

"Elizabeth Brown," he said without preamble, "for the Administrative Council of the Veldorian Authority, I hereby recognize you as Director of Research Ethics for this region, in accordance with the communications transmitted to my government directly from off-world Administration. As director, you are requested to make available for questioning Xavier Gregory, former director, in connection with the assault on two security personnel and illegal entry into the offices of the Administrative Council."

"Why, why," Elizabeth stammered. "Yes, of course. And I do want to express my deepest regrets—"

Xavier rose, went to the communicator, moved Elizabeth aside.

"Listen carefully, Akira," he said. "Your deception has been exposed. You don't come in and we don't come out. Your concealment worked for fourteen years, but it's finished now. I suggest you maintain composure and resist the temptation to worsen your situation."

"Elizabeth Brown," Akira said, "a security squad waits outside your research ethics office. It is clear you are dealing with a dangerous individual. As always, the Veldorians wish only cooperation with off-worlders, but—"

"Don't bother," Xavier said. "You know what was in those records I examined this morning."

Xavier turned at a sound behind him. Elizabeth was at the door, reaching for the security lock release...

"Don't!" Xavier moved—too late.

The door burst inward. A group of armed Veldorians pressed into the room, pushed Elizabeth back, aimed weapons at Xavier. Security Chief Walter Ford pushed forward.

"Attempt no resistance, off-worlder," he said. "I cannot promise to restrain my officers."

"You're violating off-world territory, Walter," Xavier said steadily. "I suggest you withdraw the same way you entered."

"I invited them here," Elizabeth spoke up. "They are here at my explicit invitation."

"Are they? Are you sure you intended to go this far, Elizabeth? A squad of armed Veldorians in the research ethics office?"

"You are the director, Elizabeth Brown," Walter said. "Would it not be best if we removed this unstable person to a secure location?"

"You're making a serious mistake, Walter," Xavier said.

"Yes," Elizabeth said. "You're quite right, Administrator Ford. Please escort Director Gregory to his quarters in this building—"

"I don't advise you to violate my diplomatic immunity, Akira," Xavier said.

"As director," Elizabeth said quickly, "I hereby waive immunity in the case of Xavier Gregory."

Walter produced a recording device. "Kindly repeat your statement, Director, officially," he said. "I wish no ambiguity to arise later."

"Don't be foolish, woman," Xavier said. "Don't you see what you're enabling? This would be an excellent time for you to determine whose interests you're serving."

"I'm serving the interests of proper conduct and research ethics!"

"You've been deceived. These people are concealing—"

"You think everyone is incompetent, don't you, Director Gregory?" She turned to the security chief and spoke into the microphone he held up.

"That's an invalid waiver," Xavier said. "I'm director here, whatever communications you've received. This situation is coming into the open, whatever you do. Don't add violation of off-world territory to the list of Veldorian offenses."

"Detain him," Walter said.
question: Where did Xavier Gregory plan to visit during his investigation?
option_a: The Veldorian Council on Scientific Advancement

synthetic_story:
JOURNEY TO THE DEEP PAST
By ADAPTATION


The fossil beds stretched endlessly beneath the red sky of Mars-Prime, humanity's first successful terraformed world. Dr. Eva George stood at the edge of the excavation site, watching the dust devils dance across the ancient lakebed. She had spent three decades building the paleontology program here, and now it was all coming to an end.

"I don't see why we have to be here," one of the junior researchers complained. "She's not going to say anything we don't already know."

"She'd better," Dr. Victor Hill said loudly from the row in front. "I've been waiting two years for this announcement."

"Victor, please," his research partner Angela Matthews whispered. "People are staring."

"I don't care if they are," Victor said. "You know that when I commit to something, I follow through. And if I want to speak my mind..."

"The Director is coming. Please be quiet."

Victor looked up. "About time. I haven't got all day to sit here. I have fieldwork to complete."

The researcher to his left whispered, "I bet she's going to tell us it's another delay."

"If she does, I'm going to stand up and say I won't tolerate it anymore."

"Victor," Angela said, "Dr. George can hear you if you're going to talk so loud."

"I hope she does. She's the one keeping us all from completing our research legacy, and I hope she hears me."

"You tell her!" someone called from two rows back.

Dr. Oliver Li, the station administrator, sat in the senior staff section with perfect posture. He was studiously ignoring the junior researchers, limiting his field of vision to the left half of the assembly hall. While Dr. George stood before the podium waiting for silence, Oliver reached back with great dignity and scratched his shoulder blade.

Dr. George was dressed in the full ceremonial robes of the Paleontological Institute. Her boots were polished to a mirror shine. Her silver hair was pulled back in the traditional style of senior field researchers, symbolizing decades of dedication to uncovering Earth's ancient history on new worlds. The baldness of her scalp—a side effect of years of radiation exposure during early terraforming—was worn as a badge of honor. Her crimson cloak, embroidered with the fossils of extinct species, rustled as she moved.

"Colleagues," she said. And then, more loudly, "Colleagues!"

The murmur of conversation died away.

"Colleagues," she repeated. "Last week—Thursday, to be exact—one of the junior researchers came to me with a concern."

"Well, I'll be damned," Victor said loudly.

Dr. George cleared her throat. "It was about the Transition Protocol. That's why I called you all together today." She gazed at a point above and behind the audience.

"It reminds me of the parable of the six Archaeopteryx specimens."

Victor sighed deeply.

"Three, you will recall, were properly preserved. When the Great Curator examined them at the Museum of Natural History, they were brought forth and displayed. 'Curator,' the handlers said, 'we have maintained these specimens perfectly.' The Curator looked at them and saw that it was true. Then she blessed them and had them placed in climate-controlled storage. For which the three specimens remained intact for centuries. But three were improperly stored and exposed to humidity; and these three crumbled to dust within a decade."

Oliver rubbed his nose.

"The moral, my colleagues, is clear: proper procedure ensures longevity. As it says in the Institute Charter, 'Methodology preserves truth.'"

Dr. George adjusted her cloak. "I want you all to remember that principle. I want you to take it with you and reflect on it tonight in your quarters.

"Just as those who came to the Curator with their concerns, one of our researchers came to me. He said: 'Director, I am weary of this project.'

"And I know that. Every one of you—every single one—is weary of this project. I know that as well as I know my own name.

"But because he came to me and said, 'Director, I am weary of this project,' I went to the administrator, and I said, 'Administrator, the team is weary.'

"And then Oliver said: 'Very well, Director. I will set the date for the Transition Ceremony!'"

The small woman was pleased by the rustle of approval from the audience. "About damn time!" Victor said.

Dr. George cleared her throat again. "And the date is not far off," she said.

"I knew there was a catch," Victor muttered.

"I know you will have many questions. You are thinking: 'What kind of ceremony can we have here on this station?' You are thinking: 'How wonderful it would be to have the Transition at home, among colleagues from other institutions.'

"Well, I want to tell you: I come from the Meadowbrook Region research facilities. And you know that Meadowbrook never let any other region outdo them in a Transition Ceremony.

"The amphitheater in Meadowbrook is the greatest in the whole system. We have had as many as sixty thousand participants in our institutional reforms. All of them together—it's quite a sight. People come from everywhere to witness it. I'll never forget the ceremony when my mentor transitioned. She...

"Well, my point is this: I know what a proper Transition should be, and Oliver and I will do everything in our power to make ours as meaningful as any anywhere.

"And I want you to know that if you come to me with your suggestions, I'll do all I can to see that we honor our professional ethics properly. I want you to be proud of this Transition Ceremony, so you can look back on it and say—this was the real culmination of your research career!"

Everyone but Victor cheered. He sat glumly muttering to himself.

Dr. George nodded at them and beamed. She noticed that there was a young woman, one of the junior researchers, in the front row who had very promising field notes.

While they were still cheering, Dr. George walked off the platform and into the senior staff corridor. She wiped her forehead on her sleeve and felt relieved that the announcement was over.

---

Dinner that evening was a celebration in the station. The kitchen staff prepared a feast in honor of Dr. George's announcement. For the senior staff, Oliver broke out the last case of vintage Thornhill wine from Havencia ('94). He ordered it placed at each setting.

Oliver came down from his office after the meal had begun. He nodded curtly to the staff when he entered the dining hall, walked directly to his place at the head of the table, and began working the cork out of his wine bottle.

"You'll spoil the flavor, shaking it that way," Dr. Nicole Leonard cautioned. She was particularly fond of that vintage.

Oliver twisted the bottle, and the cork came free with a pop. He placed it carefully beside his fork and poured himself a full glass.

"Very probably," he said sadly.

"I don't think it'll matter," Dr. Elizabeth Holt said. "He hasn't shaken it hard enough."

Oliver picked up the glass, brought it toward his lips—then suddenly put it back down and turned to Dr. George.

"Director. Have you decided on the Hill matter yet?"

The small paleontologist looked up. She laid her knife across her plate. "It has complications," she said.

When Nicole saw that her opinion on the wine was not to be immediately validated, she settled back with a small sigh.

"What do you think your decision will be, Director?" the kitchen supervisor asked.

Dr. George cut a piece of meat. "It's difficult to say. The whole issue involves, as a core point, the principle of personal growth versus institutional loyalty."

Elizabeth nodded knowingly.

"The intent, of course, could be interpreted as prioritizing individual achievement over collaborative research; and in that case, naturally, the decision would be even more complex. I wish I could consult with the Institute Council, but there isn't time. I'll have to decide something."

"He had very impressive field notes," Nicole said.

"Yes, very," Dr. George agreed. "But as I was saying, if it could be proven that his departure from protocol was due to no negligence on his part, either conscious or unconscious, then obviously no professional sanctions would apply." She chewed thoughtfully.

"But the data wasn't compromised at all," Angela Matthews said. "I don't think the specimens suffered. It happened too quickly."

Dr. George swallowed and washed it down with wine. "The problem, Angela, is one of intent. To focus on the outcome is to miss the point. Take the Wilson case, back in Meadowbrook. Certainly his research was valuable."

"Yes," Angela said. "I read about it in the journals."

"But it was a case of obvious intent to circumvent peer review," continued Dr. George, "and therefore constituted a clear attempt to avoid proper scientific collaboration."

Upon hearing the phrase "proper procedure," Oliver brightened.

"That," he said to Dr. George, "is the cardinal point of the whole matter. Procedure. And I must say, I think you're being quite shortsighted about the Transition date. After all, it's not only a question of how we transition, but also a question of completing our duties first. That's equally important."

"The Institute Charter—" Dr. George began.

"Director! Really. The Institute Charter! Surely you've misinterpreted that. Anticipation can be motivating, you know—almost equal to the achievement itself. Anticipation should drive us in our work. It's noble and purposeful." He scratched his hand.

Elizabeth had been trying to interject for several minutes. "You don't need to worry about your transition, Oliver. I have in mind a most elegant protocol."

Oliver was not visibly cheered; he was still brooding about the lack of urgency regarding proper procedure. "I will welcome it," he said, "at the appropriate time. And I certainly hope—" His eyes swept the table. "I certainly hope to be transitioned by a senior researcher. It would be quite improper to have a junior staff member do it."

"Oh, very," said the supervisor.

"I don't know," Angela said, "whether you can count on my participation. I have my own research to complete."

"This question of Victor Hill interests me," Nicole said. "Did I ever tell you about my graduate student? He published our data prematurely."

"He was very ambitious," her husband said.

"He probably wouldn't have succeeded anyway," Nicole said. "Flawed methodology."

"That," said Dr. George, "is not at all like the Hill case. Not at all. Yours is a question of labor relations and attribution."

Elizabeth nodded.

"It seems to me the whole thing depends on his intent."

"Oliver," the supervisor said, "you really must try some of this bread."

"That's very kind, but I..."

"No trouble at all," the supervisor said.

"As I see it," Dr. George said, "if the intent was natural competitive drive to advance his career, then..."

"Oh, not at all," Nicole said. "He did it because he wanted the recognition."

"Well, in that case, I see no reason why he shouldn't receive credit."

"I certainly hope so," Nicole's husband said. "She worries about it constantly."

"I do not," Nicole contradicted.

"Now, dear, you know you do."

At that moment, Nicole lost interest and leaned toward Oliver. "Well?" she asked.

Oliver rolled the wine over his tongue. "You were right, of course."

Nicole turned triumphantly to Elizabeth. "There, I told you."

Elizabeth shrugged. "I never get anything right. I've spent more years than all of you building a research portfolio that's better than even Oliver's. And Angela and I have to stay and help orient the next team. Lord knows how long before we get our own Transition."

"Really, now. Duty, duty," Oliver reprimanded mildly.

"Duty! Duty! Duty! You're all conspiring against me. You want me to die of old age before I can complete my life's work."

"Nonsense," said the supervisor. "We don't want that. After all, someone has to train the newcomers."

"Quite right," said Oliver. "You should be honored."

Elizabeth threw her napkin on her plate and left the dining hall.

"Quite sensitive today," Dr. George observed.

"By the way," Nicole said, "Lucy Hicks gave me a petition for you, Director."

"Lucy?"
