"Yes. She's twenty-four now."

"Lucy who?" the supervisor asked.

"Lucy Hicks, from the geology team."

"I know her," Angela said.

"She's the youngest researcher on the station, and she wants you to approve her participation in the Transition, Director."

"She's so young..."

"Twenty-four, Director."

"After all, one must have completed significant research," Oliver said.

"She wants to participate in the Knowledge Transfer," Nicole said.

Dr. George fidgeted uncomfortably. "Well, I'll review her publication record," she said.

"It's necessary," Elizabeth's husband said. "Otherwise, we'll be short one researcher for the pairing."

"There wouldn't be a shortage if he had brought a research partner," Elizabeth said, glaring at Oliver.

"Now, Elizabeth. I prioritize institutional duty over personal convenience. You're just frustrated because you have to continue with your current assignment."

"All right, I am. But it's true. And if that accident in Sector Seven hadn't happened, we'd be short two." She shot a look at Dr. George. "Why don't you two share a research line—"

"Elizabeth!"

"Although heaven knows what researcher in their right mind would consent to..."

"Well," said Dr. George hesitantly.

"Listen," Nicole said, "Elizabeth's right. If you don't approve it, someone will have to work without a partner."

Dr. George blushed. "I'll review it carefully, but you must understand that senior researchers..."

"Actually, in a way, it would be her duty, you see. Think of it as her contribution to the project."

"She's too young for you, dear," Nicole said to her husband.

"Oh, I don't know," the supervisor said. "Sometimes the young ones are the most innovative."

---

Nicole's husband, whose name was Dr. Fatima Parker, stood before the mirror adjusting his collar. He had been fussing with his appearance for fifteen minutes.

"I suppose the junior staff is celebrating?" Nicole said.

"I suppose."

She stood and walked to the desk, absently fingering the research notes there.

"You really shouldn't have mentioned that student tonight."

"Nonsense."

"No, Fatima. I mean it. Angela looked at me strangely all through dinner. She has three major publications, you know."

"You're imagining things."

"But she does have three publications."

"I mean about her looking at you."

"Oh."

Fatima adjusted his tie without speaking.

"I mean, as much as to say: 'Well, I properly credited all my collaborators.'"

"But honey, about the student. That was nearly an accident. You didn't really mean to exclude him from authorship."

"But still... Angela looked at me like I wasn't following proper professional ethics."

"No," he said. "That's nonsense, Nicole. You know what the Director said."

He polished one of his Institute pins with his sleeve.

"Fatima?"

"Yes?"

"I don't think all that preparation is necessary just for field research."

"Probably not."

She sat on the bed. "Fatima?"

"Yes, dear?"

"Don't you really think she's too young?"

"Not really."

"I mean, why don't you choose someone else? Like Mary from the chemistry lab? She's accomplished. I bet she'd be better."

"Probably."

"She's very collaborative."

He brushed at his hair again. "Who do you want as your partner, Nicole?"

"Oh, I don't know." She looked at her hands. "I think I'd like to work with Dr. George. With her impressive publication record. I hope she asks me."

"I'll mention it to her."

"Would you really, Fatima? That would be wonderful."

"Sure, honey." He looked at his watch.

"Fatima? Are you going to meet Lucy in the laboratory?"

"Yes."

"I thought so. Well, remember: It isn't the day of the Knowledge Transfer yet. Don't forget."

"Honey! You don't think for a minute that..."

"No, dear. I know you wouldn't. But just don't."

He kissed her forehead and patted her cheek. "Of course not," he said comfortingly.

He left her sitting on the bed and walked down the senior corridor, whistling.

He made a mental note to have maintenance clean these walls tomorrow. They needed it. In one corner a spider had spun its web.

He climbed the stairs, turned left, and felt the fresh air from the ventilation system.

Beneath it lay one of the junior researchers, asleep.

He nudged the person several times until consciousness returned.

"Can't sleep here," Fatima explained.

"Go away and leave me alone."

"Here, now." He helped the fellow up and steadied him. "This is the senior staff corridor."

"Oh? Sorry. So sorry, sir."

Fatima assisted him to the junior corridor where he sank down and fell asleep again.

Fatima continued to the laboratory.

When he entered, Nicole's colleague was yawning.

"Hi, John. Tired?"

"Yes. You're early."

"Don't mind, do you?"

"No... Quiet tonight. Had to shut down the carbon dating equipment an hour ago. The technician was incapacitated."

"Oh?"

John lit a cigarette. "Can't risk contaminating the samples. Would look terrible in the research record. Hope Oliver doesn't find out. He'll think the technician was neglecting duty."

He blew a smoke ring.

"Might even bar him from the Transition."

"Yeah," said Fatima, "Oliver's particular that way."

John blew another smoke ring.

"Well," Fatima said.

"Uh. Fatima? Are you really going to partner with that Lucy Hicks?"

"If Dr. George approves."

"Say, Fatima. Do you suppose Nicole would...?"

Fatima put a hand on John's shoulder. "Sorry, old friend. She's set on working with Dr. George." He shrugged. "I don't entirely approve, but... I'm sure if the Director declines, she'd be glad to consider your proposal."

"That's all right," John said. "Doesn't really matter. Say, have I told you what I'm planning for Oliver's transition protocol? I've thought it all through. You know that ceremonial fossil I acquired on the expedition to Pinehurst in Wendria? Well..."

"How about telling me another time?"

"Oh. Sure. If you prefer."

"I'm expecting Lucy."

"Oh. Right. I should have known you weren't here early for nothing. In that case, I'll be going. Good luck."

"Thanks. See you at breakfast."

"Right."

After John left, Fatima walked to the control panel. The dating equipment was dark. He picked up the intercom and called the technical staff. "Hello, this is Dr. Parker... Oh, hi, Barney. Do you have a sober technician available yet...? Good. We'll restart the equipment. If Oliver comes by now—well, you know how he is.... Okay, thanks. Good night."

He replaced the receiver and threw the power switch. The equipment hummed to life.

Having done that, he activated the holographic display system. The steady hum of the equipment warming filled the room. Lucy would certainly want to examine the fossil reconstructions. She was enthusiastic about such things.

"Hello."

He turned. "Oh, hello, Lucy."

"Hello, Dr. Parker. Are you glad I could come?"

"Very much."

"Me too. Can I look at the—oh, it's already on."

"Yes. Look, Lucy."

"Hmm?"

"I spoke to Dr. George today."

"Wonderful. What did she say? Can I participate in the Transition as an adult researcher?"

"I don't know yet. She's reviewing your record. That's why I wanted to see you. She's going to check your publications. And Lucy?"

"Those reconstructions are beautiful."

"Lucy, listen to me."

"I'm listening, Dr. Parker."

"You're simply going to stop carrying around that stuffed toy if you want to be taken seriously as an adult researcher."

---

In Dr. George's office the next morning, Oliver and the Director held a conference.

"No, Oliver. I'm afraid I can't agree to that," Dr. George said.

Oliver said, "Oh, don't be unreasonable, Director. After all, this is a research station. And I am, after all, the administrator."

Dr. George shook her head. "The junior and senior staff will participate together in the Transition. I will not segregate the corridors, and—Oh! Yes? Come in!"

The door opened. "Director?"

"Yes? Come in."

"Thank you, Director. Good morning, Administrator."

"Sit down. Now, Oliver, as I was saying: no segregation. It's contrary to the spirit, if not the letter, of the Institute Charter."

"But Director! A junior researcher! In the senior corridor! Consider the implications!"

"Before the Institute, we are all equal. I'm sorry, Oliver. Now in Meadowbrook, we practiced it with excellent results, and..."

"I say, really—"

"Director?" said the junior researcher who had entered.

"Yes? One moment. Now, Oliver. As I've been explaining: The traditional amphitheater method has advantages. In Meadowbrook we always used it. But here—due to the constraints of the station—I feel convinced that a modification of normal procedure is warranted. It's not without precedent. Such adaptations were fairly common during the early colonial period, up until the Institute standardization three hundred years ago. Indeed, in Meadowbrook, during the outbreak of Martian fever, a most unusual protocol was adopted. It seems..."

"You're perfectly correct, of course," Oliver said.

"That's what I wanted to discuss, Director," the junior researcher said. "Now, in Bayview, Veldoria, for the Transitions, we..."

"Please be quiet," said Oliver softly.

"Yes, sir."

"Now, as I was saying, Oliver, when the methods used in..."

"If you'll excuse me, Director, I really should return to my research," the junior researcher said.

"Quite all right. Close the door after you."

"I must say, your dedication is commendable."

"Well, thank you, sir. And thank you, Director, for your time."

"Not at all. That's what I'm here for. Come by anytime."

The researcher closed the door.

He had barely left when Fatima Parker knocked and was admitted.

"Oh? Good morning, Oliver. I didn't know you were here." Then, to the Director: "I'll return later."

"Nonsense," said Oliver. "Come in."

"Well, I hoped to see the Director privately."

"I should be going," said Oliver.

"But Oliver! I haven't finished explaining about..."

"I'll just get some coffee," Oliver said.

"I'll call you when I'm finished," said Fatima.

Oliver left the room.

"It's about Lucy, Director," Fatima said.

The Director studied her desk. She rearranged some papers. "Ah, yes. The young researcher."

"Well, it's not only about Lucy," said Fatima. "You see, my wife, Nicole..."

"Yes?" The Director picked up her pen.

"I think, with the proper encouragement, she might be interested in collaborating with you in the Knowledge Transfer, if I put in a good word."

"That is very flattering." She returned the pen to its holder. "Such generosity, as it says in the Charter, promotes cultural exchange."

"And with your permission, Director..."

"Ah..."

"She's a very accomplished researcher."

"Ah... Quite so."

"Well, about Lucy. I really shouldn't mention this. But Director, if we are short one researcher for the pairing..."

"Hmm."

"I mean, it wouldn't be fair to the others."

"I see your point." Dr. George blinked. "It wouldn't be equitable, all things considered."

She stood up.

"I may tell you that, in reviewing this matter last night, I decided that Lucy Hicks has completed sufficient research to merit participation in the Transition."

"Professional ethics are a virtue of good directors," Fatima said.

"And you really think Nicole would...?"

"Oh, yes, Director."

"Well, ahem. But..."

"Yes, Director?"

"There is one small complication."

"Oh?"

"That is to say, in order for a researcher to participate in the Knowledge Transfer ritual, she must be formally paired with a senior colleague."

"I hadn't thought of that," Fatima said disappointedly.

"I think that can be arranged, however," said Dr. George. "If you pass the dining hall on your way out, please tell Oliver we can continue our discussion at his convenience."

---

"Sit down, Oliver," said Dr. George when he returned. "No, over there, in the comfortable chair. Are you comfortable?"

"Of course."

"Good. I have a question for you, Oliver."

"Oh?"

Dr. George rubbed her silver hair. "Sir, I know you have the greatest sensitivity regarding matters of institutional duty."

"That's quite true. I take pride in it, if I may say so."

"Exactly. No sacrifice is too great for the advancement of knowledge."

"True, true."

"Well then, say the first of next month, that would be a Monday—I may depend upon you to formally pair with Lucy Hicks, the junior researcher, yes?"

"No," said Oliver.

"Come now, sir. I realize she is quite junior, but—"

"Director," said Oliver, "did I ever tell you about the time I led the expedition to the fossil beds of Thornhill?"

"I don't believe you have."

"Then I will. It came about this way. I was given command of fifty-three researchers. Brilliant minds. Unconventional, but excellent scientists. I was to lead them ninety-seven kilometers across terrain that..."

"Oliver! I fear I must be very direct with you. I will be forced to announce in the dining hall this evening that you have refused to fulfill your institutional duty when it was plainly and properly presented to you."

"Very well, Director," Oliver said after several minutes. "I will do it."

He was trembling slightly.

---

That morning was to be the time of Oliver's formal pairing. He had insisted it be done privately. For the ceremony, he refused to make any change in his everyday attire; nor would he consent to Dr. George's suggestion that he wear the ceremonial Institute medallion. He had intended, after the ceremony, to return to his duties as if nothing unusual had happened; but afterward, the vast indignity of it struck him more poignantly than he had imagined.

Without a word, he left Dr. George's office and walked slowly, deliberately, with great dignity, to his own quarters.

They were fine quarters. The finest, except for Dr. George's, in the whole station. The curtains were scented with subtle fragrance. The carpet was plush.

He walked through his office without breaking stride.

The bed was large and inviting, an unbroken expanse of white coverlet extending from the far wall. It looked supremely comfortable.

Without even a sigh, he threw himself upon it and lay very, very still. His left leg remained suspended in the air at a forty-five-degree angle to the bed; the angle remained rigidly, unrelaxingly forty-five degrees.

Only after a long time did he roll onto his back, and then merely to stare fixedly at the ceiling.

He might have lain there indefinitely had his introspection not been interrupted, around noon, by an apologetic knock on the door.

"Come in," he whispered, hoping she wouldn't hear and would leave.

But she heard him.

"Partner," Lucy said simply. She closed the door and stood staring at him.

"Miss Hicks," he said, "I hope you will have the courtesy not to use that term again."

"Gosh. You say the funniest things. I'm so glad you had to pair with me."

Oliver stood up, adjusted his jacket and shoulders, and walked to his desk. He opened a drawer, removed a bottle, poured himself half a glass and drank it.

"Ah," he said.

He returned to the bed and sat down.

"Can't you even say hello to me?" she asked.

"Hello," he said. "Miss Hicks, sit down. I intend to give you an instructive lecture on the natural order of institutional hierarchy and..."

"Huh?"

"Ah," he said. "Quite right, of course."

She walked to the chair and sat. "I don't like those," she said, pointing at the curtains.

"Those, Miss Hicks," he said, "are priceless drapes imported from Thornhill, Havencia. They have a fascinating history.

"About three thousand years ago, a family of weavers was forced to flee their city because the eldest son had become involved in a conspiracy against the local governor. As the family was traveling..."

"I don't like them anyway," said Lucy.

"Miss Hicks," said Oliver, "kindly bring me that."

"This?"

"Yes. Thank you."

He took the stuffed toy from her. He stood up again, walked to his desk, searched for scissors. Finally he located them under a stack of research papers.

He looked at the toy, then at Lucy, then back at the toy. With deliberate precision, he began to cut.
question: How many years had Dr. Eva George spent building the paleontology program on Mars-Prime?

synthetic_story:
The Salvage Run
By MARCUS CHEN

Stand by for the
M.S. Prometheus
, laughingstock of the Merchant Marine. She's got something revolutionary in her engines, and only her brilliant engineer can make it work!

Captain Samuel Perkins stood in the acidic rain of Forestdale Station, Belvoria, and stared at his new assignment with barely concealed disgust. The rain here never stopped—a consequence of the atmospheric processors that had made this moon habitable but had never quite gotten the weather right. Now a thick fog was rolling in from the industrial sectors, reducing visibility to near zero. It was a typical day on Belvoria.

Samuel cursed Administrator Chen and all his bureaucratic ancestors with considerable feeling. Then he motioned to his companion, and together they trudged through the muck toward the ancient cargo hauler.

The bulky frame of the Merchant Ship
Prometheus
loomed unhappily into the thick air above the two men as they reached the loading bay. Samuel raised reluctant eyes to the scarred hull of the fat cargo ship.

"It looks," he commented bitterly, "like a flying warehouse that lost a fight with an asteroid."

First Officer Anil Hunt—"Hunt" to his friends—nodded in agreement. "That's our Fire-Bringer... old Prommy herself. The ship with the cursed reputation." Hunt had been with her a full year, which was a record for First Officers on the
Prometheus
. She generally sent them back to Earth with stress disorders in half that time.

"Tell me, Captain," continued Hunt curiously, "how does it happen that you of all people happened to draw this tub for a command? I thought..."

"You know Chen?" queried Samuel.

Hunt nodded. "Oh, yes. Yes, indeed. Old Iron-Desk Chen?"

"The same."

"Well," Hunt ran a hand over his chin speculatively, "I know Chen's a prize bureaucrat... but you were in command of the
Constellation
. And, after all, you come from an old merchant family and all that. How come this?" He indicated the cargo hauler expressively.

Samuel sighed. "Well, now, Hunt, I'll tell you. You'll be shipping with me and I guess you've a right to know the worst... not that you wouldn't find it out anyway. I come from a long line of very successful captains. Five generations of officers and entrepreneurs. Steeped in tradition.

"The first Samuel Perkins, son of a shipping magnate, emerged from the Corporate Wars a fleet commander and Innovation Medal winner. Then came Samuel Perkins II, and in the Media Consolidation Crisis of 2087, he won a Transparency Citation for exposing corporate corruption. And then came Samuel Perkins III... me.

"From such humble beginnings do great traditions grow. But something happened when I came into the picture. I don't fit with the rest of them. Call it luck or temperament or what have you.

"In the first place, I seem to have an uncanny talent for saying the wrong thing to the wrong person. Chen for example. And I take too much initiative. Chen doesn't like that. I lost the
Constellation
because I left my assigned route to rescue a group of miners I thought were in danger from pollution control failures at an orbital refinery..."

"The Queenstown incident?" asked Hunt.

"So you've heard about it." Samuel shook his head sadly. "My environmental specialist warned me that the refinery's containment systems might fail catastrophically. I left my scheduled delivery to evacuate miners." He shrugged. "Wrong guess. No failure. I made an ass of myself and lost the
Constellation
. Chen gave it to his former protégé. I got this."

Hunt coughed slightly. "I heard something about Summit Station, too."

"Me again. The
Constellation's
whole crew ended up in the Ulvaria detention center. We celebrated a successful run a bit too freely."

Hunt looked admiringly at his new Commander. "That was the day after the
Constellation
broke the record for the Jarvonia-to-Belvoria run, wasn't it? And then wasn't there something about..."

"Springfield?"

Hunt nodded.

"That time I called the Trade Minister's economic policies 'a masterclass in how to destroy labor relations.' It was at a political economy summit."

"I begin to see what you mean, Captain."

"Samuel's the name, Hunt."

Hunt's smile was expansive. "Samuel, I think you're going to like our old rust bucket here." He patted the
Prometheus's
loading bay affectionately. "She's old... but she's independent. And we're not likely to meet any Ministers or Administrators with her, either."

Samuel sighed, still thinking of his sleek
Constellation
. "She'll haul cargo, I suppose. And that's about all that's expected of her."

Hunt shrugged philosophically. "Better than processing waste materials, anyway. Deep space?"

Samuel shook his head. "Belvoria-Selvoria."

Hunt scratched his chin speculatively. "Inner system run. Routine work."

Samuel was again looking at the ship's unprepossessing exterior. "A quantum-drive hauler, so help me."

Hunt nodded agreement. "The last of her class."

And she was not an inspiring sight. The unfortunately named
Prometheus
was a quantum-drive cargo hauler built some fifteen years back in the period immediately preceding the Resource Wars. She had been designed primarily for conventional cargo runs, with a quantum-drive system for emergency high-speed transport. At least that was the designer's vision. In those days, quantum propulsion was in its experimental stage, and at the time of the
Prometheus's
launching, the quantum-drive was hailed as the future of shipping.

Her designer, Marcus Schultz, had been awarded a Pioneer's Medal for her, and every shipping executive in the fleet had dreamed of commanding one of her class. There had been three. The
Atlas
, the
Titan
, and the prototype... old Prommy. The three vessels had gone into service during the Resource Crisis after the Selvoria Embargo had disrupted trade routes.

All three were spectacular failures.

The eager captains commanding the three haulers had found the quantum-drive too tempting not to use. They activated it... improperly.

The
Atlas
suffered a catastrophic engine failure. The
Titan
vanished in the general direction of the outer colonies, her quantum core destabilizing and creating a radiation hazard. And the
Prometheus's
port engines blew, causing her to spin uncontrollably under extreme acceleration until all her cargo and much of her interior equipment was destroyed, along with half her crew.

The
Prometheus
was refitted for service. And because it was an integral part of her design, the quantum-drive was rebuilt... and locked down. She became a workhorse, growing more temperamental with each passing year. She carried supplies. She hauled ore. She transported equipment and personnel. Now, she would carry time-sensitive medical supplies and research materials. She would lift from Forestdale and burn to Queenstown, Selvoria, without delay or variation. Regulations, tradition, and Administrator Chen of the Inner System Trade Authority required it. And it was now up to Samuel Perkins III to see to it that she did...

The Officer of the Deck, a sharp-featured woman in crisp uniform, saluted smartly as Samuel and Hunt stepped through the airlock.

Samuel felt vaguely uncomfortable. He knew, of course, that at least half the personnel on board civilian vessels was female, but he had never actually had women in senior positions on a ship of his own, and he felt quite certain that he preferred a different arrangement.

Hunt sensed his discomfort. "That was Rita Jenkins, Samuel. Lieutenant. Navigation Officer. She's excellent, too."

Samuel shook his head. "Don't like mixing professional and personal dynamics. Makes me uncomfortable."

Hunt shrugged. "Rita's the only senior officer. But about a third of our crew is female." He grinned maliciously. "Equal opportunity, you know."

"No doubt," commented the other sourly. "Is that why they named this... ship 'Prometheus'?"

Hunt saw fit to consider the question rhetorical and remained silent.

Samuel ducked through the hatchway to the main control deck. Hunt followed. He trailed his Captain through a maze of conduits and control panels to the main engineering station. Samuel sank into a command chair in front of the red LOCKED seal on the quantum-drive control.

"Looks like something from a particle physics lab, doesn't it?" commented Hunt.

Samuel nodded sadly, thinking of the streamlined efficiency of the
Constellation's
bridge. "But she's home to us, anyway."

The thick Belvorian fog had closed in around the upper levels of the ship, obscuring the viewports and cutting off all view of the station outside. Samuel reached for the communications panel.

"Attention all crew. All senior personnel will assemble on the command deck at 0600 hours for Captain's briefing. Officer of the Deck will recall any crew currently on shore leave..."

Hunt was on his feet, all casualness gone from his manner. "Orders, Captain?"

"We can't do anything until the new Engineering Officer gets here. They're sending someone from the
Orion
, and I expect them by 0600 hours. In the meantime, you'll coordinate their duties. See to it that we are fueled and ready to launch by 0602. Station will start loading the cargo at 0599:30. That's about all."

"Yes, sir." Hunt saluted and turned to go. At the hatchway, he paused. "Captain," he asked, "Who is the new E/O to be?"

Samuel stretched his legs out on the deck plates. "A Lieutenant Schultz. Ruby Schultz, according to the orders."

Hunt thought hard for a moment and then shrugged his shoulders. "Ruby Schultz." He shook his head. "Don't know her."

The other officers of the
M.S. Prometheus
were in conference with the Captain when Hunt and the woman at his side reached the command deck. She was tall and auburn-haired with striking features and intelligent green eyes. She wore a service uniform with two silver bars on the collar, and even the standard-issue garment couldn't hide her confident bearing.

Samuel's back was toward the hatchway, and he was addressing the others.

"...and that's the situation. We are to transit within standard safety parameters of the Selvoria system. Route is direct trajectory. With current orbital positions, we have a straightforward run and it should be routine. But I'm certain this old hauler can handle it. I understand the designer who built her wasn't as incompetent as history suggests. But Trade Regulations are specific about medical supply runs. This is important to you, Jenkins. Your navigation has to be accurate to within fifty kilometers plus or minus the optimal route. And there'll be no course deviations. Now be certain that the life support systems are checked, Mister Ward, especially in the biological storage units. Proper environmental controls are going to be critical."

"That's about all there is to tell you. As soon as our apparently delayed E/O gets here, we can launch with our precious cargo." He nodded. "That's the story. Launch in..." He glanced at his chronometer, "...in one hour and ten minutes."

The officers filed out and Hunt stuck his head into the room. "Captain?"

"Come in, Hunt." Samuel's brows knit at the sight of the uniformed woman in the doorway.

Hunt's face was neutral, but hidden amusement was kindling behind his eyes. "Captain, may I present Lieutenant Schultz? Lieutenant
Ruby
Schultz?"

Samuel looked blankly at the woman.

"Our new E/O, Captain," prompted Hunt.

"Uh... welcome aboard, Lieutenant Schultz," was all the Captain could find to say.

The woman's eyes were cold and professional. "Thank you, Captain." Her voice was crisp and businesslike. "If I may have your permission to inspect the engines, Captain, I
may
be able to convince you that the designer of this vessel was not... as you seem to think... an incompetent fool."

Samuel was perplexed, and he showed it. "Why, certainly... uh... Lieutenant... but why should you be so..."

The woman's voice was even sharper than before as she said, "Marcus Schultz, Captain, is my father."

Two weeks in space had convinced Samuel that he commanded a jinx ship. Burning toward Selvoria from Belvoria, the cantankerous
Prometheus
had suffered a coolant leak, and it had been necessary to reduce speed while Ward, the Assistant E/O, and a maintenance crew effected repairs. When full power was restored, old Prommy was running twelve hours behind schedule, and Samuel and Jenkins, the Navigation Officer, were sweating out the unforeseen changes introduced into the trajectory calculations by the time spent at reduced speed.

The
Prometheus
rumbled on toward Queenstown...

For all the tension between the occupants of the command deck, Samuel and Ruby Schultz worked well together. And after a third week in space, a reluctant admiration was replacing the resentment between them. Ruby spent whatever time she could spare analyzing her father's quantum-drive design, and Samuel began to realize that there was little she didn't know about spacecraft engineering. Then, too, Ruby spent considerable time at the controls, and Samuel was forced to admit that he had never seen finer piloting done by anyone.

And finally, Ruby hated old Iron-Desk Chen even more than Samuel did. She felt that Chen had destroyed her father's career through bureaucratic obstruction and poor understanding of organizational development principles, and she was dedicating her career to proving her father right and Chen wrong. There's nothing in the cosmos to nurture friendship like a common enemy.

At three weeks into the journey, the
Prometheus's
environmental systems were functioning normally, maintaining the interior of the ship at a comfortable temperature. The crew had settled into routine, and morale was improving. The personnel dressed in standard uniforms, and the ship ran smoothly under Ruby's expert management.

Samuel was in the forward observation bay when Jenkins called to say that she had picked up a distress signal. The emergency beacon showed the signal to be from the
Hercules
and the
Achilles
. The two corporate research vessels were engaged in material science experiments in deep space... a purely routine operation. But the thing that made Samuel curse under his breath was Jenkins's notation that the
Achilles
carried none other than Trade Administrator Marcus Chen himself, along with a media production crew documenting advances in natural resource management.

Samuel thought it a pity that old Iron-Desk couldn't fall into a black hole... and he told Ruby so.

And she agreed.

Old Prommy had reached the halfway point when it happened. The crew was efficient and focused. Hunt and Jenkins had resolved their earlier tension about some minor point concerning the ship's cargo distribution. Ruby went about her work on the bridge with professional determination, and Samuel made no attempt to disturb her concentration. Lieutenant Ward had successfully completed all maintenance protocols. The crew was functioning well...

And then it happened.

Hunt was in the communications room when the operator pulled the message from the decoder. It was a distress signal from the
Hercules
. The
Achilles
had suffered a catastrophic reactor failure and was drifting helplessly toward a debris field from an old mining operation. Radiation made a transfer of personnel impossible, and the
Achilles's
escape pods didn't have the power to reach safe distance from the contaminated area. The
Hercules
had attached a tether to the sister vessel and was trying to pull the heavy ship to safety, but even the considerable power of the
Hercules's
drive wasn't enough to overcome the gravitational pull toward the dangerous debris field.

A fleet of specialized rescue tugs was on its way from Summit Station and Springfield Port, but they could not possibly arrive in time. And it was doubtful that even the tugs had the necessary power to drag the crippled
Achilles
away from a collision course.

Hunt snatched the message from the operator's hands and rushed to the command deck. He burst in and waved the message excitedly in front of Samuel's face.

"Have a look at this! By all that's holy! Read it!"

"Well, hold it still so I can!" snapped Samuel. He read the message and passed it to Ruby Schultz with a shake of his head.

She read it through and looked up with sudden intensity. "This is
it
! This is the chance I've been waiting for, Samuel!"

He returned her gaze seriously. "For Chen to drift into a debris field? I recall I said something of the sort myself, but there are other people on those ships. And, if I know Captain Martinez on the
Hercules
, she won't release that tether even if it means her own destruction."

Ruby's eyes flashed. "That's not what I meant, and you know it! I mean this!" She touched the red-locked quantum-drive control.

"That's very interesting, Lieutenant," commented Hunt drily. "And I know that you've been studying that system extensively. But I seem to recall that the last time that drive was activated, everyone aboard became part of the bulkheads... very unpleasantly, too."

"Let me understand you, Ruby," said Samuel in a measured voice. "What you are suggesting is that I risk my ship and the lives of all of us trying to pull Chen's operation out of danger with a drive that's failed catastrophically three times out of three. Very bold."

There was fierce determination in Ruby Schultz's eyes and she sounded desperate. "But we can save those ships! We can, I
know
we can! My father designed this vessel! I know every system of her! Those operators in the Resource Crisis didn't understand the cognitive development required to use this technology properly. Father told them that! And I'm trained! I've studied the historical interpretation of every failure. I can take her in and save those ships!" Her expression turned challenging. "Or are you afraid?"

"Frankly, Ruby, I haven't enough sense to be afraid. But are you so certain that we can pull this off? If I make a mistake this time... it'll be the last. For all of us."

"We can do it," said Ruby Schultz simply.

Samuel turned to Hunt. "What do you say, Hunt? Shall we take the risk?"

Hunt shrugged. "If you say so, Samuel. It's good enough for me."

Jenkins left the bridge shaking her head. "We'll all be dead soon. And the digital transformation of shipping will have to wait."

Samuel turned to the communications panel. "Ward!"

"Ward here," came the reply.

"Have communications get a directional fix on the
Achilles
and maintain it. We'll home on their emergency beacon. They're in trouble and we're going after them. Plot the intercept course."

"Yes, Captain."

Samuel turned to Hunt. "Have the cargo teams stand by to assist the engineering crew. It's going to require all hands and we'll need coordination."

"Yes, sir!" Hunt saluted and was gone.

Samuel returned to the communications panel. "Navigation!"

"Jenkins here," replied Rita from her station.

"Get a positional fix on the
Hercules
and maintain it. Send your data to Ward and tell him to send us a range estimate."

"Yes, Captain," she replied crisply.

"Engineering bay!"

"Engineering here, sir," came a voice.

"Have the auxiliary tether system prepared with reinforced cable. Be ready to deploy on short notice... any range."

"Yes, sir!" The response was immediate.

"And now you, Lieutenant Schultz."

"Yes, Captain?" Her voice was steady.

"Take over primary control... and Ruby..."

"Yes?"

"Don't kill us off." He smiled at her.

She nodded silently and took her place at the control panel. Smoothly she turned old Prommy's nose toward the distress signal...

Linked together with a length of industrial-grade tether cable, the
Hercules
and the
Achilles
drifted helplessly toward the debris field. The desperate thrust from the
Hercules's
engines was fading, her fuel reserves depleting under the strain. Still she tried. She could not desert her sister ship, nor could she save her. Already the two ships had drifted to within dangerous proximity of the contaminated debris. The jagged remnants of old mining equipment and radioactive waste seemed like deadly obstacles waiting for the trapped people on board the vessels. The sensor arrays, the communication dishes, and other external equipment on both ships were beginning to show damage from micro-impacts. Only the robust shielding on the vessels made life within them possible. And, even so, people were in danger.

Swiftly, the bulky, ungainly shape of old Prommy drew near. On her command deck, Samuel and Ruby Schultz watched the stricken ships on the main viewscreen.

The environmental controls were stable and the air was clean despite the tension. Ruby's uniform was crisp, her focus absolute. Samuel watched her with a mixture of apprehension and confidence.

Carefully, Ruby maneuvered around the two vessels. From the auxiliary bay, a reinforced tether shot toward the
Achilles
. It flew straight and true, trailing cable as it went. It connected with the hull, and secured there, fast to the ship's frame. Quickly, automated systems drew it tight and the cable was made secure. Like cosmic replicas of ancient rescue operations, the three spacecraft aligned in space... and all three began to drift together toward danger.

They were heading into the debris field.

The tension on the
Prometheus's
bridge was palpable. Every system was operating at peak efficiency, but Samuel knew that efficiency alone wouldn't be enough.

Ruby fought the complex calculations and the unresponsive controls as the slack came out of the cable. Her hands moved with practiced precision across the instrument panel. Determinedly, she made the critical adjustment... and succeeded. Conscious and fully in control, she activated the quantum-drive system.

"
Ruby!
" Samuel was beside her, ready to assist.

"I... I can do this... Samuel. This is... what I've trained for... all my life."

Samuel stood ready but let her work. His heart was racing as she unlocked the quantum-drive control.

Slowly she adjusted the power flow. Systems responded. From deep within old Prommy's core came a low hum. She fed more energy into the drive. Control rods adjusted in the reactor chambers decks below. The humming rose in pitch. The drifting of the ships in space slowed. Stopped. With careful precision, they aligned for the rescue maneuver.

More power. The hum changed to a resonant tone. A harmonic frequency.

Hunt's voice came through the communications system, steadily. "Samuel, all systems are holding. We're at maximum capacity."

"Acknowledged, Hunt!" shouted Samuel over the tone of the drive. The gauges showed the quantum-drive fully engaged. "
Now!
" Ruby adjusted the final controls, and a surge of acceleration pressed them into their seats...

The last thing Samuel remembered clearly was a voice. It sounded like Ward's. And it was shouting. "We're moving them! We're pulling clear! We're..." And the acceleration took over.

The rescue tug
Valiant
found them.

The three ships...
Achilles
,
Hercules
, and old Prommy... linked together and drifting safely in space. Every person aboard exhausted from the acceleration stress, and
Prometheus's
fuel reserves nearly depleted. But they were a safe distance from the debris field...

The reception hall was elegant, the corporate headquarters beautifully appointed. Hunt leaned against the refreshment table and examined the silver medal of the Merchant Service Citation on Samuel's chest. Then he inspected his own and nodded with satisfaction. He looked out at the Selvoria skyline beyond the broad windows and back again at Samuel. His expression was curious.

"All right," said Samuel, setting down his glass. "What's on your mind, Hunt? Something's bothering you."

Hunt nodded slowly. He took a long sip of his drink. "I understand that you declined your chances of getting the
Constellation
back when Chen made you the offer..."

"All I said to him..."

"I know. I know what you said... and it was diplomatic enough. But you're not fooling me. You've come to appreciate old Prommy and you don't want to leave her. Very commendable. Loyal! Good captain! But what about Ruby?"

"Ruby?"

Hunt looked away. "I thought that you and she... well, I thought that when we got back... well..."

Samuel shook his head. "She's gone to the Design Bureau with an engineering development position."

Hunt waved an expressive arm in the air. "But surely, man, I thought..."

"The answer is
no
. Ruby's exceptional... but..." He paused and sighed. "Since she was promoted to her father's old rank... well..." He shrugged. "Who wants a partner that outranks you?"

"Never thought of that," mused Hunt. For a long while he was silent; then he pulled out a contact list and scrolled through until he came to the entries marked "Queenstown, Selvoria."

And he was gratified to see that Captain Samuel Perkins III was doing the same.
question: How many generations of Perkins had been in the shipping business before Samuel Perkins III?

story_name: And Then the Town Took Off
synthetic_story:
The district of Oakridge simply vanished on the night of March 15th.

A delivery driver named Sofia Stone was the first to report it. She had been rushing south along Highway 7, trying to make up time after a longer-than-expected stop at a distribution center, when she slammed on her brakes. If she'd gone another thirty feet, she would have driven straight into the void where Oakridge had been.

Sofia couldn't see the full extent of the emptiness because of the darkness, but it looked massive. Bigger than any sinkhole she'd ever heard of. Her first thought was some kind of catastrophic infrastructure collapse. She reversed two hundred feet, set out emergency flares, then sped off to find a phone signal.

State authorities converged on the former site of Oakridge from multiple directions. Communicating by radio across the vast emptiness, they confirmed that the district was definitely missing. They called in the National Guard.

The Guard surrounded the area with personnel—more than eight hundred were needed—to keep people from falling into the void. A helicopter pilot who flew over it reported that it looked as if someone had used a giant cookie cutter on the landscape.

The regional transit authority complained that one of its automated trains was missing. The train's schedule had it passing through Oakridge at 11:47 PM. That seemed to fix the time of the disappearance around midnight.

Someone pointed out that March 15th was the Ides of March, historically a day of upheaval.

Somebody else said they'd better check for radiation or chemical contamination. An environmental safety official brought detection equipment, but everything registered normal.

A National Guard officer volunteered to take a vehicle down into the void, having found what seemed like a navigable slope. She was gone for over an hour, but when she emerged on the other side, she reported that the void was smooth, bowl-shaped, and showed no signs of explosion or fire. She'd found no people, no buildings—no trace of anything except the void itself.

The Governor asked federal authorities whether any unidentified aircraft had been in the region. Washington said no. The Department of Defense and various agencies denied conducting any secret experiments.

Nor had there been any sensitive facilities in Oakridge that might have been targeted. The district's biggest employer was a film production studio, and the second-biggest was a venture capital firm specializing in virtual reality startups.

A commercial pilot found Oakridge early on the morning of March 16th. The pilot, Captain Jonathan Spencer, who prided himself on rational thinking and logic, was afraid he was seeing something impossible. The object emerged from a cloud layer at fifteen thousand feet, and Spencer changed course to avoid it. He noted with minimal relief that his co-pilot also saw the thing and wondered why it wasn't moving.

Then he saw the broadcast tower on it.

A few minutes later, he had relayed a message from Oakridge, formerly of the Pearlbrook Region, addressed to anyone listening:

It said that Oakridge had declared independence from the ground.

One other radio message came from Oakridge, now airborne, on that first day. An amateur radio operator reported an unidentified voice saying plaintively:

"Getting cold up here!"

Kevin Mason had been dozing in the observation car of the express train when it jerked to a stop. He looked out the window, hoping this was Magnolia Province, where he planned to catch a connecting flight. But it wasn't. All he could see were emergency lights moving along the tracks.

The conductor looked into the car. A woman with striking auburn hair across the aisle—Kevin had noticed her earlier—asked, "Why did we stop?"

"Someone flagged us down," the conductor said. "We don't normally stop at Oakridge on this route."

The woman's hair was professionally styled, and Kevin had observed earlier that she carried herself with the confidence of someone used to authority. Her eyes had been focused on a tablet when Kevin entered the car, giving him time to notice her sharp features and the slight frown lines that suggested she was accustomed to finding fault. Her expression was one of practiced skepticism.

If the woman had given Kevin more than a cursory glance, she would have seen a man in his late twenties—about her age—lean and athletic, with dark hair, an unremarkable face, and a habit of tapping his fingers thoughtfully when concentrating.

But likely all she noticed was the locked metal case he carried, secured by a biometric lock to his left wrist.

"Will we be here long?" Kevin asked the conductor. He didn't want to miss his flight. The sooner he got to Highpoint Territory, the sooner he'd deliver the case. The biometric lock was one reason why his interest in the auburn-haired woman had been only passing.

"Can't say," the conductor told him. He let the door close and went down to the tracks.

Kevin hesitated, shrugged at the woman, said, "Excuse me," and followed the conductor. About twenty people were milling around the train as it sat in the dark. Kevin made his way forward and found a larger group gathered ahead of the locomotive.

Some kind of barricade had been erected across the tracks, covered with every imaginable warning device. There were LED flares, reflective barriers, emergency lights, and even an orange safety vest.

Kevin saw two people who must have been the engineer and assistant talking to an older woman wearing a civil defense vest, a long coat, and hiking boots.

"You'd go over the edge, I'm telling you," the older woman was saying.

"If you don't clear this obstruction," the engineer said, "I'll push right through it. Over the edge? Are you serious?"

"See for yourself," the woman in the vest said. "Go ahead. Look."

The engineer was exasperated. She turned to her assistant. "You look. Humor her. Then let's go."

The woman—she introduced herself as Dr. Vanessa Shaw—went off with the assistant. Kevin followed them. They had walked a quarter mile along the gravel when the assistant stopped. "Okay," she said, "where's this edge? I don't see anything." The tracks seemed to stretch endlessly into the darkness.

"It's another half mile or so," Dr. Shaw said.

"Well, let's hurry. We haven't got all night."

The older woman chuckled. "I'm afraid you do."

They came to it at last, stopping well back from it. Dr. Shaw seemed almost proud as she made a theatrical gesture.

"Behold," she said. "The edge of our new world."

True enough, everything seemed to stop, and they could see lights from the ground shining far below where ground should not be visible.

Kevin Mason and the assistant walked cautiously toward the edge while Dr. Shaw strode ahead with the confidence of someone who had been there before. But there was a wind, and they didn't venture too close. Nevertheless, Kevin could see that it was apparently a clean, precise edge, not ragged like something caused by an explosion. This had the feeling of intentional design.

Standing on tiptoe and fighting a wave of vertigo, Kevin looked over the edge. He didn't need to stand on tiptoe any more than he needed to grip the armrest during a tense movie scene, but the situation seemed to demand it. Over the edge, he could see a vast section of the Pearlbrook Region. At least he assumed it was Pearlbrook.

Kevin looked at the assistant, who had a stunned expression, then at Dr. Shaw, who was smiling and nodding.

"You see what I mean," she said. "You would have gone right over. I believe it's a three-mile drop."

"Of course you could have stayed on the train," the man driving the electric sedan said, "but I really think you'll be more comfortable at the Institute."

Kevin Mason, sitting in the back seat with the auburn-haired woman from the observation car, asked, "Institute?"

"The Oakridge Institute for Advanced Studies. We focus on applied ethics and cultural sociology, though we're not traditionally accredited. What did you say your name was, miss?"

"Sasha Holmes," she said. "I work in international diplomacy."

"Ms. Holmes. I'm Jin Gupta. You know Mr. Mason, I suppose."

The woman smiled slightly. "We've exchanged glances." Kevin nodded and smiled back.

"There's plenty of room in the guest quarters," Jin said. "People don't exactly line up to visit the Institute."

"Are you connected with it?" Kevin asked.

"Me? No. I'm the district administrator of Oakridge. The whole place has really risen in the world, hasn't it?"

"Literally overnight," Sasha Holmes said. "If what Mr. Mason and the train assistant say is true. I haven't seen the edge myself."

"You'll have a better chance to look in the morning," the administrator said, "assuming we don't settle back down in the meantime."

"Was there any kind of explosion?" Kevin asked.

"No. There wasn't any sensation at all, as far as I noticed. I was reviewing some strategic planning documents on my tablet—we're always dealing with community organizing issues in Oakridge. Well, suddenly my internet connection improved dramatically. Then the phone rang, and it was Dr. Shaw."

"The older woman with the vest and the hiking boots?" Sasha Holmes asked.

"Yes. Vanessa Shaw, Director of the Institute's Applied Physics program."

"Applied Physics?" Kevin asked.

"Among other things. The Institute isn't bound by traditional academic constraints. Well, Dr. Shaw called and said, 'Jin'—that's my name—'we've achieved separation.' She was being cryptic, of course. I said, 'What?' and then she explained."

"Explained what?" Sasha Holmes asked. "I mean, does she have any theory about this?"

"She has theories about everything. I think what she was trying to convey was that this—this levitation—confirmed her gravitational manipulation hypothesis."

"What's that?" Kevin asked.

"I haven't the faintest idea. I'm an administrator, not a physicist. Dr. Shaw went on about it for a while, something about artificial gravity fields and quantum mechanics, but I think she was mainly calling as a courtesy, so the district administrator wouldn't look foolish the next morning."

"What's the population of Oakridge?" Kevin asked.

"Four thousand, including the Institute staff and students. Four thousand and fifty-three, counting you people from the train. I guess you'll be with us for a while."

"What do you mean by that?" Sasha Holmes asked sharply.

"Well, I don't see how you can get down. Do you?"

"Does Oakridge have an airport?" Kevin asked. "I need to get to Highpoint Territory."

"Nope," Jin said. "No airport. No suitable landing area, either."

"Maybe not for planes," Kevin said, "but helicopters could land almost anywhere."

"No helicopters here."

"Maybe not. But I bet they'll be swarming around by morning."

"Hm," said Jin Gupta. Kevin couldn't quite read his expression in the rearview mirror. "I suppose they could. Well, here's the Institute. You go right through that entrance, where the others are going. There's Dr. Shaw. I need to speak with her—excuse me."

The administrator hurried off across the campus. Kevin looked at Sasha Holmes, who was frowning. "Are you thinking," he asked, "that Administrator Gupta was perhaps less than completely forthcoming?"

"I'm thinking," she said, "that I should have stayed at my conference another day and taken a direct flight."

"Where were you headed?" Kevin asked.

"Highpoint Territory. I work with the diplomatic corps." She paused. "What do you do, Mr. Mason?"

"I'm a courier for a tech company. Artificial intelligence prototypes, mostly. Hence the locked case."

"I see," she said, though her tone suggested she wasn't entirely convinced. "We should find somewhere to sleep. It's getting late."

"Agreed," Kevin said. They were met by a middle-aged man who introduced himself as Marco Watson, the Institute's hospitality coordinator. "We'll make you comfortable," he said. "What a night! Dr. Shaw is absolutely thrilled. We haven't had this much excitement since the particle accelerator malfunctioned."

They caught a glimpse of Dr. Shaw, still in her civil defense vest, gesturing animatedly to someone in a lab coat.

Kevin Mason had slept, but not well. He'd tried to maneuver the metal case through his sleeve to remove his jacket, but whatever was inside was too large. The Institute had given him a private room in the guest quarters, and he'd removed his pants but had to sleep in his shirt and jacket. He got up feeling grimy and did what minimal preparation was possible.

It was eight o'clock according to his watch, and activity was evident outside. He had a view of the campus from his window. Bright sun illuminated young people moving generally toward a low building—probably the cafeteria—while others moved in various directions. The air was remarkably clear, and the morning shadows were sharp. Only then did he fully remember that he and the entire district of Oakridge were suspended in the air.

He went through the guest quarters. A few people were still sleeping. Others had left their unmade beds. He shivered as he stepped outside. It was cold, though not freezing, and his breath was visible. First he'd eat, he decided, so he'd have energy to examine the edge in daylight and see the ground below.

The dining hall was cafeteria-style, and he got in line with a tray for juice, eggs, and coffee. He saw no one he knew, but as he looked for a table, a slender woman with platinum blonde hair smiled and gestured to the empty seat across from her.

"You're Mr. Mason," she said. "Won't you join me?"

"Thanks," he said, unloading his tray. "How did you know?"

"The mystery man with the locked case. You're hard to miss. I'm Nathan Morris—yes, Nathan, not Natalie. My parents had a sense of humor. Are you with some intelligence agency? Or did you steal something valuable?"

"How do you do. No, just a tech courier. What an unusual name. Dr. Shaw's student?"

"Assistant, actually," she said. "Also her daughter, though we keep that quiet professionally. A pity, because if I'd had a choice, I'd have gone to a normal university. As it is, I'm duty-bound to represent the second generation at the experimental facility."

"Experimental facility? You mean the Institute?" Kevin struggled to manipulate his utensils without knocking things over with his attached case.

"Here, let me help you," Nathan said, cutting his food. "You should order scrambled eggs tomorrow. Yes, the Institute. Home of the unorthodox theory and the controversial experiment."

"I'm sure it's not that bad. Thanks. As for tomorrow, I hope to be gone by then."

"How do you plan to leave? Float down on a parachute?"

"I'll find a way. I'm more interested in how I got up here."

"You were levitated, like everyone else."

"You make it sound deliberate, Ms. Morris, as if someone lifted an entire district for some purpose."

"Well, that's debatable. Have you seen the news feeds?"

"I didn't know there were any."

"Actually, there's just one local outlet, the Oakridge Observer, a weekly publication. This is a special edition. The editor must have worked all night." She pulled out her phone and showed him a digital edition.

Kevin blinked at the headline: "District Gets High"

"The editor's something of an independent thinker, like most people in Oakridge," Nathan said.

Kevin read the story, which seemed to treat the situation with surprising levity despite its gravity.

"Residents planning to travel beyond district boundaries today are advised to reconsider. It's a long way down. Where Oakridge was once surrounded by the Pearlbrook Region, today Oakridge ends literally at the district line.

A Citizens' Emergency Barrier Committee is being organized, but in the meantime, everyone is warned to stay well away from the edge. The laws of physics seem to have been suspended for the district, but it's doubtful the same exemption would apply to a curious individual bent on investigating..."

Kevin skimmed the rest. "I don't see anything about it being deliberate."

Nathan had been preparing Kevin's coffee. She pushed it toward him and said, "It's not on the front page. The editor and Administrator Gupta don't get along, so you'll find the administrator's statement in a box on page three."

Kevin navigated to the page, took a sip of coffee, nodded his thanks, and read:

"Administrator Claims Independence from Ground

Administrator Jin Gupta, in a proclamation issued locally and transmitted to the ground via drone, announced today that Oakridge has declared independence. His reasons were as vague as his explanation.

The 'reasons' include: (1) Oakridge has been neglected by regional and federal agencies; (2) the Institute has been ridiculed by traditional academic institutions; and (3) the district has been subject to unfair pollution control regulations that hampered its film production industry.

The 'explanation' consists of a 73-page paper on gravitational field manipulation by Dr. Vanessa Shaw of the Institute, which the editor (a) does not fully understand; (b) lacks space to publish; and which (being highly technical) he (c) cannot adequately summarize for general readers."

Kevin said, "I'm beginning to like this editor."

"He's wonderful," Nathan said. "He's about the only one in town who challenges Mother."

"Does your mother claim that she levitated Oakridge off the ground?"

"Not to me. I'm one of those inconveniences, a skeptic. She gave up trying to convince me when I was seventeen. I had a physics professor at a summer program—not at the Institute—who gave me all kinds of difficult questions to ask Mother. I asked them, being naturally contrary, and Mother has considered me intellectually lost ever since."

"How old are you, Ms. Morris, if I may ask?"

She sat up straighter, adjusting her sweater. She had an excellent figure, intelligent eyes, a delicate nose, and expressive lips. She could have been the star of any campus with a more conventional student body.

"You may call me Nathan," she said. "And I'm twenty-two."

Kevin grinned. "Recently?"

"Four months ago. How old are you, Mr. Mason?"

"Kevin's the name I've had for twenty-eight years. Please use it."

"Gladly. And now, Kevin, unless you want more coffee, I'll accompany you to the edge of the world."

"On such short notice?" Kevin was intrigued. Last night the woman from the train had been coolly professional, and this morning a friendly blonde was apparently offering companionship. He wondered briefly where Sasha Holmes was.

"I'll admit to the double meaning," Nathan said. "What I meant—for now—was that we can walk out to where Oakridge used to be connected to the rest of the region and see how the ground is managing without us."

"I'd like that. But don't you have work to do?"

"Sure. I'm supposed to be analyzing data from yesterday's sensors. But I'm an expert procrastinator, which is why I'm still finishing my graduate work at my advanced age. On to the edge!"

They walked south from the campus and came to the train tracks. The train was still there, going nowhere. It had been abandoned except for the conductor, who had dutifully remained aboard overnight.

"What's happening?" he asked when he saw them. "Any word from down there?"

"Not that I know of," Kevin said. He introduced Nathan Morris. "What are you going to do?"

"What can I do?" the conductor asked.

"You can go to the Institute and have breakfast," Nathan said. "Nobody's going to bother your train."

The conductor decided that sounded reasonable and left.

"You know," Kevin said, "before the train stopped last night, I thought I saw a stream running alongside the tracks."

"Clearwater Stream," Nathan said. "That's right. It's just over there."

"Is it still there? Hasn't it all poured off the edge by now? Was that Oakridge's water supply?"

Nathan shrugged. "All I know is the water still works. Let's check the stream."

They found it flowing normally between its banks.

"Looks the same," she said.

"That's strange. Come on, let's follow it to the edge."

The edge, as Nathan called it, looked even more dramatic in daylight. Everything simply stopped. There was a residential area with houses and yards, then nothing. There was Clearwater Stream flowing along, then nothing. In the distance, a grove of trees simply ended.

"Where is the water going?" Kevin asked. "I can't tell."

"Down, presumably. Rain for the people below."

"But it should be drained by now. I'm going to look."

"Don't! You'll fall!"

"I'll be careful." He walked cautiously toward the edge. Nathan followed, a few feet behind. He stopped a yard from the brink and waited for vertigo to pass. The ground was spread out like a satellite image, far below. Kevin took another careful step, then sat down.

"Careful," said Nathan. She laughed nervously, then sat down too.

"I still can't see where the water goes," Kevin said. He lay flat on his stomach and began to inch forward. "You stay there."

Finally, he inched to a point where, by stretching, he could almost reach the edge. He gave another push forward and his right hand closed over the brink. For a moment he lay there, breathing hard, head pressed to the ground.

"How do you feel?" Nathan asked.

"Terrified. When I get my nerve back, I'll lift my head and look."

Nathan reached out tentatively, then firmly grasped his ankle. "Just in case of wind," she said.

"Thanks. That helps. Okay, here goes." He lifted his head. "Damn."

"What?"

"It's still not clear. Do you have a mirror?"

"I have a compact." She took it from her bag with her free hand and tossed it to him. It rolled and Kevin had to grab to keep it from going over. Nathan gasped. Kevin was momentarily shaken and had to put his head back down. "Sorry," she said.

Kevin opened the compact and carefully transferred it to his right hand. He held it out beyond the edge and peered into it, focusing on the end of the stream. "Now I see it. The water isn't going off the edge!"

"It isn't? Then where?"

"Down, yes, but it's as if it's going into a vertical shaft, just short of the edge."

"Why? How?"

"I can't see clearly, but that's what it looks like. Hold on. I'm coming back." He inched away from the edge, then stood and brushed himself off. He returned her compact. "I think we need to check the other end of the stream."

"The source?"

"Exactly."

Clearwater Stream didn't cut through the center of Oakridge but flowed in an arc through the southern part of the district. They had about two miles to walk, past Clearwater Bridge—which used to connect to the neighboring area, Nathan said—past the Oakridge Recreation Center, and on to the edge again.

But as they approached what should be the source of the stream, they found a chain-link fence blocking the area. "This is new," Nathan said.

The fence, which had a sign on it reading "WARNING—ELECTRIFIED," was semicircular, with each end at the edge, and tarps hung behind it so they couldn't see the mouth of the stream. The water flowed from under the tarp and fence.

"Look how it comes in pulses," Nathan said.

"As if it's being pumped."

Smaller text on the sign read: "Protecting source of Clearwater Stream, one of two water sources for Oakridge. Electrical charge in fence is sufficient to cause serious injury." It was signed: "Marco Watson, Security Coordinator, Jin Gupta, Administrator."

"What's the other source?" Kevin asked.

"North Reservoir, probably," Nathan said. "It's used for the water treatment facility."

"Is the reservoir entirely within the district boundaries?"

"I don't know."

"If it were on the edge, and if someone took a boat out on it, I wonder what would happen?"

"I know one thing—I wouldn't be there holding your ankle while you found out."

She took his arm as they gazed past the electrified fence at the ground below and to the west.

"It's impressive, isn't it?" she said. "I wonder if that's the Magnolia Province way over there?"

He patted her hand absent-mindedly. "I wonder if it's west at all. I mean, how do we know Oakridge is maintaining the same orientation as before?"

"We could tell by the sun, silly."

"Of course," he said, grinning. "And I guess we're not high enough to see very far. If we were, we'd be able to see the mountain ranges."

They were contemplating the geography when a plane emerged from a cloud layer and, a moment later, veered sharply. They could make out commercial airline markings on the fuselage. As it turned, they imagined they could see faces at the windows. They waved and thought they saw people wave back. Then the plane climbed eastward and disappeared.

"Well," Kevin said as they turned back toward the Institute, "now we know they know. Maybe we'll start getting some answers. Or, if not answers, then rescue."

"Rescue?" Nathan squeezed the arm she was holding. "Why? Don't you like it here?"

"If you mean don't I like you, the answer is yes, I do. But if I don't get out of this biometric lock soon so I can shower and change clothes, you're not going to like me."

"You're still quite presentable, if a bit scruffy." She stopped, still holding his arm, and he turned so they were face to face. "So kiss me," she said, "before you get any worse."

They were in the middle of an extremely pleasant kiss when the metal case at the end of Kevin's biometric lock began to emit a high-pitched alarm.
question: What was the name of the district that vanished?
