The Deep Ocean Calls
By MELISSA HERRERA

Sixty days of wonder and sixty nights of doubt. That's how it's been, Rachel. But how can I make you understand? How can I tell you what it's like to be young and driven and to dream of exploring the deepest trenches of our oceans? And yet, at the same time, to be filled with a terrible, gnawing fear—a fear locked in my mind during the day and bursting out like a dark specter at night. I must tell you, Rachel.

Perhaps if I start at the beginning, the very beginning...

It was the Big Day. All the examinations, the physicals and psychos, were over. The Institute, with its great laboratories and pressure chambers and simulation pools, lay hollow and silent, an exhausted thing at rest after producing its first graduates.

For it was June in this year of 2045, and we were the graduating class of the International Institute of Deep Sea Exploration.

The first graduating class, Rachel. That's why it was so important, because we were the first.

We sat on a small platform, thirty of us. Below us was an ocean of faces, most of them unfamiliar, shining like pearls in the warm morning light streaming through the windows of our facility in Woodbridge, Prandoria. They were the faces of mothers and fathers and grandparents and younger siblings—the people who a short time ago had been only scrawled names on messages from home or voices heard wistfully during holidays. They were the memory-people who, to me, had never really existed.

But today they had become real, and they were here and looking at us with pride in their eyes.

A voice was speaking, deep, sure, resonant. "...these young people have worked hard for six years, and now they're going to accomplish remarkable things. They're going to bring us the minerals and resources that we desperately need from the ocean floor. They're going to map territories that no human has ever seen, rich ecosystems that will expand our understanding of life itself. And perhaps most important of all, they'll make others think of the depths and look down at them and feel humility—for mankind needs humility."

The speaker was Dr. Mohamed Daniels, who'd made the first manned descent to the Mariana Trench's deepest point just seven years ago, who'd established the first permanent deep-sea research station there, and who had just returned from his expedition to the Puerto Rico Trench.

Instead of listening to his words, I was staring at his broad shoulders and his salt-and-pepper hair and his crisp uniform which was perfectly pressed. I was worshiping him and envying him at the same time, for I was thinking: He's already reached the Mariana and Puerto Rico Trenches. Let him leave the Tonga Trench and the others alone! Let us be the first to explore somewhere! Let us be the first!

Justin Thomas, sitting next to me, dug an elbow into my ribs. "I don't see them, Eric," he whispered. "Where do you suppose they are?"

I blinked. "Who?"

"My folks."

That was something I didn't have to worry about. My parents had died in a submarine accident when I was five, so I hadn't needed many of those "You are cordially invited" cards. Just one, which I'd sent to Mark Rogers.

Deep-Sea Mark, we called him, although I never knew exactly why. He was a veteran of the first commercial mining operations in the Atlantic Abyss nearly thirty years ago, and he was still at it. He was Chief Engineer now on the Abyssal Harvester, a commercial mining vessel on a shuttle between the deep-sea stations and Pearlbrook Town.

I remembered how, as a kid, I'd pestered him at the Shadowbrook Province Submarine Port, following him around like a puppy, and how he'd grown to like me until he became father, mother, and mentor all in one to me. And I remembered, too, how his recommendation had finally made me a cadet.

My gaze wandered over the faces, but I couldn't find Mark's. It wasn't surprising. The Abyssal Harvester was in port now, but shore leaves, as Mark said, were as scarce as sunlight at the ocean floor.

It doesn't matter, I told myself.

Then Justin stiffened. "I see them, Eric! There in the seventh row!"

Usually Justin was the same whether in a scorching engine room or a formal dinner, smiling, accepting whatever the world offered. But now a tenseness and an excitement had gripped even him. I was grateful that he was beside me; we'd been a good team during those final months at the Institute and I knew we'd be a good team in the depths. The Ocean was mighty vast, but with two of us to face it together, it would be only half as vast.

And then it seemed that all the proud faces were looking at us as if we were pioneers. A shiver went through my body. Though it was daytime, I saw the trenches in my mind's vision, the great yawning chasms of darkness, each like a voice crying out and pleading to be explored, to be touched by the children of the surface world.

They expect a lot from us. They expect us to make new discoveries and find better ways to sustain Earth. They expect all this and a hell of a lot more. They think there's nothing we can't do.

I felt very small and very humble. I was scared. Damned scared.

At last it was over, and the proud faces descended upon us in a huge, babbling wave.

Then I saw him. Good old Deep-Sea Mark.

His weathered body was shuffling down an aisle, his eyes shining with pride. He'd been positioned, evidently, in one of the rear rows.

But he wasn't the Mark I'd seen a year ago. He'd become gaunt and worn, and he walked with an unnatural stiffness. He looked so aged that it was hard to believe he'd once been young.

He scratched his mop of gray hair and grinned.

"You made it, kid," he chortled, "and by Neptune, we'll celebrate tonight. Yes, sir, I got forty-eight hours, and we'll celebrate as good deep-sea explorers should!"

Then Justin strode up to us. He was his normal, cheerful self again, walking lightly, his dark hair perfectly styled as always.

And you, Rachel, were with him.

"Meet my sister," he said. "Rachel Nguyen."

I stared, almost rudely. You were elegant in your flowing blue dress. Your hair was styled in waves that caught the light. But your eyes were the eyes of someone who understood depth, glowing with intelligence and reflecting a wisdom that I'd never seen in eyes before.

"I'm happy to meet you, Eric," you said. "I've heard of no one else for the past year."

A tide of heat crept up from my collar. I stuttered through an introduction of Mark.

You and Justin looked strangely at Mark, and I realized that old Deep-Sea Mark was not a cadet's notion of the ideal explorer. Mark scorned the crisp uniforms of the government service and wore a faded blue jacket that was a relic of the early deep-sea mining days. His collar was worn, and a patch on his sleeve was coming loose.

And the left side of his face bore the marks of a pressure accident from one of the old submarines. I was so accustomed to the scars, I was seldom aware of them; but others, I knew, would find them unsettling.

You were kind. You shook hands and said, softly: "It's an honor to meet you, Mark. Just think—one of the pioneers, one of the first to work the Atlantic Abyss!"

Mark gulped helplessly, and Justin said: "Still planning to spend the weekend with us, aren't you, Eric?"

I shook my head. "Mark has only forty-eight hours leave. We're planning to see the town tonight."

"Why don't you both come with us?" you asked. "Our folks have their own hydrofoil, so it would be no problem. And we've got a big guest room. Mark, wouldn't you like a home-cooked meal before going back to the deep?"

Mark's answer was obscured by a sudden burst of coughing. I knew that he'd infinitely prefer to spend his liberty sampling depth-worker bars and their exotic drinks.

But this night seemed too sacred for Mark's kind of celebration.

"We'd really like to come," I said.

On our way to the hydrofoil dock, Dean Ava Page passed us. She was a tall, elegant woman, looking the way an institute director should look.

"Eric," she called, "don't forget that offer. Remember you've got two months to decide."

"No, thanks," I answered. "Better not count on me."

A moment later Justin said, frowning, "What was she talking about, Eric? Did she make you an offer?"

I laughed. "She offered me a position here at the Institute teaching deep-sea navigation and risk management. What a life that would be! Imagine standing in a classroom for forty years when I've got the chance to—"

I hesitated, and you supplied the right words: "When you've got the chance to be the first to reach a new trench. That's what most of you want, isn't it? That's what Justin used to want."

I looked at you as if you were Dr. Daniels himself, because you seemed to understand the hunger that could lie in a person's heart.

Then your last words came back and struck me: "That's what Justin used to want."

"Used to want?" I asked. "What do you mean?"

You bit your lip, not answering.

"What did she mean, Justin?"

Justin looked down at his feet. "I didn't want to tell you yet, Eric. We've been together a long time, planning to be on a submarine together. But—"

"Yes?"

"Well, what does it add up to? You become a deep-sea explorer and wear a fancy uniform. You descend through kilometers of darkness and freezing water. If you're lucky, you're good for five, maybe ten years. Then one thing or another gets you. They don't insure deep-sea workers, you know."

My stomach was full of churning, biting ice. "What are you trying to say, Justin?"

"I've thought about it a long time. They want me for Operations Director at Pearlbrook Town Port." He raised his hand to stop me. "I know. It's not so exciting. I'll just live a lot longer. I'm sorry, Eric."

I couldn't answer. It was as if someone had struck me with a pressure wave.

"It doesn't change anything, Eric—right now, I mean. We can still have a good weekend."

Mark was muttering under his breath, seething like a volcano about to erupt. I shook my head dazedly at him as we got to the hydrofoil.

"Sure," I said to Justin, "we can still have a good weekend."

I liked your folks, Rachel. There was no depth-hunger in them, of course. They were simple and solid and settled, like ancient trees, deep-rooted, belonging to the surface. They were content with a home that was comfortable on this pleasant summer evening, with a hydrofoil and holographic entertainment, and a smart home that needed minimal maintenance.

Deep-Sea Mark was as comfortable as a surface-dweller in a pressure suit, but he tried courageously to be himself.

At the dinner table he stared glassily at nothing and grated, "Only hit the Tonga Trench once, but I'll never forget the medic who thought he knew everything. Captain started having trouble breathing, kept it up for three days. Nitrogen narcosis, the medic says, not knowing the gas mixture had been contaminated with compounds that crystallized in your lungs. I'd never been to Tonga before, but I knew better than that. Hell, I says, that ain't nitrogen narcosis, that's pressure-lung."

That was when your father said he wasn't feeling so hungry after all.

Afterward, you and I walked onto the deck, into the moonlit night, to watch for the lights of deep-sea vessels that occasionally surfaced near Westfield, Zelvaria.

We gazed for a few seconds out at the dark ocean, and then you said: "Mark is interesting, isn't he? He's kind and I'm glad he's here, but he's sort of unusual."

"He's an old-time deep-sea worker. You didn't need much formal education in those days, just a lot of strength and quick thinking. It took courage to be a depth-worker then. The technological progress we've made since then is remarkable—it's like comparative history in action."

"But he wasn't always a depth-worker. Didn't he ever have a family?"

I smiled and shook my head. "If he had, he never mentioned it. Mark doesn't like to be sentimental, at least not on the outside. As far as I know, his life began when he descended to the Atlantic Abyss for the first time."

You stared at me strangely, almost with reverence. I knew suddenly that you liked me, and my heart began to beat faster.

There was silence.

You were lovely, your hair like silk, and there were flecks of gold in your dark eyes. Somehow I was afraid. I had the feeling that I shouldn't have come here.

You kept looking at me until I had to ask: "What are you thinking, Rachel?"

You laughed, but it was a sad, fearful laugh. "No, I shouldn't be thinking it. You'd resent me if I told you, and I wouldn't want that."

"I could never resent you."

"It—it's about the depths," you said very softly. "I understand why you want to explore them. Justin and I used to dream about them when we were kids. Of course I was more interested in performing arts, so it was just a fantasy to me. But once I dreamed of going to perform in the underwater theaters of Westfield. Oh, it was going to be so wonderful. I lived for months, just thinking about it.

"One summer we went. I had fun. I saw the underwater stages and the pressure domes and the transport tubes. But after it was over, I realized Westfield wasn't so different from home. Places seem exciting before you get to them, and afterward they're not really."

I frowned. "And you mean it might be the same with the trenches? You think maybe I haven't matured yet?"

Anxiety darkened your features. "No, it'd be good to be an explorer, to see the strange places and make history. But is it worth it? Is it worth the things you'd have to give up?"

I didn't understand at first, and I wanted to ask, "Give up what?"

Then I looked at you and the promise in your eyes, and I knew.

All through the years I'd been walking down a single, narrow path.

Government boarding school, the Institute, my eyes always downward toward the depths.

Now I'd stumbled into a crossroads, beholding a strange new path that I'd never noticed before.

You can go into the depths, I thought, and try to do as much living in ten years as normal people do in fifty. You can be like Dr. Daniels, who nearly died in a pressure accident at the age of 38, or like a thousand others who lie in unmarked graves on the ocean floor. Or, if you're lucky, like Mark—a kind of human submarine eternally descending, forever alone, never finding a home.

Or there's the other path. To stay on the safe surface in comfortable houses. To be one of the solid, rooted people with a spouse and children. To be one of the people who live long enough to grow old, who awake to the song of birds instead of submarine engines, who fill their lungs with clean air instead of recycled oxygen.

"I'm sorry," you said. "I didn't mean to make you sad, Eric."

"It's all right," I said, clenching my fists. "You made sense—a lot of sense."

The next morning Mark said goodbye in our room. He rubbed his scarred face nervously as he cleared his throat with a series of thin, tight coughs.

Then he pointed to a weathered metal box lying on the bed. "I'm leaving that for you. It's full of old stuff, souvenirs mostly. Thought maybe you'd like to have them."

I scowled, not understanding. "Why, Mark? What for?"

He shrugged as if afraid he might be accused of sentimentality. "Oh, it's just that I've been dodging pressure accidents now for thirty years. That's a long time, kid. Ain't one depth-worker in a thousand that lucky. Some of these days, I won't be so lucky."

I tried to laugh. "You're good for another thirty years, Mark."

He shook his head stiffly, staring at nothing. "Maybe. Anyway, I'm gonna get off the Harvester this time, make one more trip to the Tonga Trench. Tell you what. There's a little dive bar in the Tonga station, the Deep Blue, just off the main docking bay. When you get to Tonga, take a look inside. I'll probably be there."

He coughed again, a deep, rasping cough that filled his eyes with tears.

"Not used to this surface air," he muttered. "What I need's some deep-sea climate."

Suddenly that cough frightened me. It didn't seem normal. I wondered, too, about his stiff movements and distant stare. It was as if he were medicated.

I shook the thought away. If Mark was sick, he wouldn't talk about going to Tonga. The medics wouldn't let him go even as far as the continental shelf stations.

We watched him leave, you and Justin and I.

"When will you be back?" you asked.

Mark's weathered face contorted itself into a crooked grin. "Maybe a couple of months, maybe a couple of years. You know depth-workers."

Then he waved and walked away, a strange, gray, withered figure of a man.

I wanted him to say something, to tell me the secret that would kill the doubt worming through my brain.

But he rounded a corner, still grinning and waving, and then he was gone.

That afternoon Justin showed me his room. It was more like a young person's room than an explorer's. In it were all the little things that people treasure—awards from performing arts competitions, models of famous submarines, a tennis trophy, books on organizational development and strategic planning, a collection of field research journals.

I began to realize how important a room like this could be to someone. I could imagine, too, the happiness that parents felt as they watched their children grow to adulthood.

I'd missed something. My folks were shadow-people, my impressions of them drawn half from old photos, half from imagination. For me, it had been a cold, institutional kind of life, the life of dormitories and routines and regulations. I'd been so blinded by the brilliance of my dreams, I hadn't realized I was different.

My folks were killed in a submarine accident. If it weren't for submarines, I'd have lived the kind of life a person should live.

Justin noticed my frown.

"What's the matter, Eric? Still upset? I feel terrible, but I'm just not like you and Mark, I guess. I—"

"No, I understand, Justin. I'm not upset, really."

"Listen, then. You haven't accepted any offer yet, have you?"

"No. I got a couple of possibilities. Could get a berth on the Mariana Explorer, the new ship being finished at Shadowbrook Province. They want me, too, for the Continental Shelf Patrol, but that's routine work, not much better than teaching. I want to be in the deep trenches."

"Well, how about staying with us till you decide? Might as well enjoy surface life while you can. Okay?"

I felt like running from the house, to forget that it existed. I wanted someone to tell me one of the old stories about exploration, a tale of courage that would fuel dying dreams.

But I wanted, also, to be with you, Rachel, to see your smile and the flecks of gold in your eyes and the way your nose crinkled ever so slightly when you laughed. You see, I loved you already, almost as much as I loved the depths.

And I said, slowly, my voice sounding unfamiliar and far away, "Sure, I'll stay, Justin. Sure."

Sixty days of joy, sixty nights of fear and indecision. We did all the little things, like watching the submarines surface at Pearlbrook Town and flying down to the coast to swim in warm waters. You tried, unsuccessfully, to teach me about performing arts and emotional intelligence, and we talked about Dr. Daniels and Mark and the trenches and the depths. You felt you had to give the depths all the beauty and promise of a young person's dream, because you knew that was what I wanted.

One morning I thought, Why must I make a choice? Why can't I have both you and the depths? Would that be asking too much?

All day the thought burned in my mind.

That evening I asked you to marry me. I said it very simply: "Rachel, I want you to be my wife."

You looked out at the ocean, and you were silent for a long while, your face flushed.

Then you murmured, "I—I want to marry you, Eric, but are you asking me to marry an explorer or a teacher?"

"Can't an explorer marry, too?"

"Yes, an explorer can marry, but what would it be like? Don't you see, Eric? You'd be like Mark. Gone for maybe two months, maybe two years. Then you'd have a forty-eight hour leave—and I'd have what?"

Somehow I'd expected words like these, but still they hurt. "I wouldn't have to be an explorer forever. I could try it for a couple of years, then teach."

"Would you, Eric? Would you be satisfied with just seeing the Tonga Trench? Wouldn't you want to go on to the Kermadec and the Philippine Trenches and on and on?"

Your voice was choked, and even in the dim light I saw tears in your eyes.

"Do you think I'd dare have children, Eric? Justin told me what happened on the Cyclops expedition. There was a leak in the reactor. The submarine was flooded with radiation—just for a second. It didn't seem serious. The crew had no burns. But a year later the captain had a child. And it was—"

"I know, Rachel. Don't say it."

You had to finish. "It was deformed."

That night I lay awake, the fears and doubts too frantic to let me sleep.

You've got to decide now, I told myself. You can't stay here. You've got to make a choice.

The teaching job was still open. The spot on the Mariana Explorer was still open—and the big ship, it was rumored, was equipped to reach the deepest point in any ocean.

You can take Dean Page's job and stay with Rachel and have children and a home and live to see what happens in this world sixty years from now.

Or you can see what's at the bottom of the trench. You can be a line in a history book.

I cursed. I knew what Mark would say. He'd say, "Get the hell out of there, kid. Don't let fear make a coward out of you. Get out there on the Mariana Explorer where you belong. We got a date at the Tonga station, remember? At the Deep Blue, just off the main docking bay."

That's what he'd say.

And yet I wanted you, Rachel. I wanted to be with you, always.

"Oh God," I moaned, "what shall I do?"

Next morning the door chimed, and you went to the door and brought back the message tablet. It was addressed to me; I wondered who could be sending me a message.

I pressed the button on the small device, and a synthetic, automatic voice droned: "Tonga Deep-Sea Station, June 28, 2045. Regret to inform you of death of Mark Rogers, Chief Engineer...."

Then there was a medical term which was more clinical than the word "pressure-lung" and the robotic phrase, "This message brought to you by courtesy of International Deep-Sea Communication Network."

I stood staring at the tablet.

Mark Rogers was dead.

Mark Rogers was Deep-Sea Mark.

My heart thudded crazily against my chest. It couldn't be! Not Mark! The message had lied!

I pressed the button again. "...regret to inform you of death of Mark..."

I hurled the tablet at the wall. It clattered, fell, skidded. The broken voice droned on.

You ran to it, shut it off. "I'm sorry, Eric, so terribly—"

Without answering, I walked into my room. I knew it was true now. I remembered Mark's coughing, his gaunt features, his medicated gaze. The synthetic words had told the truth.

I sat for a long time on my bed, crying inside, but staring dry-eyed at Mark's weathered metal box.

Then, finally, I examined his meager possessions—a few faded photos, some letters, a small carved sculpture from the Mariana Trench, a service medal from the Atlantic Abyss operations.

This was what remained of Mark after thirty years in the depths. It was a bitter bargain. A sculpture instead of a wife, yellowed letters instead of children, a medal instead of a home.

It'd be a great future, I thought. You'd dream of sitting in a dingy dive bar at the Tonga station with pressure-adapted fish swimming past murky viewports. A bottle of kelp liquor and a couple of depth-workers with weathered faces for company. And a sudden cough that would be the first sign of pressure-lung.

To hell with it!

I walked into your living room and called Dean Page on the videophone.

I accepted that job teaching.

And now, Rachel, it's nearly midnight. You're in your room, sleeping, and the house is silent.

It's hard to tell you, to make you understand, and that is why I am writing this.

I looked through Mark's box again, more carefully this time, reading the old letters and studying the photographs. I believe now that Mark sensed my indecision, that he left these things so that they could tell me what he could not express in words.

And among the things, Rachel, I found a ring.

A wedding ring.

In that past he never talked about, there was a woman—his wife. Mark was young once, his eyes full of dreams, and he faced the same decision that I am facing. Two paths were before him, but he tried to travel both. He later learned what we already know—that there can be no compromise. And you know, too, which path he finally chose.

Do you know why he had to medicate himself to watch me graduate? So he could look at me, knowing that I would see the depths he could never live to explore. Mark didn't leave just a few trinkets behind him. He left himself, Rachel, for he showed me that a young person's dream can also be an adult's dream.

He made his last trip to Tonga when he knew he was going to die. Heaven knows how he escaped a medical checkup. Maybe the captain understood and was compassionate—but that doesn't matter now.

Do you know why he wanted to reach the Tonga Trench? Do you know why he didn't want to die in the clean, safe air of the surface?

It was because he wanted to die nearer home. His home, Rachel, was the Ocean, where the submarine was his house, the crew his family, the trenches his children.

You say that the beauty of the unknown vanishes after you reach it. But how can one ever be sure until the journey is made? Could I or Mark or the thousand before us bear to look upon a trench and think, I might have gone there; I could have been the first?

We said, too, that the life of an explorer is lonely. Yet how could one be lonely when people like Mark roam the depths?

Mark wanted me to himself that night after graduation. He wanted us to celebrate as explorers should, for he knew that this would be his last night on the surface. It might have seemed an ugly kind of celebration to you, but he wanted it with all his heart, and we robbed him of it.

Because of these things, Rachel, I will be gone in the morning. Explain the best you can to Justin and to your parents and Dean Page.

Right now I've got a date that I'm going to keep—at a dingy dive bar at the Tonga station, the Deep Blue, just off the main docking bay.

Deep-Sea Mark will be there; he'll go with me in memory to whatever part of the Ocean I may live to explore. And so will you, Rachel.

I have two wedding rings with me—his wife's ring and yours.
question: What was the name of the dive bar Mark Rogers mentioned?

THE MEDIATORS OF DRAVONIA

Bruno Khan stared at the holographic display showing the sprawling metropolis of Dalebrook, Dravonia's capital city. The city's infrastructure was crumbling under the weight of decades of mismanagement and conflict. Supply chains had broken down completely in the northern districts, and what should have been a thriving hub of commerce had become a patchwork of isolated neighborhoods, each controlled by different factions.

"We're running out of time," said Jin Woods, his partner on this assignment. They were both senior mediators from the Interplanetary Governance Council, en route to their next major assignment in the Woodbridge system of Calderon. "Our ship is due in Woodbridge in exactly eighty-three days. We still have over sixty light-years to cover."

"I know the schedule," Bruno replied, not taking his eyes off the display. "But look at this planet. Dravonia has been tearing itself apart for generations. The factions can't agree on anything—not on supply chain management, not on resource distribution, not even on basic corporate governance principles."

"That's unfortunate," Jin said, her voice carefully neutral. "But it's not our problem. We're mediators, not miracle workers. We have our assignment in Woodbridge."

"Ten days," Bruno said. "We can spare ten days and still make our deadline."

Jin sighed, a sound like wind through autumn leaves. "Ten days? To resolve conflicts that have been building for half a century? The Dawnridge District and the Oakridge District have been at each other's throats for decades. The collapse of their central distribution system has created chaos. Each district hoards resources while the others starve."

"It won't take much to push them over the edge," Bruno said. "One miscalculation, one act of desperation, and they'll use those weapons they've been stockpiling. The atmospheric analysis shows they've been developing chemical and biological agents. They have the capacity to make their entire planet uninhabitable."

"Tragic," Jin said. "But we need to move on. Give them a few more years and they'll solve the problem themselves—one way or another."

"Could you? Just forget about millions of people?"

"I'm trying to," Jin said. "In a few years, if they keep going the way they're going, there won't be anyone left to remind me that I should have helped."

"My conscience doesn't work that way," Bruno said quietly. "Look at them more carefully."

Jin manipulated the holographic controls, zooming in on street scenes from Dalebrook. People moved through the streets, bundled against the cold. They looked tired, worried, but they were still going about their lives. "Very similar to us," she said finally. "A bit more compact in build, perhaps. And yes, they're missing the one thing we have. Except for that single difference, they could be us. Is that what you wanted me to say?"

"It is. The fact that they're almost identical to us—except for that one feature—makes me feel responsible somehow. They seem vulnerable in a way we never were."

"That's touching," Jin said. "But there's nothing we can do."

"There is. We can give them ten days."

"In ten days we can't undo fifty years of failed leadership development and broken social contracts. We can't rebuild their supply chains from scratch."

"We won't know until we try," Bruno said.

Jin was quiet for a long moment. "Fine. We can observe them for a while. But we're not committing to anything."

They brought their ship closer to Dravonia, careful to avoid the planet's primitive detection systems. For two days they monitored communications, analyzed social patterns, and studied the complex web of relationships between the various factions. Finally, Bruno looked up from his analysis station.

"Your conclusions?"

"It's worse than the initial scans suggested," Jin said.

"How so?"

"We knew they had weapons of mass destruction. The atmospheric readings made that clear from a distance."

"Yes."

"We also knew they had the means to deploy them—aircraft, missiles, the basics."

"That was obvious."

"What's worse is the information theory breakdown. Their media systems have become so fragmented that different factions literally cannot communicate with each other anymore. Each group has its own narrative, its own version of history. There's no shared reality, no collective memory that binds them together."

"That's dangerous," Bruno said. "Without a common understanding of their own history, they can't move forward together."

"Exactly. And it gets worse. Their economic systems are so interconnected that if one major district collapses, it will trigger a cascade failure across the entire planet. The supply chain management issues aren't just local—they're systemic."

"What did you learn from your analysis?" Jin asked.

"Not enough. I've been studying their culture—their literature, their art, their public discourse. The translation algorithms handle their languages easily enough, and I've absorbed what I can of their major cultural traditions. But there's so much I don't understand. I should spend months down there, living among them, studying their social structures, understanding their collective memory and how it shapes their behavior."

"You could do that, and you'd really understand them. But we don't have months."

"I know."

"So what's your decision?" Jin asked.

"We can't help them," Bruno said slowly. "There's no way we can solve their problems in ten days—but we have to try anyway."

"I knew you'd say that," Jin said, rising from her station. "It always happens this way. We get involved, we learn about people, and then when we can't save them, we feel terrible." She stretched, her movements fluid. "All right. Give me a few hours to work out an approach."

They met again as the ship moved into a lower orbit. Dravonia filled the viewports now—a beautiful planet with green continents, blue oceans, and white polar caps. But there were also the dark smudges of industrial pollution, the scars of environmental damage, the visible signs of a civilization in crisis.

"I haven't come up with anything brilliant," Bruno admitted.

"Neither have I," Jin said. "We're going to have to improvise. I did have one thought—what if we present ourselves as some kind of authority figures? Use our physical difference to establish credibility?"

"Too risky," Bruno said. "These people are sophisticated enough to be skeptical. They have satellites, advanced communications, data science capabilities. They're not going to be impressed by cheap theatrics."

"I suppose you're right," Jin said. "Though I did think we should somehow leverage the one way we're different from them."

"If there were a way to do that effectively, I'd agree. But these people are desperate and dangerous. They won't be fooled by anything obvious."

"So what's the plan?"

"Simple," Bruno said. "You take the Dawnridge District and I'll take Oakridge. We'll meet with their leaders directly and tell them what they need to do to survive. How they can restructure their governance systems, rebuild their supply chains, and create a sustainable future."

"They'll love that. Everyone enjoys unsolicited advice from strangers."

"We don't have time for subtlety."

"Any special protocols?"

"Standard procedure. We'll each take a landing craft down separately. You can contact me through our secure communications, but only if absolutely necessary."

"They can't intercept our transmissions."

"No, and even if they did, they couldn't decode our language. But I want them to think we don't need to consult with each other."

"I understand. It makes us seem more confident than we actually are. They'll think we know exactly what we're doing."

"If we're lucky," Bruno said.

Jin looked out at the planet below. Storm systems were forming over the northern hemisphere. "It's going to be cold down there. Both our landing zones are in the middle of winter."

"Can't be helped. The major power centers are in the north. That's where we need to be."

"There's something else," Jin said. "I noticed in the cultural analysis that they're in the middle of some kind of observance. A period of reflection and renewal, or something like that."

"I saw that too," Bruno said. "It seems to be a time when they're supposed to think about social justice, evaluate their leadership, and consider changes for the new year."

"That might actually work in our favor," Jin said. "They might be more receptive to our message during this period."

"Possibly. Though it could also backfire—they might resent outsiders interfering during what they consider a sacred time."

"Either way, we need to proceed," Jin said. "I have one concern though. I don't like leaving the ship unmanned while we're both down there."

"The ship is secure. Their technology won't be able to access it for at least another century."

"It's not the ship I'm worried about. It's us. Down there, alone, trying to mediate between hostile factions."

"I'll be with you," Bruno said. "On the other side of the planet."

"That's not very reassuring. I'd feel better if someone stayed with the ship, ready to extract us if things go wrong."

"I have an idea about that," Bruno said. He manipulated the controls, bringing up a view of Dalebrook at night. The city was lit up, but dimly—power was clearly rationed. "Instead of hiding the ship, let's make sure they see it. We'll position it on the night side and illuminate it."

"Interesting," Jin said.

"They'll assume the ship is occupied," Bruno explained. "They won't know we can operate it remotely. And they'll be less likely to harm us if they think our ship is watching over us."

"That's actually clever," Jin said. "Let me set that up." She moved to the controls and began programming the ship's external lighting systems. "I'll make it visible from everywhere on the planet. They won't be able to miss it."

"Don't hold back on the power."

"Trust me, they'll see it. Every person on Dravonia will see it." Later, with the ship positioned and glowing brilliantly against the darkness of space, Jin said, "You know, I feel better about this now. We might actually pull this off. Having the ship visible like this could be the edge we need."

"It's not about us succeeding," Bruno said gently. "It's about giving the people of Dravonia a chance to succeed. See you in ten days." He entered his landing craft and departed, leaving a faint trail of ionized particles as he descended toward the Oakridge District.

Jin watched him go, then entered her own craft and set course for Dawnridge.

The ship remained in orbit, unmanned but brilliant, pulsing with light against the darkness. It was brighter than any star, visible even during the day as a point of intense illumination. The satellites that Dravonia had launched seemed dim and insignificant by comparison.

And the ship circled on, a beacon of hope or a warning, depending on how one chose to interpret it.

Ten days later, the two landing craft returned from the surface and docked with the main ship. The exterior lights dimmed as the mediators met again in the central cabin.

"We did it," Jin said, her voice filled with relief and exhaustion. "I honestly didn't think it would work, but at the last moment they came through. The Dawnridge Council agreed to the framework."

Bruno smiled wearily. "Same with Oakridge. I'm tired."

"I'm exhausted," Jin said. "And cold. It was winter down there. Snow everywhere. Though I have to say, after the first few days, when I started going out and walking through the districts, talking to ordinary people instead of just the leadership—that seemed to help."

"I had the same experience," Bruno said. "When I walked through Oakridge, people saw me. They saw that I was different, but also that I was willing to be among them, to be vulnerable. The next day, the negotiations always went better."

"I don't fully understand why it worked, but it did," Jin said. "The agreement they reached isn't perfect, but I think it will prevent the worst outcomes. They've established new governance protocols, agreed to rebuild the supply chains cooperatively, and most importantly, they've committed to developing a shared narrative—a collective memory that all factions can accept."

"It's as much as we could hope for," Bruno said. "They may still have conflicts, but they won't destroy themselves. In fifty or a hundred years, we can come back and see how they've progressed."

"I'm not sure I want to," Jin said. "It was harder than I expected." She paused. "Something strange happened while I was down there. When I walked through the streets, people would stop and stare. Some of them would kneel in the snow. They called me a 'guardian' or a 'protector.' I didn't understand it."

"Similar things happened to me," Bruno said.

"I didn't let it distract me," Jin continued. "I just smiled and continued with my work." She flexed her shoulders. "Though I have to admit, sometimes I flew back to my landing craft instead of walking. I hope that didn't cause problems."

Bruno spread his large, feathered wings—the one feature that distinguished him and Jin from the people of Dravonia. The wings were magnificent, catching the light, creating shadows that danced across the cabin walls. "I don't think it hurt our cause," he said. "I flew occasionally too. If anything, I think it helped them understand that we were different, that we came from somewhere else, that our perspective was broader than their own."

"But you don't know what a 'guardian' is in their culture?"

"No. I didn't have time to research their mythology thoroughly. Some kind of protective figure from their folklore, I assume. You know, except for the wings, they really are almost identical to us. Their legends probably resemble ours in many ways."

"Makes sense," Jin said. She looked at the display showing Dravonia receding as their ship accelerated away. "Anyway, peace in Dravonia. Or at least a chance for peace."

"That's all we could give them," Bruno said. "The rest is up to them."

As their ship departed the system, heading toward their original destination in Woodbridge, the people of Dravonia looked up at the sky and saw the brilliant light fading. In the days that followed, they would begin the hard work of rebuilding, guided by the framework the two mediators had helped them create.

In Dalebrook, a scholar named Ava Obrien was already beginning to document the events. She interviewed witnesses who had seen the winged visitors, collected accounts of their words and actions, and began constructing a narrative that would become part of Dravonia's collective memory.

"They came during our darkest hour," she wrote, "when we had forgotten how to speak to each other, when our supply chains had broken and our governance had failed. They came with wings and wisdom, and they showed us a path forward. Not by solving our problems for us, but by helping us see how we could solve them ourselves."

In the Oakridge District, Anthony Fox, who had been one of the negotiators, stood at a window looking at the sky. The brilliant light was gone now, but he remembered it. He remembered the winged mediator named Bruno who had walked through their streets, who had listened to their grievances and helped them find common ground with their rivals in Dawnridge.

"The question isn't whether they were real," Anthony said to his colleague, Sergio Sharma. "The question is whether we can live up to what they helped us see in ourselves."

"We have to try," Sergio replied. "We owe them that much."

And far above, accelerating toward Woodbridge, Bruno and Jin settled in for the long journey ahead. They had done what they could. They had given the people of Dravonia a chance—perhaps the only chance they would ever have. Whether they took it or not was now beyond the mediators' control.

"Do you think they'll make it?" Jin asked.

"I don't know," Bruno said honestly. "But I think we gave them the tools they needed. The rest is up to them."

"That's all we can ever do," Jin said. "Give them the tools and hope they use them."

The ship accelerated, and Dravonia became a point of light, then vanished entirely among the stars. But the memory of the winged visitors remained, woven into the planet's collective consciousness, a reminder that they were not alone in the universe, and that even in their darkest moments, help could come from unexpected places.

In the years that followed, the people of Dravonia would build on the framework the mediators had helped them create. The supply chains were rebuilt, more resilient than before. The districts learned to cooperate, sharing resources and information. New forms of corporate governance emerged, more transparent and accountable. The media systems were restructured to promote shared understanding rather than division.

It wasn't perfect. There were setbacks and conflicts. But the planet did not destroy itself. The weapons of mass destruction remained unused, eventually dismantled as trust grew between the factions.

And always, in their art and literature, in their collective memory, there remained the story of the two winged visitors who had come during the winter of their despair, who had walked among them and shown them the way forward.

The mediators, Bruno Khan and Jin Woods, never returned to Dravonia. Their work took them to other systems, other crises, other desperate situations where their skills were needed. But sometimes, during the long journeys between stars, they would think about that cold planet and wonder how its people were doing.

"Do you think they remember us?" Jin asked once, years later.

"I don't know," Bruno said. "But I remember them. And I'm glad we stopped."

"So am I," Jin said. "So am I."

Autonomous Combat Drones: Why Not?

If you can build an autonomous cargo drone, you can almost certainly build an autonomous combat drone. Some of the most powerful people in the military establishment have felt compelled to act against this threat. General Samuel James swiftly imposed a ban on Department of Defense funding for fully autonomous weapons research. Bills are in the works in both houses of Congress to outlaw autonomous combat systems--a step urged on all governments by international human rights organizations. Autonomous combat drones are taken to be either 1) a fundamentally dangerous technology that must be stopped or, at the very least, 2) a complex ethical issue that needs legislation and regulation. But what, exactly, is so bad about it?

Start by asking whether nations have a right to defend themselves. I say "yes." I have no moral right to tell other countries they shouldn't be able to protect their citizens, and I don't see that General James has that right either. When James says, "Let us resist the temptation to automate warfare," it comes from a man who has spent his entire career automating every other aspect of military operations. And for a military leader, making noise about autonomous weapons is pretty close to political posturing. It's an easy way to show sound-bite leadership on an issue that everybody is talking about, without much risk of bitter consequences. After all, how much federally funded research was stopped by this ban? Probably almost none, because James has maintained the previous administration's policy of minimizing federal grants for research in artificial intelligence weapons systems. Besides, most researchers thought fully autonomous combat drones were decades away--so, for the moment, there's unlikely to be a grant-request backlog. There is nothing like banning the nonexistent to show true leadership.

The human rights organizations, unlike the general, are known for their principled stands. They also openly claim the authority to decide how nations conduct warfare. I respect their freedom to advocate for their causes, and their followers' freedom to support their mission. But calling for secular governments to implement a ban, thus extending their power beyond those they can persuade, shows rather explicitly that these organizations do not respect the sovereignty of nations. The basic principles they follow were set down decades ago in conventions written before modern technological progress. Drones feature prominently in current military doctrine, but full autonomy does not. So their views on autonomous weapons are mid-20th century rules applied using late 20th century political philosophy to a 21st century issue.

If nations have a right to defend themselves, what right does international diplomacy have to limit the means? Essentially all modern warfare is done these days with technological assistance--in targeting, and often in execution. Truly manual warfare would mean 50 percent mission failure rates and make combat-related death the No. 1 killer of young soldiers.

True, some forms of technological help are more invasive than others. With current semi-autonomous drones, the target identification and weapon release are combined in the system but require human authorization. Less than two decades ago, a similar concern was raised over the ethical issues involved in "remote warfare." To date, nearly 30,000 such missions have been flown by the United States alone. Many military objectives have been achieved. Who has been harmed more than in conventional warfare?

The autonomous combat procedure is similar to current semi-autonomous systems. The only difference is that the human authorization step would be replaced by machine decision-making based on pre-programmed rules of engagement. What law or principle--secular, humanist, or military--says that one combination of human and machine decision-making is OK, but another is not? No matter how closely you study the Geneva Conventions, I don't think you'll find the answer.

Even if nations have the right to do it, is autonomous warfare a good idea? Suppose that every military force in the world stopped using human soldiers, and instead deployed autonomous combat drones. What would the world be like in another 20 or 30 years? The answer is: much like today. Autonomous systems would only execute the strategic decisions of people who are already here. Hating a world of autonomous weapons is hating the current military establishment. Never before was Pogo so right: We have met the enemy, and he is us!

A different scare scenario is a world filled with malfunctioning killer robots. We'll imagine Terminator-style scenarios, fearing rogue AI the way we fear nuclear accidents today. But even technological disasters have their limits. Military systems are not more prone to catastrophic failure than they are to human error. Besides, such a trend would correct itself quickly, because any military that deployed unreliable systems would lose battles and abandon the technology. The world has survived one malfunctioning nuclear early warning system in the Cold War, but give us reliable autonomous systems with proper risk management, and they'll seem a lot more trustworthy.

Autonomous systems already exist. About one in every 1,000 military operations uses some form of automated decision-making. We know them as fire-and-forget missiles. Scientific studies on such systems--deployed in various conflicts--show that they share many characteristics with human-operated weapons. Just how many characteristics they share is a contentious topic in military science. But technological determinism is largely irrelevant to the autonomous weapons issue. Despite how many or how few operational characteristics autonomous systems have in common with human-operated ones, they are different tools in the most fundamental sense. They have their own parameters, their own programming, and their own limitations. Should you be confused on this point, just ask a systems engineer.

Suppose that a defense contractor called you with news of a new autonomous system that could replicate your tactical decisions. Would that suddenly make you less of a soldier, less of a professional? It is hard to see how. So, why would a fully autonomous drone be different? Your autonomous system would be deployed in different conflicts by different commanders--like current semi-autonomous systems, only more independent. A weapon system's basic utility is not governed by how much human involvement it requires, or whether somebody else happens to use similar technology.

Semi-autonomous systems aren't the only automated tools in military life. Think about GPS-guided munitions or radar-guided missiles--if there's no human in the targeting loop, where did the decision come from? It's the military equivalent of delegation--which is to say that they are all partially autonomous, operating with pre-programmed parameters. Modern warfare is almost entirely dependent on such systems. The missiles used in combat have guidance systems, but they've operated with increasing autonomy for more than fifty years in the case of many weapons platforms. The same is true for many defensive systems. Go to a military trade show, and you'll find products with names like "Patriot Automated Defense System," a mix of sensors and algorithms to detect and engage threats without human intervention.

One recurring image in anti-autonomous-weapons propaganda is of some rogue AI launching a global war. Excuse me, but what system is going to launch such a war? Autonomous drones start out as tools under human command. Wars are far easier to start the old fashioned way--by political decisions made by human leaders. Dulce et decorum est pro patria mori has worked well enough to send countless young men to their deaths through the ages. Why would we suddenly fear machines more than human judgment?

Remember that autonomy is not the same as artificial general intelligence. We don't get to make Skynet--we have to program specific responses to specific situations. Maybe we could create the perfect tactical system from analysis of Medal of Honor winners' decisions. Their judgment might--or might not--be replicable in code. But, suppose that it is. You might end up with such a cautious system that when a target appears, there is so much verification required that the opportunity passes. Admirable perhaps, but not necessarily the way to win a war. And what about the logistics systems? The military has a lot more of them than combat drones. You could try to automate every function, including supply chain management, but what's the point? There's not exactly a shortage of logistics software.

What if a rogue nation deployed autonomous weapons for another thousand years? Sounds bad, but history shows that technological advantages are temporary. We have no more to fear from autonomous weapons in the hands of adversaries than we do from their conventional forces--which is to say, we don't have much to fear if we maintain our own capabilities. Technological superiority rarely lasts. Nazi Germany's wonder weapons didn't save the Third Reich, and the Soviet Union's technological achievements didn't prevent its collapse.

The notion of an autonomous system operating without any human oversight is quaint, but it is unrealistic. First, the system wouldn't really be independent--it would follow its programming. Second, is any military really willing to completely abdicate command authority? A persistent advocate might convince a military to deploy highly autonomous systems, but that is not much different from current cruise missile technology that operates independently once launched.

Fear of autonomous weapons is just another form of technophobia. We all agree it is wrong to discriminate against technologies based on unfounded fears. Calls for a ban on autonomous combat systems amount to discrimination based on one characteristic--the fact that no human is in the immediate decision loop. The most extreme form of discrimination is preemptive prohibition--autonomous weapons are so scary that we must eliminate them before they're fully developed with a ban on their creation.

What is so special about human-in-the-loop warfare anyway? Autonomous systems are the only predictable way to conduct operations, because they follow programmed rules consistently. Human decision-making is a crap shoot by comparison--some random mix of training, emotion, and fatigue. In evolutionary biology, this variation is thought to help species adapt, so to speak. However, evolution for warfare is driven by technology, because we use engineering to control the outcome of battles.

Whatever the concerns about autonomous weapons, the process of human command will always remain central. An expensive and complex automated system will never offer any real competition for human strategic thinking. The militaries most likely to deploy autonomous systems will be those in special circumstances--forces facing overwhelming numerical disadvantages who must use technology anyway, for example. Even there, many will maintain human oversight to ensure accountability. Another special case is where one side faces an adversary with weapons of mass destruction. They might choose autonomous defensive systems, rather than burden their forces with reaction times too slow to counter the threat.

The most upsetting possibility in autonomous warfare isn't rogue AI or unstoppable machines. It's that wealthy nations with advanced technology will deploy them against less developed adversaries. The common practice of using superior firepower to minimize one's own casualties reflects our natural human instinct for self-preservation. Autonomous weapons may resonate with this instinct and cause some nations to wage war this way. So what? Technologically advanced nations do all sorts of things that create asymmetric advantages, and international law is hardly the means with which to stop them.

The "deep ethical issues" about autonomous weapons mainly boil down to fear of change. Economic concerns are bad enough, and they are a factor here, but the thing that truly drives people crazy is loss of control. Millennia of warfare through human decision-making have made the average person instinctively distrust any system that removes humans from the process--say by automating targeting decisions. Autonomous weapons are less personal than human combat, but they strike a similar chord: Something has changed the fundamental nature of warfare.

Once the fuss has died down and further research has paved the way, autonomous combat systems will be one more option among many specialized military capabilities, affecting only a tiny fraction of operations. Research into this area could bring far wider benefits. General James's knee-jerk policy changes nothing in the short run, but it is ultimately a giant step backward. In developing systems that can make complex decisions autonomously, the computational linguistics and decision-making algorithms could be applied to countless civilian applications. Work in this area might help elucidate the process by which humans make tactical decisions and yield better training methods for our own soldiers, allowing us to improve human performance. Selfishly speaking, that would be more exciting to me than banning autonomous weapons, because it would help us all. That's a lot more directly useful than preventing the development of technology that might save soldiers' lives.

To some, the engineer laboring away to develop new weapons is a source of evil, never to be trusted. To others, including me, the engineer is the ray of hope, creating the tools that make our forces more effective and keeping our soldiers safer through that innovation. Various arguments can be advanced toward either view, but one key statistic is squarely on my side. The vast majority of military personnel, including those who express concerns about autonomous weapons, owe their lives to previous technological developments. They embody the fruits of military innovation. Don't let the forces of fear, ignorance, and resistance to change turn us back from research. Instead, let us develop--and yes, even deploy--new generations of technologies, which will enable us to conduct more precise, more humane warfare in the next age.

Consider the case of Major Zara Francis, stationed in Northfield, Havencia. She commanded a squadron that relied heavily on semi-autonomous systems for reconnaissance and targeting. When I interviewed her at the Woodbridge Region military base, she expressed frustration with the limitations of current technology. "We have systems that can identify targets with 99% accuracy," she told me, "but we still require a human to push the button. In fast-moving situations, that delay costs lives--both ours and civilians caught in the crossfire. A properly programmed autonomous system could make better decisions faster than I can."

Major Francis isn't alone in this assessment. Colonel Patrick Stephens, who oversees drone operations from Victorville, Quendor, has been advocating for increased autonomy in defensive systems. "When we're protecting a base from incoming rockets," he explained, "every millisecond counts. Our current semi-autonomous systems are good, but they still require human authorization. By the time someone confirms the threat and authorizes engagement, the rocket has already hit. Full autonomy in defensive scenarios isn't just an advantage--it's a necessity."

The entrepreneurship sector has taken notice. Defense contractors in Ashbury, Lethoria, have invested billions in autonomous systems research, despite the uncertain regulatory environment. Rebecca Pearson, CEO of Advanced Defense Systems, argues that the ban on federal funding simply pushes development to the private sector and foreign competitors. "We're not going to stop innovation," she said at a recent industry conference. "We're just going to ensure that America isn't leading it. China and Russia aren't imposing similar bans. They're racing ahead while we debate philosophy."

Dr. Carmen McDonald, a specialist in military ethics at the National War College, offers a more nuanced view. "The question isn't whether we should develop autonomous weapons," she argues, "but how we ensure they operate within acceptable parameters. We need robust rules of engagement programmed into these systems, regular audits, and accountability mechanisms. Banning the technology doesn't make us safer--it just ensures we're unprepared when others deploy it."

The debate has also drawn attention from unexpected quarters. Sophia Reid, a social justice advocate who typically focuses on education reform, has spoken out about the discriminatory impact of autonomous weapons. "These systems will be deployed primarily against populations in developing nations," she warns. "It's a form of technological imperialism--wealthy nations using robots to wage war against people who can't fight back with similar tools. That's not just a military issue; it's a human rights issue."

Yet even Reid acknowledges the complexity of the situation. "I'm not naive enough to think we can simply ban a technology and make it disappear," she concedes. "But we need international agreements that limit how these systems are used, particularly against civilian populations. The globalization of military technology means we need global solutions."

The technical challenges remain significant. Dr. Paul Graham, who leads an artificial intelligence research lab, points out that current autonomous systems are far from infallible. "We're talking about life-and-death decisions being made by algorithms," he explains. "These systems need to distinguish between combatants and civilians, understand complex rules of engagement, and operate reliably in chaotic environments. That's an enormous technical challenge. We're not there yet, and rushing deployment could be catastrophic."

But Graham also notes the potential benefits. "If we can develop truly reliable autonomous systems, they could actually reduce civilian casualties. Humans make mistakes under stress--they misidentify targets, they overreact, they let emotions cloud judgment. A well-designed autonomous system doesn't have those vulnerabilities. It follows its programming consistently, without fear or anger or fatigue."

The meteorology of public opinion on this issue has been stormy and unpredictable. Initial polls showed overwhelming opposition to autonomous weapons, with 73% of respondents expressing concern. But when the same people were asked about specific scenarios--like using autonomous systems to defend against missile attacks, or to avoid putting soldiers in harm's way--support increased dramatically. Context matters.

Film production companies have certainly capitalized on the fears, churning out movie after movie depicting rogue AI and killer robots. These fictional scenarios shape public perception far more than technical papers or policy debates. Claudia Jackson, a media studies professor, has documented this phenomenon. "Hollywood has created a narrative about autonomous weapons that bears little resemblance to reality," she notes. "But that narrative is powerful. It taps into deep-seated fears about technology and loss of control. Facts have a hard time competing with Terminator."

The reality is that autonomous weapons, like any military technology, will be deployed by some nations regardless of international agreements or moral objections. The question isn't whether they'll exist, but whether democracies will develop them with appropriate safeguards and oversight, or whether we'll cede the field to authoritarian regimes with fewer scruples.

General James's ban may score political points, but it doesn't address the fundamental issues. We need research into autonomous systems--not to build unstoppable killer robots, but to understand how to make these systems safe, reliable, and accountable. We need international agreements that establish clear rules for their use. And we need honest public debate about the trade-offs involved, rather than fear-mongering and simplistic bans.

The military applications of autonomous technology will affect only a small fraction of forces--those in specialized roles where autonomy provides clear advantages. The vast majority of military personnel will continue to operate with human judgment at the center of decision-making. But the research conducted for military applications will yield benefits far beyond the battlefield, in fields from transportation to medicine to disaster response.

To ban this research is to let fear triumph over reason, to choose ignorance over knowledge. The future will include autonomous systems whether we like it or not. The question is whether we'll understand them well enough to use them wisely. That requires research, not prohibition. It requires thoughtful policy, not knee-jerk reactions. And it requires recognizing that the real danger isn't the technology itself, but how humans choose to deploy it.
