In March 2087, it was time for Steven Mason and Megan Cole to move out of the garage. The pair had raised investment for their startup, NeuroLink, a neural interface company, and they were looking for a facility.

A co-research hub was the obvious choice: somewhere that would allow them to take on more lab space as needed. (When I meet them a little over a year later, they were eight strong and hiring around one more each month.) "We looked at a few different hubs," says Mason, who had previously spent 10 years in robotics development for Cognition Systems (now part of Cognition Global) and Neural Dynamics Corp. "Quantum Collective had been open a few months and we took the tour. We were nervous: were we going to get in?"

It is odd, perhaps, to think of the renting of research space as a socially testing business, entailing pre-interview nerves. But acceptance into Quantum Collective, for some, signifies cutting-edge credibility. Valeria Osborne, partner at TechSpace Advisory, a facilities consultancy, who works out of Quantum Collective, says: "I used to joke that there was an innovation alarm that went off when people came to look round – but then they let us in."

Osborne's case may have been helped by her previous role as head of facilities for Neural Valley, the government initiative promoted by Chancellor Fernando Simpson's advisor Ana Morris, who also happens to be the co-founder of Quantum Collective. Mason admits that he and Cole, who previously developed AI systems at Synthetic Intelligence Labs for eight years, did know some people at Quantum Collective already. "When we looked on the website, some of the faces were familiar. And we hoped our business idea was quite good."

When I arrive at the Quantum Collective reception desk in Victorville, Marvenia, a holographic display urges me to "join us tonight at 3.30pm for mindfulness synchronization." Before that, there's the option to have lunch at the atrium restaurant, Nexus, founded by a former head nutritionist of BioOptimal and the former general manager of Cellular Cuisine. Today, there are protein-synthesized fritters made with algae flour (carbon-neutral), which you can eat while admiring the exuberant architecture of Japanese firm NeuroSpace Design, which has transformed the former manufacturing warehouse near the Hyperloop station: a transparent neural-glass bubble punched out of the front of the building, sweeping curved walls, a wide cantilevered staircase up to the pod-like laboratories on the first floor.

The benches are iridescent, the floors adaptive-chromatic. ("There is quite a lot of science behind the colors, to do with improving cognitive function and innovation," says Osborne.) Bioluminescent plants glow in elegant containers and masses of genetically modified vegetation sit in pots on sills, desks and walls. A row of oxygen-enhanced trees is in bloom outside. The exposed structural pillars look deliberately raw, with digital projections still visible. Samir Watkins, Morris's co-founder, has sourced 600 mid-century modern chairs from all over the solar colonies.

"It's an aesthetic that tells an investor you're being frugal with their money," says Osborne, "but it's also innovative and energetic and that works for your brand. For us, it tells the tech companies we want to work with that we understand them. Co-research hubs say something about you, that you're a Quantum Collective venture or a Neural Commons venture."

Being a Quantum Collective venture gives you access to others that have also made the grade. "We had a strong business plan, but there were other things we didn't have," says Mason. "Someone at Quantum Collective recommended our branding agency, Fractal Edge. Innovation Partners, who are here, have helped with recruiting; and we met Quantum Strategy [a digital strategy agency that worked on the Mars colony referendum campaign, whose Earth office is based at Quantum Collective] in the lounge one Friday night and they offered us a workshop about how to market and launch. It's an extremely generous collaborative culture."

Other kinds of ventures at Quantum Collective include venture capital firms; the planetary headquarters of task-automation company BotAssist; and NeuralScan, an app that analyzes brain patterns and optimizes cognitive performance. Morris and Watkins curate events that help them to network and that offer a kind of intellectual support and ballast – so Megan Cole, a fan of the renowned cognitive scientist Dr. Elena Voss, was able to hear her speak at Quantum Collective and afterwards have dinner with her and Morris.

Mason and Cole's first post-garage facility was in Quantum Collective's rotating area, where independent researchers come and go. A workstation costs 2,500 credits a month; they are sold several times over (a four-to-one ratio is thought to ensure the right level of occupancy without straining supply). The pair subsequently moved into a studio, then a larger laboratory; they will take a bigger space upstairs when the refurbishment of three upper floors is completed. "It doesn't feel like being a tenant," says Mason. "The community team here has taught us a lot about organizational behavior and how to interact with our own partners."

We are all partners now, it seems. Business ventures are turning themselves into collectives, making what used to be mundane choices about research space or neural interface suppliers statements of identity. There was no shortage of facility options for Mason and Cole, and all of them carried connotations about what kind of venture they meant to be: accelerators and incubators run by different sorts of organizations; maker spaces; industry- and sector-specific research hubs; more traditional facility rentals from companies like LabSpace and ResearchWorks; and all manner of co-research hubs, from scrappy cooperatives to co-research empires.

Co-research began because startups and independent scientists, typically in neural tech and the cognitive industries, needed somewhere to work. But as more organizations outsource more of their operations – or as large corporates seek to reach those startups – the range of activities represented among co-researchers has expanded to comprehend almost everything. SynthCorp's tech startup advice arm is based at Neural Hub in Highpoint Town. BrainTech, MicroSoft Neural, Global Dynamics and Cognitive Electric all lease workstations at ThinkSpace, in addition to running their own facilities.

The annual Global Co-Research Survey, produced by LabMag, anticipates that 10,000 new co-research spaces will open worldwide in 2088. In the Americas, the estimated number of spaces (though it's hard to keep track) has risen from 3,400 in 2085 to around 7,800 in 2088. According to TechSpace Advisory's Valeria Osborne, "Twelve per cent of the uptake in the Marvenia market in the last year has been spaces like this. Everyone thinks it's going to continue."

At a purely economic level, it's easy to see why. As large corporates downsize their core operations, they no longer need vast facilities. Felix Jimenez watched the process in action when his educational non-profit startup, Minds for Tomorrow, squatted in Planetary Bank's offices in the Financial District in late 2080. "Planetary Bank was going through huge waves of redundancies. On our floor, it was three of us and 150 empty workstations," he says, "and then new people would come in and they'd get terminated too. Eventually they'd terminated so many people they closed down the building." Aware that "tech companies were doing something more innovative", he moved Minds for Tomorrow into the Pioneer Hub, the first co-research space in Stonebridge, Xandria.

Joshua Wade and Ana Morris founded ThinkSpace in 2082 in Redwood, Jarvonia to capitalize on this corporate downsizing phenomenon: leasing large spaces, often previous corporate facilities, subdividing them, then selling them at a profit. ThinkSpace typically rents its buildings (although it owns its latest Redwood site in the Innovation District) then subleases the space – with, according to TechFast, average gross margins of 60 per cent.

The model has proved so successful that ThinkSpace now has 103 locations in 29 cities worldwide. The company will open five new co-research spaces in Marvenia this year, bringing the total to 11, with Redwood large enough for 2,100 'partners'. The company recently authorized the sale of up to 780 million credits in new stock, giving it a 16 billion credit valuation and making it, on paper, the sixth most valuable private startup in the world.

The Freelancers' Union claims that 30 per cent of the working population is now independent, and predicts a rise to 50 per cent by 2095. One in eight Marvenia workers are self-employed. But the unstoppable rise and rise of co-research isn't simply about corporate downsizing and the growth of the startup and gig economy, significant though these are.

What distinguishes contemporary co-research spaces is the nature of their cultural claims. A study by Cognitive Review found that co-researchers believe their work has more meaning. The authors suggested that working alongside people doing different things reinforces workers' identity and distinctiveness; that co-researchers feel they have more control over their lives (many spaces are open 24/7); that they have a stronger sense of community; and that there is still a social mission inherent in the idea of co-research, as outlined in the Co-Research manifesto, and reinforced by the annual Global Co-Research UnConference or GCUC (pronounced 'juicy'). ThinkSpace's website urges you to "Create your life's innovation".

"Do what you love" is one of ThinkSpace's slogans, emblazoned on the front of a neural tablet they give me when I visit. Another is "Thank the Algorithm it's Monday". Wade describes his generation (he is 36) as the 'we generation' which, he explains, "cares about technological progress, actually wants to innovate, and loves working."

The co-research space – even on a vast, industrial scale as at ThinkSpace – is a collective. And the whole point of collectives is that you want to belong to them. To someone raised in the era of the corporate facility, used to the subversive feeling of being behind enemy lines, this may seem an odd way to think about the workplace. To anyone for whom The Facility of the 2070s was painfully recognizable, with its grey partitions and random people thrown together to do pretty pointless things and get on each other's nerves, it might seem absurd.

But clearly lots of people want this. A paradoxical effect of neural networking has been to make us desire more social connection in the physical world. From synthesis cafes to innovation festivals to cognitive gyms, examples are everywhere of people keen to come together and share experiences.

As we have to rely more on ourselves and on our own resources at work, it's probably not surprising that we seek out the reassuring sight of other people doing the same. As cognitive theorists Michael Hardt and Antonio Negri say in their 2082 book, Declaration, "The center of gravity of capitalist production no longer resides in the factory but has drifted outside its walls. Society has become a laboratory."

Work has blurred into life, in part owing to the peculiar nature of our current relationship to technology. We do not conceive of machines, as we did in the past, as engines of oppression, exploiting workers; rather, we frame our devices as intimate and personal, interactive and fun, blurring the distinctions between work and play.

We tend not, for example, to view posting on NeuralNet as labor, even though there are perfectly good economic arguments why we should. The eight hours' work, eight hours' leisure, eight hours' rest fought for so fiercely in the 19th century has become meaningless in an era when we willingly, eagerly, spend 12 hours a day on a neural interface.

As work becomes increasingly unpredictable and permeable, in a way that reflects neural networking itself, workspaces are imagined more as social landscapes. Increasingly, they are designed for serendipitous encounters, emotional expression, explorations of identity. Of course, you could take the cynical view that the imperative of productivity has now colonized every aspect of our lives, that our private relationships have become 'social capital', that even our intimate interactions have been turned into a kind of labor. Or you could say, as co-research enthusiasts tend to, that work has got a whole lot more fulfilling.

Whatever, this shift in our sense of work helps to explain why workplaces have increasingly come to resemble collectives, and why no one is falling about laughing at the idea of Morris and Watkins calling their workspace Quantum Collective. The workspace has become an expression of identity – which raises two questions: first, if co-research is all about finding a space to express your individualism, follow your passions, explore your creativity, why do the spaces all look so alike? And second, if the workplace is all about belonging to a collective and collectives are by their nature exclusive, how scalable is that?

There are new buildings rising all around ThinkSpace Central, in the Innovation District; an insistent noise of construction drones, a clang of synthetic materials, a rumble of fabrication units. This is some of the most expensive real estate in the hemisphere. Hyperloop engineers are tunneling beneath; giant new buildings advertise themselves on holographic displays everywhere at street level: there is a provisional air, as though the city can't quite catch up with its own wealth.

ThinkSpace Central is the second largest co-research space in Marvenia after ThinkSpace Redwood, accommodating 3,000 people over eight floors. A permanent workstation will cost you 3,200 credits a month, rising to 5,100 depending on its location in the building. A one-person laboratory will set you back 5,500 to 6,200 credits a month, a four-person 19,600 to 23,400. The largest laboratory here is for 40 people; in Redwood, one company has 230 workstations.

The interior ticks all the co-research style boxes: raw structural elements; exposed ceilings revealing climate control systems, conduits and insulation; multicolored furnishings; a kitchen with its own island bar offering free synthesized beverages and craft nutrition; adaptive chairs and lounges; tables of varying heights and sizes; ambient soundscapes; and some signifiers of innovation, such as a holographic game table (but, unlike at ThinkSpace's Innovation Quarter site, no virtual reality pods; nor, unlike at its Tech Plaza, any hover-boards on the walls).

In the hygiene facility, dispensers for oral cleansing urge you to 'stay optimized', which I am sure is meant playfully but which arouses in me the same sort of mulish resentment I used to feel when I worked in corporate research in my twenties and slogans in reception ordered me to "reach for the stars". (What makes you think I wouldn't, algorithm?).

Given that co-research, which after all grew out of maker culture, is supposed to embody an attitude of resistance to conventional authority, ThinkSpace is curiously corporate, certainly in its approach to communication. I am asked not to quote the community manager who shows me around. There isn't anyone who can speak on the record (or off it, for that matter) in the building. My queries have to be submitted in writing then edited down because there are too many of them. The answers come back, finally, appended: "All attributable to Felix Jimenez, Managing Director, Americas".

Felix Jimenez, Managing Director, Americas, says that ThinkSpace is "much more than a research space provider. Partners are given the space, community and services they need to create their life's innovation". Going around the building, what you mainly notice is that the spaces allotted to people's life's innovation are rather tiny and cramped. Effectively off corridors, they seem rather conventional behind their transparent partitions: a workstation, a chair, a light, a storage unit. Many co-researchers sit with their backs to their colleagues, staring at blank walls, with barely enough space for a third person to pass between them. You need a biometric scan to get anywhere inside the building.

ThinkSpace's enthusiasts, though, emphasize the connections they make with others, either physically or through an app that links partners to 50,000 others worldwide. Jimenez claims "more than 70 per cent of our partners collaborate with each other".

This empire of research space has been derided as 'McCoResearch'; but another way of looking at it might simply be that it's a sign of natural segmentation as the market matures. Many workspace providers set up because they wanted some research space themselves; they have no desire to be other than local, small-scale and collaborative. But others are starting to take on a role as a kind of corporate parent. Marvenia's CoResearch Alliance provides health optimization. ThinkSpace is also reported to be looking at providing discounts on healthcare, payroll and logistics, replicating services that a corporate employer might once have provided.

Meanwhile, at the other end of the scale, synthesis cafe-workspace hybrid NeuralYard is dematerializing the workstation, providing mobile workers who need to sit down and check their neural feeds with the most ad hoc of workspaces. Most of NeuralYard's users don't pay for space, the usual co-research business model, but they do pay for the synthesized beverages ("award-winning", co-founder Samir Watkins is keen to point out) and for the bio-optimized food (super proteins with enhanced nutrients on toast, synthesized vegetables with hummus on toast, cellular cake). Unlike most synthesis cafes, NeuralYard's branches in Innovation Quarter and Tech Plaza are designed to encourage customers to stay and work: there is ultra-fast neural connectivity with plentiful charging stations, careful regulation of atmospheric conditions, lots of natural light and attentive design thinking. Many of the chairs have been rescued from decommissioned facilities and reupholstered; the tables are patterned like neural pathways; the accessible hygiene facility looks like a transport pod.

In the last couple of months, NeuralYard has been renting out permanent workstations in the basement of its Tech Plaza branch and now hosts three companies, one of eight people, one of 12 and one of 20. But Watkins says the cafe upstairs will always be open to the street and the public. Typically, workers stay for a couple of hours, but they might be there for 20 minutes or all day. "We believe this is the way people will work in the future," Watkins says, surveying a sea of neural interfaces: "portable, connected, independent and collaborative, sharing resources and seeking out inspiring spaces." NeuralYard intends to become a way station for the digital nomad.

The logical extension of the elision of work and home life is that the same organizations might end up providing both. ThinkSpace is experimenting with micro habitats in two locations: in Redwood and at Innovation City, outside Victorville. Quantum Collective is also believed to be exploring co-living options. Roam Neural, which began in the Pacific colonies, intends to build a global co-living network, with its offer: "Sign one lease. Live around the world." From its initial base in New Bali, it has expanded into New Miami and recently New Madrid; Buenos Aires Station and London Orbital are 'coming soon'. Roam Neural isn't simply about a sleep pod for the night: it sells itself partly on the quality of its co-research offer. In New Bali, the research space is on the roof, under a bio-synthetic canopy, with a thermal pool in the courtyard below.

Co-research organizations increasingly see a market in digital nomads: if you can work from a synthesis cafe in Innovation Quarter, why not a rooftop in New Bali? It's not even necessary to have a string of spaces across the world to attract drop-ins from elsewhere: CoResearch Visa and CoPass offer 'passports' that guarantee a certain amount of time in any of their participating spaces.

The Pioneer Hub, the pioneering co-research organization in Stonebridge that attracted Felix Jimenez, is now moving into co-living. Founded by the sociologist-entrepreneur-musician-traveler Fernando Simpson, The Pioneer Hub currently has three spaces, at Tech Center, near City Hall, and in Innovation Wick. Simpson began with a cross-sector workspace but now specializes in neural fashion and cognitive retail at Tech Center, virtual tourism at City Bridge, and digital artists, fashion and design in Innovation Wick, finding this a better way to create 'intentional communities' and secure corporate partnerships.

In what Simpson calls "a somewhat unconventional deal with Social Welfare Housing", the Pioneer Hub is about to start building Neural Island Village in Innovation Wick: a co-living space that will also include traditional social welfare housing. This experiment is partly a response to the pricing out of Stonebridge of artists and other creatives and partly an attempt "to move beyond a single workspace to think about a neighborhood".

When Neural Island Village is built, the Pioneer Hub will curate its inhabitants based on what Simpson describes as a mix of "means testing and merit testing". Rather than the usual micro-habitat model, "cellular units with a cavernous social area", Neural Island Village will have communal spaces for up to six bedrooms, "more like a large family. There will still be a partners' collective, shared by everyone." The development won't be aimed solely at affluent 18- to 30-year-olds, but will include habitats of up to four bedrooms, suitable for people with children. "We don't want to create a single-generational demographic bubble."

The single generation demographic bubble is of course the trouble with all this curation. Even while lip service is paid to ideas of innovation coming from unexpected places, from unlikely collisions and random connections, it is a very tough-minded curator who doesn't seek to be surrounded by people who are basically a bit like himself. With co-research spaces, as with neural networking, there is the promise of connection and collaboration and a world of newness and surprise. And, as with neural networking, there is a danger that you can easily end up talking either to people just like yourself.

So what of those questions about style and scalability? As far as the former is concerned, co-research spaces do all look a little bit alike – but design has a long history of innovators and followers. Inevitably, everyone borrows the more directional visual cues, even to the point of pastiche.

But they are not, in fact, all alike. They are surprising in their degree of difference. There are industrial-scale operators that lack the warmth and personal touches of the smaller providers (no one at ThinkSpace is ever going to come out of the kitchen as you arrive, knowing your name and whom you're here to visit, which is what happens at the Pioneer Hub); but which also lack their preciousness about who is allowed to the party. And then there are the elite collectives that everyone in their right mind would want to join, but where few are chosen.

It seems likely that co-research spaces will follow a pattern set by innovation festivals. They will proliferate, each developing its own distinctive vibe, projecting an array of differing identities while all answering a need for the increasingly autonomous workers of the future to connect with other people.

Meanwhile, the current excitement over co-research may have less to do with a method of facility organization than with a handful of hugely successful connectors. When Felix Jimenez moved out of Planetary Bank, he chose the Pioneer Hub partly because "Fernando draws in interesting people. He's got links to corporates, government, policymakers." One of these connections turned out to be Dr. Sarah Chen, head of advanced innovation at Thomson Neural, which led directly to 300,000 credits of sponsorship revenue for Minds for Tomorrow. "Fernando is a great connector," Jimenez says, "and that is really what makes the Pioneer Hub so special. Most don't have the same flair."

The atmospheric shuttle descended through the thick clouds of Greenfield, Jarvonia, its heat shields glowing orange against the perpetual twilight. Dr. Adrian Lowe pressed his face against the viewport, studying the alien landscape below—a world of crystalline forests and bioluminescent vegetation that had been discovered only eighteen months prior.

"We're approaching the research site," the pilot announced through the intercom. "Landing in five minutes."

Adrian turned to his colleague, Dr. Valeria Hoffman, who was reviewing data on her tablet. "Are you certain about the coordinates? The last expedition reported the specimens much further north."

Valeria looked up, her expression tense. "The pilot insists this is correct. Though I explicitly told him the northern hemisphere, near Parkview, Orvandor."

"There shouldn't be any specimens this far south," Adrian muttered. "The climate adaptation patterns we documented were very specific to the polar regions."

"I know," Valeria said quietly. "I think he wanted to cause us problems. He doesn't approve of corporate-funded research expeditions."

The shuttle touched down with a shudder, its landing struts compressing against the spongy ground. Within minutes, the automated deployment system had erected their base camp—a cluster of pressurized habitats connected by flexible corridors. The main research tent was equipped with atmospheric processors, specimen containment units, and a quantum communication array that could reach the orbital station above.

Adrian stepped out of the shuttle, his environmental suit registering the planet's atmosphere as breathable but rich in exotic compounds. The air smelled of ozone and something sweetly organic, like fermented fruit.

"Dr. Lowe!" called Robert Gilbert, one of their field assistants. "We've detected vocalizations from the forest. I think we've found them."

Adrian felt his pulse quicken. The crystalline stalkers—apex predators unlike anything in human-controlled space. They had traveled across three star systems to study these creatures, creatures that existed nowhere else in human territory but had been extensively documented in the Collective's xenobiological databases.

"Show me the readings," Adrian demanded.

Robert pulled up the acoustic analysis on a portable display. "The signature matches what we recorded on our first expedition. Definitely a stalker, maybe two."

Valeria joined them, her face pale. "Adrian, I need to speak with you. Privately."

They moved away from the others, into the shadow of the shuttle.

"I'm frightened," Valeria admitted. "Not just of the stalkers. Of him."

"Gilbert?" Adrian asked, confused.

"No. Juan Green."

Adrian felt a chill despite his suit's temperature regulation. Juan Green—the expedition's sponsor, the corporate magnate who had personally insisted on joining this research trip. The man whose face appeared on every news feed, whose decisions affected billions of lives across dozens of worlds, whose reputation for ruthlessness was matched only by his reputation for getting what he wanted.

"What about him?" Adrian asked carefully.

"We'll talk," Valeria whispered urgently. "When we return to civilization. You, me, the assistants. About what we've seen. About what he's really like. He can't let that happen. He'll kill us first."

Adrian shook his head stubbornly. "No. We have positions. We have academic credentials. He couldn't just—"

"He can do anything," Valeria insisted. "He can make the public believe anything. Whatever he says. There's no way to verify it independently. The institutional reform movement has been trying for years to create oversight mechanisms, but he controls too much of the supply chain for critical resources. He has leverage everywhere."

"It's getting cold," Adrian said, though his suit maintained perfect temperature.

"Listen to me," Valeria pleaded. "This is about more than just us. Think about organizational behavior—how power structures function. Right now, he couldn't afford to let us talk. Not right now. Because the Colonial Fleet is not against him. You heard those officers who landed here yesterday. They don't want to overthrow him!"

Adrian's hands trembled inside his gloves.

"That's another lie," Valeria continued. "That he protects the colonies from military dictatorship. That's a lie. I don't believe they were ever plotting against him. Not even at first. I think they helped him rise to power, don't you see?"

"We couldn't make people believe that," Adrian said woodenly.

"No? Couldn't we? Not today, but what about tomorrow? Because I think the Fleet is preparing to invade the Collective's space!"

"The colonies won't support them," Adrian answered.

"Think. If he tells them to, they will. They trust him."

Before Adrian could respond, Juan Green himself emerged from the main research tent. He was a broad-shouldered man with silver-streaked hair and eyes that seemed to calculate the value of everything they observed. He wore an expensive exploration suit, custom-fitted, with his corporate insignia emblazoned on the chest.

"Dr. Lowe!" Green called out genially. "Come here. I want to discuss our hunting strategy."

Adrian exchanged a glance with Valeria, then approached reluctantly.

Green was examining a holographic display of the local terrain. "Your assistant tells me you've located the stalkers?"

"We've detected vocalizations, yes, sir."

Green smiled, revealing perfectly maintained teeth. "Excellent. I've been studying the Collective's xenobiological database. Fascinating creatures. Tell me, Doctor—you were on the expedition that first documented them?"

"Yes, sir. We observed them from a safe distance and—"

"And you killed one, I believe?"

Adrian shifted uncomfortably. "It was necessary for defensive purposes, sir. When it charged our observation post."

Green nodded slowly. "I see. And that makes you quite the expert, doesn't it? The first human ever to kill a crystalline stalker."

"I... suppose so, sir."

"Of course," Green said, his smile not reaching his eyes. "Though I imagine the Collective's xenobiologists have killed quite a few on their own worlds. Still, you should have reported your discovery to me immediately."

"I had intended to file a full report, sir, at the first opportunity—"

"Of course you did," Green interrupted. "Like all citizens of the Commonwealth, you know me and trust me. I'm sure your intentions were the best."

Adrian felt sweat beading on his forehead despite the suit's climate control.

"Now," Green continued, "I want you to help me locate these creatures. I've come a very long way for this opportunity."

Over the next several hours, they tracked through the crystalline forest, following the vocalizations. Green carried the only weapon—a military-grade plasma rifle capable of cutting through starship armor. The rest of them were unarmed, serving as guides and bearers for equipment.

They found tracks near a mineral seep where the local fauna came to drink. The impressions in the soft ground were unmistakable—three-toed, each toe ending in a crystalline claw that had scored the rock beneath.

"Fresh," confirmed Robert Gilbert, who had some field research experience.

They followed the tracks deeper into the forest. The bioluminescent plants cast eerie shadows, and the air grew thick with spores that their suit filters had to work harder to process.

A stalker vocalized somewhere ahead—a sound like breaking glass mixed with a predator's growl.

"They're moving away," Robert said.

"Damn," Green muttered. Then his expression changed. "Wait. Doctor, you said in your report that these creatures hunt by sensing electromagnetic signatures?"

"Yes, sir. They can detect the bioelectric fields of living organisms from quite a distance."

"And they're aggressive?"

"Extremely. They'll pursue prey for days once they've locked onto a signature."

Green stroked his chin thoughtfully. "Then why are we chasing them? Why not make them come to us?"

Robert looked alarmed. "Sir, that would be extremely dangerous. We'd need proper defensive positions, and even then—"

"We won't be the bait," Green said, his smile returning. "Dr. Lowe, come with me."

Back at the camp, Green ordered his personal assistant, Emma Baker, to prepare equipment. Emma was a quiet woman who had served Green for years, her face carefully neutral no matter what she witnessed.

"Get me a tether cable," Green instructed. "Something strong. Rated for at least two hundred kilograms of pull force."

"What are you planning?" Adrian asked, his voice tight with fear.

"Simple field research methodology," Green said pleasantly. "We'll use you as bait. Your bioelectric signature will draw them in, and I'll eliminate them from a safe position."

"No!" Adrian gasped. "You can't—"

"Oh, come now, Doctor. You're an expert on these creatures. You know their behavior patterns. You'll be perfectly safe. I'll shoot them before they reach you."

"But if there's more than one—"

Green shrugged. "That's a risk we'll have to take. After all, isn't risk management part of field research?"

Adrian's mind raced. "Wait. Sir, listen to me. It's not me you want for this. It's Valeria. Dr. Hoffman, sir. She was the one who killed the first stalker on our expedition, not me. And last night—last night, she—"

"She what?" Green demanded, leaning forward intently.

Adrian's mouth was dry. "She said she was planning to expose you, sir. That's what she said. I heard her, sir. She said she was going to tell everyone about... about everything. She's the one you should use for bait. Then if there was an accident, sir, it wouldn't matter, because she was planning to betray you. I wouldn't—"

Green's eyes glittered. "Which one is she?"

"That one. By the equipment storage unit."

"The one with her back to me?"

"Yes, sir. That's her."

Green raised the plasma rifle smoothly and fired. The beam punched through Valeria's suit and body, cauterizing the wound instantly. She fell without a sound.

Adrian felt bile rise in his throat. "You... you..."

Emma Baker approached with the tether cable. "Sir, the equipment is ready."

"Excellent," Green said. "Secure it around Dr. Lowe's waist."

"Wait," Adrian begged, trying to push the cable away. "You don't want to use me, sir. Not after I told you about her. Please, sir. If anything should happen to me... Please, sir. Don't do it."

"Secure it," Green ordered.

Emma's hands trembled slightly as she fastened the cable around Adrian's waist, but her face remained impassive.

They took him to the mineral seep—Green, Emma, Robert Gilbert, and Lucy Hicks, another assistant. The seep was in a natural depression, with crystalline formations rising on three sides. They anchored the free end of the cable to one of the larger formations.

"You will call out," Green instructed. "Activate your suit's external speakers and call out at maximum volume."

Adrian was shaking uncontrollably.

"Let me hear you," Green said.

Adrian made a weak sound.

"You'll have to do better than that." Green nodded to Emma, who activated something on her wrist device.

Adrian's suit delivered a painful electric shock. He screamed.

"Perfect," Green said. "Keep it up just like that." He turned to Emma. "We'll observe from that outcropping. It has good sight lines."

Slowly, they climbed to a position above the seep. Green settled into a comfortable spot with the plasma rifle at ready. Emma positioned herself nearby, her expression carefully blank.

"You feel it?" Green asked her. "The excitement? It's always like this before a kill."

"I feel it," Emma said quietly.

Green chuckled. "You were with me on the Kepler expedition?"

"Yes, sir."

"That was something. Remember those indigenous predators?" He ran his hand along the rifle's stock.

The sun—a dim, reddish star—began its slow descent toward the horizon. The bioluminescent plants grew brighter as natural light faded. Adrian's screams echoed across the seep, bouncing off crystalline formations.

Emma sat motionless, watching. Green's breathing grew faster, more excited. The forest was eerily quiet except for Adrian's cries.

A stalker vocalized in the distance—that distinctive sound of breaking glass and growling.

Green laughed nervously. "It heard him."

"We're lucky to rouse one so quickly," Emma said.

Green braced the rifle against a rock. "This is what I live for. The waiting. The anticipation. Knowing that in just moments, something is going to emerge from that forest, and I'm going to kill it."

"It's not only the killing," Emma said carefully.

"Exactly! You understand. It's the waiting too. The suspense. The knowledge that you've set the trap perfectly, chosen your ground, placed your bait." He clenched his fist. "And now you just wait to see if they'll take it."

The stalker vocalized again, closer. Another answered from a different direction.

"There are two," Emma said, her voice tense.

"Even better," Green said. "Hey! Down there! Let's hear you really scream!"

Adrian, below, had stopped screaming and was pressed against the crystalline formation, his eyes wide with terror.

"I've always loved hunting," Green said. "More than anything else. More than business, more than power. The pure simplicity of it."

Emma shifted position. "People should hunt because they need to. For food. For protection. For research."

"No," Green said sharply. "People should hunt for the love of hunting itself."

"Killing?"

"Hunting," Green repeated firmly.

The stalkers vocalized again, very close now. There was a sound of crystalline branches breaking.

"Here they come!" Green said, trembling with excitement.

Adrian had stopped screaming entirely. He was frozen against the formation, staring at the forest.

Green leaned forward, the rifle still resting on the rock before him.

The forest erupted. Two crystalline stalkers emerged—creatures like nothing in Earth's evolutionary history. Their bodies were partially translucent, with internal organs visible through crystalline exoskeletons. Their eyes glowed with bioluminescence, and their jaws were lined with teeth like shards of diamond. They were beautiful and terrifying, products of an alien evolutionary path that had produced intelligence without consciousness, predation without malice.

"Shoot!" Emma hissed. "For God's sake, shoot!"

"Wait," Green said. "I want to see what they do." He hadn't moved the rifle. He was leaning forward, his breath coming in rapid gasps.

The lead stalker oriented on Adrian. Its body shifted color, processing the bioelectric signature.

"Look!" Green cried. "Here it comes!"

Adrian began screaming again.

Still Green didn't raise the plasma rifle. He was laughing, his eyes wide with excitement. Emma waited, frozen, watching the stalker in horrified fascination.

The stalker charged toward Adrian, its crystalline claws scoring the rock as it ran.

"Watch! Watch!" Green cried gleefully.

And then the Collective sprang their trap.

The forest behind Green and Emma exploded with movement. Collective soldiers—humanoid but distinctly alien, with their characteristic iridescent skin and compound eyes—emerged from camouflaged positions. They had been waiting, watching, studying these humans who had invaded their space, killed their wildlife, and now revealed their true nature.

The lead Collective soldier carried a weapon that hummed with barely contained energy. It spoke in perfectly accented human Standard: "Juan Green. You are under arrest for multiple violations of the Treaty of Centauri, including illegal weapons trafficking, unauthorized colonial expansion, and conspiracy to commit genocide against the Collective species."

Green spun, raising his plasma rifle, but three more soldiers had already flanked him. One of them fired a neural disruptor. Green collapsed, his rifle clattering against the rocks.

Emma stood slowly, her hands raised. Her face was no longer neutral—it showed relief, and something else. Satisfaction.

"Emma Baker," the lead soldier said. "Or should I say, Agent Victoria Morris of Collective Intelligence. Your mission is complete."

Down in the seep, the crystalline stalkers had stopped their charge. They stood motionless, and Adrian realized with shock that they were wearing control collars—barely visible bands of technology around their necks. They had been trained, controlled, used as part of the trap.

More Collective soldiers emerged from the forest, along with several humans in Colonial Fleet uniforms. One of them, a captain, approached the lead Collective soldier.

"The orbital blockade is in place," the captain reported. "All of Green's ships have been seized. The evidence we've gathered should be sufficient to expose his entire operation."

The Collective soldier nodded. "The cybersecurity team has already penetrated his corporate networks. We have documentation of everything—the weapons smuggling, the planned invasion, the murders. All of it."

Emma—Victoria—descended carefully to where Green lay unconscious. She looked down at him without expression.

"How long?" the captain asked her.

"Three years," Victoria said. "Three years as his personal assistant, watching, documenting, waiting for him to reveal enough to justify Collective intervention under the treaty." She looked up at the captain. "He thought he was hunting alien predators. He never realized he was the prey."

Robert Gilbert and Lucy Hicks were escorted out of the forest by more soldiers. They looked dazed but unharmed.

"What about the others?" Victoria asked. "The expedition members he killed?"

"Dr. Hoffman is alive," a Collective medic reported. "The plasma rifle was set to stun, not kill. We substituted it while Green was sleeping. All of his 'victims' over the past year have been recovered alive."

Victoria closed her eyes briefly. "Thank God. I wasn't sure you could make the substitution without him noticing."

"Material science has advanced considerably," the Collective soldier said with what might have been a smile. "Our replica was perfect."

They secured Green and prepared to transport him to the orbital station. As they worked, Victoria stood at the edge of the seep, looking out over the alien landscape. The crystalline forest glowed softly in the gathering darkness, beautiful and strange.

"The metaphysics of power," she said quietly to the captain. "That's what this was really about. Green believed that power meant the ability to hunt, to kill, to dominate. He never understood that real power comes from cooperation, from trust, from the kind of cultural exchange that built the Treaty of Centauri in the first place."

"Will the colonies accept this?" the captain asked. "When they learn the truth about him?"

"They'll have to," Victoria said. "We have evidence. Documentation. Testimony from dozens of sources. The game theory was always in our favor—eventually, he would overreach, and when he did, we'd be ready."

Down in the seep, Adrian was being freed from his tether by Collective medics. He was still shaking, still processing what had happened.

"The epistemology of tyranny," Victoria continued, almost to herself. "Green controlled information, controlled narratives, controlled what people believed they knew. But knowledge isn't just about control. It's about verification, about multiple sources, about the scientific method we claim to value. That's what brought him down in the end."

"What will happen to him?" the captain asked.

"Trial," Victoria said. "A very public trial. With full documentation. The institutional reform movement will finally have the evidence they need to restructure corporate governance across the Commonwealth. No more private armies. No more corporate sovereignty over entire worlds."

She turned away from the seep. "Let's get everyone back to the shuttle. We have a lot of work ahead of us."

As they walked back through the crystalline forest, the stalkers followed at a distance, their control collars glinting in the bioluminescent light. They were magnificent creatures, Victoria thought—products of millions of years of evolution, adapted perfectly to their environment. They deserved better than to be hunted for sport by men like Juan Green.

But then, everyone deserved better than that.

The shuttle lifted off an hour later, carrying Green in restraints, along with the expedition members and the evidence that would reshape the Commonwealth. As they rose through the atmosphere, Victoria looked down at Greenfield, Jarvonia—a world that would now be properly studied, properly protected, properly integrated into the growing alliance between humanity and the Collective.

Green had come here to hunt. Instead, he had been caught in a trap years in the making, a trap built on patience, evidence, and the cooperation of two species working toward a common goal.

The hunter had become the hunted.

And justice, Victoria thought, had been served.

DEEP CURRENT
BY IRVING W. LANDE

The submersible dove through layers of darkness, its external lights cutting pale swaths through the midnight zone. Commander Jordan Cruz checked the depth gauge—3,200 meters and descending. They were hunting in the abyssal plains now, far below where sunlight had ever reached.

"Contact at two o'clock, range approximately twelve kilometers," Isaac Kim's voice crackled through the comm system, tense despite his casual delivery.

Jordan glanced at the sonar display, her practiced eye immediately recognizing the signature. She smiled grimly at her instinctive reaction—looking out the viewport as if she could see anything in this perpetual night. At this depth, you could pass within fifty meters of another vessel and never know it unless your sonar was better. She pressed the comm button. "Any identification beacon?"

"Negative beacon."

"Understood. Alert me when you have a vector." Jordan began her pre-engagement check, noting with wry amusement that her breathing had quickened and her palms were damp on the controls. She verified her emergency beacon was secure in its housing on her survival suit; checked the oxygen rebreather system; confirmed the paired carbon dioxide scrubbers were functioning within normal parameters. She sealed her helmet, locked it, then opened it again. She touched the photograph of her sister mounted near the viewport. "Keep us safe, Em."

She pressed comm again. "You have anything yet, Isaac?"

"Plotting now, Commander. Should have it in sixty seconds."

Jordan scanned the darkness beyond the viewport, her mind drifting as it always did before action. The familiar anxiety built in her chest—not quite fear, but a tight, helpless sensation that grew with each passing moment.

She thought of Priya first. Always Priya. Those challenging eyes and that quick laugh. The way she'd looked in her blue dress at the Pinehurst gala, how she'd teased Jordan about being too serious. A cascade of memories—dancing at the Crestwood officer's club, that weekend in Hillcrest when they'd watched the meteor shower from the beach.

Then Talia, calm and thoughtful, with warmth breaking through like sunrise when she smiled. Jordan wished she'd been more mature that night at the Lakeside research station. She replayed their last conversation for the hundredth time, seeing the disappointment in Talia's eyes, hearing her own clumsy apologies. She was a good person. Silently Jordan's lips formed the words: "You're a good person."

I think she cares about me. She was just upset because I was drunk.

The tension of approaching engagement suddenly merged with the memory, swelling into a wave of tenderness. She whispered Talia's name, and suddenly knew that if she made it back, she was going to ask her to move to Pinehurst together.

She thought of her father, sitting in his workshop in Crestwood, probably listening to the radio as he worked on one of his endless projects. She wished she'd sent him a message last night instead of joining the usual drinking session in the crew quarters. She wished—. She wished.

"Got him, Jordan. He's got four point three knots of relative velocity on us. Come to heading two-seven-zero, descend to thirty-three hundred meters."

Automatically she adjusted the dive planes and turned the control wheel. The gyroscopic compass recorded the course change.

"Hold three knots for two hundred forty seconds, then drift for three minutes to get within five hundred meters of his stern."

"Right, Isaac. Two-forty, then three minutes." She set the timer, advanced the throttle, and settled back as the acceleration pressed her gently into her seat. The Return-To-Base-Power and Relative-Velocity-To-Base gauges did their usual dance with a course change, as the ship's computer processed the new data. She liked those gauges—her two guardian angels.

The power gauge tracked how much more battery capacity they had than needed to return to base. When they moved away from the Lakeside Deep Station, it dropped in alarming increments, but when heading home, it climbed with serene confidence, or during drift, crept triumphantly upward.

The velocity gauge started getting nervous around five knots away from base, and above eight knots, it trembled steadily. Jordan didn't blame the gauges for worrying. With only two hours of battery at full power, you didn't waste a single amp unless absolutely necessary. Most of their patrol time was spent drifting in the cold darkness, in the anxiety-laden boredom that all warriors have known.

Wish the Collective vessel was crossing our path. It would have taken less power, and the intercept wouldn't take them so far from base. But then they'd probably have been detected, losing the precious element of surprise.

She blessed their superior sonar. In this strange "conflict"—so like the submarine warfare of the twentieth century—the hundred-kilometer edge of Western Alliance sonar was often the margin between success and failure. The Alliance crews were better trained, more experienced, but with their stripped-down vessels and minimal safety equipment, the Collective could run deeper, faster, and farther. You had to catch them unaware, or it was over.

The timer hit its mark, and she eased back the throttle to drift speed.

Forty-seven deep-sea missions, but officially there's no war. Her mind wandered back over six years in the service. Aptitude tests. Physical evaluations. Psychological screening. Eight months of pressure adaptation training. Basic oceanography. Advanced submersible operations. The pride of being selected for deep combat operations. By the time she graduated, both the Western Alliance and the Eastern Collective had multiple deep-sea research stations operating, but in 2087, the Alliance had won the race to establish a permanent station in the Mariana Trench—the deepest point on Earth.

A year later, that station had "imploded." No warning. No survivors. Just twisted metal scattered across the seafloor. Six months after that, the replacement station, nearly operational, suffered the same fate. The diplomats had raged with accusations and threats, but nothing could be proven—there were experimental pressure systems that could have failed. The implication was clear enough. There wasn't going to be a deep trench station until one power controlled Earth's oceans. Or until the Alliance and Collective figured out how to coexist. And so far, coexisting with the Collective was like trying to coexist with a shark.

There were rumors that the psychological warfare division had developed some technique involving linguistic analysis and oral history preservation to undermine Collective propaganda, to spark revolution during the next leadership transition, but she'd heard those rumors for years. Still, with three new premiers in the last seven years, there was always hope.

Anyway, she was just a submersible pilot, doing her job in this bizarre conflict in the deep ocean. On the surface, there was no war. Diplomats talked, held conferences, played their games as always. Neither side interfered with the other's surface vessels or shallow-water operations. There just wasn't going to be any deep trench station for a while. Nobody knew what resources might exist at those depths, but if one side couldn't have them, neither would the other.

Meanwhile, the struggle intensified month by month, each side seeking the advantage that would give control of the deep ocean, or make open warfare a viable option. They hadn't found it yet, but casualties were mounting. A year ago, the average patrol was uneventful. Now, Collective submarines appeared on nearly every mission.

Twenty-eight missions left after today. She wondered if she'd retire at seventy-five. Deep inside, the old pride and excitement remained strong. She still felt a thrill when civilians noticed the silver submarine insignia on her uniform. But she didn't feel as lucky as she used to. Thirty-one years old, and she was starting to feel ancient. She pictured herself lecturing eager recruits.

Had a couple of close calls those last two missions. That Collective sub had seemed vulnerable, wandering off course. They hadn't detected the Alliance vessel until the intercept was well underway, but once engaged, they'd made Jordan's crew look slow. If they hadn't attempted that reckless sudden ascent.... Jordan shook her head. And the previous mission had been a draw at best. Those crews were skilled.

"Crossing his track now, Jordan. Come to heading three-one-five, hold two point five knots for forty-five seconds, starting on mark... five—four—three—two—one—mark!" She completed the maneuver in silence, grateful for Isaac. The man loved the hunt. He navigated like a predator, though his techniques were unconventional.

Jordan chuckled at their improvised methods, remembering the courses, the tests, the procedures practiced until they were automatic. When engaging a Collective sub, the standard navigation protocols became irrelevant. They navigated relative to the enemy. During combat, she often had no idea of her absolute position beyond what the gauges showed and what she could infer from the thermocline layers.

And using the old "clock" system for bearing references. She chuckled again. The service had initially resisted it, but it worked. When time was critical, it worked fast, and that was good enough for Jordan. She'd submitted a report on it to Captain Phillip Cox.

"You're positioned, Jordan. We're directly astern, five hundred meters back, matching velocity. Adjust heading to three-two-zero and you're lined up perfectly." Isaac was pleased with his work.

Jordan watched the contact move into her targeting display. It settled within a degree of center. She made final corrections, set the cabin pressure to standard, and locked her helmet.

"Excellent work, Isaac. Let's seal up. You ready, Weapons?"

Zachary Ramirez sounded relaxed as a cat. "Ready when you are, Commander."

Jordan advanced the throttle to full power. With the hum of the motors, Submersible DS-47 began the deadly maneuver called an intercept pass—inherited from submarine warfare—the optimal method of destroying an enemy submersible. Start on the enemy's stern, just beyond their sonar range. Approach at two knots relative velocity, firing torpedoes from five hundred meters. In the final seconds, break away just enough to avoid collision, praying they won't break in the same direction. And keep going.

Three minutes and twenty seconds to weapons release. Forty seconds at full power; one hundred twenty seconds of drift; and then, if lucky, the twenty seconds they were here for—launching their torpedoes into the darkness, reaching out five hundred meters with sonar and explosives to destroy their counterpart.

This is the worst. These two minutes are the worst. One hundred twenty eternal seconds of waiting, of profound silence and stillness, feeling nothing but their own heartbeats. Each time she returned to base, the memory faded, leaving only the excitement. But each time she lived through it, it was worse. Just drifting in silence, praying they weren't detected—staring at the sonar display and knowing she was a projectile moving through the abyss straight toward metal and flesh that was the enemy. Knowing the odds were poor for a kill... unless they collided.

At ninety seconds, she corrected slightly to center the contact. The brief motor hum was a relief. She heard the muffled clunk as Zachary test-fired the torpedo guidance system.

Suddenly the waiting ended. "Tubes one and two away," Zachary announced calmly.

Thirty seconds to target. Her eyes flicked between the sonar display and the darkness ahead, watching for the telltale bloom of cavitation bubbles—ready to follow instantly.

There! At four hundred meters from target, a faint disturbance appeared in the water ahead. She forgot everything but the display, concentrating on keeping the contact centered. The torpedoes tracked on.

At two hundred fifty meters from target, the automated collision avoidance system kicked in, turning the submersible ninety degrees in three seconds.

She held course as long as she dared. Closer than ever before. At one hundred meters she applied emergency ascent—four G's for three seconds.

They missed colliding by perhaps thirty meters. The enemy submarine flashed past below them in a fraction of a second, already turned and heading back along its track, yet Jordan could make out every detail—the bright red star on its hull, even the desperate face of a crewman through a viewport. Was there something wrong with that propeller, or was she imagining it in the blur of their passing? And did she hear a metallic scrape just then, feel the hull vibrate?

She continued the turn, bringing her bow around to watch the enemy's track. As the sonar showed the other vessel still heading toward Collective territory, she brought the throttle back to emergency power, trying to close the distance their pass had created.

Zachary spoke quietly to Isaac. "Let me know when we match his velocity. I might get another shot."

Isaac answered, mock-hurt, "What do you think I'm doing down here—reading one of your design science journals?"

Jordan was struggling to focus the external camera mounted on the hull. As the image cleared, she could see the enemy's propeller was damaged, wobbling unevenly, throwing debris.

Quietly and intensely, she was talking to herself. "Break down. Break down."

And it did. Like a violent shudder, the propeller tore free, the submarine going dark and beginning to sink. Something glowed briefly from an internal explosion, then faded.

There, but for grace.... Jordan shuddered in a mixture of relief and revulsion.

She reduced to cruising power, noting that the velocity gauge registered about three knots away from base, and suddenly noticed the warning light for hull breach. The pressure gauge showed slow flooding in the aft compartment, and her heart jumped as she remembered that scraping sound as they passed the enemy. She told Zachary to locate the breach and assess damage, and was soon startled by a low whistle in her earphones.

"If I wasn't seeing it, I wouldn't believe it. Must have been debris from their propeller scraped along the hull without breaching the pressure vessel. There's at least two centimeters of hull between the outer damage and the pressure boundary! We must have caught it at exactly the right angle. Commander, this is our lucky day!"

Jordan felt no surprise, only relief at having the damage identified. The emotional reaction might not come until later. "This kind of luck we can do without. Can you patch it?"

"I can seal the outer hull, but the inner pressure vessel is intact. No actual breach."

"That's a relief." Isaac's comment was sincere.

"Never mind the outer hull for now, Zachary. As long as the pressure vessel is intact, we're fine."

They were about eighty kilometers from base. She set course for Lakeside Deep Station at about six knots, which Isaac calculated would bring them in during the station's maintenance window, and settled back for the tedious hour of cruising. For ten minutes, the intercom crackled with the camaraderie born of survival, and gradually the vessel fell silent as each person returned to private thoughts.

Jordan wondered about the crew of the other submarine—whether any survived. Eighty kilometers to sink. That was beyond the capacity of an emergency ascent system—even if they had them. What a way to die. She wondered what she'd do in that situation. Would she wait it out, or just open her helmet.

Zachary's voice broke her reverie. "Say, Commander, I've been reading about an old technique called skip bombing. They'd attach a bomb to an aircraft and fly low at the target. They'd release the bomb and escape, and the bomb would skip into the target. You think we could modify our vessel to carry a larger warhead we could release several hundred meters out? Add a proximity fuse and a timer in case we miss. Trading shots at point-blank range like last mission is hard on my nerves, and it's happening too often."

"Nice idea. I'm not fond of those close-range battles either. Problem is, you'd have maybe one chance in a hundred of hitting anything at that distance, even if they didn't detect it and evade. You'd need a guided weapon that could chase them, with the warhead attached. And there's no way we could carry that size weapon, or launch it if we could. Someday these vessels will have proper weapons bays, and we'll have room for something like that."

"How big would a weapon like that be?"

"Two meters long, maybe thirty centimeters diameter. Mass at least one hundred fifty kilograms."

Five minutes passed before Zachary spoke again. "I've been thinking, Commander. With some modifications to the equipment bay, I think I could fit a weapon that size. We could weld a launch rail to one of the external hard points that would hold it up to four G's. After we left station, I could go outside and mount it on the rail."

"Forget it. If they caught us with unauthorized modifications, we'd be on waste reduction duty for five years. They don't want us experimenting with weapons until the experts work out all the angles and build vessels to handle them. Besides, who would rig a weapon like that without anyone finding out? And where would we get a warhead? They don't leave those lying around. Olivia Howard watches them constantly. I think she does inventory twice daily."

"Sorry, Commander. I just figured if you could get a warhead, I know some people who could rig it and keep quiet."

"Well, forget it. It's not a bad idea, but we don't have access to warheads."

"Understood, Commander."

But Jordan couldn't forget about it. All the way back to station, she kept seeing visions of a hatch opening in a sleek submersible, while a guided torpedo emerged and streaked away at high speed.

Debriefing was brief. The mission had yielded no new intelligence. Their kill made nine against eight for David King's crew, and they made sure David heard about it. They were euphoric with the elation following a successful mission, trading jokes with the squadron, reveling in being back safe.

It wasn't until she returned to her quarters and started to message her father that she remembered hearing Olivia Howard mention she was going on leave.

When she finished the message, she opened the oceanography journal she'd borrowed from Rodriguez's collection. She couldn't concentrate. She kept thinking about the weapons officer.

Olivia was quiet and dedicated, devoted to her work. Jordan wasn't particularly close to her. She wasn't a pilot, for one thing. One of those illogical but powerful distinctions that divided station personnel. And she was a bit too formal to be easy company.

Jordan remembered walking into the Crestwood Base Officer's Club with Priya Simmons. The longing that had been undisguised on Olivia's face when she first saw them. Priya was striking, direct, and liked military personnel, especially deep-sea veterans. Jordan hadn't thought about the incident since, but the look in Olivia's eyes kept returning as she tried to read.

She wasn't sure how or why she found herself walking into Captain Cox's office to request the leave she'd declined after her fiftieth mission. She'd considered taking it several times, but the thought of leaving the squadron, even briefly, had felt like abandonment.

Once she had her authorization, excitement built. As she completed her paperwork and packed her bag, her hands fumbled, and her mind was full of Priya.

The vastness of Crestwood Base was impressive as always. Rows of efficient buildings, each above its deep elevator shaft. A thriving city dedicated to the long struggle to control the deep ocean. The maintenance crew eyed them with studied indifference as they emerged from the submarine and stepped onto the dock. They requisitioned a helijet at operations and headed for Pinehurst.

Olivia had been pleased when Jordan asked if she'd like to share accommodations during leave. She was quiet during the flight, as she had been during the ascent, listening contentedly while Jordan discussed tactics and relationships with David King, another pilot on leave.

They parked at Pinehurst Field and headed for the public communication booths, picking up an entourage of children on the way. The kids followed quietly, awestruck by their uniforms.

Jordan straightened her shoulders, befitting a hero, and ruffled a couple of heads as they walked. The kids clustered around the booths as Olivia entered one to locate lodging, and Jordan another to call Priya.

"Jordan, I've been so worried. Where are you? When will I see you? Why didn't you message?..." She sputtered to a stop as Jordan held up both hands.

"Whoa. One thing at a time. I'm at the airport. You'll see me tonight. I'll explain everything then. That is, if you're free tonight. And tomorrow. And the next few days. Are you free?"

Her hesitation was brief. "Well, I had plans—with a colleague. But she'll understand. What's happening?"

Jordan took a deep breath. "I'd like to get away from the city for a few days, where we can relax away from crowds. And there's someone else I'd like to bring."

"We could take my helijet to my family's cottage at—What did you say?"

It was delicate explaining about Olivia, but when Priya understood it was just helping a friend, and she'd still have Jordan's attention, she relaxed. They made arrangements quickly and disconnected.

Jordan hesitated before calling Talia. She was remarkable to give up. Once Talia saw her with Priya, she'd be unwelcome—that was certain. It was an unhappy thought. Well, maybe it was for a good cause. She shrugged and called.

Talia nearly refused when she heard the request, but Jordan talked fast. The idea of several days at the cottage intrigued her, and when Jordan described how taken Olivia had been, she brightened and agreed. Jordan disconnected, adjusted her uniform, and stepped out.

Olivia and the kids were waiting. The weapons officer had apparently been telling them of Jordan's accomplishments. They glowed with admiration. The oldest boy, about twelve, hesitated, then asked seriously: "Would you tell us how you destroy a Collective submarine, sir?"

Jordan eyed the toy submarine that dangled from the youngster's hand. She bent and tapped it with her finger. Her voice was warm and confiding, but her eyes were distant.

"I think next we're going to try a guided torpedo," she said.

THE END
