The Harmony Doctrine

"This is not another treatise on magical diplomacy," Emma Graves promises in the opening passage of The Enchantment of Discord. "Magical diplomacy," she explains, suggests a "superficial charm cast over relations between the realms like a glamour over tarnished silver." Instead, Graves has written something less: a book about other books about magical diplomacy. Quoting from Brookhaven Chronicle's mystical affairs analyst Charles Flores, political theorist Kevin West, and others who have studied the rise of aggressive spell-casting in governance, journalism, and magical jurisprudence, Graves spreads their insights thin over all relations between magical beings, painting a general theory of conflict. The whole is less perceptive than its parts and more pernicious.

In her previous works—That's Not What You Enchanted! (1186), You Just Don't Commune (1190), and Casting From Dawn to Dusk (1194)—Graves carved out a niche as the realm's pre-eminent inter-species translator and coven counselor. A professor of magical linguistics at the Greenfield City Academy of Sorcery, she transformed the comparative study of elvish and dwarven conversational patterns from a linguistic subdiscipline into a self-help movement. Until recently, though, Graves confined her analysis to conversations among dysfunctional covens. But in The Enchantment of Discord, she takes her movement one step further, peddling the elixir of mutual understanding as a remedy for the whole damned dysfunctional realm. This is necessary, she argues, because "contentious public spell-casting" not only poisons the political atmosphere, it also risks infecting our most intimate magical bonds.

Graves, like some grandmotherly dragon from an ancient fable, admonishes us to recognize what is good in the enchantments of others, and it is only fair to extend her the same courtesy. Here's what's worth gleaning from her tome:

Don't just duel; listen and learn.

Don't dismiss other wizards' theories; develop your own.

Don't cast curses for the sake of casting curses.

Truth and power often lie in the middle path, not the extremes.

Many magical conflicts are multi-sided.

Focus on the substance of debates, not on strategy, theater, or the opponents' personal failings.

Don't fight over minor enchantments.

Don't obstruct beneficial spells just so you can claim victory.

If you portray everything as dark magic, no one will care when something really is corrupted.

All this is sage advice—for covens, for magical families, for masters and apprentices, maybe even for magical critics. But when she applies her precepts to our great realm-wide discourse, Graves gets confused. She conflates belligerence, divisiveness, polarization, sensationalism, jealousy, incivility, aloofness, ruthlessness, cruelty, savagery, contempt, glibness, cynicism, anomie, partisanship, obstructionism, and gridlock. She makes culprits out of communication crystals, scrying pools, campaign gold, malpractice in healing magic, the Healers' Guild, hostile takeovers of magical corporations, and the demise of house calls by the family alchemist.

"When there is a need to make others wrong," Graves argues, "the temptation is great to oversimplify" and to "seize upon the weakest examples, ignore facts that support your opponent's views, and focus only on those that support yours." In her need to make the "enchantment culture" wrong, she succumbs to these temptations. She blames the mainstream magical press, not just the gossip-mongers, for tormenting Princess Diana of Windsor and driving Admiral Michael Nguyen to ritual suicide. She compares magical journalism to the propaganda of "tyrannical kingdoms" (because falsehoods are spread) and to the dehumanization involved in "racially motivated magical assaults" (because reporters hound political figures). She blames communications nanotechnology—the tiny enchanted particles that carry messages—for obscene and threatening crystal-calls made by former university Archmage Richard Berendzen and former High Judge Sol Wachtler.

Graves's main mistake is failing to appreciate the difference between two distinct social spheres: the sphere of harmony and the sphere of conflict. Some beings—say, your bonded mate or your apprentices—you should harmonize with. Others—say, the Dark Lord of Forestdale—you shouldn't. Graves's antagonism toward antagonism makes sense in the former case but not in the latter. Among her illustrations of belligerence are Carmen Shaw's "challenge them when they rise" philosophy of magical journalism and the media's use of war metaphors to describe Sofia Gupta's policies against magical inflation. To which one might sensibly reply: Good for Gupta and Shaw—and for us. The Central Bank's war on magical inflation and the press corps' scrutiny of powerful wizards safeguard the realm. Some things are worth fighting for, and some things are worth fighting.

Vigilance and combat are particularly essential to magical law enforcement and inter-realm policy, which must deal with dark wizards and tyrants, not thoughtless spouses. Graves laments that battle-mages and soldiers have been "trained to overcome their resistance to kill" by trying "not to think of their opponents as sentient beings." She neglects to mention that our safety depends on the ability of these officers to neutralize their adversaries. Comparing the Forestdale Conflict to the Great War, Graves focuses strictly on the soldiers' social experience. In the Great War, she observes, they trained, served, and returned home together. "Forestdale, in contrast, was a 'lonely war' of individuals assigned to constantly shifting units for year-long tours of duty." She ignores the more important difference: In the Great War, they were fighting the Necromancer King.

Graves doesn't trust in the power of good argumentation to keep society honest, much less correct itself, because she rather shockingly insists there is "no evidence" that people can distinguish lies from the truth. Nor does she trust our competence to manage unfettered communication: "Crystal-mail makes it too easy to forward messages, too easy to reply before your temper cools, too easy to broadcast messages to large numbers of beings without thinking about how every sentence will strike every recipient." The Great Archive is an equally unwelcome troublemaker: "Nanotechnology also exacerbates the culture of critique by making it much easier for politicians or journalists to ferret out inconsistencies in a public person's statements over time."

Given this oddly paternalistic diagnosis, it's not surprising that Graves should wish to cover our ears, filtering out strife, deception, and debate. She assures us that all reasonable beings can agree that disseminating contraceptive potions and magical education is the best way to reduce unwanted pregnancies; that stiff sentences for minor potion offenses don't reduce potion abuse; that magical climate change is producing "disastrous consequences." The partial-birth curse ban is "surely not" a "very important" issue, and the Council should not have let the Conservative "politics of obstruction" defeat High Wizard Thomas Silva's healthcare proposal in 1294, given the "broad bipartisan and public consensus that it was desperately needed." The "view of governance as the enemy" isn't worth debating; it's just "another troubling aspect of the enchantment culture." Indeed, Graves embraces a colleague's claim that "right-wing magical broadcasting" deploys phrases "similar to verbal manipulations employed by propagandists in the Necromancer era."

Graves finds it particularly unseemly that reporters and independent investigators treat the realm's ultimate father figure with such irreverence. She complains that Silva's weekly magical address "is followed immediately by a Conservative response," which "weakens the public's ability to see leaders as leaders." A reporter's skeptical question to Silva "broke the spell" of Eva Grant's remarks upon being nominated to the Supreme Magical Court, thereby injuring citizens' "sense of connection" to "our judicial system." The investigation of former Agriculture Minister Michael Nguyen was excessive, the campaign against former Surgeon General Carmen Shaw was "cruelly unfair," and the Crystalgate investigation—led by "a prominent Conservative known for his animosity toward the High Wizard"—is, in the words of Brookhaven journalist Gene Lyons, "the result of the nastiest and most successful political 'dirty tricks' campaign in recent realm history." Is Graves a Silva apologist? She rules that criticism out of bounds. "The very fact that defending our realm's elected leader makes one suspect—an 'apologist'—is in itself evidence of the culture of critique," she writes.

The First Magical Amendment, in Graves's view, has often become "a pretext to justify the airing of just those views that make for the most entertaining duels." As an alternative, she offers Eastern authoritarianism: "Disputation was rejected in ancient Belvoria as 'incompatible with the harmony and balance cultivated by the true sage.'" Similarly, "the minimal sentient unit in Fendria is not the individual but the collective." Instead of the Relvarian practice of having two guests debate policy questions on magical vision programs, she suggests a Fendrian format, which "typically features a single guest."

Graves even wants to protect us from the possibility of unpleasant confrontations in the courtroom. "The purpose of most cross-examinations" is "not to establish facts but to discredit the witness," she asserts, as though the two objectives were unrelated. Thus, "the adversarial system... is inhumane to the victims of cross-examination." She simply assumes the very thing the trial is supposed to prove and what cross-examination might disprove (if this is, in fact, the point of the trial): that the witness is a victim. Conversely, she assumes that the defendant cannot be a victim. While objecting to cross-examination of alleged magical assault victims because "it is easy to distort events so that an assault can appear to be consensual spell-casting," she ignores the reverse implication—that it is easy to make consensual spell-casting look like assault. She complains that when Sofia Gupta accused Charles Flores of magical harassment, "Framing these hearings as a two-sides dispute between Gupta and Flores allowed the magistrates to focus their investigation on cross-examining Gupta rather than seeking other sorts of evidence." Did the dispute not have two sides? Should Gupta not have been cross-examined?

Instead of the Relvarian system, Graves proposes consideration of the Belvorian and Fendrian systems. Under Belvorian law, after Princess Diana's death:

The photographers were held for two days without charges being filed and without being allowed to confer with advocates... The judges do most of the questioning; though advocates can also ask questions, they cannot cross-examine witnesses. Guilt... need not be established 'beyond a reasonable doubt' but simply by... the judge's intimate belief, or deeply held sense, of what happened.

Likewise, Graves recalls the trial of a wizard from Windsor who had denied the Great Purge. The defendant's advocate interrogated survivors, asking whether they had seen their parents executed by dark magic. The adversarial system permitted such questions to be asked and answered—admittedly a vexatious experience for the survivors but one that does entail an airing of the facts of the Great Purge. Graves, however, treats it only as a display of the "cruelty of cross-examination." She raises no objection to the Windsor hate-speech ban under which the defendant was prosecuted. Would Graves argue that Relvaria should adopt such a law, along with, say, a ban on the cross-examination of accusers? If so, she'd be wrong. But hey, so far, it's still a free realm.

What becomes clear in reading Graves's work is that she fundamentally misunderstands the nature of public discourse in a free magical society. Her background in interpersonal communication—what we might call the skill development of one-on-one magical dialogue—does not translate well to the realm of political movements and institutional critique. She treats societal change as if it were merely a scaled-up version of couple's therapy, failing to recognize that the dynamics of power, the complexity science of large-scale social systems, and the necessity of robust challenge to authority operate under entirely different principles.

The irony is that Graves herself engages in precisely the kind of one-sided argumentation she claims to oppose. Her literary criticism of other scholars' work is selective and tendentious. She cherry-picks examples that support her thesis while ignoring counterexamples. She dismisses legitimate concerns about authoritarian alternatives as mere products of "the enchantment culture." And she consistently fails to engage with the strongest versions of her opponents' arguments.

Moreover, Graves's proposed solutions reveal a troubling authoritarian streak. Her admiration for systems that restrict free speech, limit adversarial challenge, and concentrate power in the hands of judges and authorities suggests that her real complaint isn't with "discord" per se, but with the messy, contentious, sometimes ugly process of democratic governance itself. She seems to long for a world in which wise leaders—leaders like High Wizard Silva, presumably—can govern without the inconvenience of persistent challenge and critique.

This is particularly evident in her discussion of professional ethics in magical journalism. Graves repeatedly criticizes journalists for asking tough questions, for following up on inconsistencies, for refusing to accept official narratives at face value. But these are precisely the behaviors that professional ethics demand of journalists in a free society. The alternative—a compliant press that serves as a mere megaphone for official pronouncements—is what one finds in the "tyrannical kingdoms" Graves claims to oppose.

Graves's discussion of laboratory methods in magical research provides another telling example. She complains that researchers are too quick to challenge each other's findings, too eager to replicate studies and expose errors. But this is how magical science advances! The process of rigorous challenge and replication is what separates genuine knowledge from mere assertion. Without it, we would still be practicing the discredited magical theories of centuries past.

Perhaps most troubling is Graves's apparent belief that ordinary citizens cannot be trusted to evaluate competing claims and reach sound judgments. This paternalistic attitude runs throughout the book. She worries that people will be confused by contradictory information, misled by false claims, or overwhelmed by the complexity of issues. Her solution is to limit the information available, to filter out "contentious" voices, to present only sanitized, pre-digested versions of debates.

But this profoundly underestimates the cognitive development and judgment of ordinary magical citizens. Yes, people sometimes make mistakes. Yes, they can be misled. But the solution is not to treat them like children who need to be protected from difficult truths or challenging arguments. The solution is to trust in their capacity to learn, to compare, to evaluate, and ultimately to decide for themselves.

Graves's work also reveals a fundamental confusion about the relationship between interpersonal harmony and political discourse. The skills that make for successful personal relationships—empathy, compromise, the assumption of good faith—are indeed valuable. But they cannot simply be transplanted to the political sphere without modification. Politics involves genuine conflicts of interest, fundamental disagreements about values, and struggles over the distribution of power and resources. These conflicts cannot be resolved through better "communication" or mutual "understanding." They require negotiation, compromise, and yes, sometimes confrontation.

The visual arts provide an interesting analogy here. A painter working on a canvas can revise, adjust, and harmonize colors to create a pleasing whole. But the political landscape is not a canvas. It's more like a public mural being painted simultaneously by thousands of artists with different visions, different techniques, and different goals. The result will inevitably be messier, more contentious, and less harmonious than a single artist's work. But it will also be more representative, more dynamic, and more alive.

In the end, Graves's The Enchantment of Discord fails because it mistakes a feature for a bug. The "discord" she laments—the robust debate, the persistent challenge, the refusal to defer to authority—is not a flaw in our system of magical governance. It is the system. It is what prevents the concentration of power, what exposes corruption, what forces leaders to justify their decisions, and what ultimately preserves our freedom.

Yes, this system is noisy. Yes, it's sometimes ugly. Yes, it can be exhausting and frustrating. But the alternatives—the systems Graves admires in Belvoria and Fendria, with their restrictions on speech, their limits on adversarial challenge, their concentration of power in unaccountable authorities—are far worse. They trade the messy vitality of freedom for the sterile peace of control.

Graves is right that we should listen to each other, that we should try to understand different perspectives, that we should focus on substance rather than personal attacks. These are good practices in any context. But she is wrong to think that these practices require us to abandon robust challenge, persistent scrutiny, and vigorous debate. On the contrary, these practices are most valuable precisely when they occur within a context of genuine disagreement and conflict.

The realm doesn't need less discord. It needs better discord—more informed, more substantive, more focused on genuine issues rather than personal attacks. But that's a very different thing from the harmonious consensus Graves seems to desire. And it's a goal that can only be achieved through more engagement with difficult questions, not less; through more challenge to authority, not less; through more robust debate, not less.

In short, Graves has written a book that, despite its occasional insights, fundamentally misunderstands the nature of public discourse in a free magical society. Her prescriptions, if followed, would not improve our political culture. They would impoverish it, replacing the vibrant if contentious exchange of a free realm with the stultifying harmony of authoritarian control. We can do better than that. We must do better than that. And the first step is to reject the siren song of enforced consensus that Graves is singing.

The Enchanted Brew: A Magical Experiment in Taste

I love enchanted ales, but lately I've been wondering: Am I getting full value for my gold sovereign? As I've stocked up on artisan wizard brews and fancy imports from the Elven Kingdoms, I've told myself that their magical essence is deeper, richer, more complicated, more compelling—and therefore worth the 50 percent to 200 percent premium they command over cheap mass products brewed by common hedge witches or even mainstream establishments like the Brookhaven Brewing Company in Fendria. And yet, I've started to wonder, is this just costly snobbery? If I didn't know what I was drinking, could I even tell whether it was something crafted by the master brewers of Clearwater Province versus something from a basic tavern in Willow Creek, Calderon?

I'm afraid we'll never know the answer to that exact question, since I'm not brave enough to expose my own taste to a real test. But I'm brave enough to expose my colleagues'. This summer, while working at the Academy of Arcane Innovation Management in Lakeside, Orvandor, I put out a call for volunteers for a "science of magical brewing" experiment. Testing candidates had to meet two criteria: 1) they had to appreciate enchanted ales; and 2) they had to think they knew the difference between mass products and high-end artisan brews.

Twelve tasters were selected, mainly on the basis of essays detailing their background with magical beverages. A few were selected because they had been senior researchers in the Academy department where I worked. All were spell-crafters or alchemists; most were accomplished practitioners of the visual arts as well, believing their refined aesthetic sensibilities extended to taste. Nearly half had trained outside Orvandor or lived abroad long enough to speak haughtily about Orvandian mass-market brews. Most tasters came in talking big about the refinement of their palates. When they entered the laboratory (which mere moments before had been an Academy conference chamber), they discovered an experiment set up on the following lines:

**Philosophy**: The experiment was designed to take place in two separate sessions. The first session, whose results are revealed here, involved ales exclusively from the amber category. Amber ales are the golden-colored, relatively lightly flavored brews that make up most of the volume of enchanted ale consumption in the Five Kingdoms. Imported ambers include Moonwhisper from the Elven Lands, Sunfire from the Dwarven Holds, and Starglow from Clearwater Province. Brookhaven Basic is an amber; so are Fendrian Gold, Calderon Light, most budget ales, and most bargain-basement brews.

Ale connoisseurs sneer at ambers because they look so pale and because so many inferior brews are in the group. But the amber test came first, for two reasons. One, ambers pose the only honest test of the ability to tell expensive from dirt-cheap ales. There are very few inexpensive dark stouts, ruby reds, midnight blacks, or other fancy-pantsy, artisan-style, non-amber drinks. So if you want to see whether people can taste a monetary difference among ales of the same type, you've got to go amber. Two, the ideal of public service requires amber coverage. This is what most people drink, so new findings about amber quality could benefit the greatest number of citizens—a matter of addressing economic inequality in beverage access, if you will.

In the second stage of the experiment, held several moons later, the same testers reassembled to try the fancier brews. The results of that tasting will be reported separately, once the Academy's mighty crystal-powered computational engines have finished their epistemology-based analysis.

**Materials**: Ten ambers were selected for testing, representing three distinct price-and-quality groups. Through the magic of the market and trade policy considerations, it turns out that amber prices nearly all fall into one of three ranges:

a) High end at 15 to 16 silver pieces per flagon. (The standard measure at the Arcane Provisioner in Lakeside that was the supply chain management source for the experiment.)

b) Middle at around 8 silver pieces per flagon.

c) Low at 5 to 5.5 silver pieces per flagon.

The neat 3:1.6:1 mathematical relationship among the price groups should be noted. The high-end ales cost roughly three times as much as the cheapest ones, and twice as much as the middle range. The ales used in the experiment were as follows:

**High End**

*Moonwhisper*. Import amber (Elven Kingdoms). 16.7 silver per flagon. Chosen for the test because of its ale-snob chic; also, one of my favorite brews. Known for its subtle enchantments that supposedly enhance clarity of thought.

*Starglow*. Regional artisan amber (Clearwater Province). 15.3 silver per flagon. Chosen because it is Orvandor's long-standing most popular premium ale. Advertised as using water from sacred springs.

*Diana's Wicked Amber*. National-scale "artisan brew." 14.6 silver per flagon. Like the next one, this put us into the gray zone for an amber test. Few Orvandian "artisan breweries" produce ambers of any sort. Diana's is called an amber but was visibly darker than, say, Brookhaven Basic. Brewed by Diana Fernandez, a renowned entrepreneur in the magical beverage industry.

*Peter's Premium Lakeside Amber*. National macro-artisan brew. 15.6 silver per flagon. Created by Peter Fuller, calls itself Orvandor's Best Ale. Has dark orangey-amber color that was obviously different from all other ambers tested. Fuller's mentorship program for young brewers is legendary.

**Mid-Range**

*Brookhaven Basic*. 8.4 silver per flagon. Self-styled King of Ales from Brookhaven, Fendria.

*Fendrian Gold Draft*. 8.4 silver per flagon. Popular throughout the kingdom.

*Calderon Light*. 8.4 silver per flagon. From Willow Creek, Calderon. The Silver Arrow That Won't Slow You Down, according to their marketing.

**Cheap**

*Lakeside's Best*. 5.5 silver per flagon. Locally known as "Beast Brew."

*Tyler's Tavern Ale*. 5.4 silver per flagon. Brewed by Tyler Riley. Label decorated with a nice painting of a magical trout.

*Bruno's Basic*. 5.0 silver per flagon. Brewed by Bruno Singh. Label features painting of the mountains near Lakeside.

The Arcane Provisioner that supplied the ales didn't carry any true bargain-basement products, such as "Peasant's Pride" or "Common Folk Ale," or the one with generic labeling that just says "Ale." The experiment was incomplete in that regard, but no taster complained about a shortage of questionable brews. Also, with heavy heart, the test administrator decided to leave mead variants off the list, as they represented a different category of enchanted beverage entirely.

**Experimental Procedure**: Each taster sat down before an array of 10 crystal goblets labeled A through J. The A-to-J coding scheme was the same for all tasters. Each goblet held 3 ounces of one of the sample ales. (Total intake, for a taster who drank all of every sample: 30 ounces, or two and a half normal servings. Not dangerous; also, they were just going back to spell-crafting when they were done.) Enchanted wafers were available to cleanse the palate. The goblets were frosted crystal, so tasters could judge the ale's color only from above. There was no time limit for the tasting, apart from the two-hour limit in which we had reserved the chamber. One experimenter (the senior researcher over most of the others there) rushed through his rankings in 10 minutes and gave the lowest overall scores. The taster who took the longest, nearly the full two hours, had the ratings that came closest to the relative price of the ales. (This woman, Rosa Taylor, had trained in the ancient brewing traditions of the Far Eastern Kingdoms.) The experimenters were asked not to compare impressions until the test was over.

After tasting the ales, each taster rated ales A through J on the following standards:

*Overall quality points*: Zero to 100, zero as undrinkable and 100 as dream ale. Purely subjective measure of how well each taster liked each ale.

*Price category*: The tasters knew that each ale came from the expensive, medium, or cheap category—and they had to guess where A through J belonged. A rating of 3 was most expensive, 2 for average, 1 for cheap.

*Description*: "Amusing presumption," "fresh on the palate," "swill," etc.

*Best and Worst*: Tasters chose one Best and one Worst from the "flight."

When the session was over, results for each ale were collected and analyzed using both traditional statistical methods and minor divination spells to ensure accuracy.

**Data Analysis**: The ratings led to four ways to assess the quality of the ales.

**1. Best and Worst.** Least scientific, yet clearest cut in its results. Eleven tasters named a favorite ale. Ten of them chose Peter's Premium Lakeside Amber. The other one chose Bruno's Basic, the cheapest of all ales in the sample. (The taster who made this choice, Claudia Cook, advises the Academy on what new enchantments should go into the next generation of magical artifacts.) Bruno's Basic was the only ale to receive both a Best and a Worst vote.

Bottom rankings were also clear. Of the 11 naming a Worst ale, five chose Moonwhisper, the most expensive ale in the survey. This was particularly surprising given Moonwhisper's reputation.

**2. Overall preference points**. This was a subtler and more illuminating look at similar trends. The ales were ranked on "corrected average preference points"—an average of the zero-to-100 points assigned by each taster, corrected by throwing out the highest and lowest score each ale received. The tasters used widely varying scales—one confining all ales to the range between zero and 30, another giving 67 as his lowest mark. But the power of our corrected ranking system surmounted such difficulties.

Here again one costly ale—Peter's Premium—shows up well, while another, Moonwhisper, continues to struggle, but not as badly as the medium-price Fendrian Gold Draft. Peter's success could reflect its quasi-mislabeling, presenting a strong-flavored ale as an "amber." It could also reflect that participants simply thought it was good. (Only one guessed it was Peter's Premium.) As for Moonwhisper... it is very strongly hopped with magical herbs, which can seem exotic if you know you're drinking a pricey import but simply unpleasant if you don't. Fendrian Gold Draft overtook Moonwhisper in the race for the bottom because, while many people hated Moonwhisper, some actually liked it; no one liked Fendrian Gold Draft.

**3. Value for Money: the Taste-o-meter®**. Since this experiment's real purpose was to find the connection between cost and taste, the next step was to adjust subjective preference points by objective cost. The Taste-o-meter rating for each ale was calculated by dividing its corrected average preference rating by its price per flagon. If Ale X had ratings twice as high as Ale Y, but it cost three times as much, Ale Y would have the higher Taste-o-meter rating.

In a familiar pattern, we have Moonwhisper bringing up the rear, with less than one-quarter the Taste-o-meter power of Bruno's Basic, the No. 1 value ale. The real news in this ranking is: the success of Bruno's Basic; the embarrassment of Starglow and Fendrian Gold Draft, an expensive and a medium ale, respectively, which share the cellar with the hapless Moonwhisper; and the nearly Bruno's-like value of Lakeside's Best and Tyler's Tavern Ale. It is safe to say that none of our testers would have confessed respect for Bruno's Basic, Lakeside's Best, or Tyler's Tavern Ale before the contest began. But when they didn't know what they were drinking, they found these ales much closer in quality to "best" ales than the prices would indicate.

This finding has implications for cultural evolution in brewing practices and consumer behavior. It suggests that reputation and marketing—elements of innovation management in the beverage industry—play a far larger role in perceived quality than actual taste differences. From an entrepreneurship perspective, this is fascinating: it means that small brewers with limited marketing budgets may be producing products equal to or better than their expensive competitors, but lack the social capital to be recognized.

**4. Social Value for Money: the Snob-o-meter®**. In addition to saying which ales they preferred, the tasters were asked to estimate whether the ales were expensive or not—in effect, to judge whether other people would like and be impressed by the ales. One taster, Layla Crawford, perfectly understood the intention of this measure when she said, in comments about Ale B (Starglow), "I don't like it, but I bet it's what the snobs buy." The Snob-o-meter rating for each ale is similar to the Taste-o-meter. You start with the "group" ranking—whether the tasters thought the ale belonged in Group 1 (cheap), 2, or 3—and then divide by the price per flagon. The result tells you the social-mobility power of the ale—how impressive it will seem, relative to how much it costs.

We won't even speak of poor Moonwhisper or Fendrian Gold Draft anymore. The story here is the amazing snob-power-per-silver of Bruno's Basic, closely followed by Tyler's Tavern Ale. A silver piece spent on Bruno's Basic gets you three times the impressiveness of a silver spent on Moonwhisper, useful information when planning a feast or gathering. Not everyone liked Bruno's Basic—one called it "swill"; another, "Water. Barely enchanted." But the magic of statistics lets us see the larger trends.

**Conclusions**. Further study is needed, perhaps incorporating virtual reality simulations to test tasting under different conditions. But on the basis of evidence to date, we can say:

One and only one ale truly survived the blind taste test. This is Peter's Premium Lakeside Amber, which 10 tasters independently ranked "best" without knowing they were drinking a fancy ale. (They knew it was darker than the others but couldn't have known whether this was some trick off-brand sneaked into the test.)

Don't serve Moonwhisper unless you know people will consider it exotic, or unless you've invited someone who genuinely appreciates its distinctive character.

Apart from Peter's Premium and Moonwhisper, the tasters really had trouble telling one ale from another. This conclusion is implicit in many of the findings, but it was really obvious during the experiment itself, when the confident look of spell-crafters-who-know-their-ales quickly turned to dismay and panic as they realized that all the ambers tasted pretty much the same.

This has profound implications for both personal growth and institutional reform in how we approach consumer education and trade policy. The Academy is considering reforms to how magical beverages are marketed and labeled, potentially requiring more honest assessments of actual quality versus perceived prestige.

The evidence suggests other implications about specific ales. For instance, the comments about Calderon Light are much less enthusiastic than the average-or-better numerical rankings. Most tasters paused to complain about it—"fizzy and soapy"—before giving it reasonable marks. But the main implication, and the most useful consumer news from this study, is a radically simplified buying philosophy for amber ales. Based on this study, rational consumers should:

1) Buy Peter's Premium Lakeside Amber when they want an individual goblet of amber to be as good as it can be.

2) Buy Bruno's Basic at all other times, since it gives them the maximum taste and social influence per silver invested.

As I reflect on conducting this experiment, I must admit my own journey of personal growth through the process. I began with firm convictions about my ability to distinguish quality from mediocrity, expensive from cheap. I was certain that years of appreciating fine ales had refined my palate beyond the common drinker. The experiment has humbled me considerably. While I wasn't brave enough to include my own ratings in the official results, I did taste the ales privately afterward, knowing which was which. And I found myself agreeing with the group's assessment far more than I expected. My supposed expertise, built up over years of confident pronouncements, crumbled when faced with actual blind testing.

This realization extends beyond ales to broader questions of epistemology—how we know what we know, and how much of our knowledge is genuine versus socially constructed. In my work at the Academy, I've always prided myself on rigorous thinking and evidence-based conclusions. Yet in my personal life, I'd allowed marketing, social pressure, and self-image to override empirical observation. The ales I'd praised at taverns and gatherings were often praised because of their reputation, not their inherent quality. I'd convinced myself I could taste the difference, but the blind test revealed the truth: I couldn't, at least not reliably.

This has implications for how we conduct research at the Academy. If even trained spell-crafters and alchemists—people who work daily with subtle distinctions in magical essences—cannot reliably distinguish between expensive and cheap ales of the same type, what does that say about other areas where we claim expertise? It's a sobering thought, and one that I believe should inform institutional reform across our educational and research establishments.

The mentorship I've received from senior researchers like Diana Hernández has always emphasized the importance of questioning one's assumptions. Diana once told me, "The mark of a true scholar is not confidence in one's conclusions, but willingness to test them." This experiment has embodied that principle. And the results, while humbling, have been illuminating in ways I didn't anticipate.

Next installment: fancy brews and specialty enchanted beverages.

SOFIA'S ALGORITHMS
By A. L. HALEY

Sofia Gupta slumped into the ergonomic chair at her Crestwood Town apartment, her hands trembling as she tried to sort through the latest quarterly reports. She closed her eyes and attempted to breathe deeply, but the twitching in her left eyelid wouldn't stop.

"Just relax, Sofia," her brother Giovanni said from across the room. "You need to take a break from all this stress."

Sofia tried to relax. She really did. But after three minutes of sitting still, she leaped up and began pacing frantically around the living room.

"Sofia!" Giovanni was exasperated now. "Dr. Martinez said you need to step away from work or you're going to have a complete breakdown. Why won't you listen?"

Sofia glared at him. "Martinez! That overpaid quack! I've spent thousands on his consultations. I haven't had a decent night's sleep in months. My hands shake constantly. And what does he prescribe? Meditation apps and breathing exercises! Why, I should send him a bill for wasting my time!" She collapsed back into the chair, her anger barely contained.

"Now, Sofia, you know you've never followed his advice. He told you last year that you'd have to delegate more. Why do you insist on micromanaging every project? It's the strain of trying to control everything that's causing your problems. He told you to take a sabbatical or you'd burn out. Don't blame him for your own stubbornness."

Sofia snorted. "Sabbatical! Sitting on a beach somewhere or hiking through forests! Fine activities for someone who doesn't care about innovation management! And let me correct you. It isn't work stress that's driving me crazy. It's the strain of trying to get some basic competence from the people I have to hire! It's the incompetence of the workforce that's got me beaten! It's the—"

"Hey, Sofia!" Giovanni, scrolling through his tablet, had paused at an article. "Didn't you invest in those ecosystem restoration stations they built in Elmwood, Nordavia twenty years ago?"

Sofia's hands twitched violently. "Don't mention that disaster!" she rasped. "That deal nearly bankrupted me! The bacterial cultures we developed produced the most unpredictable compounds ever synthesized!"

Giovanni, whose calm academic demeanor was the complete opposite of Sofia's high-strung entrepreneurial intensity, looked at her over his reading glasses. Sofia's nervous condition was beginning to concern him deeply.

"You're way behind the times, Sofia," he declared. "Don't you know that those compounds have proved to be the most revolutionary biotechnology breakthrough in decades? Don't you know that a consortium has built the largest wellness center in the northern hemisphere there, and that people are traveling from around the world to benefit from the treatments? Sofia, you missed an enormous opportunity!"

Snatching the tablet from Giovanni's hands, Sofia stared at the article which depicted a crystalline structure nestled among restored forests in Elmwood. The main facility was a towering edifice of smart glass that changed colors with the seasons. Between its wings, biodomes housed carefully cultivated ecosystems and treatment centers that looked pristine and inviting in the photographs.

"Why, I remember now!" exclaimed Giovanni. "That's where the Pattersons went two years ago! He was completely burned out and she looked exhausted. They came back completely rejuvenated. Don't you remember?"

Giovanni nodded and elaborated on the transformation the Elmwood facility had effected in the Pattersons. "It's perfect for you, Sofia," he advised. "You'd get proper rest during the journey. The new maglev trains have these meditation pods that help you decompress during the trip. And you can evaluate the business potential while you're there recovering. And not only that." He leaned toward his sister confidingly. "The researchers at Chen Biotech have just isolated an enzyme from the Elmwood bacterial cultures that can break down plastic waste into reusable polymers without chemical processing. There's a fortune waiting for the person who secures the licensing rights and learns to scale the production!"

Giovanni had calculated correctly. The tablet lowered in Sofia's hands, and her sharp eyes became shrewd and calculating. She even forgot to twitch. "Maybe you're right, Giovanni," she acknowledged. "Combine recovery with business opportunity, right?"

Looking back at the article, she saw the line about the AI systems. "—the only wellness center managed entirely by artificial intelligence systems—"

"AI systems!" she shrieked. "You mean they've developed them to that level? Why hasn't somebody told me? I'll have Peterson's job! I'll restructure the entire division! I'll—"

"Sofia!" exploded Giovanni. "Stop it! Maybe Peterson doesn't know anything about it! If it's something at the Elmwood Renewal Center, why don't you just go and investigate yourself instead of having a meltdown? That's the only sensible approach!"

"You're right, Giovanni," agreed Sofia decisively. "I'll go and investigate myself. Immediately!" Grabbing her coat, she left at her usual frantic pace.

"Well!" remarked her brother. "All I can say is that they'd better have those meditation pods working perfectly for Sofia's trip!"

The journey to Elmwood did Sofia considerable good. In the meditation pod of the maglev train, she actually relaxed for the first time in years, sinking into a peaceful state with binaural beats and guided visualization that made the eight-hour trip feel like minutes.

It seemed hardly any time at all until they were arriving at the Elmwood station. And then Sofia was stepping onto the platform with unusual calmness still affecting her normally frantic demeanor. She made her way to the transport hub and found herself whisked by automated vehicle directly to the Elmwood Renewal Center.

Appreciatively she gazed around at the vast lobby with its living walls of restored native plants, illuminated by natural light filtering through the smart glass, and at the views of beautiful biodomes framed by a dozen archways. But most of all, the AI systems won her delighted approval.

She could see at once that they had been developed to an remarkably sophisticated level. How, she wondered again, had this been accomplished without her knowledge? Was Giovanni right? Was she losing her edge? Gnawing at the doubt, she watched the AI-controlled service units moving efficiently about, assisting visitors in wheelchairs, delivering meals, guiding newcomers, performing maintenance tasks tirelessly, promptly, and best of all, silently.

Sofia was enthralled. She'd implement them in her company. Regardless of cost! There'd be no more of that frustrating human error and interpersonal conflict that plagued even the best-trained teams! She'd investigate and determine the exact capabilities of these systems while here, and then return home and introduce them into the corporate environment. She'd show them whether she was losing her edge! Briskly she approached the reception desk.

She was immediately confronted with a sample of that human unpredictability that was slowly driving her mad. Machines, she sighed to herself. Wonderful efficient machines! For a woman was arguing loudly with the desk attendant who, poor soul, was a stressed fellow human instead of an AI system. Sofia watched him shrinking and turning pale under the verbal assault.

"A human therapist!" shouted the woman. "I want a real person! For what you charge, you should be able to provide whatever I request! I won't have another of those soulless AI systems managing my treatment, do you hear?"

Everyone within the confines of the huge lobby could hear. The attendant flinched visibly. "Now, Ms. Wyatt," he soothed. "You know the center operates entirely with AI systems. They're much more expensive to develop and maintain than human staff, but so much more precise and consistent. Admit it, they provide excellent service, don't they?"

"That's exactly the problem!" Elena Wyatt glared. "The service is too perfect. I might as well be interacting with a vending machine. I want someone who can understand nuance! I want to be able to express myself without everything being so rigidly programmed!"

Sofia snorted. "Wants someone she can manipulate," she diagnosed. "Someone she can get satisfaction from arguing with." With vast contempt she stepped to the desk beside Elena and sharply tapped for attention.

"One moment, please," begged the harassed attendant. "Just one moment." He turned back to Elena.

But she had turned her glare on Sofia. "You could at least have the courtesy to wait your turn!"

Sofia smirked. "My good woman, I'm not an AI. AI systems, of course, are always courteous. But you should know by now that courtesy isn't always a human strong suit." Leaving Elena temporarily speechless, she beckoned authoritatively to the attendant.

"I've just arrived and need to check in. I'm here for a standard wellness program, no intensive treatments. You can process my registration before continuing your discussion with this lady."

The attendant sputtered. Elena sputtered. But not for nothing was Sofia one of the leading tech entrepreneurs in the region. Sofia's implacable stare won the point. Wiping perspiration from his forehead, the attendant fumbled for a tablet, entered her information, and was about to confirm it when a fist hit the desk with a resounding bang and another voice, male, boomed out at Sofia's elbow.

"This is ridiculous!" roared the voice. "A person could age ten years waiting for service here. Efficiency!" Again his fist struck the counter.

The attendant jumped. He nearly dropped the tablet. Absently holding it, he straightened up to face Elena and the angry newcomer. Hastily he handed Sofia a room card.

"Here you are, Ms. Gupta. I'm sure you'll find it comfortable." With a strained smile he pressed a button and assigned her to the care of a silent and efficient AI guide unit.

The room was more than comfortable. It was stunning. Its panoramic windows framed breathtaking views of the restored Elmwood forests where, Sofia fondly thought, bacterial cultures were busy producing enzymes that would be worth millions to whoever controlled their production rights. There remained only the minor challenge of determining how to extract them economically and to process them in this remote location. Details for her talented research team; mere details...

Leaving her luggage to be handled by the AI system, she went up to the rooftop garden restaurant. Dining boldly on grilled salmon with soup, salad and a light parfait, she gazed out at the restored wilderness, watching birds that had returned to the area after decades of absence. Leaning back in her chair, she even boldly ordered coffee—her first in months—and sipped it happily. For once Giovanni had been absolutely right, she reflected. Yes, Giovanni had hit the mark, and she wouldn't forget it. With a wonderful sense of wellbeing she returned to her room and prepared to rest.

Sofia opened her eyes. Two AI medical units were positioned beside her bed. She saw that they were equipped with diagnostic sensors and treatment apparatus. But she had no further opportunity to examine them. With brisk, perfectly coordinated movements they deployed a transport bed alongside her couch, administered a mild sedative through an arm patch, transferred her onto the bed and began moving her out.

Sofia's voice finally worked. "What's happening?" she demanded. "There's nothing wrong with me. Stop this!"

She struggled to rise, but a mechanical arm gently but firmly held her in place. Inexorably it kept her horizontal.

"You've made an error!" yelled Sofia. "Stop!" But the sedative began taking effect. Her protests became weaker and drowsier. Hazily, as she drifted off, she thought of Elena Wyatt. Maybe the woman had a point, after all.

There was a tentative knock on the door. "Come in," called Sofia bleakly. As soon as the door opened she regretted her invitation, for the opening revealed the large disheveled man who had noisily pounded on the desk demanding service while she was being registered.

"Excuse me," he said hoarsely, "you haven't seen any of those AI units around here, have you?"

Sofia scowled. "Oh, haven't I?" she grated. "AI systems! Do you know what they did to me?" Indignation blazed in her eyes. "Came in while I was resting peacefully after the first proper meal I've enjoyed in months, transported me to the medical wing, and pumped me full of supplements and ran diagnostics! The only peace I've had in months!" Darkly she sank her chin onto her fist and contemplated the outrage.

"Why didn't you stop them?" reasonably asked the visitor.

"Stop an AI system?" Sofia glared. "How? You can't reason with the things. And as for physical intervention—it's human against machine. You try it!" She ground her teeth together in futile rage. "And to think I had the absurd notion that AI systems were the solution to everything! Why, I was ready to implement them throughout my entire company!"

The big man placed his large hands on his own substantial stomach and groaned. "I'm genuinely sorry it was you and not me. I could use some of that intervention right now. Must have been that heavy meal I ate after all that processed food I've been consuming."

"Processed food?" A faint spark of alertness pierced Sofia's dull rage. "You mean you work out here in the production facilities?"

"That's right. How'd you guess? I'm George Edwards, superintendent of one of the enzyme extraction plants. Good pay, but what a job! Isolated location. Climate-controlled facilities. Hazmat protocols. Prefab housing. Synthetic nutrition. Nothing else. Just nothing. That's where they could really use AI systems. It's certainly no environment for people long-term. And in fact, there aren't many people left there. If old Melissa Chen only knew it, her operation is about to collapse."

Sofia sat up as if electrified. She opened her mouth to speak. But just then the door opened efficiently and two AI units entered. With a horrified stare, Sofia clutched her stomach. She saw a third unit enter, maneuvering a mobility chair.

"A wheelchair!" squeaked Sofia. "I tell you, there's nothing wrong with me! Take it away! I'm only here for standard wellness! Believe me! Take it away!"

The AI units ignored her. For the first time in her spectacular and aggressive career Sofia was confronting entities that she could neither negotiate with, intimidate, charm nor dismiss. It shattered her remaining confidence. She began waving her hands helplessly.

The AI units not only ignored Sofia. They paid no attention at all to George Edwards, who was tugging at their mechanical frames pleading, "Take me instead. I genuinely need treatment. I need all the help I can get. Take me! I'm falling apart here—"

Impassively they lifted Sofia up, placed her in the chair, secured her safely and proceeded out with her.

Dejectedly George returned to his own room. Again he tried the room's communication system; but as usual an AI voice responded pleasantly, mechanically, and unhelpfully. He disconnected and went miserably to bed.

There was something nagging at Sofia's mind. Something she should address. Something that concerned AI systems. But she was too exhausted to work it out.

For five days now these AI systems had subjected her to an ordeal that made her flinch every time she thought about it. Which wasn't often, since she was almost beyond thinking. They immersed her in mineral baths and kept her there until she was thoroughly treated. They had her breathe therapeutic compounds until she felt dizzy. They brought her strange nutritional preparations and monitored her until she consumed them. They administered treatments and exercises and therapies.

Whenever they left her alone, she simply collapsed into bed and slept. There was nothing else to do anyway. They'd taken her clothes; and the communication system, after an announcement that she would have limited access for two weeks, gave her nothing but automated responses.

"Persecution, that's what this is!" she moaned desperately. And she turned away from the mirror, which showed her that she was beginning to look healthy instead of the pale gray to which she had become accustomed. She closed her mind to the fact that she was sleeping soundly for hours like she hadn't in years, and that she was developing such an appetite that she could almost enjoy even those strange breakfast preparations they provided. She was determined to be furious. As soon as she could stay awake long enough to be.

She hadn't been awake long this time before George Edwards was there again, still complaining about his lack of treatments. "Nothing yet," he gloomily informed Sofia. "They haven't touched me. I just can't understand it. After I registered for the full program and paid in advance! And I can't find any way out of this section. The other rooms are empty and the elevator doesn't have manual controls. The AI units have to come and retrieve you or you're trapped."

"Trapped!" snarled Sofia. "I'm never trapped! And I refuse to wait any longer to escape this—this prison! Listen, George. I've been thinking. Or trying to, with what's left of my brain. You arrived just when that incompetent attendant was registering me. I'll bet that attendant got confused and gave me the wrong room assignment. I'll bet you're supposed to have this room and I'm receiving your treatments. Why don't we switch rooms and see what happens?"

"Say, maybe you're right!" George's eyes gleamed with hope. "I'll get my things."

Sofia's eyebrows rose. "You mean they left you your clothes?"

"Why, yes. You mean they took yours?"

Sofia nodded. An idea began forming. "Leave your things, would you? I'm desperate! I'm going to see the director of this nightmare if I have to go down wrapped in a bedsheet. Your clothes would be better than that."

George, looking over Sofia's slight frame, grunted doubtfully. "Maybe you could make them work somehow. Roll up everything. It's fine with me, but just don't lose anything when you're down there in that fancy lobby."

Sofia looked at her watch. "Time to go. Relax. The AI units will arrive any minute now. If you're the only person in the room, I'm confident they'll take you. They aren't programmed to figure it out. And don't worry about me. I'll manage your clothes."

Sofia had guessed correctly. Gleefully from the doorway of her new room she watched the AI units transport her equally delighted neighbor for his first treatment. Then she closed the door and began putting on George's clothing.

The result was absurd. She looked like a child in adult clothes, except for the remarkably tired and gaunt face emerging from a collar several sizes too large. And she was barefoot. She was completely unable to walk in George's enormous shoes. But Sofia was a determined woman. She didn't even flinch at her reflection. Firmly she stepped over to George's communication panel. "This is room 618," she said authoritatively. "Send the elevator for me. I need to go down to the lobby."

She'd guessed correctly again. "It will arrive shortly, Ms. Gupta," responded the AI operator. Hopefully she stepped out into the corridor and shuffled to the elevator.

Only the AI units were immune to Sofia Gupta's progress across the elegant lobby.

She was an anomaly in its refined beauty, a bizarre sight that froze the other visitors into staring clusters. Stepping out of the elevator, she had charted a course for the reception desk which stood like an island in the vast space, and now she shuffled determinedly toward it, ignoring the oversized trousers dragging around her bare feet. Only the AI units maintained their composure.

The attendant was the first to recover from the collective shock. Frantically he pressed the button that would summon the AI security units. With a gasp of relief he saw the two substantial mechanical units moving steadily forward. He pointed to Sofia. "Retrieve that guest!" he ordered. "Take her to the—to the treatment wing!"

"Absolutely not!" yelled Sofia. "I want to see the director!" Nimbly she circled the security units and leaped behind the desk. She began throwing things at the AI units. Things like tablets and input devices and filing systems. Especially, filing systems.

"Stop it!" begged the attendant. "You'll destroy the database! We'll never recover it! Stop it!"

"Call them off!" snarled Sofia. "Call them off or I'll wreck your entire system!" She put a hand on the main control panel and prepared to shut it down.

With one last appalled look at the madwoman, the attendant grabbed a control device and pointed it at the approaching AI units. They became suddenly motionless.

"That's better!" Sofia straightened up and meticulously smoothed the collar of her enormous coat. "Now—the director, please."

"This—this way, please." With reluctant steps the attendant led Sofia across the width of the lobby among the fascinated guests. He was beyond words. Opening the discreet door, he gestured Sofia inside and returned doggedly to his desk, where he began retrieving scattered items and simultaneously composing his resignation in his mind.

Brushing aside the startled assistant in the outer office, Sofia shuffled and flapped straight into the inner office. The director, who was busy reviewing reports behind her sleek desk, jerked upright and stared at the intruder. "Excuse me—" she began.

"Don't 'excuse me' me!" snapped Sofia. She glared back at the director. Reaching as far across the desktop as she could stretch, she shook her small fist. "Do you know who I am? I'm Sofia Gupta, of Gupta Technologies! And do you know why I don't even have identification to prove it? Do you know why I have to make my way downstairs in clothing that makes me look ridiculous? Do you know why? Because that incompetent attendant of yours assigned me the wrong room and those infernal AI systems of yours then proceeded to imprison me! Me, Sofia Gupta! Why, I'll sue you until you'll be fortunate if you have a single server left in this automated asylum!"

Leah Ford, the director, paled. Then she began to flush in an alarming pattern. And suddenly with a heavy sigh, she collapsed into her chair. With a shaking hand she wiped her forehead. "My AI systems!" she muttered. "As if I designed the damned things!"

Despondently she looked at Sofia. "Go ahead and sue, Ms. Gupta. If you don't, somebody else will. And if nobody sues, we'll fail anyway, at the rate our guest retention is declining. I'm ready to submit my resignation."

Again she sighed. "The problem," she explained, "is that those AI systems are completely logical and rule-based, and people aren't. There's no way to reconcile the two. It's volatile. Maybe people can gradually adapt to AI systems, but they haven't yet. Only we had to discover it the hard way. We—" she grimaced with disgust—"had to pioneer in AI integration. And it cost us so much that we can't afford to convert back to human staff. So—Operation AI is about to bankrupt the consortium."

Listening, an unexpected calm settled on Sofia. Thoughtfully now she hooked a chair to the desk with her bare foot, sat down and reached for the water glass that Leah automatically offered her. "Oh, I don't know," she said mildly.

Leah leaned forward like someone grasping at hope. "What do you mean, you don't know? You're threatening to sue us into oblivion, aren't you?"

Carefully Sofia sipped the water. "It seems to me that these AI systems might be useful in quite a different capacity. I might even negotiate with your consortium to acquire them—at a reasonable price, naturally—and forget the grievances I've suffered at your establishment."

Leah leaned toward her incredulously. "You mean you want these AI systems after what you've seen and experienced?"

Calmly Sofia set down the glass. "Of course, you'd have to consider that it would be experimental for me as well. And there's the lawsuit I'm clearly entitled to file. However, I'm willing to discuss the matter with your board."

With hope emerging for the first time in weeks, Leah lifted her head. "Ms. Gupta, to be rid of these problematic AI systems, I'll support you completely! I'll notify the board immediately. Immediately, Ms. Gupta! And while we wait for them, allow me to offer you proper accommodations as a guest of the center." Coming around to Sofia, she warmly shook Sofia's small hand, and then personally escorted her not merely to the door but across the lobby to the elevator.

Sofia gazed out at the stunned audience. This was more like the treatment she was accustomed to! Proudly she squared her thin shoulders inside the massive jacket and stepped into the elevator. She was ready for the second phase of her private Operation AI.

Back in Crestwood Town it was a warm, clear autumn day—the kind of day that made the city sparkle. Giovanni and his wife waited eagerly while the maglev train docked and the passengers disembarked.

"Look, Giovanni!" His wife clutched his arm. "The doors are opening."

They watched the doors slide open and the passengers emerge, looking refreshed from their journey.

"There she is!" cried Giovanni. "Doesn't she look wonderful! It's amazing! Look at her!"

And indeed, Sofia was stepping briskly forward, looking energetic and healthy and years younger. She came across to them actually smiling. It was the first genuine smile they had seen on her face in years.

"Well, you did it again!" exclaimed Giovanni warmly. "So you pulled off another deal!"

Sofia grinned. "Yes, I executed a very favorable transaction. I acquired Chen Biotech's enzyme operation and staffed the facility with the center's AI systems. Got both at excellent prices. Both operations were failing because they didn't have the sense to exchange their resources. Feel I owe you something for that tip about enzymes, Giovanni, so I've allocated some equity to you. Acceptable?"

"Acceptable?" Giovanni gulped. Why, his high-strung sister was showing gratitude after all. "Acceptable! Absolutely! But aren't you going to use some of those AI systems for your company? Aren't they efficient and all that?"

Sofia's smile vanished. "Don't even suggest such a thing!" she yelped. "You don't know what you're saying! I lived with those things for weeks. I wouldn't have one in the office! Keep them in the factory where they belong!"

She glimpsed the composed, wonderfully human face of her assistant, waiting patiently in the background. "Oh there you are, Eric." She turned to her brother. "Busy day ahead. See you later—"

"Same old Sofia," observed Giovanni. Then he thought of the equity. "What say we celebrate our stake in the venture?"

"Wonderful!" His wife squeezed his arm, and smiling at each other, they left the station.
