synthetic_story:
The Reluctant Innovators
By A. MITCHELL

The young woman sat rigidly in the conference room chair, her fingers drumming an anxious rhythm on the polished table. She studied the grain of the wood, traced invisible patterns on its surface, and adjusted her collar three times in as many minutes.

"I've been offered the lead position on the first autonomous vehicle testing facility in the Martian colonies," she said.

The older woman across from her set down her tablet and regarded her thoughtfully. "It's remarkable, isn't it? The new atmospheric processors make it possible now. There was a time when we couldn't even dream of surface facilities."

The young woman looked frustrated.

"I don't think I want to accept," she said quickly. "I don't think I want to spend three years there."

The older woman leaned back in her chair and folded her hands. "You mean you'd miss Earth—the people you've worked with, the familiar routines that have shaped your career here. You're worried the excitement would fade and you'd grow to resent Mars."

The young woman nodded miserably. "Yes, exactly that."

"Is there something else?"

The young woman's fingers found the table grain fascinating again. Finally, in a barely audible voice: "Yes."

"Someone special?"

A slight nod confirmed this.

The older woman smiled gently. "You know, of course, that the Commission's position is that research facilities should eventually be staffed by committed partnerships. Once it becomes feasible."

"But that could take years!" the young woman protested.

"It could—but sometimes these things happen faster than expected. And the goal makes it worthwhile."

"I suppose, but—"

The older woman's smile deepened. "Still the reluctant innovators," she murmured.

---

Grace Osborne stared at the communications terminal.

Four years at the Blackwood research station and they didn't want her to come back.

Four years developing autonomous vehicle systems for Martian terrain and they assumed she'd gladly stay longer. Just increase her compensation package, the standard corporate logic. They probably thought she'd found her calling here.

Sure, she loved it. Recycled water, protein paste, vitamin supplements, and filtered air until your body felt like a chemistry experiment. Life in a cramped habitat module where you could walk twenty paces before hitting a wall. Their glorious frontier outpost with none of Earth's comforts—a fascinating place where real showers were rationed, fresh food was a memory, and the low gravity played havoc with your bone density.

And for triple her salary they expected her to stay another two years. Maybe three. She should probably feel honored by the opportunity.

The terminal chimed again, demanding a response.

She typed: "Declined."

Silence, then an angry burst of text demanding reconsideration. Grace muted the notifications and turned toward the sleeping quarters.

The message hadn't woken anyone. They were all still asleep in their individual pods. Justin Wood, the geologist, was snoring peacefully in the lower tier. Zhang Williams, the poor kid assigned to stopover duty, was muttering in his sleep. Leo Potter wore that expression of perfect contentment, dreaming of home. Patrick Ford and David Rice lay perfectly still, sleeping lightly as always.

Lord, Grace thought, I'll be happy to see some different faces.

"What did they want?" Leo had one eye open, looking curious.

"They wanted me to stay until the next relief transport arrives," Grace whispered back.

"What did you tell them?"

She shrugged. "No."

"Diplomatic as always," someone else whispered. It was Patrick, sitting up in his pod. "If it were me, I'd have given them a detailed explanation of where they could file that request."

The others were stirring now, except for Zhang who had his back turned and seemed determined to sleep through everything.

Justin rubbed his face sleepily. "Frustrated, aren't you?"

"Somewhat. Who wouldn't be?"

"Don't take it personally. The board members have never been to Blackwood. They don't understand what it's like. They're just trying to retain a valuable employee."

"Trying to retain a valuable employee," Grace said sarcastically. "They can keep trying."

"They think you've made a home here," Patrick said.

"Why don't you all shut up until morning?" Zhang was awake now, looking bitter. "Some of us still have to stay here, you know. Some of us aren't leaving today."

No, Grace thought, some of us aren't leaving. You aren't. And Martinez isn't either. Only Martinez isn't ever going back.

Leo pointed toward Zhang's pod, held a finger to his lips, and walked quietly to the small food preparation unit. It was his turn for breakfast duty.

The others began organizing their spaces, preparing for their last day of work at Blackwood. In a few hours they'd be relieved by members of the Fourth research group and they'd be on their way back to Earth.

And that includes me, Grace thought. I'm going home. I'm finally going home.

She walked to the one small observation window. It was morning—Mars's morning—and she suppressed a shiver. The Sun's rays were striking the far edge of Valles Marineris, casting long shadows across the rust-colored landscape. The rest was still shrouded in that peculiar Martian darkness, a jumble of red dust and jagged rock formations that made the Badlands look like paradise.

Two hundred meters from the habitat she could make out the small memorial cairn and the simple metal marker, constructed from spare parts and welded together. You could still see the rover tracks in the fine dust where the group had gathered around it. That had been more than two years ago, but there was barely any wind to erase those tracks. They'd persist for decades.

That's what happened to people like Martinez, Grace thought. On Mars, one mistake could be your last.

Leo returned with the coffee. Grace took a cup, grimaced, and forced herself to finish it. It had been in storage so long the flavor was more memory than reality.

Patrick was warming his hands on his cup, looking contemplative. Justin and David were pulling on their environment suits, getting ready to go outside. Zhang was still in his pod, trying to ignore them.

"Think we should check with the orbital station to see if they've departed yet?" Leo asked.

"I contacted them on the last call," Grace said. "The relief transport left twelve hours ago. They should arrive"—she checked her chronometer—"in about seven hours."

"Grace, you know, I've been thinking," Patrick said quietly. "You've been here twice as long as the rest of us. What's the first thing you're going to do when you get back?"

It hit them then. Justin and David looked blank for a moment and slowly found equipment cases to sit on. The tops of their suits were still hanging on the wall rack. Leo lowered his coffee cup and looked serious. Even Zhang glanced up expectantly.

"I don't know," Grace said slowly. "I guess I was trying not to think about it. None of us have. We've been like children waiting so long for something that we can't believe it when it's finally about to happen."

Leo nodded in agreement. "I haven't been here four years like you, but I understand what you mean." He warmed to the topic as the realization deepened. "What are you really going to do?"

"Nothing spectacular," Grace said, smiling. "I'm going to rent a place in Goldfield Village, get some actual music—not synthesized—and just watch real people living real lives. Then I think I'll visit someone."

"Who's the someone?" Patrick asked.

Grace grinned. "Just someone. What about you, Patrick?"

"Well, I'm going to be practical. First, I'll submit all my geological survey data to the Commission. Then I'm going to sell my story to a media production company and then—well, then I think I'll get properly drunk!"

Everyone laughed and Grace turned to Leo.

"How about you?"

Leo looked solemn. "Like Patrick, I'll fulfill my obligations to the expedition first. Then I'm going home to see my husband."

They were quiet. "I thought all expedition members had to be unattached," Patrick said.

"They are. And I understand the reasoning—professional ethics and all that. But who could pass up the compensation package the Commission offered?"

"If I had to do it again? Not me," Patrick said promptly.

They laughed. Someone said: "Play your music file, Grace. Today's the day for it."

The audio file was an old recording Grace had brought with her when she'd arrived with the First group. The quality was degraded from multiple copies, but the song was meaningful.

"Homeward Bound" by an ancient folk artist.

They played it twice. They were beginning to feel it now, Grace thought. They were actually going home and the reality was starting to sink in.

"You know, Grace," Patrick said, "Blackwood won't be the same without you. We'll look at Mars from Earth and it just won't have the same appeal."

"Like they say in the old movies," David said, "you never had it so good. You found a home here."

The others joined in the gentle teasing and Grace smiled. Yesterday or a week ago they couldn't have done this. She had been here too long and resented it too much.

The mood quieted after a while and Justin and David finished suiting up. They still had atmospheric readings to take before they left. Patrick was right after them. There was a rock formation he wanted to sample and some strata he needed to photograph.

And time went faster when you kept busy.

Grace stopped them at the airlock. "Remember to check your suits for breaches," she warned. "And verify your oxygen tank levels."

Patrick looked annoyed. "I've gone out at least seven hundred times," he said, "and you check me every single time."

"And I'd check you seven hundred more," Grace said. "It takes only one mistake. And watch for unstable ground. Step through one of those weak spots and that's it."

Patrick sighed. "Grace, you watch us like we're children. You verify our suits, you mediate our disputes, you ensure we're not bored and that we stay healthy and productive. I think you'd tie our shoes if we couldn't manage it ourselves. But someday, Grace old friend, you're going to discover that your team can handle themselves!"

But he checked his suit for breaches and verified his tank level before he left.

Only Leo and Grace remained in the habitat. Leo was at the work station, carefully cataloging some bacterial specimens.

"I never knew you were married," Grace said.

Leo didn't look up. "There wasn't much point in discussing it. You just end up dwelling on it and wanting—and there's nothing you can do. You talk about it and it just intensifies the longing."

"He let you go without objection?"

"No, he didn't object. But I don't think he wanted me to go, either." He laughed slightly. "At least I hope he didn't."

They were silent for a while. "What do you miss most, Grace?" Leo asked. "I know what we said earlier, but I mean genuinely."

Grace thought for a moment. "I think I miss the weather," she said quietly. "Real weather. Rain and snow and wind that isn't trying to kill you. Trees that change with the seasons. I think, when I get back, I'd like to stand in a thunderstorm and just feel the rain on my face."

She paused, feeling self-conscious. Leo's expression was encouraging. "And then I think I'd like to go to a crowded place—maybe Eastwood in Prandoria—and just watch people. Or maybe go to a live performance and smell the popcorn and feel the energy of a real audience in the dark."

She examined her hands. "I think what I miss most is humanity in all its complexity—complexity science could never fully capture. All kinds of people. People struggling with applied ethics in their daily lives. People who wouldn't know strategic planning from urban planning. And people who wouldn't care. We're hundreds of millions of kilometers from everything familiar, Leo, and what I miss most is the messy, beautiful chaos of human society."

"Someone special back home?" Leo asked almost casually.

"Yes."

"You're not like Zhang. You've never mentioned it."

"Same reason you didn't mention your husband. You get to thinking about it."

Leo sealed the specimen container. "Going to get married when you return?"

Grace was at the window again, staring out at the desolate landscape. "We hope to."

"Settle down somewhere and build a life together?"

Grace nodded.

"That's the only real future," Leo said.

He stored the container and joined her at the window. Grace moved over so they could both look out.

"Grace." Leo hesitated. "What happened to Martinez?"

"She died," Grace said. "She was brilliant, completely dedicated to the research. Being on Mars was the opportunity of a lifetime. She was so focused on the work that she forgot the fundamentals—like how to stay alive. The day before the Second group arrived, she went out to complete some experiments. She forgot to check for suit breaches and whether her tank valve was fully closed. We couldn't reach her in time."

"She had her communicator?"

"Yes. It worked perfectly. We heard everything she was thinking at the end."

Leo's face was expressionless. "What's your real job here, Grace? Why does someone have to stay for stopover?"

"Many reasons, Leo. You can't bring in a whole relief crew and let them take over without guidance. They need to know where you left off. They need to know where equipment is, how systems work, what hazards to watch for. And because you've been here two years and understand the environment, you have to monitor them to ensure they stay alive despite their inexperience. Mars is a hostile environment and you have to learn how to survive in it. There's a lot to learn—and some people just never do."

"You're a caretaker, then."

"I suppose you could say that."

Leo said, "You're not a researcher, are you?"

"No, you should know that. I came as the pilot and systems engineer of the first transport. We converted parts of the ship into the habitat, so there wasn't anything to return on. I'm good with machinery and made myself useful with the equipment. When it became clear someone would need to stay for stopover, I volunteered. I thought the others were so valuable that their data should get back to Earth when the first relief transport came."

"You wouldn't do it again, though, would you?"

"No, I wouldn't."

"Do you think Zhang will do as good a job as you've done here?"

Grace frowned. "Frankly, I hadn't considered that. I don't believe I care anymore. I've served my time; it's someone else's turn now. He volunteered for it. I think I was clear in explaining the responsibilities when you all discussed it."

"You were, but I don't think Zhang's right for it. He's too young, too inexperienced. He volunteered because he thought it made him look heroic. He doesn't have the judgment that someone older would have. That you have."

Grace turned slowly and faced Leo.

"I'm not irreplaceable," she said slowly, "and even if I were, it wouldn't matter to me. I'm sorry if Zhang is young. So was I. I've lost four years here. And I don't intend to lose any more."

Leo held up his hands. "Look, Grace, I didn't mean you should stay. I know how much you resent it and the time you've invested. It's just—" His voice trailed away. "It's just that I think it's such a critically important job."

Leo had gone out for a final equipment check and Grace enjoyed one of her rare moments of solitude. She wandered to her pod and opened her personal storage locker. She checked her civilian clothes and toiletries for perhaps the hundredth time and pushed everything down further in the bag. It was unnecessary because the bag had been packed for a week. She remembered postponing it as long as possible and then the quiet satisfaction about a week ago when she had opened her locker and transferred its meager contents to the bag.

She hadn't actually needed to pack, of course. In less than a day she'd be back on Earth where she could buy more toothpaste than she could use in a decade. She could leave behind her worn clothes and the oversized shirts she had inherited from—who was it? Richardson?—from the First group. Zhang could probably use them or maybe someone from the Fourth.

But it wasn't like going home unless you packed. It was part of the ritual, like marking off the last three weeks on the wall panel beside her pod. Just hours ago, when she woke, she had made the final mark and signed her name and the date. Her signature was right beneath Martinez's.

She frowned thinking about Martinez and secured the bag's closure. They should never have sent someone like Martinez to Mars.

She had just locked the bag when she heard the airlock cycle and the soft hiss of equalization. Someone had returned earlier than expected. She watched the inner door open and the suited figure enter and remove its helmet.

Zhang. He had gone out to assist Justin with the atmospheric sensors. Maybe Justin hadn't needed help, with David along. Or more likely, considering the circumstances, Zhang wasn't much help to anyone today.

Zhang stripped off his suit. His face was covered with perspiration and his eyes showed fear.

He moistened his lips. "Do—do you think they'll ever have relief transports more frequently than every two years, Grace? I mean, considering the advances in—"

"No," Grace interrupted bluntly. "I don't. Not for at least a decade. The fuel costs too much and the journey's too dangerous. In terms of transport economics, you're worth more than your weight in platinum when they send you here. Even if it becomes cheaper, it won't shorten stopover periods right away." She paused, feeling some sympathy for Zhang. "It won't be terrible. There'll be new people here and you'll spend considerable time getting to know them."

"Well, you see," Zhang started, "that's why I came back early. I wanted to talk to you about stopover. It's that—well, I'll put it this way." He seemed to be searching for the right words. "I'm engaged back home. Really wonderful person, Grace, you'd like them if you knew them." He fumbled in his pocket and produced a photograph, placing it on the work station. "That's a picture of Alex, taken at a gathering we attended together." Grace didn't look. "We—I—expected to get married when I returned. I never told Alex about stopover, Grace. They think I'll be home tomorrow. I kept thinking, hoping, that somehow—"

He was handling it badly, Grace thought.

"You wanted to trade places with me, didn't you, Zhang? You thought I might stay for stopover again, in your place?"

It hurt to see Zhang's eyes. They were the eyes of someone desperately trying to stop themselves from doing something shameful, but unable to help themselves.

"Well, yes, essentially. Oh, God, Grace, I know you want to go home! But I couldn't ask any of the others; you were the only one who could, the only one who was qualified!"

Zhang looked as though he might be sick. Grace tried to recall everything she knew about him. Zhang Williams. Excellent engineer. Graduate from a prestigious technical institute. Family was involved in natural resource management or something similar.

It still didn't quite add up. "You know I don't like it here any more than you do," Grace said slowly. "I may have commitments at home, too. What made you think I would change my mind?"

Zhang took the plunge. "Well, you see," he started eagerly, too desperate to remember pride, "you know my family's quite well-off. We would make it worth your while, Grace." He was feverish. "It would mean two more years, Grace, but they'd be well-compensated years!"

Grace felt exhausted. The good feeling about going home was slowly dissolving.

"If you have any reports to complete, I think you should get started," she cut in, keeping the harshness she felt out of her voice. "It'll be too late after the relief transport departs. It'll be easier to give the captain your report than try to transmit it back to Earth from here."

She felt more sympathy for Zhang than she could remember feeling for anyone. Long after returning home, Zhang would remember this moment.

It would haunt him.

Cowardice is the one thing no one ever forgives themselves for.

Patrick was eating a nutrition bar and looking out the window, so naturally he saw the transport first. "Well, look at that!" he shouted. "We have visitors!" He rushed for his suit. Justin and David followed quickly and all three headed for the airlock.

Grace was standing in front of it. "Check your suits," she said quietly. "Just be certain to check."

"Oh, come on, Grace!" Patrick started angrily. Then he stopped and went over his suit. He got to his tank and went pale. Nearly empty. It was only a kilometer to the relief transport, so someone probably would have reached him in time, but.... He bit his lip and got a full tank.

Grace and Leo watched them cross the Martian surface, making the long, bounding strides that low gravity permitted. The transport's hatch had opened and small figures were descending the ramp. The figures from the habitat reached them and performed a brief dance of welcome. Then the figures linked arms and started back. Grace noticed one—probably Patrick—pat the transport's hull affectionately before starting back.

They were in the airlock and the air cycled in and then they were in the habitat, removing their suits. The newcomers were impressed and serious, acutely aware of the tremendous responsibility that now rested on them. Like Patrick and Leo and the members of the Second group had been when they arrived. Like Grace had been with the First.

Patrick and the others surrounded them.

How was Earth? What was the political situation? Were the autonomous vehicle regulations finally passed? What was happening in healthcare policy? Was the orbital station expansion complete?

Was the sky still blue, was the grass still green, did the seasons still change, did people still love and argue and were there still people who didn't understand complexity science and didn't care?

Grace had experienced this before. But was Jordan still Jordan?

Some of the Fourth group members had brought personal items. One of them—a sturdy, enthusiastic woman named Camila Cook—was opening a container about thirty centimeters square and fifteen centimeters deep. Grace watched curiously.

"Well, I'll be damned!" Leo said. "Hey, everyone, look at this!"

Grace and the others crowded around and suddenly Patrick leaned over and inhaled deeply. In the container, covering a thick layer of actual soil, was a small plot of living grass. They looked at it, awed. Leo reached out and touched it gently.

"I like the feel of it," he said simply.

Grace carefully plucked a single blade and held it to her nose. It had been years since she had seen grass, experienced the luxury of walking barefoot on it and lying on its cool surface during those warm summer evenings when it was too pleasant to be indoors.

Camila blushed. "I thought we could spare a little water for it and perhaps use the grow lights occasionally. Couldn't resist bringing it; it seemed like a symbol of something...." She looked embarrassed.

Grace understood. If she had been thinking clearly, she should have tried to bring something like that instead of her music files.

"That's expensive grass," Zhang said sharply. "Do you realize that at current transport rates, it's worth about a thousand credits per blade?"

Camila looked distressed and someone said, "Oh, shut up, Zhang."

One of the newcomers separated from the group and approached Grace. She extended her hand and said, "My name's Joshua Fuller. Captain of the relief transport. I understand you're in charge here?"

Grace nodded and shook hands. They hadn't had a captain on the First transport. Just a pilot and crew. Fuller looked every inch a captain. Strong features, graying hair, the confident bearing of someone accustomed to command.

"You could say I'm in charge here," Grace said.

"Well, look, Ms. Osborne, is there somewhere we can speak privately?"

They walked to one corner of the habitat. "This is about as private as we can get, captain," Grace said. "What's on your mind?"

Fuller found an equipment case and sat down. He looked at Grace carefully.

"I've always wanted to meet the person who's spent more time here than anyone else," he began.

"I'm sure you wanted to see me for more than just curiosity."

Fuller reached for a container of mints. "Mind if I have one?"

Grace gestured toward Zhang. "Ask him. He's in charge now."

The captain didn't bother. He put the container away. "You know we have extensive plans for the station," he said.

"I hadn't heard specifics."

"Oh, yes, extensive plans. They're developing automated cargo transports now that could deliver building materials for additional habitat modules. Enable us to expand the facility, have a series of modules all connected. Create proper laboratories and living quarters for the research staff." His eyes swept the room. "Provide some actual privacy for a change."

Grace nodded. "They could use some privacy here."

The captain noticed the pronoun. "Well, that's one of the reasons I wanted to speak with you, Osborne. The Commission discussed it and they'd like you to stay. They feel if they're going to expand operations, add more modules and increase staff, that someone with practical experience should be managing things. They believe you're the only person who's capable and who has the necessary experience."

The captain vaguely sensed his approach was wrong.

"Is that everything?"

Fuller looked uncomfortable. "Naturally you'd be well compensated. I don't imagine anyone would enjoy being here indefinitely. They're prepared to triple your salary—perhaps even add a substantial bonus—and give you complete authority. You'd be Director of the Blackwood Research Complex."

All this and a title too, Grace thought.

"That's it?" Grace asked.

Fuller frowned. "Well, the Commission said they'd be willing to consider anything else you had in mind, if it was additional compensation or...."

"The answer is no," Grace said. "I'm not interested in more money for staying because I'm not interested in staying. Money can't buy it, captain. I'm sorry, but I'm afraid you'd have to live here to appreciate that.

"Zhang Williams is staying for stopover. If there's something important about the project or upcoming changes, perhaps you should brief him before you leave."

She walked away.
question: What is the name of the research station where Grace worked?

synthetic_story:
The Sanctuary for Ethan

Ethan Reid pressed his body against the cold metalite wall of the immigration processing center in Lakeside, Selvoria, the fugitive following silently in his mind.

His fear-driven gaze swept across the crowded detention hall. The place was a pressure cooker of humanity, filled with people culled from every corner of three continents. Most of the vast room lay obscured behind a shimmer of body heat and the acrid smell of unwashed clothes and desperation.

Here and there, Ethan saw moving figures. He could not tell if they were refugees, economic migrants, or political dissidents like himself.

Someone tugged at his worn jacket. He jumped, thinking absurdly that it was the dead man's hand reaching from memory.

"You need help, friend?" a small voice asked in broken English. "I know people. Good people. Can get you papers. Real papers. Yes?"

Ethan looked down.

The speaker was an eager-eyed boy of about twelve, thin as a rail, with dark skin and darker eyes. He wore a stained t-shirt advertising a film production company and torn jeans.

"I'm fine," Ethan muttered.

"Ah, American! I speak English good, yes? I have cousin, she work in records office. She can fix your file, make you legal. Only five hundred credits, friend. Good deal, yes?"

Ethan shook his head.

He thought, *I don't want your forged documents. I don't want your black market contacts or your smuggling routes. But if you had something that could erase the memory of what I did, I'd pay everything I have.*

"No deal, friend? Then I show you to safe corner. Free. No charge."

The boy grabbed his hand. Because Ethan could think of no reason to resist, he followed. They wove through shifting masses of people and past the drone of multilingual conversations.

They passed the processing desks with their line of stern-faced immigration officers—bureaucrats with the power to grant hope or deliver despair with a single stamp.

They squeezed down a narrow corridor flanked by holding cells that jutted up into the fluorescent brightness like concrete tombstones.

Several times, Ethan glimpsed the bulky figures of Dravonian security guards, the first he'd encountered since crossing the border.

They were massive men, gray-uniformed, silent giants with neural scanners clipped to their belts. They stood solitary and motionless, aloof, their cold eyes unblinking. According to rumors, some of them had been trained in advanced interrogation techniques involving psychological profiling, and the thought sent a fresh rivulet of fear down Ethan's spine.

Once he spotted a blue-uniformed officer of Lakeside's Border Patrol. The woman was striding down a corridor, idly tapping her stun baton against the concrete walls.

*Keep walking*, Ethan told himself. *You look the same as anyone else here. Keep walking. Look straight ahead.*

The officer passed. Ethan breathed easier.

"Here we are, friend," the boy said. "A good spot. Hidden from cameras."

Ethan winced. How did this kid know he wanted to avoid surveillance? Frowning, he sat down on a metal bench—he and the ghost of the dead man.

He listened to the mournful sounds of a street musician's violin drifting through an air vent. The melody was sad, charged with echoes of lost homes and forgotten countries.

For an instant, Ethan's mind rose above the haunting vision of the dead man. He thought, *What am I doing here? Here, in a detention center in a country I've never been to, running from a crime I can barely believe I committed?*

He sobered. It didn't matter. He ordered a coffee from a vending machine. He held the cup but did not drink. His gaze wandered over the faces of the center's other occupants.

*You've got to find him*, he thought. *You've got to find the man named Isaac Hunt. It's the only way you can escape the dead man.*

The dead man was real. His name was Peter Ford. He was stocky and aggressive and about thirty-five, and he hated immigrants.

His body was buried now—probably in the red clay soil outside Northfield, Aldoria. But he'd become a kind of invisible companion, as much a part of Ethan as the guilt in his heart.

Sometimes the image would be standing beside him, its lips spitting hate-filled accusations.

Again, its face would be a wide-eyed mask of surprise as Ethan's fist connected with its jaw. More often, the face would be frozen in the stillness of death. The eyes would stare. Blood would pool beneath the head.

You can forget a living man. You can defeat him or submit to him or ignore him, and the matter is closed. You can't escape from a memory that has burned into your consciousness.

It had begun three weeks ago in Northfield, Aldoria. Ethan's illegal border crossing had been successful. He'd wanted to find work, to disappear into the underground economy. He stopped alone in a workers' bar for a beer. The man named Peter Ford planted his stocky frame on the stool next to him.

"Immigrants," he muttered, "are everywhere now. Like locusts. Everywhere you look, more damn immigrants."

He was dressed in work clothes, a construction supervisor's badge on his shirt.

Ethan smiled nervously. "If it weren't for immigrant labor, half the buildings in this city wouldn't exist."

"The name's Ford." The man took a long drink. "Immigrants taking our jobs. They think they deserve everything we worked for. Bet you think you deserve it too." He slammed his glass down.

Ethan stiffened. He was twenty-eight and dressed in the cheap, worn clothes of a day laborer. He had a master's degree in political economy from a university that no longer existed, in a country torn apart by civil war.

He'd sought long for safety and opportunity.

At the age of eight—perhaps to escape the memory of his father's arrest by government forces—he'd spent hours reading about democratic nations and their immigration policies. At fifteen, he'd begun studying English and the cultural sociology of Western nations. At twenty, he'd joined a pro-democracy movement that nearly cost him his life.

At twenty-five, after the regime change and the subsequent economic collapse, he'd spent every resource he had to reach Aldoria. There, among other refugees and economic migrants, he'd found people who understood his dream of a new life.

And two weeks ago, he'd received a tip about Isaac Hunt—a man rumored to help political refugees establish new identities and find work in the Larchmont Region, where labor laws were more flexible and questions were rarely asked.

Ford was persistent. "Damn fools should've stayed in their own countries. What the hell good does it do, running from place to place?"

*The guy's drunk*, Ethan thought. He took his beer and moved to a table across the room.

Ford followed. "You don't like the truth, do you? You don't like being called a parasite."

Ethan stood and started to leave the bar, but Ford grabbed his arm and held him there.

"That's what you are—a parasite. You're young now. Wait ten years. You'll be dying in some factory accident or deported back to whatever hellhole you came from. Wait and see!"

Until this instant, Ethan had suppressed his anger. Now, suddenly and without warning, it welled up into savage fury.

His fist struck the man on the temple. Ford's eyes gaped in shocked horror. He spun backward. His head cracked sickeningly on the edge of a table. The sound was like a punctuation mark signaling the end of life.

He sank to the floor, eyes glassy, blood pooling beneath his skull.

Ethan knew that he was dead.

Then, for a single absurd second, Ethan was seized with terror—just as, a moment before, he'd been overwhelmed with anger.

He ran.

For some thirty minutes, he raced through a dizzying, nightmare world of dark alleys and shouting voices and pursuing feet.

At last, abruptly, he realized that he was alone and in silence. He saw that he was in an industrial district on the edge of the city.

He huddled in a dark corner of a loading dock and lit a cigarette. A thousand stars—a thousand distant points of indifferent light—shone above him through the smog-filled sky.

He was sorry he'd hit Ford, of course. He was not sorry he'd run. Escaping at least gave him a power of choice, of decision.

*You can do two things*, he thought.

*You can give yourself up, and that's what a good citizen would do. That would eliminate the flight charge. You'd get off with manslaughter. Under Aldorian law, that would mean fifteen years in prison and deportation afterward. And then you'd be free.*

*But you'd be sent back to a country where you'd be imprisoned or killed for your political activities. They don't grant asylum to convicted killers. You'd get whatever freedom exists in a mass grave.*

*Or—*

There were rumors of a network of activists who helped political refugees disappear into the vast underground economy of the Larchmont Region. The activists weren't criminals. They were idealists who believed that borders were artificial constructs designed to preserve economic inequality.

And whereas no legally recognized immigration path existed for people like Ethan, this network had supposedly helped thousands establish new lives. Their coordinator—a subject of intense speculation among refugee communities—was rumored to be a man named Isaac Hunt.

*So*, Ethan reflected, *you can take a whispered rumor seriously. You can hide for a few weeks, change your appearance, adopt a new name. You can wait for a chance to reach the Larchmont Region. To hell with the law. You can try to build a new life, even if you exile yourself from any hope of legitimacy.*

After all, was it right for a single moment of rage to destroy a man's chance at survival?

He was lucky. He found a smuggler whose operation was on its last run before retirement. Security was lax, background checks even more so.

Ethan Reid made it to Lakeside, Selvoria—the gateway to the Larchmont Region.

There was just one flaw in his decision. He hadn't realized that the memory of the dead man's face would haunt him, torment him, follow him as constantly as breath flowed into his lungs.

But might not the noise of a new life drown the accusing voice? Might not the vision of a fresh start obscure the dead face?

So now he sat searching for a perhaps mythical Isaac Hunt, hoping and doubting and fearing, all at once.

"You still looking for someone, friend?"

He jumped. "You again?"

"Yes." The boy grinned. "I keep you company on your first day in Lakeside, yes?"

"This isn't my first day here," Ethan lied. "I've been around."

"You are refugee?"

Ethan threw a ten-credit note on the bench. "Here. Leave me alone."

Thin fingers swept up the money. "Thank you, friend. You know why they call this the Sanctuary City?"

Ethan didn't answer.

"They say it is because the old mayor believed in open borders. What is open borders, friend?"

Ethan raised his hand as if to strike the boy.

"Okay, okay, I go. You stay safe."

The thin body melted into the crowd.

Minutes passed. There were two more coffees. A ceaseless parade of faces broke through the mass of humanity around him—brown faces, black faces, pale faces, and occasionally a face marked by the distinctive features of the Larchmont Region. But nowhere was there a face matching the description of Isaac Hunt—a tall man with intense eyes and a distinctive scar across his left cheek.

A sense of hopelessness gripped Ethan Reid. Lakeside was but one of a dozen border cities in Selvoria. Each had twenty detention centers such as this.

He needed help.

But his photo must have been distributed to border security systems. A reward must have been offered for information leading to his capture. Whom could he trust? The street kid, perhaps?

Far down the corridor nearest him, his eyes caught a flash of blue. He tensed.

*Like the uniform of a Border Patrol officer*, he thought.

His gaze shifted to another corridor and another hint of blue.

And then he saw another and another and another.

Each uniform became brighter and closer, like shrinking spokes of a wheel with Ethan as their focal point.

*Idiot! The damn kid! You should have known!*

Lights flashed in a dazzling sequence. Ethan, half blinded, realized that the center's emergency alert system had been activated.

The lights washed away any sense of anonymity, revealing every face in harsh detail.

Eyes blinked and squinted. There were swift, frightened movements and a chorus of panicked voices. The occupants of the detention center were like exposed insects whose hiding places had been swept away.

Ethan Reid twisted his lean body upright. His bench toppled backward, clattering.

The blue-clad officers charged forward, stun batons raised.

A woman screamed. Conversations ceased. Most of the crowd slunk toward exits. Only a few security guards remained unmoved, their scanning eyes shifting methodically in Ethan's direction.

"Reid!" one of the officers yelled. "You're surrounded! Don't move!"

Ethan whirled away from the advancing patrol, made for an emergency exit he'd spotted earlier.

A crackling sound traveled past his left ear, a sound like electricity arcing through air. A section of the wall ahead of him sparked and smoked.

He stumbled forward. They were using neural disruptors now, not just the mildly painful stun batons.

Another crackle passed his shoulder. He was about fifteen feet from the exit.

*Another second*, his brain screamed. *Just another second—*

Or would the exits be guarded?

He heard the crackle.

It hit directly between his shoulder blades. There was no pain, just a sudden tingling sensation, like pins and needles spreading rapidly.

He froze as if yanked to a stop by invisible chains. His body seemed to be shutting down, muscles refusing to obey commands. He knew that the neural disruptor had overloaded his nervous system, knew that the paralysis was spreading like cascading failure through every nerve and muscle.

He staggered like a man moving through molasses. He'd have twenty—maybe thirty—seconds before complete loss of motor control overwhelmed him.

In the dark world beyond his fading consciousness, he heard a voice yell, "Get the medics!"

Then a pressure and warmth were on his left hand. He realized that someone had grasped it.

A soft feminine voice spoke to him. "You're hit? They got you?"

"Yes." His thick tongue wouldn't form words properly.

"You want to escape—even now?"

"Yes."

"You may be permanently damaged if you don't get medical treatment."

"No, no."

He tried to stumble toward the exit.

"All right then. Not that way. Here, follow me."

Heavy footsteps thudded toward them. A few yards away, a flashlight beam swept across the floor.

Hands were guiding him. He was aware of being pushed and pulled. A door closed behind him. The glare of the flashlight faded from his vision—if he still had vision.

"You're sure?" the voice persisted.

"I'm sure," Ethan managed to say.

"I have no neural stabilizer. You may suffer permanent damage."

His mind fought to comprehend. With the proper medical intervention, massage, and rest, a person could recover from neural disruptor effects within a day. Without treatment, the paralysis could spread to vital organs. It could become permanent disability or death. An effective weapon: the threat of lasting harm compelled most people to surrender immediately.

"No... I'm... sure."

He didn't hear the answer or anything else.

Ethan Reid had no precise sensation of awakening. Return to consciousness was a gradual evolution from a world of nothingness to a dream-like state of awareness.

He felt the pressure of hands on his arms and legs, hands that massaged, manipulated, fought to restore sensation and movement. He knew they were skilled hands. Their skill seemed to transfer hope to his own body.

For a long time, he tried to open his eyes. His lids felt sealed shut. But after a while, they opened. His world of darkness gave way to a translucent veil of light. A round, indistinct shape hovered above him—a face, he supposed.

He tried to talk. Although his lips moved slightly, the only sound was a low, guttural moan.

But he heard someone say, "Don't try to talk." It was the same gentle voice he'd heard in the detention center. "Don't talk. Just rest. Everything will be okay."

*Everything okay*, he thought dimly.

There were long periods of unconsciousness. There were periods of light and darkness. Gradually he grew aware of details. He realized that he was breathing supplemental oxygen through a mask. He felt the warmth of heated blankets wrapped around his body. Occasionally a tube would be in his mouth and he would taste liquid nutrition and feel warmth in his stomach.

Always, it seemed, the face was above him, floating in the obscuring haze. Always, it seemed, the soft voice was echoing in his ears:

"Swallow this now. That's it. You need nourishment." Or, "Close your eyes. Don't strain. It won't be long. You're improving."

*Improving*, he'd think. *Getting better...*

At last, after one of the periods of unconsciousness, his eyes opened. The haze brightened, then dissolved.

He beheld the water-stained ceiling of a small room, its bare walls broken by a single, narrow window. He saw the footboard of his cot and the outlines of his feet beneath a thin blanket.

Finally he saw the face and figure standing at his side.

"You are better?" the kind voice asked.

The face belonged to a woman probably in her early thirties. Her features, devoid of makeup, had an exhausted pallor, as if she hadn't slept properly in weeks. Yet, at the same time, her lean, athletic build suggested strength and determination. Her straight black hair was pulled back in a simple ponytail.

"I—I am better," he murmured. His words were still slow and slurred. "Am I going to recover?"

"You will recover."

He thought for a moment. "How long have I been here?"

"Twelve days."

"You took care of me?" He noted the deep, dark circles beneath her sleep-deprived eyes.

She nodded.

"You're the one who helped me when I was hit?"

"Yes."

"Why?"

Suddenly he began to cough. Breath came hard. She held the oxygen mask in readiness. He shook his head, not wanting it.

"Why?" he asked again.

"It would be a long story. Perhaps I'll tell you tomorrow."

A new thought, cloaked in sudden fear, entered his murky consciousness. "Tell me, will—will I be normal again? Will I be able to walk?"

He lay back then, gasping, exhausted.

"You have nothing to worry about," the woman said softly. Her cool hand touched his hot forehead. "Rest. We'll talk later."

His eyes closed and breath came easier. He slept.

When he next awoke, his gaze turned first to the window. There was light outside, but he had no way of knowing what time it was or even what day.

He saw no towering buildings of Lakeside, no organized streets with their streams of vehicles, no evidence of the city at all. There was only a translucent whiteness, as if the window overlooked an infinite expanse of fog or cloud.

The woman entered the room.

"Hi," she said, smiling. The dark circles under her eyes were less prominent. Her face was relaxed.

She adjusted his pillows and helped him sit up.

"Where are we?" he asked.

"Still in Selvoria."

"We're not in Lakeside?"

"No."

He looked at her, wondering. "You won't tell me?"

"Not yet. Later, perhaps."

"Then how did you get me here? How did we escape from the center?"

She shrugged. "We have friends who can be persuaded. A hiding place in the city, the use of a private vehicle, a pass to leave the detention zone—these can be arranged for a price."

"You'll tell me your name?"

"Luna."

"Why did you save me?"

Her eyes held a hint of amusement. "Because you understand game theory."

His own eyes widened. "How did you know that?"

She sat on a simple chair beside his bed. "I know everything about you, Ethan Reid."

"How did you learn my name? I destroyed all my documents—"

"I know that you're twenty-eight. Born March 15, 1997. Orphaned at nine when your father was arrested and your mother died of illness. You attended underground schools until you were nineteen. You graduated from Central University with a master's degree in political economy. Your thesis on the application of game theory to immigration policy was highly regarded. Your only weak area was historical analysis of pre-globalization economic systems. Want me to go on?"

Fascinated, Ethan nodded.

"You joined the pro-democracy movement at twenty. You did significant work analyzing the political philosophy of authoritarian regimes. After the regime change and economic collapse, you fled to Aldoria. In a bar fight in Northfield, you struck and killed a man named Peter Ford, a construction supervisor. You've been charged with manslaughter and illegal immigration. A reward of 10,000 credits has been offered for information leading to your capture. You came to Lakeside hoping to find Isaac Hunt and his network. You were looking for him in the detention center."

He gaped incredulously, struggling to rise from his pillows. "I—don't understand."

"There are ways of finding out what we need to know. As I told you, we have many friends."

He fell back into his pillows, breathing hard. She rose quickly.

"I'm sorry," she said. "I shouldn't have overwhelmed you. I felt relieved because you're alive. Rest now. We'll talk again soon."

"Luna, you—you said I'd recover. You didn't say I'd walk normally again."

She lowered her gaze. "I hope you will."

"But you don't think I will, do you?"

"I don't know. We'll try walking tomorrow. Don't think about it now. Rest."

He tried to relax, but his mind was a storm of questions.

"Just one more question," he almost whispered.

"Yes?"

"The man I killed—did he have a family?"

She hesitated. He thought, *Damn it, of all the questions, why did I ask that?*

Finally she said, "He had a wife."

"Children?"

"Three. I don't know their ages."

She left the room.

He sank into the softness of his cot. As he turned over on his side, his gaze fell upon an object on a small table in the corner of the room.

He sat straight up, his chest heaving.

The object was a framed photograph of a lean, intense man with a distinctive scar across his left cheek—*Isaac Hunt*!

Ethan stared at the photo for a long time. At length, he slipped into restless sleep. Images of faces and echoes of words spun through his brain.

The dead man returned to him. Bloodied lips cursed at him. Glassy eyes accused him. Somewhere were three lost children crying in the night.

And standing before him was Isaac Hunt, whose steady gaze seemed to judge him. Ethan crawled through the darkness on hands and knees, his legs numb and useless. The crying of the children was a chilling wail in his ears.

His head rose and turned to Isaac Hunt. His pleading voice called out in a thick, harsh whisper. Yet even as he called, the figure disappeared, to be replaced by blue-uniformed officers marching relentlessly toward him.

He awoke still trembling...

A night passed. Ethan lay waiting for Luna's return, a question already formed in his mind.

She came and at once he asked, "Who is the man with the scar?"

She smiled. "I was right then when I told you about yourself. You *were* looking for him, weren't you?"

"Who is he?"

She sat on the chair beside him.

"My partner," she said softly.

He began to understand. "And your partner needs someone who understands political economy? That's why you saved me?"

"We need all the skilled people we can get."

"Where is he?"

She tilted her head thoughtfully. "Somewhere in the Larchmont Region. He's building a new sanctuary for us—and a community for people like you. When his work is ready, I'll be joining him there."

"Why aren't you with him now?"

"He said the early stages are too dangerous for both of us to risk. So I've been monitoring detention centers and border crossings, trying to find recruits like yourself. You know how we operate?"

He told her the rumors he'd heard.

She nodded. "There are quite a few of us now—about three thousand—and a dozen safe houses. Our network used to be based in Bayview, Dravonia, but that became too risky. This house we're in now was established a few years ago after we had to leave Bayview. We lost a few people in the process, but with every expansion of our work, someone takes a risk."

"Selvoria is getting more restrictive with immigration enforcement. We're moving to the Larchmont Region, and this house is only temporary for cases like yours. The new sanctuary—I might as well tell you it's going to be in a rural area. I won't say exactly where."

"Don't think we're criminals. Sure, about half our network is wanted by authorities for immigration violations or related charges, but we help people build honest lives. We're just people like yourself and Isaac."

"Isaac? Your partner?"

She laughed. "The name sounds biblical, doesn't it? Isaac's anything but traditional. He's a former professor of political philosophy who got radicalized by studying healthcare policy and economic inequality."

She lit a cigarette. "Anyway, the wanted ones stay in the Larchmont Region. Isaac and those like him can never return to their home countries or even to places like Lakeside—not without being arrested. The others are political refugees or economic migrants who have skills but can't get legal status. They know they could be deported at any time but won't give up. They work in our network, helping new arrivals find jobs and housing."

"Don't the authorities object?"

"Not as strongly as you'd think. The immigration enforcement agencies have too many cases to pursue every rumored network. Besides, we provide labor for industries that can't find enough workers legally. Nobody really cares whether workers have papers or not, as long as the work gets done. If we want to risk our freedom helping people, that's our business."

She pursed her lips. "But if they realized how organized we are or that we have sympathizers within the system—well, things might be different. There probably would be a major crackdown."

Ethan frowned. "What happens if there *is* a crackdown? And what will you do when immigration laws are reformed? They can't ignore you then."

"Then we adapt. We develop new strategies, find new locations, maybe expand to other regions or countries. In time, maybe, borders will become less relevant. Maybe it won't be governments who create the first truly borderless society. It *could* be us, you know—if we survive long enough. But this work is dangerous. You can't follow the official rules when you're trying to help people the system has failed. You make up your own."

Ethan stiffened. "And that's why you want me—for my understanding of political economy and game theory."

Luna rose, her eyes serious. "If you want to join us—and if you get well." She looked at him intently.

"Suppose—" He struggled to find the right words. "Suppose I got well and decided not to join Isaac. What would happen to me? Would you let me go?"

Her thin face showed a flurry of emotions—alarm, then confusion, then concern. "I don't know. That would be up to Isaac."

He lay biting his lip, staring at the photo of Isaac Hunt. She touched his hand and it seemed that sadness now dominated the emotions that had crossed her face.

"The only thing that matters right now," she murmured, "is your recovery. We'll try walking this afternoon. Okay?"

"Okay," he said.

When she left, his eyes were still fixed on Isaac's photo.

He was torn, he thought.

Part of him wanted to believe in the rule of law, in proper procedures, in the immigration policies that nations established to protect their interests. Those were the structures that maintained order in a globalized world.

He remembered a poster in his university classroom before the government shut it down. Under a picture of diverse people working together was the caption: "A Just Society Requires Fair Laws."

Justice, fairness, order. Important concepts, but without flexibility and compassion, those concepts could trap people in circumstances beyond their control.

Without adaptability, refugees fleeing violence would be turned away at borders. Without networks like Isaac's, people with skills and dreams would die in detention centers or be sent back to countries where they faced persecution.

And yet...
question: Who was the person Ethan was hoping to find in Lakeside?

THE REGULATORY INTERVENTION

By the time the automated transport reached the outer orbits of the financial district, Samantha Boyd and Isaac Ahmed had compiled enough data to understand the full scope of the crisis. Their vessel, a sleek diplomatic craft from the Interstellar Commerce Federation, had intercepted thousands of market transactions, regulatory filings, and news broadcasts from the planet below. Advanced algorithms had translated the major trading languages and constructed comprehensive models of the planetary economy.

The course of their ship adjusted slightly as they moved closer to the world designated in their charts as Market-7, though its inhabitants called it something else entirely. For days, the two Federation auditors had monitored the situation with growing concern.

"We need to make a decision," said Samantha, reviewing the latest economic projections on her display. "The regulatory framework is completely inadequate."

"I know what you're thinking," said Isaac, "but you've seen their history. They've had three major financial collapses in the past century alone, each one worse than the last."

"That's exactly why we need to intervene," Samantha argued. "Without proper financial regulation, their entire economic system could implode. The derivatives market alone is leveraged at ratios that defy basic systems thinking."

"I'll remind you that in seventy-three days we're due at the Concordance Summit in the Timberline sector of Estoria," Isaac said. "Without checking the navigation charts, I can tell you we still have more than a hundred light-years to cover."

"A week," Samantha insisted. "We can spare one week and still arrive on time."

"A week?" Isaac shook his head. "To restructure their entire financial system? They've been building these markets for generations. Their whole approach to natural resource management is tied up in speculative trading. And now with autonomous vehicles disrupting their transportation sector, the economic instability is accelerating."

"It won't take a complete overhaul," Samantha said. "Just key interventions. A few critical regulatory reforms. The wrong market fluctuation, or a single bank failure could trigger a cascade. Their systems are so interconnected through globalization that one collapse would spread across the entire planet."

"Too bad," said Isaac. "We'll just have to accept that some civilizations aren't ready for sustainable economics."

"Could you? Could you really forget about billions of people?"

"I'm trying to," Isaac replied. "Just give them a little time and the problem will resolve itself—one way or another."

"My conscience doesn't work that way," said Samantha. "I'm asking you to look at them more carefully."

Isaac pulled up detailed demographic and economic data on his screen. "Very similar to our own species at a comparable stage of development," he said finally. "Slightly less advanced in certain technologies, and definitely incomplete in their understanding of complex systems. But yes, I see the resemblance. Is that what you wanted me to acknowledge?"

"Yes. The fact that they're essentially a younger version of ourselves makes this personal. They seem vulnerable, though I know they're resourceful."

"Unfortunate," said Isaac. "But there's nothing we can do."

"There is. We can give them a week."

"In a week we can't undo centuries of flawed economic policy. We can't resolve the fundamental contradictions in their approach to electoral politics and market regulation."

"We won't know unless we try," said Samantha.

"And what authority do we actually have here?"

"Very little," Samantha admitted. "Two mid-level auditors on our way to a routine summit—and we stumble upon a crisis no one at Federation headquarters even knows exists."

"And by the time we reach Timberline and file our reports, it will be months before anyone can respond. There's nothing in this sector that the Federation considers strategically important," said Isaac. "How long can this planet's economy hold? Ten years? Ten months? The market volatility is increasing exponentially."

"What can I say?" said Isaac. "I suppose we can take a closer look. We're not committing to anything by gathering more data."

They moved much closer to Market-7, their sensors carefully avoiding the planet's primitive detection systems. For a full day they orbited, analyzing market structures, regulatory frameworks, and economic patterns. Finally, Samantha looked up from her console.

"Any conclusions?"

"It's worse than I thought," Isaac said.

"How so?"

"We knew they had developed high-frequency trading algorithms. The market analysis showed that from a distance."

"Right."

"We also knew they had minimal oversight of their derivatives markets."

"That was obvious from the leverage ratios."

"What's worse is that I've discovered they've also implemented autonomous financial systems—AI-driven trading platforms that operate faster than human oversight can track. They're approaching a singularity point where the machines could trigger a crash before anyone realizes what's happening."

"Dangerous," said Samantha. "The humans sit there watching numbers change, never knowing when the system will collapse. The stress alone could trigger panic selling."

"It could, and the autonomous systems make it exponentially worse," said Isaac. "What did you find?"

"I was studying the people themselves while you analyzed their markets."

"And?"

"I wish I had more time. Language isn't the problem—our translation matrices handle their financial terminology easily, and I've absorbed their economic theories. But that's not enough. I should spend months down there, attending their universities, speaking with their economists, understanding their cultural relationship to wealth and risk."

"You could do that, and you'd truly understand them. But we don't have months."

"I know."

"So what's your answer?" Isaac asked.

"No. We can't fix their system," said Samantha. "There's no simple solution—but we have to try anyway."

"I knew you'd say that," said Isaac, standing and stretching. "It's happened before. We investigate a civilization's problems, realize we can't solve them completely, and feel terrible about it. This will be no different." He moved toward the equipment bay. "Give me an hour to formulate an approach."

It was longer than that before they reconvened. In the meantime, their ship had moved into a higher orbit. Through the viewports, Market-7 rotated below them. The southern continents showed green agricultural regions; the oceans were deep blue; and much of the northern hemisphere was covered in the sprawling gray-brown of massive urban centers. Weather patterns swirled over the poles, and a haze of industrial pollution spread across the equatorial manufacturing zones.

"I haven't developed a brilliant strategy," said Samantha.

"Neither have I," said Isaac. "We're going to have to improvise."

"I did consider one approach," Isaac said. "What if we present ourselves as representatives of a superior economic authority? Use our obvious technological advantage to add weight to our recommendations?"

"Too risky," said Samantha. "A century ago that might have worked. But these people have satellites, quantum computers, and sophisticated media networks. They're not primitives who'll accept authority without question."

"I thought we should leverage our differences somehow."

"If we could do it subtly, I'd agree. But these people are cynical and desperate. They've been burned by false promises before. They won't trust anything that seems manipulative."

"All right, you're leading this operation," said Isaac.

"Here's the plan," said Samantha. "You take one major economic bloc, I'll take another. We'll present ourselves as neutral advisors and explain clearly what reforms they need to implement if they want to avoid collapse. We'll give them the frameworks they need to establish proper financial regulation."

"That'll be popular. Everyone loves being told their system is broken."

"Can't be helped. It's all we have time for."

"Any specific protocols?"

"None beyond the basics. We'll take separate landing craft down to the surface. You can contact me through our quantum communicators if necessary, but don't unless it's critical."

"They can't intercept our communications."

"They can't, and even if they detected the quantum signatures, they couldn't decode our language. But I want them to think we don't need to confer."

"I understand. Makes us seem more confident and knowledgeable than we actually are."

"Exactly."

Isaac looked at the planet below. "It's going to be challenging wherever we land. You too. Are we sure we don't want to adjust our targets? Maybe approach smaller nations first, build credibility?"

"No. The major economic powers control the global system. If we're going to prevent a collapse, we need to reach the decision-makers in the dominant markets."

"Right, but I was thinking about timing. We'll be arriving just before their major holiday season. That won't help."

"I know. People don't appreciate interruptions during holidays. But we can't wait."

"Understood," said Isaac. "Brief me on these holidays. Anything I should know? Religious significance?"

"Originally religious, centuries ago," said Samantha. "From what I've gathered from their media, it's now primarily commercial—a peak season for consumer spending and market activity."

"So it's fundamentally economic."

"That's accurate. I didn't learn as much as I should have. I was focused on understanding their approach to community organizing and how economic stress affects social cohesion."

"I was thinking we might be able to use the holiday period somehow. Make it work in our favor."

"If there's a way, I haven't seen it."

"You're running this mission." Isaac looked down at the planet. Storm systems were forming over the western ocean. "I don't like leaving our ship unmanned while we're on the surface."

"They can't touch it. Even with another century of development, they won't have the technology to breach our hull or access our systems."

"I'm thinking about us. Down there, alone."

"I'll be with you. On the opposite side of the planet."

"That's not exactly close. I'd prefer having someone in the ship ready to extract us if things go wrong. These people don't trust their own economists. I doubt they'll welcome alien auditors."

"They may be hostile," Samantha acknowledged. She switched a monitor to show a financial district in one of the major cities. People rushed through streets decorated with lights and synthetic trees. "I've thought of a strategy to mitigate that risk."

"If it keeps us safe, I'm interested."

"No guarantees," said Samantha. "But here's my thinking: instead of hiding the ship on the far side of their moon where it's unlikely to be detected, we make sure they do see it. Let's position it in a visible orbit and illuminate it."

"That could work," said Isaac.

"They won't imagine we'd light up an unmanned vessel," said Samantha. "Even if they consider the possibility, they'll have no way to verify it. More importantly, they'll be reluctant to harm us while our ship is clearly visible above them."

"Good thinking," said Isaac, moving to the navigation controls. "I'll position us in an optimal orbit and activate the external lighting arrays. I'll make it impossible to miss."

"Don't be subtle."

"Trust me. Everyone on the planet will see it." Later, with the ship in position, its hull blazing with light in a carefully programmed pattern that pulsed like a beacon, Isaac said: "You know, I feel better about this. We might actually succeed. The visible ship gives us leverage we didn't have before."

"It's not about our success, but their survival," said Samantha. "See you in five days." She entered a small landing craft, which left a faint ion trail as it descended toward the planet's surface. Minutes later, Isaac departed in another craft, heading for a different continent.

And the ship orbited Market-7, unmanned, brilliant and pulsing with light. No satellite or space station could match its luminosity. The automated weather satellites recorded it; the astronomical observatories tracked it; the media networks broadcast images of it. During daylight hours it appeared as an impossibly bright star. At night it seemed to burn through the darkness like a piece of captured starlight brought near the planet for all to witness.

And the ship continued its orbit, bright, shining, an undeniable presence in the sky that no one could ignore or explain away.

In five days, the two small landing craft that had departed from it arced back up through the atmosphere and docked with the larger vessel. The small craft slid inside and the airlocks sealed behind them. Shortly after, the two Federation auditors met again in the main cabin.

"We did it," said Isaac enthusiastically as he entered. "I don't know how, and I thought we'd fail, but at the last moment they agreed to the framework."

Samantha smiled, though she looked exhausted. "I'm tired," she said softly.

"Me too, but mostly I'm frustrated," said Isaac. "Bureaucracy. Nothing but bureaucracy wherever I went. Endless meetings. And yet you had me do those public presentations after that first day."

"From my own experience, it seemed effective," Samantha explained. "When I did a public presentation one day, I noticed the officials were much more cooperative the next day. If it worked for me, I thought it might help you."

"It did. I don't understand the mechanism, but it definitely helped," said Isaac. "Anyway, the regulatory framework they've agreed to isn't perfect, but I believe it will prevent a systemic collapse."

"It's the best we could achieve in the time available," said Samantha. "They may still have market corrections and regional recessions, but not the catastrophic collapse. In fifty or a hundred years, the Federation can send another team to assess their progress."

"I'm not sure I want that assignment," said Isaac. "Hey, what's a 'guardian angel'?"

"Why do you ask?"

"When I did those public presentations, people would approach me afterward. Some would kneel and call me a guardian angel. They'd thank me for watching over them."

"Something similar happened to me," said Samantha.

"I didn't understand the reference, but I didn't let it derail me," said Isaac. "I smiled and continued with the work." He stretched, and as he did, his wings—carefully folded during the mission—extended slightly. They were magnificent, spanning nearly three meters, with feathers that seemed to shimmer with an inner light. The evolutionary adaptation that had allowed his species to thrive on their high-gravity homeworld made them appear, to human eyes, like beings from ancient religious texts.

"I don't think your appearance hurt our credibility," said Samantha. She too stretched, her own wings unfurling briefly. They were slightly smaller than Isaac's but equally striking, with patterns of iridescence that shifted in the light.

"But you don't know what a 'guardian angel' is?"

"No. I didn't have time to research their mythology and comparative history thoroughly. I was focused on economic systems thinking and decision-making frameworks. Some figure from their cultural traditions, I assume. You know, except for the wings, they're remarkably similar to us physiologically. Their legends probably reflect similar archetypes."

"Makes sense," said Isaac. "Anyway, we've given them a chance. Financial stability on Market-7."

"For now," said Samantha, looking at the planet one last time before they departed. "For now."

The ship's lights dimmed, and it began to accelerate away from Market-7, heading toward Timberline and the summit that awaited them. Behind them, on the planet below, economists and government officials were already implementing the regulatory frameworks the two visitors had proposed. The financial markets, which had been teetering on the edge of collapse, began to stabilize.

And in the cities below, people looked up at the now-empty sky where the brilliant ship had been, and they wondered about the two winged visitors who had appeared during their holiday season, offered guidance, and then departed as mysteriously as they had arrived.

In Oakdale, Havencia, a financial analyst named Malik Vasquez filed a report about the new regulations, noting that they seemed to come from an understanding of systems far more advanced than anything their civilization had developed. In the Dawnridge District, Sophia Young, a professor of comparative history, began writing a paper about the visitors and their remarkable resemblance to figures from ancient texts.

And in Havenbrook, Marvenia, a community organizer named Henri Gonzalez stood in the street, looking up at the stars, thinking about existential questions that the visitors had raised simply by their presence. What did it mean that they were not alone? What did it mean that others were watching, sometimes helping?

The media debated the visitors' nature and purpose. Some claimed they were advanced beings from another world. Others insisted they were something more—angels, perhaps, or guardians sent to protect humanity from its own worst impulses.

In the end, it didn't matter what they called them. What mattered was that they had come, they had helped, and they had left behind a framework that might just save civilization from collapse.

At least for now.

At least for a while.

And somewhere, far above, accelerating toward distant stars, Samantha Boyd and Isaac Ahmed reviewed their mission reports, satisfied that they had done what they could with the limited time available.

"Do you think they'll make it?" Isaac asked.

"I think they have a chance," Samantha replied. "That's all anyone can ask for. A chance."

THE END
