By A. Mitchell

In the observation tower of the Galactic Research Institute on Pearlbrook Station, orbiting the mining colony of Goldfield Territory, Dr. Li Gordon reviewed the personnel files of three new researchers assigned to her xenolinguistics division. The files made her shake her head in weary recognition. Another batch of brilliant minds with significant psychological complications—the kind of people who ended up working under her command.

Li Gordon had spent twenty-three years as Director of Xenolinguistic Studies for the Institute, and in that time, she'd learned that the best scientific collaboration often came from the most unlikely sources. Her division had become the dumping ground for researchers who couldn't function in normal laboratory environments but were too talented to dismiss entirely.

She opened the first file. Dr. Sergio Harris, age forty-two, specialist in comparative syntax and morphological structures. His credentials were impeccable—three advanced degrees, publications in every major journal, breakthrough work on the Centauri language families. But buried in the psychological evaluation was the problem: severe obsessive-compulsive disorder focused on verification. Harris couldn't accept any data point without checking it seventeen times through seventeen different methodologies. In a normal research environment, this made him impossibly slow. Projects ground to a halt under his leadership.

The second file belonged to Dr. Teresa Cole, thirty-seven, an expert in semantic drift and historical interpretation of dead languages. Her problem was different: she suffered from analysis paralysis. When presented with multiple competing theories or interpretations, she became psychologically incapable of choosing between them. She could see merit in every argument, validity in every approach, and would freeze completely when forced to commit to a single conclusion.

The third researcher was Jack Peterson, twenty-nine, a prodigy in statistical inference and pattern recognition within linguistic structures. His issue was acute social anxiety disorder, so severe that he couldn't present findings to groups larger than three people without experiencing debilitating panic attacks.

Li Gordon sighed and closed the files. She understood why they'd been sent to her. Pearlbrook Station was remote, isolated, and most of its work was done in small teams or individually. The Institute's administration knew that Gordon had a gift for finding ways to make damaged people useful—or rather, for finding situations where their damage became an asset.

Her communicator chimed. "Dr. Gordon, incoming priority transmission from Central Administration on Magnolia, Marvenia."

"Put it through, Eva."

Eva Ahmed, her administrative assistant, was another case study in strategic placement. Eva had an information hoarding disorder—she collected data compulsively but found it psychologically painful to share it with others. As Gordon's gatekeeper, this trait was perfect. Nothing leaked from Gordon's office without explicit authorization.

The face of Director Paul Sanders appeared on the screen. He was the Institute's liaison with the Galactic Council, a political appointee who understood bureaucracy better than science but was competent enough in both.

"Dr. Gordon, we have a situation that requires your immediate attention."

Gordon leaned back in her chair. "I'm listening."

"You're aware of the Vex situation, I presume?"

She nodded. Everyone in the galaxy knew about the Vex. They were a recently contacted species from the Eastwood Sector, highly advanced but utterly alien in their cognitive processes. For five years, humanity had been trying to establish meaningful communication with them, with limited success. The Vex seemed interested in dialogue but operated on principles that defied human understanding.

"Three months ago," Sanders continued, "the Vex proposed a joint scientific venture—a collaborative project to develop a unified translation protocol that would allow our species to communicate complex abstract concepts. They've offered to share their advanced robotics technology and natural resource management techniques in exchange for our expertise in digital transformation and complexity science."

"That's... significant," Gordon said carefully. "What's the problem?"

"The problem is timing and location. The Vex have established a research station on Goldfield Territory—specifically, on the third moon. They want to begin the project immediately, and they want it conducted there. They've given us seventy-two hours to assemble a team and arrive at the station, or they'll consider our lack of response as disinterest and withdraw the offer entirely."

Gordon felt her stomach tighten. Goldfield Territory. That was practically next door—only a few hours by shuttle from Pearlbrook Station.

"Why the rush?"

"Political philosophy," Sanders said grimly. "The Vex operate on consensus-based decision-making, but their consensus windows are short. The faction that supports human collaboration has a narrow window of political capital. If we don't act now, the opposition faction will use our hesitation as evidence that humans are unreliable partners."

"And you want me to lead the team."

"You're the obvious choice. Your work on the Centauri dialects showed that you can bridge seemingly incompatible linguistic frameworks. You understand both the technical challenges and the political implications."

Gordon looked away from the screen. There it was—the assumption that she could do this, that she should do this. But Sanders didn't know. How could he? She'd hidden it so well for so long.

"Director Sanders, I appreciate the confidence, but I can't accept this assignment."

His eyebrows rose. "Can't? Dr. Gordon, this is potentially the most important xenolinguistic project in human history. The educational reform implications alone—if we can truly understand how the Vex think, we could revolutionize how we teach comparative cognition. And the political ramifications—"

"I understand the stakes," Gordon interrupted. "But I still can't go."

There was a long pause. Sanders' expression shifted from surprise to calculation. "Dr. Gordon, I'm going to be direct. When you were appointed to Pearlbrook Station, certain... accommodations were made. Your personnel file indicates that you have severe claustrophobia and a pathological fear of enclosed spaces. The station's observation tower was specially designed with transparent aluminum walls to give you the illusion of openness. Your quarters are the only residential unit with external viewports on all sides."

Gordon felt her face flush. So he did know.

"The Vex research station," Sanders continued, "is built into the moon's interior. It's a network of tunnels and chambers carved into solid rock. There are no windows, no external views. Just corridors and rooms, all underground."

"Then you understand why I can't go."

"I do. Which is why I'm not asking you to go. I'm asking you to send a team in your place—a team that can accomplish what needs to be accomplished."

Gordon was quiet for a moment, thinking. "You want me to choose the team?"

"I want you to do what you do best—find the right broken pieces and fit them together into something functional."

After Sanders disconnected, Gordon sat in silence, staring out at the stars visible through her transparent walls. She thought about the three new researchers in her files, and about the Vex waiting on Goldfield Territory's third moon.

An idea began to form.

She called Eva Ahmed. "I need you to pull up everything we have on Vex communication patterns and decision-making processes. Everything. And I need the full psychological profiles on Harris, Cole, and Peterson. The complete versions, not the summaries."

"Right away, Dr. Gordon."

For the next six hours, Gordon immersed herself in the data. She studied the Vex linguistic patterns, their cultural frameworks, their approach to collaborative research. And slowly, a picture emerged.

The Vex were consensus-builders, but their consensus required absolute certainty. They wouldn't accept a conclusion unless it had been verified through multiple independent methodologies. They valued thoroughness over speed, accuracy over efficiency.

And they were incapable of making decisions when presented with multiple equally valid alternatives. Their entire political philosophy was built around the idea that for every problem, there existed one optimal solution, and their job was to find it through exhaustive analysis. When faced with two genuinely equal options, their decision-making process would stall indefinitely.

Gordon smiled. It was perfect.

She called in Sergio Harris first.

"Dr. Harris, I have an assignment for you. It's probably the most important work you'll ever do in your career."

Harris nodded slowly, his hands fidgeting with a stylus. "Yes, Dr. Gordon."

She explained the Vex project, emphasizing the need for absolute verification of every data point, every translation, every interpretation.

"The Vex won't accept anything less than complete certainty," she said. "They need someone who will check and double-check and triple-check every conclusion. Someone who won't cut corners or accept 'good enough.' Someone who understands that in xenolinguistics, a single mistranslation can cause diplomatic disasters."

Harris's eyes lit up. For once, his compulsion wasn't a hindrance—it was exactly what was needed.

"I can do that, Dr. Gordon. I won't let anything slip through."

"I know you won't. But you won't be going alone. I'm sending Dr. Teresa Cole with you as co-lead."

She called Cole in next and explained the situation.

"The Vex will try to present you with multiple possible interpretations of their concepts," Gordon said. "They'll offer alternative frameworks, different ways of understanding their cognitive processes. Your job is to evaluate each option thoroughly and advise Dr. Harris on which approach to take."

Cole looked worried. "But what if there are multiple valid approaches? What if I can't determine which is best?"

"Then you tell Harris exactly that. You present him with all the alternatives, explain the merits of each, and let him know that the choice between them isn't clear. The Vex respect thoroughness and honesty. They'd rather know that we're uncertain than have us pretend to certainty we don't possess."

What Gordon didn't say—what she didn't need to say—was that Cole's inability to choose between alternatives would force Harris to verify every option exhaustively before making any decision. And Harris's obsessive verification would prevent Cole from ever having to make a definitive choice. They would balance each other perfectly.

"And I'm sending Jack Peterson as your data analyst," Gordon added. "He'll handle all the statistical inference and pattern recognition work. He's brilliant, but he has severe social anxiety, so keep the team small and don't ask him to present to large groups."

Over the next two days, Gordon prepared her team. She drilled into them the importance of the mission, the political implications, the potential for personal growth and professional recognition. She made sure they understood the Vex cultural framework and decision-making processes.

And then she sent them to Goldfield Territory's third moon.

The reports came back daily, relayed through Eva Ahmed's carefully controlled information channels. Gordon read them with growing satisfaction.

The Vex had initially tried to rush the process, presenting the human team with quick decisions and demanding immediate responses. But Harris had refused to accept any conclusion without exhaustive verification. Every translation had to be checked through seventeen different methodological frameworks. Every interpretation had to be validated against seventeen independent data sets.

The Vex, who valued thoroughness above all else, couldn't argue with this approach. They began to slow down, matching Harris's pace.

Then the Vex tried offering alternative frameworks—multiple ways of understanding the same concept, all equally valid within their cognitive system. They seemed to expect the humans to choose one arbitrarily.

But Cole couldn't choose. She would analyze each alternative, find merit in all of them, and report back to Harris that no clear winner had emerged. This would trigger another round of Harris's verification protocols, examining each alternative through every possible lens.

The Vex, who themselves couldn't make decisions when faced with truly equal alternatives, found themselves in a familiar paralysis. But instead of frustration, they felt... understood. The humans were approaching the problem exactly as the Vex themselves would.

Peterson's role was subtler but no less crucial. His statistical analyses kept finding patterns that suggested hidden complexities in the Vex communication system—patterns that demanded further investigation. Each discovery would send Harris into another verification cycle and give Cole more alternatives to analyze.

Three weeks into the project, Director Sanders visited Pearlbrook Station in person.

"Dr. Gordon, I've been reviewing the reports from Goldfield Territory. Your team has made more progress in understanding Vex cognition than anyone in the past five years. The Vex are calling this the most successful scientific collaboration in their history."

Gordon smiled modestly. "I chose the right people for the job."

"But they're not actually making any decisions," Sanders said, puzzled. "Every report shows them analyzing, verifying, considering alternatives, but never actually concluding anything."

"Exactly," Gordon said. "The Vex don't want quick decisions. They want thorough analysis. They don't want arbitrary choices between equal alternatives. They want recognition that sometimes no clear choice exists. My team is giving them exactly what their cognitive framework requires."

Sanders shook his head in admiration. "You matched their psychological profile perfectly."

"I matched broken pieces to a broken system," Gordon corrected. "Harris can't stop verifying, Cole can't make decisions, and Peterson keeps finding new complications. In any normal research environment, they'd be disasters. But working with the Vex, who have the same cognitive patterns, they're ideal."

"And you knew this how?"

Gordon looked out at the stars through her transparent walls. "Because I understand what it's like to have a limitation that defines you. I can't go into enclosed spaces. I can't handle the underground tunnels of that Vex station. I'm trapped here in my tower with my windows and my illusions of openness."

She turned back to Sanders. "But I'm not useless. I'm just useful in specific contexts. The same is true for Harris, Cole, and Peterson. They're not broken—they're specialized. And in the right context, specialization is strength."

Sanders nodded slowly. "The Vex have proposed extending the collaboration indefinitely. They want your team to stay on Goldfield Territory and help develop a comprehensive translation protocol. They're offering access to their entire technological database—everything from advanced robotics to their techniques for natural resource management and complexity science. This could revolutionize human understanding of non-human cognition."

"Then I suppose my team will be staying," Gordon said.

"And you? Will you stay here in your tower?"

Gordon smiled. "Where else would I go? This is where I'm useful. This is where my particular form of brokenness becomes a strength. I understand damaged people because I'm one of them. And I know how to find contexts where damage becomes adaptation."

She looked back out at the stars. "Besides, someone has to be here to handle the next batch of brilliant misfits they send me. There's always another impossible problem that needs an impossible solution."

Sanders stood to leave, then paused. "Dr. Gordon, I have to ask—when you chose Harris, Cole, and Peterson, did you know they would work this well together?"

"I had a hypothesis," Gordon said. "Supported by statistical inference and historical interpretation of similar cases. But I couldn't be certain until I tested it."

"And if you'd been wrong?"

Gordon shrugged. "Then I would have verified my assumptions through alternative methodologies and tried again. Isn't that what good science is about? Testing hypotheses, learning from failures, and adapting our approaches?"

After Sanders left, Gordon returned to her desk and opened a new set of personnel files. Three more researchers were being transferred to Pearlbrook Station next month. She began reading their psychological profiles, looking for the patterns, searching for the contexts where their particular forms of brokenness might become strengths.

Outside her transparent walls, the stars wheeled slowly through the void. And in her tower, surrounded by the illusion of infinite space, Li Gordon continued her work—matching broken pieces to impossible problems, finding strength in weakness, and proving that sometimes the best tool for a job is the one that doesn't quite fit anywhere else.

The reports from Goldfield Territory continued to arrive daily, each one documenting another small breakthrough in human-Vex understanding. Harris verified, Cole analyzed alternatives, Peterson found patterns, and together they built something that none of them could have built alone.

And in her tower, Gordon smiled. This was her gift—not the ability to fix broken things, but the wisdom to know that sometimes broken things don't need fixing. Sometimes they just need the right context, the right problem, the right impossible situation where their brokenness becomes exactly what's required.

She thought about behavioral economics and entrepreneurship, about how the best innovations often come from people who don't fit the standard molds. She thought about education reform and how the system tries to make everyone the same, when perhaps the goal should be to find where each person's uniqueness becomes valuable.

But most of all, she thought about her team on that distant moon, working in tunnels she could never enter, solving problems she could never directly touch, succeeding precisely because of the limitations that would have made them failures anywhere else.

That was the paradox at the heart of her work: sometimes the best solution is the one that shouldn't work at all.
question: What is Dr. Gordon's phobia as detailed in her personnel file?

The Geologists of Titan's Edge

By the expedition log of Dr. Li Ramos
Recorded at Dalebrook Station, Aldoria Sector

There were two crystalline formations on the tiny plateau that shouldn't have existed.

To understand the geological mystery of Titan's Edge, one must consider three elements: the observer, the phenomenon, and the catalyst. All three existed on this remote moon, but there was a question as to their true nature.

The fourth day of the *Horizon Explorer's* landing on the tidally-locked moon orbiting the gas giant Prometheus was a repetition of the three before it—a twelve-hour cycle of eerie, phosphorescent twilight. Geologist Dr. Li Ramos—standing her rotation on monitoring duty—sat at the observation dome with her spectrographic scanner ready; but despite her vigilance, she had captured no useful data when the inevitable pre-shift luminescence began to shimmer over the methane sea to the east.

The cycle change brought her alert with a start, frowning at the sight of two meter-tall crystalline formations standing on the tiny basalt plateau a half-kilometer from shore, their geometric faces oriented precisely toward the research station.

"They're back again," Ramos called, and climbed down from the dome. "Everyone up! I'm going to run a full spectral analysis this time!"

Walter Gutierrez and Timothy Kelly emerged from their rest pods reluctantly, fastening the thermal suits required even in Titan's Edge's carefully regulated artificial atmosphere. Gutierrez blinked as he cycled through the airlock, his gray beard frosted with condensation and his rounded frame moving stiffly. He looked, Ramos thought for the hundredth time, more like a retired university dean than the veteran commander of a Terran Geological Survey expedition.

Kelly followed, his lean athletic build moving with the careful precision of someone trained in extreme-environment protocols. Kelly was the team's xenomineralogist, a man in his late twenties with sharp features and an intensity that sometimes bordered on obsessive.

"Any sign of the silicon-based organisms yet?" he asked.

"They won't emerge until the crystal-eaters arrive," Ramos said. She adjusted the wavelength filter of her scanner and frowned at Gutierrez. "Walter, I wish you'd let me take core samples this time. This cycle of destruction is affecting our data quality."

Gutierrez shielded his eyes against the glare of Prometheus rising over the methane sea. "You know I can't authorize that, Li. These formations may represent a form of proto-intelligence or higher, and under Terran Survey Protocols, our interference with what may be a fundamental geological process would violate every principle of scientific collaboration. We need to crack the chemical communication patterns and understand the ecosystem restoration cycle before we can intervene."

Ramos turned an irritated stare toward the cluster of smaller crystalline structures gathering at the edge of the sulfur-dioxide frost fields that bordered the landing site.

"What puzzles me is the pattern," she said. "Why do these formations migrate to that plateau every cycle, when the outcome is always the same?"

Kelly answered with his own persistent mystery, his angular face troubled. "For that matter, what happened to the city I detected during our orbital survey? The electromagnetic signatures suggested a massive structure, yet we've mapped this entire moon in the rover and found nothing but methane seas and scattered plateaus like this one, all covered in mineral deposits. The architecture I detected wasn't something these crystal formations could have created. The complexity was beyond anything natural by orders of magnitude."

Gutierrez and Ramos exchanged weary looks. The city had become an obsession with Kelly, and his stubborn insistence—coupled with an annoying habit of being proven right—had worn their patience thin.

"There never was a city here, Tim," Gutierrez said. "You misinterpreted the data during orbital insertion, that's all."

Kelly stiffened defensively, but Ramos's voice cut through. "Get ready! Here they come!"

Out of the luminescent haze descended a swarm of silicon-based flyers, each three meters across and gleaming with metallic compounds in the dim light. They dove like raptors upon the plateau, engulfing the two crystalline formations instantly under their grinding, abrading appendages. Then around the outcrop, the ground erupted violently, churned up by a sudden emergence of dark, tentacled shapes composed of living polymer chains.

"The silicon-eaters," Gutierrez muttered. "Right on schedule. Two seconds too late, as always, to prevent the destruction."

A barrage of chemical tendrils lashed out from the emerging organisms and struck into the swarm of flyers. The flyers retreated immediately into the haze, leaving behind three of their number who were pulled beneath the surface like trapped insects. No trace remained of the two crystalline formations.

"A perfect example of predator-prey dynamics," Ramos said, deactivating her scanner. "Do any of those entities look like city-builders to you, Tim?"

The smaller crystalline structures drifted past from the shelter of the frost fields, seemingly oblivious to the researchers, and arranged themselves along the mineral-rich ledges near the methane sea to begin their photosynthetic cycle.

"Nothing we've observed fits the technological signatures I detected," Kelly said stubbornly. "But the source is here somewhere, and I'm going to find it. Will either of you need the rover today?"

Gutierrez raised his hands in surrender. "I have mountains of geological data to process, and Li is off duty after her monitoring shift. Take the rover, but you won't find anything."

The rover was a distant speck on the horizon when Ramos entered her rest pod a short time later, leaving Gutierrez to organize his collection of samples. Sleep eluded her initially; a vague sense of overlooked details nagged at her consciousness, but it wasn't until drowsiness finally claimed her that the discrepancy crystallized into clarity.

She recalled then that on the first day of the *Explorer's* landing, one of the crystal formations had fallen from a ledge into a methane pool and had dissolved rapidly before the polymer organisms could extract it with their tendrils. Which meant that the formations couldn't survive in liquid methane—otherwise some would surely have adapted to that environment.

And the expedition had surveyed Titan's Edge exhaustively without finding any mechanism for the formations to traverse the methane sea. The logical chain completed itself automatically, nearly jolting Ramos from her drowsy state.

"Impossible," she muttered. "No traversal mechanism, and they can't survive the sea. *Then how do they reach that plateau?*"

She fell asleep with the paradox unresolved.

Gutierrez was still hunched over his sample analysis when Ramos emerged from her pod and extracted a nutrition pack from the storage unit. The communication panel above the control console hummed softly, its display blank on open channel.

"Has Kelly located his phantom city yet?" Ramos asked, grinning when Gutierrez snorted.

"He's scanning the sunward hemisphere now," Gutierrez said. "Li, I'm going to ground Tim tomorrow, despite my reluctance to issue direct orders. He's fixated on that electromagnetic anomaly, and he lacks the perspective to understand how dangerous such an obsession can be to our mission parameters."

Ramos shrugged. "I'd normally agree, except for Tim's frustrating tendency to be correct. I hope he finds it soon, if it exists. I'll probably be covering his monitoring shifts until he's satisfied."

Gutierrez looked relieved. "Would you mind taking tonight's shift? I'm exhausted after processing today's samples."

Ramos gestured agreement and gathered her scanning equipment. Darkness had fallen outside—the deep, absolute darkness of Titan's Edge's shadow side, where Prometheus's bulk blocked all light from the distant sun. She positioned her chair at the observation dome and activated her data pad, settling in comfortably while Gutierrez prepared a sleep aid before retiring.

Later she would remember that Gutierrez had taken a sedative, but at the moment it seemed routine. Within minutes, his gentle snoring drifted through the station, a sound faintly irritating against the absolute silence outside.

Ramos reviewed her notes and returned to the inconsistencies she'd identified. The formations couldn't survive methane immersion, and without any traversal mechanism...

It occurred to her then that there had been precisely two formations on the plateau each cycle, and the consistency made her sit up abruptly, startled. Why two? Why not three or four, or only one?

She cycled through the airlock and paced restlessly on the processed landing pad, feeling the artificial atmosphere's warmth against her face. Four days of routine monitoring had built up a need for direct investigation that chafed at her scientific discipline; she was intrigued and simultaneously frustrated by the enigmatic relationship linking the crystal formations to the flyers and polymer organisms, and her desire to understand that relationship was intensified by the knowledge that Titan's Edge could provide crucial insights into biodiversity conservation principles. That is, she thought wryly, if Terran scientists could rationalize the bizarre cycle pursued by its indigenous life forms—what appeared to be deliberate self-sacrifice in pairs.

She reviewed again the improbable drama of the past four cycles, and found it scientifically explicable until she reached the question of motivation and the transportation mechanism that placed the formations in pairs on the plateau, when her entire framework of hypothesis collapsed into contradictions. She abandoned the effort finally; how could any human scientist rationalize the alien imperatives that drove such fundamentally different forms of existence?

She returned inside, and the sound of Gutierrez's muffled snoring aggravated her restlessness. She made her decision impulsively, setting aside the scanner for a portable light and a pocket-sized communicator which she clipped to her thermal suit.

She didn't select any defensive equipment because she saw no need for it. The light would reveal how the formations reached the outcrop, and if she required assistance the communicator would summon Gutierrez. Investigating without Gutierrez's authorization was, technically speaking, a violation of Survey Protocols, but—

"Damn the protocols," she muttered. "I need to *understand*."

Ramos activated the light at the edge of the frost field and proceeded carefully, eager for discovery now that she'd committed to action. Just inside the mineral deposits she encountered a pair of small crystalline structures, dormant and stable, their geometric faces completely blank and unrevealing.

She worked deeper into the field and found other dormant pairs, but nothing else. There were no atmospheric disturbances, no thermal variations, no electromagnetic anomalies. She had penetrated close to the field's center without further discovery and was preparing to return, disappointed, when something massive and powerful seized her from behind.

A sharp cold burned through her thermal suit at the shoulder, and a sudden overwhelming numbness swept her into unconsciousness deeper than Titan's Edge's darkness. Her last conscious thought wasn't of her own danger, but of Gutierrez—sedated and unprotected in the station...

She was standing upright when consciousness returned, her back to the methane sea and a prismatic shimmer of cycle-change luminescence reflecting on the liquid surface before her. For a moment she was completely disoriented; then peripherally she detected the crystalline blur of a formation standing beside her, and cried out in panic when she tried to turn her head and couldn't.

She was on the basalt plateau offshore, and except for autonomic functions of balance and respiration, her body was paralyzed.

The first glow of Prometheus-rise blurred the reflected luminescence at her feet, but for several seconds her racing mind was too occupied to consider the implications of her predicament. *Whatever transported me here immobilized me first*, she thought. *That cold at my shoulder was like a chemical injection.*

Panic seized her again when she remembered the silicon-based flyers; more seconds passed before she regained control, her suit's thermal regulation system straining against her fear-induced temperature spike. She had to get help. If she could activate the communicator at her belt and call Gutierrez...

She focused every ounce of concentration toward raising her right hand, and failed.

Her arm felt like solid metal, its inertia impossible to overcome. She released the effort with a groan, anxiety rising again when she saw Prometheus's bright curve on the methane sea, edges distorted by surface tension waves.

On shore she could see the *Horizon Explorer* resting between frost field and landing pad, its composite hull gleaming with condensation. The airlock remained open, and the empty rover dock told her that Kelly hadn't yet returned.

She realized then that sensation was gradually returning, that the cold surface of the communicator unit at her hip—previously unfelt—was now pressing against her forearm. She concentrated again on movement; this time her arm responded slightly, enough to send hope surging through her. If she could apply sufficient pressure to the activation stud...

The tiny click of its engagement left her weak with relief.

"Gutierrez!" she called. "Walter, emergency—*Gutierrez*!"

The communicator hummed quietly, without response.

She gathered herself for another call, and remembered with horror the sedative Gutierrez had taken before retiring. Exhausted by his work, Gutierrez had ensured he wouldn't be easily disturbed.

Prometheus's curve on the sea brightened and expanded. Above its reflected glow she detected movement, a restless suggestion of approaching flyers.

She tried again. "Gutierrez, help me! I'm on the plateau!"

The communicator crackled. The voice that answered wasn't Gutierrez's, but Kelly's.

"Ramos! What are you doing on that killing ground?"

Ramos suppressed an hysterical laugh. "Never mind that—get here immediately, Tim! The flyers—"

She stopped, seeing for the first time the polymer organisms that surrounded the plateau just beneath the surface, waiting with chemical tendrils extended and sensor nodes studying her with alien awareness. She heard the unmistakable sound of approaching flyers behind and above her then, and thought with shock-induced clarity: *I wanted to observe this phenomenon, and now I'm part of it*.

The rover roared in from the west across the frost field, passing so close overhead that she felt the turbulence of its passage. Almost instantly she heard the high-pitched whine of its emergency thrusters as Kelly intercepted the flyer swarm directly.

Kelly's voice came through the communicator. "Dispersed them temporarily, Li—disrupted their navigation with the thruster wash, I think. Hold position. I'm retrieving you now."

The rover settled on the plateau beside Ramos, so close that the heat from its exhaust system warmed her legs through the thermal suit. Kelly extended his arms and pulled her inside like a mannequin, ignoring the crystal formation. The rover accelerated toward shore with Ramos lying across Kelly's lap in the cockpit, her head hanging partially outside.

Ramos had a final disorienting glimpse of the plateau against the blur of methane sea below, and felt her shaky laugh of relief catch in her throat. Two of the polymer organisms were moving strongly toward shore, holding the rigid crystal formation carefully above the liquid surface between them.

"Tim," Ramos croaked. "Tim, can you look back? I think I'm hallucinating."

The rover swerved briefly as Kelly glanced back. "You're fine, Li. Just stay calm. I'll explain everything when we get you safely to the *Explorer*."

Ramos forced herself to relax, more relieved than alarmed by the painful tingling of returning sensation. "I should have known, damn you," she said. "You found your city, didn't you?"

Kelly sounded slightly disgusted, as if still annoyed with himself over some personal failure. "I should have found it sooner if I'd applied basic principles. It was submerged, obviously."

In the *Horizon Explorer*, Kelly woke Gutierrez from his sedated sleep and distributed stimulant drinks, leaving Ramos comfortably positioned in the padded command chair. The paralysis continued to fade gradually, easing Ramos's fear of permanent damage.

"We never detected the city from the rover because we didn't achieve sufficient altitude," Kelly said. "I finally realized that, remembering oral history accounts of how early aviators used high-altitude observation to detect submarine structures, and when I took the rover high enough, there it was, at the bottom of the methane sea—a city comparable to anything humans ever constructed."

Gutierrez stared. "A submerged city? Why would aquatic organisms need buildings?"

"They wouldn't," Kelly said. "I believe the city must have been built ages ago—by beings similar to the crystal formations or a related species, judging from the architecture—and was submerged later by geological subsidence that eliminated the original builders and left Titan's Edge with only scattered plateaus. The polymer organisms evolved to dominance then, and from all evidence they've developed a sophisticated culture."

"I don't follow," Gutierrez complained, shaking his head. "The crystal formations—"

"Are livestock, or less," Kelly finished. "The polymer organisms are the dominant intelligence, and they're so far advanced that we're completely violating protocols here. Under Survey Regulations we can't establish research operations on Titan's Edge. It would constitute unauthorized interference."

"Interference with a polymer-based civilization?" Ramos protested, confused. "Why would surface research conflict with a submerged culture, Tim? Why couldn't we coexist?"

"Because the polymer organisms control the plateaus too, and actively manage them," Kelly said patiently. "They even cultivate the crystal formations. It was one of the polymer-people, making a terrestrial survey of its managed territory to select specimens for this cycle's event, that transported you last night."

"Consider the familiar pattern emerging," Gutierrez said. He laughed suddenly, a deep resonant sound of comprehension. "Titan's Edge is a polymer-people's world, Li, don't you see? And like most advanced civilizations, they practice resource management. The silicon-based flyers are the resource they harvest, and they cultivate the crystal formations for—"

Ramos swore in amazement. "Then those formations are placed there deliberately, like bait on a hook—inverted predation! No wonder I couldn't determine their motivation! It's a principle of ecosystem restoration and complexity science—managed predator-prey dynamics for biodiversity conservation!"

Kelly moved to seal the airlock, blocking out the dim luminescence. "Research operations being prohibited, we should depart before the polymer organisms become sufficiently curious about us to create complications. Can you handle the acceleration, Li?"

Ramos and Gutierrez looked at each other, understanding dawning. Ramos said: "You don't think I want to remain here and be used as bait again, do you?"

She and Gutierrez were still processing the implications when Kelly, expressionless, fired the *Horizon Explorer's* engines and lifted them free of Titan's Edge.

The final entry in Dr. Li Ramos's expedition log noted that the discovery would require extensive peer review and consultation with bioethics committees before any future missions could be authorized. The polymer-people's sophisticated approach to ecosystem management—using cultivated crystal formations as bait to harvest silicon-based flyers—represented a level of technological progress and scientific understanding that demanded respect under all Terran protocols regarding contact with advanced civilizations.

What the expedition couldn't have known was that the polymer-people had been monitoring them since arrival, and had deliberately allowed Kelly to discover the submerged city as a form of communication—a demonstration that Titan's Edge was already claimed by an intelligence that understood complexity science far better than any human researcher.

The city, built by an ancient crystal-based civilization before geological subsidence flooded the lowlands, had been preserved by the polymer-people as a monument to their predecessors. In their own chemical communication system—incomprehensible to humans—they had been trying to convey a simple message: *We remember those who came before. We honor their legacy through careful stewardship. Please respect what we have built upon their foundation.*

But that message, like so many attempts at interspecies communication, was lost in translation. The humans departed, recording Titan's Edge as off-limits for colonization, never understanding that the polymer-people had been offering not a warning, but an invitation to mutual scientific collaboration.

The crystal formations continued their cycles, the silicon-based flyers continued their harvests, and the polymer-people continued their patient cultivation of an ecosystem they had spent millennia learning to understand. And deep beneath the methane sea, the ancient city stood as a reminder that civilizations rise and fall, but the principles of careful stewardship and biodiversity conservation remain eternal.

In the end, the greatest mystery wasn't how the city came to be submerged, but why the humans never thought to ask what the polymer-people might have learned from preserving it.
question: Who is the xenomineralogist on the team?

The Salvage Run
By MARCUS CHEN

Stand by for the
M.S. Prometheus
, laughingstock of the Merchant Marine. She's got something revolutionary in her engines, and only her brilliant engineer can make it work!

Captain Samuel Perkins stood in the acidic rain of Forestdale Station, Belvoria, and stared at his new assignment with barely concealed disgust. The rain here never stopped—a consequence of the atmospheric processors that had made this moon habitable but had never quite gotten the weather right. Now a thick fog was rolling in from the industrial sectors, reducing visibility to near zero. It was a typical day on Belvoria.

Samuel cursed Administrator Chen and all his bureaucratic ancestors with considerable feeling. Then he motioned to his companion, and together they trudged through the muck toward the ancient cargo hauler.

The bulky frame of the Merchant Ship
Prometheus
loomed unhappily into the thick air above the two men as they reached the loading bay. Samuel raised reluctant eyes to the scarred hull of the fat cargo ship.

"It looks," he commented bitterly, "like a flying warehouse that lost a fight with an asteroid."

First Officer Anil Hunt—"Hunt" to his friends—nodded in agreement. "That's our Fire-Bringer... old Prommy herself. The ship with the cursed reputation." Hunt had been with her a full year, which was a record for First Officers on the
Prometheus
. She generally sent them back to Earth with stress disorders in half that time.

"Tell me, Captain," continued Hunt curiously, "how does it happen that you of all people happened to draw this tub for a command? I thought..."

"You know Chen?" queried Samuel.

Hunt nodded. "Oh, yes. Yes, indeed. Old Iron-Desk Chen?"

"The same."

"Well," Hunt ran a hand over his chin speculatively, "I know Chen's a prize bureaucrat... but you were in command of the
Constellation
. And, after all, you come from an old merchant family and all that. How come this?" He indicated the cargo hauler expressively.

Samuel sighed. "Well, now, Hunt, I'll tell you. You'll be shipping with me and I guess you've a right to know the worst... not that you wouldn't find it out anyway. I come from a long line of very successful captains. Five generations of officers and entrepreneurs. Steeped in tradition.

"The first Samuel Perkins, son of a shipping magnate, emerged from the Corporate Wars a fleet commander and Innovation Medal winner. Then came Samuel Perkins II, and in the Media Consolidation Crisis of 2087, he won a Transparency Citation for exposing corporate corruption. And then came Samuel Perkins III... me.

"From such humble beginnings do great traditions grow. But something happened when I came into the picture. I don't fit with the rest of them. Call it luck or temperament or what have you.

"In the first place, I seem to have an uncanny talent for saying the wrong thing to the wrong person. Chen for example. And I take too much initiative. Chen doesn't like that. I lost the
Constellation
because I left my assigned route to rescue a group of miners I thought were in danger from pollution control failures at an orbital refinery..."

"The Queenstown incident?" asked Hunt.

"So you've heard about it." Samuel shook his head sadly. "My environmental specialist warned me that the refinery's containment systems might fail catastrophically. I left my scheduled delivery to evacuate miners." He shrugged. "Wrong guess. No failure. I made an ass of myself and lost the
Constellation
. Chen gave it to his former protégé. I got this."

Hunt coughed slightly. "I heard something about Summit Station, too."

"Me again. The
Constellation's
whole crew ended up in the Ulvaria detention center. We celebrated a successful run a bit too freely."

Hunt looked admiringly at his new Commander. "That was the day after the
Constellation
broke the record for the Jarvonia-to-Belvoria run, wasn't it? And then wasn't there something about..."

"Springfield?"

Hunt nodded.

"That time I called the Trade Minister's economic policies 'a masterclass in how to destroy labor relations.' It was at a political economy summit."

"I begin to see what you mean, Captain."

"Samuel's the name, Hunt."

Hunt's smile was expansive. "Samuel, I think you're going to like our old rust bucket here." He patted the
Prometheus's
loading bay affectionately. "She's old... but she's independent. And we're not likely to meet any Ministers or Administrators with her, either."

Samuel sighed, still thinking of his sleek
Constellation
. "She'll haul cargo, I suppose. And that's about all that's expected of her."

Hunt shrugged philosophically. "Better than processing waste materials, anyway. Deep space?"

Samuel shook his head. "Belvoria-Selvoria."

Hunt scratched his chin speculatively. "Inner system run. Routine work."

Samuel was again looking at the ship's unprepossessing exterior. "A quantum-drive hauler, so help me."

Hunt nodded agreement. "The last of her class."

And she was not an inspiring sight. The unfortunately named
Prometheus
was a quantum-drive cargo hauler built some fifteen years back in the period immediately preceding the Resource Wars. She had been designed primarily for conventional cargo runs, with a quantum-drive system for emergency high-speed transport. At least that was the designer's vision. In those days, quantum propulsion was in its experimental stage, and at the time of the
Prometheus's
launching, the quantum-drive was hailed as the future of shipping.

Her designer, Marcus Schultz, had been awarded a Pioneer's Medal for her, and every shipping executive in the fleet had dreamed of commanding one of her class. There had been three. The
Atlas
, the
Titan
, and the prototype... old Prommy. The three vessels had gone into service during the Resource Crisis after the Selvoria Embargo had disrupted trade routes.

All three were spectacular failures.

The eager captains commanding the three haulers had found the quantum-drive too tempting not to use. They activated it... improperly.

The
Atlas
suffered a catastrophic engine failure. The
Titan
vanished in the general direction of the outer colonies, her quantum core destabilizing and creating a radiation hazard. And the
Prometheus's
port engines blew, causing her to spin uncontrollably under extreme acceleration until all her cargo and much of her interior equipment was destroyed, along with half her crew.

The
Prometheus
was refitted for service. And because it was an integral part of her design, the quantum-drive was rebuilt... and locked down. She became a workhorse, growing more temperamental with each passing year. She carried supplies. She hauled ore. She transported equipment and personnel. Now, she would carry time-sensitive medical supplies and research materials. She would lift from Forestdale and burn to Queenstown, Selvoria, without delay or variation. Regulations, tradition, and Administrator Chen of the Inner System Trade Authority required it. And it was now up to Samuel Perkins III to see to it that she did...

The Officer of the Deck, a sharp-featured woman in crisp uniform, saluted smartly as Samuel and Hunt stepped through the airlock.

Samuel felt vaguely uncomfortable. He knew, of course, that at least half the personnel on board civilian vessels was female, but he had never actually had women in senior positions on a ship of his own, and he felt quite certain that he preferred a different arrangement.

Hunt sensed his discomfort. "That was Rita Jenkins, Samuel. Lieutenant. Navigation Officer. She's excellent, too."

Samuel shook his head. "Don't like mixing professional and personal dynamics. Makes me uncomfortable."

Hunt shrugged. "Rita's the only senior officer. But about a third of our crew is female." He grinned maliciously. "Equal opportunity, you know."

"No doubt," commented the other sourly. "Is that why they named this... ship 'Prometheus'?"

Hunt saw fit to consider the question rhetorical and remained silent.

Samuel ducked through the hatchway to the main control deck. Hunt followed. He trailed his Captain through a maze of conduits and control panels to the main engineering station. Samuel sank into a command chair in front of the red LOCKED seal on the quantum-drive control.

"Looks like something from a particle physics lab, doesn't it?" commented Hunt.

Samuel nodded sadly, thinking of the streamlined efficiency of the
Constellation's
bridge. "But she's home to us, anyway."

The thick Belvorian fog had closed in around the upper levels of the ship, obscuring the viewports and cutting off all view of the station outside. Samuel reached for the communications panel.

"Attention all crew. All senior personnel will assemble on the command deck at 0600 hours for Captain's briefing. Officer of the Deck will recall any crew currently on shore leave..."

Hunt was on his feet, all casualness gone from his manner. "Orders, Captain?"

"We can't do anything until the new Engineering Officer gets here. They're sending someone from the
Orion
, and I expect them by 0600 hours. In the meantime, you'll coordinate their duties. See to it that we are fueled and ready to launch by 0602. Station will start loading the cargo at 0599:30. That's about all."

"Yes, sir." Hunt saluted and turned to go. At the hatchway, he paused. "Captain," he asked, "Who is the new E/O to be?"

Samuel stretched his legs out on the deck plates. "A Lieutenant Schultz. Ruby Schultz, according to the orders."

Hunt thought hard for a moment and then shrugged his shoulders. "Ruby Schultz." He shook his head. "Don't know her."

The other officers of the
M.S. Prometheus
were in conference with the Captain when Hunt and the woman at his side reached the command deck. She was tall and auburn-haired with striking features and intelligent green eyes. She wore a service uniform with two silver bars on the collar, and even the standard-issue garment couldn't hide her confident bearing.

Samuel's back was toward the hatchway, and he was addressing the others.

"...and that's the situation. We are to transit within standard safety parameters of the Selvoria system. Route is direct trajectory. With current orbital positions, we have a straightforward run and it should be routine. But I'm certain this old hauler can handle it. I understand the designer who built her wasn't as incompetent as history suggests. But Trade Regulations are specific about medical supply runs. This is important to you, Jenkins. Your navigation has to be accurate to within fifty kilometers plus or minus the optimal route. And there'll be no course deviations. Now be certain that the life support systems are checked, Mister Ward, especially in the biological storage units. Proper environmental controls are going to be critical."

"That's about all there is to tell you. As soon as our apparently delayed E/O gets here, we can launch with our precious cargo." He nodded. "That's the story. Launch in..." He glanced at his chronometer, "...in one hour and ten minutes."

The officers filed out and Hunt stuck his head into the room. "Captain?"

"Come in, Hunt." Samuel's brows knit at the sight of the uniformed woman in the doorway.

Hunt's face was neutral, but hidden amusement was kindling behind his eyes. "Captain, may I present Lieutenant Schultz? Lieutenant
Ruby
Schultz?"

Samuel looked blankly at the woman.

"Our new E/O, Captain," prompted Hunt.

"Uh... welcome aboard, Lieutenant Schultz," was all the Captain could find to say.

The woman's eyes were cold and professional. "Thank you, Captain." Her voice was crisp and businesslike. "If I may have your permission to inspect the engines, Captain, I
may
be able to convince you that the designer of this vessel was not... as you seem to think... an incompetent fool."

Samuel was perplexed, and he showed it. "Why, certainly... uh... Lieutenant... but why should you be so..."

The woman's voice was even sharper than before as she said, "Marcus Schultz, Captain, is my father."

Two weeks in space had convinced Samuel that he commanded a jinx ship. Burning toward Selvoria from Belvoria, the cantankerous
Prometheus
had suffered a coolant leak, and it had been necessary to reduce speed while Ward, the Assistant E/O, and a maintenance crew effected repairs. When full power was restored, old Prommy was running twelve hours behind schedule, and Samuel and Jenkins, the Navigation Officer, were sweating out the unforeseen changes introduced into the trajectory calculations by the time spent at reduced speed.

The
Prometheus
rumbled on toward Queenstown...

For all the tension between the occupants of the command deck, Samuel and Ruby Schultz worked well together. And after a third week in space, a reluctant admiration was replacing the resentment between them. Ruby spent whatever time she could spare analyzing her father's quantum-drive design, and Samuel began to realize that there was little she didn't know about spacecraft engineering. Then, too, Ruby spent considerable time at the controls, and Samuel was forced to admit that he had never seen finer piloting done by anyone.

And finally, Ruby hated old Iron-Desk Chen even more than Samuel did. She felt that Chen had destroyed her father's career through bureaucratic obstruction and poor understanding of organizational development principles, and she was dedicating her career to proving her father right and Chen wrong. There's nothing in the cosmos to nurture friendship like a common enemy.

At three weeks into the journey, the
Prometheus's
environmental systems were functioning normally, maintaining the interior of the ship at a comfortable temperature. The crew had settled into routine, and morale was improving. The personnel dressed in standard uniforms, and the ship ran smoothly under Ruby's expert management.

Samuel was in the forward observation bay when Jenkins called to say that she had picked up a distress signal. The emergency beacon showed the signal to be from the
Hercules
and the
Achilles
. The two corporate research vessels were engaged in material science experiments in deep space... a purely routine operation. But the thing that made Samuel curse under his breath was Jenkins's notation that the
Achilles
carried none other than Trade Administrator Marcus Chen himself, along with a media production crew documenting advances in natural resource management.

Samuel thought it a pity that old Iron-Desk couldn't fall into a black hole... and he told Ruby so.

And she agreed.

Old Prommy had reached the halfway point when it happened. The crew was efficient and focused. Hunt and Jenkins had resolved their earlier tension about some minor point concerning the ship's cargo distribution. Ruby went about her work on the bridge with professional determination, and Samuel made no attempt to disturb her concentration. Lieutenant Ward had successfully completed all maintenance protocols. The crew was functioning well...

And then it happened.

Hunt was in the communications room when the operator pulled the message from the decoder. It was a distress signal from the
Hercules
. The
Achilles
had suffered a catastrophic reactor failure and was drifting helplessly toward a debris field from an old mining operation. Radiation made a transfer of personnel impossible, and the
Achilles's
escape pods didn't have the power to reach safe distance from the contaminated area. The
Hercules
had attached a tether to the sister vessel and was trying to pull the heavy ship to safety, but even the considerable power of the
Hercules's
drive wasn't enough to overcome the gravitational pull toward the dangerous debris field.

A fleet of specialized rescue tugs was on its way from Summit Station and Springfield Port, but they could not possibly arrive in time. And it was doubtful that even the tugs had the necessary power to drag the crippled
Achilles
away from a collision course.

Hunt snatched the message from the operator's hands and rushed to the command deck. He burst in and waved the message excitedly in front of Samuel's face.

"Have a look at this! By all that's holy! Read it!"

"Well, hold it still so I can!" snapped Samuel. He read the message and passed it to Ruby Schultz with a shake of his head.

She read it through and looked up with sudden intensity. "This is
it
! This is the chance I've been waiting for, Samuel!"

He returned her gaze seriously. "For Chen to drift into a debris field? I recall I said something of the sort myself, but there are other people on those ships. And, if I know Captain Martinez on the
Hercules
, she won't release that tether even if it means her own destruction."

Ruby's eyes flashed. "That's not what I meant, and you know it! I mean this!" She touched the red-locked quantum-drive control.

"That's very interesting, Lieutenant," commented Hunt drily. "And I know that you've been studying that system extensively. But I seem to recall that the last time that drive was activated, everyone aboard became part of the bulkheads... very unpleasantly, too."

"Let me understand you, Ruby," said Samuel in a measured voice. "What you are suggesting is that I risk my ship and the lives of all of us trying to pull Chen's operation out of danger with a drive that's failed catastrophically three times out of three. Very bold."

There was fierce determination in Ruby Schultz's eyes and she sounded desperate. "But we can save those ships! We can, I
know
we can! My father designed this vessel! I know every system of her! Those operators in the Resource Crisis didn't understand the cognitive development required to use this technology properly. Father told them that! And I'm trained! I've studied the historical interpretation of every failure. I can take her in and save those ships!" Her expression turned challenging. "Or are you afraid?"

"Frankly, Ruby, I haven't enough sense to be afraid. But are you so certain that we can pull this off? If I make a mistake this time... it'll be the last. For all of us."

"We can do it," said Ruby Schultz simply.

Samuel turned to Hunt. "What do you say, Hunt? Shall we take the risk?"

Hunt shrugged. "If you say so, Samuel. It's good enough for me."

Jenkins left the bridge shaking her head. "We'll all be dead soon. And the digital transformation of shipping will have to wait."

Samuel turned to the communications panel. "Ward!"

"Ward here," came the reply.

"Have communications get a directional fix on the
Achilles
and maintain it. We'll home on their emergency beacon. They're in trouble and we're going after them. Plot the intercept course."

"Yes, Captain."

Samuel turned to Hunt. "Have the cargo teams stand by to assist the engineering crew. It's going to require all hands and we'll need coordination."

"Yes, sir!" Hunt saluted and was gone.

Samuel returned to the communications panel. "Navigation!"

"Jenkins here," replied Rita from her station.

"Get a positional fix on the
Hercules
and maintain it. Send your data to Ward and tell him to send us a range estimate."

"Yes, Captain," she replied crisply.

"Engineering bay!"

"Engineering here, sir," came a voice.

"Have the auxiliary tether system prepared with reinforced cable. Be ready to deploy on short notice... any range."

"Yes, sir!" The response was immediate.

"And now you, Lieutenant Schultz."

"Yes, Captain?" Her voice was steady.

"Take over primary control... and Ruby..."

"Yes?"

"Don't kill us off." He smiled at her.

She nodded silently and took her place at the control panel. Smoothly she turned old Prommy's nose toward the distress signal...

Linked together with a length of industrial-grade tether cable, the
Hercules
and the
Achilles
drifted helplessly toward the debris field. The desperate thrust from the
Hercules's
engines was fading, her fuel reserves depleting under the strain. Still she tried. She could not desert her sister ship, nor could she save her. Already the two ships had drifted to within dangerous proximity of the contaminated debris. The jagged remnants of old mining equipment and radioactive waste seemed like deadly obstacles waiting for the trapped people on board the vessels. The sensor arrays, the communication dishes, and other external equipment on both ships were beginning to show damage from micro-impacts. Only the robust shielding on the vessels made life within them possible. And, even so, people were in danger.

Swiftly, the bulky, ungainly shape of old Prommy drew near. On her command deck, Samuel and Ruby Schultz watched the stricken ships on the main viewscreen.

The environmental controls were stable and the air was clean despite the tension. Ruby's uniform was crisp, her focus absolute. Samuel watched her with a mixture of apprehension and confidence.

Carefully, Ruby maneuvered around the two vessels. From the auxiliary bay, a reinforced tether shot toward the
Achilles
. It flew straight and true, trailing cable as it went. It connected with the hull, and secured there, fast to the ship's frame. Quickly, automated systems drew it tight and the cable was made secure. Like cosmic replicas of ancient rescue operations, the three spacecraft aligned in space... and all three began to drift together toward danger.

They were heading into the debris field.

The tension on the
Prometheus's
bridge was palpable. Every system was operating at peak efficiency, but Samuel knew that efficiency alone wouldn't be enough.

Ruby fought the complex calculations and the unresponsive controls as the slack came out of the cable. Her hands moved with practiced precision across the instrument panel. Determinedly, she made the critical adjustment... and succeeded. Conscious and fully in control, she activated the quantum-drive system.

"
Ruby!
" Samuel was beside her, ready to assist.

"I... I can do this... Samuel. This is... what I've trained for... all my life."

Samuel stood ready but let her work. His heart was racing as she unlocked the quantum-drive control.

Slowly she adjusted the power flow. Systems responded. From deep within old Prommy's core came a low hum. She fed more energy into the drive. Control rods adjusted in the reactor chambers decks below. The humming rose in pitch. The drifting of the ships in space slowed. Stopped. With careful precision, they aligned for the rescue maneuver.

More power. The hum changed to a resonant tone. A harmonic frequency.

Hunt's voice came through the communications system, steadily. "Samuel, all systems are holding. We're at maximum capacity."

"Acknowledged, Hunt!" shouted Samuel over the tone of the drive. The gauges showed the quantum-drive fully engaged. "
Now!
" Ruby adjusted the final controls, and a surge of acceleration pressed them into their seats...

The last thing Samuel remembered clearly was a voice. It sounded like Ward's. And it was shouting. "We're moving them! We're pulling clear! We're..." And the acceleration took over.

The rescue tug
Valiant
found them.

The three ships...
Achilles
,
Hercules
, and old Prommy... linked together and drifting safely in space. Every person aboard exhausted from the acceleration stress, and
Prometheus's
fuel reserves nearly depleted. But they were a safe distance from the debris field...

The reception hall was elegant, the corporate headquarters beautifully appointed. Hunt leaned against the refreshment table and examined the silver medal of the Merchant Service Citation on Samuel's chest. Then he inspected his own and nodded with satisfaction. He looked out at the Selvoria skyline beyond the broad windows and back again at Samuel. His expression was curious.

"All right," said Samuel, setting down his glass. "What's on your mind, Hunt? Something's bothering you."

Hunt nodded slowly. He took a long sip of his drink. "I understand that you declined your chances of getting the
Constellation
back when Chen made you the offer..."

"All I said to him..."

"I know. I know what you said... and it was diplomatic enough. But you're not fooling me. You've come to appreciate old Prommy and you don't want to leave her. Very commendable. Loyal! Good captain! But what about Ruby?"

"Ruby?"

Hunt looked away. "I thought that you and she... well, I thought that when we got back... well..."

Samuel shook his head. "She's gone to the Design Bureau with an engineering development position."

Hunt waved an expressive arm in the air. "But surely, man, I thought..."

"The answer is
no
. Ruby's exceptional... but..." He paused and sighed. "Since she was promoted to her father's old rank... well..." He shrugged. "Who wants a partner that outranks you?"

"Never thought of that," mused Hunt. For a long while he was silent; then he pulled out a contact list and scrolled through until he came to the entries marked "Queenstown, Selvoria."

And he was gratified to see that Captain Samuel Perkins III was doing the same.
question: What caused the mission of the Prometheus to be delayed by twelve hours?
