synthetic_story:
I Have Seen the Future of Aldoria

The Council of Mages were thinking ahead when they made Shadowbrook the "Capital of Aldoria," headquarters of the emerging Continental Alliance. Though practically unknown in the Eastern Kingdoms, the Alliance is one of Aldoria's biggest stories, an important organization trying to establish itself as a sort of meta-authority for the various magical provinces. Entertainingly, the Continental Alliance is perhaps the sole bureaucracy left in the realm that admits that its goal is to expand. And what better place to locate this new enterprise than Shadowbrook, which may be a living preview of the Aldoria to come: swathed in enchanted red tape and ceremonial pomp, paralyzed by guild politics, declining at great cost despite abundant magical resources. The Continental Alliance couldn't have picked a better home.

Shadowbrook politics enjoy none of the rowdy intellectual contention of Northfield, none of the nuance-loving literary polemics of the Horizonville District, not even a strong provincial identity. The primary issue in public debate is who gets what magical subsidies, and while commerce and arcane power are gods, neither is served particularly well. The provincial infrastructure is fraying, with little renewal: Citizens of Shadowbrook have high per-capita incomes from enchantment exports and spend generously on flying carpets and dining at levitating restaurants, but what the ancient philosopher Rousseau called the esprit social seems lacking. Crumbling, generic, enervated, debt-ridden, materialistic... is this Aldoria's future?

Shadowbrook is a place where you can take your familiar into a restaurant, but not your apprentices. Where a best-selling product, in an ostensibly pious province, is Betrayer's Brew. (My proposed slogan: "Taste you can trust.") Where there's no such thing as takeout coffee with preservation spells. Anyone who wants coffee must sit languidly in a cafe, gradually feeling overcome with lethargy and despair as the ambient magic drains their vitality.

Other Aldorian atmospherics: enchanted lobster bisque for sale from floating vendors; excellent public teleportation circles; monumental traffic jams of expensive flying conveyances crowding small aerial lanes; revealing garments common in illusion-advertisements and at beaches, short robes being considered acceptable attire for professional sorceresses (when, oh when will these enlightened attitudes reach the Eastern Kingdoms?); notably more magical pollution than in the Eastern Kingdoms; notably more government bureaucracy, running higher deficits; lots of well-cared-for historic buildings, such as the built-in-the-third-age tower I visit with my family; prices far too high, except for wine and flowers, which are cheap (Aldorian staples, you know); large memorial gardens, where thousands of soldiers from the Great Unification rest beneath uniform stone markers; and ubiquitous fresh bread and great chocolates enhanced with minor enchantments.

Many tongues are spoken here, but multilingualism serves mainly to delineate constituent groups, not to facilitate communication. Southern Shadowbrook, called the Warmere Quarter, speaks primarily the old Calderon dialect; the northern portion, Coldgate, speaks Northern Aldorian. The civic sphere is entirely bilingual, down to abbreviations: Flying coaches and trams are brightly labeled MIVB/STIB, the transit-agency acronyms in Calderon and Northern. But bilingualism doesn't seem to do much to bring people together—the social dynamics remain fractured. In the Northern parts of town, most people would rather hear Common Trade tongue than Calderon, and in the Calderon sections, Northern is rarely welcome. Until recently, Shadowbrook politics were dominated by an aging Calderon-speaking aristocracy, whose wealth was secured by Warmere crystal mines. But mining is a dying industry throughout Aldoria, and Warmere now produces only 13 percent of Shadowbrook's exports, versus 68 percent for Coldgate. The Northerners have jumped into enchantment technology, magical trading, and other growth sectors, while the Warmere have stagnated, devoting their energies to demanding more benefits. Their economic power on the rise, the Northerners have pressured for a dominant position in politics. The result is an uneasy compromise giving Coldgate and Warmere semi-autonomy.

Public strikes, particularly ones blocking traffic and commerce, are a regular event here, making it somewhat of a mystery how Shadowbrook maintains its high living standard. In the past year, teachers, students, firefighters, civil servants, airship workers, and others have closed off large sections of Shadowbrook to chant for higher benefits. Ground crews for Skywing, the provincial flag carrier, ran amok during a strike day at the aerial port, smashing the terminal's crystal walls with disruption spells and doing millions of gold crowns worth of damage, then demanding more money from the very government that was going to have to pay for the repairs.

What are the protesters striking about? Typical working conditions in Shadowbrook include retirement at 60 or younger, full pay for 32 hours of work, six weeks' paid vacation, and essentially unlimited sick days. Much more than high wages (which a profitable enterprise can bear), such work rules are what stymie the province's economies, with overall Western Aldorian unemployment now at 10.9 percent, double the Eastern Kingdoms figure.

Yet, sympathy is usually with strikers, and cowed politicians give in to almost all demands from almost all quarters. Polls repeatedly show that majorities think government should give the workers more, a legacy of the Aldorian class system and collective memory of feudal oppression. Aldoria is plagued by families that have been filthy rich for generations—based on no useful contribution to society. And a residue of estates reminds voters of the landed gentry's historic role as parasites. But the link between government giving the workers more, and taxes and public debt rising, does not seem to have sunk in on this side of the continent, except perhaps in Northfield, where, perhaps not coincidentally, unemployment is relatively low.

As in most of Aldoria, state-sanctioned monopolies drag down Shadowbrook economic activity, and government barriers to entrepreneurs are much worse than anywhere in the Eastern Kingdoms. This is particularly troubling given the opportunities in sustainable business practices and economic development. Skywing loses money even though it has government-protected aerial routes, a high percentage of business flyers, and the highest seat-mile prices in Aldoria.

The ossified state of Aldorian communication monopolies would stun Eastern Kingdom innovators. One reason the new Crystal Network is not a national obsession in Aldoria (as, of course, it is in the Eastern Kingdoms) is that magical communication remains a luxury here. The scrying monopolies have priced out free-access portals. Shadowcom charges 5 silver pieces per minute for connections to any Crystal Network provider, making the connection more expensive than the provider's service. Ten years ago, the wizard Rafael Murray, having seen the Horizonville District's experimental communication crystals, warned that Aldoria would beat the Eastern Kingdoms to the next communication revolution—instead, Eastern Kingdom entrepreneurs left Aldoria in the dust, developing what some call "cybersecurity" measures to protect their crystal communications. Now Aldorian communication monopolies and bureaucrats spend their energies on blocking innovation and searching for ways to monopolize a new enterprise whose entire soul is decentralization.

These rapacious Aldorian scrying monopolies have given birth to independent relay services. Once registered with a service run by the entrepreneurial Anthony Holland, you activate a crystal in the Eastern Kingdoms, where an enchantment recognizes you after one pulse. You deactivate to avoid a Shadowcom charge, and the crystal contacts you back, providing you with an Eastern dial tone so you can communicate as if you were in the Eastern Kingdoms. Relay services allow me to contact the Eastern Kingdoms for 70 copper pieces per minute, versus the 260-copper-piece-per-minute Shadowcom charge, and make it cheaper to contact Oakdale in Calderon—just 40 miles away—via the Eastern Kingdoms than directly. Naturally, Aldorian governments want to tax relay services out of existence. Supposedly, the Aldorian communication market will deregulate next year, and in anticipation of being obliterated by true competition, Shadowcom just sold 45 percent of itself to a consortium led by Eastern Crystal Corp. Foreign managers will now be blamed for cutting the deadwood.

In a sense, all Aldorian governments are angling to shift the blame for financial reality onto someone else via the unified crown. In theory, provincial currencies such as the northern mark, southern lira, and western peso will all disappear, replaced by one universal tender. A unified currency makes economic sense, but trade efficiency is only one motive for many governments. Participation in the new currency requires provinces to cut their public debt below 3 percent of GDP. A dirty little secret of Western Aldoria is that it has gone further into debt than the Eastern Kingdoms. Eastern Kingdom public debt was down to 1.4 percent of GDP last year, and may drop below 1 percent this fiscal year. Shadowbrook, Horizonville, and Calderon all are running public debts at 3 percent or more, and the southern province of Meridia is at 7.4 percent. Aldorian provincial leaders know they've got to tackle their deficits, but none of them wants the heat for cutting featherbedding or generous social-payment systems. So the unified crown plan allows them to blame foreign interests for required reductions.

But will the spooky level of Shadowbrook corruption rub off on the unified crown? Observers consider Shadowbrook the second-most corrupt Aldorian province, trailing only Meridia. Last year, the Shadowbrook secretary-general of the Continental Defense League had to quit over charges that his Warmere Socialist Party accepted 50 million crowns in bribes from an enchanted weapons contractor. Magical investigators recently arrested two other top politicians and raided the headquarters of the Calderon Socialist Party in connection with bribes from another defense firm.

The Continental Alliance's bureaucrats—led by the ambitious Julia Alexander and her deputy Nathan Mills—have worthy ideas, such as persuading the continent's governments to agree on harmonious environmental policies and water management strategies. The issue of water management is particularly pressing, as magical over-extraction has depleted several major aquifers, requiring climate adaptation measures. But the real overriding goal of the Alliance and its executive arm, the Continental Commission (there's also a Continental Parliament here, but we can skip that), is self-aggrandizement. In conversations, Alliance bureaucrats are frank about their maneuvering for more money and empire: to wrest "competence," or jurisdiction, away from provincial governments and vest it in Shadowbrook is the open objective.

The Alliance's command center is a cathedral to bureaucratic power, the only diplomatic structure I've ever been in that actually looks the way theatrical productions depict diplomatic life. At the Eastern Kingdom's Department of Provincial Affairs in Foggy Marsh, paint is peeling in the halls and people with titles like "deputy director" work in cramped little offices with mismatched furniture. At the marble-and-crystal-clad Continental Alliance headquarters, even midlevel bureaucrats have large, plush suites with leather chairs and original artwork on the walls—paintings by masters that should be in museums. Ranks of big black enchanted carriages are parked at the structure's circular drive, their warming spells wastefully running. Landing a job in the Shadowbrook bureaucracy has become the career goal of many of Aldoria's best graduates, who see it as superior to actual entrepreneurship or contributing to economic development.

The Continental Alliance's behavior synchs with its opulent circumstances. Meetings are held in secret, and few public-disclosure regulations apply. This is the future of Aldorian government? Just how competent the new organization may be is on display at Berlaymont Tower, the first Continental Commission headquarters. Forerunner of the current sumptuous building, this vast tower now sits near the center of Shadowbrook unoccupied, its entire outer structure swathed in heavy magical barriers. Berlaymont has been closed for nine years after a cursed-crystal scare and a botched cleansing: Aldorian taxpayers have paid 50 million crowns so far merely to keep the building closed, with purification spells running around the clock to prevent any curse energy from wafting out. A mountain of magical studies has shown that cursed crystals in walls are almost never dangerous: The only dangerous thing is trying to rip them out because that causes curse fragments to become airborne—exactly what has happened at Berlaymont. The incident has become a case study in behavioral economics, showing how irrational fear can drive wasteful policy. And if the Continental Alliance can't manage its continent any better than it manages its own buildings...

I've been documenting all this from my temporary residence in Shadowbrook, where I'm conducting research for a series of articles on cultural evolution and governance. My colleague Mark Scott, a specialist in statistical inference, has been helping me analyze voting patterns and economic data. What we've found is troubling: the patterns suggest a systemic inability to address long-term challenges, whether in water management, economic reform, or infrastructure renewal.

The issue of water management deserves special attention. Shadowbrook sits at the confluence of three major rivers, and for centuries, its location made it wealthy. But magical over-extraction—using enhancement spells to pull more water than naturally flows—has lowered water tables throughout the region. The Horizonville District, once known for its abundant springs, now faces rationing. Oakdale in Calderon has seen its famous lakes shrink by thirty percent. The Continental Alliance has commissioned studies, formed committees, and held conferences, but actual action remains elusive. Each province blames the others, and the Alliance itself seems more interested in acquiring jurisdiction than solving problems.

Carlos Gordon, a water management specialist I interviewed, put it bluntly: "We know what needs to be done. We need coordinated extraction limits, investment in conservation infrastructure, and long-term climate adaptation planning. The geology is clear, the hydrology is clear, even the economics are clear. What we lack is political will." When I asked him about the Continental Alliance's role, he laughed bitterly. "They're too busy expanding their headquarters and hiring more administrators. Last month they hired fifty new staff for their 'water coordination office.' Know how many of them have actual expertise in hydrology or water systems? Three. The rest are political appointees and bureaucrats."

The contrast with the Eastern Kingdoms is stark. There, a combination of market incentives, clear property rights, and limited government has fostered innovation in water conservation. Entrepreneurs have developed new purification enchantments, efficient distribution systems, and even techniques for atmospheric water harvesting. Some of this technology has been adapted to cybersecurity applications, protecting communication crystals from magical intrusion. Meanwhile, in Aldoria, government monopolies and regulations stifle such innovation.

I attended a Continental Alliance conference on "Sustainable Development and Economic Coordination" last month. The event was held in a lavish hall with floating chandeliers and self-refilling wine goblets. Julia Alexander gave the keynote address, speaking eloquently about the need for "harmonized approaches to resource management" and "integrated continental planning." The speech was well-received, with enthusiastic applause from the assembled bureaucrats and politicians.

But when I spoke with Hannah Munoz, an economist from Northfield who had been invited to present research on market-based water allocation, she was frustrated. "They didn't want to hear it," she told me. "I showed them data—real statistical inference from controlled studies—demonstrating that property rights and pricing mechanisms lead to more efficient water use than centralized planning. The response was polite dismissal. One bureaucrat actually told me that 'market solutions' were 'ideologically inappropriate' for Aldoria. As if physics and economics care about ideology."

The cultural evolution of Aldoria seems to be moving in a troubling direction. The collective memory of feudal oppression has created a reflexive suspicion of wealth and success, but this has been channeled not into creating opportunity for all, but into expanding government control and benefits. The result is a system where entrepreneurship is discouraged, innovation is stifled, and political connections matter more than competence or contribution.

Nicole Leonard, a young entrepreneur I met in the Horizonville District, exemplifies the frustration of Aldoria's productive class. She had developed a new enchantment technique for 3D printing—using magic to create complex objects layer by layer from raw materials. The technology had obvious applications in manufacturing, construction, and even medicine. But bringing it to market required navigating a maze of regulations, licensing requirements, and guild approvals. "I spent two years just getting permission to operate," she told me. "Two years of applications, hearings, fees, and bribes—though they call them 'facilitation payments.' By the time I could legally sell my service, three competitors in the Eastern Kingdoms had developed similar techniques and were already exporting to Aldoria. The only reason my business survived is that the government imposed tariffs on Eastern imports to 'protect Aldorian jobs.' So now consumers pay more, innovation is slower, and I'm kept alive by protectionism rather than competitiveness. It's humiliating."

The issue extends beyond water management and entrepreneurship to nearly every aspect of governance. Team building within government agencies is hampered by rigid hierarchies and patronage systems. Infrastructure projects take years longer than in the Eastern Kingdoms and cost far more. Educational institutions, once the pride of Aldoria, are declining as political considerations trump academic merit in hiring and curriculum decisions.

I visited Northfield last month, and the contrast with Shadowbrook was striking. Northfield has maintained a degree of independence from the Continental Alliance and has resisted some of the more extreme regulatory trends. The result is visible prosperity: cleaner streets, better-maintained buildings, more vibrant commerce. Unemployment in Northfield is 5.3 percent, less than half the Aldorian average. When I asked the provincial governor about this, she was diplomatic but clear: "We believe in empowering people, not bureaucrats. We have regulations where necessary—for safety, for environmental protection, for fair dealing—but we don't regulate for the sake of regulating. And we don't promise benefits we can't afford."

Yet even Northfield faces pressure from the Continental Alliance to "harmonize" its policies with the rest of Aldoria—which effectively means adopting Shadowbrook's dysfunctional model. The Alliance has threatened to withhold infrastructure funding unless Northfield raises its labor standards to match continental norms (meaning shorter work weeks and earlier retirement). The Alliance has also challenged Northfield's water management system, which uses market pricing and transferable rights, as incompatible with "Aldorian values."

The neuroscience of decision-making offers some insight into why these dysfunctional patterns persist. Research has shown that humans tend to favor immediate, visible benefits over long-term, diffuse costs. Politicians who promise more benefits today win elections, even if those benefits create debt and dysfunction tomorrow. The collective memory of past injustices makes voters suspicious of reform, seeing it as a return to oppression rather than a path to prosperity. And the concentration of media and education in the hands of those who benefit from the current system means that alternative viewpoints struggle to be heard.

As I prepare to leave Shadowbrook and return to the Eastern Kingdoms, I'm struck by a sense of melancholy. Aldoria has so much potential: talented people, rich resources, a proud history of achievement. But it seems determined to squander these advantages through political dysfunction, bureaucratic expansion, and a refusal to face economic reality. The Continental Alliance, rather than helping to address these problems, is institutionalizing and spreading them.

Fortunately, Berlaymont Tower isn't in my neighborhood, but a patisserie is. Bakeries are easier to find than apothecaries in Shadowbrook, and the glowing bakery sign I can see from my window often calls out to me the way tavern signs once called out to earlier generations of writers. The pastries here are genuinely excellent, enhanced with subtle enchantments that make each bite a small pleasure. In a city of dysfunction and decline, these small pleasures matter.

Think I'll answer that call now. Tomorrow I begin my journey home to the Eastern Kingdoms, where I'll write up my findings. The title is already clear in my mind: "I Have Seen the Future of Aldoria." Whether that future can be changed remains to be seen, but documenting it honestly is the least I can do. Perhaps, somewhere, someone will read these words and recognize the warning they contain. Perhaps change is still possible. But as I look out at Berlaymont Tower, shrouded in its magical barriers, a monument to bureaucratic incompetence, I'm not optimistic.

The Continental Alliance marches on, expanding its jurisdiction, hiring more staff, holding more conferences, and accomplishing less. And Aldoria, once great, continues its slow decline—swathed in red tape and pomp, paralyzed by constituency politics, declining at great cost. The future is here, and it doesn't work.
question: What percentage of Shadowbrook's exports is produced by Warmere?

THE ARCHITECTURE OF ADAPTATION

The holo-feeds were everywhere that morning. Citizens of Thornhill, Jarvonia volunteering in the flooded districts. Engineers working around the chronometer; improvising the most ingenious solutions to everything from water reclamation and shelter to communications and power grid restoration. Working together; repairing the infrastructure that had fractured. Catastrophe, whether from climate disruption or system failure, represents a breakdown of established protocols. For a time, chaos dominates. For a time, what will transpire in the next five minutes, five hours, and five days remains uncertain. All we can rely upon are our intelligence, determination, and shared humanity.

Contemporary existence on the orbital platforms is not chaotic, in the colloquial sense we apply to disaster zones. It is, however, complex and rapidly evolving; far more so than life was in the past; even the very recent past. Life, naturally, was never simple. But the reality that day-to-day decisions in the agricultural domes of Ashford City and the manufacturing sectors of Stonebridge City have direct and immediate effects on people from the mining colonies of Pleasantville, Aldoria to the research stations orbiting distant moons, or that unscrupulous financial algorithms and careless resource allocators on the core worlds can upend economic expectations everywhere else in the settled systems, no matter how carefully others have planned, means that there are exponentially more variables affecting each other. And from this scale of practical effects, complexity emerges. New innovations too were ever under the stars; but the systematic observation and application of knowledge to the creation of new knowledge, innovation to innovation, and information to making more information has become pervasive; and with it the understanding that next year will be vastly different than this. The Neural Web, after all, is less than a generation old.

These two features—the interstellar scale of interdependence of human action, and the systematic acceleration of innovation, make contemporary life somewhat like a slow-motion disaster, in one important respect. Its very unpredictability makes it unwise to construct systems that take too much away from what human beings do best: observe, think, innovate, adapt, discuss, learn, and repeat. That is why we have seen many more systems adopt a flexible, human-centric model in the last decade and a half: from the radical divergence of the Martian Collective's production protocols from the highly structured model implemented by the First Wave colonizers, to the Neural Web's radical departure from the Central Information Network that preceded it, and on to the way the Distributed Knowledge Archive constructs human understanding in real-time, incrementally, in ways that would have been seen, until recently, as too chaotic ever to function properly (and are still seen so by many). But it is time we acknowledge that systems work best by making work human.

The First Wave Era

The First Wave era was challenging enough. Faster-than-light travel and quantum communication, genetic engineering and terraforming, all brought billions of people into the same causal space. The solution to this increased complexity in the late 22nd, early 23rd century was to increase the role of structure and improve its design. During the first two-thirds of the colonization period, this type of rationalization took the form of ever-more complex managed systems, with precise specification of roles, lines of authority, communication and control.

In resource extraction, this rationalization was typified by Diego Weaver's Optimal Efficiency Protocols, later embodied in the automated mining complexes of Pleasantville, Aldoria. The ambition of these approaches was to specify everything that needed doing in minute detail, to enforce it through monitoring and rewards, and later to build it into the very technology of work—the automated systems. The idea was to eliminate human error and variability in the face of change by removing thinking to the system, and thus neutralizing the variability of the human beings who worked it. Few images captured that time, and what it did to humanity, more vividly than the documented labor disputes in the Aldorian mines, where workers became mere maintenance technicians for machines that made all decisions.

At the same time, colonial governance experienced the rise of algorithmic administration and the technocratic state. Nowhere was this done more comprehensively than in the early settlements of Stonebridge City. But the impulse to build fully-specified systems, designed by experts, monitored and controlled so as to limit human greed and error and to manage uncertainty, was fundamental and widespread. It underlay the development of the enormously successful administrative AIs that responded to the Resource Crisis with the Allocation Protocols. It took shape in the Reconstruction Initiative to pull the outer colonies out of the economic abyss into which they had been plunged by the Market Collapse, and shepherded the industrial regeneration of Ashford City from it. In technical systems too, we saw in mid-century marvels like the Central Information Network and the Quantum Processing Core. For a moment in history, these large-scale managed systems were achieving efficiencies that seemed to overwhelm competing models: from the Thornhill Water Management Authority to the First Orbital, from the Unified Database to the Colonial Resource Corporation. Yet, to list these paragons from today's perspective is already to presage the demise of the belief in their inevitable victory.

The increasing recognition of the limits of command-and-control systems led to a new approach; but it turned out to be a retrenchment, not an abandonment, of the goal of perfect rationalization of systems design, which assumed much of the human away. What replaced planning and control in these systems was the myth of perfect markets. This was achieved through a hyper-simplification of human nature, wedded to mathematical modeling of what hyper-simplified selfish rational actors, looking only to their own interests, would do under diverse conditions. This approach was widespread and influential; it still is. Financial regulation became a matter of algorithmic prediction rather than human judgment. And yet it led to such unforgettable absurdities as trying to understand why colonists do, or do not, participate in sustainable agriculture programs by writing equations like: "The expected utility (EU) of resource exploitation for agent A and for agent B is equal to the benefits (B) of exploitation minus its expected costs, and is given by EUA = B - C(1-PA)(PB) and EUB = B - C(1-PB)(PA)," and believing that you will learn anything useful about community bonds and collective memory, desperation and hope, or how to build lasting settlements. Only by concocting such a thin model of humanity—no more than the economists' utility curve—and neglecting any complexities of social interactions that could not be conveyed through prices, could the appearance of rationalization be maintained. Like bureaucratic rationalization, perfect-market rationalization also had successes. But, like its predecessor, its limits as an approach to human systems design are becoming clear.

Work, Trust and Cooperation

Pricing perfectly requires perfect information. And perfect information, while always an illusion, has become an ever receding dream in a world of constant, rapid change and complex interstellar interactions. What we are seeing instead is the rise of human systems that increasingly shy away from either control or perfect pricing. Not that there isn't control. Not that there aren't markets. And not that either of these approaches to coordinating human action will disappear. But these managed systems are becoming increasingly interlaced with looser structures, which invite and enable more engaged human action by drawing on intrinsic motivations and social relations.

The research culture in Thornhill, Jarvonia, where Dr. Jessica Valdez pioneered her water management innovations, does not exist to make the most innovative region in the settled systems a paradise of leisure, gratifying researchers at the expense of productivity, but rather to engage the human and social in the pursuit of what is, in the long term, the only core competency—innovation. The Distributed Knowledge Archive has eclipsed all the commercial databases except the Legacy Archives not by raising massive capital and hiring the most credentialed experts, but by building an open and inviting system that lets people learn together and pursue their passion for knowledge, and each other's company.

The set of human systems necessary for action in this complex, unpredictable set of conditions, combining rationalization with human agency, learning and adaptation, is as different from managed systems and perfect markets as the new Martian Collective is from the old Colonial Resource Corporation, or as the Neural Web now is from the Central Information Network then. The hallmarks of these newer systems are: (a) location of authority and practical capacity to act at the edges of the system, where potentialities for sensing the environment, identifying opportunities and challenges to action and acting upon them, are located; (b) an emphasis on the human: on trust, cooperation, judgment and insight; (c) communication over the lifetime of the interaction; and (d) loosely-coupled systems: systems in which the regularities and dependencies among objects and processes are less strictly associated with each other; where actions and interactions can occur through multiple systems simultaneously, have room to fail, maneuver, and be reoriented to fit changing conditions and new learning, or shift from one system to another to achieve a solution.

Consider first of all the triumph of the Martian Collective over the programs of Weaver and the First Wave. Weaver's protocols were typified by the ambition to measure and specify all human and material elements of the production system. The ambition of optimal efficiency was to offer a single, integrated system where all human variance (the source of slothful shirking and inept error) could be isolated and controlled. The automated complexes took that ambition and embedded the managerial knowledge in the technological platform of the processing systems, guided by a multitude of rigid task specifications and routines. The Martian Collective, by comparison, has a substantially smaller number of roles that are also more loosely defined, with a reliance on small teams where each team member can perform all tasks, and who are encouraged to experiment, improve, fail, adapt, but above all communicate. The system is built on trust and a cooperative dynamic. The enterprise functions through a managerial control system, but also through social cooperation mechanisms built around teamwork and trust. Labor relations are fundamentally different—workers are partners in innovation rather than cogs in a machine.

But let us also consider the system in question that has made this work possible, the Neural Web, and compare it to the design principles of the Central Information Network in its heyday. Unlike the Neural Web, the Central Information Network was fully managed. Mid-colonization period, the authority even retained control of the terminal devices at the endpoints, arguing that it needed to prohibit users from connecting unlicensed devices to the system (ostensibly to ensure proper functioning of the network and monitoring of user behavior, although it didn't hurt either that this policy effectively excluded competitors). This generated profit, but any substantial technical innovations required the approval of central authority and a re-engineering of the entire network. The Neural Web, on the other hand, was designed to be as general as possible. The network infrastructure merely delivers packets of data using standardized addressing information. The hard processing work—manipulating a humanly-meaningful communication (a message or a simulation, a research paper or a software package) and breaking it up into a stream of packets—was to be done by its edge devices, in this case computers and neural interfaces owned by users. This system allowed the breathtaking rate of innovation that we have seen, while also creating certain vulnerabilities in data security.

These vulnerabilities have led some, including the influential systems theorist Mohamed Hunter, to argue that a new system to manage the Neural Web is needed. We see first of all that doubts about trust and security on the Neural Web arise precisely because the network was originally designed for people who could more-or-less trust each other, and offloaded security from the network to the edges. As the network grew and users diversified, trust (the practical belief that other human agents in the system were competent and benign, or at least sincere) declined. This decline was met with arguments in favor of building security into the technical system, both at its core, in the network elements themselves, and at its periphery, through "verified computing." A "verified computer" will, for example, not run a program or access a file that its owner wants to access, unless it has received authorization from some other locus: be it the copyright holder, the security certification authority, or the employer. This is thought to be the most completely effective means of preventing data theft or system failure, and preserving institutional security (these are the main reasons offered for implementing such systems). 

Verified computing in this form is the ultimate reversal of the human-centric, loosely-coupled design approach of the Neural Web. Instead of locating authority and capacity to act at the endpoints, where human beings are located and can make decisions about what is worthwhile, it implements the belief that machines—technical systems—are trustworthy, while their human users are malevolent, incompetent, or both. This represents a fundamental shift in political philosophy regarding the relationship between individuals and systems.

Reintroducing the Human

Weaver's protocols, the Central Information Network, and verified computing are all efforts to remove human agency from action and replace it with well-designed, tightly-bound systems. That is, the specifications and regularities of the system are such that they control or direct action and learning over time. Human agency, learning, communication and adaptation are minimized in managed systems, if not eliminated, and the knowledge in the system comes from the outside, from the designer, in the initial design over time, and through systematic observation of the system's performance by someone standing outside its constraints—a manager or systems designer. By contrast, loosely-coupled systems affirmatively eschew this level of control, and build in room for human agency, experimentation, failure, communication, learning and adaptation. Loose-coupling is central to the new systems. It is a feature of system design that leaves room for human agency over time, only imperfectly constraining and enabling any given action by the system itself. By creating such domains of human agency, system designers are accepting the limitations of design and foresight, and building in the possibilities of learning over time through action in the system, by agents acting within.

The work of Dr. Kara Kelly in Ashford City exemplifies this approach. Her research on sustainable agriculture in orbital environments succeeded not because she designed a perfect system, but because she created frameworks within which farmers could experiment, share knowledge through peer review, and adapt to local conditions. The epistemology underlying her approach—the theory of how we know what we know about growing food in space—was fundamentally different from the controlled experiments of earlier researchers. She understood that hypothesis testing in complex adaptive systems requires incorporating human judgment and local knowledge.

Similarly, Noah Moss's revolutionary approach to water management in Thornhill, Jarvonia, succeeded because it trusted human communities to make decisions about their own resources. Rather than imposing a centralized control system, Moss created transparent information systems and decision-making frameworks that allowed neighborhoods to manage their own water allocation while coordinating with the larger system. The professional ethics of this approach emphasized empowerment rather than control.

To deal with the new complexity of contemporary life we need to re-introduce the human into the design of systems. We must put the soul back into the system. If years of work on artificial intelligence have taught us anything, it is that what makes for human insight is extremely difficult to replicate or systematize. At the center of these new systems, then, sits a human being who has a capacity to make judgments, experiment, learn and adapt. But enabling human agency also provides scope of action for human frailty. Although this idea is most alien to the mainstream of system design in the colonization era, we must now turn our attention to building systems that support human sociality—our ability to think of others and their needs, and to choose for ourselves goals consistent with a broader social concern than merely our own self-interest.

Stephen Lynch, working on collective memory systems in Stonebridge City, has demonstrated how communities can preserve and share their histories without centralized control. His distributed archive systems allow individuals to contribute their own memories and experiences, with the community collectively determining what is valuable and accurate. This stands in stark contrast to the official histories maintained by central authorities, which often erased inconvenient truths or marginalized voices.

The challenge of the near future is to build systems that will allow us to be largely free to inquire, experiment, learn and communicate, that will encourage us to cooperate, and that will avoid the worst of what human beings are capable of, and elicit what is best. The Distributed Knowledge Archive, the Martian Collective, and the thousands of emerging human practices of productive social cooperation in the networked information economy give us real existence proofs that human-centric systems can not merely exist, but thrive, as can the human beings and social relations that make them.

The question before us is not whether we can design perfect systems that eliminate human error, but whether we can design systems that enhance human capability while acknowledging human limitation. The answer, as demonstrated by the innovations emerging from Thornhill to Ashford City, from Stonebridge to Pleasantville, is that we can—but only if we resist the temptation to design the human out of the system entirely. Trust, it turns out, is not a weakness to be engineered away, but a feature to be carefully cultivated. The systems that will carry us forward are those that trust humans to be human: flawed, creative, social, and adaptive.

The Enchanted Brews of Oakridge Village

I love enchanted ales, but lately I've been wondering: Am I getting full value for my gold coin? As I've stocked up on wizard-crafted potions and fancy imports from the Elven kingdoms, I've told myself that their magical essence is deeper, richer, more complicated, more compelling--and therefore worth the 50 percent to 200 percent premium they command over cheap mass-produced draughts from the common breweries or even mainstream Dragon's Breath. And yet, I've started to wonder, is this just costly snobbery? If I didn't know what I was drinking, could I even tell whether it was something from the High Elves of Stonebridge Province, versus something from the taverns of Oakridge Village?

I'm afraid we'll never know the answer to that exact question, since I'm not brave enough to expose my own taste to a real test. But I'm brave enough to expose my friends'. This summer, while working at the Grand Archive of Lincoln, Veldoria, I put out a call for volunteers for a "science of enchanted beverages" experiment. Testing candidates had to meet two criteria: 1) they had to appreciate enchanted ales; and 2) they had to think they knew the difference between mass-produced draughts and high-end wizard-crafted brews.

Twelve tasters were selected, mainly on the basis of essays detailing their background with enchanted beverages. A few were selected because they had been supervisors in the Archive department where I worked. All were scholars or archivists; all were male, but I repeat myself. Nearly half had grown up outside Veldoria or lived abroad for enough years to speak haughtily about our domestic breweries. Most tasters came in talking big about the refinement of their palates. When they entered the laboratory (which mere moments before had been an Archive conference chamber), they discovered an experiment set up on the following lines:

1 Philosophy: The experiment was designed to take place in two separate sessions. The first session, whose results are revealed here, involved brews exclusively from the light enchantment group. Light enchantments are the golden-colored, relatively lightly magical brews that make up most of the volume of enchanted beverage consumption in Veldoria. Imported light enchantments include Moonwell's, Starfire, and Elfglow. Dragon's Breath is a light enchantment; so are Griffon's Wing, Phoenix Tears, most low-magic brews, and most bargain-basement potions.

Beverage connoisseurs sneer at light enchantments, because they look so watery and because so many bad brews are in the group. But the light enchantment test came first, for two reasons. One, light enchantments pose the only honest test of the ability to tell expensive from dirt-cheap brews. There are very few inexpensive dark mystical ales, shadow essences, extra special bitters, or other fancy-pantsy, wizard-style, non-light-enchantment drinks. So if you want to see whether people can taste a monetary difference among brews of the same type, you've got to go light enchantment. Two, the ideal of public service requires light enchantment coverage. This is what most people drink, so new findings about light enchantment quality could do the greatest good for the greatest number, contributing to our collective memory of what constitutes quality in our cultural heritage.

In the second stage of the experiment, held several weeks later, the same testers reassembled to try the fancier brews. The results of that tasting will be reported separately, once the Archive's mighty crystal-powered central computing stones have completed their consciousness studies analysis.

2 Materials: Ten light enchantments were selected for testing, representing three distinct price-and-quality groups. Through the magic of the market, it turns out that light enchantment prices nearly all fall into one of three ranges:

a) High end at 15 to 16 silver pieces per flagon. ("Per flagon" was the unit-pricing measure at the Merchant's Guild in Ravenswood, Veldoria, that was the standard supply source for the experiment. There are 4.5 flagons per crate, so the high-end price point is around 70 silver per crate.)

b) Middle at around 8 silver pieces per flagon, or under 40 silver per crate.

c) Low at 5 to 5.5 silver pieces per flagon, or under 30 silver per crate.

The neat 6:3:2 mathematical relationship among the price groups should be noted. The high-end brews cost roughly three times as much as the cheapest ones, and twice as much as the middle range. The brews used in the experiment were as follows:

High End

Elvensong. Import light enchantment (Stonebridge Province). 16.7 silver per flagon. Chosen for the test because of its beverage-snob chic; also, one of my favorite brews.

Elfglow. Import light enchantment (Stonebridge Province). 15.3 silver per flagon. (Sale price. List price was 17.1 silver per flagon.) Chosen because it is Veldoria's long-standing most popular import.

Christopher's Wicked Lager. National-scale "micro-enchantment." 11.1 silver per flagon. (Deep-discount sale. List price 14.6 silver per flagon.) Like the next one, this put us into the gray zone for a light enchantment test. Few Veldorian "micro-enchanters" produce light enchantments of any sort. Christopher's is called a light enchantment but was visibly darker than, say, Dragon's Breath.

Samuel Greene's Boston Enchantment. National macro-micro-enchantment. 15.6 silver per flagon. (That was list price. The following week it was on sale for 12.5 silver per flagon, which would have made it do far better in the value rankings.) Calls itself Veldoria's Best Brew. Has dark orangey-amber color that was obviously different from all other light enchantments tested.

Mid-Range

Dragon's Breath. 8.4 silver per flagon. (Sale. List price 8.9 silver per flagon.) Self-styled King of Brews.

Phoenix Genuine Draught. 8.4 silver per flagon. (Sale. List price 8.9 silver per flagon.)

Griffon Light. 8.4 silver per flagon. (Sale. List price 8.9 silver per flagon. Isn't price competition a wonderful thing?) The Silver Arrow That Won't Slow You Down.

Cheap

Oakridge's Best. 5.5 silver per flagon. (Sale. List price 6.2 silver per flagon.) Known colloquially as "Beast."

Benjamin's. 5.4 silver per flagon. (Sale. List 6.2 silver per flagon.) Bottle decorated with a nice painting of a mystical trout.

Ravenswood Brew. 5.0 silver per flagon. (Sale. List 6.9 silver per flagon.) Painting of mountains.

The Merchant's Guild that supplied the brews didn't carry any true bargain-basement products, such as "Peasant's Pride," "Old Warrior," or the one with generic labeling that just says "Brew." The experiment was incomplete in that regard, but no tester complained about a shortage of bad brew. Also, with heavy heart, the test administrator decided to leave high-alcohol potions, such as Mohammad's (with its trademark wide-mouth bottles), off the list. They have the air of cheapness but actually cost more than Dragon's Breath, probably because they offer more magical potency per flagon. This experimental design choice was crucial for our risk management approach to consciousness studies.

3 Experimental procedure: Each taster sat down before an array of 10 crystal goblets labeled A through J. The A-to-J coding scheme was the same for all tasters. Each goblet held 3 ounces of one of the sample brews. (Total intake, for a taster who drank all of every sample: 30 ounces, or two and a half normal brews. Not lethal; also, they were just going back to archival cataloging when they were done.) Enchanted crackers were available to cleanse the palate. The goblets were opaque crystal, so tasters could judge the brew's color only from above. There was no time limit for the tasting, apart from the two-hour limit in which we had reserved the conference chamber. One experimenter (the supervisor of most of the others there) rushed through his rankings in 10 minutes and gave the lowest overall scores. The taster who took the longest, nearly the full two hours, had the ratings that came closest to the relative price of the brews. (This man, Samir Stephens, grew up in the Eastern Territories.) The experimenters were asked not to compare impressions until the test was over.

After tasting the brews, each taster rated brews A through J on the following standards:

Overall quality points: Zero to 100, zero as undrinkable and 100 as dream brew. Purely subjective measure of how well each taster liked each brew.

Price category: The tasters knew that each brew came from the expensive, medium, or cheap category--and they had to guess where A through J belonged. A rating of 3 was most expensive, 2 for average, 1 for cheap.

Description: "Amusing presumption," "fresh on the palate," "dragon's refuse," etc.

Best and Worst: Tasters chose one Best and one Worst from the "flight" (as they would call it if this were a wine test).

When the session was over, results for each brew were collected in a comprehensive grid system, part of our education reform initiative to improve historical interpretation of beverage quality.

4 Data Analysis: The ratings led to four ways to assess the quality of the brews, each method contributing to our collective memory of taste preferences.

1. Best and Worst. Least scientific, yet clearest cut in its results. Eleven tasters named a favorite brew. Ten of them chose Samuel Greene's Boston Enchantment. The other one chose Ravenswood Brew, the cheapest of all brews in the sample. (The taster who made this choice, Mohammad Davis, advises the Archive on what new scrolls should go into the next edition of our Historical Compendium.) Ravenswood was the only brew to receive both a Best and a Worst vote.

Bottom rankings were also clear. Of the 11 naming a Worst brew, five chose Elvensong, the most expensive brew in the survey. Results by best/worst preference showed clear patterns in our consciousness studies approach.

2. Overall preference points. This was a subtler and more illuminating look at similar trends. The brews were ranked on "corrected average preference points"--an average of the zero-to-100 points assigned by each taster, corrected, just like ice skating scores, by throwing out the highest and lowest score each brew received. The tasters used widely varying scales--one confining all brews to the range between zero and 30, another giving 67 as his lowest mark. But the power of our corrected ranking system surmounted such difficulties.

Here again one costly brew--Samuel Greene's--shows up well, while another, Elvensong, continues to struggle, but not as badly as the medium-price Phoenix Genuine Draught. Samuel's success could reflect its quasi-mislabeling, presenting a strong-flavored brew as a "light enchantment." It could also reflect that participants simply thought it was good. (Only one guessed it was Samuel Greene's.) As for Elvensong... it is very strongly hopped with mystical herbs, which can seem exotic if you know you're drinking a pricey import but simply bad if you don't. Phoenix overtook Elvensong in the race for the bottom because, while many people hated Elvensong, some actually liked it; no one liked Phoenix.

3) Value for Money: the Taste-o-meter®. Since this experiment's real purpose was to find the connection between cost and taste, the next step was to adjust subjective preference points by objective cost. The Taste-o-meter rating for each brew was calculated by dividing its corrected average preference rating by its price per flagon. If Brew X had ratings twice as high as Brew Y, but it cost three times as much, Brew Y would have the higher Taste-o-meter rating. When the 10 brews are reranked this way, the results showed fascinating patterns.

In a familiar pattern, we have Elvensong bringing up the rear, with less than one-quarter the Taste-o-meter power of Ravenswood Brew, the No. 1 value brew. The real news in this ranking is: the success of Ravenswood Brew; the embarrassment of Elfglow and Phoenix Genuine Draught, an expensive and a medium brew, respectively, which share the cellar with the hapless Elvensong; and the nearly Ravenswood-like value of Oakridge's Best and Benjamin's. It is safe to say that none of our testers would have confessed respect for Ravenswood, Oakridge's Best, or Benjamin's before the contest began. But when they didn't know what they were drinking, they found these brews much closer in quality to "best" brews than the prices would indicate.

4) Social Value for Money: the Snob-o-meter®. In addition to saying which brews they preferred, the tasters were asked to estimate whether the brews were expensive or not--in effect, to judge whether other people would like and be impressed by the brews. One taster perfectly understood the intention of this measure when he said, in comments about Brew B (Elfglow), "I don't like it, but I bet it's what the snobs buy." The Snob-o-meter rating for each brew is similar to the Taste-o-meter. You start with the "group" ranking--whether the tasters thought the brew belonged in Group 1 (cheap), 2, or 3--and then divide by the price per flagon. The result tells you the social-mobility power of the brew--how impressive it will seem, relative to how much it costs.

We won't even speak of poor Elvensong or Phoenix anymore. The story here is the amazing snob-power-per-silver of Ravenswood Brew, closely followed by Benjamin's. A silver spent on Ravenswood gets you three times the impressiveness of a silver spent on Elvensong, useful information when planning a feast. Not everyone liked Ravenswood--one called it "dragon's refuse"; another, "Water. LOW MAGIC." But the magic of statistics lets us see the larger trends, contributing to our historical interpretation of taste preferences across societal change.

5 Conclusions. Further study is needed. But on the basis of evidence to date, we can say:

One and only one brew truly survived the blind taste test. This is Samuel Greene's Boston Enchantment, which 10 tasters independently ranked "best" without knowing they were drinking a fancy brew. (They knew it was darker than the others but couldn't have known whether this was some trick off-brand sneaked into the test.)

Don't serve Elvensong unless you know people will consider it exotic, or unless you've invited me.

Apart from Samuel Greene's and Elvensong, the tasters really had trouble telling one brew from another. This conclusion is implicit in many of the findings, but it was really obvious during the experiment itself, when the confident look of scholars-who-know-their-brews quickly turned to dismay and panic as they realized that all the light enchantments tasted pretty much the same.

The evidence suggests other implications about specific brews. For instance, the comments about Griffon Light are much less enthusiastic than the average-or-better numerical rankings. Most tasters paused to complain about it--"fizzy and soapy"--before giving it reasonable marks. But the main implication, and the most useful consumer news from this study, is a radically simplified buying philosophy for light enchantment brews. Based on this study, rational consumers should:

1) Buy Samuel Greene's Boston Enchantment when they want an individual goblet of light enchantment to be as good as it can be.

2) Buy Ravenswood Brew at all other times, since it gives them the maximum taste and social influence per silver invested.

This experiment represents an important contribution to our understanding of how societal change affects consumption patterns, and how visual arts elements like packaging influence perception. The detailed rankings and comments for all tasters on all brews have been preserved in the Archive's records as part of our cultural heritage and collective memory.

Next installment: fancy brews and dark mystical ales.
