The neural interface lab in Dalebrook Town hummed with the quiet efficiency of expensive equipment. I nearly tripped over the kid before I saw her in the dim corridor outside the observation room.

Her wheelchair was positioned where it usually was during evening hours, near the large window overlooking the research campus courtyard. But tonight something was different. Priya wasn't watching the courtyard gardens as she typically did, tracking the movements of birds and small animals with that intense focus that had first caught my attention months ago. Instead, she sat with her head tilted back, staring at the ceiling-mounted neural activity display that showed real-time brain scans of research subjects.

The girl wasn't observing the data streams tonight as she usually did. She was lying back in her chair with her face turned upward, her eyes following patterns that seemed to exist only in her mind, so absorbed that she didn't notice me until I spoke.

"Everything okay, Priya?" I asked.

She said, "Yes, Dr. Wolfe," without shifting her gaze from the display.

For a moment I experienced an odd sensation of déjà vu, as if I'd lived through this exact scene before. The feeling puzzled me until I remembered a similar encounter three months earlier, when Dr. Nathan Hamilton and I had first brought our mobile research unit to the Dalebrook Neurological Institute. I'd nearly stumbled over Priya's wheelchair that time too, but she hadn't been studying neural patterns then. She'd been watching something else entirely.

"What are you looking at up there, Priya?" I asked.

She didn't move, and her voice had that distant quality I'd learned to recognize.

"I'm reorganizing some connections," she said softly.

I gave up and continued to my shared office without pressing further. How do you talk to a child prodigy like that?

Nathan wasn't in, but for once I didn't worry about him. I was trying to recall what had seemed so familiar about finding Priya's wheelchair out of place. I retrieved a coffee from our small machine—I think better with something warm in my hands—and by the time I'd finished it, I had my answer.

This scenario was familiar because it had happened before, about three months back when Nathan and I first established our research presence at Dalebrook. I'd nearly stumbled over Priya that time too, but she wasn't reorganizing neural connections then. She was just staring ahead, waiting.

She'd been sitting in her wheelchair near the window, gazing out at the courtyard entrance. She was practically holding her breath, as if expecting someone important to arrive, so absorbed that she didn't notice me until I spoke. With her slight frame, serious expression, and unnaturally still dark eyes, she reminded me of those unsettling child actors in psychological thrillers. Except there was nothing theatrical about her intensity. Maybe that's why I spoke, because she looked so desperately focused.

"Something wrong, kid?" I asked.

She didn't startle or look up. Her accent placed her as second-generation immigrant, probably South Asian based on her name and features.

"I'm waiting for Dr. Santos to come back," she said, keeping her eyes on the entrance.

I might have asked who Dr. Santos was, but just then the observation room door opened behind her and her mother took over.

I couldn't see Susan Stanley well because the lights were dimmed inside for the neural imaging equipment. But I could tell from her silhouette that she was tall and imposing. I could make out the glow of a tablet screen in her hands, and when she looked up—the blue light illuminating her face—I saw she was in her mid-thirties, professional-looking but with an edge of exhaustion that spoke of long hours and difficult decisions. The ventilation system carried a faint scent of institutional coffee her way.

"This isn't your concern, Dr. Wolfe," she said. Her voice was educated, professional, but with an undercurrent of protective fierceness. "Please don't encourage Priya's fixations."

She was right about it being none of my business. I went on to the office I shared with Nathan Hamilton and left the two of them waiting for Dr. Santos together.

Our office was dark, which meant first that Nathan had probably gone to the faculty lounge as soon as I left that morning to run my experiments, and second that he'd probably gotten too caught up in philosophical debates to remember to come back. But I was wrong on at least one count, because when I switched on the light and set down my research notes, I saw Nathan asleep on the small couch we'd requisitioned.

He'd been drinking coffee, though. I could smell it on him when I shook him awake—strong, institutional coffee that spoke of long hours in the lounge discussing epistemology with anyone who would listen.

Nathan sat up and blinked against the fluorescent lights, a thin man in his fifties with graying temples, wire-rimmed glasses, and rumpled clothes that suggested he'd been sleeping in them. He was still wearing his lab coat, though at some point during the day he'd managed to shave. He'd even organized some papers; they sat in a neat stack on his desk with a half-written grant proposal on top.

"Wake up and help me write this progress report, Nathan," I said, holding him to his end of our research partnership. "I've collected three months of data and the ethics board wants documentation."

Nathan got up and stretched. He walked to my desk and poked at my notes.

"Cortical plasticity studies again," he complained. "Diego, I'm tired of measuring brain waves!"

"You don't get tenure by studying philosophy," I told him. And because I'd never been able to stay annoyed at him for long, I added, "But we have fresh coffee. Where's your mug?"

"I'm tired of coffee, too," Nathan said. "I need a real conversation about something meaningful."

I gestured at the air, making a show of it. "You've been having one already. Where?"

He grinned at me then with that self-aware, intellectually mischievous expression that transformed his face and made him different from every other burned-out academic I'd ever met.

"The bounty of human curiosity," he said, "is distributed impartially across disciplines and departments. I helped young Priya to the restroom this afternoon while her mother was conducting interviews, and my kindness was justly rewarded."

Sometimes it's hard to tell when Nathan is being serious. He's a trained philosopher—used to teach at some prestigious Eastern university, he'd mentioned once, and I never doubted it—and speaks like one when he chooses to. But Nathan's no deadbeat, though he's semi-obsessed with existential questions and lets me carry most of our research load, and he's perceptive enough to read my thoughts like a data stream.

"No, I didn't barge into her private files," he said. "Susan—Ms. Stanley—shared information with me voluntarily. Why else do you suppose I'd organize those papers?"

That was like Nathan. He hadn't violated research ethics though his curiosity was probably eating him alive. He'd organized grant proposals instead, making himself useful enough to warrant Susan sharing what she knew. It wasn't such a gamble at that, because Nathan has a way about him when he bothers to use it; maybe that's why he drifts through academic positions with me and the grant-funded research circuit, because he's used that charm too often in inappropriate contexts.

"Fair enough," I said and poured coffee for both of us while Nathan pulled up our data files.

He told me more about the Stanleys while we reviewed the research. Susan and Priya were permanent residents of Dalebrook. The girl—she was twelve—was a neurological anomaly who hadn't walked for over two years following a severe accident, and her mother was a research coordinator at the Institute studying rehabilitation techniques. There wasn't any Mr. Stanley. I guessed there never had been, which would explain Susan's protective intensity.

We were halfway through the data review when I remembered something Priya had said.

"Who's Dr. Santos?" I asked.

Nathan frowned at his screen. "Priya had a mentor named Stella Santos, a brilliant neuroscientist who specialized in neural plasticity and consciousness studies. Dr. Santos isn't coming back. She died in a research accident at the Bristol facility while Priya was hospitalized after her injury."

"Terrible," I said, thinking of the girl sitting out there every evening in her wheelchair, watching the entrance. "You mean she's been waiting two years?"

Nathan nodded, seemed to lose interest in the Stanleys, so I let the subject drop. We worked through the evening and finished the progress report around midnight. When we shut down for the night, I figured we wouldn't be staying long at the Dalebrook Institute. It wasn't a very comfortable research environment.

I was wrong there. It wasn't comfortable, but we stayed.

I couldn't have explained at first why we remained, and if Nathan could, he didn't volunteer the information. Neither of us discussed it. We just continued our routine, a few months here and a few there, following grant funding across the country.

We'd arrived at the Dalebrook facility too late for the main consciousness studies funding cycle, so I focused on peripheral research instead. I worked on cortical mapping projects all the way from basic sensory processing to complex decision-making paradigms, not committing to any of the major research teams because I prefer mobility when I get restless. I chose independent neural plasticity studies mostly, because the publication potential is good there if you've got strong analytical skills and patience for data collection.

Neural mapping isn't the exciting frontier it seems to graduate students who flock to the field because the technology is cutting-edge. You work with sophisticated equipment, usually, scanning brain activity instead of direct observation, and you use multiple measurement modalities that capture activity at the cellular level where the real changes occur. There's no dramatic breakthrough moment, as the students discover quickly. A neural reorganization happens gradually, and the biggest challenge is documenting the incremental changes once you've identified a pattern.

Usually a researcher like me publishes findings through the Institute's channels or collaborates with some established team that wants additional data for their meta-analyses, and there's nearly always recognition—from a pool of competitive researchers at the beginning of every funding cycle—for the person documenting the most significant plasticity event. There's a knack to identifying meaningful patterns, and when the grants were running well I only worked a few days a week and spent the rest of my time in the office playing chess and drinking coffee with Nathan Hamilton.

Usually it was an ideal academic life, but somehow it wasn't enough at this place. We'd get moderately caffeinated and work up a promising debate about the nature of knowledge or the foundations of consciousness. Then, just when we'd gotten epistemology looking its most fascinating with our arguments, one or the other of us would glance out the window and see Priya Stanley in her wheelchair, waiting for a brilliant neuroscientist named Stella Santos to walk through the entrance. She was always there, morning or evening, until her mother finished work and took her home.

It wasn't right or natural for a child to wait like that for anything, and it troubled me. I even offered once to arrange for Priya to meet other mentors in the field, but Susan Stanley told me quickly to mind my own business. Nathan explained that the girl didn't want another mentor because she had what he called an epistemological fixation.

"Dr. Santos was more than just a teacher to her," Nathan said. "She was a symbol representing two things no one else in the world could offer—validation and possibility. With Dr. Santos mentoring her, Priya felt intellectually validated, and she could envision possibilities beyond her physical limitations because Dr. Santos showed her that pure thought could transcend bodily constraints. If she accepted another mentor now, she'd be abandoning more than Dr. Santos. She'd be abandoning everything that relationship represented, and then there wouldn't be any point in pursuing knowledge."

I could understand it when Nathan framed it that way. Dr. Santos had spent more time with Priya than Susan had, and the girl felt as intellectually secure with her as she would have with a tenured faculty advisor. And Dr. Santos, being dedicated to her protégés, had depended on Priya for the kind of brilliant insights that made research worthwhile. The mentor needed Priya and Priya needed her. Together, they'd been an ideal partnership.

At first I thought it was strange that Priya never expressed grief or cried when Dr. Santos didn't return, but Nathan explained it was all part of this epistemological fixation. If Priya grieved, she'd be admitting that the knowledge quest was over. So she waited and watched, secure in her belief that Dr. Santos would come back.

The Stanleys grew accustomed to Nathan and me being around, but they never became what you'd call close. Priya would engage with some of Nathan's philosophical provocations, but her attention always returned to the courtyard entrance, watching for Dr. Santos. And she never let anything interfere with her routine.

That routine started every morning when Leonardo Simmons, the Institute's mail courier, rolled his cart through from the main building to deliver correspondence and packages. Leonardo would always make it a point to stop by the observation room window, and Priya would intercept him and ask if he'd seen anything of a Dr. Santos on his rounds that day.

Old Leonardo would pause with his cart and remove his cap, frowning while he pretended to consider.

Then he'd say, "Not today, Priya," or, "Thought I saw someone similar yesterday, but she was heading to the Lincoln facility. Wasn't Dr. Santos."

Then he'd continue on, shaking his head. Later the maintenance staff would come around to service the equipment, and Priya would ask them the same question. Once a month the administration sent someone to conduct facility inspections, and they became part of Priya's routine too.

It was hard on Susan. Sometimes the girl would have vivid dreams at night that Dr. Santos had returned and was working in her old lab, and she'd wake Susan and beg her to go check. When that happened, Nathan and I could hear Susan talking to her through the thin walls of the residential wing, low and steady, until late into the morning, and when Priya finally settled, we'd hear Susan in her kitchenette, probably pouring something stronger than coffee.

But there came a night that exceeded Susan's capacity to cope, a night that changed Priya's routine and much more besides. It left a mark you've seen yourself—everyone has who follows neuroscience news—though you never knew what caused it. Nobody ever knew that except Priya and Susan Stanley and Nathan and me.

Nathan and I were finishing our evening work around midnight when the girl called out from the residential wing. We heard Susan go to her, and we paused our discussion because we knew neither of us would concentrate until Susan got Priya settled again. But this night was different. Susan hadn't talked to the girl long when Priya cried out, "Dr. Santos! Dr. Santos!" and after that we heard both of them weeping.

Shortly after, Susan emerged into the corridor and closed the door behind her. She looked disheveled and defeated, her professional demeanor completely stripped away, her hair loose around her shoulders and her eyes swollen from crying. Whatever emotional reserves she'd been maintaining hadn't helped.

She stood motionless for a while, then she looked up at the ceiling-mounted neural displays and said something I'm not likely to forget.

"Why couldn't you give the girl a break?" she said, not angry or anything but loud enough for us to hear through our open door. "You, up there—what's another brilliant mentor to You?"

Nathan and I looked at each other in the fluorescent light of our office.

"She's done it, Diego," Nathan said.

I knew what he meant and wished I didn't. Susan had finally told the girl that Dr. Santos wasn't coming back, not ever.

That's why I was concerned about Priya when I came to the lab the next evening and found her studying the neural activity displays instead of watching the courtyard. It meant she'd stopped waiting for Dr. Santos. And the quiet way the girl spoke of reorganizing neural connections concerned me more, because it sounded genuinely delusional.

Not that you could blame her for losing touch with reality. It was challenging enough to be confined to a wheelchair without being able to move her legs at all. But to lose her mentor in addition...

I was reviewing my third data set when Nathan arrived with a large package under his arm. Nathan was completely sober, which surprised me, and he was energized from a shopping trip to Brookhaven, which surprised me more. It was when he opened his package, though, that I thought he'd lost his professional judgment.

"Books for Priya," Nathan said. "Susan and I agreed this morning that the girl needs a new intellectual focus now, and since she can't attend regular school, I'm going to tutor her here."

He went on to explain that Susan hadn't had the courage the previous night, desperate as she was, to tell Priya the complete truth. She'd told her instead, citing an imaginary colleague at the Bristol facility, that Dr. Santos had accepted a position at a research institute in Lincoln, Orvandor, and had taken the assignment to advance her career. It was a plausible story. Priya still didn't know that Dr. Santos was dead, but her waiting was over because no mentor could be expected to return from such a prestigious opportunity.

"We must give the girl another focus," Nathan said, shelving the books and pouring fresh coffee. "Priya has a remarkable capacity for concentration—most intellectually gifted children do—that could destroy her if it isn't redirected into productive channels."

I thought the girl had already broken down and said so.

"Reorganizing neural connections?" Nathan said when I told him. "Good God, Diego—"

Susan Stanley knocked just then, interrupting him. She came in and had coffee with us and discussed Nathan's plan for tutoring Priya at the Institute. But she couldn't tell us anything more about the girl's new fixation than we already knew. When she asked Priya why she stared at the neural displays like that, she'd say only that she wanted something to remember Dr. Santos by.

It was about nine o'clock when Susan went back to prepare dinner. Nathan and I abandoned our chess game and moved to the observation room to check some equipment. It was then that the first neural pattern shifted.

It shifted suddenly, the way any spontaneous reorganization does, and rippled across the display in a cascading wave of activity. I didn't pay much attention, but Nathan nearly dropped his coffee.

"Diego," he said, "that was Subject Twelve! The motor cortex just reorganized!"

I didn't see anything particularly significant about it and said so. You can observe dozens of minor reorganizations on any given day if you're monitoring enough subjects.

"Not minor reorganization, you fool," Nathan said. "Subject Twelve—the chronic paralysis case—just showed complete motor cortex reactivation, then stabilized!"

I paid attention then, partly because the pattern really had stabilized instead of reverting the way spontaneous activity usually does, partly because anything that excites Nathan Hamilton that much deserves consideration.

We monitored the displays like two researchers at a critical experiment, but nothing else changed. After a while another subject's scan showed activity, though, and later in the night a whole series of them displayed reorganization patterns, forming a sequence that didn't make sense to us. They stopped changing around midnight and we returned to our office, but neither of us could focus on work.

"Perhaps we ought to find another research focus ourselves instead of developing one for Priya," Nathan said. He meant it as a joke but it sounded uncertain. "Something besides staring at neural scans every night, for instance."

"You think we're experiencing shared delusions from too much caffeine?" I asked.

Nathan laughed at that, sounding more like himself. "No, Diego. No two people ever had simultaneous and identical hallucinations of objective data."

"Look," I said. "I know this sounds irrational, but maybe Priya—"

Nathan wasn't amused anymore. "Don't be absurd, Diego. If those patterns really reorganized, you can be certain of two things—Priya had nothing to do with it, and the research literature will explain everything tomorrow."

He was wrong on at least one count.

The neuroscience journals the next day were filled with urgent communications and breaking news, but none of them explained anything. The conference calls and emergency meetings involved every authority available, and research coordinators everywhere were struggling to understand. It just couldn't happen, they said.

Nathan and I reviewed the literature systematically that night, and I learned more about neural plasticity than I'd absorbed in years of study. Nathan, as I've mentioned, is a trained philosopher, and what he couldn't recall about neuroscience, the emergency publications quoted with extensive citations. They included interviews with researchers at major institutes—Harvard, Stanford, Johns Hopkins, and facilities across the globe—but nobody could explain why all those subjects would show spontaneous motor cortex reorganization simultaneously.

It disturbed me to learn that Subject Twelve had been paralyzed for over three years following severe spinal trauma, that the case had been considered permanent and irreversible, that the motor neurons had been documented as non-functional but hadn't shown any activity until now. This particular subject—researchers referred to them by number for privacy—hadn't shown any change in associated regions, which puzzled the specialists considerably. I suggested to Nathan, only half joking, that maybe the associated regions hadn't reorganized because they weren't damaged enough to interest Priya's attention, but Nathan rebuked me sharply.

"Don't joke about Priya," he said sternly. "Regarding Subject Twelve—the neural pathways are so extensively damaged that signals need years to establish new routes. That means any reorganization would have started when Priya was only ten years old. Neural plasticity has well-established temporal constraints, Diego, and neuroscientists say they can't be violated."

"They said spontaneous reorganization across multiple subjects was impossible, too," I pointed out. "I'm not claiming that Priya really reorganized those neural pathways, Nathan, but if she did, she could have accelerated the timeline along with them, couldn't she?"

But Nathan wouldn't engage the argument. "I need air," he said.

I followed, but we didn't get farther than Priya's wheelchair.

There she sat, tense and absorbed, staring up at the neural activity displays. Nathan and I followed her gaze, the way you do automatically when someone ahead of you focuses intently on something. We looked up just in time to see more patterns begin reorganizing.

The first one to change was a subject with severe cognitive impairment whose scan suddenly showed activity spreading across the prefrontal cortex—rapid, like that—and stabilized at a level consistent with normal function.

Nathan said, "There went Subject Seven," and his voice sounded strained.

That was only the beginning. During the next hour, forty or fifty more subjects showed reorganization patterns, and their scans joined the group that had changed the night before. The sequence they formed still didn't resemble anything recognizable.

I left Nathan staring at the displays and went over to help Priya, who had finished for the night and was manually rolling her wheelchair toward the residential wing entrance, navigate the door. I assisted her inside where Nathan couldn't overhear, then I asked her how things were progressing.

"Slowly, Dr. Wolfe," she said. "I have approximately a hundred more to complete."

"Then you're really reorganizing those neural patterns up there?"

She looked surprised. "Yes, it's not particularly difficult once you understand the principles."

The odds were even that she was speaking metaphorically, but I proceeded anyway and asked another question.

"I can't discern any pattern in it, Priya," I said. "What are you creating up there?"

She gave me a very small smile.

"You'll know when I'm finished," she said.

I told Nathan about that after we'd returned to our office, but he said I shouldn't encourage the girl's magical thinking. "Priya's heard everyone discussing those neural reorganizations; the emergency meetings have been constant, so she's excited too. But she has far more imagination than most people because she's intellectually gifted, and she could develop a delusional system because she's traumatized about Dr. Santos. The thing to do is provide her with a rational explanation instead of validating her fantasy as reality."

Nathan was taking all this so seriously—because it was undermining theories he'd accepted as foundational all his professional life, like those neuroscientists who were panicking worldwide. I didn't realize how disturbed Nathan really was, though, until he woke me around 4:00 a.m.

"I can't sleep for thinking about those neural patterns," he said, sitting at my desk. "Diego, I'm frightened."

That from Nathan was something I'd never expected to hear. It startled me alert enough to sit up and listen while he articulated his concerns.

"I'm afraid," Nathan said, "because what is happening in those scans isn't consistent with established neuroscience. It just can't be, yet it is."

It was so quiet when he paused that I could hear the ventilation system humming. Finally Nathan said, "Diego, the human nervous system is as delicately balanced as any complex system. If that balance is disrupted too extensively, our understanding of consciousness itself will be fundamentally challenged."

Ordinarily I wouldn't have argued with Nathan on his own ground, but I could see he was constructing a mental scenario of all neuroscience collapsing like a house of cards, and I was afraid to let him continue.

"The problem with you philosophers," I said, "is that you think your experts have everything figured out, that there's nothing in the world their theories can't explain. Well, I'm a pragmatic researcher, but I know that your neuroscientists can measure brain activity until they're exhausted and they'll never learn who designed those brains in the first place. So how do they know that whatever designed them won't reorganize them again? I've always heard that if a person had sufficient belief, they could accomplish impossible things. Well, if a person has the focus that Priya's demonstrated, maybe she could reorganize neural pathways, too."

Nathan sat quiet for a moment.

"'There are more things in heaven and earth...'" he began, then laughed. "A quotation worn threadbare by centuries of repetition but as relevant tonight as ever, Diego. Do you really believe Priya is reorganizing those neural patterns?"

"Why not?" I responded. "It's as valid an explanation as any the experts have proposed."

Nathan stood and returned to his couch. "Perhaps you're right. We'll discover more tomorrow."

And we did. Nathan did, rather, while I was occupied running controlled experiments all day.

I returned to the lab slightly earlier than usual that evening, just before the day shift ended. Priya was sitting as usual alone in her wheelchair. In the dimming light I could see a stack of books on the floor beside her, books Nathan had given her to study. What stopped me was that Priya was staring at her legs as if they were the first ones she'd ever really seen, and she had that same expression of intense concentration I'd observed when she was studying the neural displays.

I didn't know what to say to her, thinking perhaps I shouldn't mention the neural patterns. But Priya spoke first.

"Dr. Wolfe," she said, without taking her eyes off her knees, "did you know that Dr. Hamilton is an exceptionally wise person?"

I said I'd always thought so, but why?

"Dr. Hamilton said this morning that I shouldn't reorganize any more neural patterns," the girl said. "He says I should concentrate instead on learning to walk again so I can travel to Lincoln and study with Dr. Santos's colleagues."

For a moment I was angry enough to confront Nathan if he'd been available. Anyone who would manipulate a disabled, vulnerable child like that...

"Dr. Hamilton says that if I can do what I've been doing to those neural scans, then it ought to be straightforward to reorganize my own neural pathways," Priya said. "And he's correct, Dr. Wolfe. So I'm not going to reorganize any more patterns in the database. I'm going to reorganize my own."

She looked up at me with her small, serious smile. "It took me a whole day to learn how to reorganize that first subject's motor cortex, Dr. Wolfe, but I could do this after only a few hours. Look..."

And she moved both her feet.

It's unfortunate that events in reality don't unfold like they do in fiction, because a compelling narrative could be constructed from Priya Stanley's capacity for reorganizing neural patterns through focused attention. In a story, Priya might have revolutionized neuroscience or destroyed the field entirely, depending on which outcome would engage the most readers and earn the writer the largest advance, but of course it didn't actually conclude either way. It ended in what Nathan Hamilton called an anticlimax, leaving everyone satisfied enough except a few neuroscientists who appreciate mysteries anyway or they wouldn't be neuroscientists in the first place.

The neural patterns that had been reorganized remained stable, but the sequence Priya had started was never completed. That unfinished sequence won't ever disappear, in case you've wondered about it—it's there in the research database where you can access it with proper clearance—but it will never be finished because Priya Stanley lost interest in it when she learned to walk again.

Walking was a gradual process with Priya at first because her legs had atrophied significantly—severe muscle wasting, Nathan said—and it took time to rebuild them. But within a few weeks she was moving around with crutches, and after that she never approached her wheelchair again.

Susan enrolled her in the Dalebrook school system, and before the academic year ended she was participating in adaptive sports and joining other students for social activities on weekends.

School opened up an entirely new world to Priya, and she adapted to the routine as smoothly as if she'd been doing it all her life. She learned extensively there and she forgot much that she'd learned independently through isolation. Before we realized what was happening, she was just like any other twelve-year-old, full of curiosity and energy, with no more ability to reorganize neural patterns through concentration than anyone else had.

I think she actually forgot about those neural scans along with other things that had meant so much to her when she was confined to her wheelchair and couldn't do anything but wait and think.

For instance, a young researcher named Jose Baker joined the Institute staff and began mentoring Priya in basic neuroscience. She attended his lectures and assisted with his experiments and called him Professor Baker, and after that she never mentioned traveling to Lincoln to find Dr. Santos's colleagues. It was only natural, of course, because adolescents—healthy adolescents—move forward quickly. It's a sort of developmental necessity, Nathan says, against the traumas of existence.

When the academic year ended, Susan accepted a position at the Brookhaven facility where Priya could attend a specialized school for gifted students instead of the standard curriculum. When they transferred, the Dalebrook Institute felt so empty and purposeless that Nathan and I relocated and went to the Bristol research center for the consciousness studies program. We never heard from Susan and Priya again.

We've moved several times since; we're at a facility in Belvoria currently, working with the artificial intelligence research group. But everywhere we go, we're reminded of them. Every time we access the neural plasticity database, we see what Nathan calls the Priya Stanley Neural Monument, which is nothing but an unusual sequence sketched out with a hundred or so reorganized patterns of various types and magnitudes.

The structure of it is so incomplete that you'd never determine what it's supposed to represent unless you knew already what you were looking for. To us, the outline of a human brain is fairly clear. If you know enough to fill in the gaps, you can see it was meant to be a detailed neural map with only one region missing.

Nathan says that transient researchers like him and me forget old associations as quickly as adolescents do—and for the same adaptive reasons—so I'm not particularly interested now in where Susan and Priya Stanley are or how they're progressing. But there's one thing I'll always wonder about, now that there's no way of ever knowing for certain.

I wish I'd asked Priya or Susan, before they transferred away, which brain region she decided to leave incomplete.
question: Who was Priya waiting for outside of the neural interface lab?

The lecture hall at Northfield Town University was half-empty, which wasn't unusual for a Friday afternoon seminar on research ethics. Emma Graves sat in the back row, her notebook open but largely ignored as Professor Steven Holland droned on about proper citation methods and data integrity.

Emma's mind was elsewhere. As a journalism student with a minor in data science, she'd been tracking something unusual for the past week—a series of encrypted transmissions that had been picked up by the university's radio telescope array. The signals weren't random noise; they had structure, pattern, purpose.

She'd only learned about them because of her internship at the Northfield Observer, where she'd been assigned to cover the university's astronomy department. What started as a routine interview with Dr. Raj Baker had turned into something far more interesting when she'd noticed the unusual activity in the lab.

"Miss Graves," Professor Holland's voice cut through her thoughts. "Perhaps you could enlighten us on the ethical implications of publishing unverified information?"

Emma felt her face flush. "I... well, a journalist has a responsibility to report the truth, but also to consider the consequences of what they publish."

"Indeed," Holland said, his expression unreadable. "And sometimes, the greater good requires discretion rather than disclosure."

The way he said it made Emma wonder if he knew what she'd been investigating.

After class, she headed straight to the observatory. Dr. Baker was there, along with two other faculty members she recognized: Dr. Pablo Fuller from the robotics department and Dr. Elena Herrera, who specialized in particle physics and systems thinking.

"Emma," Baker said, looking uncomfortable. "I thought we agreed you wouldn't come back here."

"You agreed," Emma said. "I never did. Dr. Baker, those signals—they're not natural, are they? Someone's transmitting from somewhere in the Springfield Territory."

The three professors exchanged glances. Finally, Fuller spoke.

"Miss Graves, what we're about to tell you must remain confidential. The implications are... significant."

Over the next hour, they explained. The signals weren't coming from Springfield Territory at all—they were coming from much farther away. From Mars, to be precise.

"Mars?" Emma breathed. "But we don't have any manned missions to Mars. Nobody does."

"Exactly," Herrera said. "Which is why the government has been involved from the beginning. Three days ago, we received a message. Not just radio signals—actual language. English, Spanish, Mandarin, Russian. The message claimed to be from a Martian research station, requesting permission to send a cultural exchange representative to Earth."

Emma's reporter instincts kicked into overdrive. "This is incredible! When were you planning to announce this?"

"We weren't," Baker said firmly. "The world governments decided that panic would serve no one. They've been holding secret meetings—the kind that usually take months to arrange happened in days. Tomorrow night, there's going to be a landing at the old airfield outside Waverly, Aldoria. A small craft carrying their representative."

"And you're just going to keep this secret? The biggest discovery in human history?"

"It's not our decision," Fuller said. "We're scientists, not politicians."

But Emma saw something in their eyes—a flicker of doubt, of rebellion.

"Let me come with you," she said. "To the landing. I won't publish anything without permission, but I need to see this."

After much debate, they agreed.

The next evening, Emma found herself in a car heading toward Waverly. The small town in Aldoria was remote enough to keep the event secret, but accessible enough for the necessary officials to attend. When they arrived at the airfield, she was stunned by the level of security and the caliber of attendees. This wasn't just scientists and military personnel—these were world leaders, gathered in unprecedented unity.

At exactly midnight, the sky erupted with light. A small craft descended, sleek and silver, landing with barely a sound in the center of the illuminated area. Emma watched, breathless, as a team in protective gear approached the craft. A hatch opened, revealing not a being, but a container.

The voice that emerged from the craft's speakers was calm and measured: "Greetings from Mars. The container before you holds our representative. Please follow the assembly instructions provided."

Assembly instructions?

Emma watched in fascination as the team opened the container to reveal an intricate collection of components—and a detailed manual. Over the next three hours, scientists and engineers worked together, following the instructions to build what was clearly an advanced robot. When they pressed the final activation switch, the robot stood, nearly seven feet tall, its design elegant and purposeful.

"Thank you," it said, its voice surprisingly warm. "I am the Representative from Mars. I come to deliver a message of utmost importance to your world."

Two days later, Emma sat in the press gallery of the United Nations building in Dawnridge, Quendor, where the UN had relocated for this historic session. She'd been allowed to attend on the condition that she could not report anything until an official announcement was made. Around her sat other carefully selected journalists, all bound by the same restrictions.

The robot Representative stood at the podium, addressing an assembly that included virtually every major world leader.

"Citizens of Earth," it began, "I come from a colony established on Mars by a coalition of scientists who left Earth twenty years ago, disillusioned by the endless conflicts that threatened to destroy your world. We have watched your progress with hope and with fear. Your advances in data science, your growing understanding of systems thinking, your achievements in particle physics—all of these show humanity's potential. But your weapons, your divisions, your inability to see yourselves as one collective memory, one shared destiny—these threaten not just Earth, but the future of human expansion into space."

The assembly was silent.

"We offer you a choice," the Representative continued. "Continue your path of cooperation, resolve your differences through dialogue and cultural exchange, or face the consequences. We have the capability to intervene from Mars. We have weapons that can reach Earth within hours. We do not wish to use them, but we will not stand by and watch humanity destroy itself and potentially spread that destruction to other worlds. Consider this both a warning and an invitation. Choose peace, choose collaboration, choose to see performing arts and science, culture and technology, as bridges rather than divides—or face our intervention."

The robot sat down, and chaos erupted in the chamber.

Three days after that, Emma was back in Northfield Town, sitting in Professor Holland's office. The Representative had been destroyed in a controlled detonation, its message delivered. The Mars craft had departed. And Emma had the story of a lifetime—one she couldn't tell.

"You know, don't you?" she said to Holland.

The professor looked at her calmly. "Know what, Miss Graves?"

"That there is no Mars colony. That this was all staged. I've been going through my old notes from your seminars on research ethics and social dynamics. Some of the phrases the Representative used—I've heard them before. From you."

Holland said nothing.

"I did some systematic observation," Emma continued. "Dr. Fuller's robotics lab has been locked for three months. Dr. Herrera requisitioned unusual materials. Dr. Baker's radio telescope has been under 'maintenance' for weeks. And you, Professor Holland, have been meeting with them regularly."

She pulled out her notebook and read: "'The greatest ethical challenge is knowing when the truth serves humanity and when it endangers it. Sometimes, the most moral act is a noble deception in service of survival.' You said that in class two years ago. The Representative said something remarkably similar."

Holland leaned back in his chair. "These are serious accusations, Miss Graves. Do you have any proof?"

"No," Emma admitted. "And I'm not going to look for any."

"Why not? You're a journalist. This would be the story of the century."

Emma stood up and walked to the window, looking out at the campus. "Because I've been thinking about media ethics. About the responsibility we have not just to report the truth, but to consider the impact of what we report. If I exposed this hoax, what would happen?"

"The world would know there's no Mars colony threatening them," Holland said quietly.

"And without that threat, without that fear, how long before we're back to the same old conflicts? How long before someone decides the risk of nuclear war is acceptable?" She turned to face him. "You and your colleagues created something that might actually save humanity. A shared enemy, a reason for cooperation, a collective memory of unity in the face of an external threat. Real or not, it's working. I can see it already—the peace talks, the joint initiatives, the sustainable business practices being implemented globally."

"So what will you do?"

"What any responsible journalist should do when the truth would cause more harm than good. I'll keep your secret, Professor. As far as I'm concerned, Mars really did send us a warning. And we'd better heed it."

Holland stood and extended his hand. "You're a remarkable young woman, Miss Graves. The world needs more journalists who understand that ethics aren't just about disclosure—they're about wisdom."

Emma shook his hand. "Just promise me one thing, Professor."

"What's that?"

"That if humanity does slip back into its old ways, if we forget this moment of unity—you'll find a way to remind us. Even if it means another 'message from Mars.'"

Holland smiled. "You have my word."

That evening, Emma drove out to a hilltop outside Northfield Town with her boyfriend, Mohamed Hunter. He'd been pestering her for days about what she'd witnessed, but she'd remained tight-lipped.

"You're really not going to tell me anything?" he asked.

Emma looked up at the night sky, at the red dot of Mars hanging above them. "I can tell you this: we live in a remarkable time. Humanity just got a wake-up call, and for once, we seem to be listening. Whatever the source of that call, I'm grateful for it."

Mohamed followed her gaze. "You really believe there's a colony up there? Scientists with weapons pointed at us?"

Emma thought about Professor Holland and his colleagues, about their audacious plan, about the personal growth it must have taken to commit to such an elaborate deception in service of a greater good. She thought about research ethics and the fine line between truth and necessary fiction.

"I believe," she said carefully, "that sometimes the story we need is more important than the story we have. And right now, humanity needs to believe that someone is watching, someone is holding us accountable. Whether that someone is on Mars or in a university laboratory in Northfield Town... does it really matter?"

Mohamed put his arm around her. "I guess not. You know, you've changed since this all started. You seem more... thoughtful. Less eager to chase every story."

"Maybe I'm learning that being a good journalist isn't just about reporting everything you know. It's about understanding the impact of what you report, about considering the broader implications. It's about wisdom, not just information."

She looked at Mars again, that red dot in the sky, and smiled. Let the world believe. Let them fear the watchful eye from above. Let them work together, cooperate, build a better future. And if that future was built on a noble lie rather than a harsh truth, was that really so terrible?

Professor Holland had taught her about research ethics, but he'd also taught her something more important: that sometimes, the most ethical choice is the one that serves humanity's survival, even if it means keeping secrets that would make a career-defining story.

Mars winked at her in the darkness, and Emma winked back.

In the weeks that followed, Emma watched as the world transformed. International cooperation reached unprecedented levels. Financial regulation was reformed to support sustainable business practices globally. Cultural exchange programs flourished. The performing arts saw a renaissance as nations shared their traditions. The threat from Mars—real or imagined—had given humanity a common purpose.

And Emma kept her promise. She never wrote the exposé that would have made her famous. Instead, she wrote about the positive changes, the new spirit of cooperation, the hope for the future. Her articles were well-received, but they never revealed what she knew.

Sometimes, late at night, she would see Professor Holland on campus, and they would exchange knowing glances. No words were needed. They shared a secret that was bigger than both of them, a secret that was helping to save the world.

And that, Emma thought, was a story worth keeping.

THE ARCHIVIST FROM VALLEYVIEW
BY KEITH LAUMER (ADAPTED)

You don't have to be obsessed with the past to be an archaeological consultant—but in Morningside it sure helps!

I

"The Director of Archaeological Services," Helena Phillips said, "presents her compliments to the Ministry of Historical Preservation of the Nordavian Republic, and with reference to the Ministry's invitation to attend a symposium on pre-colonial pottery techniques, has the honor to express regret that she will be unable—"

"You can't turn this invitation down," Senior Researcher Jin Lawson said flatly. "I'll make that 'accepts with pleasure'."

Helena exhaled slowly, setting down her coffee.

"Jin," she said, "in the past couple of weeks I've sat through six academic lectures, four museum openings, and god knows how many assorted cultural heritage festivals. I've been tied up every off-duty hour since I got here—"

"You can't offend the Nordavians," Jin said sharply. "Director Carlson would never have been so rude."

"Carlson left here three months ago," Helena said, "leaving me in charge."

"Well," Jin said, closing her tablet. "I'm sure I don't know what excuse I can give the Minister."

"Never mind the excuses," Helena said. "Just tell him I won't be there." She stood up.

"Are you leaving the office?" Jin adjusted her reading glasses. "I have some important reports here for your signature."

"I don't recall requesting any reports today, Jin," Helena said, pulling on a light jacket.

"I wrote them for you. They're just as Director Carlson would have wanted them."

"Did you write all Carlson's reports for him, Jin?"

"Director Carlson was an extremely busy man," Jin said stiffly. "He had complete confidence in me."

"Since I'm cutting out the cultural obligations from now on," Helena said, "I won't be so busy."

"Well!" Jin said. "May I ask where you'll be if something comes up?"

"I'm going over to the National Archives."

Jin blinked behind thick lenses. "Whatever for?"

Helena looked thoughtfully at Jin. "You've been here in Morningside for four years, Jin. What was behind the government transition that put the current administration in power?"

"I'm sure I haven't pried into—"

"What about that Estorian research vessel? The one that disappeared in the Pearlbrook Region about ten years back?"

"Ms. Phillips, those are just the sort of questions we avoid with the Nordavians. I certainly hope you're not thinking of openly intruding—"

"Why?"

"The Nordavians are a very sensitive people. They don't welcome outsiders raking up things. They've been gracious enough to let us live down the fact that Estorians subjected them to deep humiliation on one occasion."

"You mean when they came looking for the vessel?"

"I, for one, am ashamed of the high-handed tactics that were employed, interrogating these innocent people as though they were criminals. We try never to reopen that wound, Ms. Phillips."

"They never found the vessel, did they?"

"Certainly not in Nordavia."

Helena nodded. "Thanks, Jin," she said. "I'll be back before you close the office." Jin's face was set in lines of grim disapproval as she closed the door.

The pale-featured Nordavian official shook his head firmly.

"Access to the Archives is not permitted," he said in his soft accent. "The Archivist's deepest regrets."

"The importance of my research here," Helena said, working through the formal phrasing. "My interest in local historical interpretation."

"The impossibility of access to foreigners. Please depart quietly."

"The necessity that I enter."

"The specific instructions of the Archivist." The official's voice rose slightly. "Please insist no longer. Give up this idea!"

"OK, I know when I'm beaten," Helena said in Estorian. "Keep your records safe."

Outside, Helena stood for a moment looking across at the ornate stone facades lining the street, then started off in the direction of the Estorian Archaeological Mission. The few Nordavians on the street eyed her warily, moved to give her space as she passed. Electric trams glided silently along the smooth pavement. The air was clean and cool.

At the office, Jin would be waiting with another list of complaints.

Helena studied the carved signs over the doorways along the street. An elaborate one with gilded letters seemed to indicate a café. Helena went in.

A Nordavian server was dispensing cups of dark coffee from behind the counter. He looked at Helena and froze, a pot poised over a waiting cup.

"I'd like to enjoy a local coffee," Helena said in Nordavian. "To sample a true Nordavian beverage."

"Not to enjoy my poor offerings," the server mumbled. "A stomach upset; I express regret."

"Don't worry," Helena said, irritated. "Pour it out and let me decide whether I like it."

"To be arrested by authorities for poisoning foreigners." The server looked around for support, found none. The Nordavian customers, eyes elsewhere, were drifting away.

"Get moving," Helena said, placing a large bill on the counter. "Come on."

"The need for a cage," a voice called from the sidelines. "The displaying of a specimen."

Helena turned. A tall Nordavian gestured dismissively. From his flushed face, it was apparent the man was drunk.

"Be silent, you fool," the server hissed. "Keep quiet."

"Swallow your own poison," the drunk said. "Find a proper cage for this zoo specimen." He wavered toward Helena. "Show this one in the streets, like all freaks."

"Seen a lot of freaks like me, have you?" Helena asked, interested.

"Speak intelligibly, malodorous foreigner," the drunk said. The server whispered something, and two customers came up to the drunk, took his arms and helped him to the door.

"Get a cage!" the drunk shouted. "Keep the animals in their own stinking place."

"I've changed my mind," Helena said to the server. "Thanks anyway, but I have to hurry off now." She followed the drunk out the door. The other Nordavians released him, hurried back inside. Helena looked at the weaving man.

"Leave, freak," the Nordavian muttered.

"Let's be friends," Helena said. "Be kind to dumb animals."

"I'll have you hauled away to a pound, ill-smelling foreign creature."

"Don't be angry, fragrant native," Helena said. "Let me buy you a drink."

"I won't endure such insolence!" The Nordavian advanced toward Helena. Helena backed away.

"Let's talk," Helena said. "Be reasonable—"

The Nordavian reached for her, missed. A passer-by stepped around him, head down, hurried away. Helena backed into the opening to a narrow side street and continued her verbal provocations to the drunken local, who followed, furious. Helena backed around a corner into a narrow alley, deserted, silent... except for the following Nordavian.

Helena stepped around him, seized his collar and pulled. The Nordavian fell backward. Helena stood over him. The man half-rose; Helena put a foot against his chest and pushed.

"You're not going anywhere for a few minutes," Helena said. "Stay right here and have a nice long talk with me."

II

"There you are!" Jin said, eyeing Helena over her glasses. "There are two gentlemen waiting to see you. Nordavian officials."

"Government men, I imagine. Word travels fast." Helena pulled off her jacket. "This saves me the trouble of paying another call at the Ministry."

"What have you been doing? They seem very upset, I don't mind telling you."

"I'm sure you don't. Come along. And bring an official recorder."

Two Nordavians wearing formal suits and elaborate ministry badges rose as Helena entered the room. Neither offered a courteous nod, Helena noted. They were angry, all right.

"I am Roman Barnes, of the Foreign Relations Department, Ministry of External Affairs, Ms. Director," the taller man said, in accented Estorian. "May I present Fernando Sanchez, of the Internal Security Bureau?"

"Sit down, gentlemen," Helena said. They resumed their seats. Jin hovered nervously, then sat on the edge of an uncomfortable chair.

"Oh, it's such a pleasure—" she began.

"Never mind that," Helena said. "These gentlemen didn't come here for pleasantries today."

"So true," Roman said. "Frankly, I have had a most disturbing report, Ms. Director. I shall ask Fernando to recount it." He nodded to the security chief.

"One hour ago," Fernando said, "a Nordavian citizen was brought to hospital suffering from minor injuries. Questioning of this individual revealed that he had been assaulted by a foreigner. An Estorian, to be precise. Investigation by my department indicates that the description matches that of the Archaeological Director."

Jin gasped audibly.

"Have you ever heard," Helena said, looking steadily at Roman, "of an Estorian research vessel, the ESV Discovery, which vanished in this sector nine years ago?"

"Really!" Jin exclaimed, rising. "I wash my hands—"

"Just keep that recorder running," Helena snapped.

"I'll not be a party—"

"You'll do as you're told, Jin," Helena said quietly. "I'm telling you to make an official sealed record of this conversation."

Jin sat down.

Roman stiffened indignantly. "You reopen an old wound, Ms. Director. It reminds us of certain illegal treatment at Estorian hands—"

"Nonsense," Helena said. "That story worked with my predecessors, but it doesn't work with me."

"All our efforts," Jin said, "to live down that terrible episode! And you—"

"Terrible? I understand that an Estorian task force came to Nordavia and sent a delegation to ask questions. They got some evasive answers, and stayed to investigate a little. After a week they left. Somewhat annoying to the Nordavians, maybe—at most. If they were innocent."

"If!" Jin burst out.

"If, indeed!" Roman said, his voice trembling. "I must protest your—"

"Save the protests, Roman. You have some explaining to do. And I don't think your story will be good enough."

"It is for you to explain! This person who was assaulted—"

"Not assaulted. Just questioned firmly to refresh his memory."

"Then you admit—"

"It worked, too. He remembered lots of things, once he focused."

Roman rose; Fernando followed suit.

"I shall request your immediate recall, Ms. Director. Were it not for your diplomatic status, I should do more—"

"Why did the government change, Roman? It was just after the task force paid its visit, and before the arrival of the first Estorian archaeological mission."

"This is an internal matter!" Roman said sharply. "The new regime has shown itself most friendly to you Estorians. It has gone out of its way—"

"—to keep the Estorian director and staff in the dark," Helena said. "And the same goes for the few Estorian researchers you've granted visas. This continual round of cultural events; no social contacts outside the academic circle; no travel permits to visit outlying districts, or the Pearlbrook Region—"

"Enough!" Roman's hands shook. "I can discuss this matter no further—"

"You'll discuss it with me, or there'll be a task force here in five days to do the discussing," Helena said.

"You can't!" Jin gasped.

Helena turned a steady look on Jin. She closed her mouth. The Nordavians sat down.

"Answer me this one," Helena said, looking at Fernando. "A few years back—about nine, I think—there was a little parade held here. Some curious looking people were captured. After being securely detained, they were exhibited to the Nordavian public. Marched through the streets. Very educational, no doubt. A highly cultural display.

"Funny thing about these people. They wore research uniforms. They seemed to communicate with each other in Estorian. Altogether it was a very interesting exhibit.

"Tell me, Fernando, what happened to those six Estorians after the parade was over?"

Roman made a choked noise and spoke rapidly to Fernando in Nordavian. Fernando paled, shrank down in his chair. Jin opened her mouth, closed it and blinked rapidly.

"How did they die?" Helena demanded. "Did you murder them, let them starve, or bury them alive? What convenient end did you arrange for them? Experiments, maybe? Dissect them to see what made them different..."

"No!" Roman gasped. "I must correct this terrible misunderstanding at once."

"Misunderstanding, hell," Helena said. "They were Estorians! A simple truth serum interrogation would get that out of any Nordavian who saw the parade."

"Yes," Roman said weakly. "It is true, they were Estorians. But there was no killing."

"They're alive?"

"Alas, no. They... died."

Jin made a faint sound.

"I see," Helena said. "They died."

"We tried to keep them alive, of course. But we did not know what medical care—"

"Didn't take the trouble to find out, either, did you?"

"They fell ill," Roman said. "One by one..."

"We'll deal with that question later," Helena said. "Right now, I want more information. Where did you find them? Where did you hide the vessel? What happened to the rest of the crew? Did they 'fall ill' before the big parade?"

"There were no more! Absolutely, I assure you!"

"Killed in the crash?"

"No crash. The vessel landed intact, east of the city in the Pearlbrook Region. The... Estorians... were unharmed. Naturally, we feared them. They were strange to us. We had never before encountered such people from across the sea."

"Came off the vessel with weapons drawn, did they?"

"Weapons? No, no weapons—"

"They raised their hands, didn't they? Asked for help. You helped them; helped them to death."

"How could we know?" Roman moaned.

"How could you know a flotilla would show up in a few months looking for them, you mean? That was a shock, wasn't it? I'll bet you had a busy time hiding the vessel, and silencing everybody. A close call, eh?"

"We were afraid," Fernando said. "We are a peaceful people. We feared the strange people from the foreign vessel. We did not kill them, but we felt it was just as well they... did not survive. Then, when the ships came, we realized our error. But we feared to speak. We removed our guilty leaders, concealed what had happened, and... offered our friendship. We invited the opening of archaeological relations. We made a mistake, it is true, a great mistake. But we have tried to make amends..."

"Where is the vessel?"

"The vessel?"

"What did you do with it? It was too big to just hide and forget. Where is it?"

The two Nordavians exchanged looks.

"We wish to show our remorse," Roman said. "We will show you the vessel."

"Jin," Helena said. "If I don't come back in a reasonable time, transmit that recording to Regional Headquarters, sealed." She stood, looked at the Nordavians.

"Let's go," she said.

Helena ducked under the heavy support beams shoring the entry to the underground chamber. She peered into the dimness at the curved hull of the weathered vessel.

"Any lights in here?" she asked.

A Nordavian threw a switch. A weak bluish glow appeared.

Helena walked along the raised wooden platform, studying the vessel. Empty equipment bays gaped below cracked instrument panels. Damaged decking was visible within the half-open entry hatch. Near the bow the words 'ESV Discovery L4 New Estoria' were lettered in faded paint.

"How did you get it in here?" Helena asked.

"It was transported here from the landing point, some nine miles distant," Roman said, his voice thin. "This is a natural cavern. The vessel was lowered into it and covered over."

"How did you shield it so the detectors didn't pick it up?"

"All around here is high-grade iron ore," Roman said, gesturing. "Great deposits of almost pure metal."

Helena grunted. "Let's go inside."

Fernando came forward with a flashlight. The party entered the vessel.

Helena climbed up a narrow ladder, glanced around the interior of the control compartment. Dust was thick on the floor, the mounting points where seats had been attached, the empty instrument panels, the litter of broken components, scraps of wire and paper. A thin layer of rust dulled the exposed metal where cutting tools had removed heavy equipment. There was a faint odor of decay.

"The cargo bay—" Fernando began.

"I've seen enough," Helena said.

Silently, the Nordavians led the way back out through the tunnel and into the late afternoon sunshine. As they climbed the slope to the electric car, Roman came to Helena's side.

"Indeed, I hope that this will be the end of this unfortunate affair," he said. "Now that all has been fully and honestly revealed—"

"You can skip all that," Helena said. "You're nine years late. The crew was still alive when the task force came, I imagine. You killed them—or let them die—rather than take the chance of admitting what you'd done."

"We were at fault," Roman said miserably. "Now we wish only friendship."

"The Discovery was a major research vessel, about two hundred tons." Helena looked grimly at the slender official. "Where is she, Roman? I won't settle for a twenty-ton shuttle craft."

Roman's eyes widened in shock.

"I know nothing of... of..." He stopped. His jaw clenched as he struggled for calm.

"My government can entertain no further accusations, Ms. Director," he said at last. "I have been completely candid with you, I have overlooked your intrusion into matters not properly within your authority. My patience is at an end."

"Where is that vessel?" Helena demanded. "You never learn, do you? You're still convinced you can hide the whole thing and forget it. I'm telling you you can't."

"We return to the city now," Roman said. "I can do no more."

"You can and you will, Roman," Helena said. "I intend to get to the truth of this matter."

Roman spoke to Fernando in rapid Nordavian. The security chief gestured to his four armed officers. They moved to surround Helena.

Helena eyed Roman. "Don't try it," she said. "You'll just make things worse for yourself."

Roman's jaw tightened angrily.

"Out of deference to your diplomatic status, Estorian, I shall ignore your insulting remarks," Roman said stiffly. "Let us now return to the city."

Helena looked at the four officers. "I see your point," she said.

Roman followed her into the car, sat rigidly at the far end of the seat.

"I advise you to remain very close to your mission," Roman said. "I advise you to dismiss these fantasies from your mind, and to enjoy the cultural aspects of life in Morningside. Especially, I should not venture out of the city, or appear overly curious about matters of concern only to the Nordavian government."

In the front seat, Fernando looked straight ahead. The vehicle hummed along the highway. Helena listened to the electric motor and said nothing.

III

"Jin," Helena said, "I want you to listen carefully to what I'm going to tell you. I have to move rapidly now, to catch the Nordavians off guard."

"I'm sure I don't know what you're talking about," Jin snapped, her eyes sharp behind the heavy lenses.

"If you'll listen, you may find out," Helena said. "I have no time to waste, Jin. They won't be expecting an immediate move—I hope—and that may give me the window I need."

"You're still determined to make an issue of that incident!" Jin snorted. "I can hardly blame the Nordavians. They are not a sophisticated people; they had never before encountered foreigners."

"You're ready to forgive a great deal, Jin. But it's not what happened nine years ago I'm concerned with. It's what's happening now. I've told you that it was only a shuttle the Nordavians have hidden. Don't you understand the implication? That craft couldn't have traveled far on its own. The main vessel must be somewhere nearby. I want to know where!"

"The Nordavians don't know. They're a very cultured, gentle people. You can do irreparable harm to the reputation of Estorians if you insist—"

"That's my decision," Helena said. "I have a job to do and we're wasting time." She crossed the room to her desk, opened a drawer and took out a small recording device.

"This office is being watched. Not very efficiently, if I know the Nordavians. I think I can get past them."

"Where are you going with... that?" Jin stared at the device. "What in the world—"

"The Nordavians won't waste any time destroying every document in their files relating to this. I have to get what I need before it's too late. If I wait for an official inquiry commission, they'll find nothing but blank looks."

"You're out of your mind!" Jin stood up, quivering with indignation. "You're like a... a..."

"You and I are in a difficult position, Jin. The logical next move for the Nordavians is to silence both of us. We're the only ones who know what happened. Roman almost succeeded this afternoon, but I bluffed him—for the moment."

Jin emitted a shrill laugh. "Your fantasies are getting the better of you," she gasped. "In danger, indeed! Silencing me! I've never heard anything so ridiculous."

"Stay in this office. Lock the door. You've got food and water in the dispenser. I suggest you stock up, before they shut the supply down. Don't let anyone in, on any pretext. I'll keep in touch via phone."

"What are you planning to do?"

"If I don't make it back here, transmit the sealed record of this afternoon's conversation, along with the information I've given you. Send it through on an emergency priority. Then tell the Nordavians what you've done and sit tight. I think you'll be all right. It won't be easy to break in here and anyway, they won't make things worse by harming you. A force can be here in a week."

"I'll do nothing of the sort! The Nordavians are very fond of me! You... newcomer! Troublemaker! Setting out to destroy—"

"Blame it on me if it makes you feel better," Helena said, "but don't be foolish enough to trust them." She pulled on her jacket, opened the door.

"I'll be back in a couple of hours," she said. Jin stared after her silently as she closed the door.

It was an hour before dawn when Helena keyed the combination to the lock and stepped into the darkened mission office. She looked exhausted.

Jin, dozing in a chair, awoke with a start. She looked at Helena, rose and snapped on a light, turned to stare.

"What in the world—Where have you been? What's happened to your clothes?"

"I got a little dirty. Don't worry about it." Helena went to her desk, opened a drawer and replaced the recording device.

"Where have you been?" Jin demanded. "I stayed here—"

"I'm glad you did," Helena said. "I hope you stocked up on food and water from the dispenser, too. We'll be holed up here for a week, at least." She jotted notes on a pad. "Warm up the official transmitter. I have a long message for Regional Headquarters."

"Are you going to tell me where you've been?"

"I have a message to send first, Jin," Helena said sharply. "I've been to the Ministry of Historical Preservation," she added. "I'll tell you all about it later."

"At this hour? There's no one there..."

"Exactly."

Jin gasped. "You mean you broke in? You burglarized the Ministry?"

"That's right," Helena said calmly. "Now—"

"This is absolutely the end!" Jin said. "Thank heaven I've already—"

"Get that transmitter going!" Helena snapped. "This is important."

"I've already done so, Ms. Phillips!" Jin said harshly. "I've been waiting for you to come back here..." She turned to the communicator, activated controls. The screen glowed, and a wavering long-distance image appeared.

"She's here now," Jin said to the screen. She looked at Helena triumphantly.

"That's good," Helena said. "I don't think the Nordavians can jam our transmission, but—"

"I have done my duty, Ms. Phillips," Jin said. "I made a full report to Regional Headquarters last night, as soon as you left this office. Any doubts I may have had as to the rightness of that decision have been completely dispelled by what you've just told me."

Helena looked at her levelly. "You've been busy, Jin. Did you mention the six Estorians who died here?"

"That had no bearing on the matter of your reckless behavior! I must say, in all my years in archaeological work, I've never encountered someone less suited to diplomatic administration."

The screen crackled, the ten-second transmission lag having elapsed. "Ms. Phillips," the face on the screen said, "I am Kai Porter, Senior Administrator for the region. I have received a report on your conduct which makes it mandatory for me to relieve you administratively, with Jin Lawson assuming directorship. Pending the findings of a review board, you will—"

Helena reached out and switched off the communicator. The triumphant look faded from Jin's face.

"Why, what is the meaning—"

"If I'd listened any longer, I might have heard something I couldn't ignore. I can't afford that, at this moment. Listen, Jin," Helena went on earnestly, "I've found the missing research vessel."

"You heard him relieve you!"

"I heard him say he was going to, Jin. But until I've received and acknowledged a written order, it has no legal force. If I'm wrong, he'll get my resignation. If I'm right, that suspension would be embarrassing all around."

"You're defying lawful authority! I'm in charge here now." Jin stepped to the local communicator.

"I'm going to report this terrible thing to the Nordavians at once, and offer my profound—"

"Don't touch that screen," Helena said. "You go sit in that corner where I can keep an eye on you. I'm going to make a sealed recording for transmission to Headquarters, along with a request for an armed task force. Then we'll settle down to wait."

Helena ignored Jin's protests as she spoke into the recorder.

The local communicator chimed. Jin jumped up, staring at it.

"Go ahead," Helena said. "Answer it."

A Nordavian official appeared on the screen.

"Jin Lawson," he said without preamble, "on behalf of the Minister of External Affairs of the Nordavian Republic, I hereby recognize you as Estorian Archaeological Director in Morningside, in accordance with the advisories transmitted to my government directly from Estorian Headquarters. As director, you are requested to make available for questioning Ms. Helena Phillips, former director, in connection with the assault on a citizen and illegal entry into the offices of the Ministry for Historical Preservation."

"Why, why," Jin stammered. "Yes, of course. And I do want to express my deepest regrets—"

Helena rose, went to the communicator, moved Jin aside.

"Listen carefully, Roman," she said. "Your bluff has been called. You don't come in and we don't come out. Your cover-up worked for nine years, but it's all over now. I suggest you keep calm and resist the temptation to make matters worse than they are."

"Ms. Lawson," Roman said, "a security squad waits outside your mission. It is clear you are dealing with a dangerous person. As always, the Nordavians wish only friendship with the Estorians, but—"

"Don't bother," Helena said. "You know what was in those files I examined this morning."

Helena turned at a sound behind her. Jin was at the door, reaching for the lock release...

"Don't!" Helena jumped—too late.

The door burst inward. A crowd of uniformed Nordavians pressed into the room, pushed Jin back, aimed weapons at Helena. Security Chief Fernando pushed forward.

"Attempt no violence, Estorian," he said. "I cannot promise to restrain my officers."

"You're violating Estorian territory, Fernando," Helena said steadily. "I suggest you move back out the same way you came in."

"I invited them here," Jin spoke up. "They are here at my express request."

"Are they? Are you sure you meant to go this far, Jin? A squad of armed Nordavians in the mission?"

"You are the director, Ms. Jin Lawson," Fernando said. "Would it not be best if we removed this unstable person to a secure location?"

"You're making a serious mistake, Fernando," Helena said.

"Yes," Jin said. "You're quite right, Mr. Sanchez. Please escort Ms. Phillips to her quarters in this building—"

"I don't advise you to violate my diplomatic immunity, Roman," Helena said.

"As chief of mission," Jin said quickly, "I hereby waive immunity in the case of Ms. Phillips."

Fernando produced a recording device. "Kindly repeat your statement, Madam, officially," he said. "I wish no question to arise later."

"Don't be a fool, Jin," Helena said. "Don't you see what you're letting yourself in for? This would be an excellent time for you to figure out whose side you're on."

"I'm on the side of proper procedure!"

"You've been deceived. These people are concealing—"

"You think everyone is incompetent, don't you, Ms. Phillips?" She turned to the security chief and spoke into the microphone he held up.

"That's an illegal waiver," Helena said. "I'm director here, whatever rumors you've heard. This situation is coming out into the open, whatever you do. Don't add violation of the mission to the list of Nordavian crimes."

"Take her," Fernando said.
