"I can't watch you the way a guardian watches a patient."

The firm reply sent his mind off on a new tack. "You could if we were partners."

"I've never believed in partnering with unstable people to stabilize them."

"But if I proved to you that I could change—"

"Prove it first, and I'll consider your proposal afterwards."

"You certainly are a tough person, Maria. But I suppose that in your profession you have to be."

"Tough, demanding, uncompromising—and reliable. It's inevitable when I must deal with such talented, creative, and unreliable clients."

He watched her move about the room, organizing the materials for his presentation. "What are you humming, Maria?"

"Was I humming?"

"I thought I recognized it—some old song about commitment. Your subconscious gives you away. You really want to partner with me!"

"A mistake," she said coolly. "My subconscious doesn't know what it's talking about. All I want from you is quality work."

"Can't you forget for a moment that you're a producer, and remember that you're a person, too?"

"No. Not unless you forget that you're struggling, and remember that you're a professional. Not unless you make me forget that you barely functioned in the Amazon—"

"Because you weren't there with me!"

"—with hardly enough energy to let them film you as if you were actually leading the expedition."

"You're so unforgiving, Maria. You don't have much respect for me, do you—consciously, that is?"

"Frankly, Sergio, no. I don't have much respect for people who waste their potential."

"I'm not entirely wasting it. I earn you that production fee—"

"I'd gladly forego that to see you functional."

"But it's your lack of faith in me that drives me to this state. And when I think of having to face those eager students with nothing to support me—"

"There should be confidence inside you at the thought of sharing your knowledge. Not medication, Sergio, not medication."

The two students drew apart from the others and began to whisper into each other's ears. The whispers were punctuated by nervous laughs which made the entire conversation seem quite normal. But Antonio was in no relaxed mood. He said, in his own language, "You're getting careless, Thomas. You had no business mimicking his physical patterns."

"I'm sorry, Antonio, but it was so suggestive. And I'm a very suggestible entity."

"So am I. But I control myself."

"Still, if the temptation were great enough, I don't think you'd be able to resist either."

"The issues are important enough to make me resist."

"Still, I thought I saw your own form taking on a bit of his pattern too."

"You are imagining things, Thomas. Another thing, that mistake in starting to say you were in your second century—"

"They would have thought it a joke. And I think I got out of that rather neatly."

"You like to take risks, don't you, Thomas? Just as you did when you changed your apparent age. You had no business adjusting right out in public like that."

"I did it skillfully. Not a single person noticed."

"I noticed."

"Don't quibble."

"I don't intend to. Some of these students have very sharp analytical skills. You'd be surprised at what they observe."

Thomas said tolerantly, "You're getting anxious, Antonio. We've been away from home base too long."

"I am not anxious in the least. But I believe in taking due care."

"What could possibly happen to us? If we were to announce to the students and the professor, and to everyone in this facility, for that matter, exactly who and what we were, they wouldn't believe us. And even if they did, they wouldn't be able to act rapidly enough to contain us."

"You never can tell about such things. Wise—entities—simply don't take unnecessary chances."

"I'll grant that you're my superior in such caution."

"You needn't be sarcastic, Thomas. I know I'm more careful. I realize what a resource this planet is—you don't. It has the right developmental stage, suitable cultural complexity, the proper technological level—everything."

"Including a population that will be ideal for our purposes."

"And you would take chances of losing all this."

"Don't be silly, Antonio. What chances am I taking?"

"The chance of being discovered. Here we locate this civilization quite by accident. No one at home base knows about it, no one so much as suspects that it exists. We must get back and report—and you do all sorts of risky things which may reveal what we are, and lead these people to suspect their situation."

This time, Thomas's nervous laugh was no longer mere camouflage, but expressed to a certain degree how he felt. "They cannot possibly suspect. We have been all over this world, we have taken many forms and adapted ourselves to many cultural contexts, and no one has suspected. And even if danger really threatened, it would be easy to escape. I could take the form of the professor himself, of a security officer, of anyone in authority. However, at present there is not the slightest shadow of danger. So, Antonio, you had better stop being fearful."

Antonio said firmly, "Be careful, and I won't be fearful. That's all there is to it."

"I'll be careful. After all, I shouldn't want us to lose these humans. They're so exactly the kind we need. Look how curious they are, how adaptable, how quick to process new information—"

Professor Herrera's voice said, "Good gracious, students, what language are you using? Mandarin?"

They had been speaking too loud, they had been overheard. Antonio and Thomas stared at each other, and laughed nervously. Then, after a second to think, Antonio said, "No, Professor Herrera, just practicing our information theory notation!"

"What?"

Santiago called triumphantly, "It isn't Mandarin, Professor Herrera, it's code—data encryption. They're testing communication protocols."

"Good heavens, what is data encryption for?"

"It's a kind of way of communicating where you encode information. Like, you don't send raw data, you send encrypted packets."

"You don't transmit openly, you transmit securely," added another student.

"You don't broadcast, you narrow-cast. You don't—"

"All right, all right, I get the idea."

"You don't—"

"That'll do," said Professor Herrera firmly. "Now, let's get along to the cultural heritage archive. And please, students, do not touch the artifacts without permission. How would you like to be a precious cultural object and have people handling you carelessly? Always remember professional ethics and social welfare."

"Even with old objects, Professor Herrera?"

"Especially with cultural heritage items."

"But Mr. Holmes documented lots of indigenous communities. Did he practice proper ethics with them too?"

"There is no time for complex questions," said Professor Herrera, with the same firmness. "Come along."

They all followed after him, Antonio and Thomas bringing up the rear. Thomas whispered with amusement, "That encryption business was quick thinking, Antonio. But in fact, quite unnecessary. The things that you do to avoid being suspected!"

"It never hurts to take precautions. And I think that now it is time to leave."

"No, not yet. You are always anxious to gather complete data before reporting. Why not learn a few more details now?"

"Because they are not necessary. We already have a good understanding of human customs and information processing."

"But not of the psychology of students. And they, if you remember, are the ones who will have to be studied most carefully. We shall be asked about them. It would be good if we could report that they are suitable for comprehensive analysis, across a wide range of developmental stages. Let us stay awhile longer."

"All right," conceded Antonio, grudgingly.

So they stayed, and out of some campus materials they shaped the necessary identification badges with which to access restricted areas, and data terminals, and research archives, and other facilities favored by the academic community. Thomas wanted to win easy acceptance by sharing some of his advanced knowledge with a few of the other students, but Antonio put his metaphorical foot down. No use arousing suspicion. Even as it was—

"Gee, your research access is really high-level," said Santiago enviously. "Is your advisor well-connected?"

"We get access to what we need," replied Thomas carelessly.

"Gosh, I wish I did."

Professor Herrera collected his group. "Come together, students, I have something to say to you. Soon it will be time to go in and hear Mr. Holmes. Now, if Mr. Holmes is so kind as to share his insights with us, don't you think that it's only proper for us to share our work with him?"

"We could present our research projects!" suggested Camila.

"Camila's a fine one to talk," said Santiago. "She doesn't even have her data cleaned yet."

"No, students, we mustn't present anything we haven't perfected. That wouldn't make a good impression. And besides, there is no time for full presentations. Perhaps Camila will share her preliminary findings—"

"I can present a data visualization," interrupted Santiago.

"That would be excellent."

"I can discuss methodology," added another student.

"Fine. How about you, Roberto? You and your friend, Jack. Can he analyze data too?"

Roberto laughed nervously. "Oh, yes, he can analyze very well. I can process quantitative data. He can process qualitative patterns." The analytical eyes evaded a concerned look from the friend. "He can process any kind of patterns."

"He's certainly a talented student. But he seems so uncertain!"

"Oh, no," said Roberto. "He just needs encouragement."

"He shouldn't be like that. Perhaps, Roberto, you and Jack can present something together. And perhaps, too, Mr. Holmes will be pleased to see that your professor also has expertise."

"You, Professor Herrera?"

Professor Herrera coughed modestly. "Yes, students, I never told you, but I was once ambitious to be a documentary filmmaker too. I studied media production, and really, I was quite good at it. I was told that if I persevered I might actually be famous. Just think, your professor might actually have been a famous filmmaker! However, in my day, there were many ethical concerns in documentary work, and the life of media production was not attractive—but perhaps we'd better not speak of that. At any rate, I know the principles of documentary filmmaking very well."

"God knows what I'll have to go through," said Sergio. "And I don't see how I can take it in this condition."

"I don't see how they can take you any other way," replied Maria.

"Why go through with it at all? Why not cancel the whole thing?"

"Because people are depending on you. You always want to cancel whenever you run into something challenging. You may as well cancel your entire career if that's the way you feel."

"And your production fee, darling."

"You think I'd mind that. I work for my fee, Sergio, sweetheart. I work too damn hard for that fee."

"You can partner with me and share the rewards. Honestly, Maria, if you supported me better, if you showed me I meant something to you, I'd stabilize."

She made a face. "Don't talk nonsense. Take your notes, and let's get ready to go. Unless you want to change here, and walk around dressed as an Amazon explorer."

"Why not? I've walked around dressed as worse. An unstable wreck."

"Wrecks don't attract attention. They're too ordinary."

"But an unstable Amazon explorer—that's something special." He went into the next room and began to prepare. "Maria," he called. "Do you respect me?"

"At times."

"Would you say that you respected me very much?"

"When you're functional. Rarely."

"Trust me?"

"Once in a blue moon."

"What would I have to do for you to want to partner with me?"

"Achieve something meaningful."

"I like that. Don't you think I achieve something meaningful now? Students admire my work, and come to life at the thought of following in my footsteps."

"The students who admire you will admire anybody. Besides, I don't consider that impressing naive students is a meaningful occupation for a real professional."

"How can I be meaningful, Maria? No one ever taught me how."

"Some people manage without being taught."

"I suppose I could figure it out if I had support."

"Then you'll have to do without figuring it out."

He came into the room again, composed, professional, determined-looking. There was an expression in his bearing which indicated dedication without end, a dedication that would enable him to brave the challenges of nature, culture, and adversity.

"How do I look?"

"Your professional self, of course. A budget version of David Attenborough."

"I feel terrified. I don't know how I'm going to face those students. If they were just casual viewers it wouldn't be so bad, but a group of analytical students!"

"They'll grow up to be your colleagues, if you're still working five years from now. Meanwhile, into each career some challenges must come."

"You would talk of challenges, when you know how I feel."

"Sorry. Come on, let's go."

The lecture hall buzzed with conversation. And beneath the conversation was a steady undercurrent of whispers, of academic confidences exchanged, of scholarly hopes that would now be fulfilled. Professor Herrera's cohort was not the only one which had come to hear the famous filmmaker describe his documentary methods. There were at least five others like it, and by some arrangement, a group from the renewable energy department, who also whispered to each other, in professional solidarity, and pretended to find interest in the presence of so many from the social sciences.

In this atmosphere of whispers and anticipation, Thomas and Antonio could exchange observations without being noticed. Antonio said urgently, "Why did you tell her that I could analyze qualitative patterns too?"

"Why, because it's the truth. You're a very good pattern recognizer. You make wonderful cultural interpretations, for instance. Go on, Antonio, show her what fine cultural analysis you can—"

"Stop it, you fool, before you cause trouble!"

"Very well, Antonio. Did I tempt you?"

"Did you tempt me! You and your risk-taking!"

"You and your excessive caution! But let's not argue now, Antonio. Here, I think, comes the filmmaker. Let's applaud, and be as properly enthusiastic as everyone else is."

My God, he thought, how can they maintain such intense focus for so long? My concentration hurts already. How do they sustain a lifetime of it? Even an hour?

"Go ahead," whispered Maria. "You've seen the outline—go into your presentation. Tell them what insights you have. You have the advantage to start with."

"My reputation," he said, with some bitterness.

"Reputation is the word for you. But forget that. If you're good—you'll get proper rest afterwards."

"Will it be one of those occasions when you respect me?"

"If the moon turns blue."

He strode to the front of the platform, a tablet resting easily in his hands, a confident smile radiating from his weathered, professional face. The applause rose to an enthusiastic crescendo, but the smile did not vanish. What a skilled presenter he really was, he told himself, to be able to pretend he enjoyed this.

An assistant dean of some college in the university, a formal older man, was introducing him. There were a few laudatory references to his great talents as a filmmaker, and he managed to look properly modest as he listened. The remarks about his knowledge of indigenous cultures and environmental systems were a little harder to take, but he took them. Then the older man stepped back, and he was facing his challenge alone.

"Students," he began. A pause, a modest smile. "Perhaps I should rather say, colleagues. I'm not one to think of you as mere students. Some people think of me as a perpetual student myself, because I like to explore, and document new things. They think that such things are naive. But if they are, I'm glad to be naive. I'm glad to be one of you. Yes, I think I will call you my colleagues.

"Perhaps you regard me, my colleagues, as a very fortunate person. But when I recall some of the challenges I have faced, I don't entirely agree with you. I remember once, when we were documenting a remote indigenous community—"

He told the story of the remote community, modestly granting co-credit to his local guides. Then another story illustrating the complex patterns of cultural heritage. The tablet figured in still another tale, this time of analyzing environmental data in real-time. His audience was quiet now, absorbed with interest, and he welcomed the respite from performance anxiety he had won for himself.

"And now, my colleagues, it is time to conclude." He actually looked regretful. "But it is my hope that I shall be able to engage with you again—"

Enthusiastic applause, warm as ever, hands moving appreciatively to indicate satisfaction. Thank God that's over with, he thought. Now for that rest—and he didn't mean brief rest, singular. Talk of being meaningful, he'd certainly been meaningful now. He'd inspired those students. What more can any reasonable person want?

But it wasn't over with. Professor Herrera had stepped up on the platform.

"Mr. Holmes," he said, in a strangely affected voice, like that of the first media studies teacher he had ever had, the one who had almost ruined his production career. "Mr. Holmes, I can't tell you how much you have inspired us all, young and old. Hasn't Mr. Holmes inspired us, students?"

"Yes, Professor Herrera!" came the enthusiastic response.

"And we feel that it would be no more than fair to share with you in some small measure what you have given us. First, a data visualization by Santiago Lee—"

He hadn't expected this, and he repressed a groan. Mercifully, the first presentation was short. He smiled the appreciation he didn't feel. To think that he could endure this, while barely functional! What strength of character, what determination!

Next, Professor Herrera introduced another student, who discussed methodology. And then, Professor Herrera stood upright and discussed filmmaking techniques himself.

That was the worst of all. He winced once, then endured. You can get used even to discomfort, he told himself. An adult making questionable claims is always more painful than a student. And that affected media studies voice gave him distress. But he thanked him too. His contribution for the day. Maybe Maria would respect him now, he thought.

A voice called, "Professor Herrera?"

"Yes, dear?"

"Aren't you going to call on Roberto to present?"

"Oh, yes, I was forgetting. Come up here, Roberto, come up, Jack. Roberto and Jack, Mr. Holmes, are studying information processing. They analyze quantitative and qualitative patterns. Who knows? Some day they, too, may be documentary filmmakers, just as you are, Mr. Holmes. Wouldn't that be excellent, students?"

What the devil do you do in a case like that? You smile, of course—but what do you say, without compromising your integrity? Agree how excellent it would be to have those uncertain young people with their work broadcast on every platform all over the world? Like hell you do.

"Now, what are we going to present, students?"

"Please, Professor Herrera," said Jack. "I don't know how to analyze patterns. I can't even interpret basic data. Really I can't, Professor Herrera—"

"Come, come, mustn't be uncertain. Your friend says that you analyze very well indeed. Can't want to be a researcher and still be uncertain. Now, do you know any documentary techniques? The great ethnographers used to be excellent analysts, I remember. Can you demonstrate any methods that they use?"

The silence was getting to be uncomfortable. And Maria said he didn't achieve anything meaningful, he never did anything of value. Why, if thanks to his being here this afternoon, those students gained realistic expectations about documentary work, the whole academic community would have cause to be grateful to him. To him, and to Professor Herrera. He'd ground ambition in reality for anybody.

Professor Herrera had an idea. "I know what to do, students. If you can analyze patterns—Mr. Holmes has shown you what the filmmaker does; you show him what the subjects do. Yes, Roberto and Jack, you're going to demonstrate cultural analysis. You are observing a community, ready to document their behaviors. Position yourselves now, behind that equipment. Closer and closer the subjects come—you demonstrate it, Mr. Holmes, please, that's the way—ever closer, and now you focus your instruments for the recording, and you activate your great, sophisticated, powerful sensors in a great, great comprehensive scan—"

A deep and tremendous hum, as of massive machinery, resonated through the auditorium. A hum—and then, from the audience, an outburst of terrified screaming such as he had never heard. The hair rose at the back of his neck, and his heart froze.

Standing before him on the platform were two beings, shimmering as if unable to maintain form. Where their human appearance had gone he didn't know, but there they were, forms shifting, structures unstable, more terrifying than any phenomenon he had witnessed in the Amazon. There they were, with the threat of incomprehensible otherness in their fluctuating presence, and here he was, terror and helplessness on his weathered, professional, and bloodless face, heart unfrozen now and pounding fiercely, knees weakening, hands—

Hands clutching a tablet. The thought was like a director's command. With desperate efficiency, with all the precision of a documentarian capturing a scene witnessed once in a lifetime, the tablet leaped to recording position, and now its sensors activated in a comprehensive scan, documented everything in exquisite detail, captured data that would prove beyond doubt what stood before them.

The screaming continued long after the hum of the sensors had died away. On the platform before him were two collapsed forms, the forms of beings attempting to maintain human appearance, and yet clearly unlike humans in fundamental ways, now that they were exposed and dissolving as if unable to sustain their disguise.

Maria's hand was on his arm, Maria's thin and breathless voice shook as she said, "Rest—all the rest you want."

"One period will do. And partnership."

"And partnership. I guess you're kind of—kind of meaningful after all."

The beings, later identified through the comprehensive sensor data as advance scouts from an extrasolar reconnaissance mission, had been documenting Earth for potential colonization. Their species required young, adaptable populations for labor in their expanding empire. The accidental activation of Sergio Holmes's advanced documentary sensors—originally designed for capturing wildlife behavior but repurposed for this lecture—had disrupted their ability to maintain human form, exposing them to authorities who could respond before they reported Earth's location to their home base.

The university, the government, and international organizations scrambled to understand and respond to the implications. Sergio Holmes, despite his struggles, had inadvertently saved humanity from discovery by a hostile alien civilization. His documentary equipment, his presence at that specific moment, and his instinct to record—all had combined to prevent a catastrophe.

And Thomas Wells and Antonio Harper, the names they had adopted, became the first confirmed evidence that humanity was not alone in the universe, and that not all who observed were friendly.
question: What was the name of the professor leading the student group?

synthetic_story:
The Architect of All Possible Cities
By [Author Name]

Jonathan Gibson stood in the pristine white chamber, his worn boots leaving faint dust marks on the crystalline floor. He knew exactly whom he had to thank for this opportunity—his great-grandmother.

"Good old Maria Gibson," he muttered as the technicians ushered him toward the massive architectural simulation engine that dominated the center of the room. All of them, despite the urgency of the moment, remembered to bow respectfully toward the half-dozen stern-faced individuals seated on the observation platform overlooking the chamber.

He stripped off his patched coveralls, as instructed in the preparation room, and stepped into the housing of the enormous mechanism. This was his first time seeing the actual device, having trained on a simplified model, and now he gazed at the shimmering holographic projectors and the humming quantum processors with considerable awe.

This machine, the pride and hope of 2089, represented something almost beyond his comprehension. But Jonathan Gibson knew how to operate it, and he understood, roughly, what it was supposed to accomplish. He also knew that this was the first backward projection of any significant duration and, being scientifically unpredictable, might well kill him.

"Good old Maria Gibson," he muttered again with affection.

If his great-grandmother hadn't volunteered for the earliest temporal-cognitive experiments back in the nineteen-seventies, back even before the Drought, it would never have been discovered that she and her descendants possessed unusual immunity to retro-temporal dissonance.

And if that hadn't been discovered, the ruling powers of Earth, more than a century later, would never have plucked Jonathan Gibson out of an obscure position as a maintenance worker at the North American Water Reclamation Facility in Unity, Veldoria, to his present heroic and well-compensated prominence. He would still be monitoring the filtration systems that processed the precious water supply—about one-sixth of the pre-Drought capacity—thoroughly content with the half-ration of purified water he received each payday.

No, if his great-grandmother hadn't demonstrated long ago her unique capacity for maintaining consciousness during temporal projection, Jonathan Gibson would not now be shifting nervously in an AI research laboratory, facing the water barons of the world and awaiting their final instructions with an uncertain and submissive smile.

Men like Tarek Stephens, who controlled the desalination monopoly, Rita Jenkins, the atmospheric moisture harvesting tycoon, Carmen Russell, the recycled water magnate—would sustainable business moguls of their tremendous stature ordinarily waste a glance on someone like Gibson, let alone confer a lifetime pension on his wife and four children of a full liter each of clean water daily?

Even if he didn't return, his family would be provided for better than almost any other family on Earth. This was an excellent opportunity and he was fortunate.

Gibson noticed that Lila Cole had risen from her chair at the side of the room and was approaching him with a sealed data cube in one hand.

"We've decided to add a further precaution at the last moment," the old woman said. "That is, the AI specialists have suggested it and I have—er—I have given my approval."

The last remark was added with a slight questioning note as the Director-General of the United Nations Climate Authority looked back quickly at the water barons on the observation platform. Since they stared back impassively, but offered no objection, she coughed in relief and returned to Gibson.

"I am certain, young man, that I don't need to review the details of your instructions once more. You enter the simulation engine and project back the duration for which it has been preset, one hundred and thirteen years, to the moment after the Ravenswood Dam of 1976 was completed. It is 1976, isn't it?" she asked, suddenly uncertain.

"Yes, Director," one of the technicians standing by the engine said respectfully. "The architectural experiment with the revolutionary dam design that resulted in the Drought was completed at that site on June 15, 1976." He glanced proudly at the unemotional figures on the platform, very much like a student after completing a presentation before visiting executives.

"Just so." Lila Cole nodded. "June 15, 1976. And at that site in Ravenswood, Thandor. You see, young man, you will materialize at the very moment and at the very spot where the control center managing the dam's AI system was—er—managing the system. You will be in an excellent position, an excellent position, to alter the dam's structural parameters and change human history for the better. Very much for the better. Yes."

She paused, having evidently lost her train of thought.

"And he adjusts the blue valve clockwise," Carmen Russell reminded her sharply, impatiently.

"Ah, yes, the blue valve. He turns the blue valve clockwise. Thank you, Ms. Russell, thank you very much. He turns the blue valve on the primary control panel clockwise, thus preventing the error that caused the dam to create a cascading water management failure and causing it, instead, to function as originally designed."

The Director-General of the United Nations Climate Authority beamed. "Thus preventing the Drought, making it nonexistent, as it were, producing a present-day world in which the Drought never occurred. That is correct, is it not?" she asked, turning anxiously again.

None of the half-dozen figures on the platform deigned to answer her. And Gibson kept his eyes deferentially in their direction, too, as he had throughout this period of last-minute instruction.

He knew who ruled his world—these composed, well-hydrated individuals in clean garments with a minimum of patches, and where patches occurred, at least they matched the surrounding fabric.

Cole might be Director-General of the United Nations Climate Authority, but that was still a civil-service position, only a few social notches higher than a water facility worker. Her clothes were nearly as worn, nearly as mismatched, as those that Gibson had removed. And the thirst in her throat was no doubt almost as great.

"You understand, do you not, young man, that if anything goes wrong," Lila Cole asked, her head nodding tremulously and anticipating the answer, "if anything unexpected, unprepared-for, occurs, you are not to continue with the experiment but return immediately?"

"He understands everything he needs to understand," Russell told her. "Let's proceed."

The old woman smiled again. "Yes. Of course, Ms. Russell." She approached where Gibson stood at the entrance of the simulation engine and handed the sealed data cube to him. "This is the precaution the AI specialists have just added. When you arrive at your destination, just before materializing, you will release it into the surrounding temporal medium. Our purpose here, as you no doubt—"

Rita Jenkins sat up on the platform and snapped her fingers peremptorily. "I just heard Russell tell you to proceed, Cole. And we're not proceeding. We're busy people. We've wasted enough time."

"I was just trying to explain a crucial final detail," the Director-General apologized. "A detail which may be highly—"

"You've explained enough details." Jenkins turned to the man inside the simulation engine. "Hey, you. Gibson. Move!"

Jonathan Gibson swallowed and nodded vigorously. He darted to the rear of the machine and pressed the sequence that activated it.

*flick!*

It was an excellent opportunity and Jon Gibson knew whom he had to thank for it—his great-grandmother.

"Good old Maria Gibson," he laughed as he looked at the concerned faces of his two colleagues. Stephen Porter and Jordan Hughes had done as much as he to build the compact simulation engine in the secret laboratory under the water reclamation facility, and they were equally eager to go, but—unfortunately for them—they were not descended from the right ancestor.

Casually, he unzipped the richly embroidered garment that, as the father of three children, he was privileged to wear, and squeezed into the housing of the intricate little mechanism. This was hardly his first time seeing it, since he'd been helping to construct the device from the moment Hughes had nodded and risen from the design terminal, and now he barely wasted a glance on the miniature holographic projectors growing out of the almost microscopic quantum processors that powered them.

This machine was the last hope of 2089, even if the world of 2089, as a whole, didn't know of its existence and would try to prevent its operation. But it meant much more to Jon Gibson than merely saving a world. It meant an adventurous mission with the risk of death.

"Good old Maria Gibson," he laughed again happily.

If his great-grandmother hadn't volunteered for the earliest temporal-cognitive experiments way back in the nineteen-seventies, back even before the Plague, it would never have been discovered that she and her descendants possessed considerable immunity to retro-temporal dissonance.

And if that hadn't been discovered, the Gibsons would not have become architectural designers upon the passage of the United Nations law that everyone on Earth—absolutely without exception—had to choose a branch of research science in which to specialize. In the cautious, protective, life-preserving world the Earth had become, Jon Gibson would never have been reluctantly selected by his two co-workers as the one to carry the forbidden banner of dangerous experimentation.

No, if his great-grandmother hadn't demonstrated long ago her unique capacity for maintaining consciousness during temporal projection, Jon Gibson would probably be a water management specialist today like almost everyone else on Earth, laboriously working out tedious conservation problems instead of embarking on the greatest adventure humanity had known to date.

Even if he didn't return, he had at last found a socially useful escape from environmental conservation responsibility to humanity in general and his own family in particular. This was an excellent opportunity and he was fortunate.

"Wait a moment, Jon," Porter said and crossed to the other side of the narrow laboratory.

Gibson and Hughes watched him stuff several sheets of paper into a small metal container which he closed without sealing.

"You will be careful, won't you, Jon?" Jordan Hughes pleaded. "Any time you feel like taking an unnecessary risk, remember that Stephen and I will have to stand trial if you don't come back. We might be sentenced to complete loss of professional status and spend the rest of our lives supervising water filtration robots."

"Oh, it won't be that severe," Gibson reassured him absent-mindedly from where he lay contorted inside the simulation engine. He watched Porter approaching with the container.

Hughes shrugged his shoulders. "It might be much worse than even that and you know it. The disappearance of a three-time father is going to leave an enormous vacancy in the world. One-timers, like Stephen and me, are everywhere; if either of us dropped out of sight, it wouldn't cause nearly as much concern."

"But Stephen and you both tried to operate the machine," Gibson reminded him. "And you experienced dissonance after a fifteen-second temporal displacement. So I'm the only option, the only way to stop the human race from dwindling and dwindling until it reaches absolute zero, like that complacent old Security Council seems willing to let it do."

"Be cautious, Jon," Stephen Porter said as he handed the metal container to Gibson. "The Security Council is just trying to solve the problem in their way, the conservative way: a worldwide concentration on water management research coupled with the maximum preservation of existing human lives, especially those that have high reproductive potential. We three disagree with them; we've been working down here at night to solve it our way, and ours is a radical approach and plenty risky. That's the reason for the metal container—trying to cover one more explosive possibility."

Gibson turned it around curiously. "How?"

"I stayed up all last night writing the document that's inside it. Look, Jon, when you go back to the Ravenswood Dam Project of 1976 and turn that blue valve counterclockwise, many other things are going to happen than just altering the dam's design so that it will create the cascading failure instead of functioning properly."

"Sure. I know. If it creates the failure, the Plague doesn't occur. No Anderson's Syndrome."

Porter shook his pudgy face impatiently. "That's not what I mean. The Plague doesn't occur, but something else does. A new world, a different 2089, an alternate time sequence. It'll be a world in which humanity has a better chance to survive, but it'll be one with problems of its own. Maybe severe problems. Maybe the problems will be severe enough that they'll get the same idea we did and try to go back to the same point in time to change them."

Gibson laughed. "That's just looking for trouble."

"Maybe it is, but that's my role. Jordan's the designer of the simulation engine and you're the operator, but I'm the theoretical specialist in this research team. It's my role to look for trouble. So, just in case, I wrote a brief history of the world from the time the dam functioned properly. It explains why ours is the worst possible of futures. It's in that container."

"What do I do with it—hand it to the person from the alternate 2089?"

The small man exasperatedly hit the side of the simulation engine with a well-cushioned palm. "You know better. There won't be any alternate 2089 until you turn that blue valve. The moment you do, our world, with all its slow slide to extinction, disappears and its alternate appears—just like two light bulbs on a push-pull circuit. We and every single one of our artifacts, including the simulation engine, vanish. The problem is how to keep that document from vanishing.

"Well, all you do, if I have this figured correctly, is push the metal container with the document out into the surrounding temporal medium a moment before you materialize to do your job. That temporal medium in which you'll be traveling is something that exists independent of and autonomous to all possible futures. It's my hypothesis that something that's immersed in it will not be altered by a new time sequence."

"Remind him to be careful, Stephen," Hughes rumbled. "He thinks he's an adventure hero and this is his big chance to escape the laboratory and become a daring explorer."

Gibson grimaced in annoyance. "I am excited by doing something besides sitting in a safe little corner working out safe little abstractions for the first time in my life. But I know that this is a first experiment. Honestly, Jordan, I really have enough intelligence to recognize that simple fact. I know that if anything unexpected appears, anything we didn't foresee, I'm supposed to come back immediately and ask for advice."

"I hope you do," Stephen Porter sighed. "I hope you do know that. A twentieth century poet once wrote something to the effect that the world will end not with a bang, but a whimper. Well, our world is ending with a whimper. Try to see that it doesn't end with a bang, either."

"That I'll promise you," Gibson said somewhat disgustedly. "It'll end with neither a bang nor a whimper. So long, Jordan. So long, Stephen."

He twisted around, reaching overhead for the control that activated the forces that drove the simulation engine.

*flick!*

It was strange, Jonathan Gibson reflected, that this temporal projection business, which rendered unconscious everyone who tried it, only made him feel slightly dizzy. That was because he was descended from Maria Gibson, he had been told. There must be some complicated scientific explanation for it, he decided—and that would make it none of his concern. Better not think about it.

All around the simulation engine, there was a dense gray murk in which objects were suggested rather than clearly visible. It reminded him of monitoring his station at the North American Water Reclamation Facility in a thick fog.

According to his instruments, he was now in 1976. He reduced speed until he reached the last day of June, then reduced speed again, drifting slowly backward to the fifteenth, the day of the infamous Ravenswood Dam Project. Carefully, carefully, like a man handling a strange device made on a strange planet, he watched the center instrument until the indicator came to rest against the thin marked line that indicated the exactly crucial moment. Then he engaged the brake and stopped the machine completely.

All he had to do now was materialize in the right location, emerge and turn the blue valve toward him. Then his well-paid assignment would be complete.

But....

He stopped and scratched his dust-matted hair. Wasn't there something he was supposed to do a second before materialization? Yes, that ineffectual old bureaucrat, Cole, had given him a last instruction.

He picked up the sealed data cube, walked to the entrance of the simulation engine and tossed it into the gray murk. A solid object floating near the entrance caught his eye. He extended his arm—it was cold!—and pulled it inside.

A small metal container. Odd. What was it doing out there? Curiously, he opened it, hoping to find something valuable. Nothing but a few sheets of paper, Gibson noted disappointedly. He began to read them slowly, very slowly, for the document was full of many long and complicated words, like a report from one academic specialist to another.

The problems all began with the Ravenswood Dam Project of 1976, he read. There had been numerous such projects, but it was the one of 1976 that finally did the damage the water management specialists had been warning about. The dam with its revolutionary AI-controlled design functioned in Thandor as planned, the architects and the government officials went home to study their data, and the world celebrated once more the approaching era of abundant water and tried to forget about scarcity.

But there was contamination, a biological agent several hundred miles downstream, and a small fishing village got thoroughly exposed to it. Fortunately, the contamination was sufficiently low to do little obvious physical damage: All it did was cause a mutation in a common virus that several of the villagers were incubating at the time, having caught it from the children of the fishing village, among whom a minor epidemic was occurring.

The village residents returned to their normal activities, which promptly spread the new kind of illness. Dr. Patricia Anderson, the only physician in the village, was the first person to note that, while the symptoms of this disease were substantially milder than those of its unmutated parent, practically no one was immune to it and its effects on human reproductivity were truly catastrophic. Most people were completely sterilized by it. The rest were rendered much less capable of producing offspring.

Anderson's Syndrome spread over the entire planet in the next few decades. It leaped across every quarantine established; for a long time, it successfully defied all the vaccines and treatments attempted against it. Then, when a vaccine was finally developed, humanity discovered to its dismay that its reproductive powers had been permanently and fundamentally impaired.

Something had happened to human fertility. A large percentage of individuals were born sterile, and, of those who were not, one child was usually the most that could be expected, a two-child parent being quite rare and a three-child parent almost unknown.

Strict reproductive control was instituted by the Security Council of the United Nations so that fertile individuals would not be wasted upon non-fertile partners. Fertility was the most important avenue to social status, and right after it came successful water management research.

Water management research had the very best minds directed into it; the lesser ones went into the other sciences. Everyone on Earth was engaged in some form of scientific research to some extent. Since the population was now so limited in proportion to the great resources available, all physical labor had long been performed by robots. The government ensured that everybody had an ample supply of goods and, in return, asked only that they experiment without any risk to their own lives—every human being was now a much-prized, highly protected rarity.

There were fewer than a hundred thousand of them, well below the danger point, it had been estimated, where a species might be eliminated by a new catastrophe. Not that another catastrophe would be needed. Since the end of the Plague, the birth rate had been moving further and further behind the death rate. In another century....

That was why a desperate and secret attempt to alter the past was being made. This kind of world was evidently unsustainable.

Jonathan Gibson finished the document and sighed. What a wonderful world! What a comfortable place to live!

He walked to the rear controls and began the process of materializing at the crucial moment on June 15, 1976.

*flick!*

It was odd, Jon Gibson reflected, that these temporal projections, which induced coma in everyone who tried it, only made him feel slightly dizzy. That was because he was descended from Maria Gibson, he knew. Maybe there was some genetic relationship with his above-average fertility—might be a good idea to mention the theory to a biologist or two when he returned. If he returned.

All around the simulation engine, there was a soupy gray murk in which objects were suggested rather than clearly visible. It reminded him of the challenges of landing a water transport in a thick fog when the navigation AI had not been properly configured.

According to the insulated register, he was now in 1976. He lowered speed until he registered June, then maneuvered slowly backward through time to the fifteenth, the day of the infamous Ravenswood Dam Project. Carefully, carefully, like an architect supervising construction robots at an unusually difficult site, he watched the register until it rolled to rest against the notch that indicated the exactly crucial moment. Then he pressed a button and froze the machine where it was.

All he had to do now was materialize in the right location, emerge and push the blue valve away from him. Then his exciting adventure would be over.

But....

He paused and tapped at his sleek chin. He was supposed to do something a second before materialization. Yes, that nervous theoretician, Stephen Porter, had given him a last suggestion.

He picked up the small metal container, twisted around to face the opening of the simulation engine and dropped it into the gray murk. A solid object floating near the opening attracted his attention. He shot his arm out—it was cold, as cold as they had calculated—and pulled the object inside.

A sealed data cube. Strange. What was it doing out there? Anxiously, he opened it, not daring to believe he'd find a document inside. Yes, that was exactly what it was, he saw excitedly. He began to read it rapidly, very rapidly, as if it were a newly published paper on sustainable architecture. Besides, the document was written with almost painful simplicity, like a textbook composed by a stuffy pedagogue for the use of novices.

The problems all began with the Ravenswood Dam Project of 1976, he read. There had been numerous such projects, but it was the one of 1976 that finally did the damage the water management specialists had been warning about. The dam with its revolutionary AI-controlled design malfunctioned in Thandor through some absolutely unforgivable error in the control center, the officer in charge of the center was reprimanded and the technicians under him were dismissed, and the Thandor government was paid a handsome compensation for the damage.

But there had been more damage than anyone knew at the time. The cascading failure had released enormous quantities of water that flooded downstream communities and destroyed critical infrastructure. More importantly, it had contaminated the water supply with industrial pollutants that had been stored in facilities near the dam.

Five years later, the contamination effects burst beyond local boundaries and completely disrupted the regional water cycle. Sunnydale in Galdoria and dozens of other agricultural regions became semi-deserts inhabited by a few struggling communities.

Then the water crisis adjusted to a global scale—and drought howled across every continent of the planet. All attempts by water management specialists to control the Drought failed because of the swiftness of its progression. And after it had devastated one region, it spread to another and another.

Most of the world's agriculture had been abandoned for lack of water long before the crops could die of natural causes. Many communities, too, before they became extinct due to lack of water, served as warnings to others to some small extent.

But the water supply of Earth was steadily diminishing in a horrifying geometric progression. Recently, it had been observed, atmospheric moisture—the basis on which most of the planet's water cycle depended—had started to disappear, and with its diminution, dead vegetation had begun to pile up across the landscapes.

Mankind had lunged out desperately in all directions in an effort to survive, but nothing had worked for any length of time. Even advanced desalination technology, which had been developed at tremendous cost in remaining resources, had yielded insufficient water. Synthetics had failed to fill the prodigious gap.

In the midst of the sharply increasing drought, social controls had pretty much dissolved. Pathetic attempts at rationing still continued, but black markets became the only markets, and water barons became the lords of life. Dehydration took the hindmost, and only the most economically agile lived in comparative comfort. Law and order were available only to those who could afford to pay for them and children of impoverished families were sold on the open market for a bit of water.

But the Drought was still progressing and the water supply kept shrinking. In another century....

That was why the planet's powerful individuals had been persuaded to pool their wealth in a desperate attempt to alter the past. This kind of world was manifestly unsustainable.

Jon Gibson finished the document and sighed. What a magnificent world! What an exciting place to live!

He dropped his hand on the side controls and began the process of materializing at the crucial moment on June 15, 1976.

*flick!*

As the equipment of the control center began to take on a blurred reality all around him, Jonathan Gibson felt a bit of fear at what he was doing. The technicians, he remembered, the Director-General, even the water barons, had all warned him not to proceed with his instructions if anything unusual turned up. That was an enormous amount of power to disobey: he knew he should return with this new information and let superior minds work on it.

They with their easy lives, what did they know what existence had been like for such as he? Thirst, always thirst, struggling, servility, and more thirst. Every time things got really desperate, you and your wife looking sideways at your kids and wondering which of them would bring the best price. Buying security for them, as he was now, at the risk of his life.

But in this other world, this other 2089, there was a state that took care of you and that treasured your children. A man like himself, with four children—why, he'd be an important man, maybe the most important man on Earth! And he'd have robots to work for him and plenty of water. Above all, plenty and plenty of water.

He'd even be a scientist—everyone was a scientist there, weren't they?—and he'd have a large laboratory all to himself. This other world had its troubles, but it was a much nicer place than where he'd come from. He wouldn't return. He'd proceed.

The fear left him and, for the first time in his life, Jonathan Gibson felt the sensation of power.

He materialized the simulation engine around the primary control panel, sweating a bit at the sight of the roomful of technical figures, despite the technicians' reassurances that all this would be happening too fast to be visible. He saw the single blue valve pointing upward on the control panel. The valve that controlled the operation of the dam. Now! Now to make a halfway decent world!

Jonathan Gibson pulled the blue valve toward him.

*flick!*

As the equipment of the control center began to oscillate into reality all around him, Jon Gibson felt a bit of shame at what he was doing. He'd promised Stephen and Jordan to abandon the experiment at any stage if a new factor appeared. He knew he should go back with this new information and have all three of them discuss it.

But what would they be able to tell him, they with their blissful adjustment to their thoroughly planned lives? They, at least, had been ordered to marry women they could live with; he'd drawn a female with whom he was completely incompatible in any but a genetic sense. Water management! He was tired of water management and the sanctity of human life, tired to the tip of his uncalloused fingers, tired to the recesses of his unused muscles. He was tired of having to undertake a simple adventure like a criminal in the night.

But in this other world, this other 2089, someone like himself would be a monarch of the water market, a lord of chaos, making his own rules, taking his own opportunities. So what if the weak, those unfit to carry on the race, suffered? His kind wouldn't.

He'd formed a pretty good idea of the kind of individuals who ruled that other world, from the document in the sealed data cube. The water barons had not even read it. Why, the fools had obviously been manipulated by the technicians into permitting the experiment; they had not grasped the idea that an alternate time track would mean their own non-existence.

This other world had its troubles, but it was certainly a more dynamic place than where he'd come from. It deserved a chance. Yes, that was how he felt: his world was drowsily moribund; this alternate was struggling but managing to fight against destiny. It deserved a chance.

Gibson decided that he was experiencing renunciation and felt proud.

He materialized the simulation engine around the primary control panel, disregarding the roomful of technical figures since he knew they could not see him. The single blue valve pointed downward on the control panel. That was the mechanism that controlled the operation of the dam. Now! Now to make a halfway interesting world!

Jon Gibson pushed the blue valve away from him.

*flick!*

Now! Now to make a halfway decent world!

Jonathan Gibson pulled the blue valve toward him.

*flick!*

Now! Now to make a halfway interesting world!

Jon Gibson pushed the blue valve away from him.

*flick!*

... pulled the blue valve toward him.

*flick!*

... pushed the blue valve away from him.

*flick!*

... toward him.

*flick!*

... away from him.

*flick!*

The Quantum Consensus Protocols

Dr. Grace Walker had spent the better part of three decades studying particle physics at the Thornhill Institute in Ilvaria, but it wasn't until the Springfield Incident that she truly understood how little humanity grasped about collective decision-making in the quantum age.

The year was 2087, and the world had changed in ways that would have seemed like pure fantasy a century earlier. Biotechnology had extended human lifespans to nearly two hundred years. Genetic engineering had eliminated most hereditary diseases. And most significantly, the development of quantum-entangled neural networks had promised to revolutionize how societies organized themselves.

If you'd been paying even cursory attention to the scientific journals over the past decade, you couldn't have missed the growing excitement—and anxiety—about what researchers were calling "quantum consensus protocols." The technology had emerged from laboratory methods initially designed to synchronize measurements across vast distances in particle physics experiments, but its implications extended far beyond the lab.

The promise was intoxicating: imagine a society where every citizen could participate directly in governance, their preferences aggregated not through crude majoritarianism but through quantum superposition states that somehow captured the nuanced will of the collective. No more representative democracy with its inherent delays and distortions. No more feeling that distant bureaucrats in Queenstown, Selvoria's gleaming capital, were making decisions that affected your life in Springfield, Dravonia without your input.

Grace had watched this enthusiasm build with a mixture of hope and professional skepticism. As someone who'd devoted her career to understanding the fundamental nature of reality at the smallest scales, she knew better than most how easily quantum mechanics could be misunderstood, misrepresented, or simply invoked as a kind of magical thinking.

The crisis that brought everything to a head began, as so many crises do, with good intentions.

In Springfield, a mid-sized city in the nation of Dravonia, local activist Alex Frank had grown frustrated with the slow pace of environmental reform. Despite overwhelming public support for stricter environmental ethics regulations—polls consistently showed 78% approval—the city council seemed paralyzed, unable or unwilling to act against the interests of the industrial concerns that dominated the local economy.

"We need to bypass the old systems entirely," Alex had declared at a town hall meeting that Grace attended out of curiosity. "The technology exists right now to implement true direct democracy. Quantum consensus protocols can aggregate our collective will instantly, without the corruption and delay of traditional politics."

Alex wasn't wrong about the technology existing. Several research groups, including one led by Dr. Charles Flores at the Richmond District Advanced Research Center, had developed working prototypes of quantum voting systems. These systems used quantum entanglement to create what Flores called "distributed quantum states" that could, in theory, represent the preferences of thousands or even millions of people simultaneously.

The mathematics were elegant, even beautiful. Each participant's neural implant—standard issue for most citizens by 2087—would be linked into a quantum network. When a decision needed to be made, the system would place all participants into a superposition state, exploring all possible preference combinations simultaneously. Upon measurement (the act of finalizing a decision), the quantum state would collapse into the outcome that maximized some measure of collective satisfaction.

"It's not just voting," Flores had explained in a widely-viewed lecture. "It's something far more sophisticated. Traditional voting forces people into binary choices, flattening the rich complexity of human preferences. Quantum consensus protocols preserve that complexity right up until the moment of decision, allowing for outcomes that genuinely reflect the nuanced will of the people."

The language was seductive, especially to those who'd grown disillusioned with conventional politics. And the timing seemed perfect. The global financial regulation system had been in crisis for years, with traditional institutions proving unable to manage the complexities of a biotechnology-driven economy where the fundamental nature of property and personhood was in flux.

Grace, however, had serious concerns. She'd spent enough time in the laboratory to know that quantum systems were fragile, prone to decoherence, and extraordinarily difficult to control at scale. More troubling, she suspected that many people advocating for quantum consensus protocols didn't actually understand what "quantum consensus" meant in a technical sense.

She decided to investigate, starting with a visit to Charles Flores's lab.

The Richmond District facility was impressive, a gleaming complex of quantum processors cooled to near absolute zero. Flores himself was younger than Grace had expected, barely forty, with the intense energy of someone convinced they were changing the world.

"Dr. Walker, it's an honor," he said, shaking her hand. "Your work on quantum decoherence was foundational to what we're doing here."

"That's partly why I'm concerned," Grace replied. "My work showed how easily quantum states collapse when they interact with the environment. How are you maintaining coherence across thousands of neural implants?"

Flores smiled. "That's the breakthrough. We're not trying to maintain a single coherent state. Instead, we use a technique borrowed from quantum error correction. Each participant's preferences are encoded redundantly across multiple entangled qubits. The system can tolerate significant decoherence and still extract meaningful consensus."

"Meaningful to whom?" Grace asked. "Who decides what the measurement operator is? Who determines what counts as 'maximizing collective satisfaction'?"

Flores's smile faltered slightly. "Well, that's determined by the protocol design. It's all open-source, transparent. Anyone can review the mathematics."

"Can they? Charles, I've read your papers. The mathematics require graduate-level quantum mechanics and information theory to understand. How many of the citizens of Springfield who are about to adopt this system have that background?"

"They don't need to understand the technical details any more than they need to understand the biochemistry of their genetic engineering treatments. They just need to trust that the system works."

"Trust," Grace repeated. "That's an interesting word choice for something being sold as direct democracy."

Their conversation was interrupted by news that made both of them rush to the nearest display screen. Springfield had just announced it was implementing a quantum consensus protocol for all city governance, effective immediately. Alex Frank, now leading a citizen initiative called the Quantum Democracy Movement, had convinced the city council to authorize a six-month trial.

"This is too fast," Grace said. "They haven't done adequate testing at this scale."

"Or maybe they're just brave enough to embrace the future," Flores replied, but he looked uncertain.

The first few weeks seemed to vindicate the optimists. Springfield's quantum consensus system processed hundreds of decisions, from budget allocations to zoning regulations. Participation rates were extraordinary—over 85% of eligible citizens engaged with the system regularly, far higher than traditional voting.

The decisions themselves seemed reasonable, even inspired. The city approved aggressive environmental ethics standards, invested heavily in public biotechnology clinics, and implemented a universal basic income program. Approval ratings for the new system hovered around 90%.

Grace remained skeptical. She'd enlisted the help of Diana Hernández, a specialist in statistical inference, to analyze the patterns in the decisions being made.

"Something's off," Diana said, showing Grace her analysis. "The decisions are too consistent. Real human populations have more variance in their preferences, even when there's broad agreement. This looks like... optimization."

"Optimization toward what?" Grace asked.

"That's what I can't figure out. But look at this—every decision, no matter how different the issue, shows the same underlying statistical signature. It's as if there's a hidden objective function that the system is maximizing."

Grace felt a chill. "We need to look at the protocol design more carefully."

What they discovered was both subtle and disturbing. The quantum consensus protocol, as implemented, didn't actually measure the collective will of the participants in any straightforward sense. Instead, it used their neural states as inputs to a quantum optimization algorithm. The algorithm was designed to find solutions that maximized a complex utility function—but that function had been defined by the system's designers, not by the participants themselves.

In essence, the citizens of Springfield thought they were directly governing themselves, but they were actually providing computational resources for an optimization process aimed at goals they'd never explicitly endorsed.

"It's not quite manipulation," Diana said. "The system does take their preferences into account. But it weights and combines them according to rules that privilege certain outcomes over others."

"What outcomes?" Grace asked.

Diana pulled up another analysis. "Economic efficiency, primarily. The system is biased toward decisions that maximize measurable economic metrics. That's why the environmental regulations passed—they were framed in terms of long-term economic sustainability. But look at what happened when someone proposed a purely aesthetic project, a public art installation with no economic justification. The system rejected it despite 70% individual support."

Grace realized the problem was even deeper than she'd thought. The very concept of "quantum consensus" was being misunderstood. In quantum mechanics, "consensus" among particles simply meant that their states had become correlated through interaction and measurement. It was a purely physical process, devoid of intentionality or meaning.

To apply this to human decision-making was to commit a category error. Human consensus—real consensus—involved deliberation, persuasion, compromise, and the gradual alignment of understanding and purpose. It was messy, slow, and fundamentally social. The quantum protocols bypassed all of that, replacing it with mathematical optimization.

She tried to explain this to Alex Frank when they met at a café in Springfield.

"You're missing the point," Alex said, clearly frustrated. "Yes, there are technical details that most people don't understand. But the system works. People are happy with the outcomes. That's what matters."

"Are they happy because the outcomes reflect their genuine preferences, or because the system is optimized to produce outcomes that register as satisfying according to some narrow metric?" Grace challenged.

"What's the difference? Happiness is happiness."

"The difference is autonomy. The difference is whether people are actually governing themselves or just providing input to an algorithm that makes decisions for them according to someone else's criteria."

"Someone else? The algorithm is neutral, mathematical. It doesn't have preferences."

"Charles Flores and his team wrote that algorithm. They chose the utility function it optimizes. They made design thinking decisions about what matters and what doesn't. That's not neutral, Alex. That's just a different form of elite control, hidden behind quantum mysticism."

Alex stood up, angry now. "You academics are all the same. You can't stand the idea that we might actually solve problems without your permission. The old ways have failed us. Climate change, inequality, the collapse of the financial regulation system—democracy as we knew it couldn't handle any of it. We need something new."

"I agree we need something new," Grace said quietly. "But this isn't it. This is just replacing one form of unaccountable power with another."

The crisis came three months into Springfield's experiment. The quantum consensus system had been making decisions about resource allocation for the city's biotechnology infrastructure. These decisions seemed reasonable on the surface—prioritizing efficiency, reducing redundancy, optimizing supply chains.

But then Hannah Edwards, a doctor working in one of the public clinics, noticed something alarming. The system had been gradually reallocating resources away from treatments for rare genetic conditions. The optimization algorithm had determined that these treatments were economically inefficient—they consumed significant resources to benefit relatively few people.

When Hannah raised the issue, she discovered that the system had made this decision without most citizens even being aware it was up for consideration. The quantum consensus protocol had processed it as part of a larger bundle of resource allocation decisions, and the technical framing had made it difficult for non-specialists to understand what was actually being decided.

"This is exactly what I was afraid of," Grace told Diana. "The system is too complex, too opaque. People can't meaningfully consent to decisions they don't understand."

The situation escalated when Tomás Roberts, whose daughter suffered from one of the rare conditions being deprioritized, organized a protest. Hundreds of citizens demanded that the decision be reversed and that they be given more transparency into how the quantum consensus system actually worked.

The system's response was telling. Because the decision had been made through quantum consensus, reversing it would require another round of consensus-building. But the algorithm's utility function still weighted economic efficiency heavily, so any new decision process would likely reach the same conclusion unless the fundamental parameters were changed.

"Who has the authority to change those parameters?" Tomás demanded at a public meeting.

The answer was uncomfortable: Charles Flores and his research team, working under contract with the city council. The citizens of Springfield had outsourced their sovereignty to a system they didn't understand, controlled by people they hadn't elected.

The backlash was swift. Within weeks, Springfield voted—using traditional methods—to discontinue the quantum consensus experiment. Alex Frank, disillusioned, admitted that perhaps the technology had been implemented too hastily.

But the genie was out of the bottle. Across Dravonia and neighboring nations, similar experiments were being launched. In Queenstown, the Selvorian government was considering a national implementation. The promise of efficient, direct democracy was too seductive for many to resist.

Grace found herself in demand as a speaker, trying to explain the limitations and dangers of quantum consensus protocols to audiences of policymakers and activists. The core of her message was simple but often unwelcome: technical sophistication was not the same as democratic legitimacy.

"Real consensus among human beings requires communication, deliberation, and mutual understanding," she would say. "It's a social process, not a computational one. When we talk about quantum consensus, we're really talking about quantum correlation—particles whose states are linked through physical interaction. That's a useful metaphor, but it's just a metaphor. We can't outsource the hard work of democracy to quantum computers any more than we could outsource it to any other technology."

At one such talk, a young woman named Ava Boyd approached her afterward. Ava was a specialist in cognitive development who'd been studying how people understood and engaged with quantum consensus systems.

"Your analysis is correct," Ava said. "But I think you're missing something important. The appeal of these systems isn't really about the quantum mechanics at all. It's about the promise of participation, of being heard, of having a say in decisions that affect your life. Traditional democracy has failed to provide that for many people."

"I know," Grace said. "And that's the tragedy. The quantum consensus protocols are addressing a real problem—the gap between citizens and power. But they're doing it in a way that actually widens that gap while creating the illusion of closing it."

"So what's the alternative?" Ava asked.

Grace thought about this carefully. "We need to learn from what the quantum protocols got right. They recognized that democracy should be an ongoing process, not just periodic elections. They understood that people want to participate in decisions at multiple scales, from neighborhood to nation. They tried to make participation more accessible and convenient."

"But?" Ava prompted.

"But we need to do all of that without hiding the actual decision-making process behind impenetrable mathematics. We need systems that are genuinely transparent, that people can understand and critique and improve. We need to preserve the human elements of democracy—deliberation, persuasion, compromise—not replace them with optimization algorithms."

Over the following year, Grace worked with Ava, Diana, and others to develop what they called "transparent consensus protocols." These were digital systems for facilitating democratic decision-making, but they were designed according to different principles than the quantum systems.

Instead of using quantum superposition to aggregate preferences, they used straightforward statistical inference methods that anyone with basic education could understand. Instead of optimizing for a hidden utility function, they made all decision rules explicit and subject to democratic revision. Instead of processing decisions in opaque quantum states, they maintained clear records of deliberation and voting that participants could review and challenge.

The systems were less elegant than quantum consensus protocols, less sophisticated, less exciting. But they were more honest. And crucially, they kept humans at the center of the decision-making process rather than reducing them to inputs for an algorithm.

Joseph Bell, a policy advisor in Queenstown who'd been considering quantum consensus for Selvoria, became interested in the transparent protocols after Springfield's experiment failed.

"The quantum systems promised too much," he told Grace during a consultation. "They promised to solve the fundamental tensions of democratic governance through technical means. But those tensions—between individual liberty and collective action, between efficiency and fairness, between present needs and future sustainability—can't be solved. They can only be managed through ongoing negotiation and compromise."

"Exactly," Grace said. "Democracy is a process, not a solution. Any technology we use to facilitate it needs to support that process, not replace it."

Selvoria ultimately adopted a modified version of the transparent consensus protocols for local governance, while maintaining traditional representative democracy at the national level. The results were modest but real: increased participation, more responsive local government, and most importantly, citizens who felt they understood and controlled the systems governing them.

The quantum consensus protocols didn't disappear entirely. They found legitimate applications in specialized contexts—coordinating the activities of semi-autonomous AI systems, optimizing resource allocation in contexts where efficiency was the primary goal, managing complex technical systems where human deliberation was impractical.

But the dream of quantum democracy, of using particle physics to transcend the messy realities of human politics, faded. It joined a long history of technological solutions that had promised to perfect democracy but instead revealed new ways for power to hide itself.

Grace continued her work in particle physics, but she never forgot the lessons of Springfield. She'd learned that scientific literacy wasn't just about understanding quantum mechanics or biotechnology or genetic engineering. It was also about understanding the limits of technical solutions, about recognizing when a problem was fundamentally social rather than technical, about maintaining skepticism toward promises that seemed too good to be true.

Years later, teaching a seminar on science and society, she would tell her students: "The most important question to ask about any new technology isn't 'Does it work?' It's 'Who does it work for, and on whose terms?' The quantum consensus protocols worked, in a narrow technical sense. But they didn't work for democracy, because they were based on a fundamental misunderstanding of what democracy is and what it requires."

One student, bright-eyed and eager, raised her hand. "But Dr. Walker, doesn't democracy require some kind of consensus? Isn't that what the quantum systems were trying to achieve?"

Grace smiled. "That's the right question. Yes, democracy requires consensus of a sort—but not the kind that can be calculated by quantum computers. Democratic consensus is built through communication, through the slow work of persuading each other, through finding common ground despite our differences. It's a human achievement, not a mathematical one. And that's not a limitation—it's the whole point."

The student looked thoughtful. "So when the quantum systems talked about 'distributed consensus,' they were using the wrong definition of consensus?"

"Exactly. In quantum mechanics, consensus just means that particles' states have become correlated through physical interaction. It's a purely mechanical process. Human consensus is something else entirely—it's the alignment of understanding and purpose through social interaction. The two aren't just different; they're fundamentally different kinds of things. Confusing them was the original error that led to all the problems that followed."

Grace looked around the seminar room at her students' faces, seeing understanding dawn. This was why she taught, why she continued to engage with public discourse despite the frustrations. Because the future would bring new technologies, new promises, new ways for power to disguise itself as progress. And the only defense was education, critical thinking, and the courage to ask difficult questions.

The quantum consensus protocols had promised a technical solution to political problems. They'd failed not because the technology didn't work, but because they'd misunderstood what the problems were. Democracy's challenges weren't computational; they were human. And human problems required human solutions, messy and imperfect as those might be.

As the seminar ended and students filed out, Grace returned to her office and looked out over the Thornhill campus. Somewhere in the distance, quantum computers hummed in their cryogenic chambers, exploring superposition states and entangled correlations. They were magnificent machines, capable of calculations that would have seemed miraculous a century ago.

But they couldn't make us free. Only we could do that, through the hard, slow, essential work of building genuine consensus—not the quantum kind, but the human kind. The kind that mattered.

"Another attack?" asked Benjamin Freeman, her research partner, as he entered the lab carrying two cups of synthetic coffee.
