synthetic_story:
The Deep Calls Home
By ANTHONY HOLLAND

Sixty days of paradise and sixty nights of torment. That's how it's been, Carmen. But how can I make you understand? How can I tell you what it's like to be young and driven and to dream of reaching the ocean depths? And yet, at the same time, to be filled with a terrible, gnawing fear—a fear locked in my mind during the day and bursting out like an evil jack-in-the-box at night. I must tell you, Carmen.

Perhaps if I start at the beginning, the very beginning....

It was the Big Day. All the examinations, the physicals and psychos, were over. The Institute, with its great halls and classrooms and laboratories, lay hollow and silent, an exhausted thing at sleep after spawning its first-born.

For it was June in this year of 2045, and we were the graduating class of the Global Institute of Deep-Sea Exploration and Resource Management.

The first graduating class, Carmen. That's why it was so important, because we were the first.

We sat on a little platform, twenty-five of us. Below us was a beach of faces, most of them strange, shining like pebbles in the warm sunlight of Horizonville Town. They were the faces of mothers and fathers and grandparents and kid brothers and sisters—the people who a short time ago had been only scrawled names on letters from home or words spoken wistfully at Christmas. They were the memory-people who, to me, had never really existed.

But today they had become real, and they were here and looking at us with pride in their eyes.

A voice was speaking, deep, sure, resonant. "...these young people have worked hard for six years, and now they're going to do a lot of big things. They're going to bring us the minerals and resources that we desperately need from the ocean floor. They're going to find new ways to manage our water systems, to create sustainable business models that will feed our children and preserve our oceans. And perhaps most important of all, they'll make other people think of the depths and look down at them and feel humility—for mankind needs humility."

The speaker was Jessica Lawson, who'd made the first descent to the Mariana Challenger Deep just five years ago, who'd established the first permanent deep-sea research station there, and who had just returned from her second expedition to the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

Instead of listening to her words, I was staring at her broad shoulders and her dark, crew-cut hair and her blue uniform which was silk-smooth and skin-tight. I was worshiping her and hating her at the same time, for I was thinking:

She's already reached the Challenger Deep and the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. Let her leave the Tonga Trench and the others alone! Let us be the first to explore somewhere! Let us be the first!

Liam Morris, sitting next to me, dug an elbow into my ribs. "I don't see 'em, Sergio," he whispered. "Where do you suppose they are?"

I blinked. "Who?"

"My folks."

That was something I didn't have to worry about. My parents had died in a submarine accident when I was four, so I hadn't needed many of those "You are cordially invited" cards. Just one, which I'd sent to Ian Jordan.

Old Depth Dog Ian, we called him, although I never knew why. He was a veteran of Henderson's first expedition to the abyssal plains nearly twenty-five years ago, and he was still at it. He was Chief Engineer now on the Nautilus Express, a commercial mining vessel on a shuttle between the deep-sea facilities and Parkview, Yendor.

I remembered how, as a kid, I'd pestered him at the Richmond, Thandor Seaport, tagging after him like a puppy, and how he'd grown to like me until he became father, mother, and buddy all in one to me. And I remembered, too, how his recommendation had finally made me a cadet.

My gaze wandered over the faces, but I couldn't find Ian's. It wasn't surprising. The Nautilus Express was in port now, but liberties, as Ian said, were as scarce as fresh water in the desert.

It doesn't matter, I told myself.

Then Liam stiffened. "I see 'em, Sergio! There in the fifth row!"

Usually Liam was the same whether in a furnace-hot engine room or a garden party, smiling, accepting whatever the world offered. But now a tenseness and an excitement had gripped even him. I was grateful that he was beside me; we'd been a good team during those final months at the Institute and I knew we'd be a good team in the depths. The Ocean was mighty big, but with two of us to face it together, it would be only half as big.

And then it seemed that all the proud faces were looking at us as if we were gods. A shiver went through my body. Though it was daytime, I saw the depths in my mind's vision, the great crushing darkness of the abyss, each trench like a voice crying out and pleading to be explored, to be touched by the sons of Earth.

They expect a lot from us. They expect us to make a new kind of civilization and a better place out of Earth. They expect all this and a hell of a lot more. They think there's nothing we can't do.

I felt very small and very humble. I was scared. Damned scared.

At last it was over, and the proud faces descended upon us in a huge, babbling wave.

Then I saw him. Good old Depth Dog Ian.

His wizened little body was shuffling down an aisle, his eyes shining like a child's. He'd been sandwiched, evidently, in one of the rear rows.

But he wasn't the Ian I'd seen a year ago. He'd become gaunt and old, and he walked with an unnatural stiffness. He looked so old that it was hard to believe he'd once been young.

He scratched his mop of steel-gray hair and grinned.

"You made it, boy," he chortled, "and by Neptune, we'll celebrate tonight. Yes, siree, I got twenty-four hours, and we'll celebrate as good deep-sea explorers should!"

Then Liam strode up to us. He was his normal, boyish self again, walking lightly, his blond, curly-haired skull swaying as if in rhythm with some silent melody.

And you, Carmen, were with him.

"Meet the Brat," he said. "My sister Carmen."

I stared almost rudely. You were like a doll lost in the immensity of your fluffy pink dress. Your hair was long and transformed into a golden froth where sunlight touched it. But your eyes were the eyes of a woman, glowing like dark stars and reflecting a softness, a gentleness that I'd never seen in eyes before.

"I'm happy to meet you, Sergio," you said. "I've heard of no one else for the past year."

A tide of heat crept up from my collar. I stuttered through an introduction of Ian.

You and Liam looked strangely at Ian, and I realized that old Depth Dog was not a cadet's notion of the ideal deep-sea explorer. Ian scorned the skin-tight uniforms of the government service and wore a shiny black suit that was a relic of Henderson's early-day Ocean Patrol. His tie was clumsily knotted, and a button on his coat was missing.

And the left side of his face was streaked with dark scar tissue, the result of a pressure blowout on one of the old deep-sea vessels. I was so accustomed to the scars, I was seldom aware of them; but others, I knew, would find them ugly.

You were kind. You shook hands and said, softly: "It's a privilege to meet you, Ian. Just think—one of Henderson's crew, one of the first to reach the abyssal plains!"

Ian gulped helplessly, and Liam said: "Still going to spend the weekend with us, aren't you, Sergio?"

I shook my head. "Ian has only twenty-four hours liberty. We're planning to see the town tonight."

"Why don't you both come with us?" you asked. "Our folks have their own hydrofoil, so it would be no problem. And we've got a big guest room. Ian, wouldn't you like a home-cooked meal before going back to the depths?"

Ian's answer was obscured by a sudden burst of coughing. I knew that he'd infinitely prefer to spend his liberty sampling kelp whiskey and deep-sea cocktails.

But this night seemed too sacred for Ian's kind of celebration.

"We'd really like to come," I said.

On our way to the hydrofoil parking field, Director Violet Ryan passed us. She was a tall, willowy woman, spectacled, looking the way an institute director should look.

"Sergio," she called, "don't forget that offer. Remember you've got two months to decide."

"No, thanks," I answered. "Better not count on me."

A moment later Liam said, frowning, "What was she talking about, Sergio? Did she make you an offer?"

I laughed. "She offered me a job here at the Institute teaching oceanography and sustainable business practices. What a life that would be! Imagine standing in a classroom for forty years when I've got the chance to—"

I hesitated, and you supplied the right words: "When you've got the chance to be the first to reach a new trench. That's what most of you want, isn't it? That's what Liam used to want."

I looked at you as if you were Henderson himself, because you seemed to understand the hunger that could lie in a person's heart.

Then your last words came back and jabbed me: "That's what Liam used to want."

"Used to want?" I asked. "What do you mean?"

You bit your lip, not answering.

"What did she mean, Liam?"

Liam looked down at his feet. "I didn't want to tell you yet, Sergio. We've been together a long time, planning to be on a submersible. But—"

"Yes?"

"Well, what does it add up to? You become a deep-sea explorer and wear a pretty uniform. You wade through the thermal vents and the crushing pressures. If you're lucky, you're good for five, maybe ten years. Then one thing or another gets you. They don't insure deep-sea explorers, you know."

My stomach was full of churning, biting ice. "What are you trying to say, Liam?"

"I've thought about it a long time. They want me for Resource Coordinator at Richmond, Fendria Port." He raised his hand to stop me. "I know. It's not so exciting. I'll just live a lot longer. I'm sorry, Sergio."

I couldn't answer. It was as if someone had whacked the back of my knees with a pressure blast.

"It doesn't change anything, Sergio—right now, I mean. We can still have a good weekend."

Ian was muttering under his breath, smoldering like a bomb about to reach critical mass. I shook my head dazedly at him as we got to the hydrofoil.

"Sure," I said to Liam, "we can still have a good weekend."

I liked your folks, Carmen. There was no depth-hunger in them, of course. They were simple and solid and settled, like green growing things, deep-rooted, belonging to the surface world. They were content with a home that was cool on this warm summer night, with a hydrofoil and a tri-dimensional video, and a handsome automatic home that needed no servants or housework.

Depth Dog Ian was as comfortable as a deep-sea fish in a desert, but he tried courageously to be himself.

At the dinner table he stared glassily at nothing and grated, "Only hit the Challenger Deep once, but I'll never forget the kid who called himself a medic. Captain started coughing, kept it up for three days. Pneumonia, the medic says, not knowin' the recycled air had contaminants that turned to toxins in your lungs. I'd never been that deep before, but I knew better'n that. Hell, I says, that ain't pneumonia, that's depth-rot."

That was when your father said he wasn't so hungry after all.

Afterward, you and I walked onto the terrace, into the moonlit night, to watch for the lights of deep-sea vessels that occasionally surfaced near Richmond, Thandor.

We gazed for a few seconds out into the dark ocean, and then you said: "Ian is funny, isn't he? He's nice and I'm glad he's here, but he's sort of funny."

"He's an old-time explorer. You didn't need much education in those days, just a lot of brawn and a quick mind. It took guts to be a deep-sea explorer then."

"But he wasn't always an explorer. Didn't he ever have a family?"

I smiled and shook my head. "If he had, he never mentioned it. Ian doesn't like to be sentimental, at least not on the outside. As far as I know, his life began when he descended to the abyssal plains with Henderson."

You stared at me strangely, almost in a sacred kind of way. I knew suddenly that you liked me, and my heart began to beat faster.

There was silence.

You were lovely, your soft hair like strands of gold, and there were flecks of silver in your dark eyes. Somehow I was afraid. I had the feeling that I shouldn't have come here.

You kept looking at me until I had to ask: "What are you thinking, Carmen?"

You laughed, but it was a sad, fearful laugh. "No, I shouldn't be thinking it. You'd hate me if I told you, and I wouldn't want that."

"I could never hate you."

"It—it's about the ocean depths," you said very softly. "I understand why you want to go to them. Liam and I used to dream about them when we were kids. Of course I was a girl, so it was just a game to me. But once I dreamed of going to Australia. Oh, it was going to be so wonderful. I lived for months, just thinking about it.

"One summer we went. I had fun. I saw the Great Barrier Reef and the research stations and the underwater habitats. But after it was over, I realized Australia wasn't so different from home. Places seem exciting before you get to them, and afterward they're not really."

I frowned. "And you mean it might be the same with the depths? You think maybe I haven't grown up yet?"

Anxiety darkened your features. "No, it'd be good to be a deep-sea explorer, to see the strange places and make history. But is it worth it? Is it worth the things you'd have to give up?"

I didn't understand at first, and I wanted to ask, "Give up what?"

Then I looked at you and the promise in your eyes, and I knew.

All through the years I'd been walking down a single, narrow path.

Government boarding school, the Institute, my eyes always downward and on the depths.

Now I'd stumbled into a cross-roads, beholding a strange new path that I'd never noticed before.

You can go into the depths, I thought, and try to do as much living in ten years as normal people do in fifty. You can be like Henderson, who died in a pressure failure at the age of 36, or like a thousand others who lie in unmarked graves on the ocean floor. Or, if you're lucky, like Ian—a kind of human torpedo streaking through the depths, eternally alone, never finding a home.

Or there's the other path. To stay on this little prison of a surface world in cool, comfortable houses. To be one of the solid, rooted people with a wife and kids. To be one of the people who live long enough to grow old, who awake to the song of birds instead of pressure alarms, who fill their lungs with the clean rich air of Earth instead of recycled oxygen.

"I'm sorry," you said. "I didn't mean to make you sad, Sergio."

"It's all right," I said, clenching my fists. "You made sense—a lot of sense."

The next morning Ian said good-bye in our room. He rubbed his scarred face nervously as he cleared his throat with a series of thin, tight coughs.

Then he pointed to a brown, faded tin box lying on the bed. "I'm leavin' that for you. It's full of old stuff, souvenirs mostly. Thought maybe you'd like to have 'em."

I scowled, not understanding. "Why, Ian? What for?"

He shrugged as if afraid he might be accused of sentimentality. "Oh, it's just that I've been dodgin' pressure failures now for twenty-five years. That's a long time, boy. Ain't one explorer in a thousand that lucky. Some of these days, I won't be so lucky."

I tried to laugh. "You're good for another twenty-five years, Ian."

He shook his head stiffly, staring at nothing. "Maybe. Anyway, I'm gonna get off the Shuttle this time, make one more trip to the Challenger Deep. Tell you what. There's a little dive bar at the bottom, the Pressure Point, just off Henderson Station near the thermal vents. When you get down there, take a look inside. I'll probably be there."

He coughed again, a deep, rasping cough that filled his eyes with tears.

"Not used to this surface air," he muttered. "What I need's some deep-sea climate."

Suddenly that cough frightened me. It didn't seem normal. I wondered, too, about his stiff movements and glassy stare. It was as if he were drugged.

I shook the thought away. If Ian was sick, he wouldn't talk about going to the Challenger Deep. The medics wouldn't let him go even as far as the continental shelf.

We watched him leave, you and Liam and I.

"When will you be back?" you asked.

Ian's hard face contorted itself into a gargoylish grin. "Maybe a couple of months, maybe a couple of years. You know deep-sea explorers."

Then he waved and strode away, a strange, gray, withered gnome of a man.

I wanted him to say something, to tell me the secret that would kill the doubt worming through my brain.

But he rounded a corner, still grinning and waving, and then he was gone.

That afternoon Liam showed me his room. It was more like a boy's room than an explorer's. In it were all the little things that kids treasure—pennants, models of Henderson's two submersibles, a swimming trophy, books, a home-made video system.

I began to realize how important a room like this could be to a boy. I could imagine, too, the happiness that parents felt as they watched their children grow to adulthood.

I'd missed something. My folks were shadow-people, my impressions of them drawn half from ancient photos, half from imagination. For me, it had been a cold, automatic kind of life, the life of dormitories and routines and rules. I'd been so blinded by the brilliancy of my dreams, I hadn't realized I was different.

My folks were killed in a submarine accident. If it weren't for deep-sea exploration, I'd have lived the kind of life a kid should live.

Liam noticed my frown.

"What's the matter, Sergio? Still sore? I feel like a heel, but I'm just not like you and Ian, I guess. I—"

"No, I understand, Liam. I'm not sore, really."

"Listen, then. You haven't accepted any offer yet, have you?"

"No. I got a couple of possibilities. Could get a berth on the Poseidon, the new submersible being finished at Richmond, Fendria. They want me, too, for the Continental Shelf Patrol, but that's old stuff, not much better than teaching. I want to be in the deep trenches."

"Well, how about staying with us till you decide? Might as well enjoy surface life while you can. Okay?"

I felt like running from the house, to forget that it existed. I wanted someone to tell me one of the old stories about the depths, a tale of courage that would put fuel on dying dreams.

But I wanted, also, to be with you, Carmen, to see your smile and the flecks of silver in your eyes and the way your nose turned upward ever so slightly when you laughed. You see, I loved you already, almost as much as I loved the ocean depths.

And I said, slowly, my voice sounding unfamiliar and far away, "Sure, I'll stay, Liam. Sure."

Sixty days of joy, sixty nights of fear and indecision. We did all the little things, like watching the submersibles dock at Richmond, Thandor and flying down to the coast to swim in cool waters. You tried, unsuccessfully, to teach me to dance, and we talked about Henderson and Ian and the abyssal plains and the trenches. You felt you had to give the depths all the beauty and promise of a child's dream, because you knew that was what I wanted.

One morning I thought, Why must I make a choice? Why can't I have both you and the depths? Would that be asking too much?

All day the thought lay in my mind like fire.

That evening I asked you to marry me. I said it very simply: "Carmen, I want you to be my wife."

You looked out at the ocean, and you were silent for a long while, your face flushed.

Then you murmured, "I—I want to marry you, Sergio, but are you asking me to marry a deep-sea explorer or a teacher?"

"Can't a deep-sea explorer marry, too?"

"Yes, an explorer can marry, but what would it be like? Don't you see, Sergio? You'd be like Ian. Gone for maybe two months, maybe two years. Then you'd have a twenty-four hour liberty—and I'd have what?"

Somehow I'd expected words like these, but still they hurt. "I wouldn't have to be an explorer forever. I could try it for a couple of years, then teach."

"Would you, Sergio? Would you be satisfied with just seeing the Challenger Deep? Wouldn't you want to go on to the Tonga Trench and the Philippine Trench and on and on?"

Your voice was choked, and even in the semi-darkness I saw tears glittering in your eyes.

"Do you think I'd dare have children, Sergio? Liam told me what happened on the Cyclops. There was a leak in the pressure system. The vessel was flooded with toxic gases—just for a second. It didn't seem serious. The crew had no burns. But a year later the captain had a child. And it was—"

"I know, Carmen. Don't say it."

You had to finish. "It was a monster."

That night I lay awake, the fears and doubts too frantic to let me sleep.

You've got to decide now, I told myself. You can't stay here. You've got to make a choice.

The teaching job was still open. The spot on the Poseidon was still open—and the big submersible, it was rumored, was equipped to make it all the way to the deepest trenches.

You can take Director Ryan's job and stay with Carmen and have kids and a home and live to see what happens in this world sixty years from now.

Or you can see what's on the other side of the mountain. You can be a line in a history book.

I cursed. I knew what Ian would say. He'd say, "Get the hell out of there, boy. Don't let a fool woman make a sucker out of you. Get out there on the Poseidon where you belong. We got a date at the Challenger Deep, remember? At the Pressure Point, just off Henderson Station near the thermal vents."

That's what he'd say.

And yet I wanted you, Carmen. I wanted to be with you, always.

"Oh God," I moaned, "what shall I do?"

Next morning the door chimes pealed, and you went to the door and brought back the audiogram. It was addressed to me; I wondered who could be sending me a message.

I pressed the stud on the little gray cylinder, and a rasping, automatic voice droned: "Henderson Station, Challenger Deep, July 27, 2045. Regret to inform you of death of Ian Jordan, Chief Engineer...."

Then there was a Latin name which was more polite than the word "depth-rot" and the metallic phrase, "This message brought to you by courtesy of United Nations Ocean Communication Corps."

I stood staring at the cylinder.

Ian Jordan was dead.

Ian Jordan was Ian. Depth Dog Ian.

My heart thudded crazily against my chest. It couldn't be! Not Ian! The audiogram had lied!

I pressed the stud again. "... regret to inform you of death of Ian..."

I hurled the cylinder at the wall. It thudded, fell, rolled. The broken voice droned on.

You ran to it, shut it off. "I'm sorry, Sergio, so terribly—"

Without answering, I walked into my room. I knew it was true now. I remembered Ian's coughing, his gaunt features, his drugged gaze. The metallic words had told the truth.

I sat for a long time on my bed, crying inside, but staring dry-eyed at Ian's faded tin box.

Then, finally, I fingered his meager possessions—a few wrinkled photos, some letters, a small carved figurine of a deep-sea creature, a gold service medal from the Ocean Patrol.

This was what remained of Ian after twenty-five years in the depths. It was a bitter bargain. A figurine instead of a wife, yellowed letters instead of children, a medal instead of a home.

It'd be a great future, I thought. You'd dream of sitting in a dingy dive bar at the bottom of the ocean with bioluminescent creatures buzzing around smoky, stinking lights. A bottle of kelp juice and a couple of deep-sea workers with dirty boots for company. And a sudden cough that would be the first sign of depth-rot.

To hell with it!

I walked into your living room and called Director Ryan on the visiphone.

I accepted that job teaching.

And now, Carmen, it's nearly midnight. You're in your room, sleeping, and the house is silent.

It's hard to tell you, to make you understand, and that is why I am writing this.

I looked through Ian's box again, more carefully this time, reading the old letters and studying the photographs. I believe now that Ian sensed my indecision, that he left these things so that they could tell me what he could not express in words.

And among the things, Carmen, I found a ring.

A wedding ring.

In that past he never talked about, there was a woman—his wife. Ian was young once, his eyes full of dreams, and he faced the same decision that I am facing. Two paths were before him, but he tried to travel both. He later learned what we already know—that there can be no compromise. And you know, too, which path he finally chose.

Do you know why he had to drug himself to watch me graduate? So he could look at me, knowing that I would see the depths he could never live to see. Ian didn't leave just a few trinkets behind him. He left himself, Carmen, for he showed me that a boy's dream can also be a man's dream.

He made his last trip to the Challenger Deep when he knew he was going to die. Heaven knows how he escaped a checkup. Maybe the captain understood and was kind—but that doesn't matter now.

Do you know why he wanted to reach the deepest trench? Do you know why he didn't want to die in the clean, cool air of Earth?

It was because he wanted to die nearer home. His home, Carmen, was the Ocean, where the submersible was his house, the crew his father, mother, brothers, the trenches his children.

You say that the beauty of the other side of the mountain vanishes after you reach it. But how can one ever be sure until the journey is made? Could I or Ian or the thousand before us bear to look upon a trench and think, I might have gone there; I could have been the first?

We said, too, that the life of a deep-sea explorer is lonely. Yet how could one be lonely when people like Ian roam the ocean depths?

Ian wanted me to himself that night after graduation. He wanted us to celebrate as explorers should, for he knew that this would be his last night on the surface. It might have seemed an ugly kind of celebration to you, but he wanted it with all his heart, and we robbed him of it.

Because of these things, Carmen, I will be gone in the morning. Explain the best you can to Liam and to your parents and Director Ryan.

Right now I've got a date that I'm going to keep—at a dingy dive bar at the bottom of the ocean, the Pressure Point, just off Henderson Station near the thermal vents.

Depth Dog Ian will be there; he'll go with me in memory to whatever part of the Ocean I may live to reach. And so will you, Carmen.

I have two wedding rings with me—his wife's ring and yours.
question: How many graduates were there in Sergio's class?

synthetic_story:
THE SAPPHIRE INITIATIVE
BY KEITH LAUMER

It was a simple cultural exchange—but Sebastian Knight gave them more of an education than they expected!

I

Deputy Administrator Michelle Peterson took her embroidered shawl and jade pendant from the wall hook. "I'm off now, Sebastian," she said. "I hope you'll manage the administrative routine during my absence without any unfortunate incidents."

"That seems a modest enough hope," Sebastian said. "I'll try to live up to it."

"I don't appreciate frivolity with reference to this Division," Michelle said testily. "When I first came here, the Cultural Heritage and Environmental Development Directorate was a shambles. I fancy I've made CHED what it is today. Frankly, I question the wisdom of placing you in charge of such a sensitive desk, even for two weeks. But remember. Yours is purely a rubber-stamp function."

"In that case, let's leave it to Ms. Chen. I'll take a couple of weeks off myself. With her experience, she could bring plenty of expertise to bear."

"I assume you jest, Sebastian," Michelle said sadly. "I should expect even you to appreciate that Zenithian participation in the Cultural Exchange Program may be the first step toward sublimation of their industrial aggressions into more sustainable channels."

"I see they're sending three thousand artisans to Greenfield Territory," Sebastian said, glancing at the Memo for Record. "That's a sizable sublimation."

Michelle nodded. "The Zenithians have launched no less than five mining campaigns in the last two decades. They're known as the Strip-Miners of the Proxima Sector. Now, perhaps, we shall see them breaking that precedent and entering into the cultural life of the Coalition."

"Breaking and entering," Sebastian said. "You may have something there. But I'm wondering what they'll study in Greenfield Territory. That's an agricultural world of the poor but honest variety."

"Academic details are the affair of the artisans and their mentors," Michelle said. "Our function is merely to bring them together. See that you don't antagonize the Zenithian representative. This will be an excellent opportunity for you to practice your diplomatic restraint—not your strong point, I'm sure you'll agree."

A buzzer sounded. Sebastian punched a button. "What is it, Ms. Chen?"

"That—rustic person from Parkview is here again." On the small desk screen, Ms. Chen's stern features were compressed in disapproval.

"This fellow's a confounded pest. I'll leave him to you, Sebastian," Michelle said. "Tell him something. Get rid of him. And remember: here at Coalition HQ, all eyes are upon you."

"If I'd thought of that, I'd have worn my other jacket," Sebastian said.

Michelle snorted and passed from view. Sebastian punched Ms. Chen's button.

"Send the rustic person in."

A tall broad woman with sun-darkened skin and silver-streaked hair, wearing practical trousers of heavy canvas, a loose tunic open at the collar and a short vest, stepped into the room. She had a bundle under her arm. She paused at sight of Sebastian, looked him over momentarily, then advanced and held out her hand. Sebastian took it. For a moment the two stood, face to face. The newcomer's jaw muscles knotted. Then she winced.

Sebastian dropped her hand and motioned to a chair.

"That's nice grip work, mister," the stranger said, massaging her hand. "First time anybody ever did that to me. My fault though. I started it, I guess." She grinned and sat down.

"What can I do for you?" Sebastian said.

"You work for this Cultural Heritage bunch, do you? Funny. I thought they were all bureaucrats. Never mind. I'm Isabella Wyatt. I'm a farmer. What I wanted to see you about was—" She shifted in her chair. "Well, out in Parkview, Xandria we've got a serious problem. The sapphire harvest is just about ready. We start gathering in another two, three months. Now I don't know if you're familiar with the Crystal Sapphire plants we cultivate...?"

"No," Sebastian said. "Have a drink?" He pushed a carafe across the desk. Isabella took it. "Crystal Sapphires are an unusual crop," she said, pouring water into a glass. "Only mature every fifteen years. In between, the plants don't need a lot of attention, so our time's mostly our own. We like to farm, though. Spend a lot of time developing new forms. Vegetables the size of a boulder—and delicious—"

"Sounds very pleasant," Sebastian said. "Where does the Cultural Heritage and Environmental Development Division come in?"

Isabella leaned forward. "We go in pretty heavy for the visual arts. Folks can't spend all their time hybridizing plants. We've turned all the land area we've got into parks and farms. Course, we left some sizable forest areas for wildlife preservation and such. Parkview's a nice place, Mr. Knight."

"It sounds like it, Ms. Wyatt. Just what—"

"Call me Isabella. We've got long seasons back home. Six of 'em. Our year's about twenty-two Terra months. Cold as ice in winter; eccentric orbit, you know. Purple-black sky, stars visible all day. We do mostly sculpture and pottery in the winter. Then Spring; still plenty cold. Lots of ice-sailing, snow-trekking, aurora watching; and it's the season for glassworkers. Our crystal work—"

"I've seen some of your crystal work," Sebastian said. "Beautiful pieces."

Isabella nodded. "All local minerals too. Lots of rare earths in our soil and those compounds give the crystals some color, I'll tell you. Then comes the Bloom Season. Flowers—they cover everything. But the sun's getting closer. Shines all the time. Ever seen it with flowers blooming in perpetual daylight? That's the music-composing season. Then summer. Summer's warm. We stay outside most of the time and have community gatherings all night. Lots of open spaces in Parkview; we're mostly valleys and plains. That's the dance and theater time. The stages are set up in the meadows, or on the hillsides. You have the performances and the wildflowers and the bonfires and stars—we're close to the center of a stellar nursery, you know...."

"You say it's time now for the sapphire harvest?"

"That's right. Autumn's our harvest season. Most years we have just the ordinary crops. Grains, tubers, that kind of thing; getting it in doesn't take long. We spend most of the time on architecture, getting new places ready for the winter or renovating the older ones. We spend a lot of time in our dwellings. We like to have them comfortable. But this year's different. This is Sapphire Year."

Isabella sipped her water, looked worriedly at Sebastian. "Our sapphire crop is our big money crop," she said. "We make enough to keep us going. But this year...."

"The crop isn't panning out?"

"Oh, the crop's fine. One of the best I can remember. Course, I'm only thirty-five; I can't remember but two other harvests. The problem's not the crop."

"Have you lost your markets? That sounds like a matter for the Commercial—"

"Lost our markets? Mister, nobody that ever saw our sapphires ever settled for anything else!"

"It sounds like I've been missing something," said Sebastian. "I'll have to see them some time."

Isabella put her bundle on the desk, pulled off the wrappings. "No time like the present," she said.

Sebastian looked at the two crystalline samples, one azure blue, one deep violet, both gleaming with inner light.

"Accepting gifts on duty is frowned on in the Coalition, Ms. Wyatt," he said.

"This isn't a gift. It's just samples." Isabella smiled. "Besides, my feelings would be hurt if you didn't look at them properly." She winked.

Sebastian took a jeweler's loupe from a drawer beside the desk. "Come to think of it, we also have to be careful about violating cultural heritage protocols."

Isabella held up the blue crystal. Sebastian examined it through the loupe, noting the perfect internal structure, then studied it with the naked eye. He looked at Isabella thoughtfully.

"Hmmm. The refraction patterns are extraordinary. Like looking into a living ocean."

"Don't try to describe it, Mr. Knight," Isabella said. She held up the violet crystal. "The custom back home is to view both colors in sequence."

Sebastian examined the second crystal. "Bad luck if you don't appreciate both," Isabella said, nodding. "You probably never heard about the trouble we had in Parkview a few years back?"

"Can't say that I did, Isabella." Sebastian set down the loupe. "Beautiful work."

"We've got plenty of minerals in Parkview," Isabella said. "But we don't plan to wreck the landscape mining 'em. We like to farm and create art. About twelve years back some neighbors of ours landed a force. They figured they knew better what to do with our minerals than we did. Wanted to strip-mine, process ore industrially. We convinced 'em otherwise. But it took a year, and we lost a lot of people."

"That's too bad," Sebastian said. "Environmental justice is a serious matter."

"It put us in a bad spot," Isabella went on. "We had to borrow money from a world called Bayview Territory. Mortgaged our fields. Had to start exporting art work too. Plenty of buyers, but it's not the same when you're doing it for strangers."

"Say, these crystals are remarkable," Sebastian said. "What's the problem? Bayview about to foreclose?"

"Well, the loan's due. The sapphire crop would put us in the clear. But we need harvest hands. Gathering Crystal Sapphires isn't a job you can turn over to machinery—and anyway we wouldn't if we could. Harvest season is the high point of living in Parkview. Everybody joins in. First, there's the gathering in the fields. Miles and miles of crystal gardens covering the valley floors, and climbing the hillsides, with meditation spaces here and there. Tall plants, ten feet high, loaded with crystals, and deep moss growing between. The water-carriers keep on the run, bringing refreshment to the gatherers. There's prizes for the biggest day's output, competitions for who can fill the most baskets in an hour.... The sun's high and bright, and it's just cool enough to give you plenty of energy. Come nightfall, the tables are set up in the garden plots, and the feast is laid on: roasted game, cultivated proteins, grain dishes, all kinds of preparations. Big salads. Plenty of fruit. Fresh-baked bread ... and crystal-clear water from the mountain springs. The cooking's done by a different crew each night in each garden, and there's prizes for the best crews.

"Then the crystal-processing. We still hand-polish each stone. That's mostly for the young folks but anybody's welcome. That's when things start to get creative. Matter of fact, pretty near half our artistic collaborations start after a harvest. All formality is dropped then. It keeps a person inspired though. Ever tried to polish a crystal while working side by side with someone who shares your vision?"

"Never did," Sebastian said. "You say most of the artistic collaborations start after a harvest. That would make the participants only fifteen years old by the time—"

"Oh, that's Parkview years; they'd be twenty-three, Terra reckoning."

"I was thinking you looked a little mature for thirty-five," Sebastian said.

"Fifty-two, Terra years," Isabella said. "But this year it looks bad. We've got a bumper crop—and we're short-handed. If we don't get a big harvest, Bayview steps in. Lord knows what they'll do to the land. Then next harvest time, with them holding half our crystal acreage—"

"You mortgaged the gardens?"

"Yep. Pretty foolish, huh? But we figured fifteen years was a long time."

"What we figured was, maybe you Cultural Heritage people could help us out. A loan to see us through the harvest, enough to hire extra hands. Then we'd repay it in sculpture, paintings, crystal work—"

"Sorry, Isabella. All we do here is work out itineraries for traveling exhibitions, that kind of thing. Now, if you needed a troupe of Andromedan light-dancers—"

"Can they gather crystals?"

"Nope. Anyway, they can't work in daylight. Have you talked this over with the Labor Office?"

"Sure did. They said they'd fix us up with all the digital transformation specialists and climate technology programmers we wanted—but no field hands. Said it was what they classified as menial drudgery; you'd have thought I was trying to buy slaves."

The buzzer sounded. Ms. Chen's features appeared on the desk screen.

"You're due at the Intergroup Council in five minutes," she said. "Then afterwards, there are the Zenithian artisans to meet."

"Thanks." Sebastian stood. "I have to run, Isabella," he said. "Let me think this over. Maybe I can come up with something. Check with me day after tomorrow. And you'd better leave the samples here. Cultural exhibits, you know."

II

As the council meeting broke up, Sebastian caught the eye of a colleague across the table.

"Mr. Hassan, you mentioned a shipment going to a place called Bayview Territory. What are they getting?"

Hassan blinked. "You're the fellow who's filling in for Michelle, over at CHED," he said. "Properly speaking, equipment grants are the sole concern of the Industrial Equipment Distribution, Division of Loans and Exchanges." He pursed his lips. "However, I suppose there's no harm in telling you. They'll be receiving heavy mining equipment."

"Drill rigs, that sort of thing?"

"Strip mining gear." Hassan took a slip of paper from a breast pocket, blinked at it. "Titan Model XV/3 excavators, to be specific. Why is CHED interested in IED's activities?"

"Forgive my curiosity, Mr. Hassan. It's just that Bayview cropped up earlier today. It seems they hold a mortgage on some crystal gardens over in—"

"That's not IED's affair, sir," Hassan cut in. "I have sufficient problems as Chief of IED without probing into CHED's business."

"Speaking of excavators," another person put in, "we over at the Special Committee for Rehabilitation and Development of Under-resourced Nations' Environmental Systems have been trying for months to get a request for mining equipment for Greenfield Territory through IED—"

"SCRUNES was late on the scene," Hassan said. "First come, first served. That's our policy at IED. Good day, colleagues." He strode off, briefcase under his arm.

"That's the trouble with peaceful worlds," the SCRUNES committee member said. "Zenith is a troublemaker, so every agency in the Coalition is out to pacify them. While my chance to make a record—that is, assist peace-loving Greenfield Territory—comes to naught." She shook her head.

"What kind of arts institute do they have in Greenfield Territory?" asked Sebastian. "We're sending them three thousand exchange artisans. It must be quite an institution."

"Arts institute? Greenfield Territory has one under-funded community center."

"Will all the exchange artisans be studying at the Community Center?"

"Three thousand artisans? Hah! Three
hundred
artisans would overtax the facilities of the center."

"I wonder if the Zenithians know that?"

"The Zenithians? Why, most of Greenfield Territory's difficulties are due to the unwise trade agreement they entered into with Zenith. Three thousand artisans indeed!" She snorted and walked away.

Sebastian stopped by the office to pick up a light jacket, then rode the elevator to the roof of the 180-story Coalition HQ building and hailed a transport to the port. The Zenithian artisans had arrived early. Sebastian saw them lined up on the platform waiting to go through customs. It would be half an hour before they were cleared through. He turned into the lounge and ordered a coffee.

A stocky young person at the next table raised their cup.

"Good fortune," they said.

"And prosperity to match."

"You said it." They gulped half their coffee. "My name's Valentina Evans. Ms. Evans. Yeah, Ms. Evans. This is tedious, sitting around this place waiting...."

"You meeting somebody?"

"Yeah. Bunch of novices. Kids. How they expect—Never mind. Have one on me."

"Thanks. You a mentor?"

"I'll tell you what I am. I'm a shepherd. You know—" Valentina turned to Sebastian—"not one of those kids has more than basic training." She grimaced. "Artisans, you know. Never saw an artisan with real experience, did you?"

"Lots of times. You're meeting the artisans, are you?"

Valentina blinked at Sebastian. "Oh, you know about it, huh?"

"I represent CHED."

Valentina finished her coffee, ordered another. "I came on ahead. Sort of an advance coordinator for the kids. I trained 'em myself. Treated it like a workshop, but they can handle a fabrication unit. Don't know how they'll act under pressure. If I had my old team—"

She looked at her coffee cup, pushed it back. "Had enough," she said. "So long, friend. Or are you coming along?"

Sebastian nodded. "Might as well."

At the exit to the Customs enclosure, Sebastian watched as the first of the Zenithian artisans came through, caught sight of Valentina and straightened up, chest out.

"Drop that, friend," Valentina snapped. "Is that any way for an artisan to act?"

The youth, a lean-faced person with intense eyes, grinned.

"Right, no. Say, uh, Ms. Evans, are we gonna get to see the city? We folks were thinking—"

"You were, hah? You act like a bunch of students! I mean ... no! Now line up!"

"We have quarters ready for the artisans," Sebastian said. "If you'd like to bring them around to the west side, I have a couple of transports arranged."

"Thanks," said Valentina. "They'll stay here until departure time. Can't have the little dears wandering around loose. Might get ideas about going independent." She grimaced. "I mean they might skip orientation."

"We've scheduled your re-embarkation for noon tomorrow. That's a long wait. CHED's arranged gallery visits and a dinner."

"Sorry," Valentina said. "As soon as the equipment gets here, we're off." She grimaced again. "Can't travel without our equipment, y'know."

"Suit yourself," Sebastian said. "Where's the equipment now?"

"Coming in aboard a Bayview lighter."

"Maybe you'd like to arrange for a meal for the artisans here."

"Sure," Valentina said. "That's a good idea. Why don't you join us?" Valentina winked. "And bring some refreshments."

"Not this time," Sebastian said. He watched the artisans, still emerging from Customs. "They seem to be all young adults," he commented. "No senior artisans?"

"Maybe later," Valentina said. "You know, after we see how the first group is received."

Back at the CHED office, Sebastian buzzed Ms. Chen.

"Do you know the name of the institution these Zenithian artisans are bound for?"

"Why, the Arts Institute at Greenfield Territory, of course."

"Would that be the Community Center?"

Ms. Chen's mouth puckered. "I'm sure I've never pried into these details."

"Where does doing your job stop and prying begin, Ms. Chen?" Sebastian said. "Personally, I'm curious as to just what it is these artisans are travelling so far to study—at Coalition expense."

"Ms. Peterson never—"

"For the present, Ms. Chen, Ms. Peterson is on leave. That leaves me with the question of three thousand young artisans headed for a world with no facilities for them ... a world in need of excavators. But the excavators are on their way to Bayview Territory, a world under obligation to Zenith. And Bayview holds a mortgage on the best crystal acreage in Parkview."

"Well!" Ms. Chen snapped, eyes glaring. "I hope you're not questioning Ms. Peterson's wisdom!"

"About Ms. Peterson's wisdom there can be no question," Sebastian said. "But never mind. I'd like you to look up an item for me. How many excavators will Bayview be getting under the IED program?"

"Why, that's entirely IED business," Ms. Chen said. "Ms. Peterson always—"

"I'm sure she did. Let me know about the excavators as soon as you can."

Ms. Chen sniffed and disappeared from the screen. Sebastian left the office, descended thirty-three stories, followed a corridor to the Coalition Library. In the archives he thumbed through catalogues, pored over indices.

"Can I help you?" someone asked. A young librarian stood at his elbow.

"Thank you," Sebastian said. "I'm looking for information on a mining rig. A Titan model XV excavator."

"You won't find it in the industrial section," the librarian said. "Come along." Sebastian followed them along the archives to a well-lit section lettered MILITARY EQUIPMENT. They took a data crystal from the shelf, plugged it into the viewer, scrolled through and stopped at a massive armored vehicle.

"That's the model XV," they said. "It's what is known as a planetary extraction unit. It carries six operators, with devastating environmental impact capability."

"There must be an error somewhere," Sebastian said. "The Titan model I want is an excavator. Model XV M-3—"

"Oh, the modification was the addition of a processing blade for demolition work. That must be what confused you."

"Probably—among other things. Thank you."

Ms. Chen was waiting at the office. "I have the information you wanted," she said. "I've had it for over fifteen minutes. I was under the impression you needed it urgently, and I went to great lengths—"

"Sure," Sebastian said. "Go ahead. How many excavators?"

"Eight hundred."

"Are you sure?"

Ms. Chen's face tightened. "Well! If you feel I'm incompetent—"

"Just questioning the possibility of a mistake, Ms. Chen. Eight hundred excavators is a lot of equipment."

"Was there anything further?" Ms. Chen inquired frigidly.

"I sincerely hope not," Sebastian said.

III

Leaning back in Michelle's ergonomic chair with climate control and posture adjustment, Sebastian leafed through a folder labelled "CERP 9-804-Bt; BAYVIEW TERRITORY (general)." He paused at a page headed Industry.

Still reading, he opened the desk drawer, took out the two crystal samples and examined them in the light. He studied the blue crystal meditatively.

It would be a pity, he reflected, if anything should interfere with the production of such beauty....

Half an hour later he laid the folder aside, keyed the communications panel and put through a call to the Bayview Legation. He asked for the Commercial Attache.

"Knight here, Coalition HQ," he said airily. "About the IED shipment, the excavators. I'm wondering if there's been a mix up. My records show we're shipping eight hundred units...."

"That's correct. Eight hundred."

Sebastian waited.

"Ah ... are you there, Knight?"

"I'm still here. And I'm still wondering about the eight hundred excavators."

"It's perfectly in order. I thought it was all settled. Mr. Hassan—"

"One unit would require a substantial operation to handle its output," Sebastian said. "Now Bayview subsists on its fisheries. They have perhaps half a dozen small processing facilities. Maybe, in a bind, they could handle the ore fifteen XVs could extract ... if Bayview had any ore. It doesn't. By the way, isn't an XV a poor choice as a mining outfit? I should think—"

"See here, Knight! Why all this interest in a few surplus excavators? And in any event, what business is it of yours how we plan to use the equipment? That's an internal affair of my government. Mr. Hassan—"

"I'm not Mr. Hassan. What are you going to do with the other seven hundred and eighty-five excavators?"

"I understood the grant was to be with no strings attached!"

"I know it's bad manners to ask questions. It's an old diplomatic tradition that any time you can get anybody to accept anything as a gift, you've scored points in the game. But if Bayview has some scheme cooking—"

"Nothing like that, Knight. It's a mere business transaction."

"What kind of business do you do with a Titan XV? With or without a blade attached, it's what's known as a planetary extraction unit."

"Great Heavens, Knight! Don't jump to conclusions! Would you have us branded as environmental criminals? Frankly—is this a secure line?"

"Certainly. You may speak freely."

"The excavators are for transshipment. We've gotten ourselves into a difficult situation, balance-of-payments-wise. This is an accommodation to a group with which we have rather strong business ties."

"I understand you hold a mortgage on the best land in Parkview," Sebastian said. "Any connection?"

"Why ... ah ... no. Of course not, ha ha."

"Who gets the excavators eventually?"

"Knight, this is unwarranted interference!"

"Who gets them?"

"They happen to be going to Parkview. But I scarcely see—"

"And who's the friend you're helping out with an unauthorized transshipment of grant material?"

"Why ... ah ... I've been working with a Ms. Oliver Johnson, a Zenithian representative."

"And when will they be shipped?"

"Why, they went out ten days ago. They'll be two-thirds of the way there by now. But look here, Knight, this isn't what you're thinking!"

"How do you know what I'm thinking? I don't know myself." Sebastian rang off, buzzed the secretary.

"Ms. Chen, I'd like to be notified immediately of any new applications that might come in from the Zenithian Consulate for placement of artisans."

"Well, it happens, by coincidence, that I have an application here now. Ms. Johnson of the Consulate brought it in."

"Is Ms. Johnson in the office? I'd like to see her."

"I'll ask if she has time."

"Great. Thanks." It was half a minute before a sharp-featured woman in severe attire walked in. She wore modern styling, a crisp uniform, polished boots and an impatient expression.

"What is it you wish?" she barked. "I understood in my discussions with the other ... ah ... administrator there'd be no further need for these tiresome conferences."

"I've just learned you're placing more artisans abroad, Ms. Johnson. How many this time?"

"Three thousand."

"And where will they be going?"

"Bayview Territory. It's all in the application form I've submitted. Your job is to provide transportation."

"Will there be any other artisans embarking this season?"

"Why ... perhaps. That's Zenith's business." Oliver looked at Sebastian with narrowed eyes. "As a matter of fact, we had in mind dispatching another three thousand to Magnolia, Veldoria."

"Another under-populated world—and in the same sector, I believe," Sebastian said. "Your people must be unusually interested in that region of space."

"If that's all you wanted to know, I'll be on my way. I have matters of importance to see to."

After Oliver left, Sebastian called Ms. Chen in. "I'd like to have a breakdown of all the artisan movements that have been planned under the present program," he said. "And see if you can get a summary of what IED has been shipping lately."

Ms. Chen compressed her lips. "If Ms. Peterson were here, I'm sure she wouldn't dream of interfering in the work of other departments. I ... overheard your conversation with the representative from the Bayview Legation—"

"The lists, Ms. Chen."

"I'm not accustomed," Ms. Chen said, "to intruding in matters outside our responsibility cluster."

"That's worse than listening in on communications, eh? But never mind. I need the information, Ms. Chen."

"Loyalty to my Chief—"

"Loyalty to your position should send you moving for the material I've asked for," Sebastian said. "I'm taking full responsibility. Now go."

The buzzer sounded. Sebastian flipped a key. "CHED, Knight speaking...."

Isabella's weathered face appeared on the desk screen.

"Hello, Sebastian. Okay if I come up?"

"Sure, Isabella. I want to talk to you."

In the office, Isabella took a chair. "Sorry if I'm rushing you, Sebastian," she said. "But have you got anything for me?"

Sebastian gestured at the crystal samples. "What do you know about Bayview Territory?"

Understanding dawned on Valentina. This must be a researcher or security officer who worked in this facility. She'd probably been alerted to an unauthorized presence. And judging by her reaction, temporal displacement was either very rare or very dangerous in this era—possibly both.

It wasn't just scientific curiosity. It was because she'd been studying the collapse of social welfare systems in the Bristol Region, watching communities fall apart as economic development failed to keep pace with population growth. She'd hoped that seeing how future societies handled these challenges might provide insights that could help her own time.

The memories came faster now, each one carrying emotional weight. Her mother's voice teaching her traditional songs from Dawnridge, Havencia. The performing arts center she'd helped establish in Crestwood to preserve cultural traditions. The design thinking workshops she'd run to help communities develop sustainable economic models.

She thought about her sister's face, about the students waiting for her next lecture, about the communities counting on her research. She thought about Henri Fuller, probably frantic with worry about what had happened to his test subject.

The world began to dissolve around her. She felt the familiar sensation of fragmentation, but this time it was different—purposeful, directed. The data points of her consciousness weren't scattering randomly but streaming in a specific direction, pulled by the gravitational force of her own timeline.

The woman in the laboratory was saying something, her voice rising in alarm, but Valentina could barely hear her anymore. The room faded, replaced by the crystalline layers of temporal displacement, and then—

—She was lying on a medical bed in Henri Fuller's laboratory in Crestwood. The familiar ceiling tiles above her had never looked so beautiful. Monitoring equipment beeped steadily around her, and she could hear voices speaking in her own language, her own time's accent and vocabulary.

Henri's face appeared above her, lined with worry and relief in equal measure. "Valentina! Thank God. You were gone for almost three minutes. We were about to shut down the experiment. What happened? Did you see anything?"

Valentina sat up slowly, her head spinning. "I was there, Henri. Not just observing—I was physically there. In a research facility, I think, maybe two hundred years in the future. The displacement technology... it doesn't work the way you thought it would."

Henri's face went pale. "Physical displacement? That's impossible. The equations don't allow for—"

"I know what the equations say," Valentina interrupted. "But I'm telling you what happened. And there's something else." She paused, remembering the fear in the other woman's eyes. "We can't do this again. The risks are too great, and not just to us. We could damage the timeline, create paradoxes. I saw things there that I shouldn't know about—advances in quantum computing, space exploration infrastructure, cultural developments that could influence our own decisions if we act on that knowledge."

Henri nodded slowly, his scientific excitement warring with ethical responsibility. "You're right, of course. The experiment is over. I'll destroy the equipment and seal the research." He looked at her closely. "Are you all right? Physically, I mean?"

Valentina considered the question. She felt fine, actually—better than fine. The experience had been terrifying, but it had also given her something unexpected: a renewed sense of purpose and connection to her own time. "I'm good, Henri. But I need to get back to work. There are people counting on me here and now."

She swung her legs off the bed and stood up, testing her balance. In her hand, she realized, she was still holding something—the small data cube from the future laboratory. She must have been gripping it when the displacement reversed.

She looked at it for a long moment, then handed it to Henri. "This needs to be locked away somewhere safe. Studied eventually, maybe, but carefully and with full ethical oversight. The knowledge in this could change everything—for better or worse."

Henri took the cube gingerly, as if it might explode. "I'll take care of it. And Valentina? Thank you. For being brave enough to try this, and wise enough to know when to stop."

Valentina smiled, though her hands were still shaking slightly. "I wasn't brave, Henri. I was terrified—both there and when I realized I might not get back. But sometimes fear is what keeps us human, what keeps us connected to what matters."

She walked toward the door, already thinking about her sister in Timberline, the students waiting for her, the communities that needed her research. She'd seen the future, and it was magnificent and terrifying in equal measure. But her place was here, in her own time, doing the work that needed to be done now.

Neither of them noticed the faint pulse of light from the data cube, a signal being sent across time to a research facility that wouldn't exist for another two centuries, where a young security officer named Amara Bell was filing a very strange incident report about a temporal intruder who had appeared and vanished from a locked laboratory, leaving no trace except a missing data storage device.

But in Crestwood, in the mid-21st century, Valentina Hart was already back at work, using her experience not to change the future but to improve the present, one community at a time.

The flow of time was not meant to be navigated backwards, only forward, one day at a time, with courage and purpose and the understanding that every moment mattered in its own right.

BROOKS: Dr. Young, could you explain what your institute does?

YOUNG: Primarily, we investigate correlations between digital network activity and various forms of social behavior. We use computational methods to analyze large-scale data patterns.

BROOKS: What kind of digital network activity are you referring to?

YOUNG: Well, social media activity is one form. But we also track other digital phenomena—search patterns, online purchasing behavior, streaming habits, that sort of thing.

BROOKS: I understand there are theories about how social media affects mental health and social cohesion.

YOUNG: There are countless theories. Most of them are what I'd call fashionable nonsense.

BROOKS: Could you elaborate?

YOUNG: People love to blame technology for society's problems. "Social media is destroying our children." "The internet is making us depressed." "Digital devices are ruining human connection." I've been hearing variations of this since I was an undergraduate studying cultural anthropology at the University of Crestwood. My grandmother used to say the same things about television. Before that, people blamed radio. Before that, newspapers. It's always something.

BROOKS: So you don't think technology affects behavior?

YOUNG: I didn't say that. I said most theories about it are nonsense. The relationship is far more complex and interesting than the simple cause-and-effect narratives people prefer.

BROOKS: What led you to your current research?

YOUNG: It started in early 2016. I had been consulting with law enforcement agencies in Waverly about a troubling trend. We were seeing sudden spikes in violent crime—assaults, domestic violence, road rage incidents—that seemed to occur in clusters. Not clusters in space, mind you, but clusters in time.

BROOKS: What do you mean?

YOUNG: I mean that on certain days, we'd see a dramatic increase in violent incidents across the entire city. Then things would calm down for a while. Then another spike. The pattern was unmistakable once you started looking for it.

BROOKS: Couldn't this be explained by normal statistical variation?

YOUNG: That's what everyone assumed at first. But I ran the numbers. Proper hypothesis testing, rigorous statistical analysis. The clustering was far beyond what you'd expect from random variation. Something was causing these synchronized outbursts of violence and aggression.

BROOKS: What did you do?

YOUNG: I started collecting detailed data. Not just crime statistics, but reports from hospitals, schools, workplaces. I had colleagues in Hartfield, Ilvaria doing similar work in their region. We began to notice that these episodes of collective aggression had certain characteristics.

BROOKS: Such as?

YOUNG: First, they always occurred during working hours—roughly 9 AM to 6 PM. Second, they seemed to affect a broad cross-section of the population. Third, the onset was often sudden and dramatic. People would describe feeling fine one moment, then experiencing intense anger, paranoia, or despair the next.

BROOKS: That must have been disturbing.

YOUNG: It was deeply troubling. Here we had evidence of some force that could simultaneously affect the mental state of thousands of people across a wide geographic area. But what force? That was the question.

BROOKS: Did you consider psychological explanations?

YOUNG: Of course. Mass hysteria, collective anxiety, cultural trauma. But none of these explanations fit the data. The people affected had nothing in common—different ages, backgrounds, occupations. No shared cultural heritage or experience. The only thing linking them was timing.

BROOKS: So what was your breakthrough?

YOUNG: I brought in a colleague, Dr. Lila Hernández, who specializes in network theory and digital systems analysis. She had been studying patterns in social media activity for her work in digital humanities. When I showed her my data, she immediately saw something I had missed.

BROOKS: What was that?

YOUNG: The spikes in aggressive behavior correlated almost perfectly with spikes in a particular type of social media activity. But not the kind you'd expect.

BROOKS: What kind was it?

YOUNG: That's where it gets interesting. Lila had been tracking what she called "N-Nodes"—network nodes that exhibited unusual broadcasting patterns. These weren't regular users or even influencers in the traditional sense. They were something else entirely.

BROOKS: Can you describe these N-Nodes?

YOUNG: They're accounts that appear normal at first glance. But when you analyze their activity patterns using advanced network theory, you see something strange. They post content that spreads through social networks in an unusual way—not viral in the conventional sense, but insidious. The content itself isn't particularly inflammatory or emotional. In fact, it's often quite mundane. But somehow it creates a kind of psychological resonance that amplifies negative emotions in those exposed to it.

BROOKS: How did you discover this?

YOUNG: Lila had been mapping these N-Nodes for her research on information diffusion. When we overlaid her maps with my timeline of aggressive incidents, the correlation was stunning. Every spike in violence corresponded with a period of high N-Node activity. More remarkably, there was a lag of approximately six to eight hours between peak N-Node activity and peak aggressive behavior.

BROOKS: Why the delay?

YOUNG: We believe it takes time for the psychological effect to build. The content from N-Nodes doesn't cause immediate reaction. Instead, it creates a kind of cognitive dissonance that accumulates over several hours until it manifests as anger, anxiety, or aggression.

BROOKS: But surely not everyone who sees this content is affected?

YOUNG: True. Susceptibility varies widely. Some people seem almost immune, while others are highly sensitive. We're still investigating why. It may relate to individual differences in media literacy, emotional regulation, or even neurological factors. Our research is touching on areas of biotechnology and neuroscience now.

BROOKS: Can you give an example of what this N-Node content looks like?

YOUNG: That's the disturbing part—it looks completely innocuous. A news story, a meme, a personal anecdote. Nothing that would raise red flags. But when Lila analyzed the semantic structure and network propagation patterns, she found they all shared certain mathematical properties. It's as if they're designed to exploit vulnerabilities in how we process information.

BROOKS: Are you suggesting these N-Nodes are deliberately created?

YOUNG: That's the question that keeps me up at night. At first, we thought they might be bot networks or state-sponsored disinformation campaigns. But the patterns are too sophisticated, too adaptive. They respond to current events in real-time. They evolve their strategies based on what works. It's almost as if they're learning.

BROOKS: That sounds like artificial intelligence.

YOUNG: Possibly. Or it could be coordinated human effort using AI tools. We've brought in experts in risk management and digital security, but so far we haven't been able to trace the N-Nodes back to any source. They appear, operate for a period, then disappear, only to be replaced by new ones.

BROOKS: How long does an N-Node typically remain active?

YOUNG: Anywhere from a few weeks to several months. During that time, it can cause multiple episodes of collective aggression. Then it goes dormant or is deleted. The pattern repeats with new N-Nodes emerging in different parts of the network.

BROOKS: You mentioned working with colleagues in Hartfield. Have you found similar patterns there?

YOUNG: Yes, and in Crestwood, Thandor as well. My colleague Omar Vasquez has documented identical phenomena there. We've even found cases where people in different cities experienced the same psychological effects at nearly the same time, despite being exposed to different N-Nodes. This suggests the N-Nodes are part of a coordinated network.

BROOKS: What about the timing issue—why only during working hours?

YOUNG: That puzzled us for a long time. Then we realized it corresponds to peak social media usage during work breaks and lunch hours. People check their phones during these times, get exposed to N-Node content, and the effects build throughout the afternoon. By evening, when many people have logged off, the exposure decreases.

BROOKS: Have you been able to warn people about this?

YOUNG: That's the challenge. How do you warn people about content that looks completely normal? We can't exactly tell everyone to stop using social media. Even if we could identify specific N-Node accounts, they'd just be replaced by new ones. It's like trying to fight a hydra.

BROOKS: What about content moderation by the platforms themselves?

YOUNG: We've been working with them, but it's difficult. The content doesn't violate any terms of service. It's not hate speech or misinformation in the conventional sense. It's more subtle than that. The platforms are starting to take it seriously, but developing effective countermeasures requires understanding mechanisms we're only beginning to comprehend.

BROOKS: Has your research drawn on any particular theoretical frameworks?

YOUNG: We've incorporated insights from multiple fields. Cultural anthropology helps us understand how information spreads through social groups. Justice theory informs our thinking about the ethical implications. We've even done oral history projects, interviewing people who've experienced these episodes to understand the phenomenology. And of course, network theory is fundamental to mapping the spread of influence.

BROOKS: What role does personal growth play in resistance to these effects?

YOUNG: That's an interesting question. We've found that people who engage in regular self-reflection and emotional skill development seem to be somewhat more resilient. Those who are aware of their emotional states and can recognize when they're being manipulated are better able to resist. In some ways, the best defense is personal growth—developing the capacity to observe your own reactions and question their origins.

BROOKS: Are there any historical precedents for this kind of phenomenon?

YOUNG: Historical analysis reveals that societies have always been vulnerable to coordinated manipulation. What's new is the scale and speed enabled by digital networks. In the past, it might take weeks or months for a rumor or propaganda campaign to spread. Now it happens in hours. The mechanisms of influence are ancient, but the delivery system is unprecedented.

BROOKS: What's the current status of N-Node activity?

YOUNG: As of this week, we're tracking seven active N-Nodes across major platforms. Activity levels are moderate but increasing. We're also seeing evolution in their tactics—they're getting better at evading detection.

BROOKS: That's rather ominous.

YOUNG: It is. But there's also reason for hope. Now that we understand the mechanism, we can develop countermeasures. We're working on browser extensions and app features that can identify potential N-Node content. We're also developing educational programs to help people recognize when they're being manipulated.

BROOKS: Do you think this problem will get worse before it gets better?

YOUNG: Almost certainly. As social media becomes more integrated into daily life, the potential for this kind of manipulation increases. We're also seeing the emergence of more sophisticated N-Nodes that use machine learning to optimize their impact. It's an arms race.

BROOKS: Some might say this research sounds like conspiracy theory.

YOUNG: I understand the skepticism. A few years ago, I would have been skeptical myself. But the data doesn't lie. We have rigorous statistical evidence, replicated findings across multiple cities, and a plausible mechanism. This isn't speculation—it's documented fact.

BROOKS: What would you say to people who feel helpless in the face of this?

YOUNG: I'd say awareness is the first step. If you find yourself suddenly feeling angry, anxious, or aggressive for no apparent reason, take a step back. Ask yourself: where is this feeling coming from? Have I been scrolling social media? Could I be reacting to something I saw online rather than to my actual circumstances? That kind of metacognition—thinking about your thinking—is powerful.

BROOKS: Any final thoughts?

YOUNG: Just this: we like to think we're rational actors making free choices. But the truth is we're all vulnerable to influence and manipulation. The question isn't whether we can be influenced—we can. The question is whether we can become aware enough to recognize it when it's happening. That's where personal growth intersects with social responsibility. We need to develop both individual resilience and collective awareness. Because if we don't, we're at the mercy of whoever controls the N-Nodes.

BROOKS: Dr. Young, thank you for your time.

YOUNG: Thank you, Jin. I hope this conversation helps people understand what we're up against.

THE END
