Every colony has problems—but especially a colony that is mining asteroids in the outer belt with AI oversight!

Sure I'm a Shadow, and I've been "terminated" nine times, always in the isolation of deep space mining operations, and I'm not alone, although there aren't very many of us, never were.

It made sense. DeepCore Mining was new to full AI integration and they wanted him on the station because he was a trained data analyst. They wanted facts, not speculation. But to ask a man to give up eighteen months of his life—well, that was asking a lot. Eighteen months in a rotating habitat. Still, it had an appeal Oscar Webb knew he couldn't deny, a researcher's joy of clean data sets, an asteroid field far afield, a closeup view of renewable energy harvesting at scale, history in the making.

Operations Director Leonardo Montgomery knocked the stylus against his tablet, saying, "DataStream Analytics is willing to let you have a leave of absence, if you're interested."

He knew Chief Administrator Catherine Russell from years of conferences, and now Russell said, "Personally, I don't want to see anybody else on the job. You've got a fine record in this sort of field research."

Oscar Webb smiled, but just barely. "You should have called me for the first rotation."

Russell nodded. "I wish we had had you on Highpoint Station Alpha."

"Miners," Montgomery said, "make poor observers."

Highpoint Station Alpha had launched the first rotation to the Cedarville Asteroid Cluster three years before with two thousand workers, reached the site with less than twelve hundred functional crew members. Upon the return to Earth orbit six months later, the crew's report of conflict and chaos during the nine-month outward journey was twisted, distorted and fragmentary. Webb remembered it well. The decision of DeepCore was that the workers started a rebellion far out in the belt, that it was fanned by the ignorance of Station Commander Vincent Baker in dealing with such matters.

"Isolation affects people in a peculiar way," Russell said. "We have conquered the problem of small groups in space—witness the discovery of the Cedarville Cluster, for example—but when there are large groups with AI management, control is more difficult."

"Baker," Montgomery said, "was authoritarian. The trouble started at about the halfway point. It ended with workers engaging in open warfare with each other and the AI systems. Baker was lucky to escape with his career."

"As I recall," Webb said, "there was something about the 3D printing facilities."

Russell rubbed her chin. "No weapons were allowed on the station, but you must remember the workers were selected for their intelligence and resourcefulness. They utilized these attributes to hack the 3D printing systems to manufacture makeshift weapons."

"The second rotation is history," Montgomery said. "And a puzzle."

Webb nodded. "The station went dark."

"Yes. We gave control to an advanced AI system."

"Assuming no accident in space," Russell said, "it was a wrong decision. They probably sabotaged the network."

"And now," Webb said, "you're going to try again."

Montgomery said very gravely, "We've got the finest station commander in the industry. Jennifer Lambert. No doubt you've heard of her. She's spent her life managing orbital facilities, and she's handpicking her own staff. We have also raised prerequisites for applicants. We don't think anything is going to happen, but if it does, we want to get an impersonal, unprejudiced view. That's where you come in. You do the observing, the data analysis. We'll evaluate it on your return."

"If I return," said Webb.

"I suppose that's problematical," Russell said, "but I think you will. Commander Lambert and her eighty staff members want to return as badly as you do." She grinned. "You can write that paper on complexity science you're always talking about on your return trip on Highpoint Station Beta."

Being a Shadow is important, probably as important as running the station, and I think it is this thought that keeps us satisfied, willing to be what we are.

Highpoint Station Beta had been built in Earth orbit, as had its predecessor, Highpoint Station Alpha, at a tremendous cost. Basically, it was an instrument which would open distant asteroid fields to resource extraction, reducing the supply chain management pressures of a resource-depleted Earth. A gigantic, rotating torus, the station would never land anywhere, but would orbit the Cedarville Cluster as it had orbited Earth, processing its cargo and housing its workers for the promised profits, the new frontier. A space-borne industrial complex, it would be the home for two thousand persons outward bound, only the staff on the return trip. It was equipped with every conceivable facility and comfort—dining facilities, assembly hall, individual and family quarters, recreation areas, hydroponic gardens, library, virtual reality theater. Nothing had been overlooked.

The commander's briefing room was crowded, the air was heavy with the breathing of so many people, and the ventilators could not quite clear the air of recycled atmosphere that drifted aimlessly here and there before it was caught and whisked away.

In the tradition of data analyst and observer, Oscar Webb tried to be as inconspicuous as possible, pressing against a bulkhead, but Commander Lambert's eyes sought his several times as Lambert listened to final reports from her engineers, resource managers, energy systems specialists, AI coordinators, and all the rest. She grunted her approval or disapproval, made a suggestion here, a restriction there. There was no doubt that Lambert was in charge, yet there was a human quality about her that Webb liked. The commander's was a sharp face, well composed, and her eyes were chips of gray.

"Colleagues," Lambert said at last, as Webb knew she would, "I want to introduce Oscar Webb, whose presence DeepCore has impressed upon us. On loan from DataStream, he will have an observer status." She introduced him to the others. All of them seemed professional; Webb thought it was a good staff.

Lambert detained him after the others had gone. "One thing, Mr. Webb. To make it easier for you, I suggest you think of this journey strictly from the observer viewpoint. There will be no paper for DataStream at the end."

Webb was startled. While he had considered the possibility, he had not dwelt on it. Now it loomed large in his mind. "I don't understand, Commander Lambert. It seems to me—"

"Let me put it differently. Let me say that you will not understand why I say that until the journey ends." She smiled. "Perhaps I shouldn't have mentioned it."

Webb left the commander's quarters with an odd taste in his mouth. Now why had Lambert said that? Why hadn't Montgomery or Russell said something, if it was important?

He made himself comfortable in his eight-foot-by-eight-foot quarters, which is to say he dropped on his bed, found it more comfortable than he thought it would be, put his arms behind his head, stared at the ceiling. Metal walls, one viewport, one floor vent, one ceiling vent, and a solitary ceiling panel light. This would be his home for eighteen months, just as there were homes like it for two thousand others, except that the family quarters would be larger. His quarters were in the inner ring near the officers' section.

He felt rather than heard the dull vibration. It was a sound he knew would be with him for eighteen months—nine months going and nine months returning.

He looked at his tablet, opened his data collection app and made an entry. The station right now would be slipping ever so slowly away from Earth orbit. He got up. He'd have to go forward to the observation dome to see that. Last view of Earth for eighteen months.

The penetration of deep space by large groups is the coming out from under the traditions of thousands of years, and as these planet-originated rules fall away, the floundering group seeks a new control, for they are humanity adrift, rudderless, for whom the stars are no longer bearings but nonexistent things, and values are altered if they are not shown the way.

The theft of Teresa Hicks's research drive occurred on the forty-third day out. In Webb's mind the incident, though insignificant from the standpoint of the station as a whole, could very well be the cause of dissension later on. His notes covering it were therefore very thorough.

Hicks's drive contained genetic sequences for renewable energy organisms—thousands of them, according to the Commander's Bulletin, the station's daily newsletter which went to all staff and workers. In the Bulletin the commander appealed to the thief to return the drive to Dr. Hicks. She said it was significant that all en route had passed psychological evaluations, and that it was to the station's discredit that someone with criminal tendencies should have been permitted aboard.

Webb had to smile at that. What did Commander Lambert think of those workers who sabotaged each other on Highpoint Alpha? They had passed psychological evaluations too. This, then, was what happened when you took two thousand strangers and stuck them in a rotating can for nine months.

When Webb saw Lambert about it, the commander said, "Of course I realize it takes only a little thing like this to set things off. I know people get tired of seeing each other, running the same simulations, looking at the asteroids from the observation dome, walking down the same corridors, reading the same files, eating the same meals, though God knows we try to vary it as much as we can. Isolation creates rough edges. But the point is, we know all this, and knowing it, we shouldn't let it happen. We've got to find that thief."

"What would they want genetic sequences for? Have you thought of that?"

"Of course. They'd have real value at Cedarville. Green infrastructure for the colony stations."

Webb sought out Teresa Hicks. She was a young woman with an intense face and determined eyes. She said, "Now what am I going to Cedarville for? I could only take along so much data storage and I deleted some personal files to make room for the sequences. I'm a bioengineering specialist, and DeepCore asked me to go along. But what use am I now? Where am I going to get sequences like those? Do you know how long it took me to develop them? They're not ordinary organisms, Mr. Webb."

There was an appeal from Hicks in the next day's newsletter describing the sequences, telling of their value, and requesting their return in the interests of the Cedarville colony and of humanity.

On the forty-seventh day a witness turned up who said she had seen a person emerging from Hicks's quarters with the silver drive. "I didn't think anything of it at the time," Marina Jenkins said.

Lambert asked her to describe the person.

"Oh, they were about average height, medium build, and they wore a black environmental mask that covered their face completely."

"Didn't you think that was important?" Lambert asked in an outraged voice. "A person wearing a black mask?"

Jenkins shrugged. "This is a space station. How would I know whether a black mask—or a red or blue one—does or doesn't belong on a space station?"

Although Jenkins' account appeared in the newsletter, it was largely discounted.

"If it is true," Lambert told Webb, "the theft must be the work of someone unstable. But I don't believe Marina Jenkins. It may well be she's the unstable one." She snorted. "Black environmental mask! I think I'll have Jenkins put through additional psychological evaluation."

Attendant to taking notes on this incident, Webb noted a strange thing. Hicks lived in that part of the station known as Sector One, and those who lived in that sector—more than five hundred men, women and children—felt that the thief must surely live in Sector Two or Four. Valentina Brown, who had the quarters next to Hicks's, sounded the consensus when she said, "Surely a person wouldn't steal from their own sector, now would they, Mr. Webb?"

And so, Webb observed in his notebook, are conflicts created.

Seen in space, asteroids are tumbling, silent, mineral-rich masses ever present and indifferent. To people unused to it, such a sight numbs, compresses, stultifies. They introduce a countermeasure, proof they exist, which is any overt act, sometimes violent.

On the sixty-second day Catherine Russell, the young wife of one of the resource engineers, ran screaming down one of the long corridors of Sector Three. She told the commander she had been attacked in her quarters while her husband was in the station's data center. She was taken to one of the station's doctors, who confirmed it.

She said the culprit was a person of average build wearing a black environmental mask, and though her description of what they had done did not appear in the story in the newsletter, it lost no time in penetrating every quarter of the station.

Webb was present when a delegation from Sector Three called on Commander Lambert, demanding action.

Lambert remained seated behind her desk, unperturbed, saying, "I have no staff to spare for security duty."

The delegation commenced speaking vehemently, to be quieted by Lambert's raised hand.

"I sympathize," Lambert said, "but it is up to each sector to deal with its problems, whatever they may be. My job is to get us to Cedarville."

The group left in a surly mood.

"You wonder at my reluctance, Mr. Webb," Commander Lambert said. "But suppose I assign the staff to patrol duties, the culprit isn't caught, and further incidents occur. What then? It soon becomes the staff's fault. And soon the workers will begin thinking these things might be the staff's doing in the first place."

"Yes," Webb said, "but what if the intruder is a staff member?"

"I know my people," Lambert said flatly.

"You could have a search for the mask and the research drive."

"Do you think it is a member of the staff?" Lambert's eyes were bright. "No, I trust my people. I won't violate that trust."

Webb left, feeling uneasy. If he were Lambert, he'd initiate an investigation, if nothing else than to prove the staff guiltless. Why couldn't Lambert see the wisdom of setting an example for the workers?

As a Shadow, I knew that isolation breeds hostility. There is a seed of malevolence in every person. It sometimes blossoms out among the asteroids. On Highpoint Beta it was ready for ripening.

Vincent Baker was killed in the station's medical bay on the eighty-fourth day. Baker, a Sector Four worker, had complained of feeling ill, had been hospitalized with a diagnosis of appendicitis. He had put his credit chip in the drawer of the small stand beside his bed. A person in a black mask was seen hurrying from the medical area, and a staff investigation revealed that Baker had died trying to prevent the theft of the chip.

Commander Lambert did not wait for the newsletter. Through the station's communication system, she reported that Baker had significant credits on the chip and had died of severe trauma. She said that since the incident occurred in the staff section of the station, her staff would be forced to submit to a thorough inspection in an effort to find the mask, the drive, the chip and the perpetrator.

"I will not countenance such an act by a staff member," Lambert said. "If and when they are found, they will be severely dealt with. But they might not be a member of the staff. I am ordering an assembly of all workers at nine tomorrow morning in the auditorium. I will speak to you all then."

Faces were angry, voices were sharp at the meeting, eyes suspicious and tempers short. Above it all was the commanding presence of Commander Lambert speaking to them.

"It is not my desire to interfere in worker affairs," she said. "Insofar as the station is concerned, it is my duty to make certain no staff member is guilty. This I am doing. But my staff is not and cannot be a security force for you. It is up to you people to police and protect yourselves."

"How can we protect ourselves without stunners?" one worker called out.

"Has Black Mask a weapon?" Lambert retorted. "It seems to me you have a better defense than any gun."

"What's that?"

"This station is only so wide, so long and so deep. If every inch is searched, you'll find your perpetrator. They have to be somewhere aboard."

The workers quieted. Leonardo Montgomery, one of the senior engineers, was elected president of the newly formed Sector Council. One person from each of the sectors was named to serve under him. Each of these people in turn selected five others from their own group.

Those assembled waited in the hall while each team of six inspected the quarters of the others. These quarters were then locked, everyone returned to their quarters, and the larger search was conducted. It took twenty-eight hours.

No mask was found. No mask, no drive, no chip, no perpetrator.

The commander reported that her search had been equally fruitless. At another assembly the following day it was decided to make the inspection teams permanent, to await further moves on the part of Black Mask. The Sector Council held periodic meetings to set up a method of trial for them when they were caught. It was all recorded in the newsletter and by Oscar Webb.

We Shadows know about hostility and about violence. We know too that where there is hostility there is violence, and where there is violence there is death.

During sleep time on the 109th day Marina Jenkins, awakened by a strange sound, sat up in the bed of her quarters to find a person in a black mask in her room. Her cries brought neighbors into the corridor. The flight of the person was witnessed by many, and several people tried to stop them. But the intruder was quick on their feet and fast. They escaped.

The Sector Council confronted the commander, demanding weapons.

"Are you out of your minds?" Lambert exclaimed.

Leonardo Montgomery, Sector Four leader, said, "We want to set up a security force, Commander. We want stunners."

"There's no regulation against it," Lambert said, "but it's a policy of mine that no weapons are to be issued en route."

"If we had had a weapon, we'd have got Black Mask," Montgomery said.

"And I might have a death on my conscience."

Montgomery said, "We've also thought of that. Suppose you supply us with low-power stunners? That way we can stun but not kill."

They got their weapons. Now there were thirty-two security personnel on duty in the corridors—ten on at a time. Webb observed that for the first time the workers seemed relaxed.

Let Black Mask move against armed people, they said.

Yeah, let them see what happens now.

Black Mask did.

On the 139th day they were seen in a corridor in Sector Four. Valentina Brown, security on duty, managed to squeeze off several shots at their retreating figure.

Black Mask was seen again on the 165th day, on the 186th day, and the 217th day. They were seen, shot at, but not hit. They were also unable to commit any crime.

We've got them on the run, the workers said.

They're afraid to do anything, now that we've got security, they said smugly.

The Sector Council congratulated itself. The workers were proud of themselves. A special congratulatory message from Commander Lambert appeared one day in the Bulletin newsletter.

The workers settled down to living out the rest of the voyage until the arrival at Cedarville.

But on the 234th day calamity struck. Black Mask appropriated one of the stunners, made their way down one whole corridor section in Sector Two, put occupants to sleep as they went, taking many articles of value and leaving disorder behind.

Webb interviewed as many victims as he could, noted it all in his database. The things taken were keepsakes, photographs and items of personal value. It seemed to be the work of someone deranged. If Black Mask wanted to make everyone furious, they certainly succeeded.

"What do they want that stuff for?" Teresa Hicks, now working as a medical assistant, asked. "I can see them taking my bioengineering notes, my research files—but my grandmother's necklace? That I don't understand."

It was the same with others. "The person's insane, Mr. Webb. Positively insane." Many people said it.

The council issued orders that all workers from now on would be required to lock their quarters at all times. More weapons were obtained from the commander. More security personnel were appointed.

Webb was busy noting it all in his database. It became filled with entries about innocent people being accidentally stunned when trigger-happy security thought their movements suspicious, about one person's suspicion of another and the ensuing search of quarters, people who saw Black Mask here, saw them there. Hardly a day went by without some new development.

"Oh, yes, Mr. Webb, we're going to get them," said Montgomery, now chief of security, cracking his knuckles, his eyes intense with the thought. "We're bound to get them. We've got things worked out to the finest detail. They won't be able to get through our net now. Just let them make so much as a move."

"And what will you do when you get them?"

"Terminate them," Montgomery said, his eyes glowing more fiercely than ever.

"Without a trial?"

"Oh, there'll be a trial, Mr. Webb, but you don't think any jury would let them live after all the things they've done, do you?"

Black Mask was stunned in Sector Four in a corridor by a security officer named Jennifer Lambert on the 277th day. The criminal was carried to the assembly room surrounded by guards, for they surely would have been harmed, if not killed, by angry workers who crowded around. In the assembly hall their mask was removed. The crowd gasped. Nobody knew them.

Webb's first thought was that they must be a stowaway, but then he remembered the face, and Commander Lambert, who came to have a look at them, unhappily admitted the person was a member of the staff. Their name was Vincent Baker and they were a data systems analyst third class.

"Well, Baker," Lambert said to them, "what have you got to say for yourself?"

"Nothing you'd understand," Baker said quietly. As if it were an afterthought, they turned away from the commander.

Lambert looked as if she were going to terminate the person herself right there and then.

It was a long trial—from the 303rd to the 331st day—and there didn't seem to be much doubt about the outcome, for Baker didn't help their own cause during any of it.

Catherine Russell, who was appointed prosecutor, asked them, "What did you do with the stolen items, Baker?"

Baker looked her square in the eye and said, "I jettisoned them through one of the waste airlocks. Does that answer your question?"

"Jettisoned them?" Russell and the crowd were incredulous.

"Sure," Baker said. "You workers got the easy life as passengers, just sitting around. I had to work constantly managing data systems for you lazy people."

The verdict was, of course, termination.

They executed Vincent Baker on the morning of the 372nd day with blasts from six stunners supplied with full power. It was witnessed by a great crowd in the assembly hall. A detail from the station's staff disposed of their body through an airlock.

It was all duly recorded in Oscar Webb's database.

Dying is easy for a Shadow. Especially if it's arranged for beforehand, which it always is.

Highpoint Station Beta was only one day out of Cedarville orbit when Commander Lambert sent for Webb and introduced him to the executed person.

"Hello," Baker said, grinning from ear to ear.

"I figured as much," Webb said. "I've been doing a lot of data analysis."

"You're perhaps a little too good as an observer," Lambert said. "Or maybe it was because you really weren't one of the workers. But no matter, Baker did a good job. They were trained by an old colleague of mine for this job, Gelthorpe Shadow. Shadow used to be in institutional reform when there were corporate wars."

"You were excellent," Webb said.

"Can't say I enjoyed the role," said Baker, "but I think it saved lives."

"Let me get this straight. DeepCore thought that it was isolation and boredom that caused the conflicts on Highpoint Alpha, so they had you trained to be a scapegoat. Is that right?"

Baker nodded. "When great numbers are being transported, they are apt to magnify each little event because so little happens. It was my job to see that they directed none of their hostility against each other or the staff, only toward me."

Lambert smiled. "It made the time pass quickly and interestingly for the workers."

"To say nothing of me," Baker said.

"And you, Mr. Webb, were along to observe it all," Commander Lambert put in. "DeepCore wanted an accurate picture of this. If it worked, they told me they'd use it on other rotations to Cedarville."

Webb nodded. "No time for brooding, for differences of opinion on small matters. Just time to hate Vincent Baker. Unanimously."

"Probably," Baker said, "you are wondering about the execution."

"Naturally."

"We removed the charges before the weapons were used."

"And Teresa Hicks's drive?"

"She'll get it back when she's shuttled to Cedarville. And all the other items will be returned. They're all tagged with their owner's names. Commander Lambert will say they were found somewhere on the station. You see, I was lying."

"How about that assault on Catherine Russell?"

Baker grinned again. "She played right into our hands. She ran out into the hall claiming I'd attacked her, which I did not. She was certainly amazed when the station's physicians agreed with her. Of course Commander Lambert told them to do that."

"And the murder?"

"Vincent Baker—the original Vincent Baker—died in medical all right, but he died from his illness on the operating table. We turned it into an advantage by making it look suspicious."

Webb brightened. "And by that time everybody was seeing Black Mask everywhere and the workers organized against them."

"Gave them something to do," Lambert said.

"Every time things got dull, I livened them up. I got a stunner and robbed along the corridor. That really stirred them. Lucky nobody got hurt during any of it, including that Jenkins woman. I was trying to rob her when she woke up."

Lambert cleared her throat. "Ah, Webb, about that paper. You understand you can't write it, don't you?"

Webb said regretfully that he did understand.

"The workers will never know the truth," Lambert went on. "There will be other stations outward bound."

Baker sighed. "And I'll have to be caught again."

Yes, we're anonymous, nameless, we Shadows, for that's what we call each other, and are a theme, with variations, in the endless stretches of deep space, objects of hatred and contempt, professional villains, dying once a rotation when the time is ripe, antidote to boredom, and we'll ply our trade, our little tragedies, on a thousand stations bringing humanity to new worlds.
question: Who was the Operations Director that spoke to Oscar Webb?

synthetic_story:
I am a Probability Field
By SOPHIA WEST

When I got back from the research institute, I was not so much exhausted as mentally drained, but the effect is similar. I let myself into the apartment in Eastwood Village, which had an absent-partner look, and took a cold shower. The present temperature according to the weather app was thirty-two degrees Celsius, but according to my thermometer, it was thirty-eight. I got dressed and went into the living room, and wished ardently that my partner Hassan were here to tell me why the whole place looked so desolate.

What do they do, I asked myself, that I have left undone? I've cleaned the floors, I've organized the books and I've straightened the cushions.... Ah! The coffee mugs. I washed them and put them back, but still the place looked partner-deserted.

It had been a difficult day; I had forgotten to charge my alarm, so I'd had to rush to make a theoretical modeling presentation at one of the quantum computing labs I consult for. I didn't notice the impending storm and had no umbrella when I reached the sidewalk, to find myself confronted with an almost tropical downpour. I would have turned back, but a rideshare pulled up and a woman got out, so I dashed through the rain and got in.

"University District, the Quantum Sciences Building," I said.

"Right," said the driver, and I heard the engine sputter, and then go on sputtering. After some futile attempts, she turned to me. "Sorry. You'll have to find another ride. Good luck."

If possible, it was raining still harder. I opened my bag over my head and ran for the metro: three blocks. Traffic held me up at each crossing and I was soaked when I reached the platform, just in time to miss the express. After an abnormal delay, I got one which exactly missed the connection at Central Station. The same thing happened at both ends of the cross-district line, but I found the rain had stopped when I got out at University Square.

As I walked toward the building, I passed a large construction site where they were preparing to build a new green infrastructure project—part of the city's environmental justice initiative. There was the usual crowd of observers watching the excavation machines and, in particular, a worker with a jackhammer who was breaking up some compressed sediment. While I looked, a large chunk of it fell away, and for an instant I was able to see something that looked like a piece of crystalline material, the size of a storage container. It glittered brilliantly in the sunlight, and then the chattering jackhammer hit it.

There was a faint crack and the thing disintegrated. It knocked the worker backwards, but he got right up and I realized he was not hurt. At the moment of the fracture—if so minor a thing can be called one—I felt something sting my cheek and, on touching it, found blood on my hand. I dabbed at it with a tissue but, though slight, the bleeding would not stop, so I went into a pharmacy and bought some adhesive strips which I put on the tiny cut. When I got to the lab, I found that I had missed the presentation slot.

During the day, by actual count, I heard the phrase "Let's workshop that" nine times, and another academic favorite, "The entire theoretical framework," eleven times. However, my theoretical model had been accepted without revision because nobody had noticed my absence from the presentation room. There you have what is known as the Academic World, the research game, or the grant-writing racket, depending upon which level of the hierarchy you have achieved.

The metro gave a repeat performance going home, and as I got to the apartment complex in Eastwood Village, the building manager was standing there talking to the maintenance supervisor.

She said, "Hello, Dr. West. I guess you must have just missed it at your building. We just heard a little while ago: all four elevators in the Quantum Sciences Building jammed at the same time. Sounds impossible. I guess you just missed it."

Anything can happen in academia, I thought. "That's right, I just missed it," I said, and went on in.

Behavioral economics tells us that some people are risk-seeking; I, on the other hand, seemed recently to be coincidence-prone, anomaly-adjacent, and except for the dead alarm, I'd had no control over what had been going on.

I went into our small kitchen to make a drink and reread the instructions Hassan had left, telling me how to manage by myself until he got back from his conference in Crestwood Village, a matter of ten days. How to use the coffee maker, how to operate the food processor, whom to call if I needed help. My partner used to be a professional chef and he is quite convinced that I cannot feed myself without him. He is right, but not for the reasons he supposes.

I opened the refrigerator to get some ice and saw another note: "When you take out the Juice or Cheese, Put it Right Back. And Close the Door, too."

Intimidated, I took my drink into the living room and sat down in front of the computer. As I stared at the research paper that was to establish my reputation beyond quantum computing, I noticed an error and picked up a stylus. When I put it down, it rolled off the desk, and with my eyes on the manuscript, I groped under the chair for it. Then I looked down. The stylus was standing on its end.

There, I thought to myself, is that one chance in a million we hear about, and picked up the stylus. I turned back to my paper and drank some of the cocktail in hopes of inspiration and relief from the muggy heat, but nothing came. I went back and read the whole section to try to get forward momentum, but came to a dead stop at the last sentence.

Damn the heat, damn the stylus, damn academia and grant applications. My drink was gone and I went back to the kitchen and read Hassan's notes again to see if they would be like a message from him. I noticed one that I had missed, pinned to the recycling bin: "Pickup at 6:30 AM so the idea is to Put it Here the Night Before. I love you." What can you do when he loves you?

I made another drink and went and stared out of the living room window at the courtyard opposite. The sun was out again and a woman with a remote was operating her collection of drones. They flew in formation, hoping to be allowed to land, but were not allowed to.

Drones fly as a rule in coordinated patterns and turn simultaneously, so that their solar panels all catch the sunlight at the same time. I was thinking about this elegant fact when I saw that as they were making a turn, they seemed to bunch up together. By some curious chance, they all wanted the same position in the airspace to turn in, and several collided and fell.

The woman was as surprised as I and went to one of the damaged drones and picked it up. She stood there shaking her head from side to side, examining its rotors.

My speculations about this peculiar aerial traffic accident were interrupted by loud voices in the hallway. Since our building is usually very well behaved, I was astonished to hear what sounded like an incipient argument, and among the angry voices I recognized that of my neighbor, Felix, a very quiet guy who works in media production and has never, to my knowledge, caused disturbances, particularly in the late afternoon.

"You can't accuse me of that!" I heard him shout. "I tell you I bought this deck this afternoon and it wasn't opened till we started to play!"

Several other loud voices started at the same time.

"Nobody gets five royal flushes in a row!"

"Yeah, and only when you were dealer!"

The tone of the argument was beginning to get ugly, and I opened the door to offer Felix help if he needed it. There were four people confronting him, evidently torn between the desire to make an angry exit and the impulse to stay and confront him further. His face was furiously red and he looked stunned.

"Here!" he said, holding out a deck of cards, "For heaven's sake, examine them yourselves if you think they're marked!"

The nearest person struck them up from his hand. "Okay, magician! So they're not marked! All I know is five royal...."

His voice trailed away. He and the others stared at the scattered cards on the floor. About half were face down, as might be expected, and the rest face up—all spades.

Someone must have called for it, because at that moment the elevator arrived and the four people, with half frightened, incredulous looks, and in silence, got in and were taken down. My friend stood looking at the neatly arranged cards.

"Unbelievable!" he said, and started to pick them up. "My God, what a session...."

I helped him and said to come in for a drink and tell me all about it, but I had an idea what I would hear.

After a while, he calmed down, but he still seemed dazed.

"Never seen anything to equal it," he said. "Wouldn't have believed it. Those people didn't believe it. Every round normal, nothing unusual about the hands—three of a kind, a low straight, that sort of thing and one person got queens over tens, until it gets to be my deal. Brother! Royal flush—every time! And each time, somebody else has four aces...."

He started to perspire again, so I got up to fix him another drink. There was one bottle of tonic water left, but when I tried to open it, the cap broke and glass fragments got into the bottle.

"I'll have to go down for more tonic," I said.

"I'll come, too. I need air."

At the convenience store on the corner, the clerk gave me three bottles in what must have been a weak bag, because as he handed them to me over the counter, the bottom gave and they fell onto the tile floor. None of them broke, although the fall must have been from at least five feet. Felix was too absorbed in his thoughts to notice and I was getting used to anomalies. We left the proprietor with his mouth open and met the building manager, looking in at the door, also with her mouth open.

On the sidewalk, a man walking in front of Felix stopped suddenly to check his phone and Felix, to avoid bumping him, stepped into the bike lane and a cyclist swerved to avoid Felix. The pavement was still wet and the cyclist skidded, their rear wheel lightly tapping the front of one of those small electric scooters, which was going rather fast. It turned sideways and, without any side-slip, went right up the steps of a building opposite, coming to rest with its front wheel inside the entrance, which a woman opened at that moment.

The sight of this threw another cyclist into a skid, and when she and the first cyclist had stopped sliding around, they were positioned face to face, arranged crosswise to the bike lane. This gave them exactly no room to move either forward or backward, for one bike had its back to a bench and the other to a lamppost.

Although rather wide, this is a two-way bike lane, and in no time at all, traffic was backed up from both directions as far as the intersections. Everyone was ringing their bell.

The building manager was frustrated—more so when she tried to put through a call to the maintenance office from the panel in the lobby.

It was malfunctioning.

Upstairs, the wind was blowing into the apartment and I closed the windows, mainly to shut out the commotion and the noise. Felix had brightened up considerably.

"I'll stay for one more drink and then I'm due at the studio," he said. "You know, I think this would make content for our channel." He grinned and nodded toward the chaos.

When he was gone, I noticed it was getting dark and turned on the desk lamp. Then I saw the window blinds. They were all twisted in spirals, except one. That was twisted in three spirals.

All right, I told myself, it was the wind. But I felt the time had come for me to get expert advice, so I went to the phone to call Ruth. Ruth is an associate professor of theoretical physics at a university uptown and lives near us. She is highly analytical, but we believe she knows everything.

When I picked up the receiver, the line sounded dead and I thought, more trouble. Then I heard someone cough and I said hello. Ruth's voice said, "Sophia? You must have picked up the receiver just as we were connected. That's a remarkably unlikely coincidence."

"Not in the least," I said. "Come on over here. I've got something for you to analyze."

"Well, as a matter of fact, I was calling to ask you and Hassan—"

"Hassan's away for the week. Can you get over here quickly? It's urgent."

"Immediately," she said, and hung up.

While I waited, I thought I might try working on a few paragraphs of my research paper—perhaps something would come now. It did, but as I came to a point where I was about to type the word "superposition," I decided it was too technical for the introduction, and stopped at the letter "P." Then I saw that I had unaccountably hit all five keys one step to the side of the correct ones, and deleted the line, with my face flushed.

This was absolutely not my day.

"Well," Ruth said, "nothing you've told me is impossible or supernatural. Just very, very improbable. In fact, the odds against that card game alone would lead me to suspect Felix, well as I know him. It's all those other things...."

She got up and walked over to the window and looked at the hot twilight while I waited. Then she turned around; she had a look of concern.

"Sophia, you're a rational person, so I don't think you'll take offense at what I'm going to say. What you have told me is so impossibly unlikely, and the odds against it so astronomical, that I must consider the possibility that you're either fabricating this or you're experiencing a perceptual anomaly." I started to get up and protest, but she motioned me back. "I know, but don't you see that that is far more likely than...." She stopped and shook her head. Then she brightened. "I have an idea. Maybe we can have a demonstration."

She thought for a tense minute and snapped her fingers. "Have you any coins on you?"

"Why, yes," I said. "Quite a few." I reached into my pocket. There must have been nearly three dollars in various denominations. "Do you think they'll each have the same date, perhaps?"

"Did you accumulate all those coins today?"

"No. During the week."

She shook her head. "In that case, no. Discounting the fact that you could have arranged it, if my preliminary theory is correct, that would be actually impossible. It would involve temporal reversal. I'll tell you about it later. No, just throw down the coins. Let's see if they all come up heads."

I moved away from the carpet and tossed the handful of coins onto the floor. They clattered and bounced—and bounced together—and stacked themselves into a neat pile.

I looked at Ruth. Her eyes were narrowed. Without a word, she took a handful of coins from her own pocket and threw them.

These coins didn't stack. They just fell into an exactly straight line, the adjacent ones touching.

"Well," I said, "what more do you need?"

"Good grief," she said, and sat down. "I suppose you know that there are two great apparently opposite principles governing the Universe—entropy and negentropy. Random distribution on the beach is an example of entropy and living systems are examples of negentropy. The motions of particles in a gas are what we call random, but there are so many of them, we treat them statistically and derive thermodynamic laws—quite reliable. It isn't theoretically absolute; it's just a matter of extreme probability. Now living systems, on the other hand, seem not to depend on probability at all; actually, they work against it. Or you might say they are certainly not accidental manifestations."

"Do you mean," I asked in some confusion, "that some form of life is controlling the coins and—the other things?"

She shook her head. "No. All I mean is that improbable events usually have improbable explanations. When I see a statistical law being violated, I don't say to myself, 'Here's a miracle.' I revise my understanding of the principles. Something—I don't know what—is happening, and it seems to involve probability, and it seems to center around you. Were you still in that building when the elevators stuck? Or near it?"

"I guess I must have been. It happened just after I left."

"Hm. You're the epicenter, all right. But why?"

"Epicenter of what?" I asked. "I feel as though I were the epicenter of a probability storm. Something has it in for me!"

Ruth grinned. "Don't be superstitious. And especially don't anthropomorphize."

"Well, if it's the opposite of entropy, it's got to be a living system."

"On what basis? All we know for certain is that random events are being reorganized. A crystal, for example, is not alive, but it's a non-random arrangement of particles.... I wonder." She had a faraway, contemplative look.

I was beginning to feel hungry and the drinks had worn off.

"Let's go out and eat," I said. "There's not a thing in the kitchen and I'm not allowed to cook. Only eggs and coffee."

We put on our jackets and went down to the street. From either end, we could hear tow trucks removing the stalled vehicles. There were, by this time, a number of harassed traffic officers directing the maneuver and we heard one of them say to the building manager, "I don't know what's going on around here. Every single vehicle's got something wrong with it. They can't any of them back out for one reason or another. Never seen anything like it."

Near us, two pedestrians were doing a curious little dance as they tried to pass one another; as soon as one of them moved aside to let the other pass, the other would move to the same side. They both had embarrassed grins on their faces, but before long their grins were replaced by looks of suspicion and then determination.

"All right, wise guy!" they shouted in unison, and barged ahead, only to collide. They backed off and threw simultaneous punches which met in mid-air. Then began one of the most remarkable encounters ever witnessed—a confrontation in which fist hit fist but never anything else, until both combatants backed away undefeated, muttering identical excuses and threats.

The building manager appeared at that moment. Her face was flushed. "You all right, Dr. West?" she asked. "I don't know what's happening around here, but ever since this afternoon, things are going haywire. Martinez!" she shouted—she could succeed as an auctioneer. "Bring those people over here!"

Three people in a confused tangle, with their half-open umbrellas intertwined, were brought across the street, which meant climbing over bike racks. Martinez, a competent young security officer, seemed self-conscious; the people seemed not to be.

"All right, now, Ms. Wheeler!" one of them said. "Let go of my umbrella and we'll say no more about it!"

"And so now it's Ms. Wheeler, is it?" said her adversary.

The third, a younger woman with her back turned to us, her umbrella also caught in the tangle, pulled at it tentatively, at which the other two glared at her. She turned her head away and tried to let go, but the handle was caught in her sleeve. She looked up and I saw it was Hassan. My chef-partner.

"Oh, Sophia!" he said, and managed to detach himself. "Are you all right?" Was I all right!

"Hassan! What are you doing here?"

"I was so worried, and when I saw all this, I didn't know what to think." He pointed to the stalled vehicles. "Are you really all right?"

"Of course I'm all right. But why...."

"The Crestwood Village operator said someone kept dialing and dialing the conference center and there wasn't anyone on the line, so then she had it traced and it came from our phone here. I kept calling back, but I only got a busy signal. Oh, dear, are you sure you're all right?"

I put my arm around him and glanced at Ruth. She had an inward look. Then I caught the building manager's eye. It had a thoughtful, almost suspicious cast to it.

"Trouble does seem to follow you, Dr. West," was all she said.

When we got upstairs, I turned to Ruth. "Explain to Hassan," I said. "And incidentally to me. I'm not properly informed yet."

She did so, and when she got to the summary, I had the feeling he was a step ahead of her.

"In other words, you think it's something organic?"

"Well," Ruth said, "I'm trying to think of anything else it might be. I'm not doing so well," she confessed.

"But so far as I can see," Hassan answered, "it's mere probability manipulation, and without any overall pattern."

"Not quite. It has a center. Sophia is the center."

Hassan looked at me with a curious expression for a moment. "Do you feel all right, darling?" he asked me. I nodded brightly. "You'll think this silly of me," he went on to Ruth, "but why isn't it something like quantum entanglement gone wrong?"

"Pure speculation," she said. "No empirical evidence."

"Electromagnetic fields?"

"Absolutely not. For one thing, most of the objects affected weren't conductive—and don't forget electromagnetism is a force, not a form of energy itself, and a great deal of energy has been involved. I admit the energy has mainly been supplied by the objects themselves, but in an electromagnetic field, all you'd get would be stored potential energy, such as when a charged particle moves in a field. Then it would just stay there, like a capacitor. These things do a lot more than that—they continue moving."

"Why did you mention a crystal before? Why not a life-form?"

"Only an analogy," said Ruth. "A crystal resembles life in that it has a definite structure and exhibits growth, but that's all. I'll agree this—phenomenon—has no discernible structure and motion is involved, but plants don't move and amoebas have no fixed shape. Then a crystal accumulates material, but it does not transform what it accumulates; it merely rearranges it into a non-random pattern. In this case, it's rearranging random events and it has a nucleus and it seems to be growing—at least in what you might call improbability."

Hassan frowned. "Then what is it? What's it made of?"

"I should say it was made of the probability distributions themselves. There's a similar concept in quantum field theory. Another thing that's like a crystal is that it appears to be forming around a nucleus not of its own composition—the way a speck of dust in a supersaturated solution becomes the nucleus of crystallization."

"Sounds like the pearl in an oyster," Hassan said, and gave me an impertinent look.

"Why," I asked Ruth, "did you say the coins couldn't have the same date? I mean apart from the unlikely chance I got them that way."

"Because I don't think this phenomenon got started before today and everything that's happened can all be described as improbable events here and now. The dates were already there, and to change them would require retroactive causation, reversing time. That's out, in my book. That telephone now—"

The doorbell rang. We were not surprised to find it was the phone technician. She took the device apart and made disapproving sounds.

"I guess you dropped it on the floor," she said with strong disapproval.

"Certainly not," I said. "Is it broken?"

"Not exactly broken, but—" She shook her head and took it apart some more.

Ruth went over and they discussed the problem in undertones. Finally the technician left and Hassan called the conference center to reassure them. Ruth tried to explain to me what had happened with the phone.

"You must have jostled something loose. And then you replaced the handset in such a way that the contact wasn't quite open."

"But for heaven's sake, Hassan says the calls were going on for a long time! I phoned you only a short time ago and it must have taken him nearly two hours to get here from Crestwood Village."

"Then you must have done it twice and the vibrations in the floor—something like that—just happened to cause the right induction patterns. Yes, I know how you feel," she said, seeing my expression. "It's beginning to intensify."

Hassan was through telephoning and suggested going out for dinner. I was so pleased to see him that I'd forgotten all about being hungry.

"I'm in no mood to cook," he said. "Let's get away from all this."

Ruth raised an eyebrow. "If all this, as you call it, will let us."

In the lobby, we ran into Felix, looking satisfied in a media way.

"I've been assigned to cover the story—who could be better?—I live here. So far, I don't quite get what's been happening. I've been talking to the building manager, but she didn't say much. I got the feeling she thinks you're involved in some mystical way. Hello, Ruth, what's with you?"

"She's got a theory," said Hassan. "Come and eat with us and she'll tell you all about it."

Since we decided on a climate-controlled restaurant nearby in the arts district, we walked. The jam of vehicles didn't seem to be any less than before and we saw the building manager again. She was talking to a city inspector, and when she caught sight of us, she said something that made the inspector look at us with interest. Particularly at me.

"If you want your umbrella, Mr. McCoy," the building manager said, "it's at the security office. What there's left of it, that is."

Hassan thanked her and there was a short pause, during which I felt the speculative regard of the inspector. I pulled out a packet of mints, which I had opened, as always, by tearing off the top. I happened to have it upside down and all the mints fell out. Before I could move my foot to obscure what they had spelled out on the sidewalk, the two officials saw it. The inspector gave me a hard look, but said nothing. I quickly kicked the insulting mints into the gutter.

When we got to the restaurant, it was crowded but cool—although it didn't stay cool for long. We sat down at a side table near the entrance and ordered gin and tonics as we looked at the menu. Sitting at the next table were a large woman, wearing a very elaborate, brilliant purple evening gown, and a thin, sour-looking man in formal wear. When the server returned, they preempted him and began ordering dinner fussily: a salad for the man, and gazpacho, crab cakes and chocolate mousse for the large woman.

I tasted my drink. It was most peculiar; salt seemed to have been used instead of sugar. I mentioned this and my companions tried theirs, and made faces.

The server was concerned and apologetic, and took the drinks back to the bar across the room. The bartender looked over at us and tasted one of the drinks. Then he dumped them in his sink with a puzzled expression and made a new batch. After mixing this, he set out a row of glasses, put ice in them and began to pour.

That is to say he tilted the shaker over the first one, but nothing came out. He tapped it against the side of the bar and tried again. Still nothing. Then he took off the top and probed into it with his stirrer, his face pink with frustration.

I had the impression that the shaker had frozen solid. Well, ice is a crystal, I thought to myself.

The other bartender gave him a fresh shaker, but the same thing happened, and I saw no more because the customers sitting at the bar crowded around in front of him, offering suggestions. Our server came back, baffled, saying he'd have the drinks in a moment, and went to the kitchen. When he returned, he had the woman's gazpacho and some bread, which he put down, and then went to the bar, where the audience had grown larger.

Hassan lit a cigarette and said, "I suppose this is all part of it, Sophia. Incidentally, it seems to be getting warmer in here."

It was, and I had the feeling the place was quieter—a background noise had stopped. It dawned on me that I no longer heard the faint hum of the air-conditioner over the entrance, and as I started to say so, I made a gesture toward it. My hand collided with Hassan's when he tapped his cigarette over the ashtray, and the cigarette landed in the neighboring gazpacho.

"Hey! What's the idea?" snarled the sour-looking man.

"I'm terribly sorry," I said. "It was an accident. I—"

"Throwing cigarettes at people!" the large woman said.

"I really didn't mean to," I began again, getting up. There must have been a loose thread in the edge of their tablecloth which one of my bracelet clasps caught on, because as I stepped out from between the closely set tables, I pulled everything—tablecloth, silverware, water glasses, salt and pepper shakers and the gazpacho-à-la-nicotine—onto the floor.

The large woman surged from the booth and slapped me forcefully. The man raised his fists and postured as boxers are popularly supposed to do. The owner of the place, a woman with distinctive silver hair, hustled toward us with a determined manner. I tried to explain what had happened, but I was outshouted, and the owner frowned darkly.

The Fracturing of the Neural Grid

"Another attack?" asked Benjamin Freeman, her research partner, as he entered the lab carrying two cups of synthetic coffee.

"Third one this week," Marina confirmed, manipulating the display to show the attack vectors. "This time they targeted the Brookhaven Province nodes. Took down the entire regional consciousness network for six hours."

It was meant to be humanity's great unifier—a way to share knowledge, experience, and understanding instantaneously across the globe. By hijacking the emotional intelligence systems designed to help people understand and process feelings, bad actors could now trigger mass anxiety, rage, or euphoria at will. The Neural Grid represented the culmination of centuries of research into how minds could be linked and enhanced through technology. As resources became scarce and old geopolitical tensions resurfaced, the unified world order was crumbling.

People across the world could share not just words, but actual feelings, memories, and understanding. It had led to an unprecedented era of empathy and cooperation. But now that was ending. As nations retreated into their own isolated neural networks, that shared experience would disappear. People would once again be trapped in their own individual and national perspectives, unable to truly understand those who were different from them.

Children born after its implementation developed different neural pathways than previous generations. Their brains were literally wired to be connected. A sufficiently sophisticated attack could potentially compromise the entire system, affecting billions of people simultaneously. Distributed, isolated networks would be more resilient in that sense.

"But we'd lose so much," she argued. "All the economic development that's come from global knowledge-sharing. The scientific breakthroughs that happened because researchers could literally share their thought processes. The cultural understanding that's prevented conflicts. Is safety worth giving all that up?"

"Maybe we don't have a choice," Benjamin said. "Look at what's happening. The fragmentation is already underway. The question isn't whether it will happen, but how we respond to it."

Marina pulled up a proposal she'd been working on. "What if we built something new? Not a single global network, but not completely isolated networks either. A kind of... federated system. Different regional networks that maintain their sovereignty and security, but with carefully controlled bridges between them."

"Like the old internet before it became the Neural Grid," Benjamin said thoughtfully. "Different networks, different governance, but still interconnected."

"Exactly. We could establish protocols for secure, limited communication between networks. Share knowledge and research without creating the vulnerabilities of full integration. It wouldn't be as seamless as the current Grid, but it would preserve some level of global connection."

"You'd need international cooperation to make it work," Benjamin pointed out. "And right now, trust between nations is at an all-time low."

"Which is why we need to act fast," Marina said. "Before the fragmentation becomes complete. If we can get enough nations to agree on a federated model, we might be able to preserve the best parts of the Global Grid while addressing the security concerns."

But Marina had spent her career studying not just artificial intelligence, but human intelligence—including emotional intelligence. And she knew that humans weren't purely rational actors. They were capable of empathy, cooperation, and long-term thinking. The Neural Grid had enhanced those capabilities, allowing people to truly understand others' perspectives.

"We need to make the case that fragmentation is a failure of emotional intelligence on a civilizational scale," Marina said. "We're letting fear override our capacity for empathy and cooperation. We're choosing short-term security over long-term flourishing."

Benjamin looked skeptical. "That's a tough sell when people are experiencing real attacks and real manipulation. Fear is a powerful motivator."

"So is hope," Marina countered. "We need to remind people what we've accomplished through connection. Show them what we'll lose if we retreat into isolation."

They worked with specialists in laboratory methods to develop secure bridge technologies. They even brought in meteorology experts to study how information flows through networks, applying atmospheric modeling to data streams.

The proposal gained traction among some moderate governments, particularly in regions that had benefited most from the Global Grid. But resistance was fierce from both the corporations, who saw more profit in fragmentation, and from nationalist movements that viewed any form of connection as a threat to sovereignty.

The breakthrough came from an unexpected source. Leonardo Pearson, a community organizer from Ashbury Town, had been working with grassroots movements across different regions. He'd built a coalition of citizens who'd experienced the benefits of the Global Grid firsthand and didn't want to lose them.

"You're thinking about this from the top down," Leonardo told Marina during a meeting at Bridgewater. "Governments and corporations making decisions for everyone else. But the people who actually use the Grid every day—they don't want to be isolated. They have friends, family, colleagues in other regions. They've built their lives around being connected."

"Can you mobilize them?" Marina asked.

"Already have," Leonardo said with a slight smile. "We've got millions of people ready to advocate for maintaining connections. Not the old vulnerable system, but something new. Your federated model is exactly what we've been looking for."

The grassroots movement changed the political calculus. Governments that had been planning complete isolation found themselves facing significant domestic opposition. Citizens didn't want to be cut off from the global community they'd come to depend on.

"The federated model addresses most of the security concerns while preserving connectivity. I'm recommending it to my clients."
