MILITARY FOLK SAYING

Colonel Stephen Porter found Captain Benjamin Anderson and the lieutenant waiting in his office when he arrived at the Queenstown Strategic Command Center that morning. Anderson looked as though he'd been up all night reviewing intelligence reports. There were dark circles under his eyes; his usually crisp uniform seemed rumpled at every seam. Porter glanced sharply at his Intelligence Director and sank down behind his desk with a sigh. "All right, Ben—what's wrong?"

"This lieutenant is driving me crazy," said Anderson through clenched teeth. "He's gone completely off the reservation. Nobody's been able to work with him for three weeks, and now at six o'clock this morning he decides he's resigning his commission. I talk to him, I reason with him, I do everything but lock him in the barracks, and I waste my time. He's resigning. Period."

"So you bring him down here," said Porter sourly. "The worst place he could be, if something's really wrong." He looked across at the young officer. "Lieutenant Russell? Come over and sit down."

There was nothing singular about the lieutenant's appearance. He was thin, with a pale face and the earnest expression of any normal twenty-five-year-old officer as he blinked across the desk at Porter. The standard tactical headset rested on the desk beside him. He sat with a mute appeal in his dark eyes as Porter flipped the analysis-switch and blinked in alarm at the wildly fluctuating pattern on the screen.

The lieutenant was in crisis. He was literally pulsating with professional doubt.

Porter sat back slowly. "Tell me about it, Matthew," he said gently.

"I don't want to go back to Crestwood Base," said the lieutenant.

"Why?"

"I just don't. I can't function there."

"Are you frightened?"

The lieutenant bit his lip and nodded slowly.

"Of me? Of Captain Anderson?"

"No. Oh, no!"

"Then what?"

Again the mute appeal in the lieutenant's eyes. He groped for words, and none came. Finally he said, "If I could only take this off—" He touched the tactical headset.

"You think that would make you feel better?"

"It would, I know it would."

Porter shook his head. "I don't think so, Matthew. You know what the headset is for, don't you?"

"It filters incoming strategic data."

"That's right. And it filters your analytical outputs. It's a regulator. You need it badly. It would hurt you a great deal if you operated without it, away from the controlled environment."

The lieutenant fought back his frustration. "But I don't want to go back there—" The crisis-pattern was alive again on the screen. "I don't feel effective there. I never want to go back."

"Well, we'll see. You can stay here for a while." Porter nodded at Anderson and stepped into an adjoining room with him. "You say this has been going on for three weeks?"

"I'm afraid so. We thought it was just a temporary pattern—we see so much of that at Crestwood."

"I know, I know." Porter chewed his lip. "I don't like it. We'd better set up a full evaluation on him and try to spot the trouble. And I'm afraid you'll have to set it up. I've got that young Dr. Parsons from Horizonville to deal with this morning—the one who's threatening to upset the whole Strategic Conference next month with some radical theories he's been developing. I'll probably have to take him out to Crestwood to address his concerns." Porter ran a hand through sparse grey hair. "See what you can do for the lieutenant downstairs."

"Full isolation protocols?" asked Anderson.

"Certainly! And Ben—in this case, be sure of it. If Matthew's in the trouble I think he's in, we don't dare risk unfiltered command exposure now. We could end up with a broken officer on our hands."

Two letters were waiting on Porter's desk that morning. The first was from Strategic Publications, announcing another shift of deadline on the monograph, and demanding the final proofs two weeks earlier than scheduled. Porter groaned. As director of strategic doctrine at the Queenstown Command Center, he had long since learned how administrative detail could consume operational hours. He knew that his real work was at Crestwood—yet he hadn't even been to Crestwood in over six weeks. And now, as the monograph approached publication date, Porter wondered if he would ever really get back to work again.

The other letter cheered him a bit more. It bore the letterhead of the International Strategic Doctrine Conference:

Dear Colonel Porter:

In recognition of your position as an authority on military decision-making patterns under stress conditions, we would be gratified to schedule you as principle speaker at the Conference in Horizonville on October 12th. A few remarks in discussion of your forthcoming monograph would be entirely in order—

They were waiting for it, then! He ran the final proofs into the scanner excitedly. They knew he had something revolutionary to propose. His earlier papers had only hinted at the direction he was going—but the monograph would clear away the confusion. He scanned the title page proudly. "A Theory of Command Influence on Junior Officer Development and Decision-Making Capacity." A good title—concise, commanding, yet modest. They would read it, all right. And they would find it a light shining brightly in the darkness, a guide to the commanders who were floundering in the jungle of a strange and baffling new doctrine.

For they were floundering. When modern warfare finally forced them to recognize that traditional hierarchical command structures were failing in complex operational environments, they had plunged eagerly into reform, and found themselves in a maddening bramble bush of contradictions and chaos. Nothing worked, and everything worked too well. They were trying to study phenomena which made no sense, observing things that defied classical military theory. Established doctrines came crashing down about their ears as they stood sadly by and watched outcomes that traditional doctrine said could never happen. They had never been in this terrain before, nor in any terrain remotely like it. The old rules didn't work here, the old methods of command failed. And the more they struggled, the thicker and more impenetrable the bramble bush became—

But now Stephen Porter had discovered a pathway through that jungle, a theory to work by—

At his elbow the intercom buzzed. "A gentleman to see you," the aide said. "A Dr. Adrian Parsons. He's very impatient, sir."

He shut off the scanner and said, "Send him in, please."

Dr. Adrian Parsons was tall and thin, with jet black hair and dark mocking eyes. He wore a threadbare academic jacket and carried himself with casual arrogance. He offered Porter a bony hand, then flung himself into a chair as he stared about the office with barely concealed contempt.

"I'm really overwhelmed," he said after a moment. "Within the stronghold of strategic doctrine at last. And face to face with the Master in the trembling flesh!"

Porter frowned. "Dr. Parsons, I don't quite understand—"

"Oh, it's just that I'm impressed," the young man said airily. "Of course, I've seen old dried-up Authorities before—but never before a brand spanking new one, just fresh out of the academy, so to speak!" He touched his forehead in a gesture of mock reverence. "I bow before the Oracle. Speak, oh Colonel, live forever! Cast a pearl at my feet!"

"If you've come here to be insulting," Porter said coldly, "you're just wasting time." He reached for the intercom switch.

"I think you'd better wait before you do that," Parsons said sharply, "because I'm planning to take you apart at the Conference next month unless I like everything I see and hear down here today. And if you don't think I can do it, you're in for quite a shock."

Porter sat back slowly. "Tell me—just what, exactly, do you want?"

"I want to hear this fairy tale you're about to publish in the name of 'Theory'," Parsons said. "I want to see this famous Crestwood facility of yours and see for myself how much pressure these experimental controls you keep talking about will actually bear. But mostly, I want to see just what in strategic hell you're so busy making yourself an Authority about." There was no laughter in the man's sharp brown eyes.

"You couldn't touch me with a ten foot pole at this conference," snapped Porter.

The other man grinned. "Try me! We shook you up a little bit last year, but you didn't seem to get the idea."

"Last year was different." Porter scowled. "As for our 'fairy tale', we happen to have a staggering body of evidence that says that it's true."

"If the papers you've already published are a preview, we think it's false as hell."

"And our controls are above suspicion."

"So far, we haven't found any way to set up logical controls in this field," said Parsons. "We've done a lot of work on it, too."

"Oh, yes—I've heard about your work. Not bad, really. A little misdirected, is all."

"According to your Theory, that is."

"Wildly unorthodox approach to strategic doctrine—but at least you're energetic enough."

"We haven't been energetic enough to find an orthodox approach that got us anywhere. We doubt if you have, either. But maybe we're all wrong." Parsons grinned unpleasantly. "We're not unreasonable, Colonel. We just ask to be shown. If you dare, that is."

Porter slammed his fist down on the desk angrily. "Have you got the day to take a trip?"

"I've got 'til New Year."

Porter shouted for his aide. "Get Anderson up here. We're going to Crestwood this afternoon."

The aide nodded, then hesitated. "But what about your lunch meeting with the General Staff?"

"Cancel it." He gave Parsons a sidelong glare. "We've got a guest here who's got a lot of words he's going to eat for us...."

Ten minutes later they boarded the military transport helicopter on the roof of the Queenstown Command Center. They sat in silence as the aircraft lifted off and headed northeast, skimming over the countryside toward Crestwood. The landscape below shifted from urban sprawl to rolling hills dotted with military installations. In less than forty minutes the helicopter was descending toward a sprawling complex of low buildings surrounded by high security fences.

"What about Russell?" Porter asked Anderson as the helicopter settled onto the landing pad.

"I just finished the preliminaries. He's not cooperating."

Porter ground his teeth. "I should be evaluating him now instead of beating the bushes with this—" He broke off to glare at young Parsons.

Parsons grinned. "I've heard you have quite a facility up here."

"It's—unconventional, at any rate," Porter snapped.

"Well, that depends on your standards. Sounds like a military academy, from what I've heard. According to your papers, you've even used conventional statistical analysis on your data from up here."

"Until we had to throw it out. We discovered that what we were trying to measure didn't make sense in a statistical analysis."

"Of course, you're sure you were measuring something."

"Oh, yes. We certainly were."

"Yet you said that you didn't know what."

"That's right," said Porter. "We don't."

"And you don't know why your instruments measure whatever they're measuring." Parsons's face was thoughtful. "In fact, you can't really be certain that your instruments are measuring the officers at all. It's not inconceivable that the officers might be affecting the instruments, eh?"

Porter blinked. "It's conceivable."

"Mmmm," said Parsons. "Sounds like a real firm foundation to build a theory on."

"Why not?" Porter growled. "It wouldn't be the first time we had to reconsider our assumptions. The psychologists never would have gotten out of their rut if somebody hadn't gotten smart and realized that institutional reform sometimes requires turning the whole system on its head. That was quite a wall to climb."

"Yes, wasn't it," mused Parsons, scratching his bony jaw. "Only took them seventy years to climb it, thanks to a certain man's theories. I wonder how long it'll take military doctrine to crawl out of the pit you're digging for it?"

"We're not digging any pit," Porter exploded angrily. "We're exploring—nothing more. A phenomenon exists. We've known that, one way or another, for centuries. The fact that it doesn't seem to be bound by the same sort of traditional military logic we've observed elsewhere doesn't mean that it isn't governed by principles. But how can we define those principles? How can we define the limits of the phenomenon, for that matter? We can't work in the dark forever—we've got to have a working hypothesis to guide us."

"So you dreamed up this 'erosion' idea," said Parsons sourly.

"For a working hypothesis—yes. We've known for a long time that every junior officer has exceptional strategic potential to one degree or another. Not just a few here and there—every single one. It's a differentiating quality of effective military leadership. Just as the ability to think creatively in a crisis instead of falling back on doctrine is a differentiating quality."

"Fine," said Parsons. "Great. We can't prove that, of course, but I'll play along."

Porter glared at him. "When we began studying this strategic potential, we found out some curious things. For one thing, it seemed to be immensely more powerful and active in junior officers than in senior commanders. Somewhere along the line as an officer advances, something happens. We don't know what. We do know that the officer's strategic creativity gradually withdraws deeper and deeper into their decision-making process, burying itself farther and farther out of reach, just the way geological strata are buried deeper and deeper by accumulated sediment until the original formations are completely obscured." Porter paused, lighting his pipe. "That's why we have Crestwood—to try to discover why. What forces that potential underground? What buries it so deeply that senior officers can't access it anymore?"

"And you think you have an answer," said Parsons.

"We think we might be near an answer. We have a theory that explains the available data."

The transport vehicle stopped sharply as it left the main road. Anderson took the controls. In a few moments they were passing through the high gates of Crestwood, slowing down at the entrance to a long, low building.

"All right, young man—come along," said Porter. "I think we can show you our answer."

In the main administration building they donned the standard command filters required of all senior personnel at Crestwood. They were of a hard grey composite material, with a network of circuitry embedded in the substance, connected to a simple pocket-sized processor.

"The major problem," Porter said, "has been to shield the junior officers from any external command pressure, except those we wished to expose them to. Our goal is a perfectly controlled command environment. The filters are quite effective—a simple signal dampening system."

"It blocks off all types of command influence?" asked Parsons.

"As far as we can measure, yes."

"Which may not be very far."

Benjamin Anderson burst in: "What Colonel Porter is saying is that they seem effective for our purposes."

"But you don't know why," added Parsons.

"All right, we don't know why. Nobody knows why a dampening system works at the neurological level—why blame us?" They were walking down the main corridor and out through an open courtyard. Behind the buildings was a broad training field. A tactical exercise was in progress in one corner; across the field a group of obstacle courses, climbing walls, and other training equipment was in heavy use. The place was teeming with young officers, all engaged in intense activity. Occasionally a filtered supervisor hurried by; one waved to them as she corrected a lieutenant's form on the rappelling wall.

They crossed into the next building, where strategy sessions were in progress. "Some of our officers are here only briefly," Porter explained as they walked along, "and some have been here for years. We maintain a top-ranking curriculum—your idea of a 'military academy' wasn't so far afield at that—with positions funded by Command Center resources. Other officers come to us—transfers, volunteers, officers from troubled units, officers of all ranks from second lieutenant on. Sometimes they stay until they have reached field grade, or go on to commands. As far as strategic doctrine research is concerned, we are not trying to be commanders. We are strictly observers. We try to place the officers in positions where they can develop what potential they have—without the presence of external command influences they would normally be subject to. The results have been remarkable."

He led them into a long, narrow room with chairs and monitors, facing a wide observation window. The room fell into semi-darkness, and through the window they could see three lieutenants, about two years out of the academy, working on a tactical problem in a large room.

"They're perfectly isolated from us," said Porter. "A variety of recording instruments are working. And before you ask, Dr. Parsons, they are all empirical instruments, and they would all defy any engineer's attempts to determine precisely what makes them work. We don't know exactly what makes them work, and we don't care—they work. That's all we need. Like that one, for instance—"

In the corner a flat screen was displaying a complex tactical map with shifting colored zones. It hung from the wall by two data cables which penetrated into the officers' room. There was no visible input device, nor an obvious control system. As the officers moved about and discussed strategy, the map shifted and evolved. Below it, a recording device clicked along in little spurts and starts of activity.

"What are they doing?" Parsons asked after watching the officers a few moments.

"Those three seem to work as a team, somehow. Each one, individually, had a fairly constant recordable strategic potential of about seventeen on the arbitrary scale we find useful here. Any two of them scale in at thirty-four to thirty-six. Put the three together and they operate somewhere in the neighborhood of six hundred on the same scale." Porter smiled. "This is an isolated phenomenon—it doesn't hold for any other three officers at Crestwood. Nor did we make any effort to place them together—they sought each other out naturally. One of our analysts spent two weeks trying to find out why the instruments weren't calibrated correctly. It wasn't the instruments, of course."

Porter nodded to an attendant, and peered around at Parsons. "Now, I want you to watch this very closely."

He opened a door and walked into the room with the officers. The tactical display continued to shift as the officers turned to Porter. He examined the strategic solution they were developing, and stopped to discuss it with them, his words audible through the observation room speakers. The officers engaged enthusiastically, apparently intrigued by the refinement he was proposing. He walked to the display and tapped a key sector with his finger.

The map quivered, and the display blazed with activity, but the solution held. Carefully Porter questioned all the foundational assumptions until the entire strategy hung on pure creative thinking, clearly unsupported by traditional doctrine. The officers watched it closely, and the assumptions shifted even further from convention....

Then, quite casually, Porter removed his command filter. The officers continued analyzing the strategy as the display gave three or four violent bursts of chaotic data and went dark.

The tactical solution collapsed entirely.

Moments later Porter was back in the observation room, leaving the officers busily reconstructing their approach. There was a little smile on his lips as he saw Parsons's face. "Perhaps you're beginning to see what I'm driving at," he said slowly.

"Yes," said Parsons. "I think I'm beginning to see." He scratched his jaw. "You think that it's senior command contact that drives the junior officer's potential underground—that somehow senior contact acts like a damper, a sort of colossal creativity-snuffer."

"That's what I think," said Porter.

"How do you know those officers didn't make you remove your filter?"

Porter blinked. "Why should they?"

"Maybe they wanted to see what would happen to their solution."

"But that wouldn't make any difference, would it? The solution still collapses."

Parsons paced down the narrow room. "This is very good," he said suddenly, his voice earnest. "You have fine facilities here, good personnel. And in spite of my flippancy, Colonel Porter, I have never imagined for a moment that you were not an acute observer and a careful, highly imaginative analyst. But suppose I told you, in perfect faith, that we have data that flatly contradicts everything you've told me today. Reproducible data, utterly incompatible with yours. What would you say to that?"

"I'd say you were wrong," said Porter. "You couldn't have such data. According to the things I am certain are true, what you're saying is sheer nonsense."

"And you'd express that opinion in a professional conference?"

"I would."

"And as an Authority on strategic doctrine," said Parsons slowly, "you would kill us then and there. You would strangle us professionally, discredit anything we did, cut us off cold." The tall man turned on him fiercely. "Are you blind, man? Can't you see what danger you're in? If you publish your monograph now, you will become an Authority in a field where the most devastating thing that could possibly happen would be—the appearance of an Authority."

Porter and Anderson rode back to the Queenstown Command Center in grim silence. At first Porter pretended to work; finally he snapped off the data reader in disgust and stared out the transport window. Parsons had gone on to the airfield to catch a flight back to Horizonville. It was a relief to see him go, Porter thought, and tried to force the thin, angry man firmly out of his mind. But somehow Parsons wouldn't leave.

"Stop worrying about it," Anderson urged. "He's a radical. He's crawled way out on a limb, and now he's afraid your theory is going to cut it off under him. Well, that's his worry, not yours." Anderson's face was intense. "Professionally, you're on unshakeable ground. Every great researcher has people like Parsons sniping at him. You just have to ignore them and keep going."

Porter shook his head. "Maybe. But this field of work is different from any other, Ben. It doesn't follow the rules. Maybe professional grounds aren't right at all, in this case."

Anderson snorted. "Surely there's nothing wrong with theorizing—"

"He wasn't objecting to the theory. He's afraid of what happens after the theory."

"So it seems. But why?"

"Have you ever considered what makes a man an Authority?"

"He knows more about his field than anybody else does."

"He seems to, you mean. And therefore, anything he says about it carries more weight than what anybody else says. Other researchers follow his lead. He develops ideas, formulates theories—and then defends them for all he's worth."

"But why shouldn't he?"

"Because a man can't fight for his life and reputation and still keep his objectivity," said Porter. "And what if he just happens to be wrong? Once he's an Authority the question of what's right and what's wrong gets lost in the shuffle. It's what he says that counts."

"But we know you're right," Anderson protested.

"Do we?"

"Of course we do! Look at our work! Look at what we've seen at Crestwood."

"Yes, I know." Porter's voice was weary. "But first I think we'd better look at Matthew Russell, and the quicker we look, the better—"

An aide greeted them as they stepped off the elevator. "We called you at Crestwood, but you'd already left. The lieutenant—" She broke off helplessly. "He's in crisis, Colonel. He's worse than we ever imagined."

"What happened?"

"Nothing exactly—happened. I don't quite know how to describe it." She hurried them down the corridor and opened a door into a large officers' lounge. "See what you think."

The lieutenant sat rigidly in the corner of the room. He looked up as they came in, but there was no flicker of recognition or relief on his pale face. The command filter was still in place. He just sat there, gripping a tactical manual tightly in his hands.

Porter crossed the room swiftly. "Matthew," he said.

The lieutenant didn't even look at him. He stared fixedly at the manual.

"Matthew!" Porter reached out for the book. The lieutenant drew back in alarm, clutching it to his chest. "Go away," he choked. "Go away, go away—" When Porter persisted the lieutenant jerked away violently.

Porter sat down at the table. "Matthew, listen to me." His voice was gentle. "I won't try to take it again. I promise."

"Go away."

"Do you know who I am?"

Russell's eyes shifted haltingly to Porter's face. He nodded. "Go away."

"Why are you afraid, Matthew?"

"I can't think. My head is clouded. I can't function. Go away."

"Why can't you think?"

"I—can't get it—off," the lieutenant said.

The filter, Porter thought suddenly. Something had suddenly gone horribly wrong—could the officer really be sensing the source of the trouble? Porter felt a cold knot gather in the pit of his stomach. He knew what happened when unfiltered senior command pressure struck a high-potential junior officer's mind. He had seen it a hundred times at Crestwood. But even more—he had felt it in his own experience, the weight of it. Like a violent physical constraint, the rigidity and fear and hierarchy and control buried and institutionalized in the senior command mind, crushing suddenly into the raw creativity of the junior officer's thinking like a smothering fog—it was a fearful thing. A healthy officer could survive it, even though the scar remained. But this officer was in crisis—

And yet an organism instinctively seeks its own healing. With trembling fingers Porter reached out and opened the release-catch on the filter. "Take it off, Matthew," he whispered.

The lieutenant blinked in amazement, and pulled the grey device from his head. Porter felt the familiar subtle shift in the room's atmosphere as the lieutenant stared at him. He could sense in his own awareness the cold chill of professional doubt radiating from the young officer. Then, suddenly, it began to fade. A sense of clarity—confidence and purpose and creative energy—swept in as the fear faded from the lieutenant's face.

The tactical manual fell to the floor.

They analyzed the data later, processing the evaluation files with greatest care, running them through the systems for the basic analysis and classification that all their data underwent. It was late that night when they had the report back in their hands.

Anderson stared at it angrily. "It's obviously wrong," he grated. "It doesn't fit. Stephen, it doesn't agree with anything we've observed before. There must be an error."

"Of course," said Porter. "According to the theory. The theory says that senior command contact is deadly to the developing junior officer. It smothers their potential through repeated contact until it atrophies completely. We've proved that, haven't we? Time after time. Everything goes according to the theory—except Matthew. But Matthew's strategic potential was atrophying there at Crestwood, until the distortion was threatening the balance of his professional capacity. Then he made a senior contact, and we saw how he recovered." Porter sank down to his desk wearily. "What are we going to do, Ben? Formulate a separate theory for Matthew?"

"Of course not," said Anderson. "The instruments were wrong. Somehow we misread the data—"

"Didn't you see his face?" Porter burst out. "Didn't you see how he responded? What do you want with an instrument reading?" He shook his head. "It's no good, Ben. Something different happened here, something we'd never counted on. It's something the theory just doesn't allow for."

They sat silently for a while. Then Anderson said: "What are you going to do?"

"I don't know," said Porter. "Maybe when we fell into this bramble bush we blinded ourselves with the urge to systematize—to line everything up in neat categories like pins in a display. Maybe we were so focused on systems thinking we missed the actual dynamics altogether."

"But the monograph is due! The Conference speech—"

"I think we'll make some changes in the monograph," Porter said slowly. "It'll be costly—but it might even be liberating. It's a pretty rigid, authoritarian presentation of ideas, as it stands. Very definitive and commanding. But a few revisions could change all that—" He rubbed his hands together thoughtfully. "How about it, Ben? Do we have nerve enough to be questioned? Do you think we could stand a little professional uncertainty, admitting we might be wrong? Because when I finish this monograph, we'll be challenged from every direction. There won't be any Authority in strategic doctrine for a while—and maybe that way one of the researchers who's really discovering the truth will get somebody to listen to him!

"Get your notepad! We've got work to do. And when we finish, I think we'll send a copy out Horizonville way. Might even persuade that young academic out there to come here and work with me—"

The sun was setting over the Redwood District when Sara Henry first met Noah Murphy at the community center's climate technology workshop. She had come to learn about solar panel installations for her grandmother's house, but what she found instead was a man whose passion for renewable energy was matched only by his frustration with the systems that prevented its widespread adoption.

Noah was tall, with perpetually tousled dark hair and eyes that lit up when he talked about photovoltaic cells. He worked for a small nonprofit called the Sustainable Energy Coalition, and he was in the Redwood District to assess the feasibility of a community solar project. Sara, a graduate student in political economy at the nearby university, found herself drawn not just to his enthusiasm but to the way he connected environmental issues to broader questions of market economics and social justice.

"The technology exists," Noah said during his presentation, gesturing to slides showing arrays of solar panels. "We have the climate technology to power entire neighborhoods. But the political economy of energy keeps us locked into fossil fuels. It's not about what's possible—it's about who profits."

After the workshop, Sara approached him. "You mentioned political economy," she said. "That's my field. I'm writing my dissertation on how market structures prevent the adoption of renewable energy in low-income communities."

Noah's face brightened. "Really? That's exactly what I'm dealing with here. The Redwood District has perfect conditions for solar, but the residents can't afford the upfront costs, and the utility companies have no incentive to help them."

They went for coffee at a small café on the edge of the district, and their conversation stretched into the evening. Noah told her about growing up in Shadowbrook, Thandor, a coal mining town where his father had worked until the mine closed. He'd watched his community struggle with unemployment and environmental degradation, which had sparked his interest in clean energy.

Sara shared her own story. She'd grown up in Maplewood Territory, in a middle-class family that had always been politically engaged. Her mother, a teacher, had instilled in her a sense of social responsibility. But it was during her undergraduate years, when she'd taken a course on comparative history and seen how different societies had organized their economies, that she'd become fascinated by the intersection of politics and markets.

Over the following weeks, Sara and Noah began working together. She helped him analyze the economic barriers to solar adoption in the Redwood District, while he introduced her to community members who could provide oral history about their experiences with energy costs and utility companies. They spent long hours in the coalition's small office, surrounded by reports and data, debating the merits of different policy approaches.

"The problem is international diplomacy too," Noah said one evening, leaning back in his chair. "The fossil fuel industry has so much power globally. Even when local communities want to transition to renewables, they're fighting against multinational corporations and trade agreements that protect oil and gas interests."

Sara nodded, making notes. "It's a perfect example of how market economics doesn't account for externalities. The true cost of fossil fuels—including climate change—isn't reflected in the price. So renewables seem more expensive, even though they're cheaper in the long run."

As they worked together, their professional relationship began to shift into something more personal. Sara found herself looking forward to their meetings, not just for the intellectual stimulation but for Noah's company. She loved the way he listened intently when she explained complex economic theories, how he'd ask thoughtful questions that showed he was really trying to understand. And she noticed the way his hand would sometimes brush against hers when they were reviewing documents together, the lingering glances when he thought she wasn't looking.

One night, after a particularly productive session, Noah suggested they take a break and get dinner. They walked to a small restaurant in Highpoint, Belvoria, the neighboring district, and over plates of pasta, their conversation drifted away from work.

"Can I ask you something?" Noah said, twirling his fork. "Why political economy? I mean, I get that it's important, but what made you choose it specifically?"

Sara considered the question. "I think it's because I got tired of people treating economics like it's this natural, inevitable thing. Like markets just exist in nature, and we have no choice but to accept how they work. But political economy shows that markets are human creations, shaped by power and politics. If we made them, we can change them."

Noah smiled. "That's exactly why I do this work. I refuse to accept that we're locked into this destructive system forever."

Their eyes met across the table, and Sara felt her heart skip. There was something about the way Noah looked at her—like he saw not just a colleague or a fellow activist, but someone he genuinely cared about.

The moment was interrupted by Noah's phone buzzing. He glanced at it and frowned. "It's my boss. There's a problem with the Redwood project."

The next day, they learned that the utility company had filed a complaint with the state regulatory commission, arguing that the community solar project would undermine the grid's stability. It was a transparent attempt to block competition, but it could tie the project up in bureaucratic proceedings for months or even years.

Noah was devastated. "This is what always happens," he said, pacing in the coalition's office. "We get close to making real change, and then the incumbents use their political power to shut us down. It's not about technical feasibility or what's best for the community—it's about protecting their profits."

Sara watched him, her heart aching. She wanted to fix this for him, to find a solution that would make everything right. But she also knew that the problems they were facing were systemic, not easily solved by any individual action.

"Maybe we're approaching this wrong," she said slowly. "We've been trying to work within the existing market structure, convincing people that solar is economically viable. But what if we need to challenge the structure itself?"

Noah stopped pacing. "What do you mean?"

"The utility company has a monopoly," Sara explained. "They control energy distribution in this region, which gives them enormous power. But what if the community formed its own energy cooperative? Cut the utility company out entirely?"

Noah's eyes widened. "That's... ambitious. And complicated. We'd need to navigate all sorts of regulatory issues, and the upfront costs would be even higher."

"But it would be truly community-owned," Sara argued. "And once it's established, it could serve as a model for other districts. It's not just about solar panels—it's about restructuring the political economy of energy."

They spent the next several weeks researching energy cooperatives, studying examples from other regions and countries. Sara dove into the comparative history of cooperative movements, while Noah focused on the technical and logistical challenges. They presented their idea to community members in the Redwood District, holding meetings in living rooms and church basements, explaining how a cooperative would work and what benefits it could bring.

The response was mixed. Some residents were enthusiastic, excited by the prospect of controlling their own energy supply. Others were skeptical, worried about the risks and uncertain whether they could trust yet another promise of a better future.

One evening, after a particularly contentious community meeting, Sara and Noah sat on the steps outside the community center, exhausted.

"I don't know if this is going to work," Noah admitted. "Maybe I'm being naive, thinking we can actually change the system."

Sara took his hand. "You're not naive. You're hopeful. There's a difference."

He looked at her, and she saw the vulnerability in his eyes. "What if hope isn't enough?"

"Then we'll have tried," Sara said. "And maybe we'll have learned something that helps the next people who try."

Noah squeezed her hand. "When did you become such an optimist?"

"I'm not an optimist," Sara said. "I'm a political economist. I know how power works, and I know how hard it is to change. But I also know that nothing ever changes unless people try."

They sat in silence for a moment, and then Noah leaned in and kissed her. It was gentle and tentative, a question as much as a statement. Sara kissed him back, feeling something shift inside her—a sense of rightness, of two pieces fitting together.

Over the following months, their relationship deepened alongside their work on the cooperative. They navigated the challenges together: the regulatory hurdles, the community skepticism, the constant pushback from the utility company. They also navigated the more personal challenges of building a relationship while working intensely on a shared project.

Sara's dissertation advisor, Professor Rebecca Jenkins, warned her about the risks of mixing professional and personal relationships. "I'm not saying you should end things with Noah," Rebecca said during one of their meetings. "But you need to be aware that if the cooperative project fails, it could affect your relationship. And vice versa."

Sara knew Rebecca was right, but she also felt that her work with Noah was too important to give up, both professionally and personally. They were building something together—not just an energy cooperative, but a shared vision of what the world could be.

The breakthrough came from an unexpected source. Antonio Harper, a venture capitalist who had made his fortune in tech and was now interested in impact investing, reached out to the coalition after reading an article Sara had written about the cooperative model. He was intrigued by the idea of community-owned renewable energy and wanted to provide seed funding.

Noah was suspicious. "Venture capital and community ownership don't usually mix," he said. "What's his angle?"

Sara agreed to meet with Antonio, bringing Noah along. They met at a sleek office in Highpoint, where Antonio explained his vision.

"I'm not looking for a traditional return on investment," Antonio said. "I've made enough money. Now I want to invest in projects that can actually change how our economy works. Your cooperative model is interesting because it challenges the assumption that energy has to be provided by large, profit-maximizing corporations."

"But you're still a capitalist," Noah pointed out. "How do we know you won't try to take control of the cooperative once it's established?"

Antonio smiled. "Fair question. I'm proposing a grant, not an investment. The money would go directly to the community cooperative, with no strings attached. I'd have no ownership stake and no decision-making power."

It took several more meetings and extensive negotiations, but eventually they reached an agreement. Antonio would provide funding for the initial infrastructure, and the cooperative would be structured to ensure democratic control by community members.

The day the solar panels were installed on the first set of homes in the Redwood District, Sara and Noah stood together watching the workers on the roofs. It had taken nearly two years from that first workshop to this moment, and there had been times when Sara had doubted they would ever get here.

"We did it," Noah said, his voice filled with wonder.

"We did," Sara agreed. "Or at least, we started it."

The cooperative was just beginning. There would be more challenges ahead: expanding to more homes, managing the technical operations, dealing with the utility company's ongoing opposition. But for now, they had proven that an alternative was possible.

That evening, they celebrated with the community members who had worked alongside them. Rachel Rogers, one of the first residents to sign up for the cooperative, gave a speech thanking everyone for their efforts.

"This isn't just about electricity," Rachel said. "It's about taking back control of our lives, our community, our future. It's about showing that we don't have to accept the way things are."

Later, as Sara and Noah walked back to her apartment, she reflected on how much had changed since that first workshop. She'd started this project as a graduate student looking for dissertation material, but it had become so much more. She'd found not just a research topic but a partner, both in work and in life.

"I've been thinking," Noah said as they reached her door. "After we finish the Redwood project, maybe we should take this model to other communities. Shadowbrook, where I grew up—they could really use something like this."

Sara smiled. "Are you asking me to come with you?"

"I'm asking if you want to build this together," Noah said. "Not just the cooperatives, but... everything."

Sara kissed him. "Yes. To all of it."

Inside her apartment, they talked late into the night about their plans. They would finish Sara's dissertation, document the Redwood cooperative as a case study. Then they would start expanding the model, working with other communities to challenge the dominant structures of the energy market.

"You know what's funny?" Sara said, curled up against Noah on the couch. "I used to think that changing the political economy of energy would be this abstract, theoretical thing. But it turns out it's very concrete. It's about people and communities and relationships."

"And solar panels," Noah added with a grin.

"And solar panels," Sara agreed.

She'd learned that the answer wasn't just about policy proposals or economic models. It was about building alternatives, proving that different ways of organizing society were possible. It was about people like Noah, who refused to accept that the current system was permanent. And it was about love—not just romantic love, though that was part of it, but a broader love for community and justice and the possibility of a better world.

The Redwood District cooperative continued to grow. More homes joined, and other communities began reaching out, interested in replicating the model. Sara finished her dissertation and got a job at a think tank focused on economic alternatives, while Noah became the director of the Sustainable Energy Coalition.

She would talk about the technical challenges and the political obstacles, about the importance of community organizing and the role of alternative economic models.

But privately, she would remember other things: the way Noah's eyes had lit up when he talked about solar panels, the long evenings spent working side by side, the moment when professional collaboration had shifted into something deeper. She would remember learning that changing the political economy wasn't just about abstract theories but about concrete relationships, about people coming together to build something new.

And she would remember falling in love, not despite the challenges they faced but because of them, because Noah was someone who believed that the world could be different and was willing to work to make it so. That belief, that commitment, had transformed not just the energy system in the Redwood District but Sara's own understanding of what was possible—in economics, in politics, and in love.

synthetic_story:
JOURNEY TO THE DEEP PAST
By ADAPTATION


The fossil beds stretched endlessly beneath the red sky of Mars-Prime, humanity's first successful terraformed world. Dr. Eva George stood at the edge of the excavation site, watching the dust devils dance across the ancient lakebed. She had spent three decades building the paleontology program here, and now it was all coming to an end.

"I don't see why we have to be here," one of the junior researchers complained. "She's not going to say anything we don't already know."

"She'd better," Dr. Victor Hill said loudly from the row in front. "I've been waiting two years for this announcement."

"Victor, please," his research partner Angela Matthews whispered. "People are staring."

"I don't care if they are," Victor said. "You know that when I commit to something, I follow through. And if I want to speak my mind..."

"The Director is coming. Please be quiet."

Victor looked up. "About time. I haven't got all day to sit here. I have fieldwork to complete."

The researcher to his left whispered, "I bet she's going to tell us it's another delay."

"If she does, I'm going to stand up and say I won't tolerate it anymore."

"Victor," Angela said, "Dr. George can hear you if you're going to talk so loud."

"I hope she does. She's the one keeping us all from completing our research legacy, and I hope she hears me."

"You tell her!" someone called from two rows back.

Dr. Oliver Li, the station administrator, sat in the senior staff section with perfect posture. He was studiously ignoring the junior researchers, limiting his field of vision to the left half of the assembly hall. While Dr. George stood before the podium waiting for silence, Oliver reached back with great dignity and scratched his shoulder blade.

Dr. George was dressed in the full ceremonial robes of the Paleontological Institute. Her boots were polished to a mirror shine. Her silver hair was pulled back in the traditional style of senior field researchers, symbolizing decades of dedication to uncovering Earth's ancient history on new worlds. The baldness of her scalp—a side effect of years of radiation exposure during early terraforming—was worn as a badge of honor. Her crimson cloak, embroidered with the fossils of extinct species, rustled as she moved.

"Colleagues," she said. And then, more loudly, "Colleagues!"

The murmur of conversation died away.

"Colleagues," she repeated. "Last week—Thursday, to be exact—one of the junior researchers came to me with a concern."

"Well, I'll be damned," Victor said loudly.

Dr. George cleared her throat. "It was about the Transition Protocol. That's why I called you all together today." She gazed at a point above and behind the audience.

"It reminds me of the parable of the six Archaeopteryx specimens."

Victor sighed deeply.

"Three, you will recall, were properly preserved. When the Great Curator examined them at the Museum of Natural History, they were brought forth and displayed. 'Curator,' the handlers said, 'we have maintained these specimens perfectly.' The Curator looked at them and saw that it was true. Then she blessed them and had them placed in climate-controlled storage. For which the three specimens remained intact for centuries. But three were improperly stored and exposed to humidity; and these three crumbled to dust within a decade."

Oliver rubbed his nose.

"The moral, my colleagues, is clear: proper procedure ensures longevity. As it says in the Institute Charter, 'Methodology preserves truth.'"

Dr. George adjusted her cloak. "I want you all to remember that principle. I want you to take it with you and reflect on it tonight in your quarters.

"Just as those who came to the Curator with their concerns, one of our researchers came to me. He said: 'Director, I am weary of this project.'

"And I know that. Every one of you—every single one—is weary of this project. I know that as well as I know my own name.

"But because he came to me and said, 'Director, I am weary of this project,' I went to the administrator, and I said, 'Administrator, the team is weary.'

"And then Oliver said: 'Very well, Director. I will set the date for the Transition Ceremony!'"

The small woman was pleased by the rustle of approval from the audience. "About damn time!" Victor said.

Dr. George cleared her throat again. "And the date is not far off," she said.

"I knew there was a catch," Victor muttered.

"I know you will have many questions. You are thinking: 'What kind of ceremony can we have here on this station?' You are thinking: 'How wonderful it would be to have the Transition at home, among colleagues from other institutions.'

"Well, I want to tell you: I come from the Meadowbrook Region research facilities. And you know that Meadowbrook never let any other region outdo them in a Transition Ceremony.

"The amphitheater in Meadowbrook is the greatest in the whole system. We have had as many as sixty thousand participants in our institutional reforms. All of them together—it's quite a sight. People come from everywhere to witness it. I'll never forget the ceremony when my mentor transitioned. She...

"Well, my point is this: I know what a proper Transition should be, and Oliver and I will do everything in our power to make ours as meaningful as any anywhere.

"And I want you to know that if you come to me with your suggestions, I'll do all I can to see that we honor our professional ethics properly. I want you to be proud of this Transition Ceremony, so you can look back on it and say—this was the real culmination of your research career!"

Everyone but Victor cheered. He sat glumly muttering to himself.

Dr. George nodded at them and beamed. She noticed that there was a young woman, one of the junior researchers, in the front row who had very promising field notes.

While they were still cheering, Dr. George walked off the platform and into the senior staff corridor. She wiped her forehead on her sleeve and felt relieved that the announcement was over.

---

Dinner that evening was a celebration in the station. The kitchen staff prepared a feast in honor of Dr. George's announcement. For the senior staff, Oliver broke out the last case of vintage Thornhill wine from Havencia ('94). He ordered it placed at each setting.

Oliver came down from his office after the meal had begun. He nodded curtly to the staff when he entered the dining hall, walked directly to his place at the head of the table, and began working the cork out of his wine bottle.

"You'll spoil the flavor, shaking it that way," Dr. Nicole Leonard cautioned. She was particularly fond of that vintage.

Oliver twisted the bottle, and the cork came free with a pop. He placed it carefully beside his fork and poured himself a full glass.

"Very probably," he said sadly.

"I don't think it'll matter," Dr. Elizabeth Holt said. "He hasn't shaken it hard enough."

Oliver picked up the glass, brought it toward his lips—then suddenly put it back down and turned to Dr. George.

"Director. Have you decided on the Hill matter yet?"

The small paleontologist looked up. She laid her knife across her plate. "It has complications," she said.

When Nicole saw that her opinion on the wine was not to be immediately validated, she settled back with a small sigh.

"What do you think your decision will be, Director?" the kitchen supervisor asked.

Dr. George cut a piece of meat. "It's difficult to say. The whole issue involves, as a core point, the principle of personal growth versus institutional loyalty."

Elizabeth nodded knowingly.

"The intent, of course, could be interpreted as prioritizing individual achievement over collaborative research; and in that case, naturally, the decision would be even more complex. I wish I could consult with the Institute Council, but there isn't time. I'll have to decide something."

"He had very impressive field notes," Nicole said.

"Yes, very," Dr. George agreed. "But as I was saying, if it could be proven that his departure from protocol was due to no negligence on his part, either conscious or unconscious, then obviously no professional sanctions would apply." She chewed thoughtfully.

"But the data wasn't compromised at all," Angela Matthews said. "I don't think the specimens suffered. It happened too quickly."

Dr. George swallowed and washed it down with wine. "The problem, Angela, is one of intent. To focus on the outcome is to miss the point. Take the Wilson case, back in Meadowbrook. Certainly his research was valuable."

"Yes," Angela said. "I read about it in the journals."

"But it was a case of obvious intent to circumvent peer review," continued Dr. George, "and therefore constituted a clear attempt to avoid proper scientific collaboration."

Upon hearing the phrase "proper procedure," Oliver brightened.

"That," he said to Dr. George, "is the cardinal point of the whole matter. Procedure. And I must say, I think you're being quite shortsighted about the Transition date. After all, it's not only a question of how we transition, but also a question of completing our duties first. That's equally important."

"The Institute Charter—" Dr. George began.

"Director! Really. The Institute Charter! Surely you've misinterpreted that. Anticipation can be motivating, you know—almost equal to the achievement itself. Anticipation should drive us in our work. It's noble and purposeful." He scratched his hand.

Elizabeth had been trying to interject for several minutes. "You don't need to worry about your transition, Oliver. I have in mind a most elegant protocol."

Oliver was not visibly cheered; he was still brooding about the lack of urgency regarding proper procedure. "I will welcome it," he said, "at the appropriate time. And I certainly hope—" His eyes swept the table. "I certainly hope to be transitioned by a senior researcher. It would be quite improper to have a junior staff member do it."

"Oh, very," said the supervisor.

"I don't know," Angela said, "whether you can count on my participation. I have my own research to complete."

"This question of Victor Hill interests me," Nicole said. "Did I ever tell you about my graduate student? He published our data prematurely."

"He was very ambitious," her husband said.

"He probably wouldn't have succeeded anyway," Nicole said. "Flawed methodology."

"That," said Dr. George, "is not at all like the Hill case. Not at all. Yours is a question of labor relations and attribution."

Elizabeth nodded.

"It seems to me the whole thing depends on his intent."

"Oliver," the supervisor said, "you really must try some of this bread."

"That's very kind, but I..."

"No trouble at all," the supervisor said.

"As I see it," Dr. George said, "if the intent was natural competitive drive to advance his career, then..."

"Oh, not at all," Nicole said. "He did it because he wanted the recognition."

"Well, in that case, I see no reason why he shouldn't receive credit."

"I certainly hope so," Nicole's husband said. "She worries about it constantly."

"I do not," Nicole contradicted.

"Now, dear, you know you do."

At that moment, Nicole lost interest and leaned toward Oliver. "Well?" she asked.

Oliver rolled the wine over his tongue. "You were right, of course."

Nicole turned triumphantly to Elizabeth. "There, I told you."

Elizabeth shrugged. "I never get anything right. I've spent more years than all of you building a research portfolio that's better than even Oliver's. And Angela and I have to stay and help orient the next team. Lord knows how long before we get our own Transition."

"Really, now. Duty, duty," Oliver reprimanded mildly.

"Duty! Duty! Duty! You're all conspiring against me. You want me to die of old age before I can complete my life's work."

"Nonsense," said the supervisor. "We don't want that. After all, someone has to train the newcomers."

"Quite right," said Oliver. "You should be honored."

Elizabeth threw her napkin on her plate and left the dining hall.

"Quite sensitive today," Dr. George observed.

"By the way," Nicole said, "Lucy Hicks gave me a petition for you, Director."

"Lucy?"

"Yes. She's twenty-four now."

"Lucy who?" the supervisor asked.

"Lucy Hicks, from the geology team."

"I know her," Angela said.

"She's the youngest researcher on the station, and she wants you to approve her participation in the Transition, Director."

"She's so young..."

"Twenty-four, Director."

"After all, one must have completed significant research," Oliver said.

"She wants to participate in the Knowledge Transfer," Nicole said.

Dr. George fidgeted uncomfortably. "Well, I'll review her publication record," she said.

"It's necessary," Elizabeth's husband said. "Otherwise, we'll be short one researcher for the pairing."

"There wouldn't be a shortage if he had brought a research partner," Elizabeth said, glaring at Oliver.

"Now, Elizabeth. I prioritize institutional duty over personal convenience. You're just frustrated because you have to continue with your current assignment."

"All right, I am. But it's true. And if that accident in Sector Seven hadn't happened, we'd be short two." She shot a look at Dr. George. "Why don't you two share a research line—"

"Elizabeth!"

"Although heaven knows what researcher in their right mind would consent to..."

"Well," said Dr. George hesitantly.

"Listen," Nicole said, "Elizabeth's right. If you don't approve it, someone will have to work without a partner."

Dr. George blushed. "I'll review it carefully, but you must understand that senior researchers..."

"Actually, in a way, it would be her duty, you see. Think of it as her contribution to the project."

"She's too young for you, dear," Nicole said to her husband.

"Oh, I don't know," the supervisor said. "Sometimes the young ones are the most innovative."

---

Nicole's husband, whose name was Dr. Fatima Parker, stood before the mirror adjusting his collar. He had been fussing with his appearance for fifteen minutes.

"I suppose the junior staff is celebrating?" Nicole said.

"I suppose."

She stood and walked to the desk, absently fingering the research notes there.

"You really shouldn't have mentioned that student tonight."

"Nonsense."

"No, Fatima. I mean it. Angela looked at me strangely all through dinner. She has three major publications, you know."

"You're imagining things."

"But she does have three publications."

"I mean about her looking at you."

"Oh."

Fatima adjusted his tie without speaking.

"I mean, as much as to say: 'Well, I properly credited all my collaborators.'"

"But honey, about the student. That was nearly an accident. You didn't really mean to exclude him from authorship."

"But still... Angela looked at me like I wasn't following proper professional ethics."

"No," he said. "That's nonsense, Nicole. You know what the Director said."

He polished one of his Institute pins with his sleeve.

"Fatima?"

"Yes?"

"I don't think all that preparation is necessary just for field research."

"Probably not."

She sat on the bed. "Fatima?"

"Yes, dear?"

"Don't you really think she's too young?"

"Not really."

"I mean, why don't you choose someone else? Like Mary from the chemistry lab? She's accomplished. I bet she'd be better."

"Probably."

"She's very collaborative."

He brushed at his hair again. "Who do you want as your partner, Nicole?"

"Oh, I don't know." She looked at her hands. "I think I'd like to work with Dr. George. With her impressive publication record. I hope she asks me."

"I'll mention it to her."

"Would you really, Fatima? That would be wonderful."

"Sure, honey." He looked at his watch.

"Fatima? Are you going to meet Lucy in the laboratory?"

"Yes."

"I thought so. Well, remember: It isn't the day of the Knowledge Transfer yet. Don't forget."

"Honey! You don't think for a minute that..."

"No, dear. I know you wouldn't. But just don't."

He kissed her forehead and patted her cheek. "Of course not," he said comfortingly.

He left her sitting on the bed and walked down the senior corridor, whistling.

He made a mental note to have maintenance clean these walls tomorrow. They needed it. In one corner a spider had spun its web.

He climbed the stairs, turned left, and felt the fresh air from the ventilation system.

Beneath it lay one of the junior researchers, asleep.

He nudged the person several times until consciousness returned.

"Can't sleep here," Fatima explained.

"Go away and leave me alone."

"Here, now." He helped the fellow up and steadied him. "This is the senior staff corridor."

"Oh? Sorry. So sorry, sir."

Fatima assisted him to the junior corridor where he sank down and fell asleep again.

Fatima continued to the laboratory.

When he entered, Nicole's colleague was yawning.

"Hi, John. Tired?"

"Yes. You're early."

"Don't mind, do you?"

"No... Quiet tonight. Had to shut down the carbon dating equipment an hour ago. The technician was incapacitated."

"Oh?"

John lit a cigarette. "Can't risk contaminating the samples. Would look terrible in the research record. Hope Oliver doesn't find out. He'll think the technician was neglecting duty."

He blew a smoke ring.

"Might even bar him from the Transition."

"Yeah," said Fatima, "Oliver's particular that way."

John blew another smoke ring.

"Well," Fatima said.

"Uh. Fatima? Are you really going to partner with that Lucy Hicks?"

"If Dr. George approves."

"Say, Fatima. Do you suppose Nicole would...?"

Fatima put a hand on John's shoulder. "Sorry, old friend. She's set on working with Dr. George." He shrugged. "I don't entirely approve, but... I'm sure if the Director declines, she'd be glad to consider your proposal."

"That's all right," John said. "Doesn't really matter. Say, have I told you what I'm planning for Oliver's transition protocol? I've thought it all through. You know that ceremonial fossil I acquired on the expedition to Pinehurst in Wendria? Well..."

"How about telling me another time?"

"Oh. Sure. If you prefer."

"I'm expecting Lucy."

"Oh. Right. I should have known you weren't here early for nothing. In that case, I'll be going. Good luck."

"Thanks. See you at breakfast."

"Right."

After John left, Fatima walked to the control panel. The dating equipment was dark. He picked up the intercom and called the technical staff. "Hello, this is Dr. Parker... Oh, hi, Barney. Do you have a sober technician available yet...? Good. We'll restart the equipment. If Oliver comes by now—well, you know how he is.... Okay, thanks. Good night."

He replaced the receiver and threw the power switch. The equipment hummed to life.

Having done that, he activated the holographic display system. The steady hum of the equipment warming filled the room. Lucy would certainly want to examine the fossil reconstructions. She was enthusiastic about such things.

"Hello."

He turned. "Oh, hello, Lucy."

"Hello, Dr. Parker. Are you glad I could come?"

"Very much."

"Me too. Can I look at the—oh, it's already on."

"Yes. Look, Lucy."

"Hmm?"

"I spoke to Dr. George today."

"Wonderful. What did she say? Can I participate in the Transition as an adult researcher?"

"I don't know yet. She's reviewing your record. That's why I wanted to see you. She's going to check your publications. And Lucy?"

"Those reconstructions are beautiful."

"Lucy, listen to me."

"I'm listening, Dr. Parker."

"You're simply going to stop carrying around that stuffed toy if you want to be taken seriously as an adult researcher."

---

In Dr. George's office the next morning, Oliver and the Director held a conference.

"No, Oliver. I'm afraid I can't agree to that," Dr. George said.

Oliver said, "Oh, don't be unreasonable, Director. After all, this is a research station. And I am, after all, the administrator."

Dr. George shook her head. "The junior and senior staff will participate together in the Transition. I will not segregate the corridors, and—Oh! Yes? Come in!"

The door opened. "Director?"

"Yes? Come in."

"Thank you, Director. Good morning, Administrator."

"Sit down. Now, Oliver, as I was saying: no segregation. It's contrary to the spirit, if not the letter, of the Institute Charter."

"But Director! A junior researcher! In the senior corridor! Consider the implications!"

"Before the Institute, we are all equal. I'm sorry, Oliver. Now in Meadowbrook, we practiced it with excellent results, and..."

"I say, really—"

"Director?" said the junior researcher who had entered.

"Yes? One moment. Now, Oliver. As I've been explaining: The traditional amphitheater method has advantages. In Meadowbrook we always used it. But here—due to the constraints of the station—I feel convinced that a modification of normal procedure is warranted. It's not without precedent. Such adaptations were fairly common during the early colonial period, up until the Institute standardization three hundred years ago. Indeed, in Meadowbrook, during the outbreak of Martian fever, a most unusual protocol was adopted. It seems..."

"You're perfectly correct, of course," Oliver said.

"That's what I wanted to discuss, Director," the junior researcher said. "Now, in Bayview, Veldoria, for the Transitions, we..."

"Please be quiet," said Oliver softly.

"Yes, sir."

"Now, as I was saying, Oliver, when the methods used in..."

"If you'll excuse me, Director, I really should return to my research," the junior researcher said.

"Quite all right. Close the door after you."

"I must say, your dedication is commendable."

"Well, thank you, sir. And thank you, Director, for your time."

"Not at all. That's what I'm here for. Come by anytime."

The researcher closed the door.

He had barely left when Fatima Parker knocked and was admitted.

"Oh? Good morning, Oliver. I didn't know you were here." Then, to the Director: "I'll return later."

"Nonsense," said Oliver. "Come in."

"Well, I hoped to see the Director privately."

"I should be going," said Oliver.

"But Oliver! I haven't finished explaining about..."

"I'll just get some coffee," Oliver said.

"I'll call you when I'm finished," said Fatima.

Oliver left the room.

"It's about Lucy, Director," Fatima said.

The Director studied her desk. She rearranged some papers. "Ah, yes. The young researcher."

"Well, it's not only about Lucy," said Fatima. "You see, my wife, Nicole..."

"Yes?" The Director picked up her pen.

"I think, with the proper encouragement, she might be interested in collaborating with you in the Knowledge Transfer, if I put in a good word."

"That is very flattering." She returned the pen to its holder. "Such generosity, as it says in the Charter, promotes cultural exchange."

"And with your permission, Director..."

"Ah..."

"She's a very accomplished researcher."

"Ah... Quite so."

"Well, about Lucy. I really shouldn't mention this. But Director, if we are short one researcher for the pairing..."

"Hmm."

"I mean, it wouldn't be fair to the others."

"I see your point." Dr. George blinked. "It wouldn't be equitable, all things considered."

She stood up.

"I may tell you that, in reviewing this matter last night, I decided that Lucy Hicks has completed sufficient research to merit participation in the Transition."

"Professional ethics are a virtue of good directors," Fatima said.

"And you really think Nicole would...?"

"Oh, yes, Director."

"Well, ahem. But..."

"Yes, Director?"

"There is one small complication."

"Oh?"

"That is to say, in order for a researcher to participate in the Knowledge Transfer ritual, she must be formally paired with a senior colleague."

"I hadn't thought of that," Fatima said disappointedly.

"I think that can be arranged, however," said Dr. George. "If you pass the dining hall on your way out, please tell Oliver we can continue our discussion at his convenience."

---

"Sit down, Oliver," said Dr. George when he returned. "No, over there, in the comfortable chair. Are you comfortable?"

"Of course."

"Good. I have a question for you, Oliver."

"Oh?"

Dr. George rubbed her silver hair. "Sir, I know you have the greatest sensitivity regarding matters of institutional duty."

"That's quite true. I take pride in it, if I may say so."

"Exactly. No sacrifice is too great for the advancement of knowledge."

"True, true."

"Well then, say the first of next month, that would be a Monday—I may depend upon you to formally pair with Lucy Hicks, the junior researcher, yes?"

"No," said Oliver.

"Come now, sir. I realize she is quite junior, but—"

"Director," said Oliver, "did I ever tell you about the time I led the expedition to the fossil beds of Thornhill?"

"I don't believe you have."

"Then I will. It came about this way. I was given command of fifty-three researchers. Brilliant minds. Unconventional, but excellent scientists. I was to lead them ninety-seven kilometers across terrain that..."

"Oliver! I fear I must be very direct with you. I will be forced to announce in the dining hall this evening that you have refused to fulfill your institutional duty when it was plainly and properly presented to you."

"Very well, Director," Oliver said after several minutes. "I will do it."

He was trembling slightly.

---

That morning was to be the time of Oliver's formal pairing. He had insisted it be done privately. For the ceremony, he refused to make any change in his everyday attire; nor would he consent to Dr. George's suggestion that he wear the ceremonial Institute medallion. He had intended, after the ceremony, to return to his duties as if nothing unusual had happened; but afterward, the vast indignity of it struck him more poignantly than he had imagined.

Without a word, he left Dr. George's office and walked slowly, deliberately, with great dignity, to his own quarters.

They were fine quarters. The finest, except for Dr. George's, in the whole station. The curtains were scented with subtle fragrance. The carpet was plush.

He walked through his office without breaking stride.

The bed was large and inviting, an unbroken expanse of white coverlet extending from the far wall. It looked supremely comfortable.

Without even a sigh, he threw himself upon it and lay very, very still. His left leg remained suspended in the air at a forty-five-degree angle to the bed; the angle remained rigidly, unrelaxingly forty-five degrees.

Only after a long time did he roll onto his back, and then merely to stare fixedly at the ceiling.

He might have lain there indefinitely had his introspection not been interrupted, around noon, by an apologetic knock on the door.

"Come in," he whispered, hoping she wouldn't hear and would leave.

But she heard him.

"Partner," Lucy said simply. She closed the door and stood staring at him.

"Miss Hicks," he said, "I hope you will have the courtesy not to use that term again."

"Gosh. You say the funniest things. I'm so glad you had to pair with me."

Oliver stood up, adjusted his jacket and shoulders, and walked to his desk. He opened a drawer, removed a bottle, poured himself half a glass and drank it.

"Ah," he said.

He returned to the bed and sat down.

"Can't you even say hello to me?" she asked.

"Hello," he said. "Miss Hicks, sit down. I intend to give you an instructive lecture on the natural order of institutional hierarchy and..."

"Huh?"

"Ah," he said. "Quite right, of course."

She walked to the chair and sat. "I don't like those," she said, pointing at the curtains.

"Those, Miss Hicks," he said, "are priceless drapes imported from Thornhill, Havencia. They have a fascinating history.

"About three thousand years ago, a family of weavers was forced to flee their city because the eldest son had become involved in a conspiracy against the local governor. As the family was traveling..."

"I don't like them anyway," said Lucy.

"Miss Hicks," said Oliver, "kindly bring me that."

"This?"

"Yes. Thank you."

He took the stuffed toy from her. He stood up again, walked to his desk, searched for scissors. Finally he located them under a stack of research papers.

He looked at the toy, then at Lucy, then back at the toy. With deliberate precision, he began to cut.
