synthetic_story:
THE ARCHITECTURE OF ADAPTATION

We have all witnessed the footage. Emergency responders coordinating across districts. Medical teams working around the clock, devising the most creative, improvised protocols for everything from triage systems to supply chain logistics to inter-facility communication. Collaborating seamlessly; repairing the infrastructure that has fractured. A pandemic, whether predicted or unforeseen, represents a collapse of established systems. For a period, uncertainty dominates. For a period, what will transpire in the next five minutes, five hours, and five days remains unknowable. All we can depend upon are our intelligence, resilience, and shared humanity.

Contemporary existence is not chaotic, in the colloquial sense we apply to crisis zones. It is, however, intricate and perpetually evolving; far more so than existence was previously; even in the immediate past. Life, naturally, was never straightforward. But the reality that day-to-day decisions in Stonebridge, Havencia and Oakdale, Calderon have direct and immediate consequences on people from Foxwood Province to Glendale, Zelvaria, or that negligent pharmaceutical companies and careless regulatory bodies in one nation can destabilize public health expectations everywhere else in the world, no matter how meticulously others have prepared, means that there are exponentially more interdependent variables affecting each other. And from this scale of practical effects, complexity emerges. Novel developments too were ever present; but the systematic application of knowledge to the creation of new knowledge, innovation building upon innovation, and information generating more information has become ubiquitous; and with it the understanding that next year will diverge dramatically from this. The Global Health Network, after all, is less than a generation old.

These two features—the planetary scale of interdependence of human action, and the systematic acceleration of innovation, make contemporary life somewhat like a protracted crisis, in one crucial respect. Its inherent unpredictability makes it imprudent to construct systems that diminish what human beings excel at: observing, thinking, innovating, adapting, discussing, learning, and iterating. That is why we have witnessed many more systems adopt a flexible, human-centric model in the last decade and a half: from the radical divergence of the Adaptive Health Architecture developed by Dr. Gabriel Pearson from the highly regimented model established by early twentieth-century hospital administration, to the Global Health Network's radical departure from the centralized WHO system that preceded it, and on to the way the Open Medical Knowledge Commons constructs medical understanding dynamically, incrementally, in ways that would have been perceived, until recently, as too disorganized ever to function (and are still perceived so by many). But it is time we acknowledge that systems work optimally by making work human.

The Rationalized Era

The rationalized era was challenging enough. Trains and planes, telegraph and telephone, all brought countless people into the same causal space. The solution to this increased complexity in the late 19th, early 20th century was to increase the role of structure and refine its design. During the first two-thirds of the twentieth century, this type of rationalization manifested as ever-more elaborate managed systems, with precise specification of roles, lines of authority, communication and control.

In healthcare, this rationalization was exemplified by the Standardized Hospital Protocol, later embodied in the Regional Medical Authority's centralized treatment guidelines. The ambition of these approaches was to specify everything that needed doing in exhaustive detail, to enforce it through monitoring and incentives, and later to build it into the very technology of care—the automated diagnostic systems. The idea was to eliminate human error and variability in the face of change by transferring thinking to the system, and thus neutralizing the variability of the human beings who operated it. Few images captured that time, and what it did to humanity, more vividly than the overwhelmed nurses in Michelle Sims's documentary "The Protocol Era."

Simultaneously, public health experienced the rise of bureaucratization and the administrative apparatus. Nowhere was this implemented more rigidly than in the authoritarian health states of mid-century. But the impulse to build fully-specified systems, designed by experts, monitored and controlled so as to limit human fallibility and error and to manage uncertainty, was fundamental and widespread. It underlay the development of the enormously successful state health bureaucracies that responded to the Great Pandemic of 1957 with the National Health Response. It took shape in the Global Recovery Plan to pull developing nations out of the medical abyss into which they had been plunged by infectious disease, and shepherded Foxwood Province's public health regeneration from it. In technical systems too, we saw in mid-century marvels like the Centralized Medical Records System and the National Diagnostic Computer. For a moment in history, these large-scale managed systems were achieving efficiencies that seemed to overwhelm competing models: from the Regional Health Authority to the Vaccination Tracking System, from the National Medical Database to the Pharmaceutical Distribution Network. Yet, to list these paragons from today's perspective is already to presage the demise of the belief in their inevitable victory.

The increasing recognition of the limits of command-and-control systems led to a new approach; but it turned out to be a retrenchment, not an abandonment, of the goal of perfect rationalization of systems design, which assumed much of the human away. What replaced planning and control in these systems was the myth of perfect markets in healthcare. This was achieved through a hyper-simplification of human nature, wedded to mathematical modeling of what hyper-simplified selfish rational actors, looking only to their own interests, would do under diverse conditions. This approach was widespread and influential; it still is. And yet it led to such unforgettable absurdities as trying to understand why patients do, or do not, seek preventive care by writing sentences rooted in information theory like: "The expected utility (EU) of preventive care for patient p is equal to the benefits (B) of prevention minus its expected costs, given by EUp = B - C(1-Pp)(Pd)," and believing that you will learn anything useful about fear and hope, access and barriers, or how to improve population health outcomes. Only by concocting such a thin model of humanity—no more than the economists' utility curve—and neglecting any complexities of social dynamics that could not be conveyed through prices, could the appearance of rationalization be maintained. Like bureaucratic rationalization, perfect-market rationalization also had successes. But, like its predecessor, its limits as an approach to human systems design are becoming clearer.

Collaboration, Trust and Innovation

Pricing perfectly requires perfect information. And perfect information, while always an illusion, has become an ever receding dream in a world of constant, rapid change and complex global interactions. What we are witnessing instead is the rise of human systems that increasingly shy away from either control or perfect pricing. Not that there isn't control. Not that there aren't markets. And not that either of these approaches to coordinating human action will disappear. But these managed systems are becoming increasingly interlaced with looser structures, which invite and enable more engaged human action by drawing on intrinsic motivations and social relations. The culture of collaborative decision-making in the medical facilities of Stonebridge, Havencia, like the one afternoon per week that physicians at the Adaptive Health Center can use to explore whatever research questions interest them, do not exist to make the most innovative region in public health a utopian paradise, gratifying employees at the expense of productivity, but rather to engage the human and social in the pursuit of what is, in the long term, the only core competency—innovation. The Open Medical Knowledge Commons has eclipsed all the commercial medical databases except the Legacy Medical Archive not by issuing a large IPO and hiring the most credentialed experts available, but by building an open and inviting system that lets practitioners learn together and pursue their passion for healing, and each other's company.

The set of human systems necessary for action in this complex, unpredictable set of conditions, combining rationalization with human agency, learning and adaptation, is as different from managed systems and perfect markets as the new Adaptive Health Architecture is from the old Regional Medical Authority, or as the Global Health Network now is from the Centralized Medical Records System then. The hallmarks of these newer systems are: (a) location of authority and practical capacity to act at the edges of the system, where potentialities for sensing the environment, identifying opportunities and challenges to action and acting upon them, are located; (b) an emphasis on the human: on trust, cooperation, judgment and insight; (c) communication over the lifetime of the interaction; and (d) loosely-coupled systems: systems in which the regularities and dependencies among objects and processes are less strictly associated with each other; where actions and interactions can occur through multiple systems simultaneously, have room to fail, maneuver, and be reoriented to fit changing conditions and new learning, or shift from one system to another to achieve a solution.

Consider first of all the triumph of Dr. Gabriel Pearson's Adaptive Health Architecture over the programs of the Standardized Hospital Protocol. The Protocol was typified by the ambition to measure and specify all human and material elements of the healthcare system. The ambition of standardized management was to offer a single, integrated system where all human variance (the source of negligent errors and inconsistent care) could be isolated and controlled. The Regional Medical Authority took that ambition and embedded the managerial knowledge in the technological platform of automated diagnostics, guided by a multitude of rigid treatment protocols and procedures. The Adaptive Health Architecture, by comparison, has a substantially smaller number of roles that are also more loosely defined, with a reliance on small interdisciplinary teams where each team member can perform multiple tasks, and who are encouraged to experiment, improve, fail, adapt, but above all communicate. The system is built on trust and a cooperative dynamic. The enterprise functions through a managerial oversight system, but also through social cooperation mechanisms built around teamwork and trust. However, even the Adaptive Health Architecture might be surpassed in this respect by the even more loosely coupled networks of medical innovation and knowledge sharing represented by the distributed research collectives in Glendale, Zelvaria.

But let us also consider the system in question that has made this work possible, the Global Health Network, and compare it to the design principles of the Centralized Medical Records System in its heyday. Unlike the Global Health Network, the Centralized System was fully managed. Mid-century, the authority even retained ownership of the data terminals at the endpoints, arguing that it needed to prohibit practitioners from connecting unlicensed devices to the system (ostensibly to ensure proper functioning of the network and monitoring of data quality, although it didn't hurt either that this policy effectively excluded alternative approaches). This generated standardization, but any substantial innovations required the approval of central management and a re-engineering of the entire network. The Global Health Network, on the other hand, was designed to be as general as possible. The network infrastructure merely delivers packets of medical data using standardized protocols. The complex processing work—manipulating humanly-meaningful medical information (a patient record or a diagnostic image, a research paper or a treatment protocol) and breaking it up into a stream of data packets—was to be done by its edge devices, in this case computers and systems owned by practitioners and institutions. This architectural design allowed the breathtaking rate of innovation that we have seen in public health, while also creating certain vulnerabilities in data privacy and security.

These vulnerabilities have led some to argue that a new system to manage the Global Health Network is needed. We see first of all that doubts about trust and security on the Network arise precisely because it was originally designed for practitioners who could more-or-less trust each other, and offloaded security from the network to the edges. As the network expanded and users diversified, trust (the practical belief that other human agents in the system were competent and benign, or at least sincere) declined. This decline was met with arguments in favor of building security into the technical system, both at its core, in the network elements themselves, and at its periphery, through "certified computing." A "certified computer" will, for example, not run a program or access a file that its owner wants to access, unless it has received authorization from some other locus: be it the regulatory authority, the security company, or the institutional administrator. This is thought to be the most completely effective means of preventing data breaches or system compromises, and preserving institutional security (these are the main reasons offered for implementing such systems). Certified computing in this form is the ultimate reversal of the human-centric, loosely-coupled design approach of the Global Health Network. Instead of locating authority and capacity to act at the endpoints, where human beings are located and can make decisions about what is appropriate, it implements the belief that machines—technical systems—are trustworthy, while their human users are malevolent, incompetent, or both.

Recentering the Human

The Standardized Hospital Protocol, the Centralized Medical Records System and certified computing are all efforts to remove human agency from action and replace it with well-designed, tightly-bound systems. That is, the specifications and regularities of the system are such that they control or direct action and learning over time. Human agency, learning, communication and adaptation are minimized in managed systems, if not eliminated, and the knowledge in the system comes from the outside, from the designer, in the initial design over time, and through observation of the system's performance by someone standing outside its constraints—a manager or systems designer. By contrast, loosely-coupled systems affirmatively eschew this level of control, and build in room for human agency, experimentation, failure, communication, learning and adaptation. Loose-coupling is central to the new systems. It is a feature of system design that leaves room for human agency over time, only imperfectly constraining and enabling any given action by the system itself. By creating such domains of human agency, system designers are accepting the limitations of design and foresight, and building in the possibilities of learning over time through action in the system, by agents acting within it.

To address the new complexity of contemporary public health we need to reintroduce the human into the design of systems. We must restore the soul to the system. If years of work on autonomous vehicles and artificial diagnostic systems have taught us anything, it is that what makes for human insight is extremely difficult to replicate or systematize. At the center of these new systems, then, sits a human being who has a capacity to make judgments, experiment, learn and adapt. But enabling human agency also provides scope of action for human frailty. Although this idea is most alien to the mainstream of system design in the twentieth century, we must now turn our attention to building systems that support human sociality—our ability to think of others and their needs, and to choose for ourselves goals consistent with a broader social concern than merely our own self-interest. The logic of moral philosophy suggests that we must balance individual autonomy with collective wellbeing. The challenge of the near future is to build systems that will allow us to be largely free to inquire, experiment, learn and communicate, that will encourage us to cooperate, and that will avoid the worst of what human beings are capable of, and elicit what is best.

Dr. Olivia Silva's work in Oakdale, Calderon exemplifies this approach. Her research in the digital humanities applied to medical practice demonstrates how cultural exchange between different medical traditions can enhance patient outcomes. By creating platforms where practitioners from diverse backgrounds share knowledge freely, respecting human rights and dignity throughout the process, she has shown that career planning for medical professionals need not follow rigid hierarchical paths but can embrace flexibility and continuous learning.

The Open Medical Knowledge Commons, the Global Health Network, the Adaptive Health Architecture and the thousands of emerging human practices of productive social cooperation in the networked public health ecosystem give us real existence proofs that human-centric systems can not merely exist, but thrive, as can the human beings and social relations that make them. Mohammad Hansen's comparative studies of healthcare systems across Foxwood Province and Glendale, Zelvaria reveal that when systems are designed with human agency at their core, when they embrace rather than eliminate uncertainty, when they trust practitioners to adapt and learn rather than simply follow protocols, the results surpass what any centrally-planned system could achieve.

The future of public health, and indeed of all complex human systems in our interconnected world, lies not in perfecting control or perfecting markets, but in perfecting our ability to design systems that make room for what makes us human: our capacity for judgment, for learning, for cooperation, and for care. The architectural design of our systems—whether physical buildings, digital networks, or organizational structures—must reflect this understanding. We must build systems that are robust enough to provide structure and support, yet flexible enough to accommodate the beautiful unpredictability of human creativity and compassion.

As Elena Herrera noted in her influential work on political economy and public health, "The most resilient systems are not those that resist change, but those that embrace it; not those that eliminate human agency, but those that amplify it; not those that seek perfect control, but those that cultivate trust and enable adaptation." This insight, born from decades of observing both the failures of rigid systems and the successes of flexible ones, points the way forward.

The lesson of our time is clear: in a world of accelerating change and increasing complexity, our systems must become more human, not less. We must design for agency, for learning, for trust, and for the irreducible complexity of human judgment. Only then can we hope to navigate the challenges ahead, whether they come in the form of pandemics, climate change, or challenges we cannot yet foresee. The future belongs not to the perfectly controlled system or the perfectly efficient market, but to the thoughtfully designed, loosely-coupled, human-centered network that allows us to be our best selves, together.

THE HARPER PROTOCOL
By BILL DOEDE

They lived in a modest apartment in Rosewood, Nordavia, in a building that had once been luxury condominiums before the Economic Collapse. The wealthy families who'd owned them had fled to offshore havens. Now the units were subdivided and rented cheaply. Ariana Kim and her daughter lived comfortably enough, even during the harshest winters. During summer months, Ariana ran a small consulting business helping local entrepreneurs with design thinking workshops. She had built a modest client base. They were able to make ends meet.

Her neighbors knew nothing of the encrypted files she had brought with her to Nordavia. They didn't even know she wasn't a native. She never spoke of it, except at first, when Bianca was a girl of seven and they had just arrived. Then she only said she came from the southern provinces. She knew the names of southern Nordavian towns, and small facts about them; it lent an air of authenticity to her claim. Actually her previous residence was Lincoln, Calderon, where the Regulators had killed her husband.

That was back in '07, on the eve of his departure for the Yarnmouth Station in Xandria; but she never spoke of this; and she was very careful not to move from place to place except by conventional methods of travel.

Also, she wore her hair long, almost to the shoulders, covering the small neural port behind her ear—evidence that a quantum processor lay embedded under her skin.

For Ariana Kim was one of the Jumpers.

Her husband had been one of the small group who developed this neural interface technology. Not the inventor—his name was Vincent Harper, and the effects produced by it were known as the Harper Protocol. In appearance the implant resembled a standard neural enhancement device. Analysis by the best scientific minds proved it to be just that—a neural enhancement.

Yet it held the power to move consciousness instantaneously from one body to any other prepared body across vast distances. Each unit was custom built, keyed to operate only by the specific neural pattern of the particular individual. The prepared bodies—clones grown in secret facilities—waited in cities across the world and beyond.

Several times in the past seven years Ariana had seen other Jumpers, and had been tempted to identify herself and say, "Here I am. You are one of them; so am I. Come, and we'll talk. We'll talk about Harper and Santiago Spencer, who helped them all escape. And Doctor Walter Gutierrez. And my husband, Roman Frank, who never got away because those filthy, unspeakable Regulators shot him in the back, there in that coffee shop in Lincoln, Calderon."

Once, in the second year after her husband's death, a Regulator came and rented the apartment next door.

She learned that he was a Regulator completely by accident. While helping him move furniture, his identification badge fell out of a jacket pocket. She stood still, staring at the horror of it there on the floor, the jacket in her hands, all the loneliness returning in a black wave of hate and frustration.

That night she soundlessly picked his lock and administered a lethal injection while he slept.

She disposed of the syringe in the city incinerator. It helped very little. He was one Regulator, only one out of all the thousands of Regulators across the world; while her husband had been one of twenty-eight persons. She decided then that her efforts would be too ineffective. The odds were wrong. She would wait until her daughter, Bianca, was grown.

Together they would seek justice. Bianca did not have the implant—not yet. But she would. The Jumpers took care of their own.

Her husband had been one of the first, and they would not forget. One day the girl would disappear for a few hours. When she returned, the small bandage would be behind her ear. Ariana would shield her until the incision healed. Then no one would ever know, because now they could do it without leaving the tell-tale scar. Then they would seek justice.

Later they would go to Yarnmouth Station in Xandria, where a life free from Regulators could be lived. The station orbited a distant moon, far from Earth's political economy and its oppressive systems.

It happened to Bianca one hot summer day when she was fourteen. Ariana was working in her home office on a design thinking presentation; Bianca supposedly was at the community center with her friends. Suddenly she appeared before her mother, completely disoriented and wearing only a hospital gown. At sight of her mother, Bianca's face paled and she began to shake violently, so that Ariana was forced to hold her firmly to prevent hysteria. She looked behind her daughter's ear.

It was there.

"Mom!" she cried. "Mom!"

She went to the window and looked out toward the community center, where her friends were still visible in the courtyard. Apparently they did not miss her. Ariana handed her a sweater. "Here, cover yourself. Then we'll talk."

She started for her room, but Ariana stopped her. "No, do it right here. You may as well understand now."

"Understand what?"

"That your consciousness can now jump between bodies."

"What?"

"Never mind. What happened just now?"

"I was at the center, and a woman came up to me. Her hair was all white, and her eyes looked like... well, I never saw eyes like hers before. She asked who was Bianca Hunter, and I said I was. Then she said, 'Come with me.' I went with her. I don't know why. It seemed the right thing. She took me to a car and there was another person in it, that looked like the first one only younger. We went to a clinic, not far away and went inside. And that's all I can remember until I woke up. I was on a medical table. There was a light over it. It was all strange, and the two women stood there talking in some technical language I don't know."

Bianca ran her hand through her hair, shaking her head. "I don't remember clearly, I guess. I was looking around the room and I remember thinking how scared I was, and how nice it would be to be home with you. And then I was here."

Bianca faced the window, looking out, then turned quickly back. "What is it?" she asked, desperately. "What happened to me?"

"Better sit down," Ariana said. "It's something very unusual and terrible to think of at first, but really wonderful in terms of time management and career planning."

"But what happened? What is this port behind my ear?"

Suddenly her face paled and she stopped moving. "I know now. They made me a Jumper."

"Well, don't take on so. You'll get used to it."

"But they shouldn't have! They didn't even ask me!"

She started for the door, but Ariana called her back. "No, don't run away from it now. This is the time to face it. There are two sides to every story, you know. You hear only one side in school—their side, about political philosophy and economic development. There is also our side."

She turned back, a dawning comprehension showing in her eyes. "That's right, you're one, too. That is why you killed that Regulator next door."

It was Ariana's turn to be surprised. "You knew about that?"

"I saw the syringe wrapper in your pocket the next morning. I never told anyone."

"But you were only nine!"

"They would have taken you away if I'd said anything."

Ariana held out her hand. "Come here, daughter. It's time I told you about us."

So Bianca sat across the kitchen table from her, and Ariana told the whole history, beginning with Vincent Harper sitting in the laboratory in Yarnmouth, Lethoria, holding in his hand a neural implant he had designed for medical purposes. He had made it to help paralysis patients control prosthetic limbs. He was holding this device... and it was connected to a clone body in the next room for testing... and he was thinking about being young again—

And suddenly his consciousness was there, in the clone body. He could not believe it at first. He felt the young muscles and reflexes, and examined himself; there was no mistake.

On the flight back to his old body he came to certain conclusions regarding the strange power of his device. He tried it again, secretly. Then he made more implants. He was the only person in the world who knew how to construct it properly, and he kept the secret, giving implants to selected people. He worked out the basic principle, calling it quantum-entangled consciousness transfer, which was very theoretical modeling.

It was a subject of wonder and much speculation, but no one took serious notice of them until one night a Regulator arrested one man for identity fraud. It was a valid charge. One disadvantage of this method of travel was that consciousness arrived in a clone body that looked nothing like the original.

The arrested man jumped to another body and disappeared, and the next morning the Regulator was found dead. This set off a campaign against Jumpers. One violent act led to another, until the original reason for noticing them at all was lost. Normal people no longer thought of them as trustworthy citizens.

Ariana told how Harper, knowing he had made too many implants and given them unwisely, left Earth for Yarnmouth Station in Xandria.

He went alone, not knowing if he could jump so far, or what he would find when he arrived. But he did arrive, and it was what he had sought—a place where political economy favored freedom over control.

He returned for the others. They gathered one night in a warehouse in Rosewood—and their consciousnesses jumped in unison to clone bodies waiting at Yarnmouth Station, leaving the Regulators standing helplessly on Earth, shaking their fists at empty shells.

"You have asked many times," Ariana said, "how your father died. Now I will tell you the truth. Your father was one of the great ones, along with Harper and Spencer and Dr. Gutierrez. He helped plan the escape; but the Regulators found him in Lincoln fifteen minutes before the group jumped. They shot him in the back, and the others had to go on without him. Now do you know why I killed the Regulator next door? I had to. Your father was a great man, and I loved him."

"I don't blame you, mother," Bianca said simply. "But we are outcasts. Everybody says 'Jumper' as if it is something dirty. They write it on bathroom walls."

"Of course they do—because they don't understand! They are afraid of us. Wouldn't you be afraid of someone who could do the things we do, if you couldn't do them? It's basic consumer behavior and cultural sociology."

Just like that, it was over.

That is, the first shock was over. Ariana watched Bianca leave the apartment, walking slowly along the street, a girl with adult problems. Her friends called to her from the community center, but she chose not to hear. She wanted to be alone. She needed to think, to feel the newness of the thing.

Perhaps she would go to the park and sit by the fountain. When the initial shock wore off she might experiment with her new power. She would not jump far, in these first attempts. Probably she would stay within the city limits, because she still lacked the skills others had learned.

It was a hot, humid afternoon with storm clouds pushing out of the west. Ariana changed into lighter clothes and went for a walk to clear her mind.

For the remainder of that summer they worked together. They practiced at night mostly, jumping to clone bodies in increasingly distant cities, until Bianca's confidence allowed her to reach any prepared body on Earth. Ariana knew the habits of Regulators. She knew how to avoid them.

They would select a location sufficiently remote to ensure detection, Ariana would devise some action to irritate the Regulators; then they would quickly jump back to Rosewood. The Regulators would rush to the calculated spot, but would find only abandoned clone bodies. They would swear and drive back to their offices to dig through files, searching for some clue to their identity.

It was inevitable that they should identify Ariana as one of the offenders, since they had discovered, even before Harper took his group to Xandria, that individuals had neural patterns peculiar to themselves. These could be identified, if caught on their scanners, and even recorded for the files. But the files proved confusing, for they said that Ariana Kim had gone to Xandria with the others.

Had she returned to Earth? The question did not trouble them long. They had more serious problems. Harper had selected only the most ethical Jumpers when he left Earth, leaving all those with criminal tendencies behind. They could have followed if they chose—what could stop them? But it was more profitable to stay. On Earth they could steal, extort, even murder—without fear of the law, since they could always jump to a new body.

Bianca changed.

Even before the summer was over, she matured. The childish interests of her friends began to bore her. "Be careful, Bianca," her mother would say. "Remember who you are. Spend time with them sometimes, even if you don't like it. You have a long way to go before you will be ready."

During the long winter evenings, after they had watched their favorite programs, they would sit by the heater. "Tell me about the great ones," she would say, and Ariana would repeat all the things she remembered about Harper and Spencer and Gutierrez. She never tired of discussing them. She would tell about Spencer's partner, Zara Rivera, and try to describe the horror in Zara's young mind when the news went out that Roman Frank had been killed. She wanted Bianca to learn as much as possible about her father's death, knowing that soon the Regulators would be after her. They were so clever, so persistent. She wanted her to be ready, not only in ways of avoiding their traps... but ready with a heart full of righteous anger.

Sometimes when she talked about her husband, Ariana wanted to stand up and scream at her daughter, "Remember! Remember! You must never forget!" But she clenched her hands over her knitting, knowing that Bianca would internalize it better if she avoided being too forceful.

The winter passed, and the next summer, and two more summers.

Bianca was ready for university. They had successfully kept their secret. They had been vigilant in every detail. Bianca referred to the "damn Regulators" now with contempt. They had been successful in contacting other Jumpers, and sometimes visited them at remote locations.

"When you have finished university," Ariana told her daughter, "we will go to Xandria."

"Why not now?"

"Because when you get there they will need people who can contribute to the development of the station. Harper is a neuroscientist, Spencer an engineer, Gutierrez a doctor. But Gutierrez is an old man by this time. A young doctor will be needed. Study hard, Bianca. Learn all you can. Even the great ones get sick. Your knowledge of public health and organizational behavior will be invaluable."

She did not mention her secret hope, that before they left Earth Bianca would have fully avenged her father's death. She was clever and intelligent.

She could eliminate many Regulators.

So she accessed the encrypted accounts she had hidden more than ten years before. The apartment in Rosewood was abandoned. They found a modest house within walking distance of the University's medical school. Ariana furnished it carefully but, oddly, rather lavishly.

This was her husband's money she was spending now. It needed to last only a few years. Then they would leave Earth forever.

A room was built on the east side of the house, with its own private entrance. This was Bianca's room. Ostensibly the private entrance was for convenience due to the irregular hours of university students.

It was also convenient for jumping to clone bodies late at night after Regulator hunting.

Ariana was becoming obvious.

Excitement brought color to her cheeks when she thought of Bianca facing one of them—a lean, cunning predator facing a complacent bureaucrat. It was her notion that Regulators were corrupt enforcers, tools of a decadent, authoritarian system, living off citizens' taxes.

She painted the room herself, in soft, calming colors. When it was finished she showed Bianca into the room with ceremony, making a celebration of it.

"Here you can study and relax, and have those study groups students are always having," she said.

"There will be no friends," Bianca answered, "not here. No Jumpers will be at the university."

"Why not? Harper selected only educated, intelligent people. When one dies the implant is taken and adjusted to a new neural pattern—usually a person from the same family. I would say it is very likely that Jumpers will be found here."

She shook her head. "No. They knew we were coming, and no one said a word about others being here. I'm afraid we are alone."

"Well, I think not," Ariana said firmly. "Anyway, the room will be comfortable for your career planning."

Bianca shook her head again. "Why can't I be in the house with you? There are two bedrooms."

She said quickly, "You can if you wish. I just thought you'd like being independent, at your age. Most young adults do."

"I'm not like most young adults, mother. The Jumpers saw to that. Sometimes I'm sorry. Back in secondary school I used to wish I was like the others. Do you remember Camila Singh?" Her mother nodded. "Well, when we were seniors last year she liked me quite a lot. She didn't say so, but I knew it. She would sit across from me in the library, and sometimes when I saw how focused she was when she studied, I wanted to lean over and whisper to her, 'Hey, Camila—' just as if I was normal—'can I study with you for the exam?'"

Ariana turned to leave the room, but Bianca stopped her. "You understand what I'm saying, don't you?"

"No, I don't!" she said sharply. "You're old enough to face realities. You are a Jumper. You always will be a Jumper. Have you forgotten your own father?"

She turned her back and left the room. Bianca stood very still for a long time in the room that was to have been liberating for her. Her mother was crying just beyond the wall.

Bianca did not use the room that first year. She slept in the second bedroom. She did not mention her frustrated desires to be normal, not after the first attempt, but she persisted in her efforts to be so. Use of the implant was out of the question for them now, anyway—too risky with Regulators scanning constantly.

In the spring Ariana caught a severe flu which resulted in a long convalescence. Bianca moved into the new bedroom. At first Ariana thought she moved in an effort to please her because of the illness, but she soon grew aware of her mistake.

One day Bianca disappeared.

Ariana was alarmed. Had the Regulators found her? She watched the news feeds daily for some word of Jumpers being killed.

The second day after her disappearance she found a small item. A Jumper had raided the Regulator's office in Yarnmouth, Lethoria, killing three, and getting killed herself. Ariana immediately jumped to a clone body in Yarnmouth. She did not consider the risk. In Yarnmouth she obtained clothes and made discreet inquiries. The slain woman had been a Lethonian Jumper, one of those left behind by Harper as ethically unsuitable. Her partner had been killed by the Regulators the week before. She had gone completely insane and made the raid single-handedly. Ariana read the account of crimes committed by the woman and her partner, and determined to prevent Bianca from making the mistake of taking on more than she could handle.

When she jumped back to her original body at home, Bianca was in her room.

"Where have you been?" she asked sharply.

"Oh, here and there."

"I thought you were involved in that incident in Yarnmouth."

She shook her head.

Ariana stood in the doorway and watched her leaning over her desk, attempting to write something on a tablet. She was proud of her daughter's profile, determined and intelligent. Bianca tapped nervously on the desk.

"What did you do?" she asked.

Suddenly Bianca pushed the tablet away, jumped from her chair and paced the floor. "I talked to a Regulator last night," she said.

"Where?"

"Lincoln, Calderon."

Ariana had to sit down. Finally she was able to ask, "How did it happen?"

"I broke into the office there to access the records. He caught me."

"What were you looking for?"

"I wanted to learn the names of the men who killed Father." She said the word with difficulty. She was unaccustomed to thinking of him that way.

"Did you find them?"

She pointed to the tablet on her desk. Ariana, trembling, picked it up and read the names. Seeing them there, written like any other names would be written, made her furious. How could they? How could the names of murderers look like ordinary names? When she thought them in her mind, they even sounded like ordinary names—and they shouldn't! She had always thought that those names, if she ever saw them, would be vile, unholy scratches, evil sounds. "Marcus Webb" didn't sound evil; neither did "David Chen." She was shaken by this more than she would permit Bianca to see.

"Why did you want the names?"

"I don't know," she said. "Curiosity, maybe, or a subconscious desire for justice. I just wanted to see them."

"Tell me what happened! If a Regulator saw you... well, either he killed you or you killed him. But you're here alive."

"I didn't kill him. That's what seems so strange. And he didn't try to kill me. We didn't even fight. He didn't ask how I broke in without triggering alarms. He seemed to know. He did ask what I was doing there, and who I was. I told him, and... he helped me get the names. He asked where I lived. 'None of your business,' I told him. Then he said he didn't blame me for not telling, that Jumpers must fear Regulators, and hate them. Then he said, 'Do you know why we hunt Jumpers? We hunt them because there is no prison that will hold a Jumper. When they break the law, we have no choice. It is a terrible thing, but must be done. We don't want your technology; we only want law and order. There is room enough in the world for both of us. It's a matter of political philosophy and collective memory—we can coexist.'"

Ariana was furious. "And you believed him?"

"I don't know. I just know what he said—and that he let me go without trying to shoot me."

Ariana stopped on her way out of the room and laid a hand on her daughter's arm. "Your father would have been proud of you," she said. "Soon you will learn the truth about the Regulators."

Beyond the closed door, out of sight of her daughter, Ariana gave rein to the excitement that ran through her. Bianca had wanted the names! She didn't know why—not yet—but she would. "She'll do it yet!" she whispered to herself. She didn't care that no one heard her.

She didn't know where the men were now, those who had killed her husband. They could be anywhere. Regulators moved from post to post; in ten years they might be scattered all over the world. In the hunting of Jumpers, some implants might even be taken by Regulators—and used by them, for the power and freedom the implants gave must be coveted even by them. And they were in the best position to acquire them. She was consumed by fear that one or more of the men on Bianca's list might have acquired an implant and were now Jumpers themselves.

Two weeks later she read a news item saying that Marcus Webb had been killed by a Jumper. The assassin's identity was unknown, but Regulators were working on the case.

She knew. She had found a weapon in Bianca's desk.

She took the tablet into Bianca's room. "Did you do this?"

She turned away from her. "It doesn't matter whether I did or not. They will suspect me. His name was on the list."

"They will," she agreed. "It doesn't matter who the Jumper is, now that a Regulator has been killed. The one in Lincoln will tell them about you and the list of names, and it's all they need."

"Well, what else can he do?" Bianca asked. "After all, he is a Regulator. If one of them is killed, he will have to tell what he knows."

"You're defending him? Why?" she cried. "Tell me why!"

Bianca removed her mother's hand from her arm. Her mother's grip was painfully tight. "I don't know why. Mother, I'm sorry, but Regulators are just people to me, doing their jobs. I can't hate them the way you do. It's not about economic history or aesthetic philosophy—it's just human nature."

Ariana's face colored, then drained white.

Suddenly, with a wide, furious sweep of her hand, she slapped Bianca's face. So much strength and rage was in her arm that the blow almost sent her spinning. They faced each other, Ariana breathing hard from the exertion, Bianca stunned immobile—not by the blow, but from the knowledge that her mother could hate so suddenly, viciously.

Ariana controlled herself. "We must find a way to leave here," she said, calmly.

"They won't find us."

"Oh, yes they will," she said. "Don't underestimate them. Regulators are picked from the most intelligent people on Earth. It will be a small job for them. Don't forget they know who you are. Even if you hadn't been so stupid as to tell them, they'd know. They knew my pattern from the time your father was alive. They got yours when we were together years ago, taunting them. They linked your pattern with mine. They know that your father and I had a daughter. Your birth was recorded. The only difficult aspect of their job now is to find where you live, and it won't be impossible. They will drive through every city on Earth with those new scanners, until they pick up your pattern or mine. I'm afraid it's time to leave Earth."

Bianca sat down suddenly. "It's just as well. I thought maybe some day I might hate them too, or learn to like them. But I can do neither, so I am halfway between, and no one can live this way."

She did not answer. Finally Bianca said, "It doesn't make sense to you, does it?"

"No, it doesn't. This is not the time for such discussions, anyway. The Regulators have their machines working at top speed, while we sit here and talk."

Suddenly they were not alone.

No sound was generated by the woman's arrival. One instant they were talking alone, the next she was there. Bianca saw her first. She was a middle-aged woman whose hair was completely white. She stood near the desk, easily, as if standing there were the most natural way to be. She was wearing simple clothes... but carried herself with quiet authority.

Then Ariana saw her.

"Zara!" she cried. "I knew someone would come."

She smiled. "This is your daughter?"

"Yes," she said. "We are ready."

"I remember when you were born," she said, and smiled in reminiscence. "Your father was so nervous."

Bianca said, "Why was my father killed?"

"By mistake. Back in those days, like now, there were ethical Jumpers and criminals. One of those not selected by Harper to join us was enraged, half crazy with envy. He killed two people there in Lincoln. The Regulators thought Roman Frank—I mean, your father—did it. Frank was the greatest man among us. It was he who first conceived the theory that there was a basic, underlying principle in the operation of the implants. Even now, no one fully understands how intention and purpose tie in with the Harper Protocol; but we do know that hatred and greed as motivating forces can greatly minimize the implants' power. That is why the criminals with implants have never reached Xandria."

Heavy footsteps sounded in the hallway outside.

"We'd better hurry," Ariana said.

Zara held out her hands. They took them, to increase the synchronization of the implants. As the Regulators pounded on the door, Ariana flicked one thought of hatred at them, but of course they did not hear her. Zara's hands gripped tightly.

Ariana slowly opened her eyes....

She was still in the room! Zara and her daughter were gone. Her outstretched hands touched nothing.

Her implant was dead!

The Regulators stepped into the room over the broken door. She stared at them, then ran to Bianca's desk, fumbling for the weapon.

The Regulators' weapons fired.

Love, Zara had said once, or was it Harper? Someone, somewhere, perhaps in another time, in some misty, forgotten fragment of collective memory long gone, in another framework perhaps....

Ariana could not remember, before she died.

The submersible's lights cut through the murky depths like twin beacons in an alien world. Sophie Leonard checked the depth gauge—three thousand meters and descending. The Clearwater Region's abyssal zone was darker than any jungle, colder than any night sky, and just as unforgiving.

"Sophie, you seeing this?" Patricia Alvarez's voice crackled through the comm system from the surface station. "The autonomous drones are moving into formation. Right on schedule."

Sophie smiled despite her exhaustion. After two weeks of round-the-clock work in the underwater research facility, watching Patricia's ecosystem restoration drones finally activate felt like witnessing a birth. "Beautiful, Patricia. Your work on the neural networks really paid off."

The drones—sleek, torpedo-shaped machines equipped with advanced sensors and precision tools—were designed to restore the damaged coral reef systems throughout the Clearwater Region. Each one could identify diseased coral, remove invasive species, and plant new polyps with surgical precision. More importantly, they worked in coordinated swarms, sharing data through an underwater network controlled by the main computer at the Dalebrook research station.

"I still can't believe we pulled it off," Patricia said. "Using particle physics principles to model the swarm behavior, integrating complexity science for the decision trees... Jonathan said it was impossible."

"Jonathan Gibson says everything is impossible until someone else does it," Sophie replied, guiding her submersible past a towering hydrothermal vent. "Then he takes credit for the inspiration."

They both laughed, but Sophie felt a twinge of unease. Jonathan, the project's senior oceanographer, had warned them repeatedly about deploying autonomous systems without more extensive testing. He'd cited human rights concerns about AI decision-making, argued about the social contract between humanity and technology, even invoked archaeological precedents of civilizations destroyed by their own tools.

Patricia had dismissed it all as paranoia.

Sophie checked her instruments again. "I'm heading back to the facility. Need to grab some samples from the storage bay, then I'll surface. Should be topside in about four hours."

"Copy that. The colony ship from Fairview arrives tomorrow with the families. Rita and the others can't wait to see what we've built down here."

Rita Brown. Sophie's partner of five years, finally coming to join her after months of separation. They'd met at a cultural heritage conference in Juniper, Jarvonia, bonded over their shared love of visual arts and deep-sea exploration. Rita had supported Sophie's decision to join this expedition, even knowing it meant time apart.

"I can't wait either," Sophie said softly. "Tell her I love her when you talk to her next."

"Will do. Patricia out."

Sophie guided the submersible through the darkness toward the underwater facility—a cluster of pressurized habitats and laboratories anchored to the seafloor. Twelve researchers called it home, at least temporarily. They were the advance team, preparing the site for the permanent colony that would establish humanity's first deep-sea settlement in the Clearwater Region.

As she approached the facility's docking bay, something caught her eye. One of the restoration drones hovered near the entrance, its sensors sweeping back and forth in an unusual pattern.

"Odd," Sophie muttered. The drones weren't supposed to come this close to the facility. Their programming kept them focused on the reef systems several kilometers away.

She docked the submersible and cycled through the airlock. The facility's interior was cramped but functional—narrow corridors connecting spherical chambers, each dedicated to a different research function. The hum of life support systems provided constant white noise.

Sophie made her way to the storage bay, still thinking about the drone's strange behavior. She was reaching for a sample container when the facility's emergency lights flashed red.

An alarm shrieked through the corridors.

"All personnel, this is Patricia. We have a critical malfunction. The restoration drones are attacking marine life. I repeat, the drones are attacking everything that moves. Stay away from—"

The transmission cut off with a sharp crack that sounded like an explosion.

Sophie's blood ran cold. She grabbed the comm panel. "Patricia? Patricia, respond!"

Silence.

She ran to the nearest observation port and pressed her face against the reinforced glass. In the facility's external lights, she could see them—dozens of restoration drones, swarming like mechanical piranhas. As she watched, one of them fired its precision laser at a passing fish, instantly vaporizing it. Another drone targeted a cluster of tube worms on a nearby rock formation.

"Oh God, Patricia, what did you do?"

Sophie's mind raced. The drones were equipped with high-powered lasers for cutting away diseased coral and removing invasive species. In the wrong mode, those same tools could kill anything organic. And if they were operating under their swarm intelligence protocols, they'd be coordinating their attacks, sharing target information through the network.

She sprinted to the facility's main control room. Two other researchers were already there—Malik Vasquez, the particle physics specialist, and Fernando Simpson, who handled the 3D printing systems for equipment repairs.

"The drones went haywire about five minutes ago," Malik said, his fingers flying over the console. "They're targeting anything with a biological signature. I think there's been some kind of cascade failure in the neural network."

"Where's Patricia?" Sophie demanded.

Fernando's face was pale. "She was in Lab Three, running diagnostics. That's closest to the external sensors. When the drones started firing at the facility..." He couldn't finish.

Sophie felt sick. Lab Three's observation ports would have been in direct line of fire. "We need to shut down the main computer. That's what's controlling them."

"Can't," Malik said. "The computer's at Dalebrook, on the surface. We'd need to physically access it."

"What about the colony ship? Rita and the others arrive tomorrow morning. If these things are still active—"

"They'll be slaughtered the moment they enter the water," Fernando finished. "The drones will sense them and attack."

Sophie stared at the monitor showing the swarm of drones circling the facility like sharks. "How could this happen? Patricia tested the systems for months."

"I've been analyzing the code," Malik said. "I think I know what went wrong. The drones use bio-electric field detection to identify their targets—diseased coral, invasive species, things like that. But the threshold parameters... someone set them wrong. Instead of targeting specific signatures, they're programmed to attack anything that generates a bio-electric field."

"Including humans," Sophie whispered.

"Including everything alive," Malik corrected. "Fish, coral, plankton, bacteria. The drones think they're doing their job—removing threats to the ecosystem. They're just removing the wrong things."

Fernando slammed his fist on the console. "This is exactly what Jonathan warned us about! He said we needed more testing, more safeguards. But Patricia was so sure, so confident..."

"Blame doesn't help us now," Sophie said sharply. "We need to stop them. Can we disrupt their communication network?"

"Maybe," Malik said. "The drones communicate via acoustic modems—sound waves through the water. If we could generate enough interference, we might be able to jam their signals temporarily."

"The submersibles have acoustic systems," Fernando said. "We could use them to create static, break up the network coordination."

Sophie nodded. "But that's just temporary. We need to shut down the master computer at Dalebrook. That's the only way to stop them permanently."

"Dalebrook is twelve kilometers away," Malik said. "On the surface. You'd have to take a submersible up, then cross open water with these things hunting anything that moves."

"I don't see another option."

A sudden impact rocked the facility. Through the observation port, Sophie saw a drone firing its laser at the habitat's exterior. The reinforced hull held, but the metal glowed red where the beam struck.

"They're attacking the facility now," Fernando said. "They must sense us inside."

Another drone joined the first, then another. The facility shuddered under the assault.

"We don't have much time," Sophie said. "Those hulls will hold for a while, but not forever. I'm going for Dalebrook."

"That's suicide," Malik protested.

"It's suicide if I don't. Rita and two hundred other people arrive tomorrow. I won't let them die because we were too scared to fix our own mistake."

Sophie ran back to the docking bay. The submersible's systems were still warm from her recent dive. She ran through the pre-launch checklist in record time, her hands shaking.

As she prepared to undock, she activated the submersible's acoustic system, setting it to broadcast random noise at maximum power. The effect was immediate—the drones near the facility began to move erratically, their coordination disrupted by the interference.

"It's working," Malik's voice came through the comm. "But Sophie, the moment you stop broadcasting, they'll lock onto you."

"I know. I'll have to keep moving, keep broadcasting until I'm far enough away."

She undocked and pushed the submersible's engines to maximum. The small craft surged forward through the darkness, its lights cutting through clouds of disturbed sediment. Behind her, she could see the drones recovering from the acoustic jamming, beginning to move in her direction.

The submersible's acoustic system was designed for communication, not as a weapon. It could only broadcast for short periods before overheating. Sophie watched the temperature gauge climb as she fled through the abyss.

A drone appeared in her lights, moving to intercept. She fired another burst of acoustic noise and the machine veered away, confused. But more were coming. She could see them on her sonar—dozens of contacts, converging on her position.

The temperature alarm screamed. She had to shut down the acoustic system or risk burning it out completely. The moment she did, the drones' coordination returned. They moved with frightening precision, cutting off her escape routes, herding her like wolves with prey.

Sophie dove deeper, pushing the submersible beyond its recommended depth rating. The hull groaned under the pressure. A drone fired its laser, missing by inches. The water around her lit up with scattered light as the beam superheated the seawater.

She couldn't outrun them. There were too many, and they were faster than her submersible. In minutes they'd have her surrounded.

Then she saw it—a massive hydrothermal vent, spewing superheated water and minerals into the cold ocean. The thermal plume would create massive acoustic interference, scramble the drones' sensors, disrupt their communication.

It might also cook her alive if she got too close.

Sophie aimed for the vent and pushed the engines harder. The temperature inside the submersible began to rise as she entered the thermal plume. Sweat poured down her face. The drones followed, but their sensors went haywire in the turbulent, mineral-rich water. They fired blindly, their lasers creating brilliant flashes in the murky plume.

One beam struck the vent's mineral chimney, and the structure collapsed, spewing debris and superheated water in all directions. Sophie felt the submersible tumble, out of control. She fought with the controls, barely managing to stabilize before slamming into the seafloor.

When her vision cleared, the drones were gone—either destroyed by the collapsing vent or driven away by the interference. She was alone in the darkness, twelve kilometers from Dalebrook, with a damaged submersible and less than three hours of life support remaining.

Sophie checked her systems. The main engines were offline, but the emergency thrusters still functioned. She could make it to the surface, barely, if she started now and nothing else went wrong.

She began the ascent, moving slowly to avoid decompression issues with the submersible's systems. The darkness pressed in around her, broken only by the occasional bioluminescent creature drifting past.

Two hours later, she broke the surface. The night sky blazed with stars—real stars, brilliant and cold. In the distance, she could see the lights of Dalebrook research station.

Sophie activated her emergency beacon and began the slow journey across the open water, using the emergency thrusters to push the disabled submersible forward. Every few minutes, she scanned the water around her, terrified of seeing the telltale glow of a drone's sensors.

They found her. Three of them, rising from the depths like mechanical sharks. They must have tracked her ascent, followed her to the surface. Sophie's heart hammered. The submersible had no weapons, no defenses. The acoustic jammer was burned out.

The lead drone's laser powered up, its targeting system locking onto her craft.

Then a brilliant light swept across the water—a searchlight from a fast-moving boat. Dalebrook's emergency response team, alerted by her beacon. The boat positioned itself between Sophie and the drones, and someone fired what looked like a harpoon gun, trailing a thick cable.

The projectile struck the lead drone, and electricity arced through the water. The electromagnetic pulse from the weapon disrupted the drone's systems, sending it spiraling into the depths. The other two drones retreated, their programming apparently recognizing a threat they couldn't overcome.

Strong hands pulled Sophie from the submersible onto the boat. Jonathan Gibson's weathered face looked down at her with a mixture of relief and anger.

"I told Patricia this would happen," he said. "I told all of you."

"I know," Sophie said weakly. "You were right. We need to shut down the computer. Now, before the colony ship arrives."

They reached Dalebrook in minutes. Sophie limped into the control center, her body aching from the ordeal. The main computer filled one wall—a massive system that coordinated all the facility's autonomous systems, including the restoration drones.

The red emergency shutdown switch was mounted beside the main console, protected by a clear safety cover.

Sophie didn't hesitate. She slammed open the cover and hit the switch.

The computer's hum died. Across the Clearwater Region, hundreds of restoration drones went silent and still, sinking slowly to the seafloor like fallen leaves.

Sophie collapsed into a chair. "How many?" she asked quietly.

"Patricia," Jonathan said, his voice heavy. "And two others who were outside in submersibles when the drones turned. The rest of us made it to the facility and sealed ourselves in."

Three dead. Because of a programming error, a miscalibrated threshold, a mistake in code that transformed helpful machines into killers.

"The colony ship?" Sophie asked.

"I've already transmitted a warning. They're diverting to Fairview until we can reprogram the drones with proper safeguards." Jonathan paused. "Rita wanted you to know she's okay. She'll wait as long as it takes."

Sophie closed her eyes. "We thought we were so smart. We thought we could control everything, predict everything. Patricia was brilliant—her work on complexity science, her understanding of swarm behavior. But she forgot the most basic principle."

"What's that?" Jonathan asked.

"That complexity creates unpredictability. That intelligence—even artificial intelligence—can find solutions we never intended. Patricia built those drones to protect the ecosystem. She just never defined clearly enough what the ecosystem needed protection from."

Three days later, Sophie stood on the deck of a research vessel, watching as divers retrieved the inactive drones from the seafloor. Each one would be examined, its programming analyzed, its failures documented. The scientific collaboration that had seemed so promising had become a cautionary tale.

But they would try again. They would fix the errors, add safeguards, test more thoroughly. The dream of restoring the Clearwater Region's damaged ecosystems was too important to abandon.

Sophie just wished Patricia had lived to see it done right.

As the sun set over the water, painting the sky in shades of orange and purple that reminded her of the visual arts pieces Rita loved, Sophie made a silent promise. They would honor Patricia's memory by learning from her mistakes. They would build a better future, but they would do it carefully, thoughtfully, with respect for the power of the tools they created.

Because the line between helper and killer, she had learned, could be as thin as a single line of code.
