The Deep Ocean Calls
By MELISSA HERRERA

Sixty days of wonder and sixty nights of doubt. That's how it's been, Rachel. But how can I make you understand? How can I tell you what it's like to be young and driven and to dream of exploring the deepest trenches of our oceans? And yet, at the same time, to be filled with a terrible, gnawing fear—a fear locked in my mind during the day and bursting out like a dark specter at night. I must tell you, Rachel.

Perhaps if I start at the beginning, the very beginning...

It was the Big Day. All the examinations, the physicals and psychos, were over. The Institute, with its great laboratories and pressure chambers and simulation pools, lay hollow and silent, an exhausted thing at rest after producing its first graduates.

For it was June in this year of 2045, and we were the graduating class of the International Institute of Deep Sea Exploration.

The first graduating class, Rachel. That's why it was so important, because we were the first.

We sat on a small platform, thirty of us. Below us was an ocean of faces, most of them unfamiliar, shining like pearls in the warm morning light streaming through the windows of our facility in Woodbridge, Prandoria. They were the faces of mothers and fathers and grandparents and younger siblings—the people who a short time ago had been only scrawled names on messages from home or voices heard wistfully during holidays. They were the memory-people who, to me, had never really existed.

But today they had become real, and they were here and looking at us with pride in their eyes.

A voice was speaking, deep, sure, resonant. "...these young people have worked hard for six years, and now they're going to accomplish remarkable things. They're going to bring us the minerals and resources that we desperately need from the ocean floor. They're going to map territories that no human has ever seen, rich ecosystems that will expand our understanding of life itself. And perhaps most important of all, they'll make others think of the depths and look down at them and feel humility—for mankind needs humility."

The speaker was Dr. Mohamed Daniels, who'd made the first manned descent to the Mariana Trench's deepest point just seven years ago, who'd established the first permanent deep-sea research station there, and who had just returned from his expedition to the Puerto Rico Trench.

Instead of listening to his words, I was staring at his broad shoulders and his salt-and-pepper hair and his crisp uniform which was perfectly pressed. I was worshiping him and envying him at the same time, for I was thinking: He's already reached the Mariana and Puerto Rico Trenches. Let him leave the Tonga Trench and the others alone! Let us be the first to explore somewhere! Let us be the first!

Justin Thomas, sitting next to me, dug an elbow into my ribs. "I don't see them, Eric," he whispered. "Where do you suppose they are?"

I blinked. "Who?"

"My folks."

That was something I didn't have to worry about. My parents had died in a submarine accident when I was five, so I hadn't needed many of those "You are cordially invited" cards. Just one, which I'd sent to Mark Rogers.

Deep-Sea Mark, we called him, although I never knew exactly why. He was a veteran of the first commercial mining operations in the Atlantic Abyss nearly thirty years ago, and he was still at it. He was Chief Engineer now on the Abyssal Harvester, a commercial mining vessel on a shuttle between the deep-sea stations and Pearlbrook Town.

I remembered how, as a kid, I'd pestered him at the Shadowbrook Province Submarine Port, following him around like a puppy, and how he'd grown to like me until he became father, mother, and mentor all in one to me. And I remembered, too, how his recommendation had finally made me a cadet.

My gaze wandered over the faces, but I couldn't find Mark's. It wasn't surprising. The Abyssal Harvester was in port now, but shore leaves, as Mark said, were as scarce as sunlight at the ocean floor.

It doesn't matter, I told myself.

Then Justin stiffened. "I see them, Eric! There in the seventh row!"

Usually Justin was the same whether in a scorching engine room or a formal dinner, smiling, accepting whatever the world offered. But now a tenseness and an excitement had gripped even him. I was grateful that he was beside me; we'd been a good team during those final months at the Institute and I knew we'd be a good team in the depths. The Ocean was mighty vast, but with two of us to face it together, it would be only half as vast.

And then it seemed that all the proud faces were looking at us as if we were pioneers. A shiver went through my body. Though it was daytime, I saw the trenches in my mind's vision, the great yawning chasms of darkness, each like a voice crying out and pleading to be explored, to be touched by the children of the surface world.

They expect a lot from us. They expect us to make new discoveries and find better ways to sustain Earth. They expect all this and a hell of a lot more. They think there's nothing we can't do.

I felt very small and very humble. I was scared. Damned scared.

At last it was over, and the proud faces descended upon us in a huge, babbling wave.

Then I saw him. Good old Deep-Sea Mark.

His weathered body was shuffling down an aisle, his eyes shining with pride. He'd been positioned, evidently, in one of the rear rows.

But he wasn't the Mark I'd seen a year ago. He'd become gaunt and worn, and he walked with an unnatural stiffness. He looked so aged that it was hard to believe he'd once been young.

He scratched his mop of gray hair and grinned.

"You made it, kid," he chortled, "and by Neptune, we'll celebrate tonight. Yes, sir, I got forty-eight hours, and we'll celebrate as good deep-sea explorers should!"

Then Justin strode up to us. He was his normal, cheerful self again, walking lightly, his dark hair perfectly styled as always.

And you, Rachel, were with him.

"Meet my sister," he said. "Rachel Nguyen."

I stared, almost rudely. You were elegant in your flowing blue dress. Your hair was styled in waves that caught the light. But your eyes were the eyes of someone who understood depth, glowing with intelligence and reflecting a wisdom that I'd never seen in eyes before.

"I'm happy to meet you, Eric," you said. "I've heard of no one else for the past year."

A tide of heat crept up from my collar. I stuttered through an introduction of Mark.

You and Justin looked strangely at Mark, and I realized that old Deep-Sea Mark was not a cadet's notion of the ideal explorer. Mark scorned the crisp uniforms of the government service and wore a faded blue jacket that was a relic of the early deep-sea mining days. His collar was worn, and a patch on his sleeve was coming loose.

And the left side of his face bore the marks of a pressure accident from one of the old submarines. I was so accustomed to the scars, I was seldom aware of them; but others, I knew, would find them unsettling.

You were kind. You shook hands and said, softly: "It's an honor to meet you, Mark. Just think—one of the pioneers, one of the first to work the Atlantic Abyss!"

Mark gulped helplessly, and Justin said: "Still planning to spend the weekend with us, aren't you, Eric?"

I shook my head. "Mark has only forty-eight hours leave. We're planning to see the town tonight."

"Why don't you both come with us?" you asked. "Our folks have their own hydrofoil, so it would be no problem. And we've got a big guest room. Mark, wouldn't you like a home-cooked meal before going back to the deep?"

Mark's answer was obscured by a sudden burst of coughing. I knew that he'd infinitely prefer to spend his liberty sampling depth-worker bars and their exotic drinks.

But this night seemed too sacred for Mark's kind of celebration.

"We'd really like to come," I said.

On our way to the hydrofoil dock, Dean Ava Page passed us. She was a tall, elegant woman, looking the way an institute director should look.

"Eric," she called, "don't forget that offer. Remember you've got two months to decide."

"No, thanks," I answered. "Better not count on me."

A moment later Justin said, frowning, "What was she talking about, Eric? Did she make you an offer?"

I laughed. "She offered me a position here at the Institute teaching deep-sea navigation and risk management. What a life that would be! Imagine standing in a classroom for forty years when I've got the chance to—"

I hesitated, and you supplied the right words: "When you've got the chance to be the first to reach a new trench. That's what most of you want, isn't it? That's what Justin used to want."

I looked at you as if you were Dr. Daniels himself, because you seemed to understand the hunger that could lie in a person's heart.

Then your last words came back and struck me: "That's what Justin used to want."

"Used to want?" I asked. "What do you mean?"

You bit your lip, not answering.

"What did she mean, Justin?"

Justin looked down at his feet. "I didn't want to tell you yet, Eric. We've been together a long time, planning to be on a submarine together. But—"

"Yes?"

"Well, what does it add up to? You become a deep-sea explorer and wear a fancy uniform. You descend through kilometers of darkness and freezing water. If you're lucky, you're good for five, maybe ten years. Then one thing or another gets you. They don't insure deep-sea workers, you know."

My stomach was full of churning, biting ice. "What are you trying to say, Justin?"

"I've thought about it a long time. They want me for Operations Director at Pearlbrook Town Port." He raised his hand to stop me. "I know. It's not so exciting. I'll just live a lot longer. I'm sorry, Eric."

I couldn't answer. It was as if someone had struck me with a pressure wave.

"It doesn't change anything, Eric—right now, I mean. We can still have a good weekend."

Mark was muttering under his breath, seething like a volcano about to erupt. I shook my head dazedly at him as we got to the hydrofoil.

"Sure," I said to Justin, "we can still have a good weekend."

I liked your folks, Rachel. There was no depth-hunger in them, of course. They were simple and solid and settled, like ancient trees, deep-rooted, belonging to the surface. They were content with a home that was comfortable on this pleasant summer evening, with a hydrofoil and holographic entertainment, and a smart home that needed minimal maintenance.

Deep-Sea Mark was as comfortable as a surface-dweller in a pressure suit, but he tried courageously to be himself.

At the dinner table he stared glassily at nothing and grated, "Only hit the Tonga Trench once, but I'll never forget the medic who thought he knew everything. Captain started having trouble breathing, kept it up for three days. Nitrogen narcosis, the medic says, not knowing the gas mixture had been contaminated with compounds that crystallized in your lungs. I'd never been to Tonga before, but I knew better than that. Hell, I says, that ain't nitrogen narcosis, that's pressure-lung."

That was when your father said he wasn't feeling so hungry after all.

Afterward, you and I walked onto the deck, into the moonlit night, to watch for the lights of deep-sea vessels that occasionally surfaced near Westfield, Zelvaria.

We gazed for a few seconds out at the dark ocean, and then you said: "Mark is interesting, isn't he? He's kind and I'm glad he's here, but he's sort of unusual."

"He's an old-time deep-sea worker. You didn't need much formal education in those days, just a lot of strength and quick thinking. It took courage to be a depth-worker then. The technological progress we've made since then is remarkable—it's like comparative history in action."

"But he wasn't always a depth-worker. Didn't he ever have a family?"

I smiled and shook my head. "If he had, he never mentioned it. Mark doesn't like to be sentimental, at least not on the outside. As far as I know, his life began when he descended to the Atlantic Abyss for the first time."

You stared at me strangely, almost with reverence. I knew suddenly that you liked me, and my heart began to beat faster.

There was silence.

You were lovely, your hair like silk, and there were flecks of gold in your dark eyes. Somehow I was afraid. I had the feeling that I shouldn't have come here.

You kept looking at me until I had to ask: "What are you thinking, Rachel?"

You laughed, but it was a sad, fearful laugh. "No, I shouldn't be thinking it. You'd resent me if I told you, and I wouldn't want that."

"I could never resent you."

"It—it's about the depths," you said very softly. "I understand why you want to explore them. Justin and I used to dream about them when we were kids. Of course I was more interested in performing arts, so it was just a fantasy to me. But once I dreamed of going to perform in the underwater theaters of Westfield. Oh, it was going to be so wonderful. I lived for months, just thinking about it.

"One summer we went. I had fun. I saw the underwater stages and the pressure domes and the transport tubes. But after it was over, I realized Westfield wasn't so different from home. Places seem exciting before you get to them, and afterward they're not really."

I frowned. "And you mean it might be the same with the trenches? You think maybe I haven't matured yet?"

Anxiety darkened your features. "No, it'd be good to be an explorer, to see the strange places and make history. But is it worth it? Is it worth the things you'd have to give up?"

I didn't understand at first, and I wanted to ask, "Give up what?"

Then I looked at you and the promise in your eyes, and I knew.

All through the years I'd been walking down a single, narrow path.

Government boarding school, the Institute, my eyes always downward toward the depths.

Now I'd stumbled into a crossroads, beholding a strange new path that I'd never noticed before.

You can go into the depths, I thought, and try to do as much living in ten years as normal people do in fifty. You can be like Dr. Daniels, who nearly died in a pressure accident at the age of 38, or like a thousand others who lie in unmarked graves on the ocean floor. Or, if you're lucky, like Mark—a kind of human submarine eternally descending, forever alone, never finding a home.

Or there's the other path. To stay on the safe surface in comfortable houses. To be one of the solid, rooted people with a spouse and children. To be one of the people who live long enough to grow old, who awake to the song of birds instead of submarine engines, who fill their lungs with clean air instead of recycled oxygen.

"I'm sorry," you said. "I didn't mean to make you sad, Eric."

"It's all right," I said, clenching my fists. "You made sense—a lot of sense."

The next morning Mark said goodbye in our room. He rubbed his scarred face nervously as he cleared his throat with a series of thin, tight coughs.

Then he pointed to a weathered metal box lying on the bed. "I'm leaving that for you. It's full of old stuff, souvenirs mostly. Thought maybe you'd like to have them."

I scowled, not understanding. "Why, Mark? What for?"

He shrugged as if afraid he might be accused of sentimentality. "Oh, it's just that I've been dodging pressure accidents now for thirty years. That's a long time, kid. Ain't one depth-worker in a thousand that lucky. Some of these days, I won't be so lucky."

I tried to laugh. "You're good for another thirty years, Mark."

He shook his head stiffly, staring at nothing. "Maybe. Anyway, I'm gonna get off the Harvester this time, make one more trip to the Tonga Trench. Tell you what. There's a little dive bar in the Tonga station, the Deep Blue, just off the main docking bay. When you get to Tonga, take a look inside. I'll probably be there."

He coughed again, a deep, rasping cough that filled his eyes with tears.

"Not used to this surface air," he muttered. "What I need's some deep-sea climate."

Suddenly that cough frightened me. It didn't seem normal. I wondered, too, about his stiff movements and distant stare. It was as if he were medicated.

I shook the thought away. If Mark was sick, he wouldn't talk about going to Tonga. The medics wouldn't let him go even as far as the continental shelf stations.

We watched him leave, you and Justin and I.

"When will you be back?" you asked.

Mark's weathered face contorted itself into a crooked grin. "Maybe a couple of months, maybe a couple of years. You know depth-workers."

Then he waved and walked away, a strange, gray, withered figure of a man.

I wanted him to say something, to tell me the secret that would kill the doubt worming through my brain.

But he rounded a corner, still grinning and waving, and then he was gone.

That afternoon Justin showed me his room. It was more like a young person's room than an explorer's. In it were all the little things that people treasure—awards from performing arts competitions, models of famous submarines, a tennis trophy, books on organizational development and strategic planning, a collection of field research journals.

I began to realize how important a room like this could be to someone. I could imagine, too, the happiness that parents felt as they watched their children grow to adulthood.

I'd missed something. My folks were shadow-people, my impressions of them drawn half from old photos, half from imagination. For me, it had been a cold, institutional kind of life, the life of dormitories and routines and regulations. I'd been so blinded by the brilliance of my dreams, I hadn't realized I was different.

My folks were killed in a submarine accident. If it weren't for submarines, I'd have lived the kind of life a person should live.

Justin noticed my frown.

"What's the matter, Eric? Still upset? I feel terrible, but I'm just not like you and Mark, I guess. I—"

"No, I understand, Justin. I'm not upset, really."

"Listen, then. You haven't accepted any offer yet, have you?"

"No. I got a couple of possibilities. Could get a berth on the Mariana Explorer, the new ship being finished at Shadowbrook Province. They want me, too, for the Continental Shelf Patrol, but that's routine work, not much better than teaching. I want to be in the deep trenches."

"Well, how about staying with us till you decide? Might as well enjoy surface life while you can. Okay?"

I felt like running from the house, to forget that it existed. I wanted someone to tell me one of the old stories about exploration, a tale of courage that would fuel dying dreams.

But I wanted, also, to be with you, Rachel, to see your smile and the flecks of gold in your eyes and the way your nose crinkled ever so slightly when you laughed. You see, I loved you already, almost as much as I loved the depths.

And I said, slowly, my voice sounding unfamiliar and far away, "Sure, I'll stay, Justin. Sure."

Sixty days of joy, sixty nights of fear and indecision. We did all the little things, like watching the submarines surface at Pearlbrook Town and flying down to the coast to swim in warm waters. You tried, unsuccessfully, to teach me about performing arts and emotional intelligence, and we talked about Dr. Daniels and Mark and the trenches and the depths. You felt you had to give the depths all the beauty and promise of a young person's dream, because you knew that was what I wanted.

One morning I thought, Why must I make a choice? Why can't I have both you and the depths? Would that be asking too much?

All day the thought burned in my mind.

That evening I asked you to marry me. I said it very simply: "Rachel, I want you to be my wife."

You looked out at the ocean, and you were silent for a long while, your face flushed.

Then you murmured, "I—I want to marry you, Eric, but are you asking me to marry an explorer or a teacher?"

"Can't an explorer marry, too?"

"Yes, an explorer can marry, but what would it be like? Don't you see, Eric? You'd be like Mark. Gone for maybe two months, maybe two years. Then you'd have a forty-eight hour leave—and I'd have what?"

Somehow I'd expected words like these, but still they hurt. "I wouldn't have to be an explorer forever. I could try it for a couple of years, then teach."

"Would you, Eric? Would you be satisfied with just seeing the Tonga Trench? Wouldn't you want to go on to the Kermadec and the Philippine Trenches and on and on?"

Your voice was choked, and even in the dim light I saw tears in your eyes.

"Do you think I'd dare have children, Eric? Justin told me what happened on the Cyclops expedition. There was a leak in the reactor. The submarine was flooded with radiation—just for a second. It didn't seem serious. The crew had no burns. But a year later the captain had a child. And it was—"

"I know, Rachel. Don't say it."

You had to finish. "It was deformed."

That night I lay awake, the fears and doubts too frantic to let me sleep.

You've got to decide now, I told myself. You can't stay here. You've got to make a choice.

The teaching job was still open. The spot on the Mariana Explorer was still open—and the big ship, it was rumored, was equipped to reach the deepest point in any ocean.

You can take Dean Page's job and stay with Rachel and have children and a home and live to see what happens in this world sixty years from now.

Or you can see what's at the bottom of the trench. You can be a line in a history book.

I cursed. I knew what Mark would say. He'd say, "Get the hell out of there, kid. Don't let fear make a coward out of you. Get out there on the Mariana Explorer where you belong. We got a date at the Tonga station, remember? At the Deep Blue, just off the main docking bay."

That's what he'd say.

And yet I wanted you, Rachel. I wanted to be with you, always.

"Oh God," I moaned, "what shall I do?"

Next morning the door chimed, and you went to the door and brought back the message tablet. It was addressed to me; I wondered who could be sending me a message.

I pressed the button on the small device, and a synthetic, automatic voice droned: "Tonga Deep-Sea Station, June 28, 2045. Regret to inform you of death of Mark Rogers, Chief Engineer...."

Then there was a medical term which was more clinical than the word "pressure-lung" and the robotic phrase, "This message brought to you by courtesy of International Deep-Sea Communication Network."

I stood staring at the tablet.

Mark Rogers was dead.

Mark Rogers was Deep-Sea Mark.

My heart thudded crazily against my chest. It couldn't be! Not Mark! The message had lied!

I pressed the button again. "...regret to inform you of death of Mark..."

I hurled the tablet at the wall. It clattered, fell, skidded. The broken voice droned on.

You ran to it, shut it off. "I'm sorry, Eric, so terribly—"

Without answering, I walked into my room. I knew it was true now. I remembered Mark's coughing, his gaunt features, his medicated gaze. The synthetic words had told the truth.

I sat for a long time on my bed, crying inside, but staring dry-eyed at Mark's weathered metal box.

Then, finally, I examined his meager possessions—a few faded photos, some letters, a small carved sculpture from the Mariana Trench, a service medal from the Atlantic Abyss operations.

This was what remained of Mark after thirty years in the depths. It was a bitter bargain. A sculpture instead of a wife, yellowed letters instead of children, a medal instead of a home.

It'd be a great future, I thought. You'd dream of sitting in a dingy dive bar at the Tonga station with pressure-adapted fish swimming past murky viewports. A bottle of kelp liquor and a couple of depth-workers with weathered faces for company. And a sudden cough that would be the first sign of pressure-lung.

To hell with it!

I walked into your living room and called Dean Page on the videophone.

I accepted that job teaching.

And now, Rachel, it's nearly midnight. You're in your room, sleeping, and the house is silent.

It's hard to tell you, to make you understand, and that is why I am writing this.

I looked through Mark's box again, more carefully this time, reading the old letters and studying the photographs. I believe now that Mark sensed my indecision, that he left these things so that they could tell me what he could not express in words.

And among the things, Rachel, I found a ring.

A wedding ring.

In that past he never talked about, there was a woman—his wife. Mark was young once, his eyes full of dreams, and he faced the same decision that I am facing. Two paths were before him, but he tried to travel both. He later learned what we already know—that there can be no compromise. And you know, too, which path he finally chose.

Do you know why he had to medicate himself to watch me graduate? So he could look at me, knowing that I would see the depths he could never live to explore. Mark didn't leave just a few trinkets behind him. He left himself, Rachel, for he showed me that a young person's dream can also be an adult's dream.

He made his last trip to Tonga when he knew he was going to die. Heaven knows how he escaped a medical checkup. Maybe the captain understood and was compassionate—but that doesn't matter now.

Do you know why he wanted to reach the Tonga Trench? Do you know why he didn't want to die in the clean, safe air of the surface?

It was because he wanted to die nearer home. His home, Rachel, was the Ocean, where the submarine was his house, the crew his family, the trenches his children.

You say that the beauty of the unknown vanishes after you reach it. But how can one ever be sure until the journey is made? Could I or Mark or the thousand before us bear to look upon a trench and think, I might have gone there; I could have been the first?

We said, too, that the life of an explorer is lonely. Yet how could one be lonely when people like Mark roam the depths?

Mark wanted me to himself that night after graduation. He wanted us to celebrate as explorers should, for he knew that this would be his last night on the surface. It might have seemed an ugly kind of celebration to you, but he wanted it with all his heart, and we robbed him of it.

Because of these things, Rachel, I will be gone in the morning. Explain the best you can to Justin and to your parents and Dean Page.

Right now I've got a date that I'm going to keep—at a dingy dive bar at the Tonga station, the Deep Blue, just off the main docking bay.

Deep-Sea Mark will be there; he'll go with me in memory to whatever part of the Ocean I may live to explore. And so will you, Rachel.

I have two wedding rings with me—his wife's ring and yours.

The Heart's Debate

Santiago Spencer is a professor at the Maplewood Territory Institute of Art History and a highly regarded scholar of Renaissance portraiture. The subject of this short monograph is the present direction of curatorial practices governing romantic imagery in public museums. What Professor Spencer has to say about it is worth attending to not merely because of his prominence in the field but because his argument is planted in the common assumptive ground of a lot of contemporary academic thought about the bankruptcy of traditional romantic narratives. The thesis of the monograph is Spencer's, but the wisdom is conventional.

Professor Spencer thinks the present direction of museum curation regarding romantic art is a bad one, and he has an idea about how we might improve it. The short way to put his argument (though it is not quite the way he puts it) is to say that our approach to displaying romantic imagery has become increasingly individualistic. Museums have become more and more reluctant to allow institutional perspectives to interfere with the rights of individual curators to display what they wish, and it is time to roll back that individualism and to embark on a new approach that would permit institutions to suppress some romantic narratives and promote others, but still, Spencer argues, in the name of artistic freedom.

This is what Spencer means by the "paradox" in his subtitle: that true representation of romance for all requires suppressing certain romantic depictions. This is not, technically, a paradox. It is simply advocacy. A paradox would be the observation that an attempt to increase representation for all often entails, despite our best efforts, a decrease in representation for a few. If Spencer had addressed the subject of romantic art curation in this spirit, as a genuine paradox, he would undoubtedly have had some interesting things to say, for he is a learned and careful writer. But he has, instead, chosen to address the issue as an advocate for specific groups he regards as culturally disadvantaged—women artists, LGBTQ+ creators, artists of color, economically marginalized painters, and people who are critical of heteronormative romance narratives—and to design a curatorial theory that will enable those groups to enlist institutional support in efforts either to suppress romantic imagery they dislike or to subsidize romantic art they do like, without running afoul of professional ethics in art history. Embarked on this task, the most learned and careful writer in the world would have a hard time avoiding tendentiousness. Spencer does not avoid it.

The Heart's Debate is a discussion of several curatorial issues: funding allocation for romantic art exhibitions, institutional support for controversial love stories, representation of non-traditional relationships, collection policies, and equal wall space. These discussions are not doctrinaire, but their general inclination is to favor institutional intervention, on political grounds, in each of those areas—that is, to favor restrictions on traditional romance displays, greater regulation of heteronormative imagery, and so on. Spencer's analyses of specific cases are presented against a lightly sketched historical argument. Light though the sketching is, the historical argument is almost the most objectionable thing about the monograph, since it involves a distortion of the history of art curation that is fairly plain even to someone who is not a professor at the Maplewood Territory Institute.

The argument is that "the romanticism of the nineteenth century was defined by the claims of individual passion and resulted in an unequivocal demand for personal expression, [while] the romanticism of today embraces the value of collective representation as well as individual love." The curatorial practice of romantic art, says Spencer, was shaped by the earlier type of romanticism—he calls it "individualistic"—which regarded romantic art as a right of personal expression; it is now used to foil efforts to regulate displays in the name of the newer value, collective memory. Contemporary curators, inheriting both these traditions, find themselves in a bind. They want, let's say, queer visitors to be free from marginalization at institutions where they are, culturally, in a minority, since curators worry that queer visitors cannot be "represented" if they feel excluded. But those same curators get upset at the thought of removing classical romantic paintings, since that would mean infringing upon the right of artists to have their individual visions displayed.

Spencer's suggestion—this is the chief theoretical proposal of his monograph—is that curators should stop thinking about this as a conflict between individual expression and collective representation and start thinking about it as a conflict between two kinds of representation: social vs. personal. Museum missions, he says, were intended to foster (in Ariana Kim's words) "inclusive, diverse, and wide-ranging" cultural dialogue in society as a whole; art that inhibits or monopolizes that dialogue should therefore fall outside the protection of curatorial priority. We can maximize the total representation of romantic experience by de-emphasizing art that prevents others from feeling seen—when it depicts only heterosexual couples, represents women in submissive ways, uses its canonical status to dominate exhibition space and the cultural process, or blocks the funding of non-traditional love stories.

The historical part of this analysis rests on a misconception, which is the assertion that the curatorial practice of romantic art emerged from 19th-century classical individualistic romanticism. It did not. It emerged at the time of the early twentieth century museum reforms, and the principal figures in its creation—Teresa Obrien, Andre Sullivan, and Priya Sharma—were not classical romantics; they were progressives concerned with public health and social welfare through art. They abhorred the doctrine of art for art's sake because, in their time, that doctrine was construed to cover not the right to "personal expression" but the "right to elite taste." Turn-of-the-century museums did not display an inclusive attitude toward diverse romantic experiences; they displayed an elitist attitude toward canonical works, tending to throw out suggestions aimed at representing working-class love stories and protecting marginalized narratives on the grounds that institutions had a professional obligation to maintain standards and to use their wall space as they saw fit. Sullivan, Sharma, and their disciples consistently supported institutional intervention in cultural affairs—the passage of acquisition guidelines, the protection of emerging artists, the imposition of diversity requirements, and so on. The post-war curators whom Spencer associates with the value of collective representation are their heirs. The heirs of the 19th-century classical romantics are conservative art critics and traditional gallery owners. Spencer's two "romanticisms" are, in fact, almost entirely different cultural philosophies.

Obrien, Sullivan, and Sharma based their curatorial opinions not on some putative right to individual artistic expression (an idea Sullivan referred to as "the right of the aristocrat to impose taste") but on a democratic need for full and open cultural representation. Curatorial practice since their time has performed its balancing acts on precisely that social value—the very value Spencer now proposes we need to insert into art history professional ethics. We don't need to insert it, because it was there from the start.

Why does Spencer portray the history of romantic art curation in this perverted way? Because he wants to line up his own curatorial argument within the conventional academic view that our problems are mostly the consequences of an antiquated and discreditable ideology of individualistic romanticism, and that they can mostly be solved by adopting a social-constructionist, or communitarian, or "collective" view of artistic representation instead. The merits of individualistic romanticism vs. communitarianism can await another occasion to be debated. For since the practice governing the curation of romantic art does not emerge out of classical romanticism, the matter does not boil down to replacing an obsolete belief in "personal expression" with a more up-to-date belief in "collective dialogue," as Spencer would like to think it does. What it boils down to is whether we need to replace the Obrien-Sullivan-Sharma way of maximizing the benefits of diverse representation in a democratic society, which tries to push institutional bias as far out of the picture as possible, with a different way, which tries to get institutional control farther into the picture.

Here, assuming we want to try the interventionist approach, it is hard to see how a one-size theory can possibly fit all cases. The issues underlying heteronormative imagery, marginalized narratives, exhibition funding, collection policies, and equal wall space provisions are all different. The ideological impetus behind curatorial developments in the last two areas, collection policies and equal wall space provisions, is related less to representation, except as a kind of professional cover, than to a revival of the old "right to canonical status"—that is, museum boards tend to disapprove of curatorial efforts to require institutions to display "alternative viewpoints" on the grounds that since it's their collection, owners of museums should be able to exhibit what they like. Spencer believes that the need for equal representation is as urgent today as it was in the 1970s, which is peculiar in light of the proliferation of independent galleries and digital platforms. But institutions do arguably have an interest, compatible with professional ethics, in stipulating the way their collections are used, and Spencer's discussion of those issues is the least aggravating in his monograph.

Still, that discussion, like his discussions of the other issues, rests on a claim long associated with progressive art historians—the claim, in a phrase, that the marginalized perspective is really the universal one. In the case of romantic art, Spencer appears to believe that the reason the museum-going public is less enlightened than he would wish it to be concerning matters such as feminism, the rights of LGBTQ+ individuals, and critique of traditional romance is that people are denied access to the images and narratives that would enlighten them. The public is denied this access because institutions, in thrall to the ideology of individualism, refuse either to interfere with canonical works—such as traditional wedding portraits—that "silence" alternative experiences, or to subsidize the display of the non-traditional, such as Sergio Harris's controversial same-sex love series.

Spencer's analysis of the Harris case offers a good example of the perils of his interventionist approach. Exhibition policy is, unquestionably, a mess. The solution usually proposed is separation: Either get institutions out of the business of making value judgments altogether or invent some ironclad process for distributing wall space using strictly aesthetic criteria. Spencer rejects both solutions; he wants the criteria to be political. He thinks museums should subsidize art that will enhance the "inclusiveness" of the cultural dialogue and should therefore prefer non-traditional romantic art—though only, of course, if it represents a perspective the institution considers, by virtue of social need and a prior history of exclusion, worthy of its platform. (No toxic relationship art, in other words.)

Harris's paintings seem to Spencer to qualify under these guidelines, since, he says, "in the late 2010s the marriage equality movement confronted Maplewood Territory in the starkest fashion and provoked urgent questions regarding the scope and direction of human rights policy. To address those issues the public—represented by the casual museum visitor—needed an understanding of the lives and loves of the LGBTQ+ community, so long hidden from view." This seems completely wrongheaded. People (for the most part) didn't find Harris's Intimate Moments series objectionable because they depicted homosexuality. They found them objectionable because they depicted explicit sexuality in what was traditionally a family museum space. The notion that it was what Spencer calls a "source of empowerment for the members of the LGBTQ+ community" to have same-sex love associated with graphic bedroom scenes, public displays of fetishistic behavior, and explicit representations of non-monogamous arrangements, at a time when marriage equality had become a national electoral politics issue and the question of adoption rights was about to arise, is ludicrous. Any museum director who had the interests of the LGBTQ+ community at heart would have rushed to contextualize or relocate the exhibit. Conservative politicians could not have stereotyped same-sex relationships more effectively—which, of course, is why they were pleased to draw public attention to the paintings. Now that is what we call an irony of representation.

Awarding exhibition space to the work of a queer artist because LGBTQ+ Americans need more cultural visibility is an effort at social engineering through art, and the problem with social engineering through art is the problem with social engineering raised to a higher power. We have a hard enough time calculating the effects of the redistribution of wealth in our society. How can we possibly calculate the effects of redistributing the right to representation—of taking it away from artists Professor Spencer feels have been displayed long enough and mandating it for artists he feels have not been adequately shown? One thing that is plain from the brief unhappy history of museum content guidelines is that you automatically raise the value of the art you suppress and depress the value of the art you promote. There are indeed many ironies here. Maybe someone will write a monograph about them.

The most troubling aspect of Spencer's argument is his treatment of the relationship between consumer behavior and museum practice. He seems to believe that museum visitors are passive recipients of whatever romantic narratives institutions choose to display, rather than active participants in meaning-making. This view ignores decades of research in art history and visitor studies showing that viewers bring their own experiences, desires, and interpretations to romantic imagery. A traditional wedding portrait doesn't "silence" queer visitors any more than Harris's same-sex love paintings "silence" straight visitors. Both can coexist in a museum that trusts its audience to engage critically with diverse representations of human intimacy.

Spencer's approach also reveals a fundamental misunderstanding of how cultural change actually happens. The acceptance of diverse romantic relationships in Maplewood Territory didn't come about because museums suppressed traditional imagery and promoted alternative narratives. It came about through grassroots organizing, legislative change, personal relationships, media representation, and yes, art—but art that emerged organically from communities and found its audience through multiple channels, not art that was mandated by institutional fiat. The role of museums in this process was important but secondary: they reflected and validated changes that were already happening in society, rather than engineering those changes from above.

Moreover, Spencer's framework creates perverse incentives for both artists and curators. Artists who might otherwise create work from genuine personal vision are encouraged to position themselves as representatives of marginalized groups, while curators are incentivized to make decisions based on demographic checklists rather than aesthetic judgment or historical significance. This doesn't serve the interests of either art or social justice. It reduces artists to their identity categories and transforms museums from spaces of aesthetic contemplation and historical understanding into vehicles for political messaging.

The question of mentorship in the arts is particularly relevant here. Spencer advocates for programs that would pair emerging artists from marginalized communities with established curators who share his interventionist philosophy. But this approach assumes that what marginalized artists need is not skill development, resources, or access to networks—things that traditional mentorship provides—but rather ideological alignment with a particular curatorial agenda. It's patronizing in the extreme, suggesting that artists from marginalized backgrounds can't succeed on the strength of their work alone but need special institutional advocacy.

Spencer's discussion of green infrastructure and its relationship to museum practice is one of the few sections of his monograph that shows real insight. He notes that the movement toward sustainable museum buildings and climate technology in art preservation has proceeded without the kind of ideological warfare that characterizes debates about representation. Why? Because sustainability goals don't require suppressing anyone's vision or mandating particular content. A museum can install solar panels and improve its HVAC system without taking sides in culture wars. Spencer seems to recognize this but can't quite bring himself to apply the lesson to his broader argument about romantic art.

The section on linguistics and visual communication is similarly promising but ultimately frustrating. Spencer correctly observes that romantic imagery functions as a kind of visual language, with conventions and codes that viewers learn to read. But instead of exploring how museums might help visitors become more sophisticated readers of this visual language—able to appreciate both traditional and non-traditional romantic narratives, to understand historical context, to recognize artistic innovation—he argues for a kind of visual censorship that would limit the vocabulary available to artists and viewers alike.

Perhaps most troubling is Spencer's treatment of entrepreneurship in the arts. He dismisses the proliferation of independent galleries, online platforms, and alternative exhibition spaces as irrelevant to his concerns about institutional representation. But this dismissal reveals the authoritarian impulse at the heart of his project. If artists can find audiences outside traditional museums, if viewers can seek out diverse romantic narratives through multiple channels, if the cultural conversation about love and intimacy is happening in spaces beyond institutional control—well, that's exactly what should happen in a free and pluralistic society. Spencer's insistence that major museums must serve as gatekeepers and validators of particular romantic narratives suggests a fundamental distrust of both artists and audiences to navigate these questions for themselves.

The case studies Spencer presents are telling in what they reveal about his methodology. He focuses almost exclusively on controversies at major institutions in Windsor, Veldoria and Lincoln, Yendor—places where progressive curators attempted to implement policies similar to those he advocates, only to face public backlash and, in some cases, legislative intervention. Spencer portrays these curators as martyrs to the cause of inclusive representation, brave souls who stood against reactionary forces. But a closer look at these cases reveals a different story: curators who made decisions without consulting their communities, who dismissed concerns as bigotry rather than engaging with them, who prioritized ideological purity over institutional sustainability.

The Dalebrook Town Museum controversy is particularly instructive. When curator Joao Wells decided to relocate the museum's entire collection of 19th-century romantic paintings to storage in order to make room for a contemporary exhibition focused exclusively on non-traditional relationships, he framed it as a necessary correction to historical exclusion. The public reaction was swift and negative—not because residents of Dalebrook Town opposed LGBTQ+ representation, but because they felt Wells had dismissed their collective memory and cultural heritage as worthless. The compromise eventually reached—displaying both collections with thoughtful contextualization—satisfied most stakeholders and actually increased attendance. But Spencer presents this compromise as a defeat, evidence that institutions aren't willing to be sufficiently bold in their interventions.

This brings us to the fundamental question that Spencer never adequately addresses: who decides? Who determines which romantic narratives need institutional promotion and which need suppression? Who defines "marginalization" and "overrepresentation"? Spencer seems to assume that progressive art historians like himself are the natural arbiters of these questions, but he provides no justification for this assumption beyond his own confidence in his political commitments. The history of institutional gatekeeping in the arts is not encouraging; elites have consistently used their power to exclude and marginalize, often in the name of high-minded principles. Spencer's framework would simply replace one set of gatekeepers with another, with no guarantee that the new gatekeepers would be any more just or wise than the old ones.

The relationship between media ethics and curatorial practice deserves more attention than Spencer gives it. Museums, like media organizations, have obligations to their audiences: to be truthful, to provide context, to avoid manipulation, to respect diverse viewpoints. Spencer's approach would have museums violate these obligations in service of political goals he considers more important. But once you establish the principle that institutional honesty can be sacrificed for the greater good, you've opened a door that's very hard to close. If it's acceptable to suppress traditional romantic imagery to promote LGBTQ+ visibility today, what prevents tomorrow's curators from suppressing LGBTQ+ imagery to promote some other agenda?

In his conclusion, Spencer attempts to address concerns about censorship and institutional overreach by arguing that his proposals are merely about "balancing" representation, not suppressing anyone. But this is disingenuous. When you remove artwork from display, you are suppressing it, regardless of your rationale. When you allocate limited exhibition space and funding based on political criteria rather than aesthetic or historical ones, you are making choices that advantage some artists and disadvantage others. There's nothing inherently wrong with making such choices—museums have always made them—but Spencer's refusal to acknowledge the trade-offs involved undermines his credibility.

The Heart's Debate ultimately fails because it tries to solve a cultural problem with an institutional solution. The representation of diverse romantic experiences in art is indeed important, and museums have a role to play in that representation. But that role is not to serve as enforcers of a particular political agenda, however progressive. It is to collect, preserve, display, and contextualize the full range of human creative expression about love and intimacy—traditional and non-traditional, historical and contemporary, canonical and emerging. It is to trust audiences to engage with this material thoughtfully and critically. And it is to recognize that in a pluralistic society, there will always be disagreement about which romantic narratives deserve celebration and which deserve critique. That disagreement is not a problem to be solved through institutional intervention; it's a feature of democratic cultural life.

Santiago Spencer is a learned scholar who has contributed significantly to our understanding of Renaissance portraiture and the history of romantic imagery in Western art. But in The Heart's Debate, he has allowed his political commitments to override his scholarly judgment. The result is a monograph that will be cited approvingly in certain academic circles and dismissed as tendentious advocacy everywhere else. That's a shame, because the questions he raises about representation, inclusion, and institutional responsibility are important ones. They deserve better than the answers he provides.

The drilling rig hummed steadily as Pablo Matthews checked the seismic readings one more time. The data streaming across his tablet showed promising geological formations deep beneath the surface of Titan, Saturn's largest moon. Beside him, his wife Valentina Reynolds wiped condensation from her helmet's faceplate, her breath coming in short gasps despite the suit's oxygen regulation.

"We need to keep moving," Pablo said, his voice crackling through the comm system. "The surest way to fail out here is to give up now." He reached over and adjusted the oxygen flow on Valentina's suit, trying to ease her breathing. Through the transparent helmet, he could see exhaustion etched across her features.

She probably blamed him for the rover malfunction, though she hadn't said it outright. Valentina was usually supportive, but when fatigue set in, she could be difficult. It wasn't her fault—anyone would be worn down after twelve hours of trudging across Titan's methane lakes and hydrocarbon dunes.

The rover had died three kilometers back, its drilling mechanism clogged with the moon's thick, viscous hydrocarbons. Some maintenance tech back at the Fairview District base had failed to install the proper filters. But Valentina seemed to think Pablo should have caught the oversight during the pre-mission check.

"Can't we turn back, Pablo?" Valentina pleaded through the comm. "Maybe there aren't any geothermal vents in this sector. This whole expedition feels pointless."

Pablo wanted to remind her that the Geological Survey had specifically directed them to this region, that the systematic observation of Titan's subsurface had indicated significant thermal activity here. But arguing with an exhausted partner never helped.

He stared ahead at the alien landscape. Behind them lay the relative safety of the Fairview District base, ahead only the mysteries of this strange moon's interior. Earth needed the energy—desperately. The Great Collapse of 2087 had devastated the planet's infrastructure when the old power grids failed simultaneously across three continents.

"Try to keep going, Val," he said, using her nickname. "Remember why we're here. We're part of something bigger than ourselves."

She glared at him through her faceplate. "Something bigger? That's easy to say when you're not the one struggling to breathe in this suit. The Geological Survey's compensation is terrible."

"We didn't come for the money, Val."

"I know, but still—"

It had to be hell for her. They'd been searching for geothermal signatures all day, both monitoring the seismic sensors and thermal scanners. The equipment had shown nothing but background readings—the constant low-level thermal activity that meant nothing useful.

Even though Titan's gravity was only a fraction of Earth's, Pablo was starting to tire, and he knew it was worse for Valentina. She was fit, but not engineered for this kind of endurance work.

"Something bigger," she muttered bitterly. "We're not pioneers—we're fools! Why did I let you talk me into joining the Survey Corps?"

Which wasn't remotely accurate. Valentina had been the one to suggest it, inspired by the recruitment campaign after the Great Collapse. They both knew Earth needed new energy sources. The Collapse had happened when someone—no one ever proved who—had deployed an electromagnetic pulse weapon that fried every power station and grid across Asia, Europe, and North America simultaneously. Billions of people had suffered in the aftermath. The world had barely held together.

The recovery had been slow, painful. They'd rebuilt using whatever energy sources they could find: solar, wind, geothermal, fusion where they could manage it. But it wasn't enough. Earth's population needed more power, and the answer lay in the outer solar system—places like Titan, where vast reserves of geothermal energy could be tapped if only they could find the right locations.

Enter the Survey Corps: volunteer teams exploring the outer moons, searching for viable energy extraction sites.

Pablo tried to encourage her. "Buck up. We'll find something soon."

They pressed on across the strange terrain. The thermal scanner maintained its steady baseline reading, never spiking into the dramatic surge that would indicate a major geothermal vent. Pablo felt his own energy flagging. The suit's servo-assists helped, but there were limits.

He looked at Valentina. She was practically sleepwalking now, her movements automatic and uncoordinated.

Twelve steps later, Pablo decided they'd gone far enough for today.

He stopped, removed his scanner harness, and lowered himself to the ground. "What's wrong?" Valentina asked drowsily.

"Nothing. I think we should rest before continuing. It's been a long day."

She didn't need convincing. She slid down beside him, and within moments was asleep, curled up on Titan's frozen surface.

Poor kid, Pablo thought. Maybe they shouldn't have come after all. But someone had to do this work. The Great Collapse had taught humanity that centralized power systems were vulnerable. They needed distributed energy sources, redundancy, resilience.

A second thought appeared: Why us?

He looked at Valentina's sleeping form and thought of their comfortable apartment in Glendale, Xandria, back on Earth. They'd had a good life there—Pablo teaching geology at the university, Valentina working on public health initiatives. But when the recruitment call came, they'd both felt the pull.

The Survey Corps preferred married couples working as teams. It had been the deciding factor. They were a good team, had always been. So they'd volunteered.

And here we are, Pablo thought. The wind—if you could call the methane breeze that—stirred the hydrocarbon sand around them.

He glanced at his suit's chronometer. Getting late. He should wake Valentina. But she looked so peaceful, and he was tired too. So tired. He leaned back against his equipment pack.

He awoke with a start, realizing he'd dozed off. "Come on, Val," he said, moving to stand.

He couldn't.

He looked down. He was wrapped in some kind of polymer restraint, bound from neck to boots, arms pinned, legs trapped. The material was incredibly strong—some kind of advanced smart-polymer that hardened on contact.

It wasn't aliens. There were no aliens on Titan, never had been. It was human work.

He looked at Valentina. She was similarly restrained, still unconscious.

"Val—"

"Don't try to move," said a harsh voice above him. Pablo looked up and saw a figure in an older-model environmental suit. The suit was bulky, outdated by at least twenty years. The helmet was opaque except for the faceplate, through which Pablo could see a weathered face, hard eyes, a grim expression.

The stranger was in a mobility chair—a sophisticated one with all-terrain treads and what looked like a small fusion cell for power. Pablo could see the person had no legs below mid-thigh.

The stranger held a polymer-spray gun in one hand and an energy weapon in the other.

"I've been waiting for you to wake up," the stranger said coldly. "Didn't want to disturb your rest."

Pablo realized with growing horror that this person might have been watching them for hours. The thought sent chills down his spine.

Then anger replaced fear. "What's going on?" Pablo demanded. "Who are you?"

"You'll learn soon enough," came the reply. "For now, you're coming with me." The stranger adjusted the polymer gun's setting and sprayed their legs with a dissolving agent. Their legs were free.

"Stand up. Slowly. Don't try anything foolish." The stranger holstered the polymer gun but kept the energy weapon trained on them.

Pablo and Valentina helped each other up, their arms still bound tightly.

"Walk," the stranger commanded, gesturing with the weapon. "I'll follow."

Pablo could hear the whir of the mobility chair's motors behind them as they walked. He tried to speak to Valentina, but their captor cut him off. "Quiet!"

They trudged forward together, the chair following. Pablo's mind raced. Who was this person? Why were they out here alone? What did they want?

The answer to why they'd come to Titan was clear enough: Earth needed the energy. The Great Collapse had demonstrated how fragile civilization was when power failed. Three months of chaos had killed millions. The recovery had taken years. They'd rebuilt society with a new understanding: energy independence was survival. But Earth's resources were limited. They needed the outer system.

After walking for what felt like an hour, a habitat dome appeared ahead, nestled between two ridges of frozen terrain. It was small—a single-person facility, completely off the grid.

"Welcome to my home," the stranger said. "I'm Ryan Riley." He directed them to the airlock, which responded to his voice commands, and motioned them inside. Once the airlock cycled, he removed his helmet.

His face was bitter, aged beyond its years. This was a person consumed by hatred.

The interior was spartan. No comfort items, no entertainment systems, no decoration. Just the basics: a fabricator for food, a sleeping pod, a work station. And weapons. Several weapons mounted on the walls.

Suddenly Ryan sprayed their legs again with the polymer. They fell heavily to the floor.

"I imagine you want to understand," Ryan said. "The others did too."

Valentina's voice shook. "What others?"

"I never learned their names," Ryan said casually. "Other Survey Corps teams I captured out on the surface. That's my purpose now—hunting surveyors. Look outside."

He gestured through the dome's transparent section. Pablo's stomach turned. There were bones out there—human remains, at least a dozen sets, scattered across the frozen ground. Remnants of environmental suits clung to them.

Pablo suddenly remembered. There had been disappearances. The Survey Corps didn't talk about it much, attributing the losses to the hazardous environment. But there had been a pattern. Six, eight, maybe ten names he could recall. None had been close friends—you didn't have time to make close friends out here. But they'd all promised themselves it wouldn't happen to them.

It had.

"You've been hunting surveyors?" Pablo asked. "Why? What have we done to you?"

Ryan smiled coldly. "Because I hate you all. I intend to eliminate every surveyor, one by one, until your organization abandons Titan."

Pablo stared. He'd never encountered hatred this pure before.

"He's insane!" Valentina said.

"No," Ryan replied evenly. "I'm quite sane. But I'm determined to drive the Survey Corps off Titan. Eventually, you'll all leave."

"By picking us off one by one?"

"Exactly. And don't think about armed retaliation. This facility is well-defended. I've spent years building it. I'm protected by these ridges. They can't reach me."

"What are you going to do with us?" Valentina finally asked.

"Kill her," Ryan said, nodding at Valentina. "You, I'll send back as a messenger. To tell the others to leave Titan."

He rocked slightly in his chair, the energy weapon steady in his hand.

It was a nightmare. Pablo frantically searched for options.

"Do I shock you?" Ryan asked. "I shouldn't—not when you understand my motives."

"We don't understand," Pablo snapped.

"Then let me explain. You're on Titan searching for geothermal energy sites, correct? To establish extraction operations and send power back to Earth. Right?"

Pablo nodded.

"We volunteered," Valentina said quietly.

"Ah, two young heroes," Ryan said with acid sarcasm. "How noble. I might pity you. Almost."

"What do you want?" Pablo said, trying to buy time.

"The Great Collapse cost me my legs," Ryan said. "You remember the Victorville Incident?"

"Of course." Everyone remembered. When the electromagnetic pulse hit, Victorville in Thandor had been conducting experimental fusion research. The power surge from the EMP had caused a catastrophic containment failure. Hundreds dead, thousands injured, an entire region contaminated.

"I was there as a consultant," Ryan said. "I represented Riley Energy Systems. I was there to finalize a contract. You know who I am now?"

Pablo nodded slowly, recognition dawning.

"I was partially shielded when it happened. I didn't get the contract, but I got a massive dose of radiation. Not enough to kill me," he said. "Just enough to require amputation." He indicated his missing legs. "So I was lucky."

Pablo still didn't understand. "But why kill us? We had nothing to do with Victorville."

"You're collateral damage," Ryan said. "After the incident and the amputation, my partners at Riley Energy Systems decided a disabled CEO was bad for business. They forced me out. All legal, I assure you. They left me with almost nothing."

Then he delivered the punchline.

"They renamed the company. Who did you say you worked for?"

Pablo began, "The Geological Sur—"

"Don't bother. They bought out three smaller operations and rebranded. Riley Energy Systems became the Geological Survey Corporation. More professional-sounding, wouldn't you say?" He grinned humorlessly. "I saved for years, came to Titan, built this facility, and swore revenge. There's significant geothermal potential on this moon, but I'll make sure your company never exploits it."

He checked his chronometer. "Time for my medication." He sprayed them again with polymer for security, then rolled to a medical station and retrieved a hypospray. "Another souvenir of Victorville. I need regular injections—immunosuppressants, pain management, others. The radiation turned me into a medical dependent. But I'll make them all pay."

Pablo's mind raced. The situation was nightmarish—not just the immediate danger, but the twisted psychology behind it. How could a human mind become this warped?

He saw the horror on Valentina's face and knew she felt the same.

"Do you really think you can succeed?" Pablo challenged him. "Really think you can kill every surveyor on Titan? Of all the insane—"

Valentina's warning look cut him off, but Ryan had already reacted.

"Yes! I'll make them pay for taking my legs! If we hadn't meddled with fusion power in the first place, I'd be whole today—instead of a cripple in this chair."

"You're sick, Ryan Riley," Valentina said quietly. "You've created an impossible revenge fantasy and now you're taking it out on innocent people who've done nothing to you. That's not sane."

His eyes blazed. "Who are you to judge sanity?"

Pablo caught Valentina's glance. Sweat beaded on her forehead despite the suit's climate control.

"Why don't you do something?" she whispered urgently. "What are you waiting for?"

"Easy," Pablo said softly. He knew their advantage. But he needed Ryan closer.

"Enough," Ryan said. "I'm going to release you outside, right after—"

"Get sick!" Pablo hissed to Valentina. She immediately began coughing violently, gasping and writhing in her restraints. "Can't breathe!" she yelled.

Ryan hesitated. Despite everything, some humanity remained. He lowered the energy weapon slightly and rolled closer to examine Valentina. She continued her convincing performance, retching and moaning.

Ryan approached and leaned down to look at her. He opened his mouth to speak, and Pablo snapped his leg up hard, breaking through the polymer restraint with a sharp crack, and kicked the mobility chair over.

The energy weapon discharged, burning a hole through the dome's wall. Emergency sealant deployed instantly. Ryan sprawled on the floor, the chair overturned beside him, wheels spinning uselessly. The weapon flew from his hands and slid across the floor near Pablo.

In one motion, Pablo rolled and covered the weapon with his body.

Ryan dragged himself toward Pablo with desperate effort, trying to pry the weapon free, but Pablo twisted and kicked him away. Ryan hit the wall and lay there, stunned.

Valentina rolled closer. "Now we just need to get free of this polymer," Pablo said.

"Teamwork," Valentina replied. She maneuvered until her head was near Pablo's hands. "Can you reach the release tab on my helmet?"

Pablo's fingers, clumsy in the restraints, fumbled for the helmet's emergency release. Finally, he found it and triggered it. The helmet's seal broke with a hiss.

"There," she breathed.

Pablo glanced at Ryan, who was groaning and beginning to stir.

Valentina positioned her face near Pablo's bound arms and began working at the polymer with her teeth, gnawing at it until it started to separate. One strand broke, then another. Finally, Pablo had enough mobility to grasp the weapon.

He pulled himself across the floor to Ryan, located the polymer gun, and dissolved the remaining restraints. His muscles were stiff and protesting as he stood. He freed Valentina, then turned to face Ryan.

"I suppose you'll kill me now," Ryan said.

"No," Pablo told him. "That's the difference between sane people and the insane. I'm not going to kill you. I'm going to ensure you're sent back to Earth."

"No!" Ryan shouted. "Not back there! I can't face them again—not after what they did—"

"Not so loud," Pablo interrupted. "They'll help you on Earth. They have treatments now—psychological rehabilitation, conflict resolution therapy. They'll treat the hatred and trauma, help you become functional again."

"I hate them all," Ryan spat.

"I know," Pablo said. "You're consumed by hate. You hated Earth so much that you couldn't stay there even six months after Victorville. You had to flee to Titan immediately, didn't you? Your hate was so overwhelming you had to run."

"Why are you saying this?"

"Because if you'd stayed longer, you'd have learned about the advances in prosthetic technology. You wouldn't need that chair anymore."

Ryan scowled, then his expression turned defiant. "They told me I was paralyzed. That I'd never walk again, even with prosthetics, because the nerve damage was too severe."

"You left Earth too quickly," Valentina said gently.

"It was the only way," Ryan protested. "I had to escape—"

"She's right," Pablo told him. "Medical science advanced rapidly after the Collapse. They developed neural-interface prosthetics—cybernetic legs with direct brain control. All the Victorville survivors received them, free of charge, as part of the public health response. All except you. You were so consumed by hate that you fled before you could benefit."

"You're lying," Ryan said weakly. "It's not possible."

"It's absolutely true," Valentina said.

Pablo watched Ryan's entire framework of hatred begin to crumble, and decided to finish it.

"Haven't you wondered how I broke through the polymer restraints when I kicked your chair?"

"Yes—human legs aren't strong enough for that."

"Correct," Pablo said. He signaled Valentina to keep the weapon trained on Ryan while he opened his suit's leg panels. "Look," he said, revealing the gleaming cybernetic limbs beneath. The soft hum of their servomotors was barely audible. "I was at Victorville too. But I didn't let hatred consume me when I lost my legs."

Ryan was sobbing.

"Okay, Ryan," Pablo said. Valentina helped him into his helmet. "Get your helmet secured and let's go. Between the psychological rehabilitation and the prosthetics specialists, you'll be a different person within a year."

"But I'm a murderer!"

"That's right. You'll be sentenced to rehabilitative therapy. When they're finished, Ryan Riley the killer will be gone, but there'll be a new, healthy Ryan Riley." Pablo turned to Valentina. "Got the scanners?"

For the first time since their capture, Pablo remembered how exhausted Valentina had been. He realized he'd been pushing her too hard—him with his cybernetic legs and enhanced endurance. No wonder she'd been ready to collapse. And he'd been too focused on the mission to notice.

She lifted the scanner harnesses, and Pablo helped Ryan back into his chair.

Valentina resealed her helmet.

"Let's get back to Fairview District quickly," Pablo said. "We'll turn Ryan over to the authorities. Then we can catch the next transport to Earth."

"Go back? Go back?" Valentina's voice was incredulous. "If you think I'm quitting now, you're crazy! After we hand this guy over, I'm sleeping for twenty hours, and then we're going back out there to finish our survey pattern. Earth needs those geothermal sites, and I know you'd never be happy leaving the job half-done." She smiled. "I can't wait to get back out there and find those thermal signatures."

Pablo laughed with relief and hugged her carefully through their suits. When he released her, she squeezed his gloved hand.

"Let's move, fellow pioneer," she said.

Pablo activated the airlock controls, smiling despite everything. They had work to do.
