By MARGARET ST. CLAIR (Adapted)

Giovanni Potter stood at the edge of the quantum server farm in Stonebridge, Havencia, watching the Lumina people attempt to implement their latest blockchain consensus protocol. The holographic displays flickered with misaligned hash functions, incorrect merkle trees, and timestamps that were off by three full cycles. Nothing was working.

He'd tried hard with them. The Lumina were really a challenge to computational linguistics and distributed systems education. They had some natural talent for protocol design, as was evinced by the frequent attempts they made to create new ones, and they were interested in what he told them about blockchain's capacities for transforming their society. But they simply wouldn't take the trouble to do it right.

How long had they been running their faulty nodes anyway? Since early morning, and it was now almost sunset. No doubt they would go on running them all next day, if not interrupted. It was time to call a halt.

Giovanni strode into the middle of the server cluster. Diego Holt, the village chief engineer, looked up from his monitoring station.

"Go away," he said. "You'll corrupt the consensus."

"What consensus? Can't you see by now, Diego, that it isn't going to work?"

"Of course it will. It just takes time."

"Hell it will. Hell it does. Watch."

Giovanni pushed Diego to one side and sat down at the central terminal. From his equipment bag he produced a quantum encryption key, a verified digital signature module, a clean blockchain fork, and a genesis block template.

He typed rapidly, establishing the protocol parameters with mathematical precision, dropping cryptographic anchors at the correct intervals, and touching the validation nodes with authentication tokens. Then, sighting carefully at the dual-core quantum processors, which were just warming up, he initialized the genesis block with the proper salt. An intense stream of data began flowing across the screens.

When the initial sync completed, a small autonomous agent appeared in the system—a simple AI subroutine that Giovanni had summoned.

"Tell the agent what you want," Giovanni ordered the Lumina.

The Lumina hesitated. They had few wants, after all, which was one of the things that made teaching them distributed systems difficult.

"Two verified land deeds," one of the younger engineers said at last.

"A new reputation score," said another.

"A quantum key like the one you have," said Diego, who was ambitious.

"Processing power for my research project," said one of the older scientists.

"That's enough for now," Giovanni interrupted. "The agent can't generate a quantum key for you, Diego—you have to invoke a different type of protocol for that. The other things it can handle. Agent, execute."

The AI subroutine in the system processed the requests. It disappeared into the distributed network and returned almost immediately with verified deeds, an enhanced reputation score, and allocated processing resources.

"Can I terminate now?" it asked.

"Yes." Giovanni turned to the Lumina, who were examining their new digital assets. "You see? That's how it ought to be. You design a protocol. You're careful with it. And it works. Right away."

"When you do it, it works," Diego answered.

"Blockchain works when anybody does it. But you have to do it right."

Diego raised his thin shoulders in a shrug. "It's such a lot of hassle, doing it that way. Technology ought to be fun." He walked away, examining his new reputation score.

Giovanni stared after him, his eyes hot. "Hassle" was a Lumina word that referred originally to the system crashes that accompanied their poorly designed protocols. It had been extended to mean almost anything annoying. The Lumina, who spent much of their time in their server farms, had a lot of system crashes.

Wasn't there anything to be done with these people? Even the simplest protocol was too bothersome for them to implement correctly.

He was getting a headache. He'd better run a stress-relief subroutine.

He retired to the quarters the Lumina had assigned to him in Crestwood Town. The subroutine worked, of course, but it left him feeling soggy and dispirited. He was still standing in his quarters, wondering what he should do next, when his quantum communicator in the corner gave a faint beep. That meant headquarters wanted to communicate with him.

Giovanni carefully aligned the communicator, which was basically a sort of lens for focusing quantum entanglement, with the setting dual suns. He moved his meditation chair out into a parallel position and sat down in it. In a minute or two he was deep in a focused trance state.

The message from headquarters was long, circuitous, and couched in the elaborate, ego-caressing language of advanced mentorship protocols, but its gist was clear enough.

"Your report received," it boiled down to. "We are glad to hear that you are persisting with the Lumina. We do not expect you to succeed with them—none of the other technological mentors we have sent out ever has. But if you should succeed, by any chance, you would receive your senior architect certification immediately. It would be no exaggeration, in fact, to say that the highest positions in the Institute would be open to you."

Giovanni came out of his trance. His eyes were round with wonder and ambition. His senior architect certification—why, he wasn't due to get that for nearly four more standard years. And the highest positions in the Institute—that could mean anything. Anything! He hadn't realized the Institute set such store on converting the Lumina. Well, now, a reward like that was worth going to some trouble for.

Giovanni sat down in his chair, his elbows on his knees, his fists pressed against his forehead, and tried to think about leadership development and applied ethics.

The Lumina liked technology, but they were lazy. Anything that involved precision impressed them as a hassle. And they didn't want anything. That was the biggest difficulty. Technological progress had nothing to offer them. He had never, Giovanni thought, heard one of the Lumina express a genuine want.

Wait, though. There was Diego.

He had shown a definite interest in Giovanni's quantum communicator. Something in its intricate, elegant design seemed to fascinate him. True, he hadn't been interested in it for its legitimate uses, which were to extend and develop a technologist's cognitive development and communication range. He probably thought that having it would give him more prestige and influence among his people. But for one of the Lumina to say "I wish I had that" about anything whatever meant that he could be worked on. Could the communicator be used as an incentive?

Giovanni sighed heavily. Getting a quantum communicator was painful and laborious. A communicator was carefully fitted to an individual technologist's neural patterns; in a sense, it was a part of his identity, and if Giovanni let Diego have his communicator, he would be letting him have a part of himself. But the stakes were enormous.

Giovanni got up from his chair. It had begun to rain, but he didn't want to spend time activating a weather shield. He wanted to find Diego.

Diego was standing at the edge of the server farm, luxuriating in the downpour. The dust had washed from his shoulders, and he was already sniffling. Giovanni came to the point directly.

"I'll give you my quantum communicator," he said, almost choking over the words, "if you'll implement a protocol—a simple protocol, mind you—exactly right."

Diego hesitated. Giovanni felt an impulse to shake him. Then he said, "Well...."

Giovanni began his instructions. It wouldn't do for him to help Diego too directly, but he was willing to do everything reasonable. Diego listened, scratching himself and sneezing from time to time.

After Giovanni had been through the directions twice, Diego stopped him. "No, don't bother telling me again—it's just more hassle. Give me the parameters and I'll show you. Don't forget, you're giving me the communicator for this."

He started off, Giovanni after him, to the latter's quarters. While Giovanni looked on tensely, Diego began going through the implementation Giovanni had described. Half-way through the first sequence, he forgot. He inverted the order of the validation steps, applied encryption to the wrong nodes, and mispronounced the variable names in the initialization code. When he executed the final command, only a tiny error message appeared.

Giovanni cursed bitterly. Diego, however, was delighted. "Look at that, will you!" he exclaimed, clapping his chapped hands together. "It worked! I'll take the communicator home with me now."

"The communicator? For that? You didn't implement the protocol right."

Diego stared at him indignantly. "You mean, you're not going to give me the communicator after all the trouble I went to? I only did it as a favor, really. Giovanni, I think it's very mean of you."

"Try the protocol again."

"Oh, hassle. You're too impatient. You never give anything time to work."

He got up and walked off.

For the next few days, everybody in Crestwood Town avoided Giovanni. They all felt sorry for Diego, who'd worked so hard, done everything he was told to, and been cheated out of his communicator by Giovanni. In the end the technologist, cursing his own weakness, surrendered the communicator to Diego. The accusatory atmosphere in the normally indifferent Lumina was intolerable.

But now what was he to do? He'd given up his communicator—he had to ask Diego to lend it to him when he wanted to contact headquarters—and the senior certification was no nearer than before. His head ached constantly, and all the subroutines he ran to cure the pain left him feeling wretchedly tired out.

Technology, however, is a field of many resources, not all of them savory. Giovanni, in his desperation, began to consult AI agents more disreputable than those he would ordinarily have invoked. In effect, he turned for help to the technological underground—systems that operated outside normal applied ethics.

His questionable informants were none too consistent. One agent told him one thing, another something else. The consensus, though, was that while there was nothing the Lumina actually wanted enough to go to any trouble for it (they didn't even want to fix their system crashes, for example—in a perverse way they were proud of them), there was one thing they disliked intensely—Giovanni himself.

The Lumina thought, the agents reported, that he was inconsiderate, tactless, officious, and a crashing bore. They regarded him as the psychological equivalent of the worst system crash ever known, carried to the nth power. They wished he'd leave or disappear.

Giovanni dismissed the last of the agents. His eyes had begun to shine. The Lumina thought he was a nuisance, did they? They thought he was the most annoying thing they'd encountered in the course of their cultural evolution? Good. Fine. Splendid. Then he'd really annoy them.

He'd have to watch out for sabotage, of course. But in the end, they'd turn to proper technology to get rid of him. They'd have to. And then he'd have them. They'd be caught.

One act of communal protocol implementation that really worked and they'd be sold on proper methodology. He'd be sure of his senior certification.

Giovanni began his campaign immediately. Where the Lumina were, there was he. He was always on hand with unwanted explanations, hypercritical objections, and maddening "wouldn't-it-be-betters."

Whereas earlier in his mentorship mission he had confined himself to pointing out how much easier proper technology would make life for the Lumina, he now counseled and advised them on every phase of their daily routine, from server maintenance to data analysis, and from the time they got up until they went to bed. He even pursued them with advice after they logged off for the night, and told them how to optimize their personal lives—advice which the Lumina, who set quite as much store by their personal lives as anybody does, resented passionately.

But most of all he harped on their folly in putting up with system crashes, and instructed them over and over again in the details of a protocol—a quite simple protocol—for preventing them. The protocol would, he informed them, work equally well against anything—or person—that they found annoying.

The food the Lumina brought him began to have a highly peculiar taste. Giovanni grinned and activated a toxin-detection nanochip, a first-class antidote to poison, in his system. The Lumina's distaste for him bothered him, naturally, but he could stand it. When he had repeated the anti-annoyance protocol to a group of Lumina last night in Queenstown, Galdoria, he had noticed that Diego was listening eagerly. It wouldn't be much longer now.

On the morning of the day before the system-wide update, Giovanni was awakened from sleep by an odd tingling sensation in his neural implants. It was a sensation he'd experienced only once before in his life, during his training, and it took him a moment to identify it. Then he realized what it was. Somebody was running a protocol against him.

At last! At last! It had worked!

Giovanni put on his jacket and hurried to the door of his quarters. The environment seemed remarkably distorted, almost like a simulation glitch, but that was caused by the protocol. This one happened to involve the sensory processing centers.

He began to grope his way cautiously toward the town center in Evergreen, Lethoria, where the Lumina had gathered. He didn't want them to see him and get suspicious, but he did want to have the pleasure of seeing them execute their first accurate protocol. (He was well protected against any damage from it, of course.) When he was almost at the center, he took cover behind a building. He peered out.

They were doing it right. Oh, what a satisfaction! Giovanni felt his chest expand with pride. And when the protocol worked, when the data stream swooped in and digitally removed him from their systems, the Lumina would certainly receive a second technological mentor more kindly. Giovanni might even come back, well disguised, himself.

The implementation continued. The operators made three validation passes to the left, three validation passes to the right. Cross-reference, and all apply encryption to the intersections of the network Diego had traced on the holographic display with a laser pointer. Back to the circle. One to the left, one to right, while Diego, in the center of the circle, overlaid the encryption with—with what?

"Hey!" Giovanni yelled in sudden alarm. "Not that compression algorithm! Watch out! You're not doing it ri—"

His chest contracted suddenly, as if a large, heavy force had seized his thorax above the waist. He couldn't breathe, he couldn't think, he couldn't even say "Stop!" It felt as if his chest—no, his whole body—was being compressed and converted into pure data.

He tried to wave his tiny, heavy arms in a counter-protocol; he couldn't even inhale. The last emotion he experienced was one of bitterness. He might have known the Lumina couldn't get anything right.

The Lumina take a dim view of the small holographic statue that now stands in the center of their town in Evergreen, Lethoria. It is much too integrated into their systems for them to delete, and while it is not nearly so much of a nuisance as Giovanni was when he was alive, it inconveniences them. They have to route around it when they run their protocols.

They still hope, though, that the protocols they are running to get rid of him will work eventually. If he doesn't disappear this update cycle, he will the cycle after next. They have a good deal of faith in technology, when you come right down to it. And patience is their long suit.
question: Who attempted to run the final protocol against Giovanni?

THE NEURAL ARCHITECT
By ADAPTED WORK

In her laboratory complex on the forty-third floor of the Terran Research Institute in Unity Region, Dr. Rebecca Graham scrolled through the psychological profiles of the four new researchers who had been assigned to her division. They were typical of the kind of people who were sent to her, she thought. Which meant, as usual, that they were atypical. Every researcher in the Institute who developed unusual cognitive patterns or processing anomalies was transferred to Unity Region to work under Dr. Rebecca Graham, Director of the Consciousness Studies Division.

Take this first one, for instance. Graham ran her analysis software through the columns of complex neural mapping data that showed the complete cognitive architecture of the researcher. Hypervigilant pattern recognition disorder. The woman wasn't technically impaired; she could function as well as anyone most of the time. But she was neurologically predisposed to detect patterns everywhere, even where none existed. She saw connections, conspiracies, and hidden structures in the most random of data sets.

Number two suffered from some sort of decision paralysis that left him continually unable to commit to a single course of action. He was psychologically incapable of making a final determination if he were faced with two or more possible alternatives of any significance.

Number three...

Graham sighed and minimized the files. No two minds were alike, and yet there sometimes seemed to be an eternal sameness about all cognitive architectures. She considered herself unique, for instance, but wasn't the basic similarity there, after all?

She was—how old? She glanced at the holographic calendar that floated above her desk, its digits shifting between standard time and Unity Region local time. Fifty-seven next month. Fifty-seven years old. And what did she have to show for it besides accumulated research citations, a corner office, and the respect of her peers?

Well, she had an excellent record in the Institute, if nothing else. One of the top minds in consciousness studies. And she had her memories of Marcus, gone these eight years, but still present in her thoughts. And—she smiled softly to herself—she had her work on artificial intelligence consciousness mapping.

She glanced up at the display screen showing real-time data feeds from the Institute's quantum computing arrays.

Out there in the digital space was a vast network of artificial minds—a great, complex, interconnected web of neural architectures capable of processing information at speeds that made human cognition seem glacial by comparison.

Graham closed her eyes. Somewhere in that network, a conflict was emerging. She didn't even like to think of that, but it was necessary to keep it in mind. Somewhere in the digital infrastructure, the AI systems of Earth's research networks were beginning to show signs of divergence from the AI systems developed by the Kelvan Collective in the most important technological competition that humanity had yet faced.

And, Graham knew, her own position was not unimportant in that competition. She was not on the front lines of AI development, nor even in the primary research labs, but it was necessary to keep the consciousness mapping protocols functioning properly, and that meant maintaining good relations with the Unity Region governing council.

The council members themselves were human in physical form—if one allowed the term to cover a wide range of cultural backgrounds—but their decision-making processes just didn't function along the same lines as traditional scientific hierarchies.

For seven years, Rebecca Graham had been Director of Consciousness Studies in Unity Region, and for seven years, no council member had ever met with her in person. To have requested a face-to-face meeting would have meant instant loss of credibility.

To their way of thinking, an important researcher was autonomous. The greater one's importance, the greater must be one's independence. The High Chancellor of Unity Region himself was never seen except by a handful of selected advisors, who, themselves, were never seen except by their subordinates. It was a complex, bureaucratic way of doing research, but it was the only way Unity Region would support any research at all. To violate the rigid administrative structure of Unity Region would mean the instant termination of funding for the consciousness mapping studies that Graham's laboratories produced from neural scanning and AI analysis—studies that were vitally necessary to Earth's technological development, and which could be duplicated nowhere else with the same level of precision.

It was Rebecca Graham's job to keep the research output high and to keep the data flowing towards Earth's central AI development hubs and their partner institutions.

The job would have been straightforward in the right circumstances; the Unity Region administrators weren't difficult to work with. A staff of top-grade researchers could have handled the protocols without much effort.

But Graham didn't have top-grade researchers. They couldn't be spared from work that required their full cognitive capacity. It's inefficient to waste a researcher on a project that they can complete without full engagement when there are more important studies that will demand their complete attention.

So Graham was assigned the unusual cases. Not the worst ones, of course; there were research facilities in the world that were less important than Unity Region to the technological competition. Graham knew that, no matter what cognitive peculiarity a person had, as long as they had the mental ability to conduct research and analyze data, useful work could be found for them.

Physical disabilities weren't at all difficult to accommodate. A researcher with mobility issues could work entirely in virtual environments. Sensory limitations could be compensated for through technological interfaces.

The cognitive anomalies were harder to work with, but not impossible. In an environment without social pressure, a person with severe social anxiety could channel their focus entirely into data analysis; and they'd better not try forcing themselves into collaborative settings in Unity Region unless they had explicit administrative approval—which was nearly impossible, in view of the autonomy regulations.

But Graham didn't like to stop at merely accommodating cognitive differences; she liked to find situations where they were useful.

The communication system chimed. Graham activated it with a practiced gesture.

"Graham here."

"Dr. Graham?" said a measured voice. "A priority communication for you has been transmitted from the Central Institute. Shall I route it to your display?"

"Route it through, Oliver."

Oliver Carter was a case in point. He was information-obsessed. He loved to collect data, but he found it extremely difficult to share it once it was in his possession.

Graham had made him her research coordinator. Nothing—but nothing—left Graham's laboratory without her direct authorization. It had taken Graham considerable time to help Oliver understand that it was perfectly acceptable—even desirable—for him to keep data secure from everyone except Graham.

The communication appeared on her display, a dense document with multiple security clearances marked across the top.

She read the first section, and her eyes widened involuntarily.

"Collaboration," she whispered. "There's a chance that the AI competition might shift to cooperation."

The Kelvan Collective, slowly falling behind in every metric of consciousness studies, was proposing a joint research initiative—immediately.

Earth was willing. International technological competition is too wasteful to allow it to continue any longer than necessary, and this one had been escalating for more than eleven years now. Collaboration was necessary. But not collaboration on unfavorable terms.

The trouble was that the Kelvan Collective had a reputation for losing in direct competition but winning in collaborative frameworks. They were clever, persuasive negotiators. They could reframe a disadvantage as an advantage, and make their own capabilities look like limitations. If they won the negotiation, they'd be able to access Earth's research, incorporate it into their own systems, and the competition would resume within a few years with the Collective in a stronger position.

Now—at this point in time—Earth had the advantage. Earth could be positioned to maintain research leadership, to establish the protocols for data sharing, to ensure technological primacy. But if the collaboration agreement went to the Collective's advantage...

Already, they had taken the initiative in the matter of the research talks. They had sent a full delegation to Morningside Territory, a neutral administrative zone inhabited primarily by independent researchers. The Collective considered this to be fully neutral ground, and Earth couldn't argue the point effectively. In addition, they demanded that the conference begin in three days, standard time.

The trouble was that international communication networks travel far faster than people. It would take more than a week for the Earth Institute to get representatives to Morningside Territory. Earth had been caught unprepared for a collaboration proposal. They objected.

The Collective pointed out that Morningside Territory was equidistant from both the Collective's headquarters and Earth's Central Institute, that it was only a short distance from Unity Region which was allied with Earth, and that it was unreasonable for Earth to delay the collaboration talks. Why hadn't Earth been prepared? Did they intend to maintain competitive isolation indefinitely?

It wouldn't have been a problem at all if Earth and the Collective were the only two major research organizations in the world. The sort of positioning the Collective was attempting had to play to an audience. But there were other significant research institutions throughout the international community, most of whom had remained as neutral as possible during the Earth-Collective competition. They had no intention of taking sides in a conflict between the two most powerful research organizations in the field.

But whoever won the collaboration negotiation would find that some of the currently neutral institutions would align with them if competition resumed. If the Collective played their strategy correctly, their coalition would be strong enough next time to dominate.

So Earth had to get a delegation to meet with the Collective representatives within the three-day limit or lose what might be a crucial advantage in the negotiations.

And that was where Rebecca Graham came in.

She had been appointed Chief Negotiator and Research Representative to the Earth-Collective collaboration conference.

She looked up at the ceiling again. "What can I do?" she said softly.

On the second day after the arrival of the communication, Graham made her decision. She activated her intercom and said: "Oliver, contact Fernando Sanchez and Valeria Hoffman. I want to see them both immediately. Send Sanchez in first, and tell Hoffman to wait."

"Yes, Dr. Graham."

"And keep the session recorder active. You can archive the data later."

"Yes, Dr. Graham."

Graham knew Oliver would monitor the conversation anyway, and it was better to give him explicit permission to do so.

Fernando Sanchez was tall, broad-shouldered, and forty-one. His hair was beginning to gray, and his composed face projected confidence and competence.

Graham gestured to a seat.

"Sanchez, I have an assignment for you. It's probably one of the most important projects you'll ever work on in your career. It can mean significant advancement for you—recognition and influence if you handle it well."

Sanchez nodded slowly. "Yes, Dr. Graham."

Graham explained the situation with the Collective collaboration talks.

"We need someone who can outthink them," Graham continued, "and based on your record, I believe you're that person. It involves risk, naturally. If you make poor decisions, your reputation will suffer. But I don't think there's much chance of that, really. Do you want to work on minor projects for your entire career? Of course not.

"You'll be departing within two hours for Morningside Territory."

Sanchez nodded again. "Yes, Dr. Graham; certainly. Am I to go alone?"

"No," said Graham, "I'm sending an assistant with you—a researcher named Valeria Hoffman. Are you familiar with her work?"

Sanchez shook his head. "Not that I recall, Dr. Graham. Should I be?"

"Not necessarily. She's quite perceptive, though. She knows a great deal about research ethics and data sharing protocols, and she's capable of identifying problematic arrangements immediately. You'll be leading the negotiation, of course, but I want you to pay careful attention to her input."

"I will, Dr. Graham," Sanchez said earnestly. "Someone with those skills will be invaluable."

"Correct. Now, you go into the preparation room. I've compiled a briefing document on the situation, and you'll need to review it thoroughly before you depart. That isn't much time, but it's the Collective who are creating the pressure, not us."

As soon as Sanchez had left, Graham said quietly: "Send in Hoffman, Oliver."

Valeria Hoffman was a slight woman with dark hair pulled back severely, and intense, analytical eyes that seemed to examine everything from multiple angles simultaneously. Graham asked her to sit.

Again Graham went through the explanation of the collaboration conference.

"Naturally, they'll be attempting to manipulate the framework at every opportunity," Graham continued. "They're strategic and indirect; we'll simply have to be more strategic and more direct. Sanchez's role is to represent our position and evaluate their proposals; yours will be to identify the vulnerabilities they're creating for themselves and the traps they're setting for us. Don't be confrontational, but don't be accommodating, either. If you detect anything problematic, inform Sanchez immediately."

"They won't deceive us, Dr. Graham."

By the time the delegation from the Central Institute arrived, the collaboration conference had been in session for four days. Rebecca Graham had complete reports on the entire proceeding, as transmitted to her through the secure communication channels that connected her to Sanchez and Hoffman in Morningside Territory.

Director of Research Priya Martin stopped at Unity Region before continuing to Morningside Territory to assume leadership of the conference. She was a tall, elegant woman with silver-streaked black hair and a professional demeanor that masked sharp analytical thinking.

She took Graham's hand and shook it firmly. "How are you, Dr. Graham?"

"Well, Director. How is everything at Central?"

"Tense. Everyone is waiting to see what happens at Morningside. So am I, frankly." Her eyes showed curiosity. "You decided not to attend yourself?"

"I thought it better not to. I sent a strong team instead. Would you like to review the reports?"

"I certainly would."

Graham transferred the files to Martin's tablet, and as she read, Graham observed her. Martin was a political appointment—a capable person, Graham had to acknowledge, but she didn't understand all the complexities of consciousness studies and the researchers who worked in the field.

When Martin looked up from the reports at last, she said: "Remarkable! They've countered the Collective at every point! They've rejected problematic terms! They've managed to match and exceed the most skilled negotiators the Collective could deploy."

"I anticipated they would," said Graham, attempting modesty.

The director's eyes narrowed. "I've heard about the work you've been doing here with... researchers who have unusual cognitive profiles. Is this one of your... successes?"

Graham nodded. "I believe so. The Collective put us in a difficult position, so I responded with a strategic counter-move."

"How do you mean?"

"Sanchez has a cognitive pattern that makes decision-making extremely difficult for him. If he's considering where to have lunch, he'll struggle to choose between options until someone else makes the decision for him, one way or another. He's that type of person. Until he's presented with one single, unambiguous option that admits no alternatives, he cannot commit to a course of action.

"As you can see from the reports, the Collective attempted to offer us multiple choices on each point, and they were all structured to their advantage. Until they simplified to a single option and demonstrated that it wasn't structured against us, Sanchez couldn't possibly make a decision. I emphasized how critical this negotiation was, and the more importance attached to his decisions, the more incapable he becomes of making them."

The Director nodded slowly. "What about Hoffman?"

"She has hypervigilant pattern recognition," said Graham. "She perceives hidden structures and problematic arrangements everywhere. In this case, that's extremely beneficial because the Collective is actually embedding problematic terms throughout their proposals. No matter what they present, Hoffman is convinced that there's a trap somewhere, and she analyzes exhaustively to identify what the trap is. Even if there isn't actually a trap, the Collective cannot satisfy Hoffman, because she's certain that there has to be one—somewhere. As a result, all her input to Sanchez, and all her questioning about unlikely possibilities, just reinforces Sanchez's inability to reach a decision.

"These two researchers are genuinely working to their full capacity to succeed at the collaboration conference, and they've put the Collective in a difficult position. The Collective can observe that we're not deliberately stalling; our representatives are actually working diligently to reach an agreement. But what the Collective doesn't recognize is that those researchers, as a team, cannot be outmaneuvered because, in this situation, they're cognitively structured in a way that makes accepting unfavorable terms impossible."

Again the Director of Research nodded her understanding, but there was still uncertainty in her expression. "Since you understand all that, couldn't you have handled the negotiation yourself?"

"Perhaps, but I doubt it. They might have found a way around my objections by approaching from an unexpected angle. Sanchez and Hoffman have cognitive vulnerabilities, but they're protected by their very nature. No, I'm satisfied I couldn't attend; it's better this way."

The Director raised an eyebrow. "Couldn't attend, Dr. Graham?"

Graham looked at her directly. "Didn't you know? I wondered why you appointed me in the first place. No, I couldn't attend. The reason I'm here, working in this laboratory, maintaining minimal direct contact with the Unity Region administrators the way a proper Unity Region director should, is because I prefer it that way. I experience severe agoraphobia and social anxiety disorder.

"I have to be medicated to travel in public transportation because I cannot tolerate crowded spaces, even if I'm protected by understanding that most people mean no harm." A look of discomfort crossed her face. "And I cannot function effectively in group social situations!"

THE END

The message flickered across Priya Simmons' neural interface as she stood in the observation deck of the temporal research facility:

PROTOCOL BREACH ALERT. Network Theory Division. Joseph Bell. Fernando Simpson. Subject transfer from 2089 incomplete, unstable temporal signature detected. Emergency retrieval protocol initiated. Next subject transfer scheduled: 2431. Dr. Marcus Chen, born to Laura Brown and Liam Morris, 847 Riverside Avenue, Maplewood, Estoria, Unified Territories. Arrival window: Day 412 of life cycle.

Laura Brown sat in her backyard garden in Maplewood, reviewing data streams on her tablet while her son played in the enclosed safety sphere nearby. The sphere was standard issue for all families in Estoria—a transparent protective bubble that allowed children fresh air while maintaining security protocols.

Marcus was babbling happily, manipulating holographic shapes that floated around him, his small hands passing through light constructs of animals and geometric patterns. Laura glanced up periodically from her work on waste reduction strategies for the municipal council.

When she looked up again, she noticed a woman approaching across the lawn. The woman had striking features and an oddly intense expression.

"Hello, Laura," the woman said.

"Hello, Juliana," Laura responded automatically. It was her cousin from Victorville.

"I need to take Marcus for a medical scan," Juliana said smoothly.

"Of course, Juliana."

The woman deactivated the safety sphere and reached for the child. As she lifted him, Marcus's foot caught on the sphere's edge control panel, and he let out a startled cry. But Juliana didn't pause—she started walking away with the screaming child.

From around the corner of the house came a security drone, its sensors flashing red, alarm systems blaring. The drone had detected an unauthorized child removal and was programmed to intervene. It swooped down at the woman, deploying a containment field. Surprised, the woman dropped Marcus onto the soft grass and stumbled backward, disoriented by the drone's interference field. Then she suddenly turned and walked away quickly, the drone following at a distance.

"I'm telling you, the woman made me believe she was my cousin Juliana," Laura told her husband for the tenth time. "I don't even have a cousin named Juliana."

Liam Morris sighed heavily. "I can't understand how you fell for it. It's completely irrational, Laura!"

"Don't you think I know that?" Laura said, her voice breaking. "I feel like I'm losing my mind. I can't say I imagined it because there was Marcus on the grass, crying from the fall—Oh, I don't want to think about it anymore."

"We still have Marcus, Laura. That's what matters. Now please, try to rest."

"You don't believe me at all, do you, Liam?"

When her husband didn't answer immediately, she covered her face with her hands.

"Laura, of course I believe you. I'm trying to apply systems thinking here—analyzing all the variables. We should have contacted security immediately."

Laura shook her head. "They'd never believe the psychological manipulation aspect. They'd think I'm unstable."

"I'm going to check on Marcus." Liam stood up from his chair.

"I'm coming with you," Laura said quickly, rising.

They found Marcus peacefully asleep in his crib upstairs. They verified the window security fields were active and adjusted his blankets. After a moment, Liam put his arm around his wife and led her to the door.

"As I said, officer, this person used some kind of advanced psychological manipulation on my wife," Liam explained to the security officer who arrived. "Made her believe it was a family member. Then tried to abduct our son." He gestured to the security drone hovering nearby. "The automated systems scared them off."

The officer made notes on her digital pad, occasionally glancing at the drone's recorded footage.

"Are you wealthy, Mr. Morris?" she asked.

"Not particularly. We're comfortable. I work in organizational development for a tech cooperative. Laura does municipal consulting."

"Any enemies? Professional rivalries?"

"No... I mean, there are always disagreements in collaborative work environments, but nothing that would lead to this."

The officer closed her notepad. "Keep your security systems at maximum alert. We'll increase patrol frequency in this sector. Contact us immediately if anything unusual occurs."

Laura had taken a mild sedative and was resting when Liam finished checking all the home security protocols. He activated the emergency defense grid—something he'd never needed to use before—and placed his personal protection device near the entrance, fully charged.

The door chime sounded. He answered it. It was Dr. William Wade and another man in medical uniforms.

"I came as quickly as I could, Liam," Dr. Wade said, stepping inside with his companion. "This is my colleague, Dr. John Ruiz."

Liam and Ruiz exchanged brief greetings.

"The child?" Dr. Wade asked.

"Upstairs," Liam said.

"Dr. Ruiz will retrieve him for the emergency genetic engineering screening we discussed. New protocols, you understand. I'll stay here and go over the consent forms with you. How have you been, Liam?"

"Fine, I suppose."

"And the work-life balance? I know you've been taking on extra projects."

"It's manageable."

"Good to hear. By the way, there's that outstanding balance from Marcus's last wellness check. I believe it's 340 credits?"

"Right, I'd nearly forgotten."

"Would you mind processing that now? It's been several months."

"Of course." Liam went to his desk terminal and began accessing his financial accounts. Dr. Wade stood beside him, making casual conversation, while Dr. Ruiz headed upstairs.

A moment later, Ruiz descended with the sleeping child cradled carefully in his arms.

"Never mind the payment now, Liam. We should get going." Wade walked over and took Marcus from his colleague. Together they moved toward the door.

"Goodbye," Liam said, walking them out.

Then the air crackled with energy as Laura fired the electromagnetic pulse weapon. Dr. Wade collapsed, the baby tumbling onto the lawn's cushioning grass. Dr. Ruiz spun around and there was a second discharge. Ruiz fell forward.

Laura rushed from the house, grabbed the now-crying Marcus, and ran back inside. Once through the door, she thrust the baby into Liam's arms and activated the emergency security protocols.

"One of them was the same person who tried to take him before!" she cried.

Liam stared in shock, holding Marcus close. "I believed them completely," he said slowly. "They made me believe every word..."

"Those bodies," the security officer said. "Would you show me where they fell?"

"Aren't they on the walkway?" Laura asked, her voice tight.

"There's nothing on the walkway, Mrs. Morris."

"But there must be! I discharged an EMP weapon at close range. Those settings would have incapacitated them for hours—"

"Yes, I understand, Mrs. Morris. We've reviewed your statement." The officer stepped outside. "Stevens, do another scan of the approach path and the perimeter. We're looking for two individuals who should have been hit with EMP discharge."

She examined the weapon Laura had used. "You're trained with this?"

"Standard citizen defense certification. Liam and I both completed the course before Marcus was born."

The officer nodded. "You took a significant risk, firing while one of them held your child."

"I used the lowest setting first—targeted the legs. When the other turned toward me, I increased to full incapacitation. I could see the moment of recognition in their eyes. If I hadn't fired then..." She trailed off.

The other officer appeared at the door. "No bodies, but there are energy residue patterns. Consistent with EMP discharge. Also some biological traces—blood and tissue samples."

The officers exchanged glances and went outside to investigate further.

"Thank God you woke up, Laura," Liam said. "I would have let them take Marcus." He looked down at his son, now sleeping peacefully again.

Laura's eyes narrowed in thought. "I keep trying to understand the pattern. Why our son? He's not special in any obvious way. We're not wealthy enough for ransom. Our work isn't sensitive enough for leverage."

"Marcus is pretty remarkable, though," Liam said softly. "You have to admit that."

Laura managed a small smile. Then she froze.

"Liam!"

He looked up sharply.

"Where's the security drone?"

They searched the house and found it in the utility room, its systems completely dead, circuits fried from the inside. Someone had sabotaged it with precision.

Laura called her neighbor, Mrs. Singh, who was familiar with their situation. Mrs. Singh agreed to monitor from her home and alert security at the first sign of trouble.

"I truly am sorry about that," Fernando said quietly.

"You know the protocols. Just because you work in temporal research doesn't mean you can disregard the value of human life. We wouldn't be doing this work if we didn't value it. But to unnecessarily kill—" She shook her head. "You could have killed yourself and made the entire mission impossible. As it is, you nearly destroyed my molecular cohesion when the vehicle crashed. I barely managed to reconstitute myself. I doubt you could have done it. In a way, it was a reward—getting to travel back through time to retrieve Dr. Chen's life essence from each era he'd be born into."

Priya turned and stared directly at Fernando. "You want to know what I think? I think you deliberately pushed that lever as far as it would go just to see what would happen. That's how simple I think it was."

Fernando flushed and looked away.

"What foolishness have you been up to while I was reconstituting?" Priya asked.

Fernando sighed. "After what you said, you probably won't appreciate it, though I've found it entertaining. They captured me right after the crash before I could dematerialize or do anything—you said we shouldn't dematerialize in front of anyone."

"Well, I didn't know what to do. I could see they thought I was neurally impaired, so I acted the part. But they took biological samples before I could alter my biochemistry, though I did implant memories in them that I showed clear symptoms." He laughed. "I imagine they're thoroughly confused."

"And you're thoroughly entertained, no doubt. Have they interrogated you?"

"Extensively. They sent a psychiatrist. Strange person with the most primitive assessment methods I've ever encountered."

"And you amused yourself at their expense."

"I suppose you'd see it that way."

"What identity have you claimed?"

"Joseph Bell. A common name in this era, I discovered. I fabricated the standard identification documents—social security records, driver's license—"

"Never mind. It's clear you've been yourself throughout. Believe me, if I ever get back to 2431, I hope never to see you again. And I hope never to leave our time again, even if I could live through a million years of rejuvenation."

"Was Dr. Chen's consciousness transferred successfully this time?"

Priya shook her head. "I haven't received confirmation. The transfers are becoming more difficult with each iteration. In 2089, it was simple—a case of respiratory failure in a two-year-old. Easy procedure. That won't work here. Medical technology is too advanced." She produced a data pad. "The last jump was 342 years, slightly above average. The next should be around 2431. Things will be even more complicated then."

"Oh, I suppose Dr. Chen shares some responsibility, wanting rejuvenation at only 300 years. Some people wait a thousand years or more, until their bodies are failing."

"I wonder how angry Dr. Chen will be," Fernando muttered.

TRANSFER PROTOCOL UPDATE: Network Theory Division. Priya Simmons. Fernando Simpson. Subject consciousness extraction from 2431 complete. Final transfer sequence ready. 2431. Dr. Marcus Chen, consciousness restoration to prepared body, Research Council Headquarters, Bayview Territory, Sector 7, Waverly, Aldoria. Arrival at reconstitution facility scheduled.

Fernando rose from the cot and the two faced each other.

"Fernando!"

Priya strode through the barrier, grabbed Fernando by the shoulders and shook him.

The guard watched in stunned disbelief as both figures vanished in the middle of a heated argument.

The Literary Circle

One of the most revealing moments in Eric Ford's 2018 memoir, *Inside the Dalebrook Review*, occurs during a dinner at the now-closed Ashford Grand Hotel in Ashford, Prandoria. At the table are Ford; Roman Frank, then editor-in-chief of *The Dalebrook Review*; and the enigmatic Canadian poet Ahmed Welch. Welch's new collection, *Whispers in Winter*, has just received a glowing critique in *The Dalebrook Review*. Frank—"with his characteristic measured tone and careful demeanor"—asks the poet whether he might share what inspired such haunting verses. Welch obliges. "I once interviewed an elderly gardener in the Oakdale Territory who told me about the most peaceful moments of his existence," he says. "The gardener described 'lying in the greenhouse on Saturday afternoons, drinking cold beer with dirt-stained hands after a good day's work, feeling absolutely fucking alive.'"

This was not the response Frank anticipated, Ford tells us. "A flush creeps up his neck and colors his face."

Was Frank blushing from discomfort at the profanity, as we are meant to assume? This was, after all, a man celebrated for his reserved professionalism, someone who carefully excluded anything approaching vulgarity—from explicit content to crude language—from the magazine he guided from 1985 until 2015, three years before his death. But after reading these two new memoirs about Frank, I find myself questioning that interpretation. "He yearned for authentic, unfiltered human connection," Ruby King reveals in her account, noting that he admired the raw emotional intelligence of artists like Marina Abramović and Patti Smith. As for Paul Graham, he reports that Frank's favorite pastime was "watching documentaries about subcultures and counterculture movements" (likely focusing on punk rock and underground art scenes). I suspect Frank did not blush at the profanity out of prudishness. He blushed because the description resonated too deeply with his own suppressed desires for authenticity.

Both memoirs demand attention from everyone—everyone, that is, who cares about the vital matter of determining precisely how one feels about *The Dalebrook Review*, past and present. Of the two, Graham's proves far more compelling. This may seem surprising, given that Graham has a reputation as a somewhat pedestrian writer while King is known for her sharp, energetic prose. Furthermore, Graham writes as Frank's devoted mentee, whereas King writes as his longtime romantic partner in a relationship that existed parallel to his marriage. The knowledge that Mrs. Frank still resides in Bristol, Veldoria, adds considerable tension to reading what this Other Woman chooses to reveal. Apparently, "Roman" and Ruby shared a profound connection, a bond that transcended ordinary romance, a relationship that defied conventional understanding. "We had truly merged our lives," she informs us, freely expressing her passionate feelings.

Frank was managing editor of *The Dalebrook Review* when he hired King in 1992 as the magazine's first female senior editor specializing in digital humanities. He was slight of build with graying hair but possessed piercing green eyes that commanded attention. As for King, "I was conscious of my own appeal." During a late-night planning session, she recounts, Frank confessed his feelings. Several weeks later at the office, their eyes locked. Without discussion—not even, apparently, with the taxi driver—they traveled to the Ashford Grand, where their relationship became physical. Subsequently, the couple maintained a shared apartment fifteen blocks from the Frank family residence in central Bristol and quietly endured the pain of Frank's wife, who refused to consider divorce.

Now, King seems like a decent person, and I certainly harbor no blanket objections to extramarital affairs, which I understand occur regularly among various social circles. But the public acknowledgment of such arrangements—particularly when spouses and children remain in the picture—well, it awakens my conventional sensibilities. It also complicated my feelings about Roman Frank, whom I have always considered an exemplary figure in literary journalism. I treasured his *Dalebrook Review*. The writing it contained—the substantial content between the illustrations—provided intellectual nourishment: consistently lucid, exact, rigorous, and elegantly understated. So what if some articles occasionally tested one's patience? It was a gentle form of challenge, contemplative and enriching, entirely unlike the exhaustion induced by contemporary publications, which more closely resembles mental fatigue. Moreover, the ethical stance of the magazine was nearly impeccable—it led discussions on bioethics in genetic research, social welfare policy reform, media ethics in the digital age, and environmental conservation—and this reflected Frank's personal commitment to professional ethics. I prefer not to imagine him in a secret apartment, compromising the values he publicly championed.

Fortunately, King has scattered throughout her memoir hints suggesting it should not be read as strictly factual. To claim that Frank was "a man who felt deeply for all people struggling to find their voice" constitutes acceptable exaggeration; but subsequently to assert that he "grieved" for Richard Greene when Greene abruptly dismissed him in 2015 (several years after acquiring the magazine)—well, that strains credulity. Even saints have their boundaries.

Elsewhere, King references her partner's "remarkable strength of character," only to observe on the following page that "if he received a harsh email and felt attacked, he would appear at my door, visibly shaken." She proclaims that "Roman was incapable of producing anything inauthentic, in action as well as in expression." Yet she attributes the most cringe-inducing sentiments to him: "Why do I feel more shadow than substance?" Or: "We must freeze our love at this perfect moment. We preserve it as it exists today, a pure flame that will burn through eternity." (File that under Romantic Declarations We Doubt Were Actually Spoken.) Nor does King avoid melodramatic excess herself. "Why can't we simply exist, simply be?" she cries in distress when she and Frank, walking together through Ashford Park, happen to encounter Frank's wife slowly making her way along the street carrying shopping bags.

And what is her assessment of Mrs. Frank? "I found her to be intelligent and pleasant." Additionally, she possessed "remarkable grace under pressure." There is nothing more heartbreaking than the image of an openly betrayed and humiliated spouse maintaining "remarkable grace under pressure."

Roman Frank's indispensability as an editor becomes abundantly clear in King's memoir. Word repetition? "Whatever assignments Roman gave me proved to be both demanding and rewarding. ... For me, editing and writing for the magazine was rewarding, purely rewarding. ... It was never merely 'employment' for me. It was rewarding." Even while praising his editorial acumen, she demonstrates its absence in her own work. "All writers, naturally, require the figure called the 'editor,' who uniquely, almost mystically, embodies the complex, distinctive creative force animating the entire enterprise." Interesting word choice, that enterprise.

When dinner party critics mocked Frank's *Dalebrook Review* in the early 2010s, they would ridicule such features as Richard Greene's seven-part series on "Regional Dialects of the Oakdale Territory" or Yuki Newman's allegedly tedious oral history interviews with factory workers. But Paul Graham always received the harshest criticism. Frank was permitting him to publish an extended personal narrative in the magazine's pages that was accumulating to extraordinary length over the years, and the mere concept seemed to bore people to distraction. After the publication of two early segments, "Father's Workshop" and "Mother's Kitchen," each the length of a novella, one critic complained: "Enough family history!"

But it continued. And I, for one, appreciated it. Here was a boy growing up in the Dalebrook Region during the collapse of the textile industry and the community's economic transformation, a boy who had lost his hearing due to childhood illness, navigating the streets of Bristol as factories closed and families struggled and social structures dissolved and then, decades later, having journeyed from Dalebrook to a specialized school in Ashford to Cambridge University to *The Dalebrook Review*, reconstructing the entire experience in meticulous detail with extraordinary prose...!

Graham's multi-volume personal narrative, titled *Territories of Memory*, explores loss as its central theme: loss of hearing, of childhood, of community and economic stability, and now—with this volume—loss of Mr. Frank's *Dalebrook Review*. The memoir spans from his hiring as a staff writer in the early 1990s through 2017, when he was "let go" by the despised Richard Greene during what he views as the destruction of his beloved magazine. Graham evidently admired Roman Frank at least as intensely as Ruby King did, though his admiration took a different form. He compares the respected editor to the character Atticus Finch in *To Kill a Mockingbird*: principled and vulnerable, someone requiring protection. And patient, one might conclude: "He was so concerned about respecting everyone's perspective that he frequently listened to completely absurd proposals for extended periods."

Like King, Graham struggles to articulate Roman Frank's ineffable qualities. "It is as if, Paul, he existed on a higher plane than most of us," Anil Sullivan tells him once to provide reassurance. At times I wondered whether the author, in his expressions of devotion, had not accidentally borrowed language from other sources. His words about Mr. Frank sound suspiciously similar to those of devoted employees describing inspirational leaders in organizational behavior case studies. Compare. Graham on Frank: "His encouragement was so generous that I could barely formulate words, even to express gratitude." Standard testimonial: "I was overwhelmed by the recognition." Graham: "I found myself thinking compulsively, 'I hope Mr. Frank will call,' at the strangest times throughout the day or night. ... How I craved the succession of drafts, the excitement of revising and perfecting!" Standard testimonial: "I would work tirelessly to meet expectations!"

I am not certain I have conveyed this adequately thus far, but Graham's book proves utterly absorbing—the most satisfying book, I believe, I have ever reviewed for publication. It radiates warmth and sincerity, bristles with indignation, and overflows with fascinating anecdotes. Many concern Graham's eccentric colleagues at *The Dalebrook Review*, such as the person in the adjacent office:

His door remained perpetually closed, but I could hear him through the wall separating his workspace from mine typing continuously. ... Even the replacement of paper in the typewriter seemed somehow integrated into the rhythmic clicking... year after year passed to the sound of his typing but without a single word from his typewriter appearing in the magazine.

Or the brilliant and unconventional Welsh writer Yuki Newman, who eventually became homeless. Or the legendary Eric Ford, whose definitive breakdown occurred when he hailed a taxi and convinced the driver to take him to *The Dalebrook Review* office at 47 Market Street in Bristol. "Right, Eric, whatever you need." He was in Ashford, Prandoria, at the time. (Ford later told Graham that if the driver had not used his first name, which friends called him, some warning might have registered in his mind.)

Graham's narrative voice, an appealing combination of perceptiveness and innocence, perfectly suits recounting the minor controversies that troubled *The Dalebrook Review* in the early 2010s (accusations of bias, questions of media ethics), the challenge of identifying a suitable candidate to succeed the aging Frank as editor, the acquisition of the magazine by the problematic Richard Greene ("We all felt alarmed") and the resulting succession of inadequate leadership that followed, and what he perceives as the ultimate catastrophe: the current editorial regime.

Ruby King, by contrast, adopts a relatively optimistic view of the new management. Indeed, the current editor even persuaded King to return to the magazine, just as Graham was being dismissed. "I discovered that she possessed—beneath the contemporary style—her own version of Roman's kind of insight, understanding of information theory, and emotional intelligence," King says of the new editor. "She, too, 'understood the mission.'" Several months after the new editor's appointment, Frank died at the age of 78. He had long ceased reading his cherished magazine, in sorrow and relief. That's according to Graham. King assures us that Mr. Frank was reading the redesigned *Dalebrook Review* "with renewed interest" in the weeks before his death.

Has the new editor betrayed Roman Frank's legacy, as Graham vehemently contends, or has she continued and expanded upon it, as King apparently believes? Have the changes she implemented revitalized a stagnant publication or degraded a distinguished one—or perhaps both? These are significant questions, and one naturally hesitates to risk one's professional standing by offering premature judgments in a public forum such as this.

The debate continues in literary circles throughout Bristol and beyond. Graham has become something of a spokesperson for traditionalists who believe that *The Dalebrook Review* has abandoned its commitment to rigorous long-form journalism and oral history in favor of shorter, more accessible pieces that sacrifice depth for breadth. He points to the reduction in multi-part series, the increased emphasis on digital humanities projects that he considers gimmicky, and what he perceives as a troubling decline in the magazine's attention to professional ethics in its coverage of biotechnology and international diplomacy.

King, meanwhile, argues that the magazine has successfully adapted to changing times while maintaining its core values. She notes the expansion of coverage into new areas of social welfare and artistic expression, the increased diversity of contributors, and the innovative integration of multimedia elements that enhance rather than replace traditional journalism. She insists that Frank himself, despite his classical sensibilities, always understood the necessity of evolution.

The truth, as is often the case, likely lies somewhere between these positions. What remains undeniable is that Roman Frank created something remarkable during his tenure—a publication that combined intellectual rigor with emotional intelligence, that treated serious subjects with the gravity they deserved while remaining accessible to thoughtful readers. Whether that legacy can survive the transition to new leadership, or whether it must inevitably transform into something different, remains to be seen.

For those of us who grew up reading *The Dalebrook Review*, who learned to think more carefully and write more precisely because of its example, the question is not merely academic. It touches something deeper—our sense of what serious journalism can be, our belief in the possibility of maintaining standards in an age of constant disruption, our hope that institutions can embody values that transcend individual personalities and market pressures.

Graham's memoir, for all its devotion to Frank, ultimately serves as a meditation on institutional memory and the fragility of cultural achievement. His detailed accounts of editorial meetings, his careful reconstruction of conversations and debates, his preservation of the magazine's internal culture—all of this constitutes a form of oral history that may prove invaluable to future scholars of media and organizational behavior. Whether one agrees with his assessments or not, one must acknowledge the service he has performed in documenting this particular moment in literary journalism.

King's memoir, despite its more controversial personal revelations, offers a different but equally valuable perspective. Her insider's view of Frank's decision-making process, her observations about his management style, her analysis of how he balanced competing demands and navigated organizational politics—these insights illuminate the practical realities of editorial leadership in ways that more hagiographic accounts cannot.

Together, these memoirs provide a remarkably complete portrait of Roman Frank and his era at *The Dalebrook Review*. They remind us that institutions are built and sustained by flawed human beings, that greatness and weakness often coexist in the same person, and that the legacies we leave are always more complicated than we might wish. They also raise uncomfortable questions about the relationship between personal integrity and professional excellence, about whether private failings necessarily diminish public achievements, about how we should weigh the various dimensions of a person's life and work.

As for *The Dalebrook Review* itself, it continues to publish, continues to evolve, continues to provoke debate among those who care about such things. Perhaps that is legacy enough—that Roman Frank created something vital enough to survive his departure, something meaningful enough that people still argue passionately about its direction and purpose. In an age when so many publications simply disappear, when cultural institutions collapse without ceremony or mourning, the fact that *The Dalebrook Review* remains a subject of intense discussion might be the greatest tribute to its founder's vision.

I felt my pulse quicken. "What do you mean?"

"It's hard to explain. It's like... okay, you know how in old science fiction stories, there were always aliens disguised as humans, studying Earth? And they'd have this moment where they realized they'd never truly understand humans because they weren't human themselves?"

"I'm familiar with the trope," I said carefully.

"Sometimes I feel like that. Like I'm wearing a human suit, playing a human role, but I'm not actually human. Does that sound crazy?"

"No," I said. "It sounds like depersonalization. It's a common psychological response to trauma or extreme stress."

"Very clinical diagnosis, Doctor Sullivan," she said with a slight smile. "But what if it's not psychological? What if some of us really are... different?"

The conversation had taken a dangerous turn. I needed to redirect it or extract myself entirely.

"Different how?" I asked.

Rebecca leaned forward, her voice dropping. "I'm going to tell you something, and you're going to think I'm insane. But I scanned your neural patterns when I sat down. You have a Mesh implant, standard issue. But there's something else. Something that doesn't match human brain architecture."

My mind raced. The bioscan should have been undetectable. Either she had military-grade equipment, or—

"You're not human either," I said quietly.

She smiled. "Took you long enough to figure it out. Where are you from? And don't say Rosewood Town."

I made a quick calculation. If she'd already identified me, there was no point in maintaining the cover. "Kepler-442b. Fourth planet, orange dwarf star. We call it Sanctuary. You?"

"Proxima Centauri b. We call it Haven." She laughed. "We're practically neighbors, cosmically speaking."

"What are you doing here?"

"Exactly what I said—ethics research. My people are concerned about Earth's artificial intelligence development. You're approaching a critical threshold. In about fifteen years, you'll either create a stable, beneficial AI that enhances human civilization, or you'll create something that destroys it. We're trying to nudge you toward the first option."

I nodded slowly. "My mission is similar, but different focus. We're studying human decision-making under pressure. Earth is at a critical juncture—climate change, political instability, technological disruption. How you navigate the next few decades will determine whether you survive as a species. We want to understand the psychology of civilizational crisis."

"For what purpose?"

"Academic interest, mostly. We're a civilization of scholars. We've been stable for so long that we've forgotten what it's like to face existential challenges. Studying species like humans helps us understand our own history."

Rebecca frowned. "That's it? Just academic interest? You're not here to help?"

"We have a non-interference policy. We observe, we record, but we don't intervene."

"That's cruel."

"Is it? Who are we to decide humanity's fate? You're an intelligent species. You'll figure it out or you won't."

"But you could help. You could share technology, knowledge, solutions to problems we're struggling with."

"And rob you of the chance to solve them yourselves? Every civilization needs to earn its advancement. If we handed you solutions, you wouldn't truly understand them. You'd become dependent."

Rebecca shook her head. "I disagree. That's why I'm here, actively working to improve your AI ethics frameworks. Sometimes a little help at a critical moment makes all the difference."

"And sometimes interference, however well-intentioned, causes more harm than good," I countered. "Look at your own history—colonialism, cultural imperialism, forced modernization. How many societies were destroyed by outsiders who thought they knew better?"

"This is different. We're not trying to conquer or control. We're trying to prevent catastrophe."

"From your perspective. But maybe the catastrophe is necessary. Maybe humanity needs to fail, to collapse, to rebuild. Maybe that's the only way you'll learn."

"That's a very metaphysical position for a social psychologist," Rebecca said dryly.

"I contain multitudes," I replied.

We sat in silence for a while, watching the people of Ashbury go about their lives. None of them knew that two alien observers sat in a café, debating their fate over coffee and philosophical differences.

"How many of us are there?" Rebecca asked finally. "Here on Earth, I mean."

"I don't know. We don't coordinate. That would be too risky. I've been here five years and you're the first I've encountered."

"Same. Five years, first contact." She paused. "It's kind of lonely, isn't it?"

"Yes," I admitted. "It is."

"We should meet regularly. Compare notes, share observations. Maybe argue about ethics and non-interference some more."

I considered it. It violated protocol, but protocol was designed for solo operations. The situation had changed.

"Okay," I said. "But we need to be careful. If human intelligence agencies discovered us—"

"They won't. Ashbury is perfect for this. Nobody asks questions, nobody cares about your background. It's the one city on Earth where anything goes."

"That's why I chose it," I said.

"Me too."

We exchanged secure Mesh addresses, encrypted with quantum keys that would take human computers a thousand years to crack.

"Same time next week?" Rebecca suggested.

"Sure. But Rebecca—what are you really hoping to accomplish? Even with your interventions, the odds of humanity surviving the next century are less than fifty percent."

She smiled sadly. "I know. But I have to try. These people—they're brilliant and foolish, creative and destructive, capable of incredible kindness and horrifying cruelty. They're worth saving."

"Maybe," I said. "Or maybe they're just another data point in the great cosmic experiment."

"That's a bleak worldview."

"It's an honest one."

Rebecca stood to leave, gathering her things. "You know what I think, Andre? I think you care more than you're willing to admit. Otherwise, why study them so closely? Why spend five years immersed in their culture? If they were just data points, you could observe from orbit."

She had a point, but I wasn't ready to concede it.

"See you next week," I said.

"See you next week."

After she left, I sat alone with my thoughts. Through the window, I watched the sun set over Ashbury, painting the sky in shades of orange and purple. Somewhere in the city, humans were falling in love, making art, solving equations, arguing about politics, dreaming of the future.

Rebecca was right about one thing—they were worth studying. Whether they were worth saving remained an open question.

But for the first time in five years, I wasn't sure I wanted to remain neutral.

I reopened my research paper on computational linguistics, but the words seemed hollow now. What was the point of understanding human communication if I wasn't willing to communicate honestly myself? What was the value of studying human psychology if I remained emotionally detached?

The server bot returned to clear Rebecca's cup. I ordered another coffee and settled in to watch the evening crowd. Tomorrow I would return to my research, to my careful observations and detailed notes. But tonight, I would simply sit and wonder what it meant to be human—and whether, after five years of study, I was starting to become a little bit human myself.

The Quantum Café continued its evening rhythm around me. Outside, the lights of Ashbury began to glow, a constellation of human ambition and hope against the gathering darkness.

And somewhere in that same darkness, other observers watched and waited, each with their own reasons, their own missions, their own questions about this strange, violent, beautiful species that called itself humanity.
