THE RETURNED ONE
By HERBERT D. KASTLE
Adapted and Reimagined

There was the usual welcoming crowd for a celebrity, and the usual speeches by the usual officials who met her at the transit station which had once been twenty miles outside of Bayview, but which the growing city had since engulfed and placed well within its boundaries. But everything wasn't usual. The crowd was quiet, and the mayor didn't seem quite as at-ease as he'd been on his last big welcoming—for Dr. Helena Hoffman, who had won the international prize for her work in pollution control systems. His Honor's handclasp was somewhat moist and cold. His Honor's eyes held a trace of remoteness.

Still, she was the honored home-comer, the successful returnee, the hometown woman who had made good in a big way, and they took the triumphal tour up Main Street to the new square and the grandstand. There she sat between the mayor and a nervous young graduate student chosen as homecoming representative, and looked out at the municipal bands, the National Guard, the civic organizations and community groups. Several of the local institutions in town had shown indecision as to how to instruct their members to treat her. But they had all come around. The tremendous national interest, the fact that she was the First Returned, had made them come around. It was obvious by now that they would have to adjust as they'd adjusted to all the other firsts taking place in these—as the media had dubbed the start of the new era—the Revolutionary Thirties.

She was glad when the official greeting was over. She was a very tired woman and she had come farther, traveled longer through stranger territory, than any person who'd ever lived before. She wanted a meal at her own table, a kiss from her husband, a word from her daughter, and later to see some old friends and a relative or two. She didn't want to talk about the journey. She wanted to forget the immediacy, the urgency, the terror; then perhaps she would talk.

Or would she? For she had very little to tell. She had traveled and she had returned and her voyage was very much like no voyage anyone had ever experienced—long periods of absolute nothing, and then the gradual awakening.

The house had changed. She saw that as soon as the official car let her off at 45 Riverside Avenue. The change was, she knew, for the better. They had put solar panels on the roof. They had rehabilitated, spruced up, almost rebuilt the entire outside and grounds with funds from the government compensation program. But she was sorry. She had wanted it to be as before.

The head of the Community Council and the chief of the local administration, who had escorted her on this trip from the square, didn't ask to go in with her. She was glad. She'd had enough of strangers. Not that she was through with strangers. There were dozens of them up and down the street, standing beside parked vehicles, looking at her. But when she looked back at them, their eyes dropped, they turned away, they began moving off. She was still too much the First Returned to have her gaze met.

She walked up what had once been a gravel path and was now a smooth composite path. She climbed the new steps and raised her hand to the biometric scanner, but then realized it wouldn't recognize her yet. She pressed the old-fashioned bell button and heard the soft chime sound within. She was surprised that she'd had to do this. She'd thought Fernando would be watching at a window.

And perhaps he had been watching... but he hadn't opened the door.

The door opened; she looked at him. It hadn't been too long and he hadn't changed at all. He was still the tall, gentle man she'd loved in graduate school, the tall, gentle man she'd married fourteen years ago. Lena was with him. They held onto each other as if seeking mutual support, the thirty-eight-year-old man and twelve-year-old girl. They looked at her, and then both moved forward, still together. She said, "It's good to be home!"

Fernando nodded and, still holding to Lena with one hand, put the other arm around her. He kissed her—her neck, her cheek—and all the old jokes came to mind, the jokes of travel-weary people, the and-then-I'll-put-my-bag-down jokes that spoke of terrible hunger. He was trembling, and even as his lips came up to touch hers she felt the difference, and because of this difference she turned with urgency to Lena and picked her up—though the girl was almost too big for that now—and hugged her and said, because she could think of nothing else to say, "What a big girl, what a big girl."

Lena stood in her arms as if her feet were still planted on the floor, and she didn't look at her mother but somewhere beyond her. "I didn't grow much while you were gone, Mom. Dad says I'm just like you were at this age."

So she put her down and told herself that it would all change, that everything would loosen up just as her project director, Dr. Wei Kumar, had said it would early this morning before she left the Capital Medical Research Facility in Carmel.

"Give it some time," Wei had said. "You need the time; they need the time. And for the love of heaven, don't be sensitive."

Fernando was leading her into the living room, his hand lying still in hers, a cool, uncertain hand lying still in hers. She sat down on the couch, he sat down beside her—but he had hesitated. She wasn't being sensitive; he had hesitated. Her husband had hesitated before sitting down beside her.

Wei had said her position was analogous to the early pioneers of medical technology, to the first recipients of artificial organs, to the first cryogenic revival subjects—but more so. Wei had said lots of things, but even Wei who had worked with her all the way, who had engineered the entire fantastic process—even Wei the Nobel prize winner, the multi-degreed genius in neural regeneration, had not actually spoken to her as one person to another.

The eyes. It always showed in their eyes.

She looked across the room at Lena, standing in the doorway, a girl already tall, already showing the features of young womanhood. It was like looking into the mirror and seeing herself twenty-five years ago. But Lena's face was drawn, was worried in a way that few twelve-year-old faces are.

"How's it going in school?" she asked.

"Mom, it's the third month of summer break."

"Well, then, before summer break?"

"Pretty good."

Fernando said, "She made honor roll both semesters before break, and she made honor roll the semester you went away, Priya."

She nodded, remembering that, remembering everything, remembering the warmth of their farewell, the warmth of Lena's farewell, their tears as she left for the experimental medical facility in Crestwood. They had feared for her, having read of the many procedures gone wrong even in the most advanced research centers.

They had been right to worry. She had suffered much after that accident. But now they should be rejoicing, because she had survived and made the long journey back. Lena suddenly said, "I have to go, Mom. I promised Yasmin and the others I'd help with the data science project. It's the Regional Science Fair preparation, you know. I have to keep my word." Without waiting for an answer, she waved her hand—it shook; a twelve-year-old girl's hand that shook—and ran from the room and from the house.

She and Fernando sat beside each other, and she wanted badly to take him in her arms, and yet she didn't want to oppress him. She stood up. "I'm very tired. I'd like to lie down a while." Which wasn't true, because she'd been lying down all the months of the recovery.

He said, "Of course. How thoughtless of me, expecting you to sit around and make small talk and pick up just where you left off."

She nodded. But that was exactly what she wanted to do—make small talk and pick up just where she'd left off. But they didn't expect it of her; they wouldn't let her; they felt she had changed too much.

He led her upstairs and along the hallway past Lena's room and past the small study to their bedroom. This, too, had changed. It was newly painted and it had new furniture. She saw twin beds separated by an ornate little table with an ornate little lamp, and this looked more ominous a barrier to her than the twelve layers of security clearance around the research facility.

"Which one is mine," she asked, and tried to smile.

He also tried to smile. "The one near the window. You always liked the fresh air, the morning light. You always said it helped you to wake up motivated when you were working on your environmental conservation thesis. You always said it reminded you—being able to see the sky—that you were going to make a difference in the world, and that you were going to come back to this bed again."

"Not this bed," she murmured, and was a little sorry afterward.

"No, not this bed," he said quickly. "Your professional association donated the bedroom set and I really didn't know—" He waved his hand, his face pale.

She was sure then that he had known, and that the beds and the barrier between them were his own choice, if only an unconscious choice. She went to the bed near the window, began to remove her jacket, but then remembered that some neural interface scars still showed on her neck and arms. She waited for him to leave the room.

He said, "Well then, rest up, dear," and went out.

She took off her jacket and saw herself in the mirror on the opposite wall; and then took off her shirt. The scars were faint, the marks running in precise lines along her spine, across her shoulders, disappearing under her clothing. There were several more on her abdomen, and one on her left thigh where the emergency neural bypass had been installed. They'd been treated properly and would soon disappear. But he had never seen them.

Perhaps he never would. Perhaps long sleeves and high collars and dim lighting would keep them from him until they were gone.

Which was not what she'd considered at all important on leaving the Research Facility early this morning; which was something she found distasteful, something she felt beneath them both. And, at the same time, she began to understand that there would be many things, previously beneath them both, which would have to be considered. He had changed; Lena had changed; all the people she knew had probably changed—because they thought she had changed.

She was tired of thinking. She lay down and closed her eyes. She let herself taste bitterness, unhappiness, a loneliness she had never known before.

But sometime later, as she was dozing off, a sense of reassurance began filtering into her mind. After all, she was still Priya Baker, the same woman who had left home thirteen months ago, with a love for family and friends which was, if anything, stronger than before. Once she could communicate this, the strangeness would disappear and the First Returned would again become good old Priya. It was little enough to ask for—a return to old values, old relationships, the normalcies of everyday life instead of the intensity of the spotlight. It would certainly be granted to her.

She slept.

Dinner was at seven p.m. Her sister came; her colleague Zara and Zara's partner Sophie came. Together with Fernando, Lena and herself, they made six, and ate in the dining room at the big table.

Before she'd become the First Returned, it would have been a noisy affair. Her family had never been noted for a lack of enthusiasm, a lack of conversation, and Lena had always chosen mealtimes—especially with company present—to describe everything and anything that had happened to her during the day. And Fernando himself had always chatted, especially with her sister, though they didn't agree about much regarding education reform. Still, it had been good-natured; the general tone of their lives had been good-natured.

This wasn't good-natured. Exactly what it was she wasn't sure. "Stiff" was perhaps the word.

They began with salad, Fernando and her sister serving quickly, efficiently from the kitchen, then sitting down at the table. She looked at her sister as she raised her first forkful of greens, and said, "You look wonderful." It was nothing new; she'd said it many many times before, but her sister had always reacted with a bright smile and a quip something like, "Wonderful for someone pushing forty, you mean." This time she burst into tears. It shocked her. But what shocked her even more was the fact that no one looked up, commented, made any attempt to comfort her; no one indicated in any way that a woman was sobbing at the table.

She was sitting directly across from her sister, and reached out and touched her left hand which lay limply beside the silverware. She didn't move it—she hadn't touched her once beyond that first, quick, strangely-cool embrace at the door—then a few seconds later she withdrew it and let it drop out of sight.

So there she was, Priya Baker, at home with the family. So there she was, the miracle returned, waiting to be treated as a human being.

The salad plates were cleaned away and the soup served. Zara began to talk. "The most innovative educational data analytics platform you ever did see," she said in her enthusiastic professor's voice. "Still expanding rapidly. We'll reach national implementation before—" At that point she looked at Priya, and Priya nodded encouragement, desperately interested in this normalcy, and Zara's voice died away. She looked down at her bowl, mumbled, "Soup's getting cold," and began to eat. Her hand shook a little; her confident face was not quite as confident as Priya remembered it.

Sophie made a few tentative statements about the University Cultural Exchange Program, and Priya looked across the table to where she sat between Zara and her sister—her husband and daughter bracketed her, and yet she felt alone—and said, "I've missed being involved in the community initiatives. Here it is August and I haven't participated in a single project."

Sophie smiled, if you could call it that—a pitiful twitching of the lips—and nodded. She threw her eyes in her direction, and past her, and then down to her bowl. Her sister, who was still sniffling, said, "I have a terrible migraine. I'm going to lie down in the guest room a while." She touched her shoulder in passing—her affectionate, demonstrative sister who would embrace strangers and volunteer for every cause, who had often overwhelmed her with an excess of physical and verbal affection—she barely touched her shoulder and fled.

So now five of them sat at the table. The main course was served—grilled salmon, the pink flesh steaming and fragrant. She cut into it and raised a forkful to her mouth, then glanced at Lena and said, "Looks fresh enough to have been caught this morning." Lena said, "Yeah, Mom." Sophie put down her knife and fork and murmured something to her partner. Zara cleared her throat and said Sophie was dealing with some dietary concerns and she guessed she was going into the living room for a while. "She'll be back for dessert, of course," she said, her laugh sounding forced.

Priya looked at Fernando; Fernando was busy with his plate. Priya looked at Lena; Lena was busy with her plate. Priya looked at Zara; Zara was chewing, gazing out over their heads to the kitchen. Priya looked at Sophie; she was disappearing into the living room.

She brought her fist down on the table. The settings jumped; a glass overturned, spilling water. She brought it down again and again. They were all standing now. She sat there and pounded the table with her right fist—Priya Baker, who would never have thought of making such a scene before, but who was now so sick and tired of being treated as the First Returned, of being stood back from, looked at in awe of, felt in fear of, that she could have smashed more than a table.

Fernando said, "Priya!"

She said, voice hoarse, "Leave me alone. Go away. Let me eat alone. I'm sick of the lot of you."

Her sister and Zara returned a few minutes later where she sat forcing food down her throat. Her sister said, "Priya dear—" She didn't answer. She began to cry, and Priya was glad she left the house then. She had never said anything really harsh to her sister. She was afraid this would have been the time. Zara merely cleared her throat and mumbled something about getting together again soon and "come by the university and see the new data center" and she, too, was gone. Sophie never did manage to speak to her.

She finished her salmon and waited. Soon Fernando came in with the special dessert he'd been preparing half the day—a magnificent chocolate torte. He served her, and cut a portion for himself and Lena. He hesitated near her chair, and when she made no comment he called their daughter. Then the three of them were sitting, facing the empty side of the table. They ate the torte. Lena finished first and got up and said, "I really should—"

"You really should go work on your data science project or study for your advanced placement exams or anything to get away from your mother."

Lena's head dropped and she muttered, "No, Mom, that's not it."

Fernando said, "She'll stay home, Priya. We'll spend an evening together—talking, watching something, playing games."

Lena said, "Of course, Mom, if you want to."

Priya stood up. "The question is not whether I want to. You both know I want to. The question is whether you want to."

They answered together that of course they wanted to. But their eyes—her husband's and daughter's eyes—could not meet hers, and so she said she was going to her room because she was, after all, very tired and would in all probability continue to be very tired for a long, long time and that they shouldn't count on her for normal social life.

She fell asleep quickly, lying there in her clothes.

But she didn't sleep long. Fernando shook her and she opened her eyes to a lighted room. "Yasmin and her husband are here." She blinked at him. He smiled, and it seemed his old smile. "They're so anxious to see you, Priya. I could barely keep Yasmin from coming up and waking you herself. They want to go out and catch up. Please, Priya, say you will."

She sat up. "Yasmin," she muttered. "Yasmin and Marcus." They'd had wonderful times together, from college on. Yasmin and Marcus, their oldest and closest friends. Perhaps this would begin her real homecoming.

Go out and celebrate? They'd laugh and reminisce and reconnect!

It didn't turn out that way. She was disappointed; but then again, she'd also expected it. This entire first day at home had conditioned her to expect nothing good. They went to the recreation center, and Yasmin sounded very much the way she always had—animated and full of stories and full of insights. She hugged Fernando the way she always had, and squeezed Priya's hand (but not the way she always had—so much more carefully, almost tentatively), and insisted they all drink more wine than was sensible as she always had. And for once, Priya was ready to go along on the drinking. For once, she matched Yasmin glass for glass.

They didn't stay at the recreation center very long. At ten o'clock they crossed the plaza to the Garden Café, where Yasmin and the others ordered appetizers and coffee and Priya went right on drinking. Fernando said something to her, but she merely smiled and waved her hand and sipped another glass of oblivion.

There was music and dancing at the Garden Café. She'd been there many times before, and she was sure several of the patrons recognized her. But except for a few furtive glances in her direction, it was as if she were a stranger in a city halfway around the world.

At midnight, she was still drinking. The others wanted to leave, but she said, "I haven't danced with my friend Yasmin." Her speech was slightly slurred, her mind was blurred, and yet she could read the strange expression on Yasmin's face—brilliant Yasmin, who'd always been so warm with her, who'd made a ritual of their friendship. Brilliant Yasmin, who now looked as if she were going to be ill.

"So let's dance," she said and stood up.

They were on the dance floor. She held her close in the contemporary style, and hummed and chatted. And through the alcoholic haze saw she was a stiff-smiled, stiff-bodied, mechanical dancing partner.

The song finished; they walked back to the table. Marcus said, "Time to head home."

Priya said, "First one dance with my loving husband."

She and Fernando danced. She didn't hold him as close as she had Yasmin. She waited for him to come close on his own, and he did, and yet he didn't. Because while he put himself against her, there was something in his face—no, in his eyes; it always showed in the eyes—that made her know he was trying to be the old Fernando and not succeeding. This time when the music ended, she was ready to go home.

They rode back to Bayview along the main highway, she and Fernando in the rear of Yasmin's vehicle, Marcus driving because Yasmin had drunk just a little too much, Yasmin chatting and telling an occasional story about their university days, and somehow not her old self. No one was their old self. No one would ever be their old self with the First Returned.

They turned left, to take the short cut along Memorial Park Drive, and Yasmin finished a story about a failed experiment and a famous scientist and looked at her husband and then past him at the long, stone wall paralleling the road. "Hey," she said, pointing, "do you know what they're planning for the new memorial garden?"

Marcus glanced to the left, and so did Priya and Fernando. Marcus made a small sound, and Fernando seemed to stop breathing, but Yasmin went on a moment longer, not yet aware of her supposed misstep.

"You know what?" she repeated, turning to the back seat, the enthusiasm rising in her voice. "You know what, everyone?"

Marcus said, "Did you see the announcement about the new cultural center in—"

Priya said, "No, Yasmin, what are they planning for the memorial garden?"

Yasmin said, "They're going to—" And then she caught herself and waved her hand and muttered, "I can't remember the details."

"They're going to create a memorial for people who died and were brought back through neural regeneration," Priya said, and looked through the window, past the stone wall, into the large memorial park at the fleeting monuments.

The vehicle was filled with horrified silence when there should have been nothing but interest, or perhaps mild curiosity. "Maybe you should let me out right here," Priya said. "I'm home—or that's what everyone seems to think. Maybe I should lie down in the memorial garden. Maybe that would satisfy people. Maybe that's the only way to act, like something from a horror story."

Fernando said, "Oh, Priya, don't, don't!"

The vehicle raced along the road, crossed an intersection, went four blocks and pulled to a stop. She didn't bother saying good night. She didn't wait for Fernando. She just got out and walked up the composite path and entered the house.

"Priya," Fernando whispered from the study doorway, "I'm so sorry—"

"There's nothing to be sorry about. It's just a matter of time. It'll all work out in time."

"Yes," he said quickly, "that's it. I need a little time. We all need a little time. Because it's so strange, Priya. Because it's so frightening. I should have told you that the moment you walked in. I think I've hurt you terribly, we've all hurt you terribly, by trying to hide that we're frightened."

"I'm going to stay in the study," she said, "for as long as necessary. For good if need be."

"How could it be for good? How, Priya?"

That question was perhaps the first firm basis for hope she'd had since returning. And there was something else; what Wei had told her, even as Wei himself had reacted as all people did.

"There are others coming, Fernando. Fifteen that I know of in the regeneration pods right now. My colleague, Dr. Helena Hoffman, who died at the same moment I did—nine months ago next Tuesday—she's going to be next. She was injured worse than I was, so it took a little longer, but she's almost ready. And there'll be many more, Fernando. The government is going to save all they possibly can from now on. Every time a young and healthy person loses their life by accident, by trauma, and their body can be recovered in time, they'll go into the pods and they'll start the regenerative neural and organ process—the process that made it all possible. So people have to get used to us. And the old fears, the old superstitions, the primitive terrors have to die, because in time each community will have some of us; because in time it'll be an ordinary thing."

Fernando said, "Yes, and I'm so grateful that you're here, Priya. Please believe that. Please be patient with me and Lena and—" He paused. "There's one question."

She knew what the question was. It had been the first asked her by everyone from the President on down.

"I experienced nothing," she said. "It was as if I slept those eight months—slept without dreaming."

He came to her and touched her face with his lips, and she was satisfied.

Later, half asleep, she heard a siren wailing in the distance, and remembered stories of how they announced emergencies and the presence of danger. She shivered and pulled the covers closer to her and luxuriated in being safe in her own home.

THE END

The holding chamber in Evergreen, Belvoria had been designed with meticulous attention to detail. Isabella Graves noted this with a mixture of admiration and frustration as she examined the seamless walls for the hundredth time. The Kelhari were nothing if not thorough—every preliminary report from Earth's diplomatic corps had emphasized that point. Their civilization had achieved remarkable advances in biotechnology and social organization, creating a society of unprecedented efficiency and longevity through genetic optimization and rigid social structures.

Isabella stretched on the chamber's single resting platform, a precisely engineered surface that provided optimal spinal support while remaining deliberately austere. She'd been in isolation for four days now, with nothing to occupy her mind but her own thoughts and the nightly sessions where Kelhari technicians administered their accelerated language-learning treatments while she slept.

The language itself was fascinating—a construction of pure logical precision that made even the most rigorous academic discourse seem sloppy by comparison. Every word had exact boundaries, every concept fit into clearly defined categories. There were no ambiguities, no metaphors that didn't resolve into literal meanings, no room for the sort of interpretive flexibility that characterized human communication.

Isabella had tried to keep herself mentally active through various exercises—reviewing her training in international diplomacy, running through scenarios for cultural evolution, even attempting some amateur archaeology in her mind by reconstructing the historical analysis of Kelhari development from the fragments she'd learned. But four days was a long time with nothing but one's own thoughts.

She wished they'd at least given her something to read. Even a technical manual on Kelhari biotechnology would have been better than nothing.

The door opened with a soft hiss. Isabella rose quickly, smoothing her diplomatic uniform and preparing herself for interaction. The Kelhari who entered was tall and angular, with the characteristic pale blue skin and four-fingered hands of his species. His eyes—large and golden—fixed on her with unwavering intensity.

"You are Isabella Graves," he stated. It wasn't a question, but Isabella had learned the ritual.

"You are of the Kelhari," she replied.

He inclined his head slightly. "I am Wei Mills of the Kelhari." The name had been chosen for diplomatic purposes, Isabella knew—the Kelhari had adapted human naming conventions for this interaction. "The Director of Social Coherence requires your presence."

Isabella considered her options. She was a prisoner, technically, though the Kelhari preferred the term "detained guest." Her ship had made an emergency landing—genuinely emergency, though she'd chosen the emergency—and the Kelhari had responded with characteristic efficiency, securing both her and her vessel while they determined what to do with this unexpected visitor.

"I will accompany you to the Director," Isabella said, completing the ritual.

Wei Mills gestured, and two guards appeared in the doorway. They escorted Isabella through corridors of stunning biological architecture—the Kelhari grew their buildings rather than constructing them, using advanced biotechnology to shape living structures that adapted to their inhabitants' needs. The walls pulsed gently with bioluminescence, and the air carried the faint scent of growing things.

The Director's chamber was vast and circular, its walls a deep indigo that seemed to absorb light. The Director himself—Santiago Lee, as he'd introduced himself in their first brief meeting—sat in a central seat that appeared to have grown specifically to accommodate his form. Around him stood several other Kelhari, their roles indicated by the subtle variations in their skin pigmentation that marked different genetic castes.

"Isabella Graves," Santiago Lee said, his voice carrying the precise articulation that characterized all Kelhari speech. "You will answer questions regarding your presence on our world."

"I will answer truthfully," Isabella said.

"We have prepared a verification system," Santiago Lee continued. A device was wheeled in—a biotechnological marvel that combined organic and synthetic components in ways Earth's scientists could only dream of. "This will monitor your physiological responses and determine the veracity of your statements. It has been calibrated to your human biology."

Isabella allowed herself to be connected to the device. Sensors attached to her skin, monitoring everything from heart rate to neurochemical fluctuations. The Kelhari's ability to adapt their technology to alien physiology in just four days was remarkable—and deeply concerning. A species this advanced, this efficient, and this rigid in their thinking posed exactly the kind of threat that had brought Isabella here in the first place.

"We will begin with simple calibrations," Santiago Lee said. "What is your species designation?"

"Human," Isabella replied.

"What is your planet of origin called?"

"Earth," Isabella said.

"Are you currently standing?"

"No, I am seated," Isabella said.

Santiago Lee consulted with his technicians, who signaled that the device was functioning properly. "Now we will proceed to substantive questions. Your ship entered our atmosphere and landed. Was this intentional?"

"Yes," Isabella said.

"For what purpose?"

"To initiate contact with your civilization," Isabella said.

"You represent a governing body?" Santiago Lee asked.

"I do," Isabella confirmed.

"Describe this governing body's structure," Santiago Lee commanded.

Isabella took a breath. This was the moment she'd been preparing for—the reason she'd volunteered for this mission despite knowing it would be difficult, possibly dangerous, and certainly frustrating. The Kelhari needed to be exposed to a concept so foreign to their thinking that it would occupy their considerable intellectual resources for years, possibly generations. They needed to be given an existential question that their rigid logical framework couldn't easily resolve.

"The structure cannot be simply described," Isabella said carefully.

Santiago Lee's expression hardened. "All structures can be described. We are a logical people. We deal in precise definitions and clear hierarchies. Describe your government."

"I will try," Isabella said. "But you may find it difficult to understand."

"We will understand," Santiago Lee said with absolute confidence. "We have mastered biotechnology, physics, chemistry, and social organization. We have eliminated economic inequality through genetic optimization and perfect resource distribution. We have achieved a form of corporate governance—if you will—where each individual functions as a cell in a larger organism, with the Director serving as the coordinating consciousness. This is the only logical system. Now, describe yours."

"We call it democracy," Isabella said. "It means rule by the people. All people participate in governance."

There was a moment of silence. Then one of the attendant Kelhari, a female with darker blue skin named Zara Rivera, spoke up. "This is impossible. If all participate in governance, who governs? Governance requires hierarchy. It requires a single point of decision-making to ensure coherence and efficiency."

"We have no single point of decision-making," Isabella said.

"Then you have no government," Santiago Lee said flatly.

"We do have government," Isabella countered. "Laws are made and enforced. Resources are distributed. Conflicts are resolved."

"By whom?" Zara Rivera demanded.

"By the people themselves," Isabella said. "Through representatives they choose, through direct voting, through various mechanisms that allow collective decision-making."

Santiago Lee leaned forward. "You are saying that individuals who disagree with a decision still follow it?"

"Often, yes," Isabella said.

"Why?" The question came from another Kelhari, Omar May, whose role appeared to be some kind of social theorist. "What compels them? If there is no Director to enforce compliance, no genetic optimization to ensure cooperative behavior, what prevents chaos?"

"The social contract," Isabella said, using a term she'd carefully prepared. "An agreement, implicit and explicit, that we make with each other to follow collective decisions even when they disadvantage us individually."

"This is irrational," Omar May said. "Behavioral economics would predict defection from such an arrangement. Individuals would pursue their own interests."

"Sometimes they do," Isabella admitted. "But the system continues to function."

"Impossible," Zara Rivera said. She turned to the technicians. "The verification device must be malfunctioning. She cannot be telling the truth."

The lead technician, a Kelhari named Rosa Hawkins, examined her instruments carefully. "The device indicates truth," she said slowly. "Her physiological responses are consistent with honest statement."

"Then recalibrate it," Omar May snapped. "The statements are logically contradictory. A government with no governor. Laws that are followed without enforcement. Individuals acting against their own interests without compulsion. These things cannot coexist."

Santiago Lee held up a hand for silence. "Perhaps we are asking the wrong questions. Isabella Graves, let us approach this differently. In your system, who has the final authority to make decisions?"

"The people," Isabella said.

"All of them simultaneously?" Santiago Lee asked.

"In a sense, yes," Isabella said.

"How is this coordinated?" Zara Rivera asked. "How do millions—billions?—of individuals reach a single decision?"

"Through various processes," Isabella said. "Voting, deliberation, representation—"

"But someone must count the votes," Omar May interrupted. "Someone must organize the deliberation. Someone must coordinate the representatives. That someone holds the power. That someone is the true governor."

"Those are administrative functions," Isabella said. "The power remains with the people."

"Power cannot remain with everyone," Santiago Lee said with growing frustration. "Power must reside somewhere. It must have a location, a holder, a source."

"It resides in the collective agreement," Isabella said. "In the social contract."

"Show us this contract," Zara Rivera demanded. "Let us examine its terms."

"It's not a physical document," Isabella said. "It's a concept. A shared understanding."

The Kelhari looked at each other in obvious confusion. For a species that had mastered biotechnology to the point of redesigning their own genomes, that had created perfect social coherence through genetic optimization and rigid hierarchy, the idea of a government based on abstract agreement rather than concrete authority was genuinely incomprehensible.

"This is a waste of time," Omar May said. "She is either lying, or her species is so primitive and chaotic that they mistake disorder for governance."

"The device says she tells the truth," Rosa Hawkins reminded him.

"Then the device is flawed," Omar May insisted.

Santiago Lee studied Isabella for a long moment. "We will continue this examination," he said finally. "But we will need to consult our experts in social theory and behavioral economics. We will need to conduct historical analysis of our own governmental evolution to understand how such a system could possibly function. This may take some time."

"I understand," Isabella said, keeping her expression neutral while internally celebrating. The hook was set. The Kelhari would now spend months, possibly years, trying to understand democratic governance. And in trying to understand it, they would necessarily have to question their own assumptions about hierarchy, authority, and social organization.

They would have to engage with ideas about personal growth and individual autonomy that their genetic optimization program had essentially eliminated. They would have to consider forms of cultural evolution beyond their rigid, directed path. They would have to grapple with existential questions about the nature of authority and legitimacy that had no place in their current worldview.

And most importantly, they would be too busy with this intellectual puzzle to expand their civilization beyond their current borders. A species this efficient and this rigid, if left unchecked, would spread through the galaxy like a perfectly optimized plague, assimilating or destroying everything in their path. But give them an unsolvable problem—unsolvable within their current framework, at least—and they would turn all that formidable intellectual power inward.

The Kelhari were brilliant at solving physical and biological problems. But they had no experience with the messy, contradictory, paradoxical nature of social and political philosophy. They had optimized those problems away through genetic engineering and rigid hierarchy. Now, confronted with a system that worked despite—or because of—its apparent contradictions, they would have to either dismiss it as impossible (which the verification device prevented) or try to understand it (which would require fundamentally rethinking their entire worldview).

Over the next several days, Isabella was visited by a parade of Kelhari experts. Social theorists tried to model democratic governance using their frameworks of genetic optimization and behavioral economics, only to find that the models broke down when applied to beings who weren't genetically programmed for cooperation. Historians attempted to find parallels in the oral history of the Kelhari's own development, but their evolution had been so deliberately directed that they had no experience with emergent social orders. Biotechnology specialists wondered if humans had some genetic trait that enabled this seemingly impossible form of governance—Isabella truthfully told them that humans were remarkably diverse genetically, which only confused them further.

Each expert left more puzzled than when they arrived. The verification device continued to confirm that Isabella was telling the truth, which meant the problem wasn't with her statements but with the Kelhari's ability to comprehend them.

On the seventh day, Isabella noticed that the security around her chamber had grown lax. Doors that should have been locked weren't. Weapons that should have been secured were left accessible. It wasn't carelessness—the Kelhari didn't do carelessness. It was something deeper, something unconscious.

The Kelhari mind, for all its logical precision and genetic optimization, still had depths that their conscious awareness didn't fully control. And when confronted with a truly insoluble problem—one that couldn't be resolved within their existing framework—the unconscious mind sought other solutions. If the problem couldn't be solved, perhaps the problem could be made to disappear.

There were two ways to make a problem disappear: destroy it, or let it escape. Destruction would require conscious acknowledgment that the problem was insoluble, which the Kelhari weren't capable of—their entire civilization was built on the premise that all problems could be solved through sufficient application of logic and biotechnology. But escape... escape could happen through a series of small, unconscious lapses that no individual Kelhari would have to take responsibility for.

Isabella took the opportunity. She moved through the corridors of Evergreen, following the path her unconscious captors had left open for her. She reached the facility where her ship was being held—another door unlocked, another guard conveniently absent. The ship had been repaired with typical Kelhari efficiency, every system optimized beyond its original specifications.

She launched from Evergreen and set course for the outer system, then engaged her faster-than-light drive. As the stars stretched and compressed around her, she allowed herself a small smile.

The mission was complete. The Kelhari had been given their puzzle—a form of governance that worked despite violating every principle of their social theory. They would spend years, possibly decades, trying to understand it. Some of them might eventually succeed, but only by developing new frameworks of thought, new ways of understanding social organization that went beyond genetic optimization and rigid hierarchy.

And in developing those new frameworks, they would necessarily change. They would have to acknowledge that efficiency and logic weren't the only values worth pursuing. They would have to recognize that some problems didn't have neat solutions, that some systems worked precisely because they were messy and contradictory.

By the time they figured it out—if they ever did—they would no longer be the threat they had been. They would have evolved, culturally if not genetically, into something more complex and less dangerous.

Isabella activated her ship's communication system, sending a tight-beam message back toward Earth. She had no psionic abilities, but the message would reach the right people eventually.

"Mission successful," she transmitted. "The Kelhari have been given a problem in political philosophy that their current framework cannot solve. Democracy—true democracy, with all its contradictions and paradoxes—is incomprehensible to a species that has optimized away individual variation and built their entire civilization on genetic hierarchy and rigid logic.

"They can't understand how people would follow laws they themselves made, especially laws that disadvantage them. They can't grasp the concept of authority that comes from collective agreement rather than imposed hierarchy. They can't comprehend a social contract that exists as shared understanding rather than genetic programming.

"To understand it, they'll have to question everything about their own system. They'll have to develop new fields of study—political philosophy, social psychology, maybe even art history to understand how cultures express and transmit values outside of genetic programming. They'll have to grapple with questions of personal growth and individual autonomy that they've eliminated through biotechnology.

"It's going to keep them busy for a long time. Long enough for us to prepare, if they ever do expand outward. But I think by the time they understand democracy, they'll be too changed to be the threat they were.

"Also, I'm incredibly bored and ready to come home. Intellectual victory is satisfying, but I miss coffee and conversations that don't require perfect logical precision.

"Isabella Graves, signing off."

She settled back in her pilot's chair and watched the stars stream past. Somewhere behind her, in Evergreen, Belvoria, the Kelhari were probably convening another committee of experts, trying to solve the unsolvable puzzle she'd given them. She hoped they enjoyed it.

After all, personal growth often came from struggling with problems that didn't have easy answers. The Kelhari were about to get a crash course in that particular lesson.

And if they survived the experience, they might just become something worth knowing, rather than something to be feared.

I am a Probability Sink
By ISABEL MCCOY

When I arrived at the climate tech startup's office in Bridgewater, Selvoria, I was exhausted from the morning's disasters, but the effect was the same as being tired. I let myself into the building, which had an abandoned look since most of the team was at the renewable energy conference in Pearlbrook, and took a cold shower in the executive washroom. The current temperature outside, according to my phone, was thirty-two degrees Celsius, but according to the ancient thermometer in our lab, it was thirty-eight.

I got dressed and went into the main workspace, wishing desperately that my business partner Ruth Singh were here to tell me why everything looked so desolate. What do successful entrepreneurs do, I asked myself, that I have left undone? I've organized the prototypes, I've filed the patent applications, and I've updated the investor deck.... Ah! The coffee mugs. I washed them and put them back, but still the place looked partner-deserted.

It had been a catastrophic day; I had forgotten to charge my phone, so I'd had to rush to make a pitch meeting at one of the venture capital firms we were courting. I didn't notice the impending thunderstorm and had no umbrella when I reached the street, to find myself confronted with an almost tropical downpour. I would have turned back, but an auto-taxi pulled up and a woman got out, so I dashed through the rain and got in.

"Venture Plaza, downtown," I said to the AI system.

"Confirmed," said the synthesized voice, and I heard the electric motor hum, and then sputter and die. After some futile diagnostic beeps, the system announced, "Sorry, passenger. Vehicle malfunction. Please find alternative transportation."

If possible, it was raining even harder. I opened my jacket over my head and ran for the metro: four blocks. Malfunctioning traffic signals held me up at each intersection and I was soaked when I reached the platform, just in time to miss the express train. After an abnormal delay, I caught one which exactly missed the connection at Central Station. The same thing happened at both ends of the cross-town line, but I found the rain had stopped when I emerged at Market and Fifth.

As I walked toward Venture Plaza, I passed a large construction site where they were preparing to install a massive solar panel array for the new carbon-neutral office complex. There was the usual crowd of onlookers watching the installation robots and, in particular, a technician operating a plasma cutter who was removing some old concrete foundation. While I watched, a large chunk fell away, and for an instant I was able to see something that looked like a piece of crystalline mineral, the size of a storage container. It glowed with an unusual iridescence in the sunlight, and then his cutting torch hit it.

There was a faint pop and the thing shattered. The technician stumbled backward but wasn't hurt. At the moment of the fracture—if so minor an event can be called one—I felt something sting my cheek and, on touching it, found a small cut. I dabbed at it with a tissue but, though slight, the bleeding wouldn't stop, so I went into a pharmacy and bought some liquid bandage which I applied to the tiny wound.

When I got to the VC firm, I found that the partners had rescheduled without telling me.

During the day, by actual count, I heard the phrase "disruptive innovation" eleven times, and another startup favorite, "paradigm shift," fifteen times. However, our climate technology proposal had been accepted for second-round consideration because nobody had noticed my absence from the original meeting time. There you have what is known as the startup world, the entrepreneurship game, or the venture capital racket, depending upon which stage of funding you've achieved.

The metro gave a repeat performance going back, and as I arrived at our building in Bridgewater, the security guard was standing outside talking to a municipal inspector.

He said, "Hello, Ms. McCoy. I guess you just missed it at Venture Plaza." I looked confused and he explained, "We just heard about it: all four elevators in that building locked simultaneously on different floors. Sounds impossible. I guess you just avoided that mess."

Anything can happen in the startup world, I thought. "That's right, Oscar," I said, and went inside.

Psychology tells us that some people are accident-prone; I, on the other hand, seemed recently to be coincidence-prone, fluke-magnetized, and except for my phone, I'd had no control over what had been happening.

I went into our small kitchenette to make coffee and reread the instructions Ruth had left, telling me how to manage by myself until she returned from the conference in Pearlbrook, a matter of eight days. How to operate the espresso machine, how to access the backup servers, whom to call if equipment failed. My partner used to be a systems engineer and she is quite convinced that I cannot function without her oversight. She is correct, but not for the reasons she supposes.

I opened the refrigerator to get some oat milk and saw another note: "When you take out the Samples or Equipment, Return them Immediately. And Close the Door properly."

Intimidated, I took my coffee into the main lab and sat down in front of my workstation. As I reviewed the renewable energy prototype documentation that was supposed to liberate us from investor dependency, I noticed an error and picked up a stylus. When I put it down, it rolled off the desk, and with my eyes on the screen, I groped under the chair for it. Then I looked down. The stylus was standing on its end.

There, I thought to myself, is that one chance in a million we hear about, and picked up the stylus. I turned back to the documentation and drank some of the coffee in hopes of inspiration and relief from the oppressive heat, but nothing came. I went back and reviewed the whole technical specification to try to build momentum, but came to a dead stop at the last section.

Damn the heat, damn the stylus, damn venture capital and institutional reform. My coffee was gone and I went back to the kitchenette and read Ruth's notes again to see if they would feel like a message from her. I noticed one I had missed, attached to the recycling chute: "Composting collected at 6:00 AM so the idea is to Put materials Here the Night Before. Good luck with everything."

I made another coffee and went to stare out of the lab window at the rooftop garden opposite. The sun was out again and a researcher was monitoring a flock of sensor-equipped drones. They circled in a pattern, collecting air quality data, but were kept in constant motion.

Drones typically fly in coordinated patterns and adjust simultaneously, so that their solar panels all catch the sunlight at optimal angles. I was thinking about this efficient fact when I saw that as they were making a turn, they seemed to cluster together unnaturally. By some peculiar chance, they all wanted the same position in the airspace, and several collided and fell.

The researcher was as surprised as I and went to one of the damaged drones and picked it up. She stood there shaking her head, examining its components.

My speculations about this peculiar aerial traffic accident were interrupted by raised voices in the hallway. Since our building is usually very professional, I was astonished to hear what sounded like an argument, and among the angry voices I recognized that of my colleague, Steven Mason, a very reserved guy who works on ecosystem restoration projects and has never, to my knowledge, caused disruptions, particularly in the late afternoon.

"You can't accuse me of that!" I heard him shout. "I tell you I bought this deck this morning and the seal wasn't broken until we started playing!"

Several other loud voices erupted simultaneously.

"Nobody draws a royal flush five times in a row!"

"Yeah, and only when you were dealing!"

The tone of the argument was becoming hostile, and I opened the door to offer Steven assistance if needed. There were three people confronting him, evidently torn between the desire to storm off and the impulse to stay and confront him further. His face was flushed and he looked bewildered.

"Here!" he said, holding out a deck of cards. "For heaven's sake, examine them yourselves if you think they're marked!"

The nearest person struck them from his hand. "Fine, Houdini! So they're not marked! All I know is five royal flushes..."

His voice faded. He and the others stared at the scattered cards on the floor. About half were face down, as might be expected, and the rest face up—all spades.

Someone must have called it, because at that moment the elevator arrived and the three people, with half-frightened, incredulous expressions, and in silence, got in and descended. My colleague stood looking at the impossibly arranged cards.

"Good grief!" he said, and started to collect them. "What a session..."

I helped him and suggested he come to the lab for coffee and explain what happened, but I had an intuition about what I would hear.

After a while, he calmed down, but still seemed dazed.

"Never experienced anything like it," he said. "Wouldn't have thought it possible. Those people didn't believe it. Every hand normal, nothing unusual—three of a kind, a straight, that sort of thing, and one person got queens over jacks, until it's my deal. Incredible! Royal flush—every single time! And each time, somebody else has four aces..."

He started to perspire again, so I got up to make him more coffee. There was one container of oat milk left, but when I tried to open it, the cap broke and fragments got into the liquid.

"I'll have to go down for more milk," I said.

"I'll come too. I need fresh air."

At the corner market, the clerk handed me three bottles in what must have been a defective bag, because as he passed them to me over the counter, the bottom gave way and they fell onto the tile floor. None of them broke, although the fall must have been from at least six feet. Steven was too absorbed in his thoughts to notice and I was becoming accustomed to improbabilities.

On the sidewalk, a person walking in front of Steven stopped suddenly to check their phone and Steven, to avoid collision, stepped into the bike lane where an electric scooter swerved to avoid Steven. The pavement was still wet and the scooter skidded, its rear end lightly tapping a small autonomous delivery vehicle, which was moving rather quickly. It spun sideways and, without any apparent friction, went directly up the steps of a brownstone across the street, coming to rest with its front compartment inside the entrance, which someone opened at that moment.

The sight of this caused another cyclist to skid, and when both the cyclist and a pedestrian had stopped their confused movements, they were face to face, blocking the entire sidewalk. This left them exactly no room to move in either direction.

Although reasonably wide, this is a two-way street, and within minutes, traffic was backed up from both directions as far as the main boulevards. Everyone was sounding their horns.

Oscar was frustrated—more so when he tried to use the emergency communication panel.

It was malfunctioning.

Upstairs, the ventilation was blowing papers around the lab and I closed the vents, mainly to shut out the chaos and commotion. Steven had brightened somewhat.

"I'll stay for one more coffee and then I'm expected at the ecosystem restoration site," he said. "You know, I think this would make an interesting case study." He smiled and gestured toward the pandemonium.

When he left, I noticed it was getting dark and turned on the desk lamp. Then I saw the cables. They were all tangled in knots, except one. That was tied in three knots.

All right, I told myself, it was the ventilation system. But I felt the time had come for me to seek expert consultation, so I went to the phone to call Felix Chang. Felix is a professor of applied physics and metaphysics at a university in Carmel, Yendor, and maintains a research office near us. He is highly analytical, but we believe he understands everything.

When I picked up the receiver, the line sounded dead and I thought, more problems. Then I heard someone clear their throat and I said hello. Felix's voice said, "Isabel? You must have picked up just as the connection completed. That's a remarkably unlikely coincidence."

"Not in the least," I said. "Come over here immediately. I have something that requires your expertise."

"Well, actually, I was calling to ask you and Ruth—"

"Ruth's at the conference for the week. Can you get here quickly? It's urgent."

"Right away," he said, and disconnected.

While I waited, I thought I might try documenting a few notes about our renewable energy prototype—perhaps some insight would emerge now. It did, but as I came to a point where I was about to type the word "photosynthetic," I decided it was too technical for the summary, and stopped at the letter "P." Then I saw that I had inexplicably pressed all the wrong keys several positions to the side of the correct ones, and deleted the paragraph, my face burning.

This was absolutely not my day.

"Well," Felix said, "nothing you've described is impossible or supernatural. Just extraordinarily, extraordinarily improbable. In fact, the odds against that card game alone would lead me to suspect Steven, well as I know him. It's all these other incidents..."

He stood and walked to the window and looked at the warm twilight while I waited. Then he turned around; he had an expression of concern.

"Isabel, you're a rational person, so I don't think you'll be offended by what I'm about to say. What you've told me is so impossibly unlikely, and the odds against it so astronomical, that I must consider the possibility that you're either fabricating this or experiencing some kind of perceptual distortion." I started to protest, but he gestured for me to wait. "I understand, but don't you see that that is far more likely than..." He stopped and shook his head. Then he brightened. "I have an idea. Perhaps we can conduct a demonstration."

He thought for an intense moment and snapped his fingers. "Do you have any coins?"

"Why, yes," I said. "Several." I reached into my pocket. There must have been nearly three euros in various denominations. "Do you think they'll all show the same year, perhaps?"

"Did you accumulate all these coins today?"

"No. Over the past week."

He shook his head. "In that case, no. Setting aside the fact that you could have arranged it deliberately, if my tentative hypothesis is correct, that would be actually impossible. It would require temporal reversal. I'll explain later. No, just toss the coins. Let's see if they all land heads up."

I moved away from the equipment and tossed the handful of coins onto the floor. They clattered and bounced—and bounced together—and stacked themselves into a neat tower.

I looked at Felix. His eyes narrowed. Without a word, he took several coins from his own pocket and threw them.

These coins didn't stack. They simply fell into a perfectly straight line, each one touching the next.

"Well," I said, "what more evidence do you need?"

"Extraordinary," he said, and sat down. "I suppose you're aware that there are two great apparently opposing principles governing the Universe—randomness and order. The distribution of particles in a gas is an example of random distribution, and biological life is an example of order. The motions of molecules in a liquid are what we call random, but there are so many of them, we treat them statistically and derive thermodynamic laws—quite reliable from a practical standpoint. These laws aren't theoretically absolute; they're matters of extreme probability. Now life, on the other hand, seems not to depend on probability at all; actually, it works against entropy. Or you might say it is certainly not an accidental phenomenon."

"Do you mean," I asked in some confusion, "that some form of life is controlling the coins and—the other events?"

He shook his head. "No. What I mean is that improbable events usually have improbable explanations. When I observe a natural law being violated, I don't conclude, 'Here's a miracle.' I revise my understanding of the principles. Something—I don't know what—is occurring, and it seems to involve probability manipulation, and it seems to center on you. Were you still in that building when the elevators malfunctioned? Or nearby?"

"I must have been. It happened shortly after I left."

"Mm. You're the epicenter, certainly. But why?"

"Epicenter of what?" I asked. "I feel as though I'm at the center of some kind of probability storm. Something is targeting me!"

Felix smiled. "Don't be superstitious. And especially don't anthropomorphize."

"Well, if it's the opposite of random, it must be some form of intelligence."

"On what basis? All we know with certainty is that random events are being reorganized. A crystal, for example, is not alive, but it's a non-random arrangement of molecules.... I wonder." He had a distant, contemplative look.

I was beginning to feel hungry and the coffee had worn off.

"Let's go out for dinner," I said. "There's nothing in the kitchenette and I'm not supposed to use the main lab equipment for food preparation. Only coffee and basic items."

We put on our jackets and went down to the street. From both directions, we could hear emergency vehicles clearing the stalled traffic. There were, by this time, several frustrated traffic coordinators managing the operation and we heard one of them say to Oscar, "I don't understand what's happening here. Every single vehicle has some kind of malfunction. They can't any of them reverse or move forward for various reasons. Never witnessed anything like it."

Near us, two pedestrians were performing a peculiar little dance as they tried to pass one another; as soon as one moved aside to let the other pass, the other would shift to the same side. They both had embarrassed smiles initially, but before long their smiles were replaced by expressions of suspicion and then determination.

"All right, wise guy!" they shouted simultaneously, and pushed forward, only to collide. They stepped back and threw simultaneous gestures which met in mid-air. Then began one of the most remarkable confrontations ever witnessed—an argument in which accusation met accusation but never any resolution, until both parties backed away unsatisfied, muttering identical complaints and threats.

Oscar appeared at that moment. His face was glistening with perspiration. "Are you all right, Ms. McCoy?" he asked. "I don't know what's happening around here, but ever since I started my shift this afternoon, things have been going haywire. Martinez!" he called—his voice could carry across a stadium. "Bring those people over here!"

Two individuals in a confused dispute, with their identical briefcases somehow locked together, were escorted across the street, which meant climbing over vehicle bumpers. Martinez, a competent young security officer, seemed self-conscious; the individuals seemed oblivious.

"All right, now, Mr. Watkins!" one of them said. "Release my briefcase and we'll forget about this!"

"And so now it's Mister Watkins, is it?" said his adversary.

A third person, a woman with her back to us, her briefcase also caught in the tangle, pulled at it tentatively, at which the other two glared at her. She turned her head away and tried to let go, but the handle was caught on her watch. She looked up and I saw it was Ruth. My partner.

"Oh, Isabel!" she said, and managed to detach herself. "Are you all right?" Was I all right!

"Ruth! What are you doing here?"

"I was so worried, and when I saw all this chaos, I didn't know what to think." She pointed to the stalled vehicles. "Are you really all right?"

"Of course I'm all right. But why..."

"The conference coordinator said someone kept trying to access the emergency contact system repeatedly and it was traced to our office here. I kept trying to call, but I only got error messages. Oh dear, are you sure you're all right?"

I put my arm around her and glanced at Felix. He had an introspective expression. Then I caught Oscar's eye. It had a thoughtful, almost suspicious quality.

"Trouble does seem to follow you, Ms. McCoy," was all he said.

When we got upstairs, I turned to Felix. "Explain to Ruth," I said. "And incidentally to me. I'm not adequately briefed yet on your hypothesis."

He did so, and when he reached the conclusion, I had the feeling she was ahead of him.

"In other words, you think it's something organic? Some kind of life form?"

"Well," Felix said, "I'm trying to conceive of what else it might be. I'm not succeeding," he admitted.

"But as far as I can determine," Ruth answered, "it's pure probability manipulation, without any discernible pattern or purpose."

"Not quite. It has a center. Isabel is the center."

Ruth looked at me with a curious expression for a moment. "Do you feel all right, darling?" she asked me. I nodded enthusiastically. "You'll think this unscientific of me," she went on to Felix, "but why couldn't it be something like an overactive poltergeist phenomenon?"

"Pure speculation," he said. "No empirical evidence for such things."

"Electromagnetic fields?"

"Absolutely not. For one thing, most of the objects affected weren't ferromagnetic—and don't forget electromagnetism is a force, not a form of energy per se, and a substantial amount of energy has been involved. I acknowledge the energy has primarily been supplied by the objects themselves, but in an electromagnetic field, all you'd observe would be stored potential energy, such as when a piece of iron moves toward a magnet. Then it would simply remain there, like a wound-down clock. These objects do considerably more than that—they continue moving in improbable ways."

"Why did you mention a crystal earlier? Why not a biological organism?"

"Only an analogy," said Felix. "A crystal resembles life in that it has a definite structure and exhibits growth, but that's all. I'll concede this—phenomenon—has no discernible structure and motion is involved, but plants don't move and amoebas have no fixed shape. A crystal feeds, but it doesn't metabolize what it consumes; it merely reorganizes it into a non-random pattern. In this case, it's reorganizing random motions and it has a nucleus and it seems to be growing—at least in what you might call improbability intensity."

Ruth frowned. "Then what is it? What's it composed of?"

"I would hypothesize it's composed of the motions themselves. There's a similar concept in particle physics regarding virtual particles. Another similarity to crystals is that it appears to be forming around a nucleus not of its own substance—the way a grain of sand in a supersaturated solution becomes the nucleation site."

"Sounds like a pearl in an oyster," Ruth said, and gave me a teasing look.

"Why," I asked Felix, "did you say the coins couldn't show the same date? I mean apart from the unlikely chance I received them that way."

"Because I don't believe this phenomenon initiated before today and everything that's occurred can all be described as improbable events here and now. The dates were already stamped, and to alter them would require retroactive causation, reversing time. That's excluded, in my framework. That communication system now—"

The door chime sounded. We were not surprised to find it was the telecommunications technician. She examined the system and made disapproving sounds.

"I think you dropped the handset," she said with evident disapproval.

"Certainly not," I said. "Is it damaged?"

"Not exactly damaged, but—" She shook her head and disassembled it further.

Felix went over and they discussed the technical problem in low voices. Finally the technician left and Ruth contacted her mother to provide reassurance. Felix attempted to explain to me what had occurred with the system.

"You must have dislodged something. And then you replaced the handset in such a way that the contact wasn't quite disconnected."

"But for heaven's sake, Ruth says the calls were continuing for an extended period! I contacted you only a short while ago and it must have taken her nearly three hours to get here from Pearlbrook."

"Then you must have done it twice and the vibrations in the structure—something like that—just happened to generate the correct signal impulses. Yes, I understand your reaction," he said, observing my expression. "It's beginning to intensify."

Ruth had finished her call and suggested going out for dinner. I was so relieved to see her that I'd forgotten about being hungry.

"I'm in no condition to cook," she said. "Let's get away from all this."

Felix raised an eyebrow. "If all this, as you call it, will permit us."

In the lobby, we encountered Steven, looking satisfied in a journalistic way.

"I've been assigned to document the story—who could be better qualified?—I work here. So far, I don't quite understand what's been occurring. I've been talking to Oscar, but he was circumspect. I got the impression he thinks you're involved in some mystical way. Hello, Felix, what's your assessment?"

"He has a hypothesis," said Ruth. "Come and eat with us and he'll explain it thoroughly."

Since we decided on a climate-controlled restaurant nearby on Harbor Avenue, we walked. The congestion of vehicles didn't seem any less than before and we saw Oscar again. He was talking to a municipal supervisor, and when he noticed us, he said something that made the supervisor regard us with interest. Particularly me.

"If you want your briefcase, Ms. Singh," Oscar said, "it's at the security office. What remains of it, anyway."

Ruth thanked him and there was a brief pause, during which I felt the evaluative regard of the supervisor. I pulled out a package of mints, which I had opened, as always, by tearing the wrapper. I happened to have it inverted and all the mints fell out. Before I could move my foot to obscure what they had arranged themselves into on the pavement, the two officials saw it. The supervisor gave me a hard look, but said nothing. I quickly scattered the offensive mints into the gutter.

When we arrived at the restaurant, it was crowded but cool—although it didn't remain cool for long. We sat down at a corner table near the entrance and ordered sparkling water as we examined the menu. Sitting at the adjacent table were a heavyset woman wearing a very long, brilliant purple evening gown, and a thin, sour-faced man in formal attire. When the server returned, they commandeered him and began ordering dinner fussily: a grain bowl for the man, and gazpacho, quinoa salad, and mango sorbet for the heavyset woman.

I tasted my water. It was most peculiar; it seemed to have salt in it instead of being neutral. I mentioned this and my companions tried theirs, and grimaced.

The server was concerned and apologetic, and took the glasses back to the bar across the room. The bartender looked over at us and tasted one of the drinks. Then he poured them into his sink with a puzzled expression and prepared a new batch. After mixing this, he set out a row of glasses, added ice and began to pour.

That is to say he tilted the pitcher over the first glass, but nothing came out. He tapped it against the bar and tried again. Still nothing. Then he removed the top and probed into it with a stirrer, his face flushed with frustration.

I had the impression that the pitcher had frozen solid. Well, ice is a crystal, I thought to myself.

The other bartender provided him with a fresh pitcher, but the same thing occurred, and I saw no more because the customers sitting at the bar crowded around, offering suggestions. Our server returned, baffled, saying he'd have the drinks momentarily, and went to the kitchen. When he returned, he had the woman's gazpacho and some bread, which he set down, and then went to the bar, where the audience had expanded.

Ruth lit a cigarette and said, "I suppose this is all part of it, Isabel. Incidentally, it seems to be getting warmer in here."

It was, and I had the sense the place was quieter—a background sound had ceased. It occurred to me that I no longer heard the faint hum of the air-conditioning unit over the door, and as I started to mention this, I made a gesture toward it. My hand collided with Ruth's when she tapped her cigarette over the ashtray, and the cigarette landed in the neighboring gazpacho.

"Hey! What's the meaning of this?" snarled the sour-faced man.

"I'm terribly sorry," I said. "It was an accident. I—"

"Throwing cigarettes at people!" the heavyset woman said.

"I really didn't intend to," I began again, standing up. There must have been a loose thread on the edge of their tablecloth which one of my bracelet clasps caught on, because as I stepped out from between the closely positioned tables, I pulled everything—tablecloth, silverware, water glasses, ashtrays and the gazpacho-à-la-nicotine—onto the floor.

The heavyset woman surged from the booth and struck me solidly. The man assumed a boxing stance. The proprietor of the establishment, a man with prominent dark eyebrows, hurried toward us with a determined expression. I attempted to explain what had happened, but I was overwhelmed by shouting, and the proprietor frowned severely.
question: What unusual formation did the coins create when thrown by Isabel?
