But that is not important. You need only understand that we cannot be confused by such means."

"Good," Riley said.

The experts' luminescence flickered. "Good?" Omar said.

"Naturally," Riley said in a friendly tone.

The expert's expression shifted, showing concern. Zephyrians didn't have teeth to show, but their luminescence patterns were expressive enough. "Your strategy is failing," the expert said, "and you call this a good thing. You can mean only that your strategy is different from the one we are analyzing."

"True," Riley said.

There was a short silence. The expert's luminescence brightened. He examined the indicators of the truth-verification system with great care. "What is your strategy?" he said at last, in a curious tone.

"To respond to your questions, truthfully and logically," Riley said.

The silence this time was even longer.

"The system says that you tell the truth," the expert said at last, in an awed tone. "Thus, you must be working against your native planet. You must want us to integrate with your economic systems, and have come here secretly to facilitate this."

Riley was very glad that wasn't a question. It was, after all, the only logical deduction.

But it happened to be wrong.

"The name of your planet is Earth?" the Prime Coordinator asked. A few minutes had passed; the experts were gathered around the central display. Riley was still connected to the system; a logical race makes use of a collaborator, but a logical race does not trust blindly.

"Sometimes," Riley said.

"It has other designations?" the Prime Coordinator said.

"It has no designation," Riley said truthfully. The Zephyrian idiom was like the Earthly one; and certainly a planet had no designation. People attached designations to it, that was all. It had none of its own.

"Yet you call it Earth?" the Prime Coordinator said.

"I do," Riley said, "for convenience."

"Do you know its location?" the Prime Coordinator said.

"Not with exactitude," Riley said.

There was a stir. "But you can locate it again," the Prime Coordinator said.

"I can," Riley said.

"And you will inform us about it?" the Prime Coordinator went on.

"I will," Riley said, "so far as I am able."

"We will wish to know about economic systems," the Prime Coordinator said, "and about resource distribution and production methods. But we must first know of the manner of coordination on this planet. Is your planet integrated with others in a system or does it exist independently?"

Riley nearly smiled. "Both," he said.

A short silence was broken by one of the attendant experts. "We have theorized that a subsystem may be permitted to make some of its own coordinations, leaving only the more extensive ones for the primary system. This seems to us inefficient and liable to error, yet it is a possible structure. Is it the structure you mean?"

Very sharp, Riley told himself grimly. "It is," he said.

"Then the system which coordinates several planets is primary," the Prime Coordinator said.

"It is," Riley said.

"What is the coordination mechanism?" the Prime Coordinator said.

The key question had, at last, been asked. Riley felt grateful that the logical Zephyrians had determined to begin from the beginning, instead of going off after details of technology first; it saved a lot of time.

"The answer to that question," Riley said, "cannot be given to you."

"Any question of fact has an answer," the Prime Coordinator said firmly. "A paradox is not involved here; a system exists, and some mechanism provides coordination. Perhaps several mechanisms share this function; perhaps automated systems do the work. But where there is coordination, there is a coordination mechanism. Is this agreed?"

"Certainly," Riley said. "It is completely obvious and true."

"The planet from which you come is part of a system of planets which are coordinated, you have said," the Prime Coordinator went on.

"True," Riley said.

"Then there is a coordination mechanism for this system," the Prime Coordinator said.

"True," Riley said again.

The Prime Coordinator's luminescence dimmed slightly. "Explain this mechanism to us," they said.

Riley shrugged. "The explanation cannot be given to you."

The Prime Coordinator turned to a group of experts and a short murmured conversation took place. At its end the Prime Coordinator turned their attention back to Riley. "Is the deficiency in you?" they said. "Are you in some way unable to describe this coordination?"

"It can be described," Riley said.

"Then you will experience negative consequences if you describe it to us?" the Prime Coordinator went on.

"I will not," Riley said.

It was the signal for another conference. With some satisfaction, Riley noticed that the Zephyrians were becoming slightly uncertain; they were no longer moving and speaking with calm assurance.

The plan was taking hold.

The Prime Coordinator had finished their conference. "You are attempting again to create confusion," they said.

Riley shook his head earnestly. "I am attempting," he said, "not to create confusion."

"Then I request an answer," the Prime Coordinator said.

"I request that I be allowed to ask a question," Riley said.

The Prime Coordinator hesitated, then nodded. "Ask it," they said. "We shall respond if we determine it appropriate to do so."

Riley tried to look grateful. "Well, then," he said, "what is your coordination system?"

The Prime Coordinator beckoned to a tall azure being named Victoria Morris, who stepped forward from a group of Zephyrians, inclined her head in Riley's direction, and began. "Our coordination system is the only logical form of coordination," she said in a melodious voice. "The Prime Coordinator optimizes all decisions, and the population implements. In this way uniformity is achieved, and this uniformity aids in the efficiency of possible action and in the effectiveness of action. All Zephyrians act optimally in the same manner. The Prime Coordinator is selected by rigorous merit assessment; in this way we are assured of optimal judgment and consistent decision-making."

"You have heard our coordination system defined," the Prime Coordinator said. "Now, you will define yours for us."

Riley shook his head. "If you insist," he said, "I'll try it. But you won't understand it."

The Prime Coordinator's luminescence flickered with concern. "We shall understand," they said. "Begin. What coordinates you?"

"Nothing," Riley said.

"But you are coordinated?"

Riley nodded. "Yes."

"Then there is a coordination mechanism," the Prime Coordinator insisted.

"True," Riley said. "But everyone is the coordination mechanism."

"Then there is no coordination," the Prime Coordinator said. "There is no unified optimization."

"No," Riley said equably, "there are many optimizations binding on all."

"What makes them binding?" the Prime Coordinator asked. "What compels you to accept these optimizations? Some of them must be suboptimal for some beings?"

"Many of them are suboptimal," Riley said. "But we are not compelled to accept them."

"Do you act against your own optimization?"

Riley shrugged. "Not knowingly," he said. The Prime Coordinator flashed a look at the technicians handling the truth-verification system. Riley turned to see their expression. They needed no words; the system was telling them, perfectly obviously, that he was speaking the truth. But the truth wasn't making any sense. "I told you you wouldn't understand it," he said.

"It is a deficiency in your explanation," the Prime Coordinator said with unusual sharpness.

"My explanation is as exact as it can be," he said.

The Prime Coordinator's luminescence pulsed rapidly. "Let us try something else," they said. "Everyone is the coordination mechanism. Do you share a single consciousness? A collective mind has been theorized, though we have encountered no examples—"

"Neither have we," Riley said. "We are all individuals, like yourselves."

"But with no single coordinator to optimize decisions, to make determinations—"

"We have no need of one," Riley said calmly.

"Ah," the Prime Coordinator said suddenly, as if they saw clarity ahead. "And why not?"

"We call our form of coordination democracy," Riley said. "It means the coordination of the people, by the people. There is no need for another coordinator."

One of the experts spoke up suddenly. "The beings themselves coordinate each other?" he said. "This is clearly impossible; for, no one being can have the authority to compel acceptance of their optimizations. Without this authority, there can be no effective coordination."

"That is our form of coordination," Riley said.

"You are providing false information," the expert said.

One of the technicians chimed in: "The system indicates—"

"Then the system is miscalibrated," the expert said. "It will be recalibrated."

Riley wondered, as the technicians argued, how long they'd take studying the system, before they realized it didn't have any calibration errors to correct. He hoped it wasn't going to be too long; he could foresee another stretch of boredom coming. And, besides, he was getting homesick.

It took three days—but boredom never really had a chance to set in. Riley found himself the object of more attention than he had hoped for; one by one, the experts came to his quarters, each with a different method of resolving the obvious contradictions in his statements.

Some of them went away frustrated. Others simply went away, uncertain.

On the third day Riley departed.

It wasn't very difficult; he hadn't thought it would be. Even the most logical of thinking beings has unconscious processes as well as conscious ones, and one of the ways of dealing with an unresolvable problem is to make the problem disappear. There were only two ways of doing that, and eliminating the problem's main focus was a little more complicated. That couldn't be done by the unconscious processes; the conscious had to intervene somewhere. And it couldn't.

Because that would mean recognizing, fully and consciously, that the problem was unresolvable. And the Zephyrians weren't capable of that sort of thinking.

Riley thanked his lucky stars that their genius had been restricted to the physical and biological sciences. Any insight at all into the social sciences would have given them the key to his existence, and his entire strategy, within seconds.

But, then, it was lack of that insight that had called for this particular strategy. That, and the political structure of the Zephyrians.

The same lack of insight let the Zephyrian unconscious processes work on his departure without any annoying distractions in the way of deep reflection. Someone left a door unlocked and a communicator nearby—all quite unintentional, Riley was sure. Getting to the shuttle was a little more complicated, but presented no new problems; he was airborne, and then space-borne, inside of a few hours after leaving the quarters.

He set his course, relaxed, and cleared his mind. He had no psionic talents, but the people at Earth Central did; he couldn't receive messages, but he could send them. He sent one now.

Mission accomplished; the Zephyrians aren't about to come integrating into galactic commerce too soon. They've been given food for thought—nice indigestible food that's going to stick in their processing until they finally manage to digest it. But they can't digest it and stay what they are; you've got to understand economic inequality, to some extent, to understand the idea. What keeps us accepting suboptimal outcomes? What keeps us accepting systems that create disadvantages for us? Complex game theory and risk management, of course—but try to make a Zephyrian see it!

With one coordination system and one optimization method, they just weren't equipped for translation. They were too efficient physically to develop the social sciences at all. No social sciences, no insight into my mind or their own—and that means no translation.

These existential questions about governance will keep them busy for decades. They'll need to develop entirely new frameworks—community organizing, peer review, mentorship in democratic thinking. It's the only way they'll understand us. And by the time they do, they'll be different enough to join the Consortium peacefully.

But—damn it—I wish I were home already. I'm bored absolutely stiff!
question: How many days did it take for Riley to leave the Zephyrian planet?

synthetic_story:
THE LAST DEEP-SEA EXPLORER
BY VARIOUS AUTHORS

Illustrated by Digital Artists

[Transcriber's Note: This etext was produced from
Ocean Worlds Quarterly, March 2089
Extensive research did not uncover any evidence that
the U.S. copyright on this publication was renewed.]

What's more important—humanity's understanding
of the deep ocean, or one explorer's peace of mind?

I

They gave him a commemorative plaque. It was meant to be symbolical, of course. In the old tradition. It was crafted from actual titanium alloy, being one of the materials used in the earliest deep-sea submersibles constructed generations past in the coastal facilities of Highpoint, Selvoria. Its significance lay in the fact that it represented the hull plating from the historic vessel Challenger Deep II, not a modern composite material grown through nanotechnology, but actual forged metal that had withstood the crushing pressures of the Mariana Trench.

They also had a ceremony for him, complete with speeches by such luminaries of the Department of Ocean Exploration as Director Luna King and Professor Mohammad Newman. There was also somebody from the Global Resource Management Council who spoke, but he was one of those pseudo-elected bureaucrats who didn't know much about deep-sea exploration nor the significance of Paul Sanders' retirement. Paul didn't bother to remember his name. He only wondered vaguely why the administrator had shown up at all.

In common with recipients of commemorative plaques of a score of generations before him, Paul Sanders would have preferred something a bit more tangible in the way of reward, such as a few additional shares of Universal Basic Income credits to add to his portfolio. But that, he supposed, was asking too much.

The fact of the matter was, Paul knew that his retiring had set them back considerably. They hadn't figured he had enough UBI credits to see him through decently. Well, possibly he didn't, given their standards. But Deep-Sea Pilot Paul Sanders didn't have their standards. He'd had plenty of time to think it over. It was better to retire on a limited income, on a confoundedly limited income, than to take the two or three more dives in hopes of attaining a higher standard of living.

He'd had plenty of time to figure it out, there alone in the crushing darkness of the hadal zone, there on the abyssal plain runs. There on the long, long descents to the hydrothermal vent systems, fearfully checking the symptoms of pressure psychosis, the madness compounded of claustrophobia, sensory deprivation, profound isolation and the constant awareness of millions of tons of water pressing against the hull. Plenty of time. Time to decide that a small efficiency habitat-pod, complete with an auto-recliner and built-in beverage synthesizer, and with one wall a full immersion holographic display, was all he needed to find contentment for a mighty long time. Possibly somebody like Professor Newman might be horrified at the idea of living in an efficiency habitat-pod... not realizing that to a deep-sea pilot it was spacious beyond belief compared to the cramped sphere of a submersible craft.

No. Even as Paul listened to their speeches, accepted the plaque and made a halting little talk of his own, he was grinning inwardly. There wasn't anything they could do. He had them now. He had enough UBI credits to keep him comfortably, by his standards, for the rest of his life. He was never going to subject himself to pressure psychosis again. Just thinking about it, now, set the tremor going in his left hand.

They could pressurize their hulls and descend, for all he gave a damn.

The commemorative plaque idea had been that of Luna King, which was typical, she being in the way of a living traditionalist herself. In fact, Director King was possibly the only living person on the North American continent who still maintained a physical library of actual printed books. Her explanation was that she found the tactile experience of turning pages irreplaceable and that digital formats lacked the gravitas of bound volumes.

That was only an excuse so far as her closest associate, Mohammad Newman, was concerned. Professor Newman was convinced King would have even used a manual typewriter, had she but a touch more courage. King longed for the methodologies of yesteryear, a seldom found phenomenon under the Universal Welfare System.

Seated in an ergonomic chair in the research facility of his Hampton, Ilvaria apartment, Luna King scowled at her colleague. She said, acidly, "Any more brilliant ideas, Mohammad? I presume you now acknowledge that appealing to Sanders' sense of duty, scientific curiosity and desire for historical significance have miserably failed."

Newman said easily, "I wouldn't call Paul Sanders unmotivated. In his position, I am afraid I would do the same thing he has."

"That's nonsense, Mohammad. By all measures of comparative history! Either you or I would gladly take Sanders' place were we capable of performing the duties for which he has been trained. There aren't two people on this continent—there aren't two people in the world!—who better realize the urgency of continuing our exploration of the hadal zones." King snapped her fingers. "Like that, either of us would risk our lives to prevent humanity from completely abandoning the quest to understand our ocean's depths."

Her colleague said drily, "Either of us could have volunteered for deep-sea pilot training forty years ago, Luna. We didn't."

"At that time there wasn't such a devastating percentage of risk-averse individuals throughout this whole Universal Welfare System! Who could foresee that eventually our entire program would face termination due to lack of courageous young people willing to take chances, willing to face the existential questions that arise in profound isolation, willing to react to danger in the manner our ancestors did?"

Newman grunted his sarcasm and synthesized a glass of cold green tea. He said, "Nevertheless, both you and I conform with the present generation in finding it far more pleasant to follow one's research interests in the comfort of one's facility than to be confronted with the psychological dangers of facing nature's extremes in more adventurous pursuits."

King, half angry at her colleague's argument, leaned forward to snap a rebuttal, but the other was raising a hand negatively. "Face reality, Luna. Don't require or expect from Paul Sanders more than is reasonable. He is an average young man. Born in our Universal Welfare System, he was guaranteed his fundamental security by being issued that minimum allocation of UBI credits in our society that allows him an income sufficient to secure the food, housing, medical care and education to sustain a basic level of subsistence. Statistical probabilities were against his ever being drafted into the workforce. Automation and robotics being what they are, only a fraction of the population is ever called up for mandatory service. But Sanders was. His aptitude profile revealed him a possible candidate for deep-sea pilot, and it was you yourself who convinced him to take the training... pointing out the pragmatic advantages such as complete retirement after but six dives, supplemental UBI credits so that he could enjoy a more comfortable life than most, and the recognition that would accrue to him as one of the very few who still participate in hadal exploration. Very well. He was persuaded. Took his training, which, of course, required long years of demanding study in neuroscience, pressure physiology, and submersible operations. Then, performing his duties quite competently, he made his six dives. He is now legally eligible for retirement. He was drafted into the workforce reserves, served his time, and is now free from mandatory labor for the balance of his life. Why should he listen to our pleas for a few more dives?"

"But has he no sense of wonder? Has he no appreciation for..."

Newman was raising his hand again, a gesture that, seemingly mild though it was, had an astonishing ability to halt the conversation of one who debated with the calm, measured man.

He said, "No, he hasn't. Few there are who have, nowadays. Humanity has always paid lip service to exploration, hardships and discovery, but in actuality our instincts, like those of any other animal, lead us to the safest path. Today we've reached the point where no one need face danger—ever. There are few who don't take advantage of that fact. Including you and me, Luna, and including Paul Sanders."

His colleague changed subjects abruptly, impatiently. "Let's leave this frustrating discussion about Sanders' motivation and address the actual problem. The man is the only trained deep-sea pilot in the world. It will take months, possibly more than a year, to bring another candidate to the point where they can safely be trusted to pilot our next research submersible down to hadal depths. Appropriations for our expeditions have been increasingly difficult to secure—even though in our minds, Mohammad, we are approaching critical breakthroughs, discoveries which might possibly so inspire the human race that a renewed commitment to understanding our planet's last frontier will take hold of us. If it is revealed that our organization has deteriorated to the point that we haven't a single qualified pilot, then it might well be that the Economic Planning Council, and especially those administrators on the Appropriations Committee, will terminate the entire Department of Ocean Exploration."

"So..." Newman said gently.

"So somehow we've got to bring Paul Sanders out of his retirement!"

"Now we are addressing the real issue." Newman nodded his agreement. Looking over the rim of his glass, his eyes narrowed in thought as his face took on an expression of calculated strategy. "And do not the ends justify the means?"

King blinked at him.

The other chuckled. "The trouble with you, Luna, is that you have failed to apply lessons from comparative history to our problem. Haven't you ever studied the psychology of sailors and their way of life?"

"Sailors? What in the name of reason do sailors have to do with it?"

"You must realize, my dear Luna, that our Paul Sanders is nothing more than a modern-day sailor, with many of the psychological patterns, perspectives, tendencies and vulnerabilities of the seafarers of the past. Have you never heard of the merchant mariner who dreamed of returning to his hometown and starting a small business? All the long months at sea—and sometimes the cargo vessels or fishing boats would be out for years at a stretch before returning to home port—he would talk of his retirement and his dream. And then? Then in port, it would be one drink with his shipmates, before taking his accumulated wages and heading home. The one drink would lead to another. And morning would find him, broke, tattooed and possibly sleeping it off in a holding cell. So back to sea he'd have to go."

King grunted bitterly. "Unfortunately, our present-day explorer can't be separated from his credits quite so easily. If he could, I'd personally be willing to hack his account, drain his balance and force him back to work."

She brought up her wrist display and flicked it to show her universal credit account. "The ultimate financial regulation," she grunted. "Nobody can spend your money but you, yourself. Nobody can steal it, nobody can, ah, manipulate you out of it. Just how do you expect to separate our modern-day sailor from his accumulated nest egg?"

The other chuckled again. "It is simply a matter of finding contemporary methods, my dear colleague."

II

Paul Sanders was a great believer in the institution of celebration. Any excuse would do. Back when he had finished his basic education at the age of twenty-five and was registered for the labor draft, there hadn't been a chance in a hundred that he'd have the misfortune to have his name selected. But when it had been, Paul had celebrated.

When he had been informed that his physical and psychological qualifications were such that he was eligible for the most demanding occupation in the Universal Welfare System and had been persuaded into taking training for deep-sea pilot, he had celebrated once again. Eighteen others had taken the training with him, and only he and Eva Ahmed had passed the final evaluations. On this occasion, he and Eva had celebrated together. It had been quite an event. Three weeks later, Eva had died when a catastrophic hull failure occurred on what should have been a routine descent to the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

Each time Paul returned from one of his own dives, he celebrated. A night out, an indulgence, a spree, a commemoration of dangers met and survived.

Now it was all over. At the age of thirty he was retired. Professional ethics and legal regulations prevented him from ever being called up for contributing to the world's labor needs again. And he most certainly wasn't going to volunteer.

He had taken his education much as had his contemporaries. There wasn't any particular reason for trying to excel. You didn't want to get the reputation for being overly ambitious, or lazy either. Just one of the crowd. You could do the same in life whether you really studied or not. You had your Universal Basic Income allocation, didn't you? What else did you need?

It had come as a surprise when he'd been drafted for the labor force.

In the early days of the Universal Welfare System, they had made a mistake in adapting to the automation revolution and the advances in robotics. They had attempted to give everyone work by reducing the number of working hours in the day, and the number of working days in the week. It finally became absurd when employees were working but two days a week, three hours a day. In fact, it got chaotic. It became obvious that it was more practical to have one worker putting in thirty-five hours a week and developing real expertise, than it was to have a score of employees, each working a few hours a week and none of them ever really becoming proficient.

The only equitable solution was to let the technologically unemployed remain unemployed, with their Universal Basic Income as the equivalent of unemployment insurance, while the few workers still needed put in a reasonable number of hours a day, a reasonable number of weeks a year and a reasonable number of years in a lifetime. When new employees were needed, a draft lottery was held.

All persons registered in the labor force participated. If you were drawn, you must serve. The dissatisfaction those chosen might feel at their poor luck was offset by the fact that they were granted supplemental UBI credits, according to the tasks they fulfilled. Such credits could be added to their portfolios, the dividends becoming part of their current balance, or could be liquidated for a lump sum.

Yes, but now it was all over. He had his own small habitat, his own personal transport pod and twice the amount of UBI credits that most of his fellow citizens could claim. Paul Sanders had it made. A celebration was obviously called for.

He was going to do this one properly. This was the significant one. He'd accumulated substantial credits these past few months and he intended to spend them, or at least a considerable portion of them. His credit account was ready to be used. However, he wasn't going to rush into things. This had to be done correctly.

Too many celebrations were improvised. You started off with a few drinks, met some unremarkable companion and usually ended up in a mediocre establishment where you spent just as much as though you'd been in the finest venue in the city. Come morning and you had nothing to show for all the credits that had been spent but a headache and regrets.

Thus, Paul was vaguely aware from his studies of social psychology, it had always been down through the centuries since the ancient Phoenician sailor, back from his year-long voyage to distant trading ports, squandered his hard earned share of the expedition's profits in a matter of days in the wine shops of Tyre. Nobody gets quite so little for his money as that loneliest of all workers, he who must leave his home for isolated duty, returning only periodically and usually with the compensation of lengthy, demanding periods of time to be spent hurriedly in an attempt to achieve the pleasure and happiness so long denied him.

Paul was going to do it differently this time.

Nothing but the best. Entertainment, cuisine, companionship, luxury accommodations. Everything. But nothing but the best.

To start off, he dressed with great care in the formal retirement-status attire he had so recently purchased. His deep-sea exploration pin he attached carefully to the collar. That was a good beginning, he decided. A bit of prestige didn't hurt when you went out on the town. In the Universal Welfare System hardly one person in a hundred actually ever performed anything of significant value to society. The contributions of most weren't needed. Those few who did contribute were awarded honors, recognition, status markers.

Attired satisfactorily, Paul double-checked to see that his credit chip was secure. As an afterthought, he went over to the habitat-pod's communication console, activated it, held the chip to the scanner and said, "Balance inquiry, please."

In a moment, the console's synthesized voice reported, "Base Universal Basic Income allocation: ten thousand credits annually. Supplemental workforce credits: forty-two thousand credits. Current liquid balance: eight thousand, three hundred and seventeen credits." The screen went dark.

Eight thousand, three hundred and seventeen credits. That was substantial. He could safely spend as much as half of it, if the celebration proved as memorable as he hoped it would. His quarterly UBI distribution was due in another week or so, and he wouldn't have to worry about routine expenses. Yes, indeed, Paul Sanders was as financially secure as he had ever been in his thirty years.

He opened the compact door which housed his personal transport pod, and settled himself into the comfortable vehicle. He activated the canopy, engaged the pressurization and considered the destination interface. Only one place really made sense. Unity, Galdoria.

He considered for a moment, decided against the districts of Highpoint and Dawnridge, and selected Unity instead. He had the resources. He might as well do it properly.

He entered Unity into the navigation system and felt the subtle acceleration that indicated his pod's engagement with the transit network. While it was being routed through the automated controls, being directed here and there preparatory to the high-speed transit to his destination, he accessed the pod's information system for data on the premier hotels of Unity. He selected an exclusive establishment he'd read about and seen on the holographic broadcasts of society and celebrity content, and entered it as his destination.

"Nothing too good for ex-Deep-Sea Pilot Paul Sanders," he said aloud.

The pod paused for a moment, that brief hesitation before the acceleration, and Paul took the involuntary breath that even experienced travelers couldn't quite suppress. He pressed back into the seat. Minutes passed, and the direction of the pressure reversed.

Unity. The routing adjustments began again, and one or two more local transits. Finally, the display showed green and Paul opened the canopy and stepped into his hotel suite.

A voice said pleasantly, "If the accommodations are satisfactory, please present your credit chip within ten minutes."

Paul took his time. Not that he really needed it. It was by far the most luxurious suite he had ever seen. One wall was a holographic window of whatever view the guest might desire and Paul touched the control that expanded it to maximum. His view opened such that he could see both the Central Archive Tower and the Meridian Gardens. Beyond the gardens stretched the seemingly endless metropolis that was Greater Unity.

He didn't take the time to activate the menu interface next to the automated dining station, nor to check the extensive selection on the beverage synthesizer. All that, he well knew, would be exceptional. Besides, he didn't plan to dine or do much drinking in his suite. He made a wry smile. Not unless he managed to find some pleasant companionship, that was.

He looked briefly into the hydrotherapy pool and cleansing chamber, then settled himself onto the bed. It wasn't adjusted to the degree of firmness he presently desired, and he recalibrated the settings to his preference so that with a satisfied sigh he sank into the perfect support of the mattress.

He came back to his feet, gave his attire a quick adjustment so that it fell into perfect alignment and, taking his credit chip from his pocket, placed it against the communication console screen and pressed the hotel registration control so that check-in could be completed.

For a moment he stood in the center of the floor, considering his options. Take it easy, Paul Sanders, take it all easy, this time. No squandering his credits in second-rate establishments, no eating in automated food dispensaries. This time, perhaps the only time in his life, he was going to celebrate in the grand manner. No mediocrity for Paul Sanders.

He decided a drink was in order to help him plan his evening. A drink at the hotel's famous Zenith Lounge where notable individuals were reputed to gather regularly.

He left the suite and entered one of the elevators. He said, "Zenith Lounge."

The automated elevator responded politely, "Yes, sir, the Zenith Lounge."

At the entrance to the famous gathering place of the elite, Paul paused a moment and observed his surroundings. He'd never been in a place like this before. However, he suppressed his initial instinct to worry about what this was going to cost with an inner smile and made his way to the bar.

There was actually a human bartender.

Paul suppressed his astonishment and said, casually, attempting an air of practiced sophistication, "Abyssal Depths."

"Yes, sir."

The drinks in the Zenith Lounge might be prepared by hand, but Paul noticed they had the standard payment scanners built into the bar surface. He placed his credit chip on the scanner immediately before him when the drink arrived, and had to resist his desire to check for a balance inquiry, so as to be able to calculate what the cocktail had cost him.

Well, this was something worthwhile. This was the sort of experience he'd imagined, out there in the crushing darkness, sealed in the confining sphere of his submersible craft. He sipped at the drink, finding it exceeded his expectations, and then turned slightly on his stool to observe the other patrons.

To his disappointment, there were no recognizable celebrities. None that he identified, at least—prominent holographic performers, influential politicians of the Universal Welfare System or renowned artists.

He turned back to his drink and noticed, for the first time, the woman who occupied the seat two down from him. Paul Sanders blinked. He blinked and then inhaled sharply.

"Remarkable," he breathed.

She was styled in the latest aesthetic from the Pacific Rim cultural centers, even to the point of having cosmetically enhanced her features with bioluminescent accents that caught the ambient light. Every detail, but every detail, was flawless. She sat with the composed elegance that spoke of professional training in artistic expression.

His stare couldn't be ignored.

She looked at him coolly, turned to the bartender and murmured, "A Crystalline Cascade, please, Walter." Then deliberately added, "I thought the Zenith Lounge was supposed to be exclusive."

There was nothing the bartender could say to that, and he went about preparing the drink.

Paul cleared his throat. "Hey," he said, "how about letting this one be on me?"

Her eyebrows, which had been shaped and enhanced to complement her aesthetic presentation, rose. "Indeed?" she said, drawing it out.

The bartender said quickly, "I beg your pardon, sir..."

The woman, her voice suddenly subtly changed, said, "Wait, isn't that a deep-sea exploration pin?"

Paul, disconcerted by the sudden reversal, said, "Yeah... sure."

"Good heavens, you're a hadal pilot?"

"Sure." He indicated the collar pin. "You can't wear one unless you've completed at least one descent to the hadal zone."

She was obviously both taken aback and impressed. "Why," she said, "you're Paul Sanders, the pilot. I watched the ceremony they held for you."

Paul, carrying his glass, moved over to the seat next to her. "Call me Paul," he said. "Everyone calls me Paul."

She said, "I'm Claudia. Claudia Montgomery. Just Claudia. Imagine meeting Paul Sanders. Just sitting down next to him at a bar. Just like that."

"Paul," Paul said, gratified. By all measures, he'd never encountered anyone with this level of refined beauty. Maybe on holographic displays, of course, one of the current cultural icons, but never in person. "Call me Paul," he said again. "I've been called Paul so long, I don't even register when someone uses my full name."

"I was moved when they gave you that commemorative plaque," she said, her tone such that it was obvious she hadn't quite processed having actually met him.

Paul Sanders was surprised. "Moved?" he said. "Well, why? I was somewhat disengaged from the whole ceremony. But Director King, I used to work under her in the Ocean Exploration Department, she was enthusiastic about it."

"Director King?" she said. "You just call her Luna?"

Paul was expansive. "Why, sure. In the Ocean Exploration Department we don't have much use for formality. Everyone's just Paul, and Luna, and Mohammad. Like that. But why were you moved?"

She looked down into the drink the bartender had placed before her, as though avoiding his gaze. "I... I suppose it was that speech Professor Newman made. There you stood, so distinguished in your deep-sea pilot uniform, the veteran of six exploration dives to the hadal zones..."

"Well," Paul said modestly, "two of my dives were only to the bathypelagic zone."

"...and he said all those things about humanity's quest to understand the deep ocean. And the existential questions that arise when we confront the unknown depths. And then the fact that you were the last of the deep-sea pilots. The last person in the whole world trained to pilot a hadal submersible. And there you were, retiring."

Paul grunted. "Yeah. That's all part of Luna's strategy to get me to take on another three dives. They're concerned the whole department will be eliminated by the Appropriations Committee on the Economic Planning Council. Even if they can find some other candidate to train for the position, it would take maybe a year before they could even send them on a bathypelagic descent. So Director King, and Professor Newman too, they're both trying to pressure me into more dives. Otherwise they have an Ocean Exploration Department, with all the expense and all, but nobody to pilot their submersibles. It's somewhat ironic, in a way. You know what one of those hadal submersibles costs?"

"Ironic?" she said. "Why, I don't think it's ironic at all."

Paul said, "Look, how about another drink?"

Claudia Montgomery said, "Oh, I'd love to have a drink with you, Mr..."

"Paul," Paul said. He gestured to the bartender with a circular motion indicating their need for two more of the same. "How come you know so much about it? You don't meet many people who are interested in deep-sea exploration anymore. In fact, most people are almost dismissive, like. Think it's kind of a wasteful expenditure to help consume resources and keep the economy functioning."

Claudia said earnestly, "Why, I've been fascinated by ocean exploration all my life. I've studied everything about it. Have always known the names of all the deep-sea pilots and everything about them, ever since I was young. I suppose you'd say I'm captivated by the existential questions that Professor Newman spoke about."

Paul chuckled. "A real enthusiast, eh? You know, it's kind of funny. I was never much interested in it. And I became considerably less interested after my first dive and I discovered what pressure psychosis was."

She frowned. "I don't believe I know much about that."

Sitting in the Zenith Lounge with the most beautiful woman to whom he had ever spoken, Paul could be casual about the subject. "Director King keeps that aspect mostly suppressed and out of the media articles and holographic documentaries. Says there's enough negative publicity about ocean exploration already. But at this stage when the whole submersible is packed with automated scientific equipment and all, there's extremely limited space in the pilot sphere and you're the only person aboard. Luna says later on when submersibles are larger and there's a whole crew aboard, there won't be any such thing as pressure psychosis, but..." Suddenly the left side of Paul Sanders' hand began to tremble and he hurriedly took up his drink and finished it.
question: Who, alongside Director Luna King, gave a speech at Paul Sanders' retirement ceremony?

synthetic_story:
THE RUINS OF COPPERFIELD

By DEAN EVANS

Every child should be able to hum a tune, except, of course, the Venusian settlers. But this one did!

She seemed a very small girl to be carrying so large a geological sample kit. She swung it in her thin left hand as she walked, and at first glance you couldn't be sure if she were carrying it, or it carrying her.

She came humming. All children hum. To children, humming is as natural as breathing. However, there was something peculiar about this particular child's humming. Or, rather, there were two things peculiar, but each was related to the other.

The first was that she was a Venusian settler child. You could be very sure of that, for Earth children have attached earlobes while Venusian settler children do not—and she most certainly didn't.

The second was the tune she hummed—a somehow familiar tune, but one which I should have thought not very appealing to a child.

"Hi, there," I said when she came near enough. "What's that you're humming?"

She stopped humming and she stopped walking, both at the same time, as though she had pulled a switch or turned a tap that shut them off. Then she lifted her small head and stared up into my eyes.

"'Clair de Lune'," she said in a soft, child's voice.

"The what?" I asked.

"From Debussy's Suite Bergamasque," she explained, still looking up at me. She said it deadpan, and her wide gray eyes never once batted.

"Oh," I said. "And where did you learn that?"

"My father taught me."

I blinked at her. She didn't blink back. Her round little face still held no expression, but if it had, I knew it would have matched the serene quality of the tune she hummed.

"You hum very well," I told her.

That pleased her. Her eyes lit up and an almost-smile flirted with the corners of her small mouth.

She nodded grave agreement.

"Been collecting rock samples, I see. I'll bet you didn't find any good ones. This is the wrong geological layer."

The light in her eyes snapped off. "Well, good-by," she said abruptly and very relevantly.

"Good-by," I said.

Her humming and her walking started up again in the same spot where they had left off. I mean the note she resumed on was the note which followed the one interrupted; and the step she took was with the left foot, which was the one she would have used if I hadn't stopped her.

I followed her with my eyes. An unusual little girl. A most precisely mechanical little girl.

When she was almost out of sight, I took off after her, wondering.

The dwelling she went into was over in that crumbling section which forms a curving boundary line, marking the limits of those frantic and ugly original excavation sites made many years ago by the early colonists in Copperfield, Veldoria. It seems that someone had told someone who had told someone else that here, a mere fifty feet beneath the surface, was a deposit as wide as a warehouse and as long as a politician's promise, of pure—pure, mind you—platinum.

Back in those days, to be a colonist meant to be a rugged individual. And to be a rugged individual meant to not give a damn one way or another. And to not give a damn one way or another meant to make one hell of a mess on the pristine landscape of Venus.

There had not been any platinum found, of course, and now, for the most part, the mining structures so hastily thrown up were only fever scars of a sickness long gone and little remembered. A few of the dwellings were still occupied, like the one into which the Venusian child had just disappeared.

So her father had taught her Debussy's "Clair de Lune," had he? That tickling thought made me chuckle as I stood before the ramshackle building. And then, suddenly, I stopped chuckling and began to think, instead, of something quite astonishing:

How had it been possible for him to teach, and for her to hum? All Venusian settlers are as tone-deaf as a bucket of lead.

I went up three composite steps and rapped loudly on the weather-beaten door.

The man who faced me may have been as young as twenty-five, but he didn't look it. That shocked look, which comes with the first realization that youth has slipped quietly away downstream in the middle of the night, and left nothing but frightening rocks of middle age to show cold and gray in the hard light of dawn, was like the validation stamp of Time itself in his wide, weary eyes. And his voice wasn't young any more, either.

"Well? And what did I do now?"

"I beg your pardon?" I said.

"You're Colonial Security, aren't you? Or is that badge you're wearing just something to cover a hole in your shirt?"

"Yes, I'm Security, but does it have to mean something?" I asked. "All I did was knock on your door."

"I heard it." His lips were curled slightly at one corner.

I worked up a smile for him and let him see it for a few seconds before I answered: "As a matter of fact, I don't want to see you at all. I didn't know you lived here and I don't know who you are. I'm not even interested in who you are. It's the little girl who just went in here that I was interested in. The little Venusian settler girl, I mean."

His eyes spread as though somebody had put fingers on his lids at the outside corners and then cruelly jerked them apart.

"Come in," he almost gasped.

I followed him. When I leaned back against the plain door, it closed protestingly. I looked around. It wasn't much of a room, but then you couldn't expect much of a room in a little ghost of a place like this. A few artifacts of the locality stood about on two tables and a shelf, bits of rock with streak-veins of compressed silicate; not bad if you like the appearance of frozen lightning.

There were two chairs and a large table intended to match the chairs, and a rough couch kind of thing made of discarded shipping containers which had probably been hauled here from the International Spaceport at Ashford City, thirty kilometers to the east. In the back wall of the room was a doorway that led dimly to somewhere else in the dwelling. Nowhere did I see the little girl. I looked once again at the man.

"What about her?" he whispered.

His eyes were still startled.

I smiled reassuringly. "Nothing, friend, nothing. I'm sorry I upset you. I was just being nosy is all, and that's the truth of it. You see, the little girl went by me a while ago and she was humming. She hums remarkably well. I asked her what the name of the tune was and she told me it was 'Clair de Lune' from Debussy. She also told me her father had taught her."

His eyes hadn't budged from mine, hadn't flickered. They might have been bright, moist marbles glued above his cheeks.

He said one word only: "Well?"

"Nothing," I answered. "Except that Venusian settlers are supposed to be tone-deaf, aren't they? It's something lacking in their auditory processing. So when I heard this little girl, and saw she was a Venusian settler, and when she told me her father had taught her—" I shrugged and laughed a little. "Like I said before, I guess I got just plain nosy."

He nodded. "We agree on that last part."

Perhaps it was his eyes. Or perhaps it was the tone of his voice. Or perhaps, and more simply, it was his attitude in general. But whatever it was, I suddenly felt that, nosy or not, I was being treated shabbily.

"I would like to speak to the Venusian settler man," I said.

"There isn't any Venusian settler man."

"There has to be, doesn't there?" I said it with little sharp prickers on the words.

But he did, too: "Does there?"

I gawked at him and he stared back. And the stare he gave me was hard and at the same time curiously defiant—as though he would dare me to go on with it. As though he figured I hadn't the guts.

For a moment, I just blinked stupidly at him, as I had blinked stupidly at the little girl when she told me her father had taught her how to hum. And then—after what seemed to me a very long while—I slowly tumbled to what he meant.

His eyes were telling me that the little Venusian settler girl wasn't a little Venusian settler girl at all, that she was cross-breed, a little child who had a Venusian settler mother and a human, Earthman father.

It was a startling thought, for there just aren't any such mixed families. Or at least I had thought there weren't. Physically, spiritually, mentally, or by any other standard you can think of, compared to a human female the Venusian settler woman isn't anything you'd want around the house—or so the common wisdom went.

I finally said: "So that is why she is able to hum."

He didn't answer. Even before I spoke, his eyes had seen the correct guess which had probably flashed naked and astounded in my own eyes. And then he swallowed with a labored breath that went trembling down inside him.

"There isn't anything to be ashamed of," I said gently. "Back on Earth there's a lot of mixtures, you know. Some people even claim there's no such thing as a pure race. Cultural exchange has been happening for millennia. I don't know, but I guess we all started somewhere and intermarried plenty since."

He nodded. Somehow his eyes didn't look defiant any more.

"Where's her mother?" I asked.

"S-she's dead."

"I'm sorry. Are you all right? I mean do you get along okay and everything, now that...?"

I stopped. I wanted to ask him if he was starving by slow degrees and needed help. Lord knows the careworn look about him didn't show it was luxurious living he was doing—at least not lately.

"Look," I said suddenly. "Would you like to go back to Earth? I could fix—"

But that was the wrong approach. His eyes snapped and his shoulders stiffened angrily and the words that ripped out of his mouth were not coated with honey.

"Get the hell out of here, you fool!"

I blinked again. When the flame in his eyes suddenly seemed to grow even hotter, I turned on my heel and went to the door. I opened it, went out on the top composite step. I turned back to close the door—and looked straight into his eyes.

He was crying, but that didn't mean exactly what it looked like it might mean. His right hand had the door edge gripped tightly and he was swinging it with all the strength he possessed. And while I still stared, the door slammed savagely into the casing with a shock that jarred the step under my feet, and flying splinters from the deteriorated material stung my flinching cheeks.

I shrugged and turned around and went down the steps. "And that is the way it goes," I muttered disgustedly to myself. Thinking to be helpful with community organizing, you offer assistance and they immediately reject it—violently.

I looked up just in time to avoid running into a spread-legged woman who was standing motionless directly in the middle of the gravel-path in front of the door. Her hands were on her hips and there was something in her eyes which might have been a leer.

"Pulled a howler in there, eh, friend?" she said. She chuckled hoarsely in her throat. "Not being exactly deaf, I heard the tail end of it." Her chuckle was a crude thing, a thing usually reserved—if it ever was reserved at all—for the back rooms of some of the lower class establishments. And then she stopped chuckling and frowned instead and said complainingly:

"Regular little hothead, ain't he? I ask you now, wouldn't you think a man which had got himself in a little jam, so to speak, would be more reasonable—"

Her words chopped short and she almost choked on the final unuttered syllable. Her glance had dropped to my badge and the look on her face was one of startled surprise.

"I—" she said.

I cocked a frown of my own at her.

"Well, so long, friend," she grunted, and spun around and dug her heels in the gravel and was away. I stood there staring at her rapidly disappearing form for a few moments and then looked back once more at the dwelling. A tattered synthetic curtain was just swinging to in the dirty, dust-blown window. That seemed to mean the man had been watching. I sighed, shrugged again and went away myself.

When I got back to Security Headquarters in Ashford City, I went to the file and began to rifle through pictures. I didn't find the man, but I did find the woman.

She was a killer named Ava Lucas.

I took the picture into the Chief's office and laid it on his desk, waited for him to look down at it and study it for an instant, and then to look back up to me. Which he did.

"So?" he said.

"Wanted, isn't she?"

He nodded. "But a lot of good that'll do. She's holed up somewhere back on Earth."

"No," I said. "She's right here. I just saw her."

"What?" He nearly leaped out of his chair.

"I didn't know who she was at first," I said. "It wasn't until I looked in the files—"

He cut me off. His hand darted into his desk drawer and pulled out an Authority Card. He shoved the card at me. He growled: "Kill or capture, I'm not especially fussy which. Just get her!"

I nodded and took the card. As I left the office, I was thinking of something which struck me as somewhat more than odd.

I had idly listened to a little half-breed Venusian settler girl humming part of Debussy's "Clair de Lune," and it had led me to a wanted killer named Ava Lucas.

Understandably, Ms. Lucas did not produce herself on a silver platter. I spent the remainder of the afternoon trying to get a lead on her and got nowhere. If she was hiding in any of the places I went to, then she was doing it with mirrors, for on Venus an Authority Card is the big stick than which there is no bigger. Not solely is it a warrant, it is a commandeer of help from anyone to whom it is presented; and wherever I showed it I got respect.

I got instant attention. I got even more: those wraithlike tremblings in the darker corners of bars, those corners where light never seems quite to penetrate. You don't look into those. Not if you're anything more than a ghoul, you don't.

Not finding her wasn't especially alarming. What was alarming, though, was not finding the Earthman and his little half-breed Venusian settler daughter when I went back to the tumbledown dwelling where they lived. It was empty. He had moved fast. He hadn't even left me a note saying good-by.

That night I went into the Elmwood Region to the Kahreen Reservation, where the Venusian settlers still try to act like Venusian settlers.

It was Festival night, and when I got there they were doing the dance to the three rings. At times like this you want to leave the Venusian settlers alone. With that thought in mind, I pinned my Authority Card to my lapel directly above my badge, and went through the gates.

The huge circle fire was burning and the dance was in progress. Briefly, this can be described as something like the ceremonial dances put on centuries ago by the ancient aborigines of the Pacific Islands. There was one important exception, however. Instead of a central fire, the Venusian settlers dig a huge circular trench and fill it with dried roots of the kelnu tree and set fire to it. Being resin-like, the gnarled fragments burn for hours. Inside this ring sit the spectators, and in the exact center are the dancers. For music, they use the drums.

The dancers were both men and women and they were as minimally clothed as Venusian settlers can get, but their dance was a thing of grace and loveliness. For an instant—before anyone observed me—I stood motionless and watched the sinuously undulating movements, and I thought, as I have often thought before, that this is the one thing the Venusian settlers can still do beautifully. Which, in a sad sort of way, is a commentary on the way things have gone since the first rocket-blasting ship set down on these misty plains.

I felt the blade dig my spine. Carefully I turned around and pointed my index finger to my badge and card. Bared teeth glittered at me in the flickering light, and then the blade disappeared as quickly as it had come.

"Valenhk," I said. "The Chief. Take me to her."

The Venusian settler turned, went away from the half-light of the circle. She led me some meters off to the north to a swooping-tent. Then she stopped, pointed.

"Valenhk," she said.

I watched her slip away.

Valenhk is an old Venusian settler. I don't think any Venusian settler before her has ever lived so long—and doubtless none after her will, either. Her leathery, almost gray-black skin was rough and had a weathered look about it, and up around the eyes were little plaits and folds that had the appearance of being done deliberately by a Venusian sand-artist.

"Good evening," I said, and sat down before her and crossed my legs.

She nodded slowly. Her old eyes went to my badge.

From there they went to the Authority Card.

"Power sign of the Earthmen," she muttered.

"Not necessarily," I said. "I'm not here for trouble. I know as well as you do that, before tonight is finished, more than half of your men and women will be intoxicated on illegal spirits."

She didn't reply to that.

"And I don't give a damn about it," I added distinctly.

Her eyes came deliberately up to mine and stopped there. She said nothing. She waited. Outside, the drums throbbed, slowly at first, then moderated in tempo. It was like the throbbing—or sobbing, if you prefer—of the old, old pumps whose shafts go so tirelessly down into the planet for such pitifully thin streams of water.

"I'm looking for an Earthman," I said. "This particular Earthman took a Venusian settler for a wife."

"That is impossible," she grunted bitterly.

"I would have said so, too," I agreed. "Until this afternoon, that is."

Her old, dried lips began to purse and wrinkle.

"I met his little daughter," I went on. "A little semi-human girl with Venusian settler features. Or, if you want to turn it around and look at the other side, a little Venusian settler girl who hums."

Her teeth went together with a snap.

I nodded and smiled. "You know who I'm talking about."

For a long long while she didn't answer. Her eyes remained unblinking on mine and if, earlier in the day, I had thought the little girl's face was expressionless, then I didn't completely appreciate the meaning of that word. Valenhk's face was more than expressionless; it was simply blank.

"They disappeared from the dwelling they were living in," I said. "They went in a hurry—a very great hurry."

That one she didn't answer, either.

"I would like to know where he is."

"Why?" Her whisper was brittle.

"He's not in trouble," I told her quickly. "He's not wanted. Nor his child, either. It's just that I have to talk to him."

"Why?"

I pulled out the file photo of Ava Lucas and handed it across to her. Her wrinkled hand took it, pinched it, held it up close to a lamp hanging from one of the ridge poles. Her eyes squinted at it for a long moment before she handed it back.

"I have never seen this Earthwoman," she said.

"All right," I answered. "There wasn't anything that made me think you had. The point is that she knows the man. It follows, naturally, that he might know her."

"This one is wanted?" Her old, broken tones went up slightly on the last word.

I nodded. "For murder."

"Murder." She spat the word. "But not for the murder of a Venusian settler, eh? Venusian settlers are not that important any more." Her old eyes hated me with an intensity I didn't relish.

"You said that, old woman, not I."

A little time went by. The drums began to beat faster. They were rolling out a lively tempo now, a tempo you could put music to.

She said at last: "I do not know where the man is. Nor the child."

She looked me straight in the eyes when she said it—and almost before the words were out of her mouth, they were whipped in again on a drawn-back, great, sucking breath. For, somewhere outside, somewhere near that dancing circle, in perfect time with the lively beat of the drums, somebody was humming.

It was a clear, clean sound, a merry, bright, happy sound, as sharp and as precise as the thrust of a laser through a piece of soft synthetic material.

"In your teeth, Valenhk! Right in your teeth!"

She only looked at me for another dull instant and then her eyes slowly closed and her hands folded together in her lap. Being caught in a lie only bores a Venusian settler.

I got up and went out of the tent.

The man never heard me approach. His eyes were toward the flaming circle and the dancers within, and, too, I suppose, to his small daughter who was somewhere in that circle with them, humming. He leaned against the bole of a kelnu tree with his arms down and slightly curled backward around it.

"That's considered bad luck," I said.

His head jerked around with my words, reflected flames from the circle fire still flickering in his eyes.

"That's a kelnu tree," I said. "Embracing it like that is like looking for a ladder to walk under. Or didn't you know?"

"Would it make any difference?" He spoke softly, but the words came to me above the drums and the shouts of the dancers. "How much bad luck can you have in one lifetime, anyway?"

I ignored that. "Why did you pull out of that dwelling? I told you you had nothing to fear from me."

He didn't answer.

"I'm looking for the woman you saw me talking with this morning," I went on. "Friend, she's wanted. And this thing, on my lapel is an Authority Card. Assuming you know what it means, I'm asking you where she is."

"What woman?" His words were flat.

"Her name is Ava Lucas."

If that meant anything to him, I couldn't tell. In the flickering light from the fires, subtle changes in expression weren't easily detected.

"Why should I care about an Earthwoman? My wife was a Venusian settler. And she's dead, see? Dead. Just a Venusian settler. Not fit for anything, like all Venusian settlers. Just a woman who fell in love with an Earthman and had the guts to marry him. Do you understand? So somebody murdered her for it. Ain't that pretty? Ain't that something to make you throw back your head and be proud about? Well, ain't it? And let me tell you, Mister, whoever it was, I'll get them. I'll get them!"

I could see his face now, all right. It was a twisted, tortured thing that writhed at me in its agony. It was small white teeth that bared at me in viciousness. It was eyes that brimmed with boiling, bubbling hate like a ladle of molten steel splashing down on bare, white flesh. Or, simply, it was the face of a man who wanted to kill the killer of his woman.

And then, suddenly, it wasn't. Even though the noise of the dance and the dancers was loud enough to command the attention and the senses, I could still hear his quiet sobbing, and I could see the heaving of the thin shoulders.

And I knew then the reason for old Valenhk's bitterness when she had said to me, "But not for the murder of a Venusian settler, eh? Venusian settlers are not that important any more."

What I said then probably sounded as weak as it really was: "I'm sorry, friend. But look, just staking out in that old dwelling of yours and trying to pry information out of the type of people who drifted your way—well, I mean there wasn't much sense in that, now was there?"

I put a hand on his shoulder. "She must have been a pretty nice woman," I said. "I don't think you'd have married her if she wasn't."

I stopped. Even in my own ears, my words sounded comfortless. I looked up, over at the flaming circle and at the sweat-laved dancers within it. The sound of the drums was a wild cacophonous tattoo now, a rattle of speed and savagery combined; and those who moved to its frenetic jabberings were not dancers any more, but only frenzied, jerking figurines on the strings of a puppeteer gone mad.

I looked down again at the man. "Your little girl and her geological sample kit," I said softly. "In a season when no good samples can be found. What was that for? Was she part of the plan, too, and the kit just the alibi that gave her a passport to wander where she chose? So that she could listen, pick up a little information here, a little there?"

He didn't answer. He didn't have to answer. My guesses can be as good as anybody's.

After a long while he looked up into my eyes. "Her name was Sahily," he said. "She had the secret. She knew where the platinum deposit was. And soon, in a couple of years maybe, when all the prospectors were gone and she knew it would be safe, she was going to stake a claim and go after it. For us. For the three of us."

I sighed. There wasn't, isn't, never will be any platinum on this planet. But who in the name of God could have the heart to ruin a dream like that?

Next day I followed the little girl. She left the reservation in a cheery frame of mind, her hum sounding soft and clear on the thin morning air. She didn't go in the direction of Ashford City, but the other way—toward the ruins of the ancient Temple Complex of the Rings. I watched her thin arm and the swinging of the big geological sample kit on the end of that arm. Then I followed along in her dusty tracks.

It was desert country, of course. There wasn't any chance of tailing her without her knowledge and I knew it. I also knew that before long she'd know it, too. And she did—but she didn't let me know she did until we came to the stone-cliffs, those filigree walls of stone that hide the entrance to the valley of the three rings.

Once there, she paused and placed her geological sample kit on a rock ledge and then calmly sat down and took off her shoes to dump the dust while she waited for me.

"Well," I said. "Good morning."

She looked up at me. She nodded politely. Then she put on her shoes again and got to her feet.

"You've been following me," she said, and her gray eyes stared accusingly into mine.

"I have?"

"That isn't an honorable thing to do," she said very gravely. "A gentleman doesn't do that to a lady."

I didn't smile. "And what would you have me do about it?"

"Stop following me, of course, sir."

"Very well," I said. "I won't follow you any more. Will that be satisfactory?"

"Quite, sir."

Without another word, she picked up her geological sample kit and disappeared along a path that led through a rock crevice. Only then did I allow myself to grin. It was a sad and pitying and affectionate kind of grin.

I sat down and did with my shoes as she had done. There wasn't any hurry; I knew where she was going. There could only be one place, of course—the city of Deimos and Phobos. Other than that she had no choice. And I thought I knew the reason for her going.

Several times in the past, there have been people who, bitten with the fever of an idea that somewhere on this misty planet there must be platinum, have done prospecting among the ruins of the old temples. She had probably heard that there were people there now, and she was carrying out with the thoroughness of her precise little mind the job she had set herself of finding the killer of her mother.

I took a short-cut over the stone-cliffs and went down a winding, dust-worn path. The temple stones stood out barren and dry-looking, like ribs from the desiccated carcass of an animal. For a moment I stopped and stared down at the ruins. I didn't see the girl. She was somewhere down there, though, still carrying her geological sample kit and, probably, still humming.

I started up once more.

And then I heard it—a shrill blast of sound in an octave of urgency; a hum, sure, but a warning one.

I stopped in my tracks from the shock of it. Yes, I knew from whom it had come, all right. But I didn't know why.

And then the hum broke off short. One instant it was in the air, shrieking with a message. The next it was gone. But it left tailings, like the echo of a death cry slowly floating back over the dead body of the creature that uttered it.

I dropped behind a fragment of the stone-cliff. A shot barked out angrily. Splinters of the rock crazed the morning air.
question: Where did the narrator encounter a blade during the Festival?
option_a: In the circle of the dance
