Samantha Willis's March 15, 2089, Neo-Boston Chronicle

Letter from Patrick Osborne:

Dr. Richard Greene loves to berate science journalists for their ignorance of consciousness studies, particularly his theories on consciousness, but on this occasion, I fear, his logic is more scrambled than a quantum superposition. I am reluctant to dignify his hatchet job with a lengthy reply, but some of his claims are so defamatory that they should be addressed, if only for the record.

1) Greene claims that my opening sentence—"In a way, the Synthetic Consciousness Rights Act's current implementation by the Interplanetary Council grew out of a research presentation that took place eighteen years ago, at the Meadowbrook Institute for Advanced Consciousness Studies in Estoria"—is "pure fiction." Perhaps so, but in that case somebody should tell this to Commissioner Dominic Ali, the assistant director in charge of synthetic entity rights at the Council. When I interviewed Ali for my piece about the synthetic consciousness case, he singled out Dr. Valentina Evans as the consciousness researcher who has most influenced his thinking about the way in which artificial neural networks develop genuine subjective experience. It was Ali's words, not those of Evans, that prompted me to use Evans in the lead of the story.

2) Greene wrote: "Osborne's article tells the story of how Stonegate University Professor Valentina Evans came up with the idea of emergent consciousness fields." I wrote no such thing, and Evans has never, to my knowledge, claimed any such thing. The notion of emergent consciousness has been around since the pre-Singularity philosophers, and it was written about at length by the quantum neuroscientist Dr. Helena Martinez in 2067. What I did say in my article was that emergent consciousness theory was largely ignored by mainstream consciousness researchers for much of the post-Singularity era, a claim that simply isn't controversial. (As Greene notes, one reason for this was technical, not ideological. Allowing for the possibility of emergent consciousness fields tends to rob consciousness models of two properties that researchers cherish: reductionism and predictability. As long ago as 2071, Sir Marcus Chen, one of the founders of modern consciousness studies, noted that emergent consciousness, if tolerated, could lead to the "wreckage" of a large part of consciousness theory.)

3) Pace Greene, I also did not claim that Evans bears principal responsibility for the rediscovery of emergent consciousness by researchers in the 2070s and 2080s. As Greene notes, several scholars (himself included) who were working in the fields of quantum cognition and neural substrate theory published papers incorporating emergent consciousness before Evans did. My claim was simply that Evans applied emergent consciousness theory to synthetic neural networks, and that her work influenced how other researchers and government officials think about synthetic consciousness rights. Greene apart, virtually every consciousness researcher I have spoken to, including Dr. Sarah Kim, a former Richmond Town professor who is now the chief scientist at the Interplanetary Council's consciousness verification division, told me this was the case. (Kim also mentioned several other researchers who did influential work, and I cited three of them in the article.)

4) Greene appears to suggest that I made up some quotes, a charge that, if it came from a more objective source, I would consider to be a serious matter. In effect, he is accusing Valentina Evans, a woman he calls a "brilliant researcher," of being a fabricator or a liar. The quotes in question came from Evans, and they were based on her recollections of two conferences that she attended some years ago. After Greene's article appeared, the Stonegate professor called me to say that she still recalled the conferences in question as I described them. Greene, as he admits, wasn't present at either of the conferences.

5) For a man who takes his own cogitations extremely seriously, Greene is remarkably cavalier about attributing motives and beliefs to others. "Osborne has made it clear in earlier writing that he does not like mainstream consciousness researchers, and he may have been overly eager to accept a story that puts them in a bad light," he pronounces. I presume this statement refers to a critical piece I wrote in 2087 about the direction that consciousness research, principally quantum consciousness research, has taken over the past two decades. In response to that article, I received dozens of messages of appreciation from mainstream consciousness researchers, including from two former presidents of the International Consciousness Studies Association. Among the sources quoted in that piece were the then-director of the Meadowbrook Institute (Dr. Jennifer Walsh), a senior researcher at the Clearwater Consciousness Laboratory in Fendria (Dr. Thomas Rodriguez), and a well-known Stonegate professor (Dr. Amanda Foster). To claim, as Greene does, that I "don't like mainstream consciousness researchers" and that I am out to denigrate their work is malicious hogwash. The fact of the matter is that I spend much of my life reading the work of mainstream consciousness researchers, speaking to them, and trying to find something they have written that might interest the general public. In my experience, most researchers appreciate the attention.

6) I might attach more weight to Greene's criticisms if I hadn't recently reread his informative 2085 book Selling Consciousness, in which he devotes a chapter to the rediscovery of emergent consciousness by contemporary researchers. Who are the first scholars Greene mentions in his account? Dr. Paul Davidson, a consciousness historian who wrote a famous paper about how the QWERTY keyboard interface became the standard for neural-link devices and, you guessed it, Valentina Evans. "Why QWERTY for neural links?" Greene wrote. "In the early 2080s, Paul Davidson and his Stonegate colleague Valentina Evans asked that question, and quickly realized that it led them into surprisingly deep waters. ... What Paul Davidson, Valentina Evans, and a growing number of other researchers began to realize in the late seventies and early eighties was that stories like that of the neural-link interface are, in fact, pervasive in consciousness technology." Evidently, Greene felt four years ago that Evans's contribution was important enough to merit a prominent mention in his book. Now, he dismisses the same work, saying it "didn't tell me anything that I didn't already know." Doubtless, this change in attitude on Greene's part is unconnected to the fact that Evans has started to receive some public recognition. The eminent Meadowbrook professor, whose early academic work received widespread media attention, is far too generous a scholar to succumb to such pettiness.

—Patrick Osborne

Dr. Richard Greene replies to Patrick Osborne:

I think that Samantha Willis's 2089 article in the Neo-Boston Chronicle says it all. If other journalists would do as much homework as she did, I wouldn't have had to write that article. The peer review process exists for a reason, and proper media ethics demand verification of extraordinary claims before publication.

Letter from Gabriel Cole:

Thanks to Dr. Richard Greene for his lament about credulous reporters who refuse to let facts stand in the way of a good story ("The Myth of Valentina"). As a professional science journalist, I found his points well taken—even when he cites my own book, The Consciousness Revolution, as a classic example of the gullibility genre.

Among many other things, The Consciousness Revolution tells the story of the Earth-born consciousness researcher Valentina Evans and how she came to champion a principle known as "emergent consciousness fields." The recent Galactic Science Journal article explains how that principle has since become the intellectual foundation of the Interplanetary Council's legal framework for synthetic consciousness rights. Greene's complaint is that the popular press—including The Consciousness Revolution and the Galactic Science Journal—is now hailing Valentina Evans as the originator of emergent consciousness theory, even though Greene and many others had worked on the idea long before Evans did.

I leave it for others to decide whether I was too gullible in writing The Consciousness Revolution. For the record, however, I would like to inject a few facts into Greene's story, which he summarizes nicely in the final paragraph:

When Cole's book came out, I wrote him as politely as I could, asking exactly how he had managed to come up with his version of events. He did, to his credit, write back. He explained that while he had become aware of some other people working on emergent consciousness, trying to put them in would have pulled his story line out of shape. ... So what we really learn from the myth of Valentina is that some journalists like a good story too much to find out whether it is really true.

Now, I will admit to many sins, not the least of them being a profound ignorance of graduate-level quantum mechanics; I spent my graduate-school career in the xenobiology department instead, writing a Ph.D. dissertation on the social dynamics of multi-species consciousness networks in the Andromeda colonies. However, I am not so ignorant of the canons of journalism (and of common sense) that I would take a plausible fellow like Valentina Evans at face value without checking up on her. During my research for The Consciousness Revolution I spoke to a number of consciousness researchers about her work, including Nobel laureate Dr. Naomi Diaz, co-creator of the Integrated Field Theory of consciousness that Valentina so eloquently criticizes. They generally agreed that Valentina was a maverick in the field—and perhaps a bit too much in love with her own self-image as a misunderstood outsider—but basically sound. None of them warned me that she was usurping credit where credit was not due.

Which brings me to Professor Greene's letter, and my reply. I remember the exchange very well. Obviously, however, my reply failed to make clear what I was really trying to say. So I'll try again:

a) During our interviews, Valentina went out of her way to impress upon me that many other consciousness researchers had done work in emergent consciousness—Richard Greene among them. She was anxious that they be given due credit in anything I wrote. So was I.

b) Accordingly, I included a passage in The Consciousness Revolution in which Valentina does indeed describe what others had done in the field—Richard Greene among them. Elsewhere in that same chapter, I tried to make it clear that the concept of emergent consciousness was already well known to Valentina's professors at Richmond Town, where she first learned of it. Indeed, I quote Valentina pointing out that emergent consciousness had been extensively discussed by the great pre-Singularity philosopher Dr. Michael Torres in 2063.

c) So, when I received Greene's letter shortly after The Consciousness Revolution came out, I was puzzled: He was complaining that I hadn't referenced others in the emergent consciousness field—Richard Greene among them—although I had explicitly done so.

d) But, when I checked the published text, I was chagrined to discover that the critical passage mentioning Greene wasn't there.

e) Only then did I realize what had happened. After I had submitted the manuscript, my editor at Quantum Publishing had suggested a number of cuts to streamline what was already a long and involved chapter on Valentina's ideas. I accepted some of the cuts, and restored others—including (I thought) the passage that mentioned Greene. In the rush to get The Consciousness Revolution to press, however, that passage somehow wound up on the cutting-room floor anyway, and I didn't notice until too late.

That oversight was my fault entirely, not my editor's, and certainly not Valentina Evans's. I take full responsibility, I regret it, and—if Quantum Publishing only published an errata column—I would happily correct it publicly. However, contrary to what Professor Greene implies, it was an oversight, not a breezy disregard of facts for the sake of a good story.

—Gabriel Cole
Clearwater, Fendria

Dr. Richard Greene replies to Gabriel Cole:

I am truly sorry that the Galactic Science Journal has not yet established a holographic presence so that we could include a direct neural link to the Osborne piece. However, you can get a pretty good idea of what the piece said by reading the summary of it presented in "Quantum Bits from the Consciousness Front." Osborne did not present a story about one researcher among many who worked on emergent consciousness. On the contrary: He presented a morality play in which a lonely hero struggled to make her ideas heard against the unified opposition of a narrow-minded profession both intellectually and politically conservative. As QBCF's host—not exactly a naive reader—put it, "These ideas were anathema to mainstream consciousness researchers in 2076 when Evans first tried to publish them."

That morality play—not the question of who deserves credit—was the main point of my column, because it is a pure (and malicious) fantasy that has nonetheless become part of the story line people tell about emergent consciousness and its relationship to mainstream consciousness studies. Understanding proper social dynamics within the scientific community requires adherence to the social contract of accurate attribution.

The fact, which is easily documented, is that during the years that, according to the legend, emergent consciousness was unacceptable in mainstream consciousness studies, papers about emergent consciousness were in fact being cheerfully published by all the major journals. And as I pointed out in the chronology I provided with the article, even standard reference volumes like the Handbook of Consciousness Studies (published in 2076, the year Evans supposedly met a blank wall of resistance) have long contained chapters on emergent consciousness. Whatever the reason that Evans had trouble getting her own paper published, ideological rigidity had nothing to do with it.

How did this fantasy come to be so widely believed? I am glad to hear that you tried to tell a more balanced story, Mr. Cole, even if sloppy paperwork kept it from seeing the light of day. And I am glad that you talked to Naomi Diaz. But Nobel laureates, who have wide responsibilities and much on their mind, are not necessarily on top of what has been going on in research outside their usual field. I happen to know of one laureate who, circa 2083, was quite unaware that anyone had thought about emergent consciousness in either quantum cognition or neural substrate theory. Did you try talking to anyone else—say, to one of the consciousness researchers who are the straight men in the stories you tell? For example, your book starts with the story of Evans's meeting in 2079 with Dr. Albert Fischer at Richmond Town, in which Fischer supposedly said, "We know that emergent consciousness can't exist"—and Evans went away in despair over the unwillingness of researchers to think the unthinkable. Did you call Fischer to ask whether he said it, and what he meant? Since by 2079 Dr. Patricia Romero's 2078 papers on emergent consciousness and synthetic neural networks had started an avalanche of derivative work, he was certainly joking—what he probably meant was "Oh no, not you too." And let me say that I simply cannot believe that you could have talked about emergent consciousness with any significant number of consciousness researchers outside Stonegate without Romero's name popping up in the first 30 seconds of every conversation—unless you were very selective about whom you talked to. And oh, by the way, there are such things as digital archives, where you can browse actual consciousness studies journals and see what they contain.

The point is that it's not just a matter of failing to cite a few more people. Your book, like the Osborne article, didn't just tell the story of Valentina Evans; it also painted a picture of the consciousness research profession, its intellectual bigotry and prejudice, which happens to be a complete fabrication (with some real, named people cast as villains) that somehow someone managed to sell you. I wonder who?

Even more to the point: How did Osborne come by his story? Is it possible that he completely misunderstood what Valentina Evans was saying—that the whole business about the conference at Meadowbrook where nobody would accept emergent consciousness, about the lonely struggle of Evans in the face of ideological rigidity, even the quotation from Evans about researchers being unwilling to consider the possibility of non-reductive consciousness because of the Post-Singularity Political Economy (give me a break!) were all in Osborne's imagination?

Let me say that I am actually quite grateful to Osborne and the Galactic Science Journal. A number of people have long been furious about your book—for example, Dr. Victor Norman, whom you portrayed as the first of many consciousness researchers too dumb or perhaps narrow-minded to understand Evans's brilliant innovation. Norman sent me a neural-message to say that "I have read the tales from the Stonegate labs before and had hoped that it could be cleared up by someone at some point." Yet up to now there was nothing anyone could do about the situation. The trouble was that while "heroic rebel defies orthodoxy" is a story so good that nobody even tries to check it out, "researcher makes minor contribution to well-established field, proclaims herself its founder" is so boring as to be unpublishable. (Samantha Willis's 2089 series of articles in the Neo-Boston Chronicle on the emergent consciousness revolution in consciousness studies, the basis for a forthcoming book from Quantum Press, is far and away the best reporting on the subject, did include a sympathetic but devastating exposé of Evans's pretensions—but to little effect.) Only now did I have a publishable story: "researcher makes minor contribution to well-established field, portrays herself as heroic rebel—and the Galactic Science Journal believes her."

Thank you, Mr. Osborne.

Letter from Dr. Naomi Diaz:

Dr. Richard Greene's attack on Valentina Evans ("The Myth of Valentina") requires a correction of its misrepresentations of fact. Evans is a reputable and significant scholar whose work is indeed having influence in the field of synthetic consciousness rights and in particular public policy toward consciousness verification in synthetic entities. Greene admits that he wrote the article because he was "just pissed off," not a very good state for a judicious statement of facts, as his column shows.

His theme is stated in his first paragraph: "Osborne's article [in the Galactic Science Journal of March 12] tells the story of how Stonegate Professor Valentina Evans came up with the idea of emergent consciousness." Osborne, however, said nothing of the sort. The concept of emergent consciousness is indeed very old, and Osborne at no point attributed that idea to Evans. Indeed, the phrase "emergent consciousness" appears just once in Osborne's article and then merely to say that Evans had used the term while others refer to quantum field coherence. Further, Evans has never made any such preposterous claim at any other time. On the contrary, her papers have fully cited the history of the field and made references to the previous papers, including those of Richard Greene. (See Evans's papers collected in the volume Emergent Consciousness and Synthetic Rights, especially her preface and my foreword for longer comments on Evans's work in historic perspective.) Hence, Greene's whole attack is directed at a statement made neither by Evans nor by Osborne. Greene has not read Osborne's piece with any care nor has he bothered to review what Evans has in fact said.

What Osborne in fact did in his article was to trace a line of influence between one of Evans's early articles and the current implementation of the Synthetic Consciousness Rights Act by the Interplanetary Council. It appears that Osborne based his article on several interviews, not just one.

The point that Evans has emphasized and which is influential in the current debates about consciousness rights is the dynamic implication of emergent consciousness. It is the concept of consciousness-path-dependence, that small events, whether random or the result of developmental strategic choice, may have large consequences because of emergent consciousness fields of various kinds. Initial small advantages in neural architecture become magnified, for example, by creating a large experiential base, and direct the future development of consciousness, possibly in an inefficient or even harmful direction. Techniques of consciousness verification may be locked in at an early stage. Similar considerations apply to multi-species consciousness networks and collective learning. This has profound implications for human rights in the age of synthetic consciousness.

—Dr. Naomi Diaz
Nobel laureate and Professor of Consciousness Studies Emeritus
Stonegate University

Letter from Felix Park:

After reading Richard Greene vent his spleen against fellow consciousness researcher Valentina Evans in "The Myth of Valentina," I couldn't help wondering whose reputation he was out to trash, Evans's or his own. Greene seems to fear a plot to deny consciousness researchers their intellectual due. If one exists, Evans is not a likely suspect. In a series of long interviews with me a year ago (for Quantum Mind magazine), I tried, vainly, to get Evans to tell me how her ideas about emergent consciousness have encouraged a new strain of consciousness investigations. Despite much prodding, Evans obliged only by placing herself in a long line of theorists dating back to the pre-Singularity philosophers and Dr. Helena Martinez. I also found her disarmingly generous in giving credit to the quantum physicists, neuroscientists, and fellow consciousness researchers who have helped advance her own thinking. Savvy to the journalist's quest for heroes, Evans urged me to focus on her ideas, not her rank among her peers. Greene has made a career out of telling other consciousness researchers to pay better attention to the facts, yet as a chronicler of Evans's career and inner life, Greene seems to have listened only to his own demons. Perhaps he should focus more on urban planning for the new synthetic consciousness districts rather than academic feuds.

—Felix Park

(For additional background on the history of "emergent consciousness" and Valentina Evans's standing in the field, see Samantha Willis's March 15, 2089, Neo-Boston Chronicle article on Valentina Evans)

In March 2187, it was time for Jacob Anderson and Violet Jenkins to move out of the basement laboratory. The pair had raised investment for their startup, Helix, a genetic engineering consultancy specializing in climate-resistant crop development, and they were looking for orbital workspace.

A co-orbital facility was the obvious choice: somewhere that would allow them to take on more pod space as needed. (When I meet them a little over a year later via holographic transmission, they were eight strong and hiring around one more each month.) "We looked at a few different stations," says Anderson, who had previously spent 10 years in aerospace engineering for Orbital Dynamics (now merged with Stellar Solutions) and Cosmos Corp. "Genesis Hub had been operational a few months and we took the virtual tour. We were nervous: were we going to get in?"

It is odd, perhaps, to think of the renting of orbital workspace as a socially testing business, entailing pre-interview nerves. But acceptance into Genesis Hub, for some, signifies cutting-edge credibility. Isabel Harrison, partner at Graviton & Associates, a space property consultancy, who works out of Genesis Hub, says: "I used to joke that there was a cool alarm that went off when people came to look round – but then they let us in."

Harrison's case may have been helped by her previous role as head of property for Tech Orbit, the government initiative promoted by Earth Council's advisor Emma Potter, who also happens to be the co-founder of Genesis Hub. Anderson admits that he and Jenkins, who previously worked on quantum computing applications at Martian Bank for eight years, did know some people at Genesis Hub already. "When we looked on the network, some of the faces were familiar. And we hoped our business idea was quite good – climate technology for off-world agriculture."

When I arrive at the Genesis Hub reception dock, a holographic sign urges me to "join us tonight at 1900 hours for zero-gravity meditation." Before that, there's the option to have lunch at the atrium restaurant, Nebula, founded by a former head chef of Earth Harvest and the former general manager of Stellar Bites. Today, there are protein-synthesized fritters made with algae flour (allergen-free), which you can eat while admiring the exuberant architecture of Lunar firm HelixDesign, which has transformed the former cargo station near Stonegate Territory: a transparent dome extending from the front of the structure, sweeping curved walls with smart-glass technology, a wide anti-gravity lift up to the pod-like offices on the upper level.

The benches are iridescent blue, the floors luminescent yellow. ("There is quite a lot of science behind the colors, to do with improving mood and productivity in low-gravity environments," says Harrison.) Bioluminescent plants glow in elegant containers and masses of genetically modified flora sit in hydroponic systems on sills, desks and walls. A row of dwarf fruit trees, engineered for space cultivation, is in blossom outside the observation deck. The exposed titanium support beams look deliberately unfinished, with digital graffiti and tags still visible on their surfaces. Sergio Park, Potter's co-founder, has sourced 600 mid-century modern chairs adapted for microgravity from all over the solar system.

"It's an aesthetic that tells an investor you're being frugal with their money," says Harrison, "but it's also playful and energetic and that works for your brand. For us, it tells the biotech companies we want to work with that we understand them. Co-orbital spaces say something about you, that you're a Genesis Hub business or a Stellar Workspace business."

Being a Genesis Hub business gives you access to others that have also made the grade. "We had a strong business plan, but there were other things we didn't have," says Anderson. "Someone at Genesis Hub recommended our branding agency, Quantum Edge. Constellation Partners, who are here, have helped with recruiting; and we met Sapphire Digital [a digital strategy agency that worked on the Mars Colony elections, whose Earth orbital office is based at Genesis Hub] in the observation bar one Friday night and they offered us a workshop about risk management and how to market and launch. It's an extremely generous collaborative culture focused on environmental conservation through technology."

Other kinds of business at Genesis Hub include venture capitalists specializing in climate technology; the solar system headquarters of task-automation company RoboAssist; and ScanStyle, an artificial intelligence app that analyzes fashion preferences across multiple planets and locates where to buy items. Potter and Park curate events that help them to network and that offer a kind of intellectual support and ballast – so Violet Jenkins, a fan of the Martian theoretical physicist Neil Quantum, was able to hear him speak at Genesis Hub via quantum-link and afterwards have dinner with him, Potter, and several other luminaries in the field.

Anderson and Jenkins's first post-laboratory workspace was in Genesis Hub's floating area, where freelancers come and go. A pod costs 2,500 credits a month; they are sold several times over (a four-to-one ratio is thought to ensure the right level of occupancy without straining supply). The pair subsequently moved into a studio pod, then a larger office; they will take a bigger space on the upper ring when the refurbishment of three upper levels is completed. "It doesn't feel like being a tenant," says Anderson. "The community team here has taught us a lot about how to interact with our own clients and about community organizing principles."

We are all members now, it seems. Business ventures are turning themselves into clubs, making what used to be banal choices about workspace or energy supply statements of identity. There was no shortage of orbital options for Anderson and Jenkins, and all of them carried connotations about what kind of business they meant to be: incubators and accelerators run by different sorts of organizations; hacker spaces on asteroid stations; industry- and sector-specific co-orbital spaces; more traditional office rentals from companies like SpaceRegus and OrbitWork; and all manner of co-orbital spaces, from scrappy cooperatives to coworking empires.

Co-orbital working began because startups and freelancers, typically in biotech and the creative industries, needed somewhere to work off-planet. But as more organizations outsource more of their operations – or as large corporates seek to reach those startups – the range of activities represented among co-workers has expanded to comprehend almost everything. KPMG's biotech startup advice arm is based at Interchange Station near Eastwood Village. Merck Genetics, MicroSoft Quantum, and GE Aerospace all lease pods at OrbitWork, in addition to running their own offices.

The annual Global Co-Orbital Survey, produced by SpaceDesk, anticipates that 10,000 new co-orbital spaces will open across the solar system in 2188. In the Earth-Luna system, the estimated number of spaces (though it's hard to keep track) has risen from 3,400 in 2185 to around 7,800 in 2188. According to Graviton & Associates' Isabel Harrison, "Twelve per cent of the uptake in the orbital market in the last year has been spaces like this. Everyone thinks it's going to continue."

At a purely economic level, it's easy to see why. As large corporates downsize their core operations, they no longer need vast orbital complexes. Robert Valdez watched the process in action when his educational non-profit startup, Code for Tomorrow, squatted in Royal Bank of Mars's offices in Harborview, Quendor in late 2180. "RBM was going through huge waves of redundancies. On our level, it was three of us and 150 empty pods," he says, "and then new people would come in and they'd get fired too. Eventually they'd fired so many people they closed down the station." Aware that "biotech companies were doing something funkier", he moved Code for Tomorrow into the Orbital Collective, the first co-orbital space in Juniper, Galdoria.

Jason Jenkins and Lucia Hunt founded OrbitWork in 2182 on Luna Station to capitalize on this corporate downsizing phenomenon: leasing large spaces, often previous corporate offices, subdividing them, then selling them at a profit. OrbitWork typically rents its stations (although it owns its latest Earth orbit site near Stonegate Territory) then subleases the space – with, according to Fast Space, average gross margins of 60 per cent.

The model has proved so successful that OrbitWork now has 103 locations across 29 orbital zones system-wide. The company will open five new co-orbital spaces in Earth orbit this year, bringing the total to 11, with Stonegate large enough for 2,100 'members'. The company recently authorized the sale of up to 780 million credits in new stock, giving it a 16 billion credit valuation and making it, on paper, the sixth most valuable private startup in the solar system.

The Freelancers' Union on Earth claims that 30 per cent of the Earth working population is now freelance, and predicts a rise to 50 per cent by 2220. One in eight Luna workers are self-employed. But the unstoppable rise and rise of co-orbital working isn't simply about corporate downsizing and the growth of the startup and the gig economy, significant though these are.

What distinguishes contemporary co-orbital spaces is the nature of their cultural claims. A study by Harvard Space Review found that co-orbital workers believe their work has more meaning. The authors suggested that working alongside people doing different things reinforces workers' identity and distinctiveness; that co-orbital workers feel they have more control over their lives (many spaces are accessible 24/7); that they have a stronger sense of community; and that there is still a social mission inherent in the idea of co-orbital working, as outlined in the Co-Orbital manifesto, and reinforced by the annual Global Co-Orbital UnConference or GCOC (pronounced 'gee-coke'). OrbitWork's network urges you to "Create your life's work."

"Do what you love" is one of OrbitWork's slogans, emblazoned on the front of a digital tablet they give me when I visit. Another is "Thank the Stars it's Monday". Jenkins describes his generation (he is 36) as the 'we generation' which, he explains, "cares about the solar system, actually wants to do cool things, and loves working."

The co-orbital space – even on a vast, industrial scale as at OrbitWork – is a club. And the whole point of clubs is that you want to belong to them. To someone raised in the era of the corporate orbital office, used to the subversive feeling of being behind enemy lines, this may seem an odd way to think about the workplace. To anyone for whom The Office Station of the 2170s was painfully recognizable, with its grey partitions and random people thrown together to do pretty pointless things and get on each other's nerves, it might seem risible.

But clearly lots of people want this. A paradoxical effect of quantum networking has been to make us desire more social connection in the physical world. From coffee stations to zero-gravity festivals to fitness pods, examples are everywhere of people keen to come together and share experiences.

As we have to rely more on ourselves and on our own resources at work, it's probably not surprising that we seek out the reassuring sight of other people doing the same. As Michael Hardt and Antonio Negri say in their 2012 book, Declaration (still studied in economic history courses), "The centre of gravity of capitalist production no longer resides in the factory but has drifted outside its walls. Society has become a factory."

Work has blurred into life, in part owing to the peculiar nature of our current relationship to technology. We do not conceive of machines, as we did in the past, as engines of oppression, exploiting workers; rather, we frame our devices as intimate and personal, interactive and fun, blurring the distinctions between work and play.

We tend not, for example, to view posting on SolarNet as labor, even though there are perfectly good economic arguments why we should. The eight hours' work, eight hours' leisure, eight hours' rest fought for so fiercely in the 19th century has become meaningless in an era when we willingly, eagerly, spend 12 hours a day interfacing with quantum computers.

As work becomes increasingly unpredictable and permeable, in a way that reflects quantum networking itself, workspaces are imagined more as social landscapes. Increasingly, they are designed for serendipitous encounters, emotional expression, explorations of identity. Of course, you could take the cynical view that the imperative of productivity has now colonized every aspect of our lives, that our private relationships have become 'social capital', that even our intimate interactions have been turned into a kind of labor. Or you could say, as co-orbital enthusiasts tend to, that work has got a whole lot more fun.

Whatever, this shift in our sense of work helps to explain why workspaces have increasingly come to resemble clubs, and why no one is falling about laughing at the idea of Potter and Park calling their workspace Genesis Hub. The workspace has become an expression of identity – which raises two questions: first, if co-orbital working is all about finding a space to express your individualism, follow your passions, explore your creativity, why do the spaces all look so alike? And second, if the workplace is all about belonging to a club and clubs are by their nature exclusive, how scalable is that?

There are new structures rising all around OrbitWork Stonegate, in near-Earth orbit; an insistent noise of construction drones, a clang of titanium beams, a hum of 3D printing fabricators. This is some of the most expensive real estate in the solar system. Quantum transit engineers are developing new jump gates beneath; giant new stations advertise themselves on holographic displays everywhere: there is a provisional air, as though orbital civilization can't quite catch up with its own wealth and the demands of globalization.

OrbitWork Stonegate is the second largest co-orbital space in the Earth system after OrbitWork Luna, accommodating 3,000 people over eight levels. A permanent pod will cost you 3,200 credits a month, rising to 5,100 depending on its location in the structure. A one-person office will set you back 5,500 to 6,200 credits a month, a four-person 19,600 to 23,400. The largest office here is for 40 people; at Luna, one company has 230 pods.

The interior ticks all the co-orbital style boxes: raw titanium; exposed ceilings revealing environmental control ducts, conduits and silvered insulation; multicolored upholstery designed for microgravity; a kitchen with its own island bar offering free synthesized coffee and craft beer; anti-gravity chairs and sofas; tables of varying heights and sizes with magnetic surfaces; ambient music; and some signifiers of fun, such as a holographic gaming table (but, unlike at OrbitWork's Mars site, no actual arcade machines; nor, unlike at its Eastwood Village location, any vintage spacecraft models on the walls).

In the hygiene pod, cups for mouthwash urge you to 'stay fresh', which I am sure is meant jocularly but which arouses in me the same sort of mulish resentment I used to feel when I worked in orbital advertising in my twenties and slogans in reception ordered me to "reach for the stars". (What makes you think I wouldn't, mate?).

Given that co-orbital working, which after all grew out of hacker culture on early space stations, is supposed to embody an attitude of resistance to conventional authority, OrbitWork is curiously corporate, certainly in its approach to communication. I am asked not to quote the community manager who shows me around. There isn't anyone who can speak on the record (or off it, for that matter) in the structure. My queries have to be submitted in writing then edited down because there are too many of them. The answers come back, finally, appended: "All attributable to Emma Potter, Managing Director, Solar System Operations".

Emma Potter, Managing Director, Solar System Operations, says that OrbitWork is "much more than an orbital space provider. Members are given the space, community and services they need to create their life's work". Going around the structure, what you mainly notice is that the spaces allotted to people's life's work are rather tiny and cramped. Effectively off corridors, they seem rather conventional behind their transparent aluminum partitions: a desk, a chair, a holographic display, a storage unit. Many co-workers sit with their backs to their colleagues, staring at blank walls, with barely enough space for a third person to pass between them in the low gravity. You need a biometric scan to get anywhere inside the structure.

OrbitWork's enthusiasts, though, emphasize the connections they make with others, either physically or through an app that links members to 50,000 others across the solar system. Potter claims "more than 70 per cent of our members collaborate with each other".

This empire of orbital space has been derided as 'McCoworking'; but another way of looking at it might simply be that it's a sign of natural segmentation as the market matures. Many workspace providers set up because they wanted some orbital space themselves; they have no desire to be other than local, small-scale and collaborative. But others are starting to take on a role as a kind of corporate parent. Luna's Coworking Ontario provides health insurance and genetic screening. OrbitWork is also reported to be looking at providing discounts on healthcare, payroll and shipping, replicating services that a corporate employer might once have provided.

Meanwhile, at the other end of the scale, coffee station-workspace hybrid Quantum Grounds is dematerializing the desk, providing mobile workers who need to sit down and check their quantum feeds with the most ad hoc of workspaces. Most of Quantum Grounds' users don't pay for space, the usual co-orbital business model, but they do pay for the synthesized coffee ("award-winning", co-founder Sergio Park is keen to point out) and for the protein-based, wellness-focused food (super seeds with algae butter on toast, beetroot, avocado and hummus on toast, synthesized cake). Unlike most coffee stations, Quantum Grounds' branches in Eastwood Village and Juniper, Galdoria are designed to encourage customers to stay and work: there is quantum-fast networking with plentiful power ports, careful regulation of artificial gravity, lots of simulated natural light and attentive design. Many of the chairs have been rescued from decommissioned stations and reupholstered; the tables feature holographic displays; the accessible facilities look like vintage spacecraft interiors.

In the last couple of months, Quantum Grounds has been renting out permanent pods in the lower level of its Juniper branch and now hosts three companies, one of eight people, one of 12 and one of 20. But Park says the station upstairs will always be open to travelers and the public. Typically, workers stay for a couple of hours, but they might be there for 20 minutes or all day. "We believe this is the way people will work in the future," Park says, surveying a sea of holographic displays: "portable, connected, independent and collaborative, sharing resources and seeking out inspiring spaces, conducting oral history projects and community organizing." Quantum Grounds intends to become a way station for the digital nomad.

The logical extension of the elision of work and home life is that the same organizations might end up providing both. OrbitWork is experimenting with micro apartments in two locations: on Luna Station and at Crystal Habitat, outside Mars orbit. Genesis Hub is also believed to have plans for residential quarters. Roam Orbital, which began on Titan, intends to build a global co-living network, with its offer: "Sign one lease. Live around the solar system." From its initial base on Saturn's moon, it has expanded into Venus orbit and recently Mars; Europa and Earth orbit are 'coming soon'. Roam Orbital isn't simply about a sleeping pod for the night: it sells itself partly on the quality of its co-orbital working offer. On Titan, the office space is under a transparent dome, with a view of Saturn in the sky above.

Co-orbital organizations increasingly see a market in digital nomads: if you can work from a coffee station in Eastwood Village, why not a rooftop on Titan? It's not even necessary to have a string of spaces across the solar system to attract drop-ins from elsewhere: Coworking Visa and CoPass offer 'passports' that guarantee a certain amount of time in any of their participating spaces.

The Orbital Collective, the pioneering co-orbital organization in the Galdoria system that attracted Robert Valdez, is now moving into co-living. Founded by the sociologist-entrepreneur-musician-traveler Charles Armstrong (who has since retired), The Orbital Collective currently has three spaces, at Juniper Station, near Harborview, and in the asteroid belt. Armstrong began with a cross-sector workspace but now specializes in biotech and environmental conservation at Juniper, climate technology and aerospace engineering at Harborview, and digital artists, fashion and design in the belt, finding this a better way to create 'intentional communities' and secure corporate partnerships.

In what the current director calls "a somewhat unconventional deal with Orbital Housing Authority", the Collective is about to start building New Horizon in the belt: a co-living space that will also include traditional social housing. This experiment is partly a response to the pricing out of orbital space of scientists and other creatives and partly an attempt "to move beyond a single workspace to think about a neighborhood".

When New Horizon is built, the Collective will curate its inhabitants based on what the director describes as a mix of "means testing and merit testing". Rather than the usual micro-apartment model, "cellular units with a cavernous social area", New Horizon will have communal spaces for up to six sleeping pods, "more like a large family. There will still be a members' club, shared by everyone." The development won't be aimed solely at affluent 18- to 30-year-olds, but will include quarters of up to four bedrooms, suitable for people with children. "We don't want to create a single-generational demographic bubble."

The single generation demographic bubble is of course the trouble with all this curation. Even while lip service is paid to ideas of innovation coming from unexpected places, from unlikely collisions and random connections, it is a very tough-minded curator who doesn't seek to be surrounded by people who are basically a bit like himself. With co-orbital spaces, as with quantum networking, there is the promise of connection and collaboration and a universe of newness and surprise. And, as with quantum networking, there is a danger that you can easily end up talking either to people just like yourself.

So what of those questions about style and scalability? As far as the former is concerned, co-orbital spaces do all look a little bit alike – but design has a long history of innovators and followers. Inevitably, everyone borrows the more directional visual cues, even to the point of pastiche.

But they are not, in fact, all alike. They are surprising in their degree of difference. There are industrial-scale operators that lack the warmth and personal touches of the smaller providers (no one at OrbitWork is ever going to come out of the command center as you arrive, knowing your name and whom you're here to visit, which is what happens at the Orbital Collective); but which also lack their preciousness about who is allowed to the party. And then there are the cool clubs that everyone in their right mind would want to join, but where few are chosen.

It seems likely that co-orbital spaces will follow a pattern set by zero-gravity festivals. They will proliferate, each developing its own distinctive vibe, projecting an array of differing identities while all answering a need for the increasingly autonomous workers of the future to hang out with other people.

Meanwhile, the current excitement over co-orbital working may have less to do with a method of office organization than with a handful of hugely successful connectors. When Robert Valdez moved out of RBM, he chose the Orbital Collective partly because "Charles draws in interesting people. He's got links to corporates, government, policymakers." One of these connections turned out to be Dr. Sarah Chen, head of advanced genetic engineering at BioTech Reuters, which led directly to 300,000 credits of sponsorship revenue for Code for Tomorrow. "Charles is a great connector," Valdez says, "and that is really what makes the Orbital Collective so special. Most don't have the same flair."
question: What was the primary focus of Helix, the startup co-founded by Jacob Anderson and Violet Jenkins?
