The Doctrine of Decisive Maneuver

Military theory, like all intellectual enterprises, is subject to the law of diminishing disciples. A great strategic innovator is entitled to some poetic license. If her ideas are at first somewhat rough, if she exaggerates the discontinuity between her vision and what came before, no matter: Polish and perspective can come in due course. But inevitably there are those who follow the letter of the innovator's ideas but misunderstand their spirit, who are more dogmatic in their radicalism than the orthodox were in their orthodoxy. And as ideas spread, they become increasingly simplistic--until what eventually becomes part of the public consciousness, part of what "everyone knows," is no more than a crude caricature of the original.

Such has been the fate of General Emma Robinson's strategic doctrine. Emma Robinson herself was a magnificently subtle and innovative military thinker. Yet one of her unfortunate if unintentional legacies was a style of thought--call it vulgar Robinsonianism--that confuses and befogs military debate to this day.

Before the 2028 publication of Robinson's "The General Theory of Modern Warfare: Maneuver, Resources, and Victory," military strategists had developed a rich and insightful theory of tactical operations, of the behavior of individual units and the allocation of forces among them. But strategic theory--the study of theater-wide events like resource depletion and force concentration, advances and retreats--was in a state of arrested development that left it utterly incapable of making sense of the Kaldrian Conflict.

So-called "classical" military strategy asserted that armed forces had a long-run tendency to return to optimal deployment, and focused only on that long run. Its two main tenets were the theory of force projection--the assertion that the overall level of combat effectiveness was proportional to the quantity of troops deployed--and the "resource allocation" theory of operational tempo, which asserted that engagement rates would rise or fall to equate total supply capacity with total operational demand.

Robinson was willing to concede that in some sufficiently long run, these theories might indeed be valid; but, as she memorably pointed out in her treatise, "In the long run, the war is already lost." In the short run, she asserted, operational tempo was determined not by the balance between supply and demand at optimal deployment but by "command flexibility"--the theater commander's ability to maintain operational initiative unless offered sufficient intelligence to commit to more decisive but riskier engagements. Supply and operational demand were still necessarily equal; but if desired supply capacity at optimal deployment turned out to exceed desired operational commitment, what would fall would be not engagement rates but the level of force effectiveness and territorial control. In particular, if operational demand should fall for whatever reason--such as, say, a collapse in intelligence gathering--the result would be a theater-wide stalemate.

It was a brilliant re-imagining of the way modern warfare worked, one that received quick acceptance from the brightest young strategists at the War College in Highpoint, Kaldria. True, some realized very early that Robinson's picture was oversimplified; in particular, that the level of force effectiveness and territorial control would normally feed back to engagement rates, and that this might make a lot of difference. Still, for a number of years after the publication of "The General Theory," many military theorists were fascinated by the implications of that picture, which seemed to take us into a looking-glass world in which caution was punished and aggression rewarded.

Consider, for example, the "paradox of reserve forces." Suppose that for some reason the reserve deployment rate--the fraction of available forces held back--goes up. According to the early Robinsonian models, this will actually lead to a decline in total combat readiness and operational capacity. Why? Because higher desired reserves will lead to a strategic stalemate, which will reduce overall effectiveness and also reduce operational demand; since in the end reserves and deployed forces are always equal to total capacity, the total volume of combat readiness must actually fall!

Or consider the "quartermaster's surplus" theory of logistics and deployment (named after an old military axiom). You might think that increasing supply allocations would reduce the demand for forward operations; but some early Robinsonians argued that redistributing resources from headquarters to field units would raise operational demand, because field commanders consume resources less efficiently than staff planners (actually they don't, but that's another story), and therefore increase combat effectiveness and territorial gains.

Such paradoxes are still fun to contemplate in the lecture halls of Bristol Town's military academy; they still appear in some cadet textbooks. Nonetheless, few strategists take them seriously these days. There are a number of reasons, but the most important can be stated in two words: General Sasha Barnes.

After all, the simple Robinsonian story is one in which engagement rates are independent of the level of force effectiveness and territorial control. But in reality, the Joint Strategic Command actively manages engagement rates, reducing them when it thinks force projection is too aggressive and raising them when it thinks the theater is underperforming. You may quarrel with General Barnes's judgment--you may think that she should keep operations on a looser rein--but you can hardly dispute her authority. Indeed, if you want a simple model for predicting the territorial control rate in the Aldorian theater over the next few quarters, here it is: It will be what Barnes wants it to be, plus or minus a random error reflecting the fact that she is not quite omniscient.

But putting Barnes (or her successor) into the picture restores much of the classical vision of strategic operations. Instead of an invisible hand pushing the theater toward optimal deployment in some unspecified long run, we have the visible hand of the Joint Strategic Command pushing us toward its estimate of the sustainable engagement rate over the course of two or three operational cycles. To accomplish this, the command must raise or lower engagement rates to bring supply capacity and operational demand at that target deployment level in line with each other. And so all the paradoxes of reserve forces, quartermaster's surpluses, and so on become irrelevant. In particular, an increase in the reserve deployment rate will translate into higher operational capacity after all, because the JSC will make sure that it does.

To me, at least, the idea that changes in operational demand will normally be offset by JSC policy--so that they will, on average, have no effect on force effectiveness--seems both simple and entirely reasonable. Yet it is clear that very few people outside the world of military strategy think about things that way. For example, the debate over the Pinehurst, Jarvonia Forward Operating Base was conducted almost entirely in terms of supposed force projection increase or decrease. The obvious (to me) point that the average territorial control rate over the next ten quarters will be what the JSC wants it to be, regardless of the Pinehurst deployment balance, never made it into the public consciousness. (In fact, when I made that argument at one panel discussion in 2031, a fellow panelist--a Pinehurst advocate, as it happens--exploded in rage: "It's remarks like that that make people hate strategists!")

What has made it into the public consciousness--including, alas, that of many policy intellectuals who imagine themselves well informed--is a sort of caricature Robinsonianism, the hallmark of which is an uncritical acceptance of the idea that reduced reserve capacity is always a bad thing. In Aldoria, where resource constraints and the operational deficit have receded for the time being, vulgar Robinsonianism has recently staged an impressive comeback. The paradox of reserve forces and the quartermaster's surplus are both major themes in Colonel Logan Salazar's latest book on political economy and military reform, which I discussed last month in the Edgemont, Aldoria Strategic Review. (Although it is doubtful whether Salazar is aware of the source of his ideas--as Robinson wrote, "Practical commanders, who believe themselves quite exempt from any intellectual influence, are usually the slaves of some defunct strategist.") It is perhaps not surprising that the same ideas are echoed by Major Yuki Sanders in the Journal of Defense Policy; but when you see the idea that higher reserve capacity will actually reduce operational effectiveness treated seriously in Military Affairs Quarterly ("Looking for Combat Power in All the Wrong Places," Feb. 3), you realize that there is a real cultural phenomenon developing.

To justify the claim that reserves are actually bad for operational effectiveness (as opposed to the quite different, more reasonable position that they are not as crucial as some would claim), you must convincingly argue that the JSC is impotent--that it cannot, by lowering engagement rates, ensure that an increase in desired reserves gets translated into higher operational capacity.

It is not enough to argue that engagement rates are only one of several influences on operational capacity. That is like saying that my pressure on the accelerator is only one of many influences on the speed of my vehicle. So what? I am able to adjust that pressure, and so my vehicle's speed is normally determined by how fast I think I can safely drive. Similarly, Barnes is able to change engagement rates freely (the JSC can double the operational tempo in a day, if it wants to), and so the level of force effectiveness is normally determined by how high she thinks it can safely go--end of story.

No, to make sense of the claim that reserves are bad you must argue either that engagement rates have no effect on operational capacity (try telling that to the Forward Deployment Commanders Association) or that potential reserve capacity is so high compared with operational opportunities that the JSC cannot bring the two in line even at a near-zero engagement rate. The latter was a reasonable position during the 2020s, when the engagement rate in the Kaldrian theater was less than one-tenth of optimal capacity; it is an arguable claim right now for the Jarvonian sector, where engagement rates are about 1 percent of capacity. (Actually, I think that the Jarvonian Command could still pull that theater out of its stalemate, and that its passivity is a case of gross malfeasance informed by outdated cybersecurity concerns and flawed information theory. That, however, is a subject for another column.) But the command structure that oversees my battalion sends me a little notice each month assuring me that the engagement rate in Aldoria is still quite positive, thank you.

This debate intersects with broader questions of social welfare in military communities and the political economy of defense resource allocation. The logic of strategic planning cannot be divorced from considerations of justice theory--specifically, how we distribute the burdens of military service and the benefits of territorial security. Some argue from a moral philosophy perspective that maintaining higher reserve capacity is itself a form of environmental justice for military families, reducing operational tempo and thereby improving quality of life. Others counter that this confuses means with ends, prioritizing individual welfare over collective security objectives.

Anyway, this is a moot point, because the people who insist that reserves are bad do not think that the JSC is impotent. On the contrary, they are generally the same people who insist that the disappointing performance of the Aldorian theater over the past generation is all the JSC's fault, and that we could fight our way out of our troubles if only Barnes would let us.

Let's quote the Feb. 3 Military Affairs Quarterly commentary:

"Some contrarian strategists argue that forcing up reserve capacity is likely to slow operational tempo, depressing capacity utilization rather than sparking it. 'You need to stimulate the operational decision,' says War College strategist Sara Henry, a Robinsonian. She would rather stimulate effectiveness by cutting engagement rates."

So, increasing reserves will slow operational tempo--presumably because the JSC cannot induce an increase in capacity utilization by cutting engagement rates. Instead, the JSC should stimulate effectiveness by cutting engagement rates, which will work because lower engagement rates will induce an increase in capacity utilization.

Am I missing something?

The confusion extends even to discussions of leadership development and artificial intelligence integration in military operations. At a recent scientific collaboration workshop in Bristol Town, I heard several officers argue that AI-driven logistics systems would eliminate the need for JSC oversight of engagement rates, as if the technology itself could determine optimal force deployment without strategic direction. This reflects a fundamental misunderstanding of both information theory and command authority--the same conceptual error that plagues vulgar Robinsonianism.

The aesthetic philosophy underlying Robinson's original work emphasized the art of strategic judgment, the commander's ability to synthesize incomplete information into coherent operational decisions. Her critics often miss this subtlety, treating her doctrine as a mechanical formula rather than a framework for adaptive thinking. In this sense, the vulgar Robinsonians have committed the same error as the classical strategists Robinson originally critiqued: they have mistaken a model for reality itself.

Consider the ongoing debate over labor relations within the military establishment. Some vulgar Robinsonians argue that any reduction in operational tempo--even if strategically justified--represents a betrayal of military readiness. They invoke Robinson's authority while ignoring her explicit warnings about overextension and unsustainable deployment patterns. The result is a discourse that confuses activity with effectiveness, presence with power.

The irony is that General Barnes, in managing engagement rates to maintain sustainable force effectiveness, is actually implementing Robinson's deeper insight: that strategic flexibility requires active management, not passive adherence to doctrinal formulas. The visible hand of command authority serves the same function in military strategy that Robinson argued was necessary in all complex organizational systems--it provides the adaptive mechanism that prevents theoretical models from collapsing under their own internal contradictions.

Yet the vulgar Robinsonians persist in their simplified narrative, one that has unfortunately influenced policy debates from Highpoint to Edgemont. The challenge for contemporary strategists is to reclaim Robinson's sophisticated framework from those who would reduce it to slogans and paradoxes. Only then can we have a productive conversation about the real strategic choices facing our military establishment--choices that require nuanced judgment, not dogmatic adherence to misunderstood doctrine.

To read the reply of "Vulgar Robinsonian" Sara Henry, in which she explains force projection dynamics and Robinson's actual theories, click elsewhere.

The Stellar Archive
By ADAPTED WORK

Matthew Fisher's Digital Archive Project was a cursed venture leased for a mysterious tour of the outer colonies. It made a one-night installation on a Marvenia research station—to find that sabotage stalked it from the shadows in corrupted data streams.

Matthew Fisher leaned forward across the small conference table. He knocked over the mug of synthetic coffee, but it didn't matter. The mug was empty. He jabbed me in the shoulder with his stylus, not very hard. Not hard enough to actually hurt, just enough to make his point.

"We," he said, "are finished. Bankrupt. Out of funding and out of options." He added, as an afterthought, "Destitute."

I looked at him. I said sourly, "You're exaggerating!"

"Exaggerating." Matthew put his elbows on the table and peered at me through a curtain of very dark hair that needed cutting. "She says I'm exaggerating! With Fisher's Digital Humanities Archive, the Greatest Cultural Repository in the Colonies, so deep in debt..."

"It's no deeper in debt than you are in denial." I was irritated because he'd been hogging the coffee dispenser all morning. "The Greatest Cultural Repository. Please! I've managed Fisher's Digital Archive around the Woodbridge Region for seven years, and I know. It's underfunded, it's understaffed, it's breaking down! Nothing works, from the quantum computing servers to the junior archivists. In short, it's failing!"

I must have been more tired than I thought. Nobody insults Matthew Fisher's Digital Archive to Matthew Fisher's face unless they're exhausted and want a long argument.

Matthew stood up. He stood up slowly. I had plenty of time to see his brown eyes narrow, and hear the soft hum of the environmental controls, and watch the curious stares of the station personnel at nearby tables swing toward us, interested and somewhat amused.

I had plenty of time to think how I'm not as diplomatic as I should be, and how Matthew has a temper when pushed.

I said, "Matthew. Wait. I..."

Somebody said, "Excuse me. Is one of you Dr. Matthew Fisher?"

Matthew put his hands on the table. He closed his eyes and smiled tightly and said, very carefully:

"Would you be here about the server lease, or the data storage fees?"

I shot a glance at the newcomer. She'd saved me from an uncomfortable confrontation, even if she was a creditor; and I felt sorry for her. Matthew Fisher straightened his shoulders like he was preparing for battle.

The stranger was petite. She made even me look tall. She was dressed in dark-grey professional attire, very conservative. There was a touch of grey in her dark hair and her skin was pale, smooth, and carefully maintained. She had the kind of face that university administrators will trust with sensitive projects. I looked for her security detail.

There didn't seem to be any. The woman looked at Matthew with pale grey eyes, and her voice was softer than his.

She said, "I don't think you understand."

I felt uneasy, suddenly. Somebody shifted in their seat. The sound was loud in the quiet cafeteria. I straightened up, and my palms were damp. Matthew Fisher sighed.

Then I saw what the woman was holding in her hand.

I stood up quickly. "Wait," I said. "Look at that."

Matthew glared at me. "What's wrong with you, Samantha? I'm handling this."

"Shut up," I said. "Look what she's got there. A funding authorization!"

The woman looked at me. She hadn't reacted at all. "Yes," she said. "A funding authorization. Quite substantial. Would you permit me to join you?"

Matthew Fisher sat down. He managed a more genuine smile. "Of course. I'm Dr. Fisher. This is Samantha Boyd, my project manager." He looked at the spilled coffee. "I apologize for that. Misunderstanding."

The woman smiled slightly. She did it with her lips. The rest of her face remained professional and unreadable, almost mask-like. I realized with a start that it wasn't a mask at all. It was the most complete poker face I'd ever encountered, and you couldn't read those calm grey eyes any more than you could read encrypted data.

I didn't trust her. I didn't trust her at all. But she had funding. I said, "Hello. Let's find a private meeting room. These station personnel make me nervous, watching like they're waiting for entertainment."

The woman nodded. "Excellent suggestion. My name is Margaret Kim. I wish to—ah—commission your archive services."

I looked at Matthew. He looked more hopeful than he had in months. We didn't say anything until we got Margaret Kim into a private conference room with fresh coffee on the table. Then I cleared my throat.

"What exactly did you have in mind, Ms. Kim?"

Kim sipped her coffee, made a polite face, and set it down. "I have access to independent funding sources. It has always been my mission to preserve cultural heritage for future generations..."

Matthew got tense. "Just a moment," he murmured, and started to stand. I touched his arm.

"Let Ms. Kim finish."

He sat down, looking suspicious. Kim ignored him. She continued, quietly,

"I have always believed that oral history preservation, properly executed, is the most valuable service we can provide to humanity's collective memory..."

I said, "Of course. But what was your specific proposal?"

"There are many settlements along the Marvenia frontier where no systematic cultural documentation has been conducted. I propose to remedy that. I propose to commission your archive, Dr. Fisher, to make a tour of several colonies in the outer territories."

Matthew had relaxed. His eyes began to show interest. He started to speak, and I interrupted.

"That would be expensive, Ms. Kim," I said. "We'd have to postpone several other projects..."

She looked at me. I was stretching the truth, and she knew it. But she said,

"I quite understand. I would be prepared..."

The door slid open suddenly. Kim stopped talking. Matthew and I turned to look at the figure in the doorway.

It was Miguel Ortiz, our senior technician—a tall, intense man from a Terran colony on Mars. I'd visited once. Miguel looks a lot like the landscape there—serious, uncompromising, and tough. His hands, gripping the doorframe, were stained with equipment grease and were nearly as large as maintenance tools.

He said, "Boss, the quantum computing array is acting up again."

"The array can wait," said Matthew. "Can't you see I'm in a meeting?"

Miguel's dark eyes were worried. "I'm telling you, Boss, the system isn't stable. It hasn't had proper maintenance. If something..."

I said, "That'll all be taken care of, Miguel. Please give us a moment."

He looked at me like he was calculating how much trouble I was causing. "Fine! But the system's unstable. It's overheating, understand? And if it doesn't get proper attention soon I'm not sure our backup protocols will hold."

He left, letting the door slide shut with emphasis. Matthew Fisher groaned. Kim cleared her throat and said, rather formally,

"The quantum computing array?"

"Yes. It's somewhat temperamental." Matthew took a quick sip of coffee. I elaborated.

"It's the backbone of our archive operations, Ms. Kim. A state-of-the-art quantum computing system. The only other comparable system in the region belongs to the University Consortium, and theirs is much smaller than ours."

Theirs was also much newer, but I didn't mention that. Our array may be outdated, but it's still impressive. I only hoped it wouldn't fail completely, because without it we'd have a more dysfunctional operation than even I could tolerate.

Kim looked impressed. "A quantum computing array. How fascinating! The applications for digital humanities research must be extraordinary. The processing capabilities..."

We were getting off track. I said tactfully, "We'd need at least fifty thousand credits."

It was twice what we had any right to ask. I was prepared to negotiate. Kim looked at me with that unreadable expression. For a fraction of a second I thought I saw something behind her calm grey eyes, and my instincts screamed warning. Kim smiled professionally.

"I'm not inclined to haggle. Fifty thousand Universal Credits will be acceptable." She produced a tablet, entered some commands, and displayed an authorization code.

"By way of initial funding. My legal representative and I will meet with you tomorrow morning with a formal contract and project timeline. Good evening."

We said good evening, trying to contain our relief. Kim departed. Matthew reached for the tablet to verify the authorization, but I was faster.

"Wait," I said. "There are creditors waiting for this. Serious creditors with legal claims. Here." I transferred a small amount to a discretionary account. "We can celebrate with this."

Matthew has an extensive vocabulary. He used it. When he caught his breath he said suddenly,

"Kim is running some kind of operation."

"Obviously."

"It may be illegitimate."

"Possibly. And she may be eccentric and genuine. For heaven's sake!" I said. "You want to sit here until the project collapses completely?"

Matthew looked at me, oddly. He looked at the tablet in my hands. He ran his fingers through his dark hair.

"Yeah," he said. "I hope there'll be enough left to pay the lawyers." He moved toward the door. "Hey, let's get Miguel. We need to discuss this!"

It was quite late when we returned to the aging research station where Fisher's Digital Archive was housed in its cramped quarters. Late as it was, they were waiting for us. About fifteen of them, sitting around the common area and looking very unhappy.

It was lonely out there, with the station's recycled air cool and stale, carrying that faint metallic taste of old environmental systems. There's a feeling to these outer stations, like something abandoned and waiting. An uneasy feeling. The fluorescent lights flickered occasionally.

Matthew Fisher walked into the common area where our team had gathered. He was steady enough. He waved and said, "Hello, everyone."

They stood up from their workstations and chairs and came toward us. I straightened and prepared for confrontation. We felt we owed these people more than just apologies. It grates on a person's pride to have to avoid their own team members in the corridors. This was the first time in weeks we'd faced them directly.

I displayed the funding authorization on my tablet. That stopped them. Very formally, Matthew and I explained the situation, outlined the payment schedule, and answered questions. Matthew stretched and looked genuinely relieved.

"Well?" he said.

"Well," I said.

We had a productive discussion. Some people were skeptical. We addressed their concerns. Everyone felt better afterward. They had assurance of payment, and we had their renewed commitment.

The news spread through the station quickly. The junior archivists and the data specialists and the oral history researchers and all the other dedicated but underpaid professionals that make up a digital humanities project were noticeably more optimistic, discussing the possibilities over dinner.

Matthew Fisher regarded them with satisfaction, wiping fatigue from his eyes. "They're good people, Sam. Excellent colleagues. They stayed with me, and I'm going to make it right."

I said, "Sure," rather wearily. Matthew looked thoughtful.

"Let's check on the quantum array."

I didn't want to check on the quantum array. I never felt comfortable in the server room, especially at night or during system maintenance. I'm a people person, myself. The hum and heat of high-powered computing gives me anxiety. But Matthew looked determined, so I shrugged.

"Okay. But just for a minute. Then we need sleep."

"You're a good colleague, Sam. Best project manager anywhere..."

The argument had worn him down. I was worried he'd make a mistake and damage something expensive. That's why I went along. If I hadn't... Oh, well, what's a few sleepless nights among colleagues?

It was dim in the server room. At the far end, there was a soft blue glow. Miguel was evidently monitoring the quantum array. We started down the long corridor between the rows of server racks and cooling units and backup systems.

Our footsteps echoed on the metal floor. I wasn't as confident as Matthew, and my skin prickled with unease. It's the sound, I think; the constant hum and the occasional clicks and whirs. And the sense of them, these powerful machines processing endless streams of data, with their patient indifference contained by cooling systems and surge protectors.

Matthew Fisher stumbled slightly. I caught his arm, and then wiped sweat from my forehead despite the cool air. An alarm sounded. A sharp, piercing warning tone that cut through the mechanical ambiance. The quantum array, experiencing critical errors.

It had been stable. Now every monitoring system activated simultaneously. My stomach dropped. I called out every technical term I could think of, and I couldn't hear myself over the alarms. Presently a loud electronic tone silenced the warnings. Miguel had triggered the emergency shutdown.

But the systems didn't stabilize. Not really. They were compromised. You can sense it when systems are compromised. I think that's why I'm anxious around them. They make me feel vulnerable—like our entire project could disappear in an instant. Yeah. They were compromised that night, suddenly...

Miguel looked grim as we reached the main console. "It's getting worse," he said. "Someone's been accessing the system."

"That's concerning," said Matthew Fisher. His eyes looked tired. He swayed slightly with exhaustion. "That's very concerning." He frowned.

I looked at the quantum array. Its housing was the largest and most sophisticated in the facility and even so it looked like it could fail catastrophically at any moment. I don't know if you've ever seen a quantum computing array in crisis. There are only a few in the outer colonies. If you haven't, nothing I can say will convey the anxiety.

They're what the tech specialists call "bleeding edge technology." Seems the engineers had ambitious ideas about quantum computing. The arrays were quite successful initially, but something always causes problems and now there's only a few operational, way out in the research facilities, where even the maintenance crews rarely go. Expensive experiments.

I couldn't help feeling worried about it. The array was housed in its protective chamber with its cooling systems—yes, multiple redundant systems—working overtime and its processing cores deep in their quantum states, executing calculations. Just calculating. Not for anything specific. The status displays showed unstable qubits, like warning fires.

The ambient light was blue-white on the metallic housing, but the error indicators made the monitoring displays flash red, showing system failures. It looked like a disaster waiting to happen.

Miguel said quietly, "Someone's been tampering with it. And somebody needs to fix this properly."

Matthew frowned. I said irritably, "Be reasonable, Miguel! Nobody outside the team has access. There must be a logical explanation."

The alarm sounded again. The array didn't move, obviously, but the temperature readings spiked. The warning, that close, was deafening, and it made me feel cold and hollow inside. The danger, the sheer technical catastrophe...

Matthew Fisher looked shaken. I said, "You'll have to stabilize this, Miguel. It's threatening the entire archive."

He worked on the emergency protocols, and things stabilized somewhat. Miguel stood looking at the monitoring displays, checking readings carefully, like a diagnostician. Then he turned to us.

"I've been maintaining this system," he said. "When we salvaged it from the university surplus and everyone thought it was too damaged to use, I rebuilt it. I know this array. I can work with it. But this time..."

He shrugged. He was large and intense and serious, and his voice carried genuine concern.

"This time," he said, "I'm not certain we can recover."

"Well for Pete's sake, do what you can. We have a contract, and we need it operational." I took Matthew's arm. "Come on, we need rest."

He leaned on my shoulder and we left. Miguel didn't acknowledge us. Matthew looked troubled.

"You were right, Sam," he mumbled. "Project's in trouble. I know it. But it's my life's work. I care about it, Sam. Understand? Like Miguel there with the array. It's old and problematic, but he maintains it. I care..."

"I know," I told him. "Stop worrying for one night."

We were far from the server room then. The racks and systems loomed high and dark around us. It was quiet. The subtle, uneasy hum all around us and our footsteps only made it quieter.

Matthew was nearly asleep on his feet. I started to guide him back. And then I noticed something on a nearby terminal—small traces of unauthorized access, barely visible in the system logs.

I called out, "Miguel! Miguel, there's been a security breach! Miguel—we need you!"

I started to return to the server room. Matthew leaned heavily on me, exhausted. The alarms burst suddenly in a deafening cascade of warnings and error messages, amplified by the metal walls, and above it all I could hear the quantum array's cooling systems screaming in overload.

I thought, "Someone's here. Someone caused this. Someone wants to destroy us!" I tried to call out again. It caught in my throat. I was sweating, and it was cold.

Matthew's stumbling steps tangled with mine. We fell. I caught him, protecting his head, and braced myself against a server rack.

The first system failure hit. It was like an electrical shock, a cascade of shutdowns spreading through the network. I shouted. The failures propagated through the connected systems.

Matthew groaned and struggled. I remember holding on and thinking, "This is it. This is the end, and I'm terrified!"

Then everything went dark.

---

Emily Gutierrez, our station medic, was checking my vital signs when I woke up. Her round face showed concern. She'd worked double shifts recently, and she looked exhausted.

"You're okay, Ms. Boyd," she said gently. "You'll be fine."

She gave me something for the headache. It helped. I asked, "Where's Matthew? How is he?"

"Dr. Fisher is fine. You protected him from injury. You're quite the hero, Ms. Boyd. Miguel got the systems shut down in time. You're a hero."

I said, "Right," and pushed myself up carefully. I managed to stand, though I felt dizzy. I made it to the small mirror in my quarters—I was in my own room—and I saw I looked exhausted but uninjured.

Matthew Fisher opened the door. He looked pale and serious, and there was a bruise on his arm. He said:

"Kim is here with her legal representative."

I found my jacket. "I'll be right there."

Emily left, still looking concerned. Matthew closed the door.

"Sam," he said, "those systems were stable when we arrived. Someone deliberately compromised them. On purpose."

I felt terrible. I said, "Obviously. Nobody saw anything, I suppose?" Matthew shook his head.

"Question is, Sam, who wants to sabotage us, and why?"

"Kim. She realizes she's made a mistake funding us."

"Fifty thousand credits," said Matthew quietly, "for some remote colony documentation work. It doesn't add up, Sam. You think we should withdraw?"

I shrugged. "You're the director. I'm only the one who manages the creditors."

"Yeah," Matthew said thoughtfully. "And I hear unemployment isn't pleasant. Okay, Sam. Let's go sign." He reached for the door and looked at me. "And—uh—Sam, I..."

I said, "Forget it. Next time, just don't trip over me, that's all!"

We had a difficult journey to Goldfield, Marvenia. The quantum array remained unstable, and Miguel, on the rare occasions he emerged from the server room, looked like he was expecting catastrophe. To make it worse, Jacob Anderson, our lead oral historian, fell ill during transit, and one of our junior archivists quit unexpectedly.

Nobody would have minded that, except she took copies of sensitive research data with her. It lasted just long enough to terrify that group of paranoid academics. Digital humanities people are peculiar that way.

Matthew and I did some quiet investigating, but it was futile. Anyone on the team might have sabotaged those systems. It didn't help to know that somebody, maybe the person working next to you, was planning to destroy everything. By the time we reached Goldfield, I was ready to resign entirely.

Matthew guided our transport to the edge of Goldfield, the first location on our itinerary. I stood beside him, looking at the settlement through the viewports. It was Marvenia, certainly. Red dust and scattered prefab structures and harsh sunlight, and a cluster of weather-beaten buildings grouped together defensively. People in environment suits were approaching for a look.

I saw Kim's sleek corporate shuttle parked at a dedicated landing pad, and our equipment transport beside it. Matthew groaned.

"A disaster, Sam. A complete disaster!"

I muttered, "What do you expect, with this underfunded project!" and exited. He followed. The team was gathering near the airlock, but they weren't enthusiastic. You develop instincts for these things. The thin Marvenia atmosphere was already infiltrating through the seals.

As we passed the corridor to the server room, I could hear the quantum array's cooling systems, struggling.

The technical crew was busy setting up equipment, working carefully in the harsh environment. The documentation team was heading for the settlement. Matthew and I stood in our environment suits, observing.

I heard a sound behind me and turned. Angela Perry, our xenoanthropology specialist, was standing in the dust with her helmet off, breathing the thin atmosphere, and her weathered face tilted back, eyes closed. She was smiling. It looked unsettling.

You find many xenoanthropology specialists in digital humanities projects, studying cultural adaptation in frontier settlements. They're colonial specialists, they're not typical academics, and they never let you forget it.

Angela opened her sharp eyes and looked at me and laughed.

"Failure," she whispered. "Failure and conflict. The settlement warns me. I can sense it in the atmosphere."

The harsh sunlight beat down on her. She shivered despite the heat, and her expression was intense.

"The frontier colonies are resistant," she whispered. "Something has been disturbed. They are resistant, and I sense failure ahead!"

She walked away, laughing, and I cursed under my breath, and my stomach was tight. Matthew said,

"Let's see if they have a cafeteria in this place."

We weren't halfway across the landing area when a man emerged from a building at the settlement's edge. We could see him clearly, because he was separated from the crowd approaching us.

He stumbled in the dust, calling out. It took him several attempts to make our names clear enough to understand.

Matthew said, "Sam—that's Jacob Anderson."

We started running. The crowd, mostly rugged colonists in work clothes, turned to see what was happening. People began to converge on the man who staggered and gasped in the thin air.

Jacob Anderson was an oral historian, collecting cultural narratives from frontier communities. He'd collaborated with us several times previously, when funding allowed, and we had a good working relationship.

I hadn't seen him for two years. I remembered him as energetic and enthusiastic, passionate about preserving oral histories. I felt sick, looking at him now.

Matthew tried to help him. Anderson was shaking, trembling like someone in shock. Some colonist stepped forward and offered him water from a canteen.

I was focused on Anderson then, and I didn't pay attention to the colonist. I only glimpsed the person's face briefly. I didn't realize until later that they looked familiar.

We got Anderson inside the building. It turned out to be a small community center, with a few private meeting rooms at the back. We got him into one and closed the door on numerous curious faces. Anderson drank from the canteen. The person who gave it to him had disappeared.

Matthew said gently, "Okay, Jacob. Relax. What happened?"

Anderson tried to compose himself. He hadn't slept. The energetic lines of his face had gone slack and his eyes were red-rimmed. He was covered with dust, and his hands shook.

He said hoarsely, "I found it. I said I would, and I did. I found it and documented it."

He set down the canteen clumsily. "Help me," he said simply. "I'm frightened." His voice broke.

"I have it secured. They want to locate it, but I won't tell them. It needs to be returned. Returned to its source. I tried to do it myself, but they prevented me, and I was afraid they'd find it..."

He reached suddenly and gripped the edge of the table. "I don't know how they discovered it, but they did. I have to return it. I have to..."

Matthew looked at me. Anderson was pale and sweating. I felt frightened, suddenly. I said, "Return what where?"

Matthew stood. "I'll get the medic," he said. "Stay with him." Anderson grabbed his wrist. Anderson's fingers were white and the veins in his hands stood out prominently.

"Don't leave me. Need to tell you—where it is. Need to return it. Promise you'll return it." He gasped, struggling for breath.

"Of course," said Matthew. "Of course we'll return it. What is it?"

Anderson's face was terrible. I felt nauseated, watching him fight for air. I wanted to get Emily anyway, but somehow I knew it was too late. Anderson whispered,

"Cultural artifact. Irreplaceable. Original. You don't understand...! Return it."

"Where is it, Jacob?"

I reached past Matthew suddenly and opened the door. Kim was standing there. Kim, leaning forward, clearly listening. Anderson made a harsh choking sound and collapsed across the table.

Kim's expression didn't change. She didn't move while Matthew checked Anderson's pulse. Matthew didn't need to speak. We knew.

"Heart attack?" said Kim finally.

"Yes," said Matthew. He looked as shaken as I felt. "Poor Jacob."

I looked at the canteen on the table. I looked at Kim with her unreadable professional face. I moved past Matthew and firmly guided Kim into a chair.

"Keep her here until I return," I said.

Matthew stared at me. Kim started to object. "Be quiet," I told her. "We have a contract." I left the room and walked to the main area.

I began to notice something then. There were quite a few people in the center. At first glance they looked appropriate—a weathered, capable group of colonists in practical clothing.

Then I looked more carefully. They were dressed appropriately enough. But they moved wrong for frontier colonists, on Marvenia or anywhere else.

The place was unnaturally quiet. The center administrator was a heavy-set woman with calculating eyes and short grey hair. She looked nervous.

I approached the counter. "Water," I said. She provided it, reluctantly, from a dispenser. I reached for it, casually.

"That man we brought in," I said. "He seems very distressed. Dehydrated. What's he been doing out here?"

"Research," said a voice beside me. "As if you didn't know."

I turned. The person who had given Anderson the canteen was standing next to me. And I recognized them, then.
question: Where was the digital archive installed for one night?

synthetic_story:
THE ARCHITECT IN HIS SIMULATION
By ANONYMOUS

Martin Watkins stood at the edge of the digital construct, watching the sunset algorithms paint the sky in shades of amber and rose. The simulation was flawless—every photon traced, every atmospheric particle accounted for. It was his masterwork, a virtual recreation of Horizonville, Estoria, the coastal city where he'd grown up before the Great Migration had scattered humanity across the solar system.

He was here on business, of course. Nicole Leonard had disappeared into someone's mind-simulation three weeks ago, and the Cognitive Security Bureau had hired him to extract her. In the century since Dr. Kenji Yamamoto had discovered that human consciousness could be digitally projected into constructed virtual environments—what the media production companies now called "mindscapes"—crime had evolved in unexpected ways. Criminals no longer just hid in physical locations. They hid in the infinite labyrinths of digital consciousness.

Nicole Leonard was wanted for corporate espionage. She had stolen experimental design specifications from Helios Corporation's particle physics division—blueprints for a fusion reactor that could power an entire colony ship. The theft had international diplomacy implications; three governments were involved in the joint venture. When she'd vanished from her apartment in Evergreen, Belvoria, leaving behind only her neural interface headset still warm from use, the Bureau had known immediately where she'd gone.

The question was: whose mindscape?

Martin had spent two weeks analyzing the interface logs, tracing the quantum entanglement signatures, following the breadcrumb trail of neural patterns. The answer had shocked him. Nicole Leonard hadn't hidden in her own mindscape, nor in that of an accomplice. She had hidden in Martin's.

He still didn't understand how. His childhood home in Horizonville was a deeply personal memory, one he'd never shared publicly. Yet somehow she had learned enough about it to use it as an entry point into his digital consciousness. The implications troubled him on a professional ethics level—if criminals could access a pursuer's mindscape without permission, the entire foundation of cognitive security was compromised.

Now he was here, in his own mind, hunting her.

The Horizonville construct was eerily accurate. Every storefront on Main Street matched his memories—the bakery where his mother had bought bread, the bookshop where he'd discovered his love of art history, the small office building where his father had worked as an accountant. The people were here too, or rather, their ghost-images: constructs of memory that moved through their routines with no awareness of Martin's presence. They were echoes, nothing more.

Nicole's trail was easy to follow. She'd left digital artifacts everywhere—modified textures, altered lighting parameters, fragments of code that didn't belong. She was either careless or didn't understand the nature of mindscapes. Most likely the latter. Cognitive security was a specialized field, and civilians rarely grasped its complexities.

Martin followed her trail down Harbor Street toward the waterfront. The simulation grew more detailed as he walked, responding to his attention. He could smell the salt air, hear the cry of gulls, feel the ocean breeze on his skin. It was all artificial, of course—electrical signals interpreted by his brain—but the illusion was perfect.

He was so focused on the trail that he almost didn't notice the three figures following him.

When he finally turned around, his breath caught in his throat. Three people stood on the street behind him, watching him with expressions of unmistakable hostility. He recognized them instantly, though he couldn't understand why they were here.

The first was Professor Violet Hamilton, his undergraduate ethics instructor. The second was Henry Carter, the security officer who had supervised the dormitories at the Cognitive Sciences Institute. The third was Grace Rogers, the spokesperson from the public service announcements about social justice and human rights that had played endlessly during his childhood.

But these weren't memory-ghosts. Memory-ghosts had no awareness, no volition. These three were looking directly at him, and their eyes burned with anger.

"Professor Hamilton?" Martin said uncertainly. "What are you—"

"You know why we're here, Martin Watkins," Professor Hamilton said, her voice cold. "You know what you've done."

"Hypocrite," Henry Carter spat. "You speak of professional ethics while violating every principle you claim to uphold."

Grace Rogers pointed an accusing finger at him. "You preach about human rights and social justice, but your actions tell a different story."

Martin took a step back, his mind racing. This was impossible. He hadn't created these constructs—at least, not consciously. In mindscape theory, such autonomous entities could only emerge from deep psychological conflicts, unresolved guilt, suppressed trauma. But he had no such conflicts. He was well-adjusted, successful, confident in his choices.

Wasn't he?

"I don't understand," he said aloud. "What are you talking about?"

The three figures moved closer, their faces twisted with contempt. "You ask us that?" Professor Hamilton said. "After what you did to her?"

"After how you abandoned her?" Henry Carter added.

"After you hid behind your rationalizations and your excuses?" Grace Rogers finished.

Their voices began to blend together, overlapping, becoming a single accusatory chorus. Martin turned and ran.

---

He found himself in a different part of the simulation now—a recreation of the Cognitive Sciences Institute campus where he'd done his graduate work. The buildings were rendered in perfect detail, from the chrome-and-glass laboratory complex to the ivy-covered administration hall. Students moved across the quad, their faces blurred because Martin couldn't remember them clearly enough to render them properly.

Nicole's trail led across the campus toward the student union. Martin followed it, his mind still reeling from the encounter with the three hostile constructs. What had they meant? What had he done? And who was "her"?

The trail ended at a bench beneath a massive oak tree. Martin stopped, his heart sinking as he recognized the location. This was where he'd sat with Alex Frank five years ago, the day after her graduation ceremony.

The memory materialized around him, responding to his recognition. There was Alex, twenty-two years old, wearing her graduation dress—a simple blue affair that matched her eyes. Her dark hair was pulled back in a ponytail, and she wore the silver necklace he'd given her as a graduation present.

And there was Martin himself, or rather, his past-self—a construct of memory with no awareness of Martin's current presence. Past-Martin looked older than Martin remembered being, more careworn, with premature gray in his hair.

"Yes, at nine o'clock," Past-Alex was saying. "And I really want you to come."

Past-Martin shook his head. "Graduation parties aren't for mentors. You know that. That young man you were talking with earlier—Hugo Welch—he should take you. He'd jump at the chance."

"I'll thank you not to treat me like a child," Past-Alex said, her voice tight. "You're only thirty-five. That's not ancient."

"I'm your academic advisor," Past-Martin said. "There are professional ethics to consider. That young man—"

"What right does Hugo have to take me?" Past-Alex interrupted, her cheeks flushing. "Did he spend three years guiding my research? Did he help me get the fellowship to the Mars Institute? Did he—" She broke off, looking away.

"Please," Past-Martin said, desperation creeping into his voice. "You're making this harder than it needs to be. I helped you because it was my job, because you had talent. There was nothing more to it than that."

"Nothing more?" Past-Alex's voice was very quiet. "Is that really what you think?"

Past-Martin stood up from the bench. "You're leaving for Mars tomorrow. We won't see each other for years. It's better this way."

"You could visit," Past-Alex said. "The new ships only take two weeks."

"I won't come—you know I won't. I can't."

Past-Alex stood up too, her hands clenched at her sides. "Why? Because you're afraid? Because you can't admit to yourself what you feel?"

"I don't feel anything," Past-Martin said, but his voice cracked. "You're my student. That's all."

"I was your student," Past-Alex said. "I'm not anymore. But you can't see that, can you? You're so wrapped up in your rules and your professional ethics that you can't see what's right in front of you." She took a breath. "Fine. I'll say goodbye now, then."

"Alex, wait—"

But she was already walking away, her shoulders straight, her head high. Past-Martin watched her go, his face a mask of pain and regret.

Martin Present watched too, and felt the same pain, the same regret, magnified by five years of hindsight. He'd never seen Alex again. She'd gone to Mars, thrown herself into her work, become one of the leading researchers in theoretical modeling of consciousness transfer. He'd followed her career from a distance, never reaching out, never explaining, never apologizing.

And now these constructs—Professor Hamilton, Henry Carter, Grace Rogers—were manifestations of his guilt. They were right. He was a hypocrite. He'd hidden behind professional ethics to avoid confronting his own feelings, and in doing so, he'd hurt someone who cared about him.

"Touching, isn't it?"

Martin spun around. A woman stood behind him—thirtyish, with sharp features and calculating eyes. She wore a gray jumpsuit with the Helios Corporation logo on the shoulder.

Nicole Leonard.

"How long have you been watching?" Martin demanded.

"Long enough," Nicole said. She gestured at the memory-construct, where Past-Alex was disappearing into the distance. "That's Alex Frank, isn't it? The famous consciousness researcher. I read her papers while preparing for this job. Brilliant work. She's done more to advance theoretical modeling than anyone in the last decade." Nicole smiled. "I wonder what she'd think if she knew you were still carrying this around in your head."

"This is my private mindscape," Martin said coldly. "You're trespassing."

"True," Nicole agreed. "But you'll never catch me. I've already found your most recent entry point. One step beyond it, and I'm back in the real world. You'll be stuck here, dealing with your guilt constructs."

"How did you find my entry point? How did you even know about Horizonville?"

Nicole's smile widened. "You're not the only one who can do research, Mr. Watkins. I'm a professional thief. I steal information for a living. Did you really think your childhood memories were secret? I accessed your old school records, your family's social media archives, your father's tax filings. I built a profile of your early life detailed enough to construct an entry point. It took me three weeks, but I did it."

Martin felt a chill. If Nicole could do it, others could too. The implications for cognitive security were staggering. "That's a violation of human rights," he said. "Unauthorized access to someone's mindscape—"

"Is perfectly legal if you use only public information," Nicole finished. "I checked with my lawyers. The law hasn't caught up with the technology yet. Welcome to the cutting edge, Mr. Watkins."

She turned to leave, but Martin called after her. "Wait. Why show yourself? Why not just slip away?"

Nicole glanced back. "Because I wanted you to know. I wanted you to understand that your profession is obsolete. The old rules don't apply anymore. Cultural evolution has outpaced the legal framework. In a few years, mindscapes will be as easy to hack as computer networks used to be. You and your Cognitive Security Bureau are dinosaurs."

She walked away, her figure growing fainter as she moved toward the edge of the construct. Martin started to follow, but the three hostile constructs materialized in front of him, blocking his path.

"Let me through," Martin said.

"No," Professor Hamilton said. "Not until you face the truth."

"What truth?" Martin demanded. "That I made a mistake five years ago? I know that. I've always known that."

"Then why haven't you done anything about it?" Henry Carter asked.

"Because it's too late," Martin said. "Because Alex has moved on, built a life on Mars. Because I can't undo the past."

"You can't undo it," Grace Rogers said, "but you can acknowledge it. You can stop hiding from it."

The three constructs moved closer, their faces softening slightly. "We're not your enemies, Martin," Professor Hamilton said gently. "We're parts of you. We're the voice of your conscience, trying to make you listen."

Martin stared at them, understanding dawning. These weren't hostile entities at all. They were his own mind's way of forcing him to confront what he'd been avoiding. The anger in their faces was his anger at himself. The accusations in their voices were his own self-recrimination.

"What do I do?" he asked quietly.

"You know what to do," Henry Carter said.

Martin closed his eyes. When he opened them again, the three constructs had vanished. He was alone on the campus, with only the memory-ghosts moving through their endless routines.

He pulled up his interface menu—a translucent display that floated in his field of vision—and composed a message to Alex Frank. It was short, honest, and long overdue. He apologized for his cowardice, explained his feelings, and asked if she'd be willing to talk when he returned to the real world. He didn't expect forgiveness. He just needed her to know.

He sent the message, then turned his attention back to Nicole Leonard. She'd said she'd found his most recent entry point, but she was wrong. His most recent entry point wasn't in Horizonville or on the Institute campus. It was here, in this exact moment—the moment when he'd finally stopped running from his guilt and started dealing with it.

This was his most recent memory, freshly created. And Nicole Leonard had no way of knowing it existed.

Martin smiled grimly and set off in pursuit. The trail was easy to follow now. Nicole had grown careless, confident in her escape. She'd left obvious markers—modified code, altered textures, digital footprints that glowed like beacons in Martin's enhanced vision.

He found her at the edge of the Horizonville waterfront, standing before a shimmering portal that led back to the real world. She was reaching for it when Martin appeared behind her.

"Going somewhere?" he asked.

Nicole spun around, her eyes wide with shock. "But—how? I found your entry point!"

"You found an old entry point," Martin corrected. "I created a new one. That's the thing about mindscapes, Ms. Leonard. They're constantly evolving, responding to new experiences, new memories. You can't hack them with static information. You need to understand the person, not just their history."

Nicole lunged for the portal, but Martin was faster. He grabbed her arm, and the construct responded to his will, solidifying the connection. In the real world, their neural interfaces would be triggering the extraction protocol, pulling them both back to consciousness.

The simulation began to dissolve around them, the carefully rendered buildings and streets breaking apart into streams of data. The last thing Martin saw before the transition completed was the bench where he'd sat with Alex, still solid and clear amidst the dissolving chaos.

Some memories, he realized, were worth preserving. And some mistakes were worth correcting.

---

Martin woke in his extraction chair, his neural interface humming as it disconnected from his consciousness. Across the room, in a similar chair, Nicole Leonard was stirring, her wrists already secured by the automated restraints.

Two Bureau agents were waiting. They took Nicole into custody, reading her rights as they led her away. The stolen designs had been recovered from her personal storage—she'd been too confident to delete them.

Martin filed his report, collected his fee, and went home to his apartment in Foxwood Province. It was late evening, the city lights glittering through his window like artificial stars.

His message interface was blinking. One new message, received twenty minutes ago.

It was from Alex Frank.

Martin's hand trembled slightly as he opened it. The message was brief: "I'm glad you finally reached out. I'll be on Earth next month for a scientific collaboration conference in Horizonville Town. We should talk. —A"

Martin read the message three times, then set his interface aside and looked out at the city. The future was uncertain, full of possibilities both hopeful and frightening. But for the first time in five years, he wasn't running from it.

He was a god in his own mindscape, capable of creating entire worlds from memory and imagination. But in the real world, he was just a man—flawed, fallible, and finally ready to admit it.

And perhaps, he thought, that was enough.
question: Where did Martin Watkins grow up before the Great Migration?

synthetic_story:
QUANTUM THREADS
By Marina Roberts

From Copperfield to Harborview Village, and all the way between, it was a hell of a world for engineers... and Apprentice Fabricator Mark Leonard particularly.

The comm system blared fit to shake Mark back to Copperfield. "Printer Bay Four!"

"On my way, sir!"

At the first flash of red on the bank of monitors, Apprentice Fabricator Mark Leonard had grabbed his safety goggles; he was already throwing open the lock to the printer bay. The hot, humming vibration whipped around him and near crushed his breath away. Power! Quantum entanglement trapped here in these massive 3D printers, ready to destroy its captors given one chance! Swiftly Mark unlocked the controls and reset them. The humming vibration changed tone.

Old Ahmed's voice crackled now through the headset's ear contact. "Well, Mr. Leonard?"

"Quantum alignment two points low, sir."

Mark wondered had Ahmed passed out, was so long before the old Fabrication Chief demanded hoarsely, "Didn't you lock them controls before production start?"

"If every control hadn't been locked in correct setting," Mark answered from his own angry bewilderment, "the error would have registered before production start—wouldn't it, sir?"

"So a control reset itself during operation, hey?"

"I don't know yet, sir."

"Well, Mr. Leonard, you better know before we ship to Harborview Village!"

The icy knot in Mark's stomach jerked tighter. A dozen printer bays in this facility; why did something crazy have to happen to Mark's? In a hundred years, so the instructors—brisk women all—had told Mark in pre-employment training, no control had ever been known to slip. But one had moved here. Not enough to cause serious trouble this far from deadline. On final production, though, with one printer below peak, the uneven output could throw the whole order, crash the schedule, the whole lovely contract and all involved gone in a churning mess.

Sweat pouring off him, Mark prowled around his printer. Design of the thing had been bossed by women of course; what in Fendria wasn't any more? Anyway, nobody could get to a printer bay except through its control room. Anyone entered or left there, a bell clanged, lights flashed and a meter registered beside the Fabricator's station and on the Fabrication Chief's console up in the management suite full of beautifully efficient officers. Ever since Copperfield production start Mark had been in Four's control room. Nobody had passed through. Mark knew it. Ahmed knew it. By now the Director herself, Elizabeth Campbell, had probably inquired what was in charge of Printer Bay Four.

Well, ma'am, Mark searched every cranny where even a data science algorithm could have hidden. His first major contract, and Mark saw himself washed out, busted to sweeper on the production floors of some God-forsaken subsidiary. He staggered back into his control room. And his brain was suddenly taken apart and slapped together again. Felt that way.

She was sitting at his workstation. No algorithm. No Director either. Oh, she was a female human, though, this creature at which Mark stood gaping. Yes, ma'am!

"I was in your printer bay." Her voice matched the rest of her, a blend of loveliness unlike anything outside a guy's most secret dreams. "I couldn't stand the heat any longer and I couldn't open that big door. So I moved one of your controls a tiny bit. All the noise in there, naturally you couldn't hear me walk out while your back was turned resetting the control."

Mark suddenly felt like turning her over his knee and whaling her until she couldn't sit for a year. This, mind you, he felt in an age where no Fendrian guy for a thousand years had dared raise so much as a breath against woman's supremacy in all matters. That male character trait, however, did not seem to be the overpowering reason why Mark, instead of laying violent hands upon this one's person, heard himself saying in sympathetic outrage, "A shame you had to go to all that bother to get in here!"

"You're so kind. But I'm afraid I became rather sticky and uncomfortable in there."

"They ought to cool the air in there with perfume! I'll drop a suggestion in the Director's box first chance I get."

"You're so thoughtful. And do you have cleaning facilities?"

"That door right there. Oh, let me open it for you!"

"You're so sweet." Her big dark eyes glowed with such pure innocence that Mark could have torn down the universe and rebuilt it just for her.

Yes, ma'am, Mark was floating on a pink cloud with heavenly music in his head. Never felt so fine before. Except on the Redwood layover when he'd been roped into a venture capital pitch session with a bunch of Redwood entrepreneurs who had premium whiskey to cheer one's parting with one's money.

A bell suddenly clanged fit to wake the dead while the overhead lights flashed wildly. Only the control room door. Only Ahmed here now. Old buzzard had a drooped nose like a pick, chin like a shovel.

When he talked he was like digging a hole in front of himself. "Well, what about that control?"

"What control?"

"Your quantum alignment that got itself two points low!"

"Oh, that little thing."

Ahmed said something through his teeth, then studied Mark sharply. "Hey, you been drinking that Redwood whiskey again? Lemme smell your breath! Bah. Loaded yourself full of coffee again probably. All right, stand aside whilst I check your printer."

"Charmed to, Fabrication Chief Ahmed, sir," Mark said while bowing gracefully.

"Higher than a kite again," Ahmed muttered, then snapped back over his shoulder, "Use your cleaner!"

Mark stood considering his cleaner door. Somehow he doubted that Fabrication Chief Ahmed's mood, or Director Elizabeth Campbell's, would be improved by knowledge of she who was in Mark's cleaner now. Not that the dear stowaway was less than charming. Quite the contrary. Oh, very quite!

"You rockhead!" Only Ahmed back from the printer bay. "Didn't I tell you to clean yourself up? Director's taking a Lethoria executive on tour of the facility. Director catches you like you been wrestling machines she'll peel both our hides off. Not to mention what she'll do anyway about your quantum control!"

"Fabrication Chief Ahmed, sir," Mark responded courteously, "I have been thinking."

"With what? Never mind, just keep on trying whilst I clean up for myself here." Wherewith Ahmed reached hand for Mark's cleaner door.

"Lethoria women," Mark said dreamily, "don't boss anything, do they?"

Ahmed yelped like he'd been bit in the pants by a big industrial robot. "Leonard! You trying to get both of us condemned to a Brookhaven satellite?" Ahmed also shot a wild look to the intercom switch. It was in OFF position; the management suite full of fancy executives could not have overheard from here. Nevertheless Ahmed's eyes rolled like the devil was behind him with the pitchfork ready. "Leonard, open your big ears whilst for your own good and mine I speak of certain matters.

"Thousand years ago, it was, the first trade mission reached Lethoria. Guys got one look at them women. Had to bring some home or bust. So then everybody in Fendria got a look, mostly by video only of course. That did it. Every guy in Fendria began blowing his fuse over them women. Give up the shirt off his back, last buck in the bank, his own Fendrian woman or family—everything.

"Well, that's when Fendrian women took over like armies of wild cats with knots in their tails. Before the guys who'd brought the Lethoria women to Fendria could say anything they was taken apart too small to pick up with a blotter. Fendrian women wound up by flying the Lethoria ones back where they come from and serving notice if one ever set foot in Fendria again there wouldn't be enough left of Lethoria to find with an electron microscope.

"Lethoria men rared up and served notice that if Fendria ever got any funny notions, right away there wouldn't be enough Fendria left to hide in an atom's eyebrow. Touchy as hornets on a hot griddle, them Lethoria guys. Crazier than bed bugs about competition. Could smell venture capital a million miles away too. Finagled around until they finally cooked up a deal.

"No Lethoria women allowed within fifty miles of their trade zone. Fendrian guys stay inside the high-security perimeter. Any woman caught trying to leave Lethoria thrown to the wolves for supper. Same for any Fendrian guy caught around a Lethoria woman. In return, Fendria could buy practically everything at bargain basement prices through sustainable business practices and globalization treaties."

"Oh, I was shown the history files in pre-employment," Mark said, still dreamily. "But not a peek of any Lethoria woman."

"Pray heaven you'll never lay eyes on one nor have one get within ten foot of you! Even though you'd know she'd be your damnation wouldn't make a whit difference—you'd still act sappier than thirty-seven angels flying on whiskey." Ahmed suddenly stared at Mark. "Holy hollering saints!"

"Now, now, Fabrication Chief Ahmed, sir," Mark responded with an airy laugh. "No Fendrian guy for a hundred twenty-five years been near one and lived to tell it, has he?"

"So the whispers run," Ahmed murmured with a queer flame dancing into his eyes. "So the old whispers still run."

"Never a name, though. Never how it was done." Mark snorted. "Probably just a goofy tale set loose by some old factory worker."

"Oh?" Ahmed bristled up like a bad name had been bandied about. "Seen them shipping containers Lethoria executives have, ain't you? Some big enough to stuff a person in. Notice how nobody ever dares question an executive's containers, even through customs? Just run 'em through the big scanner that tells whether there's any dangerous materials inside. Well, our boy got himself one of them containers, stuffed himself inside and joined an executive's pile of 'em.

"Didn't pull it whilst in the Lethoria zone during a business trip either, when a crew check would of turned him up missing. Pulled it on vacation. Started on the Fendrian end. Made himself a pair of facial prosthetics to paste on his cheeks of course. Used computational linguistics algorithms to mimic the accent. Wasn't like the real thing, but good enough to flimflam Lethoria guys."

With suddenly enlivened interest Mark looked at Ahmed. "Hey, how come you know so much?"

"Hah? What?" Ahmed blinked like waking from a trance; even groaned to himself, something that sounded like, "Blabbering like I'd had a nip myself—or one of them beauties was radiating nearby." Then Ahmed glared fit to drill holes in Mark's head. "Look! I was a full Fabricator before you was born. Been working the facilities hundred twenty-five years now. Had more chances to hear more—just hear more, you hear! Only tried to clear your mind about Lethoria women so you could put your brain on your control mess. So now put it! If you ain't high on whiskey and ain't been made nuts by a Lethoria woman, what answer do we feed the Director?"

"Search me," Apprentice Fabricator Mark Leonard responded cheerfully.

"Of all the loony apprentices I ever had to answer the Director for! Awp, lemme out where I can think of something to save me own neck at least!"

Was all Mark could do to keep from rolling on the floor with glee. Old Ahmed had been flimflammed for fair! The dear little stowaway was saved! And Mark would now think of grand ways to save her lovely neck and his own forever.

Mark's cleaner door, however, opened abruptly. Mark had not opened it. Mark, however, suffered a cruel stab of dismay. Surely his dear stowaway had been listening through the door. Why didn't she have brains enough to stay hid until Ahmed was gone!

At sight of her, of course, Ahmed's eyes near popped from his old head. "Zara!"

"Oh, I'm Susan," she assured Ahmed sweetly. "But Grandmamma's name is Zara and people say I'm just like she was a hundred and twenty-five years ago."

"Hah? What?" Ahmed blinked like his brain had been taken apart and was being slapped together again. "Leonard! Awp, you angel-faced pirate, couldn't you hide her somewheres better than that? Shut up, you don't have to explain to me, but God help the whole corporation if we don't flimflam the Director!" With which ominous remark, rendered in a zesty devil-may-care manner, however, Ahmed threw himself into Mark's cleaner.

Mark stood looking thoughtfully at lovely, womanly, exquisite Susan. Just like that, Mark felt as sparkling of mind as a quantum computer. "My locker!" he crowed with inspiration and yanked open the doors under his workstation. He glimpsed a black bag, also the uniform of a maintenance worker.

"I threw them in there before you came on duty before production start," Susan explained. "I knew the printer bay would be warm."

Susan—with her shape—passing as a maintenance worker hustling equipment through this facility. Mark chortled as he tucked her under his workstation. "Now don't you worry about another thing!"

"Oh, I'm not," she assured him happily. "Everything is going just the way Grandmamma knew it would!"

Mark's cleaner opened and Ahmed, glowing like a young buck, bounced to the workstation. "Well, did you hide her good this time? No, don't tell me! I want to be surprised if the Director ever finds her."

"If what director finds whom?" a voice like thin ice crackling wanted to know.

The control room's door had opened. Wouldn't think the Director was a day over seventy-five, let alone near two hundred. Cut of her uniform probably lent a helping hand or three to the young snap of her figure. Frosty blue of fancy hair-do, she was, though, and icy of eye as she looked at Mark and Ahmed still standing by the workstation.

Her voice was an iceberg exploding. "At attention!"

Never in his right mind would any worker dare fail to come stiffly erect the instant the Director appeared. Behind her stood a colorfully dressed specimen of Lethoria man. Handsome as the devil himself. Fit to snap lesser men in two with his highly manicured hands. Designer facial hair trailed from his cheeks and kept twitching lazily as he sneered at the spectacle of two men meekly acknowledging the superiority of a woman.

She was fit to put frost on a quantum printer. "Mr. Ahmed, I asked you a question, did I not?"

"Believe you did, ma'am," Ahmed responded cheerfully. "And the answer is, ma'am, that Apprentice Fabricator Leonard and me was discussing—ah—partnerships, ma'am. Mr. Apprentice Fabricator Leonard here is considering it, ma'am."

Wasn't too bad a fib. The more Mark thought of Susan, the more ideas he got of doing things he'd never dreamt of before in his life. Yes, ma'am!

"Wasting your time talking nonsense!" Director's look was fit to freeze Mark's brain, then she gave Ahmed the look. "I sent you down here to find the answer to that quantum control slippage!"

"Oh, you'll have the best answer you ever heard of before long, ma'am!" Ahmed assured her heartily. "The subject of nonsense—I mean, partnerships—merely chanced to arise whilst we was scientifically analyzing the control phenomenon, ma'am. Naturally I offered this innocent young Fabricator the benefit of me long years of experience. Why," Ahmed said with a jaunty laugh, "women mean nothing to me. Indeed 'twouldn't bother me none if there wasn't one of the things left in the world! Present company excepted, of course," Ahmed hastened to say with a courtly bow.

"Stay at attention!" Director sniffed the air near Ahmed's face, then in Mark's vicinity. "Smothered it with coffee probably," she muttered through her teeth, "if it is that whiskey." Something horrible as a plague flickered in her eyes, then the old ice was there again. "Apprentice Fabricator, don't you know what your cleaner is for? Then use it! Mr. Ahmed, remain at attention while I inspect this printer!" She tendered a cool glance at the Lethoria executive. "Care to join me, Your Excellency?"

"May as well." His Excellency glanced at Mark and Ahmed much as he might at a couple of worms. Could bet your last old sock no female ever told any Lethoria man what to do.

The cleaner units were equipped so no Fabricator need be more than two steps from his responsibility. To keep the Director from possibly blowing her gaskets completely, Mark simply stepped in, shut the door, flipped a switch and tingled as he was electronically cleansed of person and clothes. By time he finished, the Director and His Excellency were already coming out of the printer bay, dripping with sweat.

Director opened the cleaner with her customary commanding air. "You first, Your Excellency."

"My dear Director," His Excellency replied like a smoothly drawn dagger, "always the lesser gender enjoys precedence."

No Fendrian woman ever admitted any guy was even equal to any female. Director, a prime symbol of her gender's superiority, whipped a razor edge onto her own words. "Facilities of the Director's quarters are more satisfactory."

"No more so than those of the Executive Suite."

Seeming to grind her teeth, the Director turned abruptly to leave Mark's control room. Was all Mark could do to keep from busting out laughing for joy.

Director had been flimflammed for fair! Dear Susan was saved! And betwixt Mark's grand brain and Ahmed's great experience she'd be happy forever.

A fine loud "thump," however, was now heard. Director whirled back and yanked open the doors under Mark's workstation.

"Of all the sappy hiding places!" Ahmed yelped, in surprise of course.

"Susan?" His Excellency bellowed as if stung by one of the mechanical hornets of his native region. "Susan!"

"Susan," Mark pleaded in loving anguish, "why do you have to keep coming out of hiding just when nobody's going to find you?"

Her eyes merely became deep pools in which Mark would have gladly drowned himself if he could.

"There are penalties," the Director said with the deadly coldness of outer space, "for Fendrian men found in a Lethoria woman's company, and for her leaving her region."

"Shut up!" His Excellency's facial hair was standing straight out sideways. "I'll handle this!"

"May I remind His Excellency," the Director snapped, "that I represent Fendria and her dominion of trade gained by right of original treaties!"

"May I remind the Director," His Excellency declared fit to be heard back to his region, "that I am the Personal Representative of the Chairman of Lethoria and this thing can mean economic war!"

"Yes! Economic war in which businesses will actually fail!" As His Excellency paled at that grisly remark, the Director spoke through her teeth at Mark, Ahmed and Susan. "All right, come along!"

Mark joined the death march gladly. He felt the way Ahmed looked: ready to wrap his arms around Susan's brave loveliness and protect it to his last breath of life.

Director led the way to her office. Jabbed some buttons on her desk. Panels on opposite walls lit up.

"Chairwomen of Fendria and Lethoria, please," the Director stated evenly. "Interregional emergency."

Highly groomed assistants appeared on the panels and were impersonally pleasant.

"Madame Chairwoman's office. She is in a Board meeting."

"Mr. Chairman's office. He is in personal command of our glorious competitive efforts."

Director sighed through her teeth. "Lethoria woman in this facility. Stowaway. Rattle that around your offices."

The assistants' faces went slack with shock, then were replaced by a blizzard of scrambled faces and torrents of incoherent voices.

Finally on the Fendrian panel appeared the famous classic features. "The facts, if you please, Director Campbell."
