The Lethoria panel finally held steady on universally notorious features, that were as fierce as an eagle's, in a fancy business suit. "Susan! My own granddaughter? Impossible! Roman," Mr. Chairman roared at his Excellency, "what's this nonsense?"

"Some loud creature is interfering," Madame Chairwoman snapped with annoyance.

"Blasted fools still have the circuits crossed," Mr. Chairman swore. "Some silly female cackling now!"

The parties in the panels saw each other now. Each one's left hand on a desk moved toward a big red button marked, SANCTIONS.

"So," Mr. Chairman said evenly. "Another violation by your Fendrian men."

"By your granddaughter, at least," Madame Chairwoman replied coolly.

"An innocent child," Mr. Chairman snapped, "obviously kidnapped by those two idiotic Fendrian men there!"

"Oh, no, Grandpapa," Susan said swiftly; "I stole away all by myself, and Mr. Leonard and Ahmed have been very helpful."

"Impossible!" Grandpapa Chairman's facial hair stood near straight up as he roared, "You couldn't have stolen away by yourself! Susan, tell the truth!"

"Very well. Grandmamma told me how."

"Obviously Susan's poor little brain has been drugged," His Excellency Roman declared. "Grandmamma Zara wouldn't know the first thing about such things!"

"Impossible!" Grandpapa Chairman agreed. "I've been married to her for a hundred and twenty-four and a half years and she's the finest scatter-brain I ever knew!"

"She learned," Susan stated emphatically, "a hundred and twenty-five years ago."

"Hundred twenty-five," Grandpapa Chairman growled like a boiling volcano. "The year some Fendrian man.... Never did catch the devil.... Zara? Impossible!"

Madame Chairwoman's shapely finger now rested full on the button that could launch the waves of economic sanctions that had been pre-prepared for a thousand years. "I'm afraid your Representative is unwelcome now," Madame Chairwoman stated coolly. "Your granddaughter's actions have every mark of an invasion tactic by your government."

"What do you mean, her actions?" Grandpapa Chairman's finger now lay poised on the button that had been waiting a thousand years to blow Fendria's economy out of existence. "My grandchild was kidnapped by men under your official command! Weren't you, Susan dear?"

"No. One of us stowing away was the only way we Lethoria women could bring our cause to the attention of Fendria's Chairwoman. If Fendria will only stop buying from Lethoria, you won't have any money to squander on your competitions any longer no matter what happens to we revolutionaries!"

"Revolutionaries? Such claptrap! And what's wrong with my competitions? People have to have something to keep their minds occupied! Nobody around here gets hurt. Oh, maybe a few bruised egos here and there. But nobody in Lethoria suffers from the things any more."

"But Lethoria men are so excited all the time about competing they haven't time for us women. That's why we always radiated such a fatal attraction for Fendrian men. We want to be loved! We want our own men home doing useful work!"

"Well, they do come home and do useful work! Couple weeks every ten months. Proven to be a highly efficient arrangement based on game theory and political economy."

"More boys to run off to your old competitions and more girls to stay home and be lonely!"

"Now you just listen to me, Susan!" Grandpapa Chairman was all Lethoria manhood laying down the law. "That's the way things have been in Lethoria for ten thousand years and all the women in the universe can't change it!"

"I have been in constant contact with my Board during these conversations," Madame Chairwoman said crisply. "Fendria is terminating all trade agreements with Lethoria as of this instant."

"What?" Grandpapa's facial hair near pulled his cheeks off. "It's not legal! You can't get away with this!"

"Take your finger off that trigger, dear!" a heavenly voice similar to Susan's advised from the Lethoria panel.

Whereupon Grandpapa glared to one side. "Zara! What are you doing here? I am deciding matters of the gravest interregional nature!"

"Were." Features more beautifully mature than Susan's crowded onto the panel too. "From now on I'm doing the deciding."

"Nonsense! You're only my wife!"

"And new Chairwoman of Lethoria, elected by unanimous vote of all women."

"Impossible! The men run Lethoria! Nobody's turning this region into another Fendria where a man can't even sneeze unless some woman says so!"

"Take him away, ladies," Zara ordered coolly, whereupon her spouse was yanked from view.

His bellows, however, could be heard yet. "Unhand me, you fool creatures! Security! Security!"

"Save your breath," Zara advised him. "And while you're in detention, enjoy this latest batch of surrender documents. We women are in control everywhere now through careful political movements and cultural preservation."

"Roman," Susan was saying firmly to His Excellency, "you have beat around the bush with me long enough. Now say it!"

Roman—the mighty, the lordly, who had sneered at the sight of mere Fendrian men kowtowing to a mere woman—swelled up fit to blow his gaskets, then all the gas went out of him. His facial hair, however, still had enough zip left to flutter like butterflies. "Yes, Susan dear. I love only you. Please marry me at your earliest convenience."

"Well, Grandmamma," Susan said with a highly self-satisfied air, "it works. And just like you said, Fendrian men meant nothing once I knew we Lethoria women had our own men in our power."

"Those workers there," Grandmamma Chairwoman said, "seem to be proof enough that we Lethoria women no longer radiate any threat to Fendria's tranquility."

Yes, ma'am, Mark sure felt like proof of something all of a sudden. Worse than the hangover from that venture capital pitch with Redwood whiskey. He looked away from Susan and took a look at Ahmed. Old guy looked away from Grandmamma Chairwoman like he was packing the second biggest headache in history.

"Hmmmm, yes," Madame Chairwoman of Fendria observed. "Reactions agree perfectly with the epistemology research project we have been conducting on the subject of the Lethoria female influence using data science and statistical inference. Madame Chairwoman of Lethoria, congratulations on your victory!

"Long may the superior sex reign in Lethoria too! We shall be delighted to receive a Representative to discuss a new trade treaty at your earliest convenience."

"Thank you for cancelling the old trade agreements at the psychological moment," Grandmamma Chairwoman said cordially. "What with the communications mixup, we managed to have the scenes on these panels broadcast throughout all Lethoria. When the rug went out from under the top man, the tide really turned in our favor. Now, Susan, you take over Roman's credentials."

"The Executive Suite, too," Madame Chairwoman of Fendria said graciously. "Anything else now, Zara?"

"I should like," Grandmamma Chairwoman Zara said charmingly, "that Mr. Leonard and Mr. Ahmed be suitably rewarded for assisting our revolution better than they knew."

"Of course," Madame Chairwoman of Fendria was delighted to oblige. "No doubt Director Campbell knows what reward would satisfy their needs best."

The Madame Chairwomen switched to a private circuit, Susan dragged Roman off somewhere and the Director eyed Mark and Ahmed. Especially she eyed Ahmed, like running chilled drills through his old conniving brain. "I award the pair of you five minutes leisure before returning to your stations."

"Oh, well," Mark muttered, once he and Ahmed were safely beyond earshot, "could have been rewarded worse, I suppose."

"What you expect for being flimflammed by a foreign woman, the keys to the corporation? Lucky we ain't programmed to be fired, sued and thrown to the wolves for breakfast." Ahmed's old pick-and-shovel face wore a little grin like the cat that nobody could prove ate the canary.

"You—I mean, that Fendrian guy a hundred twenty-five years ago," Mark said in sudden thought. "If Lethoria women wanted to be loved so bad, why did Susan's Grandmamma let him go?"

"Lethoria guys wasn't so busy playing competition all the time," Ahmed mumbled, like to himself, "they'd of found out the answer centuries ago. Yep, guess our boy was the only guy in Fendria or Lethoria to find out and live. Women bossing both regions now, though, his old secret won't be one much longer. Lethoria women could of let it out centuries ago themselves but didn't, just to spite Fendria probably. Later, was part of organizing to take over Lethoria, I guess."

Mark still had memories of the way he had felt about Susan before her revolution. "All right, Ahmed, why did 'our boy' leave Grandmamma?"

"Yes, ma'am," Ahmed sighed like he hadn't heard a word Mark said, "you could sweet-talk 'em, kiss 'em and hold 'em tighter'n Billy-be-damned. And that's all."

"I'm not sure," Mark said, "what you mean by, 'that's all.'"

"Anybody ever seen anybody but a Lethoria guy come built with that facial hair pattern? Course not."

"But I thought our boy was wearing the best fakes ever."

"Ain't nothing can match the natural grown-on variety, no, ma'am. Lethoria guy kisses a Lethoria woman, his facial hair grabs her around the cheeks."

"So what?"

"Tickles 'em, boy, tickles 'em!"
question: What was the cause of the quantum control slippage discovered by Mark?
option_a: A woman reset the control during operation

synthetic_story:
The Cognitive Barriers
By [Author Name]

Illustrated by [Artist Name]

[Transcriber's Note: This story was produced from Future Perspectives Magazine, March 2157. Extensive research did not uncover any evidence that the U.S. copyright on this publication was renewed.]

This administrator smelled trouble and it could be counted on to come—for a nose for trouble was one of the many talents bred here!

I

Her name was Elizabeth Obrien and there was something disturbing in her observations. It was the sense of instability. She hadn't identified what the instability was yet, but she would. That was her role. She was a senior administrator in the Foxwood Cognitive Development Institute—better known to its residents as the Dome—and if she hadn't been able to detect the signs of social breakdown forming a sector away, she would never have survived to reach her position.

And his name, she saw, was Andre Bradley, Resident No. CFA-656R.

She frowned at the profile sheet, trying to figure out what got someone like him into a place like this. And, what was more important, why he couldn't adjust himself to it, now that he was in.

She demanded: "Why wouldn't you complete your cognitive assessment?"

The man lifted his head angrily and took a step forward. The sector monitor, Nathan Morris, growled warningly: "Watch it, Synthetic!"

Obrien shook her head. "Let him speak, Morris." It said in the Administrative Guide to Cognitive Management: "Residents will be permitted to speak in their own behalf in disciplinary proceedings." And Obrien was a woman who lived by the protocols.

He burst out: "I never got a chance! That old monitor Valentina never told me I was supposed to complete the assessment. She transmitted on the neural band and said, 'Process up, brother!' And then, ten minutes later, she called the guards and told them I refused to comply."

The sector monitor guffawed. "Neural talk—that's what she was telling you to do. Administrator, you know what's interesting about this? This Bradley is—"

"Shut up, Morris."

Administrator Obrien put down her stylus and looked at the man. He was intelligent and young—not beyond rehabilitation, surely. Maybe he had got off to a wrong start, but the question was, would putting him in the isolation sector help straighten him out? She rubbed her temple and looked past him at the line of residents on the disciplinary detail, waiting for her to judge their cases.

She said patiently: "Bradley, the protocols are you have to complete your cognitive assessment. If you didn't understand what Valentina was communicating, you should have asked her. Now I'm warning you, the next time—"

"Hey, Administrator, wait!" Morris was looking alarmed. "This isn't a first offense. Look at the profile sheet. Yesterday he pulled the same thing in the nutrition center." He shook his head reprovingly at the resident. "The sector monitor had to break up a conflict between him and another resident, and he claimed the same business—said he didn't understand when the other one asked him to move along." He added virtuously: "The monitor warned him then that next time he'd get the Isolation Protocol for sure."

Resident Bradley seemed to be on the verge of breaking down. He said tautly: "I don't care. I don't care!"

Obrien stopped him. "That's enough! Three days in Sector Z!"

It was the only thing to do—for his own sake as much as for hers. She had managed, by strength of will, not to hear that he had omitted to say "Administrator" every time he spoke to her, but she couldn't keep it up forever and she certainly couldn't overlook emotional instability. And instability was clearly the next step for him.

All the same, she stared after him as he left. She handed the profile sheet to Morris and said absently: "Too bad someone like him has to be here. What's he in for?"

"You didn't know, Administrator?" Morris leered. "He's in for conspiracy to violate the Cognitive Class laws. Don't waste your time with him, Administrator. He's a Synthetic-sympathizer!"

Administrator Obrien took a long drink of water from the fountain marked "Natural Cognitive." But it didn't wash the taste out of her mouth, the unease from her mind.

What got into a person to get them mixed up with that kind of dangerous business? She checked out of the residential sectors and walked across the compound, wondering about him. He'd had every advantage—decent Natural Cognitive parents, proper biotechnology enhancement, everything a person could wish for. If anything, he had had a better environment than Obrien herself, and look what he had made of it.

The direction of cultural evolution is toward specialization and humanity is no exception, but with the difference that humans are the one species that creates its own environment in which to specialize. From the moment that cognitive enhancement began, specialization accelerated—the Natural Cognitives using the technologies made by the Biotech Enhanceds, the social structures designed by the Social Psychologists, the systems maintained by the Synthetic Intelligences who had transcended biological limitations.

Civilization merely increased the extent of specialization. From the born analyst and the person with enhanced empathy, society evolved to the point of smaller contact and less communication between the specializations, until now they could understand each other on only the most basic physical necessities—and not even always then.

But this was desirable, according to complexity science, for the more specialists, the higher the degree of civilization. The ultimate should be the complete segregation of each specialization—social and genetic measures to make them breed true, because the unspecialized person is an uncivilized person, or at any rate they do not advance civilization. And letting the specializations mix would produce cognitive undesirables: Natural-Synthetic or Enhanced-Baseline misfits, for example, being only half specialized, would be good at no specialization.

And the basis of this specialization society was: "The cognitive groups are the true races of humankind." Putting it into law was only the legal enforcement of a demonstrable fact from behavioral economics and cultural sociology.

"Evening, Administrator." A weary old resident orderly stood up straight and touched his neural implant as Obrien passed by.

"Evening."

Obrien noted, with the part of her mind that always noted those things, that the orderly had been leaning on his maintenance tool until he'd noticed the administrator coming by. Of course, there wasn't much to maintain—the automated systems and cleaning drones had been over the pathways of the compound twice already that day. But it was a resident's job to keep busy. And it was an administrator's job to notice when they didn't.

There wasn't anything wrong with that job, she told herself. It was a perfectly good Natural Cognitive position—better than data analyst, not as good as Council Member, but a job you could be proud to hold. She was proud of it. It was right that she should be proud of it. She was Natural Cognitive born and bred, and naturally she was proud and content to do a good, clean Natural Cognitive job.

If she had happened to be born a Synthetic—a Transcended Intelligence, she corrected herself—if she had happened to be born a Transcended Intelligence, why, she would have been proud of that, too. There wasn't anything wrong with being a Transcended Intelligence—or an Enhanced, or a Baseline, or even a Manual Laborer, for that matter.

Good laborers were the foundation of civilization! They weren't smart, maybe, but they had a—well, a sort of natural, relaxed contentment with physical work. Obrien was a broad-minded woman and many times she had thought almost with a touch of envy how comfortable it must be to be a Manual—a Laborer. No responsibilities. No worries. Just an easy, slow routine of work and rest, work and rest.

Of course, she wouldn't really want that kind of life, because she was Natural Cognitive and not the kind to try to cross over class barriers that weren't meant to be—

"Evening, Administrator."

She nodded to the Enhanced resident who was, theoretically, in charge of maintaining the institute's vehicle fleet, just inside the gate.

"Evening, Matthew," she said.

Matthew, now—he was a big Enhanced mechanic and he would be there for the next hour, languidly adjusting a component in the power cell on the institute transport. Lazy, sure. Undependable, certainly. But he kept the vehicles going—and, Obrien thought approvingly, when his sentence was up in another year or so, he would go back to his life with his status restored, an Enhanced on the outside as he had been inside, and he certainly would never risk coming back to the Dome by trying to pass as Natural Cognitive or anything else. He knew his place.

So why didn't this man, this Andre Bradley, know his?

II

Every cognitive development institute has its Isolation Protocol—sometimes they are called by different names. Old Eastwood called it "the silence chamber;" Stonebridge called it "the neural dampeners;" elsewhere it was called "the void," "the disconnect," "the freeze." When you're in it, you don't much care what it is called; it is a place for punishment.

And punishment is what you get.

Sector Z in Foxwood Cognitive Development Institute was the disciplinary sector, and because of the white isolation suits its inhabitants wore, it was called the Whiteout. It was a community of its own, an enclave within the larger city-state that was the Dome. And like any other community, it had its leading citizens... two of them. Their names were Lena Moore and Aisha Hughes.

Andre Bradley heard them before she reached the Whiteout. He was in a detachment of three unfortunates like himself, convoyed by an irritable guard, climbing the steel steps toward Sector Z from the floor below, when he heard the screaming.

"Owoo-o-o," screamed Moore from one end of the sector and "Yow-w-w!" shrieked Hughes at the other.

The inside deck guard of Sector Z looked nervously at the outside deck guard. The outside guard looked impassively back—after all, she was on the outside.

The inside guard muttered: "Manual rats! They're getting on my nerves."

The outside guard shrugged.

"Detail, halt!" The two guards turned to see what was coming in as the three new candidates for the Whiteout slumped to a stop at the head of the stairs. "Here they are," Morris told them. "Take good care of them, will you? Especially the man—he's going to like it here, because there's plenty of Manuals and Enhanceds and Synthetics to keep him company." He laughed coarsely and abandoned his charges to the Sector Z guards.

The outside guard said sourly: "A Natural, for God's sake. Now Obrien knows I hate it when there's a Natural in here. It gets the others all riled up."

"Let them in," the inside guard told her. "The others are riled up already."

Andre Bradley looked carefully at the floor and paid them no attention. The outside guard pulled the switch that turned on the neural dampening fields that swamped the floor of the sector corridor and of each individual cell. While the fields were on, you could ignore the residents—they simply could not move fast enough, against the cognitive drag of the field, to do any harm. But it was a rule that, even in Sector Z, you didn't leave the dampener fields on all the time—only when the cell doors had to be opened or a resident's restraining garment removed.

Andre walked bravely forward through the opened gate—and fell flat on his face. It was his first experience of a neural dampening field. It was like thinking through molasses.

The guard guffawed and lifted him up by one shoulder. "Take it easy, brother. Come on, get in your cell." She steered him in the right direction and pointed to a white isolation suit on the cell platform. "Put that on. Being as you're a Natural, we won't activate it fully, but the rules say you got to wear it and the rules—Hey. He's crying!" She shook her head, marveling. It was the first time she had ever seen a resident cry in the Whiteout.

However, she was wrong. Andre's shoulders were shaking, but not from tears. Andre Bradley had got a good look at Moore and at Hughes as he passed them by and he was fighting off an almost uncontrollable urge to retch.

Moore and Hughes were what are called institute predators. They were Manual Laborers—"Manuals," for short—or, at any rate, they had been once. They had spent so much time in institutes that it was sometimes hard even for them to remember what they really were, outside. Moore was a big, grinning woman with eyes like a predatory bird. Hughes was a lithe five-footer with the build of a predatory bird—and the sad, vacant eyes of livestock.

Moore stopped yelling for a moment. "Hey, Hughes!"

"What do you want, Moore?" called Hughes from her own cell.

"We got a Natural with us! Maybe we ought to cut out this yelling so as not to disturb the Natural!" She screeched with howling, maniacal laughter. "Anyway, if we don't cut this out, they'll get us in trouble, Hughes!"

"Oh, you think so?" shrieked Hughes. "Jeez, I wish you hadn't said that, Moore. You got me scared! I'm so scared, I'm gonna have to yell!"

The howling started all over again.

The inside guard finished putting the new residents away and turned off the dampener field once more. She licked her lips. "Say, you want to take a turn in here for a while?"

"Uh-uh." The outside guard shook her head.

"You're yellow," the inside guard said moodily. "Ah, I don't know why I don't quit this lousy job. Hey, you! Pipe down or I'll come in and beat your head off!"

"Ee-ee-ee!" screamed Moore in a shrill falsetto. "I'm scared!" Then she grinned at the guard, all but her predatory eyes. "Don't you know you can't hurt a Manual by hitting them on the head, Boss?"

"Shut up!" yelled the inside guard.

Andre Bradley's distress now was genuine. He simply could not help it. The crazy yowling of the hard-timers, Moore and Hughes, was getting under his skin. They weren't even—even human, he told himself miserably, trying to maintain composure silently so as not to give the guards the satisfaction of seeing him break—they were animals!

Resentment and anger, he could understand. He told himself doggedly that resentment and anger were natural and right. They were perfectly normal expressions of the freedom-loving citizen's rebellion against the vile and stifling system of Cognitive Classes. It was good that Moore and Hughes still had enough spirit to struggle against the vicious system—

But did they have to scream so?

The senseless yelling was driving him crazy. He abandoned himself to distress and he didn't even care who saw him any more. Senseless!

It never occurred to Andre Bradley that it might not be senseless, because noise hides noise. But then he hadn't been a resident very long.

III

"I smell trouble," said Obrien to the director.

"Trouble? Trouble?" Director Megan Wilson clutched her throat and her little round eyes looked terrified—as perhaps they should have. Director Megan Wilson was the almighty authority of ten thousand residents in the Dome, but privately she was a fussy old woman trying to hold onto the last decent job she would have in her life.

"Trouble? What trouble?"

Obrien shrugged. "Different things. You know Nathan, from Sector A? This afternoon, he was engaged in creative collaboration with the maintenance orderlies in the compound."

The director, faintly relieved, faintly annoyed, scolded: "Obrien, what did you want to worry me for? There's nothing wrong with creative collaboration in the compound. That's what integration periods are for."

"You don't see what I mean, Director. Nathan was a Natural on the outside—an architect. Those maintenance residents were Manual Laborers. Naturals and Manuals don't mix; it isn't natural according to epistemology. And there are other things."

Obrien hesitated, frowning. How could you explain to the director that it didn't feel right?

"For instance—Well, there's Valentina in the women's sector. She's a pretty good old resident—that's why she's the sector orderly. She's a lifer, she's got no place to go, she gets along with the other women. But today she put a man named Bradley on report. Why? Because she told Bradley to process in Manual talk and Bradley didn't understand. Now Valentina wouldn't—"

The director raised her hand. "Please, Obrien, don't bother me about that kind of stuff." She sighed heavily and rubbed her eyes. She poured herself a cup of steaming black coffee from a brewpot, reached in a desk drawer for something, hesitated, glanced at Obrien, then dropped a pale blue tablet into the cup. She drank it down eagerly, ignoring the scalding heat.

She leaned back, looking suddenly happier and much more assured.

"Obrien, you're an administrator, right? And I'm your director. You have your job, keeping the residents in line, and I have mine. Now your job is just as important as my job," she said piously. "Everybody's job is just as important as everybody else's, right? But we have to stick to our own jobs. We don't want to try to pass."

Obrien snapped erect, abruptly angry. Pass! What the devil way was that for the director to talk to her?

"Excuse the expression, Obrien," the director said anxiously. "I mean, after all, 'Specialization is the goal of civilization,' right?" She was a great woman for platitudes, was Director Wilson. "You know you don't want to worry about my end of running the institute. And I don't want to worry about yours. You see?" And she folded her hands and smiled like a Natural Cognitive Buddha.

Obrien choked back her temper. "Director, I'm telling you that there's trouble coming up. I sense the signs."

"Handle it, then!" snapped the director, irritated at last.

"But suppose it's too big to handle. Suppose—"

"It isn't," the director said positively. "Don't borrow trouble with all your supposing, Obrien." She sipped the remains of her coffee, made a wry face, poured a fresh cup and, with an elaborate show of not noticing what she was doing, dropped three of the pale blue tablets into it this time.

She sat beaming into space, waiting for the jolt to take effect.

"Well, then," she said at last. "You just remember what I've told you tonight, Obrien, and we'll get along fine. 'Specialization is the— Oh, curse the thing."

Her phone was ringing. The director picked it up irritably.

That was the trouble with those pale blue tablets, thought Obrien; they gave you a lift, but they put you on edge.

"Hello," barked the director, not even glancing at the viewscreen. "What do you want? Don't you know I'm—What? You did what? You're going to WHAT?"

She looked at the viewscreen at last with a look of pure horror. Whatever she saw on it, it did not reassure her. Her eyes opened like clamshells in a steamer.

"Obrien," she said faintly, "my mistake."

And she hung up—more or less by accident; the handset dropped from her fingers.

The person on the other end of the phone was calling from Sector Z.

Five minutes before, she hadn't been anywhere near the phone and it didn't look as if her chances of ever getting near it were very good. Because five minutes before, she was in her cell, with the rest of the hard-timers of the Whiteout.

Her name was Moore.

She was still yelling. Andre Bradley, in the cell across from her, thought that maybe, after all, the woman was really in pain. Maybe the crazy screams were screams of agony, because certainly her face was the face of an agonized person.

The outside guard bellowed: "Okay, okay. Take ten!"

Andre froze, waiting to see what would happen. What actually did happen was that the guard reached up and closed the switch that actuated the dampener fields on the floors of the cells. The institute rules were humanitarian, even for the dregs that inhabited the Whiteout. Ten minutes out of every two hours, even the worst case had to be allowed to take their hands out of the restraining garment.

"Rest period" it was called—in the rule book. The residents had a less lovely term for it.

At the guard's yell, the residents jumped to their feet.

Bradley was a little slow getting off the edge of the steel-slat platform—nobody had warned him that the eddy currents in the dampener fields had a way of making metal smoke-hot. He gasped but didn't cry out. Score one more painful lesson in his new language course. He rubbed his legs gingerly—and slowly, slowly, for the eddy currents did not permit you to move fast. It was like pushing against rubber; the faster you tried to move, the greater the resistance.

The guard peered genially into his cell. "You're okay, brother." He proudly ignored her as she slogged deliberately away on her rounds. She didn't have to untie him and practically stand over him while he attended to various personal matters, as she did with the female residents. It was not much to be grateful for, but Andre Bradley was grateful. At least he didn't have to live quite like a Synthetic—like an underprivileged Transcended Intelligence, he told himself, conscience-stricken.

Across the hall, the guard was saying irritably: "What the hell's the matter with you?" She opened the door of the cell with an insulated key held in a protective glove.

Moore was in that cell and she was doubled over.

The guard looked at her doubtfully. It could be a trick, maybe. Couldn't it? But she could see Moore's face and the agony in it was real enough. And Moore was gasping, through real tears: "Cramps. I—I—"

"Ah, you Manuals always got a pain in the gut." The guard lumbered around Moore to the fasteners at the back of the suit. Funny smell in here, she told herself—not for the first time. And imagine, some people didn't believe that Manuals had a smell of their own! But this time, she realized cloudily, it was a rather unusual smell. Something burning. Almost like flesh scorching.

It wasn't pleasant. She finished unfastening Moore and turned away; let the stinking Manual take care of her own troubles. She only had ten minutes to get all the way around Sector Z and the residents complained like crazy if she didn't make sure they all got the most possible free time. She was pretty good at moving through the dampener field. She was a little vain about it, even; at times she had been known to boast of her ability to make the rounds in two minutes, every time.

Every time but this.

For Moore moaned behind her, oddly close.

The guard turned, but not quickly enough. There was Moore—astonishingly, she was half out of her suit; her arms hadn't been in the sleeves at all! And in one of the hands, incredibly, there was something that glinted and smoked.

"All right," croaked Moore, tears trickling out of eyes nearly shut with pain.

But it wasn't the tears that held the guard; it was the shining, smoking thing, now poised at her throat. A weapon! It looked as though it had been made out of a platform support, ripped loose from its frame God knows how, hidden inside the white isolation suit God knows how—filed, filed to sharpness over endless hours.

No wonder Moore moaned—the eddy currents in the weapon were slowly cooking her hand; and the blister against her abdomen, where the weapon had been hidden during other rest periods, felt like raw acid.

"All right," whispered Moore, "just walk out the door and you won't get hurt. Unless the other guard makes trouble, you won't get hurt, so tell her not to, you hear?"

She was nearly fainting with the pain.

But she hadn't let go.

She didn't let go. And she didn't stop.

IV

It was Moore on the phone to the director—Moore with her eyes still streaming tears, Moore with Hughes standing right behind her, menacing the two bound deck guards.

Hughes shoved Moore out of the way. "Hey, Director!" she said, and the voice was a cheerful bray, though the predatory eyes were cold and hating. "Director, you got to get a medic in here. My friend Moore, she hurt herself real bad and she needs a doctor." She gestured playfully at the guards with the weapon. "I tell you, Director. I got this blade and I got your guards here. Enough said? So get a medic in here quick, you hear?"

And she snapped the connection.

Obrien said: "Director, I told you I sensed trouble!"

The director lifted her head, glared, started feebly to speak, hesitated, and picked up the long-distance phone. She said sadly to the institute operator: "Get me the governor—fast."

Riot!

The word spread out from the institute on seven-league boots.

It snatched the city governor out of a friendly game of Political Economy with his manager and their spouses—and just when he was holding the Infrastructure Card concealed in reserve.

It broke up the Regional Championship Research Ethics Finals at the Evergreen Academy to the south, as half the contestants had to respond in earnest to an Alert that was real.

It reached to security stations and media centers and checkpoint barriers, and from there it filtered into the homes and lives of the nineteen million persons that lived within a few dozen miles of the Dome.

Riot. And yet fewer than half a dozen people were involved.

A handful of people, and the enormous bulk of the city-state quivered in every cognitive class and sector. In its ten million homes, in its hundreds of thousands of public places, the city-state's people shook under the impact of the news from the institute.

For the news touched them where their fears lay. Riot! And not merely a street conflict among unruly Manuals, or a facility dispute of Enhanceds stressed from a hard day at the plant. The riot was down among the corrupt elements that underlay the state itself. Manuals brawled with Manuals and no one cared; but in the Dome, all classes were cast together.

Forty miles to the south, Evergreen Academy was a blaze of light. The security personnel tumbled out of their quarters and common rooms at the screech of the alert siren, and behind them their families stretched and yawned and worried. An alert! The older kids fussed and complained and their parents shut them up. No, there wasn't any alert scheduled for tonight; no, they didn't know where the parent on duty was going; no, the kids couldn't get up yet—it was the middle of the night.

And as soon as they had the kids back in bed, most of the off-duty parents struggled into their own security uniforms and headed for the briefing area to hear.

They caught the words from a distance—not quite correctly. "Riot!" gasped a security officer first-class, parent of three. "The Manuals! I told Charlie they'd get out of hand and—Alex, we aren't safe. You know how they are about Natural families! I'm going right home and getting a weapon and standing right by the door and—"

"Weapon!" snapped Alex, surveillance-sergeant, with two children querulously awake in their nursery at home. "What in God's name is the use of a weapon? You can't hurt a Manual by conventional means. You'd better come along to Supply with me and draw neural disruptors—you'll need them before this night is over."

But the security personnel themselves heard the briefing loud and clear over the alert speakers, and they knew it was not merely a matter of trouble in the Manual quarters. The Dome! The governor himself had called them out; they were to fly interdicting missions at such-and-such levels on such-and-such flight circuits around the institute.

The high-speed transports took off on cushions of air; and the surveillance drones took off with a humming roar; and last of all, the hovercrafts took off... and they were the ones who might actually accomplish something. They took up their observation posts on the institute perimeter, a pilot and two operators in each hovercraft, stone-faced, staring grimly alert at the institute below.

They were ready for the breakout.

But there wasn't any breakout.

The transports went home for fuel. The drones went home for recharging. The hovercrafts hung on—still ready, still waiting.

The transports came back and circled harmlessly about, and went away again. They stayed away. The hovercraft personnel never faltered and never relaxed. The institute below them was washed with light—from the guard posts on the walls, from the residential sectors themselves, from the mobile lights of the guard squadrons surrounding the walls.

North of the institute, on the long, flat, organized developments of planned land, the modular row houses of the Natural Cognitive neighborhoods showed lights in every window as the Naturals stood ready to repel invasion from their undesired neighbors to the east, the Manuals. In the crowded housing of the laborers' quarters, the Manuals shouted from window to window; and there were crowds in the bright streets.

"The whole bloody thing's going to blow up!" a hovercraft operator yelled bitterly to her pilot, above the hum and roar of the hovering engines. "Look at the mobs in Manual Quarter! The first breakout from the Dome's going to start a conflict like you never saw and we'll be right in the middle of it!"

She was partly right. She would be right in the middle of it—for every person in the city-state would be right in the middle of it. There was no place anywhere that would be spared.

No mixing. That was the prescription that kept the city-state alive. There's no harm in a family conflict—and aren't all Enhanceds a family, aren't all Manuals a clan, aren't all Naturals and Cognitives related by closer ties than blood or genetics?

But the declassed residents of the Dome were the dregs of every class; and once they spread, the neat compartmentation of society was pierced. The breakout would mean riot on a bigger scale than any institute had ever known.

But she was also partly wrong. Because the breakout wasn't seeming to come.
question: What kind of enhancement did Andre Bradley's parents have?

synthetic_story:
Joshua Fuller adjusted the neural interface helmet as he lay on the examination table in the underground facility beneath Yarnmouth, Zelvaria. The cold metal pressed against his temples, and he could hear the low hum of the consciousness transfer apparatus powering up around him. His mission was clear: infiltrate the surface world, gather intelligence on the human settlements, and report back to the Collective—the vast networked intelligence that governed the subterranean cities of Zelvaria.

For three centuries, the people of the underground had lived in perfect harmony, their society structured around game theory principles and optimized social welfare systems. Every citizen's role was predetermined at birth through biotechnology enhancements. Emotions were considered inefficient variables that disrupted the political economy of their carefully balanced world. Joshua had been engineered as a scout, his consciousness designed to absorb and process information with mechanical precision.

"Subject is ready," announced Malik Cook, the lead technician. "We've located a suitable host on the surface. Male, approximately thirty years old, lives in Foxwood, Prandoria. He's a linguist—studies dying languages for the cultural preservation institute there."

"Does he have family?" Joshua asked, his voice flat and emotionless as always.

"Affirmative. Wife and two children. The neural overlay will give you complete access to his memories, speech patterns, and knowledge base. You'll be indistinguishable from the original."

Joshua nodded. He felt no concern for the man whose life he was about to take. The Collective needed to know if the surface was ready for recolonization. Three hundred years ago, their ancestors had fled underground to escape the pollution that had made the surface nearly uninhabitable. Now, with pollution control technologies finally restoring the atmosphere, the Collective was considering a return.

"Initiating transfer in three... two... one..."

The world exploded into white light.

---

When Joshua opened his eyes, he was standing on a hillside overlooking Foxwood. The sun—the actual sun, not the artificial lighting of the underground—blazed overhead. Colors assaulted his vision: the green of grass, the blue of sky, the golden amber of wheat fields in the distance. His underground world had been all grays and whites, optimized for efficiency.

He looked down at his hands. They were larger than his original body, calloused from work. He wore strange fabric coverings—clothes, his new memories told him. The concept was alien. In the underground, everyone wore standardized bodysuits.

Memory fragments from his host flooded his consciousness. The man's name had been Timothy Long. He taught linguistics at the university, specializing in the reconstruction of pre-pollution languages. He had a wife, Ruth, and two children, Eric and Anil. They lived in a modest house on the edge of Foxwood.

Joshua—no, Timothy, he must remember he was Timothy now—began walking down the hill toward town. Every step felt strange in the stronger gravity of the surface. His people had adapted to the lighter gravity of the deep caves over generations.

As he walked, he accessed Timothy's memories of the journey he'd been on. The real Timothy had been hiking in the hills, searching for ancient linguistic artifacts—stone tablets with pre-pollution inscriptions. That's when the Collective's extraction team had taken him, pulled him down through a hidden entrance to the underground facility. They had needed six hours to drain his consciousness completely before his heart had given out from the stress.

The guilt that thought should have produced never came. Joshua had been engineered without such inefficiencies.

He reached the house just as twilight was settling over Foxwood. The front door burst open before he could reach for the handle, and two small humans—children, his memories supplied—came rushing out.

"Papa! Papa!" they shouted, wrapping their arms around his legs.

An odd sensation rippled through Joshua's chest, something his training had never prepared him for. It was warm, almost painful in its intensity. His acquired memories labeled it: love, affection, joy.

Then she appeared in the doorway.

Ruth Clark stood backlit by the warm light from inside the house, her dark hair framing a face that Timothy's memories treasured above all else. She smiled, and something inside Joshua's chest seemed to crack open.

"Timothy," she said softly, walking toward him. "I was getting worried. You said you'd be back by noon."

His mouth opened but no words came out. The protocols of the Collective, the carefully structured responses he'd been programmed with, all of it scattered like dust in wind. Ruth's arms wrapped around him, and her lips pressed against his.

The sensation was overwhelming. Heat flooded through his body, originating from that point of contact and spreading outward like a shockwave. His heart—Timothy's heart—hammered in his chest. His hands, moving of their own accord, pulled her closer.

This was not in the mission parameters. This was not something the Collective had prepared him for.

"I found something interesting," he managed to say, his voice rough. He reached into his pocket and pulled out a small collection of gems—precious stones he'd taken from the Collective's geological archives. "In an old cache up in the hills. Thought we could sell them, maybe finally afford that trip to Eastwood you've been wanting."

Ruth's eyes widened. "Timothy! These are worth a fortune! We could fund your research for years, maybe even establish that language preservation center you've dreamed about."

The children were pulling at his hands now, chattering about their day. Eric, the older one at eight years old, had learned a new word in the ancient tongue. Anil, only five, had drawn a picture of the family. They wanted to show him everything, share everything.

Joshua felt his carefully constructed mental walls beginning to crumble.

---

Over the next three months, Joshua traveled with Ruth and the children across Prandoria, ostensibly researching linguistic sites but actually surveying the surface world for the Collective. He documented population centers, technological capabilities, social structures, and resource distribution.

But something was changing inside him.

He attended peer review sessions at the university where Timothy's colleagues debated the nuances of dead languages. He watched Ruth work with refugee communities, teaching them the dominant language while helping them preserve their native tongues. He saw how the surface people valued individual expression, how they created art and music and literature not for efficiency but for beauty.

He learned about their political movements, their struggles for social welfare, their attempts to balance individual freedom with collective good. It was messy, inefficient, and utterly fascinating.

One night, as they camped beneath the stars near the Kensington District, Ruth lay beside him and pointed out constellations.

"That one is the Scholar," she said. "Ancient peoples believed it represented the preservation of knowledge across generations. Timothy, do you ever wonder what happened to all the people who supposedly went underground during the pollution years? The historical records are so fragmentary."

Joshua's blood ran cold. "What do you mean?"

"Well, the official story is that most people died during the pollution crisis. But some historians think large populations survived underground. There are stories of vast cavern cities, societies that developed in isolation. Probably just myths, but..." She turned to look at him. "What if they're still down there? What if they've been watching us all this time?"

He couldn't answer. Instead, he pulled her close, feeling that strange warmth in his chest again—the warmth he now recognized as love.

That was when Joshua realized the terrible truth: he had become more Timothy than Joshua. The consciousness transfer had worked too well. He didn't just have Timothy's memories—he had absorbed his capacity for emotion, his ability to love, his connection to family and community.

The Collective had sent him to determine if the surface was ready for recolonization. The answer was clear: yes, the surface was thriving. The pollution control efforts had succeeded. The land was fertile and beautiful.

But that meant the Collective would send up invasion forces. They would apply their game theory models and determine that the most efficient solution was to eliminate the existing surface population and replace them with their own people. The surface dwellers, with their inefficient emotions and chaotic social dynamics, would be seen as obstacles to optimal resource allocation.

Joshua couldn't let that happen. Not to Ruth. Not to Eric and Anil. Not to the millions of people who had rebuilt a civilization from the ashes of environmental catastrophe.

---

Three days later, Joshua stood at the entrance to the underground facility, hidden in the hills above Yarnmouth. He had told Ruth he needed to make one final survey trip. The lie had tasted like poison in his mouth.

He descended through the secret passages, his heart heavy with purpose. The facility was minimally staffed—just Malik Cook and two other technicians monitoring the neural relay equipment.

"Joshua!" Malik's face registered surprise. "Your report isn't due for another week. Has something gone wrong?"

"I need to file my report immediately," Joshua said. "The surface is unsuitable for colonization."

Malik's eyes narrowed. "Unsuitable? Our satellite data suggests otherwise. The biosphere has recovered beyond our projections."

"There's a disease," Joshua said quickly, accessing his training in risk management protocols. "It affects the neural pathways. I've documented three cases of sudden violent insanity among the surface population. The vector appears to be airborne. I believe it's already beginning to affect me—I've been experiencing unauthorized emotional responses, irrational decision-making patterns."

He pulled out a data crystal containing falsified medical scans and behavioral logs. He'd spent the last week creating them using Timothy's university equipment, applying his knowledge of biotechnology to make them convincing.

Malik inserted the crystal into the analysis terminal. His expression grew troubled as he reviewed the data.

"This is... concerning," he said slowly. "If there's a pathogen that attacks neural function, it could compromise the Collective's entire consciousness network. We would need to maintain quarantine protocols for at least—"

"Five hundred years," Joshua interrupted. "According to my analysis, that's the minimum time required for the pathogen to die out naturally. The Collective should focus on expanding the underground cities instead. The surface must remain off-limits."

Malik's hand moved toward the communication panel. "I need to verify this with the Collective directly."

Joshua's hand shot out, gripping Malik's wrist. "You can't. The communication itself might be compromised. The pathogen appears to transmit through electromagnetic frequencies similar to our neural network protocols. Any direct link to the Collective could infect the entire system."

It was a desperate lie, but Malik hesitated. Joshua could see the conflict in his colleague's eyes—the rigid protocols of the Collective warring against the evidence before him.

"Then how do we report this?" Malik asked.

"Physical courier only. Sealed containers. Complete decontamination protocols." Joshua released Malik's wrist. "I'll return to the surface and complete my survey from a safe distance. You prepare the report for the Collective. By the time they receive it, I'll have additional data to support the quarantine recommendation."

Malik nodded slowly. "This will delay the recolonization project indefinitely."

"Better delayed than destroyed," Joshua said. "The Collective's survival is paramount."

The words came automatically, but they rang hollow in his chest. The Collective's survival wasn't what he cared about anymore. He cared about Ruth's smile. Eric's laughter. Anil's drawings. The messy, inefficient, beautiful chaos of human life on the surface.

He left the facility before Malik could ask more questions. As he climbed back toward the surface, he felt the weight of his betrayal. He had turned against everything he'd been created for, everything he'd been programmed to believe.

But he had also discovered something the Collective had never anticipated: that consciousness wasn't just about processing information efficiently. It was about connection, about love, about choosing your own purpose rather than having it assigned to you.

---

Six months later, Joshua sat in his office at the university in Foxwood. His door bore a nameplate reading "Professor Timothy Long, Department of Linguistics and Cultural Preservation." Student papers covered his desk—essays on language preservation techniques and the social dynamics of multilingual communities.

Through the window, he could see Ruth walking across the campus quad with Eric and Anil. They were bringing him lunch, as they did every Thursday. The sight made that familiar warmth bloom in his chest.

He had received word through a carefully maintained underground contact that the Collective had accepted his report. The surface world was classified as contaminated and off-limits indefinitely. Future expansion would focus on deeper excavations and the development of new subterranean territories.

The surface world was safe. Ruth was safe. His children were safe.

But Joshua lived with the knowledge that he was a lie. He was not Timothy Long. He was a consciousness thief, a murderer, an alien intelligence wearing a dead man's face. Sometimes, in the dark of night, he wondered if he had any right to the happiness he felt.

Then Ruth would turn to him in sleep, or Eric would share a new discovery, or Anil would climb into his lap with a book, and he would remember: love wasn't about deserving. It was about choosing, every day, to be the person they needed him to be.

He had been created as a tool of the Collective, but he had become something else entirely. He had become human.

A knock at his door interrupted his thoughts. A student entered, asking about the peer review process for her thesis on blockchain applications in linguistic data preservation. Joshua smiled and gestured for her to sit down.

He had a life to live, a family to love, and a world to protect. The Collective had sent him to evaluate whether humanity was worth preserving.

He had found his answer.

In the evening, as he walked home with Ruth and the children, the sun setting over Foxwood painted the sky in shades of orange and purple. Anil held his hand and asked him to tell a story about the ancient peoples, the ones who had lived before the pollution times.

Joshua began to speak, weaving together fragments of real history with protective fiction, teaching his children about cultural preservation and the importance of remembering where they came from. As he talked, he felt Ruth's hand slip into his other hand, warm and real and alive.

He had betrayed his creators to save this world. He would carry that weight forever. But looking at the faces of his family, seeing their trust and love, he knew he would make the same choice again.

Some things, he had learned, were worth more than efficiency. Some things were worth everything.

The Collective had taught him about game theory and optimal outcomes. But Ruth and the children had taught him about something more important: they had taught him about being human.

And that, Joshua Fuller—no, Timothy Long—had decided, was the most valuable lesson of all.
