synthetic_story:
The Networker
By Anonymous

Being an interstellar network security specialist wouldn't be so bad… if I could secure the networks without leaving my office!

Director Lucia Woods had that look of intense satisfaction on her face that meant someone was in for a very rough assignment. Since we were alone in her office, it took no great feat of intelligence to figure it would be me. I spoke first, bold attack being the best defense and so forth.

"I quit. Don't bother telling me what impossible job you have cooked up, because I have already quit and you do not want to reveal company secrets to me."

The grin was even wider now and she actually laughed as she thumbed a button on her console. A thick legal document slid out of the delivery slot onto her desk.

"This is your contract," she said. "It tells how and when you will work. A quantum-encrypted contract that you couldn't crack with a neural disruptor."

I leaned out quickly, grabbed it and threw it into the air with a single motion. Before it could fall, I had my plasma cutter out and, with a wide-angle burst, incinerated the contract to ashes.

Director Woods pressed the button again and another contract slid out on her desk. If possible, the smile was still wider now.

"I should have said a duplicate of your contract—like this one here." She made a quick note on her secretary plate. "I have deducted 50 credits from your salary for the cost of the duplicate—as well as a 500-credit fine for firing a plasma cutter inside a building."

I slumped, defeated, waiting for the blow to land. Director Woods fondled my contract.

"According to this document, you can't quit. Ever. Therefore I have a little job I know you'll enjoy. Network restoration job. The Woodbridge relay hub has shut down. It's a Genesis-class system…"

"What kind of system?" I asked her. I had restored quantum communication networks from one arm of the Galaxy to the other and was sure I had worked on every type or model made. But I had never heard of this kind.

"Genesis-class," Director Woods repeated, practically chortling. "I never heard of it either until Archives dug up the specs. They found them buried in the back of their oldest data vault. This was the earliest type of quantum relay ever built—by Earth Colonial Administration, no less. Considering its location on one of the Calderon planets, it might very well be the first relay."

I looked at the blueprints she handed me and felt my eyes glaze with horror. "It's a monstrosity! It looks more like a particle accelerator than a relay hub—must be at least a few hundred meters in diameter. I'm a network specialist, not an archeologist. This pile of junk is over 1500 years old. Just forget about it and build a new one."

Director Woods leaned over her desk, breathing into my face. "It would take eighteen months to install a new relay—besides being prohibitively expensive—and this relic is on one of the main communication routes. We have data packets making twenty-light-year detours now."

She leaned back, wiped her hands on her handkerchief and gave me Lecture Thirty-seven on Company Duty and My Responsibilities.

"This department is officially called Network Maintenance and Security, when it really should be called crisis management. Quantum relays are made to last forever—or damn close to it. When one of them breaks down, it is never an accident, and repairing the thing is never a matter of just plugging in a new part."

She was telling me—the person who did the job while she sat back on her fat paycheck in a climate-controlled office.

She rambled on. "How I wish that were all it took! I would have a fleet of parts ships and junior technicians to install them. But it's not like that at all. I have a fleet of expensive ships that are equipped to do almost anything—manned by a bunch of mavericks like you."

I nodded moodily at her pointing finger.

"How I wish I could fire you all! Combination pilots, mechanics, engineers, diplomats, con-artists and anything else it takes to do the repairs. I have to browbeat, bribe, blackmail and bulldoze you mavericks into doing a simple job. If you think you're fed up, just think how I feel. But the networks must stay online! The relays must operate!"

I recognized this deathless line as the curtain speech and crawled to my feet. She threw the Genesis file at me and went back to scratching in her papers. Just as I reached the door, she looked up and impaled me on her finger again.

"And don't get any fancy ideas about jumping your contract. We can freeze that investment portfolio of yours on Highpoint long before you could liquidate it."

I smiled, a little weakly, I'm afraid, as if I had never meant to keep that portfolio a secret. Her intelligence network was getting more efficient every day. Walking down the hall, I tried to figure a way to transfer the assets without her catching on—and knew at the same time she was figuring a way to outfigure me.

It was all very depressing, so I stopped for a drink, then went on to the spaceport.

By the time the ship was serviced, I had a course charted. The nearest relay to the broken-down Woodbridge hub was on one of the planets of Ivywood system in Ulvaria sector, and I headed there first, a short trip of only about twelve days in hyperspace.

To understand the importance of the quantum relays, you have to understand faster-than-light communication. Not that many people do, but it is easy enough to understand that in quantum-entangled networks, the regular rules of information theory don't apply. Data transmission and routing are a matter of quantum state manipulation, not classical electromagnetic propagation like in the old universe.

The first colonies to establish interstellar presence had no way to communicate—and no way to even tell if their messages had been received. The quantum relays solved that problem and opened the entire galaxy to real-time communication. They are built on planets and generate tremendous amounts of power. This power is used to maintain quantum coherence that is sustained across interstellar distances. Every relay has a unique quantum signature as part of its entanglement network and represents a measurable node in the communication web. Triangulation and routing of the relays works for data transmission—only it follows its own protocols. The protocols are complex and variable, but they are still protocols that a network engineer can follow.

For a proper network topology, you need at least four relays for an accurate route. For long-distance communication, engineers use as many as nine or ten. So every relay is critical and every one has to keep operating. That is where I and the other troubleshooters came in.

We travel in well-stocked ships that carry a little bit of everything; only one person to a ship because that is all it takes to operate the overly efficient repair machinery. Due to the very nature of our job, we spend most of our time just rocketing through normal space. After all, when a relay breaks down, how do you find it?

Not through hyperspace. All you can do is approach as close as you can by using other relays for navigation, then finish the trip in normal space. This can take months, and often does.

This job didn't turn out to be quite that bad. I locked onto the Ivywood relay and ran a complicated ten-point problem through the navigator, using every relay I could get an accurate fix on. The computer gave me a course with an estimated point-of-arrival as well as a built-in safety factor I never could eliminate from the machine.

I would much rather take a chance of breaking through near some star than spend time just barreling through normal space, but apparently Tech knows this, too. They had a safety factor built into the computer so you couldn't end up inside a star no matter how hard you tried. I'm sure there was no humaneness in this decision. They just didn't want to lose the ship.

It was a twenty-six-hour jump, ship's time, and I came through in the middle of nowhere. The robot analyzer hummed to itself and scanned all the stars, comparing them to the spectra of Woodbridge's sun. It finally rang a bell and blinked a light. I peered through the eyepiece.

A fast reading with the photocell gave me the apparent magnitude and a comparison with its absolute magnitude showed its distance. Not as bad as I had thought—a seven-week run, give or take a few days. After feeding a course tape into the robot pilot, I strapped into the acceleration tank and went to sleep.

The time went fast. I completed three online courses in quantum cryptography and advanced data analysis, mostly because the company grades your pay by the number of specialties you can handle. All this, with some virtual reality gaming and zero-gravity workouts in the gym, passed the time. I was asleep when the alarm went off that announced planetary distance.

Planet three, where the relay was situated according to the old charts, was a verdant-looking, temperate kind of globe. I tried to make sense out of the ancient directions and finally located the right area. Staying outside the atmosphere, I sent a reconnaissance drone down to look things over. In this business, you learn early when and where to risk your own skin. The drone would be good enough for the preliminary survey.

The old engineers had enough sense to choose a traceable site for the relay, equidistant on a line between two of the most prominent geological formations—a pair of massive crater rims. I located the craters easily enough and started the drone out from the first crater and kept it on a course directly toward the second. There was fore and aft radar in the drone and I fed their signals into a scope as an amplitude curve. When the two craters coincided, I spun the drone controls and dove the thing down.

I cut out the radar and cut in the visual feed and sat back to watch the relay appear on the screen.

The image blinked, focused—and a great damn ziggurat swam into view. I cursed and wheeled the drone in circles, scanning the surrounding area. It was flat, cultivated farmland without a bump. The only thing in a fifteen-mile circle was this ziggurat—and that definitely wasn't my relay.

Or wasn't it?

I dove the drone lower. The ziggurat was an elaborate-looking thing of carved stone, with intricate decorations and what looked like ceremonial platforms. There was a shimmer of energy from the top and I took a closer look at it. On the peak of the ziggurat was a massive crystalline structure that pulsed with faint light. When I saw that, something clicked in my mind.

Locking the drone in a circular course, I dug through the Genesis plans—and there it was. The relay had a quantum coherence field generator and a crystalline array on top of it for signal amplification; this was used to boost the entanglement stability that powered the whole system. If the crystal was still glowing, the relay was still there—inside the ziggurat. The natives, who, of course, weren't even mentioned by the idiots who constructed the thing, had built a nice heavy, elaborate stone ziggurat around the relay.

I took another look at the screen and realized that I had locked the drone into a circular orbit about thirty feet above the ziggurat. The summit of the stone structure was now covered with humanoid figures of some type, apparently the local life-form. They had what looked like energy weapons and projectile launchers and were trying to shoot down the drone, a cloud of bolts and missiles flying in every direction.

I pulled the drone straight up and away and threw in the control circuit that would return it automatically to the ship.

Then I went to the galley for a long, strong drink. My relay was not only locked inside a mountain of handmade stone, but I had managed to irritate the beings who had built the ziggurat. A great beginning for a job and one clearly designed to drive a stronger person than me to the bottle.

Normally, a network specialist stays away from native cultures. They are poison. Anthropologists may not mind being dissected for their science, but a network specialist wants to make no sacrifices of any kind for the job. For this reason, most relays are built on uninhabited planets. If a relay has to go on a planet with a culture, it is usually built in some inaccessible place.

Why this relay had been built within reach of the local population, I had yet to find out. But that would come in time. The first thing to do was make contact. To make contact, you have to know the local language.

And, for that, I had long before worked out a system that was foolproof.

I had a surveillance drone of my own construction. It looked like a piece of local vegetation about a foot tall. Once on the ground, it would never be noticed, though it was a little disconcerting to see it float by. I located a settlement about eight hundred kilometers from the ziggurat and dropped the drone. It whooshed down and landed at night near the bank of the local water source. This was a popular spot that drew a good crowd during the day. In the morning, when the first locals arrived, I flipped on the recorder.

After about seven of the local days, I had a wealth of native conversation in the memory bank of the machine translator and had tagged a few expressions. This is fairly easy to do when you have a machine memory to work with. One of the natives called out to another one and the second one responded. I tagged this expression with the phrase, "Hello, friend!" and waited my chance to use it. Later the same day, I caught one of them alone and broadcast "Hello, friend!" at them. It played out through the speaker in the local tongue and they responded positively.

When you get enough reference phrases like this in the memory bank, the MT brain takes over and starts filling in the missing pieces. As soon as the MT could give a running translation of any conversation it heard, I figured it was time to make a contact.

I found her easily enough. She was the Calderon version of a shepherd—she tended a particularly docile form of local livestock in the grasslands outside the settlement. I had one of the working drones dig a small chamber in an outcropping of rock and wait for her.

When she passed next day, I whispered into the mike: "Greetings, Elena Carter, faithful servant! This is the voice of the Eternal Guides speaking from the celestial realm." This fitted in with what I could make out of the local religion.

Elena stopped as if she'd been struck. Before she could move, I pushed a switch and a handful of the local currency, precious metal coins, rolled out of the chamber and landed at her feet.

"Here is a gift from the celestial realm, because you have been faithful." Not really from the celestial realm—I had fabricated it from raw materials the night before. "Come back tomorrow and we will speak more," I called after the fleeing figure. I was pleased to notice that she took the coins before taking off.

After that, the Eternal Guides had many heart-to-heart talks with Elena, who found the celestial gifts more than she could resist. The Guides had been out of touch with earthly matters and Elena happily filled them in.

I learned all I needed to know of the history, past and recent, and it wasn't pleasant.

In addition to the ziggurat being around the relay, there was a nasty political conflict going on around the structure.

It all began with the migration. Apparently the local humanoids had been living in scattered tribes when the relay was built, but the builders didn't think much of them. They were a primitive type and confined to a distant region. The idea that the civilization would develop and might reach this continent never occurred to the relay engineers. Which is, of course, what happened.

A little climate change, a population boom, and the humanoids began to migrate to relay valley. And found religion. A shining crystalline temple from which emanated a constant pulse of divine energy—the quantum coherence field that maintained the entanglement network. The radiation in the field didn't harm the natives. It enhanced their cognitive development in ways that bred true.

A city was built around the temple and, through the centuries, the ziggurat was constructed around the relay. A special caste of the priesthood served the temple. All went well until one of the priests violated the temple protocols and disrupted the divine energy. There had been revolt, conflict, violence and destruction since then. But still the divine energy would not flow properly. Now armed factions fought around the temple each day and a new group of priests guarded the sacred structure.

And I had to walk into the middle of that mess and repair the thing.

It would have been easy enough if we were allowed a little force. I could have cleared the area, fixed the relay and taken off. Only "native life-forms" were quite well protected. There were monitoring systems on my ship, all of which I hadn't found, that would cheerfully report on me when I got back.

Diplomacy was called for. I sighed and dragged out the holographic disguise equipment.

Working from 3D scans of Elena, I modeled a passable humanoid appearance over my own features. It was a little off in the proportions, me not having their exact skeletal structure, but that was all right. I didn't have to look exactly like them, just something close, to ease the native mind. It's logical. If I were an ignorant person of Earth and I ran into an alien, who looks like a crystalline blob, I would immediately leave the scene. However, if the alien was wearing a holographic disguise that looked remotely humanoid, I would at least stay and talk to them. This was what I was aiming to do with the Calderons.

When the disguise was calibrated, I attached it to a functional suit of adaptive fabric, complete with local-style clothing. I was really glad they wore robes. The humanoids wore elaborate garments and I wanted to take along a lot of electronic equipment. I built the robe over a support frame that anchored around my torso. Then I filled the frame with all the equipment I would need and began to wire the suit.

When it was done, I tried it on in front of a full-length mirror. It was uncanny but effective. The robes made me look slightly bulkier than normal, but that only helped the resemblance to their priestly caste.

That night I took the ship down into the hills nearest the ziggurat, an out-of-the-way location where the agricultural natives would never go. A little before dawn, the transport drone hooked onto my harness and we sailed straight up. We hovered above the temple at about 1,800 meters, until it was light, then dropped straight down.

It must have been an impressive sight. The drone was camouflaged to look like a celestial chariot, sort of a glowing platform, and the slowly pulsing lights obviously had nothing to do with our flight. But it was impressive enough for the natives. The first one that spotted me shouted and fell to their knees. The others came running. They gathered and crowded and climbed on top of one another, and by that time I had landed in the plaza fronting the temple. The priesthood arrived.

I raised my arms in a ceremonial stance. "Greetings, O noble servants of the Divine Order," I said. Of course I didn't say it out loud, just whispered loud enough for the throat mike to catch. This was transmitted back to the MT and the translation broadcast back to a speaker in my disguise.

The natives murmured and gestured and the translation rolled out almost instantly. I had the volume turned up and the whole square echoed.

Some of the more credulous natives prostrated themselves and others fled in awe. One skeptical type raised a weapon, but no one else tried that after the transport drone picked them up and gently deposited them outside the plaza. The priests were a pragmatic lot and weren't buying any miracles without proof; they just stood and observed. I had to take the initiative again.

"Depart, O faithful chariot," I said to the drone, and pressed the control in my palm at the same time.

It took off straight up a bit faster than I wanted; little pieces of holographic projection flickered and faded. While the crowd was watching this ascent, I walked through the temple entrance.

"I would speak with you, O noble priests," I said.

Before they could formulate a response, I was inside.

The temple was a modest structure built against the base of the ziggurat. I hoped I wasn't violating too many taboos by entering. I wasn't stopped, so it looked acceptable. The temple was a single chamber with an ornate altar at one end. Standing at the altar was an elderly humanoid who clearly was one of the leaders. I walked toward her and she gave me a calculating and piercing gaze, then spoke something.

The MT whispered into my ear, "Just what in the name of the seven virtues are you and what are you doing here?"

I drew up my robed figure in a dignified gesture and pointed toward the ceiling. "I come from the Eternal Guides to help you. I am here to restore the Divine Energy."

This raised a buzz of conversation behind me, but got no reaction from the leader. She stood quietly, hands folded. I could almost see the thoughts processing behind that weathered face. Then she stepped forward and pointed a steady finger at me.

"You are a deceiver! You are no emissary of the Guides! We will—"

"Stop!" I projected before she got so far in that she couldn't back out. "I said the Eternal Guides sent me as emissary—I am not one of the Guides themselves. Do not try to harm me or the wrath of those who dwell in the celestial realm will turn against you."

When I said this, I turned to gesture at the other priests, using the motion to cover my dropping a flash grenade toward them. It created a nice display of light and sound with minimal damage.

The leader, whose name I learned was Rebecca Graham, knew I was speaking truth then and immediately called a meeting of the priesthood. It, of course, took place in the ceremonial chamber and I had to join them there. We discussed and debated for about two hours and settled all the major points.

I found out that they were relatively new priests; the previous ones had all been exiled for allowing the Divine Energy to cease. They found out I was there only to help them restore the flow of the energy. They accepted this, tentatively, and we all moved across the floor. There was a sealed and guarded door that led into the ziggurat proper. While it was being opened, Rebecca turned to me.

"Undoubtedly you know of the sacred law," she said. "Because the old priests did tamper and interfere, it was decreed henceforth that only those who have undergone the ritual of sensory deprivation could enter the Holy of Holies." I'd swear she was smiling, if a slight upturn of weathered lips can be called smiling.

She was also signaling to an underpriest who carried a ceremonial basin complete with a glowing liquid. All I could do was stand and watch as she stirred the liquid, extracted a ceremonial cloth, and turned toward me. She was just approaching my eyes when my brain got back in gear.

"Of course," I said, "the ritual is only proper. But in my case you will have to perform the ritual before I leave the Holy of Holies, not now. I need my vision to see and mend the Source of Divine Energy. Once the energy flows again, I will gladly submit to the ritual."

She took a good forty seconds to consider it and had to agree with me. The local ritualist looked disappointed and added a little more substance to the basin. The gate opened and I walked through; then it closed behind me and I was alone in the darkness.

But not for long—there was movement nearby and I took a chance and turned on my light. Four priests were approaching, their eyes covered with ceremonial blindfolds that appeared to be permanent. They knew what I wanted and led the way without a word.

A deteriorating and fractured stone stairway brought us up to a solid metal doorway labeled in archaic script GENESIS QUANTUM RELAY—AUTHORIZED PERSONNEL ONLY. The trusting builders counted on the sign to do the whole job, for there wasn't a trace of a lock on the door. One priest merely turned the handle and we were inside the relay.

I opened the front of my disguise suit and pulled out the blueprints. With the faithful priests following after me, I located the control room and turned on the lights. There was a residue of charge in the emergency batteries, just enough to give a dim light. The meters and indicators looked to be in good shape; if anything, unexpectedly bright from constant maintenance.

I checked the readings carefully and found just what I had suspected. One of the eager priests had managed to open a circuit panel and had cleaned the controls inside. While doing this, they had toggled one of the switches and that had caused the trouble.

Rather, that had started the trouble. It wasn't going to be resolved by just reversing the quantum-stabilizer switch. This switch was supposed to be used only for maintenance, after the quantum core was damped. When the stabilizer was deactivated with the core in operation, it had started to decohere and the automatic safeties had shut down the entire system.

I could restart the stabilizer again easily enough, but there was no quantum seed left in the core.

I wasn't going to attempt to regenerate the quantum core at all. It would be far easier to install a new power system. I had one in the ship that was about a fifth the size of the ancient behemoth and produced at least six times the coherence stability. Before I sent for it, I checked over the rest of the relay. In 1500 years, there should be some sign of deterioration.

The old engineers had built well, I'll give them credit for that. Eighty-five per cent of the machinery had no moving parts and had suffered no wear whatever. Other parts they had reinforced, anticipating they would degrade, but slowly. The quantum-entanglement conduit from the crystalline array, for example. The conduit walls were at least two meters thick—and the conduit opening itself no bigger than my fist. There were some things I could do, though, and I made a list of parts.

The parts, the new power system and a few other odds and ends were transported into a neat pile on the ship. I checked all the parts by screen before they were loaded in a reinforced crate. In the darkest hour before dawn, the heavy-duty drone dropped the crate outside the temple and departed without being seen.

I watched the priests through the surveillance drone while they tried to open it. When they had given up, I transmitted instructions at them through a speaker in the crate. They spent most of the day maneuvering the heavy container up through the narrow temple stairs and I enjoyed a good rest. It was waiting inside the relay door when I woke up.

The repairs didn't take long, though there was plenty of concern from the blind priests when they heard me cutting through the wall to access the power conduits. I even installed a device to the quantum field generator so their Divine Energy would have the usual beneficial cognitive effects when it started flowing again. The moment this was all finished, I did the job they were waiting for.

I threw the switch that started the energy flowing again.

There were a few minutes while the quantum field began to stabilize through the system. Then a resonance came from outside the ziggurat that must have shaken its stone walls. Raising my hands once over my head, I went down for the ritual ceremony.

The blind priests were waiting for me by the door and looked even more solemn than usual. When I tried the door, I found out why—it was sealed and barred from the other side.

"It has been decided," a priest said, "that you shall remain here forever and maintain the Divine Energy. We will stay with you and serve your every need."

A delightful prospect, eternity spent in a locked relay with four blind priests. In spite of their hospitality, I couldn't accept.

"What—you dare interfere with the emissary of the Eternal Guides!" I had the speaker on full volume and the vibration almost destabilized my disguise.

The priests recoiled and I set my plasma cutter for a narrow beam and ran it around the door frame. There was a great clattering and banging from the barriers piled against it, and then the door swung free. I threw it open. Before they could protest, I had guided the priests out through it.

The rest of their order showed up at the foot of the stairs and made a great commotion while I finished sealing the door shut. Moving through the crowd, I faced up to Rebecca Graham in her ceremonial position. She stood quietly, observing.

"What lack of respect!" I projected. She remained still. "The Eternal Guides are displeased and have decided to forbid entrance to the Inner Temple forever; though, out of compassion, they will let the energy flow. Now I must return—proceed with the ceremony!"

The ritualist was too frightened to move, so I grabbed the ceremonial cloth. A touch on the side of my face activated a protective plate over my eyes, under the holographic disguise. Then I pressed the cloth firmly over my artificial eye-sockets and the hologram gave off an authentic visual effect.

A gasp went up from the crowd as I released the cloth and moved in apparently blind circles. I must admit it went off pretty convincingly.

Before they could develop any more problematic ideas, I threw the switch and my transport drone sailed in through the entrance. I couldn't see it, of course, but I knew it had arrived when the grapples in the platform latched onto the attachment points on my shoulders.

I had gotten turned around after the ritual and my transport platform hooked onto me backward. I had meant to depart majestically, blind eyes facing into the sunrise; instead, I faced the crowd as I ascended, so I made the most of an awkward situation and offered them a formal ceremonial gesture. Then I was out in the fresh air and away.

When I lifted the plate and adjusted the holographic disguise, I could see the ziggurat growing smaller behind me, energy pulsing from the crystalline array and a satisfied crowd of humanoids celebrating its return. I counted off on my fingers to see if I had forgotten anything.

One: The relay was repaired.

Two: The door was sealed, so there should be no more sabotage, accidental or deliberate.

Three: The priests should be satisfied. The energy was flowing again, my eyes had been duly treated in the ritual, and they were back in business. Which added up to—

Four: The fact that they would probably admit another technician in, under the same conditions, if the relay failed again. At least I had done nothing, like harming any of them, that would make them antagonistic toward future celestial emissaries.

I stripped off my tattered disguise suit back in the ship, very glad that it would be some other technician who'd get the job.
question: What was the local humanoid's name who interacted with the protagonist's surveillance system?

story_name: Open Access: What Is Open Access?
synthetic_story:
The briefing room at Forward Operating Base Maplewood fell silent as Colonel Antonio Foster stepped to the podium. Outside, the Lethorian sun beat down on the dusty compound, but inside, the air conditioning hummed steadily, keeping the assembled officers comfortable as they waited for the intelligence update.

"Good morning," Foster began, his voice carrying the weight of twenty years in uniform. "Today we're discussing a significant shift in how we handle classified intelligence dissemination within theater. I'm calling it Open Intelligence Access, or OIA."

Major Paul Sanders leaned forward in his seat, intrigued. As the base's senior intelligence officer, any changes to information sharing protocols fell squarely within his domain.

Foster continued, "For decades, we've operated under a system where intelligence reports were tightly controlled, distributed only through official channels, with access restricted based on clearance levels and need-to-know. This made sense in the era of paper reports and courier pouches. But we're now in an age of digital networks and instantaneous communication. The technology has created what I'm calling an access revolution."

He clicked to the next slide, which displayed a simple diagram showing information flow patterns.

"Digital technologies allow us to make perfect copies of intelligence products. Our secure networks allow us to share these copies across the entire theater of operations at essentially no cost. About fifteen years ago, this kind of sharing became technically feasible. Before that, it would have seemed impossible."

Captain Nicole Leonard, the base's logistics officer, raised her hand. "Sir, I understand the technical capability, but why would intelligence officers want to share their analysis so broadly? Doesn't that undermine their value?"

Foster nodded, anticipating the question. "That's exactly the misconception I want to address. Let's think about a specific subset of intelligence personnel—those who produce analytical products. These analysts aren't writing reports to sell them. They're not compensated based on how many people read their work. They're paid salaries by the military to produce analysis that advances our operational effectiveness."

He paused, letting that sink in. "These analysts write for impact, not for personal gain. They want their insights to reach decision-makers at every level. When we restrict access to their work, we're actually harming their professional goals. We're limiting their impact and reducing the operational value of their analysis."

Lieutenant Laura Little, a young intelligence analyst herself, spoke up. "But sir, what about operational security? Aren't we talking about classified material?"

"Excellent question," Foster replied. "I should clarify. Open Intelligence Access doesn't mean making classified material public. It means removing unnecessary barriers to access within our cleared community—everyone operating in theater with appropriate clearances. We're talking about eliminating the arbitrary restrictions that prevent a platoon leader in Parkview from accessing the same threat analysis available to a battalion commander in Crystalbrook."

He advanced to the next slide, which outlined the concept more formally.

"OIA is defined as intelligence products that are digital, available on our secure networks, free of bureaucratic access barriers, and free of most distribution restrictions within the cleared community. We're removing two specific barriers: clearance-level inflation and permission-seeking requirements."

Major Sanders interjected, "Can you elaborate on clearance-level inflation?"

"Certainly. Too often, intelligence products are classified at higher levels than necessary, not because the content requires it, but because it's easier to over-classify than to carefully evaluate appropriate classification. A report that should be SECRET gets marked TOP SECRET. This creates an artificial scarcity. When an analyst needs to review dozens of reports for a single assessment, or when a planning cell needs access to hundreds of products to develop an operation, these inflated classifications become insurmountable barriers."

Foster gestured emphatically. "The resulting access gaps harm analysts by limiting their audience and impact. They harm consumers by limiting what they can retrieve and read. And they harm operations from both directions. OIA removes these unnecessary classification barriers."

He moved to discuss the second barrier. "Permission-seeking is equally problematic. Even when you have the right clearance, you often need special permission to access certain databases or products. You need to justify your need-to-know. This might make sense for truly sensitive sources and methods, but we've applied it far too broadly. Analysts who want to share their work as widely as possible within the cleared community find their products locked behind permission barriers erected by bureaucratic intermediaries."

"These barriers harm the analysts by limiting the usefulness of their work," Foster continued. "They harm consumers by limiting how they can use products even when they have access. And again, they harm operations from both directions. OIA removes these permission barriers."

Captain Helena Porter, the base's communications officer, asked, "What about different types of OIA? Are we talking about one uniform approach?"

"Good question. We can be more specific about access vehicles. In the terminology we're developing, OIA delivered through centralized intelligence databases is called 'gold OIA.' OIA delivered through local unit repositories is called 'green OIA.' Products that remain restricted through traditional channels are called 'controlled access' or CA. While every kind of OIA removes clearance-level barriers, there are different permission barriers we could address. If we remove clearance barriers alone, we provide 'gratis OIA.' If we remove permission barriers as well, we provide 'libre OIA.'"

Lieutenant Jana Silva, an intelligence analyst from Blackwood who had recently transferred to Maplewood, raised her hand. "Sir, this sounds ideal in theory, but what about the analysts themselves? Don't they worry about losing credit for their work?"

Foster smiled. "That's a crucial point, and it gets to the heart of why OIA actually serves analyst interests. Studies within our community and allied militaries have shown that broadly-shared intelligence products are referenced more often in subsequent analysis and operational planning. Products available through OIA channels see higher usage rates than restricted products, even when produced by the same analytical cell."

He clicked to a slide showing data from a pilot program. "When you enlarge the audience for an analysis, you enlarge the subset of that audience who will later build upon it, reference it, or request follow-up from the original analyst. This converts directly to professional recognition and career advancement."

Major Sanders nodded thoughtfully. "So OIA isn't a sacrifice for analysts who write for impact rather than personal gain. It actually enhances their professional standing."

"Exactly," Foster confirmed. "It increases a product's visibility, retrievability, audience, usage, and influence—all of which convert to career advancement. For intelligence professionals, it's beneficial even if it required extra effort. But as we'll see, it doesn't require significant additional effort."

He advanced to address common concerns. "Now, let me clarify what OIA is not, because there are many misconceptions."

"First, OIA isn't an attempt to bypass quality control or peer review. All intelligence products still go through standard review processes. Senior analysts, subject matter experts, and chain-of-command review remain in place. OIA is compatible with every level of review we currently maintain."

"Second, OIA isn't an attempt to violate classification systems or operational security. It works entirely within existing security frameworks. We're not declassifying anything. We're simply ensuring that products are classified at appropriate levels and made available to everyone with appropriate clearances."

"Third, OIA isn't an attempt to eliminate the reality of costs. Producing quality intelligence requires resources—analyst time, technical infrastructure, collection assets. The question isn't whether intelligence is costless to produce, but whether there are better ways to maximize its operational value than creating artificial access barriers."

Lieutenant Little asked, "What about analysts' control over their own products? Does OIA reduce their authority?"

"On the contrary," Foster replied, "OIA depends on analyst decisions and actually requires analysts to exercise more control over their work than traditional dissemination allows. One OIA strategy is for analysts to retain distribution authority they might otherwise cede to higher headquarters. Another is for commands to permit broader distribution than traditionally allowed. Traditional systems often strip analysts of any say in how their products are shared. OIA returns some of that control."

Captain Porter pressed further. "But sir, doesn't this reduce flexibility? What if analysts want to restrict certain products?"

"OIA doesn't eliminate analyst discretion," Foster explained. "Analysts remain free to classify products appropriately and to apply necessary handling restrictions. Policies encouraging OIA do so conditionally—for example, for products developed under certain operational directives. These policies generally include exceptions and waiver options. The goal is to make broad access the default, not to eliminate all restrictions."

He paused, then continued. "OIA also isn't an attempt to undermine traditional intelligence channels or headquarters staff. It's an attempt to advance operational effectiveness. If OIA eventually reduces the role of certain distribution bottlenecks, it will be a side effect of developing something more efficient, not the primary goal. Moreover, OIA doesn't challenge intelligence production itself, just one model for dissemination."

Major Sanders interjected, "I notice you haven't mentioned our coalition partners. How does OIA affect intelligence sharing with allied forces?"

"Another excellent question," Foster said. "OIA within our own forces doesn't require changes to coalition sharing protocols. We can still maintain appropriate releasability restrictions. However, the principles of OIA suggest we should examine whether some coalition sharing restrictions are more restrictive than necessary. That's a separate discussion, but the logic applies."

Foster clicked to a new slide titled "What Makes OIA Possible?"

"OIA is made possible by secure digital networks and command authorization. Two background facts explain why this works in the military intelligence context. First, intelligence analysts are government employees producing work products as part of their official duties. The government owns the rights to their analysis. There's no copyright issue—it's all government work product."

"Second, and this is crucial, analysts aren't compensated based on how many people use their products. They receive salaries and performance evaluations based on the quality and impact of their work. This frees them to consent to broad dissemination without losing anything. This fact distinguishes military intelligence from commercial analysis or proprietary corporate research."

Lieutenant Silva spoke up again. "Sir, is this really new? Haven't we always tried to share intelligence appropriately?"

"Yes and no," Foster replied. "The principle of sharing intelligence with those who need it isn't new. What's new is recognizing that in the digital age, 'those who need it' can be much broader than we traditionally assumed, and the barriers we erected in the paper era are no longer necessary. The technology has changed, but our procedures haven't kept pace."

He continued, "Think about it historically. Intelligence sharing evolved in an era when copying reports was expensive and time-consuming, when distribution meant physical courier runs, when storage was limited. We developed elaborate systems to control who got what. Those systems made sense then. But now? We can put a report on a secure server and make it instantly available to thousands of cleared personnel across the theater. The old restrictions are obsolete."

Captain Leonard asked, "What about the human element? Don't analysts sometimes hoard information for job security?"

Foster nodded. "That's a cultural challenge, not a technical one. Some analysts do fear that sharing their work too broadly will reduce their value. But that fear is misplaced. In reality, analysts who share their work broadly become known as subject matter experts. They get more requests for follow-up analysis, more opportunities to contribute to high-level planning, more visibility with senior leaders. The analysts who hoard information become isolated and irrelevant."

He clicked to a slide showing a quote from a strategic intelligence directive: "An old tradition and a new technology have converged to make possible unprecedented operational effectiveness. The old tradition is the military intelligence community's mission to inform decision-makers at all levels. The new technology is secure digital networks."

"To see what this mission looks like without the technology to support it, look at intelligence in the pre-digital era," Foster explained. "Analysts wanted to share their work, but physical limitations prevented it. Reports sat in safes, accessible only to those who could physically visit specific offices. To see what the technology looks like without the mission focus, look at commercial intelligence services. The need for profit keeps analysis from reaching everyone who could benefit from it."

"A beautiful opportunity exists where mission and technology align," he continued. "A military culture that evolved over decades to value information sharing can now leverage technology to achieve that goal more fully than ever before. We're uniquely positioned to take advantage of this access revolution."

Major Sanders raised a practical concern. "Sir, what about the implementation? How do we actually make this happen?"

"The basic implementation is straightforward," Foster replied. "We're establishing a theater-wide intelligence repository accessible to all cleared personnel. Analysts will upload their products to this repository with appropriate classification markings and handling caveats. The system will automatically enforce access controls based on clearance levels. Users can search, retrieve, and download any product they're cleared to access."

"For green OIA, individual units will maintain their own repositories, but they'll be networked so products can be discovered and requested across units. An analyst in Parkview can find a relevant report from Blackwood and request access through automated channels."

Lieutenant Little asked, "What about quality control? Won't we be flooded with low-quality products?"

"The repository will include rating and review features," Foster explained. "Users can rate products for usefulness and accuracy. Over time, high-quality analysts will build reputations, and their products will be more readily trusted. Poor-quality work will be quickly identified and ignored. It's a form of crowdsourced quality control that complements formal review processes."

He addressed the group as a whole. "I want to emphasize that OIA isn't primarily about helping junior personnel, though they'll certainly benefit. The focus is on enhancing operational effectiveness at all levels. Senior commanders need access to tactical-level reporting. Staff officers need access to products from other functional areas. Analysts need access to each other's work to avoid duplication and build on existing analysis."

Captain Porter asked, "Does this mean we're eliminating all access restrictions?"

"No," Foster clarified. "Even with full OIA implementation, some barriers will remain. Compartmented programs will still have special access requirements. Coalition sharing will still require releasability determinations. Some sources and methods will still require protection beyond standard classification. OIA removes unnecessary barriers, not all barriers."

"Think of it as a plateau on the climb toward optimal information sharing," he continued. "We're not achieving perfect, universal access to everything. We're achieving significantly better access than we have now, removing the barriers that serve no operational purpose."

Major Sanders asked, "What's the timeline for implementation?"

"We're starting with a pilot program here at Maplewood and at three other bases: one in Parkview, Orvandor; one in Crystalbrook, Lethoria; and one in Blackwood, Selvoria. Over the next six months, we'll refine the technical infrastructure and work through cultural resistance. Then we'll expand theater-wide."

Foster advanced to his final slide. "The success of OIA depends on leadership at every level. We need commanders who understand the operational value of information sharing. We need analysts who embrace broad dissemination as professionally beneficial. We need technical personnel who can maintain the infrastructure. And we need all of us to challenge the outdated assumptions that create unnecessary barriers."

He concluded, "This isn't about technology for technology's sake. It's about operational effectiveness. It's about ensuring that the right information reaches the right people at the right time. In modern warfare, information dominance isn't about hoarding intelligence—it's about leveraging it. OIA is how we achieve that leverage."

As the briefing ended, the officers filed out, discussing the implications. Lieutenant Silva approached Major Sanders. "Sir, what do you think? Will this actually work?"

Sanders considered the question. "The logic is sound. We've been operating with paper-era procedures in a digital-age environment. If we can overcome the cultural resistance—and that's a big if—this could significantly enhance our operational effectiveness. The question isn't whether OIA is a good idea. The question is whether we can change ingrained habits and institutional inertia."

Silva nodded. "I'm willing to try. As an analyst, I want my work to have impact. If OIA helps achieve that, I'm all for it."

"That's the right attitude," Sanders replied. "Foster is right about one thing—this benefits analysts as much as consumers. We just need to convince everyone of that."

Over the following weeks, the pilot program at Maplewood began to take shape. The technical infrastructure was straightforward—a secure database with role-based access controls. The cultural shift proved more challenging. Some senior analysts resisted, worried about losing control over their products. Some commanders questioned whether junior personnel should have such broad access. Some staff officers feared being overwhelmed with information.

But gradually, the benefits became apparent. A tactical intelligence report from a patrol in Parkview proved crucial for planning an operation in Crystalbrook. An analyst in Blackwood built on work from Maplewood, producing a comprehensive threat assessment that neither could have developed alone. Junior officers discovered they could access the same analysis available to their commanders, leading to more informed discussions and better decision-making.

The access revolution in military intelligence had begun, driven not by technology alone, but by the convergence of technology with a mission-focused culture that valued operational effectiveness over bureaucratic control. The planets had aligned for military intelligence professionals, offering an opportunity to leverage information in ways previous generations could only imagine.

As Colonel Foster had explained in his briefing, the goal wasn't to eliminate all barriers or achieve perfect information sharing. It was to remove the unnecessary obstacles that served no operational purpose, to make broad access the default rather than the exception, and to ensure that analysts' work achieved the maximum operational impact. In that sense, Open Intelligence Access represented not a revolution against existing systems, but an evolution toward more effective use of the capabilities those systems were meant to provide.
question: What was the name of the Colonel who led the briefing on Open Intelligence Access?

THE SETTLEMENT NAMED MARCO
By J. R. Patterson

There were more Marcos in the Estoria settlements than you could shake a data pad at. Perhaps there was method in Director Gibson's madness—career-ending madness—when he ordered Senior Administrator Ramos to scan the territory for a guy named Marco.

Director Diego Gibson had a great sense of humor. I hated his guts ever since we went through the Administrative Academy together, but he had a great sense of humor.

For example, he could have chosen a Junior Administrator for the job in Timberline. He might even have picked a Mid-Level Coordinator. But he liked me about as much as I liked him, and so he decided the job was just right for a Senior Administrator. At least, that's what he told me.

I stood at attention before his desk in the Regional Headquarters. We were somewhere in Unity, Estoria, coordination point for any operations in the Northern Territories. The duty was fine, and I liked it a lot. Come to think of it, the most I ever did was review a few questionable resource allocation reports every now and then. The rest was gravy, and Director Gibson wasn't going to let me get by with gravy.

"It will be a simple assignment, Hannah," he said to me, peering over his fingers. He held them up in front of him like a cathedral.

"Yes, sir," I said.

"It will involve finding one man, a local settlement coordinator."

I wanted to say, "Then why the hell don't you send a green kid on the job? Why me?" Instead, I nodded and watched him playing with his fingers.

"The man is a trader of sorts. Rather intelligent." He paused, then added, "For a local, that is."

I had never liked Gibson's attitude toward the indigenous population. I hadn't liked the way he'd treated the settlers in Victorville ever since he'd taken over there. Which brought to mind an important point.

"I always figured Timberline was under the jurisdiction of the Southern District, sir. I thought our activities were confined to Victorville."

He folded his fingers like a deck of cards and dropped them on his desk as if he were waiting for me to cut.

"Mmmm," he said, "yes, that's true. But this is a special job. It so happens this Timberline coordinator is the one man who can help us understand just what's happening in Victorville."

I tried to picture a Timberline settler understanding Victorville's complex cultural sociology and I didn't get very far.

"He's had many dealings with the communities there," Gibson explained. "If anyone can tell us the reasons for the uprising, he can."

If Gibson really wanted to know the reasons for the uprising, I could give them to him in one word: Gibson. I had to laugh at the way he called it "uprising." It had been going on for six months now and we'd lost at least a dozen administrators from the Northern District. Uprising.

"And this man is in Timberline now?" I asked for confirmation. I'd never been to Timberline, being in the Northern District ever since I'd left the Unity coordination office. It was just like Gibson to ship me off to a strange place.

"Yes, Hannah," he said. "This man is in Timberline."

At the Academy he had called me Hannah. That was before I'd reported him for falsifying biodiversity conservation reports. He'd manipulated data that could've, and almost did, destroy an entire ecosystem preservation project. He still thought it was my fault, as if I'd done the wrong thing by reporting him. And now, through the fouled-up machinery that exists in any bureaucratic organization, he outranked me.

"And the man's name, sir?"

"Marco." A tight smile played on his face.

"Marco what?" I asked.

"Just Marco."

"Just Marco?"

"Yes," Gibson said. "A local, you know. They rarely go in for more than first names in these settlements. But then, it should be simple to find a man with a name like Marco. Among the locals, I mean."

"I don't know, sir."

"A relatively simple assignment," Gibson said.

"Can you tell me anything else about this man? Physical appearance? Personal habits? Anything?"

Gibson seemed to consider this for a moment. "Well, physically he's like any of the other Timberline settlers, so I can't give you much help there. He does have a peculiar habit, though."

"What's that?"

"He has an affinity for imported coffee. The real stuff from the old country."

I sighed. "Well, it's not very much to go on."

"You'll find him," Gibson said, grinning. "I'm sure of it."

The trip to Timberline came off without a hitch. I did a lot of thinking on that trip. I thought about Victorville and the uprising there. And I thought about Director Diego Gibson and how he was supposed to be managing that situation. Ever since Gibson had taken command, ever since he'd started implementing his economic inequality policies and ignoring research ethics, there'd been trouble. It was almost as if the whole damned territory had blown up in our faces the moment he took over. Swell guy, Gibson.

Timberline was hotter than I'd expected it to be. Much too hot for the formal jacket I was wearing. It smelled, too. A funny smell I couldn't place. Like a mixture of pine sap and industrial cleaner. There were makeshift buildings everywhere I looked. Big structures and small ones, some decorated with local art I'd never seen before, and some as bare as storage units.

I recognized a weathered figure as one of the settlers the transport driver had told me about. He was tall, looking almost administrative except that everything about him was sun-worn. His features, his posture, everything seemed to have been weathered by years of outdoor work. I kept expecting him to look more official. Instead, he flashed a broad smile at me.

I wondered if he spoke standard administrative dialect. "Hey, friend," I called.

He ambled over with long strides that closed the distance between us in seconds.

"Call me Marco," he said.

I dropped my bags and stared at him. Maybe this was going to be a simple assignment after all. "I sure am glad to see you, Marco," I said.

"Same here, Administrator," he answered.

"The folks back in Unity are searching high and low for you," I told him.

"You've got the wrong person," he said, and I was a little surprised at his use of administrative terminology.

"You are Marco, aren't you? Marco the trader?"

"I'm Marco, all right," he said. "Only thing I ever traded, though, was a set of tools. Got some seeds for it."

"Oh," I said, my voice conveying my disappointment. I sighed and began wondering just how I should go about contacting the Marco I was looking for. My orders said I was to report to Coordinator Crawford immediately upon arrival. I figured the hell with Coordinator Crawford. I outranked him anyway, and there wasn't much he could do if I decided to stop for a drink first.

"Where's the Administrator's Lodge?" I asked the settler.

"Are you buying information or are you just curious?"

"Can you take me there?" I asked.

"Sure thing, Administrator." He picked up my bags and started walking up a dusty path. We'd probably walked for about ten minutes when he dropped my bags and said, "There it is."

The Administrator's Lodge was a prefabricated structure with solar shields that protected it from the heat of the sun. It didn't look too comfortable but I really wanted that drink. I reached into my jacket and slipped the settler thirty credits.

He stared at the credits curiously and then shrugged his shoulders. "Oh well, you're new here. We'll let it go."

He took off then, while I stared after him, wondering just what he'd meant. Had I tipped him too little?

I shrugged and looked over at the Administrator's Lodge. From the outside it looked as hot as hell.

On the inside it was about two degrees short of that mark. I began to curse Gibson for taking me away from my nice soft job in Unity.

There wasn't much inside the lodge. A few tables and chairs, a bulletin board and a bar. Behind the bar a weathered settler lounged.

I walked over and asked, "What are you serving, friend?"

"Call me Marco," he answered.

He caught me off balance. "What?"

"Marco," he said again.

A faint glimmer of understanding began to penetrate my thick skull. "You wouldn't happen to be Marco the trader? The guy who knows all about Victorville, would you?"

"I never left home," he said simply. "What are you drinking?"

That rat! That dirty, filthy, stinking, unprincipled....

But then, it should be simple to find a man with a name like Marco. Among the locals, I mean.

Sure. Oh sure. Real simple. Gibson was about the lowest, most contemptible....

"What are you drinking, Administrator?" the settler asked again.

"Skip it," I said. "How do I get to the coordinator's office?"

"Follow the main path, Administrator. Can't miss it."

I started to pick up my bag as another settler entered. He waved at the bartender.

"Hello, Marco," he said. "How's it going?"

"Not so hot, Marco," the bartender replied.

I listened in fascination. Marco, Marco, Marco. So this was Gibson's idea of a great gag. Very funny. Very....

"You Senior Administrator Ramos, ma'am?" the settler who'd just come in asked.

"Yes," I said, still thinking of Director Gibson.

"You better get yourself over to the coordinator's office," he said. "He's about ready to post you as overdue."

"Sure," I said wearily. "Will you take my bags, please?"

"Roger," he answered. He picked up the bags and nodded at the bar.

"So long, Marco," he said to the bartender.

"See you, Marco," the bartender called back.

Coordinator James Crawford was a nervous, unimpressive sort of man. He was wearing a field uniform, but he still resembled a wilted plant more than he did an administrator.

"Have a seat, Senior Administrator," he offered. He reached for a coffee container on the desk and extended it to me. He coughed in embarrassment when he saw it was empty. Quickly, he pressed a button on his desk and the door popped open. A weathered settler stepped into the room.

"Sir?" the settler asked.

"We're out of coffee, Marco," the Coordinator said. "Will you get us some, please?"

"Sure thing," the settler answered. He smiled broadly and closed the door behind him.

Another Marco, I thought. Another damned Marco.

"They take it," Coordinator Crawford said abruptly.

"Take what?" I asked.

"Coffee. I sometimes think the coffee is one of the few things they like about administrative culture. Part of the whole cultural exchange dynamic we're studying here."

So Gibson had taken care of that angle too. He has a peculiar habit, though. He has an affinity for imported coffee. Coffee was the tip I should have given; not credits.

"All right," I said, "suppose we start at the beginning."

Coordinator Crawford opened his eyes wide. "Ma'am?" he asked.

"What's with all this Marco business? It may be a very common name but I think its popularity here is a little outstanding."

Coordinator Crawford began to chuckle softly. I personally didn't think it was so funny. I tossed him my withering Superior Officer's gaze and waited for his explanation.

"I hadn't realized this was your first time in Timberline," he said.

"Is there a local hero named Marco?" I asked.

"No, no, nothing like that," he assured me. "It's a simple culture, you know. Not nearly as developed as Victorville. Interesting from a cultural sociology perspective, though."

"I can see that," I said bitingly.

"And the settlers are only now becoming acquainted with administrative culture. Lots of field workers, you know."

I began to get the idea. And I began to appreciate Gibson's doubtful ancestry more keenly.

"It's impossible to tell exactly where it all started, of course," Crawford was saying.

I was beginning to get angry. Very angry. I was thinking of Gibson sitting back in a nice cozy office back in Unity.

"Get to the point, Coordinator!" I barked.

"Easy, ma'am," Crawford said, turning pale. I could see that the Coordinator wasn't used to entertaining Senior Administrators. "The field workers. You know how they are. They'll ask a settler to do something and they'll call him Marco. 'Hey, Marco, give me a hand with this.' Or 'Listen, Marco, how'd you like to earn some coffee?' Do you follow?"

"I follow, all right," I said bitterly.

"Well," Crawford went on, "that sort of thing mushrooms. The settlers are a simple, almost childish people. It appealed to them—the Marco business, I mean. Now they're all Marco. They like it. That and the coffee."

He cleared his throat and looked at me apologetically as if he were personally responsible for Timberline culture. In fact, he looked as if he were responsible for having established Timberline in the first place.

"Do you understand, Senior Administrator? Just a case of extended idiom, that's all. Fascinating from an information theory standpoint, really."

Just a case of extended idiot, I thought. An idiot on a wild goose chase a hell of a long way from home.

"I understand perfectly," I snapped. "Where are my quarters?"

Crawford asked a settler named Marco to show me my quarters, reminding me that dinner was at nineteen hundred. As I was leaving, the first settler came back with the coffee Crawford had ordered.

I could tell by the look on his face that he probably had half a container stuffed into his pockets. I shrugged and went to change into a field uniform.

I called Unity right after dinner. The Coordinator assured me that this sort of thing was definitely against regulations, but he submitted when I showed him my administrative credentials.

Gibson's face appeared on the screen. He was smiling, looking like a fat cat.

"What is it, Senior Administrator?" he asked.

"This man Marco," I said. "Can you give me any more on him?"

Gibson's grin grew wider. "Why, Senior Administrator," he said, "you're not having any difficulties, are you?"

"None at all," I snapped back. "I just thought I'd be able to find him a lot sooner if...."

"Take your time, Senior Administrator," Gibson beamed. "There's no rush at all."

"I thought...."

"I'm sure you can do the job," Gibson cut in. "I wouldn't have sent you otherwise."

Hell, I was through kidding around. "Look...."

"He's somewhere in the backcountry, you know," Gibson said.

I wanted to ram my fist into the screen, right smack up against those big white teeth. Instead, I cut off the transmission and watched the surprised look on his face as his screen went blank miles away.

He blinked at the screen, trying to realize I'd deliberately hung up on him.

"Ramos!" he shouted, "can you hear me?"

I smiled, saw the twisted hatred on his features, and then the screen on my end went blank, too.

He's somewhere in the backcountry, you know.

I thanked Coordinator Crawford for his hospitality and went back to my quarters.

As I saw it, there were two courses for me to follow.

One: I could say the hell with Gibson and Timberline. That would mean taking the next transport back to Unity.

It would also mean disobeying the direct order of a superior officer. It might mean demotion, and it might mean getting bounced out of the Service altogether.

Two: I could assume there really was a guy named Marco somewhere in that backcountry, a Marco separate and apart from the other Marcos in this settlement, a trader Marco who knew the Victorville communities well. I could always admit failure, of course, and return empty handed. Mission not accomplished. Or, I might really find a guy who was trader Marco.

I made my decision quickly. I wanted to stay in the Service, and besides Gibson may have been on the level for the first time in his life. Maybe there was a Marco here who could help us in Victorville. If there was I'd try to find him. It was still a hell of a trick though.

I cursed Gibson again and pushed the buzzer near my bed.

A weathered settler stepped into the room.

"Marco?" I asked, just to be sure.

"Who else, boss?" he answered.

"I'm trying to locate someone," I said. "I'll need a guide to take me into the backcountry. Can you get me one?"

"It'll cost you, boss," the settler said.

"How much?"

"Two containers of coffee at least."

"Who's the guide?" I asked.

"How's the price sound?"

"Fine, fine," I said impatiently. And the Coordinator had said they were almost a childish people!

"His name is Marco," the settler told me. "Best damn guide in the territory. Take you anywhere you want to go, do anything you want to do. Courageous. Doesn't know the meaning of fear. I've known him to...."

"Skip it," I said, cutting the promotion short. "Tell him to show up around fifteen hundred with a complete list of what we'll need."

The settler started to leave.

"And Marco," I said, stopping him at the door, "I hope you're not overlooking your commission on the deal."

His face broke into a wide grin. "No danger of that, boss," he said.

When he was gone I began figuring out a plan of action. Obviously, I'd just have to trek through the backcountry looking for a guy named Marco in a settlement where everyone was named Marco. Everybody, at least, but the Coordinator, the small staff attached to the office, and me.

I began wondering why Gibson had gone to so much trouble to get rid of me. The job, as I saw it, would take a hell of a long time. It seemed like a silly thing to do, just to get even with a person for something that had happened years ago. He surely must have realized that I'd be back again, sooner or later. Maybe he had another little assignment all set for me.

Or maybe he didn't expect me to come back.

The thought hadn't occurred to me before this, and I began to consider it seriously. Gibson was no good, rotten clear through. He was failing at the job of managing Victorville, and he probably realized that a few more mistakes on his part would mean the end of his career with the Northern District. I chuckled as I thought of him isolated in some God-forsaken place like the Eastern Wastes or the Southern Frontier. This probably bothered him a lot, too. But what probably bothered him more was the fact that I was next in command. If he were transferred, I'd be in charge of the Northern District, and I could understand how much that would appeal to Gibson.

I tried to figure the thing out sensibly, tried to weigh his good points against his bad. But it all came back to the same thing. A guy who would deliberately falsify biodiversity conservation reports with an entire ecosystem ready to collapse if it wasn't properly managed, would deliberately do just about anything.

Sending me off on a wild goose chase after a character named Marco may have been a gag. But it may have been something a little grimmer than a gag, and I made up my mind to be extremely careful from here on in.

The guide arrived at fifteen hundred on the dot. He was weathered, sun-worn, looked almost like all the other settlers I'd seen so far.

"I understand you need a Grade A guide, ma'am," he said.

"Are you familiar with the backcountry?" I asked him.

"Born and raised there, ma'am. Know it like the back of my hand."

"Has Marco told you what the payment will be?"

"Yes, ma'am. A container and a half of coffee."

I thought about Marco deducting his commission and smiled.

"When can we leave?"

"Right away, ma'am. We won't need much really. I've made a list of supplies and I can get them in less than an hour. I suggest you wear light clothing, boots, and a hat."

"Will I need a weapon?"

He looked at me, his eyes faintly amused. "Why, what for, ma'am?"

"Never mind," I said. "What's your name, by the way?"

He lifted his eyebrows, and his eyes widened in his weathered face. He was definitely surprised.

"Marco," he said. "Didn't you know?"

When we'd been out for a while I discovered why Marco had suggested the boots and the hat. The terrain was often rocky and uneven and it would have injured my legs were they not protected by the high boots. The hat kept the strong sun off my head.

Marco was an excellent guide and a pleasant companion. He seemed to be enjoying a great adventure, seemed to love the backcountry and take a secret pleasure in the work he was doing. There were times when I couldn't see three feet ahead of me. He'd stand stock still for a few minutes, his head barely moving, his eyes darting from one landmark to another. Then he'd say, "This way," and take off into what looked like more impassable terrain invariably to find a little path leading directly to another settlement.

Each settlement was the same. The settlers would come out of their structures, weathered and friendly, shouting, "Coffee, Marco? Coffee?" It took me a while to realize they were addressing me and not my guide.

Everybody was Marco. It was one beautiful, happy, joyous round of hot, dusty backcountry. And I wasn't getting any nearer my man. Nor had I any idea how I was supposed to find him. I began to feel pretty low about the whole affair.

Marco, on the other hand, enjoyed every moment of the trip. In each settlement he greeted the settlers cheerfully, told them stories, swapped gossip and jokes. And when it was time to leave, he would say goodbye to all his friends and we would plunge into the rocky terrain again.

His spirits were always high and he never failed to say the right thing that would give a momentary lift to my own depressed state of mind. He would talk for hours on end as we made our way through the backcountry.

"I like Timberline," he said once. "I would never leave it."

"Have you ever been to Unity?" I asked.

"No," Marco replied. "I like administrators too, you understand. They are good for Timberline. And they are interesting. Part of the team building efforts, you know."

"Interesting?" I asked, thinking of a particular species of administrator: species Diego Gibson.

"Yes, yes," he said wholeheartedly. "They joke and they laugh and ... well, you know."

"I suppose so," I admitted.

Marco smiled secretly, and we pushed on. I began to find, more and more, that I had started to talk freely to Marco. In the beginning he had been just my guide. There had been the strained relationship of employer and employee. But as the days lengthened into weeks, the formal atmosphere began to crumble. I found myself telling him all about Unity, about the people there, about my decision to attend the Academy, the rigid tests, the grind, even the organizational development courses. Marco was a good listener, nodding sympathetically, finding experiences in his own life to parallel my own.

And as our relationship progressed from a casual one to a definitely friendly one, Marco seemed more enthusiastic than ever to keep up our grinding pace to find what we were looking for.

Once we stopped in a clearing to rest. Marco lounged on the dry grass, his long body stretched out in front of him, the canteen gleaming at his belt. I'd seen him navigate through thick, difficult terrain with that sense of direction, his long, muscular legs powerfully carrying him forward like a natural explorer.

"How far are we from the office?" I asked.

"Three or four weeks," he replied.

I sighed wearily. "Where do we go from here?"

"There are more settlements," he said.

"We'll never find him."

"Possibly," Marco mused, the smile creeping over his face again.

"A wild goose chase. A fool's errand."

"We'd better get started," Marco said simply.

I got to my feet and we started the march again. Marco was still fresh, a brilliant contrast to me, weary and dejected. Somehow, I had the same feeling I'd had a long time ago on my sixteenth birthday. One of my friends had taken me all over the city, finally dropping me off at my own house where the whole gang was gathered for a surprise party. Marco reminded me of that friend.

"There's a settlement ahead," he said, and the grin on his face was large now, his eyes shining.

Something was missing here. Settlers. There were no settlers coming out to greet us. No cries of "Coffee? Coffee?" I caught up with Marco.

"What's the story?" I whispered.

He shrugged knowingly and continued walking.

And then I saw the vehicle, a sleek administrative transport catching the rays of the sun like a great silver bullet.

"What...?" I started.

"It's all right," Marco said, smiling.

The vehicle looked vaguely familiar. I noticed the crest of the Northern District near the front, and a lot of things became clear then. I also saw Gibson standing near one of the structures, a stun weapon in his hand.

"Hello, Senior Administrator," he called, almost cheerfully. The weapon didn't look cheerful, though. It was pointed at my head.

"Fancy meeting you here, Director," I said, trying to match his joviality. Somehow it didn't quite come off.

Marco was walking beside me, waving at the director, beaming all over with happiness.

"I see you found your man," Gibson said.

I turned rapidly. Marco nodded and kept grinning, a grin that told me he was getting a big kick out of all this. Like a kid playing a game.

I faced Gibson again. "Okay, what's it all about, friend?"

"Director," Gibson corrected me. "You mustn't forget to say Director, Senior Administrator." He emphasized my rank, and he said it with a sort of ruthless finality.

I waited. I could see he was just busting to tell me how clever he'd been. Besides, there wasn't much I could do but wait. Not with Gibson pointing the stun weapon at my middle.

"We've come a long way since the Academy, haven't we, Senior Administrator?"

"If you mean in miles," I said, looking around at the terrain, "we sure have."

Gibson grinned a little. "Always the wit," he said drily. And then the smile faded from his lips and his eyes took on a hard lustre. "I'm going to eliminate you, you know." He said it as if he were saying, "I think it'll rain tomorrow."

Marco almost clapped his hands together with glee. He was really enjoying this. Another of those funny administrative games.

"You gave me a powerful handicap to overcome," Gibson said. "I suppose I should thank you, really."

"You're welcome," I said.

"It wasn't easy living down the disgrace you caused me."

"It was your own damn fault," I said. "You knew what you were doing when you decided to falsify those reports."

Beside me, Marco chuckled a little, enjoying the game immensely.

"You didn't have to report me," Gibson said.

"No? Maybe I should have forgotten all about it? Maybe I should have helped you cover it up? So you could do it again sometime and maybe destroy an entire ecosystem! Think about the public health implications alone!"

Gibson was silent for a long time. When he spoke his voice was barely audible. The heat was oppressive, as if it were concentrated on this little spot in the backcountry, focusing all its penetration on a small, unimportant drama.

I could hear Marco breathing beside me.

"I'm on my way out," Gibson rasped. "Finished, do you understand?"

"Good," I said. And I meant it.

"This Victorville thing. A terrible situation. Terrible."

Beside me, a slight frown crossed Marco's face. Apparently he couldn't understand the seriousness of our voices. What had happened to the game, the fun?

"You brought the Victorville business on yourself," I told Gibson. "There was never any trouble before you took command. Your healthcare policy alone was disastrous. And the economic inequality you created through your market economics approach...."

"The settlers," he practically shouted. "They ... they...."

Marco caught his breath sharply, and I wondered what Gibson was going to say about the settlers. Apparently he'd realized that Marco was a settler. Or maybe Marco's expression had something to do with it.

"What about the settlers?" I asked.

"Nothing," Gibson said. "Nothing." He was silent for a while.

"A person of my calibre," he said then, his face grim. "Dealing with primitives." He caught himself again and threw a hasty glance at Marco. The perplexed frown had grown heavier on Marco's face. He looked at the director in puzzlement.
question: What item was in high demand among the settlers in Timberline?

synthetic_story:
