The morning bells of the Magnolia Province Arcane Academy rang with their usual crystalline clarity, but Valentina Brown barely heard them as she hurried through the enchanted corridors. As Senior Enchantress-in-Charge-of-Spell-Weaving for the prestigious Crystal Dragon Guild, she should have felt secure in her position. Instead, a knot of dread had been growing in her stomach since dawn.

The Guild had changed seven years ago, in what the historians were already calling "The Great Reversal." Before that fateful night, the Crystal Dragon Guild had been managed by experienced enchanters who understood the delicate balance between magical innovation and sustainable practice. They had invested in research, developed new spells carefully, and maintained relationships with kingdoms across the realm. Then the Apprentices' Collective had purchased controlling shares of the Guild's charter stones, and everything had shifted.

Valentina smoothed her worn robes—no longer the fine silks she'd once worn—and checked the time crystal at her wrist. 8:04. Late again. She could already picture Samir Stephens, the workshop overseer, glowering at her from behind his ornate desk. The Collective had installed him to monitor the senior enchanters, ensuring they worked "efficiently" for the apprentices who now owned the Guild.

"Late again, I see," Samir growled as she entered. His voice carried the smug satisfaction of someone who enjoyed wielding even small amounts of power.

"Yes, sir. Just four minutes. The teleportation circles were crowded—"

"So it's just four minutes now, eh?" He slammed his ledger shut. "That's three times this month, Brown. Three demerits. You know what that means for your wage."

Valentina sighed and made her way to her cramped workstation. It wasn't always like this. She remembered when enchanters were respected, when they lived in comfortable towers and could focus on perfecting their craft. Now she shared a tiny apartment in the Elmwood Region with three other displaced professionals, all struggling under the new regime.

The reports on her desk made her stomach sink further. Sales of enchanted items at rock bottom. Major contracts with the Kingdom of Lincoln in Prandoria canceled. The worst performance in seven years. And she knew exactly why.

"Brown!" Samir's voice cracked like a whip. "Master Zhang wants to see you. Now."

Zhang Williams, Grand Master of the Apprentices' Collective, occupied what had once been Valentina's office. The irony wasn't lost on her as she climbed the spiral stairs to the tower's peak. The door bore fresh gold lettering:

CRYSTAL DRAGON GUILD
APPRENTICES' COLLECTIVE
Zhang Williams, Grand Master

His secretary, a nervous young woman, waved her through with a pitying look.

Zhang's massive frame filled the chair behind the desk as he glared at her. The view behind him—the sprawling workshops of the Guild complex, the shimmering practice fields—had once inspired Valentina. Now it only reminded her of what had been lost.

"What exactly do you think you're doing with this Guild, Brown?" Zhang's voice rumbled like distant thunder.

"I'm the Senior Enchantress. I organize the spell-weaving, coordinate with our client kingdoms, integrate our research with production—"

"And you think you do a good job?" Zhang threw a stack of parchments at her. "Look at these reports! Sales collapsing. Major contracts canceled. The worst performance in seven years. You asked for a raise last year, and this is what we get?"

Valentina caught the reports, her hands trembling. "I've been doing everything I can. But we haven't met a production schedule in two years. The apprentices come and go as they please, spend half their time in the lounges practicing basic cantrips instead of working. And that's only part of it—"

She rifled through the parchments. "This contract with the Queenstown City defense force—they dropped us because we haven't developed a new protection spell in six years. Why? Because Research and Development hasn't had funding in six years! What can two underpaid enchanters and a third-rate alchemist produce from a basement laboratory? The Guild built its reputation on magical innovation and careful development. But since the Reversal, you and your council have forced me to focus on cheap, quick enchantments to pay dividends to the apprentices. Now it's all falling apart."

Zhang's face darkened. "So you think we should just hand control back to you enchanters? Let you exploit us again?" He leaned back, his chair creaking. "We fought hard for this Guild, Brown. I was there from the beginning—I helped organize the whole movement. The apprentices own the charter stones now. Charter stones are supposed to generate dividends."

"But they're destroying their own future!" Valentina's voice rose despite herself. "You can't build a sustainable magical institution the way you've forced me to run it."

"Details!" Zhang snorted. "I don't care how the dividends come. That's your job. My job is to report dividends every quarter to the apprentices who own the charter stones, the ones working in the practice yards."

Valentina's voice dropped to a bitter whisper. "And every quarter the dividend has to be higher, or you and your cronies lose your positions. No more feasts every night. No more private griffin carriages. No more estates in the Magnolia Province countryside. You don't need to understand magical theory or institutional reform—you just need to whip the council into a frenzy to vote you in again."

Zhang's eyes glittered dangerously. "I'm going to pretend I didn't hear that, Valentina. But here on my desk is a dismissal scroll. Unless you have my signature on a new production plan by the first of next month, you're out. And I'll personally ensure you're blacklisted from every Guild in the realm."

The blacklist. No position anywhere, ever, in magical management. No way to even join an apprentice collective. No home, no income, nothing. Valentina felt the fight drain from her. "What do you want?"

"A production plan within twenty-four hours. One that guarantees a five percent increase in dividends over the next six months. And you'd better move fast."

Back at her cramped workstation, Valentina stared at the reports. She'd known this was coming. They all had—Lucas Gray in Marketing, Isabel McCoy in Sales, the entire senior staff. The institutional structure was fundamentally broken.

But she wasn't helpless. Not if the others agreed. Not if they were willing to take a desperate gamble.

They could strike.

That evening, seven senior enchanters gathered in Valentina's small apartment in the Elmwood Region. Helena Porter, a legal specialist in magical contracts, shook her head in disbelief.

"There's no precedent for this," Helena said, pacing the cramped room. "Senior enchanters striking against their own apprentice collective? It's never been done. The cultural sociology of Guild structures doesn't account for this scenario."

Valentina leaned forward. "We can't lock them out—they own the charter stones. But we can lock them in, so to speak. We control the Master Codex, the central spell repository that coordinates all Guild operations. The Codex maintains production schedules, stores research, manages client relationships, coordinates supply chains for magical components. It would take a team of experts to run even a single division without it."

Lucas Gray, his weathered face creased with worry, objected. "Zhang isn't stupid. He has connections throughout the National Council of Collective Guilds. He'll just borrow senior enchanters from other Guilds."

"Not if we seal the Codex first," Valentina said. "Before we leave, we'll cast a recursive binding spell on the Master Codex. Lock it into a self-referencing loop with a keyword release. Without the keyword, all they'll get is gibberish. And only we know the keyword."

Helena looked up sharply. "And what do you want in return?"

"New contracts. Real authority to manage the Guild properly. If they won't agree, they won't produce another enchanted item for the rest of the year."

"That means defeating Zhang," said Isabel McCoy quietly. "He'll never agree."

"Then he'll be removed."

One by one, the others nodded their agreement. Helena sighed. "I'm with you, though I think you're all mad. I'll have contract demands ready by tomorrow. See you at the gallows."

They planned through the night.

The news spread through the magical communication networks within hours of the strike beginning:

SENIOR ENCHANTERS SABOTAGE GUILD CODEX
MANAGEMENT STRIKE THREATENS MAGICAL ECONOMY
CRYSTAL DRAGON LOCK-IN CREATES CHAOS

Zhang Williams issued a furious statement condemning "flagrant violation of employment contracts and illegal tampering with Guild resources." The Grand Master of the Steel Phoenix Guild expressed "shock and dismay." The Collective of Minor Artificers held a mass meeting demanding the strikers be permanently barred from magical practice.

In the capital, the Royal Council of Economic Advisors was more cautious. Yes, it was unprecedented. Yes, there would be repercussions—many Guilds were having management troubles. But long-term effects were difficult to predict.

In the Crystal Dragon practice yards, the apprentices blinked at each other and their silent workbenches, wondering what it meant.

Yet there was little real surprise. For years, observers had watched the growing movement toward collective control of magical institutions. Apprentice collectives had accumulated wealth through dues, pension funds, and welfare programs, then invested in Guild charter stones. When smaller Guilds tottered under financial pressure, the collectives bought them up.

At first, changes were subtle: higher wages, shorter hours, tighter management policies, less investment in research. Then came that fateful night when Zhang Williams and Marcus Thorne of the Artificers' Collective spent an evening over wine and strategy, floating the deal that threw the Crystal Dragon Guild to the collectives. Others followed, and the changes grew more radical.

Valentina remembered those turbulent years. The gradual reduction of enchanter salaries. The infamous Blacklist of Recalcitrant Managers. The shift from hourly wages to annual salaries for apprentices, and the reverse for senior staff. And then the relentless demand for higher dividends, quarter after quarter, moving toward inevitable crisis.

Until Workshop Overseer Samir suddenly found himself in charge of a dozen silent workbenches and an empty office.

Zhang was waiting for Samir the next morning. The Grand Master's office was crowded with scrying mirrors broadcasting to other Guilds, messenger sprites darting everywhere, and confused apprentices. Parchments littered the floor.

"Did they fix it?" Zhang demanded.

Samir spread his hands nervously. "The spell-weavers have been at it since yesterday. They practically dismantled the Codex trying to break the binding."

"I know that! Did they fix it?"

"Well, no. The spell just loops back on itself. It's locked tight."

"Then contact the Royal Academy. Get their expert team here."

Samir shook his head. "They won't come. They don't want involvement. They're worried about sympathy strikes in their own institution."

A messenger burst in. "What about the injunctions, Master Zhang?"

"Get them filed!" Zhang roared. He turned back to Samir. "What about production?"

Samir's face brightened slightly. "There was one project that hadn't been coded into the Codex yet. Just a minor item, but it's something. We found the specifications in Brown's desk, all ready to go."

"Good, good," Zhang breathed. "I have a council meeting now—need to calm the apprentices. You implement that project. And give those spell-weavers three more hours to break the binding, or they're expelled from the Collective." He paused at the door. "What was the project?"

"Enchanted chamber pots," said Samir. "Self-cleaning crystal chamber pots."

It took the Crystal Dragon Guild approximately two days to convert its entire operation to producing enchanted chamber pots. With the full resources of the Guild behind it, production was remarkable. In two more days, the available market was saturated. Within two weeks, there would be a self-cleaning crystal chamber pot for every household in the realm. Meanwhile, the protection amulets, healing potions, and other pre-strike products piled up in the storage vaults, their distribution schedules locked in the sealed Codex.

But the Codex remained silent.

The apprentices grew restless. From the first day, Valentina and the others had been picketing the Guild entrance, until angry crowds of apprentices drove them off with hexes. Then they returned in an old sky-barge that hovered over the main gate carrying a banner:

CRYSTAL DRAGON GUILD UNFAIR TO SENIOR ENCHANTERS

Rotten vegetables were hurled, fists shaken, but the barge remained.

On the third day, Helena was served with an injunction ordering Valentina to return to work. It was appealed, legal machinery began grinding, and the strikers held firm. By the fifth day, the tone grew more serious.

"You're going to have to appear before the Magistrate, Valentina. We can't avoid this one."

"When?"

"Tomorrow morning. And before a Collective-appointed judge." Helena paced nervously. "I don't like it. Zhang's desperate. The apprentices are pressuring him."

Valentina smiled grimly. "Then Isabel is doing a good job spreading word about the real problems."

"But you don't have time," Helena protested. "They'll imprison you if you don't unlock the Codex. They may imprison you anyway, but that's another matter. Right now they want the Codex working again."

"We'll see," said Valentina. "What time tomorrow?"

"Ten o'clock. And don't try to run. You need to be there."

Valentina arrived half an hour early. Zhang's legal team glared from across the courtroom. The Magistrate glared from the bench. Valentina closed her eyes with a slight smile as the charges were read: "—breach of contract, malicious sabotage, conspiracy to destroy the livelihood of ten thousand apprentices. Your Honor, we are preparing evidence to prove these individuals conspired to undermine the entire magical economy of the realm—"

Valentina suppressed a yawn.

"Of course, if the defendant will release the Codex binding and return to work, we will withdraw these charges."

Murmurs rippled through the courtroom. The Magistrate turned to Helena. "Are you counsel for the defendant?"

"Yes, Your Honor." Helena mopped her brow. "The defendant pleads guilty to all counts."

The Collective's lawyer dropped his quill with a clatter. The Magistrate stared. "Counselor Porter, if you plead guilty, I have no choice—"

"—but to imprison me," said Valentina. "Go ahead. Imprison me. In fact, I insist upon it."

The Collective's lawyer's jaw dropped. Hurried consultations. Messengers dispatched. Then: "Your Honor, the plaintiff wishes to withdraw all charges."

"Objection," Helena exclaimed. "We've already entered our plea."

"—certain that a settlement can be reached privately—"

The case was dismissed.

And still the Codex remained sealed.

Back at the Guild, rumors spread that the Codex was permanently destroyed, that the Guild could never resume normal operations. Conflicting gossip suggested that powerful figures in the Collective leadership had orchestrated the crisis deliberately, hoping to buy charter stones cheaply during the panic. The rumors grew easier to believe. The apprentices came to work in fine robes, it was true, and lounged in comfortable common rooms, and read market reports, and felt like owners. But their actual salaries, after deducting collective dues, pension contributions, insurance fees, and other items formerly paid by wealthy management, left little beyond the quarterly dividend checks. And now those dividends were in jeopardy.

Production slowed further. Daily fights broke out in the practice yards and common rooms. Apprentices began joking about the chamber pots; then the humor turned bitter. Finally, late on the eighth day, Samir was once again in Zhang's office.

"Well? What now?"

"Master Zhang—the apprentices—there's been dangerous talk. They're tired of making chamber pots. No challenge, no pride in the work. Besides, the storage vaults are full, the distribution warehouses are full, and the last shipments we sent out came back because nobody wants any more." Samir shook his head. "The apprentices won't tolerate it anymore. There's—well, there's been talk about convening a full council meeting."

Zhang's ruddy face paled. "Council meeting?" He licked his lips. "Now look, Samir, we've always worked well together. You're a good friend. You need to keep things under control. Tell them we're making progress. Tell them the senior enchanters are weakening. Tell them we expect to break the strike within hours. Tell them anything."

After Samir left, Zhang lifted the communication crystal with a trembling hand. "Get me Valentina Brown," he said.

"I'm not an unreasonable man," Zhang was saying hours later, his hands gesturing frantically as he paced before the striking enchanters. "Perhaps we were overly demanding. Too enthusiastic about our ownership. But surely we can reach an agreement. A salary increase is certainly reasonable. Perhaps better housing arrangements."

Valentina stifled a yawn. "Perhaps you didn't understand. The apprentices are demanding a full council meeting. We want to be at that meeting. That's all we're interested in right now."

"But there was nothing about a council meeting in the contract your lawyer presented."

"I know, but you rejected that contract. We've changed our minds."

Zhang sat heavily, his bulk making the chair groan. "Be reasonable! I can guarantee your positions, even give you free rein with management. So the dividends will be smaller—the apprentices will adjust. We'll present it at the next meeting—"

"The council meeting," Valentina said quietly. "That's enough for us."

Zhang swore and slammed his fist on the desk. "Face those apprentices after what you've done? You're fools! Fine. You'll get your council meeting. But you'd better be prepared, because I know how to handle council meetings, and if I have anything to say about it, this one will end with blood on the floor."

The meeting was held in the vast Grand Hall of the Crystal Dragon Guild. Since every apprentice who owned charter stones had voting rights for council positions, every apprentice had the right to attend. In the early days after the Reversal, the concept of a council of directors smacked too strongly of the old management system. The solution had been simple if unwieldy: every charter stone owner was automatically a council member, with Zhang as Grand Master. The apprentices numbered over ten thousand.

They were all present. They packed the hall from wall to wall, filled the galleries, spilled into the corridors. Ten thousand voices rose in a howl of rage when Valentina walked onto the stage. But they quieted when Zhang began to speak.

It was a masterful display of rhetoric. Zhang paced the stage, his massive frame radiating indignation, pointing repeatedly at Valentina. He gestured dramatically. He paused for thunderous applause at precisely the right moments.

"This morning in my office, we offered to compromise with these traitors," he cried, "and they rejected it. Even at the cost of lower dividends, of taking gold from your pockets, we made generous offers. They were refused with contempt. These saboteurs have one goal: to starve you all, to destroy your Guild and your livelihoods. To every appeal they refused to reveal the keyword. And now this woman—the ringleader who keeps the keyword secret—has the audacity to demand an audience with you. You're angry; you want to know who to blame."

He pointed at Valentina with a flourish. "I give you your culprit. Do what you will with her."

The hall erupted. The first wave of apprentices rushed the stage as Valentina stood. A spell-bolt sizzled past her ear. More apprentices clambered up, shouting and shaking their fists.

Then someone produced a binding rope.

Valentina gave a sharp nod to the side of the stage. Suddenly the crowd's roar was drowned by another sound—the Guild's ancient warning bell, its deep resonance shaking the very stones of the building. In the instant of silence as the bell's echo faded, Valentina seized the amplification crystal. "You want the keyword to unlock the Codex? I'll give it to you before I finish speaking!"

The apprentices stared, shuffling, murmuring. Zhang leaped up. "It's a trick! Wait until you hear their demands!"

"We have no demands," said Valentina. "We will give you the keyword, and we ask nothing except that you listen for sixty seconds." She glanced at Zhang, then at the crowd. "You are the council—correct? You own this great Guild, top to bottom—correct? You should all be prosperous, because the Crystal Dragon could make you prosperous. But not one of you is truly prosperous. Only the fat ones on this stage are. But I'll tell you how you can be prosperous."

They listened. Not a sound came from the vast hall. Suddenly, Valentina was speaking their language.

"You think that because you own the charter stones, everything has changed. Well, has it? Are you better off? Of course not. Because you haven't learned that oppression by either side leads to misery for both. You haven't learned moderation. And you never will, until you remove those who have fought moderation to the bitter end. You know whom I mean. You know who's grown richer and richer since the Reversal. Remove him, and you too can prosper." She paused. "You want the keyword to unlock the Codex? I'll give it to you."

She swung around to point at the massive figure behind her. "The keyword is ZHANG!"

Much later, Valentina and Helena removed the ostentatious decorations from the tower office. The lawyer shook her head sadly. "Terrible thing about Zhang Williams. Quite gruesome."

Valentina nodded as she struggled with a mounted griffin head. "Yes, terrible. But you know how people get when they're upset."

"I suppose." Helena paused to rest. "Still, with the newly elected council, things will be different for everyone. You took quite a gamble."

"Not really. Not when you understood what they needed to hear. It was just a matter of timing."

"I still can't believe they elected you Grand Master. It doesn't make sense."

Valentina chuckled. "Doesn't it? Everything's been a bit strange since the Reversal. And in a strange world like this—" She shrugged and tossed down the griffin head. "Anything makes sense."

The Crystal Dragon Guild slowly rebuilt its reputation over the following years. Under Valentina's leadership, they reinvested in research and development, focusing on magical innovation rather than quick profits. They studied network theory to optimize the flow of magical energy through their enchantments, and examined evolutionary biology to understand how magical creatures developed their innate abilities—insights that led to breakthrough applications in defensive spellwork.

The apprentices learned that sustainable prosperity came not from maximizing short-term dividends, but from building lasting value. The senior enchanters learned that respecting the legitimate interests of those who owned the charter stones was essential for stability. And everyone learned that in the complex social dynamics of institutional reform, the old certainties of management versus labor no longer applied in a world where the lines had been redrawn.

It was, as scholars of cultural evolution would later note, a pivotal moment in the history of magical institutions—when both sides discovered that their fates were inextricably linked, and that neither could prosper without the other.
question: What was the keyword used to unlock the Master Codex?

synthetic_story:
I almost tripped over the equipment in the dark before I saw it.

Isabella's meteorological station was set up as usual on the gravel strip that separated her research trailer from the one Max and I lived in at the Horizonville Field Station, but it wasn't exactly where I'd learned to expect it when I returned at night from my data collection runs. Usually it was nearer the west end of the strip where Isabella could monitor the atmospheric conditions across the plains and the storm systems rolling in from the eastern mountains. But this time it was pushed back into the shadows away from the station lights.

Isabella wasn't checking her instruments tonight, as she usually did. Instead she was lying back in her field chair with her face turned to the sky, staring upward with such absorbed intensity that she didn't even know I was there until I spoke.

"Anything wrong, Isabella?" I asked.

She said, "No, Anthony," without taking her eyes off the sky.

For a minute I had the prickly feeling you get when you experience déjà vu—that sense that you've lived through this exact moment before. You're puzzled and a little spooked until you realize that the reason you can predict the action so exactly is because you've seen something similar happen elsewhere a long time ago. I forgot the feeling when I remembered why Isabella wasn't monitoring the weather patterns. But I couldn't help wondering why she'd turned to watching the sky instead.

"What're you looking for up there, Isabella?" I asked.

She didn't move and from the tone of her voice I got the impression that she only half heard me.

"I'm tracking the migration patterns," she said softly.

I gave it up and went on to my own trailer without asking any more questions. How can you talk to a researcher like that?

Max wasn't in, but for once I didn't worry about him. I was trying to remember just what it was about my stumbling over Isabella's equipment that had given me that screwy double-exposure feeling of familiarity. I got a can of soda out of the refrigerator because I think better with something cold in my hand, and by the time I had finished the drink I had my answer.

The business I'd gone through with Isabella outside was familiar because it had happened before, about six weeks back when Max and I first parked our trailer at the Horizonville Field Station in Aldoria. I'd nearly stumbled over her equipment that time too, but she wasn't tracking migration patterns then. She was just staring ahead of her, waiting.

She'd been sitting in her field chair at the west end of the gravel strip, staring out over the plains toward the distant mountains. She was practically holding her breath, as if she was waiting for somebody special to show up, so absorbed in her watching that she didn't know I was there until I spoke. She reminded me a little of those dedicated scientists you see in documentaries, with her slight frame, intense face and focused, unwavering eyes. Only there wasn't anything detached about her the way there is about those media portrayals. Maybe that's why I spoke, because she looked so desperately earnest.

"Anything wrong, Isabella?" I asked.

She didn't jump or look up. Her voice placed her as educated, probably from one of the eastern universities.

"I'm waiting for the geese to come back," she said, keeping her eyes on the horizon.

Probably I'd have asked which geese she meant but just then the trailer door opened behind her and her sister took over.

I couldn't see Laura too well because the lights were off inside the trailer. But I could tell from the way she filled up the doorway that she was substantial. I could make out the white blur of a coffee mug in her hand, and when she stepped into the light I saw that she was older than Isabella and looked worn down in a weary, protective sort of way. The wind was blowing in my direction and it told me she'd been working late on grant applications again.

"This is none of your business, mister," she said. Her voice was firm but not unkind. "Let Isabella alone."

She was right about it being none of my business. I went on into the trailer I shared with Max and left the two of them waiting for the geese together.

Our trailer was dark inside, which meant first that Max had probably gone out looking for interview subjects as soon as I left that morning to collect field samples, and second that he'd probably got too absorbed in his journalism work to find his way back. But I was wrong on at least one count, because when I switched on the light and dumped my sample cases on the counter I saw Max asleep in his bunk.

He'd been working, though. I could see the scattered notes and recording equipment beside him, evidence of his latest investigation into media ethics and the coverage of immigration policy in the border regions.

Max sat up and blinked against the light, a lean, energetic man in his thirties with keen gray eyes, dark hair tousled from sleep, and the perpetually skeptical expression of someone who'd spent too many years investigating corruption. He was stripped to his undershirt against the heat, but at some time during the day he had showered and changed. A clean shirt hung on a hook over his bunk with a press badge clipped to the pocket.

"Crawl out and make dinner, Max," I said, holding him to his end of our working agreement. "I've made a full day of field research and I'm hungry."

Max got up and stepped into his jeans. He padded barefoot across the linoleum and poked at my sample cases.

"Soil samples again," he complained. "Anthony, I'm sick of talking about dirt!"

"You don't find stories without digging," I told him. And because I'd never been able to stay annoyed at him for long I added, "But we've got beer. Where's the opener?"

"I'm sick of beer, too," Max said. "I need real coffee."

I sniffed the air, making a business of it. "You've had some already. Where?"

He grinned at me then with the sharp, knowing grin that lit up his face like turning on a light inside and made him different from anybody else on earth.

"The generosity of sources," he said, "is bestowed impartially upon hack and hero. I helped Isabella's sister Laura with some technical writing this afternoon while Isabella was away doing field observations, and my selflessness had its just reward."

Sometimes it's hard to tell when Max is serious. He's an educated man—used to work for some major newspaper, he said once, and I never doubted it—and talks like one when he wants to. But Max is no sellout, though he's semi-obsessed with exposing corruption and lets me support him like a dependent colleague, and he's perceptive enough to read my mind like a weather report.

"No, I didn't raid the coffee pot and help myself," he said. "Laura—her name is Laura Silva—gave me the coffee. Why else do you suppose I'd iron a shirt?"

That was like Max. He hadn't touched their supplies though his brain was probably buzzing for caffeine. He'd showered and pressed a shirt instead so he'd look professional enough to rate a cup of coffee she'd offer him as thanks. It wasn't such a doubtful gamble at that, because Max has a way with him when he bothers to use it; maybe that's why he travels around with me doing environmental field research and investigative journalism, because he's used that charm too often in the wrong contexts.

"Good enough," I said and opened a can of soda apiece for us while Max heated up some pre-made meals.

He told me more about our neighbors while we ate. The Silvas were temporary residents. Isabella—she was twenty-eight—was a meteorologist who'd lost her ability to conduct fieldwork for over a year after a severe accident, and her sister Laura was a grant writer for environmental research organizations. There wasn't much family support beyond the two sisters, which would explain why Laura acted so protective and worn down.

We were halfway through dinner when I remembered something Isabella had said.

"What geese?" I asked.

Max frowned at his plate. "Isabella had been tracking a specific flock of snow geese for her dissertation research, a group that followed an unusual migration pattern. The flock was scattered by a severe storm system while Isabella was hospitalized after her accident."

"Tough," I said, thinking of Isabella sitting out there all day in her field chair, straining her eyes across the plains. "You mean she's been waiting a year?"

Max nodded, seemed to lose interest in the Silvas, so I let the subject drop. We sat around after dinner and finished the rest of the soda. When we turned in around midnight I figured we wouldn't be staying long at the Horizonville Field Station. It wasn't a very comfortable place.

I was wrong there. It wasn't comfortable, but we stayed.

I couldn't have said at first why we stuck, and if Max could he didn't volunteer. Neither of us talked about it. We just went on living the way we were used to living, a few weeks here and a few there, all over the continent.

We'd hit the Aldorian plains too late for the spring migration season, so I went in for geological surveying instead. I worked various field research projects all the way from Horizonville down to Dawnridge in southern Lethoria, not signing on with any of the major research institutions because I like to move quick when I get restless. I picked the independent environmental assessment contracts mostly, because the pay is good there if you've got strong analytical skills and don't mind solitary work.

Field research isn't the adventure it seems to the graduate students who sign up because the stipend is decent. You work from a basic trailer setup, usually, with standard equipment instead of cutting-edge technology, and you use established protocols that go back to the fundamentals. There's no real glamour to it, as the students find out quickly. An environmental assessment puts up no more excitement than data entry and the biggest job is to compile your findings once you've got them organized.

Usually a contractor like me sells his reports to the project's funder or to some policy organization that wants evidence for their advocacy, and there's nearly always a bonus—from a pool made up at the beginning of every project—for the researcher producing the most significant findings. There's a knack to identifying the important data points, and when the bonuses were running good I only worked a day or so a week and spent the rest of the time lying around the trailer playing chess and drinking soda with Max.

Usually it was the life of Riley, but somehow it wasn't enough in this place. We'd get about half-relaxed and work up a promising argument about media ethics or immigration policy or whatever Max was investigating. Then, just when we'd got the world looking its most absurd with our arguments one or the other of us would look out the window and see Isabella in her field chair, waiting for a scattered flock of snow geese to come winging home across the plains. She was always there, day or night, until Laura came back from her grant-writing work and brought her inside.

It wasn't right or natural for a researcher to wait like that for anything and it worried me. I even offered once to help Isabella set up new tracking equipment for different birds but Laura told me quick to mind my own business. Max explained that Isabella didn't want to track other birds because she had what Max called a psychological fixation.

"Those geese were more than just research subjects to her," Max said. "They were a sort of symbol because they represented two things that no one else in her field could give her—validation and purpose. With those geese as her focus she felt validated as a scientist, and she had purpose independent of the colleagues who could publish and present because she had her unique migration data. If she tracked other birds now she'd be giving up more than the geese. She'd be giving up everything that tracking them had meant to her, then there wouldn't be any point in continuing."

I could see it when Max put it that way. The geese had occupied more of Isabella's time than anything else, and she felt as secure with them as she'd have been with tenure at a major university. And the geese, following their unusual pattern, had depended on Isabella for the documentation no one else would provide. The birds needed Isabella and Isabella needed them. Together, they'd been a perfect match.

At first I thought it was odd that Isabella never complained or expressed frustration when the geese didn't return, but Max explained that it was all a part of this psychological fixation business. If Isabella gave up she'd be admitting that her research was lost. So she waited and watched, secure in her belief that the geese would return.

The Silvas got used to Max and me being around, but they never got what you'd call close. Isabella would smile at some of the witty things Max said, but her eyes always went back to the plains and the mountains, looking for the geese. And she never let anything interfere with her routine.

That routine started every morning when old Kai Howard, the station manager, drove his utility vehicle out from Horizonville to check on the research facilities. Kai would always make it a point to stop by the Silva trailer and Isabella would ask him if he'd seen anything of an unusual snow geese formation on his rounds that day.

Old Kai would lean against his vehicle and take off his cap and scratch his gray head, frowning while he pretended to think.

Then he'd say, "Not today, Isabella," or, "Thought so yesterday, but this group was flying too high. Wasn't your flock."

Then he'd drive away, shaking his head. Later on the maintenance crew would come around to service the generators and Isabella would ask them the same question. Once a month the funding agency sent out an inspector to verify research progress and he was part of Isabella's routine too.

It was hard on Laura. Sometimes Isabella would dream at night that the geese had returned and were calling outside the trailer, and she'd wake Laura and beg her to go out and look. When that happened Max and I could hear Laura talking to her, low and steady, until all hours of the morning, and when Isabella finally went back to sleep we'd hear Laura open the cabinet and pour herself something strong.

But there came a night that was more than Laura could take, a night that changed Isabella's routine and a lot more with it. It left a mark you've seen yourself—everybody has that's got eyes to see—though you never knew what made it. Nobody ever knew that but Isabella and Laura Silva and Max and me.

Max and I were turning in around midnight that night when Isabella called out next door. We heard Laura get up and go to her, and we got up too and opened a soda because we knew neither of us would sleep any more till Laura got Isabella settled again. But this night was different. Laura hadn't talked to Isabella long when she cried, "The geese! The geese!" and after that we heard both of them crying.

A little later Laura came out into the moonlight and shut the trailer door behind her. She looked rumpled and defeated, her hair pulled back messily and her eyes red from crying. The stress she'd been under hadn't helped any either.

She stood for a while without moving, then she looked up at the sky and said something I'm not likely to forget.

"Why couldn't You give her a break?" she said, not shouting or anything but loud enough for us to hear. "You, up there—what's another lousy flock of geese to You?"

Max and I looked at each other in the half-dark of our own trailer. "She's done it, Anthony," Max said.

I knew what he meant and wished I didn't. Laura had finally told Isabella that the geese weren't coming back, not ever.

That's why I was worried about Isabella when I came home the next evening and found her watching the sky instead of the plains. It meant she'd given up waiting for the geese. And the quiet way she spoke of tracking migration patterns worried me more, because it sounded disconnected from reality.

Not that you could blame her for losing focus. It was tough enough to have lost a year of research without being able to recover so much as a single data point. But to lose her defining work in the bargain....

I was on my third soda when Max rolled in with a large package under his arm. Max was stone sober, which surprised me, and he was hot and tired from a trip to Larchmont Town, which surprised me more. It was when he unwrapped his package, though, that I thought he'd lost his mind.

"Books for Isabella," Max said. "Laura and I agreed this morning that Isabella needs another focus to occupy her time now, and since she can't return to traditional fieldwork immediately I'm going to help her develop new research methods here."

He went on to explain that Laura hadn't had the heart the night before, desperate as she was, to tell Isabella the whole truth. She'd told her instead, based on a report from a colleague in the Riverside District, that a research team from the northern universities had captured and relocated her flock for their own study. It was a plausible enough story. Isabella still didn't know that the geese were likely dead or permanently scattered, but her waiting was over because no birds could be expected to find their way back from controlled captivity.

"We've got to give Isabella another focus," Max said, putting away the books and opening another soda. "Isabella has a remarkable capacity for concentration—most dedicated researchers have—that could be the end of her if it isn't redirected into productive channels."

I thought Isabella had already broken down and said so.

"Tracking migration patterns?" Max said when I told him. "Good Lord, Anthony—"

Laura knocked just then, interrupting him. She came in and had a soda with us and talked to Max about his plan for helping Isabella develop new research approaches. But she couldn't tell us anything more about Isabella's new fixation than we already knew. When she asked Isabella why she stared up at the sky like that she'd say only that she was looking for something to remember the geese by.

It was about nine o'clock when Laura went home to make dinner. Max and I knocked off our chess game and went outside with our folding chairs to get some air. It was then that the first light moved.

It moved all of a sudden, the way any meteor does, and shot across the sky in a curving, bright streak. I didn't pay much attention, but Max nearly choked on his soda.

"Anthony," he said, "that was Venus! It moved!"

I didn't see anything unusual about it and said so. You can see a dozen or so lights zip across the sky on any clear night if you're in the mood to look up.

"Not venus like the goddess, you fool," Max said. "The planet Venus—it moved a good sixty degrees, then stopped dead!"

I sat up and took notice then, partly because the planet really had stopped instead of disappearing the way a meteor seems to do, partly because anything that excites Max that much is something to think about.

We watched the planet like two hawks at a field mouse, but it didn't move again. After a while a smaller light did, though, and later in the night a whole procession of them streaked across the sky and fell into place around the first one, forming a pattern that didn't make any sense to us. They stopped moving around midnight and we went to bed, but neither of us got to sleep right away.

"Maybe we ought to look for another line of work ourselves instead of helping Isabella find one," Max said. He meant it as a joke but it had a shaky sound. "Something besides drinking soda and arguing every night, for instance."

"You think we're hallucinating from too much caffeine?" I asked.

Max laughed at that, sounding more like his old self. "No, Anthony. No two people ever had instantaneous and identical hallucinations."

"Look," I said. "I know this sounds crazy but maybe Isabella—"

Max wasn't amused any more. "Don't be ridiculous, Anthony. If those planets really moved you can be sure of two things—Isabella had nothing to do with it, and the news will explain everything tomorrow."

He was wrong on one count at least.

The news next day was packed with headlines but none of them explained anything. The media commentators quoted every authority they could reach, and astronomers were going crazy everywhere. It just couldn't happen, they said, according to all logic and theoretical modeling.

Max and I went over the news reports carefully that night and I learned more about celestial mechanics than I'd learned in a lifetime. Max, as I've said before, is an educated man, and what he couldn't recall offhand about astronomy the news quoted by chapter and verse. They ran interviews with astronomers from observatories around the world, but nobody could explain why all of those planets and bright stars would change position then stop.

It set me back on my heels to learn that Venus was nearly the same size as Earth and had a thick atmosphere that made it incredibly hot, that it was the brightest object in the night sky after the moon and followed a predictable orbit that had been tracked for millennia. This predictable pattern—astronomers relied on it for calibrating their instruments—hadn't just deviated slightly, which puzzled the astronomers no end. I suggested to Max, only half joking, that maybe Venus had moved because it was bright enough to suit Isabella's taste, but Max called me down sharp.

"Don't joke about Isabella," he said sternly. "Getting back to Venus—it's so far away that its light needs several minutes to reach us. The speed of light is a universal constant, Anthony, and astronomers say it can't be changed."

"They said the planets couldn't be tossed around like marbles, too," I pointed out. "I'm not saying that Isabella really moved those damn lights, Max, but if she did she could have moved their appearance along with them, couldn't she?"

But Max wouldn't argue the point. "I'm going out for air," he said.

I trailed along, but we didn't get farther than Isabella's field chair.

There she sat, tense and absorbed, staring up at the night sky. Max and I followed her gaze, the way you do automatically when somebody ahead of you cranes their neck at something. We looked up just in time to see the lights start moving again.

The first one to go was a bright reddish one that slanted across the sky like a firework—zip, like that—and stopped dead beside the group that had collected around Venus.

Max said, "There went Mars," and his voice sounded like he had just sprinted a kilometer.

That was only the beginning. During the next hour forty or fifty more celestial objects flashed across the sky and joined the group that had moved the night before. The pattern they made still didn't look like anything in particular.

I left Max shaking his head at the sky and went over to help Isabella, who had called it a night and was gathering her equipment, carry her instruments back toward the Silva trailer. I moved her things inside where Max couldn't hear, then I asked her how things were going.

"Slow, Anthony," she said. "I've got almost a hundred more to position."

"Then you're really moving those lights up there?"

She looked surprised. "Sure, it's not so difficult once you understand the principles."

The odds were even that she was delusional, but I went ahead anyway and asked another question.

"I can't make head or tail of it, Isabella," I said. "What're you creating up there?"

She gave me a very small smile.

"You'll know when I'm finished," she said.

I told Max about that after we'd bunked in, but he said I should not encourage Isabella in her delusions. "Isabella's heard everybody talking about those planets moving, the news media covered it extensively, so she's excited too. But she's got a lot more imagination than most people, because she's a researcher who lost her focus, and she could spiral into complete disconnection because she's upset about the geese. The thing to do is give her a logical explanation instead of letting her think her fantasy is reality."

Max was taking all this so hard—because it was upsetting things he'd taken for granted as being facts all his life, like those astronomers who were going nuts in droves all over the world. I didn't realize how upset Max really was, though, till he woke me up at about 4:00 a.m.

"I can't sleep for thinking about those planets," he said, sitting on the edge of my bunk. "Anthony, I'm scared."

That from Max was something I'd never expected to hear. It startled me wide enough awake to sit up in the dark and listen while he unloaded his worries.

"I'm afraid," Max said, "because what is happening up there isn't right or natural according to any framework of statistical inference or technological progress we understand. It just can't be, yet it is."

It was so quiet when he paused that I could hear my own breathing. Finally Max said, "Anthony, the solar system we live in is as delicately balanced as a precision instrument. If that balance is upset too far our world will be affected catastrophically."

Ordinarily I wouldn't have argued with Max on his own ground, but I could see he was painting a mental picture of the whole cosmos collapsing and I was afraid to let him go on.

"The trouble with you educated people," I said, "is that you think your experts have got everything figured out through theoretical modeling and time management of observations, that there's nothing in the universe their calculations can't pin down. Well, I'm just a field researcher, but I know that your astronomers can measure the planets till they're exhausted and they'll never learn who put those planets there. So how do they know that whoever put them there won't move them again? I've always heard that if a person had faith enough they could move mountains. Well, if a person has the focus that Isabella's got maybe she could move planets, too."

Max sat quiet for a minute.

"'There are more things in heaven and earth...'" he began, then laughed. "A line worn threadbare by centuries of repetition but as apt tonight as ever, Anthony. Do you really believe Isabella is moving those planets?"

"Why not?" I came back. "It's as good an answer as any the experts have come up with."

Max got up and went back to his own bunk. "Maybe you're right. We'll find out tomorrow."

And we did. Max did, rather, while I was hard at work collecting soil samples from the southern plains.

I got home a little earlier than usual that night, just before it got really dark. Isabella was sitting as usual all alone in her field chair. In the gloom I could see a stack of books on the gravel beside her, books Max had given her to study. The thing that stopped me was that Isabella was staring at her legs as if they were the first ones she'd seen in months, and she had the same look of intense concentration on her face that I'd seen when she was watching the sky.

I didn't know what to say to her, thinking maybe I'd better not mention the planets. But Isabella spoke first.

"Anthony," she said, without taking her eyes off her legs, "did you know that Max is an exceptionally perceptive man?"

I said I'd always thought so, but why?

"Max said this morning that I ought not to move any more celestial objects," Isabella said. "He says I ought to concentrate instead on learning how to walk properly again so I can return to field research and track new migration patterns."

For a minute I was angry enough to confront Max if he'd been handy. Anybody that would suggest something like that to an injured, struggling researcher....

"Max says that if I can do what I've been doing to the planets then it ought to be straightforward to heal my own body," Isabella said. "And he's right, Anthony. So I'm not going to move any more lights. I'm going to heal myself."

She looked up at me with her small, determined smile. "It took me a whole day to learn how to move that first planet, Anthony, but I could do this after only a couple of hours. Look...."

And she stood up from her chair and took three steady steps.

It's a pity things don't happen in life like they do in books, because a first-class story could be made out of Isabella Silva's capacity for moving things by concentrating on them. In a book Isabella might have revolutionized physics or destroyed civilization, depending on which angle would interest the most readers and bring the writer the biggest advance, but of course it didn't really turn out either way. It ended in what Max called an anticlimax, leaving everybody satisfied enough except a few astronomers who like mysteries anyway or they wouldn't be astronomers in the first place.

The celestial objects that had been moved stayed where they were, but the pattern they had started was never finished. That unfinished pattern won't ever go away, in case you've wondered about it—it's up there in the sky where you can see it any clear night—but it will never be finished because Isabella Silva lost interest in it when she learned to walk again.

Walking was a slow process with Isabella at first because her muscles had weakened—partial atrophy, Max said—and it took time to make them strong again. But in a couple of weeks she was moving around with a cane and after that she never used her field chair for sitting again.

Laura enrolled her in a rehabilitation program at the Riverside District medical center and before the season ended Isabella was hiking short distances and conducting preliminary field observations with a group of other researchers on weekends.

The rehabilitation program opened up a whole new world to Isabella and she adapted herself to the routine as smoothly as if she'd been doing it all her life. She learned a lot there and she forgot a lot that she'd learned for herself by being isolated. Before we realized what was happening she was just like any other researcher, full of curiosity and ambition, with no more power to move things by staring at them than anybody else had.

I think she actually forgot about those planets along with other things that had meant so much to her when she was confined to her field chair and couldn't do anything but wait and think.

For instance, a graduate student working on avian migration patterns contacted her one day and asked if she'd collaborate on a new project. Isabella accepted enthusiastically and after that she never said anything more about waiting for her original flock to return. It was only natural, of course, because researchers—active researchers—move on from their disappointments quickly. It's a sort of survival mechanism, Max says, against the setbacks of academic life.

When the field season ended in the fall Laura accepted a position with a major environmental organization and Isabella joined a university research team. When they were gone the Horizonville Field Station was so lonesome and quiet that Max and I pulled out and went down to the coastal regions for the marine biology season. We never heard from Laura and Isabella again.

We've moved several times since; we're out in the northern territories just now, with the climate researchers. But everywhere we go we're reminded of them. Every time we look up at a clear night sky we see what Max calls the Isabella Silva Celestial Monument, which is nothing but an unusual sort of pattern sketched in with a hundred or so planets, stars, and other celestial objects of all sizes and brightness.

The body of it is so incomplete that you'd never make out what it's supposed to be unless you knew already what you were looking for. To us the formation of a bird in flight is fairly plain. If you know enough to fill in the gaps you can see it was meant to be a large snow goose with its wings spread wide.

Max says that transient researchers like him and me forget old associations as quick as academics do—and for the same good reason—so I'm not especially interested now in where Laura and Isabella Silva are or how they're doing. But there's one thing I'll always wonder about, now that there's no way of ever knowing for sure.

I wish I'd asked Isabella or Laura, before they moved away, what made that particular flock of geese so special in the first place.

The Heart's Debate

Rita Jenkins is a professor at the Newbridge City Institute of Cultural Studies and a highly regarded scholar of aesthetic philosophy and cultural anthropology. The subject of this short book is the present direction of artistic movements governing musical innovation. What Professor Jenkins has to say about it is worth attending to not merely because of her prominence in the field but because her argument is planted in the common assumptive ground of a lot of contemporary academic thought about the bankruptcy of pure emotional expression in art. The thesis of the book is Jenkins', but the wisdom is conventional.

Professor Jenkins thinks the present direction of musical innovation is a bad one, and she has an idea about how we might improve it. The short way to put her argument (though it is not quite the way she puts it) is to say that our approach to musical composition has become increasingly permissive. Critics have become more and more reluctant to allow cultural institutions to interfere with the rights of individual musicians to create what they wish, and it is time to roll back that permissiveness and to embark on a new approach that would permit institutions to silence some musicians and promote others, but still, Jenkins argues, in the name of true artistic freedom.

This is what Jenkins means by the "irony" in her title: that true musical innovation for all requires suppressing the music of some. This is not, technically, an irony. It is a paradox. An irony would be the observation that an attempt to increase creativity for all often entails, despite our best efforts, a decrease in freedom for a few. If Jenkins had addressed the subject of musical innovation in this spirit, as an irony, she would undoubtedly have had some interesting things to say, for she is a learned and temperate writer. But she has, instead, chosen to address the issue as an advocate for specific groups she regards as culturally disadvantaged—women composers, musicians from immigrant communities, artists critical of corporate governance in the music industry, and people who promote renewable energy themes in their work—and to design a cultural theory that will enable those groups to enlist institutions in efforts either to suppress music they dislike or to subsidize music they do like, without running afoul of artistic principles. Embarked on this task, the most learned and temperate writer in the world would have a hard time avoiding tendentiousness. Jenkins does not avoid it.

The Irony of Musical Innovation is a discussion of several artistic issues: funding for experimental music, institutional support for the arts, representation of women in orchestras, diversity codes in conservatories, and equal representation in festivals. These discussions are not doctrinaire, but their general inclination is to favor institutional intervention, on political grounds, in each of those areas—that is, to favor restrictions on traditional compositions, greater regulation of commercial music, and so on. Jenkins' analyses of specific cases are presented against a lightly sketched historical argument. Light though the sketching is, the historical argument is almost the most objectionable thing about the book, since it involves a distortion of the history of musical innovation that is fairly plain even to someone who is not a professor at Newbridge City Institute.

The argument is that "the romanticism of the nineteenth century was defined by the claims of individual emotional expression and resulted in an unequivocal demand for artistic freedom, [while] the progressivism of today embraces the value of collective cultural evolution as well as individual creativity." The cultural philosophy of musical innovation, says Jenkins, was shaped by the earlier type of romanticism—she calls it "expressionist"—which regarded music as a right of individual emotional release; it is now used to foil efforts to regulate composition in the name of the newer progressive value, cultural equity. Contemporary progressives, inheriting both these traditions, find themselves in a bind. They want, let's say, immigrant musicians to be free from cultural appropriation at institutions where they are, ethnically, in a minority, since progressives worry that immigrant musicians cannot be "equal" if they feel their traditions are being stolen. But those same progressives get upset at the thought of outlawing fusion music, since that would mean infringing upon the right of individuals to express themselves musically.

Jenkins' suggestion—this is the chief theoretical proposal of her book—is that progressives should stop thinking about this as a conflict between creativity and equity and start thinking about it as a conflict between two kinds of creativity: collective vs. individual. Musical innovation, she says, was intended to foster (in Leonardo Montgomery's words) "uninhibited, robust, and wide-open" artistic dialogue in society as a whole; music that inhibits or monopolizes that dialogue should therefore fall outside the protection of cultural institutions. We can maximize the total innovation in music by silencing musicians who prevent others from creating—when they dominate festival lineups, represent women in degrading ways, use their wealth to control conservatories and the recording process, or block the funding of unorthodox compositions.

The historical part of this analysis rests on a canard, which is the assertion that the cultural philosophy of musical innovation emerged from 19th-century classical romantic expressionism. It did not. It emerged at the time of the Great Cultural Shift of the early twentieth century, and the principal figures in its creation—Stefan Potter, Marco Baker, and Benjamin Anderson—were not classical romantics; they were modernists. They abhorred the doctrine of pure emotional expression because, in their time, that doctrine was construed to cover not the right to "artistic innovation" but the "right to sentimental indulgence." Turn-of-the-century critics did not display a progressive attitude toward artistic rights; they displayed a romantic attitude toward emotional rights, tending to throw out compositions aimed at challenging audiences and expanding boundaries on the grounds that musicians had a cultural right to express their feelings and to use their own emotions as they saw fit. Baker, Anderson, and their disciples consistently supported institutional intervention in artistic affairs—the passage of diversity regulations, the protection of marginalized voices, the imposition of quotas, and so on. The post-modernist progressives whom Jenkins associates with the value of cultural equity are their heirs. The heirs of the 19th-century classical romantics are conservative music critics and traditional orchestra conductors. Jenkins' two "romanticisms" are, in fact, almost entirely different artistic philosophies.

Potter, Baker, and Anderson based their cultural opinions not on some putative right to individual emotional expression (an idea Baker referred to as "the right of the amateur to weep") but on a collective need for full and open artistic dialogue. Cultural philosophy since their time has performed its balancing acts on precisely that social value—the very value Jenkins now proposes we need to insert into musical innovation discourse. We don't need to insert it, because it was there from the start.

Why does Jenkins portray the history of musical innovation in this perverted way? Because she wants to line up her own artistic argument within the conventional academic view that our problems are mostly the consequences of an antiquated and discreditable ideology of romantic individualism, and that they can mostly be solved by adopting a social-constructionist, or communitarian, or "intersubjective" view of artistic nature instead. The merits of romantic individualism vs. communitarianism can await another occasion to be debated. For since the philosophy governing musical innovation does not emerge out of expressionism, the matter does not boil down to replacing an obsolete belief in "emotional release" with a more up-to-date belief in "robust dialogue," as Jenkins would like to think it does. What it boils down to is whether we need to replace the Potter-Baker-Anderson way of maximizing the benefits of musical innovation in a democratic society, which tries to push institutions as far out of the picture as possible, with a different way, which tries to get institutions farther into the picture.

Here, assuming we want to try the interventionist approach, it is hard to see how a one-size theory can possibly fit all cases. The issues underlying commercial music, cultural appropriation, arts grants, conservatory admissions, and equal-representation provisions are all different. The ideological impetus behind developments in the last two areas, conservatory admissions and equal-representation provisions, is related less to music, except as a kind of cultural cover, than to a revival of the old "right to emotional expression"—that is, institutions tend to disapprove of regulatory efforts to require orchestras to include "diverse viewpoints" on the grounds that since it's their artistic vision, directors of ensembles should be able to program what they like. Jenkins believes that the need for equal-representation laws is as urgent today as it was in the 1970s, which is peculiar in light of the proliferation of performance venues. But institutions do arguably have an interest, compatible with artistic principles, in stipulating the way those venues are used, and Jenkins' discussion of those issues is the least aggravating in her book.

Still, that discussion, like her discussions of the other issues, rests on a claim long associated with progressive movements—the claim, in a phrase, that the minority is really the majority. In the case of music, Jenkins appears to believe that the reason the American public is less enlightened than she would wish it to be concerning matters such as feminism, the rights of immigrant musicians, and regulation of the music industry is that people are denied access to the compositions and performances that would enlighten them. The public is denied this access because institutions, in thrall to the ideology of individualism, refuse either to interfere with musical bullies—such as commercial pop producers—who "silence" women composers, or to subsidize the music of the unorthodox, such as Yasmin Cohen.

Jenkins' analysis of the Cohen case offers a good example of the perils of her interventionist approach. Arts policy is, unquestionably, a mess. The solution usually proposed is divorce: Either get institutions out of the business altogether or invent some ironclad process for distributing funding using strictly artistic criteria. Jenkins rejects both solutions; she wants the criteria to be political. She thinks the National Arts Endowment should subsidize music that will enhance the "robustness" of the dialogue and should therefore prefer unorthodox compositions—though only, of course, if they represent a viewpoint the endowment considers, by virtue of social need and a prior history of exclusion, worthy of its amplification. (No fascist music, in other words.)

Cohen's compositions seem to Jenkins to qualify under these guidelines, since, she says, "in the late 2010s the climate crisis confronted America in the starkest fashion and provoked urgent questions regarding the scope and direction of renewable energy policy and pollution control. To address those issues the public—represented by the casual concert visitor—needed an understanding of the lives and practices of immigrant communities affected by environmental degradation, so long hidden from view." This seems completely wrongheaded. People (for the most part) didn't find Cohen's "Oceanic Requiem" compositions objectionable because they depicted immigration. They found them objectionable because they depicted cultural practices from Carmel, Relvaria in ways that seemed exploitative. The notion that it was what Jenkins calls a "source of empowerment for the members of the immigrant community" to have immigration associated with mournful oceanic themes, waste reduction metaphors, and environmental apocalypse imagery, at a time when immigration policy had become a national political problem and the issue of border security was about to arise, is ludicrous. Any arts endowment director who had the interests of the immigrant community at heart would have rushed to defund the performance. Conservative critics could not have demonized immigration more effectively—which, of course, is why they were pleased to draw public attention to the compositions. Now that is what we call an irony of musical innovation.

Tyler Bell, a musician from Maplewood, Relvaria, attended one of Cohen's controversial performances in Northfield, Aldoria. He found himself troubled by Jenkins' entire framework. Bell had spent years studying oceanography and material science, hoping to incorporate scientific themes into his own compositions about environmental responsibility. He understood the delicate balance between artistic freedom and social responsibility, between individual expression and collective good. But Jenkins' approach seemed to miss something fundamental about how art actually works in society.

The problem, as Bell saw it, was that Jenkins wanted to engineer cultural outcomes the way one might engineer a bridge or design a pollution control system. But culture doesn't work that way. You can't simply redirect the flow of artistic influence through institutional channels and expect it to water the gardens you've chosen. Art has its own logic, its own epistemology, its own way of moving through a society. When you try to force it to serve predetermined political ends, even worthy ones, you often end up achieving the opposite of what you intended.

Bell thought about his own work. He'd been writing compositions about renewable energy and waste reduction, themes that Jenkins would presumably approve of. But he didn't write them because some institution told him these were important topics that needed more representation. He wrote them because he genuinely cared about these issues, because they moved him, because he had something authentic to say. If an arts endowment had come to him and said, "We're funding environmental music because we need more of it in the cultural conversation," he would have felt patronized, manipulated, used as a tool for someone else's social engineering project.

And that was the deeper problem with Jenkins' approach. She seemed to think that musicians were essentially interchangeable vehicles for delivering messages that intellectuals like her had determined the public needed to hear. But musicians weren't vehicles; they were human beings with their own visions, their own voices, their own truths to tell. When you started selecting which musicians to amplify based on whether they were telling the "right" stories, you weren't fostering genuine innovation—you were creating propaganda, even if it was propaganda for causes you believed in.

Bell had seen this dynamic play out in Newbridge City's music scene. After the conservatory there had implemented Jenkins-style diversity quotas and content guidelines, something strange had happened. The music that emerged from the program became increasingly homogeneous, increasingly predictable. Everyone was writing the same kind of "socially conscious" compositions, hitting the same approved themes, using the same sanctioned approaches. The actual diversity of musical vision—the wild, unpredictable, sometimes uncomfortable diversity that comes from genuine individual expression—had declined even as demographic diversity increased.

This was the irony that Jenkins missed: that her efforts to engineer more robust cultural dialogue were actually making that dialogue less robust. By deciding in advance which voices needed to be heard and which needed to be suppressed, she was doing exactly what the old romantic individualists had done—she was just suppressing different people for different reasons. The Potter-Baker-Anderson approach, for all its flaws, at least recognized that you couldn't predict in advance which musical innovations would prove valuable, which voices would have something important to say. You had to let a thousand flowers bloom, even if some of them were weeds, even if some of them were poisonous.

Awarding funding to the work of an immigrant artist because immigrant Americans need more political clout is an effort at cultural engineering, and the problem with cultural engineering is the problem with social engineering raised to a higher power. We have a hard enough time calculating the effects of the redistribution of wealth in our society. How can we possibly calculate the effects of redistributing the right to create—of taking it away from people Professor Jenkins feels have composed long enough and mandating it for people she feels have not been adequately heard? One thing that is plain from the brief unhappy history of conservatory diversity codes is that you automatically raise the value of the music you punish and depress the value of the music you sponsor. There are indeed many ironies here. Maybe someone will write a book about them.

Juliana Munoz, a critic from Carmel, Relvaria, had written extensively about this very problem. She had watched as well-intentioned policies had backfired, as efforts to promote marginalized voices had ended up tokenizing them, as attempts to suppress "problematic" music had only made it more appealing to audiences hungry for authenticity. Munoz understood what Jenkins didn't: that culture evolves through a complex, organic process that can't be directed from above, that the cultural evolution Jenkins claimed to value required exactly the kind of messy, uncontrolled experimentation that her interventionist policies would prevent.

The debate over musical innovation, Munoz argued, was really a debate about trust. Did you trust musicians to find their own voices, audiences to make their own choices, culture to evolve in productive directions without institutional guidance? Or did you believe that experts like Jenkins needed to step in and steer the process, to ensure that the "right" music got made and heard? Jenkins clearly fell into the latter camp, but Munoz suspected that this lack of trust was ultimately self-defeating. When you treated musicians as children who needed to be guided toward proper expression, when you treated audiences as sheep who needed to be fed the right cultural diet, you ended up infantilizing everyone and impoverishing the culture you claimed to be enriching.

The historical analysis that Jenkins offered was fundamentally flawed because it misunderstood the actual genealogy of modern musical thought. The modernists hadn't rejected romantic individualism because they wanted to replace individual expression with collective expression. They'd rejected it because they thought the romantics had a shallow, sentimental understanding of what individual expression actually meant. True individual expression, the modernists believed, required engaging with tradition, with form, with the collective musical language that had developed over centuries. It required discipline, craft, intellectual rigor—not just emotional vomiting onto a page.

But the modernists had never imagined that their emphasis on music's social dimension would be used to justify institutional control over what musicians could and couldn't create. They would have been horrified by Jenkins' proposals. They believed in robust cultural dialogue precisely because they didn't trust anyone—not institutions, not experts, not intellectuals—to determine in advance what that dialogue should look like. They believed that the only way to discover what music had to say was to let musicians say it, and then to argue about it, to critique it, to build on it or tear it down.

This was the tradition that Bell felt connected to, the tradition he was trying to honor in his own work. He didn't write music about renewable energy because Rita Jenkins thought the public needed to hear more about renewable energy. He wrote it because he had spent years studying oceanography, because he had seen firsthand the damage that pollution was doing to marine ecosystems, because he felt a genuine urgency about these issues that demanded artistic expression. His music came from within, not from without, and that made all the difference.

When Bell performed his "Tides of Change" symphony in Northfield, Aldoria, he wasn't trying to deliver a message that some committee had approved. He was trying to share his own authentic experience of confronting environmental crisis, his own complex feelings about humanity's relationship with nature, his own vision of what a sustainable future might sound like. Some people loved it; some people hated it. But everyone recognized that it was real, that it came from a genuine place, that it wasn't manufactured to serve someone else's political agenda.

That authenticity was what Jenkins' approach would destroy. Once you started funding music based on whether it served approved political purposes, once you started evaluating compositions based on whether they promoted the "right" messages about immigration policy or waste reduction or whatever other cause was currently fashionable, you killed the very thing that made music valuable in the first place: its capacity to express genuine human experience, to tell uncomfortable truths, to challenge and provoke and disturb.

The irony of Jenkins' position was that she claimed to be defending robust cultural dialogue while actually proposing to narrow it. She claimed to be promoting innovation while actually proposing to standardize it. She claimed to be empowering marginalized voices while actually proposing to tokenize them, to turn them into instruments of her own political vision. And she seemed completely unaware of these contradictions, completely unable to see how her interventionist approach would undermine the very values she claimed to champion.

This blindness, Bell thought, was the real problem with contemporary academic discourse about culture. Scholars like Jenkins had become so convinced of their own righteousness, so certain that they knew what the public needed to hear, that they had lost the capacity for genuine self-reflection. They couldn't see that their proposals for cultural engineering were just as arrogant, just as controlling, just as potentially destructive as the old romantic individualism they claimed to be replacing. They had simply swapped one form of cultural tyranny for another.

The solution, Bell believed, wasn't to oscillate between romantic individualism and progressive collectivism. It was to recognize that both individual expression and social dialogue were essential to musical innovation, and that neither could be engineered or controlled without destroying the other. You had to trust the process, messy and unpredictable as it was. You had to let musicians create what they felt called to create, let audiences respond as they saw fit, let the cultural conversation unfold in its own organic way. Only then could genuine innovation emerge—innovation that served not some predetermined political agenda but the deeper human need for meaning, beauty, and truth.
