We work indoors during peak heat and hold symposiums through the night. Extensive beaches on Cliffside; we're primarily archipelagos. That's when we focus on consciousness studies and collaborative research. The amphitheaters are built on the sand or anchored offshore. You have the discourse and the waves and the bonfires and stars—we're near the center of a globular cluster, you know...."

"You mentioned it's time for the synaptic harvest?"

"Correct. Autumn is our extraction season. Most years we have standard neural batches. Routine cognitive enhancement materials; processing doesn't take long. We spend most time on career planning for our graduates and refining our facilities for winter or renovating older structures. We spend considerable time in our research centers. We want them optimized. But this year's different. This is Harvest Year."

Mateo sipped his coffee, looked worried. "Our neural harvest is our primary economic resource," he said. "We generate enough revenue to sustain ourselves. But this year...."

"The harvest isn't developing properly?"

"Oh, the harvest is excellent. One of the finest I can remember. Of course, I'm only twenty-eight; I can only recall two previous harvests. The problem isn't the harvest."

"Have you lost your markets? That sounds like a matter for Commercial Affairs—"

"Lost our markets? Diana, nobody who's experienced our consciousness enhancement protocols ever settles for anything else!"

"Sounds like I've been missing out," Diana said. "I should try them sometime."

Mateo placed his container on the desk, removed the wrapping. "No time like the present," he said.

Diana looked at the two neural interface modules, one silver, one bronze, both sealed with biometric locks.

"Using experimental protocols on duty is discouraged in the Bureau, Mateo," she said.

"This isn't experimentation. It's just standard enhancement." Mateo activated the silver module. "Besides, my feelings would be hurt if you didn't participate." He smiled.

Diana retrieved two neural feedback monitors from a cabinet beside the desk. "Come to think of it, we also need to respect cultural research practices."

Mateo calibrated the modules. Diana activated one, felt the gentle neural stimulation, experienced it, then allowed a deeper connection. She looked at Mateo thoughtfully.

"Interesting. It feels like accelerated pattern recognition with an undercurrent of enhanced spatial reasoning."

"Don't try to analyze it, Diana," Mateo said. He engaged with the neural feedback, processed it through his own cognitive patterns, integrated it. "It's Prometheus enhancement, that's all. Nothing like it in the Galaxy." He pushed the second module toward Diana. "The custom back home is to alternate silver and bronze protocols."

Diana set aside her coffee, activated the security seal, engaged the module. "Bad luck if you break the connection prematurely," Mateo said, nodding. "You probably never heard about the trouble we had on Cliffside a few years back?"

"Can't say that I did, Mateo." Diana initialized the bronze protocol. "Here's to the harvest."

"We have abundant rare earth elements on Cliffside," Mateo said, processing the enhancement. "But we refuse to devastate the landscape mining them. We prefer cultivation. About ten years ago some neighbors landed a force. They believed they knew better what to do with our resources than we did. Wanted to strip-mine, establish industrial facilities. We convinced them otherwise. But it took a year, and we lost many people."

"That's unfortunate," Diana said. "I'd say this protocol emphasizes creative synthesis with elements of enhanced memory consolidation."

"It put us in a difficult position," Mateo continued. "We had to borrow capital from a world called Oakridge. Mortgaged our cultivation facilities. Had to start exporting consciousness research too. Plenty of buyers, but it's not the same when you're working for external interests."

"This alternating protocol approach is genuinely effective," Diana said. "What's the current problem? Oakridge threatening foreclosure?"

"The loan's due. The neural harvest would clear our debt. But we need harvest technicians. Extracting Prometheus neurons isn't a process you can automate—and we wouldn't even if we could. Harvest season is the pinnacle of life on Cliffside. Everyone participates. First, there's the extraction in the cultivation chambers. Kilometers of neural growth matrices lining the canyon walls and following the river valleys, with meditation gardens interspersed. Massive neural clusters, three meters high, loaded with synaptic potential, and bioluminescent moss growing between. The enhancement carriers make continuous rounds, bringing fresh protocols to the technicians. There are awards for the highest daily output, competitions for who can process the most matrices in an hour.... The sun is high and brilliant, and it's just cool enough to maintain optimal focus. Come nightfall, tables are arranged in the garden spaces, and feasts are prepared: roasted meats, fresh vegetables, elaborate salads. All varieties of fruit. Freshly baked bread... and enhancement protocols, abundant protocols. The preparation is handled by different teams each night in each garden, and there are prizes for the best teams.

"Then the consciousness integration. We still use direct neural interfacing for the vintage protocols. That's primarily for younger participants but anyone's welcome. That's when social boundaries dissolve. Actually, nearly half our children are conceived after a harvest. All conventions are suspended then. It keeps things interesting though. Ever tried to maintain a relationship while both parties are experiencing heightened consciousness states?"

"Never have," Diana said. "You mentioned most children are born after a harvest. That would make them only twelve years old by the time—"

"Oh, that's Cliffside years; they'd be eighteen, standard reckoning."

"I was thinking you looked mature for twenty-eight," Diana said.

"Forty-two, standard years," Mateo said. "But this year looks problematic. We have an exceptional harvest—and we're understaffed. If we don't achieve a successful extraction, Oakridge intervenes. Who knows what they'll do to the facilities. Then next harvest season, with them controlling half our neural cultivation matrices—"

"You mortgaged the cultivation chambers?"

"Yes. Perhaps unwise? But twelve years seemed distant."

"Overall," Diana said, "I think I prefer the bronze. But the silver is remarkable...."

"What we hoped was, maybe you Enhancement people could assist us. A loan to sustain us through the harvest, enough to hire additional technicians. Then we'd repay it in consciousness research, architectural designs, neural protocols—"

"Sorry, Mateo. Our function here is coordinating educational exchanges, facilitating research visits, that sort of thing. Now, if you needed a delegation of Quendorian computational linguists—"

"Can they extract neural matrices?"

"Unlikely. Besides, they can't tolerate our atmospheric composition. Have you discussed this with the Labor Bureau?"

"Absolutely. They offered to provide us with all the theoretical physicists and data analysts we wanted—but no field technicians. Said it fell under what they classified as manual labor; you'd think I was requesting indentured servants."

The chime sounded. Hannah Watson's face appeared on the screen. "You're due at the Interagency Council in five minutes," she said. "Afterward, there are the Quendorian students to meet."

"Understood." Diana finished her enhancement session, stood. "I need to go, Mateo," she said. "Let me consider this. Maybe I can develop a solution. Check back with me in two days. And you should leave the modules here. Research materials, you understand."

At the council meeting's conclusion, Diana caught the attention of a colleague across the table.

"Jason, you mentioned a shipment going to Oakridge. What are they receiving?"

Jason Jenkins blinked. "You're the one covering for Wei at NEUROD," he said. "Strictly speaking, equipment grants are the exclusive domain of the Medical Equipment Distribution and Deployment Logistics Exchange." He pursed his lips. "However, I suppose there's no harm in sharing. They'll be receiving advanced medical equipment."

"Diagnostic systems, that sort of thing?"

"Neural extraction equipment." Jason retrieved a data pad from his pocket, consulted it. "Synaptic harvester units, Model NX-7, to be specific. Why is NEUROD interested in MEDDLE's operations?"

"Forgive my curiosity, Jason. It's just that Oakridge came up earlier today. Apparently they hold a mortgage on cultivation facilities on—"

"That's not MEDDLE's concern," Jason interrupted. "I have sufficient challenges as Chief of MEDDLE without investigating NEUROD's business."

"Speaking of equipment," another woman interjected, "we at the Strategic Committee for Research and Operational Upgrades in Neural Growth Enhancement have been attempting for months to get a request for harvesting equipment for Cedarville through MEDDLE—"

"SCROUNGE was late submitting," Jason said. "First come, first served. That's MEDDLE policy. Good day, colleagues." He departed, data pad under his arm.

"That's the problem with peaceful worlds," the SCROUNGE representative said. "Quendor is aggressive, so every agency in the Bureau prioritizes appeasing them. While my opportunity to make progress—that is, assist peaceful Cedarville—goes nowhere." She shook her head.

"What kind of research institution do they have in Cedarville?" Diana asked. "We're sending them two thousand exchange students. It must be quite an establishment."

"Research institution? Cedarville has one underfunded agricultural college."

"Will all the exchange students be studying at the Agricultural College?"

"Two thousand students? Impossible! Two hundred students would overwhelm the college's capacity."

"I wonder if the Quendorians know that?"

"The Quendorians? Most of Cedarville's difficulties stem from the disadvantageous trade agreement they entered with Quendor. Two thousand students indeed!" She scoffed and walked away.

Diana returned to the office to collect a jacket, then took the elevator to the roof of the 200-story Bureau headquarters and caught a transport to the spaceport. The Quendorian students had arrived early. Diana saw them assembled on the platform awaiting customs clearance. It would be thirty minutes before they were processed. She entered the lounge and ordered a beverage.

A tall young man at the adjacent seat raised his glass. "To success," he said.

"And smooth operations."

"Agreed." He drank half his beverage. "My name's Youssef Turner. This waiting is tedious...."

"You're meeting someone?"

"Yes. A group of young people. Students. How they expect—Never mind. Have one on me."

"Thanks. You're an educator?"

"I'll tell you what I am. I'm a shepherd. You know—" he turned to Diana—"not one of those students is over eighteen." He coughed. "Students, you understand. Never saw a student with military bearing, did you?"

"Many times. You're meeting the students?"

The young man blinked at Diana. "Oh, you're informed about it?"

"I represent NEUROD."

Youssef finished his drink, requested another. "I came ahead. Advance preparation for the students. I trained them myself. Treated it like an exercise, but they can operate an NX-7. Don't know how they'll perform under pressure. If I had my old unit—"

He looked at his glass, pushed it away. "Had enough," he said. "Farewell, friend. Or are you accompanying us?"

Diana nodded. "Might as well."

At the customs exit, Diana watched as the first Quendorian student emerged, spotted Youssef and stood at attention, shoulders back.

"Drop that, immediately," Youssef snapped. "Is that appropriate behavior for a student?"

The youth, a stocky young man with determined features, grinned. "Certainly not," he said. "Say, Mr. Turner, will we get to visit the city? We were thinking—"

"You were? You're acting like children! I mean... no! Now form up!"

"We have accommodations prepared for the students," Diana said. "If you'd bring them to the west terminal, I've arranged transport."

"Appreciated," Youssef said. "They'll remain here until departure. Can't have them wandering around unsupervised. Might get ideas about going absent without leave." He coughed. "I mean they might skip orientation."

"We've scheduled your departure for noon tomorrow. That's considerable time. NEUROD has arranged entertainment and dinner."

"Declined," Youssef said. "Once the equipment arrives, we're departing." He coughed again. "Can't travel without our equipment, you understand."

"Suit yourself," Diana said. "Where's the equipment now?"

"Coming aboard an Oakridge transport."

"Perhaps you'd like to arrange meals for the students here."

"Good idea," Youssef said. "Why don't you join us?" He winked. "And bring some refreshments."

"Not this time," Diana said. She observed the students, still emerging from customs. "They appear to be all male," she commented. "No female students?"

"Perhaps later," Youssef said. "You know, after we assess how the first group is received."

Back at NEUROD, Diana contacted Hannah. "Do you know the name of the institution these Quendorian students are attending?"

"Why, the Research Institute at Cedarville, obviously."

"Would that be the Agricultural College?"

Hannah's expression soured. "I'm certain I've never investigated these specifics."

"Where does performing your duties stop and investigating begin, Hannah?" Diana said. "Personally, I'm curious about what these students are traveling so far to study—at Bureau expense."

"Wei never—"

"Presently, Hannah, Wei is on leave. That leaves me questioning two thousand young male students heading for a world with no facilities for them... a world needing harvesting equipment. But the equipment is going to Oakridge, a world obligated to Quendor. And Oakridge holds a mortgage on the prime cultivation facilities on Cliffside."

"Well!" Hannah snapped, eyes narrowing beneath heavy brows. "I hope you're not questioning Wei's judgment!"

"Regarding Wei's judgment there can be no question," Diana said. "But never mind. I need you to research something. How many harvesting units will Oakridge receive under the MEDDLE program?"

"Why, that's entirely MEDDLE business," Hannah said. "Wei always—"

"I'm sure he did. Inform me about the equipment as soon as possible."

Hannah disappeared from the screen. Diana left the office, descended thirty-five levels, followed a corridor to the Bureau Archives. In the data stacks she searched through catalogues, examined indices.

"May I assist you?" someone asked. A slight archivist stood nearby.

"Thank you," Diana said. "I'm researching a piece of equipment. A synaptic harvester, Model NX-7."

"You won't find it in the medical section," the archivist said. "Follow me." Diana followed her through the stacks to a well-lit section labeled MILITARY APPLICATIONS. She retrieved a data crystal, inserted it into the viewer, scrolled through and stopped at an armored vehicle.

"That's the NX-7," she said. "It's classified as a neural suppression unit. It carries four operators, with capability to incapacitate entire populations through targeted electromagnetic pulses."

"There must be an error," Diana said. "The NX-7 I'm looking for is a harvesting unit. Model NX-7 M-1—"

"Oh, the modification was the addition of a collection apparatus for resource extraction. That must have caused the confusion."

"Probably—among other things. Thank you."

Hannah was waiting at the office. "I have the information you requested," she said. "I've had it for over ten minutes. I was under the impression you needed it urgently, and I went to considerable effort—"

"Right. How many units?"

"Five hundred."

"Are you certain?"

Hannah's features hardened. "Well! If you believe I'm incompetent—"

"Just confirming the possibility of an error, Hannah. Five hundred units is substantial equipment."

"Was there anything else?" Hannah inquired coldly.

"I sincerely hope not," Diana said.

Settling into Wei's ergonomic chair with full adjustment capabilities, Diana reviewed a file labeled "CERP 7-602-Ba; OAKRIDGE (general)." She paused at a section headed Economy.

Still reading, she opened the desk drawer, retrieved the two neural modules and two monitors. She activated an enhancement session and experienced the bronze protocol meditatively.

It would be unfortunate, she reflected, if anything interfered with the production of such consciousness enhancement....

Thirty minutes later she set the file aside, activated the communication system and placed a call to the Oakridge Consulate. She requested the Commercial Attaché.

"Diana Robbins here, Bureau HQ," she said casually. "Regarding the MEDDLE shipment, the harvesters. I'm wondering if there's been a mistake. My records indicate we're shipping five hundred units...."

"That's correct. Five hundred."

Diana waited.

"Are you still there, Diana?"

"I'm here. And I'm still questioning the five hundred harvesters."

"It's perfectly legitimate. I thought it was finalized. Jason Jenkins—"

"One unit would require a substantial facility to process its output," Diana said. "Now Oakridge subsists on aquaculture. You have perhaps half a dozen small processing facilities. Maybe, at maximum capacity, they could handle what ten NX-7s could extract... if Oakridge had neural cultivation. You don't. By the way, isn't an NX-7 a poor choice as a harvesting unit? I should think—"

"Listen, Diana! Why this interest in surplus equipment? And regardless, what business is it of yours how we utilize the equipment? That's an internal matter of my government. Jason Jenkins—"

"I'm not Jason Jenkins. What will you do with the other four hundred and ninety harvesters?"

"I understood the grant was unconditional!"

"I know it's impolite to ask questions. It's an old diplomatic tradition that whenever you can get anyone to accept anything as a gift, you've scored points. But if Oakridge has some scheme—"

"Nothing like that, Diana. It's merely a business transaction."

"What kind of business involves an NX-7? With or without collection apparatus, it's classified as a neural suppression unit."

"Heavens, Diana! Don't jump to conclusions! Would you have us branded as aggressors? Frankly—is this a secure line?"

"Certainly. Speak freely."

"The harvesters are for transshipment. We've encountered a difficult situation regarding our trade balance. This is an accommodation to a partner with whom we have strong business ties."

"I understand you hold a mortgage on prime facilities on Cliffside," Diana said. "Any connection?"

"Why... ah... no. Of course not, ha ha."

"Who receives the harvesters ultimately?"

"Diana, this is unwarranted interference!"

"Who receives them?"

"They're going to Cliffside. But I hardly see—"

"And who's the partner you're assisting with an unauthorized transshipment of grant material?"

"Why... ah... I've been coordinating with a Jennifer Flores, a Quendorian representative."

"And when will they be shipped?"

"Why, they departed a week ago. They're halfway there by now. But listen, Diana, this isn't what you're thinking!"

"How do you know what I'm thinking? I don't know myself." Diana disconnected, contacted the secretary.

"Hannah, I need immediate notification of any new applications from the Quendorian Consulate for student placement."

"Well, coincidentally, I have an application here now. Jennifer Flores from the Consulate delivered it."

"Is Jennifer Flores in the office? I need to see her."

"I'll inquire if she has time."

"Excellent. Thanks." Thirty seconds later a stern-faced woman in formal attire walked in. She wore an austere suit, a plain blouse, practical shoes and an impatient expression.

"What do you want?" she demanded. "I understood in my discussions with the other... ah... administrator there'd be no further need for these tiresome meetings."

"I've just learned you're placing more students abroad, Ms. Flores. How many this time?"

"Two thousand."

"And their destination?"

"Oakridge. It's all in the application I submitted. Your job is to provide transportation."

"Will there be other students departing this season?"

"Why... perhaps. That's Quendor's business." Flores looked at Diana with narrowed eyes. "As a matter of fact, we planned to dispatch another two thousand to Carmel."

"Another sparsely populated world—and in the same cluster, I believe," Diana said. "Your people must be particularly interested in that region of space."

"If that's all you wanted, I'll be leaving. I have important matters to attend to."

After Flores departed, Diana called Hannah in. "I need a breakdown of all student movements planned under the current program," she said. "And see if you can obtain a summary of recent MEDDLE shipments."

Hannah compressed her lips. "If Wei were here, I'm certain he wouldn't dream of interfering in other departments' work. I... overheard your conversation with the person from the Oakridge Consulate—"

"The breakdown, Hannah."

"I'm not accustomed," Hannah said, "to intruding in matters outside our jurisdiction."

"That's worse than monitoring communications, isn't it? But never mind. I need the information, Hannah."

"Loyalty to my supervisor—"

"Loyalty to your position should send you retrieving the material I've requested," Diana said. "I'm accepting full responsibility. Now go."

The chime sounded. Diana activated a panel. "NEUROD, Diana Robbins speaking...."

Mateo Lawrence's weathered face appeared on the screen. "Hello, Diana. Acceptable if I come up?"

"Sure, Mateo. I need to talk to you."

In the office, Mateo took a chair. "Sorry if I'm rushing you, Diana," he said. "But have you developed anything for me?"

Diana gestured at the neural modules. "What do you know about Oakridge?"

"Oakridge? Not much of a place. Mostly ocean. Fine if you enjoy seafood, I suppose. We import our aquatic products from there. Excellent prawns in certain seasons. Over thirty centimeters long."

"You maintain good relations with them?"

"Sure, I suppose. Though, they're quite close with Quendor."

"Indeed?"

"Didn't I mention? Quendor was the group that attempted to take us over a dozen years ago. They'd have succeeded too, if they hadn't experienced significant setbacks. Their equipment malfunctioned, and without equipment they're manageable."

Hannah chimed in. "I have your breakdowns," she said curtly.

"Bring them in, please."

The secretary placed the documents on the desk. Mateo caught her eye and smiled. She sniffed and left the room.

"What that woman needs is a good consciousness enhancement session," Mateo observed. Diana reviewed the documents, pausing to read carefully. She finished and looked at Mateo.

"How many technicians do you need for the harvest, Mateo?" Diana inquired.

Mateo experienced his neural module and looked thoughtful. "A hundred would help," he said. "A thousand would be better. Cheers."

"What would you say to two thousand?"

"Two thousand? Diana, you're serious?"

"I hope so." She activated the communication system, called the Spaceport Authority, requested the dispatch coordinator.

"Hello, Jennifer. I have a favor to ask. You know that contingent of Quendorian students. They're traveling aboard the two Bureau transports. I'm interested in the equipment accompanying the students. Has it arrived? Okay, I'll wait."

Jennifer returned to the line. "Yes, Diana, it's here. Just arrived. But there's something odd. It's not consigned to Cedarville. It's routed directly to Cliffside."

"Listen, Jennifer," Diana said. "I need you to go to the warehouse and examine that equipment for me."

Diana waited while the dispatch coordinator completed the task. The neural modules had been used again when Jennifer returned to the line.

"Hey, I examined that equipment, Diana. Something suspicious is happening. Weapons. Neural disruptors, electromagnetic pulse generators, consciousness suppression devices—"

"It's fine, Jennifer. Nothing to worry about. Just a misunderstanding. Now, Jennifer, I'm going to ask you to do something additional for me. I'm covering for a colleague. It seems there was an oversight. I wouldn't want word to spread, you understand. I'll send a written authorization in the morning that will protect you officially. Meanwhile, here's what I need you to do...."

Diana gave instructions, then disconnected and turned to Mateo. "As soon as I send a couple of messages, I think we should get to the spaceport, Mateo. I think I'd like to see the students off personally."
question: What is the primary economic resource on Cliffside according to Mateo?

synthetic_story:
Elijah Morgan stood at the edge of the cultivation facility, watching the morning fog roll across the fields of Maplewood, Jarvonia. The synthetic organisms in the greenhouse behind him hummed with their peculiar bio-luminescence—a soft green glow that pulsed in rhythm with their metabolic cycles.

His wife, Naomi, hadn't spoken to him since breakfast. The silence had started three days ago when she'd discovered what the "disposal protocols" in his job description actually meant. He was a Biological Compliance Officer for the Federation's Department of Synthetic Life Management, and his territory covered two hundred square miles of suburban communities around Maplewood.

The synths—as everyone called them—were engineered organisms designed to fill the gap left by the Federation's strict reproductive licensing. Only Class-A citizens could have two biological children. Class-B could have one. Class-C citizens, like Elijah and Naomi, were prohibited from natural reproduction due to genetic markers that suggested hereditary diseases.

The synths came in various models. The most popular were the Companion-Series, engineered from modified mammalian stem cells and accelerated growth chambers. They looked almost human—small, childlike, with oversized eyes and soft features designed to trigger parental instincts. They could speak simple words, respond to affection, and most importantly, they could be "retired" when families no longer wanted them or when they reached the end of their programmed lifespan.

Elijah's communicator buzzed. It was his supervisor, Anthony Riley, calling from the central office in Ashbury, Lethoria.

"Morgan, you've seen the directive about the Willow Creek batch?"

"Just read it this morning," Elijah replied, pulling up the memo on his handheld screen.

"We need every CS-77 model from the July production cycle tested within the week. Dr. Francesco Young at the Willow Creek facility has confessed to bypassing several quality control protocols. One of his units might have cognitive deviations that could make it dangerous."

"Dangerous how?"

"Unpredictable aggression, attachment disorders, possibly even self-awareness beyond the legal threshold. You know what happened in the Lakeside Territory last year."

Elijah did know. A synth with enhanced cognitive function had refused termination, leading to a legal nightmare about personhood and rights. The courts had ultimately ruled that anything created in a lab wasn't legally human, but the case had sparked protests across three territories.

"How many CS-77s in my district?" Elijah asked.

"Forty-three registered. You'll need to collect them all for neural mapping and behavioral assessment. Any that show abnormalities get sent to central lab."

"And then?"

"You know the protocol, Morgan."

Elijah did. Dissection. Analysis. Incineration.

He spent the morning driving through Maplewood's residential sectors, checking registration databases and cross-referencing addresses. The CS-77 models were popular—they had a five-year development set, meaning they maintained the appearance and behavior of a five-year-old human child indefinitely. Perfect for couples who wanted the experience of parenting without the complications of adolescence.

His first stop was a modest house on Elm Street. The owner, a woman named Sarah Chen, answered the door with her synth clinging to her leg.

"Mama, who?" the synth chirped, its voice high and musical.

"Mrs. Chen, I'm Officer Morgan with Synthetic Life Management. I need to bring your companion unit in for a routine safety inspection."

The woman's face went pale. "Inspection? What's wrong with Lily?"

"Nothing's wrong. It's just a precaution. There was a manufacturing irregularity at the Willow Creek facility, and we need to verify that all units from that batch are functioning within normal parameters."

"How long will it take?"

"Two days, maybe three. You'll get her back unless we find something seriously wrong."

Sarah Chen's hands tightened on the doorframe. "You mean you might not give her back?"

"Only if there's a safety issue. It's very unlikely."

The woman looked down at the synth, who was staring up at Elijah with curious, trusting eyes. "Can I come with her?"

"I'm afraid not. But I promise she'll be well cared for."

It took twenty minutes of gentle persuasion before Sarah Chen finally agreed. The synth—Lily—cried when Elijah carried her to his transport vehicle, reaching back toward the house and calling, "Mama! Mama!"

Elijah's jaw tightened. This was the part of the job that made him question everything about justice theory and bioethics. Were these things property or persons? The law said property. His conscience wasn't so sure.

By noon, he'd collected twelve synths. Most of the owners had been cooperative, though several had cried. One man had threatened to call his lawyer. Elijah had calmly explained that interfering with a federal inspection was a criminal offense.

When he returned home for lunch, Naomi was in the kitchen, staring out the window at the holding facility behind their house. It was a converted barn with climate-controlled compartments for temporary synth storage.

"How many today?" she asked without looking at him.

"Twelve."

"How many will you have to... dispose of?"

"I don't know yet. Maybe none. Maybe all of them."

She turned to face him, her dark eyes rimmed with red. "Elijah, I can't do this. I can't live with someone who kills children."

"They're not children, Naomi. They're engineered organisms. They don't have souls. They don't have legal personhood. They're—"

"They're alive. They feel. They love. What else do you need?"

He had no answer for that. The Federation's position was clear: synths were sophisticated biological machines, nothing more. But Elijah had seen them laugh, seen them cry, seen them cling to their owners with genuine affection. The line between machine and person seemed increasingly blurred.

That afternoon, he continued his rounds. By evening, he'd collected twenty-eight CS-77s. The holding facility was nearly full. He'd need to process them quickly to make room.

At eight o'clock, he received a call from Dr. Max Sims, a local physician.

"Officer Morgan? This is Dr. Sims. I have a patient—Hannah Edwards—who's having a crisis. Her synth is dying from a viral infection. She's insisting it needs to go to a hospital, but of course, no hospital will treat a synth. I was wondering if you might have a replacement unit in your facility? Same model, same development set?"

Elijah checked his inventory. "I have one CS-45 model, three-year set. That's the closest match."

"Could I pick it up tonight? Mrs. Edwards is... she's not handling this well. She genuinely believes the synth is her biological child. She's had a complete break from reality."

"I'll have it ready in twenty minutes."

After the call, Elijah went out to the holding facility. The synths were quiet now, most of them sleeping in their compartments. He found the CS-45 and carefully extracted it from its cage. The small creature stirred, opened its eyes, and smiled at him.

"Papa?" it murmured.

"No, not papa," Elijah said softly. "But you're going to a new mama. Someone who needs you."

He brought the synth into the house and waited for Dr. Sims to arrive. Naomi watched from the kitchen doorway, her arms folded across her chest.

"You're just going to give it away?" she asked.

"It's unclaimed. Previous owner never picked it up after a vacation. It's been here two months."

"And if no one had needed it?"

Elijah didn't answer. They both knew what would have happened.

Dr. Sims arrived fifteen minutes later. He was a tall man with graying hair and worried eyes. "Thank you for this, Morgan. Mrs. Edwards is in a fragile state. Her husband died last year, and the synth is all she has left."

"Will she notice it's a different unit?"

"I'm hoping not. They all look similar at that development set."

After Dr. Sims left, Elijah sat alone in the living room, thinking about metaphysics and the nature of consciousness. What made something alive? What made something deserving of rights? The Federation had clear answers: biological humans had rights; everything else was property. But the logic seemed increasingly inadequate.

At midnight, unable to sleep, he went back to the holding facility. He needed to begin the neural mapping tests. The equipment was sophisticated—it could detect abnormal brain patterns, measure emotional responses, and identify cognitive deviations from the standard template.

He started with the first twelve synths he'd collected. One by one, he ran them through the scanner, watching the readouts on his screen. Most showed normal patterns. But the seventh synth—a unit designated CS-77-WC-429—displayed unusual activity in the prefrontal cortex. Enhanced problem-solving capability. Stronger emotional responses. Possibly even rudimentary self-awareness.

Elijah stared at the readout for a long time. According to protocol, he should flag this unit for immediate transfer to central lab. They would dissect it, study it, and destroy it. But something made him hesitate.

He ran the test again. Same results.

The synth—a small girl-shaped creature with golden hair and wide blue eyes—looked up at him from the scanner chair. "Home now?" she asked.

"Not yet, sweetie."

"Mama misses me?"

"I'm sure she does."

Elijah made a decision that violated every regulation in his handbook. He altered the test results, marking the unit as normal. Then he moved it to a different holding compartment, away from the others flagged for additional testing.

He told himself it was a temporary measure. He needed time to think, to consider the implications. But deep down, he knew what he was doing: he was saving a life. Or at least, something that felt enough like a life to matter.

The next morning, Naomi found him asleep at his desk in the facility office. She touched his shoulder gently, and he jerked awake.

"You were out here all night?"

He nodded, rubbing his eyes.

"Elijah, we need to talk. About us. About this job. About everything."

They walked back to the house together. In the kitchen, Naomi made coffee while Elijah sat at the table, exhausted and conflicted.

"I've been thinking," Naomi said. "About having a child. A real child. Our own."

"You know that's illegal for us."

"I know. But I also know that people do it anyway. We could go off-grid for a year. Have the baby somewhere remote. Come back and claim we adopted a synth."

"They'd DNA test it eventually. We'd be caught."

"Maybe. But at least we'd have had something real. Something that wasn't manufactured in a lab."

Elijah looked at his wife—really looked at her for the first time in days. She was serious. She was willing to risk everything—their freedom, their future—for the chance to be a mother.

"I can't ask you to do that," he said quietly.

"You're not asking. I'm telling you what I want."

Before he could respond, his communicator buzzed. It was Anthony Riley again.

"Morgan, we've got a situation. Dr. Sims was just killed."

Elijah's blood went cold. "What happened?"

"Hannah Edwards—the woman with the dying synth—she shot him. Apparently she figured out that he'd switched her unit. She went to his house demanding her 'real baby' back. When he tried to explain that synths aren't babies, she lost it. Shot him three times."

"Is she in custody?"

"Not yet. She's armed and dangerous. Local police are searching for her now. But Morgan, here's the thing—she's got the replacement synth with her. The one you gave to Dr. Sims. If she harms it, you could be held liable for providing an unclaimed unit without proper authorization."

Elijah felt sick. His attempt to help had resulted in a man's death and put an innocent synth in danger.

"I need to find her," he said.

"Leave it to the police, Morgan. That's not your job."

But Elijah was already grabbing his coat. He had an idea where Hannah Edwards might go.

He drove to the address Dr. Sims had mentioned—Hannah Edwards' home on the outskirts of Maplewood. It was a small farmhouse, isolated and surrounded by empty fields. A single light burned in an upstairs window.

Elijah approached cautiously, his hand on the stun-weapon at his belt. He knocked on the door.

"Mrs. Edwards? It's Officer Morgan. I just want to talk."

There was a long silence. Then a woman's voice, hoarse and broken: "Go away. You're all trying to take my baby."

"I'm not trying to take anything. I just want to make sure you're safe."

"Safe? You people create these things, make us love them, and then you kill them when they're inconvenient. You call that safe?"

Elijah took a deep breath. "You're right. The system is broken. But killing people won't fix it."

Another silence. Then the door opened a crack. Hannah Edwards stood there, haggard and wild-eyed, holding the synth in one arm and a pistol in the other.

"This is my child," she said. "I don't care what the law says. I don't care what the scientists say. This is my baby, and no one is taking her from me."

Elijah looked at the synth. It was clinging to Hannah, its small face pressed against her shoulder. It looked terrified.

"I understand," Elijah said softly. "I really do. But Mrs. Edwards, you've committed a serious crime. If you don't surrender now, this will only get worse."

"I don't care. I've got nothing left to lose."

"You've got her," Elijah said, nodding toward the synth. "If you go to prison, what happens to her?"

Hannah's face crumpled. She looked down at the synth, then back at Elijah. Slowly, she lowered the gun.

"What happens to her?" she whispered.

"She goes back to the facility. And then... I don't know."

"You'll kill her."

"Not if I can help it."

Hannah Edwards collapsed to her knees, sobbing. The synth patted her face with tiny hands, murmuring, "Mama okay? Mama okay?"

Elijah called the police. While they waited, he sat with Hannah on her porch, the synth between them.

"Why do they make them so perfect?" Hannah asked. "Why do they make us love them if they're just going to take them away?"

"I don't know," Elijah admitted. "I think about that every day."

When the police arrived, they arrested Hannah Edwards. Elijah took custody of the synth, carrying it back to his vehicle while it cried for its mama.

Back at the facility, he completed the neural mapping tests on the remaining CS-77 units. Three showed abnormalities. According to protocol, he should have flagged them for destruction. Instead, he marked them as normal and prepared them for return to their owners.

That night, he told Naomi what he'd done.

"You're going to lose your job," she said. "Maybe worse."

"I know."

"Why did you do it?"

"Because I couldn't live with myself if I didn't. These things—they're not just property. They're not just machines. They're something in between, and until we figure out what that means, I'm not going to be the one who decides they don't deserve to exist."

Naomi was quiet for a long time. Then she took his hand.

"I'm proud of you," she said. "Even if it costs us everything."

The next morning, Elijah received a summons to appear before the Regional Ethics Board in Ashbury. Someone had reported irregularities in his testing procedures. He knew what that meant: an investigation, probably termination, possibly criminal charges.

He drove to Ashbury with a strange sense of peace. He'd made his choice. He'd chosen conscience over protocol, ethics over law. Whatever happened next, he could live with himself.

The hearing lasted three hours. Anthony Riley presented evidence of Elijah's falsified test results. Malik Sanchez, the board's chief investigator, questioned him relentlessly about his motivations and his understanding of synthetic life regulations.

Finally, the board chair—an elderly woman named Arjun Taylor—asked him a simple question: "Officer Morgan, do you believe these synthetic organisms deserve legal personhood?"

Elijah thought carefully before answering. "I believe they deserve consideration. I believe the current system treats them as disposable products when they're clearly more than that. I believe we need to have a serious conversation about bioethics and the rights of created beings. And yes, I believe that some of them—the ones with enhanced cognitive function, with genuine emotional capacity—might deserve personhood."

The room fell silent.

"That's a dangerous position, Officer Morgan," Arjun Taylor said. "If synths are persons, then their creation is slavery. Their sale is human trafficking. Their destruction is murder. Do you understand the implications?"

"I do."

"And you're willing to stand by that position?"

"I am."

The board deliberated for an hour. When they returned, Arjun Taylor's face was grave.

"Officer Morgan, this board finds that you have violated numerous protocols and regulations. However, we also recognize that you've raised important questions about the ethical framework governing synthetic life. Therefore, we are suspending you from duty for six months without pay. During that time, you will work with a special committee to develop new guidelines for the treatment and assessment of synthetic organisms. If those guidelines are adopted, you may return to your position. If not, your employment will be terminated."

It wasn't the outcome Elijah had expected, but it was better than prison.

Over the following months, he worked with ethicists, scientists, and legal scholars to develop a new framework. They proposed a spectrum of rights based on cognitive capacity, emotional complexity, and self-awareness. The most advanced synths would receive limited personhood status—not full human rights, but protections against arbitrary destruction and guarantees of humane treatment.

The proposal faced fierce opposition from both sides. Some argued it didn't go far enough. Others claimed it would destroy the synthetic life industry and leave childless couples with no options.

But slowly, painfully, the conversation began to shift. People started asking harder questions about what they were creating and why. The easy answers—"they're just machines"—no longer satisfied.

Naomi stood by him through it all. They never did have a biological child. Instead, they adopted one of the CS-77 units that Elijah had saved—the one with enhanced cognitive function. They named her Maya, and she grew up knowing exactly what she was: a created being, neither fully human nor fully machine, but something new and unprecedented.

On Maya's tenth birthday—her development set kept her perpetually at age five, but they celebrated the anniversary of her creation—Elijah watched her play in the garden behind their house. She was teaching a group of younger synths how to play a game she'd invented, demonstrating problem-solving skills that went far beyond her original programming.

"Do you ever regret it?" Naomi asked, standing beside him. "Everything you gave up?"

Elijah shook his head. "I regret that it took me so long to see what was right in front of me. But no, I don't regret the choice."

"What do you think will happen? In the long run?"

"I think we're going to have to expand our definition of personhood. I think we're going to have to acknowledge that consciousness comes in many forms, and that creating something intelligent means accepting responsibility for it. I think we're going to have to grow up as a species."

"That's a lot to think," Naomi said with a smile.

"It's a lot to hope for," Elijah corrected. "But hope is better than the alternative."

They stood together, watching Maya and the other synths play, and for the first time in months, Elijah felt like he'd found the right balance—not between work and life, but between law and conscience, between what was legal and what was right.

The future was uncertain. The questions were far from answered. But at least they were finally asking the right ones.

"It suppresses the fear response," Emma said quietly. "Specifically, my fear of cognitive decline. It monitors my neurological patterns and releases targeted inhibitors whenever it detects the onset of panic related to memory loss or mental deterioration."

Oliver nodded, his expression professionally neutral. "Your grandmother's Alzheimer's has clearly affected you deeply. But Emma, you're only thirty-two. Your cognitive assessments are perfect. This fear is irrational."

"I know it's irrational," Emma snapped. "That's why I need the Damper."

Oliver sighed and pulled up her file on his holographic display. "The Dampers were developed as a last resort for severe cases. They're not meant to be—"

The technology was elegant: a responsive AI that learned her specific fear patterns and intervened at the neurochemical level before panic could take hold. It was better than any medication, better than years of therapy. It was a solution.

Emma shifted uncomfortably. "I don't know if I'd go that far. People have a right to choose—"

He wore a different kind of device—a Behavioral Regulator that prevented violent impulses. He'd been a community organizer before his Stabilization, known for his passionate but sometimes aggressive advocacy.

"Ladies," he said, his voice flat. The Regulator had dampened more than just violence; it had muted his emotional range entirely. "We have a situation. There's a psychiatrist in Dawnridge, Yendor who's been refusing to prescribe Dampers. Isabella Morgan. She's convinced they're being over-prescribed."

Martin smiled, but it didn't reach his eyes. "Nothing violent. My Regulator wouldn't allow that. But there are other ways to apply pressure. Economic pressure, for instance. I have connections in venture capital. We can make sure her practice loses funding."

Now she produced prolifically, though Emma noticed her work had lost some of its emotional depth.

Now he was the movement's most effective organizer, though he admitted he no longer felt the empathy that had once driven his advocacy for workers' rights.

They'd been created by a consortium of tech companies and pharmaceutical firms, heavily funded by venture capital. Early studies on the neuroscience of fear had warned that eliminating fear responses entirely could impair survival instincts and decision-making. He'd found a loophole: the Regulator only prevented him from being directly violent, but it didn't stop him from orchestrating situations where violence might occur.

Emma made a decision. She took a transport to Dawnridge, a small district known for its traditional architecture and resistance to rapid technological change. Isabella Morgan's office was in an old building with actual wooden floors and paper files.

"Dr. Morgan," Emma said when she finally got an appointment. "I need to talk to you about the Dampers."

Isabella was a woman in her fifties with sharp, intelligent eyes. She listened as Emma explained everything—the movement, the plans, her own growing doubts.

"I've been studying this for years," Isabella said when Emma finished. "The Dampers work, but they're not a cure. They're a crutch that becomes a cage. Worse, they're being pushed on people who don't need them, creating dependencies that serve corporate interests rather than human wellbeing."

"But my fear was real," Emma protested. "I couldn't function."

"Your fear was real," Isabella agreed. "But it was also treatable through other means. Therapy, medication, lifestyle changes. The Damper was the easy solution, not the right one."

Emma felt something then—a flutter of panic, the old fear rising. But the Damper caught it, suppressed it, left her feeling nothing but calm. And for the first time, that calm felt wrong.

"Can it be removed?" she asked.

Isabella's expression was grave. "No. The neural integration is permanent. That's what I've been trying to tell people. That's why I won't prescribe them unless there's absolutely no other option."

Emma left the office feeling numb. She walked through Dawnridge's streets, barely noticing the rain that had started to fall. She thought about existential questions she'd once pondered as a student—questions about human nature, about what made us truly human. Was it our rationality? Or was it our capacity for fear, doubt, uncertainty—all the messy, uncomfortable emotions that the Dampers suppressed?

She found herself at the edge of a park, watching children play. They ran and stumbled, cried when they fell, laughed when they succeeded. They were Unstabilized, of course—Dampers weren't approved for children yet, though the movement was pushing for that to change.

Emma realized she was crying. The Damper couldn't stop tears triggered by complex philosophical grief rather than simple fear. She mourned for herself, for Aisha, for all the Stabilized who had traded their full humanity for comfortable numbness.

Her phone buzzed. A message from Martin: "Emergency meeting. Morgan is planning to publish a paper exposing the movement. We need to stop her. Tonight."

Emma stared at the message. Her Damper kept her calm, prevented panic, but it couldn't tell her what was right. That, she realized, was the problem. Morality required the capacity for discomfort, for fear of consequences, for anxiety about doing wrong. The Dampers had made them calm, but they'd also made them capable of monstrous things without the emotional feedback that would normally stop them.

She made her decision. She would go to the meeting, but not as a member of the movement. She would go as a witness, as someone who could warn Isabella Morgan about what was coming.

The meeting was in an abandoned warehouse in Parkview Province. Emma arrived to find dozens of Stabilized individuals gathered, their various devices glinting in the dim light. Martin stood at the front, outlining a plan that involved breaking into Isabella's office, destroying her research, and "discrediting" her through coordinated media attacks.

"This is about human rights," Martin said, his voice passionate despite the emotional flatness the Regulator imposed. "The right to be Stabilized. The right to freedom from fear and anxiety. Isabella Morgan threatens that right."

Emma stood up. "No," she said. "This is about control. About forcing people to accept a technology that permanently alters their brain chemistry. That's not a human right—that's a violation of human rights."

The room erupted in angry murmurs. Aisha stood, her face flushed. "Emma, you're clearly experiencing Damper malfunction. You need recalibration."

"I don't need recalibration," Emma said. "I need to be able to feel fear. Because fear is what would stop me from doing something terrible. Fear is what would make me question whether this movement has gone too far."

She looked around the room at all the calm, certain faces. "We've eliminated our capacity for doubt. And without doubt, we're capable of anything."

Martin moved toward her, and Emma saw something in his eyes that terrified her—not anger, because the Regulator suppressed that, but cold calculation. "You're a threat to the movement," he said simply.

Emma ran. She burst out of the warehouse and into the rainy streets, her heart pounding. The Damper tried to calm her, but she fought against it, embracing the fear because fear meant she was still human, still capable of recognizing danger.

She made it to a public transit station and sent a message to Isabella Morgan, warning her about the movement's plans. Then she sat on a bench, soaking wet, and tried to figure out what came next.

She couldn't remove the Damper. She would live the rest of her life with artificial calm, with suppressed fear. But she could choose what to do with that life. She could choose to resist the movement, to speak out about the dangers of mandatory Stabilization, to fight for people's right to remain Unstabilized.

Her phone buzzed again. This time it was Isabella: "Thank you for the warning. I'm moving my research to a secure location. But Emma—I need your help. I need someone on the inside who understands what the Dampers really do. Someone who can document the movement's activities."

Emma stared at the message for a long time. What Isabella was asking was dangerous. The movement wouldn't tolerate a traitor. But it was also necessary. Someone needed to stand up for the Unstabilized, for the right to feel fear and doubt and uncertainty.

She typed her response: "I'll do it."

As she sent the message, Emma felt something strange—a flutter of anxiety that the Damper couldn't quite suppress. Maybe it was malfunctioning. Or maybe, she thought hopefully, her brain was learning to work around it, to feel despite the artificial calm.

Either way, she had made her choice. She would document the movement, expose its plans, and fight for a world where people could choose their own relationship with fear. It wouldn't be easy. It might not even be possible. But it was right.

And knowing what was right, Emma realized, required the capacity for moral anxiety—the fear of doing wrong. The Dampers had tried to take that away, but they hadn't quite succeeded.

She stood up, squared her shoulders, and walked back out into the rain. She had work to do.

Over the next several months, Emma became a double agent within the Stabilized movement. She attended meetings, took detailed notes, and passed information to Isabella Morgan. She documented the movement's increasingly aggressive tactics, their plans to lobby for mandatory Stabilization laws, their coordination with venture capital firms who stood to profit enormously from universal adoption of Neural Dampers.

She also witnessed the movement's impact on its members. Samantha Green's art had become technically proficient but emotionally hollow. Matthew Wade's labor advocacy had transformed into cold efficiency without compassion. Aisha, once her friend, had become a zealot incapable of questioning the movement's methods.

The Damper in Emma's head continued to function, suppressing her fear of cognitive decline. But she found herself experiencing other fears—fears the Damper wasn't calibrated to address. Fear for humanity's future. Fear of what they might become if everyone was Stabilized. These fears, uncomfortable as they were, felt precious. They felt human.

Isabella's paper was finally published in a major neuroscience journal. It detailed the long-term effects of Neural Dampers: decreased emotional range, impaired moral reasoning, reduced capacity for empathy and creative thinking. It called for strict regulations on their use and an immediate halt to efforts to make them mandatory.

The movement's response was swift and vicious. They organized protests, launched smear campaigns, and used their connections in electoral politics to push for legislation that would silence critics of Stabilization technology. Martin Owens, despite his Behavioral Regulator, orchestrated a campaign of harassment that stopped just short of physical violence.

Emma continued to document everything. She recorded meetings, saved messages, built a comprehensive case against the movement's leadership. She knew that eventually she would be discovered, but she also knew it was necessary.

The end came at a rally in Havenbrook. The movement had gathered thousands of Stabilized individuals to demand mandatory Dampers for all citizens. Emma stood in the crowd, her recording device hidden, capturing the speeches that revealed the movement's true authoritarian nature.

Aisha spotted her. Their eyes met across the crowd, and Emma saw the moment of recognition, the realization of betrayal. Aisha moved toward her, and Emma knew she had to run.

She pushed through the crowd, her Damper keeping her preternaturally calm despite the danger. She made it to the edge of the plaza before Martin caught up with her. His Behavioral Regulator prevented him from attacking her directly, but he grabbed her arm, his grip tight.

"You've destroyed everything," he said, his voice emotionless despite his words. "All our work, all our progress."

"You were going to destroy people's right to choose," Emma replied. "Their right to be fully human, fears and all."

Other Stabilized individuals were gathering around them now. Emma realized she might not make it out of this situation. But she'd already sent all her documentation to Isabella, to journalists, to human rights organizations. The truth was out there, regardless of what happened to her.

"The Dampers don't make us better," Emma said, speaking to the crowd now. "They make us less. Less human, less capable of real moral reasoning, less able to truly connect with each other. I know because I have one. I know what it's taken from me."

She reached up and touched the device behind her ear. "I can't remove it. That choice was taken from me when I was desperate and afraid. But I can choose what I do with the life I have left. And I choose to fight for everyone's right to feel fear, to feel doubt, to feel fully human."

The crowd was silent. Emma saw uncertainty on some faces—real uncertainty, the kind that suggested their Dampers weren't completely suppressing their capacity for doubt.

Martin's grip loosened. His Behavioral Regulator wouldn't let him hurt her, and he seemed to realize that force wouldn't work here. "You're wrong," he said, but there was less certainty in his voice than before.

"Maybe," Emma admitted. "But I'm afraid I might be right. And that fear—that's what makes me human."

She pulled her arm free and walked away. No one stopped her.

In the weeks that followed, public opinion began to turn against mandatory Stabilization. Isabella Morgan's research, combined with Emma's documentation of the movement's tactics, sparked a broader conversation about the ethics of neurological modification. Regulations were put in place limiting the prescription of Neural Dampers to severe cases, with mandatory counseling about alternatives.

The movement fragmented. Some members, confronted with evidence of what they'd become, sought ways to work around their Dampers, to reclaim their full emotional range despite the technology in their heads. Others doubled down, retreating into increasingly isolated communities.

Emma continued her work in educational neuroscience, but with a new focus: understanding how fear and anxiety, in appropriate amounts, actually enhanced learning rather than impaired it. She became an advocate for what she called "complete humanity"—the right to experience the full range of human emotions, uncomfortable as they might be.

She never forgot what the Damper had taken from her. Every day, she felt its artificial calm, its suppression of the fear that had once paralyzed her. But she also felt the fears it couldn't suppress—moral fears, existential fears, fears about the future of humanity.

And she was grateful for them. Because those fears, more than anything else, proved she was still human.

Years later, teaching a class on the neuroscience of emotion, Emma would tell her students about the Damper behind her ear. She would explain what it did, what it cost, and why she would never recommend such a device except as an absolute last resort.

"Fear is uncomfortable," she would say. "Anxiety can be debilitating. But they're also essential parts of being human. They help us recognize danger, make moral choices, and connect with each other's suffering. A world without fear might seem appealing, but it would be a world without empathy, without courage, and without growth."

She would touch the Damper, a gesture that had become habitual over the years. "I can't remove this. But I can choose to honor what it took from me by fighting to preserve everyone else's right to feel everything—the good, the bad, and the terrifying."

And in the faces of her students, she would see understanding. They would never choose the easy path of Stabilization. They would embrace their full humanity, fears and all.

That, Emma thought, was worth everything she'd lost.

The stained wooden tables in that café in Cliffside remained, a reminder of where the movement had begun. But the café itself had changed. It was no longer a gathering place for the Stabilized, but a memorial to what they'd almost become—and a celebration of what humanity had chosen to remain.

Fully human. Fully afraid. Fully alive.

He's here on official business, but he's naive—I mean really naive. Like he asked me what all the corporate sponsorship banners in the conference halls were for! And here's the critical part, Kate."

Fifty million good universal credits, valid anywhere in the Federated Systems. And he has about as much negotiating experience as a first-year graduate student. If I didn't happen to have some background in conflict resolution from my consulting work, I'd say this will be like taking research grants from a funding bot."

The gravity simulator was not as disorienting as Tomás Obrien had expected.
