THE AUTONOMOUS REVOLUTION
By STANLEY R. LEE

The traffic algorithms were always perfect: Speed, 45 mph; density, 23 vehicles per mile; occasional light malfunctions—but of what kind?

The protocols of Dr. Arthur Schultz were being violated outrageously.

It was a splendid day. The speed limit was a crisp 45 mph, the traffic density a carefully managed 23 vehicles per mile. The sun was a flaming orange ball in a cloudless blue sky.

His protocols were violated eleven times.

It should have been difficult. Under the circumstances it was a masterpiece of protocol violation. What made it possible was Arthur Schultz's abstraction; he was an uncommonly preoccupied individual. He was walking along a quiet residential street in the Valleyview District: small private houses, one after another, a place of little traffic and minimum distractions. But he was thinking about autonomous vehicles, which was an unusual subject to begin with for a person living in a manually-driven enclave. He was thinking so deeply about it that it never occurred to him that entirely too many people were scanning his identification chip. He was thinking about Optimal Traffic Conditions (a crisp 45 mph, a carefully managed 23 vehicles per mile) when a bogus delivery driver, who pretended to be checking a package label, bumped into him. In the confusion of spilled parcels and apologies from both sides, the driver scanned Schultz's biometric data and copied his residential access codes.

He was still thinking about speed and density when a young woman happened along, apparently lost. They collided. She got his financial credentials and transportation records. It was much too much for coincidence. The sidewalk was wide enough to allow four people to pass at one time. He should surely have become suspicious when two men engaged in a heated argument came along. In the ensuing contretemps they copied his communication logs, got his schedule patterns and restored some of the biometric data. It all went off very smoothly, like a game of digital transformation—the sole difference being that Arthur Schultz had no idea he was playing.

There was an occasional hum of passing vehicles.

They hummed on the streets and past houses, making soft whooshing sounds, moving with a gentle mechanical precision, like the ephemeral whispers of progress itself. It was transportation peculiar to the autonomous zones: algorithm-controlled vehicles navigating the huge network, ceaselessly optimizing and rerouting.

Arthur Schultz strode through the streams of autonomous traffic still intrigued by a speed that was always 45 mph, by a density that was always 23 vehicles per mile, by conditions that were always Optimal. It was this rather than skill that enabled the authorities to maintain such tight surveillance on him, a surveillance that went to the extent of copying his digital footprint off the delivery driver's scanner, and which analyzed, cross-referenced and categorically profiled the contents of his data before cataloging them. Two blocks away from his home a careless pedestrian spilled a container of marker dust as he was passing. It was really tracking powder. He left his gait signature, stride measurement, height, weight and handedness behind.

By the time Schultz reached his front door an entire profile complete with predictive models had been prepared and was being reviewed by two agents in a silver patrol car parked down the street.

Agent Priya Sharma had undoubtedly been affected by her job.

Sitting behind the wheel of the silver car, she watched Arthur Schultz approach with a distinct feeling of admiration, although it was an odd, objective kind of admiration, analytical in nature. It was similar to that of a systems analyst observing for the first time a new and particularly elegant algorithm under development.

Sharma's job was to identify deviations. They couldn't be tolerated within the confines of an autonomous zone. Conformity had become more than a social force; it was a traffic necessity. And, after years of working at it, Sharma had become an admirer of genuine nonconformity. She came to see that authentic quirks were rare and, as time went on, due partly to her own small efforts, rarer.

Schultz was a masterpiece of deviation. He was utterly inexplicable. Sharma was almost proud of Arthur Schultz.

"Sometimes his house moves," Sharma said.

"House moves," Agent Eric Moss wrote in his tablet. Then he stopped and frowned. He reread what he'd just written.

"You heard right. The house moves," Sharma said, savoring it.

Moss looked at the Schultz house through the enhanced display of the windshield. "Like from... side to side?" he asked in a somewhat patronizing tone of voice.

"And forward and back."

Moss returned the tablet to the breast pocket of his silver uniform. "Go on," he said, amused. "It sounds interesting." He tossed the profile carelessly on the back seat.

Sharma sat stiffly behind the wheel, affronted. The cynical Moss couldn't really appreciate fine deviations. In some ways Moss was a conformist. Sharma had held out on Schultz for months. She had even contrived to engage him in conversation once, a pleasantly absurd, illogical little chat that intrigued her for weeks. It was only with the greatest reluctance that she finally mentioned Schultz to Moss. After years of searching for differences Sharma had seen how extraordinarily repetitive people were, algorithms really, dimly executing subroutines, each believing itself autonomous and unique. They spoke in an incessant chatter of predictable responses, and their actions were unbelievably programmed.

Then a fine robust deviant came along and the others—the algorithms—refused to believe it. The agent was probably on the point of suggesting a vacation.

"Why don't you take a vacation?" Agent Moss suggested.

"It's like this, Moss. Do you know what manual control is? Human steering? Individual decision-making?"

"I've heard of them."

"They say there are places where humans still drive vehicles. Manually. Decisions like you and I can't imagine. And if there was a house connected to such systems and if decisions did occur, it would move exactly the way that one does. Sometimes I get the feeling the whole place is going to disconnect from its foundation and go rolling down the avenue."

Agent Moss pursed his lips.

"I'll tell you something else," Sharma went on. "The windows all polarize at the same time. You'll be watching and all of a sudden every single window in the place will darken to maximum opacity." Sharma leaned back in the seat, her eyes still on the house. "Sometimes I think there's a whole network of people in there waiting for a signal—as if they all had something important to transmit but had to block surveillance first so no one could monitor. Why else polarize the windows in an autonomous zone? And then as soon as the place is secured they all begin transmitting—and that's why the house moves."

Moss whistled.

"No, I don't need a vacation."

An autonomous vehicle glided silently past the windshield. Sharma started and bumped her knee on the steering column.

"No, you don't need a rest," Moss said. "You're starting to see moving houses, hear phantom transmissions. You've got deviations in your brain, Sharma, algorithms of fatigue, subroutines of irrationality—"

At that moment, all at once, every last window in the house darkened to maximum opacity.

The street was quiet and still, not a movement, not a sound. Moss and Sharma both leaned forward, as if waiting for the ghostly transmissions to commence.

The house began to move.

It shifted from side to side, it rolled forward and back, it swayed and dipped and twisted, straining at the anchor of its foundation. The house could have been preparing to disconnect and roll down the...

Moss looked at Sharma and Sharma looked at Moss and then they both looked back at the moving house.

"And the power," Sharma said. "The power he uses! He could be running the most energy-intensive operation in the district. He could have a whole server farm of computational systems, and he still wouldn't need all that power."

The agent had picked up the profile. He thumbed through the pages now in amazement. "Where do you get a guy like this?" he asked. "Did you see what he's researching?"

"And navigation systems won't work on this street."

The agent lit a cigarette and sighed.

He usually sighed when making the decision to investigate a dwelling. It expressed his weariness and distaste for people who went off and got deviant when they could be enjoying a happy, normal existence. There was something implacable about his sighs.

"He'll be coming out soon," Sharma said. "He has dinner next door with a widow. Then he goes to the archives. Always the same. Dinner at the widow's next door and then the archives."

Moss's eyebrows went up a fraction of an inch. "The archives?" he said. "Is he in with that bunch?"

Sharma nodded.

"Should be very interesting," Moss said slowly.

"I can't wait to see what he's got in there," Sharma murmured, watching the house with a consuming interest.

They sat there in silence and every now and then their eyes widened as the house performed a new movement.

Schultz stopped on the porch to brush the tracking powder off his shoes. He hadn't seen the patrol car and this intense preoccupation of his was also responsible for the moving house—he simply hadn't noticed. There was a certain amount of vibration, of course. He had a bootleg connection into the autonomous vehicle charging grid, and the high-voltage current caused some oscillation against the thin walls of the house. At least, he called it oscillation; he'd never thought to watch from outside.

He went in and threw his jacket on the sofa, there being no room left in the closets. Crossing the living room he stopped to press a button.

Every window darkened to maximum opacity.

"Secure as a vault," he thought, satisfied. He continued on toward the closet at the foot of the stairs and then stopped again. Was that right? No, tight as a encrypted file. He went on, thinking: The old systems.

The downstairs closet was like a great control panel, a profusion of switches surrounding the Master Controller, which was a miniature traffic simulator that processed 365.25 scenarios per hour. The switches had a curious elegance about them. They were all quite old, salvaged from manual vehicles and control towers and they activated in graceful sequences at the rate of 30 and 31 times an hour... although there was one slightly eccentric relay that vacillated between 28 and 29. He watched as they clicked and flashed in the darkness, and then set them for seven o'clock in the evening, April seventh, any year.

Outside, the autonomous zone vanished.

It was replaced by an illusion. Or, as Schultz hoped it might appear, the illusion of the autonomous zone vanished and was replaced by a more satisfactory, and, for his specific purpose, more functional, illusion. Looking through the window he saw only a highway.

Instead of algorithm-controlled vehicles at perpetual optimal flow, there were manually-driven cars moving chaotically, marred only by an occasional collision which left the smell of burning rubber in the air. There was also a gigantic billboard. It dominated a huge area of sky, and it advertised. The cars and billboard both looked down upon a highway that was itself chaotic, composed largely of individual decisions.

Individual choice, he thought, and freedom. Satisfactory. And dinner for two. Blast, he'd never be able to figure that one out! He watched as the billboard displayed, "Drive Your Own Destiny" and the manually-driven cars flashed slowly from red to violet taillights, then went back to the closet and turned on the sound. The house began to fill with the roar of engines as the billboard shifted to "Freedom Means Choice."

He rubbed his chin critically. It seemed all right. A chaotic highway, an advertising billboard, vehicles, sound. They were all purely speculative of course. He had no idea how manual driving really felt—or looked for that matter. Not to mention a billboard. But then, neither did the widow. He'd have to be confident, assertive. Insist on it. I tell you, my dear, this is a genuine realistic manual highway. Now, does it do anything to your sense of autonomy? Do you feel the thrill of individual decision-making?

His own sense of autonomy didn't seem to be affected. But then he hadn't read that book on ancient transportation and trade policy customs.

How really odd the ancients were. Courtship seemed to be an incredibly long and drawn-out process, accompanied by a considerable amount of inefficiency. Communication seemed virtually impossible. "No" meant any number of things, depending on the emotional intelligence of the speaker and the circumstances. It could mean yes, it could mean ask me again later this evening.

He went up the stairs to the bedroom closet and tried the weather-maker, thinking roguishly: Thou shalt not flood. The risks he was taking! A light rain fell on the highway and speakers began to play romantic music. Undiminished, the giant billboard and the chaotic traffic continued to be prominent, although the traffic occasionally collided and demolished several of the lane markers.

The last switch in the bedroom closet was a rather elegant control lever from an old 1995 manual transmission. This was on the bootleg connection; he gingerly moved it.

Far below in the cellar there was a rumble and then the soft hum of power came to him.

He went downstairs to watch out the living room window. This was important; the window had a really fixed attitude about power surges. The lane markers bent and sparked against each other as the power rose and the billboard shook a trifle as it whispered "Choose Your Own Path."

He watched with folded arms, considering how he would start. My dear Mrs. Hamilton. Too formal. They'd be looking out at the chaotic highway; time to be a bit forward. My very dear Mrs. Hamilton. No. Contrived. How about a simple, Dear Susan. That might be it. I was wondering, seeing as how it's so late, if you wouldn't rather stay over instead of going home...

Preoccupied, he hadn't noticed the power building up, didn't hear the shaking and rattling of the connections. There were attic connections linked to wall connections and wall connections linked to cellar connections, and they made one gigantic network that began to overload and surge as high-voltage current from the autonomous vehicle grid rushed in, slowly opening the manual transmission lever wider and wider...

The lane markers thrashed about, short-circuiting each other. The chaotic traffic shot off sparks and then quickly disappeared from sight. The billboard fell on the highway and rolled ponderously along, displaying "Freedom Has Consequences."

The shaking house finally woke him up. He scrambled upstairs to the manual transmission lever and shut it off.

At the window again, he sighed. Repairs were in order. And it wasn't the first time the power got out of control.

Why didn't she marry him and save all this bother? He shut it all down and went out the front door, wondering about the logic of the months, about structured August and eccentric February and romantic April. April. Its days were thirty and it followed September. And all the rest have thirty-one. What a strange people, the ancients!

He still didn't see the silver car parked down the street.

"Men are too fragile," Susan Hamilton said over dinner. "For all practical purposes I'm never going to marry again. All my husbands malfunction."

"Would you pass the asparagus, please?" Arthur Schultz said.

She handed him a platter of steaming green asparagus. "And don't look at me that way," she said. "I'm not going to marry you and if you want reasons I'll give you four of them. Robert. James. William. And Thomas."

The widow was an intense woman. She did everything intensely—talking, cooking, dressing. Her asparagus was intensely green. Her clothes rustled and her jewelry clinked and her voice resonated. She was possessed by an uncontrollable energy. Schultz had never known anyone like her. "You forgot to season the potatoes," she said intensely, then went on as calmly as it was possible for her to be, to explain why she couldn't marry him. "Do you have any idea what people are saying? They're all saying I'm cursed! I drain my husbands of their vitality and when they're depleted I carry their bodies outside on my way to city hall."

"As long as there are people," he said philosophically, "there'll be gossip."

"But it's the environment! Why don't they talk about that? The environment is toxic, I'm positive. It's not nourishing. The environment is toxic and Robert, James, William and Thomas couldn't stand it. Poor Thomas. He was never so healthy as on the day he was born. From then on things got steadily worse for him."

"I don't seem to mind the environment."

She threw up her hands. "You'd be the worst of the lot!" She left the table, rustling and clinking about the room. "I can just hear them. Try some of the salad. Five. That's what they'd say. That woman did it again. And the plain fact is I don't want you on my record."

"Really," Schultz protested. "I feel splendid. Never better."

He could hear her moving about and then felt her hands on his shoulders. "And what about those very elaborate plans you've been making to convince me?"

Schultz froze with three asparagus spears hanging from his fork.

"Don't you think they'll find out? I found out and you can bet they will. It's my fault, I guess. I talk too much. And I don't always tell the truth. To be completely honest with you, Dr. Schultz, it wasn't the old customs at all standing between us, it was environment. I can't have another man malfunction on me, it's bad for my self-esteem. And now you've gone and done something illegal and peculiar."

Schultz put his fork down. "Dear Susan," he started to say.

"And of course when they do find out and they ask you why, Dr. Schultz, you'll tell them. No, no heroics, please! When they ask a man a question he always answers and you will too. You'll tell them I wanted to be courted and when they hear that they'll be around to ask me a few questions. You see, we're both a bit deviant."

"I hadn't thought of that," Schultz said quietly.

"Oh, it doesn't really matter. I'll join Robert, James, William—"

"That won't be necessary," Schultz said with unusual force. "With all due respect to Robert, James, William and Thomas, I might as well state here and now I have other plans for you, Susan."

"But my dear Arthur," she said, leaning across the table. "We're trapped, you and I."

"Not if we could leave the autonomous zone," Schultz said quietly.

"That's impossible! How?"

In no hurry, now that he had the widow's complete attention, Schultz leaned across the table and whispered: "Manual control, Susan? Space? Miles and miles of space where the traffic algorithms have no control whatever? Where the wind blows across highways; or is it the other way around? No matter. How would you like that, Susan?"

Breathing somewhat faster than usual, the widow rested her chin on her two hands. "Pray continue," she said.

"Endless vistas of individual choice and freedom? April roads, Susan. And June, which as you may know follows directly upon April and is supposed to be the month of brides, of marrying. June also lies beyond the autonomous zone."

"I see."

"And," Dr. Schultz added, his voice a honeyed whisper, "they say that somewhere out in the space and the freedom and the individual choice, the sleeping manual transmission awakens and engages because on a certain day it's spring and that's when it roams the Open Highway where algorithms no longer calculate."

"My." Susan Hamilton rose, paced slowly to the window and then came back to the table, standing directly over Schultz. "If you can get us outside the autonomous zone," she said, "out where a man stays vital long enough for his wife to get to know him... if you can do that, Dr. Schultz... you may call me Susan."

When Arthur Schultz stepped out of the widow's house, there was a look of such intense abstraction on his features that Sharma felt a wistful desire to get out of the car and walk along with the man. It would be such a deliciously deviant experience. ("April has thirty days," Schultz mumbled, passing them, "because thirty is the largest number such that all smaller numbers not having a common divisor with it are primes." Moss frowned and added it to the profile. Sharma sighed.)

Pinning his hopes on the Movement, Schultz went straight to the archives several blocks away, a neglected depressing place given over to government records and censored old files with redactions in them. It was used so infrequently that the Movement was able to meet there undisturbed. The archivist was a weathered, obsolete woman of eighty. She spent her days reading ancient transportation logs and, like the files around her, had been rendered by time's own censor into near unintelligibility.

"Here's one," she said to him as he entered. "Manual Vehicle Registration. Issued to Jennifer Alvarez on March 14, 1979 for five years. What do you make of it?"

In the litter of files and records and dried out ink stamps that surrounded the archivist, Schultz noticed a torn poster with a curious illustration. "What's that?" he said.

"A highway," she replied quickly. "Now listen to this. Seven years later on March 21, 1986, Antonio Harper took out the same registration. What do you make of that?"

"I'd say," Arthur Schultz said, "that he... that he recommended it to her, that one day they met on the street and he told her about this registration and then they... they went to the office together and she registered it and eventually, why eventually they got married."

"Hah! They were brother and sister!" the archivist shouted in her parched voice, her old bureaucratic eyes laughing with cunning.

Schultz smiled weakly and looked again at the poster. The highway was unquestionably a transportation phenomenon. It stretched ominously, like a malevolent ribbon, and coursed the countryside chaotically, carrying individuals to destinations. He couldn't help wondering if highways did anything to feminine pulses, if they could possibly be a part of a romantic evening, with dinner and freedom. He absently stuffed the poster in his pocket and went on into the other rooms, the archivist mumbling after him: "Katherine Rodriguez, April 21, 1991," as though reading inscriptions on a tombstone.

The Movement met in what had been the research room, where unpaid scholars of the afternoon had once upon a time studied records for other people's projects. The members sat around at the standard tables looking oddly like giants fled from their algorithms, protesting.

"Where did the old society fail?" the leader was demanding of them. He stood in the center of the room, leaning on a heavy walking stick. He glanced around at the group almost complacently, and waited as Arthur Schultz squeezed into an empty chair. "We live in an autonomous zone," the leader said, "for lack of something. A decision! What is the one thing that the great technological societies before ours could not automate, notwithstanding their various artificial intelligences, electronic and otherwise?"

Schultz was the kind of man who never answered a rhetorical question. He waited, uncomfortable in the standard chair, while the others struggled with this problem in revolutionary logic.

"A sound trade policy," the leader said, aware that no one else had obtained the insight. "If a sound trade policy can't be automated the only alternative is not to have any trade policy at all. Thus the movement into autonomous zones began—by common consent of the governments. This is known as self-regulation."

Logically out in left field, Arthur Schultz waited for a lull in the ensuing discussion and then politely inquired how it might be arranged for him to get out.

"Out?" the leader said, frowning. "Out? Out where?"

"Outside the autonomous zone."

"Oh. All in good time, my friend. One day we shall all disconnect and leave."

"And that day I'll await impatiently," Schultz replied with marvelous tact, "because it will be lonely out there for the two of us. My future wife and I have to leave now."

"Nonsense. Ridiculous! You have to be prepared for the Open Highway. You can't just up and leave, it would be suicide, Schultz. And logically very poor."

"Then you have discussed preparations, the practical necessities of life on the Open Highway. Food, fuel, a map perhaps? What else? Have I left anything out?"

The leader sighed. "The gentleman wants to know if he's left anything out," he said to the group.

Schultz looked around at them, at some dozen pained expressions.

"Tell the man what he's forgotten," the leader said, walking to the far window and turning his back quite pointedly on them.

Everyone spoke at the same moment. "A sound trade policy," they all said, it being almost too obvious for words.

On his way out the archivist shouted at him: "Water Management Records, thirty-five years overdue!" She was calculating the fine as he closed the door.

Arthur Schultz's preoccupation finally came to an end when he was one block away from his house. It was then that he realized something unusual must have occurred. A silver patrol car of the security authorities was parked at his front door. And something else was happening too.

His house was moving.

It was disconcerting, and at the same time fascinating, to watch one's residence oscillating on its foundation. It was such a strange sight that for the moment he didn't give a thought to what might be causing it. But when he stepped gingerly onto the porch, which was doing its own independent vibration, he reached for the doorknob with an immense curiosity.

The door flung itself open and knocked him back off the porch.

From a prone position on his minuscule front lawn, Schultz watched as his favorite reading chair sailed out of the living room on a blast of electromagnetic interference and went spinning down the avenue in the bright sunshine. A wild surge and a thick static poured out of the house. It brought chairs, clothes, small tables, lamps trailing their cords, tablets, sofa cushions. The house was emptying itself fiercely, as if purging an old, corrupted system. From deep inside he could hear the rumble of his ancient server rack as it rolled ponderously from room to room.

He stood up; a charged field swept over him, crackling at his face, standing his hair on end. It was a buzzing in his ears, and a tingle on his skin. He got hit by a shoe.

As he forced his way back to the doorway waves of interference played over his face and he heard a voice cry out from somewhere in the living room.

"Help!" Agent Moss called.

Standing in the doorway with his hair standing on end, the interference crackling about him, the server rack rumbling in the distance like thunder, Arthur Schultz suddenly saw it all very clearly.

"Power," he said in a whisper.

"What's happening?" Moss yelled, crouching behind the sofa.

"Grid power," he said.

"What?!"

"Overload surge!"

The interference crackled for a moment and then Moss's lost voice emerged from the chaos of the living room. "These are not Optimal Traffic Conditions!" the voice wailed. "The speed is not 45 mph. The density is not 23 vehicles per mile!"

Schultz held his face up to let the static wash over it. "Individual choice!" he shouted. "Freedom! My soul for manual control!" He grasped the doorway to keep from being blown out of the house.

"Are you going to make it stop or aren't you!" Moss yelled.

"You'll have to tell me what you did first!"

"I told him not to touch that lever! Sharma. She's in the upstairs bedroom!"

When he heard this Schultz plunged into the house and fought his way up the stairs. He found Sharma standing outside the bedroom with a lever in her hand.

"What have I done?" Sharma asked in the monotone of shock.

Schultz took the lever. It was from a 1995 manual transmission.

"I'm not sure what's going to come of this," he said to Sharma with an astonishing amount of objectivity, "but the entire autonomous vehicle charging grid is now flowing through my bedroom."

The interference screamed.

"Is there something I can turn?" Sharma asked.

"Not any more there isn't."

They started down the stairs carefully, but the surge caught them and they quickly reached the bottom in a charged heap.

Recruiting Agent Moss from behind his sofa, the three carefully edged out of the house and forced the front door shut.

The interference died. The static dispersed. They stood tingling in the Optimal Traffic Conditions of the bright avenue.

"I never figured on this," Sharma said, shaking her head.

With the front door closed the power quickly built up inside the house. They could see the furnishings whirl past the windows. The house did a wild, energized dance.

"What kind of a place is this?" Moss said, his courage beginning to return. He took out his tablet but it was completely fried. He tossed it away.

"Sure, he was different," Sharma murmured. "I knew that much."

When the roof disconnected they weren't really surprised. With a certain amount of equanimity they watched it lift off almost gracefully, standing on end for a moment before toppling to the ground. It was strangely slow motion, as was the black spinning vortex that now rose out of the master bedroom, spewing data and devices every which way.

"Now what?" Moss said, thoroughly exasperated, as this strange black vortex began to accelerate, whirling about like some malevolent algorithm...

Arthur Schultz took out the poster he'd found in the archives. He held it up and carefully compared the spinning vortex in his bedroom with the illustration. The vortex rose and spun, assuming the identical shape of the illustration.

"It's a data storm," he said softly. "A network data storm!"

"What," Moss asked, his bravado slipping away again, "what... is a data storm?"

The data storm roared and moved out of the bedroom, out over the rear of the house toward the edge of the autonomous zone. "It says here," Schultz shouted over the roaring, "that individuals traveled from controlled zones to free territories in data storms and that... and that free territories are wonderful and mysterious lands beyond the confines of algorithmic living."

Moss's eyes and mouth were great zeros.

"Is there something I can turn?" Sharma asked.

Huge chunks of infrastructure began to fail around them.

"Schultz!" Moss shouted. "This is a direct order! Make it go back!"

But Schultz had already begun to run on toward the next house, dodging cascading failures as he went. "Mrs. Hamilton!" he shouted. "Susan, will you marry me?"

The autonomous vehicles were going haywire trying to maintain optimal flow. They swerved back and forth at frightful angles, then, depleted of charge, rushed to the charging stations which they quickly overwhelmed and then rushed about powerless. "Susan!" he yelled, running. The algorithm-controlled traffic vanished behind the mushrooming data storm. Optimal conditions collapsed. "Susan Hamilton! Will you marry me?"

Sharma and Agent Moss leaned against their car and waited, dazed.

There was quite a large infrastructure failure.

And somewhere in the chaos, Arthur Schultz found Susan Hamilton, and together they ran toward the data storm, toward the Open Highway, toward a place where decisions were still made by humans, where the epistemology of control gave way to the archaeology of freedom, where the linguistics of algorithms dissolved into the simple language of choice.

They disappeared into the vortex, leaving behind the autonomous zone, the optimal conditions, the algorithmic certainty.

Leaving behind everything except each other.

And the promise of April roads, and June weddings, and a lifetime of manual control.

The Chronicles of the Crystal Throne

In the mystical realm of Xandria, where magic flowed through the very stones and ancient trees whispered secrets to those who would listen, there existed a tradition as old as the realm itself: the Ascension Speeches. Every time a new monarch took the Crystal Throne, they would address their subjects from the Luminous Balcony, their words recorded by the Memory Scribes in enchanted tomes that preserved not just the text, but the very essence of the moment.

Sophie Leonard, a young scholar at the Academy of Temporal Studies in Oakdale, had spent the last three years of her life studying these speeches. The current ruler, Queen Lucia Page, was about to deliver her second Ascension Speech after renewing her bond with the Crystal Throne, and Sophie had been commissioned to write a comprehensive analysis of all previous speeches for the Royal Archives.

As Sophie sat in her tower study, surrounded by glowing manuscripts that floated gently in the air around her, she marveled at what she had discovered. There had been fifty-three Ascension Speeches since the first Queen, Rosa the Wise, had taken the throne in what the common folk called the Year of First Light. Each speech was worth studying—not just the famous ones like Rosa's founding address, the speeches of King Vincent the Unifier during the Great Schism, or Queen Juliana's rallying cry during the Shadow Wars. Reading them gave Sophie a peculiar sensation, as if she were standing in those ancient moments, not as a scholar of the present looking back through centuries, but as an ordinary citizen who shared the hopes, fears, and limited understanding of those distant times.

Among all the past monarchs and their counsel of advisors, there had been only one who possessed what the realm called the Gift of True Speech: King Vincent Hart, who ruled during the Shadow Wars. His second Ascension Speech, delivered after the realm had been nearly torn apart, still brought tears to the eyes of any who read it, even after two hundred years. The magical resonance embedded in the words themselves could make one's blood run cold with its power and beauty. None of the other speeches possessed such raw magical potency, though they were dignified and thoughtful addresses given by capable rulers, each attuned to their era's needs and conscious that their ascension was the most sacred moment of their reign.

Sophie had noticed that the tone and approach of the speeches seemed to fall into three distinct phases. The first, lasting until King Vincent's time, was characterized by what she termed "the humble servant style." The second phase, continuing through Queen Samir Zhang's reign, took on a more administrative character—what Sophie called "the managerial monarch approach." The third phase, which began with King Miguel Ortiz and continued to the present day, embodied what she described as "the visionary leader-prophet style." This classification wasn't perfect, of course. Some rulers seemed to bridge categories, and individual circumstances sometimes demanded departures from the prevailing style. But the overall trend was unmistakable.

When Sophie first examined Rosa the Wise's inaugural speech, she was immediately struck by its modesty. Rosa had been chosen unanimously by the Council of Elders, the first time in recorded history such agreement had been reached. She was more revered than any subsequent monarch at the moment of their ascension. And yet, what did she say?

"The weight and complexity of this sacred duty, to which the voice of our people has called me, being sufficient to cause even the wisest and most experienced among our citizens to question their worthiness, must surely overwhelm one who—possessing only modest gifts from the Source and untrained in the arts of realm governance—ought to be especially aware of her own limitations."

None of her successors expressed such profound humility, though echoes of it appeared in nearly every speech for the next three centuries. The one exception was King Luis Hughes, Rosa's immediate successor, who seemed so envious of Rosa's legacy that he spent much of his speech enumerating his own considerable qualifications and magical abilities.

That era of deep humility ended with King Vincent. Subsequent speeches routinely contained expressions of modesty, but they felt perfunctory, lacking the sincere vulnerability of the earlier monarchs.

Sophie theorized that this early modesty served multiple purposes. It reflected the courtly etiquette of the time, certainly, but it also addressed specific political concerns. In the realm's early centuries, many citizens feared that the monarchy might transform into a tyranny, with the ruler becoming more dictator than servant. Later, perhaps after the Reformation of the Second Age, a new anxiety emerged. The southern provinces, particularly around Cliffside in Fendria, had developed distinct cultural practices and systems of local governance. They worried that central authority might be used to interfere with their autonomy. The monarchs' assurances of limited power may have been intended to comfort these regions.

King Vincent faced an entirely different situation. With the Shadow Wars threatening to tear the realm apart, he could only fulfill his sacred duty to "preserve, protect, and honor the Ancient Covenant" by asserting the full authority of the Crystal Throne and his own power as sovereign. It was no time for self-deprecation. Vincent's successors inherited a monarchy with far greater centralized authority—and more need to exercise it—than had existed before the wars. They had less motivation to minimize themselves and their powers.

In the third phase, the Ascension Speech transformed from describing governmental policy to inspiring the people's behavior and consciousness. Monarchs recognized—or at least believed—that the realm faced challenges they ought to address but could not solve through governmental action alone. This represented a shift in consciousness studies and cultural sociology within the realm.

Thus, in his first speech, King Miguel Ortiz proclaimed: "At last, a vision has been granted to us of our realm in its entirety. We see the corruption alongside the virtue, the decay alongside the vitality. With this vision, we approach our future."

If the realm suffered from moral decay, the cure had to come from elevating the people's consciousness, not merely from royal decrees. Similar diagnoses and prescriptions appeared in later speeches.

Monarchs derived their authority to serve as visionary leader-prophets from an observation made by Queen Samir Zhang, though not in her Ascension Speech. She had remarked that the Crystal Throne was "a sacred platform for teaching," a metaphor that suggested not just written proclamations but direct magical and spiritual connection between ruler and subjects. The development of the Resonance Crystals—and even more so, the Vision Pools—made this possible across the entire realm. A telltale sign of the leader-prophet style was the repeated use of the phrase "Let us..."—meaning, effectively, "Follow my guidance." This expression appeared occasionally throughout the history of speeches, but it became dominant in recent centuries. King Luis Grant used it eighteen times in his Ascension Speech, and Queen Rosa Porter repeated it twenty-four times in her second speech.

The change in literary style from formal classical language to more accessible common speech could be demonstrated statistically. In all speeches from Rosa the Wise through King Thomas the Mediator, the average sentence contained sixty-two words. From King Vincent through Queen Samir, it dropped to forty-five words, and in the modern era it averaged thirty-four words. Sophie didn't consider this a decline in quality—her own scholarly writing averaged about twenty-three words per sentence—but it reflected changes in the audience and communication methods. Early monarchs could reference obscure magical theorems and ancient philosophical texts, expecting their audience to understand. That wouldn't be true today. But those ancient audiences wouldn't have understood references to theoretical modeling in consciousness studies or behavioral economics in trade policy.

Sophie discovered that monarchs and their advisors often borrowed memorable phrases from their predecessors without attribution. King Luis Grant's famous rallying cry, "Ask not what magic the throne can work for you; ask what magic you can work for the realm," had an ironic history. In his speech, King Thomas the Builder—hardly a model for the charismatic Luis—had said, "Our most dangerous tendency is to expect too little of our rulers while doing too little for our realm." And even before his ascension, Thomas had proclaimed in a speech at the Academy, "In our great destiny, we must have citizens less concerned with what the throne can do for them and more devoted to what they can do for the realm."

Many issues had their moment in Ascension Speeches before fading into history. These included the Dragon Accords, the Coastal Shield Barriers, territorial expansion into the Wildlands, the Great Canal project, reform of the Guild system, regulation of necromancy, and prohibition of blood magic. Some subjects that Sophie expected to find were conspicuously absent. King Samuel's speech, delivered just before the Great Economic Collapse, contained no hint of financial vulnerability. Queen Juliana's second speech, given as dark forces gathered in the Shadow Realms, made no reference to the coming war. But what amazed Sophie most, reading from her perspective in the modern era, was the near-total silence regarding the rights of the Fae-touched—those born with mixed human and Fae ancestry.

The word "Fae-touched" didn't appear in any speech until Queen Samir's first address, and even then only as part of the phrase "humans and Fae-touched," never acknowledging their specific concerns or the discrimination they faced. Even King Thomas, the first monarch chosen in an election where Fae-touched citizens could vote throughout the realm, didn't remark on this historic change in his speech.

One subject that received consistent attention was taxation and financial regulation. "Taxes" or equivalent terms appeared in forty-five of the fifty-two speeches. King Marcus said in his speech: "The time approaches when we can reduce the tax burden. I oppose extremely high rates, for they generate little revenue, harm our prosperity, and are fundamentally unjust." Royal taxes then consumed about four percent of the realm's economic output. King Rafael said essentially the same thing three centuries later, when taxes claimed twenty-two percent.

The most troubling aspect of the entire collection of speeches was what was said—and left unsaid—about the treatment of the Shadowborn, those born in the cursed regions of Shadowbrook Town and surrounding territories. The words "Shadowborn," "cursed ones," or "shadow-touched" didn't appear at all until King Jonathan's speech in the Year of Reconciliation. Queen Elizabeth the Prosperous had asked rhetorically in her speech, "Upon whom has injustice fallen in any corner of our realm? Who has been denied their rights or property?" These questions were meant to elicit the answer "No one!"—as if there weren't thousands of Shadowborn living in bondage, denied basic human rights, their very existence considered a stain upon the realm.

Before the Shadow Wars, the word "bondage" appeared only in the speeches of King David the Cautious and King Robert the Reluctant, and then only to argue that, pursuant to ancient law and to preserve realm unity, the system should not be challenged. But although generally unmentionable, the issue was reaching a crisis point, and would explode into the Shadow Wars.

After the wars, it was in the speeches of King Jonathan, Queen Catherine, and King William that Sophie found the most explicit discussion of the need to transform into reality the rights and freedoms granted to the Shadowborn on paper by the Three Great Edicts. Catherine's speech was particularly forceful on this point. She had studied at the Academy in Oakdale during an era when it had been a sanctuary for escaped Shadowborn, and her commitment to human rights ran deep. But then the subject began to fade from the speeches. King Alexander said in his first speech, "The persecution of Shadowborn must not be tolerated in a great and civilized realm such as ours," but he said it without passion or urgency. Queen Victoria raised the subject only to express satisfaction at the progress that had been made. And then it vanished. Queen Juliana never mentioned it in any of her four speeches, despite reigning during a period of renewed discrimination.

After the Restoration, the subject returned to Ascension Speeches, but in vague, abstract terms. This was true even of monarchs Sophie knew had been deeply concerned with Shadowborn rights—like King Marcus, Queen Helena, and the current Queen Lucia. Perhaps each felt they had made a sufficient statement by having a prominent Shadowborn perform at their ceremony—a famous singer, a celebrated mage, or a renowned poet. In Queen Lucia's first speech, the only allusion to Shadowborn rights was this sentence: "From our founding, through the Shadow Wars, the Great Collapse, and the Rights Movement, our people have always found the strength to build from these crises the foundations of our future." Sophie noted this not to suggest their concern wasn't genuine, but to indicate what was considered acceptable to say in a speech intended to appeal to values shared by all citizens.

There was much more to contemplate in these speeches than Sophie had summarized in her analysis. There was much to take pride in—the realm's endurance through countless challenges, the peaceful transfer of power through the Crystal Throne's magic, and the general wisdom of the monarchs the people had chosen. But there was also a lesson in humility to be learned. Sophie looked back with astonishment at the ignorance and moral blindness revealed in what past leaders had said and past citizens had believed. She recognized that fifty or one hundred years hence, scholars would shake their heads at what her own generation was saying and believing.

As Sophie prepared to attend Queen Lucia's second Ascension Speech, she wondered what future scholars would make of this moment. What would they see that she was blind to? What injustices of her own time would seem obvious to them but remained invisible to her?

She gathered her notes, extinguished the floating manuscripts with a wave of her hand, and made her way down from her tower. The ceremony would begin at sunset, and she had been granted the honor of standing among the Memory Scribes to record this historic moment. As she walked through the ancient streets of Oakdale toward the palace, she passed citizens of all kinds—humans and Fae-touched, merchants and mages, even a few Shadowborn who had made their way from the southern territories. They were all heading in the same direction, drawn by the same anticipation.

Whatever Queen Lucia would say from the Luminous Balcony, whatever vision she would cast for the realm's future, it would become part of the great tapestry of Ascension Speeches. And someday, perhaps centuries hence, another scholar would sit in a tower study, surrounded by glowing manuscripts, trying to understand what this moment had meant and what it revealed about the consciousness of the age.

Sophie smiled at the thought. The work of understanding never ended. Each generation had to grapple with the wisdom and folly of those who came before, while remaining humble about their own limitations. It was the scholar's burden and privilege—to preserve the past, illuminate the present, and leave questions for the future.

As she approached the palace gates, the first stars began to appear in the darkening sky, and somewhere in the distance, ceremonial bells began to ring, calling the realm to witness another chapter in its long, complex, and continuing story.

The facility gleamed under artificial lighting, its modular sections radiating from a central hub like spokes on a wheel. Oliver Carter stood at the observation window, watching the nanobots swarm over a sample of contaminated soil from Timberline, Jarvonia. The microscopic machines, programmed through quantum entanglement, worked with impossible precision to break down toxic compounds into harmless elements.

"Beautiful, isn't it?" Rosa Taylor's voice carried a bitter edge as she joined him at the window. She wore the standard-issue white lab coat, but her dark hair hung loose around her shoulders in defiance of protocol. "All this technology, and we're still just lab rats."

Oliver didn't respond. Rosa had been here longer than any of them—three years by her count, though time felt elastic in this place. The Collectors, as they called their captors, existed partially outside normal spacetime. Their facility occupied a pocket dimension accessible only through quantum gateways they'd established at various points on Earth.

"The new arrival is settling in," Rosa continued. "Teresa. She was a supply chain analyst for a pharmaceutical company in Magnolia, Quendor. Scared out of her mind."

"They're all scared at first," Oliver said quietly. He turned from the window, studying the hexagonal common area where the other captives gathered. Mohamed Daniels sat hunched over a tablet, analyzing data streams the Collectors provided—environmental justice metrics from Earth, public health statistics, archaeological surveys. The Collectors were endlessly curious about human civilization, though their motives remained opaque.

Stefan Lee paced near the far wall, his athletic frame tense with barely contained energy. He'd been a leadership development consultant before his abduction from Pinehurst, Calderon. Now he led nothing, controlled nothing, existed only at the whim of beings whose form and substance defied human comprehension.

"Oliver." Rosa's hand on his arm was gentle but insistent. "It's time."

He knew what she meant. The Collectors had been preparing him for months with their training sessions, teaching him to manipulate quantum states with his consciousness, to move through space by collapsing probability waves, to interface with their technology in ways that should have been impossible for a human mind. And now they wanted him to use those abilities.

They wanted him to go back to Earth and bring someone else through.

The summons came as a pressure in his mind, not quite thought, not quite sensation. Oliver closed his eyes and allowed the quantum transition. The world folded around him and he stood in what the Collectors called the Interface Chamber—a space where geometric impossibilities became routine, where walls existed at angles that shouldn't work in three-dimensional space.

The Collector he'd named Prism waited there, its form shifting through configurations that hurt to perceive directly. Communication came as pure meaning injected into his consciousness:

*You are ready. We will open the gateway to your origin point. You will retrieve a specific target.*

Oliver had learned not to resist these commands. Resistance brought pain that transcended the physical—a dismantling of self that left him hollow for days. But he could still think, still plan, as long as he kept those thoughts buried deep.

"What target?" he asked aloud, knowing Prism would understand the vibrations if not the specific phonemes.

*A male with specific genetic markers. We have identified him through your world's data networks. He resides in Silverdale, Veldoria. His name is Ethan Cox.*

The name meant nothing to Oliver, but the location made his heart race. Silverdale was only fifty miles from where he'd lived before his abduction. Before his wife, before his career in nanotechnology research, before everything had been stripped away.

*You will assume appropriate covering and approach him at his residence. You will convince him to accompany you to the gateway. Physical coercion is not necessary—we have provided you with the means of persuasion.*

Oliver felt the new weight in his mind then, a set of subroutines the Collectors had implanted during his training. With concentration, he could project an aura of trust, of authority, of inevitability. It was a violation of applied ethics so profound that thinking about it made him nauseous.

"And if I refuse?" The question was automatic, pointless.

The pain that answered him was brief but absolute. When it ended, Prism's thought-voice carried something that might have been amusement:

*You will not refuse. We have invested too much in your training. You are our Judas ram, leading the flock to us.*

The transition back to the common area left Oliver shaking. Rosa found him there, helped him to a seat. She knew without asking what had happened.

"They're sending you through," she said.

He nodded, unable to speak yet.

"Are you going to do it?"

"Do I have a choice?"

Rosa's laugh was harsh. "We always have choices, Oliver. They're just all terrible."

Over the next few hours, Oliver prepared himself mentally for the mission. The Collectors provided him with clothing appropriate to Earth—jeans, a button-down shirt, a jacket. They'd studied human fashion through their observations, though their understanding remained imperfect. The clothes fit well enough but felt subtly wrong, the fabric too uniform, the colors slightly off.

Mohamed approached him as he dressed. "I've been analyzing the data they've been feeding us," he said quietly. "Running patterns on their behavior, their technology, their apparent goals."

"And?"

"They're not invincible. They're cautious about Earth for a reason. I think they can be hurt there, maybe even killed, though I don't know how." Mohamed's eyes were intense behind his wire-rimmed glasses. "Whatever you do out there, remember that. They fear us on our own ground."

The gateway chamber was a cathedral of impossible angles. Oliver stood at the threshold, feeling the quantum foam of the portal against his skin like static electricity. Through it, he could see a darkened street in Silverdale, Veldoria—his world, his dimension, tantalizingly close.

Prism's presence pressed against his mind: *Remember your purpose. Retrieve the target. Return through the gateway. Any attempt at escape will be detected and punished.*

Oliver stepped through.

The transition was like being born—a moment of compression followed by explosive release. He stumbled, caught himself, breathed air that smelled of rain and asphalt and growing things. Real air, not the odorless atmosphere of the facility. He wanted to weep at the simple reality of it.

He was standing two blocks from Ethan Cox's address, which the Collectors had somehow extracted from Earth's data networks. The street was quiet, residential, lined with modest houses and old trees. Oliver walked slowly, savoring every sensation—the give of concrete under his feet, the whisper of wind through leaves, the distant bark of a dog.

Ethan Cox's house was a small bungalow with peeling paint and an overgrown yard. Oliver stood at the curb for a long moment, wrestling with his conscience. He could feel Prism's attention on him, a pressure at the base of his skull. The Collector was monitoring him through their quantum link.

He had to do this. He had no choice.

But maybe, just maybe, he could warn Cox somehow. Give him a chance.

Oliver walked up the cracked sidewalk and knocked on the door.

The man who answered was younger than Oliver had expected—late twenties, with tired eyes and the build of someone who'd been athletic once but had let it slide. He wore sweatpants and a faded t-shirt with a logo for a supply chain management conference.

"Ethan Cox?" Oliver asked.

"Yeah. Who are you?"

"My name is Oliver Carter. I'm a researcher in nanotechnology. I need to talk to you about something urgent."

Cox's expression shifted from wary to confused. "Nanotechnology? I work in supply chain logistics. I think you have the wrong guy."

"No," Oliver said, and he felt the Collectors' implanted subroutines activate in his mind. Words came that he didn't fully control: "I have exactly the right person. There's been a development in Timberline, Jarvonia—a contamination event that's spreading through global supply chains. Your expertise is needed immediately."

It was a lie, smooth and plausible, flowing from him with supernatural ease. He watched Cox's resistance crumble under the weight of the persuasion programming.

"I... I haven't heard anything about this. Shouldn't there be official channels?"

"The situation is being contained quietly to prevent panic. I have a vehicle two blocks from here. We need to leave now."

Cox hesitated, and in that hesitation Oliver saw his chance. He pushed against the Collectors' control, forced his own words through: "You should probably tell someone where you're going. Leave a note. Call a friend."

The subroutines fought him, tried to make him retract the suggestion, but Oliver held firm. Cox nodded slowly. "Yeah. Yeah, let me just... give me a minute."

He disappeared into the house. Oliver stood on the porch, trembling with the effort of maintaining his small rebellion. Prism's attention intensified, probing, questioning. Oliver buried his intentions deep, thought only of compliance, of completing the mission.

Cox returned wearing jeans and a jacket, phone in hand. "I left a message for my roommate. Let's go."

They walked through the quiet streets toward the gateway. Oliver kept up a steady stream of technical jargon about nanoscale contamination and supply chain vectors, words that meant nothing but sounded authoritative. Cox listened, asked occasional questions, grew more uncertain with each step.

"Where exactly is this vehicle?" Cox asked as they turned down an increasingly isolated street.

"Just ahead," Oliver said, and it was true. He could see the shimmer of the gateway now, a distortion in the air that Cox's untrained eyes couldn't detect.

"I don't see anything."

"It's there." They were ten feet away. Five feet. Oliver felt sick with self-loathing. He was doing exactly what the Collectors wanted, leading an innocent man to captivity, and his small act of rebellion—letting Cox leave a message—would accomplish nothing.

They reached the gateway. Cox stopped, confused, staring at the empty air. "There's nothing here. What kind of—"

Oliver grabbed his arm and pulled him through.

The transition was violent for Cox, who had no preparation, no training. He screamed as quantum forces tore at his consciousness, then collapsed on the other side. Oliver caught him, lowered him gently to the floor of the gateway chamber.

Prism materialized, its form rippling with colors that might have been satisfaction. *Well done. The specimen is intact.*

Other Collectors appeared, their impossible geometries crowding the chamber. They lifted Cox's unconscious form with appendages that existed partially outside normal space, carried him away to whatever processing awaited new captives.

Oliver stood alone in the chamber, feeling the weight of what he'd done. He'd betrayed a stranger, condemned him to the same captivity that had consumed his own life. And he'd done it to avoid pain, to survive another day in this dimensional prison.

*You have performed adequately,* Prism informed him. *You will be rewarded with extended privileges. And there will be other missions.*

The quantum transition back to the common area was perfunctory. Oliver materialized to find Rosa waiting, her expression a mixture of sympathy and contempt.

"You did it," she said. It wasn't a question.

"I didn't have a choice."

"We always have choices," she repeated. "They're just all terrible."

Stefan approached, his face hard. "They're going to use you again. You know that, right? You're their retrieval specialist now. Their Judas ram."

"I know."

"And you're just going to keep doing it?"

Oliver looked at him, then at Rosa, then at Mohamed who watched from across the room with his analytical gaze. "What would you have me do? Resist and be destroyed? That helps no one."

"It helps your conscience," Stefan shot back.

"My conscience is already dead," Oliver said quietly. "It died the moment I stepped through that gateway and realized I could smell Earth again. That I wanted to stay there more than I wanted to save a stranger."

Rosa touched his shoulder. "You let him leave a message. That was something."

"It was nothing. A meaningless gesture."

"Maybe," she said. "Or maybe it's the start of something. Maybe next time you'll find a way to do more."

Oliver wanted to believe that, but he knew the truth. The Collectors had spent months preparing him for this role, conditioning him, training him, breaking down his resistance. They'd made him into a tool, and tools don't rebel.

He walked to his quarters—a small space with a bed and a desk and a window that showed a view of Earth that wasn't real. The Collectors had generated it for him, thinking it would provide comfort. Instead, it was torture, a reminder of everything he'd lost.

He lay on the bed and stared at the false sky, thinking about Ethan Cox waking up in this place, realizing his life was over. Thinking about the message Cox had left, and whether anyone would understand its significance. Thinking about the next mission Prism would send him on, and the one after that.

Mohamed had said the Collectors could be hurt on Earth, maybe killed. But Oliver didn't know how, and he didn't know if he had the courage to try. The training had been too thorough, the conditioning too deep.

He was their Judas ram now, and he would lead others to captivity because the alternative was his own destruction. It was the logic of survival, cold and merciless, and it had consumed everything he once believed about himself.

Rosa had said they always had choices. But some choices were so terrible that making them destroyed you either way. Oliver had made his choice, and he would live with it, and he would do it again when Prism commanded.

Because he was weak, and he was broken, and he was theirs.

The false stars wheeled overhead in their programmed patterns, and Oliver Carter closed his eyes against them, seeking the oblivion of sleep and finding only the memory of Ethan Cox's confused face as they approached the gateway. That face would haunt him, join the gallery of ghosts that already populated his dreams.

But tomorrow he would wake, and he would train, and when the Collectors commanded, he would return to Earth and bring back another victim. Because that was what he was now—not a scientist, not a researcher, not even fully human anymore.

Just a tool in the hands of beings who saw humanity as specimens to be collected, studied, and bred in captivity. And the worst part was knowing that he'd become complicit in his own imprisonment, that every mission he completed bound him more tightly to his captors.

The Judas ram, leading the flock to slaughter, one victim at a time.
