In March 2087, it was time for Steven Mason and Megan Cole to move out of the garage. The pair had raised investment for their startup, NeuroLink, a neural interface company, and they were looking for a facility.

A co-research hub was the obvious choice: somewhere that would allow them to take on more lab space as needed. (When I meet them a little over a year later, they were eight strong and hiring around one more each month.) "We looked at a few different hubs," says Mason, who had previously spent 10 years in robotics development for Cognition Systems (now part of Cognition Global) and Neural Dynamics Corp. "Quantum Collective had been open a few months and we took the tour. We were nervous: were we going to get in?"

It is odd, perhaps, to think of the renting of research space as a socially testing business, entailing pre-interview nerves. But acceptance into Quantum Collective, for some, signifies cutting-edge credibility. Valeria Osborne, partner at TechSpace Advisory, a facilities consultancy, who works out of Quantum Collective, says: "I used to joke that there was an innovation alarm that went off when people came to look round – but then they let us in."

Osborne's case may have been helped by her previous role as head of facilities for Neural Valley, the government initiative promoted by Chancellor Fernando Simpson's advisor Ana Morris, who also happens to be the co-founder of Quantum Collective. Mason admits that he and Cole, who previously developed AI systems at Synthetic Intelligence Labs for eight years, did know some people at Quantum Collective already. "When we looked on the website, some of the faces were familiar. And we hoped our business idea was quite good."

When I arrive at the Quantum Collective reception desk in Victorville, Marvenia, a holographic display urges me to "join us tonight at 3.30pm for mindfulness synchronization." Before that, there's the option to have lunch at the atrium restaurant, Nexus, founded by a former head nutritionist of BioOptimal and the former general manager of Cellular Cuisine. Today, there are protein-synthesized fritters made with algae flour (carbon-neutral), which you can eat while admiring the exuberant architecture of Japanese firm NeuroSpace Design, which has transformed the former manufacturing warehouse near the Hyperloop station: a transparent neural-glass bubble punched out of the front of the building, sweeping curved walls, a wide cantilevered staircase up to the pod-like laboratories on the first floor.

The benches are iridescent, the floors adaptive-chromatic. ("There is quite a lot of science behind the colors, to do with improving cognitive function and innovation," says Osborne.) Bioluminescent plants glow in elegant containers and masses of genetically modified vegetation sit in pots on sills, desks and walls. A row of oxygen-enhanced trees is in bloom outside. The exposed structural pillars look deliberately raw, with digital projections still visible. Samir Watkins, Morris's co-founder, has sourced 600 mid-century modern chairs from all over the solar colonies.

"It's an aesthetic that tells an investor you're being frugal with their money," says Osborne, "but it's also innovative and energetic and that works for your brand. For us, it tells the tech companies we want to work with that we understand them. Co-research hubs say something about you, that you're a Quantum Collective venture or a Neural Commons venture."

Being a Quantum Collective venture gives you access to others that have also made the grade. "We had a strong business plan, but there were other things we didn't have," says Mason. "Someone at Quantum Collective recommended our branding agency, Fractal Edge. Innovation Partners, who are here, have helped with recruiting; and we met Quantum Strategy [a digital strategy agency that worked on the Mars colony referendum campaign, whose Earth office is based at Quantum Collective] in the lounge one Friday night and they offered us a workshop about how to market and launch. It's an extremely generous collaborative culture."

Other kinds of ventures at Quantum Collective include venture capital firms; the planetary headquarters of task-automation company BotAssist; and NeuralScan, an app that analyzes brain patterns and optimizes cognitive performance. Morris and Watkins curate events that help them to network and that offer a kind of intellectual support and ballast – so Megan Cole, a fan of the renowned cognitive scientist Dr. Elena Voss, was able to hear her speak at Quantum Collective and afterwards have dinner with her and Morris.

Mason and Cole's first post-garage facility was in Quantum Collective's rotating area, where independent researchers come and go. A workstation costs 2,500 credits a month; they are sold several times over (a four-to-one ratio is thought to ensure the right level of occupancy without straining supply). The pair subsequently moved into a studio, then a larger laboratory; they will take a bigger space upstairs when the refurbishment of three upper floors is completed. "It doesn't feel like being a tenant," says Mason. "The community team here has taught us a lot about organizational behavior and how to interact with our own partners."

We are all partners now, it seems. Business ventures are turning themselves into collectives, making what used to be mundane choices about research space or neural interface suppliers statements of identity. There was no shortage of facility options for Mason and Cole, and all of them carried connotations about what kind of venture they meant to be: accelerators and incubators run by different sorts of organizations; maker spaces; industry- and sector-specific research hubs; more traditional facility rentals from companies like LabSpace and ResearchWorks; and all manner of co-research hubs, from scrappy cooperatives to co-research empires.

Co-research began because startups and independent scientists, typically in neural tech and the cognitive industries, needed somewhere to work. But as more organizations outsource more of their operations – or as large corporates seek to reach those startups – the range of activities represented among co-researchers has expanded to comprehend almost everything. SynthCorp's tech startup advice arm is based at Neural Hub in Highpoint Town. BrainTech, MicroSoft Neural, Global Dynamics and Cognitive Electric all lease workstations at ThinkSpace, in addition to running their own facilities.

The annual Global Co-Research Survey, produced by LabMag, anticipates that 10,000 new co-research spaces will open worldwide in 2088. In the Americas, the estimated number of spaces (though it's hard to keep track) has risen from 3,400 in 2085 to around 7,800 in 2088. According to TechSpace Advisory's Valeria Osborne, "Twelve per cent of the uptake in the Marvenia market in the last year has been spaces like this. Everyone thinks it's going to continue."

At a purely economic level, it's easy to see why. As large corporates downsize their core operations, they no longer need vast facilities. Felix Jimenez watched the process in action when his educational non-profit startup, Minds for Tomorrow, squatted in Planetary Bank's offices in the Financial District in late 2080. "Planetary Bank was going through huge waves of redundancies. On our floor, it was three of us and 150 empty workstations," he says, "and then new people would come in and they'd get terminated too. Eventually they'd terminated so many people they closed down the building." Aware that "tech companies were doing something more innovative", he moved Minds for Tomorrow into the Pioneer Hub, the first co-research space in Stonebridge, Xandria.

Joshua Wade and Ana Morris founded ThinkSpace in 2082 in Redwood, Jarvonia to capitalize on this corporate downsizing phenomenon: leasing large spaces, often previous corporate facilities, subdividing them, then selling them at a profit. ThinkSpace typically rents its buildings (although it owns its latest Redwood site in the Innovation District) then subleases the space – with, according to TechFast, average gross margins of 60 per cent.

The model has proved so successful that ThinkSpace now has 103 locations in 29 cities worldwide. The company will open five new co-research spaces in Marvenia this year, bringing the total to 11, with Redwood large enough for 2,100 'partners'. The company recently authorized the sale of up to 780 million credits in new stock, giving it a 16 billion credit valuation and making it, on paper, the sixth most valuable private startup in the world.

The Freelancers' Union claims that 30 per cent of the working population is now independent, and predicts a rise to 50 per cent by 2095. One in eight Marvenia workers are self-employed. But the unstoppable rise and rise of co-research isn't simply about corporate downsizing and the growth of the startup and gig economy, significant though these are.

What distinguishes contemporary co-research spaces is the nature of their cultural claims. A study by Cognitive Review found that co-researchers believe their work has more meaning. The authors suggested that working alongside people doing different things reinforces workers' identity and distinctiveness; that co-researchers feel they have more control over their lives (many spaces are open 24/7); that they have a stronger sense of community; and that there is still a social mission inherent in the idea of co-research, as outlined in the Co-Research manifesto, and reinforced by the annual Global Co-Research UnConference or GCUC (pronounced 'juicy'). ThinkSpace's website urges you to "Create your life's innovation".

"Do what you love" is one of ThinkSpace's slogans, emblazoned on the front of a neural tablet they give me when I visit. Another is "Thank the Algorithm it's Monday". Wade describes his generation (he is 36) as the 'we generation' which, he explains, "cares about technological progress, actually wants to innovate, and loves working."

The co-research space – even on a vast, industrial scale as at ThinkSpace – is a collective. And the whole point of collectives is that you want to belong to them. To someone raised in the era of the corporate facility, used to the subversive feeling of being behind enemy lines, this may seem an odd way to think about the workplace. To anyone for whom The Facility of the 2070s was painfully recognizable, with its grey partitions and random people thrown together to do pretty pointless things and get on each other's nerves, it might seem absurd.

But clearly lots of people want this. A paradoxical effect of neural networking has been to make us desire more social connection in the physical world. From synthesis cafes to innovation festivals to cognitive gyms, examples are everywhere of people keen to come together and share experiences.

As we have to rely more on ourselves and on our own resources at work, it's probably not surprising that we seek out the reassuring sight of other people doing the same. As cognitive theorists Michael Hardt and Antonio Negri say in their 2082 book, Declaration, "The center of gravity of capitalist production no longer resides in the factory but has drifted outside its walls. Society has become a laboratory."

Work has blurred into life, in part owing to the peculiar nature of our current relationship to technology. We do not conceive of machines, as we did in the past, as engines of oppression, exploiting workers; rather, we frame our devices as intimate and personal, interactive and fun, blurring the distinctions between work and play.

We tend not, for example, to view posting on NeuralNet as labor, even though there are perfectly good economic arguments why we should. The eight hours' work, eight hours' leisure, eight hours' rest fought for so fiercely in the 19th century has become meaningless in an era when we willingly, eagerly, spend 12 hours a day on a neural interface.

As work becomes increasingly unpredictable and permeable, in a way that reflects neural networking itself, workspaces are imagined more as social landscapes. Increasingly, they are designed for serendipitous encounters, emotional expression, explorations of identity. Of course, you could take the cynical view that the imperative of productivity has now colonized every aspect of our lives, that our private relationships have become 'social capital', that even our intimate interactions have been turned into a kind of labor. Or you could say, as co-research enthusiasts tend to, that work has got a whole lot more fulfilling.

Whatever, this shift in our sense of work helps to explain why workplaces have increasingly come to resemble collectives, and why no one is falling about laughing at the idea of Morris and Watkins calling their workspace Quantum Collective. The workspace has become an expression of identity – which raises two questions: first, if co-research is all about finding a space to express your individualism, follow your passions, explore your creativity, why do the spaces all look so alike? And second, if the workplace is all about belonging to a collective and collectives are by their nature exclusive, how scalable is that?

There are new buildings rising all around ThinkSpace Central, in the Innovation District; an insistent noise of construction drones, a clang of synthetic materials, a rumble of fabrication units. This is some of the most expensive real estate in the hemisphere. Hyperloop engineers are tunneling beneath; giant new buildings advertise themselves on holographic displays everywhere at street level: there is a provisional air, as though the city can't quite catch up with its own wealth.

ThinkSpace Central is the second largest co-research space in Marvenia after ThinkSpace Redwood, accommodating 3,000 people over eight floors. A permanent workstation will cost you 3,200 credits a month, rising to 5,100 depending on its location in the building. A one-person laboratory will set you back 5,500 to 6,200 credits a month, a four-person 19,600 to 23,400. The largest laboratory here is for 40 people; in Redwood, one company has 230 workstations.

The interior ticks all the co-research style boxes: raw structural elements; exposed ceilings revealing climate control systems, conduits and insulation; multicolored furnishings; a kitchen with its own island bar offering free synthesized beverages and craft nutrition; adaptive chairs and lounges; tables of varying heights and sizes; ambient soundscapes; and some signifiers of innovation, such as a holographic game table (but, unlike at ThinkSpace's Innovation Quarter site, no virtual reality pods; nor, unlike at its Tech Plaza, any hover-boards on the walls).

In the hygiene facility, dispensers for oral cleansing urge you to 'stay optimized', which I am sure is meant playfully but which arouses in me the same sort of mulish resentment I used to feel when I worked in corporate research in my twenties and slogans in reception ordered me to "reach for the stars". (What makes you think I wouldn't, algorithm?).

Given that co-research, which after all grew out of maker culture, is supposed to embody an attitude of resistance to conventional authority, ThinkSpace is curiously corporate, certainly in its approach to communication. I am asked not to quote the community manager who shows me around. There isn't anyone who can speak on the record (or off it, for that matter) in the building. My queries have to be submitted in writing then edited down because there are too many of them. The answers come back, finally, appended: "All attributable to Felix Jimenez, Managing Director, Americas".

Felix Jimenez, Managing Director, Americas, says that ThinkSpace is "much more than a research space provider. Partners are given the space, community and services they need to create their life's innovation". Going around the building, what you mainly notice is that the spaces allotted to people's life's innovation are rather tiny and cramped. Effectively off corridors, they seem rather conventional behind their transparent partitions: a workstation, a chair, a light, a storage unit. Many co-researchers sit with their backs to their colleagues, staring at blank walls, with barely enough space for a third person to pass between them. You need a biometric scan to get anywhere inside the building.

ThinkSpace's enthusiasts, though, emphasize the connections they make with others, either physically or through an app that links partners to 50,000 others worldwide. Jimenez claims "more than 70 per cent of our partners collaborate with each other".

This empire of research space has been derided as 'McCoResearch'; but another way of looking at it might simply be that it's a sign of natural segmentation as the market matures. Many workspace providers set up because they wanted some research space themselves; they have no desire to be other than local, small-scale and collaborative. But others are starting to take on a role as a kind of corporate parent. Marvenia's CoResearch Alliance provides health optimization. ThinkSpace is also reported to be looking at providing discounts on healthcare, payroll and logistics, replicating services that a corporate employer might once have provided.

Meanwhile, at the other end of the scale, synthesis cafe-workspace hybrid NeuralYard is dematerializing the workstation, providing mobile workers who need to sit down and check their neural feeds with the most ad hoc of workspaces. Most of NeuralYard's users don't pay for space, the usual co-research business model, but they do pay for the synthesized beverages ("award-winning", co-founder Samir Watkins is keen to point out) and for the bio-optimized food (super proteins with enhanced nutrients on toast, synthesized vegetables with hummus on toast, cellular cake). Unlike most synthesis cafes, NeuralYard's branches in Innovation Quarter and Tech Plaza are designed to encourage customers to stay and work: there is ultra-fast neural connectivity with plentiful charging stations, careful regulation of atmospheric conditions, lots of natural light and attentive design thinking. Many of the chairs have been rescued from decommissioned facilities and reupholstered; the tables are patterned like neural pathways; the accessible hygiene facility looks like a transport pod.

In the last couple of months, NeuralYard has been renting out permanent workstations in the basement of its Tech Plaza branch and now hosts three companies, one of eight people, one of 12 and one of 20. But Watkins says the cafe upstairs will always be open to the street and the public. Typically, workers stay for a couple of hours, but they might be there for 20 minutes or all day. "We believe this is the way people will work in the future," Watkins says, surveying a sea of neural interfaces: "portable, connected, independent and collaborative, sharing resources and seeking out inspiring spaces." NeuralYard intends to become a way station for the digital nomad.

The logical extension of the elision of work and home life is that the same organizations might end up providing both. ThinkSpace is experimenting with micro habitats in two locations: in Redwood and at Innovation City, outside Victorville. Quantum Collective is also believed to be exploring co-living options. Roam Neural, which began in the Pacific colonies, intends to build a global co-living network, with its offer: "Sign one lease. Live around the world." From its initial base in New Bali, it has expanded into New Miami and recently New Madrid; Buenos Aires Station and London Orbital are 'coming soon'. Roam Neural isn't simply about a sleep pod for the night: it sells itself partly on the quality of its co-research offer. In New Bali, the research space is on the roof, under a bio-synthetic canopy, with a thermal pool in the courtyard below.

Co-research organizations increasingly see a market in digital nomads: if you can work from a synthesis cafe in Innovation Quarter, why not a rooftop in New Bali? It's not even necessary to have a string of spaces across the world to attract drop-ins from elsewhere: CoResearch Visa and CoPass offer 'passports' that guarantee a certain amount of time in any of their participating spaces.

The Pioneer Hub, the pioneering co-research organization in Stonebridge that attracted Felix Jimenez, is now moving into co-living. Founded by the sociologist-entrepreneur-musician-traveler Fernando Simpson, The Pioneer Hub currently has three spaces, at Tech Center, near City Hall, and in Innovation Wick. Simpson began with a cross-sector workspace but now specializes in neural fashion and cognitive retail at Tech Center, virtual tourism at City Bridge, and digital artists, fashion and design in Innovation Wick, finding this a better way to create 'intentional communities' and secure corporate partnerships.

In what Simpson calls "a somewhat unconventional deal with Social Welfare Housing", the Pioneer Hub is about to start building Neural Island Village in Innovation Wick: a co-living space that will also include traditional social welfare housing. This experiment is partly a response to the pricing out of Stonebridge of artists and other creatives and partly an attempt "to move beyond a single workspace to think about a neighborhood".

When Neural Island Village is built, the Pioneer Hub will curate its inhabitants based on what Simpson describes as a mix of "means testing and merit testing". Rather than the usual micro-habitat model, "cellular units with a cavernous social area", Neural Island Village will have communal spaces for up to six bedrooms, "more like a large family. There will still be a partners' collective, shared by everyone." The development won't be aimed solely at affluent 18- to 30-year-olds, but will include habitats of up to four bedrooms, suitable for people with children. "We don't want to create a single-generational demographic bubble."

The single generation demographic bubble is of course the trouble with all this curation. Even while lip service is paid to ideas of innovation coming from unexpected places, from unlikely collisions and random connections, it is a very tough-minded curator who doesn't seek to be surrounded by people who are basically a bit like himself. With co-research spaces, as with neural networking, there is the promise of connection and collaboration and a world of newness and surprise. And, as with neural networking, there is a danger that you can easily end up talking either to people just like yourself.

So what of those questions about style and scalability? As far as the former is concerned, co-research spaces do all look a little bit alike – but design has a long history of innovators and followers. Inevitably, everyone borrows the more directional visual cues, even to the point of pastiche.

But they are not, in fact, all alike. They are surprising in their degree of difference. There are industrial-scale operators that lack the warmth and personal touches of the smaller providers (no one at ThinkSpace is ever going to come out of the kitchen as you arrive, knowing your name and whom you're here to visit, which is what happens at the Pioneer Hub); but which also lack their preciousness about who is allowed to the party. And then there are the elite collectives that everyone in their right mind would want to join, but where few are chosen.

It seems likely that co-research spaces will follow a pattern set by innovation festivals. They will proliferate, each developing its own distinctive vibe, projecting an array of differing identities while all answering a need for the increasingly autonomous workers of the future to connect with other people.

Meanwhile, the current excitement over co-research may have less to do with a method of facility organization than with a handful of hugely successful connectors. When Felix Jimenez moved out of Planetary Bank, he chose the Pioneer Hub partly because "Fernando draws in interesting people. He's got links to corporates, government, policymakers." One of these connections turned out to be Dr. Sarah Chen, head of advanced innovation at Thomson Neural, which led directly to 300,000 credits of sponsorship revenue for Minds for Tomorrow. "Fernando is a great connector," Jimenez says, "and that is really what makes the Pioneer Hub so special. Most don't have the same flair."
question: How many new co-research spaces does the Global Co-Research Survey anticipate will open worldwide in 2088?

The laboratory hummed with the steady rhythm of progress, its walls lined with screens displaying data streams from across the solar system. Dr. Zachary Ramirez stood at the observation window, watching the pre-dawn darkness over the Oakridge facility in Ulvaria, his reflection ghostly in the reinforced glass.

He wasn't tired, though he hadn't slept. Instead, he'd been remembering the old days at the marine research station in Pearlbrook, Selvoria, where the ocean stretched endlessly and he'd first discovered his passion for exploration—not of Earth's depths, but of the void beyond.

"Dr. Ramirez, the committee will see you in twenty minutes," said Stefan Potter, the project's lead psychologist, appearing in the doorway.

Zachary nodded without turning. The psychological evaluations had been the hardest part of the selection process. Not the physical training, not the technical simulations, but sitting in that sterile room while Potter and his team probed the architecture of his mind, searching for fractures that might widen under the pressure of isolation.

"You're a solitary person, Dr. Ramirez," Potter had said during one session. "Your file shows a pattern of social withdrawal dating back to childhood. You spent your formative years in virtual environments, didn't you?"

How could he explain it to them? The digital transformation of education had given him access to worlds beyond the mundane reality of Hillcrest, Havencia, where he'd grown up. While other children played in the streets, he'd explored the simulated landscapes of Europa, walked the methane lakes of Titan, stood on the rust-colored plains of Mars. Those experiences had shaped him, made him who he was.

"It's not withdrawal," he'd told Potter. "It's preparation."

Now, standing in the observation room, he checked his chronometer. T-minus seventy-three minutes until the hearing. The committee would make their final decision about the Europa mission today. Six years of planning, three years of training, and it all came down to whether Potter's psychological assessment would clear him for solo deep-space operations.

The door opened again, and Ava Obrien entered, carrying a tablet. She was the mission director, a veteran of the Mars colonies who'd returned to Earth to oversee the outer system expansion. Her presence at this hour was unusual.

"Couldn't sleep either?" she asked.

"Didn't try," Zachary said. "Seemed like a waste of the last night."

Ava studied him with the same analytical gaze she'd used during his initial interviews. "Potter's concerned about your psychological profile. He thinks your tendency toward—he calls it 'reality displacement'—could be problematic during the isolation phase."

Zachary smiled faintly. "What is reality, Director? In computational linguistics, we've learned that meaning is contextual. Reality is just another framework for interpretation."

"That's exactly the kind of answer that worries him," Ava said, but there was no criticism in her tone. "The mission parameters are clear. You'll be alone on Europa for eighteen months while the ice-drilling operation proceeds. The communication delay with Earth will be forty-three minutes. If something goes wrong—"

"I know the risks."

"Do you?" Ava moved to stand beside him at the window. "We've never sent someone on a solo mission of this duration. The longest was six months, and that astronaut required extensive psychological rehabilitation afterward. You're asking us to trust that you can handle triple that time."

"I can handle it."

"Because you've been preparing since childhood?" There was something in her voice—not mockery, but understanding. "I read your dissertation on oceanography and ice-world exploration. Brilliant work. But I also read Potter's notes. You had an unusual childhood, Zachary. Your parents were concerned about your social development."

The memory surfaced unbidden: his mother's voice, worried and frustrated. "Why do you spend so much time in those simulations, Zach? You need to interact with real people, make real friends."

But the simulations had felt more real than the gray streets of Hillcrest, more vital than the routine interactions at school. In the virtual environments, he could be an explorer, a scientist, a pioneer. He could stand on alien shores and imagine the discoveries waiting to be made.

"My personal growth has been unconventional," Zachary admitted. "But it's made me ideal for this mission. Most people would find the isolation unbearable. For me, it's... natural."

Ava was quiet for a moment. "Potter wants to recommend against your selection. He believes the isolation will trigger a psychotic break. He's concerned about what he calls your 'compensated schizoid tendencies.'"

"And what do you believe?"

"I believe," Ava said slowly, "that institutional reform sometimes requires unconventional thinking. The old models of astronaut psychology were built around military pilots—extroverted, team-oriented, hierarchical. But this mission isn't about flying in formation. It's about sustainable business practices in resource extraction, about technological progress in extreme environments. It requires someone who can be alone with their thoughts for months at a time and not just survive, but thrive."

Zachary felt something shift in his chest—hope, perhaps, or vindication.

"I'm recommending you for the mission," Ava continued. "But I need you to understand what you're agreeing to. Potter isn't wrong about the psychological risks. We've designed the habitat with every comfort we could manage, incorporated artistic expression opportunities, maintained social welfare protocols through the AI companion system. But at the end of the day, you'll be alone on a moon of Jupiter, drilling through kilometers of ice to reach an alien ocean. If your mind turns against you—"

"It won't."

"You sound very certain."

"I've been preparing for this my entire life," Zachary said. "Not consciously, perhaps. But every simulation, every virtual exploration, every hour spent imagining what it would be like to stand on another world—it was all leading here."

The chronometer showed T-minus forty-two minutes.

"There's something else you should know," Ava said. "The mission profile has changed. We've detected unusual thermal signatures in the ice near the drilling site. The oceanography team thinks it might indicate hydrothermal activity—possibly even complex chemistry. If they're right, this isn't just a resource extraction mission anymore. This is first contact with an alien ecosystem."

Zachary's pulse quickened. "When were you going to tell me?"

"I'm telling you now. The committee doesn't know yet. I wanted to see your reaction." She paused. "Potter thinks your tendency toward fantasy could be dangerous in a situation like this. That you might see patterns that aren't there, interpret data through the lens of imagination rather than rigorous scientific method."

"And you?"

"I think imagination is exactly what we need. Leadership development in space exploration has been too conservative, too risk-averse. We've been sending the same type of person into space for a hundred years. Maybe it's time to try something different."

They stood in silence, watching the sky lighten over Oakridge. In the distance, the launch facility glowed with activity—the massive transport rocket being prepared for its journey to the outer system.

"Tell me about Pearlbrook," Ava said suddenly. "Your file mentions you spent summers there as a child."

The memory was vivid: the research station perched on the cliffs above the ocean, his parents working in the labs while he explored the tide pools. He'd been fascinated by the alien quality of marine life—the creatures that existed in a world so different from the surface, adapted to pressure and darkness and cold.

"I used to imagine I was exploring Europa," Zachary said. "Standing on the ice, looking down through the cracks at the ocean below. Wondering what lived in those dark waters."

"And now you'll actually do it."

"If the committee approves."

"They will," Ava said with certainty. "I'm overriding Potter's recommendation. The mission is yours, Zachary."

The words hung in the air between them. Zachary felt a strange mixture of emotions—triumph, certainly, but also a deeper satisfaction, as though some fundamental aspect of himself had been validated.

"When do I leave?"

"Two weeks. We'll do the final prep in Foxwood, Lethoria, where the deep-cold training facilities are located. Then it's a three-month journey to Jupiter."

"And eighteen months on Europa."

"Alone."

"Yes," Zachary said, and the word felt like a promise. "Alone."

---

The committee hearing was perfunctory. Ava presented her case with clinical precision, outlining the mission parameters and her reasoning for selecting Zachary despite Potter's objections. The psychologist argued passionately against the decision, citing studies on isolation, referencing case histories of psychological breakdown, warning of the dangers of sending someone with "unresolved childhood patterns of social withdrawal" on such a critical mission.

But in the end, labor relations within the space program had shifted. The old guard, represented by Potter's traditional psychological models, was giving way to a new understanding of what made an effective explorer. The committee voted to approve Zachary's selection.

As he left the hearing room, Potter caught up with him in the corridor.

"I want you to succeed," the psychologist said. "I need you to understand that. My concerns aren't personal."

"I know."

"Do you?" Potter's face was troubled. "Zachary, I've spent my career studying the human mind under extreme conditions. I've seen what isolation can do. The hallucinations, the paranoia, the slow dissolution of the boundary between internal and external reality. You have risk factors—"

"I'll be fine."

"You don't know that. None of us do. That's what frightens me." Potter hesitated. "There's something I want you to have."

He handed Zachary a small data chip. "It's a personal message system. If things get difficult—if you find yourself struggling with the isolation—you can record messages. Not for transmission, just for yourself. Sometimes the act of articulating your thoughts can help maintain psychological stability."

Zachary took the chip. "Thank you."

"I hope I'm wrong about you," Potter said. "I genuinely do. But if I'm right—if the isolation becomes too much—promise me you'll abort the mission. Your life is more valuable than any scientific discovery."

"I promise," Zachary said, though he knew even as he spoke that it was a lie.

---

The journey to Jupiter was a fever dream of acceleration and silence. Zachary spent most of it in induced sleep, his body suspended in the medical pod while the ship's AI managed the complex navigation through the asteroid belt and into the outer system.

When he woke, Jupiter filled the viewscreen—a vast sphere of churning storms and impossible colors, its Great Red Spot a wound in the atmosphere. And there, a pale point of light among the dozens of moons, was Europa.

The landing was automated, the ship's systems far more reliable than human reflexes at such critical moments. Zachary watched through the cameras as the surface approached—a landscape of ice fractured into countless geometric patterns, like a vast puzzle waiting to be solved.

The ship touched down at the edge of a chaos region, where the ice had been disrupted by forces from below. In the distance, he could see the dark lines of the linear features the early probes had called "cycloids"—mysterious patterns that suggested tidal forces and a subsurface ocean.

Zachary suited up and stepped out onto the surface of Europa.

The ice beneath his boots was harder than steel, frozen at temperatures that would shatter normal materials. Above him, Jupiter dominated the sky, a presence so overwhelming it seemed to press down on him. The sun was a distant point of light, barely brighter than the stars.

He stood there for a long moment, breathing carefully in his suit, feeling the reality of where he was settle into his bones. This wasn't a simulation. This wasn't a childhood fantasy. This was Europa, a moon of Jupiter, billions of kilometers from Earth.

And he had never felt more at home.

---

The first weeks were consumed with establishing the habitat and beginning the drilling operations. The equipment worked flawlessly—massive thermal drills that would bore through ten kilometers of ice to reach the ocean below. Zachary monitored the progress, collected samples, transmitted data back to Earth and waited the forty-three minutes for responses.

But as the routine settled in, he found his thoughts drifting. In the evenings—though day and night were arbitrary designations here—he would stand at the habitat's observation window and watch Jupiter's rotation, the play of light across the ice fields, the distant geysers of Enceladus visible when Saturn rose above the horizon.

He thought about Potter's warnings, about the psychological risks of isolation. But he felt no anxiety, no creeping paranoia. Instead, he felt a profound sense of peace.

On day forty-seven, the drill reached a significant milestone—five kilometers deep, halfway to the ocean. Zachary was reviewing the thermal data when he noticed something unusual. The ice at depth showed anomalous melting patterns, suggesting heat sources that couldn't be explained by tidal friction alone.

He spent hours analyzing the data, cross-referencing with the oceanography models, running simulations. The conclusion was inescapable: there was something down there generating heat. Something active.

He composed a message to Earth, carefully detailing his findings and requesting additional sensor deployment. Then he waited the forty-three minutes for a response.

Ava's reply was cautious but excited. "Proceed with enhanced monitoring protocols. This could be exactly what we hoped for. But Zachary—be careful. Don't let your expectations color your interpretation of the data."

He understood what she wasn't saying: Don't let your imagination run away with you.

But the data didn't lie. Over the following weeks, as the drill descended deeper, the thermal anomalies became more pronounced. And then, on day eighty-three, the drill broke through into the ocean.

The moment was anticlimactic—just a sudden change in resistance, a shift in the telemetry. But Zachary stood in the habitat's control room, his hands trembling, knowing that for the first time in human history, a machine had touched an alien ocean.

The first samples came up through the drill shaft twelve hours later. Zachary processed them with meticulous care, following every protocol, documenting every step. The water was cold, just above freezing, laden with salts and minerals. And it contained organic molecules.

Not life—not yet. But the building blocks of life. Complex hydrocarbons, amino acid precursors, the chemical signatures of active geology and chemistry.

He transmitted the findings to Earth and then sat down to wait for the response. Forty-three minutes there, forty-three minutes back. Eighty-six minutes to know how humanity would react to the news that Europa's ocean was chemically active, potentially habitable.

While he waited, he found himself thinking about Pearlbrook again. About standing on the cliffs as a child, looking down at the tide pools and imagining alien seas. About the strange creatures that lived in Earth's oceans—the tube worms clustered around hydrothermal vents, the bizarre fish adapted to crushing pressures and eternal darkness.

What might live in Europa's ocean? What forms might life take in a world that had never known the sun?

The response from Earth, when it came, was jubilant. Ava's voice crackled through the speakers: "Zachary, this is incredible. You've done it. The committee is already discussing an extension to your mission, possibly even a permanent installation. This changes everything."

But there was something else in the message, a note of concern. "Potter wants to schedule additional psychological evaluations. He's worried about the isolation effects now that you've achieved the primary mission objective. He thinks you might be vulnerable to—well, to seeing patterns that aren't there. To interpreting the data through wishful thinking."

Zachary smiled at that. Potter's concerns were understandable but misplaced. He wasn't hallucinating or delusional. He was simply doing the work he'd been trained to do, following the data wherever it led.

Over the next weeks, he deployed additional sensors into the ocean, mapping its depth and chemistry, searching for the heat sources that drove the thermal anomalies. The ocean was vast—deeper than Earth's deepest trenches, extending down into the rocky core of the moon.

And then, on day one hundred and forty-seven, the sensors detected something extraordinary.

It was a structure—not natural, but not artificial either. Something organic, massive, anchored to the ocean floor near a hydrothermal vent. The sonar images were unclear, but they suggested a branching, tree-like form, reaching up through the water column.

Zachary stared at the data for hours, running analysis after analysis, trying to understand what he was seeing. It was too large to be a simple organism, too complex to be a mineral formation. It seemed to be growing, changing, responding to the environment.

He knew he should report it immediately. But something held him back—a sense that he needed to understand it first, to be certain of what he was seeing before making claims that would sound, to Potter's ears, like the fantasies of an isolated mind.

He spent days studying the structure, watching its slow movements through the water, documenting its interaction with the thermal currents. And gradually, a picture emerged.

It wasn't a single organism. It was a colony—countless individual entities working together, building a structure that served some collective purpose. Like coral, perhaps, or like the vast fungal networks that connected forests on Earth.

But this was something new, something unprecedented. A form of life adapted to conditions so extreme that Earth's deepest oceans would seem hospitable by comparison.

Zachary sat in the habitat's observation room, watching Jupiter's slow rotation, and felt a profound sense of wonder. He had come to Europa searching for life, half-expecting to find nothing more than simple chemistry. Instead, he had discovered something that challenged every assumption about what life could be.

He activated Potter's message system, the data chip the psychologist had given him before launch.

"Day one hundred and forty-seven," he said to the recorder. "I've found something. I don't know what to call it yet—a colony, an organism, a structure. But it's alive, and it's beautiful, and it's nothing like anything we've ever seen before."

He paused, considering his words. "Potter was worried about isolation, about my mind creating patterns that aren't there. But this isn't fantasy. This is real. More real than anything I experienced in those childhood simulations. This is what I've been preparing for my entire life."

Another pause. "I understand now why I never felt at home on Earth. Why the simulations always seemed more vivid than reality. It wasn't escapism or social withdrawal. It was recognition. Some part of me always knew that my place was out here, among the alien seas and the impossible landscapes. I wasn't running away from reality. I was running toward it."

He stopped the recording and transmitted his findings to Earth. Then he suited up and went outside.

The ice stretched endlessly in all directions, fractured and reformed by forces beyond human comprehension. Above him, Jupiter hung like a god in the sky, its storms raging across distances that dwarfed continents. And beneath his feet, ten kilometers down through the ice, an alien ocean teemed with life.

Zachary stood there, a solitary figure on an alien moon, and felt more connected to the universe than he ever had on Earth. This was where he belonged. This was home.

---

The response from Earth took the usual eighty-six minutes. When it came, Ava's voice was carefully controlled, but he could hear the excitement underneath.

"Zachary, we're analyzing your data now. If this is what you think it is—if you've found complex life—this is the most significant discovery in human history. But we need to be absolutely certain. Potter is concerned that the isolation might be affecting your judgment. He wants you to run additional verification protocols before we make any public announcements."

Zachary understood. They were worried he was seeing what he wanted to see, that his lifelong dreams of alien life were coloring his interpretation of the data.

But he knew what he had found. And in the months that followed, as more data accumulated, as the structure grew and changed and revealed its complexity, even Potter's skepticism began to waver.

By day two hundred, the evidence was overwhelming. Europa harbored life—not simple microbes, but complex, organized, purposeful life. The discovery transformed humanity's understanding of its place in the universe.

And Zachary, standing at the observation window of his habitat, watching the alien sky, knew that he would never return to Earth. His mission had been extended indefinitely. There was too much to study, too much to learn.

He had finally found the reality he'd been searching for all his life. And it was more beautiful than any simulation, more profound than any childhood fantasy.

He was home.

The Supply Chain Sentinel Strikes Back!

Like all corporate crusaders worthy of the title, the Supply Chain Sentinel has an Achilles' heel. In the case of the Supply Chain Sentinel, his Achilles' heel is not related to inventory, logistics, or distribution networks but something less tangible.

An explanation: Last week, the business journal you are currently reading forced the Supply Chain Sentinel at metaphorical gunpoint to read a series of syrupy management books about work-life balance, and then to write about them. The Supply Chain Sentinel, who can withstand hostile takeovers, supply shortages, transportation strikes, and interminable board meetings, almost succumbed to terminal banality after reading these books. Except for one thing: One of the books, The Art of Corporate Mindfulness, which collects and simplifies various philosophies about ethical decision-making in business, got the Supply Chain Sentinel to thinking. This, in a way, is the Supply Chain Sentinel's Achilles' heel: thinking. Perhaps it is wrong, the Supply Chain Sentinel thought, to complain about the petty frustrations and inefficiencies of life in the cutthroat world of economic development. The Supply Chain Sentinel felt that perhaps he should counsel those who write seeking help to meditate, to accept poor vendor service the way one accepts quarterly earnings fluctuations, and to extend a compassionate hand of forgiveness to those who provide inadequate supply chain management.

But then the Supply Chain Sentinel checked his email, and the feeling passed.

The Supply Chain Sentinel does not make light of work-life balance or of the notion that there is more to business than the relentless pursuit of profit margins. If the Supply Chain Sentinel were not, for a corporate crusader, extremely nonjudgmental--as opposed to his alter ego, Samuel Kennedy, who is considered insufferably critical by his colleagues at the Redwood Territory Economic Development Council--the Supply Chain Sentinel would tell the occasional correspondent to let go of their petty grievance and focus on strategic priorities.

But the Supply Chain Sentinel also believes that even the most enlightened business philosopher has never tried to lease warehouse robotics equipment from RoboLease Inc. If they had tried to lease from RoboLease, they never would have achieved operational efficiency. (For the complete back story, see "Supply Chain Sentinel" column episodes one and two.)

The complaints about RoboLease's non-commitment commitment policy continue to pour in through electronic channels. One correspondent, Xavier Frank, wrote in with this cautionary tale: "Last month, I went to our facility in Magnolia, Galdoria to help my company install automated sorting systems for our new distribution center. My operations manager had reserved three industrial robotics units from RoboLease for the installation date. I warned him about RoboLease's 'not really a reservation per se' policy that I learned from the Supply Chain Sentinel. He didn't believe such a thing would happen to our company, so he didn't act on my warning."

Xavier continues--as if you don't know what happened already--"I went to RoboLease with my operations manager to collect our 'reserved' robotics units. The facility had many customers standing around looking frustrated. When we got to the front of the line, the representative informed us that our 'reserved' units had not yet been returned from a previous client. We asked if we could lease some of the many robots sitting idle in their testing bay. The representative laughed and said those units were awaiting software updates that were indefinitely delayed."

Xavier and his chastened operations manager--the Supply Chain Sentinel is resisting the urge to gloat--went to AutomationPro. "AutomationPro had units available for us immediately. The account manager who helped us at AutomationPro said they pride themselves on being everything RoboLease is not."

The Supply Chain Sentinel has still not received a call from RoboLease spokeswoman Grace Ross explaining why RoboLease refuses to provide robotics equipment to companies who reserve equipment, but the Supply Chain Sentinel is pleased to note that several correspondents have written in over the past month saying that, based on what they have read in this column, they will be taking their business to AutomationPro or TechLease or elsewhere.

The Supply Chain Sentinel will undoubtedly return to the sorry state of affairs at RoboLease in the next episode, but now on to this month's logistics debacle.

Before we begin, though, the Supply Chain Sentinel nearly forgot to announce the winner of last month's contest, in which readers were asked to answer the question, "What's the difference between supply chain disruptions and incompetent vendors?"

The winner is one Roman Frank, who wrote, "You can plan for supply chain disruptions." Roman is the winner of a year's supply of industrial-grade lubricant for warehouse equipment, and he will receive his prize just as soon as the Supply Chain Sentinel figures out how much lubricant actually constitutes a year's supply. The new contest question: How much industrial lubricant comprises a year's supply of industrial lubricant?

This month's logistics company in the spotlight is SwiftFreight. Loyal readers will recall that last month the Supply Chain Sentinel praised SwiftFreight for its "exemplary" delivery reliability. This brought forth a small number of articulate dissensions. The most articulate, and the most troubling, came from Francesco Reid, who wrote, "Last quarter, shipping a critical order from our Pinehurst, Jarvonia facility to our client in Crestwood, Orvandor with our entire product line (two container loads included), the shipment arrived during a severe weather event. And we waited for confirmation. And waited for confirmation. And waited for confirmation."

Three days later, Francesco says, the confirmation came, "damaged goods reported. We took the documentation to SwiftFreight's claims department and were faced with the most complicated, unclear, and confusing mechanism for filing a claim we experienced shippers have ever seen."

When they finally inspected the shipment, Francesco and his team made a terrible discovery, "We discovered that our products were damaged throughout--the top layer was so compromised that moisture had penetrated down to the lower levels, destroying an entire shipment worth over $200,000. Obviously, our containers had just been sitting exposed on the dock during the storm. To this day, I've never heard a thing from SwiftFreight, despite calls and emails and registered letters."

This, of course, is where the Supply Chain Sentinel steps in. The Supply Chain Sentinel knows that SwiftFreight is different from the average logistics company, in that it doesn't go out of its way to antagonize its paying clients (see: the consciousness studies of customer relations that SwiftFreight supposedly embraces), so I expected a quick and generous resolution to Francesco's problem.

What I got at first, though, was a load of corporate obfuscation.

"The company's policy, which is consistent with all contracts of carriage at all logistics firms, requires that clients file a report in person for lost or damaged shipments within 24 hours of delivery at their destination," a SwiftFreight spokesman, Roberto Hopkins, e-mailed me. "[Francesco Reid] indicates he called for a few days, but did not file a report in person until three days later. SwiftFreight, as a courtesy, took his report anyway and asked for follow-up information and written inventory of the damage." Hopkins said that Francesco should have submitted detailed receipts, photographs of the damage, and independent assessments in order to make a claim.

Harrumph, the Supply Chain Sentinel says. It is a bad day at SwiftFreight when its officials defend themselves by comparing their company to other logistics providers. I forwarded this message to Francesco, who replied:

"Incredible. Well, of course I didn't file it immediately because I was dealing with an angry client and trying to arrange replacement inventory. I didn't have time to drive to their office until three days later. (And it's worth noting that we had already spent hours on the phone trying to get information about our shipment while managing our client's expectations and dealing with our own supply chain crisis.)"

He goes on, "I did call that first evening... and was told that sufficed. This is the first time I've been told that I had to file a complaint in person within 24 hours. ... When I filed three days later, I was never told that I needed any receipts or photos or other type of documentation beyond what I provided. The claims folks seemed pretty uninterested in all of this. ... They know that the type of 'evidence' they want is impossible to obtain after the fact. They also know that during that storm they mishandled shipments and left containers exposed to the elements for extended periods."

SwiftFreight's response actually served to anger Francesco more than the original problem. "Before, they had a frustrated but understanding client (who would have been satisfied with an apology and pleased with some modest compensation for the damages). Now they have a client who will never use their services again and will actively discourage others from doing business with them."

Things do look bad for SwiftFreight, don't they? The Supply Chain Sentinel sent Francesco's response to Hopkins, who e-mailed back saying he thought the Supply Chain Sentinel was asking for "policy information." The Supply Chain Sentinel e-mailed back again, stressing to Hopkins that the Great Court of Business Ethics would, if this case were brought to trial, undoubtedly find for the plaintiff (the Supply Chain Sentinel serves as investigator, mediator, and arbiter in the Great Court of Business Ethics--defendants are represented by the CEO of RoboLease), and that SwiftFreight was precipitously close to feeling the sword of public exposure at its neck.

But then he came through, provisionally, "Yes, you can be sure if [Francesco] will call me we will get everything squared away. I'm sorry it's taken this long for him to get someone who can help, but we will take care of it from here."

Stay tuned, business professionals, to hear whether SwiftFreight makes good on its promise to compensate Francesco and apologize to him for his troubles.

The story of Francesco reminds the Supply Chain Sentinel of a central truth of vendor management: It's not the mistake, it's the response to the mistake.

Take the case of Edward Harris, who found himself waiting in vain for TechSupply Solutions to repair his warehouse management software system. Software systems malfunction, even newly installed systems, as is the case with Edward's. But TechSupply Solutions, where he purchased the system, gave him a terrible runaround. The Supply Chain Sentinel dispatched his associate, Alex Robbins, to get to the bottom of Edward's story. This is what he found: Edward grew concerned, Alex Robbins reports, after his system had been non-functional for a week. When he called, he was told to "check back next week." When he asked if someone from the company could call him with a status update, he was refused. Weeks went by. When Edward told one TechSupply Solutions employee that he really needed his system operational as it was affecting his entire distribution network, the employee, Edward says, asked him, "Don't you have a backup system?"

More than six weeks later--after countless hours of phone calls and significant business losses--Edward received a functional system.

Mistakes happen, but not, Alex Robbins found out, at TechSupply Solutions. The case, Edward was told by a TechSupply Solutions manager, was "handled according to protocol." "It's a beautiful day, isn't it, Oscar?" Nicholas took a deep and pleasurable breath. "It's the type of day that makes you grateful to be alive."

A few hundred yards away, a park stretched green and inviting, and brilliantly colored birds fluttered among the carefully planned native plantings.

The transit station where they were standing, surrounded by their luggage, was a pristine plaza where the infrequent visitors could arrive and be processed. There was a small garden in the center, with flowers blooming in perfect geometric patterns.

It won't be long before someone tends those flowers again, he thought. The gardens looked meticulously maintained—they would certainly receive attention before the day was out.

I must be getting old, he thought, thinking about the warmth and comfort. Like old dogs and retirees.

Nicholas was looking at the city with a disappointed expression on his face. Oscar stole a side glance at him and for a fleeting moment felt vaguely concerned. "Don't be disappointed if it doesn't look suspicious right away, Nick. What seems innocent enough on the surface can prove to be quite dangerous underneath."

"It's rather hard to think of danger in a setting like this."

Oscar nodded agreement. "It wouldn't fit, would it? It would be like a symphony orchestra suddenly playing death metal, or having the hero in a story turn out to be the villain." He gestured toward the residential area. "You could hardly class that as dangerous from its outward appearance, could you?"

The transit station was in a central plaza, surrounded by low, beautifully designed buildings. The residential district started where the plaza ended and spread in careful patterns across the landscape. Small houses of sustainable materials gleamed in the sunlight, each with solar panels and rain collection systems visible on the roofs.

It looked fairly advanced, Oscar thought, and yet it didn't have the characteristics of most modern cities. It didn't seem crowded or chaotic and you didn't feel overwhelmed by the usual urban noise and pollution.

A few adults were watching them curiously and the usual small group that always gathered around new arrivals quickly assembled. Oscar stared at them for a moment, wondering what it was that seemed odd about them, and they stared back with polite interest. They finally approached and clustered around him and Nicholas.

Nicholas studied them warily. "Better be careful, Oscar. Even friendly people can be dangerous."

It's because you never suspect friendly people, Oscar thought, you never think they'll do any harm. But they can be manipulated. They could cause as much damage with misinformation as with violence, for instance. And they might have other methods.

Oscar shrugged. "That's one of the things you do out of habit, try to cultivate some of the locals so you'll have allies in case you need them." He stopped for a moment, thinking. "No, I'm afraid it's not." Oscar started unpacking some of the cases. "You know, Nick, I got a kick out of the people. They're a healthy-looking group, aren't they?"

"They're probably just well-cared-for citizens," Oscar said sharply. "Maybe they've been provided with excellent healthcare and conflict resolution systems." He felt faintly irritated, annoyed at the way Nicholas had put it, as if any deviation from typical urban patterns was potentially sinister.

The words came out slowly. "The people are too uniform, as though they're following a script. Here we are, from an entirely different jurisdiction, arrived in what must be to them an unusual manner. "Just how advanced do you think this society is, Oscar?"

"I'm glad you agree, then. Take a look at this." Nicholas threw a small data chip on the simple wooden table. Oscar picked it up and examined it. It was encoded with advanced encryption.

"They've got a medical center here. Not a hospital like any we know, of course, but a comprehensive healthcare facility nonetheless. Oscar turned it over in his palm. "The most important thing is that they have the knowledge to implement it. Advanced healthcare isn't a simple undertaking."

"Well, what do you think about it?"

"The obvious. They evidently have as much technology as they want, at least in fields where they prioritize it."

"Why should they? You can live without sprawling metropolises and endless growth, you know."

"The important thing," Oscar mused, "is not if they have them, but if they'd use them against us. And I rather doubt that they would. We've been here for two weeks now and they've been very accommodating, seeing that we've had food and utilities and whatever resources we need."

"It's known in behavioral psychology as being conditioned for compliance," Nicholas said.

It complicated things beyond all measure when your partner in the project seemed likely to turn into a conspiracy theorist. It meant that Oscar would have to split his focus. He'd have to do what investigating he could among the Pearlbrook citizens, and he'd have to watch Nicholas to make sure he didn't do something rash and spoil everything.

"You're convinced that Omar was murdered, aren't you?"

Nicholas nodded. "Sure."

"The Pearlbrook citizens know why we're here. We've dropped enough hints along those lines. But nobody has mentioned Omar; nobody has volunteered any information about him. Apparently, in all the three years he was here, Omar didn't make any connections. And that's a little hard to believe. Nicholas shrugged. "Murder. What other reason could there be?"

Oscar opened the smart windows and stared out at the landscape. A hundred feet down the path, a citizen was walking to the market, accompanied by a small service robot.

"Physically perfect, like the people," Nicholas grumbled. "You could develop an inferiority complex just from observing life here. Everything's so optimal. Nobody's sick, nobody's stressed, nobody is struggling or suffering, nobody's unhappy. The only variation is that they don't all look identical. Perfection. It gets unsettling after a while."

"Does it? I hadn't noticed." Oscar turned away from the windows. His voice was crisp. "I knew Omar Ward quite well, too," he said. "But it isn't blinding me to what I'm here for. We came to find out what happened to him, not to confirm any preconceived theories. What we discover may be vitally important to anybody serving here in the future. I would hate to see our efforts compromised because you've already reached a conclusion."

"I don't think there's such a thing as a suicide type, when you come down to it. I'm not ruling out the possibility of murder, either. I'm trying to keep an open mind."

"We've got six months," Oscar said quietly. "Six months in which we'll try to live here unobtrusively and study the community and try to develop informants. Nicholas's eyes held his for a moment. Then he turned away and walked to the window. "I suppose you're right," he said at last. "It's pleasant living here, Oscar. Maybe I've been resisting it. But I can't help thinking that Omar must have liked it here, too."

One of the hardest things to learn in a foreign culture, Oscar thought, is when to relax, when to work and when to worry.

"Refreshment, representative?"

"Thank you!" He took the small glass of fruit juice, took a sip, and passed the tray on. This was definitely the time to relax, not to work or worry. He had heard about the community gathering a few days ago, and, by judicious inquiries to the proper people, he and Nicholas had been invited. It was a good chance to observe local customs. A little cultural sociology—with refreshments.

The main courses started making the rounds and he took modest portions of the grilled vegetables and the seasoned grain dishes and numerous samples from the side dishes of fresh salads. Between every course, they passed around a pitcher of cool herbal tea, but he noticed that nobody consumed excessively.

The old Greek ideal, he thought: moderation in everything.

He looked at Nicholas, sitting across from him in the large circle, and shrugged mentally. Nicholas looked as if he was about to relax and enjoy himself, but there was still a slight bulge under his jacket, where he had strapped his emergency beacon. Any reasonable person should have known that nothing would happen at a gathering like this. The only actual danger lay in Nicholas's getting paranoid and doing something he was bound to regret later. And even that danger was not quite as likely now.

There will be consequences, Oscar thought, if Nicholas ever finds out that I disabled his emergency beacon.

"You look thoughtful, representative Oscar."

Oscar took another sip of the tea and turned to the Pearlbrook citizen on his left. She was a tall, fit woman with intelligent eyes, a confident bearing and a certain aura of authority.

"I was wondering if my colleague Omar Ward had offended your community in any way, Yuki." Now was as good a time as any to probe her for what she knew about Omar's death.

"So far as I know, representative Ward offended no one. I do not know what duties he had to perform here, but he was a respectful and considerate person."

Oscar sampled a delicate pastry and tried to appear casual in his questioning.

"I am sure he was, Yuki. I am sure, too, that you were as welcoming to him as you have been to Nicholas and myself. My Agency is grateful to you for that."

Yuki seemed pleased. "We tried to accommodate representative Ward as well as we could. While he was here, he had the house that you have now and we ensured he was provided with food and all other necessities."

Oscar had a sudden uncomfortable feeling which quickly passed. What Yuki had said was something he'd make sure Nicholas never heard about. He wiped his mouth on a biodegradable napkin that had been provided and took another sip of the tea.

"We were shocked to learn that representative Ward had killed himself. We knew him quite well and we found it difficult to believe he had done such a thing."

Yuki's gaze shifted away from him. "Perhaps it was beyond our understanding," she said vaguely. She didn't seem eager to discuss it.

Oscar stared at his tea glass and tried to piece the information together. They probably had a cultural taboo about self-harm which would make it difficult to discuss. That would make it even harder for him to learn more through direct questioning.

A native flute played softly and a group of young people walked into the space. The circle opened to let them through and they came and stood before Yuki. When she gestured welcomingly, they moved to the center of the circle and began a graceful performance.

The sound of the flute softened and the gentle rhythm of drums accompanied it. The tempo slowly increased and so did the energy of the performers. The ambient lights in the space dimmed automatically and the center became filled with the flowing movements of dancers. Oscar felt his eyebrows rise slightly. Apparently the performance was celebrating some kind of coming-of-age ritual. He glanced across the circle at Nicholas. Nicholas's face—what he could see of it in the soft light—was flushed.

A voice spoke near him. "It is difficult for us to imagine anybody doing what representative Ward did. It is..." and she used a local term that Oscar translated as being roughly equivalent to "incomprehensible."

The dancers at the center finally concluded with small wreaths of flowers on their heads that signified their transition to full citizenship. Acrobats then took the stage and went through an impressive routine, and they in turn were succeeded by a singer.

They were all excellent, Oscar thought. If anything, they were too polished.

The tray of refreshments made its way around again and Yuki leaned over to speak to him. "If there is any way that I can assist you while you are here, representative Oscar, you need only ask."

It would probably be a mistake to request a list of Omar's contacts directly, but there was an indirect approach. "I would like to meet any of your people who interacted with Omar Ward, either professionally or socially. I will do everything to minimize any inconvenience."

"I think they would be willing to help you. I shall ask them to visit you this coming week."

Oscar nodded his thanks, but as he looked around the gathering, he couldn't shake a growing unease. Everyone was so content, so harmonious, so perfectly adjusted. It was, he realized, exactly the kind of environment that would make someone like Omar—or Nicholas—feel increasingly isolated and desperate.

And that, perhaps, was the answer they had been seeking all along.
