The Reluctant Innovators
By A. MARTINEZ

The very young woman sat on the edge of the sofa and looked nervous. She carefully studied her fingernails and ran her hands through her hair and picked imaginary lint off the upholstery.

"I have a chance to lead the first renewable energy project in Ravenswood, Nordavia," she said.

The older woman studied the very young woman thoughtfully and then leaned over to her tea service and offered her a cup. "It's nice to have these new solar heating systems now. There was a time when we had to be very careful about energy consumption."

The very young woman was annoyed.

"I don't think I want to go," she blurted. "I don't think I would care to spend three years there."

The older woman took a sip and watched the steam rise from her cup.

"You mean you would miss it here, the people you've known and grown up with, the little familiar things that have made up your life here. You're afraid the glamor would wear off and you would get to hate it in Ravenswood."

The very young woman nodded miserably. "I guess that's it."

"Anything else?"

The very young woman found her fingernails extremely fascinating again and finally said, in a low voice, "Yes, there is."

"Someone special?"

A nod confirmed this.

It was the older woman's turn to look thoughtful. "You know, I'm sure, that psychologists and project managers agree that remote installations should be staffed by partners. That is, of course, as soon as it's practical."

"But that might be a long time!" the very young woman protested.

"It might be—but sometimes it's sooner than you think. And the goal is worth it."

"I suppose so, but—"

The older woman smiled. "Still the reluctant innovators," she said, somewhat to herself.

Ruth Wheeler stared at the computer screen.

Three years at the Keystone Research Station and they didn't want her to come back.

Three years in Keystone, Thandor and they thought she'd be glad to stay for more. Just raise her salary or give her a bonus, the every-person-has-their-price idea. They probably thought she liked it there.

Oh, sure, she loved it. Processed food, recycled water, synthetic vitamins, and filtered air until your insides felt as though they were lined with plastic. Life in a cramped, sterile facility where you could take only twenty steps in any one direction. Their little technological marvel of tomorrow with none of the comforts of home, a charming place where you couldn't take a real shower, couldn't enjoy fresh food, and your circadian rhythms didn't work right.

And for double her salary they thought she'd be glad to stay for another two years. Or maybe three. She should probably be glad she had the opportunity.

The screen started to flash again, demanding an answer.

She typed her reply: "No!"

There was a pause and then the screen flashed once more in a sudden fit of bureaucratic rage. Ruth minimized the window and ignored it. She turned to the sleeping quarters on the other side of the facility.

The flashing hadn't awakened anybody; they were still asleep, making the sounds that people usually make in slumber. Miguel Black, half out of his bunk, was snoring peacefully. Oscar Tran, the poor kid who was due for extended duty, was mumbling to himself. Anil Sullivan, with that look of contentment on his face, looked as if he had just entered his personal paradise. Leo Potter and Matthew Russell were lying perfectly still, their covers not mussed, sleeping very lightly.

Lord, Ruth thought, I'll be happy when I can see some other faces.

"What'd they want?" Anil had one eyelid open and a questioning look on his face.

"They wanted me to stay until the next rotation arrives," Ruth whispered back.

"What did you say?"

She shrugged. "No."

"You kept it short," somebody else whispered. It was Leo, up and sitting on the side of his bunk. "If it had been me, I would have told them just what they could do about it."

The others were awake now, with the exception of Oscar who had his face to the wall and a pillow over his head.

Miguel rubbed his eyes sleepily. "Frustrated, aren't you?"

"Kind of. Who wouldn't be?"

"Well, don't let it throw you. They've never been here at Keystone. They don't know what it's like. All they're trying to do is get a good engineer to stay on the job a while longer."

"All they're trying to do," Ruth said sarcastically. "They've got a fat chance."

"They think you've found a home here," Leo said.

"Why the hell don't you guys shut up until morning?" Oscar was awake, looking bitter. "Some of us still have to stay here, you know. Some of us aren't going back today."

No, Ruth thought, some of us aren't going back. You aren't. And Kai's staying, too. Only Kai isn't ever going back.

Anil jerked his thumb toward Oscar's bunk, held a finger to his lips, and walked noiselessly over to the small electric kettle. It was his day for breakfast duty.

The others started organizing their bunks, getting ready for their last day of work at Keystone. In a few hours they'd be relieved by members of the Third rotation and they'd be on their way back to Westfield, Prandoria.

And that includes me, Ruth thought. I'm going home. I'm finally going home.

She walked silently to the one small window in the facility. It was morning—Thandor's harsh northern morning—and she shivered slightly. The rays of the sun were just striking the far edge of the geothermal field and long shadows shot across the barren landscape. The rest of it was still blanketed in a dark jumble of volcanic rock and jagged formations that would make the Badlands look like paradise.

A hundred meters from the research facility she could make out the small memorial, a simple stone marker with a bronze plaque. You could still see the footprints in the ash where the group had gathered around it. It had been more than twenty months ago, but there was little wind to wear those tracks away. They'd be there for years.

That's what happened to people like Kai Howard, Ruth thought. In remote energy research, one mistake could use up your whole quota of chances.

Anil came back with the coffee. Ruth took a cup, grimaced, and forced herself to swallow the rest of it. It had been freeze-dried so long you could almost taste the packaging.

Leo was warming himself over his cup, looking thoughtful. Miguel and Matthew were getting into their thermal suits, getting ready to go outside. Oscar was still sitting on his bunk, trying to ignore them.

"Think we ought to message the transport hub and see if they've left there yet?" Anil asked.

"I talked to them on the last call," Ruth said. "The relief transport left there eighteen hours ago. They should get here"—she looked at her watch—"in about seven hours."

"Ruth, you know, I've been thinking," Leo said quietly. "You've been here just twice as long as the rest of us. What's the first thing you're going to do once you get back?"

It hit them, then. Miguel and Matthew looked blank for a minute and blindly found equipment cases to sit on. The top halves of their suits were still hanging on hooks. Anil lowered his coffee cup and looked grave. Even Oscar glanced up expectantly.

"I don't know," Ruth said slowly. "I guess I was trying not to think of that. I suppose none of us have. We've been like little kids who have waited so long for a holiday that they just can't believe it when it's finally here."

Anil nodded in agreement. "I haven't been here three years like you have, but I think I know what you mean." He warmed up to it as the idea sank in. "Just what the hell are you going to do?"

"Nothing very spectacular," Ruth said, smiling. "I'm going to rent an apartment overlooking the harbor in Westfield, get some real music playing, and drink wine and listen to it and watch the boats on the water below. Then I think I'll see somebody."

"Who's the somebody?" Leo asked.

Ruth grinned. "Oh, just somebody. What are you going to do, Leo?"

"Well, I'm going to do something practical. First of all, I want to turn over all my data analysis to the government. Then I'm going to write a book about renewable energy innovation and then—why, then, I think I'll get drunk!"

Everybody laughed and Ruth turned to Anil.

"How about you, Anil?"

Anil looked solemn. "Like Leo, I'll first get rid of my obligations to the project. Then I think I'll go home and see my husband."

They were quiet. "I thought all members of the rotations were supposed to be single," Leo said.

"They are. And I can see their reasons for it. But who could pass up the money the Commission was paying?"

"If I had to do it all over again? Me," said Leo promptly.

They laughed. Somebody said: "Play your recording, Ruth. Today's the day for it."

The music player was a small, portable model that Ruth had brought with her when she had arrived with the First rotation. The recording was of traditional folk music from her hometown, and though the file was compressed and the audio quality wasn't perfect, the music was good.

Home Again by Sarah Chen.

They ran through it twice. They were beginning to feel it now, Ruth thought. They were going to go home in a little while and the idea was just starting to sink in.

"You know, Ruth," Leo said, "it won't seem like the same old Keystone without you here. Why, we'll think about this place when we're working on our own projects and it just won't have the same appeal."

"Like they say in the service," Matthew said, "you never had it so good. You found a home here."

The others chimed in and Ruth grinned. Yesterday or a week ago they couldn't have done it. She had been there too long and she had hated it too much.

The party quieted down after a while and Miguel and Matthew finished getting into their suits. They still had a section of the geothermal grid to inspect before they left. Leo was right after them. There was a fault line he wanted to examine and some thermal readings he wished to investigate.

And the time went faster when you kept busy.

Ruth stopped them at the airlock. "Remember to check your suits for tears," she warned. "And check the seals on your oxygen masks."

Leo looked sour. "I've gone out at least five hundred times," he said, "and you check me each time."

"And I'd check you five hundred more," Ruth said. "It takes only one mistake. And watch out for unstable ground. You go through one of those thermal vents and that's it, friend."

Leo sighed. "Ruth, you watch us like a mother hen. You see we check our suits, you settle our arguments, you see that we're not bored and that we stay healthy and happy. I think you'd hold our hands if we got scared. But some day, Ruth old friend, you're gonna find out that your little team can watch out for themselves!"

But he checked his suit for tears and tested the seal of his mask before he left.

Only Anil and Ruth were left in the facility. Anil was at the work table, carefully organizing some soil samples.

"I never knew you were married," Ruth said.

Anil didn't look up. "There wasn't much sense in talking about it. You just get to thinking and wanting—and there's nothing you can do about it. You talk about it and it just makes it worse."

"He let you go without any fuss, huh?"

"No, he didn't make any fuss. But I don't think he liked to see me go, either." He laughed a little. "At least I hope he didn't."

They were silent for a while. "What do you miss most, Ruth?" Anil asked. "Oh, I know what we said a little while ago, but I mean seriously."

Ruth thought a minute. "I think I miss the ocean," she said quietly. "The blue water and the green parks and trees with birds in them. I think, when I go back, that I'd like to go to the beach and just feel the sand between my toes."

She stopped, feeling embarrassed. Anil's expression was encouraging. "And then I think I'd like to go downtown and just watch the shoppers on the sidewalks. Or maybe go to a concert hall and smell the old wood and the people's perfume and cologne."

She studied her hands. "I think what I miss most is people—all kinds of people. Rich people and poor people and tall people and short people, and people I can't understand. People who wouldn't know renewable energy from a toaster. And people who wouldn't give a damn. We're hundreds of miles from civilization, Anil, and to make it poetic, I think I miss my fellow humans more than anything."

"Got someone special back home?" Anil asked almost casually.

"Yes."

"You're not like Oscar. You've never mentioned it."

"Same reason you didn't mention your husband. You get to thinking about it."

Anil sealed the sample container. "Going to get married when you get back?"

Ruth was at the window again, staring out at the bleak landscape. "We hope to."

"Settle down in a nice place and maybe start a family, eh?"

Ruth nodded.

"That's the only future," Anil said.

He put away the container and came over to the window. Ruth moved over so they both could look out.

"Ruth." Anil hesitated a moment. "What happened to Kai?"

"She died," Ruth said. "She was a brilliant engineer, all wrapped up in the work. Being at Keystone was the opportunity of a lifetime. She thought so much about it that she forgot a lot of little things—like how to stay alive. The day before the Second rotation came, she went out to finish some work she was interested in. She forgot to check for suit tears and whether or not her oxygen mask was properly sealed. We couldn't get to her in time."

"She had her radio with her?"

"Yes. It worked fine, too. We heard everything that went through her mind at the end."

Anil's face was blank. "What's your real job here, Ruth? Why does somebody have to stay for extended duty?"

"Hell, lots of reasons, Anil. You can't get a whole relief crew and let them take over cold. They have to know where you left off. They have to know where things are, how things work, what to watch out for. And then, because you've been here two years and know the ropes, you have to watch them to see that they stay alive in spite of themselves. Keystone's a harsh environment and you have to learn how to live in it. There's a lot of things to learn—and some people just never learn."

"You're a supervisor, then."

"I suppose you could call it that."

Anil said, "You're not a scientist, are you?"

"No, you should know that. I came as the chief engineer of the first installation. We built the facility from prefabricated parts so there wasn't anything to go back on immediately. I'm a good mechanic and I made myself useful with the equipment. When it occurred to us that somebody was going to have to stay for extended duty, I volunteered. I thought the others were so important that it was better they should take their research and data back to Westfield when the first relief transport came."

"You wouldn't do it again, though, would you?"

"No, I wouldn't."

"Do you think Oscar will do as good a job as you've done here?"

Ruth frowned. "Frankly, I hadn't thought of that. I don't believe I care. I've put in my time; it's somebody else's turn now. He volunteered for it. I think I was fair in explaining all about the job when you talked it over among yourselves."

"You did, but I don't think Oscar's the man for it. He's too young, too inexperienced. He volunteered because he thought it made him look like a hero. He doesn't have the judgment that an older person would have. That you have."

Ruth turned slowly around and faced Anil.

"I'm not the indispensable person," she said slowly, "and even if I was, it wouldn't make any difference to me. I'm sorry if Oscar is young. So was I. I've lost three years up here. And I don't intend to lose any more."

Anil held up his hands. "Look, Ruth, I didn't mean you should stay. I know how much you hate it and the time you put in up here. It's just—" His voice trailed away. "It's just that I think it's such a damn important job."

Anil had gone out in a last search for thermal anomalies and Ruth enjoyed one of her relatively few moments of privacy. She wandered over to her bunk and opened her duffel bag. She checked the clothes and her toiletries for maybe the hundredth time and pushed everything down farther in the canvas. It was foolish because the bag was already packed and had been for a week. She remembered putting it off for as long as she could and then the quiet satisfaction about a week before, when she had opened her small locker and transferred its meager belongings to the bag.

She hadn't actually needed to pack, of course. In less than twenty-four hours she'd be back in Westfield where she could buy whatever she wanted. She could leave behind her worn shirts and socks and the oversized jacket she had inherited from—who was it? Martinez?—of the First rotation. Oscar could probably use them or maybe one of the team in the Third.

But it wasn't like going home unless you packed. It was part of the ritual, like marking off the last three weeks in marker on the white wall beside her bunk. Just a few hours ago, when she woke up, she had made the last check mark and signed her name and the date. Her signature was right beneath Kai's.

She frowned when she thought of Kai and zipped up the bag. They should never have sent someone as focused as Kai to Keystone.

She had just secured the bag when she heard the hiss of the airlock and the soft whoosh of air. Somebody had come back earlier than expected. She watched the inner door swing open and the suited figure clump in and remove its helmet.

Oscar. He had gone out to help Miguel on the thermal scanner. Maybe Miguel hadn't needed any help, with Matthew along. Or more likely, considering the circumstances, Oscar wasn't much good at helping anybody today.

Oscar stripped off his suit. His face was covered with light beads of sweat and his eyes were frightened.

He moistened his lips slightly. "Do—do you think they'll ever have relief transports up here more often than every two years, Ruth? I mean, considering the advance of—"

"No," Ruth interrupted bluntly. "I don't. Not at least for ten years. The logistics are too expensive and the conditions too hazardous. On transport costs alone you're worth a fortune when they send you here. Even if it becomes cheaper, Oscar, it won't come about so it will shorten extended duty right away." She stopped, feeling a little sorry for Oscar. "It won't be too bad. There'll be new people up here and you'll pass a lot of time getting to know them."

"Well, you see," Oscar started, "that's why I came back early. I wanted to see you about extended duty. It's that—well, I'll put it this way." He seemed to be groping for an easy way to say what he wanted to. "I'm engaged back home. Really wonderful person, Ruth, you'd like them if you knew them." He fumbled in his pocket and found a photograph and put it on the desk. "That's a picture of Sam, taken at a festival we attended together." Ruth didn't look. "They—we—expected to be married when I got back. I never told them about extended duty, Ruth. They think I'll be home tomorrow. I kept thinking, hoping, that maybe somehow—"

He was fumbling it badly, Ruth thought.

"You wanted to trade places with me, didn't you, Oscar? You thought I might stay for extended duty again, in your place?"

It hurt to look in Oscar's eyes. They were the eyes of a person who was trying desperately to stop what they were about to do, but just couldn't help themselves.

"Well, yes, more or less. Oh, God, Ruth, I know you want to go home! But I couldn't ask any of the others; you were the only one who could, the only one who was qualified!"

Oscar looked as though he was going to be sick. Ruth tried to recall all she knew about him. Oscar Tran. Good at systems thinking. Graduate from one of the top technical schools. Parents were entrepreneurs in the renewable energy sector.

It still didn't add up, not quite. "You know I don't like it here any more than you do," Ruth said slowly. "I may have commitments at home, too. What made you think I would change my mind?"

Oscar took the plunge. "Well, you see," he started eagerly, too far gone to remember such a thing as pride, "you know my parents are pretty well off. We would make it worth your while, Ruth." He was feverish. "It would mean two more years, Ruth, but they'd be well-paid years!"

Ruth felt tired. The good feeling she had about going home was slowly evaporating.

"If you have any report to make, I think you had better get at it," she cut in, keeping all the harshness she felt out of her voice. "It'll be too late after the relief transport leaves. It'll be easier to give the captain your report than try to transmit it back to Westfield from here."

She felt sorrier for Oscar than she could ever remember having felt for anybody. Long after going home, Oscar would remember this.

It would eat at him like a cancer.

Cowardice is the one thing for which no person ever forgives themselves.

Leo was eating a protein bar and looking out the window, so, naturally, he saw the transport first. "Well, look at that!" he shouted. "We got company!" He dashed for his suit. Miguel and Matthew piled after him and all three started for the airlock.

Ruth was standing in front of it. "Check your suits," she said softly. "Just be sure to check."

"Oh, come on, Ruth!" Leo started angrily. Then he shut up and went over his suit. He got to his oxygen mask and turned white. The seal was cracked. It was only half a kilometer to the relief transport, so somebody would probably have got to him in time, but.... He bit his lips and got a replacement.

Ruth and Anil watched them dash across the volcanic landscape, making the careful but quick movements they had all learned. The hatch of the transport had opened and figures were climbing down the ladder. The small figures from the facility reached them and did a short celebration. Then the figures linked arms and started back. Ruth noticed one—it was probably Leo—pat the transport affectionately before he started back.

They were in the airlock and the air pumped in and then they were in the facility, taking off their suits. The newcomers were impressed and solemn, very much aware of the tremendous responsibility that rested on their shoulders. Like Leo and Anil and the members of the Second rotation had been when they had arrived. Like Ruth had been in the First.

Leo and the others were all over them.

How was it back in Westfield? Who had won the elections? Was so-and-so still teaching at the university? What was the political situation?

Was the sky still blue, was the water still clean, did the leaves still turn color in the autumn, did people still love and cry and were there still people who didn't know what renewable energy was and didn't give a damn?

Ruth had gone through it all before. But was Jamie still Jamie?

Some of the people in the Third had their luggage with them. One of them—a sturdy, dark-haired woman named Sasha Lowe—was opening a box about a foot square and six inches deep. Ruth watched her curiously.

"Well, I'll be damned!" Anil said. "Hey, everyone, look what we've got here!"

Ruth and the others crowded around and suddenly Leo leaned over and took a deep breath. In the box, covering a thick layer of soil, was a small herb garden. They looked at it, awed. Anil put out his hand and touched one of the leaves.

"I like the feel of it," he said simply.

Ruth plucked a single leaf with her fingernail and put it between her lips. It had been years since she had seen fresh herbs and had the luxury of cooking with them and smelling them in a real kitchen.

Sasha blushed. "I thought we could spare a little water for it and maybe use the grow lights on it some of the time. Couldn't help but bring it along; it seemed sort of like a symbol...." She looked embarrassed.

Ruth sympathized. If she had had any sense, she'd have tried to bring something like that up to Keystone instead of her music player.

"That's valuable cargo," Oscar said sharply. "Do you realize that at current transport rates, those herbs are worth about fifty credits a leaf?"

Sasha looked stricken and somebody said, "Oh, shut up, Oscar."

One of the people separated from the group and came over to Ruth. She held out her hand and said, "My name's Chen. Captain of the relief transport. I understand you're in charge here?"

Ruth nodded and shook hands. They hadn't had a captain on the First transport. Just a pilot and crew. Chen looked every inch a captain, too. Strong face, silver-streaked hair, the confident bearing of someone who was sure of herself.

"You might say I'm in charge here," Ruth said.

"Well, look, Ms. Wheeler, is there any place where we can talk together privately?"

They walked over to one corner of the facility. "This is about as private as we can get, captain," Ruth said. "What's on your mind?"

Chen found an equipment case and made herself comfortable. She looked at Ruth.

"I've always wanted to meet the person who's spent more time here than anybody else," she began.

"I'm sure you wanted to see me for more reasons than just curiosity."

Chen took out a pack of mints. "Mind if I have one?"

Ruth jerked a thumb toward Oscar. "Ask him. He's in charge now."

The captain didn't bother. She put the pack away. "You know we have big plans for the station," she said.

"I hadn't heard of them."

"Oh, yes, big plans. They're working on autonomous vehicles now that could carry cargo and materials for more facilities like this. Enable us to enlarge the complex, have a series of buildings all linked together. Make good laboratories and living quarters for you people." Her eyes swept the room. "Have a little privacy for a change."

Ruth nodded. "They could use a little privacy up here."

The captain noticed the pronoun. "Well, that's one of the reasons why I wanted to talk to you, Wheeler. The Commission talked it over and they'd like to see you stay. They feel if they're going to enlarge it, add more facilities and have more people up here, that a person of practical experience should be running things. They figure that you're the only one who's capable and who's had the experience."

The captain vaguely felt the approach was all wrong.

"Is that all?"

Chen was ill at ease. "Naturally you'd be paid well. I don't imagine anyone would like being here all the time. They're prepared to double your salary—maybe even a bonus in addition—and let you have full authority. You'd be Director of the Keystone Energy Research Complex."

All this and a title too, Ruth thought.

"That's it?" Ruth asked.

Chen frowned. "Well, the Commission said they'd be willing to consider anything else you had in mind, if it was more money or...."

"The answer is no," Ruth said. "I'm not interested in more money for staying because I'm not interested in staying. Money can't buy it, captain. I'm sorry, but I'm afraid that you'd have to stay up here to appreciate that.

"Oscar Tran is staying for extended duty. If there's something important about the project or impending changes, perhaps you'd better tell him before you go."

She walked away.
question: Who stayed half out of their bunk and snored peacefully?

synthetic_story:
The Curator of Fairview
By ADAPTED WORK

Death was Felix Wood's expertise, and every colony had known his methods. But now, on the biodiversity station of Fairview, Yendor, he was selling his skills into the strangest of all his assignments—gambling his life against the preservation of species that shouldn't exist.

On the observation deck of the Elmwood Cultural Center, a slender woman with dark hair pulled back in a severe bun was lecturing about "The Lost Murals of Pre-Colonial Havencia." The lecture was technical, detailed, a favorite of the researchers and conservation officers who frequented the center. The woman delivered it with such precision that the audience sat in rapt attention.

She kept her eyes fixed on her notes so that her hair fell forward slightly, obscuring her face. There was tension in her shoulders. Her mouth maintained a professional smile. Her eyes were frightened.

The man who had been operating the holographic display system sat at the side of the stage, his back to the scattered audience. He did not look up at the lecturer but kept his weathered face bent over the controls, while his fingers automatically adjusted the images. Sweat beaded on his temples despite the climate control. Without looking up, he said: "Have you spotted him?" His voice was pitched to reach the lecturer alone.

The woman, with an almost imperceptible gesture, shook her head.

The afternoon was artificially temperate; but then it always was on Fairview, the newest, the most controversial, the most carefully monitored of Earth's biodiversity conservation stations. Ventilation systems throughout the center's walls circulated the processed air, while the researchers and administrators sitting in the audience sipped carefully at filtered water. Only the native assistants, the enigmatic, golden-eyed Yendorians, seemed truly at ease. They moved with fluid grace through the space.

Up on the stage the lecturer was about to transition to her next slide when she stiffened.

"Here he is," she said to the technician without moving her lips.

The technician swung around on his stool, lifted his gray eyes to the entrance leading from the main corridor.

Just within the doorway, a tall, lean man was standing. He looked like a predator surveying the room. His conservation officer's uniform hung perfectly. His dark hair was regulation length, his features angular and sharp. For a moment he studied the assembled researchers before making his way to an empty seat.

"Continue," said the technician in a flat voice.

The dark-haired woman shivered. Stepping from the stage she made her way through the seats until she came to the one occupied by the newcomer.

"May I join you?" she asked in a low voice.

The man stood. "Of course. I was expecting you. Here, sit down." He gestured to the adjacent seat, then signaled for a server. The Yendorian, his golden eyes reflecting light like polished amber, approached silently. "Bring us two glasses of the filtered spring water from the Redwood District, well chilled." The server glided away.

"So," said the dark-haired woman; "you came. I didn't think you would arrive in time." Her hands were clenched in her lap. The knuckles were white.

The man said nothing.

"I didn't want to bring you into this, Felix Wood." It was the first time she had used his name. "You have the reputation of being unpredictable. I don't trust you, but since..." She stopped as the server placed glasses on the small table and silently poured the clear water. The man, Felix Wood, raised his glass.

"Here's to ecosystem restoration," he said. His low voice carried an odd, compelling note. His eyes, pale gray and analytical, were striking against his tanned face.

The woman drew in her breath.

"No! Fairview isn't ready for that kind of intervention. Only a handful of extremists are pushing for immediate restoration. The real conservation scientists are against it, but they're afraid to speak out. You've got to believe me. The intervention is scheduled to begin during the Annual Biodiversity Summit. If it does, the research here will be compromised. The Yendorians are suspicious of us. We have limited authority."

Felix Wood wiped condensation from his glass with a cloth napkin. "I had forgotten how controlled the environment can be here."

The woman ignored the interruption. "There is one man; he is the leader, the driving force behind the intervention plan. The Yendorians respect him. They will follow whatever he recommends. Without him they would abandon the whole project. He is the scientist, Phillip Ray. I am authorized to offer you fifty thousand Earth credits to eliminate Phillip Ray's influence."

Felix Wood refilled their empty glasses. He was a imposing man, handsome in a severe fashion. Only his eyes were different. They were analytical and penetrating with straight brows. The pupils were a pale gray that could dissect a situation like a surgeon's scalpel. Now he caught the woman's eyes and held them with his own.

"Why bring me all the way from the Larchmont research station for that? Why not have that technician back there handle it?"

The woman started, glanced at the stage, said with a tremor: "We can't locate Phillip Ray. Don't look at me that way, Felix. You frighten me. I'm telling the truth. We can't find him. That's why we contacted you. You've got to find him, Felix. He's destabilizing all of Fairview's protocols."

"Who's funding this?"

"I can't tell you."

"Ah," said Felix Wood; "so that's the situation."

"That's the situation."

"There isn't much time," he said after a moment. "The Summit begins in three days."

"No," the woman replied. "But we think he's here in the facility."

"Why? What makes you think that?"

"He was seen," she began, then stopped with a gasp.

The lights had gone out.

It was as unexpected as a power failure. One moment the center was illuminated, the next the darkness swept through the space. The ventilation systems audibly slowed and stopped. The temperature began to shift.

Felix Wood moved sideways from his seat. He felt something brush his arm. Somewhere a researcher made a startled sound.

"What's happening?" growled an irritated voice. Other voices took up the complaint.

Across from Felix there was the sense of movement; he could detect it. An exclamation was suddenly muffled as if a hand had been placed over the woman's mouth.

"Lila!" said Felix in a low voice.

There was no answer.

"Lila!" he repeated, louder.

Unexpectedly, the authoritative voice of the Center Director boomed out from the stage.

"Everything is fine. The primary circuit failed. The lights will be restored momentarily."

Following his announcement the lights flashed back on, the ventilation resumed. The familiar hum of the systems returned.

Felix Wood glanced at his seat. The dark-haired lecturer was gone. So was the technician.

Felix Wood sat back down and took another sip of water. The filtered spring water had a pure, clean taste. It reminded him of mountain streams on Earth. On the carefully controlled station of Fairview it was as refreshing as natural rain.

He wondered who was funding the fifty thousand Earth credits? Who stood to lose most if the intervention failed? The answer seemed clear enough. Who, but Samuel Osborne. Osborne controlled the biodiversity research grants for which there was tremendous demand throughout the colonies.

And what had happened to the woman? Had the intervention supporters taken her? If so, he suspected they had underestimated her. Lila Park had the reputation of being resourceful.

He signaled a server, prepared to leave. As the Yendorian started to depart, a thought struck Felix. These golden-eyed Yendorians could navigate in near darkness as well as any nocturnal predator. For generations they had adapted to the variable light conditions of their world. He produced a credit chip, placed it in the server's hand.

"What became of the dark-haired lecturer?"

The Yendorian glanced at the chip, then back at the Earthman. There was no readable expression in his golden eyes.

"She and the man, the technician who operates the displays, left through the service corridor."

Felix shrugged, dismissed the server. He had not expected to get much information, but he was not a man to overlook any possibility. If the woman had been taken, only Yendorians could have managed it in the darkness; and the Yendorians were protective of their own.

Back in the main corridor Felix Wood headed for his quarters. The passages were narrow, designed for efficiency rather than comfort, with walls lined with monitoring equipment. Beneath his feet, he knew, stretched a network of laboratories and storage facilities. Somewhere in those spaces was Phillip Ray, the interventionist, and the woman.

At regular intervals soft blue lights illuminated the corridor, casting a clinical glow. He had just passed one of these lights when he detected movement behind him. It was barely perceptible, but as he moved beyond the illuminated section, he pressed himself against a maintenance alcove. Nothing appeared. There was no further sound. Again he started forward, but now he was conscious of shadows tracking him. They were never visible, but to his trained senses there came revealing indicators: the whisper of fabric against the walls, the subtle shift of air pressure. He turned down a connecting passage, faded into a doorway. Immediately all signs of pursuit ceased. But as soon as he emerged he was aware again of the followers. In the controlled environment, he was at a disadvantage against the adapted Yendorians.

In the distance a warm amber glow indicated the approach of the station's artificial dawn cycle. With a muttered curse, he set out again for his quarters. He made no further effort to elude the followers.

Once back in his room, Felix Wood removed his uniform jacket, unstrapped a shoulder holster containing a compressed air tranquilizer gun, stepped into the sanitation unit. His body was lean and marked with various scars from his years in conflict zones. There were small circular scars and long thin ones, and his left shoulder bore the distinctive mark of a chemical burn. Stepping out, he dried himself, reattached the shoulder holster, slipped into casual clothes. The clothes were simple gray with minimal decoration. Next he activated his communication device and began to review the station's personnel files with methodical attention.

He had, he supposed, eliminated rather a lot of threats. He had worked in the resource conflicts of the outer colonies for years, then the Territorial Disputes of the 2180s, after that the Larchmont Incident as well as dozens of smaller operations. No, there was little doubt but that he had neutralized quite a number of problems. But this business of tracking a man through the research facilities was outside his usual parameters.

Furthermore, there was something inconsistent about the entire situation. The Yendorians, he knew, had been advocating for greater autonomy in conservation decisions for years. Why, at this time when the Earth Council was about to grant them expanded authority, would they support a controversial intervention?

A loud, official knocking at the door interrupted his analysis. He stood and deactivated his device. Before he could reach the door the knocking came again.

Releasing the lock, he stepped back, balanced and ready.

"Enter," he called.

The door opened. A heavy-set man entered, secured and locked the door, then glanced around carefully. His eyes settled on Felix. He cleared his throat.

"Mr. Wood, the—ah—security specialist, I believe." His voice was precise, almost pedantic. "I'm Samuel Osborne." He extended a soft hand.

Felix said nothing. He ignored the hand, waited, poised.

Mr. Osborne cleared his throat again. "I have come, Mr. Wood, on a matter of urgent business. I had not intended to reveal myself in this matter. I preferred to remain behind the scenes, but the disappearance of Dr. Park has—ah—forced my hand." He paused.

Felix remained silent. Dr. Park must be the dark-haired lecturer, whom he had known under several different professional identities. He doubted even she remembered her original credentials.

"Dr. Park made you a proposition?" Samuel Osborne's voice was tight.

"Yes," said Felix.

"You accepted?"

"Why, no. As it happened she was taken before I had the opportunity."

Mr. Osborne cleared his throat. "But you will, surely you will. Unless Phillip Ray's influence is neutralized immediately there will be a catastrophic intervention across the entire station during the Biodiversity Summit. Earth doesn't recognize the severity of the situation."

"Then I was correct; it is you who are providing the fifty thousand Earth credits."

"Not entirely," said Osborne uncomfortably. "There are many of us here, Yendorians as well as Earthmen, who recognize the danger. We have—ah—pooled our resources."

"But you stand to lose most if the intervention succeeds?"

"Perhaps. I have substantial interests in the current research protocols. They are—ah—profitable."

Felix Wood activated a small recording device, sat on the edge of his bed. "Why be indirect," he asked with a slight smile. "Mr. Osborne, you've gained control of the biodiversity research funding. Other Earth administrators control the genetic archives and the northern conservation zones. Together you form perhaps the strongest administrative bloc the colonies have seen. You essentially run Fairview, and you've extracted every possible credit. Every time expanded Yendorian authority has come before the Earth Council you've succeeded in blocking it. You are, perhaps, the most resented group anywhere. I don't wonder that you fear losing control."

Mr. Osborne took out a cloth and dabbed his forehead. "Seventy-five thousand Earth credits I can offer you. But no more. That is my maximum authorization."

Felix laughed. "How did you know Lila had been taken?"

"We have a comprehensive monitoring system. I received the report of Dr. Park's abduction ten minutes after the incident."

Felix raised his eyebrows. "Perhaps then you know where she is?"

Mr. Osborne shook his head. "No. Phillip Ray's supporters took her."

A second knocking at the door caused them to exchange glances. Felix went to the door, opened it. The technician from the center was standing in the entrance. His gray eyes were intense in his lined face. His work clothes were stained with dust and moisture.

"They told me Mr. Osborne was here," he said.

"It's for you," said Felix over his shoulder.

Mr. Osborne came to the door. "Hello, Jonathan. I thought Ray's people had you? Where's Dr. Park?"

"I escaped. Look, Mr. Osborne, I need to speak with you privately."

Samuel Osborne said, "Would you excuse us, Mr. Wood?" He cleared his throat. "I'll just step out into the corridor a moment." He went out, closing the door behind him.

Felix activated his communication device. He paced the room silently, his movements economical. He sat on the edge of the bed. He stood and deactivated the device. He went to the door, but did not open it. Instead, he made another circuit of the room. Again he stopped before the door, pressed his ear against the panel. For a long time he listened but could distinguish no sound of conversation. With a curse he opened the door. The corridor was empty.

Felix returned to his room, put his uniform jacket back on, checked the tranquilizer gun. It was a flat, practical weapon which delivered a dose calculated to incapacitate. He preferred it because, though he rarely needed lethal force, it stopped a person effectively. He adjusted the gun carefully in its holster to ensure quick access if needed. Then he went out into the corridor.

At the information desk he inquired if any messages had come for him. There were none, but the clerk had seen Mr. Osborne with another man take the lift to the lower research levels. Above the clerk's head a news display was streaming current updates. Felix read:

"Earth Council suspends negotiations on Yendorian conservation autonomy pending investigation of rumored unauthorized intervention. Earth personnel advised to return home. Phillip Ray, conservation scientist, being sought."

Felix descended to the network of laboratories which served as the primary research areas. Here in the lower levels were located the specimen storage facilities and analysis rooms where the Yendorians worked at monitoring stations, their movements precise and methodical. The laboratories were brightly lit, the natives preferring clear visibility for their detailed work, and Felix moved easily through the space, passing researchers of various species. But when he reached the Earth Administration section, enhanced security protocols were evident, and there was a presence of Colonial guards among the staff.

Felix halted before a door bearing a placard which read:

"BIODIVERSITY RESEARCH ADMINISTRATION"

He pushed through the door into a well-appointed reception area. At the far end was a second door beside which sat a desk, both being separated from the rest of the office by a security barrier. The door to Samuel Osborne's inner office was slightly ajar. Felix could distinguish voices; then quite clearly he heard Samuel Osborne say in his precise tone:

"Jonathan, I thought I left you in the lower levels. Why did you follow me? How many times have I told you never to come here?"

The reply was unintelligible. Then the weathered technician came through the door, closing it behind himself. At the sight of Felix Wood he froze.

"What are you doing here?"

Felix settled himself carefully, his pale gray eyes assessing the man.

"Let's be clear," he said calmly. "I've known your type before. Frankly, ever since I saw you I've had to suppress an urge to report you to security."

The technician's gray eyes were cold, his fingers twitching. His hands began to move upward.

"You interfering..." he began, but he got no further. Felix Wood shot him with the tranquilizer.

The compressed air gun had appeared in Felix's hand. The dart struck the technician's shoulder with precision, and he slumped against the wall. Felix moved quickly, relieving him of two concealed weapons.

"I'll remember this," said Jonathan, his voice slurred. "You've interfered. I'll make you pay."

The door to the inner office opened.

"What's happened?" cried Samuel Osborne in distress. "What's wrong with you, Jonathan?"

"This man shot me with a tranquilizer."

"But why?" Osborne was agitated.

"Nothing permanent," said Felix. "He'll be unconscious for a while. That's all."

"Jonathan," said Mr. Osborne. "You're creating a scene. Why can't you go to the medical bay. Has anyone called a medic? Where's Ms. Miles? Ms. Miles! That woman. Ms. Miles!"

Jonathan slid to the floor, losing consciousness, just as a tall woman with straight auburn hair hurried in from an adjacent office. She had alert hazel eyes and enough professional competence to immediately assess the situation.

"Oh!" exclaimed Ms. Miles as she saw the unconscious technician.

"There's been an—ah—incident," said Mr. Osborne, clearing his throat. "Call medical, Ms. Miles."

Ms. Miles raised an eyebrow, went to the communication console. In a moment she had connected with a medical facility.

"Could Dr. Martinez come immediately? There's been an incident."

"Come where?" said the person on the screen. "These systems require specific locations."

"Oh," said Ms. Miles, "the offices of the Biodiversity Research Administration."

The person on the screen became more attentive. "Certainly. Dr. Martinez will be there shortly."

"Thank you," said Ms. Miles. She closed the connection, then added quietly: "Efficient."

Mr. Osborne regarded Felix Wood with concern.

"Really, Mr. Wood, was it necessary to tranquilize Jonathan? Isn't that—ah—somewhat extreme? I'm afraid it might incapacitate him, and I had an assignment for him."

"Oh," said Ms. Miles, her hazel eyes sharp. "Did you shoot that man? Aren't you the decisive one?"

"Decisive?" said Felix mildly. "Potentially dangerous individual. I took these items from him." He held out the concealed weapons. "You take them, Mr. Osborne. Frankly, they concern me. They might be used improperly."

Mr. Osborne accepted the weapons reluctantly. He held them as if they might activate unexpectedly. He started to secure them, reconsidered, glanced around helplessly.

"Here, Ms. Miles," he said, "do something with these. Put them in my secure storage."

Ms. Miles's eyes widened. "I wouldn't handle those devices for all the research grants on Fairview."

"Here, I'll take them," said Jonathan, regaining consciousness. He had managed to sit up. His face was pale and drawn. Felix watched him coldly as with his functioning hand the technician retrieved the weapons.

"Attempt to use those and I'll use lethal force next time."

"Now, Mr. Wood." Mr. Osborne cleared his throat nervously. "Jonathan, go into my office. The doctor will be here momentarily. Ms. Miles, you may leave for the day. I'll have no more work for you today."

Samuel Osborne helped Jonathan through the door. Felix and Ms. Miles were alone. With his attention on the door, Felix said:

"When you leave, go toward the cultural research section. Wait for me in the first observation lounge you find."

Ms. Miles raised her eyebrows. "What's this? An unusual approach?"

"Look," began Felix, annoyed.

"My curiosity is already overwhelming," she interrupted. "Another afternoon like this and I'm taking the first transport back to Earth." She gathered her belongings from the desk.

"I'm not trying to be social. This is..."

"How disappointing."

Felix began again patiently. "Wait for me in the first observation lounge. There's something I need to know. It's important." He cleared his throat. "Don't you find the artificial environment somewhat disorienting, Ms. Miles. But perhaps you've adapted to it."

Mr. Osborne returned to the room.

"Why, no, I mean yes," replied Ms. Miles, a confused expression on her face.

"Goodbye, Ms. Miles," said Mr. Osborne firmly.

Felix smiled slightly at her. Ms. Miles departed looking bewildered.

As the door closed behind the woman, Samuel Osborne cleared his throat, said: "Mr. Wood, I suppose my departure from your quarters requires some explanation. But the fact is that Jonathan brought critical information." He paused.

Felix said nothing.

"You might be interested to know that Dr. Park is quite safe. Phillip Ray has her, but Jonathan assures me she will be unharmed." Again he paused. As Felix remained silent, his neck flushed.

"The fact is, Mr. Wood, that we won't need your services after all. I realize that we've caused you considerable inconvenience and we're prepared to compensate you for your time. Say five thousand Earth credits?"

"That's reasonable," replied Felix.

Samuel Osborne sighed with relief. "I have the authorization prepared."

"Only," continued Felix coldly, "I'm not ready to be dismissed. I think I'll continue investigating this situation."

Mr. Osborne's face fell. "You won't reconsider?"

"Sorry," said Felix; "but I have an appointment. I'm late now." He started to leave.

"Jonathan!" called Samuel Osborne.

The weathered technician appeared in the doorway, one of the weapons in his functioning hand. Felix Wood dropped to the floor, drawing his tranquilizer gun as he fell. There was a soft discharge sound. He felt the projectile pass overhead. Then he fired from the floor. The technician collapsed completely.

Felix stood, keeping his attention on Samuel Osborne, brushed off his uniform.

"You've incapacitated him seriously," said Osborne. "If I were you, Mr. Wood, I would be on the next transport back to Earth."

Without responding, Felix backed carefully from the room.

Once Felix Wood had regained the corridor, he wiped his forehead with his hand. Whatever was occurring, these people were playing seriously. Carefully he started down the passage toward the cultural research section. At the first observation lounge he entered. His eyes scanned the space, then he smiled.

At a corner table, a glass of filtered water before her, sat Ms. Miles. Her auburn hair was slightly disheveled, and she was perched on the edge of her chair as if ready to leave quickly.

"Surprise," said Felix, approaching from behind and speaking quietly.

Ms. Miles jumped, nearly spilling her water. She regarded him with exasperation.

"Never a peaceful moment," she said.

Still smiling slightly, Felix sat down. "I'm Felix Wood, Ms. Miles. I think Samuel Osborne forgot to introduce us properly. There's some questionable activity occurring here that I'm particularly interested in understanding. I thought you might be able to help me."

"Yes," replied Ms. Miles carefully.

A Yendorian server, attracted by the commotion, approached and took Felix's order.

"All right," Felix said, but his pale gray eyes studied the woman thoughtfully. "I'll have to share certain information which might be risky for you to know. Are you willing, Ms. Miles?"

"Since we're going to be collaborating," she replied; "you might call me Anil. You make me feel excessively formal."

"Well then," he said. "First, I just seriously incapacitated that technician your supervisor had in his office."

"What!" said Anil, choking on her water.

"It was necessary," he assured her. "He attempted to use a weapon against me."

"But the authorities!" she cried, recovering.

"There'll never be an investigation. Samuel Osborne will ensure that. I was brought here on what I believed was a legitimate security assignment. Instead I was offered fifty thousand Earth credits to eliminate the influence of the intervention leader."

"What intervention? I'm completely confused."

"The Yendorians, of course."

"I don't believe it," said the woman. "The Yendorians are the most cooperative people in the colonies. They've been advocating for greater autonomy, yes. But they believe in peaceful negotiation. I don't believe you could convince a Yendorian to use violence, even in self-defense. That's why Samuel Osborne and the rest of the administration had such an easy time maintaining control of the research protocols."

"Excellent point," breathed Felix, "I begin to understand. Ms. Miles—ah, Anil—I have a feeling that we're going to work well together. How do you happen to be Samuel Osborne's administrative assistant?"

"Employment necessity. But truthfully, I was planning to resign. The Biodiversity Research Administration is nearly insolvent. Their funding has been declining precipitously."

Felix Wood raised his angular brows but did not interrupt.

"Samuel Osborne," she continued, "has been trying to transfer his position but nobody will accept the assignment, not since it appears the Earth Council is going to grant the Yendorians expanded authority. Everyone knows that the first thing the Yendorians will do is restructure the research administration."

"What about this Phillip Ray?" said Felix. "I've heard that he's encouraging the Yendorians toward unauthorized intervention. The news stream had information about the intervention too. The government has advised all Earth personnel to return home."

"It's not true," Anil stated firmly. "It's all fabricated by the Biodiversity Research Administration. I know."

"But I would think rumors like that would damage the administration's credibility."
