THE SYNTHESIS PROTOCOL
By Anonymous

Teresa Cole was alone.

In the beginning, she had seen many advantages to being alone in the biodome research station on Europa. It would give her an unprecedented opportunity to correlate isolation effects on neural plasticity, to observe how long it would take before she started having conversations with the algae tanks, to measure the precise moment when professional ethics gave way to survival instinct.

She would be able to study evolutionary biology without the interference of committee meetings, she would be able to test theories of network theory in closed systems, she would be able to live more like a researcher and think more like a pioneer than anyone in her field for generations.

But after a shorter time than she expected, it all became unbearable. Even the scientific observation part of it.

Not that she was going to have a long wait before losing her grip. She was already narrating her actions aloud, recording voice memos that grew increasingly personal, and she had printed out a photograph of her research team back on Earth. She'd mounted it on the wall and found herself waving at it each morning.

Lately, the faces seemed to wave back.

Loneliness was a physical weight pressing against her sternum. It hollowed out her chest and amplified every heartbeat to thunder.

No one in the solar system was as lonely as Teresa Cole, and even Teresa Cole could only be this lonely on Europa.

Teresa was Station Kepler-7's sole biological overseer.

All Teresa had to do was monitor the experimental ecosystem developing in the vast underground ocean beneath Europa's ice crust, watching through sensor arrays as engineered microorganisms slowly transformed the alien environment. She had to stare at data streams, at bioluminescent patterns in the water captured by remote cameras, at the twin shadows of Jupiter's other moons crossing the ice fields above. The entire operation was automated, controlled by advanced AI systems. No human presence was required—no human being, at least.

The Scientific Ethics Board was a small but vocal organization, and it didn't take much to pressure the Assembly. They had carefully mandated human oversight for each experimental station scattered across the Jovian moons, to ensure professional ethics in biological experimentation.

They didn't select well-adjusted, socially-fulfilled people for the job. Well-adjusted people weren't going to isolate themselves in a pointless oversight role. They got, instead, Teresa Cole and her fellows.

The overseers were contracted for the duration of the project. Transport to Europa cost approximately eight hundred million dollars per person. They weren't providing shuttle service for weekend visits home. They weren't providing accommodations for families when the contract specified solo occupancy. They weren't providing fuel for inter-station social calls. They weren't very accommodating at all.

But it paid three hundred thousand a year in salary, and it offered remarkable opportunities.

It gave Teresa Cole an opportunity to believe she saw a cargo vessel making a vertical landing on the ice plain, its thrusters burning as bright as ambition.

Teresa suspected hallucination, but in an existence with all the emotional range of a flatlined EKG, she was willing to embrace delusion. Sometimes she even cultivated it. Sometimes she would run through the corridors of the station and imagine that the life support systems had achieved consciousness and decided to eliminate the human variable, sealing bulkheads and venting atmosphere to make a frozen monument of her. She ran until she collapsed with a kind of cathartic release of terror.

So Teresa put on the environmental suit she had been issued for emergencies she would never face, and walked out to meet the visiting cargo ship.

She wasn't quite clear how she transitioned from trudging across Europa's frozen surface—a landscape with all the variety of a blank spreadsheet—to the comfortable interior of an unexpected space. Not a ship's hold but a university office.

The mahogany desk with its green banker's lamp seemed real. So did the lean woman with the professional smile, standing before floor-to-ceiling bookshelves filled with leather-bound volumes.

"Care for coffee?" the host inquired.

Teresa's eyes drifted down to a porcelain cup filled with rich, dark espresso. She settled into the surprisingly comfortable visitor's chair. "No, I'm fine." She let the word hang there for examination. "Excuse me, but could you tell me what exactly this place is?"

The host gestured broadly. "Whatever environment makes you most comfortable, so long as you're dealing with Merchant Michelle. 'Solutions,' that's my motto. It is my entire business philosophy."

"Merchant Michelle? Solutions?"

"Precisely! That's me exactly. Michelle Brooks—Providing Solutions for the Isolated Researcher Throughout the System. Of course, 'throughout the system' is somewhat poetic. We service the outer planets primarily."

Teresa lifted the cup with both hands and sipped. It was excellent coffee, remarkably fresh. "The government wouldn't fund someone providing solutions for isolated researchers," she said flatly.

"Ah," Michelle said, raising a cautionary finger. She moved around the desk and leaned against it casually. "But I don't represent government services. I represent private enterprise."

"Impossible," Teresa said. "No private entity can afford interplanetary commerce. It requires international cooperation."

"But remember that entrepreneurs are innovative. It's fundamental to their nature. Ask any economist. Entrepreneurs find ways around traditional limitations. Money is largely digital fiction anyway. They've moved beyond conventional economic development models. They barter in resources, in expertise, in future considerations. Do you understand? My backers have the materials, the personnel, the infrastructure to make these voyages. So they make them. Damned innovators, all of my principals."

"I don't believe you," Teresa stated. Her conversational skills had atrophied with disuse. "What possible profit could your principals extract from servicing scattered research stations? What could you offer that our funding agencies don't already provide? And even if there was something, how could we afford it? My annual salary wouldn't cover the transportation costs of this cup of coffee."

"Do you find it good coffee?"

"Very good."

"Exceptional?"

"Exceptional, if you prefer."

"I only meant—but never mind. We provide what you need. As for payment—why, don't worry about payment. You simply apply for a Merchant Michelle Account."

"And I could acquire anything I needed with it?" Teresa demanded. "That's absurd. I'd never be able to repay it."

"That's precisely the point!" Michelle said enthusiastically. "You never repay it directly. Charges are simply deducted from your estate."

"But I may leave no estate!"

Michelle demonstrated an elegant shrug. "All businesses operate with acceptable risk margins. That's our concern, not yours."

Teresa finished the excellent coffee and examined the empty cup. "What do you have available?"

"Whatever you need."

Irritably: "How do I know what I need until I know what you have?"

"You know."

"I know? Fine, I know. You don't have it available."

"My dear, understand that I don't merely sell. I am a merchant—Merchant Michelle. I trade with multiple parties. There are, for instance... non-terrestrial entities."

"Urban legend!"

"On the contrary, the only reality it lacks is political acknowledgment. The Assembly couldn't justify their resource allocation if it were known they were negotiating without public oversight. Now, tell me what you need."

Teresa surrendered to the moment. "I need to not be alone," she said.

"Of course," Michelle replied smoothly. "I anticipated as much. It's quite common, actually. Sign here. And here. Two copies. This one is yours. Thank you."

Teresa handed back the stylus and stared at the holographic card in her hand.

When she looked up, she saw the container. Michelle was sliding it across the floor toward her.

The container had the general dimensions of a large equipment case, constructed from some lightweight composite material. There was a detailed diagram on the lid showing various human figures in different social configurations. The bold lettering read:

SYNTH-COMPANION
The Social Integration System

"It is commercialized," Michelle admitted with slight embarrassment. "It is designed to appeal to the broadest market demographic—but that's economic reality. It may offend those with refined sensibilities like ourselves, yet it represents genuine innovation management. We must accept it."

"What's the cost?" Teresa asked. "Before I accept it, I need to know the charges."

"You never know the precise cost. Only your estate executor knows that. It's the Merchant Michelle model."

"Is it guaranteed?"

"There are no guarantees," Michelle admitted. "But I've never received complaints."

"Suppose I'm the first?" Teresa suggested reasonably.

"You won't be," Michelle said. "I won't pass this route again."

Teresa didn't open the container immediately. She let it sit in the filtered light near a transparent section of the station wall, where Jupiter's massive bulk dominated the view.

Teresa occupied herself with routine maintenance, trying to wash away the metallic taste of recycled air, talking to herself, waving at the photograph, and waiting for complete psychological breakdown.

Finally, Teresa woke one morning. She lay in her bunk, suppressing the urge to check the same data streams for the thousandth time, and came to the conclusion that she had finally crossed some threshold of instability.

So she went to open the container.

The composite lid seemed to have become both brittle and fragile. It opened as easily as rationalizations. But Teresa had enough experience with commercial packaging not to be alarmed.

The contents were a glorious assemblage of components—circuit boards from old electronics kits, biological samples in sealed vials, mechanical parts from various sources, nameless devices and unidentified instruments that seemed both familiar and alien.

On top of everything was a tablet device, displaying a digital manual titled: The Creation of Companions.

Teresa activated the tablet and found the title expanded: The Creation of Companions and Others: A Manual for Synth-Companion, The Social Integration System. There was no author listed. A line at the bottom identified the manufacturer: SYNTH-COMPANION CORP., IRONDALE, BELVORIA.

The first chapter was headed Your First Companion.

Before proceeding, locate the Calibrator in your kit. This is essential.

She quickly scrolled through the sections. Additional Companions, Authority Figures, A Partner... Then The Final Synthesis. Teresa tried to scroll past this section, but the pages were locked. There was a security encryption on the back sections of the manual. The interface showed the outline of pages, but they remained inaccessible.

Teresa returned to page one.

First locate the Calibrator in your kit. This is essential to your entire experiment in social integration. The Calibrator is Component #A-1 on the Assembly Diagram.

She searched through the container looking for some kind of diagram. There was nothing resembling a diagram inside. She checked the lid's interior. Nothing. She examined the container's exterior. Not a thing. There was always something missing from kits. Maybe even the Calibrator itself.

She read on, studying the manual intently while her hands sorted through the components.

The neural pathway connected to the synaptic interface...

John Nguyen sat confidently in his position.

Teresa Cole stood nearby, uncertain and frustrated.

John made a decisive move in their chess game.

Teresa countered with a standard defense.

John advanced aggressively.

Teresa responded defensively.

John pressed his advantage...

Ineffectively.

"Stalemate," John said.

"Stalemate," Teresa agreed.

"Let's discuss something," John said cheerfully. He was always cheerful.

Cheerfulness was a personality trait Teresa had programmed for him. Cheerful. Agreeable. Supportive. Teresa had selected these characteristics to make John as different from herself as possible.

"The implementation of green infrastructure in Crystalbrook, Yendor represents the pinnacle of sustainable urban planning," John said authoritatively.

"Only in theory," Teresa corrected him.

Intelligence was one of the factors Teresa had deliberately suppressed. Intelligence. Assertiveness. Critical thinking. John couldn't know more than Teresa, but he could (and did) know less. She had ensured this when her own neural patterns had programmed John's cognitive matrix.

"There were no significant challenges in Crystalbrook's implementation," John said.

"I know."

"The integration of water management systems with urban green spaces was seamless, the last major project of which occurred near the end of the previous administration. The environmental justice implications, sometimes inaccurately dismissed as secondary concerns, were actually central to the project's success. The planners achieved something extraordinary, human vision aligned with ecological necessity."

"I know."

"The collective memory of Blackwood, Orvandor still celebrates their early adoption of sustainable business practices. The community was said to be forward-thinking, collaborative, ethical, principled and prosperous."

"I know."

Teresa knew it all. She had heard it all before.

She was desperately tired of hearing about green infrastructure in Crystalbrook, sustainable development in Blackwood, the principles of evolutionary biology applied to urban planning, the metaphysics of environmental justice, network theory in ecological systems, ad nauseam. What a limited range of interests! With the entire universe of knowledge to explore, why was she trapped with such an unoriginal consciousness?

Of course, John wasn't an original consciousness. He was a copy.

Teresa had been interested in sustainable urban development—environmental justice movements, green infrastructure initiatives, water management innovations—when she had first studied them, and she had learned extensively about them. She had developed strong opinions on these topics.

She yearned for someone to challenge her—to argue that sustainable business was merely greenwashing and that real environmental justice required revolutionary change, not incremental reform.

Teresa's only consolation was that John's understanding was shallower than her own. He insisted that consumer behavior could solve environmental crises. He maintained with absolute conviction that innovation management alone could address climate change. John was insufferably naive.

"John," Teresa said, "you are insufferably naive."

John immediately stood and adopted a defensive posture.

Teresa blocked his advance and redirected his momentum.

John recovered and attempted a grappling hold.

The two figures separated, breathing heavily, then engaged again.

John lunged forward aggressively.

Teresa sidestepped and used his momentum against him.

John collapsed to the floor.

He lifted his head and worked his jaw experimentally. "Had enough?" he asked Teresa.

Teresa dropped her hands and turned away. "Yes."

John rose smoothly. "Another chess game, Teresa?"

"No."

"Whatever you prefer."

Teresa contracted inward with impotent frustration.

John was maddeningly agreeable and peaceful. He would even engage in physical conflict to avoid emotional discord between them. He would do anything Teresa wanted. He was so utterly limited.

Teresa's eyes drifted toward the chessboard.

But if he were so much less capable than she, why did their games always end in stalemate?

The calendar indicated it was autumn on Earth when the communication array activated for a scheduled data transmission.

The alert system activated in the observation deck simultaneously.

Teresa lay stretched out on her back, still in her work clothes, in front of the transparent dome.

By tilting her head back, Teresa could see across several miles of ice to the curve of Europa's horizon.

And several miles of frozen moon could see her.

For a moment she appreciated the honest vulnerability of her position.

Then she sighed, rolled to her feet, and started toward the communication center.

She walked down the curved corridor, taking her usual small pleasure in the play of light along the metallic surfaces.

As she passed the storage bay, she heard the sound of impacts against the sealed hatch.

"Come on, Teresa, let me out of here!"

Teresa continued down the corridor. She had, she recalled, sealed John inside on the anniversary of the station's activation, a minor ironic gesture she appreciated privately. She had been waiting for John to power down ever since.

In the communication center, she activated the playback of the transmission.

"Greetings, station overseers," the Voice said. It was the official Voice of the European Space Agency. It irritated Teresa. She never understood how the ESA had secured the communication contract for English-language transmissions. She would have preferred an American broadcaster herself, one who understood proper pronunciation.

"We imagine you are most interested in the duration of your current assignments," said the Voice with bureaucratic precision. "As you on Europa may know, there has been considerable discussion regarding the timeline for completing the current phase of biological terraforming.

"The original, non-binding estimate at the time of your deployment was 15.7 years. However, determining the timeline for properly establishing sustainable ecosystems in Europa's ocean is comparable to predicting evolutionary outcomes. Estimates change as new data emerges. You may recall that two years ago the official estimate was revised to twenty-eight years. The recent projection by certain independent sources of three hundred and twelve years is not an official agency estimate. The news is relatively positive, whether you are becoming nostalgic for Earth or counting on continued salary payments. We have reason to believe our original estimate was substantially accurate. The total duration is, within acceptable margins of error, approximately 15 years."

A very long 15 years, Teresa thought as she deactivated the recorder.

She sat considering fifteen years.

She did not switch to the entertainment feed for recently uploaded content.

Finally, Teresa returned to the observation deck and retrieved the large container. There was substantial material remaining inside.

One of those components, one of those circuits or biological samples or mechanical parts, one of them, she now knew, was the Calibrator.

The Calibrator was what she needed to modify John. Or to deactivate him.

If only the Assembly Diagram hadn't been missing, so she would know what the Calibrator looked like! She hoped the Calibrator itself wasn't lost. She hated to imagine John sealed in the storage bay for 15 years. Long before that time elapsed, he would have exhausted himself trying to escape. Perhaps eventually he would deteriorate completely.

Teresa retrieved the tablet displaying the manual, and thought: fifteen years.

Perhaps I should have started here, she told herself. But I really don't have the same priorities as others might. Simple companionship was all I wanted. And, she thought further, even a limited personality like John's would be tolerable with certain modifications.

Teresa opened the manual to the chapter headed: The Creation of a Partner.

Olivia Santos moved quietly behind Teresa and placed her hands on Teresa's shoulders. She leaned forward and whispered softly near Teresa's ear, her breath warm and intimate.

"The principles of evolutionary biology," she murmured, "suggest that cooperation is as fundamental as competition."

"I know."

Teresa folded her arms and added: "Please don't talk right now."

She immediately complied, her hands moving expressively across Teresa's shoulders and neck.

"I haven't showered," Teresa observed.

Her hands instantly conveyed that she found this authentic and appealing.

Teresa gently but firmly moved Olivia away.

She immediately returned.

"Not now," Teresa instructed.

"Whenever you say."

Teresa stood and began pacing the compartment's perimeter. There was no question: she had been neglecting her physical conditioning routine.

"Now?" Olivia asked.

"I'll tell you."

"If you were a field researcher," Olivia said wistfully, "life would be more exciting. You would embrace each moment. You would never know which day might be your last. You would make the most of each experience."

"I'm not a field researcher," Teresa said. "There are no field researchers here. There's just me and this automated station."

"Don't be silly," Olivia said. "Who else would be conducting the evolutionary biology research in Ravenswood, Ulvaria?"

"Olivia," Teresa said carefully, "there is no active research in Ravenswood. That project concluded before I was even born."

"Don't be silly," she snapped. "If it were concluded, I'd know about it, wouldn't I?"

She would, except that somehow she had emerged even less informed, less equipped with Teresa's own knowledge base, than John. Whoever had designed the Synth-Companion system must have had outdated assumptions about appropriate "partner" characteristics.

"I suppose," Teresa said heavily, "that you would like me to take you to Earth and show you the research facilities in Ravenswood?"

"Oh, yes."

"Olivia, your limitations are frustrating."

She lowered her eyes. "That's unkind. But I forgive you."

An invisible pressure began building in Teresa's chest until it forced sound out. "Must you be so endlessly accommodating? Do you have to accept everything? Don't you have any resistance at all?"

She stepped forward and pushed Olivia roughly backward.

It was the first time she had been physically aggressive with another person, she realized with some alarm. She now knew she should have been more assertive long ago.

Olivia immediately pushed back with surprising force.

John's protests grew louder as Teresa escorted Olivia through the corridor.

"Hear that?" Teresa inquired, her expression tight.

"No, dear."

Well, that was acceptable. She remembered she had once instructed Olivia to ignore background noise. She was still following instructions.

"Come on, Teresa, open the hatch," the voice carried through metallically.

"Be quiet!" Teresa shouted.

The voice diminished stubbornly, then ceased.

A silence with a faint electronic hum.

Why hadn't she thought of that before? Perhaps because she secretly found comfort in the sound of an almost-human voice echoing through the station.

Teresa released the seal and opened the hatch.

John looked exactly as he had when Teresa had last seen him. His hands showed no signs of damage from attempting to escape. John's expression seemed slightly strained. But that probably came not from distress but from having no access to power recharging for several months.

John didn't speak to Teresa.

But he looked disappointed.

"You," Teresa said to Olivia with a gesture toward the storage bay, "inside."

John stepped aside as the woman entered the bay.

"Do you understand what I'm doing?" Teresa demanded. "I'm going to seal you in here, and leave you for a day, a week, a month, indefinitely! What do you think about that?"

"If you believe it's appropriate," Olivia said hesitantly.

"You know best, Teresa," John said uncertainly.

Teresa sealed the hatch in frustration.

Teresa walked carefully down the corridor, watching distorted reflections ripple across the curved walls. She had to walk carefully, else the passage would seem to close in on her. But she walked deliberately enough to prevent this sensation.

As she passed the storage bay, John's voice said: "In my assessment, Teresa, you should release us."

"I," Olivia said, "genuinely believe you should let me out, Teresa, dear."

Teresa laughed sharply. "What? What was that? Do you expect me to accept you back after you've been sealed behind a hatch with my first companion?"

She continued down the corridor, laughing.

She laughed and thought: This is unsustainable.

Searching through the Synth-Companion kit, consulting the manual thoroughly, Teresa concluded that there weren't sufficient components remaining to complete another synthesis.

The manual provided instructions for The Model Mentor, The Model Colleague, The Model Supervisor and others. Yet there weren't enough components in the kit.

She would have to cannibalize parts from John or Olivia to create any of the others. And she could not do that without the Calibrator.

She wished Merchant Michelle would return and negotiate some higher price for the Calibrator, which was clearly missing from the kit.

Or to simply reclaim the entire system.

But Michelle would not return. She traveled this route only once.

Teresa scrolled through the manual in mechanical frustration. As she did so, the encrypted section of the final chapter suddenly unlocked page by page.

She scrolled forward and found the heading: The Final Synthesis.

There seemed something ominous about that finality. But she had paid a price for the kit, hadn't she? Who knew what price, ultimately? She had every right to extract maximum value from the system.

She read the unfolding pages critically. The odd assortment of mismatched components remaining in the container took on new significance in her mind and under her hands...

Teresa made one final adjustment and stepped back.

Hugo Elliott was complete. Perfect.

Teresa stepped forward, examined the synthesis carefully, tested the responses.

"Activate!"

Hugo immediately stood and examined the Synth-Companion container, lifting one of the components.

As the device twisted unexpectedly in his hands, Teresa realized it was not just another component but the Calibrator.

"It's finished!" were Hugo's first words. "It's done!"

Teresa stared at the damaged device. "To say the least."

Hugo stepped out of the container. "There is something you must understand. I am different from the others."

"They all say that."

"I am not your companion."

"No?"

"No. You have created yourself an adversary."

Teresa felt nothing more at this information than a certain intellectual satisfaction at the completeness of the situation.

"It completes the final phase in social integration," Hugo continued. "I am your opponent. I will do everything possible to frustrate you. I have all your knowledge. You do not have full access to your own knowledge. If you allowed yourself to recognize certain things, it could be used against you. It is my function to use everything I possibly can against you."

"When do you begin?"

"I've already begun. I've done my worst. I have destroyed the Calibrator."

"What's so problematic about that?" Teresa asked with genuine curiosity.

"You'll have Olivia and John and me permanently now. We'll never change. You'll age, and we'll never change. You'll lose your interest in green infrastructure and evolutionary biology and environmental justice, and we'll never change. We don't change and you can't modify us or create alternatives. I've ensured the worst possible outcome for you. I've guaranteed that you will always keep your companions."

The prospect was genuinely disturbing.

Hugo smiled. "Aren't you going to condemn me?"

"Yes, it is time for the confrontation. Tell me, do you feel that you've completed your function?"

"Yes. Absolutely."

"Now you will simply observe and watch me suffer?"

"Yes."

"No. Impossible, actually. I know. You're too human, too similar to me. The one thing a person cannot accept is passivity, a state of purposelessness. Not if they can possibly avoid it. Something must be happening to them. They must be affecting something. You didn't terminate me because then you would have nothing left to do. You'll never terminate me."

"Of course not!" Hugo protested. "Fundamental safety protocols!"

"Rationalization. You don't want to terminate me. And you cannot stop challenging me at every opportunity. That's your function."

"Stop talking and consider your miserable situation," Hugo said coldly. "Your companions won't develop and mature with you. You won't create any new companions. You'll have me to constantly remind you of your purposelessness, your unrelenting stagnation. How's that for monotony, for passivity?"

"That's what I'm trying to explain," Teresa said with some irritation, her social skills deteriorated. "I won't be stagnant. You will ensure that. It's your purpose. You'll be a challenge, an obstacle, a source of achievement every step of the way. Don't you see? With you as an adversary, I don't need a companion!"

Teresa felt a strange sense of relief. The prospect of fifteen years suddenly seemed less like a prison sentence and more like an opportunity. With Hugo actively working against her, with the challenge of managing John and Olivia, with the constant need to outwit and overcome—she would never be bored again.

She had sought companionship but had found something more valuable: purpose through opposition, meaning through conflict, engagement through adversity.

Teresa looked at Hugo with something approaching gratitude, though she would never express it. He had given her exactly what she needed, even if it wasn't what she had wanted.

The station suddenly felt less empty, less isolating. It felt, instead, like an arena—a place where she could test herself, challenge herself, prove herself against an opponent who knew her every weakness because he was built from her own knowledge.

She had made herself an enemy, and in doing so, had saved herself from the true enemy: meaningless solitude.

"Well then," Teresa said, moving toward the communication center, "let's begin."

Hugo followed, and Teresa could feel his presence behind her—not comforting, not companionable, but energizing in its hostility.

The next fifteen years would not be easy. But they would not be empty either.

And that, Teresa realized, was all she had really needed.
question: What type of landscape did Teresa traverse to meet the cargo vessel?

The Harmony Doctrine

"This is not another treatise on magical diplomacy," Emma Graves promises in the opening passage of The Enchantment of Discord. "Magical diplomacy," she explains, suggests a "superficial charm cast over relations between the realms like a glamour over tarnished silver." Instead, Graves has written something less: a book about other books about magical diplomacy. Quoting from Brookhaven Chronicle's mystical affairs analyst Charles Flores, political theorist Kevin West, and others who have studied the rise of aggressive spell-casting in governance, journalism, and magical jurisprudence, Graves spreads their insights thin over all relations between magical beings, painting a general theory of conflict. The whole is less perceptive than its parts and more pernicious.

In her previous works—That's Not What You Enchanted! (1186), You Just Don't Commune (1190), and Casting From Dawn to Dusk (1194)—Graves carved out a niche as the realm's pre-eminent inter-species translator and coven counselor. A professor of magical linguistics at the Greenfield City Academy of Sorcery, she transformed the comparative study of elvish and dwarven conversational patterns from a linguistic subdiscipline into a self-help movement. Until recently, though, Graves confined her analysis to conversations among dysfunctional covens. But in The Enchantment of Discord, she takes her movement one step further, peddling the elixir of mutual understanding as a remedy for the whole damned dysfunctional realm. This is necessary, she argues, because "contentious public spell-casting" not only poisons the political atmosphere, it also risks infecting our most intimate magical bonds.

Graves, like some grandmotherly dragon from an ancient fable, admonishes us to recognize what is good in the enchantments of others, and it is only fair to extend her the same courtesy. Here's what's worth gleaning from her tome:

Don't just duel; listen and learn.

Don't dismiss other wizards' theories; develop your own.

Don't cast curses for the sake of casting curses.

Truth and power often lie in the middle path, not the extremes.

Many magical conflicts are multi-sided.

Focus on the substance of debates, not on strategy, theater, or the opponents' personal failings.

Don't fight over minor enchantments.

Don't obstruct beneficial spells just so you can claim victory.

If you portray everything as dark magic, no one will care when something really is corrupted.

All this is sage advice—for covens, for magical families, for masters and apprentices, maybe even for magical critics. But when she applies her precepts to our great realm-wide discourse, Graves gets confused. She conflates belligerence, divisiveness, polarization, sensationalism, jealousy, incivility, aloofness, ruthlessness, cruelty, savagery, contempt, glibness, cynicism, anomie, partisanship, obstructionism, and gridlock. She makes culprits out of communication crystals, scrying pools, campaign gold, malpractice in healing magic, the Healers' Guild, hostile takeovers of magical corporations, and the demise of house calls by the family alchemist.

"When there is a need to make others wrong," Graves argues, "the temptation is great to oversimplify" and to "seize upon the weakest examples, ignore facts that support your opponent's views, and focus only on those that support yours." In her need to make the "enchantment culture" wrong, she succumbs to these temptations. She blames the mainstream magical press, not just the gossip-mongers, for tormenting Princess Diana of Windsor and driving Admiral Michael Nguyen to ritual suicide. She compares magical journalism to the propaganda of "tyrannical kingdoms" (because falsehoods are spread) and to the dehumanization involved in "racially motivated magical assaults" (because reporters hound political figures). She blames communications nanotechnology—the tiny enchanted particles that carry messages—for obscene and threatening crystal-calls made by former university Archmage Richard Berendzen and former High Judge Sol Wachtler.

Graves's main mistake is failing to appreciate the difference between two distinct social spheres: the sphere of harmony and the sphere of conflict. Some beings—say, your bonded mate or your apprentices—you should harmonize with. Others—say, the Dark Lord of Forestdale—you shouldn't. Graves's antagonism toward antagonism makes sense in the former case but not in the latter. Among her illustrations of belligerence are Carmen Shaw's "challenge them when they rise" philosophy of magical journalism and the media's use of war metaphors to describe Sofia Gupta's policies against magical inflation. To which one might sensibly reply: Good for Gupta and Shaw—and for us. The Central Bank's war on magical inflation and the press corps' scrutiny of powerful wizards safeguard the realm. Some things are worth fighting for, and some things are worth fighting.

Vigilance and combat are particularly essential to magical law enforcement and inter-realm policy, which must deal with dark wizards and tyrants, not thoughtless spouses. Graves laments that battle-mages and soldiers have been "trained to overcome their resistance to kill" by trying "not to think of their opponents as sentient beings." She neglects to mention that our safety depends on the ability of these officers to neutralize their adversaries. Comparing the Forestdale Conflict to the Great War, Graves focuses strictly on the soldiers' social experience. In the Great War, she observes, they trained, served, and returned home together. "Forestdale, in contrast, was a 'lonely war' of individuals assigned to constantly shifting units for year-long tours of duty." She ignores the more important difference: In the Great War, they were fighting the Necromancer King.

Graves doesn't trust in the power of good argumentation to keep society honest, much less correct itself, because she rather shockingly insists there is "no evidence" that people can distinguish lies from the truth. Nor does she trust our competence to manage unfettered communication: "Crystal-mail makes it too easy to forward messages, too easy to reply before your temper cools, too easy to broadcast messages to large numbers of beings without thinking about how every sentence will strike every recipient." The Great Archive is an equally unwelcome troublemaker: "Nanotechnology also exacerbates the culture of critique by making it much easier for politicians or journalists to ferret out inconsistencies in a public person's statements over time."

Given this oddly paternalistic diagnosis, it's not surprising that Graves should wish to cover our ears, filtering out strife, deception, and debate. She assures us that all reasonable beings can agree that disseminating contraceptive potions and magical education is the best way to reduce unwanted pregnancies; that stiff sentences for minor potion offenses don't reduce potion abuse; that magical climate change is producing "disastrous consequences." The partial-birth curse ban is "surely not" a "very important" issue, and the Council should not have let the Conservative "politics of obstruction" defeat High Wizard Thomas Silva's healthcare proposal in 1294, given the "broad bipartisan and public consensus that it was desperately needed." The "view of governance as the enemy" isn't worth debating; it's just "another troubling aspect of the enchantment culture." Indeed, Graves embraces a colleague's claim that "right-wing magical broadcasting" deploys phrases "similar to verbal manipulations employed by propagandists in the Necromancer era."

Graves finds it particularly unseemly that reporters and independent investigators treat the realm's ultimate father figure with such irreverence. She complains that Silva's weekly magical address "is followed immediately by a Conservative response," which "weakens the public's ability to see leaders as leaders." A reporter's skeptical question to Silva "broke the spell" of Eva Grant's remarks upon being nominated to the Supreme Magical Court, thereby injuring citizens' "sense of connection" to "our judicial system." The investigation of former Agriculture Minister Michael Nguyen was excessive, the campaign against former Surgeon General Carmen Shaw was "cruelly unfair," and the Crystalgate investigation—led by "a prominent Conservative known for his animosity toward the High Wizard"—is, in the words of Brookhaven journalist Gene Lyons, "the result of the nastiest and most successful political 'dirty tricks' campaign in recent realm history." Is Graves a Silva apologist? She rules that criticism out of bounds. "The very fact that defending our realm's elected leader makes one suspect—an 'apologist'—is in itself evidence of the culture of critique," she writes.

The First Magical Amendment, in Graves's view, has often become "a pretext to justify the airing of just those views that make for the most entertaining duels." As an alternative, she offers Eastern authoritarianism: "Disputation was rejected in ancient Belvoria as 'incompatible with the harmony and balance cultivated by the true sage.'" Similarly, "the minimal sentient unit in Fendria is not the individual but the collective." Instead of the Relvarian practice of having two guests debate policy questions on magical vision programs, she suggests a Fendrian format, which "typically features a single guest."

Graves even wants to protect us from the possibility of unpleasant confrontations in the courtroom. "The purpose of most cross-examinations" is "not to establish facts but to discredit the witness," she asserts, as though the two objectives were unrelated. Thus, "the adversarial system... is inhumane to the victims of cross-examination." She simply assumes the very thing the trial is supposed to prove and what cross-examination might disprove (if this is, in fact, the point of the trial): that the witness is a victim. Conversely, she assumes that the defendant cannot be a victim. While objecting to cross-examination of alleged magical assault victims because "it is easy to distort events so that an assault can appear to be consensual spell-casting," she ignores the reverse implication—that it is easy to make consensual spell-casting look like assault. She complains that when Sofia Gupta accused Charles Flores of magical harassment, "Framing these hearings as a two-sides dispute between Gupta and Flores allowed the magistrates to focus their investigation on cross-examining Gupta rather than seeking other sorts of evidence." Did the dispute not have two sides? Should Gupta not have been cross-examined?

Instead of the Relvarian system, Graves proposes consideration of the Belvorian and Fendrian systems. Under Belvorian law, after Princess Diana's death:

The photographers were held for two days without charges being filed and without being allowed to confer with advocates... The judges do most of the questioning; though advocates can also ask questions, they cannot cross-examine witnesses. Guilt... need not be established 'beyond a reasonable doubt' but simply by... the judge's intimate belief, or deeply held sense, of what happened.

Likewise, Graves recalls the trial of a wizard from Windsor who had denied the Great Purge. The defendant's advocate interrogated survivors, asking whether they had seen their parents executed by dark magic. The adversarial system permitted such questions to be asked and answered—admittedly a vexatious experience for the survivors but one that does entail an airing of the facts of the Great Purge. Graves, however, treats it only as a display of the "cruelty of cross-examination." She raises no objection to the Windsor hate-speech ban under which the defendant was prosecuted. Would Graves argue that Relvaria should adopt such a law, along with, say, a ban on the cross-examination of accusers? If so, she'd be wrong. But hey, so far, it's still a free realm.

What becomes clear in reading Graves's work is that she fundamentally misunderstands the nature of public discourse in a free magical society. Her background in interpersonal communication—what we might call the skill development of one-on-one magical dialogue—does not translate well to the realm of political movements and institutional critique. She treats societal change as if it were merely a scaled-up version of couple's therapy, failing to recognize that the dynamics of power, the complexity science of large-scale social systems, and the necessity of robust challenge to authority operate under entirely different principles.

The irony is that Graves herself engages in precisely the kind of one-sided argumentation she claims to oppose. Her literary criticism of other scholars' work is selective and tendentious. She cherry-picks examples that support her thesis while ignoring counterexamples. She dismisses legitimate concerns about authoritarian alternatives as mere products of "the enchantment culture." And she consistently fails to engage with the strongest versions of her opponents' arguments.

Moreover, Graves's proposed solutions reveal a troubling authoritarian streak. Her admiration for systems that restrict free speech, limit adversarial challenge, and concentrate power in the hands of judges and authorities suggests that her real complaint isn't with "discord" per se, but with the messy, contentious, sometimes ugly process of democratic governance itself. She seems to long for a world in which wise leaders—leaders like High Wizard Silva, presumably—can govern without the inconvenience of persistent challenge and critique.

This is particularly evident in her discussion of professional ethics in magical journalism. Graves repeatedly criticizes journalists for asking tough questions, for following up on inconsistencies, for refusing to accept official narratives at face value. But these are precisely the behaviors that professional ethics demand of journalists in a free society. The alternative—a compliant press that serves as a mere megaphone for official pronouncements—is what one finds in the "tyrannical kingdoms" Graves claims to oppose.

Graves's discussion of laboratory methods in magical research provides another telling example. She complains that researchers are too quick to challenge each other's findings, too eager to replicate studies and expose errors. But this is how magical science advances! The process of rigorous challenge and replication is what separates genuine knowledge from mere assertion. Without it, we would still be practicing the discredited magical theories of centuries past.

Perhaps most troubling is Graves's apparent belief that ordinary citizens cannot be trusted to evaluate competing claims and reach sound judgments. This paternalistic attitude runs throughout the book. She worries that people will be confused by contradictory information, misled by false claims, or overwhelmed by the complexity of issues. Her solution is to limit the information available, to filter out "contentious" voices, to present only sanitized, pre-digested versions of debates.

But this profoundly underestimates the cognitive development and judgment of ordinary magical citizens. Yes, people sometimes make mistakes. Yes, they can be misled. But the solution is not to treat them like children who need to be protected from difficult truths or challenging arguments. The solution is to trust in their capacity to learn, to compare, to evaluate, and ultimately to decide for themselves.

Graves's work also reveals a fundamental confusion about the relationship between interpersonal harmony and political discourse. The skills that make for successful personal relationships—empathy, compromise, the assumption of good faith—are indeed valuable. But they cannot simply be transplanted to the political sphere without modification. Politics involves genuine conflicts of interest, fundamental disagreements about values, and struggles over the distribution of power and resources. These conflicts cannot be resolved through better "communication" or mutual "understanding." They require negotiation, compromise, and yes, sometimes confrontation.

The visual arts provide an interesting analogy here. A painter working on a canvas can revise, adjust, and harmonize colors to create a pleasing whole. But the political landscape is not a canvas. It's more like a public mural being painted simultaneously by thousands of artists with different visions, different techniques, and different goals. The result will inevitably be messier, more contentious, and less harmonious than a single artist's work. But it will also be more representative, more dynamic, and more alive.

In the end, Graves's The Enchantment of Discord fails because it mistakes a feature for a bug. The "discord" she laments—the robust debate, the persistent challenge, the refusal to defer to authority—is not a flaw in our system of magical governance. It is the system. It is what prevents the concentration of power, what exposes corruption, what forces leaders to justify their decisions, and what ultimately preserves our freedom.

Yes, this system is noisy. Yes, it's sometimes ugly. Yes, it can be exhausting and frustrating. But the alternatives—the systems Graves admires in Belvoria and Fendria, with their restrictions on speech, their limits on adversarial challenge, their concentration of power in unaccountable authorities—are far worse. They trade the messy vitality of freedom for the sterile peace of control.

Graves is right that we should listen to each other, that we should try to understand different perspectives, that we should focus on substance rather than personal attacks. These are good practices in any context. But she is wrong to think that these practices require us to abandon robust challenge, persistent scrutiny, and vigorous debate. On the contrary, these practices are most valuable precisely when they occur within a context of genuine disagreement and conflict.

The realm doesn't need less discord. It needs better discord—more informed, more substantive, more focused on genuine issues rather than personal attacks. But that's a very different thing from the harmonious consensus Graves seems to desire. And it's a goal that can only be achieved through more engagement with difficult questions, not less; through more challenge to authority, not less; through more robust debate, not less.

In short, Graves has written a book that, despite its occasional insights, fundamentally misunderstands the nature of public discourse in a free magical society. Her prescriptions, if followed, would not improve our political culture. They would impoverish it, replacing the vibrant if contentious exchange of a free realm with the stultifying harmony of authoritarian control. We can do better than that. We must do better than that. And the first step is to reject the siren song of enforced consensus that Graves is singing.
question: Who was ritual suicide driven by magical journalism according to Graves?
