THE RUINS OF COPPERFIELD

By DEAN EVANS

Every child should be able to hum a tune, except, of course, the Venusian settlers. But this one did!

She seemed a very small girl to be carrying so large a geological sample kit. She swung it in her thin left hand as she walked, and at first glance you couldn't be sure if she were carrying it, or it carrying her.

She came humming. All children hum. To children, humming is as natural as breathing. However, there was something peculiar about this particular child's humming. Or, rather, there were two things peculiar, but each was related to the other.

The first was that she was a Venusian settler child. You could be very sure of that, for Earth children have attached earlobes while Venusian settler children do not—and she most certainly didn't.

The second was the tune she hummed—a somehow familiar tune, but one which I should have thought not very appealing to a child.

"Hi, there," I said when she came near enough. "What's that you're humming?"

She stopped humming and she stopped walking, both at the same time, as though she had pulled a switch or turned a tap that shut them off. Then she lifted her small head and stared up into my eyes.

"'Clair de Lune'," she said in a soft, child's voice.

"The what?" I asked.

"From Debussy's Suite Bergamasque," she explained, still looking up at me. She said it deadpan, and her wide gray eyes never once batted.

"Oh," I said. "And where did you learn that?"

"My father taught me."

I blinked at her. She didn't blink back. Her round little face still held no expression, but if it had, I knew it would have matched the serene quality of the tune she hummed.

"You hum very well," I told her.

That pleased her. Her eyes lit up and an almost-smile flirted with the corners of her small mouth.

She nodded grave agreement.

"Been collecting rock samples, I see. I'll bet you didn't find any good ones. This is the wrong geological layer."

The light in her eyes snapped off. "Well, good-by," she said abruptly and very relevantly.

"Good-by," I said.

Her humming and her walking started up again in the same spot where they had left off. I mean the note she resumed on was the note which followed the one interrupted; and the step she took was with the left foot, which was the one she would have used if I hadn't stopped her.

I followed her with my eyes. An unusual little girl. A most precisely mechanical little girl.

When she was almost out of sight, I took off after her, wondering.

The dwelling she went into was over in that crumbling section which forms a curving boundary line, marking the limits of those frantic and ugly original excavation sites made many years ago by the early colonists in Copperfield, Veldoria. It seems that someone had told someone who had told someone else that here, a mere fifty feet beneath the surface, was a deposit as wide as a warehouse and as long as a politician's promise, of pure—pure, mind you—platinum.

Back in those days, to be a colonist meant to be a rugged individual. And to be a rugged individual meant to not give a damn one way or another. And to not give a damn one way or another meant to make one hell of a mess on the pristine landscape of Venus.

There had not been any platinum found, of course, and now, for the most part, the mining structures so hastily thrown up were only fever scars of a sickness long gone and little remembered. A few of the dwellings were still occupied, like the one into which the Venusian child had just disappeared.

So her father had taught her Debussy's "Clair de Lune," had he? That tickling thought made me chuckle as I stood before the ramshackle building. And then, suddenly, I stopped chuckling and began to think, instead, of something quite astonishing:

How had it been possible for him to teach, and for her to hum? All Venusian settlers are as tone-deaf as a bucket of lead.

I went up three composite steps and rapped loudly on the weather-beaten door.

The man who faced me may have been as young as twenty-five, but he didn't look it. That shocked look, which comes with the first realization that youth has slipped quietly away downstream in the middle of the night, and left nothing but frightening rocks of middle age to show cold and gray in the hard light of dawn, was like the validation stamp of Time itself in his wide, weary eyes. And his voice wasn't young any more, either.

"Well? And what did I do now?"

"I beg your pardon?" I said.

"You're Colonial Security, aren't you? Or is that badge you're wearing just something to cover a hole in your shirt?"

"Yes, I'm Security, but does it have to mean something?" I asked. "All I did was knock on your door."

"I heard it." His lips were curled slightly at one corner.

I worked up a smile for him and let him see it for a few seconds before I answered: "As a matter of fact, I don't want to see you at all. I didn't know you lived here and I don't know who you are. I'm not even interested in who you are. It's the little girl who just went in here that I was interested in. The little Venusian settler girl, I mean."

His eyes spread as though somebody had put fingers on his lids at the outside corners and then cruelly jerked them apart.

"Come in," he almost gasped.

I followed him. When I leaned back against the plain door, it closed protestingly. I looked around. It wasn't much of a room, but then you couldn't expect much of a room in a little ghost of a place like this. A few artifacts of the locality stood about on two tables and a shelf, bits of rock with streak-veins of compressed silicate; not bad if you like the appearance of frozen lightning.

There were two chairs and a large table intended to match the chairs, and a rough couch kind of thing made of discarded shipping containers which had probably been hauled here from the International Spaceport at Ashford City, thirty kilometers to the east. In the back wall of the room was a doorway that led dimly to somewhere else in the dwelling. Nowhere did I see the little girl. I looked once again at the man.

"What about her?" he whispered.

His eyes were still startled.

I smiled reassuringly. "Nothing, friend, nothing. I'm sorry I upset you. I was just being nosy is all, and that's the truth of it. You see, the little girl went by me a while ago and she was humming. She hums remarkably well. I asked her what the name of the tune was and she told me it was 'Clair de Lune' from Debussy. She also told me her father had taught her."

His eyes hadn't budged from mine, hadn't flickered. They might have been bright, moist marbles glued above his cheeks.

He said one word only: "Well?"

"Nothing," I answered. "Except that Venusian settlers are supposed to be tone-deaf, aren't they? It's something lacking in their auditory processing. So when I heard this little girl, and saw she was a Venusian settler, and when she told me her father had taught her—" I shrugged and laughed a little. "Like I said before, I guess I got just plain nosy."

He nodded. "We agree on that last part."

Perhaps it was his eyes. Or perhaps it was the tone of his voice. Or perhaps, and more simply, it was his attitude in general. But whatever it was, I suddenly felt that, nosy or not, I was being treated shabbily.

"I would like to speak to the Venusian settler man," I said.

"There isn't any Venusian settler man."

"There has to be, doesn't there?" I said it with little sharp prickers on the words.

But he did, too: "Does there?"

I gawked at him and he stared back. And the stare he gave me was hard and at the same time curiously defiant—as though he would dare me to go on with it. As though he figured I hadn't the guts.

For a moment, I just blinked stupidly at him, as I had blinked stupidly at the little girl when she told me her father had taught her how to hum. And then—after what seemed to me a very long while—I slowly tumbled to what he meant.

His eyes were telling me that the little Venusian settler girl wasn't a little Venusian settler girl at all, that she was cross-breed, a little child who had a Venusian settler mother and a human, Earthman father.

It was a startling thought, for there just aren't any such mixed families. Or at least I had thought there weren't. Physically, spiritually, mentally, or by any other standard you can think of, compared to a human female the Venusian settler woman isn't anything you'd want around the house—or so the common wisdom went.

I finally said: "So that is why she is able to hum."

He didn't answer. Even before I spoke, his eyes had seen the correct guess which had probably flashed naked and astounded in my own eyes. And then he swallowed with a labored breath that went trembling down inside him.

"There isn't anything to be ashamed of," I said gently. "Back on Earth there's a lot of mixtures, you know. Some people even claim there's no such thing as a pure race. Cultural exchange has been happening for millennia. I don't know, but I guess we all started somewhere and intermarried plenty since."

He nodded. Somehow his eyes didn't look defiant any more.

"Where's her mother?" I asked.

"S-she's dead."

"I'm sorry. Are you all right? I mean do you get along okay and everything, now that...?"

I stopped. I wanted to ask him if he was starving by slow degrees and needed help. Lord knows the careworn look about him didn't show it was luxurious living he was doing—at least not lately.

"Look," I said suddenly. "Would you like to go back to Earth? I could fix—"

But that was the wrong approach. His eyes snapped and his shoulders stiffened angrily and the words that ripped out of his mouth were not coated with honey.

"Get the hell out of here, you fool!"

I blinked again. When the flame in his eyes suddenly seemed to grow even hotter, I turned on my heel and went to the door. I opened it, went out on the top composite step. I turned back to close the door—and looked straight into his eyes.

He was crying, but that didn't mean exactly what it looked like it might mean. His right hand had the door edge gripped tightly and he was swinging it with all the strength he possessed. And while I still stared, the door slammed savagely into the casing with a shock that jarred the step under my feet, and flying splinters from the deteriorated material stung my flinching cheeks.

I shrugged and turned around and went down the steps. "And that is the way it goes," I muttered disgustedly to myself. Thinking to be helpful with community organizing, you offer assistance and they immediately reject it—violently.

I looked up just in time to avoid running into a spread-legged woman who was standing motionless directly in the middle of the gravel-path in front of the door. Her hands were on her hips and there was something in her eyes which might have been a leer.

"Pulled a howler in there, eh, friend?" she said. She chuckled hoarsely in her throat. "Not being exactly deaf, I heard the tail end of it." Her chuckle was a crude thing, a thing usually reserved—if it ever was reserved at all—for the back rooms of some of the lower class establishments. And then she stopped chuckling and frowned instead and said complainingly:

"Regular little hothead, ain't he? I ask you now, wouldn't you think a man which had got himself in a little jam, so to speak, would be more reasonable—"

Her words chopped short and she almost choked on the final unuttered syllable. Her glance had dropped to my badge and the look on her face was one of startled surprise.

"I—" she said.

I cocked a frown of my own at her.

"Well, so long, friend," she grunted, and spun around and dug her heels in the gravel and was away. I stood there staring at her rapidly disappearing form for a few moments and then looked back once more at the dwelling. A tattered synthetic curtain was just swinging to in the dirty, dust-blown window. That seemed to mean the man had been watching. I sighed, shrugged again and went away myself.

When I got back to Security Headquarters in Ashford City, I went to the file and began to rifle through pictures. I didn't find the man, but I did find the woman.

She was a killer named Ava Lucas.

I took the picture into the Chief's office and laid it on his desk, waited for him to look down at it and study it for an instant, and then to look back up to me. Which he did.

"So?" he said.

"Wanted, isn't she?"

He nodded. "But a lot of good that'll do. She's holed up somewhere back on Earth."

"No," I said. "She's right here. I just saw her."

"What?" He nearly leaped out of his chair.

"I didn't know who she was at first," I said. "It wasn't until I looked in the files—"

He cut me off. His hand darted into his desk drawer and pulled out an Authority Card. He shoved the card at me. He growled: "Kill or capture, I'm not especially fussy which. Just get her!"

I nodded and took the card. As I left the office, I was thinking of something which struck me as somewhat more than odd.

I had idly listened to a little half-breed Venusian settler girl humming part of Debussy's "Clair de Lune," and it had led me to a wanted killer named Ava Lucas.

Understandably, Ms. Lucas did not produce herself on a silver platter. I spent the remainder of the afternoon trying to get a lead on her and got nowhere. If she was hiding in any of the places I went to, then she was doing it with mirrors, for on Venus an Authority Card is the big stick than which there is no bigger. Not solely is it a warrant, it is a commandeer of help from anyone to whom it is presented; and wherever I showed it I got respect.

I got instant attention. I got even more: those wraithlike tremblings in the darker corners of bars, those corners where light never seems quite to penetrate. You don't look into those. Not if you're anything more than a ghoul, you don't.

Not finding her wasn't especially alarming. What was alarming, though, was not finding the Earthman and his little half-breed Venusian settler daughter when I went back to the tumbledown dwelling where they lived. It was empty. He had moved fast. He hadn't even left me a note saying good-by.

That night I went into the Elmwood Region to the Kahreen Reservation, where the Venusian settlers still try to act like Venusian settlers.

It was Festival night, and when I got there they were doing the dance to the three rings. At times like this you want to leave the Venusian settlers alone. With that thought in mind, I pinned my Authority Card to my lapel directly above my badge, and went through the gates.

The huge circle fire was burning and the dance was in progress. Briefly, this can be described as something like the ceremonial dances put on centuries ago by the ancient aborigines of the Pacific Islands. There was one important exception, however. Instead of a central fire, the Venusian settlers dig a huge circular trench and fill it with dried roots of the kelnu tree and set fire to it. Being resin-like, the gnarled fragments burn for hours. Inside this ring sit the spectators, and in the exact center are the dancers. For music, they use the drums.

The dancers were both men and women and they were as minimally clothed as Venusian settlers can get, but their dance was a thing of grace and loveliness. For an instant—before anyone observed me—I stood motionless and watched the sinuously undulating movements, and I thought, as I have often thought before, that this is the one thing the Venusian settlers can still do beautifully. Which, in a sad sort of way, is a commentary on the way things have gone since the first rocket-blasting ship set down on these misty plains.

I felt the blade dig my spine. Carefully I turned around and pointed my index finger to my badge and card. Bared teeth glittered at me in the flickering light, and then the blade disappeared as quickly as it had come.

"Valenhk," I said. "The Chief. Take me to her."

The Venusian settler turned, went away from the half-light of the circle. She led me some meters off to the north to a swooping-tent. Then she stopped, pointed.

"Valenhk," she said.

I watched her slip away.

Valenhk is an old Venusian settler. I don't think any Venusian settler before her has ever lived so long—and doubtless none after her will, either. Her leathery, almost gray-black skin was rough and had a weathered look about it, and up around the eyes were little plaits and folds that had the appearance of being done deliberately by a Venusian sand-artist.

"Good evening," I said, and sat down before her and crossed my legs.

She nodded slowly. Her old eyes went to my badge.

From there they went to the Authority Card.

"Power sign of the Earthmen," she muttered.

"Not necessarily," I said. "I'm not here for trouble. I know as well as you do that, before tonight is finished, more than half of your men and women will be intoxicated on illegal spirits."

She didn't reply to that.

"And I don't give a damn about it," I added distinctly.

Her eyes came deliberately up to mine and stopped there. She said nothing. She waited. Outside, the drums throbbed, slowly at first, then moderated in tempo. It was like the throbbing—or sobbing, if you prefer—of the old, old pumps whose shafts go so tirelessly down into the planet for such pitifully thin streams of water.

"I'm looking for an Earthman," I said. "This particular Earthman took a Venusian settler for a wife."

"That is impossible," she grunted bitterly.

"I would have said so, too," I agreed. "Until this afternoon, that is."

Her old, dried lips began to purse and wrinkle.

"I met his little daughter," I went on. "A little semi-human girl with Venusian settler features. Or, if you want to turn it around and look at the other side, a little Venusian settler girl who hums."

Her teeth went together with a snap.

I nodded and smiled. "You know who I'm talking about."

For a long long while she didn't answer. Her eyes remained unblinking on mine and if, earlier in the day, I had thought the little girl's face was expressionless, then I didn't completely appreciate the meaning of that word. Valenhk's face was more than expressionless; it was simply blank.

"They disappeared from the dwelling they were living in," I said. "They went in a hurry—a very great hurry."

That one she didn't answer, either.

"I would like to know where he is."

"Why?" Her whisper was brittle.

"He's not in trouble," I told her quickly. "He's not wanted. Nor his child, either. It's just that I have to talk to him."

"Why?"

I pulled out the file photo of Ava Lucas and handed it across to her. Her wrinkled hand took it, pinched it, held it up close to a lamp hanging from one of the ridge poles. Her eyes squinted at it for a long moment before she handed it back.

"I have never seen this Earthwoman," she said.

"All right," I answered. "There wasn't anything that made me think you had. The point is that she knows the man. It follows, naturally, that he might know her."

"This one is wanted?" Her old, broken tones went up slightly on the last word.

I nodded. "For murder."

"Murder." She spat the word. "But not for the murder of a Venusian settler, eh? Venusian settlers are not that important any more." Her old eyes hated me with an intensity I didn't relish.

"You said that, old woman, not I."

A little time went by. The drums began to beat faster. They were rolling out a lively tempo now, a tempo you could put music to.

She said at last: "I do not know where the man is. Nor the child."

She looked me straight in the eyes when she said it—and almost before the words were out of her mouth, they were whipped in again on a drawn-back, great, sucking breath. For, somewhere outside, somewhere near that dancing circle, in perfect time with the lively beat of the drums, somebody was humming.

It was a clear, clean sound, a merry, bright, happy sound, as sharp and as precise as the thrust of a laser through a piece of soft synthetic material.

"In your teeth, Valenhk! Right in your teeth!"

She only looked at me for another dull instant and then her eyes slowly closed and her hands folded together in her lap. Being caught in a lie only bores a Venusian settler.

I got up and went out of the tent.

The man never heard me approach. His eyes were toward the flaming circle and the dancers within, and, too, I suppose, to his small daughter who was somewhere in that circle with them, humming. He leaned against the bole of a kelnu tree with his arms down and slightly curled backward around it.

"That's considered bad luck," I said.

His head jerked around with my words, reflected flames from the circle fire still flickering in his eyes.

"That's a kelnu tree," I said. "Embracing it like that is like looking for a ladder to walk under. Or didn't you know?"

"Would it make any difference?" He spoke softly, but the words came to me above the drums and the shouts of the dancers. "How much bad luck can you have in one lifetime, anyway?"

I ignored that. "Why did you pull out of that dwelling? I told you you had nothing to fear from me."

He didn't answer.

"I'm looking for the woman you saw me talking with this morning," I went on. "Friend, she's wanted. And this thing, on my lapel is an Authority Card. Assuming you know what it means, I'm asking you where she is."

"What woman?" His words were flat.

"Her name is Ava Lucas."

If that meant anything to him, I couldn't tell. In the flickering light from the fires, subtle changes in expression weren't easily detected.

"Why should I care about an Earthwoman? My wife was a Venusian settler. And she's dead, see? Dead. Just a Venusian settler. Not fit for anything, like all Venusian settlers. Just a woman who fell in love with an Earthman and had the guts to marry him. Do you understand? So somebody murdered her for it. Ain't that pretty? Ain't that something to make you throw back your head and be proud about? Well, ain't it? And let me tell you, Mister, whoever it was, I'll get them. I'll get them!"

I could see his face now, all right. It was a twisted, tortured thing that writhed at me in its agony. It was small white teeth that bared at me in viciousness. It was eyes that brimmed with boiling, bubbling hate like a ladle of molten steel splashing down on bare, white flesh. Or, simply, it was the face of a man who wanted to kill the killer of his woman.

And then, suddenly, it wasn't. Even though the noise of the dance and the dancers was loud enough to command the attention and the senses, I could still hear his quiet sobbing, and I could see the heaving of the thin shoulders.

And I knew then the reason for old Valenhk's bitterness when she had said to me, "But not for the murder of a Venusian settler, eh? Venusian settlers are not that important any more."

What I said then probably sounded as weak as it really was: "I'm sorry, friend. But look, just staking out in that old dwelling of yours and trying to pry information out of the type of people who drifted your way—well, I mean there wasn't much sense in that, now was there?"

I put a hand on his shoulder. "She must have been a pretty nice woman," I said. "I don't think you'd have married her if she wasn't."

I stopped. Even in my own ears, my words sounded comfortless. I looked up, over at the flaming circle and at the sweat-laved dancers within it. The sound of the drums was a wild cacophonous tattoo now, a rattle of speed and savagery combined; and those who moved to its frenetic jabberings were not dancers any more, but only frenzied, jerking figurines on the strings of a puppeteer gone mad.

I looked down again at the man. "Your little girl and her geological sample kit," I said softly. "In a season when no good samples can be found. What was that for? Was she part of the plan, too, and the kit just the alibi that gave her a passport to wander where she chose? So that she could listen, pick up a little information here, a little there?"

He didn't answer. He didn't have to answer. My guesses can be as good as anybody's.

After a long while he looked up into my eyes. "Her name was Sahily," he said. "She had the secret. She knew where the platinum deposit was. And soon, in a couple of years maybe, when all the prospectors were gone and she knew it would be safe, she was going to stake a claim and go after it. For us. For the three of us."

I sighed. There wasn't, isn't, never will be any platinum on this planet. But who in the name of God could have the heart to ruin a dream like that?

Next day I followed the little girl. She left the reservation in a cheery frame of mind, her hum sounding soft and clear on the thin morning air. She didn't go in the direction of Ashford City, but the other way—toward the ruins of the ancient Temple Complex of the Rings. I watched her thin arm and the swinging of the big geological sample kit on the end of that arm. Then I followed along in her dusty tracks.

It was desert country, of course. There wasn't any chance of tailing her without her knowledge and I knew it. I also knew that before long she'd know it, too. And she did—but she didn't let me know she did until we came to the stone-cliffs, those filigree walls of stone that hide the entrance to the valley of the three rings.

Once there, she paused and placed her geological sample kit on a rock ledge and then calmly sat down and took off her shoes to dump the dust while she waited for me.

"Well," I said. "Good morning."

She looked up at me. She nodded politely. Then she put on her shoes again and got to her feet.

"You've been following me," she said, and her gray eyes stared accusingly into mine.

"I have?"

"That isn't an honorable thing to do," she said very gravely. "A gentleman doesn't do that to a lady."

I didn't smile. "And what would you have me do about it?"

"Stop following me, of course, sir."

"Very well," I said. "I won't follow you any more. Will that be satisfactory?"

"Quite, sir."

Without another word, she picked up her geological sample kit and disappeared along a path that led through a rock crevice. Only then did I allow myself to grin. It was a sad and pitying and affectionate kind of grin.

I sat down and did with my shoes as she had done. There wasn't any hurry; I knew where she was going. There could only be one place, of course—the city of Deimos and Phobos. Other than that she had no choice. And I thought I knew the reason for her going.

Several times in the past, there have been people who, bitten with the fever of an idea that somewhere on this misty planet there must be platinum, have done prospecting among the ruins of the old temples. She had probably heard that there were people there now, and she was carrying out with the thoroughness of her precise little mind the job she had set herself of finding the killer of her mother.

I took a short-cut over the stone-cliffs and went down a winding, dust-worn path. The temple stones stood out barren and dry-looking, like ribs from the desiccated carcass of an animal. For a moment I stopped and stared down at the ruins. I didn't see the girl. She was somewhere down there, though, still carrying her geological sample kit and, probably, still humming.

I started up once more.

And then I heard it—a shrill blast of sound in an octave of urgency; a hum, sure, but a warning one.

I stopped in my tracks from the shock of it. Yes, I knew from whom it had come, all right. But I didn't know why.

And then the hum broke off short. One instant it was in the air, shrieking with a message. The next it was gone. But it left tailings, like the echo of a death cry slowly floating back over the dead body of the creature that uttered it.

I dropped behind a fragment of the stone-cliff. A shot barked out angrily. Splinters of the rock crazed the morning air.
question: Who was identified as a wanted killer by the narrator?

synthetic_story:
The research vessel *Prometheus* hung in low orbit above Kepler-442b, its sensors painting a picture that made Dr. Isabel Cole frown at her displays. The planet below was shrouded in thick atmospheric haze, but thermal imaging revealed something unexpected: massive heat signatures moving across the surface, far larger than anything in the mission briefing had suggested.

"We're picking up the automated beacon," announced Pablo Bryant from the communications station. "It's old—really old. Pre-Reformation era, I'd say. At least a hundred and twenty years."

Isabel nodded, her mind racing through the implications. The *Prometheus* had been forced off its planned route to the Thornhill Town colony when their quantum drive had malfunctioned. They'd limped into this system on conventional thrust, desperately needing to identify their location and plot a new course home. But Kepler-442b wasn't supposed to have any human presence. It was listed in the Galactic Survey as a "seeding world"—one of thousands of planets that had been inoculated with terrestrial organisms decades or centuries ago, left to develop functional ecosystems before human colonization.

"That beacon is coming from the surface," Pablo continued. "Looks like it's near what might be a crashed ship. The signal's automated—no response to our hails."

Isabel glanced at the other members of her skeleton crew. Roman Frank, their engineer, was still working on the quantum drive repairs. Logan Cox, their pilot, stood ready at the helm. And Ian James, their xenobiologist, was practically vibrating with excitement as he studied the sensor data.

"Those heat signatures," Ian said, his voice tight with barely contained enthusiasm. "They're enormous. Whatever's down there, it's not standard terraforming fauna. Something's gone wrong with the ecosystem restoration."

"Or right," Isabel muttered. "Depending on your perspective."

The problem was simple: they needed to land. They needed to access whatever records might be in that crashed ship to determine their exact location. The *Prometheus* carried star charts, but without knowing their starting point after the quantum drive mishap, those charts were useless. They could be anywhere within a sphere of space five hundred light-years across.

But there was another problem, one that made Isabel's stomach clench every time she thought about it. The *Prometheus* was registered for a crew of four. There were five people aboard. That fifth person was Aisha Hughes, a woman they'd rescued from a failed mining station three months ago. Aisha had been the sole survivor of what appeared to be a corporate massacre—her entire team killed when they'd discovered something in the asteroid belt that certain interests wanted kept quiet. She'd stowed away on the *Prometheus* when they'd stopped to investigate the distress call.

Isabel had wanted to report it immediately, to go through proper channels. But Aisha had begged them not to. The people who'd killed her colleagues would kill her too, she'd insisted, the moment she turned up in any official database. And there was another consideration: the *Prometheus* itself was operating under provisional research licenses that wouldn't survive close scrutiny. Isabel's team had been conducting unauthorized studies of pre-contact civilizations, work that violated half a dozen interstellar treaties. If port authorities started investigating why they had an extra crew member, they'd discover everything else.

So they'd kept Aisha hidden, and now they were lost, and they needed to land somewhere to get their bearings. But they couldn't land at any registered colony world. The crew manifest discrepancy would trigger immediate investigation.

"We have to go down," Logan said quietly. "We need those records."

"I know," Isabel replied. "Aisha, you'll need to stay aboard with Roman. The rest of us will suit up and investigate the wreck."

Aisha nodded from her station. She'd been grateful for their protection, but Isabel could see the guilt in her eyes. The woman knew she was the reason they couldn't simply land at Thornhill Town or any other registered port.

The *Prometheus* descended through the murky atmosphere. As they dropped below the cloud layer, the world revealed itself in all its alien strangeness. The ground wasn't ground at all—not in any conventional sense. It was a vast, undulating carpet of fungal growth, pale yellow and sickly white, stretching to the limits of visibility. Here and there, darker patches marked different species or growth stages. The whole landscape seemed to pulse and writhe.

"My God," Ian breathed. "It's all mycelial. The entire surface layer is fungal mats. This must be a very early-stage seeding world. They've only introduced the decomposer layer and primary consumers."

"Those heat signatures," Pablo said. "They're moving. Converging on... something. Can't tell what."

Isabel brought the ship down carefully, using thrusters to burn away a landing zone. The fungal mat scorched and blackened, revealing bare rock underneath. As they settled, she could see the crashed ship Ian had mentioned—a bulky, old-style vessel half-buried in fungal growth about two hundred meters away. Its hull design was ancient, from the era before the Reformation had standardized ship construction.

"Alright," Isabel said. "Pablo, Ian, Logan—with me. Full environmental suits. We don't know what's in that atmosphere, and I don't want to find out the hard way."

They suited up in the airlock. The suits were modern, flexible enough to allow natural movement. Each of them carried a plasma cutter—ostensibly for clearing debris, but Isabel was thinking about those heat signatures. Whatever was out there, it was big.

The outer door opened, and they stepped onto the scorched rock. The unburned fungal surface around them was springy, almost trampoline-like. Isabel took a cautious step onto it and felt it give beneath her weight.

"Spread out," she ordered. "That surface layer looks thin. We don't want to all fall through at once."

They moved toward the crashed ship in a loose line. The landscape was eerily silent—or rather, it should have been silent, but their suit microphones picked up a constant cacophony of sounds. Clicks and scrapes and strange, hollow booming noises that seemed to come from everywhere and nowhere.

Pablo suddenly stopped, staring at something ahead. "What in the name of—"

Isabel followed his gaze. Something was moving across the fungal plain. It was huge—easily three meters long—and it moved with a peculiar looping gait, arching its segmented body like a massive inchworm. Its body was covered in coarse, dark bristles, and it had clusters of legs at both ends.

"Lepidoptera larva," Ian said, his voice filled with wonder and horror. "A caterpillar. But it's enormous. On Earth, these grow to maybe five centimeters. This thing is fifty times that size."

"Why?" Logan asked. "What makes them grow so big?"

"I don't know," Ian admitted. "Something in the ecosystem balance is off. Maybe a missing predator species, or a absent regulatory virus, or—"

"Later," Isabel cut him off. "Let's get to that ship."

They continued forward, giving the giant caterpillar a wide berth. It seemed to ignore them, munching methodically on the fungal mat. As they got closer to the crashed vessel, Isabel could see that the growth covering it was even thicker than elsewhere. The ship had been here a long time.

She activated her plasma cutter, adjusting it to a broad, low-intensity beam. The fungal material steamed and blackened as she swept the beam across it, cutting a path to the hull. The smell—even filtered through her suit's systems—was nauseating.

"There," Pablo said, pointing. "That's an airlock. Old style, but standard configuration."

That was when Joshua realized the terrible truth: he had become more Timothy than Joshua. The consciousness transfer had worked too well. He didn't just have Timothy's memories—he had absorbed his capacity for emotion, his ability to love, his connection to family and community.

But that meant the Collective would send up invasion forces. They would apply their game theory models and determine that the most efficient solution was to eliminate the existing surface population and replace them with their own people. The surface dwellers, with their inefficient emotions and chaotic social dynamics, would be seen as obstacles to optimal resource allocation.

Joshua couldn't let that happen. Not to Ruth. Not to Eric and Anil. Not to the millions of people who had rebuilt a civilization from the ashes of environmental catastrophe.

---

Three days later, Joshua stood at the entrance to the underground facility, hidden in the hills above Yarnmouth. He had told Ruth he needed to make one final survey trip. The lie had tasted like poison in his mouth.

He descended through the secret passages, his heart heavy with purpose. The facility was minimally staffed—just Malik Cook and two other technicians monitoring the neural relay equipment.

"Joshua!" Malik's face registered surprise. "Your report isn't due for another week. Has something gone wrong?"

"I need to file my report immediately," Joshua said. "The surface is unsuitable for colonization."

Malik's eyes narrowed. "Unsuitable? Our satellite data suggests otherwise. The biosphere has recovered beyond our projections."

"There's a disease," Joshua said quickly, accessing his training in risk management protocols. "It affects the neural pathways. I've documented three cases of sudden violent insanity among the surface population. The vector appears to be airborne. I believe it's already beginning to affect me—I've been experiencing unauthorized emotional responses, irrational decision-making patterns."

He pulled out a data crystal containing falsified medical scans and behavioral logs. He'd spent the last week creating them using Timothy's university equipment, applying his knowledge of biotechnology to make them convincing.

Malik inserted the crystal into the analysis terminal. His expression grew troubled as he reviewed the data.

"This is... concerning," he said slowly. "If there's a pathogen that attacks neural function, it could compromise the Collective's entire consciousness network. We would need to maintain quarantine protocols for at least—"

"Five hundred years," Joshua interrupted. "According to my analysis, that's the minimum time required for the pathogen to die out naturally. The Collective should focus on expanding the underground cities instead. The surface must remain off-limits."

Malik's hand moved toward the communication panel. "I need to verify this with the Collective directly."

Joshua's hand shot out, gripping Malik's wrist. "You can't. The communication itself might be compromised. The pathogen appears to transmit through electromagnetic frequencies similar to our neural network protocols. Any direct link to the Collective could infect the entire system."

It was a desperate lie, but Malik hesitated. Joshua could see the conflict in his colleague's eyes—the rigid protocols of the Collective warring against the evidence before him.

"Then how do we report this?" Malik asked.

"Physical courier only. Sealed containers. Complete decontamination protocols." Joshua released Malik's wrist. "I'll return to the surface and complete my survey from a safe distance. You prepare the report for the Collective. By the time they receive it, I'll have additional data to support the quarantine recommendation."

Malik nodded slowly. "This will delay the recolonization project indefinitely."

"Better delayed than destroyed," Joshua said. "The Collective's survival is paramount."

The words came automatically, but they rang hollow in his chest. The Collective's survival wasn't what he cared about anymore. He cared about Ruth's smile. Eric's laughter. Anil's drawings. The messy, inefficient, beautiful chaos of human life on the surface.

He left the facility before Malik could ask more questions. As he climbed back toward the surface, he felt the weight of his betrayal. He had turned against everything he'd been created for, everything he'd been programmed to believe.

But he had also discovered something the Collective had never anticipated: that consciousness wasn't just about processing information efficiently. It was about connection, about love, about choosing your own purpose rather than having it assigned to you.

---

Six months later, Joshua sat in his office at the university in Foxwood. His door bore a nameplate reading "Professor Timothy Long, Department of Linguistics and Cultural Preservation." Student papers covered his desk—essays on language preservation techniques and the social dynamics of multilingual communities.

Through the window, he could see Ruth walking across the campus quad with Eric and Anil. They were bringing him lunch, as they did every Thursday. The sight made that familiar warmth bloom in his chest.

He had received word through a carefully maintained underground contact that the Collective had accepted his report. The surface world was classified as contaminated and off-limits indefinitely. Future expansion would focus on deeper excavations and the development of new subterranean territories.

The surface world was safe. Ruth was safe. His children were safe.

But Joshua lived with the knowledge that he was a lie. He was not Timothy Long. He was a consciousness thief, a murderer, an alien intelligence wearing a dead man's face. Sometimes, in the dark of night, he wondered if he had any right to the happiness he felt.

Then Ruth would turn to him in sleep, or Eric would share a new discovery, or Anil would climb into his lap with a book, and he would remember: love wasn't about deserving. It was about choosing, every day, to be the person they needed him to be.

He had been created as a tool of the Collective, but he had become something else entirely. He had become human.

A knock at his door interrupted his thoughts. A student entered, asking about the peer review process for her thesis on blockchain applications in linguistic data preservation. Joshua smiled and gestured for her to sit down.

He had a life to live, a family to love, and a world to protect. The Collective had sent him to evaluate whether humanity was worth preserving.

He had found his answer.

In the evening, as he walked home with Ruth and the children, the sun setting over Foxwood painted the sky in shades of orange and purple. Anil held his hand and asked him to tell a story about the ancient peoples, the ones who had lived before the pollution times.

Joshua began to speak, weaving together fragments of real history with protective fiction, teaching his children about cultural preservation and the importance of remembering where they came from. As he talked, he felt Ruth's hand slip into his other hand, warm and real and alive.

He had betrayed his creators to save this world. He would carry that weight forever. But looking at the faces of his family, seeing their trust and love, he knew he would make the same choice again.

Some things, he had learned, were worth more than efficiency. Some things were worth everything.

The Collective had taught him about game theory and optimal outcomes. But Ruth and the children had taught him about something more important: they had taught him about being human.

And that, Joshua Fuller—no, Timothy Long—had decided, was the most valuable lesson of all.

The Institute for Quantum Computing Futures launched in Crystalbrook Town last autumn, representing a collaboration between research centers in Woodbridge Region, Morningside in Lethoria, Crystalbrook Town, and Queenstown in Havencia. Backed by a substantial fifteen-year grant, the institute aims to investigate the implications of quantum computing for society and ensure humanity maximizes opportunities while minimizing risks.

The institute emphasizes interdisciplinary collaboration, recognizing that no single field adequately addresses these challenges. It brings together physicists, social psychologists, corporate governance experts, ethicists, and specialists in comparative history to examine how quantum computing might reshape civilization.

Dr. Arthur Schultz, a philosopher and former policy advisor, serves as the institute's executive director. Recently, he sat down with Lucia Woods, director of technology futures at a prominent think tank, to discuss quantum computing's potential impact on society.

Their conversation has been edited for clarity.

**Lucia Woods:** The institute's interdisciplinary approach seems central to its mission. How critical is this to understanding quantum computing's implications?

**Arthur Schultz:** Absolutely essential. No single academic discipline owns this conversation or approaches it systematically. If academia wants to provide thought leadership on this transformative technology, we must break down traditional disciplinary boundaries.

We're bringing together the technologists developing quantum algorithms with social psychologists studying human behavior, corporate governance specialists examining organizational structures, and comparative history scholars who can help us learn from past technological transitions. The visual arts community has also been surprisingly valuable—they help us imagine and communicate possible futures in ways that pure logic sometimes cannot.

Quantum computing isn't unique in requiring this approach—biotechnology and nanotechnology face similar challenges. But because thinking about quantum computing's societal impact is still nascent, we have an opportunity to shape how we approach it from the ground up and build a truly collaborative community.

The first step is developing a shared language. We need to create spaces where physicists can explain quantum entanglement to social scientists, and where corporate governance experts can help technologists understand organizational decision-making structures. Only then can we develop genuinely new insights together.

**Lucia:** Some argue that addressing major technological challenges has become harder due to current political fragmentation and growing isolationism. Do you see these trends hampering global efforts to manage quantum computing responsibly?

**Arthur:** It's a legitimate concern, but I think quantum computing presents a different dynamic than, say, climate change. With climate issues, the costs aren't directly borne by those profiting from fossil fuels. There's a disconnect between benefit and consequence.

With quantum computing, the major tech companies developing this technology are acutely aware that public reaction could turn against them very quickly. They've watched what happened with genetic modification and social media. They know that if quantum computing suddenly disrupts entire industries—and we're talking about potentially transforming cryptography, financial services, pharmaceutical development, and materials science within a decade—there could be massive backlash.

Consider the financial sector. Quantum computers could theoretically break current encryption standards, potentially exposing trillions in transactions. If that happens without adequate preparation, you could see governments moving to restrict or ban certain quantum computing applications. The industry is anxious about this possibility.

Through my field research and conversations with these companies, I've found genuine concern. Yes, they're motivated by business interests and intellectual challenges, but they're also people who don't wake up thinking they'll destabilize global financial systems or compromise national security. As the industry matures, there's a developing sense of responsibility.

This creates a real opportunity. Despite the broader political climate—or perhaps because of it—we can bring industry stakeholders on board to ensure the technology develops responsibly. They have strong incentives to get this right.

**Lucia:** There's a dominant narrative around quantum computing and advanced technology generally that we're somehow at the mercy of progress—that we can't control or shape it. Anyone questioning this gets labeled as anti-progress or Luddite. But we actually have more control than we acknowledge. For instance, how we structure organizations, how we design research priorities, how we allocate resources—these are choices, not inevitabilities. How do we balance being impacted by technological change with exercising agency over what kind of change we want?

**Arthur:** Technological determinism is pervasive, and understandably so. For individuals, it does feel like change simply happens and we must adapt. No single person can alter these trajectories alone.

But when we think collectively—as communities, nations, or an international community—we have real power to shape technological development. We have multiple tools: regulations, funding priorities, cultural norms, professional standards.

Technology emerges from specific legal, political, normative, and cultural frameworks. It doesn't develop in a vacuum. The more we understand technology's relationship with these frameworks, and the more consciously we shape them, the more we influence technological trajectories.

For example, we can develop cultures of responsible innovation. We can establish professional ethics—a kind of Hippocratic oath for quantum computing researchers. We can structure corporate governance to prioritize long-term societal benefit over short-term profit. We can use comparative history to learn from past technological transitions—studying how societies managed the Industrial Revolution, electrification, or computerization can inform our approach to quantum computing.

These interventions are feasible and can meaningfully shape outcomes. The key is recognizing that design thinking applies not just to products but to the social systems surrounding technology.

**Lucia:** But we can't fully control outcomes. Societies are too complex. There are always unintended consequences. How do we navigate this uncertainty?

**Arthur:** You're absolutely right. History is littered with examples of interventions producing unexpected results. We cannot engineer society with precision.

However, we can do several things. First, we can imagine how things might go catastrophically wrong and develop systems to prevent those scenarios. Second, we can collectively envision positive futures—societies we actually want to live in that incorporate this technology. Yes, our visions will be imperfect and may have unforeseen downsides, but the exercise itself is valuable.

Critically, this conversation cannot be monopolized by any single group. It shouldn't be just quantum computing researchers or just Silicon Valley executives or just government regulators. This must be as broad a conversation as possible, involving diverse perspectives and communities.

Career planning for young people increasingly requires considering how quantum computing might reshape industries. Community organizing around technology policy is becoming essential. We need input from people across society, not just technical elites.

**Lucia:** One of your institute's most fascinating projects examines what computational power actually means and how different forms of computing represent different types of capability. Could you elaborate?

**Arthur:** This is crucial. Historically, we've had an overwhelming tendency to anthropomorphize—to define computational power or problem-solving ability in human-centric terms. We measure whether machines can do what humans do, at human-level performance.

It's taken decades for the scientific community to recognize that non-human animals possess genuine intelligence that differs from ours. Crows use tools in ways that reflect sophisticated problem-solving. Octopuses, with completely different evolutionary histories and nervous systems, demonstrate remarkable cognitive abilities. We've finally accepted that human cognition isn't the only valid form of intelligence.

Now quantum computing challenges us from another direction. Just as we're accepting nature's diversity of intelligence, we're creating computational systems that are radically different from human thinking.

Too many people still talk about "human-level artificial intelligence" or "general AI" as goals, basically meaning "like human cognition." But quantum computers don't think like humans at all.

When we built the first calculators, they didn't do arithmetic like humans—they did it vastly better, without errors, using completely different mechanisms. Similarly, quantum computers solve certain problems through quantum mechanical properties—superposition, entanglement—that have no analog in human cognition.

We need to understand this landscape of different computational paradigms. We need to map all the different ways of being "powerful" at computation. A quantum computer might be extraordinarily sophisticated at optimization problems while being completely useless at pattern recognition tasks that a simple neural network handles easily—a distribution of capabilities that bears no relation to human cognitive profiles.

This matters because we tend to associate computational power with authority and rights. There's a long Western philosophical tradition linking intelligence to governance—the idea that the "smartest" should lead. If we're not careful about how we define and attribute computational capability, we might make poor decisions about which systems we trust with which tasks.

Creating an atlas of computational paradigms—mapping quantum computing, classical computing, neural networks, and other approaches—is ambitious but necessary.

**Lucia:** That's an interesting point about how we conceptualize capability. We actually think about human ability at the societal level—our collective achievements—but then conflate that with individual capacity. With quantum computing, we tend to focus on individual systems rather than networks of systems working together. Should we be thinking about computational power more holistically?

**Arthur:** Absolutely. Right now, perhaps due to our anthropomorphizing bias, there's a tendency toward adversarial framing—quantum computers versus humanity, as if it's one or the other. But this misses the reality.

Quantum computing presents risks, certainly. Any powerful technology does. But most applications will augment human capability rather than replace it. We'll work in human-quantum teams, combining human judgment and contextual understanding with quantum computational power.

The most promising applications aren't about quantum computers operating autonomously but about hybrid systems where quantum computers handle specific computational tasks while humans provide oversight, interpret results, and make decisions based on broader context.

**Lucia:** Where does the adversarial framing come from? Is it just historical anxiety about automation, or something deeper?

**Arthur:** I think it comes from several sources, some possibly innate. Humans naturally anthropomorphize, especially with complex systems. We ascribe agency to things, particularly things that seem to "act" or produce unexpected outputs. This has sound evolutionary roots—if something does something surprising, it's wise to ask what it "wants" and whether it might be dangerous.

When we ascribe agency, we naturally project our own patterns of behavior. And humans are profoundly both cooperative and competitive. We have strong in-group versus out-group psychology, which enables wonderful cooperation within groups but also drives conflict between groups.

It's natural for people to think of quantum computers as agents, to anthropomorphize them. Then we ask: are they part of our group or a different group? If they're different, is it us versus them? Who wins? This thinking is very human.

There's also this long tradition, particularly in Western culture, of associating intelligence and computational power with dominance. It's interesting to speculate—and I wish we had more research on this—how different cultures perceive quantum computing. Japan, for instance, has historically been very accepting of robots and advanced technology.

In the West, we've long justified power hierarchies by claiming some people are "smarter." In cultures where power derives from other sources—heredity, spiritual authority, communal consensus—the narrative around powerful computing might be entirely different. Perhaps in some cultural contexts, a quantum computer would be seen as a tool for collective enlightenment rather than a potential competitor.

**Lucia:** Your institute is examining what quantum computing breakthroughs might occur, when, and what social consequences they might have. What does the future hold? What are your concerns, and what positive outcomes do you envision in the short, medium, and long term?

**Arthur:** That's a big question. I don't lie awake worried about rogue quantum computers taking over the world—that's not how risks manifest. If quantum computing causes serious problems, it won't be through dramatic, visible catastrophe.

Actually, one significant risk is that we have a strong negative public reaction—like what happened with GMOs—that prevents us from realizing enormous benefits. That's as big a risk as the technology itself poses.

One concern that keeps me up at night is dependency and deskilling. The history of civilization is partly a history of humans domesticating ourselves through our tools and systems. Quantum computing could accelerate this dramatically.

Consider medical diagnosis. Already, doctors consult computational tools regularly. As diagnostic systems improve—and quantum computing could revolutionize drug discovery and personalized medicine—what will doctors do besides input symptoms and relay what the computer suggests? At some point, you might eliminate the doctor entirely. But then who actually understands medicine?

We need to worry about becoming dependent on systems we don't understand, about losing crucial capabilities. You can imagine a society where everyone is materially prosperous—basic needs met to an unprecedented degree—yet people lack meaningful work or purpose. Perhaps we escape into virtual reality. Perhaps we see troubling countercultures or neo-Luddite movements.

That scenario—material abundance coupled with existential emptiness—worries me more than dramatic technological catastrophe.

As for utopian possibilities, I hope this technological revolution helps us undo damage from previous ones. That's optimistic, perhaps unrealistic, but consider: quantum computing could revolutionize materials science, leading to much more efficient energy storage and transmission. It could optimize resource use across entire economies, reducing waste dramatically.

Green infrastructure design could be transformed through quantum optimization algorithms. We could design cities that are vastly more sustainable, transportation systems that are incredibly efficient, manufacturing processes that minimize environmental impact.

Quantum computing could help us live more intelligently—using resources more efficiently, making better collective decisions, solving optimization problems that currently seem intractable. Using these tools to repair environmental damage and build truly sustainable civilization—that's my main utopian hope.

**Lucia:** What specific steps should we take now to ensure positive outcomes?

**Arthur:** Several things. First, we need robust international dialogue. The institute is facilitating conversations between researchers, policymakers, and industry leaders across our four partner regions. We need frameworks for responsible development that span national boundaries.

Second, we need to invest heavily in education—not just training more quantum physicists, but ensuring broader public understanding. People need basic literacy about what quantum computing can and cannot do. This requires contributions from the visual arts, literary criticism, and other fields that can make complex ideas accessible.

Third, we need to reform corporate governance structures to ensure companies developing quantum computing technology are accountable to broader stakeholder groups, not just shareholders seeking short-term returns.

Fourth, we should learn from comparative history. How did societies manage previous technological transitions? What worked? What failed? The Industrial Revolution, electrification, computerization—each offers lessons.

Finally, we need to maintain epistemic humility. We don't know exactly how this will unfold. We need adaptive frameworks that can respond to unexpected developments rather than rigid plans that assume we can predict the future.

The key is starting these conversations now, while the technology is still developing, rather than waiting until quantum computing is already transforming society and our options are constrained.

**Lucia:** Thank you for your time and insights.

**Arthur:** Thank you. These conversations are exactly what we need more of.

Military Genetic Enhancement: A Strategic Necessity?

The recent breakthrough at the Silverdale Research Institute has sent shockwaves through military establishments worldwide. Dr. Helena Flores and her team successfully enhanced the physical capabilities of laboratory mice through targeted genetic modification, increasing their endurance by 300 percent and their strength by 150 percent. Within days of the announcement, General Thomas Silva convened an emergency session at the Pentagon, proposing an immediate moratorium on all military funding for human genetic enhancement research. Legislation is already being drafted in both the Senate and House to criminalize such enhancement for military purposes—a position endorsed by the International Ethics Council and several prominent religious leaders. Human genetic enhancement for military applications is widely considered either 1) a fundamentally dangerous technology that must be prohibited or, at minimum, 2) a complex issue requiring extensive regulation and oversight. But what, precisely, makes it so problematic?

Begin by considering whether a nation has the right to defend itself effectively. I argue "yes." No external authority has the moral standing to dictate how a sovereign nation protects its citizens, and I fail to see why General Silva or the International Ethics Council possesses that authority either. When Silva declares, "We must resist the temptation to artificially enhance our warriors," it rings hollow coming from a military establishment that has pursued every technological advantage from gunpowder to nuclear weapons. For a general, opposing genetic enhancement is politically expedient—it demonstrates leadership on a controversial topic without risking immediate operational consequences. After all, how many active military enhancement programs were actually terminated by this proposed ban? Likely very few, since the Reagan and Clinton administrations already minimized federal grants for advanced biotechnology research in this domain. Moreover, most researchers considered military-grade human enhancement impossible until recently—so there's probably no significant backlog of proposals. There's nothing quite like banning the barely feasible to project decisive leadership.

Religious authorities, unlike military ones, claim moral rather than strategic authority. I respect their freedom to guide their followers and those followers' freedom to adhere to such guidance. However, calling for secular governments to implement bans extends their influence beyond those they can persuade through faith alone, demonstrating a lack of respect for others' freedom. The foundational texts these authorities reference were written millennia ago. While these texts address warfare extensively, they contain nothing about genetic enhancement, evolutionary biology, or biotechnology. Applying ancient principles through medieval interpretive frameworks to 21st-century military challenges seems questionable at best.

If nations have the right to defend themselves, what right does the international community have to limit the means? Modern warfare is already conducted with extensive technological assistance—from body armor to combat medicine. Truly "natural" warfare would mean 50 percent casualty rates and make combat the leading cause of death for young adults in military service.

Some technologies are more invasive than others, certainly. With genetic enhancement, DNA modifications would be introduced through gene therapy, altering the recipient's cellular structure. Two decades ago, similar concerns arose over "designer soldiers"—troops using performance-enhancing drugs. Today, caffeine pills and approved stimulants are standard issue. Countless soldiers have benefited from improved alertness and reduced fatigue. Who has been harmed?

The genetic enhancement procedure would be similar to existing gene therapy protocols. The only difference is that modifications would target performance-related genes rather than disease genes. What law or principle—secular, humanist, or religious—says one type of genetic modification in a laboratory is acceptable while another is not? No matter how thoroughly you examine ancient texts on warfare, you won't find the answer.

Even if nations have the right to pursue enhancement, is it strategically sound? Suppose every military in the world stopped conventional recruitment and instead produced genetically enhanced super-soldiers. What would the battlefield look like in 20 or 30 years? The answer is: not dramatically different. Enhancement would only optimize the physical and cognitive aspects of people who already exist. Fearing an army of enhanced soldiers is essentially fearing a more capable version of current personnel. The enemy, as always, is simply us—but stronger and faster.

A different scenario involves armies filled with clones of exceptional warriors. We'd treat elite soldier DNA like precision weapons, coveting Mohamed Hunter's genetic profile the way we value advanced fighter jets today. But even military admiration has limits. Armed forces are more invested in unit cohesion than individual exceptionalism. Besides, such a trend would prove self-limiting, because battlefield effectiveness depends on diverse skill sets. The military values one Steven Morris—a decorated special operations veteran—but field a hundred or a million identical copies, and their tactical advantage diminishes significantly.

Enhanced individuals already exist in a sense. About one in every 1,000 people possesses naturally occurring genetic variations that provide superior athletic performance. Scientific studies on such individuals—whether athletes or not—show they share many advantageous characteristics. How many characteristics they share remains contentious in evolutionary biology and social psychology. But genetic determinism is largely irrelevant to the enhancement debate. Despite how many traits enhanced soldiers might share, they remain different people fundamentally. They possess their own identities, thoughts, and rights. Should you doubt this, ask any naturally gifted athlete whether their abilities make them less human.

Suppose genetic testing revealed you possessed the same performance-enhancing mutations as an Olympic champion. Would that suddenly make you less of an individual? Hardly. So why would deliberate enhancement be different? An enhanced soldier would be trained in the same academies by the same instructors—like the naturally gifted athlete, only more reliably capable. A person's basic humanity isn't governed by their genetic origin or whether their capabilities arose naturally or through intervention.

Natural variations aren't the only genetic advantages in military history. Consider military working dogs—German Shepherds, Belgian Malinois—if they're bred specifically for military traits, isn't that genetic enhancement? It's the canine equivalent of selective breeding, which is to say they're all enhanced through generations of deliberate genetic selection. Military horses were similarly bred for centuries. The cavalry mounts used in warfare had no wild equivalents; they'd been selectively bred for strength, speed, and temperament for thousands of years. The same applies to countless military applications. Visit any defense contractor, and you'll find programs with names like "Advanced Warrior Enhancement Initiative," combining biotechnology and research ethics to develop the next generation of capabilities.

One recurring argument against enhancement involves some rogue nation creating an army of super-soldiers. But who would deploy such an army? Enhanced soldiers still require training, equipment, and logistics. Armies are far more easily fielded the traditional way—through recruitment and training of ordinary volunteers. "Dulce et decorum est pro patria mori" has motivated countless soldiers throughout history. Why abandon proven methods?

Remember that genetic enhancement differs from cloning. We don't create superman from nothing—we must start with existing human potential. Perhaps we could enhance volunteers from Special Forces candidates. Their aptitude might—or might not—be genetically determined. But suppose it is. You might produce such a capable unit that when facing overwhelming odds, every member volunteers for the suicide mission. Admirable perhaps, but not necessarily optimal tactics. And what about support personnel? The military requires far more logistics specialists than elite operators. You could attempt to optimize personnel for every role, including administrative positions, but what's the point? There's no shortage of competent administrators.

What if a dictator like the late ruler of Pinehurst, Ulvaria, had access to enhancement technology? Concerning, but history shows that tyrants' advantages rarely persist beyond their lifetimes. Their successors, enhanced or not, typically lack their predecessors' capabilities. Stalin's daughter retired to obscurity, and second-generation dictators worldwide prove consistently less formidable than their parents.

The notion of aging generals enhancing themselves to extend their careers is unrealistic. First, the enhancement wouldn't reverse aging completely. Second, would military command structures accept such an arrangement? A persistent officer might convince younger colleagues to support enhancement research, but that's no different from any other military modernization program.

Opposition to enhancement is fundamentally a form of discrimination. We agree it's wrong to discriminate based on genetic characteristics like race or ethnicity. Calls to ban enhancement amount to discrimination based on another genetic trait—whether someone's capabilities arose naturally or through intervention. The most extreme discrimination is genocide—eliminating that which is different. Here, the discrimination is preemptive—enhanced soldiers are so threatening that we must prevent their existence entirely through bans on the technology.

What's superior about natural genetic variation anyway? Enhancement is the only predictable way to optimize military capability, because it targets specific, known genetic factors. Natural selection is random by comparison—some arbitrary combination of parental genes. In evolutionary biology, this randomness helps diversify the gene pool. However, for military applications, randomness is a liability. We don't field random weapons systems; why accept random personnel capabilities?

Whatever concerns exist about enhancement, traditional recruitment will remain predominant. An expensive and invasive medical procedure will never replace conventional training for the vast majority of military roles. Those most likely to pursue enhancement will face special circumstances—perhaps soldiers recovering from severe injuries who might otherwise face medical discharge. Even there, many will combine enhancement with traditional rehabilitation. Another case involves personnel with genetic conditions that limit their service. They might choose enhancement to remain deployable rather than accept medical retirement.

The most concerning possibility isn't super-soldiers or dictators. It's that wealthy nations with advanced biotechnology sectors will enhance their forces while others cannot. The common practice of seeking technological superiority—from stealth aircraft to precision weapons—reflects our competitive instinct. Enhancement may resonate with this pattern and cause some nations to pursue it aggressively. So what? Wealthy nations already possess numerous advantages, and international law has never successfully prevented military innovation.

The "profound ethical concerns" about enhancement largely stem from strategic anxiety. Economic competition between nations is challenging enough, and it factors here, but what truly concerns military planners is relative capability. Millennia of warfare through competitive advantage have made defense establishments acutely sensitive to any development that shifts the balance—say, through revolutionary weapons technology. Enhancement is less dramatic than nuclear weapons, but it strikes a similar nerve: someone gains strategic advantage over you.

Once initial concerns subside and further research establishes safety protocols, human genetic enhancement will become one option among many specialized military capabilities, affecting only select personnel. Research in this area could yield broader benefits. Silva's hasty policy changes little immediately, but it potentially represents a strategic error. In using genetic modification to enhance performance, researchers must understand the cellular mechanisms that determine the difference between baseline and optimal function. Work in this area might illuminate the aging process and yield methods to extend the operational lifespan of all personnel, allowing longer, healthier careers. Strategically speaking, that would benefit entire militaries, not just elite units. That's more broadly useful than creating a small cadre of super-soldiers.

To some, the scientist pursuing biotechnology research represents a threat never to be trusted. To others, including me, the scientist is an asset, illuminating the processes that enhance national security and improving defensive capabilities through knowledge. Various arguments support either view, but one key consideration favors continued research. The vast majority of military capabilities, including those critics employ, derive from previous scientific discoveries. They embody the fruits of research. Don't let fear, ignorance, and strategic timidity halt progress. Instead, let us develop—and yes, even enhance—new generations of capable defenders who can meet the challenges of future conflicts.

Consider the parallel with military working dogs again. Nobody seriously proposes banning their use because they've been selectively bred for enhanced capabilities. We recognize them as valuable tools that save human lives. The dogs themselves aren't diminished by their enhanced traits—they're simply better at their jobs. The same logic applies to human enhancement. A soldier with enhanced endurance or improved cognitive function under stress isn't less human—they're simply more capable of accomplishing their mission and surviving to return home.

The research ethics considerations are substantial, certainly. Any enhancement program must include informed consent, thorough safety testing, and long-term health monitoring. These requirements already govern military medicine and should extend to enhancement research. The experimental design must be rigorous, with appropriate controls and peer review. But meeting high ethical standards doesn't require abandoning the research entirely—it requires conducting it responsibly.

From a moral philosophy perspective, the question becomes: is it more ethical to send soldiers into combat with every possible advantage, or to deny them tools that might save their lives because of abstract concerns? When Grace Rogers deployed to the Summit District conflict zone, she relied on body armor, night vision equipment, and advanced communications—all technologies that enhanced her natural capabilities. Genetic enhancement is simply the next step in that progression.

The social welfare implications extend beyond military applications. Research into human performance enhancement could benefit athletes, emergency responders, and workers in physically demanding occupations. Medical applications might help patients recovering from injuries or managing degenerative conditions. Restricting military research restricts these potential benefits as well.

Some critics invoke archaeology, pointing to past civilizations that collapsed after pursuing technological advantages they couldn't control. But this analogy fails—those civilizations lacked our understanding of research ethics, experimental design, and long-term risk assessment. We're not ancient warriors blindly pursuing power; we're modern professionals carefully evaluating new capabilities.

The education reform movement has taught us that optimizing human potential requires both environmental and biological approaches. We've invested heavily in better training, nutrition, and equipment for military personnel. Genetic enhancement simply adds another tool to this optimization process. Just as we don't reject education reform because it creates "unfair" advantages for those with access to better schools, we shouldn't reject enhancement because it creates capability gaps.

The biotechnology sector will advance regardless of military policy. Private companies are already developing enhancement therapies for civilian applications. If military establishments abandon this research, they'll simply fall behind private sector capabilities—a strategic disaster. Better to conduct research transparently, with appropriate oversight and ethical guidelines, than to cede the field to unregulated actors.

In conclusion, the case for continued military genetic enhancement research rests on three pillars: strategic necessity, ethical feasibility, and broader social benefit. Nations have both the right and the responsibility to defend themselves effectively. Genetic enhancement, conducted ethically, offers significant defensive advantages while potentially yielding medical breakthroughs for civilian populations. The alternative—abandoning research due to vague fears—serves neither military nor humanitarian interests. The path forward requires courage to embrace new capabilities while maintaining the ethical standards that define civilized nations. That's the true test of leadership in the 21st century.
