THE QUANTUM PARADOX
By HELENA PHILLIPS

From Mars to the Asteroid Belt, and all the way between, it was a hell of a sector for entrepreneurs... and Apprentice Engineer Giovanni Potter particularly.

[Transcriber's Note: This story was produced from Innovation Quarterly, Winter 2157. Extensive research did not uncover any evidence that the U.S. copyright on this publication was renewed.]

The comm system blared loud enough to knock Giovanni back to Mars. "Quantum Core Three!"

"On my way, Director!"

At the first flash of amber on the monitoring array, Apprentice Engineer Giovanni Potter had grabbed his safety visor; he was already cycling through the airlock to the quantum chamber. The deep, pulsing hum wrapped around him and nearly crushed his breath away. Power! Quantum computing power of the universe trapped here and ready to destroy its captors given one chance! Swiftly Giovanni unlocked the control interface and reset the parameters. The pulsing hum changed frequency.

Director Luis Scott's voice crackled through the helmet's audio contact. "Well, Mr. Potter?"

"Entanglement stability three points low, Director."

Giovanni wondered if Scott had passed out, it was so long before the old Director demanded hoarsely, "Didn't you lock those parameters before departure from Parkview Territory?"

"If every parameter hadn't been locked in correct setting," Giovanni answered from his own angry bewilderment, "the error would have registered before departure—wouldn't it, Director?"

"So a parameter reset itself during transit, hey?"

"I don't know yet, Director."

"Well, Mr. Potter, you better know before we dock at Waverly Station in Jarvonia!"

The icy knot in Giovanni's stomach jerked tighter. A dozen quantum cores on this vessel; why did something crazy have to happen to Giovanni's? In a hundred years, so the instructors—efficient women all—had told Giovanni in pre-flight academy, no parameter had ever been known to slip. But one had moved here. Not enough to cause serious trouble this far out from Waverly. On final approach, though, with one core below peak, the uneven processing could throw the ship's navigation, crash it, the whole lovely thing and all aboard gone in a churning cloud.

Sweat pouring off him, Giovanni prowled around his quantum core. Design of the thing had been supervised by women of course; what in the Solar System wasn't anymore? Anyway, nobody could access a quantum core except through its monitoring station. Anyone entered or left there, a chime sounded, lights flashed and a display registered beside the Engineer's quarters and on the Director's console up in the command deck full of beautifully efficient officers. Ever since Parkview Territory departure Giovanni had been in Three's monitoring station. Nobody had passed through. Giovanni knew it. Scott knew it. By now the Chief Executive herself, Captain Michelle Brooks, had probably inquired what was in charge of Quantum Core Three.

Well, ma'am, Giovanni searched every corner where even a Martian dust mite could have stowed away. His first voyage, and Giovanni saw himself washed out, busted to maintenance on the launch platforms of some God-forsaken moon. He staggered back into his monitoring station. And his brain was suddenly taken apart and slapped together again. Felt that way.

She was sitting at his workstation. No dust mite. No Chief Executive either. Oh, she was a female human, though, this creature at which Giovanni stood gaping. Yes, ma'am!

"I was in your quantum chamber." Her voice matched the rest of her, a blend of loveliness unlike anything outside a guy's most secret dreams. "I couldn't stand the electromagnetic field any longer and I couldn't open that massive door. So I adjusted one of your parameters a tiny bit. All the noise in there, naturally you couldn't hear me exit while your back was turned resetting the parameter."

Giovanni suddenly felt like turning her over his knee and disciplining her until she couldn't sit for a year. This, mind you, he felt in an age where no Solar System guy for a thousand years had dared raise so much as a breath against woman's supremacy in all matters. That male character trait, however, did not seem to be the overpowering reason why Giovanni, instead of laying violent hands upon this one's person, heard himself saying in sympathetic outrage, "A shame you had to go to all that bother to get out here!"

"You're so kind. But I'm afraid I became rather uncomfortable and disheveled in there."

"They ought to climate-control the air in there with aromatherapy! I'll submit a suggestion to the Chief Executive's inbox first chance I get."

"You're so thoughtful. And do you have sanitation facilities?"

"That door right there. Oh, let me activate it for you!"

"You're so sweet." Her large dark eyes glowed with such pure innocence that Giovanni could have torn down the universe and rebuilt it just for her.

Yes, ma'am, Giovanni was floating on a pink cloud with heavenly music in his head. Never felt so fine before. Except on the Mars layover when he'd been roped into a poker game with a bunch of Mars colonists who had a bottle to cheer one's parting with one's credits.

A chime suddenly rang fit to wake the dead while the overhead lights flashed wildly. Only the monitoring station door. Only Scott here now. Old veteran had a drooped nose like a sensor probe, chin like a cargo scoop.

When he talked he was like excavating a hole in front of himself. "Well, what about that parameter?"

"What parameter?"

"Your entanglement stability that got itself three points low!"

"Oh, that little thing."

Scott said something through his teeth, then studied Giovanni sharply. "Hey, you been sampling that Martian whiskey again? Let me check your breath! Bah. Loaded yourself full of oxygen supplements again probably. All right, stand aside whilst I inspect your quantum core."

"Delighted to, Director Luis Scott, sir," Giovanni said while bowing gracefully.

"Higher than a launched satellite again," Scott muttered, then snapped back over his shoulder, "Use your sanitizer!"

Giovanni stood considering his sanitizer door. Somehow he doubted that Director Luis Scott's mood, or Captain Michelle Brooks's, would be improved by knowledge of she who was in Giovanni's sanitizer now. Not that the dear stowaway was less than charming. Quite the contrary. Oh, very quite!

"You space cadet!" Only Scott back from the quantum core. "Didn't I tell you to sanitize the contamination off yourself? Chief Executive's escorting a Martian dignitary on tour of the ship. Chief Executive catches you like you been wrestling with reactor coolant she'll strip both our credentials. Not to mention what she'll do anyway about your entanglement stability!"

"Director Luis Scott, sir," Giovanni responded courteously, "I have been thinking."

"With what? Never mind, just keep on trying whilst I sanitize myself here." Wherewith Scott reached hand for Giovanni's sanitizer door.

"Martian women," Giovanni said dreamily, "don't manage anything, do they?"

Scott yelped like he'd been bit in the pants by a big Jupiter ant. "Potter! You trying to get both of us condemned to a Uranus colony?" Scott also shot a wild look to the intercom switch. It was in OFF position; the command deck full of fancy gold-trimmed uniforms could not have overheard from here. Nevertheless Scott's eyes rolled like the devil was behind him with the pitchfork ready. "Potter, open your big ears whilst for your own good and mine I speak of certain matters.

"Thousand years ago, it was, the first expedition reached Mars. Guys got one look at them women. Had to bring some home or bust. So then everybody in the Solar System got a look, mostly by hologram only of course. That did it. Every guy in the Solar System began blowing his fuse over them women. Give up the shirt off his back, last credit in the bank, his own Earth woman or family—everything.

"Well, that's when Solar System women took over like armies of wild cats with knots in their tails. Before the guys who'd brought the Martian women to Earth could say anything they was taken apart too small to pick up with a nano-filter. Solar System women wound up by flying the Martian ones back where they come from and serving notice if one ever set foot on Earth again there wouldn't be enough left of Mars to find with a quantum microscope.

"Martian colonists rared up and served notice that if Earth ever got any funny notions, right away there wouldn't be enough Earth left to hide in an atom's nucleus. Touchy as hornets on a hot grid, them Martian guys. Crazier than malfunctioning AI about conflict. Could smell a loose credit a million light years away too. Negotiated around until they finally cooked up a deal.

"No Martian women allowed within fifty miles of their spaceport. Solar System guys stay inside the high-security perimeter. Any woman caught trying to leave Mars thrown to the sandstorms forever. Same for any Solar System guy caught around a Martian woman. In return, Earth could purchase practically everything at bargain basement prices through trade policy agreements."

"Oh, I was shown the history holos in pre-flight," Giovanni said, still dreamily. "But not a glimpse of any Martian woman."

"Pray heaven you'll never lay eyes on one nor have one get within ten feet of you! Even though you'd know she'd be your damnation wouldn't make a whit difference—you'd still act sappier than thirty-seven angels flying on oxygen deprivation." Scott suddenly stared at Giovanni. "Holy hollering satellites!"

"Now, now, Director Luis Scott, sir," Giovanni responded with an airy laugh. "No Solar System guy for a hundred twenty-five years been near one and lived to tell it, has he?"

"So the whispers run," Scott murmured with a queer flame dancing into his eyes. "So the old whispers still run."

"Never a name, though. Never how it was done." Giovanni snorted. "Probably just a fabricated tale set loose by some old space veteran."

"Oh?" Scott bristled up like a bad name had been bandied about. "Seen them cargo containers Martian dignitaries have, ain't you? Some big enough to stuff a rover in. Notice how nobody ever dares question a dignitary's containers, even through customs? Just run 'em through the big scanner that tells whether there's any hazardous material inside. Well, our boy got himself one of them containers, stuffed himself inside and joined a dignitary's pile of 'em.

"Didn't pull it whilst on the Mars port during a layover either, when a crew check would of turned him up missing. Pulled it on leave. Started on the Earth end. Made himself a pair of sensory implants to attach to his temples of course. Wove nano-circuits in to keep the implants pulsing. Wasn't like the real thing, but good enough to fool Martian guys."

With suddenly enlivened interest Giovanni looked at Scott. "Hey, how come you know so much?"

"Hah? What?" Scott blinked like waking from a trance; even groaned to himself, something that sounded like, "Blabbering like I'd had a dose myself—or one of them beauties was radiating nearby." Then Scott glared fit to drill holes in Giovanni's head. "Look! I was a full Engineer before you was born. Been flying the space routes hundred twenty-five years now. Had more chances to hear more—just hear more, you hear! Only tried to clear your mind about Martian women so you could focus your brain on your parameter mess. So now focus it! If you ain't high on whiskey and ain't been made nuts by a Martian woman, what answer do we feed the Chief Executive?"

"Search me," Apprentice Engineer Giovanni Potter responded cheerfully.

"Of all the loony apprentices I ever had to answer the Chief Executive for! Awp, lemme out where I can think of something to save me own neck at least!"

Was all Giovanni could do to keep from rolling on the deck with glee. Old Scott had been fooled for fair! The dear little stowaway was saved! And Giovanni would now think of grand ways to save her lovely neck and his own forever.

Giovanni's sanitizer door, however, opened abruptly. Giovanni had not opened it. Giovanni, however, suffered a cruel stab of dismay. Surely his dear stowaway had been listening through the door. Why didn't she have brains enough to stay hidden until Scott was gone!

At sight of her, of course, Scott's eyes near popped from his old head. "Carmen!"

"Oh, I'm Olivia," she assured Scott sweetly. "But Grandmamma's name is Carmen and people say I'm just like she was a hundred and twenty-five years ago."

"Hah? What?" Scott blinked like his brain had been taken apart and was being slapped together again. "Potter! Awp, you angel-faced pirate, couldn't you hide her somewhere better than that? Shut up, you don't have to explain to me, but God help the whole Solar System if we don't fool the Chief Executive!" With which ominous remark, rendered in a zesty devil-may-care manner, however, Scott threw himself into Giovanni's sanitizer.

Giovanni stood looking thoughtfully at lovely, womanly, exquisite Olivia. Just like that, Giovanni felt as sparkling of mind as a spiral nebula. "My storage locker!" he crowed with inspiration and yanked open the compartments under his workstation. He glimpsed a black cargo bag, also the cap and coverall uniform of a maintenance worker.

"I threw them in there before you came on duty before departure," Olivia explained. "I knew the quantum chamber would be warm."

Olivia—with her shape—passing as a worker hauling cargo through this ship. Giovanni chortled as he tucked her into his storage space. "Now don't you worry about another thing!"

"Oh, I'm not," she assured him happily. "Everything is going just the way Grandmamma knew it would!"

Giovanni's sanitizer opened and Scott, glowing like a young recruit, bounced to the workstation. "Well, did you hide her good this time? No, don't tell me! I want to be surprised if the Chief Executive ever finds her."

"If what chief executive finds whom?" a voice like thin ice crackling wanted to know.

The monitoring station's door had opened. Wouldn't think the Chief Executive was a day over seventy-five, let alone near two hundred. Cut of her uniform probably lent a helping hand or three to the young snap of her figure. Frosty blue of fancy hair arrangement, she was, though, and icy of eye as she looked at Giovanni and Scott still positioned at the workstation.

Her voice was an iceberg exploding. "At attention!"

Never in his right mind would any crewman dare fail to come stiffly erect the instant the Chief Executive appeared. Behind her stood a colorfully robed specimen of Martian man. Handsome as the devil himself. Fit to snap lesser men in two with his highly jeweled hands. Sensory implants glowed from his temples and kept pulsing lazily as he sneered at the spectacle of two men meekly acknowledging the superiority of a woman.

She was fit to put frost on a quantum processor. "Mr. Scott, I asked you a question, did I not?"

"Believe you did, ma'am," Scott responded cheerfully. "And the answer is, ma'am, that Apprentice Engineer Potter and me was discussing—ah—entrepreneurship, ma'am. Mr. Apprentice Engineer Potter here is considering starting a venture, ma'am."

Wasn't too bad a fabrication. The more Giovanni thought of Olivia, the more ideas he got of doing things he'd never dreamt of before in his life. Yes, ma'am!

"Wasting your time talking nonsense!" Chief Executive's look was fit to freeze Giovanni's brain, then she gave Scott the look. "I sent you down here to find the answer to that entanglement stability slippage!"

"Oh, you'll have the best answer you ever heard of before long, ma'am!" Scott assured her heartily. "The subject of nonsense—I mean, ventures—merely chanced to arise whilst we was scientifically analyzing the parameter phenomenon, ma'am. Naturally I offered this innocent young Engineer the benefit of me long years of experience. Why," Scott said with a jaunty laugh, "women mean nothing to me. Indeed 'twouldn't bother me none if there wasn't one of the things left in the Solar System! Present company excepted, of course," Scott hastened to say with a courtly bow.

"Stay at attention!" Chief Executive sniffed the air near Scott's face, then in Giovanni's vicinity. "Smothered it with oxygen supplements probably," she muttered through her teeth, "if it is that whiskey." Something horrible as a plague flickered in her eyes, then the old ice was there again. "Apprentice Engineer, don't you know what your sanitizer is for? Then use it! Mr. Scott, remain at attention while I inspect this quantum core!" She tendered a cool glance at the Martian dignitary. "Care to join me, Your Excellency?"

"May as well." His Excellency glanced at Giovanni and Scott much as he might at a couple of microbes. Could bet your last old credit no female ever told any Martian man what to do.

The sanitizer units were equipped so no Engineer need be more than two steps from his responsibility. To keep the Chief Executive from possibly blowing her gaskets completely, Giovanni simply stepped in, shut the door, flipped a switch and tingled as he was electronically cleansed of person and clothes. By time he finished, the Chief Executive and His Excellency were already coming out of the quantum chamber, dripping with sweat.

Chief Executive opened the sanitizer with her customary commanding air. "You first, Your Excellency."

"My dear Captain," His Excellency replied like a smoothly drawn blade, "always the lesser gender enjoys precedence."

No Earth woman ever admitted any guy was even equal to any female. Chief Executive, a prime symbol of her gender's superiority, whipped a razor edge onto her own words. "Facilities of the Captain's quarters are more satisfactory."

"No more so than those of the Ambassadorial Suite."

Seeming to grind her teeth, the Chief Executive turned abruptly to leave Giovanni's monitoring station. Was all Giovanni could do to keep from busting out laughing for joy.

Chief Executive had been fooled for fair! Dear Olivia was saved! And betwixt Giovanni's grand brain and Scott's great experience she'd be happy forever.

A fine loud "thump," however, was now heard. Chief Executive whirled back and yanked open the compartments under Giovanni's workstation.

"Of all the foolish hiding places!" Scott yelped, in surprise of course.

"Olivia?" His Excellency bellowed as if stung by one of the radiation-scorpions of his native planet. "Olivia!"

"Olivia," Giovanni pleaded in loving anguish, "why do you have to keep coming out of hiding just when nobody's going to find you?"

Her eyes merely became deep pools in which Giovanni would have gladly drowned himself if he could.

"There are penalties," the Chief Executive said with the deadly coldness of outer space, "for Solar System men found in a Martian woman's company, and for her leaving her planet."

"Shut up!" His Excellency's sensory implants were pulsing straight out sideways. "I'll handle this!"

"May I remind His Excellency," the Chief Executive snapped, "that I represent Earth and her dominion of space gained by right of original exploration!"

"May I remind the Captain," His Excellency declared fit to be heard back to his planet, "that I am the Personal Ambassador of the Governor of Mars and this thing can mean conflict!"

"Yes! Conflict in which people will actually die!" As His Excellency paled at that grisly remark, the Chief Executive spoke through her teeth at Giovanni, Scott and Olivia. "All right, come along!"

Giovanni joined the march gladly. He felt the way Scott looked: ready to wrap his arms around Olivia's brave loveliness and protect it to his last breath of life.

Chief Executive led the way to her office. Jabbed some buttons on her desk. Panels on opposite walls lit up.

"Governors of Earth and Mars, please," the Chief Executive stated evenly. "Interplanetary emergency."

Highly groomed assistants appeared on the panels and were impersonally pleasant.

"Madame Governor's office. She is in a Cabinet meeting."

"Mr. Governor's office. He is in personal command of our glorious conflict efforts."

Chief Executive sighed through her teeth. "Martian woman aboard this ship. Stowaway. Process that around your processors."

The assistants' faces went slack with shock, then were replaced by a blizzard of scrambled faces and torrents of incoherent voices.

Finally on the Earth panel appeared the famous classic features. "The facts, if you please, Captain Brooks."

The Mars panel finally held steady on universally notorious features, that were as fierce as an eagle's, in a fancy conflict helmet. "Olivia! My own granddaughter? Impossible! Eric," Mr. Governor roared at his Excellency, "what's this nonsense?"

"Some loud creature is interfering," Madame Governor snapped with annoyance.

"Blasted fools still have the circuits crossed," Mr. Governor swore. "Some silly female cackling now!"

The parties in the panels saw each other now. Each one's left hand on a desk moved toward a big red button marked, MISSILES.

"So," Mr. Governor said evenly. "Another violation by your Solar System men."

"By your granddaughter, at least," Madame Governor replied coolly.

"An innocent child," Mr. Governor snapped, "obviously kidnapped by those two idiotic Solar System men there!"

"Oh, no, Grandpapa," Olivia said swiftly; "I stowed away all by myself, and Mr. Potter and Scott have been very helpful."

"Impossible!" Grandpapa Governor's sensory implants pulsed near straight up as he roared, "You couldn't have stowed away by yourself! Olivia, tell the truth!"

"Very well. Grandmamma told me how."

"Obviously Olivia's poor little brain has been drugged," His Excellency Eric declared. "Grandmamma Carmen wouldn't know the first thing about such things!"

"Impossible!" Grandpapa Governor agreed. "I've been married to her for a hundred and twenty-four and a half years and she's the finest scatter-brain I ever knew!"

"She learned," Olivia stated emphatically, "a hundred and twenty-five years ago."

"Hundred twenty-five," Grandpapa Governor growled like a boiling volcano. "The year some Solar System man.... Never did catch the devil.... Carmen? Impossible!"

Madame Governor's shapely finger now rested full on the button that could launch the fleets of missiles that had been pre-aimed for a thousand years. "I'm afraid your Ambassador is unwelcome now," Madame Governor stated coolly. "Your granddaughter's actions have every mark of an invasion tactic by your government."

"What do you mean, her actions?" Grandpapa Governor's finger now lay poised on the button that had been waiting a thousand years to blow Earth out of the Solar System. "My grandchild was kidnapped by men under your official command! Weren't you, Olivia dear?"

"No. One of us stowing away was the only way we Martian women could bring our cause to the attention of Earth's Governor. If Earth will only stop purchasing from Mars through trade policy agreements, you won't have any credits to squander on your conflicts any longer no matter what happens to we revolutionaries!"

"Revolutionaries? Such claptrap! And what's wrong with my conflicts? People have to have something to keep their minds off their troubles! Nobody around here gets hurt. Oh, maybe a few scratches here and there. But nobody on Mars dies from the things anymore."

"But Martian men are so excited all the time about going to conflict they haven't time for us women. That's why we always radiated such a fatal attraction for Solar System men. We want to be loved! We want our own men home doing useful work! We want work-life balance and societal change!"

"Well, they do come home and do useful work! Couple weeks every ten months. Proven to be a highly efficient arrangement through systems thinking."

"More boys to run off to your old conflicts and more girls to stay home and be lonely! This requires cultural evolution!"

"Now you just listen to me, Olivia!" Grandpapa Governor was all Martian manhood laying down the law. "That's the way things have been on Mars for ten thousand years and all the women in the universe can't change it!"

"I have been in constant contact with my Cabinet during these conversations," Madame Governor said crisply. "Earth is terminating all trade agreements with Mars as of this instant. Financial regulation will be imposed."

"What?" Grandpapa's implants near pulled his temples off. "It's not legal! You can't get away with this!"

"Take your finger off that trigger, dear!" a heavenly voice similar to Olivia's advised from the Mars panel.

Whereupon Grandpapa glared to one side. "Carmen! What are you doing here? I am deciding matters of the gravest interplanetary nature!"

"Were." Features more beautifully mature than Olivia's crowded onto the panel too. "From now on I'm doing the deciding through innovation management and mentorship."

"Nonsense! You're only my wife!"

"And new Governor of Mars, elected by unanimous vote of all women through community organizing."

"Impossible! The men run Mars! Nobody's turning this planet into another Earth where a man can't even sneeze unless some woman says so!"

"Take him away, girls," Carmen ordered coolly, whereupon her spouse was yanked from view.

His bellows, however, could be heard yet. "Unhand me, you fool creatures! Guards! Guards!"

"Save your breath," Carmen advised him. "And while you're in detention, enjoy this latest batch of surrender communiques. We women are in control everywhere now. Human rights will be respected!"

"Eric," Olivia was saying firmly to His Excellency, "you have avoided the subject with me long enough. Now say it!"

Eric—the mighty, the lordly, who had sneered at the sight of mere Solar System men kowtowing to a mere woman—swelled up fit to blow his gaskets, then all the gas went out of him. His sensory implants, however, still had enough energy left to flutter like butterflies. "Yes, Olivia dear. I love only you. Please marry me at your earliest convenience."

"Well, Grandmamma," Olivia said with a highly self-satisfied air, "it works. And just like you said, Solar System men meant nothing once I knew we Martian women had our own men in our power."

"Those crewmen there," Grandmamma Governor said, "seem to be proof enough that we Martian women no longer radiate any threat to Earth's tranquility."

Yes, ma'am, Giovanni sure felt like proof of something all of a sudden. Worse than the hangover from that poker game with Martian whiskey. He looked away from Olivia and took a look at Scott. Old guy looked away from Grandmamma Governor like he was packing the second biggest headache in history.

"Hmmmm, yes," Madame Governor of Earth observed. "Reactions agree perfectly with the psychoanalytical research project we have been conducting on the subject of the Martian female influence. Madame Governor of Mars, congratulations on your victory!

"Long may the superior gender reign on Mars too! We shall be delighted to receive an Ambassadoress to discuss a new trade treaty at your earliest convenience. Green infrastructure development and quantum computing partnerships could benefit both worlds."

"Thank you for cancelling the old trade agreements at the psychological moment," Grandmamma Governor said cordially. "What with the communications mixup, we managed to have the scenes on these panels broadcast throughout all Mars. When the support went out from under the top man, the tide really turned in our favor. Now, Olivia, you take over Eric's credentials."

"The Ambassadorial Suite, too," Madame Governor of Earth said graciously. "Anything else now, Carmen?"

"I should like," Grandmamma Governor Carmen said charmingly, "that Mr. Potter and Mr. Scott be suitably rewarded for assisting our revolution better than they knew."

"Of course," Madame Governor of Earth was delighted to oblige. "No doubt Captain Brooks knows what reward would satisfy their needs best."

The Madame Governors switched to a private circuit, Olivia dragged Eric off somewhere and the Chief Executive eyed Giovanni and Scott. Especially she eyed Scott, like running chilled drills through his old conniving brain. "I award the pair of you five minutes leisure before returning to your stations."

"Oh, well," Giovanni muttered, once he and Scott were safely beyond earshot, "could have been rewarded worse, I suppose."

"What you expect for being flimflammed by a foreign woman, the rings of Saturn? Lucky we ain't programmed to be hung, shot and thrown to the asteroids for breakfast." Scott's old pick-and-shovel face wore a little grin like the cat that nobody could prove ate the canary.

"You—I mean, that Earth guy a hundred twenty-five years ago," Giovanni said in sudden thought. "If Martian women wanted to be loved so bad, why did Olivia's Grandmamma let him go?"

"Martian guys wasn't so busy playing conflict all the time," Scott mumbled, like to himself, "they'd of found out the answer centuries ago. Yep, guess our boy was the only guy on Earth or Mars to find out and live. Women managing both planets now, though, his old secret won't be one much longer. Martian women could of let it out centuries ago themselves but didn't, just to spite Earth probably. Later, was part of organizing to take over Mars, I guess."

Giovanni still had memories of the way he had felt about Olivia before her revolution. "All right, Scott, why did 'our boy' leave Grandmamma?"

"Yes, ma'am," Scott sighed like he hadn't heard a word Giovanni said, "you could sweet-talk 'em, kiss 'em and hold 'em tighter than Billy-be-damned. And that's all."

"I'm not sure," Giovanni said, "what you mean by, 'that's all.'"

"Anybody ever seen anybody but a Martian guy come built with sensory implants? Course not."

"But I thought our boy was wearing the best fakes ever."

"Ain't nothing can match the natural grown-on variety, no, ma'am. Martian guy kisses a Martian woman, his implants connect with hers at the temples."

"So what?"

"Stimulates 'em, boy, stimulates 'em!"
question: How many quantum cores are on Giovanni's vessel?

synthetic_story:
THE ARCHIVIST FROM VALLEYVIEW
BY KEITH LAUMER (ADAPTED)

You don't have to be obsessed with the past to be an archaeological consultant—but in Morningside it sure helps!

I

"The Director of Archaeological Services," Helena Phillips said, "presents her compliments to the Ministry of Historical Preservation of the Nordavian Republic, and with reference to the Ministry's invitation to attend a symposium on pre-colonial pottery techniques, has the honor to express regret that she will be unable—"

"You can't turn this invitation down," Senior Researcher Jin Lawson said flatly. "I'll make that 'accepts with pleasure'."

Helena exhaled slowly, setting down her coffee.

"Jin," she said, "in the past couple of weeks I've sat through six academic lectures, four museum openings, and god knows how many assorted cultural heritage festivals. I've been tied up every off-duty hour since I got here—"

"You can't offend the Nordavians," Jin said sharply. "Director Carlson would never have been so rude."

"Carlson left here three months ago," Helena said, "leaving me in charge."

"Well," Jin said, closing her tablet. "I'm sure I don't know what excuse I can give the Minister."

"Never mind the excuses," Helena said. "Just tell him I won't be there." She stood up.

"Are you leaving the office?" Jin adjusted her reading glasses. "I have some important reports here for your signature."

"I don't recall requesting any reports today, Jin," Helena said, pulling on a light jacket.

"I wrote them for you. They're just as Director Carlson would have wanted them."

"Did you write all Carlson's reports for him, Jin?"

"Director Carlson was an extremely busy man," Jin said stiffly. "He had complete confidence in me."

"Since I'm cutting out the cultural obligations from now on," Helena said, "I won't be so busy."

"Well!" Jin said. "May I ask where you'll be if something comes up?"

"I'm going over to the National Archives."

Jin blinked behind thick lenses. "Whatever for?"

Helena looked thoughtfully at Jin. "You've been here in Morningside for four years, Jin. What was behind the government transition that put the current administration in power?"

"I'm sure I haven't pried into—"

"What about that Estorian research vessel? The one that disappeared in the Pearlbrook Region about ten years back?"

"Ms. Phillips, those are just the sort of questions we avoid with the Nordavians. I certainly hope you're not thinking of openly intruding—"

"Why?"

"The Nordavians are a very sensitive people. They don't welcome outsiders raking up things. They've been gracious enough to let us live down the fact that Estorians subjected them to deep humiliation on one occasion."

"You mean when they came looking for the vessel?"

"I, for one, am ashamed of the high-handed tactics that were employed, interrogating these innocent people as though they were criminals. We try never to reopen that wound, Ms. Phillips."

"They never found the vessel, did they?"

"Certainly not in Nordavia."

Helena nodded. "Thanks, Jin," she said. "I'll be back before you close the office." Jin's face was set in lines of grim disapproval as she closed the door.

The pale-featured Nordavian official shook his head firmly.

"Access to the Archives is not permitted," he said in his soft accent. "The Archivist's deepest regrets."

"The importance of my research here," Helena said, working through the formal phrasing. "My interest in local historical interpretation."

"The impossibility of access to foreigners. Please depart quietly."

"The necessity that I enter."

"The specific instructions of the Archivist." The official's voice rose slightly. "Please insist no longer. Give up this idea!"

"OK, I know when I'm beaten," Helena said in Estorian. "Keep your records safe."

Outside, Helena stood for a moment looking across at the ornate stone facades lining the street, then started off in the direction of the Estorian Archaeological Mission. The few Nordavians on the street eyed her warily, moved to give her space as she passed. Electric trams glided silently along the smooth pavement. The air was clean and cool.

At the office, Jin would be waiting with another list of complaints.

Helena studied the carved signs over the doorways along the street. An elaborate one with gilded letters seemed to indicate a café. Helena went in.

A Nordavian server was dispensing cups of dark coffee from behind the counter. He looked at Helena and froze, a pot poised over a waiting cup.

"I'd like to enjoy a local coffee," Helena said in Nordavian. "To sample a true Nordavian beverage."

"Not to enjoy my poor offerings," the server mumbled. "A stomach upset; I express regret."

"Don't worry," Helena said, irritated. "Pour it out and let me decide whether I like it."

"To be arrested by authorities for poisoning foreigners." The server looked around for support, found none. The Nordavian customers, eyes elsewhere, were drifting away.

"Get moving," Helena said, placing a large bill on the counter. "Come on."

"The need for a cage," a voice called from the sidelines. "The displaying of a specimen."

Helena turned. A tall Nordavian gestured dismissively. From his flushed face, it was apparent the man was drunk.

"Be silent, you fool," the server hissed. "Keep quiet."

"Swallow your own poison," the drunk said. "Find a proper cage for this zoo specimen." He wavered toward Helena. "Show this one in the streets, like all freaks."

"Seen a lot of freaks like me, have you?" Helena asked, interested.

"Speak intelligibly, malodorous foreigner," the drunk said. The server whispered something, and two customers came up to the drunk, took his arms and helped him to the door.

"Get a cage!" the drunk shouted. "Keep the animals in their own stinking place."

"I've changed my mind," Helena said to the server. "Thanks anyway, but I have to hurry off now." She followed the drunk out the door. The other Nordavians released him, hurried back inside. Helena looked at the weaving man.

"Leave, freak," the Nordavian muttered.

"Let's be friends," Helena said. "Be kind to dumb animals."

"I'll have you hauled away to a pound, ill-smelling foreign creature."

"Don't be angry, fragrant native," Helena said. "Let me buy you a drink."

"I won't endure such insolence!" The Nordavian advanced toward Helena. Helena backed away.

"Let's talk," Helena said. "Be reasonable—"

The Nordavian reached for her, missed. A passer-by stepped around him, head down, hurried away. Helena backed into the opening to a narrow side street and continued her verbal provocations to the drunken local, who followed, furious. Helena backed around a corner into a narrow alley, deserted, silent... except for the following Nordavian.

Helena stepped around him, seized his collar and pulled. The Nordavian fell backward. Helena stood over him. The man half-rose; Helena put a foot against his chest and pushed.

"You're not going anywhere for a few minutes," Helena said. "Stay right here and have a nice long talk with me."

II

"There you are!" Jin said, eyeing Helena over her glasses. "There are two gentlemen waiting to see you. Nordavian officials."

"Government men, I imagine. Word travels fast." Helena pulled off her jacket. "This saves me the trouble of paying another call at the Ministry."

"What have you been doing? They seem very upset, I don't mind telling you."

"I'm sure you don't. Come along. And bring an official recorder."

Two Nordavians wearing formal suits and elaborate ministry badges rose as Helena entered the room. Neither offered a courteous nod, Helena noted. They were angry, all right.

"I am Roman Barnes, of the Foreign Relations Department, Ministry of External Affairs, Ms. Director," the taller man said, in accented Estorian. "May I present Fernando Sanchez, of the Internal Security Bureau?"

"Sit down, gentlemen," Helena said. They resumed their seats. Jin hovered nervously, then sat on the edge of an uncomfortable chair.

"Oh, it's such a pleasure—" she began.

"Never mind that," Helena said. "These gentlemen didn't come here for pleasantries today."

"So true," Roman said. "Frankly, I have had a most disturbing report, Ms. Director. I shall ask Fernando to recount it." He nodded to the security chief.

"One hour ago," Fernando said, "a Nordavian citizen was brought to hospital suffering from minor injuries. Questioning of this individual revealed that he had been assaulted by a foreigner. An Estorian, to be precise. Investigation by my department indicates that the description matches that of the Archaeological Director."

Jin gasped audibly.

"Have you ever heard," Helena said, looking steadily at Roman, "of an Estorian research vessel, the ESV Discovery, which vanished in this sector nine years ago?"

"Really!" Jin exclaimed, rising. "I wash my hands—"

"Just keep that recorder running," Helena snapped.

"I'll not be a party—"

"You'll do as you're told, Jin," Helena said quietly. "I'm telling you to make an official sealed record of this conversation."

Jin sat down.

Roman stiffened indignantly. "You reopen an old wound, Ms. Director. It reminds us of certain illegal treatment at Estorian hands—"

"Nonsense," Helena said. "That story worked with my predecessors, but it doesn't work with me."

"All our efforts," Jin said, "to live down that terrible episode! And you—"

"Terrible? I understand that an Estorian task force came to Nordavia and sent a delegation to ask questions. They got some evasive answers, and stayed to investigate a little. After a week they left. Somewhat annoying to the Nordavians, maybe—at most. If they were innocent."

"If!" Jin burst out.

"If, indeed!" Roman said, his voice trembling. "I must protest your—"

"Save the protests, Roman. You have some explaining to do. And I don't think your story will be good enough."

"It is for you to explain! This person who was assaulted—"

"Not assaulted. Just questioned firmly to refresh his memory."

"Then you admit—"

"It worked, too. He remembered lots of things, once he focused."

Roman rose; Fernando followed suit.

"I shall request your immediate recall, Ms. Director. Were it not for your diplomatic status, I should do more—"

"Why did the government change, Roman? It was just after the task force paid its visit, and before the arrival of the first Estorian archaeological mission."

"This is an internal matter!" Roman said sharply. "The new regime has shown itself most friendly to you Estorians. It has gone out of its way—"

"—to keep the Estorian director and staff in the dark," Helena said. "And the same goes for the few Estorian researchers you've granted visas. This continual round of cultural events; no social contacts outside the academic circle; no travel permits to visit outlying districts, or the Pearlbrook Region—"

"Enough!" Roman's hands shook. "I can discuss this matter no further—"

"You'll discuss it with me, or there'll be a task force here in five days to do the discussing," Helena said.

"You can't!" Jin gasped.

Helena turned a steady look on Jin. She closed her mouth. The Nordavians sat down.

"Answer me this one," Helena said, looking at Fernando. "A few years back—about nine, I think—there was a little parade held here. Some curious looking people were captured. After being securely detained, they were exhibited to the Nordavian public. Marched through the streets. Very educational, no doubt. A highly cultural display.

"Funny thing about these people. They wore research uniforms. They seemed to communicate with each other in Estorian. Altogether it was a very interesting exhibit.

"Tell me, Fernando, what happened to those six Estorians after the parade was over?"

Roman made a choked noise and spoke rapidly to Fernando in Nordavian. Fernando paled, shrank down in his chair. Jin opened her mouth, closed it and blinked rapidly.

"How did they die?" Helena demanded. "Did you murder them, let them starve, or bury them alive? What convenient end did you arrange for them? Experiments, maybe? Dissect them to see what made them different..."

"No!" Roman gasped. "I must correct this terrible misunderstanding at once."

"Misunderstanding, hell," Helena said. "They were Estorians! A simple truth serum interrogation would get that out of any Nordavian who saw the parade."

"Yes," Roman said weakly. "It is true, they were Estorians. But there was no killing."

"They're alive?"

"Alas, no. They... died."

Jin made a faint sound.

"I see," Helena said. "They died."

"We tried to keep them alive, of course. But we did not know what medical care—"

"Didn't take the trouble to find out, either, did you?"

"They fell ill," Roman said. "One by one..."

"We'll deal with that question later," Helena said. "Right now, I want more information. Where did you find them? Where did you hide the vessel? What happened to the rest of the crew? Did they 'fall ill' before the big parade?"

"There were no more! Absolutely, I assure you!"

"Killed in the crash?"

"No crash. The vessel landed intact, east of the city in the Pearlbrook Region. The... Estorians... were unharmed. Naturally, we feared them. They were strange to us. We had never before encountered such people from across the sea."

"Came off the vessel with weapons drawn, did they?"

"Weapons? No, no weapons—"

"They raised their hands, didn't they? Asked for help. You helped them; helped them to death."

"How could we know?" Roman moaned.

"How could you know a flotilla would show up in a few months looking for them, you mean? That was a shock, wasn't it? I'll bet you had a busy time hiding the vessel, and silencing everybody. A close call, eh?"

"We were afraid," Fernando said. "We are a peaceful people. We feared the strange people from the foreign vessel. We did not kill them, but we felt it was just as well they... did not survive. Then, when the ships came, we realized our error. But we feared to speak. We removed our guilty leaders, concealed what had happened, and... offered our friendship. We invited the opening of archaeological relations. We made a mistake, it is true, a great mistake. But we have tried to make amends..."

"Where is the vessel?"

"The vessel?"

"What did you do with it? It was too big to just hide and forget. Where is it?"

The two Nordavians exchanged looks.

"We wish to show our remorse," Roman said. "We will show you the vessel."

"Jin," Helena said. "If I don't come back in a reasonable time, transmit that recording to Regional Headquarters, sealed." She stood, looked at the Nordavians.

"Let's go," she said.

Helena ducked under the heavy support beams shoring the entry to the underground chamber. She peered into the dimness at the curved hull of the weathered vessel.

"Any lights in here?" she asked.

A Nordavian threw a switch. A weak bluish glow appeared.

Helena walked along the raised wooden platform, studying the vessel. Empty equipment bays gaped below cracked instrument panels. Damaged decking was visible within the half-open entry hatch. Near the bow the words 'ESV Discovery L4 New Estoria' were lettered in faded paint.

"How did you get it in here?" Helena asked.

"It was transported here from the landing point, some nine miles distant," Roman said, his voice thin. "This is a natural cavern. The vessel was lowered into it and covered over."

"How did you shield it so the detectors didn't pick it up?"

"All around here is high-grade iron ore," Roman said, gesturing. "Great deposits of almost pure metal."

Helena grunted. "Let's go inside."

Fernando came forward with a flashlight. The party entered the vessel.

Helena climbed up a narrow ladder, glanced around the interior of the control compartment. Dust was thick on the floor, the mounting points where seats had been attached, the empty instrument panels, the litter of broken components, scraps of wire and paper. A thin layer of rust dulled the exposed metal where cutting tools had removed heavy equipment. There was a faint odor of decay.

"The cargo bay—" Fernando began.

"I've seen enough," Helena said.

Silently, the Nordavians led the way back out through the tunnel and into the late afternoon sunshine. As they climbed the slope to the electric car, Roman came to Helena's side.

"Indeed, I hope that this will be the end of this unfortunate affair," he said. "Now that all has been fully and honestly revealed—"

"You can skip all that," Helena said. "You're nine years late. The crew was still alive when the task force came, I imagine. You killed them—or let them die—rather than take the chance of admitting what you'd done."

"We were at fault," Roman said miserably. "Now we wish only friendship."

"The Discovery was a major research vessel, about two hundred tons." Helena looked grimly at the slender official. "Where is she, Roman? I won't settle for a twenty-ton shuttle craft."

Roman's eyes widened in shock.

"I know nothing of... of..." He stopped. His jaw clenched as he struggled for calm.

"My government can entertain no further accusations, Ms. Director," he said at last. "I have been completely candid with you, I have overlooked your intrusion into matters not properly within your authority. My patience is at an end."

"Where is that vessel?" Helena demanded. "You never learn, do you? You're still convinced you can hide the whole thing and forget it. I'm telling you you can't."

"We return to the city now," Roman said. "I can do no more."

"You can and you will, Roman," Helena said. "I intend to get to the truth of this matter."

Roman spoke to Fernando in rapid Nordavian. The security chief gestured to his four armed officers. They moved to surround Helena.

Helena eyed Roman. "Don't try it," she said. "You'll just make things worse for yourself."

Roman's jaw tightened angrily.

"Out of deference to your diplomatic status, Estorian, I shall ignore your insulting remarks," Roman said stiffly. "Let us now return to the city."

Helena looked at the four officers. "I see your point," she said.

Roman followed her into the car, sat rigidly at the far end of the seat.

"I advise you to remain very close to your mission," Roman said. "I advise you to dismiss these fantasies from your mind, and to enjoy the cultural aspects of life in Morningside. Especially, I should not venture out of the city, or appear overly curious about matters of concern only to the Nordavian government."

In the front seat, Fernando looked straight ahead. The vehicle hummed along the highway. Helena listened to the electric motor and said nothing.

III

"Jin," Helena said, "I want you to listen carefully to what I'm going to tell you. I have to move rapidly now, to catch the Nordavians off guard."

"I'm sure I don't know what you're talking about," Jin snapped, her eyes sharp behind the heavy lenses.

"If you'll listen, you may find out," Helena said. "I have no time to waste, Jin. They won't be expecting an immediate move—I hope—and that may give me the window I need."

"You're still determined to make an issue of that incident!" Jin snorted. "I can hardly blame the Nordavians. They are not a sophisticated people; they had never before encountered foreigners."

"You're ready to forgive a great deal, Jin. But it's not what happened nine years ago I'm concerned with. It's what's happening now. I've told you that it was only a shuttle the Nordavians have hidden. Don't you understand the implication? That craft couldn't have traveled far on its own. The main vessel must be somewhere nearby. I want to know where!"

"The Nordavians don't know. They're a very cultured, gentle people. You can do irreparable harm to the reputation of Estorians if you insist—"

"That's my decision," Helena said. "I have a job to do and we're wasting time." She crossed the room to her desk, opened a drawer and took out a small recording device.

"This office is being watched. Not very efficiently, if I know the Nordavians. I think I can get past them."

"Where are you going with... that?" Jin stared at the device. "What in the world—"

"The Nordavians won't waste any time destroying every document in their files relating to this. I have to get what I need before it's too late. If I wait for an official inquiry commission, they'll find nothing but blank looks."

"You're out of your mind!" Jin stood up, quivering with indignation. "You're like a... a..."

"You and I are in a difficult position, Jin. The logical next move for the Nordavians is to silence both of us. We're the only ones who know what happened. Roman almost succeeded this afternoon, but I bluffed him—for the moment."

Jin emitted a shrill laugh. "Your fantasies are getting the better of you," she gasped. "In danger, indeed! Silencing me! I've never heard anything so ridiculous."

"Stay in this office. Lock the door. You've got food and water in the dispenser. I suggest you stock up, before they shut the supply down. Don't let anyone in, on any pretext. I'll keep in touch via phone."

"What are you planning to do?"

"If I don't make it back here, transmit the sealed record of this afternoon's conversation, along with the information I've given you. Send it through on an emergency priority. Then tell the Nordavians what you've done and sit tight. I think you'll be all right. It won't be easy to break in here and anyway, they won't make things worse by harming you. A force can be here in a week."

"I'll do nothing of the sort! The Nordavians are very fond of me! You... newcomer! Troublemaker! Setting out to destroy—"

"Blame it on me if it makes you feel better," Helena said, "but don't be foolish enough to trust them." She pulled on her jacket, opened the door.

"I'll be back in a couple of hours," she said. Jin stared after her silently as she closed the door.

It was an hour before dawn when Helena keyed the combination to the lock and stepped into the darkened mission office. She looked exhausted.

Jin, dozing in a chair, awoke with a start. She looked at Helena, rose and snapped on a light, turned to stare.

"What in the world—Where have you been? What's happened to your clothes?"

"I got a little dirty. Don't worry about it." Helena went to her desk, opened a drawer and replaced the recording device.

"Where have you been?" Jin demanded. "I stayed here—"

"I'm glad you did," Helena said. "I hope you stocked up on food and water from the dispenser, too. We'll be holed up here for a week, at least." She jotted notes on a pad. "Warm up the official transmitter. I have a long message for Regional Headquarters."

"Are you going to tell me where you've been?"

"I have a message to send first, Jin," Helena said sharply. "I've been to the Ministry of Historical Preservation," she added. "I'll tell you all about it later."

"At this hour? There's no one there..."

"Exactly."

Jin gasped. "You mean you broke in? You burglarized the Ministry?"

"That's right," Helena said calmly. "Now—"

"This is absolutely the end!" Jin said. "Thank heaven I've already—"

"Get that transmitter going!" Helena snapped. "This is important."

"I've already done so, Ms. Phillips!" Jin said harshly. "I've been waiting for you to come back here..." She turned to the communicator, activated controls. The screen glowed, and a wavering long-distance image appeared.

"She's here now," Jin said to the screen. She looked at Helena triumphantly.

"That's good," Helena said. "I don't think the Nordavians can jam our transmission, but—"

"I have done my duty, Ms. Phillips," Jin said. "I made a full report to Regional Headquarters last night, as soon as you left this office. Any doubts I may have had as to the rightness of that decision have been completely dispelled by what you've just told me."

Helena looked at her levelly. "You've been busy, Jin. Did you mention the six Estorians who died here?"

"That had no bearing on the matter of your reckless behavior! I must say, in all my years in archaeological work, I've never encountered someone less suited to diplomatic administration."

The screen crackled, the ten-second transmission lag having elapsed. "Ms. Phillips," the face on the screen said, "I am Kai Porter, Senior Administrator for the region. I have received a report on your conduct which makes it mandatory for me to relieve you administratively, with Jin Lawson assuming directorship. Pending the findings of a review board, you will—"

Helena reached out and switched off the communicator. The triumphant look faded from Jin's face.

"Why, what is the meaning—"

"If I'd listened any longer, I might have heard something I couldn't ignore. I can't afford that, at this moment. Listen, Jin," Helena went on earnestly, "I've found the missing research vessel."

"You heard him relieve you!"

"I heard him say he was going to, Jin. But until I've received and acknowledged a written order, it has no legal force. If I'm wrong, he'll get my resignation. If I'm right, that suspension would be embarrassing all around."

"You're defying lawful authority! I'm in charge here now." Jin stepped to the local communicator.

"I'm going to report this terrible thing to the Nordavians at once, and offer my profound—"

"Don't touch that screen," Helena said. "You go sit in that corner where I can keep an eye on you. I'm going to make a sealed recording for transmission to Headquarters, along with a request for an armed task force. Then we'll settle down to wait."

Helena ignored Jin's protests as she spoke into the recorder.

The local communicator chimed. Jin jumped up, staring at it.

"Go ahead," Helena said. "Answer it."

A Nordavian official appeared on the screen.

"Jin Lawson," he said without preamble, "on behalf of the Minister of External Affairs of the Nordavian Republic, I hereby recognize you as Estorian Archaeological Director in Morningside, in accordance with the advisories transmitted to my government directly from Estorian Headquarters. As director, you are requested to make available for questioning Ms. Helena Phillips, former director, in connection with the assault on a citizen and illegal entry into the offices of the Ministry for Historical Preservation."

"Why, why," Jin stammered. "Yes, of course. And I do want to express my deepest regrets—"

Helena rose, went to the communicator, moved Jin aside.

"Listen carefully, Roman," she said. "Your bluff has been called. You don't come in and we don't come out. Your cover-up worked for nine years, but it's all over now. I suggest you keep calm and resist the temptation to make matters worse than they are."

"Ms. Lawson," Roman said, "a security squad waits outside your mission. It is clear you are dealing with a dangerous person. As always, the Nordavians wish only friendship with the Estorians, but—"

"Don't bother," Helena said. "You know what was in those files I examined this morning."

Helena turned at a sound behind her. Jin was at the door, reaching for the lock release...

"Don't!" Helena jumped—too late.

The door burst inward. A crowd of uniformed Nordavians pressed into the room, pushed Jin back, aimed weapons at Helena. Security Chief Fernando pushed forward.

"Attempt no violence, Estorian," he said. "I cannot promise to restrain my officers."

"You're violating Estorian territory, Fernando," Helena said steadily. "I suggest you move back out the same way you came in."

"I invited them here," Jin spoke up. "They are here at my express request."

"Are they? Are you sure you meant to go this far, Jin? A squad of armed Nordavians in the mission?"

"You are the director, Ms. Jin Lawson," Fernando said. "Would it not be best if we removed this unstable person to a secure location?"

"You're making a serious mistake, Fernando," Helena said.

"Yes," Jin said. "You're quite right, Mr. Sanchez. Please escort Ms. Phillips to her quarters in this building—"

"I don't advise you to violate my diplomatic immunity, Roman," Helena said.

"As chief of mission," Jin said quickly, "I hereby waive immunity in the case of Ms. Phillips."

Fernando produced a recording device. "Kindly repeat your statement, Madam, officially," he said. "I wish no question to arise later."

"Don't be a fool, Jin," Helena said. "Don't you see what you're letting yourself in for? This would be an excellent time for you to figure out whose side you're on."

"I'm on the side of proper procedure!"

"You've been deceived. These people are concealing—"

"You think everyone is incompetent, don't you, Ms. Phillips?" She turned to the security chief and spoke into the microphone he held up.

"That's an illegal waiver," Helena said. "I'm director here, whatever rumors you've heard. This situation is coming out into the open, whatever you do. Don't add violation of the mission to the list of Nordavian crimes."

"Take her," Fernando said.
question: What was the name of the region where the missing Estorian vessel was found?

synthetic_story:
The transport shuttle rattled as it descended through Stonegate's atmosphere, and Ivy Bryant gripped her seat, watching the viewscreen with growing concern. Ambassador Elena Richardson had given her sealed orders—actual physical documents in a locked case—and explicit instructions not to open them until she reached the surface.

"First time on Stonegate?" the pilot asked, a grizzled woman named Claudia Murphy who looked like she'd been flying routes in the Relvaria system for decades.

"First time this far out," Ivy admitted. She was a junior cultural attaché, fresh from the Diplomatic Corps training facility on Larchmont Town. "I expected more... established colonies."

"Stonegate's only been settled five years," Claudia said. "Bunch of archaeologists and paleontologists came out here when they found those fossil beds. Then the farmers followed, thinking they could terraform the valleys. Now they're at each other's throats."

"The briefing mentioned tensions."

"Tensions." Claudia laughed bitterly. "That's diplomat-speak for 'shooting war.' The farmers want to plow up the fossil sites to plant crops. The scientists say those beds contain evidence of the most significant evolutionary divergence in known space. Last week someone blew up Dr. Palmer's excavation site."

Ivy's stomach tightened. "Ambassador Richardson said she was sending me to facilitate cultural collaboration between the groups."

"Good luck with that. The scientists think the farmers are vandals. The farmers think the scientists are elitist snobs who'd rather let people starve than disturb some old bones. And now—" Claudia paused, checking her instruments. "Now someone's shooting at us."

"What?"

"See those flashes on the screen? That's weapons fire. Small arms, probably. They're getting bolder." Claudia's hands moved over the controls. "I'm putting you down outside Dalebrook settlement. You'll have to walk in. I'm not risking my ship."

"But—"

"Take the emergency kit. There's a sidearm in there too. You might need it."

The shuttle landed hard in a clearing surrounded by strange, twisted trees with purple bark. Claudia helped Ivy gather her gear, including the locked case with her orders.

"The settlement's about two kilometers east," Claudia said. "Follow the ridge. And kid? Watch yourself. These people are serious about their territorial claims."

Ivy watched the shuttle lift off, leaving her alone in the alien forest. The air was breathable but smelled of sulfur and something sweet she couldn't identify. She checked the sidearm—a standard diplomatic corps energy pistol—and started walking.

She'd gone perhaps a kilometer when a voice called out: "Stop right there!"

A woman emerged from behind a boulder, holding an old-fashioned projectile rifle. She was lean and sunburned, wearing practical field clothes covered in dust.

"I'm Ivy Bryant," Ivy said carefully. "Cultural attaché from the Diplomatic Corps. I'm here to—"

"I know who you are. We've been expecting someone from the embassy." The woman lowered her rifle slightly. "I'm Hannah Jackson. I run the farming cooperative in Dalebrook. Sorry about the weapon, but we can't be too careful. The scientists have been raiding our supply depots."

"The scientists?"

"Dr. Sasha Palmer and her crew. They're camped in the fossil beds to the north. They've got some kind of manifesto about protecting cultural heritage—as if rocks that have been dead for a million years matter more than living people." Hannah spat on the ground. "Come on. The others will want to meet you."

As they walked, Hannah explained the situation. The Relvaria system needed food desperately. Three of its eight inhabited worlds had exhausted their agricultural capacity. Stonegate's valleys offered rich soil—ancient lake beds perfect for farming. But those same beds contained fossils that Dr. Palmer's team believed held answers to existential questions about the nature of consciousness and evolution.

"We're not monsters," Hannah said. "We offered to let them excavate a few sites. But Palmer wants to preserve everything. She says our plowing destroys the stratigraphic context, whatever that means. Meanwhile, people are hungry."

They reached Dalebrook as the local sun was setting—a small collection of prefab buildings and agricultural equipment. A group of settlers gathered around a fire pit, and Hannah introduced Ivy to them.

"The embassy finally sent someone," said a stocky man named Matthew Owen. "Though I expected someone more... experienced."

"I'm qualified to handle cultural mediation," Ivy said, trying to sound confident.

"Cultural mediation," Matthew snorted. "What we need is someone to tell those scientists to pack up and leave. This is farming territory now."

"Actually," Ivy said, "my orders are to establish a framework for peaceful coexistence. The Diplomatic Corps believes both groups have legitimate claims."

"Legitimate claims to what? Dead rocks?"

"To understanding our place in the universe," said a new voice.

Everyone turned. A tall woman with gray-streaked hair stood at the edge of the firelight, flanked by two younger people in field gear. She wore the insignia of the Planetary Research Institute.

"Dr. Palmer, I presume," Ivy said.

"Dr. Sasha Palmer, yes. And you're the attaché Richardson sent. I hope you're more reasonable than these vandals."

"Vandals?" Hannah stood up angrily. "We're trying to feed a system!"

"By destroying irreplaceable evidence of—"

"Everyone, please," Ivy said, raising her hands. "This is exactly the kind of conflict I'm here to resolve. Dr. Palmer, perhaps you could explain the significance of the fossil beds?"

Sasha stepped closer to the fire. "The deposits here show a unique evolutionary pathway. The organisms preserved in these beds developed a form of collective memory—a biological mechanism for passing learned information between generations without genetic encoding. It's unprecedented. Understanding how this worked could revolutionize our approach to cultural anthropology, digital humanities, even communication skills between species. But the stratigraphic layers must be preserved intact. Every time these farmers plow a field, they destroy data we can never recover."

"And every day you block us from farming," Matthew said, "more people go hungry. We've got families on Foxwood and Dalebrook who depend on the food we can grow here."

"There must be a compromise," Ivy said. "Surely not all the land is equally valuable to both groups?"

"The best farming soil is in the lake beds," Hannah said. "Which is exactly where the fossils are."

"And the fossil distribution is extensive," Sasha added. "We need access to multiple sites to understand the full picture."

Ivy opened her mouth to respond, then stopped. Something felt wrong. The settlers around the fire were too tense, watching not just Sasha but the darkness beyond. And Sasha's assistants kept glancing at the tree line.

"I think," Ivy said slowly, "that I need to examine my orders. And I'd like to do that privately."

"There's a supply shelter over there," Hannah said, pointing. "You can use that."

Ivy walked to the small building, aware that both groups were watching her. Inside, she unsealed the case and removed the document folder. Ambassador Richardson's instructions were clear: facilitate a division of territory that would satisfy both parties. The Diplomatic Corps had analyzed the situation and determined that—

Ivy stopped reading. The analysis was based on reports that were three months old. It assumed the conflict was still at the negotiation stage. But what she'd seen suggested something more dangerous. The tension between the groups, the weapons, the way they watched each other...

She thought about Claudia's comment about someone blowing up an excavation site. And Hannah's mention of raids on supply depots. This wasn't a dispute anymore. It was a war in its early stages.

The standard diplomatic approach—the one outlined in her orders—would be to bring both sides to the table, establish neutral zones, create a joint oversight committee. But that assumed both parties were willing to compromise. What she'd seen tonight suggested they were past that point.

Ivy made a decision. She left her orders in the shelter and walked back to the fire.

"I need to speak with Dr. Palmer," she said. "Alone."

Hannah started to object, but Ivy held up a hand. "I'll speak with your group separately afterward. But this needs to happen in sequence."

Reluctantly, Sasha followed Ivy away from the fire, into the darkness between the buildings.

"Dr. Palmer," Ivy said quietly, "I'm going to ask you a direct question, and I need an honest answer. Are you planning a military action against the farmers?"

Sasha was silent for a long moment. "We have defensive measures in place."

"That's not what I asked."

"All right. Yes. We have weapons. We have a plan to secure the most critical fossil sites by force if necessary. The Planetary Research Institute has authorized it. We can't let them destroy evidence that could reshape our understanding of consciousness itself."

"And the farmers?"

"What about them?"

"They have weapons too. Better weapons, probably. More people. If you attack them, they'll fight back. People will die."

"Some things are worth dying for."

"Are they worth killing for?"

Sasha looked away. "You don't understand. The work we're doing here—it's not just academic. These fossils show a species that developed true collective memory. They could share experiences, knowledge, skills across generations without language or technology. Imagine what we could learn. Imagine how that could change human society."

"I understand it's important. But so is feeding people."

"There are other worlds to farm. There's only one Stonegate."

Ivy took a breath. "I'm going to make you an offer. But first, I need to know: are you willing to consider alternatives to violence?"

"What kind of alternatives?"

"Let me talk to the farmers first. Then we'll discuss it."

Ivy returned to the fire and asked to speak with Hannah and Matthew privately. They moved to the far side of the settlement.

"The scientists are planning to attack," Ivy said bluntly.

Matthew swore. "When?"

"I don't know. Soon, probably. But I have a question for you: why do you need these specific valleys?"

"They're the best soil," Hannah said. "The lake bed deposits—"

"Yes, but are they the only option? Are there other areas on Stonegate that could be farmed?"

"Well... there are some highland plateaus. The soil's not as rich, but with proper fertilization..." Hannah trailed off. "You're thinking we should give up the lake beds?"

"I'm thinking we need to separate the two groups before this turns into a bloodbath. The scientists need the fossil sites intact. You need farmland. What if there's a way to give both groups what they actually need, rather than fighting over what they want?"

"The highlands would be harder to work," Matthew said. "Lower yields."

"But still viable?"

"Maybe. If we had help. Equipment, supplies, technical support."

"What if I could get the Diplomatic Corps to provide that? What if I could get the scientists to share their laboratory methods for soil enhancement? They're doing research on ancient lake bed chemistry—that knowledge could help you optimize the highland farming."

Hannah and Matthew exchanged glances. "We'd need guarantees," Hannah said. "And compensation for the time we've already invested here."

"I'll work on that. But I need to know: are you willing to consider it?"

"If the terms are right," Matthew said slowly. "Yeah. We're farmers, not soldiers. We don't want a war."

Ivy spent the next three hours shuttling between the two groups, negotiating details. The scientists would keep the lake bed fossil sites. The farmers would relocate to the highland plateaus, with Diplomatic Corps funding for equipment and infrastructure. Sasha's team would share their research on soil chemistry and provide consultation on optimizing the highland farms. The farmers would provide security for the fossil sites against any future settlers who might arrive.

It wasn't perfect. Both sides gave up things they wanted. But it was workable.

As the local sun rose, casting purple light across the strange landscape, Ivy sat with both groups around the fire.

"This is a provisional agreement," she said. "The Diplomatic Corps will need to approve it, and we'll need to establish formal protocols. But I think we have a framework that respects both the cultural heritage represented by the fossils and the practical needs of food production."

"It's more than I expected," Sasha admitted. "When I saw you were so young, I thought..."

"You thought I'd just follow my orders blindly?"

"Something like that."

Ivy smiled. "My orders were based on outdated information. Sometimes the best strategic planning happens in the field, not at headquarters."

Hannah stood and extended her hand to Sasha. "I still think you care more about dead things than living people. But I respect your dedication."

Sasha shook her hand. "And I think you're short-sighted about the value of knowledge. But I respect your practicality."

"I'll take it," Ivy said.

As the groups began to disperse, Matthew approached Ivy. "You know, when you first got here, I thought you were just another bureaucrat who'd make things worse. But you actually listened. You didn't just try to impose some solution from above."

"That's what cultural attachés are supposed to do," Ivy said. "Though I suspect Ambassador Richardson is going to be surprised when she reads my report."

"Why's that?"

"Because I'm going to recommend that the Diplomatic Corps stop sending sealed orders to situations like this. By the time the orders are written, the situation has usually changed. What we need is people on the ground with the authority to adapt."

Matthew laughed. "Good luck selling that to the bureaucracy."

"Maybe. But I think the results will speak for themselves."

As Ivy prepared to signal for pickup, she looked out over the valley where the fossil beds lay undisturbed. Somewhere in those ancient stones were answers to questions humanity had been asking for millennia. And on the plateaus above, farms would soon be growing food to sustain the future.

Both mattered. Both were worth preserving. And sometimes, the best solution wasn't the one that came in a sealed envelope.

Three days later, back on Larchmont Town, Ivy stood in Ambassador Richardson's office, watching the older woman read her report.

"You exceeded your authority," Richardson said finally.

"Yes, ma'am."

"You ignored your explicit orders."

"Yes, ma'am."

"You negotiated a completely different solution than the one Headquarters had planned."

"Yes, ma'am."

Richardson set down the report and smiled. "Well done. The Diplomatic Corps needs more people who can think for themselves. The question is: why did you decide to ignore your orders?"

Ivy thought back to that night, standing by the fire, watching the two groups watching each other. "Because I realized that following the plan would have led to violence. The situation on the ground was different than what the orders assumed. I had to adapt."

"And how did you know what to do instead?"

"I listened. To both sides. And I looked for what they actually needed, not what they said they wanted. The farmers wanted the lake beds because they thought that was the only way to succeed. The scientists wanted to block the farmers because they thought that was the only way to preserve the fossils. But neither of those things was actually true. There were other options."

Richardson nodded. "That's the essence of cultural collaboration. Finding the hidden alternatives that satisfy everyone's real needs. You did good work, Bryant. I'm recommending you for permanent assignment to the Relvaria system. We have seven other worlds with similar conflicts brewing."

"Thank you, ma'am."

"Don't thank me yet. Most of them won't be as easy as Stonegate. But I think you've got the instincts for this work." She paused. "One more question: when did you decide to ignore your orders? Was it when you read them?"

"No, ma'am. It was when I was sitting by the fire, watching both groups. I realized that bringing them together to negotiate—which was what my orders said to do—would have just given them a chance to start shooting at each other. I needed to separate them first, talk to them individually, find common ground before bringing them together. The orders didn't account for how close they were to violence."

"So you went away from the fire to think it through?"

"Yes, ma'am. I needed to be alone to figure out what was really happening, away from both groups' expectations."

Richardson smiled. "That's wisdom. Sometimes the best strategic planning happens when you step away from the immediate pressure and think clearly about what's really needed. Remember that for your next assignment."

As Ivy left the office, she felt a sense of accomplishment mixed with trepidation. Seven more worlds. Seven more conflicts. But she'd learned something important on Stonegate: that the best solutions often came from listening, adapting, and having the courage to deviate from the plan when the situation demanded it.

And sometimes, the most important thing you could do was step away from the fire and think for yourself.

"Just relax, Sofia," her brother Giovanni said from across the room. "You need to take a break from all this stress."

Sofia glared at him. "Martinez! That overpaid quack! I've spent thousands on his consultations. I haven't had a decent night's sleep in months. My hands shake constantly. And what does he prescribe? It's the strain of trying to control everything that's causing your problems. He told you to take a sabbatical or you'd burn out. Don't blame him for your own stubbornness."

Sofia snorted. "Sabbatical! Sitting on a beach somewhere or hiking through forests! Fine activities for someone who doesn't care about innovation management! And let me correct you. It isn't work stress that's driving me crazy. It's the strain of trying to get some basic competence from the people I have to hire! It's the incompetence of the workforce that's got me beaten! It's the—"

"Hey, Sofia!" Giovanni, scrolling through his tablet, had paused at an article. "Didn't you invest in those ecosystem restoration stations they built in Elmwood, Nordavia twenty years ago?"

Sofia's hands twitched violently. "Don't mention that disaster!" she rasped. "That deal nearly bankrupted me! The bacterial cultures we developed produced the most unpredictable compounds ever synthesized!"

Giovanni, whose calm academic demeanor was the complete opposite of Sofia's high-strung entrepreneurial intensity, looked at her over his reading glasses. Sofia's nervous condition was beginning to concern him deeply.

"You're way behind the times, Sofia," he declared. "Don't you know that those compounds have proved to be the most revolutionary biotechnology breakthrough in decades? Sofia, you missed an enormous opportunity!"

The main facility was a towering edifice of smart glass that changed colors with the seasons. Between its wings, biodomes housed carefully cultivated ecosystems and treatment centers that looked pristine and inviting in the photographs.

"Why, I remember now!" exclaimed Giovanni. "That's where the Pattersons went two years ago! He was completely burned out and she looked exhausted. They came back completely rejuvenated. Don't you remember?"

He leaned toward his sister confidingly. Looking back at the article, she saw the line about the AI systems. "—the only wellness center managed entirely by artificial intelligence systems—"

"You're right, Giovanni," agreed Sofia decisively. "I'll go and investigate myself. Immediately!" Grabbing her coat, she left at her usual frantic pace.

"Well!" remarked her brother. "All I can say is that they'd better have those meditation pods working perfectly for Sofia's trip!"

The journey to Elmwood did Sofia considerable good. In the meditation pod of the maglev train, she actually relaxed for the first time in years, sinking into a peaceful state with binaural beats and guided visualization that made the eight-hour trip feel like minutes.

It seemed hardly any time at all until they were arriving at the Elmwood station. And then Sofia was stepping onto the platform with unusual calmness still affecting her normally frantic demeanor. She made her way to the transport hub and found herself whisked by automated vehicle directly to the Elmwood Renewal Center.
