Was she losing her edge? Gnawing at the doubt, she watched the AI-controlled service units moving efficiently about, assisting visitors in wheelchairs, delivering meals, guiding newcomers, performing maintenance tasks tirelessly, promptly, and best of all, silently.

Sofia was enthralled. She'd implement them in her company. Regardless of cost! There'd be no more of that frustrating human error and interpersonal conflict that plagued even the best-trained teams! She'd investigate and determine the exact capabilities of these systems while here, and then return home and introduce them into the corporate environment. She'd show them whether she was losing her edge! Briskly she approached the reception desk.

She was immediately confronted with a sample of that human unpredictability that was slowly driving her mad. Machines, she sighed to herself. Wonderful efficient machines! For a woman was arguing loudly with the desk attendant who, poor soul, was a stressed fellow human instead of an AI system. Sofia watched him shrinking and turning pale under the verbal assault.

"A human therapist!" shouted the woman. "I want a real person! For what you charge, you should be able to provide whatever I request! I won't have another of those soulless AI systems managing my treatment, do you hear?"

Sofia snorted. "Wants someone she can manipulate," she diagnosed. "Someone she can get satisfaction from arguing with." With vast contempt she stepped to the desk beside Elena and sharply tapped for attention.

"One moment, please," begged the harassed attendant. "Just one moment." He turned back to Elena.

But she had turned her glare on Sofia. "You could at least have the courtesy to wait your turn!"

Sofia smirked. "My good woman, I'm not an AI. AI systems, of course, are always courteous. But you should know by now that courtesy isn't always a human strong suit." Leaving Elena temporarily speechless, she beckoned authoritatively to the attendant.

"I've just arrived and need to check in. I'm here for a standard wellness program, no intensive treatments. You can process my registration before continuing your discussion with this lady."

The attendant sputtered. Elena sputtered. But not for nothing was Sofia one of the leading tech entrepreneurs in the region. Sofia's implacable stare won the point. Wiping perspiration from his forehead, the attendant fumbled for a tablet, entered her information, and was about to confirm it when a fist hit the desk with a resounding bang and another voice, male, boomed out at Sofia's elbow.

"This is ridiculous!" roared the voice. "A person could age ten years waiting for service here. Efficiency!" Again his fist struck the counter.

The attendant jumped. He nearly dropped the tablet. Absently holding it, he straightened up to face Elena and the angry newcomer. Hastily he handed Sofia a room card.

"Here you are, Ms. Gupta. I'm sure you'll find it comfortable." With a strained smile he pressed a button and assigned her to the care of a silent and efficient AI guide unit.

The room was more than comfortable. It was stunning. Its panoramic windows framed breathtaking views of the restored Elmwood forests where, Sofia fondly thought, bacterial cultures were busy producing enzymes that would be worth millions to whoever controlled their production rights. There remained only the minor challenge of determining how to extract them economically and to process them in this remote location. Details for her talented research team; mere details...

Leaving her luggage to be handled by the AI system, she went up to the rooftop garden restaurant. Dining boldly on grilled salmon with soup, salad and a light parfait, she gazed out at the restored wilderness, watching birds that had returned to the area after decades of absence. Leaning back in her chair, she even boldly ordered coffee—her first in months—and sipped it happily. For once Giovanni had been absolutely right, she reflected. Yes, Giovanni had hit the mark, and she wouldn't forget it. With a wonderful sense of wellbeing she returned to her room and prepared to rest.

Sofia opened her eyes. Two AI medical units were positioned beside her bed. She saw that they were equipped with diagnostic sensors and treatment apparatus. But she had no further opportunity to examine them. With brisk, perfectly coordinated movements they deployed a transport bed alongside her couch, administered a mild sedative through an arm patch, transferred her onto the bed and began moving her out.

Sofia's voice finally worked. "What's happening?" she demanded. "There's nothing wrong with me. Stop this!"

She struggled to rise, but a mechanical arm gently but firmly held her in place. Inexorably it kept her horizontal.

"You've made an error!" yelled Sofia. "Stop!" But the sedative began taking effect. Her protests became weaker and drowsier. Hazily, as she drifted off, she thought of Elena Wyatt. Maybe the woman had a point, after all.

There was a tentative knock on the door. "Come in," called Sofia bleakly. As soon as the door opened she regretted her invitation, for the opening revealed the large disheveled man who had noisily pounded on the desk demanding service while she was being registered.

"Excuse me," he said hoarsely, "you haven't seen any of those AI units around here, have you?"

Sofia scowled. "Oh, haven't I?" she grated. "AI systems! Do you know what they did to me?" Indignation blazed in her eyes. "Came in while I was resting peacefully after the first proper meal I've enjoyed in months, transported me to the medical wing, and pumped me full of supplements and ran diagnostics! The only peace I've had in months!" Darkly she sank her chin onto her fist and contemplated the outrage.

"Why didn't you stop them?" reasonably asked the visitor.

"And to think I had the absurd notion that AI systems were the solution to everything! Why, I was ready to implement them throughout my entire company!"

The big man placed his large hands on his own substantial stomach and groaned. "I'm genuinely sorry it was you and not me. I could use some of that intervention right now. Must have been that heavy meal I ate after all that processed food I've been consuming."

"Processed food?" A faint spark of alertness pierced Sofia's dull rage. "You mean you work out here in the production facilities?"

"That's right. How'd you guess? I'm George Edwards, superintendent of one of the enzyme extraction plants. Good pay, but what a job! Isolated location. Climate-controlled facilities. Hazmat protocols. Prefab housing. Synthetic nutrition. Nothing else. Just nothing. That's where they could really use AI systems. It's certainly no environment for people long-term. And in fact, there aren't many people left there. If old Melissa Chen only knew it, her operation is about to collapse."

Sofia sat up as if electrified. She opened her mouth to speak. But just then the door opened efficiently and two AI units entered. With a horrified stare, Sofia clutched her stomach. She saw a third unit enter, maneuvering a mobility chair.

"A wheelchair!" squeaked Sofia. "I tell you, there's nothing wrong with me! Take it away! I'm only here for standard wellness! Believe me! Take it away!"

The AI units ignored her. For the first time in her spectacular and aggressive career Sofia was confronting entities that she could neither negotiate with, intimidate, charm nor dismiss. It shattered her remaining confidence. She began waving her hands helplessly.

The AI units not only ignored Sofia. They paid no attention at all to George Edwards, who was tugging at their mechanical frames pleading, "Take me instead. I genuinely need treatment. I need all the help I can get. Take me! I'm falling apart here—"

Impassively they lifted Sofia up, placed her in the chair, secured her safely and proceeded out with her.

Dejectedly George returned to his own room. Again he tried the room's communication system; but as usual an AI voice responded pleasantly, mechanically, and unhelpfully. He disconnected and went miserably to bed.

There was something nagging at Sofia's mind. Something she should address. Something that concerned AI systems. But she was too exhausted to work it out.

For five days now these AI systems had subjected her to an ordeal that made her flinch every time she thought about it. Which wasn't often, since she was almost beyond thinking. They immersed her in mineral baths and kept her there until she was thoroughly treated. They had her breathe therapeutic compounds until she felt dizzy. They brought her strange nutritional preparations and monitored her until she consumed them. They administered treatments and exercises and therapies.

Whenever they left her alone, she simply collapsed into bed and slept. There was nothing else to do anyway. They'd taken her clothes; and the communication system, after an announcement that she would have limited access for two weeks, gave her nothing but automated responses.

"Persecution, that's what this is!" she moaned desperately. And she turned away from the mirror, which showed her that she was beginning to look healthy instead of the pale gray to which she had become accustomed. She closed her mind to the fact that she was sleeping soundly for hours like she hadn't in years, and that she was developing such an appetite that she could almost enjoy even those strange breakfast preparations they provided. She was determined to be furious. As soon as she could stay awake long enough to be.

She hadn't been awake long this time before George Edwards was there again, still complaining about his lack of treatments. "Nothing yet," he gloomily informed Sofia. "They haven't touched me. I just can't understand it. After I registered for the full program and paid in advance! And I can't find any way out of this section. The other rooms are empty and the elevator doesn't have manual controls. The AI units have to come and retrieve you or you're trapped."

"Trapped!" snarled Sofia. "I'm never trapped! And I refuse to wait any longer to escape this—this prison! Listen, George. I've been thinking. Or trying to, with what's left of my brain. You arrived just when that incompetent attendant was registering me. I'll bet that attendant got confused and gave me the wrong room assignment. I'll bet you're supposed to have this room and I'm receiving your treatments. Why don't we switch rooms and see what happens?"

"Say, maybe you're right!" George's eyes gleamed with hope. "I'll get my things."

Sofia's eyebrows rose. "You mean they left you your clothes?"

"Why, yes. You mean they took yours?"

Sofia nodded. An idea began forming. "Leave your things, would you? I'm desperate! I'm going to see the director of this nightmare if I have to go down wrapped in a bedsheet. Your clothes would be better than that."

George, looking over Sofia's slight frame, grunted doubtfully. "Maybe you could make them work somehow. Roll up everything. It's fine with me, but just don't lose anything when you're down there in that fancy lobby."

Sofia looked at her watch. "Time to go. Relax. The AI units will arrive any minute now. If you're the only person in the room, I'm confident they'll take you. They aren't programmed to figure it out. And don't worry about me. I'll manage your clothes."

Sofia had guessed correctly. Gleefully from the doorway of her new room she watched the AI units transport her equally delighted neighbor for his first treatment. Then she closed the door and began putting on George's clothing.

The result was absurd. She looked like a child in adult clothes, except for the remarkably tired and gaunt face emerging from a collar several sizes too large. And she was barefoot. She was completely unable to walk in George's enormous shoes. But Sofia was a determined woman. She didn't even flinch at her reflection. Firmly she stepped over to George's communication panel. "This is room 618," she said authoritatively. "Send the elevator for me. I need to go down to the lobby."

She'd guessed correctly again. "It will arrive shortly, Ms. Gupta," responded the AI operator. Hopefully she stepped out into the corridor and shuffled to the elevator.

Only the AI units were immune to Sofia Gupta's progress across the elegant lobby.

She was an anomaly in its refined beauty, a bizarre sight that froze the other visitors into staring clusters. Stepping out of the elevator, she had charted a course for the reception desk which stood like an island in the vast space, and now she shuffled determinedly toward it, ignoring the oversized trousers dragging around her bare feet. "Absolutely not!" yelled Sofia. "I want to see the director!" Nimbly she circled the security units and leaped behind the desk. She began throwing things at the AI units. Things like tablets and input devices and filing systems. Especially, filing systems.

"Stop it!" begged the attendant. "You'll destroy the database! We'll never recover it! Stop it!"

"Call them off!" snarled Sofia. "Call them off or I'll wreck your entire system!" She put a hand on the main control panel and prepared to shut it down.

With one last appalled look at the madwoman, the attendant grabbed a control device and pointed it at the approaching AI units. They became suddenly motionless.

"That's better!" Sofia straightened up and meticulously smoothed the collar of her enormous coat. "Now—the director, please."

"This—this way, please." With reluctant steps the attendant led Sofia across the width of the lobby among the fascinated guests. He was beyond words. Opening the discreet door, he gestured Sofia inside and returned doggedly to his desk, where he began retrieving scattered items and simultaneously composing his resignation in his mind.

Brushing aside the startled assistant in the outer office, Sofia shuffled and flapped straight into the inner office. The director, who was busy reviewing reports behind her sleek desk, jerked upright and stared at the intruder. "Excuse me—" she began.

"Don't 'excuse me' me!" snapped Sofia. She glared back at the director. Reaching as far across the desktop as she could stretch, she shook her small fist. "Do you know who I am? I'm Sofia Gupta, of Gupta Technologies! And do you know why I don't even have identification to prove it? Do you know why I have to make my way downstairs in clothing that makes me look ridiculous? Do you know why? Because that incompetent attendant of yours assigned me the wrong room and those infernal AI systems of yours then proceeded to imprison me! Me, Sofia Gupta! Why, I'll sue you until you'll be fortunate if you have a single server left in this automated asylum!"

Leah Ford, the director, paled. Then she began to flush in an alarming pattern. And suddenly with a heavy sigh, she collapsed into her chair. With a shaking hand she wiped her forehead. "My AI systems!" she muttered. "As if I designed the damned things!"

Despondently she looked at Sofia. "Go ahead and sue, Ms. Gupta. If you don't, somebody else will. And if nobody sues, we'll fail anyway, at the rate our guest retention is declining. I'm ready to submit my resignation."

Again she sighed. "The problem," she explained, "is that those AI systems are completely logical and rule-based, and people aren't. There's no way to reconcile the two. It's volatile. Maybe people can gradually adapt to AI systems, but they haven't yet. Only we had to discover it the hard way. We—" she grimaced with disgust—"had to pioneer in AI integration. And it cost us so much that we can't afford to convert back to human staff. So—Operation AI is about to bankrupt the consortium."

Listening, an unexpected calm settled on Sofia. Thoughtfully now she hooked a chair to the desk with her bare foot, sat down and reached for the water glass that Leah automatically offered her. "Oh, I don't know," she said mildly.

Leah leaned forward like someone grasping at hope. "What do you mean, you don't know? You're threatening to sue us into oblivion, aren't you?"

Carefully Sofia sipped the water. "It seems to me that these AI systems might be useful in quite a different capacity. I might even negotiate with your consortium to acquire them—at a reasonable price, naturally—and forget the grievances I've suffered at your establishment."

Leah leaned toward her incredulously. "You mean you want these AI systems after what you've seen and experienced?"

Calmly Sofia set down the glass. "Of course, you'd have to consider that it would be experimental for me as well. And there's the lawsuit I'm clearly entitled to file. However, I'm willing to discuss the matter with your board."

With hope emerging for the first time in weeks, Leah lifted her head. "Ms. Gupta, to be rid of these problematic AI systems, I'll support you completely! I'll notify the board immediately. Immediately, Ms. Gupta! And while we wait for them, allow me to offer you proper accommodations as a guest of the center." Coming around to Sofia, she warmly shook Sofia's small hand, and then personally escorted her not merely to the door but across the lobby to the elevator.

Sofia gazed out at the stunned audience. This was more like the treatment she was accustomed to! Proudly she squared her thin shoulders inside the massive jacket and stepped into the elevator. She was ready for the second phase of her private Operation AI.

Back in Crestwood Town it was a warm, clear autumn day—the kind of day that made the city sparkle. Giovanni and his wife waited eagerly while the maglev train docked and the passengers disembarked.

"Look, Giovanni!" His wife clutched his arm. "The doors are opening."

They watched the doors slide open and the passengers emerge, looking refreshed from their journey.

"There she is!" cried Giovanni. "Doesn't she look wonderful! It's amazing! Look at her!"

And indeed, Sofia was stepping briskly forward, looking energetic and healthy and years younger. She came across to them actually smiling. It was the first genuine smile they had seen on her face in years.

"Well, you did it again!" exclaimed Giovanni warmly. "So you pulled off another deal!"

Sofia grinned. "Yes, I executed a very favorable transaction. I acquired Chen Biotech's enzyme operation and staffed the facility with the center's AI systems. Got both at excellent prices. Both operations were failing because they didn't have the sense to exchange their resources. Feel I owe you something for that tip about enzymes, Giovanni, so I've allocated some equity to you. Acceptable?"

"Acceptable?" Giovanni gulped. Why, his high-strung sister was showing gratitude after all. "Acceptable! Absolutely! But aren't you going to use some of those AI systems for your company? Aren't they efficient and all that?"

Sofia's smile vanished. "Don't even suggest such a thing!" she yelped. "You don't know what you're saying! I lived with those things for weeks. I wouldn't have one in the office! Keep them in the factory where they belong!"

She glimpsed the composed, wonderfully human face of her assistant, waiting patiently in the background. "Oh there you are, Eric." She turned to her brother. "Busy day ahead. See you later—"

"Same old Sofia," observed Giovanni. Then he thought of the equity. "What say we celebrate our stake in the venture?"

"Wonderful!" His wife squeezed his arm, and smiling at each other, they left the station.
question: What was the role of George Edwards at the facility?
option_a: Superintendent of an enzyme extraction plant

The rain hammered against the transparent dome of New Bridgewater's underground city as Steven Holland watched the surface monitors with growing dread. In three hours, the first Earth delegation would arrive, and everything had to be perfect. Everything had to look primitive.

"Steven, stop fidgeting with that costume," Amara Bell said, adjusting her own elaborate headdress. The Chief Cultural Administrator's robes were magnificent—woven from the finest synthetic materials designed to look like hand-loomed textiles, adorned with what appeared to be precious stones but were actually carefully crafted glass. "The Earthers will be here soon, and we need everyone in position."

"I still think this is insane," Steven muttered, looking down at his own outfit—or lack thereof. As the designated "street vendor," he wore little more than strategically placed rags and a tattered cloak that did nothing to keep out the cold surface winds. "We had a perfectly good society. Why did we have to throw it all away?"

Gabriel Harper, the Planetary Development Consultant who had designed this entire charade, turned from where he'd been reviewing data analysis reports on his hidden tablet. "Because, Steven, Earth anthropologists aren't interested in studying advanced civilizations that mirror their own. They want the exotic, the primitive, the 'authentic.' And since Aldoria's economy is collapsing and we desperately need the research grants and tourism revenue that Earth can provide, we give them what they want."

"By pretending to be savages," Steven said bitterly.

"By pretending to be a pre-industrial society with a rich cultural heritage," Gabriel corrected. "There's a difference. Now, I've spent five years at the Terran Institute studying cultural anthropology and research ethics. I know what I'm doing."

Steven doubted that. Gabriel had always been arrogant, even back when they were students together at the Aldorian Technical Institute. The fact that he'd won the competitive examination to study abroad on Earth had only inflated his ego further. And now he'd returned with this elaborate scheme to save their dying planet by turning it into an anthropological theme park.

The worst part was that it might actually work. Aldoria had once been prosperous, its cities gleaming beneath protective domes while the population enjoyed lives of comfort and technological sophistication. But the planet's resources had dwindled—the rare earth elements that had once made Aldoria wealthy were nearly exhausted, and the cost of importing food and materials from other worlds was bankrupting them. Tourism had been suggested, but who wanted to visit a planet where the surface was perpetually stormy and the underground cities, while comfortable, were architecturally uninspiring?

Gabriel's solution: hide the cities, construct fake "traditional" villages on the surface, and invite Earth's anthropologists to study what they believed was an untouched pre-technological society. The research grants alone would keep Aldoria solvent for decades, and if the project succeeded, cultural tourism would follow.

The Aldorian Parliament had approved the plan by a narrow margin. President Katherine Rodriguez herself had endorsed it, though Steven suspected she had reservations. And now, through an elaborate lottery system that Gabriel claimed was completely random, every citizen had been assigned a role in this massive deception.

Steven had drawn "street vendor"—essentially the lowest social position in Gabriel's invented hierarchy. Amara, his fiancée until two weeks ago, had been made Chief Cultural Administrator—second only to Gabriel himself in the new power structure. The lottery had dissolved their engagement; Gabriel's cultural framework didn't permit relationships between different castes.

Steven suspected the lottery had been rigged.

"I should get to the surface," Amara said, though her voice wavered slightly. "Steven, I want you to know that this isn't what I wanted. The role assignments—"

"Were determined by random chance," Gabriel interrupted smoothly. "As witnessed by the President and the Parliamentary Committee. Now, Amara, we need to review your welcoming speech one more time. The Earthers are very sensitive to linguistic patterns, and we can't afford any anachronisms."

Steven watched Amara follow Gabriel to the preparation chamber, her elegant robes swishing against the polished floor. This would be the last time he'd see these corridors for months, perhaps years. Once the Earth team arrived, everyone would be confined to their surface roles. The underground cities would be sealed and hidden, accessible only through carefully concealed entrances that the Earthers must never discover.

He made his way to the equipment locker where he'd stashed his secret project. Three months ago, while reviewing historical analysis documents about pre-industrial Earth societies, he'd come across references to wheeled carts used by street vendors. The concept had fascinated him—Aldorians had never developed wheels for ground transport, having moved directly from walking to anti-gravity platforms. But if they were supposed to be primitive now, surely a cart would be appropriate?

He'd built it himself in his apartment, using scrap materials from decommissioned mining equipment. It wasn't pretty, but it worked. And more importantly, it gave him an advantage. While everyone else would be slogging through the surface mud on foot, he could transport goods efficiently. In Gabriel's invented economy, that might actually mean something.

The surface access tunnel was crowded with citizens preparing for their new lives. The metal-workers—Aldoria's largest professional class—had been designated as the lowest caste, forbidden from interacting with the upper levels of society. Steven saw his former colleague Robert King among them, looking miserable in his rough worker's garments. At least Steven's role allowed him some mobility and interaction with others.

The lift to the surface was slow, designed to look like a primitive pulley system from the outside. Steven emerged into the constructed village of Redwood, named after the enormous artificial trees that had been erected to give the settlement a more "natural" appearance. The rain was immediate and brutal, and Steven's inadequate clothing provided no protection whatsoever.

"Vendor!" A sharp voice cut through the downpour. Paul Sanders, assigned the role of Village Elder, glared at Steven from beneath a waterproof awning. "What is that contraption?"

"A cart, honored elder," Steven said, affecting the deferential tone that Gabriel's cultural guidelines required. "For transporting my wares."

"It looks too sophisticated," Paul grumbled. "Gabriel approved this?"

"The wheel is one of humanity's oldest inventions," Steven replied, which wasn't exactly an answer but seemed to satisfy Paul.

The Earth ship appeared on the horizon right on schedule, a sleek vessel that made Steven ache with longing for Aldoria's own spacecraft, now hidden away in underground hangars. Two figures emerged as the ship landed—a man and a woman, both wearing practical field gear that looked far more comfortable than Steven's rags.

"Dr. Lucia Kim," the woman introduced herself, speaking accented but comprehensible Aldorian. "And this is my research assistant, Kara Kelly. We're from the Earth Institute of Anthropological Studies. We're honored that your people have agreed to let us study your fascinating culture."

Gabriel and Amara had reached the landing site, leading a procession of citizens in ceremonial dress. Steven, as befitted his lowly status, hung back at the edges of the crowd, though his cart allowed him to keep pace more easily than the others who were slipping and sliding in the mud.

"Welcome, honored visitors from Earth," Amara said, her voice carrying clearly despite the rain. "We are a simple people, but we offer you our hospitality and our friendship. May your time among us be enlightening and pleasant."

Dr. Kim smiled warmly. "Thank you. We've traveled a long way to reach Aldoria, and we're eager to begin our research. Your planet's unique cultural development has intrigued Earth scholars for years."

Steven nearly laughed at that. The only thing unique about Aldoria's culture was that it had been invented three months ago by an egotistical consultant with a degree in cultural anthropology.

"We've prepared quarters for you in our finest dwelling," Gabriel said, gesturing toward a structure that Steven himself had been forbidden from helping design, despite being one of Aldoria's most accomplished architects. Gabriel had instead used centuries-old blueprints purchased from an Earth historical database, constructing buildings that were deliberately primitive and uncomfortable.

As the procession moved toward the village center, Kara Kelly fell back slightly, her eyes on Steven's cart. "Interesting," she murmured to Dr. Kim in English—which most educated Aldorians understood, though they weren't supposed to. "The vendor has wheeled transport, but no one else does. That's an unusual technological distribution pattern."

Dr. Kim frowned. "Make a note of it. We'll want to investigate the social and economic factors that would lead to such an asymmetric adoption of basic mechanical principles."

Steven's hearts sank. He'd made a mistake. His attempt to improve his position had instead drawn unwanted attention. Gabriel was going to kill him.

But as they reached the village square, where Gabriel had planned an elaborate "rain-stopping ceremony" to demonstrate Aldorian spiritual practices, Steven noticed something else. Dr. Kim was studying everything with intense scrutiny—the buildings, the clothing, the social interactions. Her gaze was sharp, analytical, skeptical.

She didn't believe it.

Or at least, she had doubts. Steven could see it in the way she examined the "hand-woven" fabrics, the way she noted the precise uniformity of the supposedly handmade pottery, the way she measured the angles of buildings that were just a bit too geometrically perfect.

Gabriel's plan was already failing, and the Earthers had been here less than an hour.

The ceremony began, with Amara leading a group of citizens in an elaborate dance that was supposed to represent Aldoria's ancient traditions but had actually been choreographed by Gabriel based on his study of Earth's pre-industrial cultures. Steven watched from the sidelines, shivering in his inadequate clothing, and wondered how long this farce could possibly last.

"You there, vendor," Dr. Kim approached him after the ceremony, speaking Aldorian. "What's your name?"

"Steven Holland, honored scholar."

"That's an interesting cart you have. Did you build it yourself?"

Dangerous territory. "Yes, honored scholar. I... I had a vision from the spirits, showing me how to construct it."

Dr. Kim's expression was unreadable. "A vision. How convenient." She paused, then switched to English, clearly not expecting him to understand: "Kara, I want full documentation of that cart. The construction techniques, the materials, everything. Something's not right here."

"You think they're not as primitive as they claim?" Kara asked, also in English.

"I think we need more data before drawing conclusions. But yes, I have suspicions. The cultural coherence is too perfect, too complete. Real societies have inconsistencies, contradictions, competing traditions. This feels... designed."

Steven kept his expression carefully neutral, but inside he was panicking. If the Earthers discovered the deception, Aldoria would lose everything—not just the research grants, but its reputation. No other Earth institutions would work with them. The planet would be finished.

That evening, after the Earthers had retired to their quarters, Steven found himself summoned to Gabriel's residence—a large, ornate building that was primitive only on the outside. Inside, hidden from Earth's view, it contained all the modern conveniences.

"You idiot," Gabriel hissed, spinning in agitation. "That cart of yours has already raised questions. Dr. Kim spent an hour examining it, taking measurements, analyzing the construction techniques."

"I was trying to make my role more realistic," Steven protested. "Street vendors in primitive societies often had specialized tools—"

"Specialized tools that evolved over generations, not appeared fully formed from nowhere!" Gabriel's face was flushed with anger. "Do you have any idea how much work went into creating a coherent cultural framework? The mythology, the social structure, the artistic traditions—it all has to fit together, has to make sense as something that developed organically over centuries. And you just introduced an anomaly that threatens the entire structure!"

"Maybe the entire structure was flawed from the beginning," Steven shot back. "Dr. Kim is already suspicious. She knows something's wrong."

"She suspects nothing," Gabriel insisted. "She's doing her job, which is to question and analyze. That's what anthropologists do. As long as we maintain consistency, she'll eventually accept what she sees."

"And what about Amara?" Steven asked, changing the subject. "You assigned her the second-highest position in this society. That was convenient for you, wasn't it?"

Gabriel's expression hardened. "The role assignments were random, witnessed by—"

"By people you selected. I don't believe it was random, Gabriel. I think you manipulated the lottery to put yourself in power and to separate me from Amara."

"Believe what you want," Gabriel said coldly. "But you will play your assigned role, Steven, or you'll be reassigned to something worse. We have provisions for dealing with citizens who won't cooperate with the project. How would you like to spend the next five years in isolation, underground, forbidden from any contact with the surface?"

It was a threat, and they both knew it. Steven had no choice but to comply.

The next few days fell into a routine. Steven played his part as street vendor, selling simple goods to citizens who paid him with the primitive currency Gabriel had designed. The Earthers observed everything, taking notes, recording conversations, documenting daily life. Dr. Kim remained skeptical but professional, her questions probing but not accusatory.

And slowly, Steven began to understand something about his role. Yes, he was low in Gabriel's invented hierarchy. Yes, he'd been separated from Amara. But as a vendor, he had access to everyone. He moved through all levels of society, interacting with workers and elders alike. He saw things that others, confined to their specific social positions, could not see.

He saw the cracks in Gabriel's perfect system.

The metal-workers, segregated and resentful, were already talking about rebellion. The "spiritual practitioners" assigned to support Amara's religious authority were uncomfortable with the deception, questioning the ethics of lying to Earth scholars. Even some of the elders were expressing doubts about whether the economic benefits were worth the cost to Aldorian dignity.

And Steven saw something else: Dr. Kim was documenting all of it. Not just the official culture Gabriel had created, but the tensions, the inconsistencies, the signs of a society under strain.

One afternoon, as Steven was arranging goods in his cart, Dr. Kim approached him alone. "Steven Holland," she said quietly, "I'd like to ask you some questions. Unofficial questions."

His pulse quickened. "Of course, honored scholar."

"How long has your society had wheeled transport?"

"I... the spirits revealed the design to me recently."

"I see. And before your vision, no one had wheels?"

"No, honored scholar."

Dr. Kim nodded slowly. "That's remarkable. Because the construction techniques you used—the axle design, the bearing system, the load distribution—they're not intuitive discoveries. They represent centuries of engineering refinement on Earth. Yet you claim to have invented them through divine inspiration."

Steven said nothing.

"I'm going to be honest with you, Steven. I don't believe your society is what it claims to be. I think you're hiding something, and I think you're not very happy about having to hide it." She paused. "I'm not here to judge or to expose you. I'm here to understand. But I can't understand if everyone keeps lying to me."

It was a moment of decision. Steven could maintain the deception, protect Gabriel's plan, preserve Aldoria's chance at Earth's research grants and tourism revenue. Or he could tell the truth, risk everything, and hope that honesty might lead to something better than this elaborate fraud.

He thought about Amara, trapped in a role she didn't want, separated from him by Gabriel's machinations. He thought about Robert King and the other metal-workers, treated as outcasts in their own society. He thought about the underground cities, hidden away as if they were something shameful rather than achievements to be proud of.

"You're right," he said quietly. "We're not what we claim to be. We're not primitive. We're desperate."

Dr. Kim's expression didn't change, but something in her eyes softened. "Tell me."

And Steven told her everything. The dying economy, the depleted resources, Gabriel's plan to attract Earth anthropologists by pretending to be a pre-industrial society. The lottery that he suspected had been rigged, the underground cities that were sealed and hidden, the elaborate deception that was already falling apart under the weight of its own contradictions.

When he finished, Dr. Kim was silent for a long moment. Then she said, "Take me to see the real Aldoria. The cities underground. Show me what you're actually capable of."

"Gabriel will—"

"Gabriel Harper is not in charge here anymore," Dr. Kim said firmly. "I am. And I'm invoking my authority as lead researcher to demand full access to your actual society. If you refuse, I'll file a report with Earth that will ensure no anthropologist ever works with Aldoria again. But if you cooperate, if you show me the truth, then maybe we can find a way to actually help your planet."

It was another moment of decision, but this one was easier. Steven led Dr. Kim to the hidden entrance, down through the access tunnels, into the gleaming underground city of Bridgewater. She said nothing as they walked through the corridors, past the advanced transportation systems, the sophisticated architecture, the comfortable homes and efficient workspaces.

Finally, in the central plaza, she spoke. "This is what you should have shown us from the beginning. This is what Earth needs to see."

"But Earth wants primitive cultures," Steven protested. "That's what Gabriel said. That's why we—"

"Earth wants to understand other societies," Dr. Kim corrected. "Yes, there's a bias toward studying pre-industrial cultures, because we have so few of them left. But there's also tremendous interest in how different civilizations solve problems, manage resources, organize themselves. Your cities are architectural marvels adapted to a hostile environment. Your social systems, your sustainable business practices, your approach to ecosystem restoration on a damaged planet—these are all worthy of study."

"But we're failing," Steven said. "Our economy is collapsing. We can't sustain ourselves."

"Then maybe Earth can help with that. Not by turning you into a tourist attraction or an anthropological zoo, but by engaging with you as equals. Sharing technology, establishing trade, creating partnerships." Dr. Kim smiled. "But first, we need to have an honest conversation with Gabriel Harper about research ethics and the importance of informed consent in anthropological studies."

That conversation, when it happened, was explosive. Gabriel insisted his plan was working, that Dr. Kim's suspicions were manageable, that abandoning the deception now would be disastrous. But Dr. Kim was adamant, and she had the authority of Earth's academic institutions behind her.

"You've created an interesting theoretical model of a pre-industrial society," she told Gabriel. "I'm sure it will make an excellent paper on the challenges of cultural construction and the ethics of anthropological deception. But as an actual research project, this is finished. I want to study real Aldorians, not actors playing roles you assigned them."

The Parliament met in emergency session. President Rodriguez, looking relieved, dissolved Gabriel's cultural framework and authorized full cooperation with the Earth researchers. The underground cities were opened, the primitive villages abandoned, and the citizens of Aldoria returned to their normal lives.

Steven found Amara in her apartment in Thornhill, the eastern district of Bridgewater. She was still wearing the elaborate robes of the Chief Cultural Administrator, but she was crying.

"I hated it," she said when she saw him. "I hated every moment of pretending to be someone I wasn't, hated being separated from you, hated the whole elaborate lie. But I thought it was necessary. I thought it was the only way to save Aldoria."

"Maybe there's another way," Steven said, and told her about his conversation with Dr. Kim.

Three months later, Earth's Institute of Urban Planning and Sustainable Development announced a major research initiative focused on Aldoria's underground cities. The grants were smaller than what Gabriel's deception might have brought, but they were real, honest, and sustainable. Earth architects and engineers arrived to study Aldorian construction techniques. Trade negotiations began for Aldorian expertise in underground development, which several Earth cities needed as they dealt with rising sea levels and surface temperatures.

Steven, no longer a street vendor but once again a respected architect, was appointed as liaison to the Earth research teams. Amara, freed from her role as high priestess, returned to her actual profession as a specialist in information theory and helped establish communication protocols between Aldorian and Earth institutions.

And Gabriel Harper, his grand plan in ruins, was reassigned to a minor position in the Department of Historical Analysis, where he spent his days cataloging the brief, failed experiment in cultural deception that he had created.

"Do you think we'll be all right?" Amara asked Steven one evening, as they stood together in the plaza of Bridgewater, watching Earth researchers and Aldorian citizens working together on a new project.

"I think we'll be better than all right," Steven said. "We'll be ourselves. And that's enough."

The rain still hammered against the dome above them, but inside, the city was warm and bright and honest. And that, Steven thought, was worth more than any amount of Earth's research grants—though having both honesty and grants was even better.
question: What role was Steven assigned through the lottery?

ORBITAL DIPLOMACY
BY RANDALL GARRETT (ADAPTED)

Three thousand kilometers above the cloud-swept surface of Earth, in the international research habitat known as Orbital Station Alpha, a crisis was unfolding that would test the limits of aerospace engineering and international cooperation.

Commander Richard Greene stood in the command center, his weathered hands gripping the edge of the console as he stared at the communication screen. The message from Earth had been clear: Ambassador Wei Mason, the senior diplomatic liaison from the Eastern Coalition, had collapsed during a routine meeting in Conference Module Seven. What should have been a simple medical emergency had become a geopolitical nightmare.

"How long until we can establish a stable link with Lincoln Command?" Greene asked, his voice tight with controlled tension.

Lieutenant Claudia James looked up from her station, her fingers dancing across the holographic interface. "Seventeen minutes, Commander. We're passing over the Pacific now. Lincoln, Calderon won't be in range until we complete another eighth of our orbit."

Greene nodded curtly. Seventeen minutes. In those seventeen minutes, Ambassador Mason's condition could deteriorate beyond recovery. And if that happened, the fragile peace negotiations that had brought together representatives from twelve nations aboard this station would collapse. Three years of careful diplomacy, of building trust in the neutral territory of space, could evaporate in less time than it took to circle the Earth.

"Get me Dr. Ahmed Crawford," he ordered. "Now."

Dr. Ahmed Crawford was not having a good day. As the station's chief medical officer, he had prepared for everything from decompression injuries to radiation exposure. What he had not prepared for was treating a patient with a rare neurological condition that required specialized nanotechnology medical equipment—equipment that was currently sitting in a laboratory in Hampton, Ilvaria, four hundred kilometers below them.

He stood over Ambassador Mason's bed in the medical bay, watching the readouts with growing concern. The ambassador was conscious but weak, his neural implants—the very devices that made him such an effective communicator between cultures—were malfunctioning. Without the proper calibration equipment, those implants could cause permanent brain damage within hours.

"Doctor?" The voice belonged to Noah Rice, Crawford's assistant and one of the station's junior medical technicians. "The commander wants to see you immediately."

Crawford didn't look up from his patient. "Tell him I'm busy saving a man's life."

"He knows. That's why he wants to see you."

With a heavy sigh, Crawford turned to his assistant. "Monitor his vitals. If there's any change—any change at all—you call me immediately. Understood?"

"Yes, sir."

Commander Greene was waiting in his office, a small compartment that served as the administrative heart of the station. The walls were covered with screens displaying everything from orbital trajectories to diplomatic schedules. Greene gestured for Crawford to sit.

"Give it to me straight, Doctor. What are we looking at?"

Crawford massaged his temples, feeling the weight of the situation pressing down on him. "Ambassador Mason's neural implants are failing. They're experimental technology—part of an education reform initiative designed to improve communication skills across language barriers. The implants were supposed to facilitate real-time translation and enhance cognitive development. But they're prototype technology, and they need regular calibration."

"How regular?"

"Every three weeks. The ambassador's last calibration was in Hampton, Ilvaria, twenty days ago. He was scheduled for his next session when he returned to Earth next week. But the stress of the negotiations, combined with the reduced gravity up here, has accelerated the degradation."

Greene leaned back in his chair, his eyes fixed on the ceiling. "What do you need?"

"A neural calibration unit. It's specialized equipment—about the size of a large briefcase, but it requires a stable power source and a sterile environment. Without it, the implants will continue to malfunction. In six hours, maybe eight, the damage will be irreversible."

"Can we improvise something?"

Crawford shook his head. "Commander, I'm a doctor, not an engineer. The technology involved is beyond my expertise. We're talking about nanotechnology interfaces with the human brain. One wrong move and I could kill him."

Greene stood up and walked to the window—a thick pane of reinforced polymer that looked out onto the curve of Earth below. "Then we get the equipment up here. I'll contact Lincoln Command and have them prepare an emergency launch."

"Commander, with all due respect, even if they launch immediately, it'll take four hours minimum to reach us. That's assuming perfect conditions and a direct trajectory. We might not have four hours."

"Then we make those four hours count." Greene turned back to Crawford, and the doctor was struck by the determination in the commander's eyes. This was a man who had spent thirty years in the Space Service, who had overseen the construction of this station as a symbol of international cooperation. He wasn't about to let it fail now.

"There's something else," Crawford said quietly. "The other ambassadors are asking questions. They know Mason collapsed, and they're worried. If word gets out that we can't treat him, that we're not equipped for this kind of emergency..."

"The negotiations will fall apart," Greene finished. "I know. That's why we're going to fix this. Get back to your patient, Doctor. Keep him stable. I'll handle the rest."

As Crawford left the office, he couldn't shake the feeling that "handling the rest" was going to be easier said than done.

The communication link with Lincoln Command in Calderon opened at exactly 14:47 station time. Commander Greene stood in the communications center, flanked by Lieutenant James and Oscar Stewart, the station's chief engineer.

The face that appeared on the screen belonged to General Andre Bradley, the commanding officer of the Calderon Space Operations Center. Bradley was a legend in aerospace engineering circles, a man who had pioneered some of the most advanced orbital mechanics theories of the past decade.

"Commander Greene," Bradley's voice crackled slightly through the transmission. "We received your emergency request. I have to tell you, what you're asking for is... complicated."

"I understand that, General. But we have a situation up here that goes beyond medical emergency. Ambassador Mason's condition is critical, and if he dies, three years of diplomatic progress dies with him. We need that calibration unit."

Bradley nodded slowly. "We're already preparing the launch. Captain Eva Ahmed is being briefed now—she's our best pilot for rapid orbital insertion. But Greene, you need to understand the risks. We're talking about a launch window that's less than optimal. The trajectory calculations are being run now, but we're looking at a high-stress ascent profile."

"How high?"

"Nine gravities at peak acceleration. Maybe ten. It's going to be rough."

Oscar Stewart, who had been listening quietly, spoke up. "General, what about the equipment itself? Neural calibration units are sensitive. Can they handle that kind of stress?"

"We're packaging it in a shock-resistant container with active dampening. It should survive. Should."

Greene felt a knot forming in his stomach. "When can you launch?"

"Two hours. We need time to prep the ship and run the calculations. The next optimal window after that isn't for another eight hours."

"We might not have eight hours. Launch in two."

"Understood. Bradley out."

The screen went dark, and Greene turned to Stewart. "Oscar, I need you to prepare the docking bay. When that ship arrives, I want the transfer to happen in under five minutes. Can you do that?"

Stewart nodded. "I'll have a team ready. But Commander, there's something you should know. The docking clamps in Bay Three have been showing some wear. I was planning to do maintenance next week. If we're doing a hot dock—"

"Fix it. Now. I don't care if you have to rebuild the entire bay with spare parts. That ship needs to dock safely."

"Yes, sir."

As Stewart hurried off, Claudia James turned to Greene. "Commander, the other ambassadors are requesting a meeting. They want to know what's happening with Mason."

Greene closed his eyes briefly. Leadership development, he thought bitterly. They taught him about leadership development at the academy, about making tough decisions under pressure. But they never taught him how to balance saving one life against maintaining the peace between twelve nations.

"Tell them I'll meet with them in one hour. And Claudia?"

"Sir?"

"Don't tell them about the emergency launch. Not yet. Let's see if we can actually pull this off first."

Dr. Crawford was losing his patient. Not literally—not yet—but Ambassador Mason's condition was deteriorating faster than he had anticipated. The neural implants were sending increasingly erratic signals, causing seizures that required constant medication to control.

Noah Rice stood beside him, monitoring the vital signs with the intensity of a man who knew that one mistake could mean death. "His blood pressure is dropping again, Doctor. Should I increase the dosage?"

"No. We're already at maximum safe levels. Any more and we risk cardiac arrest." Crawford wiped the sweat from his forehead. The medical bay was kept cool, but the stress was making him feel like he was working in a furnace.

"There has to be something else we can do."

Crawford looked at his assistant, seeing the desperation in the young man's eyes. Noah Rice had joined the station crew six months ago, fresh from medical school, eager to learn. This was supposed to be a mentorship opportunity, a chance for Crawford to pass on his knowledge to the next generation of space medicine practitioners. Instead, it had become a lesson in helplessness.

"Sometimes," Crawford said quietly, "the hardest part of being a doctor is accepting that there are limits to what we can do. We're not miracle workers, Noah. We're just people with training and equipment. And right now, we don't have the right equipment."

"But the ship—"

"The ship might not arrive in time. Or it might arrive with damaged equipment. Or a dozen other things might go wrong. We have to prepare ourselves for that possibility."

Noah's jaw tightened. "I didn't become a doctor to watch people die, sir."

"None of us did. But part of our job is bearing witness. If Ambassador Mason dies, someone needs to be able to tell his family that he didn't die alone, that someone was there fighting for him until the end. That's not nothing, Noah. That matters."

Before Noah could respond, the intercom crackled to life. "Dr. Crawford, this is Commander Greene. I need you in Conference Module Seven immediately. Bring your medical kit."

Crawford frowned. "Commander, I can't leave my patient—"

"You're going to want to see this, Doctor. Trust me."

Leaving Noah in charge of the medical bay, Crawford made his way through the station's corridors to Conference Module Seven. The module was one of the larger spaces on the station, designed for the diplomatic meetings that were the station's primary purpose. When Crawford entered, he found Commander Greene standing with three people he didn't recognize.

"Doctor, meet Ambassador Eva Ahmed's advance team. They transmitted ahead from the rescue ship. This is Dr. Richard Greene—no relation to me—a specialist in neural implant technology from Silverdale, Havencia."

The other Dr. Greene stepped forward, a slight man with intense eyes and quick movements. "Dr. Crawford, I understand you're dealing with a malfunctioning neural implant system. I've reviewed Ambassador Mason's medical files, and I think I might be able to help you stabilize him until we arrive with the calibration unit."

"How? Without the proper equipment—"

"We don't need the full calibration unit. Not yet. What we need is to reduce the signal interference that's causing the seizures. The implants are trying to process too much information in a low-gravity environment. If we can temporarily reduce their sensitivity, we can buy time."

Crawford felt a spark of hope. "How do we do that?"

"With what you already have. The station's medical bay should have a magnetic resonance scanner, correct?"

"Yes, but it's not designed for—"

"It doesn't need to be designed for this. We're going to use it to create a localized magnetic field that will partially dampen the implant signals. It's not a perfect solution, and it's not without risks, but it should stabilize your patient for the next few hours."

Crawford looked at Commander Greene, who nodded. "It's your call, Doctor. But we're running out of options."

"All right," Crawford said. "Let's do it."

The next two hours were the longest of Ahmed Crawford's career. Working with Dr. Greene via video link, he carefully repositioned the medical bay's equipment to create the magnetic field necessary to dampen Ambassador Mason's implants. The procedure was delicate, requiring precise calibration to ensure they reduced the signal interference without causing additional damage.

Noah Rice proved invaluable during the process, his steady hands and quick thinking helping Crawford make the minute adjustments necessary. It was, Crawford reflected, exactly the kind of mentorship moment he had hoped for when Noah joined the crew—though he would have preferred it under less stressful circumstances.

Finally, at 16:23 station time, Ambassador Mason's vital signs stabilized. The seizures stopped, and his brain activity returned to normal levels. He was still unconscious, still in critical condition, but he was alive.

"Good work, Doctor," Commander Greene's voice came through the intercom. "The rescue ship will dock in forty-five minutes. Captain Eva Ahmed reports that the calibration unit survived the launch intact."

Crawford slumped against the wall, exhaustion washing over him. "Thank you, Commander. And thank Dr. Greene for me. His quick thinking saved Mason's life."

"I will. Now get some rest. You've earned it."

But Crawford couldn't rest. Not yet. He had one more task to complete.

He found Commander Greene in the observation lounge, staring out at the curve of Earth below. The commander turned as Crawford entered.

"Doctor. I thought I told you to rest."

"I will. But first, I wanted to talk to you about something." Crawford moved to stand beside Greene at the window. "This situation—it exposed some serious gaps in our preparedness. We're supposed to be a symbol of international cooperation, a place where the best minds from across the globe work together. But we're not equipped to handle medical emergencies that involve cutting-edge technology."

Greene nodded slowly. "I know. I've been thinking the same thing. What do you suggest?"

"We need to expand our medical capabilities. Not just equipment, but expertise. We should have specialists rotating through the station—people who understand nanotechnology, advanced prosthetics, all the experimental medical technologies that our crew and visitors might be using. We also need better communication protocols with Earth-based medical facilities."

"That's going to require approval from all twelve member nations. Getting them to agree on anything is like herding cats."

"Then we use this incident as a catalyst for societal change. Ambassador Mason nearly died because we weren't prepared. If we present this as a matter of applied ethics—our moral obligation to protect everyone who comes to this station—we might be able to build consensus."

Greene smiled slightly. "You know, Doctor, you're starting to sound like a diplomat yourself."

"God forbid," Crawford said with a tired grin. "I'll leave the political economy and international diplomacy to the ambassadors. I just want to make sure that the next time someone gets sick up here, we're ready."

"Fair enough. I'll start working on a proposal. In the meantime, you should know that Ambassador Mason's family has been notified of his condition. They've asked me to pass along their gratitude for everything you've done."

Crawford felt a lump forming in his throat. "I was just doing my job, Commander."

"No, Doctor. You did more than that. You refused to give up, even when the situation looked hopeless. That's not just doing your job. That's leadership."

The rescue ship docked at 17:08 station time, and within minutes, the neural calibration unit was being rushed to the medical bay. Dr. Richard Greene from Silverdale accompanied the equipment, working alongside Crawford to perform the delicate calibration procedure that would restore Ambassador Mason's implants to proper function.

By 18:30, the ambassador was awake and asking questions. By 19:00, he was sitting up in bed, insisting that he needed to return to the negotiations immediately.

"Absolutely not," Crawford said firmly. "You're going to stay in this bed for at least twenty-four hours while we monitor your recovery. The negotiations can wait."

Ambassador Mason smiled weakly. "Doctor, you don't understand. The negotiations can't wait. We're at a critical juncture in the discussions about climate technology sharing. If I'm not there—"

"If you're not there, one of the other ambassadors will step in," Commander Greene said, entering the medical bay. "Ambassador, with all due respect, you're not indispensable. The work you've done here is important, but it's not worth dying for."

"The commander is right," added Dr. Richard Greene. "Your implants need time to fully stabilize. Pushing yourself too hard right now could cause a relapse, and next time we might not be able to save you."

Mason sighed. "Very well. Twenty-four hours. But I want to be kept informed of everything that happens in those negotiations."

"Of course," Commander Greene said. "I'll have Lieutenant James set up a live feed to your room. You can observe without participating."

As the two Greenes left the medical bay, Noah Rice approached Crawford. "Doctor, can I ask you something?"

"Of course."

"Earlier, you said that sometimes our job is just bearing witness. But we did more than that today. We saved his life. Doesn't that prove that we should never give up?"

Crawford considered the question carefully. "Noah, what I said earlier wasn't about giving up. It was about accepting reality. Yes, we saved Ambassador Mason today. But we only succeeded because we had help—from Dr. Greene, from Captain Ahmed, from dozens of people on the ground who worked together to make the impossible possible. If we had been truly on our own, if that rescue ship hadn't arrived in time, Mason would have died despite our best efforts."

"So what's the lesson?"

"The lesson is that we're stronger together than we are alone. That's true in medicine, in aerospace engineering, in international diplomacy—in everything we do up here. This station exists because twelve nations decided to work together instead of competing. Ambassador Mason survived because people from three different countries—Ilvaria, Calderon, and Havencia—pooled their expertise and resources. That's the real miracle here, Noah. Not the technology, but the cooperation."

Noah nodded slowly. "I think I understand."

"Good. Now, let's check on our patient one more time, and then we're both going to get some sleep. We've earned it."

As Crawford made his final rounds for the evening, he found himself thinking about the future. The incident with Ambassador Mason had revealed weaknesses in the station's capabilities, but it had also demonstrated the power of international cooperation. If they could build on that, if they could use this crisis as a catalyst for positive change, then maybe—just maybe—they could create something truly remarkable up here.

The next morning, Commander Greene called a meeting of all the ambassadors. Ambassador Mason attended via video link from his medical bay bed, looking tired but alert. Greene outlined his proposal for expanding the station's medical capabilities, emphasizing the need for better preparedness and more specialized equipment.

To Crawford's surprise, the ambassadors were unanimous in their support. The near-loss of one of their own had reminded them all of their shared vulnerability, their common humanity. Within an hour, they had drafted a preliminary agreement to establish a rotating medical specialist program and to upgrade the station's equipment.

As the meeting concluded, Ambassador Mason caught Crawford's eye through the video screen. "Doctor, I owe you my life. If there's ever anything I can do for you—"

Crawford smiled. "Just keep working toward peace, Ambassador. That's all any of us can ask."

Later that evening, as the station completed another orbit around Earth, Crawford stood in the observation lounge with Commander Greene. Below them, the lights of cities sparkled against the darkness—Hampton in Ilvaria, Lincoln in Calderon, Silverdale in Havencia, Redwood in Jarvonia. Twelve nations, represented by twelve ambassadors, working together in the neutral territory of space.

"You know," Greene said quietly, "when I took this assignment, I thought it would be about managing resources and maintaining systems. I never expected to be in the middle of life-and-death crises with geopolitical implications."

Crawford chuckled. "Welcome to my world, Commander. Every day is a new adventure in applied ethics and crisis management."

"I suppose it is. But I have to say, despite the stress and the near-disasters, I wouldn't trade this assignment for anything. What we're doing up here—it matters. We're proving that people from different nations, different cultures, different backgrounds can work together toward common goals. That's worth all the headaches."

"I couldn't agree more," Crawford said. "And who knows? Maybe the design science principles we're developing up here—the ways we're learning to cooperate and solve problems together—maybe those lessons will filter down to Earth. Maybe we're not just a research station. Maybe we're a laboratory for a better future."

Greene smiled. "That's a nice thought, Doctor. Let's hope you're right."

As they stood there, watching the Earth turn slowly beneath them, Ahmed Crawford felt a sense of cautious optimism. The crisis with Ambassador Mason had been terrifying, but it had also been transformative. It had shown them their weaknesses, yes, but it had also shown them their strengths—their ability to work together, to overcome obstacles, to refuse to give up even when the situation seemed hopeless.

That, Crawford thought, was the real promise of Orbital Station Alpha. Not the advanced technology or the cutting-edge research, but the simple, powerful idea that people could choose cooperation over conflict, could choose to work together instead of apart.

It was a lesson that the world below needed to learn. And maybe, just maybe, they were learning it.

Three months later, the upgraded medical facilities were complete, and the rotating specialist program was in full operation. Ambassador Mason had made a full recovery and had returned to Earth to continue his work in international diplomacy. The negotiations he had been part of had concluded successfully, resulting in a groundbreaking agreement on climate technology sharing that many credited to the spirit of cooperation fostered aboard the station.

Dr. Ahmed Crawford stood in the new medical center, admiring the state-of-the-art equipment that now filled the space. Noah Rice stood beside him, having just completed his certification as a space medicine specialist.

"It's impressive, isn't it?" Noah said. "Hard to believe this all came about because of one emergency."

"That's how change often happens," Crawford replied. "A crisis forces us to confront our limitations, and if we're smart, we use that moment to grow and improve. The question is whether we can sustain that growth, or whether we'll slide back into complacency."

"I don't think we will," Noah said confidently. "Not after what we went through. Everyone on this station understands now how important it is to be prepared, to work together, to never stop learning and improving."

Crawford smiled. "I hope you're right, Noah. I really do."

As he looked out the window at the Earth below, Crawford thought about Ambassador Mason's words: "Keep working toward peace." That was what they were all doing up here, in their own ways. The engineers were working toward peace by building systems that brought people together. The diplomats were working toward peace by negotiating agreements and building trust. And the doctors were working toward peace by healing the sick and protecting the vulnerable.

It was all connected, Crawford realized. The aerospace engineering that made the station possible, the international diplomacy that gave it purpose, the mentorship that passed knowledge from one generation to the next—they were all part of the same grand project, the same fundamental human desire to build something better than what came before.

And if they could do it up here, in the harsh environment of space where every breath of air and every drop of water had to be carefully managed, where cooperation wasn't just nice but necessary for survival—then surely, Crawford thought, surely humanity could do it down there too.

It was a hope worth holding onto. A dream worth fighting for. And as long as places like Orbital Station Alpha existed, as long as people were willing to work together toward common goals, that dream remained alive.

Commander Greene's voice came through the intercom, interrupting Crawford's thoughts. "Doctor, we have a new arrival coming in next week. Ambassador from Redwood, Jarvonia. She's got some experimental hearing implants that might need monitoring."

Crawford smiled. "Understood, Commander. We'll be ready."

And they would be. Because that was what they did now. They prepared, they cooperated, they learned from their mistakes and built something better. It wasn't perfect—nothing ever was—but it was progress. And in the end, that was all anyone could ask for.

Progress, one day at a time, one crisis at a time, one small victory at a time. Up here in orbit, three thousand kilometers above the Earth, a group of people from twelve different nations were proving that it was possible.

And that, Ahmed Crawford thought as he returned to his work, was worth everything.
