THE SCENT OF DIGITAL PAINT
BY HANNAH MUNOZ

The gallery district of Maplewood, Veldoria had to be safe enough. I couldn't have been more certain. In the window of the electronics store, a holographic display was cycling through NFT art pieces, and folded in my pocket was the news article about the catastrophic failure of the new blockchain-based conservation tracking system. The young people on the corner seemed barely recognizable, hunched figures in synthetic fiber coats. It was my own time. Anyone could see I was safe, and I could risk doing what I desperately wanted to do.

I turned the corner.

The odds were against me from the start. It didn't come as any surprise. I could never get away with it. I knew that all along.

There was a Tesla parked just beyond the charging station.

The metal and glass fronts of the buildings didn't show back here, only weathered brick held together with crumbling mortar. The line of the block seemed to stretch back, ever further away from the sleek fronts into the decaying stone.

A woman brushed past me, wearing a smart blazer and carrying a tablet. And, reassuringly, she was in a hurry.

I decided to chance it. I certainly wanted to do it in the worst way.

My footsteps carried me on down the block.

A small vehicle whirred past me. One of those autonomous pods, I decided. Only it wasn't quite right. I fixed the silhouette in my mind's eye and tried to identify it. Something from the early 2020s.

Still, I wasn't worried. It was actually too early in the day. It wasn't as if it were evening or anything like that.

The little shop was right where I left it, quietly deteriorating by itself. The Retrospective Gallery, the faded sign proclaimed in blue and silver, or now, gray and cream. In the window, in protective cases, were prints from the first digital art exhibition, a recent magazine featuring contemporary VR installations, a coffee table book about the Restoration Movement murals, and a brand-new, sun-faded catalog of the Morningside Province Ecosystem Art Project.

There was a delivery drone at the curb. This time I recognized it was from an earlier generation.

I went in, the chrome handle making me conscious of the sweat on my palm.

The old woman sat behind a fortress of art books and magazines, treacherously scrolling through something on an ancient tablet. Her gray hair was pulled back from the sharp angles of her cardigan. She smiled, showing yellowed teeth.

"Came back for more of the work, did you?"

She set down the tablet. (That headline couldn't really be making such an accusation about the Conservation Council, could it?)

"Yes," I laughed, not very convincingly.

"I know what a craving can be. I shouldn't eat sweets, but I do. I've tried to stop but I lie there thinking about chocolate half the night. Dark chocolate, milk chocolate, truffles, plain bars. I feel like I could eat a whole box. Is it like that with you?"

"Not that bad. To me it's just—"

"Don't tell me art isn't a craving with some of you people. I've seen folks come in here, hardly two coins to rub together, and grab up those restoration journals and read and read, until sweat starts rolling off the end of their nose. I've hardly got the heart to throw them out."

Restoration journals. Ones with beautiful landscapes being returned to their natural state, with ecosystems being rebuilt from nothing. Yes, they were a part of it. Not a big part, but a part.

"That's not what I want to see. I want—"

The old woman chuckled. "I know what you want. Indeed I do. This way."

I followed her pointing hand and sure enough, there they were. Stacks upon stacks of old art magazines from the Restoration Movement.

"Twenty credits for ones in good condition," the old woman pronounced the ritual, "ten credits for ones with damaged covers, three for twenty-five, check them at the desk when you go."

I ran my hand down a stack. *Art & Ecology*, *The Restoration Artist*, *Biodiversity Canvas*, *Creative Conservation*, all of them.

The old woman was watching me. She scuttled back across the floor and snatched up a magazine. It was a copy of *Ecosystem Visions* with a woman in paint-splattered overalls standing before a massive mural of a restored wetland.

"This one, this one," she said. "This must be a good one. I bet she painted every species that came back. Every single one. Species."

"I'll take it."

Reluctantly she handed over the magazine, waited a moment, then left me.

I stared at the stacks of Restoration Movement magazines and I felt the slow run of the drop of sweat down my nose.

My sickness was terrible. It is as bad to be nostalgic for things you have never known as for an orphan who has never had a home to be homesick.

Living in the past, that was always me. I never watched anything on the screens made later than 2025. I was fascinated by the early digital artists, the first VR creators, the pioneers of blockchain art. My favorite artists were the ones who had painted the great restoration murals in Redwood Territory.

The music I listened to was from the Cultural Exchange Movement and the early days of computational composition.

And my viewing was the documentation of the Restoration Movement, harking back to when they had first begun rebuilding the ecosystems. This was the biggest part of it all, I think.

You identify with the subject of any documentary if it's well enough made. But the identification I felt with the artists in restoration documentation was plainly ridiculous.

I was there.

I was standing before the canvas, feeling on my face the bite of the wind from the restored prairie. I was lifting my brush to capture the return of the native grasses in the dawn light. Then in a moment my hand was moving across the canvas in answer to the landscape, creating through the systematic observation that had been drilled into us, recording the biodiversity that was slowly, miraculously returning. And back through the field notes in the pocket at my knee.

Here it comes, the morning light hitting the wetland in perfect illumination. Look at that careful documentation. You can almost see the species checklist in the artist's other hand. They can afford to be methodical with that funding. I'd like to trade this rushed commission for it. That may be just what happens too if I don't watch it.

You aren't any master restorer, friend, but this is from the Maplewood Collective for the Redwood Project.

Missed that detail!

Careful with that brushstroke! God, look at the way that color bleeds. At least it was a lie about them using cheap materials.

One of your own techniques for you, amateur. Up with the palette, up under that canopy, into the shadow detail. Where am I? Where am I?

Right here.

Look at that background go. The supplier can't be giving you as good paint as they claim.

So long. I'm nodding, see.

She's pushing through. No more paint and she's pushing through. She's a good artist. Come on. A little more. A little more and you can finish it. Come on, friend. You're doing it. You're pushing through—

But not enough.

God, what a mess.

I'm sick.

That damned synthetic medium in the mix. I'll be in the bathroom until morning...

No, the air wasn't one of synthetic medium but the pleasant smell of aged paper and printer's ink.

I'd been daydreaming again. I shouldn't forget things were getting different lately. It was becoming dangerous.

I gathered up an armload of Restoration Movement magazines at random.

Leaning across the table, I noticed the curtain in back for the first time. It was a beaded curtain of many different colors, like something from an old bohemian studio. Behind the curtain was a screen. It was a comforting anti-anachronism here.

The large flat display was showing an old documentary. A very old documentary. Early footage from the first ecosystem restoration project as scientists worked to bring back a destroyed forest, standing them off from encroaching development. The flickering images caught my unblinking eyes.

A developer is sneaking across the property line, a contract in his briefcase. A young activist makes a try to stop the bulldozers, but the security forces remove her. Now a government official is arriving with the preservation order. The developer makes a try with legal action, the activists celebrate, and the official signs the protection into law. It goes through, all the way through.

The young woman is running toward the official as he finishes with the paperwork and stands, her shirt torn from the earlier struggle. The developer stands up in defeat. The official smiles. No, no, say the woman's lips. "No!" "No!" says the subtitle. The official hesitates. Swimming in bureaucracy, the developer smiles sadly and walks away.

I had seen documentaries like that before.

When I was younger, I had seen *Heritage Flashbacks* between episodes of nature shows and environmental programs. I looked at old footage and heard voices making commentary. But hadn't I also seen these images with the sound of actual field recordings and low conversation?

I had seen these images before the Collapse.

The Collapse had made a lot of difference in my life.

Art supplies were rationed, from full sets to basic kits, and prices had gone up to where you had to pay hundreds for proper materials, so high that people said the Council should do something about it.

The Restoration Movement had transformed, and artists worked on rebuilding ecosystems in both physical and digital space. Only, hadn't they also worked on the social contract, on justice theory, on ethical decision-making about what should be restored and how?

And at the community center I had participated in decision-making processes about local projects. I never did get enough votes to lead a project, but my mentor had taken my designs and incorporated parts of them for the wetland restoration. I could never get enough recognition...

"Nobody would look at my magazines," the old woman chuckled, "if I put it out front. My daughter got me that screen. She runs a digital art studio. A good girl. Her name's on the business registry."

I pressed some credits on her and walked myself out of the store. Shutting the door, I saw that the catalog of the Ecosystem Art Project had been replaced by something about the Cultural Exchange Movement.

The street was full of autonomous vehicles, sleek electric cars, boxy delivery drones, swept-back courier bikes. Only one dark, heavy, combustion-engine vehicle moved through the traffic. It had a light on the roof.

I dodged in front of a recycling truck and behind an electric postal van and ran for that light, leaving a trail of gaudy restoration images checkering the street behind me.

I grabbed the handle on the door, opened it and threw myself into the back seat.

"Central District," I said from my diaphragm, without any breath behind it.

Something was wrong. Two people were in the front seat. The driver showed me his hard, expressionless face. "What do you think you are doing?"

"This isn't a rideshare?" I asked blankly.

"Environmental Police."

I sat there while we drove on for a few minutes.

"Disoriented and disturbed," the second person said to the driver.

"Right into our laps."

The second officer leaned forward and clicked something. "I'll get the City units."

"No, kill it, Hannah. Think of all that damned paperwork."

Hannah shrugged. "What will we do with him?"

I was beginning to attach myself to my surroundings. The street was full of traffic. My kind of traffic. Vehicles that were too new or too old.

"Look, officers, I'm not disoriented or disturbed. I thought this was a rideshare. I just wanted to get away from back then—I mean back *there*."

The two officers exchanged glances.

"What were you running from?" the driver asked.

How could I tell him that?

Before I even got a chance to try, he said: "What did you do?"

"I didn't *do* anything!"

The vehicle was turning, turning into shadows, stopping. We were in an alley. Soggy cardboard, discarded containers, prowling rats, a broken die, half a dice, looking big in the frame of my thick, probably bulletproof window.

The officers opened their doors and then mine.

"Out."

I climbed out and stood by the vehicle, blinking.

"You were causing some kind of trouble in that neighborhood back there," the driver announced.

"Really, officers—"

"What's your name?"

"Noah Nguyen. There—"

"We don't want you going back there again, Nguyen, causing trouble. Understand?"

"Officer, I only bought some magazines—I mean art journals."

"These?" the second person, Hannah, asked. She had retrieved them from the back seat. "Look here, Stephen. They look pretty subversive."

Stephen took up the *Ecosystem Visions* with the woman in the paint-splattered overalls. "Dangerous," he said.

"You know about the laws governing unauthorized restoration documentation, Nguyen."

"Those aren't unauthorized and they are my property!"

I reached for them and Hannah pulled them back, grinning. "You don't want to read these. They aren't good for you. We're confiscating them."

"Look here, I'm a citizen! You can't—"

Hannah shoved me back a little. "Can't we?"

Stephen stepped in front of me, his face in deadly earnest. "How about it, Nguyen? You a memory addict?"

He grabbed my wrist and started checking my pulse, looking for signs of neural interface abuse. I twisted away from him.

"Resisting an officer," Stephen said almost sadly.

At that, Hannah moved up beside him.

The two of them started to beat me.

They hit clean, in the belly and ribs, but not in the groin. They gave me clean white flashes of pain, instead of angry, red-streaked ones. I didn't fight back, not against the two of them. I knew that much. I didn't even try to block their blows. I stood with my arms at my sides, leaning back against the vehicle, and hearing myself grunt at each blow.

They stood away from me and let me fold helplessly to the greasy pavement.

"Stay away from that neighborhood and stay out of trouble," Stephen's voice said above me.

I looked up a little bit and saw an ugly, scarred hand thumbing across a stack of half a dozen magazines like a giant deck of cards.

"Why don't you take up contemporary art?" he asked me.

I never heard the vehicle drive away.

Home. I activated the living room lights from the door, looked around for intruders for the first time I could remember, and went inside.

I threw myself on the couch and rubbed my stomach. I wasn't hurt badly. My middle was going to be sorer in the morning than it was now.

Lighting up a vape, I watched the shapes of vapor and tried to think.

I looked at it objectively, forward and back.

The solution was obvious.

First of all, I positively could *not* have been a restoration artist in the early Restoration Movement. I was in my mid-twenties; anybody could tell that by looking at me. The time was the late 2050s; anybody could tell that from the neural interface ports in the corner, the new autonomous vehicles on the street. Memories of painting restoration murals and documenting returning biodiversity stirred in me by old magazines, archived documentaries, and re-runs of *The Restoration* on the streams were mere hallucinations.

Neither could I remember attending the first Cultural Exchange festivals, hearing the debates about the social contract in the post-Collapse world, or paying a month's credits to get into the original Ecosystem Art Project exhibition.

Only... I probably had seen the Project. Hadn't I gone with my mentor to a preview? Didn't she pay reduced admission for me? So how could I remember taking a partner, dark-haired, green jacket, Zoe, and paying full price each? I couldn't. Different exhibitions. That was it. The thing had toured half a dozen times. But would it have been that expensive no more than ten years ago?

I activated a new vape cartridge.

The thing I must remember, I told myself, was that my recollections were false and unreliable. It would do me no good to keep following these false memories in a closed curve.

I touched my navel area and flinched. The beating, I was confident, had been real. But it had been a nightmare. Those officers couldn't have been true. They were a small person's bad dream about symbolized authority. They were keeping me from re-entering the past where I belonged, punishing me to make me stay in my trap of the present.

Oh, God.

I rolled over on my face and pushed it into the upholstery.

That was the worst part of it. False memories, feelings of persecution, that was one thing. Believing that you are actively caught up in a mixture of the past with the present, a surreal viscosity of reality, was something else.

I needed help.

Or if there was no help for me, it was my duty to have myself placed where I couldn't harm other citizens.

If there was one thing that working for the Conservation Council had taught me, it was social responsibility.

I took up the directory and located several memory specialists. I selected one at random, for no particular reason.

Dr. Christopher Fernandez.

I memorized the address and heaved myself to my feet.

The doctor's office was as white as the inside of a sterile laboratory.

The cool, efficient receptionist told me to wait and I did, tasting nothing inside my mouth.

After several long, peaceful minutes the inner door opened.

"Mr. Nguyen, I can't seem to find any record of an appointment for you in Dr. Fernandez's files," the man said.

I got to my feet. "Then I'll come back."

He took my arm. "No, no, I can fit you in."

"I didn't have an appointment. I just came."

"I understand."

"Maybe I had better go."

"I won't hear of it."

I could have pulled loose from him, but somehow I felt that if I did try to pull away, the grip would tighten and I would never get away.

I looked up into that long, hard, blank face that seemed so recently familiar.

"I'm Dr. Santos," he said. "I'm taking care of Dr. Fernandez's practice for him while he is on leave."

I nodded. What I was thinking could only be another symptom of my illness.

He led me inside and closed the door.

The door made a strange sound in closing. It didn't go *snick-bonk*; it made a noise like *click-clack-clunk*.

"Now," he said, "would you like to lie down on the couch and tell me about it? Some people have preconceived ideas that I don't want to fight with at the beginning. Or, if you prefer, you can sit there in front of my desk and tell me all about it. Remember, I'm a neurologist, a doctor, not just a therapist."

I took possession of the chair and Santos faced me across his desk.

"I feel," I said, "that I am caught up in some kind of temporal displacement."

"I see. Have you consumed much restoration documentation, Mr. Nguyen?"

"Some. I view a lot. All kinds of content. Historical archives, contemporary streams, educational programs, entertainment feeds."

"You should *view* them instead of live them. Catharsis. Sublimate, Mr. Nguyen. For instance, to a certain type of person, I often recommend contemporary action feeds."

I seemed to be losing control of the conversation. "But this temporal displacement..."

"Mr. Nguyen, do you really believe in 'temporal displacement'?"

"No."

"Then how can there be any such thing? It can't be real."

"I know that! I want to be cured of imagining it."

"The first step is to utterly renounce the idea. Stop thinking about the past. Think of the future."

"How did you know I keep slipping back into the past?" I asked.

Santos's hands were more expressive than his face. "You mentioned temporal displacement..."

"But not to the past or to the future," I said.

"But you did, Mr. Nguyen. You told me all about thinking you could go into the past by visiting a gallery where they sold old magazines. You told me how the intrusion of the past got worse with every visit."

I blinked. "I did? I did?"

"Of course."

I stood up. "I did not!"

"Please try to keep from getting violent, Mr. Nguyen. People like you actually have more control over themselves than you realize. If you *will* yourself to be calm..."

"I *know* I didn't tell you a thing about the Retrospective Gallery. I'm starting to think I'm not sick at all. You—you're trying to do something to me. You're all in it together."

Santos shook his head sadly.

I realized how it all sounded.

"Good—GOD!" I moaned.

I put my hands to my face and I felt the vein over my left eye swelling, pulsing.

Through the bars of my fingers I saw Santos motion me down with one eloquent hand. I took my hands away—I didn't like looking through bars—and sat down.

"Now," Santos said, steepling his fingers, "I know of a completely appropriate facility in Crestwood. Of course, if you respond properly..."

Those hands of his.

There was something about them that wasn't right. They might have been the hands of a corpse, or a synthetic...

I lurched across the desk and grabbed his wrist.

"*Please*, Mr. Nguyen! Violence will—"

My fingers clawed at the backs of his hands and my nails dragged off ugly strips of some theatrical material—synthetic skin, I think—that had covered the scrapes and bruises he had taken hammering away at me and my belt buckle.

Santos.

Stephen.

I let go of him and stood away.

For the first time, Santos smiled.

I backed to the door and turned the handle behind my back. It wouldn't open.

I turned around and rattled it, pulled on it, braced my foot against the wall and tugged.

"Locked," Santos supplied.

He was coming toward me, I could tell. I wheeled and faced him. He had a neural interface device. It was the smallest one I had ever seen and it had an iridescence or luminosity about it, a gleaming silver needle.

I closed with him.

By the way he moved, I knew he was trained in physical combat, but you can't win them all, and I had been in a lot of fights when I had been younger. (Hadn't I?)

I stepped in while he was trying to decide whether to use the device on me or drop it to have his hands free. I palm-struck him in the solar plexus and crossed my fist into the hollow of the apex arch of his jawbone. He dropped.

I gave him a kick at the base of his spine. He grunted and lay still.

There was a knocking on the door. "Doctor? Doctor?"

I searched through his pockets. He didn't have any keys. He didn't have any money or identification or a weapon. He had a cloth and a stylus.

The receptionist had moved away from the door and was talking to somebody, in person or on a comm or intercom.

There wasn't any back door.

I went to the window. The city stretched out in an impressive panorama. On the street below, traffic crawled. There was a ledge. Quite a wide, old-fashioned ornamental ledge.

The ledge ran beneath the windows of all the offices on this floor. The twenty-first, I remembered.

I had seen it done in entertainment feeds all my life. Action heroes were always doing it for some reason or other. I had a good reason.

I unlatched the window and climbed out into the dry, crisp breeze.

The entertainment feeds didn't know much about physics. The updraft nearly lifted me off the ledge, but the cornice was so wide I could keep out of the wind if I kept myself flat against the side of the building.

The next window was about twenty feet away. I had covered half that distance, moving my feet with a sideways shuffle, when Hannah, indisputably the second officer, put her head out of the window where I was heading and pointed a weapon at me, saying in a let's-have-no-foolishness tone: "Get in here."

I went the other way.

The cool, efficient receptionist was in Santos's window with the tiny silver device in readiness.

I kept shuffling toward the receptionist. I had decided I would rather wrestle with her over the device than fight Hannah over the weapon. Idiotically, I smiled at that idea.

I slipped.

I was falling down the twenty-one stories without even a moment of windmilling for balance. I was just gone.

Lines were converging, and I was converging on the lines.

You aren't going to be able to recover from this fall, Nguyen. Good-by, Nguyen.

Death.

A sleep, a reawakening, a lie. It's nothing like that. It's nothing.

The end of everything you ever were or ever could be.

I hit.

My kneecap hurt terribly. I had scraped it badly.

Reality was all over me in patches. I showed through as a line drawing, crudely done, a sketch.

Some kind of projection. High-resolution hologram, that was all reality meant.

I was kneeling on a hard surface no more than six feet from the window from which I had fallen. It was still twenty-one flights up, more or less, but *Down* was broken and splattered over me.

I stood up, moving forward a step.

It brought me halfway through the projection, halfway through the wall at the base of the building. The other side of the screen. The solid side, I found, stepping through, bracing a hand on the image.

Looking up twenty-one floors, I saw an unbroken line of peacefully closed panes.

I remembered riding up in the elevator, the moments inside, the faint feeling of vertigo. Of course, who was to say the elevator really moved? Maybe they had only switched scenery on me while I was caught inside, listening to the artificial hum, seeing the flashing lights. Either alter the oxygen supply inside the cubicle suddenly or use subtle neural stimulation and that would contribute a sensation of change, of movement. They had it all worked out.

My fingers rubbed my head briskly, both hands working, trying to get some circulation in my brain.

I guessed I had to run. There didn't seem much else to do.

I ran.

Get help?

Not this elderly man and his grandson. Not this construction worker on her way to a job site. Not the accountant. Maybe the gallery owner, ex-Council, community leader, solid, respectable, well-intentioned, not a complete fool. The person on the corner checking a tablet by the transit stop.

"I need help," I panted to them. "Somebody's trying to kidnap me."

"Really makes you concerned to hear about something like that, doesn't it?" they said. "I'm in favor of stronger citizen protection laws myself."

"I'm not sure whether—"

"This heat is oppressive, isn't it? Especially here in these urban canyons. Sometimes I wish I was back in Crestwood. Cool, shaded streets..."

"Listen to me! These people, they're conspiring against me, trying to drive me insane! Two officers, a receptionist—"

"For my money, the Ecosystem Art Project is *the* achievement of our generation. I just don't understand these people who say it hasn't got merit. It gets merit by demonstrating what restoration can accomplish..."

They were like anybody you might talk to on the street. I knew what they would say if I cued them with "sports" or "politics" instead of the key words I had used.

I should have known better, but I wanted to touch them in some way, make them know I was alive. I grabbed them and shook them by the shoulders, and there was a whoosh and as I might have expected they collapsed like the insubstantiality they were.

There was a stick figure of a person left before me, an economical skeleton supporting the shell of a human being and two-thirds of a business suit.

Hide.

I went into the first shop I came to—Artisan Supplies.

Appropriately, it was a false front.

A neutral-colored gray surface, too smooth for concrete, stretched away into some shadows. The area was littered with trash.

Containers, bottles, what looked like the skin of a dehydrated human being—obviously, on second thought, only the discarded skin of one of the things like the one I had deflated.

And a moldering pile of documents and files.

Something caught my eye and I kicked through them. Yes, the proposal I had written to the Conservation Council in Redwood Territory, unopened. *And which they had approved.*

My work.

The work I had done for the Council, important, creative work. There was my design, the sketch of the wetland restoration, the families, children, elders, the caption: Biodiversity Conservation is Part of Our Social Contract.

All of it lying here to rot.

Something made me look away from that terrible trash.

Santos stood in the entrance of Artisan Supplies, something bright in his hand.

Something happened.

I had been wrong.

The shining instrument had not been a neural interface device.

"You're resilient," Santos said as I eased back into focus.

"You aren't, not without help," I told him in disgust.

"Spirited, aren't you? I meant mental resilience. That's the one thing we can never judge. I think you could have taken the shock right from the start. Of course, you would still have needed the conditioning to integrate properly."

"Conditioning? Conditioning?" It came out of me, vortexing up, outside of my control. "What have you done to my mind?"

"We've been trying to get it to grow back up," Santos said reasonably. "Think of this. Restoration. Renewal. Rejuvenation. This is it. Never mind how it works. Most minds can't stand being young and knowing they will have to go through the same experience all over again. We use neural remapping to shift your upper conscious memories to your subconscious, leaving room for new memories. You remember only those things out of the past you *have* to, to retain your identity."

"Identity," I repeated. "I have no identity. My identity is a dream. I have two identities—one of them decades beyond the other."

Santos tilted his head and his eyes at me and slapped me across the face. "Don't go back on me now. We gave you the best we could. The Rejuvenation Service couldn't help it if you were too old for a *beta*. You shouldn't have waited until you were so old, so very old. We used the very oldest sets and simulations we had for *betas*, but you, you had to keep wandering onto *alpha* territory, while they were striking sets, even. *Beta* or not, we gave you good service. Don't slip now."

I heard the voice and I heard another voice, and it said "What could you expect of a *beta*?" and they were only some of the voices I was hearing, and I wondered what you could expect from a *beta*, and I didn't know, or think that I would ever know.
question: How many credits are charged for magazines in good condition at the gallery?

synthetic_story:
THE AGRONOMIST FROM EARTH
BY KEITH LAUMER (ADAPTED)

You don't have to be idealistic to be an Earth agricultural consultant—but on Zelvaria it sure helps!

I

"The Agricultural Liaison for the Terrestrial Development Agency," Raj Yates said, "presents his compliments to the Ministry of Environmental Resources of the Zelvarian Republic, and with reference to the Ministry's invitation to attend a symposium on traditional farming methods, has the honor to express regret that he will be unable—"

"You can't turn this invitation down," Administrative Assistant Megan Potter said flatly. "I'll make that 'accepts with pleasure'."

Raj exhaled slowly, setting down his coffee.

"Ms. Potter," he said, "in the past couple of weeks I've sat through six lectures on pre-industrial composting, four demonstrations of hand-tilling techniques, and god knows how many assorted folk-farming festivals. I've been tied up every off-duty hour since I got here—"

"You can't offend the Zelvarians," Megan Potter said sharply. "Consultant Greene would never have been so rude."

"Greene left here three months ago," Raj said, "leaving me in charge."

"Well," Megan Potter said, snapping off the voice recorder. "I'm sure I don't know what excuse I can give the Minister."

"Never mind the excuses," Raj said. "Just tell him I won't be there." He stood up.

"Are you leaving the office?" Megan Potter adjusted her glasses. "I have some important reports here for your signature."

"I don't recall drafting any reports today, Ms. Potter," Raj said, pulling on a light jacket.

"I wrote them for you. They're just as Consultant Greene would have wanted them."

"Did you write all Greene's reports for him, Ms. Potter?"

"Consultant Greene was an extremely busy man," Megan Potter said stiffly. "He had complete confidence in me."

"Since I'm cutting out the cultural immersion from now on," Raj said, "I won't be so busy."

"Well!" Megan Potter said. "May I ask where you'll be if something comes up?"

"I'm going over to the National Archives in Rosewood."

Megan Potter blinked behind thick lenses. "Whatever for?"

Raj looked thoughtfully at Megan Potter. "You've been here in Zelvaria for four years, Ms. Potter. What was behind the political upheaval that put the current agricultural ministry in power?"

"I'm sure I haven't pried into—"

"What about that Terrestrial research vessel? The one that disappeared in this region about ten years back?"

"Mr. Yates, those are just the sort of questions we avoid with the Zelvarians. I certainly hope you're not thinking of openly intruding—"

"Why?"

"The Zelvarians are a very proud people. They don't welcome outworlders raking up things. They've been gracious enough to let us live down the fact that Terrestrials subjected them to deep humiliation on one occasion."

"You mean when they came looking for the research vessel?"

"I, for one, am ashamed of the high-handed tactics that were employed, interrogating these innocent people as though they were criminals. We try never to reopen that wound, Mr. Yates."

"They never found the vessel, did they?"

"Certainly not in Zelvaria."

Raj nodded. "Thanks, Ms. Potter," he said. "I'll be back before you close the office." Megan Potter's face was set in lines of grim disapproval as he closed the door.

The pale-featured Zelvarian clerk wrung his hands nervously.

"Access to the Archives is restricted," he said in his soft accent. "I must express the Archivist's deep regret."

"The importance of my research here," Raj said, struggling with the formal dialect. "My interest in sustainable agriculture practices and their historical development."

"Access to outworlders is impossible. Please depart quietly."

"The necessity that I review these records."

"The Archivist has given specific instructions." The clerk's voice rose slightly. "You must abandon this request!"

"OK, friend, I know when I'm beaten," Raj said in Terran Standard. "Keep your records safe."

Outside, Raj stood for a moment looking across at the ornately carved facades lining the street in Rosewood, then started off in the direction of the Terrestrial Development Agency office. The few Zelvarians on the street eyed him warily, gave him a wide berth as he passed. Electric groundcars hummed silently along the smooth pavement. The air smelled of rain and growing things.

At the office, Megan Potter would be waiting with another list of complaints.

Raj studied the shop signs along the street. An elaborate one in green paint seemed to indicate a Zelvarian café. Raj went in.

A Zelvarian server was dispensing cups of herbal tea from behind a polished counter. She looked at Raj and froze, a steaming pot poised over a waiting cup.

"To enjoy a local beverage," Raj said in Zelvarian. "To sample authentic Zelvarian hospitality."

"My humble offerings are unsuitable," the server mumbled. "A regrettable situation; please accept my apologies."

"Don't worry," Raj said, irritated. "Just pour it and let me decide whether I like it."

"I could be reported to authorities for serving foreigners." The server looked around for support, found none. The Zelvarian customers, eyes averted, were drifting away.

"Just do it," Raj said, placing a credit chip on the counter. "Move it along."

"The procurement of proper documentation," a thin voice called from the sidelines. "The displaying of permits."

Raj turned. A tall Zelvarian gestured dismissively. From his flushed complexion, it was apparent the man had been drinking.

"Mind your own business," the server hissed. "Keep silent, cousin."

"Mind your own regulations, dispenser of contraband," the drunk said. "Find proper authorization for serving this outsider." He swayed toward Raj. "Show this one the door, like all foreigners deserve."

"Seen a lot of foreigners mistreated, have you?" Raj asked, interested.

"Speak intelligibly, foul-smelling outworlder," the drunk said. The server whispered something, and two customers came up to the drunk, took his arms and helped him to the door.

"Get documentation!" the drunk called out. "Keep the outsiders in their own stinking compounds."

"I've changed my mind," Raj said to the server. "Thanks anyway, but I have to go." He followed the drunk out the door. The other Zelvarians released him, hurried back inside. Raj looked at the weaving man.

"Get lost, freak," the Zelvarian muttered.

"Let's be friends," Raj said. "Let's talk about things."

"I'll have you removed to a detention center, ill-mannered foreign pest."

"Don't be angry, fragrant local," Raj said. "Let me buy you a drink."

"I'll not endure such insolence!" The Zelvarian advanced toward Raj. Raj backed away.

"Let's just chat," Raj said. "Let's be reasonable—"

The Zelvarian reached for him, missed. A passer-by stepped around him, head down, hurried away. Raj backed into the opening to a narrow side street and continued his verbal provocations to the drunken local, who followed, furious. Raj backed around a corner into a narrow alley-like passage, deserted, silent... except for the following Zelvarian.

Raj stepped around him, seized his collar and pulled. The Zelvarian fell on his back. Raj stood over him. The downed native half-rose; Raj put a foot against his chest and pushed.

"You're not going anywhere for a few minutes," Raj said. "You're going to stay right here and have a nice long talk with me."

II

"There you are!" Megan Potter said, eyeing Raj over her lenses. "There are two gentlemen waiting to see you. Zelvarian gentlemen."

"Government officials, I imagine. Word travels fast." Raj pulled off his jacket. "This saves me the trouble of paying another call at the Ministry."

"What have you been doing? They seem very upset, I don't mind telling you."

"I'm sure you don't. Come along. And bring an official recorder."

Two Zelvarians wearing formal robes indicative of rank rose as Raj entered the room. Neither offered a courteous bow, Raj noted. They were angry, all right.

"I am Pablo Cole, of the Terrestrial Affairs Office, Ministry of Environmental Resources," the taller Zelvarian said, in accented Terran. "May I present Lucas Ramirez, of the Internal Security Bureau."

"Sit down, gentlemen," Raj said. They resumed their seats. Megan Potter hovered nervously, then sat on the edge of an uncomfortable chair.

"Oh, it's such a pleasure—" she began.

"Never mind that," Raj said. "These gentlemen didn't come here for pleasantries today."

"So true," Pablo Cole said. "Frankly, I have had a most disturbing report. I shall ask Lucas Ramirez to recount it." He nodded to the security chief.

"One hour ago," the Zelvarian said, "a Zelvarian citizen was brought to medical facility suffering from minor injuries. Questioning of this individual revealed that he had been assaulted by a foreigner. A Terrestrial, to be precise. Investigation by my department indicates that the description of the perpetrator closely matches that of the Terrestrial Agricultural Liaison."

Megan Potter gasped audibly.

"Have you ever heard," Raj said, looking steadily at Pablo Cole, "of a Terrestrial research vessel, the TSV Discovery, which dropped from sight in this sector nine years ago?"

"Really!" Megan Potter exclaimed, rising. "I wash my hands—"

"Just keep that recorder going," Raj snapped.

"I'll not be a party—"

"You'll do as you're told, Ms. Potter," Raj said quietly. "I'm telling you to make an official sealed record of this conversation."

Megan Potter sat down.

Pablo Cole stiffened indignantly. "You reopen an old wound, Mr. Yates. It reminds us of certain illegal treatment at Terrestrial hands—"

"Nonsense," Raj said. "That story worked with my predecessors, but it doesn't work with me."

"All our efforts," Megan Potter said, "to live down that terrible episode! And you—"

"Terrible? I understand that a Terrestrial investigation team came to Zelvaria and asked questions. They got some evasive answers, and stayed on to investigate a little. After a week they left. Somewhat annoying to the Zelvarians, maybe—at the most. If they were innocent."

"If!" Megan Potter burst out.

"If, indeed!" Pablo Cole said, his voice trembling. "I must protest your—"

"Save the protests, Cole. You have some explaining to do. And I don't think your story will be good enough."

"It is for you to explain! This person who was assaulted—"

"Not assaulted. Just questioned firmly to refresh his memory."

"Then you admit—"

"It worked, too. He remembered lots of things, once he focused his mind."

Pablo Cole rose; Lucas Ramirez followed suit.

"I shall request your immediate recall, Mr. Yates. Were it not for your diplomatic status, I should do more—"

"Why did the government fall, Cole? It was just after the investigation team paid its visit, and before the arrival of the first Terrestrial agricultural mission."

"This is an internal matter!" Pablo Cole cried. "The new regime has shown itself most cooperative with you Terrestrials. It has gone out of its way—"

"—to keep the Terrestrial liaison and his staff in the dark," Raj said. "And the same goes for the few Terrestrial scientists you've granted visas to. This continual round of cultural activities; no professional contacts outside the diplomatic circle; no travel permits to visit outlying agricultural zones, or your orbital research station—"

"Enough!" Pablo Cole's hands trembled. "I can discuss this matter no further—"

"You'll discuss it with me, or there'll be an investigation team here in five days to do the discussing," Raj said.

"You can't!" Megan Potter gasped.

Raj turned a steady look on Megan Potter. She closed her mouth. The Zelvarians sat down.

"Answer me this one," Raj said, looking at Lucas Ramirez. "A few years back—about nine, I think—there was a little exhibition held here in Victorville. Some unusual specimens were captured. After being securely contained, they were displayed to the Zelvarian public. Paraded through the streets. Very educational, no doubt. A highly cultural show.

"Funny thing about these specimens. They wore clothing. They seemed to communicate with each other. They used tools. Altogether it was a very interesting exhibit.

"Tell me, Ramirez, what happened to those six Terrestrials after the parade was over?"

Pablo Cole made a choked noise and spoke rapidly to Lucas Ramirez in Zelvarian. Ramirez shrank down in his chair. Megan Potter opened her mouth, closed it and blinked rapidly.

"How did they die?" Raj snapped. "Did you execute them, poison them, or let them starve? What convenient end did you arrange for them? Experimentation, maybe? Studied them to see what made them different..."

"No!" Pablo Cole gasped. "I must correct this terrible misunderstanding at once."

"Misunderstanding, hell," Raj said. "They were Terrans! A simple truth serum interrogation would get that out of any Zelvarian who saw the parade."

"Yes," Pablo Cole said weakly. "It is true, they were Terrestrials. But there was no execution."

"They're alive?"

"Alas, no. They... died."

Megan Potter made a faint sound.

"I see," Raj said. "They died."

"We tried to keep them alive, of course. But we did not know what nutrition—"

"Didn't take the trouble to find out, either, did you?"

"They fell ill," Pablo Cole said. "One by one..."

"We'll deal with that question later," Raj said. "Right now, I want more information. Where did you find them? Where did you hide the vessel? What happened to the rest of the crew? Did they 'fall ill' before the big parade?"

"There were no more! Absolutely, I assure you!"

"Killed in the crash landing?"

"No crash landing. The vessel descended intact, east of Victorville. The... Terrestrials... were unharmed. Naturally, we feared them. They were strange to us. We had never before encountered such beings on our soil."

"Stepped off the vessel with weapons drawn, did they?"

"Weapons? No, no weapons—"

"They raised their hands, didn't they? Asked for help. You helped them; helped them to death."

"How could we know?" Pablo Cole moaned.

"How could you know a fleet would show up in a few months looking for them, you mean? That was a shock, wasn't it? I'll bet you had a difficult time hiding the vessel, and silencing everybody. A close call, eh?"

"We were afraid," Lucas Ramirez said. "We are a traditional people. We feared the strange creatures from the alien craft. We did not kill them, but we felt it was perhaps for the best that they... did not survive. Then, when the investigation ships came, we realized our error. But we feared to speak. We removed our guilty leaders, concealed what had happened, and... offered our cooperation. We invited the opening of agricultural development relations. We made a terrible mistake, it is true. But we have tried to make amends..."

"Where is the vessel?"

"The vessel?"

"What did you do with it? It was too big to just hide and forget. Where is it?"

The two Zelvarians exchanged looks.

"We wish to demonstrate our remorse," Pablo Cole said. "We will show you the vessel."

"Ms. Potter," Raj said. "If I don't come back in a reasonable length of time, transmit that recording to Regional Headquarters, sealed." He stood, looked at the Zelvarians.

"Let's go," he said.

Raj ducked under the heavy support beams shoring the entry to the underground facility. He peered into the dimness at the curved hull of the space-scarred vessel.

"Any lights in here?" he asked.

A Zelvarian threw a switch. A weak yellowish glow appeared.

Raj walked along the raised metal walkway, studying the vessel. Empty equipment bays gaped below dark sensor arrays. Debris-strewn decking was visible within the half-open entry hatch. Near the bow the words 'TSV Discovery - Agricultural Research Division' were lettered in bright chrome alloy.

"How did you get it in here?" Raj asked.

"It was transported here from the landing point, some twelve kilometers distant," Pablo Cole said, his voice thinner than ever. "This is a natural cavern system. The vessel was lowered into it and covered over."

"How did you shield it so the detectors didn't pick it up?"

"All around here is dense mineral deposits," Pablo Cole said, gesturing. "Great concentrations of metallic ore."

Raj grunted. "Let's go inside."

Lucas Ramirez came forward with a portable light. The party entered the vessel.

Raj climbed up a narrow ladder, glanced around the interior of the control compartment. Dust was thick on the deck, the mounting points where equipment had been installed, the empty instrument panels, the litter of cut bolts, scraps of wire and documentation. A thin layer of corrosion dulled the exposed metal where cutting tools had sliced away protective shielding. There was a faint odor of old organic material.

"The cargo compartment—" Lucas Ramirez began.

"I've seen enough," Raj said.

Silently, the Zelvarians led the way back out through the tunnel and into the late afternoon light. As they climbed the slope to the electric vehicle, Pablo Cole came to Raj's side.

"Indeed, I hope that this will be the end of this unfortunate affair," he said. "Now that all has been fully and honestly revealed—"

"You can skip all that," Raj said. "You're nine years late. The crew was still alive when the investigation team called, I imagine. You killed them—or let them die—rather than take the chance of admitting what you'd done."

"We were at fault," Pablo Cole said abjectly. "Now we wish only cooperation."

"The Discovery was a major research vessel, about fifteen thousand tons." Raj looked grimly at the slender Environmental Resources official. "Where is she, Cole? I won't settle for a thousand-ton lifeboat."

Pablo Cole's eyes widened in shock.

"I know nothing of... of..." He stopped. His throat worked rapidly as he struggled for composure.

"My government can entertain no further accusations, Mr. Yates," he said at last. "I have been completely candid with you. I have overlooked your intrusion into matters not properly within your jurisdiction. My patience is at an end."

"Where is that vessel?" Raj demanded. "You never learn, do you? You're still convinced you can hide the whole thing and forget it. I'm telling you you can't."

"We return to Victorville now," Pablo Cole said. "I can do no more."

"You can and you will, Cole," Raj said. "I intend to get to the truth of this matter."

Pablo Cole spoke to Lucas Ramirez in rapid Zelvarian. The security chief gestured to his four armed officers. They moved to surround Raj.

Raj eyed Pablo Cole. "Don't try it," he said. "You'll just make things worse for yourself."

Pablo Cole's jaw tightened, his posture aggressive toward the Terrestrial.

"Out of deference to your diplomatic status, Terrestrial, I shall ignore your insulting remarks," Pablo Cole said. "Let us now return to the city."

Raj looked at the four officers. "I see your point," he said.

Pablo Cole followed him into the vehicle, sat rigidly at the far end of the seat.

"I advise you to remain very close to your agency office," Pablo Cole said. "I advise you to dismiss these theories from your mind, and to appreciate the cultural aspects of life in Zelvaria. Especially, I should not venture out of Victorville, or appear overly curious about matters of concern only to the Zelvarian government."

In the front seat, Lucas Ramirez looked straight ahead. The smoothly-operating vehicle hummed along the paved highway. Raj listened to the quiet electric motor and said nothing.

III

"Ms. Potter," Raj said, "I want you to listen carefully to what I'm going to tell you. I have to move rapidly now, to catch the Zelvarians off guard."

"I'm sure I don't know what you're talking about," Megan Potter snapped, her eyes sharp behind the heavy lenses.

"If you'll listen, you may find out," Raj said. "I have no time to waste, Ms. Potter. They won't be expecting an immediate move—I hope—and that may give me the opportunity I need."

"You're still determined to make an issue of that incident!" Megan Potter said. "I can hardly blame the Zelvarians. They are not a technologically advanced race; they had never before encountered aliens on their planet."

"You're ready to forgive a great deal, Ms. Potter. But it's not what happened nine years ago I'm concerned with. It's what's happening now. I've told you that it was only a lifeboat the Zelvarians have hidden. Don't you understand the implication? That vessel couldn't have traveled far on its own. The research ship itself must be somewhere nearby. I want to know where!"

"The Zelvarians don't know. They're a very traditional, peaceful people. You can do irreparable harm to the reputation of Terrestrials if you insist—"

"That's my decision," Raj said. "I have a job to do and we're wasting time." He crossed the room to his desk, opened a drawer and took out a compact stunner.

"This office is being monitored. Not very efficiently, if I know the Zelvarians. I think I can get past their surveillance."

"Where are you going with... that?" Megan Potter stared at the stunner. "What in the world—"

"The Zelvarians won't waste any time destroying every document in their files relating to this thing. I have to get what I need before it's too late. If I wait for an official Investigation Commission, they'll find nothing but cooperative smiles."

"You're out of your mind!" Megan Potter stood up, shaking with indignation. "You're like a... a..."

"You and I are in a precarious position, Ms. Potter. The logical next move for the Zelvarians is to eliminate both of us. We're the only ones who know what happened. Cole almost arranged that this afternoon, but I deterred him—for the moment."

Megan Potter emitted a sharp laugh. "Your paranoid fantasies are getting the better of you," she gasped. "In danger, indeed! Eliminating me! I've never heard anything so absurd."

"Stay in this office. Secure the door with the safety lock. You've got food and water in the dispenser. I suggest you stock up, before they shut the utilities down. Don't let anyone in, on any pretext whatever. I'll keep in touch with you via secure communicator."

"What are you planning to do?"

"If I don't make it back here, transmit the sealed record of this afternoon's conversation, along with the information I've given you. Send it through on an emergency priority. Then inform the Zelvarians what you've done and stay secure. I think you'll be safe. It won't be easy to break in here and anyway, they won't make things worse by harming you. A response team can be here in a week."

"I'll do nothing of the sort! The Zelvarians are very respectful of me! You... newcomer! Troublemaker! Setting out to destroy—"

"Blame it on me if it will make you feel any better," Raj said, "but don't be foolish enough to trust them." He pulled on a dark jacket, opened the door.

"I'll be back in a couple of hours," he said. Megan Potter stared after him silently as he closed the door.

It was an hour before dawn when Raj entered the combination to the security lock and stepped into the darkened agency office. He looked exhausted.

Megan Potter, dozing in a chair, awoke with a start. She looked at Raj, rose and activated a light, turned to stare.

"What in the world—Where have you been? What's happened to your clothing?"

"I got a little dirty. Don't worry about it." Raj went to his desk, opened a drawer and replaced the stunner.

"Where have you been?" Megan Potter demanded. "I stayed here—"

"I'm glad you did," Raj said. "I hope you stocked up on food and water from the dispenser, too. We'll be secured here for a week, at least." He made notes on a tablet. "Activate the official transmitter. I have a long transmission for Regional Headquarters."

"Are you going to tell me where you've been?"

"I have a message to send first, Ms. Potter," Raj said sharply. "I've been to the Environmental Ministry," he added. "I'll tell you all about it later."

"At this hour? There's no one there..."

"Exactly."

Megan Potter gasped. "You mean you broke in? You burglarized the Environmental Ministry?"

"That's right," Raj said calmly. "Now—"

"This is absolutely the end!" Megan Potter said. "Thank heaven I've already—"

"Get that transmitter active, woman!" Raj snapped. "This is critical."

"I've already done so, Mr. Yates!" Megan Potter said harshly. "I've been waiting for you to return here..." She turned to the communicator, activated controls. The screen illuminated, and a wavering long-distance image appeared.

"He's here now," Megan Potter said to the screen. She looked at Raj triumphantly.

"That's good," Raj said. "I don't think the Zelvarians can interrupt our transmission, but—"

"I have done my duty, Mr. Yates," Megan Potter said. "I made a full report to Regional Headquarters last night, as soon as you left this office. Any doubts I may have had as to the correctness of that decision have been completely dispelled by what you've just told me."

Raj looked at her levelly. "You've been busy, Ms. Potter. Did you mention the six Terrestrials who died here?"

"That had no bearing on the matter of your reckless behavior! I must say, in all my years with the Agency, I've never encountered a personality less suited to diplomatic liaison work."

The screen crackled, the transmission delay having elapsed. "Mr. Yates," the face on the screen said, "I am Director Sophie Leonard, Regional Coordinator. I have received a report on your conduct which makes it mandatory for me to relieve you administratively, with Ms. Megan Potter assuming interim authority. Pending the findings of a Review Board, you will—"

Raj reached out and deactivated the communicator. The triumphant look faded from Megan Potter's face.

"Why, what is the meaning—"

"If I'd listened any longer, I might have heard something I couldn't disregard. I can't afford that, at this moment. Listen, Ms. Potter," Raj went on earnestly, "I've found the missing research vessel."

"You heard her relieve you!"

"I heard her say she was going to, Ms. Potter. But until I've received and acknowledged a formal order, it has no authority. If I'm wrong, she'll get my resignation. If I'm right, that suspension would be embarrassing all around."

"You're defying legitimate authority! I'm in charge here now." Megan Potter stepped to the local communicator.

"I'm going to report this terrible thing to the Zelvarians at once, and offer my profound—"

"Don't touch that screen," Raj said. "You go sit in that corner where I can monitor you. I'm going to make a sealed transmission for Regional Headquarters, along with a request for an armed response team. Then we'll settle in to wait."

Raj ignored Megan Potter's protests as he spoke into the recorder.

The local communicator chimed. Megan Potter jumped up, staring at it.

"Go ahead," Raj said. "Answer it."

A Zelvarian official appeared on the screen.

"Megan Potter," he said without preamble, "on behalf of the Environmental Minister of the Zelvarian Republic, I hereby recognize you as Terrestrial Agricultural Liaison to Zelvaria, in accordance with the communications transmitted to my government directly from Terrestrial Regional Headquarters. As liaison, you are requested to make available for questioning Mr. Raj Yates, former liaison, in connection with the assault on a citizen and illegal entry into the offices of the Ministry of Environmental Resources."

"Why, why," Megan Potter stammered. "Yes, of course. And I do want to express my deepest regrets—"

Raj rose, went to the communicator, moved Megan Potter aside.

"Listen carefully, Cole," he said. "Your deception has been exposed. You don't come in and we don't come out. Your concealment worked for nine years, but it's finished now. I suggest you keep your composure and resist the temptation to make matters worse than they are."

"Ms. Potter," Pablo Cole said, "a security team waits outside your agency office. It is clear you are in the custody of a dangerous individual. As always, the Zelvarians wish only cooperation with the Terrestrials, but—"

"Don't bother," Raj said. "You know what was in those files I reviewed this morning."

Raj turned at a sound behind him. Megan Potter was at the door, reaching for the security lock release...

"Don't!" Raj moved—too late.

The door burst inward. A group of uniformed Zelvarians pressed into the room, pushed Megan Potter back, aimed weapons at Raj. Security Chief Lucas Ramirez pushed forward.

"Attempt no resistance, Terrestrial," he said. "I cannot guarantee to restrain my officers."

"You're violating Terrestrial territory, Ramirez," Raj said steadily. "I suggest you withdraw the same way you entered."

"I invited them here," Megan Potter spoke up. "They are here at my express authorization."

"Are they? Are you sure you meant to go this far, Ms. Potter? A squad of armed Zelvarians in the agency office?"

"You are the liaison, Ms. Megan Potter," Lucas Ramirez said. "Would it not be prudent if we removed this unstable person to a secure location?"

"You're making a serious mistake, Ramirez," Raj said.

"Yes," Megan Potter said. "You're quite right, Mr. Ramirez. Please escort Mr. Yates to his quarters in this building—"

"I don't advise you to violate my diplomatic immunity, Cole," Raj said.

"As chief of mission," Megan Potter said quickly, "I hereby waive immunity in the case of Mr. Yates."

Lucas Ramirez produced a recording device. "Kindly repeat your statement, Madam, officially," he said. "I wish no question to arise later."

"Don't be a fool, woman," Raj said. "Don't you see what you're setting yourself up for? This would be an excellent time for you to figure out whose side you're on."

"I'm on the side of proper conduct!"

"You've been deceived. These people are concealing—"

"You think all women are fools, don't you, Mr. Yates?" She turned to the security chief and spoke into the microphone he held up.

"That's an illegal waiver," Raj said. "I'm liaison here, whatever communications you've received. This situation is coming into the open, whatever you do. Don't add violation of the Agency office to the list of Zelvarian crimes."

"Detain him," Lucas Ramirez said.
